entries.title: Where four spheres meet: the pedosphere

definition.text: The outermost layer of Earth's crust, made of soil and subject to soil formation and erosion.

facts.text: It lies at the interface of the lithosphere, atmosphere, hydrosphere and biosphere, and develops only where all four interact dynamically.
The pedosphere is the foundation of terrestrial ecosystems and mediates chemical and biogeochemical fluxes into and out of the other spheres.
It lies within the Critical Zone, a wider interface running from vegetation through aquifers and regolith down into bedrock.
Soil formation begins with the chemical or physical breakdown of minerals over bedrock; it can start without life but is greatly quickened by biological reactions.
Over time the soil's bulk chemistry drifts away from that of the bedrock toward one reflecting the reactions taking place in the soil.
The chemistry of the underlying rock sets the primary conditions for soil development, and few rock types locally enrich limiting elements such as phosphorus and nitrogen.
Soil formation is dominated by chemical weathering of silicate minerals, aided by acids from pioneer organisms and by carbonic acid from the atmosphere.

entries.text: Soil forms only where four of Earth's great systems touch. The pedosphere is the outermost layer of Earth's crust, made of soil, where soil forms and wears away by erosion. It lies at the meeting point of the lithosphere, the rocky shell, with the atmosphere, the hydrosphere of Earth's waters and the biosphere of living things. Soil develops only where all four interact. The pedosphere is the foundation of every ecosystem on land, and it passes chemical and biogeochemical flows into and out of the other spheres. It sits within a wider interface that runs from vegetation through aquifers and loose material down into solid rock, described in {{ref:soil-found-115}}. Soil begins to form as minerals over solid rock break down, chemically or physically. It can start without life, but biological reactions speed it up greatly. Chemical attack on silicon-bearing minerals dominates the work. Acids from {{ref:soil-found-085}} help, and so does carbonic acid from the atmosphere. The rock below sets the starting conditions, and few rock types locally enrich scarce elements such as phosphorus and nitrogen. Over time the soil's bulk chemistry drifts away from the rock's. It comes to reflect the reactions taking place in the soil itself.

entries.title: Pedology: reading how a soil came to be

definition.text: The branch of soil science that studies how soils form and evolve and builds frameworks for describing soil bodies, often in their natural environment.

facts.text: It is one of two main branches of soil inquiry; the other, edaphology, is more agronomic and studies how soil properties influence plant communities.
Pedologists observe soil morphology, where soils occur and how they fit into wider contexts of time and space, and from this build classifications, soil maps and theories.
Its sub-disciplines include pedometrics, the quantitative characterisation and mapping of soils, and soil geomorphology, which links landform processes with soil formation.
Agronomists once saw soil as a static production medium while pedologists studied its relation to landscape history; the two approaches are now integrated.
As a soil forms, its profile slowly deepens and develops characteristic layers called horizons while it approaches a steady state.
Fallou conceived pedology in the 19th century as a fundamental science separate from agrology, the applied forerunner of edaphology.

entries.text: Every soil has a life story, and pedology sets out to read it. For a long time agronomists saw soil as a static production medium, while pedologists studied its ties to landscape history. The two approaches are now integrated. One sub-discipline characterizes and maps soils with numbers. Another, built on {{ref:soil-water-295}}, links landform processes with the way soils form.

entries.title: Edaphology: what soil does for living things

definition.text: The branch of soil science concerned with the influence of soils on living things, especially plants.

facts.text: It is one of the two main divisions of soil science alongside pedology, and covers how soil shapes people's use of land for plant growth and other purposes.
Its general subfields are agricultural soil science (agrology in some regions) and environmental soil science.
Pedology and edaphology were at first poorly distinguished: Russian soil scientists used edaphology as a synonym of pedology, and Spanish ones preferred it.
Driven out of pedology-centred soil science in the 20th century, edaphology is now recognised as a necessary branch complementary to pedology.
Xenophon and Cato were early edaphologists; Cato recommended tillage, crop rotation and legumes to build soil nitrogen, and devised the first soil capability classification for crops.
Environmental soil science covers vadose zone functions, septic fields, wastewater and stormwater, erosion control, contamination and remediation, wetland restoration and nutrient management.

conflicts.text: Xenophon lived 450–355 BCE.

entries.title: Half solid, half empty: what a soil is made of

definition.text: The proportions of solids (minerals and organic matter) and of pore space, shared between water and air, that make up a soil.

facts.text: A typical soil is about 50% solids (45% mineral and 5% organic matter) and 50% pores, half occupied by water and half by gas.
In the short term the mineral and organic shares stay constant, while water and gas trade places: a rise in one is balanced by a fall in the other.
Pore space lets air and water enter and move, both critical for soil life; compaction, especially under heavy machinery, shrinks it and keeps air and water from roots and organisms.
Mineral particles interacting with organic matter, water and gases flocculate into aggregates or peds; where these can be identified, the soil is said to be developed.
Most nutrients are held by clay and organic colloids: adsorbed on clay surfaces, bound inside clay minerals, or locked in living organisms and humus.
Apart from nitrogen fixed from the atmosphere, most plant nutrients originate in the minerals of the parent material.
Biological influences on soil properties are strongest near the surface, while geochemical influences increase with depth.

entries.text: Half of a typical soil is not solid at all. About 50% of its volume is solids, 45% mineral grains and 5% material from living things, alive or dead. The other 50% is pores, half filled with water and half with gas. Soil composition describes these proportions. In the short term the mineral and organic shares stay constant, while water and gas trade places. A rise in one is balanced by a fall in the other. Pore space matters because air and water must enter and move through it, and both are critical for soil life. Squeezing a soil, especially under heavy machinery, shrinks its pores and keeps air and water from roots and organisms. Mineral particles, interacting with the organic share, water and gases, clump together into crumbs. Where these crumbs can be identified, the soil is said to be developed. Most nutrients are held by the finest particles of clay and organic material. They cling to clay surfaces, sit bound inside {{ref:soil-chem-079}}, or are locked in living organisms and in long-decayed organic remains. Apart from nitrogen fixed from the atmosphere, most plant nutrients first came from the minerals of the rock or sediment the soil formed from. Living things shape a soil most strongly near the surface. With depth, geochemical influences take over.

entries.title: From food to foundations: how people use soil

definition.text: The many ways people rely on soil, from growing food and fibre to construction, mining and landscape work.

facts.text: In agriculture soil anchors plants and is their primary nutrient base; the soil type and available moisture determine which plants can be grown.
Soil resources produce 98.8% of the food humans consume.
Soil is the foundation for most construction and the basis of many building materials; surface mining, road building and dam construction move massive volumes of it.
Waste treatment relies on soil: septic drain fields and land application of wastewater use aerobic soil processes, and landfills use soil as daily cover.
Water percolating through soil to become groundwater is filtered of pollutants such as pesticides, hydrocarbons, heavy metals and excess nutrients.
Organic soils, especially peat, are a significant fuel and horticultural resource, and drained peatlands are farmed in Nordic countries.
Geophagy, eating soil-like substances, is practised by animals and humans; some monkeys eat soil with their foliage to ease tannin toxicity.
Aeroponics, aquaponics and hydroponics show that soil is not strictly essential for agriculture.

entries.title: Dokuchaev's idea: soil as a natural body with a history

definition.text: The view, developed by Dokuchaev, that soil is a natural body with its own genesis and history, distinct from the bedrock beneath it.

facts.text: Fallou and Dokuchaev are both credited as among the first to treat soil as a resource distinct from geology and crop production; Fallou came first, but Dokuchaev's work proved more significant.
Before them, soil was seen as a product of chemical transformations of rocks, a dead substrate from which plants draw nutrients.
For Dokuchaev, rock becomes soil under soil-forming factors: climate, vegetation, country, relief and age.
A 1914 encyclopedic definition, forms of earth formed by the weathering of rocks, shows how long the older view persisted.
In the 20th century the concept became one of earthy material altered by living processes, and it is still being refined to take in energy transport within soil.
Nikiforoff's 1959 definition of soil as the 'excited skin of the sub aerial part of the Earth's crust' fits this modern understanding.

entries.title: Everything soil does for people and ecosystems

definition.text: The general capabilities of soils that matter for agriculture, the environment, nature protection, landscape architecture and urban uses.

facts.text: They include functions for natural ecosystems, agricultural productivity, environmental quality, as a source of raw materials and as a base for buildings.
For food and biomass production, soil stores and supplies nutrients, exchanges CO2 for fresh O2 in the root zone, holds water in its pores and moderates temperature.
Soil is a biological habitat and gene reserve for many organisms, and it turns the remains of dead plants and animals into simpler mineral forms other life can use.
Soil supplies raw materials and shapes human health, since food reflects the soil it grew in; Maya ceramics, for example, inherited traits from the soils used to make them.
Productive soil is limited in area, so with growing pressure from cropping, forestry and urbanization, extracting soil as a raw material needs to be controlled.
As cultural heritage, soil gives a sense of place, preserves artifacts of the past and has guided where people settle.
About 50% of people live in houses built from soil, and roads and buildings resting on it depend on its bearing strength, compressibility, stability and shear strength.

Soils govern whether rain runs off or recharges aquifers, purify septic drain field wastes, harbor useful organisms such as antibiotic-producing bacteria and nutrient-supplying fungi, and store atmospheric carbon in organic matter.

entries.title: Soil health: treating the ground as a living system

definition.text: The state of a soil meeting its range of ecosystem functions as appropriate to its environment.

facts.text: Put simply, soil health arises from favorable interactions of all soil components, living and non-living, such as microbiota, plants and animals.
It depends on soil biodiversity and can be improved by keeping protective living covers on the soil and adding natural, carbon-containing amendments.
Inorganic fertilizers need not harm soil health if they are not used in excess and if they boost plant growth that returns more carbon-containing residues.
The term spans sustaining plant and animal productivity, enhancing biodiversity, maintaining water and air quality, and supporting human health and habitation.
Its underlying principle is that soil is a living, dynamic, ever-changing environment, not the inert growing medium that intensive farming tends to assume.
Soils highly fertile for crops are also biologically lively; temperate grassland soils hold 1–2 t/ha of bacterial and 2–5 t/ha of fungal biomass.
Some microbiologists believe that 80% of soil nutrient functions are essentially controlled by microbes.
By analogy with human health, a healthy soil is in biological, chemical and physical well-being, is not degraded, resists degradation and keeps cycling nutrients, carbon and water.

entries.contested_note: A soil can be healthy for ecosystem functioning without directly serving crop production, so sources describe a scientific debate on its terms and measurement.

Inorganic fertilizers need not harm it, if they are not used in excess and the extra plant growth returns more carbon-containing residues. The idea remains debated. By analogy with human health, a healthy soil is in biological, chemical and physical well-being. It is not degraded, it resists degradation, and it keeps cycling nutrients, carbon and water. Soil health depends on the variety of life in the soil. Keeping protective living covers on the soil and adding natural, carbon-containing amendments improve it. Inorganic fertilizers need not harm it, if they are not used in excess and the extra plant growth returns more carbon-containing residues. The idea remains debated. A soil can be healthy for its ecosystem without directly serving crop production, so scientists still disagree on how to define and measure soil health.

entries.title: Soil quality, the standard no one has fixed

definition.text: The condition of a soil judged by its capacity to perform ecosystem services that meet the needs of human and non-human life.

facts.text: It reflects how well a soil maintains biodiversity and productivity, partitions water and solute flow, filters and buffers, cycles nutrients and supports plants and structures.
Unlike water or air, which have established standards, soil quality is difficult to define or quantify.
Soil management has a major impact on soil quality; cover crops, for example, raise it by adding organic matter over time.
Soil organisms contribute to soil quality in countless ways, and the amount and diversity of the biota appears proportional to it.
Arbuscular mycorrhizae help host plants establish on degraded soil and improve its quality and health.

entries.text: Water and air have established quality standards. Soil does not, because its quality is difficult to define or quantify. Soil organisms contribute in countless ways, and the amount and diversity of soil life appears proportional to soil quality. Fungi that partner with plant roots help their hosts establish on degraded soil and improve its quality and health.

entries.title: The ground rules pedologists use to explain soils

definition.text: The working principles pedologists use to explain soil genesis, starting from the idea that external factors drive soil-forming processes and create soil patterns.

facts.text: Complexity in soil genesis is more common than simplicity, and today's soils carry imprints of past processes that may be hard to observe or measure.
Five major external factors (climate, organisms, relief, parent material and time) plus smaller ones drive soil-forming processes and create soil patterns.
Soil-forming processes both create and destroy order within soils, often at once; the profile records the balance of these processes, present and past.
Uniformitarianism applies to soils: today's soil-forming processes have run since organisms first appeared on land, though with varying intensity in space and time.
Few soils are geologically old: most soils and land surfaces are no older than the Pleistocene, though lithified paleosols occur through most of geologic time.
Soils are natural clay factories; much of the world's shale is soil clay eroded into ocean basins and later lithified.
Knowing soil genesis aids classification, mapping and management, but classifications cannot rest on genesis alone, since processes are seldom observed and change over time.

entries.text: Much of the world's shale began as soil. Soils are natural clay factories, and their clay, eroded into ocean basins, later hardened into rock. Five major factors dominate: climate, organisms, relief, the rock or sediment beneath, and time. Those processes create and destroy order within a soil, often at once, and its layers record the balance. Uniformitarianism, the idea that present processes also ran in the past, applies too: they have worked since organisms first appeared on land. Few soils are geologically old. Most date no further back than the Pleistocene. Knowing soil genesis aids classification, mapping and management. Yet classifications cannot rest on genesis alone, since its processes are seldom observed and change over time.

entries.title: What soil scientists actually do

definition.text: The practical work of soil scientists, traditionally mapping soils and increasingly addressing land and environmental problems across disciplines.

facts.text: Almost every area of the United States has a published soil survey, with tables on how soil properties support or limit uses.
Landscape tasks include protecting environmentally critical areas and valuable habitats, managing land for productivity and remediating damaged lands.
Less obvious applications include dating past activity at a site, reading archaeological stratification, vitrifying radioactive waste and using soil microbes to degrade contaminants.
The Critical Zone concept gives a framework for cross-disciplinary research on soil, rock, air, water and living resources at Earth's surface.

entries.text: Almost every area of the United States has had its soils surveyed and published, with tables on how their properties support or limit different uses. The concept of {{ref:soil-found-115}} frames research across soil, rock, air, water and living resources at Earth's surface.

entries.title: Red, hot, fat or sandy: soils by their folk names

definition.text: Folk systems that name soils either with unique names or by obvious traits such as red, hot, fat or sandy.

facts.text: They tell soils apart by appearance (colour, texture, landscape position), performance (production capability, flooding) and the vegetation growing on them.
A familiar vernacular distinction is between heavy (clayey) and light (sandy) soils.
Light soils are easier to cultivate and resist compaction by trampling cattle but erode more easily; they are not lower in bulk density or more porous than heavy soils.
The earliest known soil classification, in the Chinese Yu Gong (5th century BCE), sorted soil into three categories and nine classes by colour, texture and hydrology.

entries.text: The earliest known scheme for sorting soils comes from China. The Yu Gong, from the 5th century BCE, sorted soil into three categories and nine classes by color, grain and water. Vernacular classifications are folk systems that give soils unique names or name them by obvious traits such as red, hot, fat or sandy. They judge soils by appearance, performance and the plants growing on them. A familiar example contrasts heavy, clayey soils with light, sandy ones. Light soils are easier to cultivate and resist compaction by trampling cattle, but they erode more easily. Despite the name, they are not lighter or more porous than heavy soils.

entries.title: What the sky drops into the soil

definition.text: What the pedosphere receives from the air, mainly wind-blown sediment, rainfall and diffusing gases.

facts.text: Eolian (wind-borne) sedimentation carries aerosols, pollen and dust particles into soils.
After water, nitrogen is the most abundant constituent of rain, because water vapour uses aerosol particles to form droplets.
Carbon dioxide from roots and microbes keeps soil-water bicarbonate far above equilibrium with the air, which together with dissolved metals lowers soil pH.
Gases escaping from soil to the atmosphere come from carbonate dissolution, decomposition, redox reactions and microbial photosynthesis.

entries.text: After water itself, nitrogen is the most abundant ingredient of rain. The reason is that water vapor uses tiny airborne particles, called aerosols, to form droplets. Rain is one of three main inputs the pedosphere receives from the air. The others are wind-blown sediment and gases diffusing in. Wind carries aerosols, pollen and dust into soils, a process called eolian sedimentation. Gases move both ways. Carbon dioxide from roots and microbes keeps the bicarbonate in soil water far above balance with the air. Together with dissolved metals, this makes the soil more acid. Gases escape back to the air from dissolving carbonates, decay, chemical reactions and microbial {{ref:soil-hist-147}}.

entries.title: Forest soils, leached into sharp bands

definition.text: Soils formed under forest, usually well developed with thick humus layers.

facts.text: In forests precipitation exceeds evapotranspiration, so surplus water percolates down through the soil layers.
Slow decomposition releases much fulvic acid, which greatly enhances chemical weathering.
Percolating water and weathering leach magnesium, iron and aluminium downward (podzolization), giving marked contrasts in colour and chemistry between layers.
Forest soils can form a thick soil carbon sponge.

entries.text: In a forest, more water falls as rain and snow than evaporates or passes back out through plants. The surplus percolates down through the soil layers. Forest soils form in these conditions and are usually well developed, with thick layers of well-decayed organic remains. Slow decay releases large amounts of a soluble organic acid, which greatly enhances the chemical breakdown of minerals. Percolating water and this breakdown carry magnesium, iron and aluminum downward, a process called podzolization. The result is marked contrasts in color and chemistry between layers. Forest soils can also build a thick sponge of stored carbon.

entries.title: Grassland and desert soils, shaped by drought

definition.text: Soils formed where precipitation equals or falls short of evapotranspiration, so that soil development works under drought.

facts.text: Limited downward percolation of water and organic acids reduces leaching, chemical weathering and soil development.
Evaporation builds up calcium, which with other large cations flocculates clay minerals and fulvic acids in the upper profile.
With little leaching, calcium precipitates as calcite in lower layers to form caliche; in deserts a layer of gypsum and halite may lie beneath it.
The depth of maximum clay concentration increases where precipitation and leaching are greater.

entries.text: Drought writes itself into a soil. Grassland and desert soils form where rain and snow equal or fall short of the water lost to evaporation and plants. Little water and few organic acids percolate downward. So the washing out of dissolved substances slows, along with chemical breakdown of minerals and soil development itself. Evaporation builds up calcium in the upper profile, where it clumps clay and dissolved organic acids together. Lower down, calcium settles out as a hard layer of the mineral in {{ref:soil-found-118}}. In deserts a layer of gypsum and halite may lie beneath it. Where rain and washing out increase, the clay-richest layer sits deeper.

entries.title: Lichens, microbes and the first bite into bare rock

definition.text: The first colonisers of bare rock, such as lichens, mosses and microbes, whose acids begin turning rock into soil.

facts.text: Biological inputs may begin with lichens and other microorganisms, including cyanobacteria, green algae, fungi and bacteria, that secrete oxalic acid.
Lichens have long been seen as the pioneers of soil, yet seed-bearing plants can colonise faster; lichens tolerate harsher conditions and dominate in alpine regions.
Organic acids from roots and decay, such as citric, phenolic, humic and fulvic acids, speed chemical weathering by chelation.
As the soil thickens, earthworms, burrowing mammals and large animals above ground go on altering its chemistry and fertility.

entries.text: Bare rock starts becoming soil when living things attack it with acid. The first colonizers, such as lichens, mosses and microbes, begin the work. Lichens and other microorganisms, including cyanobacteria, green algae, fungi and bacteria, secrete oxalic acid. Lichens have long been seen as the pioneers of soil. Seed-bearing plants can colonize faster, but lichens tolerate harsher conditions and dominate in alpine regions. Organic acids from roots and decay, such as citric and phenolic acids, {{ref:soil-chem-059}} and {{ref:soil-chem-060}}, speed chemical breakdown by gripping metal atoms and pulling them from minerals. As the soil thickens, earthworms, burrowing mammals and large animals above ground go on altering its chemistry and fertility.

entries.title: Why tropical forest soils turn rusty red

definition.text: Soils of tropical forests, which receive more sunlight and rain over longer growing seasons than any other environment.

facts.text: Tropical biomass is extremely productive, producing as much as 800 grams of carbon per square meter per year (8 tons of C/hectare/year).
Heat and abundant water raise rates of chemical weathering, while fast decomposition leaves less fulvic acid to leach metals.
Unlike temperate forest soils, they show little or no podzolization and lack marked visual and chemical contrasts between layers.
Mobile magnesium, iron and aluminium instead precipitate as oxide minerals, giving the soil a rusty red colour.

entries.text: No other environment gets as much sunlight and rain over such long growing seasons as the tropical forest. Its plants produce as much as 800 grams of carbon per square meter per year, or 8 tons per hectare. Heat and abundant water speed the chemical breakdown of minerals. Decay is fast too, leaving less organic acid to wash metals downward. So unlike temperate {{ref:soil-found-087}}, tropical forest soils show little or no podzolization and lack marked contrasts between layers. Mobile magnesium, iron and aluminum instead settle out as oxides, giving the soil a rusty red color.

entries.title: How industrial farming changed soil and crop

definition.text: The ways industrialised production and farming have changed how soils interact with plants.

facts.text: Increased mechanical production has raised heavy metal levels in soils, and these metals have also been found in crops.
Greater use of synthetic fertilizers and pesticides has decreased the nutrient availability of soils.
Monocropping lowers biodiversity, which reduces the nutrients available in soils, and increases dependency on chemical fertilizer.
Intensive tillage disturbs soil microbial communities that help maintain soil moisture and air circulation.

entries.text: Heavy metals from mechanized production have built up in soils, and they have turned up in crops as well. Industrialization has changed how soils interact with plants, the core concern of {{ref:soil-found-097}}. Greater use of synthetic fertilizers and pesticides has decreased the nutrients soils make available. Growing a single crop over and over lowers biodiversity. That reduces soil nutrients further and deepens dependence on chemical fertilizer. Intensive plowing and digging disturb the soil microbes that help keep soil moist and its air circulating.

entries.title: Van Helmont's willow and a pot of soil

definition.text: An experiment in which Jan Baptist van Helmont (1577–1644) grew a willow tree in a pot of soil for five years, supplying only rainwater.

facts.text: The weight the tree gained exceeded the weight the soil lost.
Van Helmont concluded that the willow was made of water; only partly correct, the experiment reignited interest in edaphology.

entries.text: For five years Jan Baptist van Helmont (1577–1644) grew a willow tree in a pot of soil, supplying nothing but rainwater. At the end, the tree had gained more weight than the soil had lost. Van Helmont concluded that the willow was made of water. He was only partly correct, but the experiment reignited interest in edaphology, the study of how soils shape plant life.

entries.title: Biological soil crust: a living skin on bare ground

definition.text: A biological soil crust is a living surface community of fungi, lichens, cyanobacteria, bryophytes and algae in the open spaces between vascular plants.

facts.text: Biological soil crusts cover about 12% of the earth's landmass, and their species mix and appearance vary with climate, soil and disturbance.
Only cyanobacteria and cyanolichens fix nitrogen, so a crust's nitrogen contribution depends on its composition; its carbon cycling happens only when wet.
Crusts darken the surface, lowering albedo, and their roughness traps dust.
Removing stressors such as grazing, or protecting crusts from disturbance, is the easiest way to maintain them.

Crusts darken the surface, which lowers {{ref:soil-phys-177}}, and their roughness traps dust. The easiest way to keep them is to remove stressors such as grazing, or to protect them from disturbance.

entries.title: The critical zone, from living soil down to bedrock

definition.text: The near-surface environment where rock, soil, water, air and living organisms interact to regulate habitats and the availability of life-sustaining resources.

facts.text: It sustains nearly all terrestrial life and extends through the pedosphere, the unsaturated vadose zone and the saturated groundwater zone.
Critical Zone science integrates landscape evolution, weathering, hydrology, geochemistry and ecology across spatial and time scales and human influence.
These processes govern the mass and energy exchanges behind biomass production, chemical cycling and water storage.
Tsakalotos coined 'critical zone' in chemistry in 1909; Gail Ashley applied it in 1998 to the connection of vegetation to soil and weathered materials.
It is studied at Critical Zone Observatories, for which the US National Science Foundation sought proposals in 2006.
In practice the critical zone essentially equates to the pedosphere, while the biomantle is its uppermost, biota-rich layer.
It ends at some depth in bedrock, where life and water cease to change the chemistry significantly.

entries.text: Nearly all life on land depends on a zone that ends deep in solid rock, where life and water stop significantly changing the rock's chemistry. Earth's critical zone is the near-surface environment where rock, soil, water, air and living organisms interact. Together they regulate habitats and the availability of life-sustaining resources. Its uppermost, biota-rich layer is called the biomantle. Its processes govern the exchanges of mass and energy behind biomass production, chemical cycling and water storage. entries.title: Soil solution: the water that is never just water

definition.text: The water held in soil pores together with the many organic and mineral substances dissolved or suspended in it.

facts.text: Because soil water is never pure but carries hundreds of dissolved organic and mineral substances, it is more accurately called the soil solution.
Its dissolved substances, organic and inorganic, occur in ionic or molecular form in the liquid phase of the soil.
Water drives the dissolution, precipitation and leaching of minerals in the profile, making it a critical agent of soil development.
Nutrients bound to clay and organic matter buffer the solution's composition as soils wet and dry, plants take up nutrients, salts are leached or acids and alkalis are added.
Soil pH measures the hydrogen ion activity in the soil solution and affects how available plant nutrients are.

entries.text: The water in soil is never pure. It carries hundreds of dissolved substances, so soil scientists give it a more accurate name: the soil solution. It is the water held in the pores of soil, together with everything dissolved or suspended in it. These substances, organic and inorganic, sit in the liquid as ions or molecules. The solution is also a force of change. Water dissolves {{ref:soil-found-029}}, deposits new ones and washes material down through the soil, which makes it a critical agent in how soil develops. Its makeup shifts constantly. Soils wet and dry, plants take up {{ref:soil-fert-181}}, salts wash away, and acids or alkalis arrive. Plant foods held on {{ref:soil-found-040}} and on {{ref:soil-found-045}} buffer those swings, steadying the mix. One measure tracks the solution's acidity: {{ref:soil-found-014}} gauges its hydrogen ion activity, which governs how available those plant foods are.

entries.title: Can lifeless ground be called soil?

definition.text: The unsettled question of where soil ends and other loose surface material begins, in particular whether lifeless regolith can be called soil.

facts.text: One classic definition says soil has formed once organic matter accumulates and washed-down colloids leave a distinct B horizon.
That definition is somewhat arbitrary, since mixtures of sand, silt, clay and humus support biological and farming activity before a B horizon forms.
Twentieth-century thinking cast soil as earthy material altered by living processes; on that view, soil without a living component is simply part of Earth's outer layer, a regolith.
More recent definitions embrace soils without any organic matter, such as regoliths formed on Mars and in comparable Earth deserts.
Calling the surface material of the Moon and Mars soil is accepted by only part of the scientific community.
In engineering terms, soil is simply part of regolith, the loose material above bedrock, as also found on the Moon and other celestial bodies.

entries.contested_note: Sources disagree on whether material without life or organic matter, such as Martian or lunar regolith, should be called soil.
entries.text: Is the ground on Mars soil? Only part of the scientific community accepts the word for the surface material of the Moon and Mars. The question belongs to an unsettled debate over where soil ends and other loose surface material begins. One classic definition says soil has formed once dead plant and animal material accumulates and fine particles washed down from above build a distinct lower layer. That definition is somewhat arbitrary. Mixtures of mineral grains and decayed organic remains support biological and farming activity before such a layer forms. Twentieth-century thinking cast soil as earthy material altered by living processes. On that view, soil without a living component is simply part of Earth's outer layer of loose material, described in {{ref:soil-form-097}}. More recent definitions embrace soils with no organic content at all, such as loose layers formed on Mars and in comparable deserts on Earth. Engineers sidestep the question. For them, soil is simply part of the loose material above solid rock, found also on the Moon and other celestial bodies. The sources still disagree on whether lifeless material, such as the surface material of the Moon or Mars, should be called soil.

entries.title: Minerals, the crystals that build rock and soil

definition.text: A naturally occurring solid with a fairly well-defined chemical composition and a specific crystal structure.

facts.text: A mineral differs from a rock: a rock is a bulk solid geologic material made of one mineral or an aggregate of several.
Natural solids with no definite crystal structure, such as opal or obsidian, are more properly called mineraloids.
One compound with two crystal structures counts as two species: quartz and stishovite are both silicon dioxide.
The International Mineralogical Association sets mineral names and definitions; as of August 2026 it recognizes 6,228 official mineral species.
To count as a mineral, a substance must form by natural geological processes, which excludes purely human-made or biological products such as seashells.
Silicate minerals make up approximately 90% of the Earth's crust.
Minerals are classified by their key chemical constituents, chiefly in the Dana and Strunz systems.
In soil, the sand and silt fractions are mostly inert rock particles such as quartz, calcite, feldspar and mica.

entries.title: Weathering: how solid rock starts becoming soil

definition.text: The breakdown of rocks, soils and minerals through contact with water, atmospheric gases, sunlight and living things.

facts.text: Weathering happens in place, which sets it apart from erosion, where water, ice, wind, waves or gravity carry rock and mineral material away.
It is either physical, the mechanical breakdown of rock by heat, water, ice and wind, or chemical, the reaction of rock with water, gases and biological chemicals.
Water drives both kinds, though atmospheric oxygen and carbon dioxide and the activities of organisms also matter.
The material left after rock breaks down combines with organic material to create soil.
The two kinds work together: cracks widened physically expose more surface to chemical attack, speeding disintegration.
Weathering is a crucial part of the rock cycle; sedimentary rock, made from weathered rock, covers 66% of the continents.

entries.title: Chemical weathering: rock remade for life at the surface

definition.text: Weathering in which water, oxygen, carbon dioxide and other substances react with rock and change its composition.

facts.text: Most rock forms at high temperature and pressure, so its minerals are often unstable in the cool, wet, oxidizing conditions at the Earth's surface.
It turns some primary minerals into secondary minerals, carries other substances off in solution, and leaves the most stable minerals unchanged as a resistate.
The new set of minerals is closer to equilibrium with surface conditions, but true equilibrium is rare because leaching removes the dissolved products.
Water is the main agent, turning many primary minerals into clay minerals or hydrated oxides by hydrolysis; oxygen oxidizes minerals and carbon dioxide drives carbonation.
It is usually much more important than physical weathering.
Mountain uplift exposes fresh rock to air and moisture, releasing calcium and other ions into surface waters.

entries.text: Most rock is born hot and squeezed. It forms at high temperature and pressure, so its minerals are often unstable in the cool, wet, oxidizing conditions at the Earth's surface. Chemical weathering is the result. Water, oxygen, carbon dioxide and other substances react with rock and change its composition. It does three things at once. It turns some of the minerals the rock formed with, covered in {{ref:soil-form-140}}, into new minerals, of the kind described in {{ref:soil-chem-235}}. It carries other substances off in solution. And it leaves the most stable minerals unchanged, as a resistate. Water is the main agent. Through the reactions in {{ref:soil-found-060}}, it turns many of these original minerals into fine sheet minerals or hydrated oxides. Oxygen oxidizes minerals, and carbon dioxide drives carbonation. The new set of minerals sits closer to equilibrium with surface conditions. True equilibrium is rare, though, because water keeps washing the dissolved products away. Chemical weathering is usually much more important than the mechanical kind in {{ref:soil-found-053}}. Mountains show its reach. Uplift exposes fresh rock to air and moisture, releasing calcium and other ions into surface waters.

entries.title: Lichens, roots and microbes that wear down rock

definition.text: Weathering started or sped up by living things, such as soil microorganisms, lichens and plant roots.

facts.text: Soil organisms make up about 10 mg/cm3 of typical soils; albite and muscovite weather twice as fast in live soil as in sterile soil.
Lichens are among the most effective agents: hornblende granite under lichen weathered 3x–4x faster than bare rock in a New Jersey study.
Most commonly, plants release chelating compounds such as organic acids and siderophores, along with carbon dioxide.
Roots can raise carbon dioxide to 30% of all soil gases.
Chelating organic acids strip metal ions, especially aluminium and silicon, from rock; their build-up can lead to podsolisation of soils.
Mycorrhizal fungi free nutrients from minerals such as apatite or biotite and pass them to trees, and some bacteria weather minerals in ways that promote plant growth.
Physically, seedlings and roots growing in crevices push rock apart, and lichens pluck mineral grains loose with their hyphae.

entries.text: Two common minerals, albite and {{ref:soil-chem-226}}, weather twice as fast in live soil as in sterile soil. Living things make the difference. Biological weathering is weathering started or sped up by soil microorganisms, lichens and plant roots. Soil organisms make up about 10 mg/cm3 of typical soils. Lichens are among the most effective agents. In a New Jersey study, hornblende granite under lichen weathered three to four times faster than bare rock. Most commonly, plants release carbon dioxide along with chelating compounds, chemicals that grip metal ions, such as organic acids and {{ref:soil-bio-192}}. Roots can raise carbon dioxide to 30% of all soil gases. The chelating acids strip metal ions, especially aluminum and silicon, from rock. Where they build up, they can reshape whole soils. Partnerships help too. Root-dwelling fungi free nutrients from minerals such as {{ref:soil-form-144}} or apatite and pass them to trees, and some bacteria weather minerals in ways that promote plant growth. Life also works by force. Seedlings and roots growing in crevices push rock apart, and lichens pluck mineral grains loose with their hyphae, their thread-like filaments.

entries.title: Dissolution: when a mineral vanishes into water

definition.text: Chemical weathering in which a mineral dissolves completely without leaving any new solid; also called simple or congruent dissolution.

facts.text: Rainwater easily dissolves soluble minerals such as halite and gypsum, and given enough time even quartz, which goes into solution as silicic acid.
In carbonate dissolution, rainwater and carbon dioxide form weak carbonic acid, which dissolves limestone into soluble calcium bicarbonate.
Cold water holds more dissolved carbon dioxide, so carbonate dissolution is favoured at low temperature and is important in glacial weathering.
Unpolluted rain has a pH of around 5.6; sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides make acid rain that can lower it to 4.5 or even 3.0.

entries.text: Some minerals leave nothing behind when they weather. In dissolution weathering, also called simple or congruent dissolution, a mineral dissolves completely and no new solid forms. Rainwater easily dissolves soluble minerals such as halite and gypsum. Given enough time, it dissolves even quartz, which goes into solution as silicic acid. Limestone meets a special version. Rainwater and carbon dioxide form weak carbonic acid, which turns limestone into soluble calcium bicarbonate. Cold water holds more dissolved carbon dioxide, so this carbonate dissolution is favored at low temperature. That makes it important in glacial weathering. Pollution sharpens the attack. Unpolluted rain has a pH of around 5.6, where lower numbers mean more acid. Sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides make acid rain that can lower it to 4.5 or even 3.0.

entries.title: Oxidation weathering: iron that reddens and weakens rock

definition.text: Chemical weathering by oxidation of metals in minerals, most commonly iron changing from Fe2+ to Fe3+.

facts.text: Oxygen and water oxidize Fe2+ to Fe3+ oxides and hydroxides such as goethite, limonite and hematite.
This gives rock a reddish-brown surface that crumbles easily and weakens the rock.
Sulfide minerals oxidize too, as when chalcopyrite turns to copper hydroxide and iron oxides, leaving coloured deposits.
Oxidizing primary minerals, especially sulfides and those containing Fe2+, generates soil acidity.

entries.text: A reddish-brown crust on a rock is often a sign of iron changing inside it. Oxidation weathering is chemical weathering by oxidation of metals in minerals, most commonly iron changing from Fe2+ to Fe3+. Oxygen and water drive the change. They turn Fe2+ into Fe3+ oxides and hydroxides such as {{ref:soil-chem-165}}. The new surface crumbles easily, and the rock beneath grows weaker. Sulfide minerals oxidize too. Chalcopyrite, for example, turns to copper hydroxide and {{ref:soil-chem-163}}, leaving colored deposits. The process reaches into the soil. Oxidizing {{ref:soil-form-140}}, especially sulfides and those containing Fe2+, generates soil acidity.

entries.title: Physical weathering: breaking rock without changing it

definition.text: Weathering that breaks rock into smaller pieces without changing its chemistry; also called mechanical weathering or disaggregation.

facts.text: Most of it comes from expansion and contraction with temperature change, as in freeze–thaw and thermal fracturing; pressure release works without any temperature change.
It is usually much less important than chemical weathering, but can be significant in subarctic or alpine settings.
Frost weathering is its most important form, followed by wedging by plant roots that enter cracks and pry them apart.
Burrowing worms and other animals, and plucking by lichens, can also help break rock apart.

entries.text: A rock can be shattered into pieces that are chemically identical to the original. That is physical weathering, also called mechanical weathering or disaggregation: breaking rock into smaller pieces without changing its chemistry. Most of it comes from expansion and contraction as temperature changes, as in freeze–thaw and thermal fracturing. Unloading, the loss of weight from rock above, is the exception, since it works without any temperature change. Ice is the most important agent, as {{ref:soil-found-054}} explains. Next comes wedging by plant roots, which enter cracks and pry them apart. Burrowing worms and other animals help, and lichens pluck grains loose. Physical weathering is usually much less important than chemical weathering. In subarctic or alpine settings, though, it can be significant.

entries.title: What fallen leaves and roots are made of

definition.text: The water, elements and organic compounds that make up the plant debris from which soil organic matter forms.

facts.text: Plant debris is 60% to 90% water.
Carbon, oxygen and hydrogen make up about 92% of the dry weight; the rest includes nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, sulfur, calcium, magnesium and micronutrients.
Its organic compounds include carbohydrates from simple sugars to cellulose, fats, lignins from older woody parts, and proteins containing nitrogen.
Charcoal, elemental carbon left by incomplete burning, is highly resistant to decomposition.

This debris is the raw material of {{ref:soil-found-045}}. One leftover stands apart. Charcoal, the elemental carbon left by incomplete burning, is highly resistant to decomposition.

entries.title: Most soil carbon lies below the top 20 cm
entries.article: Soil organic matter#SOC distribution with depth

definition.text: How the amount, age and makeup of soil organic carbon change between the surface layer, roughly the top 20 cm, and the deeper mineral soil.

facts.text: About 70% of global soil organic carbon lies deeper than 20 cm.
Surface soil has higher carbon concentrations, but deeper soil stores more carbon overall because of its greater mass.
Radiocarbon dates show carbon growing older with depth, a sign that deep soil stores it for longer.
Living things shape organic carbon near the surface, while mineral influences dominate at depth, through mineral-associated organic matter.

entries.title: Frost weathering and the ice that splits rock

definition.text: Physical weathering caused by ice forming inside rock outcrops.

facts.text: Water expands 9.2% on freezing; a realistic upper limit on the pressure is 14 megapascals, far above granite's tensile strength of about 4 megapascals.
Frost wedging, long thought the main mechanism, needs small tortuous cracks in almost saturated rock, conditions unusual enough that it is unlikely to dominate.
In ice segregation, water drawn to growing ice lenses can exert up to ten times the pressure of frost wedging; it works best between −4 and −15 °C.
It is strongest in alpine, periglacial, subpolar maritime and polar climates, but can occur anywhere between −3 and −8 °C if water is present.

entries.contested_note: Frost wedging was long believed the main mechanism, but growing theoretical and experimental work favours ice segregation.

entries.text: Water expands 9.2% when it freezes. Inside rock, the pressure this creates has a realistic upper limit of 14 megapascals, far above granite's tensile strength of about 4 megapascals. Frost weathering is physical weathering caused by ice forming inside rock outcrops. Frost wedging, the classic explanation, was long believed the main mechanism. It needs small, twisting cracks in almost saturated rock and daily freeze–thaw cycles. Those conditions are unusual, so it is unlikely to matter in the tropics, polar regions or arid climates. Growing theoretical and experimental work now favors {{ref:soil-phys-179}} instead, though the question is still open. Water drawn to the growing ice layers covered in {{ref:soil-phys-154}} can exert up to ten times the pressure of frost wedging. It works best between −4 and −15 °C.

entries.title: Mineral hydration, water's first grip on a crystal

definition.text: Chemical weathering in which water molecules, or H+ and OH− ions, attach rigidly to the atoms of a mineral.

facts.text: Examples are iron oxides turning into iron hydroxides and anhydrite hydrating to gypsum.
Bulk hydration matters less than dissolution, hydrolysis and oxidation, but hydration of the crystal surface is the crucial first step in hydrolysis.
Water at a fresh surface splits into H+ and OH−; protons then replace surface cations, freeing them, and loosened bonds release silicic acid and aluminium hydroxides.
In the regolith, hydration turns silicate minerals such as feldspars into clay minerals; montmorillonite can take up varying water without changing its structure.

entries.text: Before water can take a crystal apart, it has to attach to it. In mineral hydration, water molecules, or H+ and OH− ions, attach rigidly to the atoms of a mineral. The minerals of {{ref:soil-chem-163}} turning into iron hydroxides, and anhydrite hydrating to gypsum, are examples. Bulk hydration matters less than dissolution, {{ref:soil-form-172}} and oxidation. But hydration of the crystal surface is the crucial first step in it. Water at a fresh surface splits into H+ and OH−. Protons then replace the positive ions at the surface, freeing them. Loosened bonds release silicic acid and aluminum hydroxides. In the mineral of {{ref:soil-form-141}}, this starts at defects on the crystal surface, in a layer only a few atoms thick.

entries.title: Pressure release: rock that peels as it rises

definition.text: Physical weathering, also called unloading, that occurs when deeply buried rock is brought to the surface and the weight on it is removed.

facts.text: Granite and other intrusive rocks form deep underground under great pressure; when erosion strips the rock above, their outer parts expand.
The expansion opens fractures parallel to the surface, and sheets of rock break away along them, a process called exfoliation or sheeting.
In buttressed rock the stress toward the free surface can reach 35 megapascals, easily enough to shatter rock.
Retreat of an overlying glacier can also cause exfoliation by pressure release.

entries.text: Granite and other intrusive rocks form deep underground, under great pressure. When erosion strips away the rock above, their outer parts expand. This is pressure release weathering, also called unloading. The expansion opens fractures parallel to the surface, and sheets of rock break away along them. Geologists call this exfoliation or sheeting. Where rock is buttressed, the stress toward the free surface can reach 35 megapascals, easily enough to shatter rock. A retreating glacier can do the same by lifting its weight off the rock beneath.

entries.title: Salt weathering: crystals that pry rock apart

definition.text: The breaking up of rock when salty water seeps into cracks and evaporates, leaving salt crystals that grow there; also called haloclasty.

facts.text: Like ice lenses, salt grains draw in more dissolved salt by capillary action and grow into lenses that press hard on the surrounding rock.
Sodium and magnesium salts are the most effective.
It occurs wherever evaporation concentrates salts, so it is most common in arid climates and along coasts.
Weathering of pyrite to iron(II) sulfate and gypsum can also grow salt lenses in sedimentary rock.

entries.text: Salt can split stone. In salt weathering, also called haloclasty, salty water seeps into cracks and evaporates, leaving salt crystals that grow there. Like {{ref:soil-phys-154}}, the grains draw in more dissolved salt through tiny gaps. They grow into lenses that press hard on the surrounding rock. Sodium and magnesium salts work best. Salt weathering happens wherever evaporation concentrates salts, so it is most common in arid climates and along coasts. In the rocks of {{ref:soil-form-136}}, weathering of {{ref:soil-chem-134}} to iron(II) sulfate and gypsum can grow salt lenses too.

entries.title: Thermal stress: rock cracked by heat and cold

definition.text: Weathering caused by rock expanding and contracting as its temperature changes.

facts.text: It takes two forms: thermal shock, where rock cracks at once, which is uncommon, and the more typical thermal fatigue, where repeated stress cycles gradually weaken rock.
It matters in deserts with large day–night temperature swings, but any large temperature change, including wildfire, can drive it, so it is likely as important in cold climates.
It works best when heated rock is buttressed by surrounding rock and can expand in only one direction.
Geologists long discounted it after early 20th-century oven experiments, since criticized as unrealistic; geomorphologists now re-emphasize it.

entries.contested_note: Its importance was long discounted on the basis of early experiments that have since been criticized as unrealistic.
entries.text: Rock swells as it warms and shrinks as it cools, and the strain adds up. Thermal stress weathering is weathering caused by these temperature changes. It takes two forms. Deserts, with their large day–night swings, are the classic setting. Yet any large temperature change can drive it, including wildfire, so it is likely as important in cold climates. It works best when heated rock is buttressed by surrounding rock and can expand in only one direction. Its reputation has swung. entries.title: Eight elements and the swaps that multiply minerals

definition.text: How the abundance of elements in the Earth's crust, and the swapping of one ion for another, control which minerals exist and how varied they are.

facts.text: Eight elements make up over 98% of the crust by weight: oxygen, silicon, aluminium, iron, magnesium, calcium, sodium and potassium, in decreasing order.
Oxygen forms 47% of the crust by weight and silicon 28%.
The minerals that form are those most stable at the temperature and pressure of formation, within the limits set by the bulk chemistry.
Ions substitute for one another only when close in size and charge; Al3+ commonly replaces Si4+, as the two are similar in charge, size and crustal abundance.
In silicates, putting Al3+ in place of Si4+ leaves a charge to balance, which is why so many different silicate minerals exist.
Weathering or hydrothermal alteration changes a rock's composition, and with it the minerals the rock contains.

entries.title: Oxide minerals, where oxygen holds the metals

definition.text: Minerals in which oxygen or hydroxide is the main anion, divided into simple oxides, hydroxides and multiple oxides.

facts.text: Hematite (Fe2O3) and corundum (Al2O3) belong to the corundum group of simple oxides.
Bauxite, the chief aluminium ore, is a mixture of hydroxides including gibbsite that forms where chemical weathering is very intense.
Magnetite is strongly magnetic because it holds iron in two oxidation states, Fe2+ and Fe3+.
Water converts many primary minerals to clay minerals or hydrated oxides through reactions called hydrolysis.

entries.text: The world's chief aluminum ore is a product of extreme weathering. This ore, {{ref:soil-chem-108}}, is a mixture of hydroxides that forms where chemical weathering is very intense. It belongs to the oxide minerals, those in which oxygen or hydroxide is the main anion, or negatively charged ion. They fall into three groups: simple oxides, hydroxides and multiple oxides. Corundum (Al2O3) and the iron oxide Fe2O3, covered in {{ref:soil-chem-112}}, belong to the corundum group of simple oxides. Magnetite is strongly magnetic because it holds iron in two charge states, Fe2+ and Fe3+, as {{ref:soil-chem-178}} explains. Oxides also form during weathering. Water converts many original rock minerals, covered in {{ref:soil-form-140}}, to fine sheet minerals or hydrated oxides through the reactions described in {{ref:soil-found-060}}.

entries.title: The handful of minerals that build most rock

definition.text: The mineral species and groups that are far more abundant in rocks than the rest.

facts.text: A rock is an aggregate of one or more minerals or mineraloids.
The main rock-forming minerals are quartz, the feldspars, micas, amphiboles, pyroxenes, olivines and calcite; all but calcite are silicates.
Some rocks are mostly one mineral, such as limestone (calcite) or quartzite (quartz); others, like granite, are defined by the proportions of key minerals.
Rocks can also be non-mineral: coal is a sedimentary rock made mainly of organically derived carbon.

entries.text: Thousands of mineral species exist, but a few do most of the building. Rock-forming minerals are the species and groups far more abundant in rocks than the rest. The main ones are quartz, {{ref:soil-chem-135}}, amphiboles, pyroxenes, and the minerals described in {{ref:soil-form-141}}, {{ref:soil-form-145}} and {{ref:soil-found-118}}. entries.title: Silicates: one building block, many ways to link it

definition.text: Minerals built from the silicon–oxygen tetrahedron, [SiO4]4−, grouped by how far those tetrahedra link together.

facts.text: Silicon almost always sits in four-fold, tetrahedral coordination with oxygen.
Tetrahedra polymerize to different degrees, forming one-dimensional chains, two-dimensional sheets and three-dimensional frameworks.
Subclasses run from isolated tetrahedra (orthosilicates) through paired tetrahedra, rings and chains to sheets (phyllosilicates) and frameworks sharing all four corners (tectosilicates).
Al3+ often replaces Si4+ in the tetrahedra because the two ions have similar radius and charge, which changes how the structure's charge must be balanced.
Single-chain silicates are mostly pyroxenes and double-chain silicates often amphiboles; pyroxenes make up about 10% of the crust.
Silicates make up approximately 90% of the Earth's crust.
Partial melting, crystallization, metamorphism, weathering and diagenesis have formed and reworked them for billions of years, and organisms such as diatoms also take part.

entries.text: Approximately 90% of the Earth's crust is silicate minerals, and all of them share one building block. It is the silicon–oxygen tetrahedron, [SiO4]4−, a silicon atom surrounded by four oxygens. Silicon almost always sits in this four-fold, tetrahedral arrangement with oxygen. What varies is how the tetrahedra link. They polymerize, or join up, to different degrees, and mineralogists group silicates by that degree. At one end are isolated tetrahedra, the orthosilicates. Then come paired tetrahedra, rings and chains. Single-chain silicates are mostly pyroxenes, which make up about 10% of the crust. Double-chain silicates are often amphiboles. Next come two-dimensional sheets, the subject of {{ref:soil-found-033}}. At the far end are three-dimensional frameworks sharing all four corners, the tectosilicates of {{ref:soil-found-032}}. One substitution adds variety. Al3+ often replaces Si4+ in the tetrahedra, because the two ions have similar radius and charge. The swap changes how the structure's charge must be balanced, as {{ref:soil-found-030}} showed.

entries.title: Quartz and feldspar, the sturdy framework silicates

definition.text: Silicate minerals whose tetrahedra share all four corners, the most polymerized class, including quartz and the feldspars.

facts.text: Strong covalent bonds make framework silicates particularly stable chemically; quartz, 12% of the crust, is the most abundant mineral species and highly resistant.
A rock rich in quartz is considered mature, because quartz is the primary mineral that survived heavy weathering.
Feldspars are the most abundant mineral group in the crust; Al3+ substituting for Si4+ is balanced by added cations such as potassium, sodium or calcium.
Weathering of feldspar is a common source of clay minerals.

entries.text: Quartz is the most abundant mineral species, making up 12% of the crust. It belongs to the framework silicates, whose tetrahedra share all four corners. This is the most polymerized class. Strong covalent bonds make these minerals particularly stable chemically, and quartz is highly resistant. That toughness makes it a marker. A rock rich in quartz is considered mature, because quartz, one of the {{ref:soil-form-140}}, is the one that survived heavy weathering. The most abundant mineral group in the crust is the one described in {{ref:soil-form-141}}. In them, Al3+ takes the place of some Si4+, and added potassium, sodium or calcium balances the charge. These minerals matter to soil for another reason: their weathering is a common source of the fine minerals in {{ref:soil-found-040}}.

entries.title: Phyllosilicates: minerals built in stacked sheets

definition.text: Sheet silicates: minerals made of sheets of linked silica tetrahedra, a class that includes the mica, chlorite and kaolinite–serpentine groups.

facts.text: Each tetrahedron is bound at three oxygen sites, giving a silicon to oxygen ratio of 2:5.
A sheet of octahedra balances the negatively charged tetrahedral sheet; these tetrahedral (T) and octahedral (O) sheets stack into layers.
The 1:1 clay minerals, the kaolinite–serpentine group, are T-O stacks held by hydrogen bonds; the 2:1 clay minerals are T-O-T stacks held by weaker van der Waals forces.
Micas are also T-O-T stacks but put aluminium in the tetrahedral sheets, whereas clay minerals hold Al3+ in octahedral sites; metal ions bond mica layers, making them harder.
Weak bonds between layers give phyllosilicates a prominent basal cleavage, so they split into thin, flexible flakes.
Octahedral sheets with every site filled are trioctahedral; those with some sites empty are dioctahedral, as in kaolinite and pyrophyllite.

entries.text: Some minerals split into thin, flexible flakes. These are the phyllosilicates, or sheet silicates, made of sheets of linked silica tetrahedra. The class includes {{ref:soil-chem-135}} and the minerals at the heart of {{ref:soil-found-040}}. Each tetrahedron is bound to its neighbors at three oxygen sites, giving a silicon to oxygen ratio of 2:5. That leaves the tetrahedral sheet negatively charged, and a sheet of octahedra balances it. These tetrahedral (T) and octahedral (O) sheets stack into layers, and the stacking defines the groups. In 1:1 minerals, T-O stacks are held together by hydrogen bonds. In 2:1 minerals, T-O-T stacks are held by weaker forces, described in {{ref:soil-chem-227}}. This peeling mineral is also a T-O-T stack, with a difference. It puts aluminum in the tetrahedral sheets, whereas the 1:1 and 2:1 minerals hold Al3+ in the octahedral sites. Metal ions bond its layers together, making them harder. Because the bonds between layers are weak, phyllosilicates show a prominent basal cleavage, a tendency to split along flat planes. Octahedral sheets come in two kinds. When every site is filled they are trioctahedral. When some sites are empty, as in pyrophyllite, they are dioctahedral.

entries.title: Clay, the finest and busiest part of soil

definition.text: A fine-grained natural soil material containing clay minerals, the hydrous aluminium phyllosilicates such as kaolinite.

facts.text: Pure clay minerals are mostly white or pale, but impurities colour natural clays; small amounts of iron oxide give red or brown tones.
Clays become plastic when wet and can be hardened by firing.
Clay soils drain poorly, which makes them generally less suited to crops, but they are more fertile because of their higher cation-exchange capacity.
Mixtures of sand, silt and less than 40% clay are called loam.
Soils rich in swelling clays, which expand as they absorb water, are a major challenge in civil engineering.
Shale, formed largely from clay, is the most common sedimentary rock.
Clay is the longest-known ceramic raw material; some of the earliest pottery shards date to around 14,000 BCE.

verification.evidence: Clay loam.—Material has 27 to less than 40 percent clay and more than 20 to 45 percent sand.

entries.title: Soil texture: the sand, silt and clay recipe

definition.text: The quality of a soil set by its make-up of sand, silt and clay particles.

facts.text: Texture considers only particles less than two millimetres across, namely sand, silt and clay.
Texture classes rest on the percentages of sand, silt and clay; the USDA and WRB systems use 12 classes and the UK-ADAS system 11.
It can be judged qualitatively, by texture by feel, or measured quantitatively, for example by the hydrometer method based on Stokes' law.
Texture is fixed by a soil's mineral component and does not change with farming, unlike soil structure.
Field capacity, the soil water content best suited to plant growth, rises as soil particles get finer, from sand to clay.
Texture helps decide which crops suit a soil and predicts its response to drought or its lime needs.
Albert Atterberg proposed the first texture classification, the international system, in 1905.

Texture and structure are called master variables because they directly influence many other soil properties; a clayey soil has more surface area, cation exchange capacity, total porosity and organic matter but less macroporosity than a sandy one.

entries.title: How rain and time turn feldspar into clay

definition.text: The making of clay minerals, most commonly by long chemical weathering of silicate-bearing rocks, and their gathering into clay deposits.

facts.text: Chemical weathering works largely by acid hydrolysis, driven by weak carbonic acid in rainwater or released by plant roots.
The acid breaks bonds between aluminium and oxygen, releasing other metal ions and silica as a gel of orthosilicic acid.
Orthoclase feldspar in granite weathers to kaolinite and silicic acid, releasing potassium ions.
Source rock and climate decide the product: feldspar-rich rock gives kaolin under warm acid weathering and illite under alkaline conditions.
Smectite forms from igneous rock under alkaline conditions, while gibbsite forms by intense weathering of other clay minerals.
Clay minerals can also form locally from hydrothermal activity.
Primary clays stay where they formed as residual soil deposits; secondary clays are carried off by water erosion and laid down elsewhere, often in large lakes or marine basins.

entries.title: Hydrolysis and carbonation, the acid attack on rock

definition.text: Chemical weathering in which only part of a mineral dissolves and the rest turns into a new solid such as a clay mineral; carbonation is the form driven by dissolved carbon dioxide.

facts.text: Most is acid hydrolysis: protons in acidic water attack the chemical bonds in mineral crystals.
Carbonic acid from dissolved carbon dioxide is the main source of protons, though organic acids also matter.
The weakest cation–oxygen bonds go first, so igneous minerals weather in roughly the order they formed, Bowen's reaction series; illite is unusually stable, silica unusually unstable.
Orthoclase feldspar, carbonic acid and water yield kaolinite, silicic acid, and potassium and bicarbonate ions in solution.
Carbonation can also turn primary minerals into secondary carbonate minerals, as when forsterite weathers to magnesite.
Silicate weathering consumes carbonic acid and leaves alkaline bicarbonate solutions, an important control on atmospheric carbon dioxide and climate.

entries.text: Weathering rock helps set how much carbon dioxide stays in the air. Silicate weathering consumes carbonic acid and leaves alkaline bicarbonate solutions, an important control on atmospheric carbon dioxide and climate. The reactions behind it are {{ref:soil-form-172}} and carbonation. In them, only part of a mineral dissolves, and the rest becomes a new solid, often one of the fine minerals of clay. Most of it is driven by acid: protons in acidic water attack the chemical bonds in mineral crystals. Carbonic acid, from dissolved carbon dioxide, is the main source of those protons, though organic acids also matter. The textbook case is the potassium mineral of {{ref:soil-form-143}}, one of the group in {{ref:soil-form-141}}. With carbonic acid and water, it yields {{ref:soil-chem-088}}, silicic acid, and potassium and bicarbonate ions in solution. The weakest bonds between metal and oxygen go first. So igneous minerals weather in roughly the order they formed, a sequence described in {{ref:soil-chem-186}}. There are exceptions, such as silica, which is unusually unstable. Carbonation is the form driven by dissolved carbon dioxide. It can also turn minerals inherited from rock ({{ref:soil-form-140}}) into the {{ref:soil-chem-235}} of {{ref:soil-found-034}}, as when forsterite weathers to magnesite.

entries.title: From granite and basalt to soil: weathering's ledger

definition.text: The conversion of rock into soil material as weathering turns its minerals into clay minerals and iron oxides.

facts.text: Granite starts weathering with the loss of hornblende; biotite then becomes vermiculite, oligoclase and microcline go last, and all end as clay minerals and iron oxides.
Soil from granite loses calcium, sodium and ferrous iron, 40% of its magnesium and 15% of its silicon compared with the bedrock.
It gains at least 50% in aluminium and potassium, triples its titanium and raises its ferric iron by an order of magnitude.
Basalt weathers more easily than granite, being formed hotter and drier, fine-grained and glassy; it turns to potassium-poor montmorillonite, then kaolinite.
Continuous intense leaching, as in rain forests, ends in bauxite; intense but seasonal monsoon rain ends in iron- and titanium-rich laterite.
Soil formation takes between 100 and 1,000 years, a brief interval in geologic time.
The chemical index of alteration, 100 Al2O3/(Al2O3 + CaO + Na2O + K2O), runs from 47 for unweathered upper crust rock to 100 for fully weathered material.

entries.text: Turning rock into soil takes between 100 and 1,000 years, a brief interval in geologic time. In that span, weathering turns the minerals of rock into {{ref:soil-chem-079}} and the minerals of {{ref:soil-chem-163}}. Granite shows the sequence. Hornblende goes first. The dark sheet mineral of {{ref:soil-form-144}} then alters to another sheet mineral, and oligoclase and microcline go last. All end as clay and oxides of iron. The chemistry shifts with them. Compared with the bedrock, soil from granite loses calcium, sodium and ferrous iron, 40% of its magnesium and 15% of its silicon. It gains at least 50% in aluminum and potassium, triples its titanium and raises its ferric iron by an order of magnitude. Basalt weathers more easily than granite. It formed hotter and drier, and it is fine-grained and glassy. It turns to potassium-poor {{ref:soil-chem-093}}, then to {{ref:soil-chem-088}}. Climate writes the ending. Continuous intense washing by rain, as in rain forests, ends in the aluminum ore of {{ref:soil-chem-108}}. Intense but seasonal monsoon rain ends in an iron- and titanium-rich material, {{ref:soil-form-065}}. Geologists track the progress with the chemical index of alteration, 100 Al2O3/(Al2O3 + CaO + Na2O + K2O). It runs from 47 for unweathered upper crust rock to 100 for fully weathered material.

Granite shows the sequence. Hornblende goes first. The dark sheet mineral of Biotite, the dark mica that yellows with age then alters to another sheet mineral, and oligoclase and microcline go last. All end as clay and oxides of iron. The chemistry shifts with them. Compared with the bedrock, soil from granite loses calcium, sodium and ferrous iron, 40% of its magnesium and 15% of its silicon. It formed hotter and drier, and it is fine-grained and glassy. It turns to potassium-poor Montmorillonite, the clay that swells tenfold, then to Kaolinite, the white clay of china and the tropics. Climate writes the ending. Continuous intense washing by rain, as in rain forests, ends in the aluminum ore of Bauxite, the rock behind the world's aluminium. Intense but seasonal monsoon rain ends in an iron- and titanium-rich material, Laterite, the brick-red earth of the tropics. entries.title: Clay walls, brick and the barrier under a landfill

definition.text: The use of clay, the defining ingredient of loam, as one of the oldest building materials on Earth.

facts.text: Between one-half and two-thirds of the world's population still live or work in buildings made with clay, often baked into brick.
Being relatively impermeable, clay seals pond linings, dam cores and landfill barriers against toxic seepage.
Clay served as mortar in brick chimneys and stone walls where protected from water.
Early 21st-century studies have tested clay's absorption capacity for removing heavy metals from waste water and purifying air.

entries.text: Between one-half and two-thirds of the world's population still live or work in buildings made with clay, often baked into brick. Clay is one of the oldest building materials on Earth. Early 21st-century studies have tested its absorption capacity for removing heavy metals from waste water and for purifying air.

entries.title: Kaolinite, smectite, illite: the main kinds of clay

definition.text: The main kinds of clay, grouped by their dominant clay minerals: kaolinite, montmorillonite–smectite and illite.

facts.text: Chlorite, vermiculite, talc and pyrophyllite are sometimes also classed as clay minerals.
There are about 30 types of pure clay, but most natural deposits mix several of them with other weathered minerals.
Clay minerals are most easily identified by X-ray diffraction rather than by chemical or physical tests.
Varved clay shows visible annual layers laid down seasonally, and is common in former glacial lakes.

entries.text: There are about 30 types of pure clay, but nature rarely serves one alone. Most natural deposits mix several of them with other weathered minerals. The main kinds of clay are grouped by their dominant {{ref:soil-chem-079}}, each with its own entry later: {{ref:soil-chem-088}}, {{ref:soil-chem-093}} and {{ref:soil-chem-094}}. A few others, among them talc and pyrophyllite, are sometimes also classed among them. Chemical and physical tests struggle to tell them apart. {{ref:soil-chem-228}} identifies them most easily. One clay keeps a calendar. Varved clay shows visible annual layers laid down seasonally, and is common in former glacial lakes.

entries.title: From Jōmon pots to pencil lead: clay at work

definition.text: The shaping and firing of clay into pottery and construction products, and its use in many industrial processes.

facts.text: Some of the earliest pottery shards, from central Honshu in Japan and linked to the Jōmon culture, date to around 14,000 BCE.
Ancient Mesopotamians adopted clay tablets, inscribed in cuneiform, as the first known writing medium.
Different clays, minerals and firing conditions produce earthenware, stoneware and porcelain.
Industry uses clay in paper making, cement production and chemical filtering, and as a filler in pencil lead.

entries.text: Some of the earliest pottery shards come from central Honshu in Japan. Linked to the Jōmon culture, they date to around 14,000 BCE. People have shaped and fired clay ever since. Different clays, minerals and firing conditions produce earthenware, stoneware and porcelain. Ancient Mesopotamians inscribed cuneiform on clay tablets, the first known writing medium. Industry still relies on clay, in paper making, cement production and chemical filtering, and as a filler in pencil lead.

entries.title: Mineralogy, the science of how minerals are built

definition.text: The branch of geology that studies the chemistry, crystal structure and physical, including optical, properties of minerals.

facts.text: It covers how minerals originate and form, how they are classified, where they occur and how they are used.
Minerals form in settings from igneous melts deep in the crust to the oxidation and weathering of rock at the surface or within soil.
Identification starts with physical properties measurable on a hand sample, such as hardness on the Mohs scale from 1 (talc) to 10 (diamond).
X-ray diffraction, demonstrated in 1912, became a tool for analysing mineral crystal structures.

entries.text: Talc sits at one end of a scale and diamond at the other. Mineralogy is the branch of geology that studies the chemistry, crystal structure and physical properties of {{ref:soil-found-029}}, optical ones included. It asks how minerals form, how to classify them, where they occur and how people use them. Some crystallize from molten rock deep in the crust; others grow as rock weathers at the surface or in soil. Identification starts with a hand sample. Hardness is a first clue, ranked on the Mohs scale from talc at 1 to diamond at 10. {{ref:soil-chem-228}}, shown in 1912, later revealed crystal structures.
