entries.title: Should minerals made by living things count?

definition.text: The dispute among geologists and mineralogists over the International Mineralogical Association's exclusion of crystalline substances made by living things.

facts.text: Lowenstam (1981) argued that organisms form a diverse array of minerals, some of which cannot form inorganically.
Skinner (2005) counts biominerals, created by organisms' metabolism, as minerals, and allows a mineral to be crystalline or amorphous.
Over 60 biominerals had been named before the IMA's listing, yet they are not on its official list of mineral names.
Mineral-forming microorganisms live on nearly every rock, soil and particle surface, can precipitate metals from solution and can catalyse mineral dissolution.

entries.contested_note: Mineralogists disagree over whether minerals made by organisms should count as minerals, which the IMA definition excludes.
entries.text: Over 60 biominerals had been named before the International Mineralogical Association drew up its listing, yet they are not on its official list. The IMA definition excludes crystalline substances made by living things, and mineralogists still disagree about that choice. In 1981, Lowenstam argued that organisms form a diverse array of minerals, some of which cannot form inorganically. In 2005, Skinner counted biominerals, created by organisms' metabolism, as minerals, and allowed a mineral to be crystalline or amorphous. The question touches soil directly. Mineral-forming microorganisms live on nearly every rock, soil and particle surface. They can precipitate metals from solution and speed up mineral dissolution.

entries.title: Carbonate minerals and the geologist's acid test

definition.text: Minerals whose main anionic group is carbonate, [CO3]2−, chiefly calcite, aragonite and dolomite.

facts.text: All carbonates react with acid, so field geologists carry dilute hydrochloric acid to tell carbonates from other minerals.
Calcite, CaCO3, is the most common carbonate and the main constituent of limestone and marble; dolomite is the double carbonate CaMg(CO3)2.
Carbonates usually form as biogenic or chemical sediments in marine settings.
Weathering of primary minerals by dissolved carbon dioxide, sometimes called carbonation, can produce secondary carbonate minerals.

entries.text: Field geologists carry dilute hydrochloric acid for a quick test. All carbonates react with acid, so a drop tells them apart from other minerals. Carbonate minerals are those whose main anionic group is carbonate, [CO3]2−. The chief ones are aragonite, dolomite and the mineral in {{ref:soil-found-118}}. That last one, CaCO3, is the most common, and the main constituent of limestone and marble. Dolomite is the double carbonate CaMg(CO3)2. Carbonates usually form as biogenic or chemical sediments in marine settings. Weathering by dissolved carbon dioxide, sometimes called carbonation, can also produce secondary carbonate minerals.

entries.title: Calcite, the mineral that fizzes in acid

definition.text: A carbonate mineral, the most stable polymorph of calcium carbonate (CaCO3).

facts.text: It is very common, particularly in limestone, and defines hardness 3 on the Mohs scale.
Acid dissolves it and releases carbon dioxide, giving a characteristic fizz.
Groundwater can dissolve or precipitate calcite depending on temperature, pH and dissolved ions; less dissolved carbon dioxide makes it precipitate.
Unusually, it becomes less soluble in water as temperature rises.

entries.text: A drop of acid on calcite starts a fizz, as the mineral dissolves and gives off carbon dioxide. Calcite is the most stable crystal form of calcium carbonate, CaCO3, and one of the {{ref:soil-found-034}}. It is very common, especially in {{ref:soil-form-147}}, and it marks hardness 3 on the Mohs scale. Water moving underground can either dissolve it or deposit it, depending on temperature, pH and the ions it carries. Less dissolved carbon dioxide makes calcite come out of solution. It also breaks a common rule: it grows less soluble as water warms.

entries.title: Scratch, streak and shine: telling minerals apart

definition.text: Telling minerals apart by physical properties such as crystal habit, hardness, lustre, colour, streak, cleavage and specific gravity.

facts.text: Some minerals can only be classified by optical, chemical or X-ray diffraction analysis, which can be costly and time-consuming.
Hardness is most often measured on the Mohs scale of scratch resistance, which runs through ten indicator minerals from talc to diamond.
Colour is the most obvious property but often not diagnostic; the streak, the colour of the powdered mineral, is independent of trace elements and weathering.
Even grains too small to see have a periodic crystal structure that X-ray diffraction can determine.

entries.text: Color is the most obvious thing about a mineral, and often not diagnostic at all. Mineral identification tells minerals apart by physical properties: crystal habit, hardness, luster, color, streak, cleavage and specific gravity. Hardness is usually measured on the Mohs scale of scratch resistance, which runs through ten indicator minerals from talc to diamond. The streak is the color of the powdered mineral, and traces of other elements and weathering do not change it. Some minerals can only be classified by optical, chemical or {{ref:soil-chem-228}} analysis, which can be costly and time-consuming. Even grains too small to see have a periodic crystal structure that it can determine.

entries.title: Sulfate minerals and the gypsum left by evaporation

definition.text: Minerals that contain the sulfate anion, [SO4]2−, of which gypsum is by far the most common hydrous member.

facts.text: Sulfates commonly form as evaporites, precipitating from evaporating saline waters.
They also occur in hydrothermal veins or as oxidation products of sulfide minerals.
Gypsum, CaSO4·2H2O, forms with other evaporites such as calcite and halite; its anhydrous counterpart is anhydrite.

entries.text: As saline water evaporates, minerals precipitate out of it. Sulfate minerals, which contain the sulfate anion [SO4]2−, commonly form this way, as evaporites. Gypsum, CaSO4·2H2O, is by far the most common hydrous sulfate. It forms alongside other evaporites such as calcite and halite, and its anhydrous counterpart is anhydrite. Sulfates also occur in hydrothermal veins, or as oxidation products of sulfide minerals.

Sulfates also occur in hydrothermal veins, or as oxidation products of sulfide minerals.

entries.title: Phytoliths, the glass skeletons plants leave behind

definition.text: A rigid microscopic mineral deposit, usually of silica, formed in plant tissue and often persisting after the plant decays.

facts.text: Plants take up dissolved silica from the soil as monosilicic acid, Si(OH)4, which can reach 0.1% to 10% of their dry weight.
Phytoliths can persist in soils for thousands of years and are abundant in the fossil record from the Late Devonian onwards.
They are used to identify palaeoenvironments and track vegetation change.
Carbon occluded in phytoliths resists decay for millennia and accumulates in soils, with stores that vary by species, biome, climate and soil.

entries.text: Plants drink stone. They take up dissolved silica from the soil as monosilicic acid, Si(OH)4, and it can make up 0.1% to 10% of their dry weight. Inside the tissue, the silica hardens into phytoliths: rigid, microscopic mineral deposits that often outlast the plant itself. They can survive in soils for thousands of years and are abundant in the fossil record from the Late Devonian onward. That durability makes them useful clues to past environments and changing vegetation. Carbon sealed inside them also resists decay for millennia. It builds up in soils, in stores that vary by species, biome, climate and soil.

entries.title: Organic matter that minerals keep for centuries

definition.text: Soil organic matter chemically stabilized by sticking to clay, iron oxide or other mineral surfaces.

facts.text: It is thought to consist of small plant and microbial molecules bonded to charged mineral surfaces or locked inside aggregates.
Binding to minerals makes it harder for decomposers to reach, so it resists microbial breakdown and loss from the soil carbon pool.
It typically persists for centuries, whereas particulate organic matter, mostly little-decomposed plant remains, lasts only a few years to decades.

entries.text: Some carbon in soil lasts a few years; some lasts centuries. The difference often lies in what it is stuck to. Mineral-associated organic matter is {{ref:soil-found-045}} chemically stabilized by sticking to clay, iron oxide or other mineral surfaces. It is thought to consist of small plant and microbial molecules. They bond to charged mineral surfaces or are locked inside aggregates, crumbs of soil particles stuck together. Binding to minerals makes this carbon harder for decomposers to reach. So it resists microbial breakdown and stays in the soil's store of carbon. It typically persists for centuries. By contrast, {{ref:soil-bio-118}}, mostly little-decomposed plant remains, lasts only a few years to decades.

Binding to minerals makes this carbon harder for decomposers to reach. So it resists microbial breakdown and stays in the soil's store of carbon. It typically persists for centuries. entries.title: Weathering rinds, the stone clocks of old gravel

definition.text: A discoloured, chemically altered outer layer of a rock fragment, formed by weathering.

facts.text: It forms on clasts from pebbles to boulders, at the surface or buried in alluvium, colluvium or till, through exposure to air or shallow groundwater.
Rinds are often enriched in iron, manganese and silica and oxidized to yellowish red or reddish colours.
Comparing rind thickness on gravel of similar rock gives relative ages of Quaternary deposits: thicker rinds mean older deposits.
Calibrated against radiocarbon-dated deposits, an age–thickness curve can date other deposits; the relation is taken to be logarithmic.

entries.text: A pebble's skin can tell its age. A weathering rind is a discolored, chemically altered outer layer on a rock fragment, formed as {{ref:soil-found-058}} works inward. Rinds grow on stones from pebbles to boulders, at the surface or buried in river, slope or glacial deposits, wherever air or shallow underground water reaches them. They are often enriched in iron, manganese and silica, and oxidized to yellowish or reddish hues. Thicker rinds on gravel of similar rock mean older deposits. Calibrated against radiocarbon-dated deposits, an age–thickness curve can date others, on the assumption that the relation is logarithmic.

entries.title: Soil pH, the number that runs soil chemistry

definition.text: A measure of how acidic or basic (alkaline) a soil is.

facts.text: pH is the negative base-10 logarithm of hydronium ion activity; for soils it is measured in a slurry with water or a salt solution such as 0.01 M CaCl2.
Soil pH normally falls between 3 and 10, with 7 neutral; ultra-acidic soils below pH 3.5 and very strongly alkaline soils above pH 9 are rare.
Because the scale is logarithmic, a solution at pH 3.5 has one million times more hydronium ions than one at pH 9.5.
Soil pH is a master variable: it controls the chemical forms of nutrients and the reactions they undergo, and so their availability to plants.
The optimum for most plants is pH 5.5 to 7.5, though many plants have adapted to thrive outside this range.
Most crops do best at pH 6.5 on mineral soils and pH 5.5 on organic soils; highly acidic soils tend to hold toxic amounts of aluminium and manganese.
High-rainfall soils tend to acidify as hydronium ions displace basic cations; in low-rainfall areas unleached calcium pushes pH to 8.5, and exchangeable sodium can raise it to 10.
Soil pH is generally lower where weathering is more advanced.

conflicts.text: In practice, soil pH ranges from 3.5 to 9.5, as values beyond those extremes are toxic to life forms.
conflicts.note: Soil#Reactivity (pH) gives a practical soil range of 3.5–9.5; the Soil pH lead says soil pH normally falls between 3 and 10.

entries.title: Soil horizons, the layers that record a soil's life

definition.text: A layer roughly parallel to the soil surface whose physical, chemical and biological characteristics differ from the layers above and below.

facts.text: Horizons are the product of soil-forming processes; layers that have not undergone such processes are simply called layers.
They are recognised mainly by colour and texture, described in absolute terms or relative to their neighbours, as coarser, sandier or darker.
Given time, an undifferentiated soil evolves a profile of two or more horizons, which differ greatly in thickness and generally lack sharp boundaries.
No soil profile has all the major horizons; some soils, such as Entisols, have only one horizon or none at all.
Erosion can strip upper horizons and bury others downslope, and tillage, tree growth and major earthworks also disturb or erase them.
Going down a profile goes back in time: pollen, testate amoebae and plant remains record past environmental change, and charcoal allows radiocarbon dating of horizons.
Most classification systems use horizons to define soil types, either as whole horizon sequences, as in the German system, or as selected diagnostic horizons.
Horizons are labelled in a shorthand of letters and numbers that describes colour, texture, structure, consistency, roots, pH, voids, boundaries and nodules.

entries.title: Buffering: why some soils shrug off acid

definition.text: A soil's resistance to a change in pH when acid or basic material is added.

facts.text: Within a soil type it rises with cation exchange capacity: pure sand has almost no buffering ability, while soils rich in mineral or organic colloids buffer strongly.
Buffering works through cation exchange and neutralisation, and carbonates also regulate pH; different buffer systems take over at different pH, from calcium carbonate to iron.
It depends on clay content, clay type and organic matter, so clay- and humus-rich soils need more lime for the same change in pH.
Lime must neutralise the acid cations held on colloids (exchangeable acidity), not just free acidity in solution, or the stored cations restore the original pH.
Once colloids are saturated with hydronium, a soil has no buffering capacity left and further acid drives pH lower; extreme rain and heat can also wash out clay and humus.
The lime needed depends on how finely it is ground (mesh size) and on buffering capacity, and can be calculated from initial pH and exchangeable aluminium.

entries.text: Add the same acid to two soils, and one barely budges while the other's pH plunges. The difference is buffering capacity, a soil's resistance to a change in pH when acid or basic material is added. It works through {{ref:soil-chem-047}} and neutralization, and carbonates also regulate pH. Different buffer systems take over at different pH, from calcium carbonate to iron. Pure sand has almost no buffering ability. Soils rich in fine mineral or organic particles, the subject of {{ref:soil-chem-154}}, buffer strongly. Within one kind of soil, buffering rises with {{ref:soil-chem-046}}. So clay- and humus-rich soils need more lime for the same change in pH. The reason is stored acidity. Lime must neutralize the acid cations held on these particles, not just the free acid in solution, or the stored cations restore the original pH. The lime needed depends on how finely it is ground and on buffering capacity. Once the particles are saturated with hydronium, the buffer is spent, and further acid drives pH lower.

entries.title: Soil color, the first thing anyone notices

definition.text: The colour of a soil, often its most visually apparent property.

facts.text: Colour does not itself change how a soil behaves, but it indicates organic matter content, mineralogy, moisture and leaching.
Soils can be brown, red, yellow, black, gray, white or even blue or green, and colour varies across landscapes, between horizons and within a single clod.
Colour develops through chemical and biological weathering, especially redox reactions, as elements released from primary minerals combine into new coloured compounds.
Ordinary conditions give uniform or gradual colour changes, while reducing environments produce disrupted, mottled patterns with points of concentrated colour.
Soil colour is primarily influenced by mineralogy and is often the first impression one has of a soil.
Because colour, especially value, changes with moisture, it may be described both moist and dry.

entries.contested_note: Sources differ on colour's diagnostic value: one says it has little use in predicting soil characteristics, another that it reveals organic matter, mineralogy, moisture and leaching.

entries.title: Aluminum, the hidden poison of acid soils

definition.text: Harm to plants from dissolved aluminium, the most widespread problem of acid soils.

facts.text: Aluminium is present in all soils, but toxic dissolved Al3+ is most soluble at low pH; above pH 5.0 most soils hold little soluble aluminium.
Aluminium inhibits root growth: lateral roots and root tips thicken, fine branching is lost and tips may turn brown.
It then disrupts the uptake and transport of calcium and other nutrients, cell division, cell wall formation and enzyme activity.
Acid soils also stress plants through hydrogen and manganese toxicity and calcium and magnesium deficiency; manganese toxicity symptoms appear below pH 5.6.
Acid rain is the main factor mobilising aluminium from natural sources.
The shift from toxic to non-toxic aluminium near pH 5 also marks the passage from acid-tolerant to acid-intolerant soil communities.

entries.text: Every soil contains aluminum, yet in most it does no harm. Aluminum toxicity is damage to plants from dissolved aluminum, and it is the most widespread problem of acid soils. The toxic form, the dissolved ion Al3+, is most soluble at low pH. Above pH 5.0 most soils hold little soluble aluminum. Roots show the damage first. Root tips and side roots thicken, fine branching is lost and the tips may turn brown. The poison then disrupts the uptake and transport of calcium and other nutrients, cell division, cell wall formation and enzyme activity. Acid soils add other stresses: hydrogen toxicity, manganese poisoning ({{ref:soil-chem-144}}), and shortages of calcium and magnesium. Manganese symptoms appear below pH 5.6. Acid rain is the main force mobilizing aluminum from natural sources. The shift near pH 5 also marks a boundary in soil life, from acid-tolerant to acid-intolerant communities.

entries.title: What pushes a soil toward acid or alkaline

definition.text: The natural and human influences that set a soil's pH, starting with the minerals of its parent material and the weathering they have undergone.

facts.text: In warm, humid climates soils acidify as weathering products are leached away; in dry climates weaker weathering and leaching leave soils neutral or alkaline.
Rain, at an average pH of 5.6 from dissolved carbon dioxide, leaches basic cations and raises the share of aluminium and hydrogen ions.
Living things add acidity: respiration and decay release CO2, and plants taking up more cations than anions release H+ ions from their roots.
Ammonium fertilizers, acid rain and oxidation of sulfide minerals, as in mine spoil or drained acid sulfate soils, also acidify soils.
Alkalinity rises with weathering or addition of minerals containing sodium, calcium, magnesium and potassium, and with irrigation water rich in bicarbonate.
Carbonates and bicarbonates build up where too little water flows through to leach salts, as under arid conditions or poor internal drainage.
Calcareous soils range from pH 7.0 to 9.5, depending on whether calcium or sodium dominates the soluble cations.

entries.text: Rain itself is slightly acidic. At an average pH of 5.6, from dissolved carbon dioxide, it washes basic cations out of soil and raises the share of aluminum and hydrogen ions. Many forces set a soil's pH, beginning with the minerals the soil formed from and the weathering they have undergone. In warm, humid climates soils acidify as weathering products wash away. In dry climates, weaker weathering and less washing leave soils neutral or alkaline. Life adds acid too. Respiration and decay release CO2, and roots release H+ ions when plants take up more cations than anions, the negatively charged ions. Ammonium fertilizers, acid rain and oxidizing sulfide minerals in mine spoil or {{ref:soil-chem-030}} acidify further. Soils turn more alkaline with minerals rich in sodium, calcium, magnesium and potassium, and with bicarbonate-rich irrigation water. Where too little water flows through, carbonates and bicarbonates build up. Soils rich in calcium carbonate range from pH 7.0 to 9.5, depending on whether calcium or sodium dominates.

entries.title: Reading pH from heather, litmus and glass electrodes

definition.text: The field and laboratory methods for determining a soil's pH, from reading the profile and its plants to electronic meters.

facts.text: Profile features hint at pH: poor mixing of the organic layer suggests strong acidity, a caliche layer alkaline conditions, and columnar structure sodic conditions.
Indicator plants help: calcifuges such as heathers, rhododendrons and gorse mark acid soils, and calcicoles such as ash, dogwoods and clematis lime-rich ones.
Cheap kits mix soil with an indicator solution that changes colour; litmus paper dipped in a soil–water mix turns red if the soil is acidic and blue if basic.
Electronic pH meters insert an electrode into moist soil or a soil–water suspension and give a digital reading.
Spectrophotometric methods, developed in the 2010s, add an indicator dye to a soil extract and avoid the drift and suspension effects of glass electrodes.
The USDA laboratory method mixes 20 g of soil with 20 mL of water (1:1), reads pH after standing 1 h, then adds CaCl2 to read it again in 0.01 M CaCl2 at 1:2.

entries.text: A soil's pH can be read before any instrument comes out. The profile gives hints. Calcifuges, plants of acid soils, such as heathers, rhododendrons and gorse, mark acid ground. Calcicoles, lime-lovers such as ash, dogwoods and clematis, mark lime-rich ground. entries.title: How pH decides which nutrients plants can reach
entries.article: Soil pH#Nutrient availability in relation to soil pH

definition.text: The control soil pH exerts over which ions are released or held, and so over the availability of plant nutrients.

facts.text: Trading off toxicity against need, most nutrients are best available at moderate pH, although most minerals are more soluble in acid soils.
In very strongly to ultra-acidic soils (pH < 5.0), aluminium-damaged roots take up less, and deficiencies of nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium and magnesium are frequent.
Molybdenum becomes more available as pH rises, while zinc, iron, copper and manganese become less available.
High pH lowers micronutrient mobility, a deficit that water-soluble chelates can correct.
Phosphorus was long thought most available near neutrality (pH 6.5–7.5), but between pH 5.5 and 6.5 raising pH may increase, decrease or not affect its availability.
In calcareous soils above 2% calcium carbonate, supplying phosphorus, iron, manganese, copper or zinc is often more efficient than trying to acidify.

entries.text: A soil can be full of nutrients and still starve a crop. Soil pH governs which ions are released or held, and so which nutrients plants can take up. Most minerals dissolve more readily in acid soils. Yet, trading toxicity against need, most nutrients are best available at moderate pH. Below pH 5.0, roots damaged by aluminum take up less, and deficiencies of nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium and magnesium are frequent. Raising pH works unevenly. Molybdenum becomes more available, while zinc, iron, copper and manganese become less so. At high pH these trace nutrients move poorly, a deficit that water-soluble chelates, compounds that hold a metal in soluble form, can correct. Phosphorus was long thought most available near neutrality, at pH 6.5–7.5. Between pH 5.5 and 6.5, though, raising pH may increase, decrease or not affect it. In soils above 2% calcium carbonate, covered in {{ref:soil-chem-035}}, supplying phosphorus, iron, manganese, copper or zinc is often more efficient than trying to acidify.

entries.title: O, A, E, B, C, R: the alphabet of a soil profile

definition.text: The main layers of a soil profile, marked with capital letters, most commonly O, A, E, B, C and R.

facts.text: Many soils have an organic surface layer (O); the mineral soil usually starts with an A horizon, the layer with most organic matter and soil life.
An E horizon is a leached layer, while a B horizon is a well-developed subsoil where substances moving down from the topsoil accumulate.
A C horizon is loose but poorly developed material below, and R is hard bedrock that cannot be excavated by hand.
Mature profiles typically have three basic master horizons, A, B and C; the solum normally comprises the A and B horizons.
Most systems define more horizons and layers than these five, and the letters may differ: the USDA field book adds L for limnic materials, W for water and M for root-limiting manufactured layers.
Suffixes of lowercase letters and figures further differentiate the master horizons.
Because the systems define their symbols differently they cannot be mixed, and none is more correct than another.

The USDA field book adds L for limnic, or lake-laid, materials, W for water and M for root-limiting manufactured layers. Because the systems define their symbols differently, they cannot be mixed, and none is more correct than another.

entries.title: Turning an alkaline soil more acid
entries.article: Soil pH#Decreasing the pH of alkaline soil

definition.text: Reducing the pH of an alkaline soil by adding acidifying agents or acidic organic materials.

facts.text: Elemental sulfur (90–99% S), applied at 300–500 kg/ha, slowly oxidises in the soil to form sulfuric acid.
Ammonium sulfate, ammonium nitrate and urea lower pH because ammonium oxidises to nitric acid; peat and sphagnum moss are acidifying organic materials.
In high-pH soils with more than 2% calcium carbonate, acidifying is very costly and ineffective.

entries.text: Sometimes the goal is a more acid soil. Lowering soil pH means adding acidifying agents or acidic organic materials to an alkaline soil. Elemental sulfur, 90–99% pure, is applied at 300–500 kg/ha and slowly oxidizes in the soil to sulfuric acid. Some fertilizers also work, because their ammonium oxidizes to nitric acid: ammonium sulfate, {{ref:soil-fert-071}} and {{ref:soil-fert-021}}. Sphagnum moss and the material described in {{ref:soil-class-070}} are acidifying organic additions. There is a limit. In high-pH soils with more than 2% calcium carbonate, acidifying is very costly and ineffective.

entries.title: Lime lovers and lime haters among plants

definition.text: The soil pH ranges to which different plant species are adapted.

facts.text: Calcifuges prefer acid soils and calcicoles lime-rich ones; there are more calcicole than calcifuge species, so plant diversity tends to increase from pH 3.5 toward pH 9.
Some species tolerate only a narrow range, such as Monterey pine at pH 4.5–5.2, while vetiver grass tolerates pH 3.0–8.0.
Tolerance can depend on the soil: soybeans may fail at pH 5.5 where molybdenum is low but grow optimally at that pH where it is sufficient.
Breeders use differences between varieties to develop aluminium- and manganese-tolerant cereals for strongly acidic soils.

entries.text: Plants take sides on pH. Each species is adapted to its own range of soil pH. Calcifuges prefer acid soils and calcicoles lime-rich ones. Calcicole species outnumber calcifuges, so plant diversity tends to rise from pH 3.5 toward pH 9. Some ranges are narrow: Monterey pine grows at pH 4.5–5.2, while vetiver grass tolerates pH 3.0–8.0. The soil matters too. Soybeans may fail at pH 5.5 where molybdenum is low, yet grow optimally at that pH where it is sufficient. Breeders use differences between varieties to develop aluminum- and manganese-tolerant cereals for strongly acidic soils.

entries.title: Soil life and pH, each shaping the other
entries.article: Soil pH#pH effects on soil biota

definition.text: The two-way relation between soil pH and the organisms living in the soil.

facts.text: Soil microbes and animals respond to pH directly and through nutrient status, metal toxicity and humus form, so community composition shifts with pH.
At low pH, aluminium-induced oxidative stress harms soft-bodied fauna without an arthropod exoskeleton, such as protists, nematodes, enchytraeids and earthworms.
Many soil fungi acidify soil by excreting oxalic acid, which locks calcium into insoluble calcium oxalate crystals.
Earthworm mucus, weakly alkaline (7.5 < pH < 8), buffers pH, and burrowing animals that mix organic and mineral matter reduce acidity, as in mull humus.

entries.text: pH shapes soil life, and soil life shapes pH. entries.title: When pH extremes leave plants thirsty
entries.article: Soil pH#Water availability in relation to soil pH

definition.text: The ways extreme soil pH reduces the water available to plants and organisms.

facts.text: Strongly alkaline soils are sodic and dispersive, with slow infiltration, low hydraulic conductivity and poor available water capacity.
They are poorly aerated when wet, and when dry they quickly lose plant-available water and become hard and cloddy.
In strongly acidic soils aluminium toxicity limits root growth so much that moisture stress occurs even when the soil is relatively moist.

entries.text: A soil can hold water that plants still cannot use, and extreme pH is one reason. Strongly alkaline soils are sodic, rich in sodium, and dispersive, their particles drifting apart. Water soaks in slowly, moves through poorly and is stored badly. When wet, these soils are poorly aerated. When dry, they quickly lose plant-available water and turn hard and cloddy. Strongly acidic soils fail differently. Aluminum toxicity stunts roots so badly that plants run short of water even when the soil is relatively moist.

entries.title: From ultra acidic to very strongly alkaline: pH classes
entries.article: Soil pH#Classification of soil pH ranges

definition.text: The named soil pH ranges of the USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service, from ultra acidic to very strongly alkaline.

facts.text: Ultra acidic is below 3.5, extremely acidic 3.5–4.4, very strongly acidic 4.5–5.0, strongly acidic 5.1–5.5, moderately acidic 5.6–6.0 and slightly acidic 6.1–6.5.
The neutral class spans pH 6.6–7.3.
Slightly alkaline is 7.4–7.8, moderately alkaline 7.9–8.4, strongly alkaline 8.5–9.0 and very strongly alkaline above 9.0.

entries.text: US soil surveyors give each stretch of the pH scale a name. The classes come from {{ref:soil-hist-050}}. On the acid side, ultra acidic is below 3.5, extremely acidic 3.5–4.4, very strongly acidic 4.5–5.0, strongly acidic 5.1–5.5, moderately acidic 5.6–6.0 and slightly acidic 6.1–6.5. Neutral is a band, not a point: pH 6.6–7.3. Above it, slightly alkaline is 7.4–7.8, moderately alkaline 7.9–8.4, strongly alkaline 8.5–9.0 and very strongly alkaline above 9.0.

entries.title: How Australia names its soil horizons
entries.article: Soil horizon#Horizons according to the Australian Soil and Land Survey Field Handbook (2009)

definition.text: The horizon scheme of the Australian Soil and Land Survey Field Handbook (2009), which adds peaty P and D horizons, drops E, and numbers sub-horizons of A and B.

facts.text: P horizons are organic layers formed under waterlogging, named after peats, with 12 to 18% or more organic carbon depending on clay content.
A horizons split into A1 (dark, most biologically active), A2 (paler) and A3 (transitional to B); B horizons split into B1, B2 and B3.
Leached layers are classed as A or B by their other properties, and D marks material below the solum unlike the solum itself.
As a rule of thumb, layers thinner than about 5 cm are described as pans or segregations within a horizon, and excessive subdivision is to be avoided.

entries.title: The international code for soil layers
entries.article: Soil horizon#Horizons and layers according to the World Reference Base for Soil Resources

definition.text: The horizon and layer symbols set out in Chapter 10 of the World Reference Base for Soil Resources manual, 4th edition (2022).

facts.text: It separates organic layers, with at least 20% organic carbon, from organotechnic layers rich in artefacts and from mineral layers.
Fine earth is the soil fraction of 2 mm or less, and the soil surface is taken below any litter layer, which is over 90% recognisable dead plant tissue.
Its master symbols are H, O, A, E, B, C and R, plus I for permanent layers of at least 75% ice and W for water.
H layers are saturated for over 30 consecutive days in most years or are drained, typically peat; O layers are not.

verification.evidence: However, most H layers underwent at least some decomposition, show < 100% (by volume) recognizable dead plant tissues and are considered to be soil horizons.

entries.title: Munsell charts: color as hue, value and chroma

definition.text: The standard way soil surveys record soil colour, using the Munsell color system, which specifies a colour by hue, value and chroma.

facts.text: Albert H. Munsell created the system early in the 20th century and the USDA adopted it for soil research in the 1930s; the soil charts keep only the colours most relevant to soil.
Hue is the dominant spectral colour, in soil generally yellow or red, and each page of the Munsell soil colour book shows one hue.
The full system has five principal hues and five intermediates such as YR, each split into steps; charts conventionally show 40 hues in steps of 2.5, such as 10R to 2.5YR.
Value, lightness or darkness, increases from the bottom of each page to the top, lower numbers being darker.
Chroma, intensity or brightness, increases from left to right, higher numbers being more vivid; a chroma of 0 is neutral gray.
General names such as yellowish brown accompany the notation, matching colour chips, but are not formally part of the Munsell system.
Soil counts as moist when adding water no longer changes its colour, and as dry when air-dried.
A colour is written as hue, then value/chroma, as in a Cecil soil horizon recorded as red (10R 4/8) clay; neutral grays are written N with a value, such as N 5/.

entries.title: What a soil's color says about its history

definition.text: Reading what a soil's colours reveal about its organic matter, iron chemistry, aeration and salts.

facts.text: Dark brown or black usually means high organic matter, which coats mineral particles and darkens them; accumulated charcoal also turns soil black.
Red indicates iron accumulation or oxidation in oxygen-rich, well-aerated soils; yellow also reflects iron, but in less oxygen-rich settings.
Gray or blue marks saturated, anaerobic soils where iron has been reduced or depleted.
Green can come from iron reduction or from minerals such as glauconite, melanterite and celadonite.
White is common where salts, carbonates or calcite accumulate, often in arid environments; jarosite can colour acidic soils yellow.
Sodium helps humus disperse and reach more minerals, so it influences how deep the dark colour extends.
A B horizon, with less organic matter than the A, takes its colour mainly from iron oxides, usually brownish or reddish.
An Illinois handheld chart links colour to organic matter: nearly black soils indicate 3.5-7%, dark brown 2-3% and yellowish brown 1.5-2.5%.

sources.title: 2.3: Organic Matter And Natural Cycles - Geosciences LibreTexts (Building Soils for Better Crops, 4th ed. (Magdoff and van Es))

entries.title: Gleying: how waterlogged soil turns gray

definition.text: The development of gray or bluish, low-chroma colours in waterlogged soils as iron is reduced or removed.

facts.text: In anaerobic soils microbes reduce iron from the ferric (Fe3+) to the ferrous (Fe2+) form, and less often manganese from Mn4+ to Mn2+.
Reduced iron is soluble and can be removed during prolonged saturation, exposing the light gray of bare silicate minerals.
When the soil dries and oxygen returns, iron re-oxidises locally into yellow-brown, reddish or orange mottles, often along root channels and burrows.
Gleyed material can begin a few centimetres below the surface and continue almost unchanged for many metres.

entries.text: Waterlogged soil turns gray, and the reason is iron. Gleying is the development of gray or bluish, low-chroma colors in waterlogged soils as iron is reduced or removed. Without oxygen, microbes convert iron from the ferric form, Fe3+, to the ferrous form, Fe2+. Less often they reduce manganese from Mn4+ to Mn2+. Reduced iron is soluble. During prolonged saturation it can be carried away, exposing the light gray of bare silicate minerals. When the soil dries and oxygen returns, iron re-oxidizes locally into yellow-brown, reddish or orange mottles, often along root channels and burrows. Gleyed material can begin a few centimeters below the surface and continue almost unchanged for many meters.

entries.title: Core samples, columns of earth pulled out intact

definition.text: A cylindrical section of a material such as sediment, rock or soil, usually obtained by drilling with a hollow tube.

facts.text: The sample is pushed more or less intact into the tube, then removed in the laboratory for inspection and analysis.
Hand coring with a hollow tube or piston corer is cheap and quick but reaches only a few decimetres in clay soils.
Coring tools often fracture the core and lose weaker intervals, complicating interpretation; cuttings-based drilling yields no undisturbed core at all.
Dated cores of ocean floor, soil and ice record changes in climate and terrain and have reshaped the history of the Pleistocene.

entries.title: Trial pits: digging down before building up

definition.text: An excavation dug to study or sample the composition and structure of the subsurface, usually during a site investigation, soil survey or geological survey; also called a test pit.

facts.text: Pits are dug before construction to find out the geology and water table of a site.
They are usually between 1 and 4 metres deep and dug by hand or with a mechanical digger.
Regulations require pits deeper than 1.2 metres to be secured against collapse if people are to enter them.

entries.text: Before a building goes up, someone often digs a hole. A trial pit, also called a test pit, is an excavation dug to study or sample what lies below the surface. Most are dug for a site investigation or a soil or geological survey. A pit reveals a site's geology and how deep the water stands, and it lays bare the layers described in {{ref:soil-found-001}}. Pits usually run 1 to 4 meters deep, dug by hand or with a mechanical digger. Regulations require any pit deeper than 1.2 meters to be secured against collapse if people will enter it.

entries.title: Bedrock, the solid floor beneath the soil

definition.text: The solid rock beneath the weathered rock and loose surface deposits, together called regolith, in the near-surface crust of Earth or another terrestrial planet.

facts.text: An exposed patch of bedrock is an outcrop; the top of the bedrock, where it meets the overlying material, is the rockhead.
Locating rockhead by digging, drilling or geophysics is important in most civil engineering projects; it can lie hundreds of metres down.
Exposed bedrock weathers physically or chemically, becoming susceptible to erosion; at its buried upper boundary, subsurface weathering forms saprolite.
Fragments detached from the bedrock and found within a weathering or soil profile are called floaters.
Geological maps show bedrock types as if all soil and superficial deposits were removed, unless the deposits are too thick to map through.
In the mapping of superficial deposits, all pre-Quaternary deposits count as bedrock.

entries.text: Dig deep enough almost anywhere and the spade strikes solid rock. Bedrock is that solid rock, lying beneath the weathered rock and loose surface deposits in the crust of Earth or another terrestrial planet. Where it breaks the surface, the exposed patch is an outcrop. Its buried top, where it meets the material above, is the rockhead. Locating rockhead by digging, drilling or geophysics matters in most civil engineering projects, and it can lie hundreds of metres down. Exposed bedrock weathers physically or chemically and then erodes. At its buried upper boundary, weathering below ground turns it into {{ref:soil-form-100}}. Fragments torn from it and found higher up, among the weathered layers and soil, are called floaters. Geological maps show bedrock as if every soil and {{ref:soil-form-103}} had been stripped away, unless the cover is too thick to map through. In mapping such cover, every deposit older than the Quaternary counts as bedrock.

entries.title: Regolith, the loose blanket over solid rock

definition.text: A blanket of loose, unconsolidated and varied surface deposits covering solid rock.

facts.text: It includes dust, broken rock and related materials and occurs on Earth, the Moon, Mars, some asteroids and other terrestrial planets and moons.
George P. Merrill defined it in 1897, from Greek rhegos, blanket, and lithos, rock, for the whole mantle of unconsolidated material whatever its origin.
On Earth it originates from weathering and biological processes and ranges from absent to hundreds of metres thick.
Its age ranges from instantaneous, for fresh ash or alluvium, to hundreds of millions of years, as with Precambrian regolith in parts of Australia.
Its uppermost part, which typically holds significant organic matter, is what is conventionally called soil.
It comprises transported cover, saprolith, interbedded volcanic deposits, duricrust, groundwater salts and biota.
Few plants grow in solid rock and animals need loose material to burrow, so regolith underpins most life.
It matters to engineers, hosts mineral deposits, supplies sand, gravel, lime and gypsum, and is the zone through which aquifers recharge and discharge.

entries.text: Few plants can grow in solid rock, and animals need loose material to burrow. Most life on land therefore rests on regolith: a blanket of loose, unconsolidated and varied surface deposits covering solid rock. George P. Merrill coined the word in 1897 from the Greek rhegos, blanket, and lithos, rock. He meant the whole mantle of loose material, whatever its origin. It includes dust, broken rock and related materials. It occurs on Earth, the Moon, Mars, some asteroids and other terrestrial planets and moons. On Earth it comes from weathering and biological processes, and it ranges from absent to hundreds of metres thick. Its age varies just as widely. Fresh ash from eruptions ({{ref:soil-form-152}}) or river sediment is instantly regolith, while parts of Australia carry Precambrian regolith hundreds of millions of years old. The blanket has several ingredients: transported cover, deeply weathered rock, interbedded volcanic deposits, hard crusts, groundwater salts and living things. Its uppermost part, which typically holds significant organic matter, is what is conventionally called soil. Regolith matters well beyond biology. Engineers build on it, mineral deposits lie in it, and it supplies sand, gravel, lime and gypsum. It is also the zone through which underground water stores recharge and discharge.

entries.title: Saprolite, the rotten rock that keeps its shape

definition.text: Chemically weathered rock, literally 'rotten rock', formed in the lower zones of soil profiles by deep weathering of the bedrock surface.

facts.text: It commonly keeps the structural details of its bedrock and inherits the texture, pH and minerals of its parent material.
Hydrolysis, chelation, hydration and freeze–thaw turn granite and other rocks into it; quartz's resistance can leave sandy soils, a process called arenization.
In the regolith, upper saprolite is fully oxidised bedrock, lower saprolite is reduced, partly weathered rock, and saprock is fractured bedrock weathered only along fractures.
Its colour comes mainly from iron compounds: fine goethite is yellow and coarse goethite brown; fine hematite is red and coarse hematite grey to black.
More intense weathering grades continuously from saprolite into laterite, whose first weathering products are kaolinized saprolites.
Being younger than its parent rock and older than any thick cover such as lava, it can sometimes be dated relatively.
Burrowing plants and animals bring saprolite up from depth to the surface.
Poorly weathered saprolite grit forms aquifers in Western Australia that can yield groundwater fit for livestock.

entries.text: Saprolite means rotten rock. It is chemically weathered rock, formed in the lower zones of soil profiles as weathering eats deep into the bedrock surface. It commonly keeps the structural details of its bedrock. It also inherits that rock's texture, pH and minerals. Hydrolysis, {{ref:soil-chem-069}}, hydration and freeze–thaw turn granite and other rocks into it. Quartz resists the attack and can be left behind as sandy soil, a process called arenization. Iron compounds supply most of its color. One, {{ref:soil-chem-104}}, is yellow when fine and brown when coarse. Another, {{ref:soil-chem-112}}, is red when fine and grey to black when coarse. Upper saprolite is fully oxidized bedrock, and lower saprolite is reduced, partly weathered rock. Below lies saprock, bedrock weathered only along its fractures. Younger than its parent rock and older than any thick cover such as lava, saprolite can sometimes be dated relatively. Burrowing plants and animals bring it up to the surface. In Western Australia, poorly weathered saprolite grit forms aquifers that can yield groundwater fit for livestock.

entries.title: Rock, the solid stuff the Earth is built from

definition.text: Any naturally occurring solid mass or aggregate of minerals or mineraloid matter.

facts.text: Rocks are categorized by the minerals they contain, their chemical composition and how they formed.
They make up the Earth's crust and most of its interior, apart from the liquid outer core and pockets of magma.
The three main groups are igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks.
Sedimentary rocks form from sediments made by the weathering, transport and deposition of existing rocks.
Sediments, from smallest to largest, are clay, silt, sand and gravel.

entries.text: Almost the whole planet is rock. It makes up the Earth's crust and most of its interior, apart from the liquid outer core and pockets of magma. A rock is any naturally occurring solid mass or aggregate of minerals or mineraloid matter, built from the crystals described in {{ref:soil-found-029}}. Geologists sort rocks by the minerals they contain, their chemical composition and how they formed. That last test gives three main groups: {{ref:soil-form-135}}, {{ref:soil-form-136}} and {{ref:soil-form-137}}. The second group matters most to soil, because it is made from the wreckage of other rocks. Weathering breaks existing rock down, and water, wind and ice carry and deposit the pieces as sediment. From smallest to largest, those sediments are clay, silt, sand and gravel, the same grains soil is made of.

entries.title: Hydrolysis: how water cracks minerals open

definition.text: Hydrolysis is any chemical reaction in which a water molecule breaks one or more chemical bonds.

facts.text: In hydrolysis one fragment of the split molecule gains a hydrogen ion and the other gains a hydroxide.
Hydrolysis is the reverse of condensation: it adds water to break molecules down, while condensation joins molecules by removing water.
Metal ions in water form aqua ions that act as acids; trivalent Al3+ and Fe3+ are weak acids with pKa comparable to acetic acid, while Na+ hydrolyses almost imperceptibly.
In acid sulfate soils, loosely bound Al3+ and Fe3+ and sparingly soluble sulfates such as jarosite release H+ by hydrolysis, adding titratable and retained acidity.
In alkali soils the carbonate anion hydrolyses in water to bicarbonate and hydroxyl ions, raising pH.
Urease catalyzes hydrolysis of urea, and highly alkaline soils (pH about 8.2 or higher) increase urea hydrolysis.

The lab manual says all minerals weather by hydrolysis, which is the primary reaction releasing most plant nutrient elements from minerals; orthoclase and water yield an aluminum silicate, K+ and OH-.

entries.title: Sedimentary rock, a thin skin over most of the land

definition.text: Rock formed by the cementation of mineral or organic particles deposited at the Earth's surface.

facts.text: Its mineral detritus comes from the weathering and erosion of existing rocks, carried by water, wind, ice or mass movement.
It covers 73% of the Earth's land surface but makes up only about 8% of the crust's volume.
Clastic sedimentary rocks are cemented rock fragments, commonly grains of quartz, feldspar, clay minerals or mica, subdivided by dominant particle size.
Mudrocks contain at least 50% silt- and clay-sized particles.

entries.text: Sedimentary rock covers 73% of the Earth's land surface, yet it makes up only about 8% of the crust's volume. It is a thin skin. This rock forms when mineral or organic particles deposited at the surface are cemented together. Its mineral debris comes from {{ref:soil-found-052}} and erosion of older rock, carried by water, wind, ice or mass movement. Clastic sedimentary rocks are cemented rock fragments, commonly grains of quartz, {{ref:soil-form-141}}, the clay-forming minerals of {{ref:soil-chem-079}} or flaky {{ref:soil-chem-135}}. They are subdivided by their dominant particle size. Mudrocks, for example, contain at least 50% silt- and clay-sized particles.

entries.title: Limestone, the rock that dissolves and sweetens soil

definition.text: A carbonate sedimentary rock made mostly of calcite and aragonite, and the main source of lime.

facts.text: About 20% to 25% of sedimentary rock is carbonate rock, most of it limestone; much of the rest is dolomite.
Partly soluble, especially in acid, it erodes into karst landscapes of pavements, caves and gorges.
Water and organic acid from the soil slowly widen its joints over thousands or millions of years, dissolving the calcium carbonate.
Pulverized limestone is used as agricultural lime to neutralize acidic soils.

entries.text: Limestone is rock that water can slowly eat. It is a carbonate sedimentary rock made mostly of calcite and aragonite, two forms of calcium carbonate, and it is the main source of lime. Water and organic acid from the soil widen its joints over thousands or millions of years, dissolving the {{ref:soil-found-118}}. The result is karst country of pavements, caves and gorges. Farmers turn the same chemistry to use: pulverized limestone, spread as {{ref:soil-fert-059}}, neutralizes acidic soils.

entries.title: Asteroid regolith, soil-like dust on tiny worlds

definition.text: The loose surface layer of asteroids, produced by impacts and other surface-altering processes.

facts.text: Spacecraft show it ranges from fine-grained deposits to coarse, boulder-rich debris.
Hayabusa's samples from Itokawa were the first asteroid regolith grains studied in the laboratory, showing space weathering and solar-wind implantation.
Hayabusa2 returned samples from Ryugu in 2020 and OSIRIS-REx from Bennu in 2023; both show organic- or carbon-rich material and water.

entries.text: Asteroids wear loose blankets too. Asteroid regolith is the loose surface layer of an asteroid, produced by impacts and other processes that alter its surface. Spacecraft show it ranging from fine-grained deposits to coarse, boulder-rich debris. The Hayabusa mission's samples from Itokawa were the first asteroid regolith grains studied in a laboratory. They showed {{ref:soil-hist-079}} and particles implanted by the solar wind. Hayabusa2 returned samples from Ryugu in 2020, and OSIRIS-REx from Bennu in 2023. Both hold organic- or carbon-rich material and water.

entries.title: Titan, where ice behaves like rock

definition.text: Loose icy material on Saturn's moon Titan, called regolith because it behaves mechanically like regolith on other bodies.

facts.text: The term traditionally covered only loose mineral grains or rock fragments; ice grains were left out because, as snow on Earth, they melt and fuse easily.
Titan is so cold that ice behaves like rock, giving an ice regolith with erosion and aeolian or sedimentary processes.
Huygens' penetrometer data suggest a surface better described as a sand of ice grains, on a plain covered in somewhat rounded pebbles.

entries.text: On Saturn's moon Titan, ice does the job of rock. The word regolith traditionally covered only loose mineral grains or rock fragments. Ice grains were left out because, like snow on Earth, they melt and fuse easily. Titan is so cold that ice behaves like rock, with its own erosion and its own wind-driven and sedimentary processes. Its loose icy material behaves mechanically like regolith elsewhere, so it earns the name. Data from an instrument the Huygens probe pushed into the ground suggest a sand of ice grains on a plain of somewhat rounded pebbles.

entries.title: Igneous rock, frozen from molten magma

definition.text: One of the three main rock types, formed by the cooling and solidification of magma or lava.

facts.text: It solidifies either below the surface as intrusive rock or at the surface as extrusive rock.
Intrusive igneous rocks have visible mineral grains, while extrusive ones are glassy or very fine-grained.
It is classified chiefly by particle size, which depends largely on cooling history, and by mineral composition.
Near the surface, acidic soil water and groundwater readily dissolve and break down igneous rocks, which are unstable there.

entries.text: Every igneous rock was once liquid. It forms when magma or lava cools and solidifies, and it is one of the three main rock types. Some freezes below the surface as intrusive rock, slowly enough to grow mineral grains the eye can see. Some freezes at the surface as extrusive rock, so fast that it ends up glassy or very fine-grained. Geologists classify it chiefly by that particle size, which depends largely on cooling history, and by its {{ref:soil-found-029}} content. Born hot and deep, igneous rock is unstable near the surface. There acidic soil water and groundwater readily dissolve it and break it down.

entries.title: Metamorphic rock, remade by heat and pressure

definition.text: Rock transformed from an existing rock into a new type by heat and pressure, a process called metamorphism.

facts.text: The protolith is heated above 150 to 200 °C, often under 100 megapascals or more, and recrystallizes while staying mostly solid.
The protolith may be igneous, sedimentary or older metamorphic rock.
Metamorphic rocks form 12% of the Earth's land surface; examples are gneiss, slate, marble, schist and quartzite.

entries.text: A metamorphic rock is a rock that has been cooked into something new. Heat and pressure transform an existing rock, a process called metamorphism. The starting rock, the protolith, may be {{ref:soil-form-135}}, {{ref:soil-form-136}} or an older metamorphic rock. It is heated above 150 to 200 °C, often under 100 megapascals of pressure or more. Its minerals then recrystallize while the rock stays mostly solid. Metamorphic rocks form 12% of the Earth's land surface. Gneiss, slate, marble, schist and quartzite are familiar examples.

It is heated above 150 to 200 °C, often under 100 megapascals of pressure or more. Its minerals then recrystallize while the rock stays mostly solid. Metamorphic rocks form 12% of the Earth's land surface. Gneiss, slate, marble, schist and quartzite are familiar examples.

entries.title: Grus, granite crumbled into coarse grit

definition.text: An accumulation of angular, coarse sand and gravel produced by the granular disintegration of crystalline rocks, especially granitoids, through weathering.

facts.text: It forms by chemical and mechanical weathering, generally in arid or semiarid regions.
Cemented grus sand forms the sandstone arkose.
Most Late Cenozoic saprolite mantles in Europe are grus, unlike older Mesozoic and Early Cenozoic saprolites of kaolinitic and ferrallitic material.

entries.text: Granite can fall apart grain by grain. The result is grus, an accumulation of angular, coarse sand and gravel left when crystalline rocks, especially granitoids, disintegrate through weathering. Both chemical and mechanical weathering make it, generally in arid or semiarid regions. Most Late Cenozoic {{ref:soil-form-100}} mantles in Europe are grus. Older Mesozoic and Early Cenozoic saprolites are different: they are made of kaolinitic and ferrallitic material, rotted much further. Cement grus sand together and it becomes a sandstone called arkose.

entries.title: Deep weathering, rock rotting for millions of years

definition.text: Long-continued chemical weathering that builds thick, deeply weathered regolith over bedrock, the product of a region's long weathering history.

facts.text: It needs relief gentle enough to prevent erosion and allow leaching, long tectonic stability, and a humid tropical to temperate climate where warmth speeds reactions.
At weathering rates of 20 m per million years, deep regoliths take several million years to form; cooler climates need longer.
Deeply weathered profiles are widespread between latitudes 35°N and 35°S, and in parts of Africa, India, South America, Australia and southeast Asia regolith has formed for over 100 million years.
Regoliths range from a few metres to over 150 m thick, depending on surface age, tectonics, climate history and bedrock.
Sulfides and carbonates leach readily, while nickel, cobalt, copper and zinc in ferromagnesian minerals stay higher and reprecipitate with iron–manganese oxides in mid to lower saprolite.
It produces secondary and supergene ores: bauxite, iron ores, saprolitic gold, supergene copper, uranium and residual heavy minerals.
Weathering formed thin kaolinitic saprolites 1,000 to 500 million years ago, thick ones 200 to 66 million years ago, and medium-thick immature ones 5 million years ago in Sweden.

entries.text: At 20 m per million years, weathering needs several million years to build a deep regolith, and cooler climates need longer. Deep weathering is that long-continued chemical attack. It builds thick, deeply weathered regolith over bedrock, the product of a region's long weathering history. Three conditions favor it. Relief must be gentle enough to prevent erosion and let water carry dissolved material down. The crust must stay tectonically stable for a long time. The climate must be humid, tropical to temperate, with warmth to speed the reactions. Deeply weathered profiles are widespread between latitudes 35°N and 35°S. In parts of Africa, India, South America, Australia and southeast Asia, regolith has been forming for over 100 million years. Regoliths range from a few metres to over 150 m thick, depending on surface age, tectonics, climate history and bedrock. The process sorts the elements as it goes. Sulfides and carbonates leave readily. Nickel, cobalt, copper and zinc held in iron- and magnesium-rich minerals stay higher. They reprecipitate with iron–manganese oxides in the middle and lower saprolite. The result is secondary and supergene ores, enriched near the surface by weathering: {{ref:soil-chem-108}}, iron ores, saprolitic gold, supergene copper, uranium and residual {{ref:soil-chem-193}}. Sweden shows the process across deep time. There it formed thin clay-rich saprolites 1,000 to 500 million years ago, thick ones 200 to 66 million years ago, and medium-thick immature ones 5 million years ago.

entries.title: Lithology, describing a rock at a glance

definition.text: The description of a rock unit's physical characteristics visible at outcrop, in hand or core samples, or under low magnification.

facts.text: The characteristics include colour, texture, grain size and composition.
Lithology can also mean a summary rock name such as sandstone, slate, basalt or limestone.
It is the basis for dividing rock sequences into lithostratigraphic units for mapping and correlation.
Site investigations describe it in standard terms, as in the European geotechnical standard Eurocode 7.

entries.title: Primary minerals, inherited unchanged from rock

definition.text: A mineral that formed during the original crystallization of its host igneous rock and has not been chemically altered since.

facts.text: Soil minerals are of two types: primary minerals are found in soil but not formed there, while secondary minerals form as primary minerals weather.
Primary mineral particles are mostly larger than 2 μm, so they make up the silt, sand and gravel fractions.
Igneous rocks contain primary minerals such as quartz, feldspar, plagioclase, muscovite, biotite, amphibole, pyroxene and olivine.
Silicates dominate the primary minerals in soil; quartz and cristobalite are common soil tectosilicates.
Primary rocks are the source of primary minerals, which are in turn the components of parent rocks.

They crystallized with their host igneous rock and have not been chemically altered since. By contrast, {{ref:soil-chem-235}} form as primary minerals weather. Primary mineral particles are mostly larger than 2 μm. They make up the silt, sand and gravel fractions. {{ref:soil-form-135}} supplies them: quartz, {{ref:soil-form-141}}, {{ref:soil-form-142}}, {{ref:soil-chem-226}}, {{ref:soil-form-144}}, amphibole, pyroxene and {{ref:soil-form-145}}. Silicates dominate the primary minerals in soil, and quartz and cristobalite are common soil tectosilicates, silicates built as a three-dimensional framework. The chain runs from primary rocks, the source of primary minerals, to the parent rocks those minerals compose.

entries.title: Feldspar: the rock mineral that becomes clay

definition.text: A group of rock-forming aluminium tectosilicate minerals that also contain cations such as sodium, calcium, potassium or barium.

facts.text: Feldspars make up about 60% of the Earth's crust and 41% of the continental crust by weight.
The commonest are the sodium–calcium plagioclase feldspars and the potassium–sodium alkali feldspars.
Chemical weathering by hydrolysis turns feldspars into clay minerals including illite, smectite and kaolinite.
Hydrolysis starts with feldspar dissolving, which goes best in acidic or basic solutions, and the dissolution rate sets the weathering rate.
Because feldspars are so abundant, clays are very abundant weathering products and an important component of soils.
Formed at high temperature, feldspars, especially plagioclase, are unstable at the surface, so they weather easily to clays.
Clay-replaced feldspar looks chalky beside glassy unweathered grains; feldspar-rich sediment points to little chemical weathering before burial.
Orthoclase and microcline are potassium feldspars (KAlSi3O8) with the same composition but different crystal forms, monoclinic and triclinic; K-Na feldspars grade to albite as the alkali feldspars.

entries.title: Olivine, the mantle mineral that fades fast at the surface

definition.text: A magnesium iron silicate mineral, (Mg,Fe)2SiO4, of the nesosilicate type.

facts.text: The main component of the upper mantle, it is common underground but weathers quickly at the surface.
It is among the least stable common surface minerals in the Goldich dissolution series, so it is rarely found in sedimentary rock.
With water it readily alters to iddingsite, a mix of clay minerals, iron oxides and ferrihydrite.
Speeding its weathering, for example by spreading fine olivine on beaches, has been proposed as a cheap way to sequester CO2.

entries.title: Plagioclase, the striped feldspar that weathers first

definition.text: A continuous solid-solution series of framework silicate minerals within the feldspar group.

facts.text: The series runs from albite, NaAlSi3O8, to anorthite, CaAl2Si2O8, with sodium and calcium substituting for each other.
It is abundant in igneous and metamorphic rock and common as a detrital mineral in sedimentary rock.
Plagioclase weathers relatively rapidly to clay minerals such as smectite, so sandstones usually hold more of the more resistant alkali feldspar.
In hand samples it is often recognized by polysynthetic twinning, a set of fine parallel striations.

entries.text: Plagioclase is a sliding scale rather than a single mineral. It is a continuous series of framework silicates within {{ref:soil-form-141}}, running from albite, NaAlSi3O8, to anorthite, CaAl2Si2O8, as sodium and calcium substitute for each other. It is abundant in igneous and metamorphic rock and common as a detrital grain in sedimentary rock. In hand samples, fine parallel striations called polysynthetic twinning often give it away. Plagioclase weathers relatively rapidly to clay-forming minerals such as {{ref:soil-chem-091}}. Sandstones therefore usually hold more of the more resistant alkali feldspar.
entries.text_plain: Plagioclase is a sliding scale rather than a single mineral. Plagioclase weathers relatively rapidly to clay-forming minerals such as Smectite, the swelling clay with an open interior. Sandstones therefore usually hold more of the more resistant alkali feldspar.

entries.title: Biotite, the dark mica that yellows with age

definition.text: A common group of dark phyllosilicate minerals in the mica group, approximately K(Mg,Fe)3AlSi3O10(OH,F)2.

facts.text: Its sheets of iron, magnesium, aluminium, silicon, oxygen and hydrogen are weakly bound together by potassium ions.
It occurs in a wide variety of igneous and metamorphic rocks and makes up as much as 7% of the exposed continental crust.
It is greenish to brown or black, turning even yellow when weathered.

entries.text: Biotite peels apart in thin, dark flakes. It is a group of phyllosilicate minerals in the family of {{ref:soil-chem-135}}, approximately K(Mg,Fe)3AlSi3O10(OH,F)2. Its sheets of iron, magnesium, aluminium, silicon, oxygen and hydrogen are held together only weakly, by potassium ions. It occurs in a wide variety of igneous and metamorphic rocks and makes up as much as 7% of the exposed continental crust. Fresh biotite is greenish to brown or black. Weathered, it can turn even yellow.

entries.title: Mafic: dark rocks rich in magnesium and iron

definition.text: Describing silicate minerals, magmas and igneous rocks rich in magnesium and iron and relatively low in silica.

facts.text: Common mafic minerals are olivine, pyroxene, amphibole and biotite; common mafic rocks are basalt, diabase and gabbro.
Mafic and felsic materials are opposite ends of a compositional spectrum; mafic rocks are dark and dense, felsic ones light and less dense.
Chemically, mafic rocks have 45 to 55 wt% silica and are enriched in iron, magnesium and calcium; felsic rocks are enriched in aluminium, silicon, potassium and sodium.
The term, from magnesium and ferric, was coined in 1912.

entries.text: Mafic is a word made from two elements: magnesium and ferric, for iron. Coined in 1912, it describes silicate minerals, magmas and igneous rocks rich in magnesium and iron and relatively low in silica. Mafic rocks have 45 to 55 wt% silica and are enriched in iron, magnesium and calcium. They are dark and dense. At the other end of the spectrum sit felsic rocks, light, less dense and enriched in aluminium, silicon, potassium and sodium. Common mafic minerals are {{ref:soil-form-145}}, pyroxene, amphibole and biotite. Common mafic rocks are basalt, diabase and gabbro.

entries.title: Stone stripes, bands of rock sorted by frost

definition.text: An elongated, unvegetated band of mostly talus-like basalt rock along a hillside or at the base of a cliff; also called a lava stringer.

facts.text: They occur mainly in north central Oregon at 900 to 1,100 m, a few metres to over 150 m long, 0.3 to 3 m wide and 20 to 65 cm deep.
They are thought to have formed under Quaternary periglacial conditions, through frost action, surface erosion, eluviation and mass wasting.
Intense freeze–thaw cycles probably sorted the rock debris, and frost penetrating no deeper than about 1 m explains their shallowness.
On level ground the same processes form stone rings around soil mounds, which grade into stripes as slope increases.

entries.text: Bare bands of broken basalt streak the hillsides of north central Oregon. A stone stripe, or lava stringer, is an elongated, unvegetated band of mostly talus-like basalt rock along a hillside or at the base of a cliff. Most lie at 900 to 1,100 m. Each runs a few metres to over 150 m long, 0.3 to 3 m wide and 20 to 65 cm deep. They probably formed in the near-glacial cold of the Quaternary, through frost action, surface erosion, the washing down of fine material and slow downhill movement under gravity. Intense freeze–thaw cycles likely sorted the rock debris. Frost reached no deeper than about 1 m, which explains their shallowness. On level ground the same processes form stone rings around soil mounds, and these grade into stripes as the slope steepens.

entries.title: Orthoclase, the potassium feldspar of granite

definition.text: A potassium feldspar, KAlSi3O8, an important tectosilicate mineral of igneous rock.

facts.text: It is a type of alkali feldspar, also called potassium feldspar or K-spar.
It is a common constituent of most granites and other felsic igneous rocks.
It commonly alters to sericite or clay.

entries.text: Orthoclase is the feldspar that carries potassium. Its formula is KAlSi3O8, and it is an important tectosilicate of {{ref:soil-form-135}}. It is a type of alkali feldspar, also called potassium feldspar or K-spar. It is a common constituent of most granites and other felsic igneous rocks, the light-coloured, silica-rich kind. Like other feldspars it does not last forever at the surface. It commonly alters to sericite, a fine-grained flaky mineral, or to clay.

entries.title: The rock cycle, from basalt to sediment and back

definition.text: The geological concept describing the transitions, through geologic time, among sedimentary, metamorphic and igneous rock.

facts.text: Each rock type changes when forced out of its equilibrium conditions; basalt, for example, breaks down and dissolves at the atmosphere.
Plate tectonics and the water cycle drive it.
Weathering and erosion break exposed rock into fragments and carry away dissolved material on the way to sedimentary rock.
On planets with life it is a biogeochemical cycle as well as a geologic one.

entries.text: No rock is permanent. The rock cycle describes how {{ref:soil-form-136}}, {{ref:soil-form-137}} and {{ref:soil-form-135}} turn into one another through geologic time. Each type changes when forced out of the conditions it formed in. Basalt, for example, breaks down and dissolves when exposed to the atmosphere. Weathering and erosion break exposed rock into fragments and carry away dissolved material, on the way to new sedimentary rock. Plate tectonics and {{ref:soil-water-079}} drive the whole loop. On planets with life, living things join in, so the loop is a {{ref:soil-fert-140}} as well as a geologic one.

On planets with life, living things join in, so the loop is a Biogeochemical cycles: how the same atoms keep coming back as well as a geologic one.

entries.title: Superficial deposits, the young loose cover

definition.text: Geologically recent, mostly unconsolidated deposits, typically of Quaternary age (less than 2.6 million years old).

facts.text: They include stream channel and floodplain deposits, beach sands, talus gravels, glacial drift and moraine, raised beaches and brickearth.
Mostly gravel, sand, silt and clay, onshore they form relatively thin, often discontinuous patches.
Geological surveys keep databases of their properties, used in farming and forestry to judge erosion, growing conditions and the risk of nutrient leaching.

entries.text: Most of the loose ground people walk on is geologically young. Superficial deposits are recent, mostly unconsolidated deposits, typically of Quaternary age, less than 2.6 million years old. They include stream channel and floodplain deposits, beach sands, talus gravels, raised beaches and {{ref:soil-class-065}}. Glacier-laid material belongs too, as {{ref:soil-form-149}} and {{ref:soil-form-150}} describe. Most are gravel, sand, silt and clay. Onshore they form relatively thin, often discontinuous patches. Geological surveys keep databases of their properties. Farmers and foresters use them to judge erosion, growing conditions and the risk of nutrients washing out.

entries.title: Parent material, the stuff every soil grows from

definition.text: The underlying geological material, generally bedrock or a superficial (drift) deposit, in which soil horizons form.

facts.text: Soils inherit much of their structure and minerals from it, so they are often classified by whether it is consolidated and how it was last transported.
It may be igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic bedrock or unconsolidated glacial, river or volcanic deposits; for metamorphic rock the original rock is the protolith.
Rock is the source of all soil minerals and of every plant nutrient except nitrogen, hydrogen and carbon.
Typical parent minerals include quartz, calcite, feldspar and mica (biotite).
Its nature strongly shapes the soil: mudstone or shale give clay-rich soils, while sandstone weathers into sandy soils.
Parent materials are classed by how they were deposited: residual (weathered in place), transported (by water, wind, ice or gravity) or cumulose (organic matter accumulated in place).
Weatherable minerals in the parent rock favour mull humus, while a shortage of them is associated with moder.
Parent material strongly influences how many basic ions a soil contains.

entries.text: Every soil carries a family likeness to the material it grew from. Rock is the source of all soil minerals and of every plant nutrient except nitrogen, hydrogen and carbon. Parent material is the underlying geological material in which soil horizons form, generally bedrock or a superficial (drift) deposit. It may be igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic rock. For a metamorphic rock, the original rock before it changed is the protolith. It may also be loose glacial, river or volcanic deposits. Typical parent minerals include quartz, calcite, feldspar and biotite, one of the minerals covered in {{ref:soil-chem-135}}. The parent leaves a clear mark. Mudstone or shale give clay-rich soils, while sandstone weathers into sandy soils. Parent material also strongly shapes how many basic ions a soil contains. Weatherable minerals in the parent rock favor one kind of {{ref:soil-bio-089}}, called mull, while a shortage of them goes with another, called moder. Soil scientists sort parent materials by how they were deposited. Residual material weathered in place. Transported material was carried by water, wind, ice or gravity. Cumulose material is organic matter that accumulated where it formed. Because soils inherit so much of their structure and minerals from their parent, they are often classified by whether it is consolidated and how it was last transported.

entries.title: Transported parent material, soil from somewhere else

definition.text: Loose, uncemented parent material moved by water, wind, ice or gravity, and classified by its last means of transport.

facts.text: Most soils form in transported material moved many miles by wind, water, ice and gravity.
Material carried by a glacier and then redeposited by streams is named for its last agent, as stream-transported or glacial fluvial parent material.
Recognized modes are wind (aeolian), water, gravity (colluvial), ice (glacial till), lakes (lacustrine) and oceans (marine).
Wind moves silt and fine sand hundreds of miles to form loess, but seldom moves clay, which forms stable aggregates.
Wind also carries sand-sized particles, typically as dunes, and volcanic ash that settles at various distances from a volcano.
Water-transported materials are classed as alluvial, lacustrine or marine.
A decrease in rock fragments with depth, especially over saprolite, suggests the soil material has moved downslope.

entries.text: Most soils form in material that wind, water, ice and gravity have carried many miles. Transported parent material is loose, uncemented material moved this way, and it is named for its last means of transport. Material a glacier carried and streams then redeposited counts as stream-transported, or glacial fluvial, parent material. The recognized carriers are wind, water, gravity, ice, lakes and oceans, and the entries ahead give each deposit its name. Water-carried material is split three ways: by rivers, in lakes or in the sea. Wind sorts its load. It moves silt and fine sand hundreds of miles to build {{ref:soil-form-106}}. It seldom moves clay, which sticks into stable clumps. Wind also piles sand-sized grains into dunes and drops {{ref:soil-form-152}} at various distances from a volcano. In the field, rock fragments that thin out with depth, especially over saprolite, suggest the soil material has moved downslope.

entries.title: Loess, the wind-blown silt that buries whole regions

definition.text: A clastic, predominantly silt-sized sediment formed by the accumulation of wind-blown dust.

facts.text: Loess or similar deposits cover ten percent of Earth's land area.
It holds 20% or less clay with roughly equal parts sand and silt, typically 20 to 50 micrometres in grain size, and is often loosely cemented by calcium carbonate.
It is homogeneous, porous, friable, pale yellow or buff and usually unstratified; its angular grains of quartz, feldspar and mica let it stand in vertical banks.
Deposits exceed a hundred metres in north-western China, reaching 350 m on the Loess Plateau, and tens of metres in the US Midwest.
Pye (1995) gave four requirements: a dust source, enough wind to carry it, a place to accumulate, and time.
Von Leonhard described Löss along the Rhine in 1823–1824 and Lyell popularized the term in 1834; its wind-blown origin was recognized later, notably by von Richthofen in China (1878).
Its vertical cleavage lets it be dug into cave dwellings in parts of China.

entries.title: Alluvium, the sediment that rivers leave behind

definition.text: Loose clay, silt, sand or gravel deposited by running water in stream beds, on floodplains, in alluvial fans or similar settings.

facts.text: It is usually geologically young and unconsolidated; sediments laid down in seas, estuaries, lakes or ponds are not called alluvium.
Floodplain alluvium can be highly fertile and supported some of the earliest human civilizations.
Alluvial parent materials form on floodplains stratified by seasonal floods, in alluvial fans that coarsen toward the uplands, and in fine-grained deltas at river mouths.
Most alluvium is Quaternary and is often called 'cover' because it hides the bedrock beneath.
Antoine Furetière's dictionary, published in 1690, defined alluvion as new land formed by sediment along rivers and seas.
In the 19th century it meant river sediment above older 'diluvium', ascribed to Noah's flood; once that idea was rejected, diluvium became 'older alluvium'.
Because running water deposits it, alluvium is generally fine-grained and well sorted, unlike colluvium.
