entries.title: Colluvium, the jumble at the foot of the slope

definition.text: Loose, unconsolidated sediment deposited at the base of hillslopes by rainwash, sheetwash, slow downslope creep or a combination of these.

facts.text: It is a heterogeneous mix of rock types and sizes, from silt to rock fragments, typically angular and loosely consolidated.
It accumulates as gently sloping aprons or fans at the foot of slopes or in gullies and hollows, sometimes several metres thick.
Gravity-moved parent material is obvious at the base of steep slopes as talus cones.
Thick colluvium often holds buried soils, plant and animal remains and archaeological deposits, recording long-term climatic change.
It differs from alluvium in not involving running water, and is poorly sorted where alluvium is well sorted.
Where the source material is fine and uniform, it can be hard to tell which process laid down a deposit.
Calcisols, cambisols and durisols develop mostly in alluvial and colluvial deposits, with aeolian deposits for the first two.

entries.title: Glacial till, the unsorted load a glacier drops

definition.text: Unsorted sediment eroded and carried by a glacier and deposited directly from the ice.

facts.text: Not carried by liquid water, it is unsorted and unstratified: mostly clay, silt and sand with scattered pebbles, cobbles and boulders, often in a bimodal size distribution.
Basal till, laid beneath the glacier, is typically very compact and slow to take in water; ablation till, dropped as the ice melts, is less compacted.
It is deposited in terminal, lateral, medial and ground moraines, and in drumlins and flutes.
Its clasts often come from outcrops hundreds of kilometres away and are faceted, striated or polished by glacial abrasion.
Archibald Geikie first applied the term to primary glacial deposits in 1863; the older name boulder clay has fallen out of favour.
Melting glaciers rework till into glaciofluvial outwash and glaciolacustrine or glaciomarine deposits such as varves.
Till follows its source rock: sandstone gives loose sandy till, granite and gneiss stony gravelly till, and limestone, clay or shale the clayey till typical of boulder clay.
Boulder clay is tough, compact and overconsolidated, from its fine rock flour and the weight of overlying ice.

entries.title: The Loess Plateau, China's yellow highland

definition.text: A plateau of some 640,000 km2 around the upper and middle reaches of China's Yellow River, covered by loess.

facts.text: Its soil has been called the most highly erodible soil on Earth.
Loess in its banks gave the Yellow River its name and colour; farmed for over a thousand years, it has produced phenomenal yields.
It holds the thickest known loess deposit, up to 350 m.
Wind-borne loess particles contribute to the Asian Dust pollution problem.

entries.text: The Yellow River owes its name and its color to the loess in its banks. Around the river's upper and middle reaches lies the Loess Plateau, some 640,000 km2 covered by loess. Wind-borne loess particles from it add to the Asian Dust pollution problem.

entries.title: Why loess soils are so fertile and so fragile

definition.text: Soils developed on loess, which tend to be very rich and, under suitable climates, among the most agriculturally productive in the world.

facts.text: The fine grains weather quickly because of their large surface area; fertility comes mainly from high cation exchange capacity and porosity rather than organic matter.
Soils underlain by loess tend to be excessively drained.
Even well-managed loess farmland can erode at well over 2.5 kg/m2 per year; Iowa's Loess Hills at times lost over 10 kg/m2 per year under autumn mouldboard ploughing.
Iowa's Loess Hills owe their fertility to 10,000 years of prairie humus; once that topsoil erodes, the loess beneath is infertile without fertilizer.

entries.text: Soils developed on loess tend to be very rich. Under suitable climates they rank among the most agriculturally productive in the world. Soils underlain by loess also tend to drain too freely. Their weakness is erosion. Even well-managed loess farmland can lose well over 2.5 kg/m2 a year. Under autumn moldboard plowing, Iowa's Loess Hills at times lost over 10 kg/m2 a year. Their fertility rests on 10,000 years of dark prairie organic matter. Once that surface layer erodes, the loess beneath is infertile without fertilizer.

entries.title: Loess–paleosol sequences, climate diaries in silt

definition.text: Stacked loess layers separated by buried soils, studied as archives of past climate and environmental change.

facts.text: In China the loess layers were laid down by a strong north-west winter monsoon, while the paleosols between them record a moist south-east monsoon.
Without robust numerical dating, even the position of the last interglacial soil in Austrian and Hungarian loess stratigraphies was long a matter of debate.
Since the 1980s luminescence methods have dated when grains were last exposed to daylight; SAR protocols give last-glacial ages with an accuracy of up to 5 and 10%.
Radiocarbon dating gives reliable loess ages for the last 40–45 ka when suitable in situ organic material such as charcoal or snail shells is found.

entries.title: Non-glacial loess, dust from deserts and volcanoes

definition.text: Loess that originates from deserts, dune fields, playa lakes or volcanic ash rather than from glacial outwash.

facts.text: Varieties include desert loess from aeolian abrasion of quartz grains, volcanic loess in Ecuador and Argentina, tropical loess and trade-wind loess.
China's thick loess deposits were blown in from deserts in the north of the country.
Loess on the Great Plains of Nebraska, Kansas and Colorado is considered non-glacial desert loess, as is loess in Australia and Africa.

entries.text: Not all loess owes its origin to ice. Non-glacial loess comes from deserts, dune fields, playa lakes or {{ref:soil-form-152}}, not from the sediment washed out of glaciers. entries.title: Residuum, weathered rock that never moved

definition.text: Weathered rock that stays in place rather than being moved by erosion, and in time helps form soil.

facts.text: It is purely mineral, unlike organic parent materials, and is not moved by wind, water or gravity.
Soils formed from it, residual soils, are expected to resemble their underlying bedrock in mineralogy and general chemistry.
Regolith covers all unconsolidated material above bedrock, transported sediments included, whereas residuum is strictly untransported.
Saprolite keeps the structural features of its bedrock; residuum has lost them, having been transformed further and shrunk in volume.
It forms mainly by chemical weathering in every climate: a thin blanket over bedrock in temperate regions, much thicker in the tropics.
Residual soils imply landscape stability; in the United States as little as three percent of soils are residual.
In limestone terrain the bedrock–residuum boundary is sharp but irregular, with pinnacles of fresh rock in reddish residual silts and clays; resistant chert or sandstone remains as float.

entries.title: Eluvial deposits, the riches weathering leaves behind

definition.text: In geology, deposits and soils derived from weathering in place, or from weathering plus gravitational movement or accumulation.

facts.text: In geology the removed material is irrelevant; the eluvial deposit is what remains.
Eluvial ore deposits such as tungsten and gold placers are enriched by winnowing away lighter material; diamonds in weathered kimberlite can count as eluvial too.
Brazil's Pitinga tin deposit, an eluvial deposit, is one of the largest tin mines in the world.
Supergene weathering of an apatite-rich carbonatite in Ontario produced a significant eluvial phosphate ore.

entries.title: River channel migration, how rivers wander

definition.text: The lateral shift of an alluvial river channel across its floodplain over time.

facts.text: It is driven mainly by bank erosion combined with point bar deposition on the opposite side of the channel.
Corkscrew-like helicoidal flow around bends undercuts banks into cut banks and moves sediment across the channel.
Cut-bank erosion usually equals point-bar deposition, and point bars push flow into the opposite bank, so meanders become better defined over time.
Its typical features are point bars, cut banks, meanders, floodplains and oxbow lakes.

entries.text: An alluvial river never stays put. River channel migration is the sideways shift of its channel across its floodplain over time. Bank erosion drives it, combined with point bar deposition, the building of a sediment bar, on the opposite side of the channel. Around each bend, water moves in a corkscrew-like helicoidal flow. It undercuts banks into cut banks and moves sediment across the channel. Cut-bank erosion usually equals point-bar deposition, and point bars push flow into the opposite bank, so meanders become better defined over time. The typical features are point bars, cut banks, meanders, floodplains and oxbow lakes.

entries.title: Volcanic ash, a fertile gift that can smother

definition.text: Fragments of rock, mineral crystals and volcanic glass under 2 mm across, produced by volcanic eruptions.

facts.text: Coarser explosive products are included in tephra, the fragmental material of an eruption whatever its composition or size.
Wind can carry ash thousands of kilometres.
Washed into the soil, ash minerals form a nutrient-rich andisol layer that is very good for farming.
Heavy ashfalls can bury pasture and sterilize the soil by oxygen deprivation; rehabilitation includes mixing ash with the buried soil.

entries.text: Wind can carry volcanic ash thousands of kilometres from the eruption that made it. Ash is fragments of rock, mineral crystals and glass chilled from lava, all under 2 mm across. Coarser explosive products fall under tephra, the fragmental material of an eruption whatever its size. Washed into the soil, ash minerals form a nutrient-rich layer that is very good for farming, the kind found in {{ref:soil-class-092}}. Too much at once does harm. Heavy ashfalls can bury pasture and sterilize the soil by cutting off its oxygen. Rehabilitation includes mixing the ash into the buried soil, adding to its {{ref:soil-form-087}}.

entries.title: Cumulose parent material, soil built from plants

definition.text: Organic parent material built up in place from plant residues, such as sphagnum moss, preserved by a high water table or other conditions that slow decay.

facts.text: It includes peat and muck soils, preserved by the low oxygen content of a high water table.
Peat may form sterile soils, while muck soils may be very fertile.
Unlike other parent materials it is not moved but originates from deposited organic material.

entries.text: Not every parent material is rock. Cumulose parent material is organic, built up in place from plant residues such as sphagnum moss. Groundwater standing high keeps oxygen low, which slows decay and preserves the residues. {{ref:soil-class-070}} and muck soils both form this way. Unlike other parent materials, it is never moved; it originates from organic material deposited where it lies. The results differ sharply. The first may form sterile soils, while muck soils may be very fertile.

entries.title: Glaciofluvial deposits, ice debris sorted by meltwater

definition.text: Boulders, gravel, sand, silt and clay from ice sheets or glaciers that meltwater streams have transported, sorted and deposited.

facts.text: They are laid down beside, below or downstream from the ice.
Retreating glaciers leave outwash plains as alluvial deposits are carried downstream from the ice.
Much of North America and Europe is underlain by Pleistocene sand and loess derived from glacial outwash.

entries.text: Meltwater sorts what the ice did not. Much of North America and Europe is underlain by Pleistocene sand and loess derived from glacial outwash.

entries.title: Periglacial loess, dust from dried-out meltwater rivers

definition.text: Loess blown from the floodplains of glacial braided rivers that carried meltwater and sediment from melting ice sheets and ice caps.

facts.text: As meltwater dwindled each autumn and winter, the bare floodplains dried and wind winnowed their glacially ground silt and clay, depositing it downwind.
The loess along both sides of the Mississippi River alluvial valley is a classic example.
The northern European loess belt, from southern England to southern Ukraine, shows strong periglacial influence; in England periglacial loess is called brickearth.
Loess ridges aligned with last-glacial winds are called paha ridges in America and greda ridges in Europe.

entries.text: Each autumn and winter, the meltwater flowing from the great ice sheets dwindled. Bare floodplains of braided rivers dried, and wind winnowed their glacially ground silt and clay, dropping it downwind. The result is periglacial loess: loess blown from the floodplains of rivers that carried meltwater and sediment from melting ice sheets and ice caps. The loess along both sides of the Mississippi River alluvial valley is a classic example. Loess ridges aligned with last-glacial winds are called paha ridges in America and greda ridges in Europe.

entries.title: Lacustrine parent material, the silt of old lakebeds

definition.text: Sediment that settled in lakes, forming a well-sorted, fine-textured parent material rich in silt and clay.

facts.text: Its high clay content gives the soils formed in it low permeability.
Beach ridges may mark where ancient lakes once washed up sand.
Lake Bonneville and many soils around the Great Lakes are examples.

definition.text: Parent material formed from glacier-derived sediment carried into lakes, typically lakes at the ice margin.

facts.text: Inflowing rivers drop their larger rocks and stones near the lake edge, while suspended sediment settles across the whole lake bed.
Annual deposition can leave clear layers called varves.

entries.title: Marine parent material, old sea floors turned to soil

definition.text: Material carried by rivers to the sea that sank to the ocean floor and later became a parent material.

facts.text: Soils along the US Gulf Coast and in California's Imperial Valley formed on ancient sea beds exposed as the land was uplifted.
Glaciomarine sediments, delivered to the ocean by glaciers or icebergs, may hold large ice-dropped boulders amid fine-grained sediment.

entries.text: Parts of the US Gulf Coast were once sea bed. Marine parent material is material that rivers carried to the sea, where it sank to the ocean floor and later became a parent material. Soils along the Gulf Coast and in California's Imperial Valley formed on such ancient sea beds, exposed as the land was uplifted. Glaciomarine sediments reached the ocean by glacier or iceberg. They may hold large ice-dropped boulders amid fine-grained sediment.

entries.title: Volcanic ash, a fast-weathering parent material

definition.text: Volcanic ash carried by the wind and settled at various distances from a volcano, the most common volcanic parent material.

facts.text: Volcanic ash and lava flows interbedded with unconsolidated material are part of Earth's regolith.
Soils of siliceous ash consist of glass bubbles and shards with high internal surface area, and weather rapidly to imogolite and smectite.
These andisols are highly fertile, rich in organic matter and of particularly low bulk density.
Volcanic ash is also a source of non-glacial loess, as in Ecuador and Argentina.

entries.text: Volcanic ash is made largely of glass, and it weathers fast. Ash carried by the wind and settled at various distances from a volcano is called tephra, the most common volcanic parent material. Volcanic ash and lava flows interbedded with loose material are part of Earth's regolith. Soils of siliceous ash consist of glass bubbles and shards with a high internal surface area. They weather rapidly to the clays {{ref:soil-chem-098}} and {{ref:soil-chem-091}}. These soils, classed as {{ref:soil-class-092}}, are highly fertile, rich in organic matter and particularly light for their volume. Volcanic ash is also a source of non-glacial loess, as in Ecuador and Argentina.

They weather rapidly to the clays Imogolite, a clay built of nanotubes and Smectite, the swelling clay with an open interior. These soils, classed as Andisols, the young, fertile soils of volcanic ash, are highly fertile, rich in organic matter and particularly light for their volume. Volcanic ash is also a source of non-glacial loess, as in Ecuador and Argentina.

entries.title: Lichens, the first soil makers on bare stone

definition.text: The part lichens, symbiotic colonies of algae or cyanobacteria and fungi, play in breaking down rock and building and stabilizing soil.

facts.text: Lichens degrade minerals chemically and disrupt them physically, slowly turning rock into soil.
Metal-binding exudates and new minerals, especially metal oxalates, make them important agents of chemical weathering that create fertile soil from stone.
They are often the first settlers where there is no soil, at high elevations and latitudes.
In deserts, lichen crusts stabilize sand and hold water, and some plant seeds establish only there.

entries.text: On bare rock high in the mountains or far toward the poles, lichens often arrive first. They are symbiotic colonies of fungi with algae or cyanobacteria, and they slowly turn stone into soil. They disrupt minerals physically and degrade them chemically, a clear case of {{ref:soil-found-063}}. Their metal-binding exudates and the new minerals they form, especially metal oxalates, make them important agents of chemical weathering. In deserts, lichen crusts stabilize sand and hold water. Some plant seeds establish only there.

entries.title: Desert varnish, a dark skin painted by dust and dew

definition.text: An orange-yellow to black coating, about one micrometre thick, on exposed rock surfaces in arid environments.

facts.text: It forms only on stable rock surfaces no longer exposed to frequent rain, fracturing or wind abrasion, and is made mainly of clay with iron and manganese oxides.
The clay can only arrive by wind; it traps other substances that react together when the rock heats in the sun, with wetting by dew also important.
Black varnish holds manganese 50 to 60 times more abundantly than the crust's 0.12%; one proposed cause is manganese-oxidizing microbes.
Where the micro-environment pH exceeds 7.5, orange varnishes poor in manganese but rich in iron develop instead.

entries.text: Desert rocks often wear a coat only about one micrometre thick. Desert varnish is that orange-yellow to black coating on exposed rock in arid places. It forms only on stable surfaces, safe from frequent rain, fracturing or sandblasting by wind, and is mostly {{ref:soil-found-040}} with iron and manganese oxides. Windblown clay traps other substances, which react as the rock heats in the sun and is wetted by dew. Black varnish holds manganese 50 to 60 times more abundantly than the crust's 0.12%. Microbes that oxidize manganese may explain it. Where the local pH exceeds 7.5, iron-rich orange varnish forms instead.

It forms only on stable surfaces, safe from frequent rain, fracturing or sandblasting by wind, and is mostly Clay, the finest and busiest part of soil with iron and manganese oxides. Windblown clay traps other substances, which react as the rock heats in the sun and is wetted by dew. Black varnish holds manganese 50 to 60 times more abundantly than the crust's 0.12%. entries.title: Glacial drift, named for a theory that sank

definition.text: All sediment, from clay to boulders, carried by a glacier and deposited by or from the ice or by its meltwater.

facts.text: It is split into unstratified drift, or till, which forms moraines, and stratified drift laid down by meltwater as outwash plains, eskers, kames and varves.
In the United Kingdom drift is used more widely for all Quaternary surficial deposits mapped apart from bedrock, including loess, river deposits and colluvium.
Murchison introduced the term in 1839, after Lyell's idea that the sediments were dropped by drifting sea ice; the name outlived the hypothesis.

entries.text: Glacial drift carries the name of a mistake. Murchison introduced the term in 1839, following Lyell's idea that the sediments were dropped by drifting sea ice. The hypothesis died; the name outlived it. Drift is now all sediment, from clay to boulders, carried by a glacier and deposited by the ice or its meltwater. It splits in two. Unstratified drift is {{ref:soil-form-090}}, which builds the ridges described in {{ref:soil-form-150}}. Stratified drift is sorted and laid down by meltwater, forming {{ref:soil-form-151}}, eskers, kames and varves. In the United Kingdom the word is broader, covering all Quaternary surface deposits mapped apart from bedrock, including loess, river deposits and colluvium.

Unstratified drift is Glacial till, the unsorted load a glacier drops, which builds the ridges described in Moraines, the rubble ridges glaciers leave behind. Stratified drift is sorted and laid down by meltwater, forming Outwash plains, where meltwater sorts the glacier's load, eskers, kames and varves. In the United Kingdom the word is broader, covering all Quaternary surface deposits mapped apart from bedrock, including loess, river deposits and colluvium.

entries.title: Moraines, the rubble ridges glaciers leave behind

definition.text: Any accumulation of unconsolidated glacial debris, often till, in currently or formerly glaciated regions.

facts.text: It ranges from boulders down to gravel and sand in a groundmass of fine clayey glacial flour.
Lateral moraines form at the side of the ice, terminal moraines at its foot, marking the glacier's furthest advance.
Ground moraines are till-covered sheets of gently rolling relief under 10 meters, laid at the ice base as lodgment till.
Recessional moraines are small ridges left where a retreating glacier paused.

entries.text: A glacier dumps what it carries along its edges and at its snout. A moraine is any such accumulation of loose glacial debris, often till, in regions that are or once were glaciated. It ranges from boulders down to gravel and sand, set in a groundmass of fine clayey glacial flour. Lateral moraines form at the side of the ice. Terminal moraines form at its foot and mark the glacier's furthest advance. Recessional moraines are small ridges left where a retreating glacier paused. Ground moraines are till-covered sheets of gently rolling relief under 10 meters, laid at the ice base as lodgment till.

entries.title: Outwash plains, where meltwater sorts the glacier's load

definition.text: A plain of glaciofluvial deposits built by meltwater outwash at the end of a glacier; also called a sandur.

facts.text: Meltwater sorts the sediment: boulders settle near the terminal moraine and the finest silt travels furthest.
Braided streams rework its surface, and kettle lakes form where buried ice blocks melted.
Fossil sandar, no longer active, lie in formerly glaciated areas.

entries.text: Meltwater pouring off a glacier sorts its load by size. Boulders settle near the {{ref:soil-form-150}} at the ice front, and the finest silt travels furthest. The result is an outwash plain, or sandur: a plain of {{ref:soil-form-091}} built at the end of a glacier. Braided streams rework its surface. Kettle lakes form where buried blocks of ice melted. Not every sandur is active. Fossil sandar lie in formerly glaciated areas, long after the ice has gone.

entries.title: Spheroidal weathering, peeling rock like an onion

definition.text: Chemical weathering of jointed bedrock that produces concentric shells of highly decayed rock within saprolite; also called onion-skin weathering.

facts.text: Water enters along joints, so blocks weather inward fastest at corners, then edges, then faces, leaving a rounded core.
The cores, called corestones or woolsacks, are left as freestanding boulders or tors once erosion strips the saprolite.
Alteration forms secondary minerals such as kaolinite and montmorillonite and increases the rock's volume.
It has often been wrongly attributed to physical weathering alone; much of it happened in past humid, even tropical, climates.

entries.text: Square blocks of rock can rot into round boulders. Spheroidal, or onion-skin, weathering is the chemical attack on jointed bedrock that leaves concentric shells of decayed rock inside {{ref:soil-form-100}}. Water enters along the joints. Each block therefore weathers inward fastest at its corners, then its edges, then its faces, leaving a rounded core. These corestones, or woolsacks, stand as freestanding boulders or tors once erosion strips away the rotten rock around them. The alteration forms {{ref:soil-chem-235}} such as {{ref:soil-chem-088}} and {{ref:soil-chem-093}}, and swells the rock's volume. It has often been wrongly blamed on physical weathering alone, yet much of it happened in past humid, even tropical, climates.

Spheroidal, or onion-skin, weathering is the chemical attack on jointed bedrock that leaves concentric shells of decayed rock inside Saprolite, the rotten rock that keeps its shape. Water enters along the joints. Each block therefore weathers inward fastest at its corners, then its edges, then its faces, leaving a rounded core. These corestones, or woolsacks, stand as freestanding boulders or tors once erosion strips away the rotten rock around them. The alteration forms Secondary minerals: what weathering builds from the wreckage such as Kaolinite, the white clay of china and the tropics and Montmorillonite, the clay that swells tenfold, and swells the rock's volume. It has often been wrongly blamed on physical weathering alone, yet much of it happened in past humid, even tropical, climates.

entries.title: Topsoil, the thin living layer that feeds plants

definition.text: The upper layer of soil, richest in organic matter and microorganisms, where most of the soil's biological activity takes place.

facts.text: A mix of mineral particles and organic matter usually 5–10 inches (13–25 cm) deep, it holds water and air that encourage biological activity.
Roots concentrate in topsoil, where plants obtain most of their nutrients; bacteria and fungi break down organic matter and insects aerate and turn the soil.
Its depth is measured from the surface to the first densely packed layer, the subsoil; classification systems call it the O or A horizon.
More organic matter strengthens soil structure; dried-out topsoil loses much of its volume and becomes more prone to wind erosion.
An optimum carbon-to-nitrogen ratio for UK topsoil is less than 20:1.
One inch (2.5 cm) of topsoil can take 500 to 1,000 years to form, and current use and erosion outpace soil generation.
The United States loses almost 3 tons of topsoil per acre per year.
Cover crops, crop rotation, conservation tillage and windbreaks are used to slow erosion and keep topsoil fertile.

Today, use and erosion strip topsoil faster than new soil forms. Cover crops, {{ref:soil-agri-004}}, {{ref:soil-agri-099}} and windbreaks slow the loss and keep it fertile.

entries.title: Subsoil, where the rain drops its cargo

definition.text: The layer of soil beneath the topsoil, a mix of sand, silt and clay with much less organic matter and humus.

facts.text: Most soil mapping systems label it the B horizon; below it lies the substratum or C horizon.
With little organic matter, its colour comes mainly from iron oxides.
Rain carries weathering products such as clay minerals and iron oxides down as solutes and colloids, and they accumulate in the subsoil, the depth of most deposition.
Physical, chemical and biological activity give the subsoil a soil structure, which sets it apart from the substratum below.
Though not sterile, it holds few soil organisms compared with humus-rich topsoil.
Human activity has mixed topsoil and subsoil in many environments.
Clay-rich subsoil has supplied adobe, cob, rammed earth and wattle and daub for millennia.

entries.text: Rain does more than wet the ground. It carries weathering products such as clay and the minerals of {{ref:soil-chem-163}} downward, dissolved or as fine suspended particles, and most of them settle in the subsoil. Subsoil is the layer beneath {{ref:soil-form-021}}, a mix of sand, silt and clay with much less {{ref:soil-found-045}}. With so little of it, the subsoil's color comes mainly from those iron minerals. Physical, chemical and biological activity cluster its particles into a definite arrangement, and that sets it apart from the barely altered substratum below. It is not sterile, but it holds few soil organisms compared with the rich layer above. Most soil mapping systems give it the letter B, with a substratum lettered C beneath; {{ref:soil-form-010}} and {{ref:soil-form-011}} return to both. Human activity has mixed topsoil and subsoil in many environments. Builders have used clay-rich subsoil for millennia, as adobe, cob, rammed earth and wattle and daub.

entries.title: Soil morphology: describing a soil by eye and hand

definition.text: The branch of soil science that describes soils technically, above all their physical properties such as texture, colour, structure and consistence.

facts.text: Descriptions are usually made in the field on a profile with several horizons, exposed by digging a pit or taking a core with a push tube or auger.
With soil formation and soil classification, soil morphology is counted as part of pedology, one of the central disciplines of soil science.
Nineteenth-century agro-geologists, who examined soils in natural settings, were the first to study soil morphology scientifically.
Dokuchaev's team saw profiles with similar horizons hundreds of kilometres apart wherever climate and vegetation were similar.
Once soils were seen as independent natural bodies, morphology was used to judge the combined influence of climate, organisms, relief, parent material and time.
Official guidelines for describing soils first appeared in the 1930s, by Charles Kellogg and the USDA Soil Conservation Service in the United States and by G.R. Clarke in the United Kingdom.
A description records site information plus horizons, colour, texture, structure and other properties; many US soil scientists use the USDA-NRCS Pedon Description field sheet.
Structure is described by shape, size and grade, best while the soil is fairly dry, because moist peds swell and press together.

entries.text: Dokuchaev's team noticed something striking. Profiles with similar horizons turned up hundreds of kilometers apart, wherever climate and vegetation were similar. Observing like that is soil morphology, the branch of soil science that describes soils technically, above all their texture, color, structure and consistence. Nineteenth-century agro-geologists, studying soils in natural settings, were the first to do it scientifically. Once soils were seen as independent natural bodies, morphology became a way to judge the combined influence of climate, organisms, relief, parent material and time. Official guidelines first appeared in the 1930s, from Charles Kellogg and the USDA in the United States and from G.R. Clarke in the United Kingdom. Today a describer works in the field on several horizons exposed by a pit, a push tube or an auger. Many US soil scientists record site, horizons, color, texture and structure on a standard USDA-NRCS field sheet. Structure is best judged fairly dry, because moist clumps swell and press together. Together with the study of how soils form and how they are classified, morphology belongs to pedology.

entries.title: Diagnostic horizons, the layers that decide a soil's name

definition.text: A horizon defined by a set of criteria, whose presence or absence at a given depth is used to assign soils to taxonomic units.

facts.text: The WRB, USDA soil taxonomy and the Australian Soil Classification pick out diagnostic horizons, whereas the German system defines soils by whole horizon sequences.
Diagnostic horizons usually carry names, such as the cambic or spodic horizon, rather than symbols.
The WRB lists 40 diagnostic horizons.
To classify a soil, each horizon is checked against the criteria, and the soil is allocated from the diagnostic horizons found.
USDA soil taxonomy separates diagnostic surface horizons, the epipedons, from subsurface ones such as the argillic, cambic, spodic and oxic horizons.
Most systems also use soil characteristics other than diagnostic horizons to define taxonomic units.

entries.text: To name a soil, a classifier checks each of its horizons against a list of criteria. A diagnostic horizon is one defined by such a set of criteria. Its presence or absence at a given depth decides which taxonomic unit the soil belongs to. The WRB lists 40 of them. The WRB, {{ref:soil-class-006}} and the {{ref:soil-class-022}} all work this way, while the German system defines soils by whole sequences of horizons. Diagnostic horizons usually carry names rather than symbols, such as the one in {{ref:soil-form-117}} or the one in {{ref:soil-form-031}}. The USDA system separates diagnostic surface horizons, covered in {{ref:soil-form-018}}, from subsurface ones. Among those are the spodic and oxic horizons and the clay-rich layer in {{ref:soil-class-045}}. Most systems also use other soil characteristics to define their units.
entries.text_plain: To name a soil, a classifier checks each of its horizons against a list of criteria. A diagnostic horizon is one defined by such a set of criteria. Its presence or absence at a given depth decides which taxonomic unit the soil belongs to. The WRB lists 40 of them. The WRB, USDA soil taxonomy: six levels from order to series and the Australia's fifteen orders for an old, weathered land all work this way, while the German system defines soils by whole sequences of horizons. Diagnostic horizons usually carry names rather than symbols, such as the one in The spodic horizon, where iron and humus settle or the one in Cambic horizons, the first signs of change below ground. The USDA system separates diagnostic surface horizons, covered in Epipedons, the diagnostic surface horizons of USDA taxonomy, from subsurface ones. Among those are the spodic and oxic horizons and the clay-rich layer in The argillic horizon, where washed-down clay collects. Most systems also use other soil characteristics to define their units.

entries.title: The O horizon, a blanket of leaves and needles

definition.text: A surface layer of organic material, built from plant residues not mixed into the mineral soil and not waterlogged for long periods.

facts.text: Organic material is defined by a minimum organic carbon content, 20% by weight in the WRB.
Its residues are typically leaves, conifer needles, twigs, mosses and lichens, partly altered by decomposition.
The upper part is often barely decomposed while the lower part may be strongly humified; the Australian system splits O horizons into O1 and O2 on that basis.
The Australian system keeps the O horizon apart from overlying leaf litter, which has no weathered mineral particles and is not part of the soil.
Organisms living in the O horizon break down organic material and release nutrients, making the soil more active.
Strong acidity, cold or pollution slow decomposition, so undecomposed organic matter builds up in an organic horizon over the mineral soil.
Though formed on top of the mineral soil, O horizons can be buried at depth by landslides, floods or wind-blown dust.
Its upper part is often relatively undecomposed litter, while the lower part may be strongly humified.

verification.evidence: The suffix symbols and their meanings follow: a Highly decomposed organic material This symbol is used with O horizons to indicate the most highly decomposed organic materials, which have a fiber content of less than 17 percent (by volume) after rubbing.
verification.note: the Manual's 17% is the fiber content of sapric (highly decomposed) material; the entry gives the WRB's 20% organic carbon threshold for organic material

entries.text: Leaves, conifer needles, twigs, mosses and lichens gather on many soils and slowly decompose in place. The result is the O horizon: a surface layer of organic material built from plant residues, not mixed into the mineral soil and not waterlogged for long periods. The WRB counts material as organic when it holds at least 20% organic carbon by weight. The upper part is often barely decomposed litter, while the lower part may be strongly humified, broken down into dark, stable organic material. The Australian system splits it into O1 and O2 on that basis. It also keeps loose leaf litter, which has no weathered mineral particles, out of the soil altogether. Organisms in the O horizon break down the residues and release nutrients. Strong acidity, cold or pollution slow them, so undecomposed material piles up over the mineral soil. Though it forms on top, an O horizon can be buried at depth by landslides, floods or wind-blown dust.

entries.title: The A horizon, where life and minerals mix

definition.text: The uppermost mineral horizon, at the surface or below an O horizon, where humified organic matter is intimately mixed with mineral material.

facts.text: It is often called topsoil and holds dark decomposed organic matter called humus.
Burrowing animals mix organic matter into the mineral matter there, a process called bioturbation.
Most biological activity happens here: earthworms, potworms, arthropods, nematodes, fungi, bacteria and archaea crowd around plant roots, so it may be called the biomantle.
Because biological activity reaches much deeper, it cannot be the chief test; A horizons are mostly defined relative to the layers beneath.
Original rock structure is fully or largely obliterated in an A horizon.
Layers changed by cultivation or pasturing count as A horizons; the suffix p marks ploughed layers.
The Australian system subdivides it into A1 (dark, most biologically active), A2 (paler) and A3 (transitional to the B horizon).

entries.text: Earthworms, potworms, arthropods, {{ref:soil-bio-193}}, fungi, bacteria and archaea crowd around plant roots in the A horizon, which is why some call it the biomantle. It is the uppermost mineral horizon, at the surface or below an O horizon, where humified {{ref:soil-found-045}} is intimately mixed with mineral material. Often called topsoil, it holds dark, decomposed matter of that kind. Burrowing animals stir it into the mineral matter, a mixing described in {{ref:soil-bio-047}}. The original rock structure is fully or largely gone. Biological activity reaches much deeper, though, so it cannot be the chief test, and A horizons are defined mostly relative to the layers beneath. Layers changed by plowing or pasturing count as A horizons, and the suffix p marks plowed ones. The Australian system divides it into A1, dark and most biologically active, A2, paler, and A3, a transition to the layer below.

entries.title: Eluviation: how percolating water empties the upper soil

definition.text: The removal of soil material from upper layers by water percolating down through the profile.

facts.text: Eluviation occurs when precipitation exceeds evaporation.
A horizon formed by it is an eluvial horizon; some sources count both the A and the E horizon as the eluvial zone.
It moves mineral and organic colloids, which sets it apart from leaching, a distinct mechanism of soil formation.
On a slope, upper facets lose salts by eluviation while lower facets gain them by illuviation.
Organic acids in acid conditions make iron and aluminium more soluble and enhance eluviation; podsolisation is an extreme case that removes iron and aluminium sesquioxides.
The material builds up lower in the profile as an illuvial deposit, a process called illuviation.
It occurs where precipitation exceeds evaporation.
It forms an eluvial horizon: a light-coloured zone at the base of the A horizon (Ae) or a separate E horizon below it, where the process is most intense.

entries.text: Where more rain falls than evaporates, water keeps moving down through the soil, and it takes things with it. That removal of soil material from upper layers by percolating water is eluviation. It carries mineral and organic particles fine enough to stay suspended in water, the kind described in {{ref:soil-chem-154}}. That sets it apart from {{ref:soil-form-050}}, a distinct soil-building mechanism. Acid conditions speed it up, because organic acids make iron and aluminum more soluble. {{ref:soil-form-061}} is the extreme case, stripping out the oxides of iron and aluminum. The layer that loses material is an eluvial horizon. It may be a light-colored zone at the base of the surface mineral horizon, labelled Ae. Where the process is most intense, it forms a separate layer beneath, lettered E and described in {{ref:soil-form-009}}. Some sources count both of these layers as the eluvial zone. What leaves must land somewhere. The material builds up lower down as an illuvial deposit, the process of {{ref:soil-form-032}}. On a slope the exchange also runs downhill: upper facets lose salts while lower facets gain them.
entries.text_plain: Where more rain falls than evaporates, water keeps moving down through the soil, and it takes things with it. That sets it apart from Leaching: how water strips a soil from the top down, a distinct soil-building mechanism. Acid conditions speed it up, because organic acids make iron and aluminum more soluble. Where the process is most intense, it forms a separate layer beneath, lettered E and described in The E horizon, a pale layer washed clean. Some sources count both of these layers as the eluvial zone. What leaves must land somewhere. The material builds up lower down as an illuvial deposit, the process of Illuviation: where washed-down material comes to rest. entries.title: The E horizon, a pale layer washed clean

definition.text: A mineral horizon that has lost clay, iron, aluminium, organic matter or a mix of these, leaving a concentration of sand and silt, mostly quartz.

facts.text: E stands for eluviated: the leached layer is usually pale and made largely of silicates or silica.
It usually lies below an O or A horizon and above a B horizon, from which it differs by higher colour value or lower chroma, coarser texture, or both.
E horizons occur only in older, well-developed soils; pedogenesis there is advanced, since the lost substances first formed or accumulated in place.
The Australian system does not use E; leached layers are labelled A or B with the suffix e.
In gravelly soils, burrowing animals commonly leave a stone layer near or at the base of the E horizon.
Where this eluviation is pronounced, a lighter-coloured E horizon appears below the A horizon.
It is usually, though not always, paler than the B horizon beneath, sometimes taking the colour of its sand and silt particles.
E stands for eluviated; such horizons occur only in older, well-developed soils, generally between the A and B horizons, and the Australian system does not use the symbol.

entries.text: Old, well-developed soils often hide a band paler than the layers around it. That is the E horizon, E for eluviated. It is a mineral horizon that has lost clay, iron, aluminum, organic material or a mix of these, leaving a concentration of sand and silt, mostly quartz. Where eluviation is pronounced, it appears below the A horizon and above a layer lettered B, covered in {{ref:soil-form-010}}. It differs from that lower layer by higher color value or lower chroma, coarser texture, or both. Sometimes it takes the color of its own sand and silt. The lost substances first had to form or collect in place, so an E horizon marks an advanced stage of soil development. In gravelly soils, burrowing animals commonly leave a stone layer near its base. The Australian system does not use E; it labels such washed-out layers A or B with the suffix e.

entries.title: Hardpans, the buried floors that stop roots

definition.text: A dense, largely water-impervious soil layer, usually lying just below the topsoil.

facts.text: Some pans form when deposits such as dissolved silica, iron oxides or calcium carbonate fuse and bind the soil particles.
Others are man-made, compacted by repeated ploughing, especially with moldboard ploughs, by heavy traffic or by pollution.
Acidic soils are most affected, because iron and calcium salts form hard complexes with soil particles under acid conditions.
Clay-rich soils compact easily, and sodium in wastewater can bind clay into a local hardpan, a common cause of septic system failure.
Hardpans impede drainage and restrict root growth on farms and in gardens.
They can be broken mechanically with a broadfork, digging fork or spade, or with a tractor-drawn chisel plough.
Manure, compost or peat improve drainage and encourage earthworms that slowly break pans; lime and gypsum help with harder pans, but amendments may take years.
Plinthite turns irreversibly into an ironstone hardpan when exposed to repeated wetting and drying.

entries.text: Some soils have a floor that roots and water cannot get through. A hardpan is a dense, largely water-impervious layer, usually lying just below the topsoil. Lime and gypsum help with harder ones, though amendments may take years. {{ref:soil-water-242}} turns irreversibly into an ironstone hardpan when wetted and dried again and again.

entries.title: Cryoturbation: how frost churns the ground

definition.text: Frost churning: the mixing of material from different soil horizons, down to bedrock, by repeated freezing and thawing in permafrost soils.

facts.text: It occurs to some degree in most Gelisols, whose name comes from Latin gelare, to freeze.
Autumn freezing forms ice wedges in the most erodible parts of the parent rock; in summer the active layer lets loosened material move both down and up.
Moisture moves from the warm surface to the cold permafrost table, drying the upper soil into a granular structure with ice lenses.
Separation of coarse from fine material produces patterned ground.
It is strongest on exposed sites and weak in sheltered valleys: Turbels show it in over one-third of the active layer, with distorted horizon boundaries, Orthels in less.
It is the dominant force in the active layer and tends to make it uniform in composition.
In frost boils it can bring base-rich water up to the surface, neutralizing acidity and replenishing nutrients.
Ice lenses grow by drawing unfrozen water along a thermal gradient, displacing and mixing mineral and organic material at the ice-water interface.

entries.text: In the frozen north, the soil mixes itself. Cryoturbation is frost churning: the mixing of material from different soil horizons, down to bedrock, by repeated freezing and thawing in soils with permanently frozen ground. It occurs to some degree in most soils of the order {{ref:soil-class-096}}, whose name comes from Latin gelare, to freeze. Autumn freezing forms wedges of ice, described in {{ref:soil-form-036}}, in the most erodible parts of the parent rock. In summer the {{ref:soil-env-146}} lets loosened material move both down and up. Moisture moves from the warm surface to the cold top of the frozen layer, drying the upper soil into a granular structure with lens-shaped bodies of ice. These lenses grow by drawing unfrozen water along a thermal gradient, displacing and mixing mineral and organic material at the ice-water interface. Separation of coarse from fine material produces {{ref:soil-phys-163}}. Cryoturbation is the dominant force in that layer and tends to make it uniform in composition. It is strongest on exposed sites and weak in sheltered valleys: Turbels show it in over one-third of that layer, with distorted {{ref:soil-form-005}}, Orthels in less. In {{ref:soil-phys-160}} it can bring base-rich water to the surface, neutralizing acidity and replenishing nutrients. In effect, ice scrambles the layers described in {{ref:soil-found-001}}.

entries.title: Illuviation: where washed-down material comes to rest

definition.text: The deposition in a lower soil layer of material, called illuvium, washed down by rainwater from a layer above.

facts.text: Removal of material from a layer is eluviation; illuviation is the matching build-up further down.
Illuvium includes organic matter, silicate clay and hydrous oxides of iron and aluminium, which collect in subsoil B horizons, the zones of illuviation.
Transport is basically vertical, unlike alluviation, the horizontal transfer by running water.
In mechanical illuviation, a drier horizon draws water from percolating suspensions by capillarity, leaving fine coatings called cutans along the channels.
In chemical illuviation, dissolved constituents carried by leaching are deposited where soil chemistry, especially pH and redox potential, changes.
Clay skins are called argillans, and horizons with enough illuvial clay are argillic horizons.
In medium-textured soils, clay is often washed down the profile and accumulates in the subsoil.

entries.text: Everything water carries out of an upper layer has to stop somewhere. Illuviation is that stopping: the deposition in a lower layer of material, called illuvium, washed down by rainwater from a layer above. It is the matching half of eluviation. Illuvium includes {{ref:soil-found-045}}, silicate clay and the iron and aluminum compounds of {{ref:soil-chem-162}}. These collect in subsoil horizons lettered B, the zones of illuviation, described in {{ref:soil-form-010}}. The movement is basically vertical, unlike alluviation, the sideways transfer by running water. It works in two ways. In mechanical illuviation, a drier horizon draws water from percolating suspensions by capillarity, the pull of water into fine pores. Fine coatings are left along the channels, the subject of {{ref:soil-found-068}}. In chemical illuviation, dissolved constituents carried down by percolating water are deposited where the chemistry of the soil changes, especially its pH and its {{ref:soil-chem-123}}. Clay skins are called argillans, and horizons with enough washed-in clay are the ones named in {{ref:soil-class-045}}. In medium-textured soils, clay is often washed down the profile and gathers in the subsoil.
entries.text_plain: Everything water carries out of an upper layer has to stop somewhere. These collect in subsoil horizons lettered B, the zones of illuviation, described in The B horizon, the soil's collecting zone. The movement is basically vertical, unlike alluviation, the sideways transfer by running water. It works in two ways. Fine coatings are left along the channels, the subject of Cutans, the coatings left by moving clay. In chemical illuviation, dissolved constituents carried down by percolating water are deposited where the chemistry of the soil changes, especially its pH and its Eh, the voltage that tells oxidizing soil from reducing soil. Clay skins are called argillans, and horizons with enough washed-in clay are the ones named in The argillic horizon, where washed-down clay collects. In medium-textured soils, clay is often washed down the profile and gathers in the subsoil.

entries.title: The B horizon, the soil's collecting zone

definition.text: A subsurface mineral horizon, formed below an A, E, H or O horizon, where the original rock structure is largely gone and soil formation has altered or enriched the material.

facts.text: Commonly called subsoil, it is brownish or reddish from iron oxides, since it holds less organic matter than the A horizon.
Its features include residual oxides or clay minerals, removal of carbonates or gypsum, and illuvial clay, iron, aluminium, organic matter, carbonates, gypsum or silica.
Where it gathers material moving down from the A and E horizons it is also called the illuvial horizon.
The B horizon generally has soil structure, and its structure or consistency differs from the horizons above and below.
Layers with gleying but no other pedogenic change, or with carbonates not contiguous to a genetic horizon above, are not B horizons.
The Australian system splits it into B1 (transitional from A), B2 (concentrated clay or oxides) and B3 (transitional to the C or D horizon).

entries.text: Brown or reddish, the B horizon takes its color from {{ref:soil-chem-163}}, because it holds less organic matter than the A horizon above. It is a subsurface mineral horizon, formed below a horizon lettered A, E, H or O. Its original rock structure is largely gone, and {{ref:soil-form-155}} have altered or enriched its material. It is commonly called subsoil. Where it gathers material moving down from the A and E horizons, it is also called the illuvial horizon. Its marks include residual oxides or clay, lost carbonates or gypsum, and washed-in clay, iron, aluminum, organic material, carbonates, gypsum or silica. It generally has a structure or consistency that differs from the layers above and below. Gleying alone does not make a B horizon, nor do carbonates cut off from a genetic horizon above. The Australian system splits it into B1, transitional from A, B2, with concentrated clay or oxides, and B3, transitional to the C or D horizon.
entries.text_plain: Brown or reddish, the B horizon takes its color from Iron oxides, the minerals that color and feed soils, because it holds less organic matter than the A horizon above. Where it gathers material moving down from the A and E horizons, it is also called the illuvial horizon. entries.title: The C horizon, raw material soil barely touched

definition.text: A layer below the soil horizons, other than hard bedrock, that is little affected by soil formation and lacks the properties of O, A, E or B horizons.

facts.text: It includes sediments, saprolite and soft bedrock that can be dug with a spade when moist and usually slake in water within 24 hours.
C horizons form in deposits such as loess, flood deposits and landslides, or from in-situ weathering of bedrock.
Without a lithologic discontinuity above it, the C horizon resembles the parent material of the solum, though C material may be unlike it.
Plant roots can penetrate C horizons, which form an important growing medium.
It may be enriched with carbonates and other soluble compounds leached down from the solum.
Layers cemented by silica, carbonates or gypsum stay C unless clearly affected by soil formation, when they become B horizons.
It forms either in deposits such as loess, flood deposits or landslides, or by in-situ weathering of residual bedrock.
Where there is no lithologic discontinuity, the C horizon resembles the parent material of the solum above.

entries.text: Below the layers that {{ref:soil-form-155}} have reshaped lies material it has barely touched. The C horizon is that layer: anything above hard bedrock that those processes have little affected and that lacks the properties of O, A, E or B horizons. It includes sediments, saprolite and soft bedrock that a spade can dig when moist and that usually slakes, crumbling in water, within 24 hours. It forms in deposits such as loess, flood deposits and landslides, or by weathering of bedrock in place. Unless a change in parent material separates them, a break covered in {{ref:soil-form-015}}, it resembles the parent material of the soil above, though C material may differ. Plant roots can penetrate it, so it is an important growing medium. It may be enriched with carbonates and other soluble compounds washed down from above. Layers cemented by silica, carbonates or gypsum stay C unless those processes have clearly affected them; then they become B horizons.

entries.title: The soil profile, a record read from the top down

definition.text: A vertical face of soil showing its horizons, layers roughly parallel to the surface; formally, one face of a pedon.

facts.text: Profiles are exposed for study by excavating a pit or by extracting a core with a hand or hydraulic push tube or an auger.
Mature profiles typically have three basic master horizons, A, B and C, but no profile has all the major horizons.
Some soils, such as Entisols, have only one horizon or none, for instance young soils on mine waste, moraines, volcanic cones, dunes or alluvial terraces.
Wind or water erosion can strip the upper horizons, burying them downslope, a natural process that tillage aggravates.
Soils reshaped by major earthworks or regular deep ploughing may lack distinct horizons almost completely.
Going down a profile goes back in time: past events are recorded in horizons much as in sediment layers.
Pollen, testate amoebae and plant remains in horizons can reveal past climate or land-use change, and large charcoal pieces allow radiocarbon dating.

entries.text: Going down a soil profile means going back in time. Like layers of sediment, its horizons record past events. A soil profile is a vertical face of soil showing its horizons, layers roughly parallel to the surface. Formally, it is one face of the three-dimensional block described in {{ref:soil-form-003}}. Soil scientists expose a profile by digging a pit or extracting a core with a hand or hydraulic push tube or an auger. Mature profiles typically have three basic master horizons, A, B and C, but no profile has all the major horizons. Some soils, such as those of the {{ref:soil-class-094}} order, have only one horizon or none. Young soils on mine waste, moraines, volcanic cones, dunes or alluvial terraces are examples. Wind or running water can strip the upper horizons and bury them downslope, a natural process that {{ref:soil-agri-095}} aggravates. Major earthworks or regular deep plowing can leave a soil almost without distinct horizons. The horizons also hold clues to the past. Pollen, {{ref:soil-bio-195}} and plant remains can reveal changes in climate or how the land was used, and large pieces of charcoal allow dating by the method in {{ref:soil-hist-120}}.
entries.text_plain: Going down a soil profile means going back in time. Like layers of sediment, its horizons record past events. entries.title: The solum, the part of the soil that formed together

definition.text: The upper part of a soil, its surface and subsoil layers, that has developed under the same soil-forming conditions.

facts.text: In horizon terms it is the A, E and B horizons, their transitional horizons and some O horizons; its base is relatively unweathered parent material.
It includes horizons of carbonate or salt accumulation if they formed at least partly in the same period of soil formation.
A solum has no minimum or maximum thickness: a 10 cm surface layer on bedrock can be the whole solum, while fresh alluvium has none.
Its lower limit should relate to the rooting depth expected for perennial plants, though in some soils it can only be set arbitrarily.
Hardened carbonate or gleying many metres down is hard to count as solum, since deep features may be relict or geological rather than pedological.
The living part of the soil is largely confined to the solum and is most prominent in the A horizon.

verification.evidence: An A horizon that is 10 cm thick overlying bedrock is by itself the solum.

entries.text: A 10 cm surface layer on bedrock can be a complete solum, while fresh alluvium has none at all. The solum is the upper part of a soil, its surface and subsoil layers, developed under the same soil-forming conditions. In horizon terms it covers the A, E and B horizons, the blended layers between them and some O horizons. Its base is relatively unweathered parent material. Layers where carbonate or salt accumulated belong too, if they formed at least partly in the same period. A solum has no minimum or maximum thickness. Its lower limit should relate to how deep the roots of perennial plants are expected to reach, though in some soils it can only be set arbitrarily. Hardened carbonate or gleying many meters down is hard to count, since such deep features may be relict or geological rather than products of soil development. The living part of the soil stays largely within the solum and is most prominent in the A horizon.

entries.title: The H horizon, peat that sits in water

definition.text: An organic layer, generally peat, that is saturated with water for long periods or has been artificially drained.

facts.text: In the WRB an H layer is saturated for more than 30 consecutive days in most years, or drained; an O horizon is saturated for no more than 30 days and not drained.
Many H horizons consist mainly of sphagnum (peat) mosses.
After drainage, O horizons may form on top of H horizons.
The Australian system calls these waterlogged organic horizons P, for peats, with at least 12 to 18% organic carbon depending on clay content.

entries.text: Not every organic layer stays dry. The H horizon is an organic layer, generally peat, that is saturated with water for long periods or has been artificially drained. In the WRB an H layer is saturated for more than 30 consecutive days in most years, or drained. An O horizon, by contrast, is saturated for no more than 30 days and not drained. Many H horizons consist mainly of sphagnum mosses. After drainage, O horizons may form on top of them. The Australian system calls these waterlogged layers P, for peats, with at least 12 to 18% organic carbon depending on clay content.

entries.title: The R layer, bedrock at the bottom of the pit

definition.text: Hard, consolidated bedrock underlying the soil at the base of the profile.

facts.text: Examples are granite, basalt, quartzite and hard limestone or sandstone; air-dry chunks do not slake in water within 24 hours.
It is too coherent to dig by hand with a spade, and its few small cracks let few roots in.
Where no lithologic discontinuity separates them, the R layer resembles the parent material of the solum.

entries.title: Horizon designations, a soil's layers written in code

definition.text: The code of letters and numbers that names each soil horizon: a capital master symbol, often followed by lowercase suffixes, with numbers for discontinuities and subdivisions.

facts.text: A capital letter gives the master horizon, such as O, A, E, B, C or R; lowercase suffixes add details of soil formation.
A numerical prefix marks a lithologic discontinuity, a change in parent material; a numerical suffix splits one horizon into subdivisions such as Bt1, Bt2 and Bt3.
Some master horizons, including O, B and L, must always carry a suffix, and several suffixes may be combined.
The horizons of a profile are joined with hyphens, as in Ah-E-Bt1-2Bt2-2BwC-3C1-3C2.
The notation summarizes colour, size, texture, structure, consistency, roots, pH, voids, boundaries and nodules or concretions.
The same horizon may be labelled differently in different classification systems; there are many systems of horizon symbols in the world.
No system is more correct than another, but because their symbols are defined differently, the systems cannot be mixed.

entries.title: Horizon suffixes, small letters with big meanings

definition.text: Lowercase letters added to a master horizon symbol to record particular features or processes of soil formation.

facts.text: In the USDA field book, t marks illuvial silicate clay, k pedogenic calcium carbonate, g strong gleying and p a plough layer.
Other USDA suffixes include b for a buried genetic horizon, f for permafrost, x for fragipan features and y for gypsum.
WRB letters borrow from other languages: k from German Karbonat, t from German Ton (clay), n from natrium and z from Dutch zout (salt).
Suffixes are combined in order of dominance, as in Btng or Btgb; the cementation suffix m follows the suffix naming the cementing agent.

entries.title: Lithologic discontinuities, numbering a change of material

definition.text: A change in parent material within a soil profile, shown in horizon designations by a numerical prefix.

facts.text: By convention the uppermost material carries no number; each lower stratum gets 2, 3 and so on, as in Oi-Oe-Ah-E-2Bt-2C-3R.
Where no discontinuity separates the solum from the C horizon below, that C horizon resembles the solum's parent material.
Numerical suffixes, by contrast, mark subdivisions within a single horizon.

entries.text: Not every profile grew from a single material. A lithologic discontinuity is a change in parent material within a soil profile, shown by a number in front of the horizon symbol. By convention the uppermost material carries no number, and each lower stratum gets 2, 3 and so on, as in Oi-Oe-Ah-E-2Bt-2C-3R. Numbers after a symbol, by contrast, mark subdivisions within a single horizon. Where no discontinuity separates the solum from the C horizon below, that C horizon resembles the solum's parent material.

entries.title: Buried horizons, old surfaces under new ground

definition.text: A genetic horizon that formed at the surface and was later covered by new mineral material, marked with the suffix b.

facts.text: A fully formed profile may be buried by wind- or water-laid sediments that later form a new profile; this is most common in coastal areas.
Numerical prefixes describe such sequences, as in O, A1, A2, B2, 2A2, 2B21, 2B22, 2C, with the buried profile starting at 2A2.
Fossil soil horizons of paleosols occur within sedimentary rock sequences and record past environments.
Soil formation is often pictured as happening in place, but burial makes the process far more complicated.

entries.text: Soils are often pictured as forming in place, but burial makes the process far more complicated. Wind- or water-laid sediments can cover a fully formed profile and later form a new profile on top, most commonly in coastal areas. A buried soil horizon is a genetic horizon that formed at the surface and was later covered by new mineral material; it carries the suffix b. Numerical prefixes describe such stacks, as in O, A1, A2, B2, 2A2, 2B21, 2B22, 2C, where the buried profile starts at 2A2. Fossil soil horizons also occur within sedimentary rock sequences, where they record past environments.

entries.title: Transitional horizons, where one layer shades into the next

definition.text: A horizon combining the properties of two master horizons, written with both capital letters, the dominant one first, as in AB or BA.

facts.text: Where separate bodies of two master horizons are intermingled, the symbols are joined with a slash, as in A/B or B/A.
The WRB writes superimposed horizons without a separator, as in AhBw, and uses a slash for separate bodies, as in Bt/E where E material interfingers into a Bt horizon.
The Australian A3, B1 and B3 transitional horizons are loosely defined and used at the describer's discretion.
I, L and W layers are never used in transitional designations.

entries.text: Some layers belong to two horizons at once. A transitional horizon combines the properties of two master horizons and is written with both capital letters, the dominant one first, as in AB or BA. Where separate bodies of the two are intermingled, a slash joins the symbols, as in A/B or B/A. The WRB writes superimposed horizons without a separator, as in AhBw. It keeps the slash for separate bodies, as in Bt/E, where E material interfingers into a Bt horizon. The Australian A3, B1 and B3 are loosely defined and used at the describer's discretion. I, L and W layers never appear in transitional designations.

entries.title: Fragipans, brittle layers that still puzzle soil scientists

definition.text: A diagnostic horizon of USDA soil taxonomy: an altered, dense subsurface layer that restricts water flow and root penetration.

facts.text: It is written Bx or Btx and limits land use much as a duripan does; the WRB counterpart is the fragic horizon.
Fragipans are firm and brittle near field capacity with virtually no roots, yet air-dry fragments slake in water, unlike duripans and petrocalcic horizons.
They contain no calcium or magnesium carbonate and do not effervesce in dilute HCl.
Proposed origins include glacial compaction, permafrost, physical ripening, inheritance from paleosols, and hydroconsolidation, the collapse of structure under loading and wetting.

entries.contested_note: Soil scientists debate how fragipans form, how to define them and whether they exist in certain landscapes (S:85fb395526b9, S:3fc191113f55).
entries.text: A fragipan holds virtually no roots, yet its air-dry fragments fall apart in water. It is a diagnostic horizon of {{ref:soil-class-006}}: an altered, dense subsurface layer that blocks water and roots. Written Bx or Btx, it limits how the land can be used much as the layer in {{ref:soil-form-027}} does. It contains no calcium or magnesium carbonate and does not fizz in dilute HCl. Proposed origins include glacial compaction, frozen ground, physical ripening, inheritance from ancient buried soils, and hydroconsolidation, the collapse of structure under loading and wetting. Soil scientists still debate how fragipans form, how to define them and whether they exist in some landscapes.

entries.title: Topsoil by the truckload

definition.text: Soil mixtures sold as topsoil, either natural topsoil mined and conditioned for use or manufactured from minerals, biosolids, compost or paper mill sludge.

facts.text: It is used to improve gardens and lawns, fill containers and grade the ground around buildings, but suits potting less well than potting soil or compost.
In the UK it must be classified under British Standard BS 3882 (2015), with thresholds for nutrients, phytotoxic elements, particle size, organic matter, pH and contamination.
The United States has no federal legal definition of topsoil sold in commerce.
Artificial growing media include terra preta and potting mix; low-quality artificial topsoil helped rehabilitate an open-cut coal mine in Victoria, Australia.

entries.text: Topsoil is also a product. Commercial topsoil is any soil mixture sold as topsoil: natural topsoil mined and conditioned for use, or a blend manufactured from minerals, {{ref:soil-fert-045}}, compost or paper mill sludge. Buyers use it to improve gardens and lawns, fill containers and grade the ground around buildings, though it suits potting less well than {{ref:soil-agri-028}} or compost. entries.title: Ice wedges, cracks that freeze and grow each winter

definition.text: A crack in the ground holding a narrow wedge of ice up to 3–4 metres long at the surface and reaching several metres down.

facts.text: By the widely accepted thermal contraction theory, winter cold opens cracks a few cm wide that fill with snowmelt, freeze, and crack again each winter.
A mean annual air temperature of −6 to −8 °C or colder is thought necessary, and the wedges usually form polygonal patterns.
Epigenetic wedges grow in existing permafrost, widening to 3–5 m; syngenetic wedges grow upward as sediment accumulates and can reach 25 m deep.
Where permafrost has gone, melted wedges fill with sediment; these ice wedge casts help estimate climates of hundreds of thousands of years ago.

These casts help estimate climates of hundreds of thousands of years ago.

entries.title: Horizon boundaries, sharp or gradual, smooth or wavy

definition.text: The lower border of a soil horizon, described in the field by how sharp it is (distinctness) and how its shape varies sideways (topography).

facts.text: Distinctness classes run from very abrupt and abrupt through clear and gradual to diffuse.
Boundaries are often not parallel to the surface and may be broken; topography classes are smooth, wavy, irregular and broken.
Official series descriptions record them, as in the Cecil series: an abrupt smooth boundary below the Ap horizon and gradual wavy boundaries further down.

entries.text: Where one horizon ends, a describer records two things. Horizon boundaries are the lower borders of horizons, described by how sharp they are, called distinctness, and how their shape varies sideways, called topography. Distinctness runs from very abrupt and abrupt through clear and gradual to diffuse. Boundaries are often not parallel to the surface and may be broken, so the topography classes are smooth, wavy, irregular and broken. Official series descriptions record them. The Cecil series, for instance, has an abrupt smooth boundary below its Ap horizon and gradual wavy boundaries further down.

entries.title: Duripans, subsoil set as hard as concrete

definition.text: A diagnostic horizon of USDA soil taxonomy in which illuvial silica has cemented the subsoil into a hardpan.

facts.text: It is usually written Bqm; the closest Canadian equivalent is the duric horizon, and the WRB counterpart is the petroduric horizon.
Duripans form almost only in arid or Mediterranean climates and can be as hard as concrete, so their soils are seldom cultivated and mostly used for grazing or wildlife.
Silica from fast-weathering volcanic glass, or from iron-magnesium minerals and feldspars, is carried into the subsoil and precipitates as microaggregates that grow into a pan.
Criteria include cementation of over half the volume, roots only along fractures 10 cm or more apart, and slaking in KOH but not HCl, which separates it from petrocalcic horizons and fragipans.

entries.text: Duripans form almost only in arid or Mediterranean climates, and they can be as hard as concrete. A duripan is a diagnostic horizon of {{ref:soil-class-006}} in which silica washed down from above has cemented the subsoil into a hardpan. Silica from fast-weathering glassy lava ({{ref:soil-chem-200}}), feldspars or iron-magnesium minerals precipitates there as microaggregates that grow into a pan. Criteria include cementation of over half the volume, roots only along fractures 10 cm or more apart, and breaking down in KOH but not HCl. That test separates it from fragipans and from the carbonate-cemented layer in {{ref:soil-form-029}}. Its soils are seldom cultivated and serve mostly for grazing or wildlife.
entries.text_plain: Duripans form almost only in arid or Mediterranean climates, and they can be as hard as concrete. A duripan is a diagnostic horizon of USDA soil taxonomy: six levels from order to series in which silica washed down from above has cemented the subsoil into a hardpan. Silica from fast-weathering glassy lava (Volcanic glass, rock that froze before it could crystallize), feldspars or iron-magnesium minerals precipitates there as microaggregates that grow into a pan. Criteria include cementation of over half the volume, roots only along fractures 10 cm or more apart, and breaking down in KOH but not HCl. That test separates it from fragipans and from the carbonate-cemented layer in Petrocalcic horizons, subsoil cemented by carbonate. Its soils are seldom cultivated and serve mostly for grazing or wildlife.

entries.title: Petrocalcic horizons, subsoil cemented by carbonate

definition.text: A diagnostic horizon of USDA soil taxonomy and the WRB in which secondary carbonates have cemented the subsoil into a hardpan.

facts.text: It is cemented by carbonates, with or without silica, and roots get through only along vertical fractures 10 cm or more apart.
Carbonates from parent material or dust are carried down by water and precipitate as it evaporates, building a massive, continuous cemented layer.
It marks advanced soil evolution in older soils, and most formed before the Holocene.
Carbonates typify alkaline soils of arid and semiarid climates and are detected in the field by fizzing with hydrochloric acid.

entries.text: Carbonates typify the alkaline soils of arid and semiarid climates, and a drop of hydrochloric acid makes them fizz. In a petrocalcic horizon, secondary carbonates have cemented the subsoil into a hardpan. It is a diagnostic horizon in {{ref:soil-class-006}} and the WRB. Water carries carbonates from parent material or dust downward, and they precipitate as it evaporates. Over time they build a massive, continuous cemented layer, with or without silica. Roots get through only along vertical fractures 10 cm or more apart. The horizon marks advanced soil evolution in older soils, and most formed before the Holocene.
entries.text_plain: Carbonates typify the alkaline soils of arid and semiarid climates, and a drop of hydrochloric acid makes them fizz. In a petrocalcic horizon, secondary carbonates have cemented the subsoil into a hardpan. It is a diagnostic horizon in USDA soil taxonomy: six levels from order to series and the WRB. Water carries carbonates from parent material or dust downward, and they precipitate as it evaporates. Over time they build a massive, continuous cemented layer, with or without silica. Roots get through only along vertical fractures 10 cm or more apart. The horizon marks advanced soil evolution in older soils, and most formed before the Holocene.

entries.title: Claypans, where water perches and topsoil washes away

definition.text: A dense, compact, slowly permeable subsoil layer with much more clay than the material above, from which a sharp boundary separates it.

facts.text: Its dense structure restricts roots and water infiltration, so a perched water table can form on top of it.
The Canadian system defines claypan as a clay-enriched illuvial B (Bt) horizon.
It covers about 4 million ha of the central United States, in states such as Kansas, Oklahoma and Illinois, and also occurs in south-west Queensland.
Bare ground, particle-size distribution and heavy rain favour it: raindrops rearrange fine sand, silt and clay until they plug the pores into a packed layer.
Dominated by montmorillonite, it shrinks hard in the dry season and swells wet and sticky in the wet season, with poor aeration.
It holds much water, but most is unavailable to plants because it evaporates and the pores are tiny.
Acidic and clay-rich, it binds phosphorus so tightly that much P fertilizer is needed, while its potassium stays available to plants.
Slow infiltration and perched water increase surface runoff, leaving claypan soils highly vulnerable to erosion of the organic-rich topsoil.

entries.text: Across about 4 million ha of the central United States, in states such as Kansas, Oklahoma and Illinois, a dense layer of clay lies beneath the fields. A claypan is a compact, slowly permeable subsoil layer with much more clay than the material above, separated from it by a sharp boundary. Bare ground, the mix of grain sizes and heavy rain favor it: raindrops rearrange fine sand, silt and clay until they plug the pores. Its dense structure restricts roots and the entry of water, so water perches on top of it and saturates the soil above. Runoff rises, leaving the organic-rich topsoil highly vulnerable to erosion. Dominated by {{ref:soil-chem-093}}, it shrinks hard in the dry season and turns wet and sticky in the wet season, with poor aeration. It holds much water, but most is unavailable to plants, because the pores are tiny and the water evaporates. Acidic and clay-rich, it binds phosphorus so tightly that much P fertilizer is needed, while its potassium stays available. It also occurs in south-west Queensland.
