Acidic and clay-rich, it binds phosphorus so tightly that much P fertilizer is needed, while its potassium stays available. It also occurs in south-west Queensland.

entries.title: Silcrete, the stone early toolmakers heated

definition.text: A hard soil duricrust formed when surface soil, sand and gravel are cemented by dissolved silica.

facts.text: It forms in a similar way to calcrete, cemented by calcium carbonate, and ferricrete, cemented by iron oxide, and looks like quartzite.
Microcrystalline silcretes form in arid settings with rising pH and lacustrine silcretes where pH falls; silcrete often caps landforms in arid Australia and Africa.
Aboriginal Australians and Middle Stone Age Africans prized silcrete for tools, heat-treating it to flake more easily, possibly the first use of pyrotechnology.
At Pinnacle Point in South Africa, heat-treated silcrete tools date to between 60,000 and 80,000 years ago.

entries.text: At Pinnacle Point in South Africa, toolmakers were heat-treating silcrete between 60,000 and 80,000 years ago. Silcrete is a hard crust, a kind of {{ref:soil-chem-039}}, formed when surface soil, sand and gravel are cemented by dissolved silica. It forms much as its cousins do: one cemented by calcium carbonate, and one cemented by iron oxide, described in {{ref:soil-form-038}}. Microcrystalline silcretes form in arid settings as pH rises, lacustrine ones where pH falls. It often caps landforms in arid Australia and Africa. Aboriginal Australians and Middle Stone Age Africans prized it for tools, heating it so it flaked more easily, possibly the first use of pyrotechnology.
entries.text_plain: At Pinnacle Point in South Africa, toolmakers were heat-treating silcrete between 60,000 and 80,000 years ago. Silcrete is a hard crust, a kind of Duricrust, the hard shell some dry soils wear, formed when surface soil, sand and gravel are cemented by dissolved silica. It forms much as its cousins do: one cemented by calcium carbonate, and one cemented by iron oxide, described in Ferricrete, the iron-cemented coffee stone. Microcrystalline silcretes form in arid settings as pH rises, lacustrine ones where pH falls. It often caps landforms in arid Australia and Africa. Aboriginal Australians and Middle Stone Age Africans prized it for tools, heating it so it flaked more easily, possibly the first use of pyrotechnology.

entries.title: Umbric horizons, dark but acid

definition.text: A thick, dark, organic-rich surface horizon that is acid and low in bases; its name comes from Latin umbra, shade.

facts.text: It normally has a pH below 5.5 and a base saturation under 50 percent.
WRB criteria include Munsell chroma and value of 3 or less when moist, at least 0.6% organic carbon, and a thickness of at least 100 mm on hard rock, otherwise 200 mm.
Roots growing horizontally can indicate its acidity.
Similar dark, base-poor horizons made by deep cultivation, kitchen middens or manuring are told apart by artifacts, spade marks or land-use history.

entries.text: Shade is in the name: umbric comes from the Latin umbra. An umbric horizon is a thick, dark, organic-rich surface horizon that is acid and low in bases. It must be at least 100 mm thick on hard rock, otherwise 200 mm. Roots growing horizontally can indicate its acidity. Similar dark, base-poor layers made by deep cultivation, manuring or the kitchen refuse heaps in {{ref:soil-hist-102}} are told apart by artifacts, spade marks or land-use history.

entries.title: Ferricrete, the iron-cemented coffee stone

definition.text: A hard, erosion-resistant layer of sedimentary rock, usually conglomerate or breccia, cemented into a duricrust by iron oxides.

facts.text: The iron oxide cement comes from the oxidation of percolating iron-salt solutions; the name joins ferruginous and concrete.
It forms at or near the land surface and may hold sediments brought from elsewhere; synonyms include ferruginous duricrust, hardpan and ironpan.
Some laterites contain ferricrete, which has been suggested to form in their wetter, leached parts.
In rural South Africa it is widely used to build roads and is known by its Afrikaans name koffieklip, coffee stone.

entries.title: Cutans, the coatings left by moving clay

definition.text: Changes in soil texture or structure at natural surfaces of particles, pores or peds, caused by illuviation.

facts.text: They are oriented deposits of any soil component: clay skins or coatings of silica, sesquioxides, manganese, organic matter or carbonate.
Clay skins are also called argillans; a horizon with enough clay illuviation is an argillic horizon.
Visible in the field, they show the degree and nature of soil formation, and reading them is a core skill in soil morphology and paleopedology.
Clay cutans show lineations from oriented clay under cross-polarized light and survive in paleosols after the original voids are lost, making them one of the most diagnostic paleosol features.

entries.text: Soil surfaces keep a record of what water carried past them. Cutans are changes in soil texture or structure at the natural surfaces of particles, pores and clumps, caused by illuviation. They are oriented deposits of any soil component: clay skins, or coatings of silica, iron and aluminum oxides, manganese, organic material or carbonate. Clay skins are also called argillans, and a horizon with enough washed-in clay is the kind named in {{ref:soil-class-045}}. Common and visible in the field, they are focal points of chemical and biological reactions. Reading them, a core skill in soil morphology and the study of ancient soils, shows the degree and nature of soil development.

entries.title: Pedocals, the carbonate soils of an older scheme

definition.text: A former class of the zonal soil order: soils of semiarid and arid regions rich in calcium carbonate and low in organic matter.

facts.text: Under a thin A horizon, calcite and other soluble minerals that water would normally remove build up in the B horizon as a cemented layer, caliche.
Marbut's classification split soils at its highest level into pedocals and pedalfers, the latter rich in aluminium and iron.
The term is not used in the current US classification but often appears in college geology texts.

entries.text: Marbut's classification split soils at its highest level into two groups: pedocals and {{ref:soil-class-042}}, the latter rich in aluminum and iron. Pedocals are soils of semiarid and arid regions, rich in calcium carbonate and low in {{ref:soil-found-045}}. They were once a class of the order described in {{ref:soil-class-015}}. Under a thin A horizon, calcite and other soluble minerals that water would normally remove build up in the B horizon. There they form a cemented layer, {{ref:soil-chem-036}}. The term is not used in the current US classification, but it often appears in college geology texts.

They were once a class of the order described in Zonal soils, shaped by regional climate. The term is not used in the current US classification, but it often appears in college geology texts.

entries.title: Paralithic horizons, weathered bedrock beneath the soil

definition.text: A weathered layer of bedrock.

facts.text: The name comes from the Greek para, "akin to", and lithic, "stony".
A paralithic contact is one of the depth limits used to define soil classes, as in the definitions of the Gelisol suborders.

entries.text: Bedrock does not always meet the soil as solid stone. A paralithic horizon is a weathered layer of bedrock. The name comes from the Greek para, akin to, and lithic, stony. A paralithic contact is one of the depth limits used to define soil classes, as in the definitions of the {{ref:soil-class-097}}.

A paralithic contact is one of the depth limits used to define soil classes, as in the definitions of the Histels, Turbels and Orthels: the three Gelisol suborders.

entries.title: Slickensides, polished cracks in swelling clay

definition.text: In pedology, the polished surfaces of cracks that form in soils with a high proportion of swelling clays.

facts.text: Slickensides are a type of cutan.
In the Australian Soil Classification, slickensides with lenticular aggregates indicate a vertisol.
In geology the name is given to fault surfaces smoothed by friction and striated in the direction of movement.

entries.text: Some soil cracks shine as if polished. In pedology, slickensides are those glossy crack surfaces, formed in soils with a high proportion of swelling clays. They are a type of {{ref:soil-found-068}}, a coating or surface feature on soil aggregates. In {{ref:soil-class-022}}, slickensides together with lens-shaped aggregates mark one soil order, {{ref:soil-class-106}}. Geologists use the same name for something larger: fault surfaces smoothed by friction and striated in the direction of movement.
entries.text_plain: Some soil cracks shine as if polished. In pedology, slickensides are those glossy crack surfaces, formed in soils with a high proportion of swelling clays. They are a type of Cutans, the coatings left by moving clay, a coating or surface feature on soil aggregates. In Australia's fifteen orders for an old, weathered land, slickensides together with lens-shaped aggregates mark one soil order, Vertisols, the clay soils that plow themselves. Geologists use the same name for something larger: fault surfaces smoothed by friction and striated in the direction of movement.

entries.title: Cambic horizons, the first signs of change below ground

definition.text: A diagnostic subsurface horizon showing early pedogenic change, recognized when it does not meet the requirements of any other diagnostic horizon.

facts.text: It lacks appreciable illuviated clay, organic carbon, iron and aluminium oxyhydroxides, carbonate, gypsum or soluble salts.
Its texture must be no coarser than loamy fine sand or very fine sand.
It is commonest in Mollisols and Inceptisols, and also occurs in Andisols, designated Bw or Bg.
With less clay than an argillic horizon, it develops into an argillic (Bt) horizon once the soil becomes an Alfisol along a chronosequence.

entries.text: The cambic horizon is the diagnostic horizon of last resort. It is a subsurface horizon showing early change by {{ref:soil-form-155}}, recognized when it does not meet the requirements of any other diagnostic horizon. It lacks appreciable illuviated clay, organic carbon, iron and aluminum oxyhydroxides, carbonate, gypsum or soluble salts. Its texture must be no coarser than loamy fine sand or very fine sand. It is commonest in {{ref:soil-class-101}} and {{ref:soil-class-100}}, also occurs in {{ref:soil-class-092}} and is written Bw or Bg. Along a {{ref:soil-form-063}}, it gains clay and develops into a clay-enriched Bt horizon once the soil becomes one of the {{ref:soil-class-090}} kind.
entries.text_plain: The cambic horizon is the diagnostic horizon of last resort. It is a subsurface horizon showing early change by Four ways soils gain, lose, change and move material, recognized when it does not meet the requirements of any other diagnostic horizon. It lacks appreciable illuviated clay, organic carbon, iron and aluminum oxyhydroxides, carbonate, gypsum or soluble salts. Its texture must be no coarser than loamy fine sand or very fine sand. It is commonest in Mollisols, the deep dark soils of the grasslands and Inceptisols, young soils just starting a subsoil, also occurs in Andisols, the young, fertile soils of volcanic ash and is written Bw or Bg. Along a Chronosequences: centuries read from months of fieldwork, it gains clay and develops into a clay-enriched Bt horizon once the soil becomes one of the Alfisols, fertile soils with a clay-rich subsoil kind.

entries.title: Tepetate, Mexico's hardened volcanic layers

definition.text: A Mexican term, from Nahuatl tepetlatl, for a horizon hardened by compaction or cementation in volcanic regions of Mexico.

facts.text: At the surface, tepetates are hard, poorly drained and infertile, which makes them a problem for farming.
Buried under soil, they raise the risk of erosion and landslides because water runs off sideways instead of soaking in.

entries.text: In the volcanic regions of Mexico, some horizons have hardened by compaction or cementation. Mexicans call such a horizon tepetate, from the Nahuatl tepetlatl. At the surface, tepetates are hard, poorly drained and infertile, which makes them a problem for farming. Buried under soil, they bring a different danger. Water runs off sideways instead of soaking in, raising the risk of erosion and landslides.

entries.title: Albic horizons, bleached layers below the surface

definition.text: A bleached, light-coloured subsurface diagnostic horizon left when soil formation moves clay minerals and oxides downward.

facts.text: It is a diagnostic horizon in both the WRB and USDA soil taxonomy.
Spodosols, acidic soils common in coniferous and boreal forests, usually have an albic horizon.
In Albeluvisols the albic horizon tongues into a clay-illuvial Bt horizon; in Stagnosols the topsoil can be completely bleached.
Plinthosols often show eluviation as an albic horizon beneath an umbric surface layer.

In {{ref:soil-class-144}}, the topsoil can be completely bleached. {{ref:soil-class-137}} often show eluviation as an albic horizon beneath an umbric surface layer.

entries.title: The calcic horizon, where lime collects in dry soils

definition.text: A horizon of secondary carbonate accumulation, above 15% calcium carbonate equivalent and at least 5% more carbonate than the layer below.

facts.text: Calcids have a calcic, hypercalcic or petrocalcic horizon whose upper boundary lies within 1.0 m of the surface.
Calciorthids, Aridisols of the U.S. Soil Taxonomy, are distinguished by a calcic horizon; most Ustolls also have one.
Aridisols have been redefined as soils with a calcic horizon less than 1 meter deep.

entries.text: In dry soils, lime washed down from above can pile up in a layer of its own. A calcic horizon is that layer of secondary carbonate accumulation, carbonate built from {{ref:soil-found-118}}. It must hold more than 15% carbonate, measured as {{ref:soil-fert-060}}, and at least 5% more carbonate than the layer below. This {{ref:soil-form-017}} marks several dryland soil groups. {{ref:soil-class-161}} have a calcic, hypercalcic or petrocalcic horizon whose upper boundary lies within 1.0 m of the surface. Calciorthids are distinguished by one, and most Ustolls have one too. {{ref:soil-class-093}} have even been redefined as soils with a calcic horizon less than 1 meter deep.

A calcic horizon is that layer of secondary carbonate accumulation, carbonate built from Calcite, the mineral that fizzes in acid. Calciorthids are distinguished by one, and most Ustolls have one too. Aridisols, the slow-forming soils of the deserts have even been redefined as soils with a calcic horizon less than 1 meter deep.

entries.title: Epipedons, the diagnostic surface horizons of USDA taxonomy

definition.text: In USDA soil taxonomy, a diagnostic surface horizon, the upper part of the soil.

facts.text: The USDA epipedons are the anthropic, folistic, histic, melanic, mollic, ochric, plaggen and umbric epipedons.
A fertile mollic epipedon, built by long additions of root-derived organic matter, is the defining feature of Mollisols.
Histosols must have a histic epipedon; an ochric epipedon is common in Entisols and Aridisols.
Inceptisols usually have an ochric or umbric epipedon over a cambic horizon; plaggen or anthropic epipedons signal intense, prolonged human activity.

entries.text: {{ref:soil-class-006}} gives the top of the soil its own set of names. An epipedon is a diagnostic surface horizon, the upper part of the soil. There are eight: the anthropic, folistic, histic, melanic, mollic, ochric, plaggen and umbric epipedons. {{ref:soil-form-118}}, fertile and built by long additions of root-derived organic material, is the defining feature of {{ref:soil-class-101}}. {{ref:soil-class-098}} must have a histic epipedon, while an ochric epipedon is common in {{ref:soil-class-094}} and {{ref:soil-class-093}}. {{ref:soil-class-100}} usually have an ochric or umbric epipedon over a cambic horizon. Plaggen or anthropic epipedons signal intense, prolonged human activity.
entries.text_plain: USDA soil taxonomy: six levels from order to series gives the top of the soil its own set of names. An epipedon is a diagnostic surface horizon, the upper part of the soil. There are eight: the anthropic, folistic, histic, melanic, mollic, ochric, plaggen and umbric epipedons. The mollic epipedon, the dark topsoil of grasslands, fertile and built by long additions of root-derived organic material, is the defining feature of Mollisols, the deep dark soils of the grasslands. Histosols, soils built from organic matter must have a histic epipedon, while an ochric epipedon is common in Entisols, soils that have barely begun and Aridisols, the slow-forming soils of the deserts. Inceptisols, young soils just starting a subsoil usually have an ochric or umbric epipedon over a cambic horizon. Plaggen or anthropic epipedons signal intense, prolonged human activity.

entries.title: The kandic horizon, a clay layer that holds little

definition.text: An argillic horizon whose clays are mainly 1:1 silicate clays, giving it a low cation exchange capacity.

facts.text: Because of its low cation exchange capacity it stores nutrients poorly.
Alfisols must have an argillic, natric or kandic horizon, and Ultisols an argillic or kandic one.
Nitisols correspond to kandic Alfisols, Ultisols and Inceptisols, and Acrisols partly to Oxisols with a kandic horizon.

entries.text: Not every clay-rich subsoil is rich in nutrients. A kandic horizon is a subsoil layer of washed-in clay, a kind of {{ref:soil-class-045}}, whose clays are mainly 1:1 silicate clays. These clays carry little exchangeable charge, so the horizon stores nutrients poorly. It is a {{ref:soil-form-017}} that helps sort soils into orders. {{ref:soil-class-090}} must have a clay-enriched, natric or kandic horizon. {{ref:soil-class-104}} must have a clay-enriched or kandic one. In the world system, {{ref:soil-class-134}} correspond to kandic soils of those two orders and of {{ref:soil-class-100}}. {{ref:soil-class-117}} correspond partly to {{ref:soil-class-103}} with a kandic horizon.

These clays carry little exchangeable charge, so the horizon stores nutrients poorly. It is a Diagnostic horizons, the layers that decide a soil's name that helps sort soils into orders. entries.title: The mollic epipedon, the dark topsoil of grasslands

definition.text: The fertile, dark surface horizon that is the defining diagnostic feature of Mollisols.

facts.text: It builds up through long-term additions of organic matter from plant roots and typically has soft, granular structure.
Mollisols must have one and a base saturation above 50%; they are common in grasslands.
Where shrink–swell clays dominate, a soil with a mollic epipedon is classed a Vertisol; in Andisols the andic properties take precedence.
Greyzems combine a mollic horizon with dry-forest vegetation, where organic accumulation outweighs leaching.

entries.text: The black topsoil of a grassland is built by roots, year after year. Long-term additions of organic matter from plant roots create a mollic epipedon, a fertile, dark surface horizon with typically soft, granular structure. It is a kind of {{ref:soil-form-018}}, a dark version of the {{ref:soil-form-008}}. It defines {{ref:soil-class-101}}, which must have one and a {{ref:soil-chem-052}} above 50%. These soils are common in grasslands. Other traits can override it. Where shrink–swell clays dominate, a soil with a mollic epipedon is classed with {{ref:soil-class-106}}. In {{ref:soil-class-092}} the andic properties take precedence. {{ref:soil-class-047}} combine a mollic horizon with dry-forest vegetation, where organic accumulation outweighs {{ref:soil-form-050}}.

entries.title: The natric horizon, a clay layer loaded with sodium

definition.text: An argillic horizon in which large amounts of exchangeable sodium have accumulated.

facts.text: Solonetz soils have a natric horizon within the upper 100 cm; the name comes from natrium, Latin for sodium.
Alfisols and Mollisols with a natric horizon belong mainly to the Solonetz.
It develops from an argillic horizon and is a diagnostic horizon in both the WRB and USDA soil taxonomy.

entries.text: Natrium is Latin for sodium, and it names a troublesome soil layer. A natric horizon is a subsoil layer of washed-in clay in which large amounts of exchangeable sodium have built up. It develops from a clay-enriched layer of the kind described in {{ref:soil-class-045}}. It is a {{ref:soil-form-017}} in both the WRB and {{ref:soil-class-006}}. {{ref:soil-class-143}} soils have a natric horizon within the upper 100 cm. Soils of two other orders, {{ref:soil-class-090}} and {{ref:soil-class-101}}, belong mainly to that group when they have one.

entries.title: The pedon, the basic block of field soil study

definition.text: The imaginary three-dimensional unit of soil large enough to show the full range of properties of a particular soil; a soil profile is one face of it.

facts.text: Pedons generally cover 1 to 10 m2 of land and are the fundamental unit of field soil study.
The Canadian system defines the pedon as a body commonly 1 metre across and 1 to 2 metres deep.
One proposal splits the pedon into a living humipedon, a copedon where most mineral weathering occurs, and a lithopedon in contact with the subsoil.
To classify a soil, every horizon of its pedon is checked against the criteria for diagnostic horizons.

entries.title: Soil monoliths, whole profiles carried into museums

definition.text: A soil profile dug from the ground in one piece, without disturbing its layers, and preserved for study or display.

facts.text: Each monolith is processed for a month or longer before it is mounted for museum display.
The World Soil Museum shows some 80 monoliths and stores about 1000 from over 70 countries, each with site data and horizon-by-horizon descriptions.
The Dokuchaev Central Museum of Soil holds about 330 monoliths representing the world's soil diversity.

entries.title: The spodic horizon, where iron and humus settle

definition.text: An iron-rich diagnostic subsurface horizon of podzols, where iron and aluminium oxides accumulate with humus.

facts.text: Spodosols must have a spodic horizon within 2 m of the surface, usually under an albic horizon; they are acidic soils of coniferous and boreal forests.
It is a diagnostic horizon in both the WRB and USDA soil taxonomy.
The Polish classification uses it to define the order of soils formed mainly by podzolisation.

entries.text: Under conifer forests, iron and aluminium travel downward and stop together. A spodic horizon is the subsurface layer of the soils in {{ref:soil-class-138}}, where iron and aluminium oxides accumulate with decayed organic matter, giving it an iron-rich look. It is a {{ref:soil-form-017}} in both the WRB and {{ref:soil-class-006}}. {{ref:soil-class-099}} must have one within 2 m of the surface, usually beneath a pale, bleached albic horizon. They are acidic soils of coniferous and boreal forests. The Polish classification uses the spodic horizon to define its order of soils formed mainly by {{ref:soil-form-061}}.
entries.text_plain: Under conifer forests, iron and aluminium travel downward and stop together. A spodic horizon is the subsurface layer of the soils in Podzol, the ash-grey soil beneath northern forests, where iron and aluminium oxides accumulate with decayed organic matter, giving it an iron-rich look. It is a Diagnostic horizons, the layers that decide a soil's name in both the WRB and USDA soil taxonomy: six levels from order to series. Spodosols, acid soils of the cool conifer forests must have one within 2 m of the surface, usually beneath a pale, bleached albic horizon. They are acidic soils of coniferous and boreal forests. The Polish classification uses the spodic horizon to define its order of soils formed mainly by Podzolisation: acid litter bleaches the upper soil.

entries.title: How bare rock slowly becomes living soil

definition.text: The development of soil, also called pedogenesis, as shaped by the effects of place, environment and history.

facts.text: It begins with the weathering of freshly accumulated parent material; new soils then deepen through further weathering and deposition, including deposition of dust.
Microbes feed on nutrients released by weathering and produce organic acids and proteins that speed mineral weathering, while their residues help form humus.
Under the Mediterranean climate of Sicily, weathering produces soil at roughly 1/10 mm per year.
As soil develops it supports pioneer species first, then more complex plant and animal communities through ecological succession.
Topsoils deepen as humus from dead plants and microbes accumulates and as organic matter mixes with weathered minerals.
As soils mature, accumulating organic matter, mineral weathering and leaching create layers called horizons that differ in colour, structure, texture and chemistry.
Biogeochemical processes both create and destroy order within soils, and differences in soil-forming factors produce patterns in the distribution of soil types.
Pedogenesis is studied as a branch of pedology; it explains soil distribution today (soil geography) and in past geological periods (paleopedology).

entries.text: In the Mediterranean climate of Sicily, weathering makes new soil at roughly 1/10 mm a year. That slow work is soil formation, also called pedogenesis: the development of soil as shaped by place, environment and history. It begins with the {{ref:soil-found-052}} of freshly accumulated parent material. New soils then deepen through further weathering and through deposition, including settling dust. Microbes feed on the nutrients that weathering releases. They produce organic acids and proteins that speed the breakdown of minerals, and their residues help build the dark, decayed organic matter of the topsoil. As the soil develops, pioneer species arrive first, then richer plant and animal communities through {{ref:soil-form-125}}. Topsoil deepens as remains of dead plants and microbes accumulate and mix with weathered minerals. With maturity come layers. Accumulating organic matter, mineral weathering and the washing of dissolved material downward create horizons that differ in color, structure, texture and chemistry. Biogeochemical processes both build and destroy order within a soil. Differences in the conditions that shape soils produce patterns in where soil types occur. Pedogenesis is studied as a branch of pedology. It explains how soils are spread across the land today and how they were spread in past geological periods.

entries.title: Leaching: how water strips a soil from the top down

definition.text: The removal of soluble materials from one zone of a soil to another by water moving through the profile.

facts.text: It is a soil-forming mechanism distinct from eluviation, which is the loss of mineral and organic colloids rather than dissolved material.
Leached and eluviated materials tend to leave the topsoil and gather in the subsoil, in a horizon called the zone of illuviation.
Laterite, which develops under high temperatures and heavy rainfall, is an example of the process.
In brown podzolic soils leaching washes mobile chemicals out of the A horizon and accumulates iron and aluminium sesquioxides in the B horizon, colouring it rusty orange-brown.
Canadian soil classification marks strongly leached layers as light grey Ae horizons, and in Solonetzic soils progressive leaching moves salts and sodium downward.
Climate directly sets the rate of leaching; it is most intense in warm, humid regions where the soil does not freeze.
Intensive leaching leaves laterite soils less fertile than other soils, and has left reclaimed acid sulfate soils infertile.
Most leaching comes from infiltrating water; it is controlled largely by hydraulic conductivity and described with solute transport models such as Darcy's law.

entries.text: Water soaking down through a soil does not travel empty. Leaching is the removal of soluble materials from one zone of a soil to another by water moving through the profile. It differs from eluviation, which moves tiny mineral and organic particles, the subject of {{ref:soil-chem-154}}, rather than dissolved material. Both tend to strip the topsoil and enrich the subsoil, in a horizon called the zone of illuviation. Climate sets the pace directly. Leaching is most intense in warm, humid regions where the soil does not freeze. The red tropical soil described in {{ref:soil-form-065}} develops under high temperatures and heavy rainfall, and intensive leaching leaves it less fertile than other soils. Its signature shows in the profile. In one brownish leached soil, {{ref:soil-class-049}}, water washes mobile chemicals out of the A horizon. Iron and aluminum oxides, the subject of {{ref:soil-form-085}}, gather in the B horizon and color it rusty orange-brown. The Canadian system for naming soils marks strongly leached layers as light gray Ae horizons. In Solonetzic soils, progressive leaching moves salts and sodium downward. The process can also defeat reclamation: intensive leaching has left reclaimed {{ref:soil-chem-030}} infertile.

entries.title: Five forces behind every soil, from climate to time

definition.text: The five classic, intertwined influences that govern how a soil develops: parent material, climate, topography, organisms and time.

facts.text: Reordered as climate, organisms, relief, parent material and time, the factors form the acronym CLORPT.
Parent material, the mineral material a soil forms from, turns into soil as it is weathered, transported, deposited and precipitated.
Climate is regarded as the dominant factor; soils show the distinctive characteristics of the climate zones in which they form.
Topography can either hasten or retard the work of climate on a soil.
Each soil has its own combination of microbial, plant, animal and human influences acting on it.
Time acts through the interactions of all the other factors, and how long a profile takes to develop depends strongly on climate, parent material, relief and biota.
The 1938 USDA soil taxonomy divided soils into three orders according to their dominant soil-forming factors.
Intrazonal soils show a local factor of relief or parent material outweighing the zonal effects of climate and vegetation.

Each soil also has its own mix of microbial, plant, animal and human influences. Time acts through all the others. How long a profile takes to develop depends strongly on climate, parent material, relief and living things. The factors once sorted the soils of a whole nation. In one of them, a local factor of relief or parent material outweighed the zonal effects of climate and vegetation.

entries.title: Paleosols, soils from vanished worlds

definition.text: An ancient soil that formed in the past.

facts.text: In geology it is a former soil buried under sediments such as alluvium or loess, or under lava or volcanic ash, and in older deposits lithified into rock.
In soil science it is a soil formed long ago whose properties bear no relation to today's climate or vegetation, found on old cratons and outliers of ancient rock.
The record reaches into the Precambrian, with rare paleosols older than 2.5 billion years.
Over the last 50 million years drying climates hardened former tropical soils across much of Australia into crusts so unweatherable that only poorly developed soils form on them.
Such relict soils are exceedingly infertile, with available phosphorus orders of magnitude lower than in younger temperate soils, yet often hold exceptional biodiversity.
Pollen, phytoliths, carbon isotopes and leaf waxes in paleosols reveal past plant life, including the balance of C3 and C4 plants.
Glacial loess layers separated by paleosols record glaciations, and stacked paleosol sequences are useful in paleoseismology.

entries.text: Some soils formed more than 2.5 billion years ago. A paleosol is an ancient soil that formed in the past. Geologists use the word for a former soil buried under sediments such as alluvium or loess, or under lava or volcanic ash. In older deposits it has hardened into rock. Soil scientists mean a soil formed long ago whose properties bear no relation to today's climate or vegetation, found on old cratons and outliers of ancient rock. Over the last 50 million years, drying climates hardened former tropical soils across much of Australia into crusts so unweatherable that only poorly developed soils form on them. These relict soils are exceedingly infertile, yet often hold exceptional biodiversity. Paleosols also keep records. Pollen, carbon isotopes and leaf waxes in them reveal past plant life, including the balance of C3 and C4 plants. Glacial loess layers separated by paleosols record glaciations, and stacked paleosols help reveal past earthquakes.

entries.title: Climate, the dominant hand in shaping soil

definition.text: The influence of climate on soil formation, chiefly through effective precipitation (precipitation minus evapotranspiration) and temperature, which set the rates of chemical, physical and biological processes.

facts.text: When warmth and abundant water coincide in the profile, weathering, leaching and plant growth are all maximized.

Water percolating through the profile carries soluble and suspended material, including clay and dissolved organic matter, from upper layers (eluviation) to lower ones (illuviation), differentiating horizons.
To act, water must penetrate the regolith; the deeper it goes, the deeper the soil is weathered and developed.
In dry regions soluble salts are not leached and may build up enough to curb plant and microbial growth; carbonates and caliche horizons also accumulate.
Colder or drier climates fix less atmospheric carbon as organic matter but also decompose less of it.
Profiles are more distinct in wet, cool climates, where organic matter accumulates, than in wet, warm climates, where it is rapidly consumed.
Climate also acts through vegetation: humid climates favour trees, subhumid and semiarid regions grasses, and arid areas shrubs and brush.
Bare tropical soils under intense evaporation can draw dissolved iron and aluminium upward into a surface hardpan of laterite or bauxite, an irreversible form of degradation.

entries.text: Where warmth and plentiful water meet in a soil, weathering, leaching and plant growth all run at their peak. Climate works chiefly through temperature and effective precipitation: rainfall minus the water lost to evaporation and plant transpiration. Together they set the rates of chemical, physical and biological processes. Water must first penetrate the regolith, and the deeper it goes, the deeper the soil weathers and develops. Percolating water carries clay and dissolved organic material from upper layers to lower ones, separating horizons. In dry regions, salts are not leached. They can build up enough to curb plant and microbial growth, while carbonates accumulate in hard layers. Colder or drier climates fix less carbon as organic matter but also decompose less of it. So profiles are more distinct in wet, cool climates than in wet, warm ones, where organic matter is quickly consumed. Climate also acts through vegetation: trees in humid climates, grasses in subhumid and semiarid regions, shrubs in arid lands.

entries.title: Snails, fungi and fire: life as a soil builder

definition.text: The influence of plants, animals, fungi, bacteria and humans on how a soil forms.

facts.text: Microorganisms drive key mineral transformations; some bacteria fix atmospheric nitrogen and some fungi extract deep phosphorus and add soil carbon as glomalin.
Plants hold soil against erosion and build humus, and with mycorrhizal fungi and rhizosphere bacteria produce chemicals that break down minerals.
Burrowing macrofauna and mesofauna mix soil and open pores for water and gases, a process called bioturbation.
Mixing by animals, sometimes called pedoturbation, tends to undo the work of the processes that create distinct horizons.
Old burrows in lower horizons often fill with material from the A horizon, leaving features called crotovinas or krotovinas.
Humans, and with them fire, belong to this factor: clearing, tillage, irrigation, fertilizer and lime can abruptly change soil formation.
In the Negev desert, lichen-grazing land snails process between 0.7 and 1.1 metric tons of limestone per hectare per year, starting soil formation.
Nearly half the humus of North American tallgrass-prairie chernozems is charcoal; Neolithic human-set fires are now accepted as helping form chernozems and terra preta.

entries.text: In the Negev desert, land snails grazing on lichens process between 0.7 and 1.1 metric tons of limestone per hectare each year, starting soil formation. Organisms, meaning plants, animals, fungi, bacteria and humans, form one of the soil-forming factors. Microorganisms drive key mineral transformations. Some bacteria fix nitrogen from the air, and some fungi extract deep phosphorus and add carbon to the soil. Plants hold soil against erosion and build organic matter. Working with fungi and bacteria around their roots, they release chemicals that break down minerals. Burrowing animals mix soil and open pores for water and gases. That mixing tends to undo the processes that create distinct horizons. Old burrows in lower horizons often fill with A-horizon material, leaving features called crotovinas or krotovinas. Humans belong here too, and with them fire. Clearing, tillage, irrigation, fertilizer and lime can change soil formation abruptly. Neolithic fires set by people are now accepted as helping form the soils of {{ref:soil-class-123}} and {{ref:soil-class-053}}.

entries.title: Time: from fresh flood mud to a developed profile

definition.text: The span over which the other soil-forming factors interact, which shapes how far a soil has developed.

facts.text: Sand, silt and clay give a soil its texture and their aggregation gives peds, but the development of a distinct B horizon marks a developing soil.
A soil takes from decades to several thousand years to develop a profile, the span depending strongly on climate, parent material, relief and biota.
Fresh flood deposits show no soil development; the old surface is buried and soil formation starts anew in the deposit.
Additions, removals and alterations continue even on stable landscapes, some lasting millions of years, so soils are always subject to new conditions.
The soil life cycle ultimately ends in conditions that leave the soil vulnerable to erosion, though most soil cycles are long.
Time is studied through chronosequences, comparing soils of different ages with small differences in the other factors; paleosols record earlier soil-forming conditions.

entries.contested_note: The notion of soil development toward a mature profile has been criticized, on the grounds that soil is constantly changing as soil-forming factors fluctuate.
entries.text: A fresh layer of flood mud shows no soil development at all. The old surface lies buried beneath it, and soil formation starts anew in the deposit. Time is the span over which the other soil-forming factors interact, and it shapes how far a soil has developed. Texture and clumping alone do not make a developing soil; a distinct B horizon does. A profile takes from decades to several thousand years to form, depending strongly on climate, parent material, relief and living things. Even stable landscapes, some lasting millions of years, keep gaining, losing and altering material. The soil life cycle ultimately ends in conditions that leave the soil vulnerable to erosion, though most cycles are long. Researchers study time by comparing soils of different ages that differ little otherwise, and through paleosols, which record earlier conditions. The very idea of development toward a mature profile has critics. They argue that soil never stops changing, because the soil-forming factors themselves keep fluctuating.

entries.title: Slope, height and aspect: how relief shapes soil

definition.text: The influence of relief (slope, elevation and aspect) on soil formation through its control of runoff, erosion and the formation of the surface profile.

facts.text: Steep slopes lose soil quickly to erosion and let less rain soak in, so their soils tend to be shallower and less developed than those on nearby level sites.
Soils at the foot of a hill get more water, and slopes facing the sun's path are drier than slopes that do not.
In swales and depressions where runoff collects, the regolith is more deeply weathered and profiles are more advanced.
In the lowest positions saturation restricts drainage and aeration, slowing weathering and decay while speeding the loss of iron and manganese; wetland soils, saline marshes or peat bogs may form.
Recurring topographic patterns produce toposequences or catenas, through differences in erosion, deposition, moisture, plant cover and exposure.
Gravity carries water, solutes and colloids downslope, raising particulate and base content at the foot of hills and mountains.

entries.text: On a steep slope, soil is lost quickly to erosion, and less rain soaks in. Soils there tend to be shallower and less developed than those on nearby level sites. Topography, or relief, shapes soil through slope, elevation and aspect, the direction a slope faces. It controls runoff, erosion and the formation of the surface profile. Soils at the foot of a hill get more water, and slopes facing the sun's path are drier than those that do not. Gravity carries water, dissolved substances and fine particles downslope, enriching the ground at the foot of hills and mountains. In swales and hollows where runoff collects, the regolith weathers more deeply and profiles are more advanced. In the lowest spots, saturation restricts drainage and aeration. Weathering and decay slow, while iron and manganese are lost faster, and wetland soils, saline marshes or peat bogs may form. Recurring patterns of relief produce repeating sequences of soils, explored in {{ref:soil-form-054}}.

entries.title: Dokuchaev writes soil as an equation

definition.text: Vasily Dokuchaev's 1898 equation expressing soil as a function of climate, organisms and parent material over relative time.

facts.text: Dokuchaev, often called the father of pedology, concluded in 1883 that soil forms over time under climate, vegetation, topography and parent material.
The equation reads soil = f(cl, o, p) tr, where tr is relative time: young, mature or old.
Jenny's later state equation differs by treating time as a factor and adding topographic relief.

entries.text: {{ref:soil-hist-001}}, often called the father of pedology, reached his conclusion in 1883: soil forms over time under climate, vegetation, topography and parent material. Jenny's later version, {{ref:soil-form-049}}, differs in two ways. It treats time as a full factor, and it adds topographic relief.

entries.title: Jenny's equation and its open-ended list of factors

definition.text: Hans Jenny's 1941 equation treating soil formation as a function of climate, organisms, relief, parent material, time and further open-ended factors: S = f(cl, o, r, p, t, ...).

facts.text: It is often remembered by the mnemonic Clorpt.
Unlike Dokuchaev's equation it treats time as a factor, adds relief, and deliberately leaves room for more state variables as understanding improves.
It can be solved by deduction or empirically; the empirical route, varying one factor while holding the others constant, is the one mostly used today.
That approach produced empirical models of soil formation: climofunctions, biofunctions, topofunctions, lithofunctions and chronofunctions.
Since 1941, soil surveyors worldwide have used it as a qualitative list of the factors behind a region's soil pattern.
Critics hold that the five-factor model, though parsimonious and useful, leaves out the biodynamic processes that produce features such as stonelayers.

entries.title: The catena: a chain of soils down one hillside

definition.text: A series of distinct but co-evolving soils arrayed down a slope, all in the same climate and on the same parent material.

facts.text: The concept arose in central Uganda, where chemist W.S. Martin described a hillslope sequence at Bukalasa; Geoffrey Milne coined the term, Latin for chain.
A slope divides into ridge, crest, midslope and toeslope; crests drain freely while toeslopes are wetter, poorly drained and richer in clay and organic matter.
A catena is an open system that forms when climate is uniform along the slope and each facet's inputs and outputs have reached equilibrium, giving a predictable sequence.
Steep middle facets erode faster and are thinner and drier; flatter top and bottom facets carry thicker, deeper soils.
Upper facets lose materials such as salts by eluviation, and lower facets gain them by illuviation.
Easily disaggregated rock and high relief favour distinct soils in source and deposition zones; on low relief, subsurface flow of dissolved and suspended solids dominates.
On acid schists in wet western Scotland a catena runs from peat bog to peaty podzols; on chalk, from brown earths to thin rendzinas and valley fen peat or alluvium.
A mature catena is in equilibrium, with deposition and erosion in balance.

entries.text: On a hillside at Bukalasa in central Uganda, the chemist W.S. Martin described soils changing in sequence from top to bottom. Geoffrey Milne named the pattern catena, Latin for chain. A catena is a series of distinct but co-evolving soils arrayed down a slope, all in the same climate and on the same parent material. The slope divides into ridge, crest, midslope and toeslope. Crests drain freely. Steep middle facets erode faster and are thinner and drier. The flatter top and bottom carry thicker, deeper soils, and toeslopes are wetter, poorly drained and richer in clay and organic matter. Upper facets lose materials such as salts by eluviation, and lower facets gain them by illuviation. A catena is an open system. Its sequence becomes predictable when climate is uniform along the slope and each facet's inputs and outputs reach equilibrium. A mature catena balances erosion and deposition. In wet western Scotland, on acid schists, one catena runs from peat bog to peaty forms of the bleached soil described in {{ref:soil-class-138}}.

entries.title: Modeling how irrigation water flushes out salt

definition.text: A hydrological model of how irrigation water leaches dissolved substances, notably salt, from soil, depending on the water regime and the soil's properties.

facts.text: It describes the process over time and as a function of the amount of water applied.
Leaching is used to reclaim saline soil or keep irrigated land's salt content favourable, since all irrigation water contains salts.
Leaching curves from the Chacupe pilot area in Peru show deeper-layer salinity first rising with salts from the topsoil, then falling as more water percolates.
Agro-hydro-salinity and leaching models such as SaltMod help determine drainage requirements.

entries.text: All irrigation water contains salts, so irrigated land must be flushed. A leaching model is a hydrological model of how irrigation water washes dissolved substances, notably salt, out of soil. It describes the process over time and against the amount of water applied, depending on the water regime and the soil's properties. Leaching is used to reclaim salty soil or keep irrigated land's salt content favorable. Curves from the Chacupe pilot area in Peru show deeper-layer salt first rising as salts arrive from the topsoil, then falling as more water percolates. Models such as {{ref:soil-water-237}} help set drainage requirements.

entries.title: Pedoturbation: the churning that blurs soil layers

definition.text: The mixing of material between soil horizons, an important factor in soil formation.

facts.text: It includes the churning of clays, cryoturbation and bioturbation.
It transforms soils through destratification, mixing and sorting, and creates preferential flow paths for soil gas and infiltrating water.
Mixing by animals tends to counteract the processes that create distinct horizons.
Precipitation of surface salts disrupts soils locally but is not counted as pedoturbation because it does not mix horizons.
With weathering and humification, pedoturbation by animals is a main process in forming oxisols.
It belongs to perturbation, the wider set of pedological and sedimentary processes that change water-borne alluvial sediments and in situ soils over time.

entries.text: Soil horizons are not sealed compartments. Clays churn, frost heaves and animals burrow, and material crosses from one layer to the next. Pedoturbation is this mixing of material between horizons, an important factor in soil formation. It includes the churning of clays, cryoturbation, and mixing by living things. It transforms soils through destratification, mixing and sorting. It also opens preferential paths for air and infiltrating water. Mixing by animals tends to counteract the processes that create distinct horizons. Together with weathering and the build-up of decayed organic matter, animal mixing is a main process in forming one order of deeply weathered tropical soils. Not every disturbance counts. When surface salts precipitate, they disrupt soils locally, but they do not mix horizons, so they are not pedoturbation. Pedoturbation belongs to a wider family called perturbation: the pedological and sedimentary processes that change water-borne alluvial sediments and soils in place over time.

entries.title: The biomantle, the living upper skin of soil

definition.text: The organic-rich, bioturbated upper part of a soil, including the topsoil, where most soil organisms live, reproduce and die.

facts.text: It is mainly a product of organic activity: faunalturbation, floralturbation and fungiturbation mix and destratify the parent material and often sort its particles.
In midlatitude A-E-B-C profiles the biomantle is the part above the B horizon: the A horizon plus any lighter E horizon.
Two-layered biomantles have a basal stonelayer and form in mixed fine and gravelly material; one-layered biomantles form in uniform sands, loess or gravels.
Midlatitude biomantles are often less than 1–2 m thick, while in stable humid tropics, with year-round termites, ants and worms, they are often 5–6 m or more.
As the main zone of bioturbation it is permeable and of low density, speeding percolation through biopores and, above dense subsoils, downslope throughflow.
As originally defined, a biomantle must show at least 50% biofabric, the pelletized fabric made by invertebrates.
In some desert, mountain and freshly eroded bedrock soils the biomantle is the whole soil, with no horizons or weathering zones beneath it.
Australian field practice may simply call the A horizon the biomantle.

entries.text: In the stable humid tropics, termites, ants and worms work year-round, and the churned upper soil often reaches 5–6 m or more. In the midlatitudes it is often less than 1–2 m thick. This is the soil biomantle: the organic-rich, animal-mixed upper part of a soil, including the topsoil, where most soil organisms live, reproduce and die. It is mainly a product of organic activity. Animals, plants and fungi mix and destratify the parent material, and often sort its particles. In a midlatitude A-E-B-C profile, the biomantle is everything above the B horizon. As originally defined, it must show at least 50% biofabric, the pelleted fabric made by invertebrates. Light and full of channels, it speeds water downward and, above dense subsoils, sideways downslope. Two-layered biomantles have a basal layer of stones and form in mixed fine and gravelly material. One-layered ones form in uniform sands, loess or gravels. In some desert, mountain and freshly eroded bedrock soils, the biomantle is the whole soil.

entries.title: Chronosequences: centuries read from months of fieldwork

definition.text: A set of sites that share similar attributes but differ in age, used to study change over time.

facts.text: In soil science it is a group of sites that have developed for different lengths of time with small differences in other soil-forming factors, used to assess time as a factor.
It assumes nothing but age differs between sites; because this often cannot be tested, its use in field successional studies has been debated.
It lets slow processes such as forest development, which take decades or centuries, be studied from field data gathered in a few months.
A classic use is tracing plant and microbial succession on recently deglaciated ground; a 2005 study used distance from a glacier's nose as a proxy for site age.
Along a chronosequence, a cambic horizon develops into an argillic (Bt) horizon once the soil becomes an alfisol.

entries.contested_note: Because the assumption that only age differs between sites often cannot be tested, the use of chronosequences in field successional studies has been debated.
entries.text: Forest development takes decades or centuries, yet a chronosequence lets researchers study it from field data gathered in a few months. A chronosequence is a set of sites that share similar attributes but differ in age. In soil science, the sites have developed for different lengths of time, with only small differences in the other soil-forming factors, so they reveal time as a factor. A classic use traces plant and microbial succession on recently deglaciated ground. One 2005 study used distance from a glacier's nose as a stand-in for site age. Along a chronosequence, a cambic horizon develops into a clay-enriched Bt horizon as the soil matures. The method has a weak point. It assumes that nothing but age differs between sites, and this often cannot be tested. Its use in field studies of succession has therefore been debated.

entries.title: Sesquioxides: the iron and aluminum oxides that color soils

definition.text: An oxide with two atoms of an element for every three of oxygen, such as the iron and aluminium oxides Fe2O3 and Al2O3.

facts.text: Many contain a metal in the +3 oxidation state; in soil, the sesquioxides that matter are those of iron and aluminium.
Podsolisation washes iron and aluminium sesquioxides out of the A horizon down to the B horizon, where they build a red-orange layer.
In ferrallitisation silica is leached away while sesquioxides stay behind, giving many tropical soils their red colour; laterite names sesquioxide-rich horizons.
Horizon notation marks their build-up with suffixes: s for illuvial and o for residual sesquioxide accumulation.

entries.text: A sesquioxide is an oxide with two atoms of an element for every three of oxygen, such as Fe2O3 and Al2O3. Many contain a metal in the +3 state ({{ref:soil-chem-178}}). In soil, the ones that matter are the oxides of iron and aluminum. Their movements show up as color. One strong form of leaching, {{ref:soil-form-061}}, washes them out of the A horizon down to the B horizon, where they build a red-orange layer. In another process, {{ref:soil-form-081}}, silica is leached away while sesquioxides stay behind, giving many tropical soils their red color. Horizon notation marks their build-up with suffixes: s for illuvial and o for residual accumulation.
entries.text_plain: A sesquioxide is an oxide with two atoms of an element for every three of oxygen, such as Fe2O3 and Al2O3. Many contain a metal in the +3 state (Oxidation states: bookkeeping for electrons). In soil, the ones that matter are the oxides of iron and aluminum. Their movements show up as color. One strong form of leaching, Podzolisation: acid litter bleaches the upper soil, washes them out of the A horizon down to the B horizon, where they build a red-orange layer. In another process, Ferrallitisation: why so many tropical soils are red, silica is leached away while sesquioxides stay behind, giving many tropical soils their red color. Horizon notation marks their build-up with suffixes: s for illuvial and o for residual accumulation.

entries.title: Laterite, the brick-red earth of the tropics

definition.text: A soil type rich in iron and aluminium that often forms in hot, wet areas, mostly in the tropics.

facts.text: Nearly all laterites are rusty red because of their high iron oxide content.
Francis Buchanan-Hamilton named a laterite formation in southern India in 1807, from Latin later, brick, because the compact soil cuts easily into building blocks.
Yves Tardy calculated that laterites cover about one-third of Earth's continental land, including most land between the tropics of Cancer and Capricorn.
Laterite covers are thick on stable shields and cratons; the cap on a plateau in Madhya Pradesh, India, is 30 m thick.
Laterites outside today's humid tropics formed when the land lay near the equator, and are read as signs of climatic change, continental drift or both.
The term has been applied to cemented sesquioxide-rich horizons, any reddish surface soil, a rock type and whole weathering profiles.
Laterites may contain pisolites and ferricrete, and relief inversion can leave them in elevated positions.

entries.contested_note: Because 'laterite' has been used for a soil, a rock, a weathering profile and even a theory of weathering, researchers such as Paton, Williams and Ollier call the usage confused and some urge abandoning the term.

entries.title: Podzolisation: acid litter bleaches the upper soil

definition.text: An extreme form of leaching that eluviates iron and aluminium sesquioxides from the upper soil.

facts.text: It generally occurs where precipitation is greater than evapotranspiration.
Decaying organic matter releases organic acids that act as chelating agents; under conifers, a thin litter layer yields acidic mor humus (pH 4.5) rich in them.
Chelating agents break down clay and release iron and aluminium, which become sesquioxides and move from the A horizon down to the B horizon.
Bases such as calcium and potassium are leached too, leaving quartz and silica in a light, eluviated AE horizon at the base of the A horizon.
The B horizon has a dark layer of illuviated organic matter and bases over a red-orange layer of iron and aluminium sesquioxides.
Waterlogging above the B horizon can saturate the A horizon, producing mottling or a gleyed podzol.
It is especially intense in boreal and cool temperate pine forests, whose litter is rich in phenolic compounds and fulvic acid; tropical forests show little or none.

entries.text: Under boreal pines, a light, ash-pale layer can form just beneath the dark surface. Podzolisation is the extreme form of leaching behind it: it eluviates iron and aluminum sesquioxides from the upper soil. It generally occurs where precipitation exceeds the water returned to the air by evaporation and plants. The chemistry starts in the litter. Decaying organic matter releases organic acids that act as chelating agents, molecules that grip metal ions. Under conifers, a thin litter layer yields an acidic decaying layer called mor, at pH 4.5, rich in these agents. They break down clay and release iron and aluminum, which become sesquioxides and move from the A horizon down to the B horizon. Bases such as calcium and potassium wash out too. Quartz and silica remain, in a light, eluviated AE horizon at the base of the A horizon. Below, the B horizon holds a dark layer of illuviated organic matter and bases over a red-orange layer of sesquioxides. If water saturates the A horizon above the B horizon, mottling or gleying follows. The process is especially intense in boreal and cool temperate pine forests, whose litter is rich in phenolic compounds and the organic acid described in {{ref:soil-chem-060}}. Tropical forests show little or none.

entries.title: Laterization: rain, drought and millions of years

definition.text: The prolonged chemical weathering of rock under tropical conditions that produces laterite.

facts.text: It needs high temperatures and heavy rainfall alternating with dry seasons: rain leaches the rock, then capillary action lifts the dissolved ions to the surface in the dry season.
Acid dissolves the host minerals, hydrolysis precipitates insoluble iron and aluminium oxides, and sodium, potassium, calcium and magnesium are leached away.
Solutions of the right pH dissolve silica in preference to aluminium and iron oxides, leaving mainly iron and aluminium behind.
The first products are kaolinized rocks called saprolites; quartz is the most abundant mineral surviving from the parent rock.
Gentle crests and plateaus favour it by protecting the weathered cover from erosion.
It was most active from the mid-Tertiary to the mid-Quaternary (35 to 1.5 million years ago), slowed with abrupt global cooling, and continues today at a reduced rate.
Mafic, iron-rich rocks yield iron oxides, granitic iron-poor rocks yield bauxites, and ultramafic rocks yield nickel laterites.

entries.text: Laterization was most active from the mid-Tertiary to the mid-Quaternary, 35 to 1.5 million years ago, and it has not stopped. It is the prolonged chemical weathering of rock under tropical conditions that produces laterite. It needs high temperatures and heavy rainfall alternating with dry seasons. Rain leaches the rock, and in the dry season {{ref:soil-phys-252}} lifts the dissolved ions to the surface. Acid dissolves the host minerals. Hydrolysis precipitates insoluble iron and aluminum oxides, while sodium, potassium, calcium and magnesium are leached away. Solutions of the right pH dissolve silica in preference to the iron and aluminum oxides, leaving mainly those two metals behind. The first products are weathered rocks called saprolites, and quartz is the most abundant mineral surviving from the parent rock. Gentle crests and plateaus help by protecting the weathered cover from erosion. The parent rock shapes the result. Mafic, iron-rich rocks yield {{ref:soil-chem-163}}, granitic iron-poor rocks yield aluminum ores, and ultramafic rocks yield nickel laterites. The process slowed with abrupt global cooling and continues today at a reduced rate.

entries.title: Stonelayers: buried stones that trace the land surface

definition.text: A subsurface soil layer dominated by particles coarser than 2 mm that generally mimics the surface topography; also called a stone line.

facts.text: It forms the basal horizon of two-layered soil biomantles.
One stone thick it shows in a pit as a 'stone line'; several stones thick it is a 'stone zone'.
Its gravel may be quartzose rock fragments, iron–manganese nodules, artifacts, shells or precious stones; where present it often acts as a subsurface drain or even an aquifer.
Stone lines in soils follow the surface and are non-imbricated, pointing to a pedogenic origin; water-laid stone lines in sediments are imbricated and geogenic.

entries.text: A stonelayer is a subsurface soil layer dominated by particles coarser than 2 mm, and it generally mimics the shape of the ground above. One stone thick, it shows in a pit as a stone line; several stones thick, it is a stone zone. Its stones may be quartz-rich rock fragments, iron–manganese nodules, artifacts, shells or precious stones. It often acts as a subsurface drain or even holds groundwater. Stone lines in soils follow the surface and their stones do not overlap like shingles, pointing to a soil origin. Water-laid stone lines in sediments do overlap, and their origin is geological.

entries.title: Biorhexistasy: climate swings between building and stripping soil

definition.text: A theory of the climatic conditions under which periods of soil formation alternate with periods of soil erosion.

facts.text: Proposed by pedologist Henry Erhart in 1951, it defines two climatic phases: biostasy and rhexistasy.
In biostasy, abundant regular rain under protective vegetation drives chemical alteration, eluviation and illuviation, building eluvial and argillic horizons and sesquioxide-rich subsoils.
In rhexistasy a drier climate thins vegetation, pedogenesis slows, physical weathering dominates, and intense rains erode soils into layers of sand and silt.
Pleistocene glacial periods are considered times of rhexistasy and interglacials times of biostasy.

entries.text: In 1951 the pedologist Henry Erhart proposed that climate switches the land between two phases, biostasy and rhexistasy. In biostasy, abundant regular rain under protective vegetation drives chemical alteration, eluviation and illuviation. Eluvial horizons, clay-enriched horizons and sesquioxide-rich subsoils build up. In rhexistasy, a drier climate thins the vegetation and soil formation slows. Physical weathering dominates, and intense rains erode soils into layers of sand and silt. Pleistocene glacial periods are considered times of rhexistasy, and interglacials times of biostasy.

entries.title: Reading ancient air from ancient soils

definition.text: The use of paleosol chemistry to infer the past composition of the atmosphere, with which soils form in near-constant contact.

facts.text: The oxidation of paleosols has served as an indicator of atmospheric oxygen, which has risen over Earth's history.
Atmospheric carbon dioxide has been reconstructed from soil gas exchange, carbon isotopes in pedogenic carbonate nodules and multi-gas mass balances.
These methods are being actively developed in early-Earth research.

entries.text: Soils form in near-constant contact with the atmosphere, so old soils hold clues to old air. Paleoatmosphere reconstruction uses paleosol chemistry to infer that past composition. How oxidized a paleosol is has served as an indicator of atmospheric oxygen, which has risen over Earth's history. Carbon dioxide has been reconstructed three ways. Researchers use gas exchange between soil and air, carbon isotopes in carbonate nodules formed in the soil, and mass balances of several gases. Researchers on the early Earth are still actively developing these methods.

entries.title: Ancient soils as rain gauges and thermometers

definition.text: The use of paleosols to gauge the climate they formed in, since rates and styles of weathering depend on climate.

facts.text: Mean annual precipitation and mean annual air temperature are the most commonly reconstructed variables.
Many proxies rely on chemical changes through the profile during weathering, burial and post-burial alteration, and not every proxy suits every paleosol.
Most proxies work only for Phanerozoic paleosols, as landscape processes changed sharply after land plants arose.
Seasonality proxies rely on pedogenic carbonate formed as soils wet and dry, and are still being tested and refined.

entries.text: Rates and styles of weathering depend on climate, so a paleosol can gauge the climate it formed in. Proxies for seasonality rely on carbonate formed in the soil as it wets and dries, and they are still being tested and refined.

entries.title: Naming ancient soils with a modern rulebook

definition.text: The naming of paleosols, which mostly borrows the orders of USDA soil taxonomy because modern systems fit ancient soils poorly.

facts.text: Geology, life and the atmosphere changed greatly over the paleosol record, notably at the Great Oxidation Event 2.42 billion years ago, so modern classification fits poorly.
An alfisol, a forest soil, could not exist before trees, and it is defined by chemical properties not preserved in rock.
A paleosol-specific naming scheme has been proposed but is used only sporadically.
The USDA hierarchy cannot be applied to paleosols below the order level.

entries.text: A forest soil could not exist before there were trees. That simple fact shows why paleosol classification is hard. It mostly borrows the top-level orders of the US system, {{ref:soil-class-006}}, because modern systems fit ancient soils poorly. Geology, life and the atmosphere changed greatly over the paleosol record, notably at the Great Oxidation Event 2.42 billion years ago. The forest soil order, {{ref:soil-class-090}}, is also defined by chemical properties that rock does not preserve. That hierarchy cannot be applied to paleosols below the order level. A naming scheme made for paleosols has been proposed but is used only sporadically.

entries.title: How to recognize a soil turned to stone

definition.text: The recognition of a fossil or buried soil from criteria such as formation in place on bedrock and up-profile changes consistent with weathering.

facts.text: Rye and Holland (1998) set out five criteria, prompted by Precambrian paleosols but applicable to paleosols of any age.
They include formation in situ on bedrock, soft-sediment deformation at the top of the profile, and up-profile changes in chemistry, texture and mineralogy matching terrestrial weathering.
Field signs include horizonation, bedrock corestones within finer overlying material, and traces of surface processes such as roots, burrows, organic matter and redox alteration.
Diagnostic horizons and features separate paleosol types; all have an A horizon, but histosols also have an O horizon above it.

entries.text: How can anyone tell that a layer of rock was once a soil? Paleosol identification answers with criteria. Rye and Holland set out five in 1998. They apply to paleosols of any age. They include formation in place on bedrock, soft-sediment deformation at the top of the profile, and up-profile changes in chemistry, texture and mineralogy that match weathering on land. In the field, signs include horizons, bedrock corestones within finer overlying material, and traces of surface processes such as roots and burrows. Diagnostic horizons and features separate paleosol types. All have an A horizon, but those of the order described in {{ref:soil-class-098}} also have an O horizon above it.

entries.title: Pedodiversity: counting soils the way ecologists count species

definition.text: The variation of soil properties within an area, usually expressed through soil classes.

facts.text: Studies began with soil series–area relationships (Beckett and Bie, 1978); McBratney developed the term in 1992 while discussing landscape preservation.
Ibáñez and colleagues (1995) first applied ecological diversity indices—richness, relative abundance and the Shannon index—treating soil classes as taxa.
It measures soil variation, is a function of soil formation, and is used to analyse soil spatial patterns, soil geography and pedogenetic theories.
In eastern North Carolina and the Ouachita Mountains, variability within plots, tied to individual trees and local lithology, outweighed differences between plots.
A 2003 US study found the West richest in soil taxa and, at the series level, taxa increasing steadily with area, indicating considerable soil endemism.
Conventional indices ignore how similar soil classes are; the mean soil taxonomic distance, which accounts for it, has been shown to be a better measure.
Knowing natural pedodiversity helps preserve the soil cover and rebuild quasi-natural soil systems on degraded land.

entries.title: How fast bedrock turns to soil under a growing blanket

definition.text: The rate at which bedrock weathers into soil, expressed as a function of soil thickness.

facts.text: A general model has bedrock weathering decline exponentially with soil thickness h, as de/dt = P0 exp(−kh), where P0 is the maximum weathering rate and k an empirical constant.
Weathering slows under thicker soil because temperature swings and average water penetration both fall off exponentially with depth.
P0 ranged from 0.08 to 2.0 mm/yr at northern California sites and 0.05–0.14 mm/yr in southeastern Australia, while k varied little, from 2 to 4 m−1; both depend on climate and parent material.
The older humped model, from G.K. Gilbert in 1877, has weathering fastest under an intermediate soil thickness, since bare rock sheds the water that chemical weathering needs.

entries.title: Laterite aquifers: groundwater held in red earth

definition.text: Thick, porous and slightly permeable laterite layers that hold and yield groundwater, especially in rural tropical areas.

facts.text: Tropical bedrock is often impermeable granite, gneiss, schist or sandstone, so the laterite above it becomes the usable aquifer.
Sri Lanka's Southwestern Laterite (Cabook) Aquifer recharges rapidly with the April–May rains and the monsoon, and supports shallow dug wells.
In some dense suburbs its water table can fall to 15 m below ground after more than 65 dry days.

entries.text: In rural tropical areas, the bedrock is often impermeable granite, gneiss, schist or sandstone. Water cannot pass through it, so the laterite above becomes the usable store of groundwater. Thick, porous and slightly permeable, these laterite layers hold water and yield it to wells. Sri Lanka's Southwestern Laterite, or Cabook, Aquifer recharges rapidly with the April–May rains and the monsoon, and supports shallow dug wells. In some dense suburbs, its water level can fall to 15 m below ground after more than 65 dry days.

entries.title: Laterite blocks that harden in the open air

definition.text: Laterite cut into blocks while moist and soft, which then harden on exposure to air into a durable building material.

facts.text: It is mined below the water table while wet and soft; as moisture evaporates, iron compounds lock into a rigid lattice that resists the weather.
Khmer builders used laterite with sandstone in the Angkor monuments, including the foundations and inner parts of Angkor Wat behind its sandstone face.
After 1000 AD Angkorian construction shifted to rectangular temple enclosures of laterite, brick and stone.
Since the mid-1970s laterite has replaced stone as a road base course in trials; Malawi saved US$40,000 per km this way in 1984.

entries.title: Red earth that scrubs phosphorus from wastewater

definition.text: The use of iron- and aluminium-rich laterite to remove phosphorus and heavy metals from wastewater.

facts.text: In Northern Ireland, where farm phosphorus enriches lakes, local laterite, a low-grade bauxite, is used in acid solution followed by precipitation at sewage works.
Laboratory tests removed 99% of phosphorus from solution, and a pilot-scale facility 96%.
Percolating laterite columns lowered cadmium, chromium and lead to undetectable concentrations.

entries.text: In Northern Ireland, phosphorus from farms enriches the lakes, and local laterite offers a fix. Rich in iron and aluminum, laterite can remove phosphorus and heavy metals from wastewater. At sewage works, this low-grade aluminum ore is used in acid solution, followed by precipitation. Laboratory tests removed 99% of phosphorus from solution, and a pilot-scale facility removed 96%. Columns of laterite with water percolating through them lowered cadmium, chromium and lead to undetectable concentrations.

entries.title: Farming laterite soils: rich in clay, poor in nutrients

definition.text: The agricultural behaviour of laterite soils, which are clay-rich but heavily leached.

facts.text: High clay gives them more cation exchange capacity, plasticity and water-holding capacity but lower permeability than sandy soils, so rain enters slowly.
Intensive leaching leaves them less fertile than other soils, but they respond readily to manure and irrigation and suit plantation crops such as oil palm, tea, coffee and cashew.
If their structure degrades, a hard surface crust forms that blocks infiltration and seedling emergence and increases runoff.
'Bio-reclamation of degraded lands', using planting pits, residues and drought-tolerant crops, has rehabilitated degraded laterite soils in Niger.

entries.text: Laterite soils are rich in clay but heavily leached, an awkward mix for farmers. Their clay helps them hold water and nutrients, and makes them more plastic than sandy soils. It also slows the passage of water, so rain enters slowly. Intensive leaching leaves them less fertile than other soils. Yet they respond readily to manure and irrigation, and suit plantation crops such as oil palm, tea, coffee and cashew. If their structure degrades, a hard surface crust forms. It blocks water entry and seedling emergence and increases runoff. In Niger, 'bio-reclamation of degraded lands', using planting pits, residues and drought-tolerant crops, has rehabilitated degraded laterite soils.

entries.title: Lateritic ores: metals concentrated by tropical weathering

definition.text: Metal ores concentrated in laterites, including aluminium, iron, manganese, nickel, copper and gold.

facts.text: Aluminium is found in bauxites, iron and manganese in iron-rich hard crusts, nickel and copper in disintegrated rock, and gold in mottled clays.
Bauxite, the main aluminium ore, is a variety of laterite averaging 45 to 60% Al2O3 and 20 to 30% Fe2O3 by weight, mainly gibbsite in newer tropical deposits.
About 70% of Earth's land-based nickel resources lie in laterites, which currently supply about 40% of world nickel production.
Northern Ireland's basaltic laterites, up to 30 m thick, were once a major source of iron and aluminium ore.

entries.title: Periglaciation, the shaping power of freeze and thaw

definition.text: The geomorphic processes that result from seasonal freezing and thawing, very often in areas of permafrost.

facts.text: Periglacial environments are anywhere freezing and thawing significantly modify the landscape, not only at the edges of former glaciers.
About a quarter of Earth's land has periglacial conditions now, and another quarter or fifth had them during the Pleistocene.
Frost heaving, solifluction and ice-wedge formation are its hallmark processes.
Walery Łoziński introduced the term in 1909.

entries.text: About a quarter of Earth's land is shaped by freeze and thaw today. Periglaciation is the set of landform processes that result from seasonal freezing and thawing, very often where the ground stays frozen year-round. Walery Łoziński introduced the term in 1909. The name suggests the edges of glaciers, but periglacial environments are anywhere freeze and thaw significantly modify the landscape. Another quarter or fifth of the land had such conditions during the Pleistocene. Its hallmark processes are {{ref:soil-phys-153}}, {{ref:soil-water-056}} and the growth of ice wedges, all driven by the force described in {{ref:soil-found-054}}.
