entries.title: Ecological succession, how life builds its own soil

definition.text: The change in species composition of an ecological community over time.

facts.text: Primary succession colonizes new surfaces with no life, such as bare rock, lava flows or freshly exposed till; secondary succession follows a disturbance.
Pioneers such as microorganisms, lichens and mosses come first, followed by grasses, shrubs and trees.
Plants change the soil as they grow, adding organic matter to litter and humus, altering nutrients and pH and allowing soil formation.
Soil properties and nutrient cycles are shaped by the community and in turn steer further succession.

entries.text: Bare rock, a fresh lava flow or newly exposed till starts with no life at all. Ecological succession is the change in a community's species over time, and on such surfaces it is called primary succession. Secondary succession follows a disturbance instead. Pioneers come first: microorganisms, lichens and mosses. Grasses, shrubs and trees follow. As plants grow they change the soil, adding organic matter to litter and {{ref:soil-bio-089}} and altering nutrients and pH. That is how {{ref:soil-form-046}} lets soil form. The soil in turn steers what grows next, since its properties and the cycling of its nutrients shape further succession.

entries.title: Lessivage: how clay travels down through a soil

definition.text: The washing of fine clay from the upper to the lower part of a soil by water moving down through the soil matrix; also called argilluviation.

facts.text: It is the main mechanism forming the clay-enriched argic, or Bt, horizon of Luvisolic soils.
Infiltrating water picks up negatively charged clay as a colloidal suspension and carries it down until a change in conditions makes it flocculate.
Clay settles where water stagnates or meets positive ions deeper down; as it accumulates, pores in the illuvial horizon become finer and trap still more clay.
It is most common in medium-textured loams under moderate to high rainfall, especially beneath deciduous and mixed forests whose organic acids disperse clay.
Very sandy soils drain too fast and lack clay, while clay-rich soils drain so slowly that clay migrates only a short way.
It is widespread in central and eastern Canada, parts of Europe and temperate Asia.
Clay deposited below raises cation exchange capacity, but a thick clay-rich layer can make soils prone to compaction, surface ponding and restricted root growth.
If the clay-enriched layer becomes too compacted, limiting traffic, subsoiling and tile drainage may be needed.

entries.text: Rain soaking into a soil can carry clay with it. Lessivage, also called argilluviation, is the washing of fine clay from the upper to the lower part of a soil by water moving down through the soil. It is the main mechanism forming the clay-enriched argic, or Bt, horizon of Luvisolic soils. Clay particles carry a negative charge. Infiltrating water picks them up as a colloidal suspension and carries them down until a change in conditions makes them clump together and settle. Clay settles where water stagnates or meets positive ions deeper down. As it accumulates, pores in the illuvial horizon become finer and trap still more clay. Texture matters. Lessivage is most common in medium-textured soils under moderate to high rainfall, especially beneath deciduous and mixed forests, whose organic acids disperse clay. Very sandy soils drain too fast and lack clay. Clay-rich soils drain so slowly that clay moves only a short way. The process is widespread in central and eastern Canada, parts of Europe and temperate Asia. Its results cut both ways. The deposited clay helps the subsoil hold nutrients, but a thick clay-rich layer can make soils prone to compaction, surface ponding and restricted root growth. If the layer becomes too compacted, limiting traffic, deep loosening and buried drain pipes ({{ref:soil-phys-227}}) may be needed.

entries.title: Ferrallitisation: why so many tropical soils are red

definition.text: The process by which rock is changed into a soil of kaolinite clay and sesquioxides, the hydrated oxides of iron and aluminium.

facts.text: In humid tropics with consistently high temperatures and rainfall, chemical weathering breaks rock down rapidly into clays, which later break down further to form silica.
The silica is leached away while iron and aluminium sesquioxides remain, giving many tropical soils their characteristic red colour.
It is the reverse of podsolisation, in which silica remains and iron and aluminium are removed.
Year-round rain in tropical rainforests produces ferrallitic soils, while savannas with alternating wet and dry seasons have ferruginous soils.

entries.text: Many tropical soils are red, and ferrallitisation explains why. It is the process that turns rock into a soil of {{ref:soil-chem-088}} clay and sesquioxides, the hydrated oxides of iron and aluminum. In the humid tropics, with consistently high temperatures and rainfall, chemical weathering breaks rock down rapidly into clays. Those clays later break down further, releasing silica. The silica is leached away, while the iron and aluminum sesquioxides remain and give the soil its characteristic red. The process is the reverse of podsolisation, in which silica remains and iron and aluminum are removed. Climate decides the details. Year-round rain in tropical rainforests produces ferrallitic soils, while savannas with alternating wet and dry seasons have ferruginous soils.

entries.title: Leaching efficiency: why some salty clays resist reclamation

definition.text: A leaching-model parameter that departs from unity where salt is unevenly distributed in the soil or the soil structure is irregular.

facts.text: Soils with low leaching efficiency are hard to reclaim; dense clay in Portugal's Tagus delta measured only 0.10 to 0.15 and was left as coarse pasture.
Clay soil in Egypt's Nile delta has a much better efficiency of 0.7 to 0.8.
The parameter is hard to measure directly and is calibrated by fitting model curves to observed salinity, as with a value of about 0.75 at Mashtul.
Tabulated values range from 0.80 for Tunisian silty clay and 0.70 for illitic clays to between 0.11 and 0.20 for smectitic clays in Peru, Portugal and Thailand.

entries.title: Tree throw, how falling trees plough the land

definition.text: A bowl-shaped pit in the subsoil made by a tree, through long root growth or when a toppled tree tears out its rootwad.

facts.text: The pit can be several meters across and 1–2 metres deep, and exposes humus-poor, mineral-rich soil.
Tree throw drives bedrock weathering and soil formation, fastest in soils of intermediate thickness; under soils deeper than roots, no bedrock is upturned.
Before trees appeared about 370 million years ago, bedrock weathering was too slow to keep thick soils on hilly terrain.
Tree-throw pits and the mounds of rotting fallen trees form the pit-and-mound topography of old-growth forest.

entries.title: Argillipedoturbation, clay that churns itself

definition.text: Soil mixing caused by the shrinking and swelling of smectite clays, sometimes called self-mulching.

facts.text: Specific to vertisolic soils, it is driven by wetting–drying cycles and needs at least 30% clay.
It opens vertical cracks up to 2 centimetres wide and 50 centimetres or more deep, which fill with sloughed-in surface material.
It can blend horizons until they are hard to tell apart, and produces gilgai topography and slickensides.
Such soils are very productive when irrigated but hard to plough and manage.

entries.title: Stone lines: geology or the work of burrowers?

definition.text: The long controversy over whether stonelayers in soils formed by geological processes or by soil-forming, largely biological, processes.

facts.text: Few Earth-science topics have caused more controversy, spanning archaeology, geology, geomorphology, ecology and pedology on every continent but Antarctica.
Sharpe coined 'stone-line' in 1938 from South Carolina, reading it as abiotic mass transfer on slopes, unaware of earlier names and drawings, including Darwin's.
It has been read as glacial evidence and as an eroded pavement buried under tropical loess, while Morrás and colleagues (2009) argue it is the base of soil biomantles.
Whether an interpreter favours a geogenic or pedogenic origin often reflects their background and training.

entries.contested_note: Stonelayers have been interpreted as geogenic (glacial deposits, erosional lags, buried pavements) or as pedogenic products of biomantle bioturbation, and the literature remains divided.

entries.title: Why most prehistoric artifacts lie in a churned layer

definition.text: The finding that most prehistoric cultural materials lie in the soil biomantle, where bioturbation has moved them out of their original context.

facts.text: The exceptions are a few stratified caves and rare open-air sites buried faster than bioturbation could destratify them.
Artifacts wider than burrows, such as cleavers, core-stones and grinding stones, settle downward and join the basal stonelayer.
Smaller flakes are spread through the upper biomantle and turn up in the spoil heaps of gophers, moles and mole-rats.
Since Darwin, the earthworm has been recognized as a key bioturbator of biomantles and artifacts.

entries.title: Gophers, termites and worms: three ways animals rework soil
entries.article: Soil biomantle#Three notable bioturbation sub-processes and associated particle comminutions

definition.text: The three overlapping sub-processes of soil bioturbation, which together abrade and reduce particles (particle comminution).

facts.text: Biomixing is the churning done by burrowing vertebrates such as pocket gophers, moles, badgers, wombats, aardvarks and pigs; tree uprooting also matters.
Biotransfer moves soil to the surface or within the biomantle, mainly by 'conveyor-belt' ants, termites and worms; termites may dig many metres for mound-building soil.
In biosorting, burrowers move only particles smaller than their burrows, so larger stones settle and form a stonelayer at the base of the biomantle.
Invertebrates are the main biosorters in tropical soils, while small fossorial vertebrates dominate in many midlatitude deserts, prairies and steppes.

entries.title: Dynamic denudation: everything happening in the biomantle at once
entries.article: Soil biomantle#Dynamic denudation, bioturbation and soil biomantle formation

definition.text: The sum of all processes acting in the soil biomantle, in which bioturbation and other organic effects are commonly dominant.

facts.text: The processes include organic matter production, eluviation and illuviation, weathering, erosion and deposition, freeze–thaw, shrink–swell and gravity movements, normally subsidiary to bioturbation.
Plants' role in soil formation is well understood, but animals' role in making soil, horizons, Mima mounds and stone lines was poorly understood until recently.

Wilkinson and Humphreys offer evidence that bioturbation appears to be the most active pedogenic process in many soils; it dominates the upper part of most soils, except possibly vertisols and cryosols.

entries.title: How a soil changes as it grows old

definition.text: How a soil's horizons, chemistry and productivity change as it ages from parent material to old soil.

facts.text: Parent material has no horizons, a young soil (about 10 to 1,000 years) a slight profile, a mature soil (1,000 to 10,000 years) a well-developed one and an old soil (10,000 to 100,000 years) an extensive one.
Typical profiles run C R, then A C R, then O A Bt C R, then O A E Bs C R as the soil ages.

In a young soil humus accumulates and carbonates leach; in a mature soil humus peaks and clays leach, with maximum illuviation; in an old soil humus declines, carbonates are gone and the surface is very acidic.
Crop productivity is low to moderate in young soil, good in young-to-mature, maximal in mature and low in old soil.
Once vegetation grew, nitrogen entered from rain and from lichens, algae and legumes, organic matter built up a dark A horizon, and rain leached calcium and magnesium carbonates.
Where soils stay highly calcareous the lime limits clay leaching, slowing profile development; on permeable material, clay moved from the A into the B and formed an argillic horizon.

entries.title: Four ways soils gain, lose, change and move material

definition.text: The soil-forming factors work through four groups of processes: additions, losses, transformations and translocations.

facts.text: Additions include organic matter, fertilizers, dust deposition and other mineral soil arriving at a soil.
Losses are soil moved away by wind or water, or chemical compounds leached, eroded or harvested from it.
Transformations are the chemical or physical weathering of soil particles or components.
Translocations are the movement of organic or mineral soil components between horizons within a profile.
These processes distinguish soils from layers of material laid down by geologic processes, and how far they have gone helps tell soils apart.
Transfers include eluviation, which removes material from a horizon, and illuviation, which deposits it; clay, and iron and aluminium organic complexes, move down with soil water.
Mixing, or turbation, is also a transfer, caused by organisms or by physical agents such as clay shrink-swell and freeze-thaw.
Weathering releases ions from minerals or turns them into secondary minerals, which may reform deeper in the soil; ions lost altogether are leached.

entries.title: Cheluviation: metals ride organic carriers downward

definition.text: The process in which metal ions in the upper soil bind with organic ligands into chelates that move downward by eluviation and are then deposited.

facts.text: Iron, aluminium, manganese, calcium, magnesium and trace elements can be chelated, mostly by ligands from soil organic matter.
Fulvic acid–metal chelates leach and deposit strongly, typically producing a grey-white leached layer above a dark brown or red deposition layer.
Iron and aluminium move easily at low pH and under reducing conditions, but precipitate as pH rises (around 7–8) or under oxidizing conditions.
Clay adsorbs chelates and weakens their leaching, while coarse-textured or water-saturated soils enhance it.

entries.text: A gray-white leached layer above a dark brown or red one is a typical signature of cheluviation. entries.title: Soil memory: a record written over and over

definition.text: The idea that soil keeps a record of past natural changes, environmental conditions and human activity.

facts.text: Nikiforoff coined the term in 1953, echoing Dokuchaev's dictum that soil is 'a mirror of the landscape'.
Soils store records palimpsest-wise (pedomemory), with successive features overprinting each other, while layered sediments store them book-wise (lithomemory), in datable order.
It is used to study climate change, land-use history and archaeological evidence; persistent environmental DNA in cultivated soils is read as a 'memory effect'.
Because most soils are polygenetic, the record is partial and 'censored', and equifinality complicates reading it, so the concept serves as an exploratory tool.

entries.text: Dokuchaev called soil 'a mirror of the landscape'. In 1953 Nikiforoff echoed him with a new term, soil memory: the idea that soil keeps a record of past natural changes, environmental conditions and human activity. Soils store that record like a page written over and over, with newer features overprinting older ones. This is pedomemory; layered sediments instead store lithomemory, like a book in datable order. The idea is used to study climate change, land-use history and archaeological evidence. Persistent genetic traces in cultivated soils, the subject of {{ref:soil-hist-090}}, are read as a 'memory effect'. Yet most soils have developed under more than one set of conditions, so the record is partial and 'censored'. Equifinality, different paths leading to the same result, complicates reading it, and the concept serves as an exploratory tool.

entries.title: Reading runoff from slope and texture

definition.text: A field method that estimates surface runoff from percent slope and the texture of the surface horizon.

facts.text: Percent slope is rise over run times 100, read directly with an Abney level or clinometer held parallel to the slope.
Runoff rises with slope and falls with infiltration rate, and soil erosion generally rises as runoff increases.
Granular, porous soils shed less water than massive, low-porosity soils because more water infiltrates.
Plant cover intercepts raindrops and reduces erosion, while a moister soil saturates sooner and so runs off sooner.
In the table, slopes of 0-1% give very slow runoff for all textures, 6-12% gives rapid runoff for loams but very rapid for clays, and over 18% is very rapid for all textures.

entries.title: From summit to toeslope: positions on a hillside

definition.text: The named positions along a hillslope, from summit to toeslope, each with its own shape and role in moving soil material.

facts.text: The summit is the level top of an upland feature and the shoulder is the convex, erosional edge leading to the backslope.
The backslope is the steepest part, shaped mainly by mass wasting and running water.
The footslope is gently inclined and concave, where colluvium and alluvium accumulate, and the toeslope is a constructional surface where alluvium collects.
A stream terrace is a level strip of an abandoned flood plain, and a flood plain is built of sediment deposited during floods.

entries.text: A hillside is not one soil but a sequence. The summit is the level top of an upland feature, and the shoulder is the convex, erosional edge leading to the backslope. The backslope is the steepest part, shaped mainly by {{ref:soil-water-053}} and running water. Below it, the footslope is gently inclined and concave, where colluvium and alluvium accumulate, and the toeslope is a constructional surface where alluvium collects. Beyond lies a flood plain, built of sediment deposited during floods, and a stream terrace is a level strip of an abandoned one. This is {{ref:soil-form-045}} made concrete.

entries.title: Effective precipitation: why wetter and cooler leaches more

definition.text: Precipitation and temperature together decide how much water moves down through a soil and how strongly it is leached.

facts.text: Leaching moves soluble salts down the profile and can carry suspended clay into the subsoil; more precipitation leaches them deeper.
Leaching lowers pH, removes basic cations (Ca2+, Mg2+, K+, Na+) and lowers nutrient content, so desert soils are little leached and humid forest soils extensively.
Higher temperature raises evapotranspiration, so with equal rainfall the cooler region has more effective precipitation and more highly leached soils.
In the Northern Hemisphere, north-facing slopes get less direct sun and so tend to be more weathered, deeper and more leached than warmer, drier south-facing ones.

All of this is Climate, the dominant hand in shaping soil in action.

entries.title: How people change soil

definition.text: Human use transforms soils, mainly through land conversion, erosion, mining and construction.

facts.text: Converting forest or grassland to cropland usually lowers soil organic matter; globally about 30% of the original soil organic carbon is lost.
Erosion removes the organically enriched surface layer, losing the most fertile soil and sometimes exposing a growth-limiting layer such as a high-sodium one.
Deposited eroded soil over-thickens lower slopes, burying the original topsoil under less fertile subsoil to give a cumulic soil.
Soils heavily disrupted by people, as by mining or pipelines, are termed anthropogenic; reconstructed soils inevitably differ from the original profile.

entries.title: Bacteria that remember an Iron Age village

definition.text: The ability of soil microbial communities to change their structure, diversity and activity in response to natural or human factors and to keep those changes over time.

facts.text: Many bacteria survive in dormant states for long periods, persisting through large environmental changes.
PCR and next-generation sequencing characterize soil bacterial communities from their DNA, well suited to detecting traces of past influences.
Distinctive bacterial communities mark an Iron Age settlement in Sicily, Iron Age cremation burials, medieval activity areas and Neolithic ditch infills.

entries.title: Polygenetic soils: one profile, several histories

definition.text: A soil, such as a paleosol, that shows evidence of continued soil development under later conditions.

facts.text: Most soils are polygenetic, so a younger pedogenic signal may overprint, mask or erase an older one.

Terra rossa has been proposed to be polygenetic, its altered parent material including volcanic ash, non-carbonate and aeolian sediments.

entries.title: Soil geography, the map of where soils lie

definition.text: The branch of physical geography that deals with how soils are distributed across the terrain.

facts.text: It studies the spatial distribution of soils in relation to topography, climate, soil life and the minerals within soils.
It sits beside geomorphology, climatology, hydrology and biogeography among the fields that study the Earth's surface.
Understanding pedogenesis explains soil distribution patterns today, the concern of soil geography, and in past geologic periods, the concern of paleopedology.
Pedodiversity was brought into pedology to analyse soil spatial patterns and soil geography and to test theories of soil formation.
The Russian Geographical Society awarded Konstantin Glinka its Lütke Gold Medal for his work on soil geography.

entries.title: Tropical soils, lush forests on poor ground

definition.text: The soils of the humid tropics, most of them strongly leached and poor in nutrients, though some areas are fertile.

facts.text: On younger substrates, especially volcanic ones, tropical soils can be quite fertile.
Most cation exchange capacity sits on clay and humus colloids; fast leaching and decomposition in hot, wet climates remove them, explaining the apparent infertility of tropical soils.
Phosphorus is often the most deficient nutrient, because intense leaching and weathering deplete the mineral pool and, unlike nitrogen, it cannot be replenished from the air.
Leaching removes silica and leaves iron and aluminium sesquioxides, giving many tropical soils their characteristic red colour.
Unlike loess, tropical soils draw their fertility almost wholly from organic matter, whose humus holds nutrient ions and releases them to roots.
Stripped of vegetation, for example by deforestation, they can develop a surface hardpan of laterite or bauxite, a known case of irreversible degradation.
Abundant deep burrowers such as ants, termites and worms mean tropical soils often lack the argillic Bt horizons of midlatitude soils, and stonelayers often mark the base of the biomantle.
Charcoal, or biochar, is used to improve nutrient-poor tropical soils, an approach modelled on the fertile Amazonian terra preta.

entries.title: Soils of British Columbia and Yukon

definition.text: British Columbia and Yukon have the greatest diversity of soils in Canada, from a varied geologic history, rugged mountain and valley terrain and wide climate range.

facts.text: The region holds all ten soil orders of the Canadian system, reflecting the full range of soil-forming factors.

Podzols have the largest extent in British Columbia, on acidic parent materials under cool, humid conditions; Luvisols are the other dominant order, on loamy glacial tills in the Interior plateaus and boreal forest.

Cryosols occur in permafrost areas of northern Yukon and on high mountain peaks; Chernozems occur only in the arid Central Interior, with Brown, Dark Brown and Black types as the climate turns more humid northward.

Regosols occur on landslide-prone and avalanche-prone slopes and the Fraser Delta; Gleysols are common in low-lying coastal areas, and artificially drained ones in the Fraser Valley are among the province's most productive farm soils.
Mining here leaves Anthroposols; in metal mining the main concern is acid rock drainage, because sulphide minerals such as pyrite weather rapidly to sulfuric acid.

entries.title: Soils of Ontario

definition.text: Ontario soils formed mostly in parent materials left by the Wisconsinan Laurentide Ice Sheet, and their distribution follows three ecozones with different dominant soil-forming factors.

facts.text: The ice retreated northeast, exposing southern Ontario as much as 13,000 years ago and the far north about 8,500 to 6,500 years ago.

In the Hudson Plains ecozone (about 25% of Ontario) cold, semi-arid climate dominates: low evapotranspiration plus water-retentive clayey and silty glacio-marine materials leave much moisture in the soil, over neutral to alkaline limestones.

The Boreal Shield (about 66%) lies on acidic, weathering-resistant Precambrian gneiss and granite, and its soils vary with climate, parent material, topography and vegetation; Dystric Brunisols dominate the west.

The Mixedwood Plains (about 9%) rest on carbonate-rich limestones, so soils depend mainly on parent material, with climate less important; it holds Ontario's most productive farmland and its major cities.
The Guelph series, a Brunisolic Gray-Brown Luvisol formed in loam to silt loam moraine, became Ontario's provincial soil in 2015 and is prime agricultural soil when not limited by slope.

entries.title: Soils of Quebec

definition.text: Quebec has seven soil orders arranged in a zonal pattern from south to north, set by climate, vegetation, time since glaciation and parent material.

facts.text: Soils formed over the last 6,000 to 10,000 years after the Laurentide Ice Sheet retreated, on parent materials that follow the geology of the Canadian Shield, the Appalachians and the sedimentary St. Lawrence valley.
After glaciation the Champlain Sea left salt-rich clay in the St. Lawrence Lowlands; leaching of the salt and river incision made these clays unstable, causing over 700 landslides and earthflows.

Podzols cover 39% of Quebec, mostly Humo-Ferric great groups on the Boreal and Taiga Shield; Brunisols cover 17%, mostly Dystric, where profile development is too weak for Podzols; Organic soils cover 8%, mainly Mesisols.
Dystric Brunisols can turn into Podzols over several thousand years, as in sandy deposits exposed by sea-level fall on the North Shore, where sesquioxide-cemented Bfc horizons replace the Bm horizon.

Only a small area has high agricultural potential: Canada Land Inventory Classes 1 to 3 total about 0.28 ha per Quebecer, the smallest of any province, and about 80% of them are cropland, so conserving them matters.

entries.title: Soils of the Atlantic Provinces

definition.text: Seven of Canada's ten soil orders occur in Atlantic Canada, but heavy precipitation and coarse, acidic glacial till make Podzols the dominant soil.

facts.text: Soils are often stony or shallow to bedrock, so the four provinces hold only about 1.5% of Canada's farmland, and only Prince Edward Island has more farmland than forest.

The region has four ecozones: Atlantic Maritime (New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island), Boreal Shield (Newfoundland), Taiga Shield (most of Labrador) and Arctic Cordillera in the far north.

The Atlantic Maritime is warmest, about 7 degrees C with 1250 mm of rain a year, on mostly sedimentary Paleozoic rock; Taiga Shield and Arctic Cordillera are colder, on Precambrian gneiss and granite with thin till and exposed rock.
Surficial geology is mostly glacial till of variable thickness, with locally important glacio-fluvial deposits.

By the Canada Land Inventory the region has no Class 1 land; Class 2 is about 588,000 ha, Class 3 about 2,275,000 ha and Class 4 about 2,507,000 ha, and most of Nova Scotia and Newfoundland is Class 7.

entries.title: Soils of the Prairie Provinces

definition.text: The soils of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba are the most heavily converted to farmland in Canada, with the soil pattern set by bedrock geology and the rain shadow of the Western Cordillera.

facts.text: In the south over 80% of the land is agricultural, and the type of farming follows soil capability; true prairie covers only the southern part of these provinces.

About one-third of the region sits on igneous and metamorphic Canadian Shield rock and two-thirds on sedimentary rock; igneous rock yields acidic sandy, gravelly parent materials, sedimentary rock neutral to alkaline loamy ones.
Chernozems dominate the southern grassland, Luvisols the northern mixed forest, Brunisols the acidic Shield, and Organic Cryosols the cold, saturated peats near Hudson Bay.
Crops once centred on spring wheat with summerfallow; today canola, pulses and flax are grown and most producers use continuous cultivation with conservation tillage or no-till.
Under the Canada Land Inventory, classes 1 to 4 sustain field crops and classes 5 and 6 suit only forage; texture decides class mainly through its effect on water availability.

entries.title: From grassland to forest: the Parkland transition

definition.text: Moving north from the grassland, soils change through the transitional Parkland zone to continuous Mixedwood forest, as tree litter replaces grass as the main organic input.

facts.text: In the Parkland the Ah horizon lightens and begins to bleach, forming an Ahe horizon; these are Dark Gray Chernozems.
Further north an LFH litter layer sits on the mineral soil over a bleached Ae horizon and a clay-richer Bt horizon, which is underlain by a carbonate-bearing C horizon; these are Gray Luvisols.
Gray Luvisols also form on glacio-lacustrine deposits in north-central Manitoba.

entries.title: Prairie dark soils and the grasses that made them

definition.text: Chernozemic great groups across the Prairies follow the zonation of native grasses, which in turn follows the regional water deficit.

facts.text: Great groups of the Chernozemic order are separated by the colour of the A horizon, which shows how much organic carbon the grasses added.
In the driest part, with an annual water deficit near 200 mm, low grasses with little biomass give Brown Chernozems; less deficit to the west and north gives Dark Brown and Black Chernozems.
Organic carbon is highest in southern Manitoba, where the annual water deficit is only about 70 mm.
Chernozems have organically enriched Ah horizons over decalcified, slightly reddened Bm horizons.

entries.title: Lithosequences, soils that differ only in their rock

definition.text: A set of soils formed under similar conditions on different parent materials, so that their profiles differ because of the parent material.

facts.text: Because the soils share similar weathering conditions, differences in composition reflect the relative weathering rates of the parent minerals.
The Goldich dissolution series, which ranks minerals by weathering rate, can be applied to lithosequences.
Studies of lithosequences give the clearest picture of the role of parent material in soil formation, including in paleosols.

entries.text: To see what rock alone does to a soil, compare soils where everything else is the same. A lithosequence is a set of soils formed under similar conditions on different {{ref:soil-form-087}}. The soils share similar weathering conditions. Lithosequence studies give the clearest picture of the role of parent material in soil formation, even in ancient buried soils.

entries.title: The soils of Australia, ancient and starved of phosphorus

definition.text: The soils of the Australian continent, many of them extremely ancient and naturally deficient in phosphorus.

facts.text: Plants with proteoid (cluster) roots can grow in these very nutrient-poor soils, and their dense root-hair networks can absorb enough rain to prevent runoff.
The Australian Soil Classification replaced earlier systems for Australian soils, including the Factual Key (1960) and the Handbook of Australian Soils (1968).
James Arthur Prescott described them in CSIR bulletin 52, The Soils of Australia in Relation to Vegetation and Climate.

entries.text: Australia's soils are among the oldest anywhere, and many are naturally short of phosphorus. Plants have adapted. Those with proteoid, or cluster, roots grow in these very nutrient-poor soils, and dense mats of fine hairs on their roots can absorb enough rain to prevent runoff. James Arthur Prescott described the continent's soils in CSIR bulletin 52. Its title was The Soils of Australia in Relation to Vegetation and Climate. {{ref:soil-class-022}} later replaced earlier systems, including the Factual Key (1960) and {{ref:soil-class-046}} (1968).

entries.title: One yardstick from clay specks to giant boulders

definition.text: The diameter of individual grains of sediment, or of the lithified particles in clastic rocks.

facts.text: Grain size differs from crystallite size, the size of a single crystal: one grain can contain several crystals.
Granular materials range from very small colloidal particles through clay, silt, sand, gravel and cobbles to boulders.
Size ranges set the limits of the named classes in the Udden-Wentworth scale used in the United States.
ISO 14688-1 classifies soils by size for engineering, from clay at 0.002 mm or less up to large boulders over 630 mm.
Grain-size data, with pore-size distribution and texture, are used to estimate hydraulic conductivity empirically, for example with Allen Hazen's formula.

verification.evidence: For soil classification purposes, weatherable minerals are determined by petrographic analysis (grain counts) of grains 0.02 to 2.0 mm in size (coarse silt to very coarse sand) or other grain size as specified in the Keys to Soil Taxonomy.
verification.note: the glossary's 0.02 mm is the coarse/fine silt boundary, not a grain-size class limit the entry states

entries.text: The finest clay and the largest boulder sit on a single scale. Engineers following ISO 14688-1 run it from clay at 0.002 mm or less to large boulders over 630 mm. That quantity is grain size: the diameter of individual grains of sediment. It also covers the particles cemented into clastic rocks, which are built from fragments of older rock. A grain is not the same as a crystal. Crystallite size is the size of a single crystal, and one grain can contain several. Above the tiny colloidal particles and clay, ever-coarser classes climb toward cobbles and boulders. The first of them is {{ref:soil-phys-013}}. The Udden-Wentworth scale, used in the United States, sets its named classes by size ranges. With texture and the spread of pore sizes, grain-size data help estimate {{ref:soil-water-193}}, the ease with which water flows through soil. One such rule of thumb is Allen Hazen's, covered in {{ref:soil-water-194}}.

entries.title: Sand, the gritty grain that records its own journey

definition.text: A granular material of finely divided mineral particles, defined mainly by grain size: coarser than silt and finer than gravel.

facts.text: By the geologists' definition, sand grains range from 0.0625 mm (1/16 mm) to 2 mm in diameter.
As a soil textural class, sand is a soil with more than 85 percent sand-sized particles by mass.
In the United States sand has five grades, from very fine (1/16-1/8 mm) to very coarse (1-2 mm), based on the Krumbein phi scale.
Its commonest mineral inland and on non-tropical coasts is quartz, whose chemical inertness and hardness make it the commonest weathering-resistant mineral.
Calcium carbonate, such as aragonite made by coral and shellfish, is the second most common sand; gypsum sands are rarer.
Sand feels gritty when rubbed between the fingers.
Freshly weathered quartz sand is angular, while grains carried far by water or wind become rounded, so grains record their origin and transport.
Sandy soils drain very well and suit crops such as watermelons, peaches and peanuts; angular sharp sand is used to loosen clay soils.

conflicts.text: The Unified Soil Classification System defines sand as 0.074 to 4.75 mm.
conflicts.note: Engineering range tied to US standard sieves.

conflicts.text: A 1938 USDA specification set the smallest sand size at 0.05 mm.
conflicts.note: USDA lower limit versus 0.0625 mm in geology.

conflicts.text: Under Albert Atterberg's early 20th-century standard, particles as small as 0.02 mm counted as sand.
conflicts.note: Historical lower limit.

conflicts.text: A 1953 AASHTO engineering standard set the minimum sand size at 0.074 mm.
conflicts.note: Engineering lower limit.

entries.title: Silt, the grain at the edge of eyesight

definition.text: A granular material finer than sand and coarser than clay, made mostly of broken quartz grains.

facts.text: Geologists define silt as detrital particles of 1/256 to 1/16 mm (about 4 to 63 microns); the USDA uses 0.05-0.002 mm.
The 63-micron upper limit is about the smallest grain the unaided eye can see; the 2-4 micron lower limit marks the change from quartz fragments to clay mineral particles.
Silt feels floury when dry, lacks plasticity when wet and feels gritty between the teeth, where clay-size particles feel smooth.
It forms by grinding of quartz grains, both in dust storms of very hot climates and by glaciers in very cold ones.
Wind-deposited silt forms loess, which makes up some of the most fertile farmland on Earth.
Silt's quartz grains supply no nutrients themselves but promote excellent soil structure, while smaller amounts of other silt-sized minerals provide nutrients.
Silt erodes easily, has poor mechanical properties and can liquefy in earthquakes; silt polluting water is called siltation.
The pipette method sizes silt by settling rate under Stokes' law: 60-micron grains settle through a metre of still water in five minutes, 2-micron grains take several days.

conflicts.text: Other geologists put silt at 2 to 63 microns (9 to 4 phi units).
conflicts.note: Lower limit 2 rather than about 4 microns.

conflicts.text: The International Society of Soil Science uses 0.02-0.002 mm.
conflicts.note: Upper limit 0.02 mm, against 0.05 mm (USDA) and about 63 microns (geology).

conflicts.text: ASTM sets silt between the No. 200 sieve and 0.005 mm.
conflicts.note: Lower limit 0.005 mm.

conflicts.text: US civil engineers call silt material passing a No. 200 sieve (0.074 mm or less) with little plasticity or cohesion.
conflicts.note: Upper limit 0.074 mm.

entries.title: Three bins for every grain: sand, silt and clay

definition.text: Set ranges of particle size, sand, silt and clay, into which a soil's mineral particles are sorted.

facts.text: Texture considers only particles smaller than two millimetres across: sand, silt and clay.
In the USDA scheme, clay particles are under 0.002 mm, silt runs from 0.002 to 0.05 mm, and sand is larger than 0.05 mm.
USDA sand is split into five grades, from very fine sand (0.05–0.10 mm) through fine, medium and coarse to very coarse sand (1.00–2.00 mm).
Other systems draw different limits; the WRB, for instance, puts the silt–sand boundary at 0.063 mm instead of 0.05 mm.
Clay particles are plate-shaped rather than spherical, which gives them a larger specific surface area.
Sand is the least active separate, with the least specific surface area, silt comes next, and clay is the most active.
Water-holding capacity is low in sand, medium to high in silt and high in clay, while drainage is respectively high, slow to medium, and very slow.

conflicts.text: Atterberg's international system set the upper limit of silt at 20 μm.
conflicts.note: Older international scheme; the USDA puts the silt–sand boundary at 0.05 mm.

conflicts.text: The WRB puts the silt–sand boundary at 0.063 mm.
conflicts.note: System difference, not an error; the USDA uses 0.05 mm.

entries.text: Soil texture ignores anything wider than two millimeters. Everything finer is sorted into soil separates: set ranges of particle size called sand, silt and clay. The USDA draws the lines at fixed sizes. Clay particles are under 0.002 mm, silt runs from 0.002 to 0.05 mm, and sand is anything larger than 0.05 mm. Each bin splits further. USDA sand has five grades, from very fine sand at 0.05 to 0.10 mm up to very coarse sand at 1.00 to 2.00 mm. Silt divides into coarse and fine at 0.02 mm. Clay divides at 0.0002 mm, with fine clay at that size or less. Not every system agrees. The WRB system, for instance, puts the silt–sand boundary at 0.063 mm instead of 0.05 mm. Shape matters too. Clay particles are flat plates rather than spheres, which gives them far more surface for their mass, an idea explored in {{ref:soil-phys-043}}. The three separates behave very differently. Sand, with the least surface, is the least active; silt comes next, and clay is the most active. Water follows the same order. Sand holds little water and drains fast. Silt holds a medium to high amount and drains slowly to moderately. Clay holds a great deal and drains very slowly.

entries.title: Two meanings of clay: a size and a mineral

definition.text: The difference between clay as a class of very fine particle sizes and clay as material made of clay minerals, two overlapping but distinct definitions.

facts.text: Clays differ from other fine-grained soils in size and mineralogy; silts contain no clay minerals and tend to be coarser than clays.
The silt–clay boundary depends on the discipline: usually 2 μm for geologists and soil scientists, often 4–5 μm for sedimentologists, and 1 μm for colloid chemists; ISO 14688 uses 2 μm.
Geotechnical engineers separate silts from clays by plasticity, measured with the Atterberg limits, rather than by size.

Size does not fix mineral makeup: textural clay may be very fine quartz or layered secondary minerals, so a size class shares surface-area properties but not chemistry-linked ones such as cation exchange.

conflicts.text: Sedimentologists often place the silt–clay boundary at 4–5 μm and colloid chemists at 1 μm.
conflicts.note: Discipline convention; soil scientists and ISO 14688 use 2 μm.

conflicts.text: The sediment grain-size scale puts clay below 3.9 μm.
conflicts.note: Sedimentological scale; soil science uses 2 μm (0.002 mm).

verification.evidence: Carbonate itself exists as crystals, predominantly calcite (CaCO3), in the size range of fine silt to coarse clay (approximately 10 to 1 µm).
verification.note: the Manual's 10 to 1 µm is the size of pedogenic carbonate crystals

entries.text: The word clay hides two different ideas. One is a class of very fine particle sizes; the other is material made of {{ref:soil-chem-079}}. The two overlap but differ. The size boundary with silt depends on the discipline: 2 μm for soil scientists, 4–5 μm for many sedimentologists, 1 μm for chemists who study {{ref:soil-chem-154}}. Geotechnical engineers separate silts from clays by plasticity rather than size, using {{ref:soil-phys-021}}. A clay-sized grain may be very fine quartz, sharing clay's surface-area traits but not its {{ref:soil-chem-047}}, the holding of nutrients.

Geotechnical engineers separate silts from clays by plasticity rather than size, using Atterberg limits: the water contents where soil changes state. entries.title: Why wet clay keeps any shape pressed into it

definition.text: Clay's capacity, when wet, to be moulded into a shape that it then keeps, its defining mechanical property.

facts.text: Plasticity comes from clay minerals, whose thin plates are tough but flexible and cling together when moist, giving clay its cohesion.
In kaolinite, a film of water molecules hydrogen-bonds the plates: weak enough to let them slip during moulding, strong enough to hold the new shape.
Drying removes most of the water so the plates bond directly, leaving clay rigid but fragile; moistened again, it becomes plastic once more.
Clay stays plastic across a range of water contents, from the plastic limit, just moist enough to mould, to the liquid limit, just dry enough to hold its shape.
For kaolinite clay, the plastic limit is about 36% to 40% and the liquid limit about 58% to 72%.
Soils, particularly clays, deform inelastically under load, mainly through rearrangement of clusters of neighbouring grains, in ways that depend on microstructure, chemistry and water content.

verification.evidence: Clay loam.—Material has 27 to less than 40 percent clay and more than 20 to 45 percent sand.
verification.note: 40 percent clay is the Manual's clay loam limit, not a plasticity claim

verification.evidence: In Frasiwassents, the Hydric subgroup is an intergrade for soils with low bearing strength (n value > 0.7, clay content > 8%) that are grading towards the Hydrowassents great group.
verification.note: the glossary's 8, 12 and 20 percent figures are not plastic or liquid limits of kaolinite

entries.text: Press wet clay into a shape, and it stays put. That is plasticity, clay's defining mechanical property: the capacity, when wet, to be molded into a shape it then keeps. It comes from {{ref:soil-chem-079}}, whose thin plates are tough but flexible and cling together when moist. In {{ref:soil-chem-088}}, a film of water molecules holds the plates together through hydrogen bonds. The bond is weak enough to let plates slip during molding, yet strong enough to hold the new shape. Drying removes most of the water, so the plates bond directly and the clay turns rigid but fragile. Wet it again, and it turns plastic. Clay stays plastic only from just moist enough to mold to just dry enough to hold a shape. For this clay, those thresholds sit near 36% to 40% and 58% to 72% water. The dry threshold has its own entry, {{ref:soil-phys-023}}. So does the wet one, {{ref:soil-phys-022}}.

entries.title: Heavy, wet and surprisingly fertile: farming on clay

definition.text: How a high clay content shapes a soil's value for farming, trading poor drainage against greater fertility.

facts.text: Clay is often seen as undesirable for farming, although some clay is a necessary part of good soil.
Clay soils hold water and drain poorly, so they often need artificial drainage and tillage before they suit crops.
Their higher cation-exchange capacity makes them more fertile and better at holding nutrients, keeping more land in production rather than fallow.
Clay soils resist wind and water erosion better than silty and sandy soils because their particles bond tightly to each other.

entries.text: Clay has a poor reputation on the farm, yet good soil needs some of it. A high clay content trades poor drainage against greater fertility. Clay soils hold water and drain poorly, so they often need artificial drainage and tillage before crops thrive. In return, their higher {{ref:soil-chem-046}}, the power to hold nutrients, makes them more fertile. That keeps more land in production rather than lying fallow. Their tightly bonded particles also resist wind and water erosion better than silty and sandy soils.

entries.title: Twelve names for every blend of sand, silt and clay

definition.text: The twelve named categories into which the USDA groups soils by their percentages of sand, silt and clay.

facts.text: The twelve classes are sand, loamy sand, sandy loam, loam, silt loam, silt, sandy clay loam, clay loam, silty clay loam, sandy clay, silty clay and clay.
A class is named after its main particle size or a mix of the most abundant sizes, as in "sandy clay" or "silty clay".
"Loam" describes a soil with roughly equal properties of sand, silt and clay, and it combines into further class names such as "clay loam" and "silt loam".
The USDA and WRB systems both use 12 textural classes, while the UK-ADAS system uses 11.
Texture classes help judge which crops suit a soil and predict its response to drought or its lime (calcium) needs.

verification.note: the Manual lists the twelve texture classes, sands to clay (fig. 3-7)

entries.text: Any soil's texture can be summed up in one name from a list of twelve. The USDA soil texture classes are those twelve named categories, assigned by a soil's percentages of sand, silt and clay. The names follow a simple logic. A class takes the name of its main particle size, or of a mix of the most abundant sizes. Sand, silt and clay each name a class of their own. Two more pair a couple of sizes, as in sandy clay and silty clay. The other seven use a fourth word for a soil with roughly equal properties of sand, silt and clay. That word stands alone or joins the others in compound names, as explained in {{ref:soil-phys-012}}. Other systems count differently. The WRB also uses 12 textural classes, while the UK-ADAS system uses 11. The names earn their keep in the field. A texture class helps judge which crops suit a soil. It also predicts how the soil will respond to drought and how much lime, a source of calcium, it needs. Turning three percentages into one class takes a chart, the subject of {{ref:soil-phys-046}}.

entries.title: Loam, the balanced blend that farmers and gardeners prize

definition.text: Soil made mostly of sand and silt with a smaller amount of clay.

facts.text: By weight a typical loam is about 40% sand, 40% silt and 20% clay, though the proportions vary.
In the USDA texture triangle, loam is the only class not dominated by sand, silt or clay.
Subtypes include sandy loam, silt loam, clay loam, sandy clay loam and silty clay loam, which drain water somewhat differently.
Loams hold more nutrients, water and humus than sandy soils, drain and aerate better than silty or clayey soils, and are easier to till than clays.
Loam is prized for farming and gardening because it keeps water and nutrients yet lets excess water drain away.
A soil dominated by one or two size groups can behave like loam if organic matter gives it strong granular structure; a textural loam loses its qualities when compacted or stripped of organic matter.
Most dictionaries, and many gardeners, define loam simply as soil containing humus, with no mention of particle size.

entries.text: Farmers and gardeners prize one soil because it keeps water and nutrients yet lets the excess drain away. Loam is soil made mostly of sand and silt with a smaller amount of clay. A typical loam is about 40 percent sand, 40 percent silt and 20 percent clay by weight. It is the only class on the USDA triangle not dominated by one size. Loams hold more nutrients, water and humus than sandy soils. They drain and aerate better than silty or clayey soils and till more easily than clays. Its subtypes, such as sandy loam, silt loam and clay loam, drain somewhat differently. Texture is not destiny. A soil dominated by one or two sizes can act like loam if organic matter gives it strong granular structure. A textural loam loses its virtues when compacted or stripped of organic matter. Most dictionaries, and many gardeners, simply call any soil containing humus loam.

entries.title: A triangle that turns three percentages into one name

definition.text: A triangular chart whose three sides give percent sand, silt and clay, used to read off a soil's texture class.

facts.text: One side of the triangle shows percent sand, another percent clay and the third percent silt.
Once a sample's sand, clay and silt percentages are known, the triangle assigns its texture class; the reading works starting from any side.
For example, a soil with 70 percent sand and 10 percent clay plots as a sandy loam.
On the USDA triangle, loam is the only class in which none of sand, silt or clay predominates.
Used in reverse, the triangle gives a rough estimate of sand, silt and clay percentages for a soil classed by feel.
It is a ternary plot: three variables that sum to a constant, usually 100%, so knowing two fixes the third and all three fit on one flat triangle.
Each component is 100% at one corner and 0% along the opposite edge; grid lines parallel to the edges make values easy to read.
For example, a sample with 50% clay and 20% silt must contain 30% sand for the three to total 100%.

verification.evidence: Definitions of Soil Texture Classes and Subclasses Sands.—Material has more than 85 percent sand, and the percentage of silt plus 1.5 times the percentage of clay is less than 15.
verification.note: 85 percent is the Manual's threshold for the sands class, not a point the entry makes

entries.title: Reading a soil's texture with thumb and forefinger

definition.text: A qualitative field method that judges a soil's texture by moistening and working a small sample by hand.

facts.text: A ball of soil is pushed between thumb and forefinger into a ribbon that extends over the finger until it breaks under its own weight.
The unbroken length of the ribbon helps indicate how much clay the sample holds.
Rubbing a wetted pinch in the palm shows the sand content: sandy soils feel gritty, silty soils smooth and clayey soils sticky.
It gives no exact sand, silt and clay values, but a trained person following its flowchart can judge their relative proportions accurately.
Needing little or no equipment, it allows quick, frequent checks that reveal variation within and between fields and boundaries between soil map units.
The method takes practice, and the WRB offers its own alternative texture-by-feel flowchart.

entries.title: Clays that heave houses and pull roots apart

definition.text: The degree to which certain clay minerals in a soil expand when wet and contract when dry.

facts.text: The capacity comes from clay minerals such as smectite, montmorillonite, vermiculite and illite, and the more of them a soil holds, the more severe its shrinking and swelling.
A soil with at least 5 percent of these minerals by weight may be able to shrink and swell.
It is measured as the coefficient of linear extensibility (COLE); a COLE above 0.06 can cause structural damage, and 0.06 means 100 inches of soil swell by 6 inches.
Among the soil separates, shrink/swell potential is very low for sand, low for silt and moderate to very high for clay.
Such soils fall in the Vertisol order: drying opens deep cracks that let water reach deeper layers, so shrinking and swelling repeat in cycles.
Contraction in dry spells can pull crop roots apart, yet the cracking also lets these soils recover quickly from compaction.
Swelling heaves structures and shrinking lets foundations settle unevenly; damage from shrink–swell clays is estimated at $7 billion a year.
Problems are worst where wet and dry seasons are sharply defined, and where pockets of wet soil sit beside dry soil and swell unevenly.

entries.text: Damage from shrinking and swelling clay soils is estimated at $7 billion a year. Shrinking can pull crop roots apart, yet the cracks help the soil recover fast from compaction.

entries.title: Gravel, the coarse rubble that water races through

definition.text: A loose aggregation of rock fragments coarser than sand.

facts.text: Definitions vary: many geologists use loose rounded particles over 2 mm, the USDA and Soil Science Society of America use 2–80 mm, and the Udden-Wentworth scale 2–64 mm.
In soil texture analysis, fragments larger than 2.0 mm are removed before the textural class is set but still appear in the name, as in gravelly sandy loam.
Most gravel comes from weathering bedrock; quartz is its commonest mineral because it is hard and inert, and river transport rounds the fragments quickly.
Natural gravel conducts water fast, sometimes above 1 cm/s, so gravel deposits make aquifers, while gravelly soils hold little moisture or nutrients and carry sparse plant life.

verification.evidence: If a size or range of sizes predominates, the class is modified (e.g., “fine gravel,” “cobbles 100 to 150 mm in diameter,” “channers 25 to 50 mm in length”).
verification.note: 25 to 50 mm is the Manual's example size for channers

verification.evidence: Rock fragments.—Discreet mineral fragments 2 mm or more in size that have a strongly coherent or higher rupture-resistance class (i.e., gravel, cobbles, stones, etc.).
verification.note: the glossary defines rock fragments, gravel included, as 2 mm or more

entries.text: Water can race through natural gravel at more than 1 cm/s. Gravel is a loose aggregation of rock fragments coarser than sand. Gravel deposits make aquifers, underground stores of water, but gravelly soils hold little moisture or nutrients. Texture tests remove fragments over 2.0 mm, yet the word "gravelly" stays in the soil's name.

entries.title: Why texture outranks color in the life of a crop

definition.text: The measurable physical traits of a soil, which in falling order of importance for crops are texture, structure, bulk density, porosity, consistency, temperature, colour and resistivity.

facts.text: These properties change with depth through the soil horizons, and most of them govern aeration and how well water enters and is held in the soil.
Texture comes from the proportions of sand, silt and clay; at the next scale up, coatings of iron oxides, carbonates, clay, silica and humus bind these separates into peds.
Bulk density measured at a standard moisture estimates compaction, and porosity is the part of the soil volume filled by gases or water.
Sand holds little water but drains fast and is well aerated; clay holds much water but drains very slowly and is poorly aerated; silt lies in between.
Clay stores plant nutrients well and resists pH change, while sand does both poorly and has a high potential for pollutant leaching.
Sandy soils warm quickly in spring and resist compaction; clay soils warm slowly and compact easily.
Silt is highly susceptible to both wind and water erosion, whereas clay resists water erosion when it is aggregated.

entries.text: A farmer sizing up a field should care more about its grains than its color. The physical properties of soil are its measurable physical traits, and for crops they rank in a clear order. Texture comes first, then structure, {{ref:soil-phys-060}}, porosity, consistency, temperature, color and resistivity. They change with depth through the soil's layers, and most govern aeration and how water enters and stays. Texture is the blend of coarse, medium and fine mineral grains. Coatings of oxides of iron ({{ref:soil-chem-163}}), carbonates, clay, silica and humus bind those grains into larger units, described in {{ref:soil-phys-003}}. Density with pores included, measured at a standard moisture, estimates compaction. Sandy soils drain fast, stay airy and warm quickly in spring, but hold little water and few nutrients. Clay soils store water and nutrients and resist pH change, yet drain very slowly and compact easily. Silty soils sit in between, and wind and rain carry them off easily.

entries.title: How grains and gaps build a living soil

definition.text: The arrangement of a soil's solid particles and of the pore spaces left between them.

facts.text: Structure depends on how individual particles clump, bind and aggregate, and that in turn sets the pattern of pores between them.
It shapes water and air movement, heat conduction, biological activity, root growth, seedling emergence and resistance to erosion.
Texture is an innate property fixed by the mineral particles, but structure can be improved or destroyed by the choice and timing of farming practices.
Structure is dynamic, changing with tillage, wheel traffic, roots, microbes and fauna, rainfall, wind erosion, wetting and drying, and freezing and thawing.
Most cultivation degrades structure: mechanical mixing compacts and shears aggregates, fills pores and exposes organic matter to faster decay and oxidation.
Continued cultivation and traffic can create compacted, impermeable layers, or hardpans, within the soil profile.
Under irrigation, structure declines as aggregates break down and clay disperses on rapid wetting, especially in sodic soils, where sodium makes wet particles repel one another.
Structure offers clues to a soil's texture, organic matter, biological activity, history, human use and the chemical and mineral conditions under which it formed.

entries.text: A farmer cannot change the mineral grains in a field, but can wreck or rebuild the way they fit together. That arrangement is soil structure: how a soil's solid particles sit, and the pore spaces left between them. Texture is innate, fixed by the mineral particles themselves, the separates described in {{ref:soil-phys-047}}. Structure is not. It depends on how particles clump, bind and gather into aggregates, small crumbs of particles stuck together. Those clumps in turn set the pattern of pores. Through that pattern, structure shapes how water and air move, how heat travels, and how roots and seedlings push through. It also governs biological activity and how well the soil resists erosion. Structure never sits still. Tillage, wheel traffic, roots, microbes and soil animals reshape it, and so do rain, wind, wetting and drying, and freezing and thawing. Most cultivation does harm. Mechanical mixing compacts and shears aggregates, fills pores and exposes organic matter to faster decay. Continued cultivation and traffic can press compacted, impermeable layers called hardpans into the soil profile. Irrigation brings its own damage, as aggregates break apart and clay disperses on rapid wetting. {{ref:soil-chem-009}} suffer most, because sodium makes wet particles push one another apart. Yet the choice and timing of farming practices can improve structure as well as destroy it. Read with care, structure is also a record. It holds clues to a soil's texture, organic matter, biology, history and human use, and to the chemistry under which it formed.

entries.title: Peds: the natural building blocks of soil

definition.text: A natural aggregate of soil particles, formed by soil-forming processes and separated from neighbouring units by pores or voids.

facts.text: The term is mostly used for visible structural units larger than 1 mm seen when soils are examined in the field.
A mass of soil made artificially, for example by cultivation, is a clod rather than a ped.
Clumping of sand, silt and clay into aggregates, and of aggregates into larger units, creates peds; the word is a contraction of pedolith.
Coatings of iron oxides, carbonates, clay, silica and humus make soil separates adhere into these larger, relatively stable secondary structures.
Peds are best described when the soil is dry or slightly moist, because they are hard to tell apart when wet.
A soil may be structureless, have simple units with no smaller components, or have compound units built of smaller ones separated by persistent planes of weakness.
Aggregation of particles into peds is one way soil macropores form, alongside roots, cracks and soil fauna.

verification.evidence: The penetrations form continuous skeletans 1 mm or more thick, mostly on the vertical faces of peds.
verification.note: the glossary's 1 mm is the thickness of skeletans on ped faces, not the size of peds

entries.text: A lump of earth gets a different name depending on who made it. When soil-forming processes build it, it is a ped: a natural aggregate of soil particles, set apart from its neighbors by pores or voids. When cultivation makes it, it is merely a clod. The word, a contraction of pedolith, is used mostly for visible units larger than 1 mm seen in the field. Peds form as sand, silt and clay clump into aggregates, and aggregates clump into larger units. Coatings of carbonates, clay, silica, humus and the minerals of {{ref:soil-chem-163}} glue them into fairly stable secondary structures. Some soils are structureless, while others have simple units or compound units built of smaller ones. The gaps between peds are one way large pores, or {{ref:soil-water-189}}, form, alongside roots, cracks and soil animals. Peds are best described when soil is dry or slightly moist, because wet peds blur together.

entries.title: Plates, prisms, blocks and crumbs: the shapes of structure

definition.text: The grouping of soil structure by the shape and arrangement of its peds, with five major classes: platy, prismatic, columnar, blocky and granular.

facts.text: Platy units are flat, usually horizontal plates, found mainly in subsoil compacted by trampling or machinery; they hinder the downward movement of water and roots.
Prismatic units are vertically elongated with flat to rounded vertical faces and flat tops; they typify clay-illuviated B horizons, cracked apart by freeze-thaw and wetting-drying cycles.
Columnar units resemble prisms but have distinct, rounded tops; common in subsoils of sodium-affected and swelling-clay soils, they are so dense that roots struggle to penetrate.
Blocky units are roughly equidimensional polyhedra, called angular when faces meet at sharp angles and subangular when corners are mostly rounded; they are common in subsoils and clay-rich topsoils.
Granular or crumb units are near-spherical with irregular faces not moulded on neighbouring peds; they dominate organic-rich grassland and garden topsoils and give good porosity.
Wedge units are interlocking elliptical lenses often bounded by slickensides; lenticular units are overlapping lenses parallel to the surface, linked to moist, silty soils prone to frost action.
Size classes depend on the type: very coarse means over 10 mm for platy and granular peds, over 50 mm for blocky and over 100 mm for prismlike peds.

entries.text: Dig a pit and the soil's architecture shows itself as plates, prisms, columns, blocks and crumbs. These are the five major soil structure types, a grouping of structure by the shape and arrangement of its peds. Platy units are flat plates, usually lying horizontally. They form mainly in subsoil packed down by trampling or machinery, and they hinder water and roots heading downward. Prismatic units stand tall, with flat to rounded vertical faces and flat tops. They typify B horizons enriched with clay washed down from above, split apart by freezing and thawing and by wetting and drying. Columnar units resemble prisms with distinct, rounded tops. Common in subsoils rich in sodium or swelling clay, they are so dense that roots struggle to enter. Blocky units are many-sided and roughly equal in every direction, common in subsoils and clay-rich topsoils. They are angular when faces meet at sharp angles and subangular when corners are mostly rounded. Granular or crumb units are nearly round, with irregular faces that do not mold to their neighbors. They dominate organic-rich grassland and garden topsoils and give good porosity. Some soils also hold wedges, interlocking elliptical lenses often bounded by slickensides, polished surfaces where soil slid past soil. Lenticular units are overlapping lenses parallel to the surface, typical of moist, silty soils prone to frost action. Size classes shift with shape. Very coarse means over 10 mm for platy and granular peds, over 50 mm for blocky ones and over 100 mm for prisms.

entries.title: A census of a soil's grains, size by size

definition.text: A list of values or a mathematical function giving the relative amount, usually by mass, of particles of each size in a granular material.

facts.text: A soil's particle-size distribution is its texture, which governs properties such as hydraulic conductivity and water potential, though mineralogy can strongly modify them.
It affects the strength and load-bearing properties of rocks and soils.
Breaking soil into its particles takes significant energy; the resulting distribution is called a grain size distribution.
A distribution is usually defined by its measuring method; sieve analysis, the simplest, reports amounts in discrete size ranges between sieve sizes.
Results are given as a range analysis, listing the amount in each size range, or cumulatively, as the total retained or passed by a notional sieve.
Real particles are irregular, so how size is characterized depends heavily on the method of measurement.
Sedimentation methods size particles by their settling velocity in a liquid and suit sizes below 10 μm, but Brownian motion prevents reliable sub-micrometre measurement.
Laser diffraction infers size from the angle of scattered light, works best between 0.1 and 3,000 μm, and now dominates industrial measurement.

entries.text: Every soil hides a recipe: so much of this grain size, so much of that. A particle-size distribution spells it out. It is a list of values, or a mathematical function, giving the relative amount of particles of each size, usually by mass. For a soil, this distribution is its texture. It governs how water moves and is held, though mineralogy can strongly modify that. It also shapes the strength and load-bearing capacity of soils and rocks. Breaking soil into separate particles takes significant energy, and real particles are irregular. So a distribution is usually defined by its measuring method. The simplest method reports amounts in set ranges between sieve sizes, as described in {{ref:soil-phys-019}}. Sedimentation methods time how fast particles settle in a liquid and suit sizes below 10 μm. Laser diffraction reads size from the angle of scattered light, works best between 0.1 and 3,000 μm, and now dominates industrial measurement.

entries.title: Shaking soil through a tower of ever-finer sieves

definition.text: A procedure that measures the particle size distribution of a granular material by passing it through a stack of progressively finer sieves and weighing what each sieve holds.

facts.text: It works on almost any granular material, from sand, clay and soil to powders and seeds, and as the simplest sizing technique it is probably the most common.
A weighed sample goes into the top, coarsest sieve of a column; each lower sieve is finer, and a pan called the receiver sits at the base.
A mechanical shaker agitates the column for a set time; the material on each sieve is then weighed and divided by the total mass to give percent retained.
Dry sieving is accurate down to #100 mesh (150 μm) but much less so for finer material, as the energy needed and particle attraction rise with smaller sizes.
Wet sieving, with a water spray rinsing the stack until the outflow runs clear, handles suspensions and fine powders (mostly under 45 μm) that clump when dry.
The method assumes near-spherical particles, so elongated or flat grains give unreliable mass-based results.
For soils, silt and clay below 60 μm need a second sizing method, usually hydrometer or pipette, on the material from the bottom sieve.
In engineering, the soil's particle size distribution from sieving helps judge its mechanical properties and whether it can support a planned structure.

entries.text: The simplest way to size grains, and probably the most common, is to shake them through holes. Sieve analysis measures particle-size distribution by passing a material through a stack of ever-finer sieves and weighing each sieve's catch. A mechanical shaker drives a weighed sample down through finer and finer sieves to a pan called the receiver. Each catch is weighed and divided by the total mass to give its percent retained. Dry sieving stays accurate down to #100 mesh, or 150 μm, but finer grains cling together. Wet sieving rinses the stack with water until it runs clear, handling fine powders mostly under 45 μm. Flat or elongated grains give unreliable results, since the method assumes near-spherical particles. Soil silt and clay below 60 μm need a second method, usually the pipette or the settling test in {{ref:soil-phys-050}}. Engineers use the results to judge whether ground can carry a planned structure.

entries.title: Timing how fast soil grains sink in a cylinder

definition.text: A laboratory sedimentation test that estimates a soil's percent sand, silt and clay from how fast dispersed particles settle, based on Stokes' law.

facts.text: Stokes' law links a particle's settling velocity to its size, so suspended particles separate by size as they sink.
The soil is shaken overnight with sodium hexametaphosphate, a dispersing agent that breaks up aggregates, then made up with water in a one-litre cylinder.
After mixing, sand (over 50 microns) settles first and silt next, while clay (2 microns or finer) stays above the silt layer.
An ASTM 152H hydrometer reads grams of suspended material per litre: at 40 seconds for silt plus clay, giving sand, and after 6–8 hours for the clay still suspended.
Percent silt is 100 minus the sum of percent clay and percent sand; subtracting a blank reading removes the need for temperature correction.
Introduced in 1927, the method is still widely used, but flaws found in the empirical 1927 protocol mean its original procedure and settling cylinder should not be used.
Platy clay particles settle broadside with extra drag, so they are sized too small and the fine fraction is overestimated; below 0.2 micron, Brownian motion stops particles settling by Stokes' law.
Sieving cannot size silt and clay on its own, so sedimentation analysis, such as the hydrometer or pipette method, covers the fine end of the size distribution.

entries.text: Within 40 seconds, the sand in a stirred soil sample has sunk, yet the clay is still suspended hours later. The hydrometer method, a laboratory sedimentation test, turns that difference into a soil's percent sand, silt and clay. It rests on Stokes' law, which links settling speed to size. First the soil is shaken overnight with sodium hexametaphosphate, a dispersing agent that breaks up clumps. Water then fills a one-liter cylinder. Sand over 50 microns settles first, then silt; clay of 2 microns or finer stays above. A hydrometer, a floating gauge, reads grams per liter: at 40 seconds for silt plus clay, giving the sand, and after 6–8 hours for the clay. Silt is 100 minus the clay and sand percentages. Introduced in 1927, it is still widely used, though flaws mean its original procedure and cylinder should not be used. Flat clay plates also sink broadside, so they are sized too small.

entries.title: Expansive clay and the builders who outwit it

definition.text: A clay soil that swells and shrinks greatly as its water content changes.

facts.text: Clays are built of tetrahedral and octahedral sheets in 1:1 or 2:1 layers; expansive clays have an expanding 2:1 lattice, though some 2:1 clays do not expand.
In the laboratory, a plasticity index above 35 or liquid limit above 50, a free swell test comparing soil volume in water and kerosene, or X-ray detection of montmorillonite reveal expansive clay.
In the field, gilgai mounds and depressions, deep shrinkage cracks, or moist soil that rolls into a 3 mm thread without crumbling indicate expansive soil.
Builders cope with deep foundations or piles, void spaces under slabs, chemical stabilizers such as lime, cement or fly ash, and steady moisture around structures.

conflicts.text: The Expansive clay lead groups kaolinite with the smectites as having the most dramatic shrink–swell capacity.
conflicts.note: Inconsistent with the page's own 2:1 expanding-lattice rule (S:296a8d21bb8e) and with Clay mineral, which classes kaolinite as a 1:1 clay (S:6d809205ff87); not used in the facts.

entries.text: Builders sometimes leave empty space under a slab on purpose. The reason is expansive clay, a clay soil that swells and shrinks greatly as its water content changes. Its minerals have an expanding 2:1 layered lattice, though not every 2:1 clay expands. Lab tests look for high plasticity, a free swell test comparing water and kerosene, or {{ref:soil-chem-093}} under X-rays. Field signs include mounds and hollows, deep cracks, and moist soil that rolls into a 3 mm thread without crumbling. Builders also use piles, lime stabilizers and steady moisture.

entries.title: Albert Atterberg draws soil's first size lines

definition.text: The first soil particle-size classification, proposed by Albert Atterberg in 1905 from his studies in southern Sweden.

facts.text: Atterberg set silt's upper limit at 20 μm: finer particles are invisible to the eye, coagulate with salts, show the fastest 24-hour capillary rise, and leave pores too small for root hairs.
Commission One of the International Society of Soil Science recommended the system at the First International Congress of Soil Science, held in Washington in 1927.
Australia adopted the system, whose equal logarithmic size intervals are seen as an attractive feature worth keeping.
The USDA adopted its own system in 1938, and the FAO used the USDA system for the FAO-UNESCO world soil map and recommended it.

entries.title: Watching grains settle with a beam of X-rays

definition.text: A hybrid particle-sizing technique that combines sedimentation with X-ray absorption.

facts.text: Particle size is calculated from terminal settling velocities using Stokes' law.
The absorption of X-rays, interpreted with the Beer–Lambert–Bouguer law, gives the relative mass concentration in each size class.
It is one of several further quantitative texture methods, alongside the pipette, particulate organic matter (POM) and rapid methods.

entries.text: Settling soil can be tracked with X-rays as well as with a floating gauge. X-ray sedimentation is a hybrid particle-sizing technique that combines sedimentation with X-ray absorption. Stokes' law turns each particle's terminal settling velocity, its steady sinking speed, into a size, as in {{ref:soil-phys-050}}. The X-rays supply the amounts. Their absorption, read through the Beer–Lambert–Bouguer law, gives the relative mass concentration in each size class. It is one of several further quantitative texture methods, alongside the pipette, {{ref:soil-bio-118}} and rapid methods.

entries.title: Well graded or poorly graded: why the size mix matters

definition.text: An engineering classification of a coarse-grained soil according to the range of particle sizes it contains.

facts.text: Gravels and sands are well graded, with a good spread of sizes from the No. 4 to No. 200 sieves, or poorly graded, which divides into uniformly graded and gap-graded soils.
Fine-grained soils, mainly silts and clays, are classed by their Atterberg limits instead.
Gradation is read from a grain-size distribution curve built from sieve or hydrometer analysis, following either the USCS or the AASHTO system.
It signals compressibility, shear strength and hydraulic conductivity: poorly graded soils drain better through more voids and liquefy more easily, while well-graded soils compact further.

entries.text: Poorly graded ground drains better than well-graded ground but liquefies more easily. Soil gradation is an engineering classification of a coarse-grained soil by the range of particle sizes it contains. Gravels and sands with a good spread of sizes, from the No. 4 to the No. 200 sieve, are well graded. The rest are poorly graded, either uniformly graded or gap-graded. Their extra voids explain the drainage, while well-graded soils compact further. Gradation is read from the grain-size curve covered in {{ref:soil-phys-020}}, using the AASHTO system or {{ref:soil-phys-036}}. Fine-grained silts and clays are classed instead by {{ref:soil-phys-021}}.
