Fine-grained silts and clays are classed instead by Atterberg limits: the water contents where soil changes state.

entries.title: Soil aggregation: turning loose grains into lasting crumbs
entries.article: Soil aggregate stability#Factors Affecting Aggregate Formation

definition.text: The joining of primary soil particles into larger aggregates through rearrangement, flocculation and cementation.

facts.text: Flocculated clumps become aggregates once cemented by agents such as carbonates, gypsum, sesquioxides, clay particles and organic matter.

Aggregation is strengthened by precipitated oxides and carbonates, biofilms and fungal hyphae, multivalent cations bridging negative particles, and hydrogen and hydrophobic bonds between organic compounds.
Calcium bridges clay and organic matter and can replace sodium on exchange sites, reducing the dispersion, crusting and slaking of sodic soils.
Iron and aluminium sesquioxides cement aggregates larger than 100 μm, an effect that becomes more pronounced in soils with more than 10% sesquioxides.
With 2:1 clays such as montmorillonite, organic matter is the main binder; with oxides and 1:1 clays such as kaolinite, electrostatic bonds also act and aggregation is weaker.
Wetting-drying and shrink-swell cycles rearrange particles, with wetting and drying able to raise or lower stability; freezing wet soil breaks aggregates into smaller ones.
Some shrink-swell soils self-mulch, forming a granular surface structure through repeated shrinking and swelling.
Earthworm casts, mite and collembola fecal pellets, roots and fungal hyphae build aggregates; such biological agents matter most in soils lacking swelling 2:1 clays.

entries.text: Earthworms, fungi, frost and chemistry all work on the same project: turning loose grains into crumbs. Soil aggregation is the joining of primary soil particles into larger aggregates through rearrangement, flocculation and cementation. Flocculated clumps become true aggregates only once something cements them. Carbonates, gypsum, clay particles, organic matter and sesquioxides, the oxides of iron and aluminum, all serve as cement. {{ref:soil-bio-050}} and fungal hyphae strengthen the bonds. So do multivalent cations bridging negatively charged particles, and hydrogen and hydrophobic bonds between organic compounds. Calcium bridges clay and organic matter. It can also replace sodium on particle surfaces, curbing the dispersion, crusting and bursting of crumbs that plague {{ref:soil-chem-009}}. The best glue depends on the clay. Organic matter is the main binder with swelling 2:1 clays such as {{ref:soil-chem-093}}, met in {{ref:soil-phys-029}}. With oxides and 1:1 clays such as {{ref:soil-chem-088}}, electrostatic bonds join in, and aggregation is weaker. Sesquioxides cement aggregates larger than 100 μm, especially in soils with more than 10% sesquioxides. Weather shuffles the pieces. Wetting and drying, and shrinking and swelling, rearrange particles and can either strengthen or weaken aggregates. Freezing wet soil breaks aggregates into smaller ones. Some shrink-swell soils even mulch themselves, building a granular surface through repeated shrinking and swelling. Life builds aggregates too, through earthworm casts, the fecal pellets of mites and collembola, roots and fungal hyphae. These biological agents matter most where swelling 2:1 clays are lacking.

entries.title: Aggregate stability: will the crumbs hold together?

definition.text: A measure of how well soil aggregates resist breaking apart under forces such as water and wind erosion, shrinking and swelling, and tillage.

facts.text: It measures soil structure, responds to management and serves as a soil-quality indicator because it combines physical, chemical and biological properties.
Aggregate stability directly controls pore-size distribution, and through it water retention, water movement and air movement.
Well-aggregated soil holds a mix of pore sizes: micropores retain and store water, while meso- and macropores let water and air move in.
Soils with good aggregate stability usually take in water faster and are not prone to ponding.
In compacted soil with few aggregates and little pore space, roots grow poorly and can be cut off from stored water and nutrients.
Tillage, machinery traffic and livestock traffic are the main disruptors; reduced or zero tillage, cover crops, perennial crops and organic inputs have been shown to improve aggregation.
Heavy or irregular rainfall, and warmer temperatures that speed decomposition and carbon loss, can lower aggregate stability.
Clay, adsorbed calcium and magnesium, and iron oxides act as cementing agents, while exchangeable sodium lowers stability by promoting dispersion between particles.

entries.title: Tilth: what makes soil fit for a crop

definition.text: The physical condition of a soil, especially how well it suits planting and growing a crop.

facts.text: Tilth depends on how well soil particles form stable aggregates, on moisture, aeration and soil life, and on rates of infiltration and drainage, and it can change quickly.
Soil in good tilth is spongy, with large pores for air and water; roots grow only where tilth allows enough oxygen, and such soil holds a reasonable store of water and nutrients.
Good tilth balances aggregate tensile strength against friability, so aggregates break readily under shallow tilling; high tensile strength gives large cemented clods.
Well-aggregated soil has a range of pore sizes: large pores drain fast and keep air moving in wet periods, while small pores hold water through dry spells.
Tillage aims to improve tilth, but the aggregation it creates is short-lived, and long-term ploughing tends to break down the soil carbon sponge and compact the soil.
In 2021 the soil volume tilled worldwide was estimated at 1840 km3 a year, against 960 km3 a year moved naturally by plant roots and earthworms.
The most stable tilth comes from roots, microbes and earthworms: root exudates feed bacteria that secrete polysaccharides and fungi whose hyphae bind particles into aggregates.
Crop rotations with grass and legume sods, deep-rooted perennials such as alfalfa, and cover crops help rebuild tilth in compacted soils.

entries.text: By one 2021 estimate, tillage turns 1840 km3 of soil a year worldwide, against 960 km3 moved by plant roots and earthworms. All that plowing chases tilth, the physical condition of a soil, especially how well it suits planting and growing a crop. Soil in good tilth is spongy, with large pores for air and water and a reasonable store of water and nutrients. Its aggregates are strong enough to hold together yet friable, crumbling readily under shallow tilling. Too much strength yields large cemented clods. Tilth depends on stable aggregates, moisture, air and soil life, and it can change quickly. Tillage improves it only briefly, and long-term plowing tends to compact the soil. The most stable tilth comes from life: substances released by roots feed bacteria that secrete sugar chains ({{ref:soil-bio-284}}), and fungi whose hyphae bind particles. Grass and legume sods, deep-rooted perennials such as alfalfa, and cover crops help rebuild compacted soil.

entries.title: Soil dispersion: how sodium makes clay wash away

definition.text: The breakdown of soil, especially sodium-rich clay, into separate fine particles that water easily washes away.

facts.text: At high levels, sodium ions break clay platelets apart, so particles repel one another when wet and aggregates disperse, whereas calcium and magnesium promote flocculation.
Dispersion is the opposite of flocculation; both are controlled mainly by soil pH, electrical conductivity and sodium content.
Dispersed soil feeds gully and tunnel erosion, degrades structure, clogs and seals surfaces where particles settle, and makes water turbid.
Dispersive layers usually lie in the subsoil, where clay and sodium concentrate, so they may go unnoticed until disturbance exposes them to running water.
Dispersive soils are commoner in old landscapes, sodium collects low in the landscape, and dispersive subsoils feel soapy and often have prismatic or columnar structure.
The key indicator is the exchangeable sodium percentage, sodium as a share of all cations: above 5% dispersion becomes possible, above 15% highly likely.
Management means avoiding disturbance, keeping vegetation cover, controlling salt, and adding gypsum where the soil has been disturbed.
Under irrigation, the decline of soil structure usually comes from aggregates breaking down and clay dispersing on rapid wetting.

verification.evidence: Another rule of thumb is that the water content at air dryness is about 10 percent of the clay percentage, assuming complete dispersion of clay.
verification.note: the Manual's 10% near the word dispersion refers to another quantity; it gives no exchangeable sodium threshold

sources.title: 1.4: Soil Physics - Geosciences LibreTexts (Digging into Canadian Soils)

entries.text: A dispersive soil can look perfectly sound until digging lets running water reach it. Soil dispersion is the breakdown of soil, especially sodium-rich clay, into separate fine particles that water easily washes away. It is the opposite of flocculation, and soil pH, electrical conductivity and sodium content control both. Sodium drives the damage. At high levels, sodium ions break clay platelets apart, so wet particles repel one another and aggregates fall to pieces. Calcium and magnesium do the reverse, promoting flocculation. The key gauge is the {{ref:soil-chem-018}}, sodium's share of all the cations a soil holds. Above 5%, dispersion becomes possible, and above 15% it is highly likely. Dispersive layers usually hide in the subsoil, where clay and sodium concentrate. They feel soapy and often have prismatic or columnar structure. Such soils are commoner in old landscapes, and sodium collects low in the landscape. Once exposed, dispersed soil feeds gully and tunnel erosion, degrades structure and turns water turbid. Where the particles settle, they clog and seal the surface. Irrigation can bring the same collapse, as aggregates break down and clay disperses on rapid wetting. Management is mostly restraint: avoid disturbance, keep vegetation cover and control salt. Where the soil has already been disturbed, gypsum is added.

entries.title: Soil crust: the hard surface that turns rain away

definition.text: A surface layer of soil, often hardened and platy, that differs from the bulk soil beneath it.

facts.text: Crusts are biological when formed by communities of surface microorganisms, or physical when formed by impacts such as those of raindrops.
Physical crusts result from raindrop or trampling impact and are often harder than uncrusted soil because salts and silica accumulate in them.
Physical crusts often cut water infiltration, hinder plant establishment and, once broken up, erode quickly.
Low infiltration on bare ground is mostly due to a soil crust or surface seal.
Surface sealing lowers infiltration capacity, so in arid and semi-arid regions intense rain readily produces infiltration-excess overland flow.
Better soil structure means less surface crusting and so better seedling emergence.
Calcium exchanging for sodium reduces the particle dispersion, surface crusting and slaking typical of sodic soils.
Coarse organic matter left on the surface helps prevent the breakdown of soil structure and the formation of crusts.

entries.text: When rain will not soak into bare ground, the culprit is usually the surface itself. A soil crust is a surface layer, often hardened and platy, that differs from the soil beneath it. Physical crusts form under the impact of raindrops or trampling. Salts and silica collect in them, so they are often harder than uncrusted soil. They cut infiltration, the soaking of water into soil, hinder plants trying to establish and erode quickly once broken. In arid and semi-arid regions, intense rain soon outpaces a sealed surface, and the excess runs off overland. Better soil structure means less crusting and better seedling emergence. Coarse organic matter left on the surface helps prevent crusts, and on {{ref:soil-chem-009}}, so does calcium swapped for sodium. Other crusts are alive, formed by communities of surface microorganisms, the subject of {{ref:soil-phys-032}}.
entries.text_plain: When rain will not soak into bare ground, the culprit is usually the surface itself. A soil crust is a surface layer, often hardened and platy, that differs from the soil beneath it. Physical crusts form under the impact of raindrops or trampling. Salts and silica collect in them, so they are often harder than uncrusted soil. They cut infiltration, the soaking of water into soil, hinder plants trying to establish and erode quickly once broken. In arid and semi-arid regions, intense rain soon outpaces a sealed surface, and the excess runs off overland. Better soil structure means less crusting and better seedling emergence. Coarse organic matter left on the surface helps prevent crusts, and on Sodic soils, where sodium rules the clay, so does calcium swapped for sodium. Other crusts are alive, formed by communities of surface microorganisms, the subject of Biological soil crust: a living skin on bare ground.

entries.title: Rebuilding the crumb: how farmers repair soil structure

definition.text: Practices that move soil toward a granular, crumb structure by raising its porosity, organic matter and microbial and faunal activity.

facts.text: Better structure means less erosion and overland flow, easier root access to water and nutrients, better seedling emergence through less crusting, and more infiltration and available water.
In cropping systems, wheat yields can rise by 10 kg/ha for every extra millimetre of rain able to infiltrate because of soil structure.
Adding mulch, manure or compost, practised since sedentary farming began, builds stable bridges between mineral particles.
Where warm, moist climates mineralize organic matter too fast, charcoal served instead, as in pre-Columbian terra preta; biochar is the modern version.
Liming increases porosity and aggregation because divalent calcium bridges negatively charged clay and organic molecules, and it also shields organic matter from mineralization.
Advised field practices include pasture phases in rotations, less tillage, not working soil when too wet or dry, and keeping ground cover against raindrop impact.
On irrigated sodic soils, gypsum is applied so calcium displaces sodium and lowers the exchangeable sodium percentage, and rapid wetting is avoided.
In irrigated horticulture, productivity under no-till or minimum tillage usually falls as structure degrades; the few exceptions are associated with high organic matter.

entries.title: Hardsetting soil: soft when wet, hard as it dries

definition.text: A soil that loses its structure when wet and sets hard into a structureless mass as it dries.

facts.text: A hardsetting horizon dries to an almost uniform mass, with occasional cracks usually more than 0.1 m apart, too hard to push a forefinger into.
It is not permanently cemented: it softens when wet, and after flood irrigation or one intense rain it sets hard again on drying.
Such soils can be tilled only in a narrow moisture range, often leave a cloddy surface, restrict seedlings and roots, and shed rain as runoff.
Crusting soils are not necessarily hardsetting: a hardsetting horizon is thicker than a crust, in cultivated soils often as thick as the cultivated layer or more.

entries.text: Some soils go soft in the rain, then dry too hard to push a forefinger into. A hardsetting soil loses its structure when wet and sets into a hard, structureless mass as it dries. Cracks are few, usually more than 0.1 m apart. It is not permanently cemented: after flood irrigation or one intense rain, it softens and then sets hard again. Such soil can be tilled only in a narrow moisture range, and it sheds rain as runoff. It runs deeper than a crust, often as thick as the cultivated layer.

entries.title: Stokes's law: why big grains sink and fine ones linger

definition.text: A law giving the drag force on a sphere moving through a viscous fluid at very small Reynolds numbers.

facts.text: George Gabriel Stokes derived it in 1851 from the Navier–Stokes equations in the limit of small Reynolds numbers.
It assumes laminar flow, no inertia, and smooth, uniform, spherical particles that do not interfere with each other.
To stay within 10% error, velocities must be limited to those giving a Reynolds number below 1.
A settling particle reaches terminal velocity when drag plus buoyancy balance its weight: v = (2/9)(ρp − ρf)gR²/μ.
Because the excess weight grows with R³ and the drag only with R, settling velocity grows with R² and so varies greatly with particle size.
It explains the sedimentation of small particles in water, and why cloud droplets stay aloft until they grow to a critical size.
Hydrometer analysis of fine soils rests on it: a grain's diameter is calculated from how far it falls in a known time.
The pipette method also uses Stokes settling to measure coarse and fine silt in a sediment sample.

entries.text: A grain's sinking speed rises with the square of its radius. That rule comes from Stokes's law. It gives the drag force on a sphere moving through a viscous fluid at very small Reynolds numbers, that is, in slow, smooth flow. Its terminal velocity is then v = (2/9)(ρp − ρf)gR²/μ. The excess weight grows with R³ but the drag only with R, so speed varies greatly with particle size. The law assumes laminar flow, no inertia, and smooth, uniform spheres that do not interfere with each other. To stay within 10% error, the Reynolds number must stay below 1. It explains how small particles settle out of water, and why cloud droplets stay aloft until they grow to a critical size. Soil laboratories rely on it. Hydrometer analysis calculates a grain's diameter from how far it falls in a known time, and {{ref:soil-phys-190}} uses the same settling to measure silt.

entries.title: Hydrophobic soil: ground that sheds water

definition.text: A soil whose particles repel water.

facts.text: It most often forms when fire or hot air drives waxy compounds out of the surface litter; these coat sandy particles in the upper soil, often beneath a layer of ash.

Sandy soils are most prone because large grains have little surface area and are easily coated, though coated silt or clay becomes severely repellent; it is reported on every continent except Antarctica.
Repellency slows infiltration, so runoff and erosion rise, wetting turns patchy and water escapes along preferential paths below the root zone; Australia has seen production losses of up to 80%.
Remedies include claying, adding clay such as calcium-bentonite, which raised one barley yield from 1.7 to 3.4 t/ha, and liming acidic soils to raise their pH.

entries.text: Fire can leave behind soil that sheds water instead of soaking it up. A hydrophobic soil is one whose particles repel water. entries.title: Soil consistency: how soil feels between the fingers

definition.text: The ability of soil to stick to itself or to other objects and to resist deformation and rupture.

facts.text: Consistency is assessed air-dry, moist and wet, and in those states it depends on clay content.
Dry soil is rubbed to test its resistance to crumbling, moist soil is pressed between thumb and finger, and wet soil is judged for stickiness and plasticity.
Standard terms run from loose to extremely hard when dry, loose to extremely firm when moist, and nonsticky to very sticky and nonplastic to very plastic when wet.
Cemented consistency, from calcium carbonate, silica, oxides or salts, hardly changes with moisture and ranges from weakly cemented to indurated, which needs hammer blows to break.
The measures are close to subjective, because they rely on how the soil feels in each state.
Consistency roughly predicts cultivation problems and a soil's ability to support buildings and roads, though more precise strength tests usually precede construction.
It is one of the traits used to describe soil horizons and to group soils into series and families.

entries.text: Squeeze a moist lump between thumb and finger, and its resistance says a good deal about the soil. Standard terms run from loose to extremely hard when dry, and from nonsticky to very sticky when wet. Cemented soils barely change with moisture, and the most cemented, called indurated, need hammer blows to break. Because these judgments rest on feel, they are close to subjective. Still, consistency roughly predicts trouble with cultivation and with supporting buildings and roads.

entries.title: Atterberg limits: the water contents where soil changes state

definition.text: A set of critical water contents (the shrinkage, plastic and liquid limits) that mark where a fine-grained soil changes from one state of consistency to another.

facts.text: Depending on how wet it is, a soil can be solid, semi-solid, plastic or liquid; each state behaves differently, so the boundaries are placed where the soil's behaviour changes.
A fine-grained soil's consistency varies with its water content, and because the transitions are gradual the standard tests define the boundaries by convention.
Albert Atterberg, a Swedish chemist and agronomist, devised the limits in 1911; Arthur Casagrande, a pioneer of soil mechanics, later refined them.
The limits separate silt from clay and different kinds of silts and clays; fine-grained soils are classified mainly by their Atterberg limits rather than by grain size.
The tests are used mostly on clayey and silty soils, because these interact with water, shrinking, swelling and changing in strength as their moisture varies.
The limits are closely related to compressibility, permeability and strength, and since they are simple to measure they serve for empirical estimates of those harder-to-measure properties.
Engineers run them early in design to check that a soil will have enough shear strength and will not change volume too much as it wets and dries.

entries.text: Add water to a dry fine-grained soil, and it passes from solid to semi-solid to plastic to liquid. The Atterberg limits are the critical water contents that mark where it crosses from one of these states to the next. A Swedish chemist and agronomist, the subject of {{ref:soil-hist-011}}, devised them in 1911. He also proposed the first soil particle-size classification, described in {{ref:soil-phys-048}}. Arthur Casagrande, a pioneer of soil mechanics, later refined them. Because the changes are gradual, standard tests fix each boundary by convention. The first of those tests appears in {{ref:soil-phys-022}}. The tests suit clayey and silty soils, which shrink, swell and change strength as their moisture varies. Fine-grained soils are classified mainly by these limits rather than by grain size. The limits are simple to measure and closely tied to compressibility, permeability and strength, so they offer quick estimates of all three.

entries.title: The Unified Soil Classification System: soil in two letters

definition.text: An engineering and geological system that classes soils by texture and grain size, giving each a two-letter symbol.

facts.text: It is the most common engineering soil classification in North America and can be applied to most unconsolidated materials.
Letters name the main material (G gravel, S sand, M silt, C clay, O organic, PT peat), and a second letter gives grading (W or P) or liquid limit (H high, L low).
Soils fall into three major groups: coarse-grained soils such as sands and gravels, fine-grained soils such as silts and clays, and highly organic soils, or peat.
A soil is coarse-grained if more than 50% is retained on the No. 200 (0.075 mm) sieve; the No. 4 sieve, with 4.75 mm openings, separates sand from gravel.
Sands and gravels are divided by grain size and grading, while silts and clays are divided by their Atterberg limits into high- and low-plasticity soils.
With 5–12% fines, both grading and plasticity matter and a dual symbol may be used, such as GW-GM for well-graded gravel with silt.
Under the USCS, silt particles measure 0.002–0.075 mm and sand particles 0.075–4.75 mm.
The European system, ISO 14688, is very similar but adds an intermediate-plasticity class for silts and clays.

conflicts.text: The USCS lead table glosses W (well-graded) as many particles of about the same size and P (poorly graded) as many different sizes.
conflicts.note: Reversed relative to Soil gradation (S:5c50677c4d23) and Soil mechanics (S:43c862203d3f), which define well-graded as a wide range of sizes; the gloss is not used in the facts.

conflicts.text: Gravel gives the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers' number 4 mesh spacing as 4.76 mm.

entries.title: Gravels and sands: the USCS coarse-grained groups
entries.article: Soil mechanics#Classification of sands and gravels

definition.text: The USCS groups for soils with more than half their weight retained on the No. 200 sieve: gravels (G) and sands (S), subdivided by grading and fines content.

facts.text: A coarse soil is gravel if more than 50% of its coarse fraction stays on the No. 4 (4.75 mm) sieve, and sand if at least 50% of it passes.
Clean gravels and sands, with under 5% fines, are well graded (GW, SW) or poorly graded (GP, SP); GW needs Cu ≥ 4 and SW Cu ≥ 6, both with 1 ≤ Cc ≤ 3.
With more than 12% fines they become silty (GM, SM) or clayey (GC, SC), according to whether the fines classify as silt or clay.
A well-graded soil has a wide range of particle sizes; sands and gravels with 5–12% fines get dual symbols such as SW-SC.

entries.title: Krumbein's phi scale, where each step halves the grain

definition.text: A logarithmic grain-size scale, created by W. C. Krumbein in 1934 from the Wentworth scale, that expresses size as minus the base-2 logarithm of diameter in millimetres.

facts.text: Sand spans phi -1 to 4 (2 mm to 62.5 μm), silt phi 4 to 8 (62.5 to 3.91 μm) and clay phi 8 to 10 (3.91 to 0.98 μm).
Above sand come granules (2-4 mm), then pebbles and cobbles, and boulders from 256 mm; some schemes call everything coarser than sand gravel.
The US sand grades divide at whole phi numbers between -1 and +4.
A reference diameter of 1 mm keeps the equation dimensionally consistent.

verification.evidence: For soil classification purposes, weatherable minerals are determined by petrographic analysis (grain counts) of grains 0.02 to 2.0 mm in size (coarse silt to very coarse sand) or other grain size as specified in the Keys to Soil Taxonomy.
verification.note: the glossary's 0.02 mm is the USDA coarse/fine silt boundary, not part of the phi scale

entries.title: How wind and rivers sift sediment by size

definition.text: The removal of a range of particle sizes from a sediment deposit by an agent such as a river or the wind.

facts.text: A sediment accumulation can be characterized by its grain size distribution.
Sorting is quantified by the Inclusive Graphic Standard Deviation, calculated in phi units from percentiles of the grain size distribution such as the 84th.
Values below 0.35 mean very well sorted and values above 4.00 extremely poorly sorted, with well, moderately, poorly and very poorly sorted in between.
Wind is very effective at separating sand from silt and clay.

entries.text: Wind is a superb sieve, very effective at separating sand from silt and clay. Above 4.00 means extremely poorly sorted, with well, moderately, poorly and very poorly sorted in between.

entries.title: One curve that captures a soil's whole spread of sizes

definition.text: A graph of the cumulative percentage of a sample passing each sieve against sieve size on a logarithmic scale.

facts.text: Percent retained on a sieve is its share of the total sample mass; adding each sieve's share to those above it gives the cumulative percent retained.
Cumulative percent passing equals 100% minus cumulative percent retained.
The curve's shape shows the gradation: a dense gradation gives an even curve, a uniform one a steep curve and a gap gradation a flat stretch in the medium sizes.
A soil's gradation is read from the grain size distribution curve produced by laboratory tests.

entries.text: A stack of sieve weighings collapses into one line. The grain-size distribution curve plots the cumulative percentage of a sample passing each sieve against sieve size, on a logarithmic scale. Adding each sieve's share of the mass to the shares above it gives the cumulative percent retained. Subtracting that from 100% gives the percent passing. The curve's shape shows the gradation, or spread of sizes. A dense gradation gives an even curve, a uniform one a steep curve, and a gap gradation a flat stretch in the medium sizes.

entries.title: Friability: soil that crumbles at a touch

definition.text: The tendency of a solid material to break into smaller pieces under stress or contact, especially rubbing.

facts.text: The opposite of friable is indurate; geologists use the pair to describe how well the fragments of soft rocks hold together.
Good tilth balances aggregate tensile strength against friability; high tensile strength gives large cemented clods of low friability.
Soil profile descriptions record it: the Cecil soil's surface horizon is described as a very friable sandy loam.
Māori dug sand and gravel into clay topsoils in Waikato to improve their drainage and friability for growing kūmara and taro.

entries.text: Good soil breaks apart easily in the hand. Friability is that tendency of a solid to break into smaller pieces under stress or contact, especially rubbing. Its opposite is indurate, and geologists use the pair to describe how well the fragments of soft rocks hold together. A good {{ref:soil-phys-039}} balances friability against the tensile strength of aggregates: high strength gives large cemented lumps that barely crumble. Soil descriptions record it. The Cecil soil's surface horizon is a very friable sandy loam. In Waikato, Māori dug sand and gravel into clay topsoils to drain better and crumble more easily for growing kūmara and taro.
entries.text_plain: Good soil breaks apart easily in the hand. Friability is that tendency of a solid to break into smaller pieces under stress or contact, especially rubbing. Its opposite is indurate, and geologists use the pair to describe how well the fragments of soft rocks hold together. A good Tilth: what makes soil fit for a crop balances friability against the tensile strength of aggregates: high strength gives large cemented lumps that barely crumble. Soil descriptions record it. The Cecil soil's surface horizon is a very friable sandy loam. In Waikato, Māori dug sand and gravel into clay topsoils to drain better and crumble more easily for growing kūmara and taro.

entries.title: Liquid limit: where clay starts to flow

definition.text: The water content at which a clayey soil passes from behaving as a plastic solid to behaving as a liquid.

facts.text: The change to liquid behaviour is gradual, and soil at its liquid limit still has some strength: remolded soil there has an undrained shear strength of about 2 kPa.
In Casagrande's cup test, the liquid limit is the moisture content at which 25 drops of the cup close a groove cut in the soil over 12.7 mm.
The fall cone test instead measures how far a standard steel cone sinks into the soil; it is preferred in Europe because it depends less on the operator.
A liquid limit of 50 divides high-plasticity (H) from low-plasticity (L) fine soils in the USCS, and values over 50 suggest significant swelling.

entries.text: Twenty-five drops of a cup can hint at whether a clay will swell. The liquid limit is the water content at which a clayey soil stops behaving as a plastic solid and starts behaving as a liquid. In Casagrande's cup test, it is the moisture content at which 25 drops close a groove cut in the soil over 12.7 mm. Europe prefers the fall cone test, which measures how far a steel cone sinks. Values over 50 suggest significant swelling. The same value of 50 divides high- from low-plasticity fine soils in {{ref:soil-phys-036}}.

entries.title: Plastic limit: the thread that breaks at 3.2 mm

definition.text: The water content below which a soil stops behaving as a plastic solid and becomes brittle, so it can no longer be rolled into a thin thread.

facts.text: It is found by rolling a thread of the soil's fine fraction on a flat, non-porous surface; as the soil dries, the thread starts breaking at larger diameters.
The plastic limit is the gravimetric moisture content at which the thread breaks apart at a diameter of 3.2 mm (about 1/8 inch).
A soil that cannot be rolled down to 3.2 mm at any moisture content is called non-plastic.
Remolded soil at the plastic limit is quite stiff, with an undrained shear strength of about 200 kPa.

conflicts.text: Soil mechanics defines the plastic limit using 3 mm diameter cylinders.
conflicts.note: Atterberg limits gives 3.2 mm (about 1/8 inch); the 3 mm figure may be a rounded value.

entries.title: Liquidity index: where a soil's water sits between limits

definition.text: An index that places a soil's natural water content on the scale between its plastic and liquid limits, LI = (W − PL)/(LL − PL).

facts.text: The liquidity index expresses how water content affects the strength of saturated remolded soil.
At an index of 1 remolded soil sits at its liquid limit with an undrained shear strength of about 2 kPa; at 0 it is at the plastic limit, near 200 kPa.
The companion consistency index, (LL − W)/(LL − PL), is 0 at the liquid limit and 1 at the plastic limit, and turns negative when the soil is in the liquid state.
The liquidity and consistency indices always add up to 1.

entries.text: Where a soil's natural water content, W, falls between its limits says much about how strong it is once remolded. The liquidity index places W on the scale from plastic to liquid limit: LI = (W − PL)/(LL − PL). At 0 the soil sits at its plastic limit, near 200 kPa of {{ref:soil-phys-103}}. At 1 it sits at its liquid limit, with only about 2 kPa. A companion consistency index, (LL − W)/(LL − PL), runs the other way, and the two always add up to 1.

entries.title: Plasticity index: the span where soil stays moldable

definition.text: The span of water contents over which a soil behaves plastically, calculated as the liquid limit minus the plastic limit.

facts.text: Soils are described by plasticity index as non-plastic (0), slightly plastic (below 7), medium plastic (7–17) or highly plastic (above 17).
It indicates how much water the soil particles can absorb and correlates with permeability, compressibility and shear strength; highly plastic clays are less permeable and hard to compact.
A plasticity index above 35 signals high expansion potential in clay soils.
In the USCS, silts and clays are classified by plotting plasticity index against liquid limit on a plasticity chart.

entries.title: Silts and clays: the USCS fine-grained groups
entries.article: Soil mechanics#Classification of silts and clays

definition.text: The USCS groups for soils with 50% or more passing the No. 200 sieve, classed as silts (M) or clays (C) by plotting plasticity index against liquid limit.

facts.text: On the plasticity chart the A-line separates clays (C) from silts (M), and a liquid limit of 50% separates high-plasticity (H) from low-plasticity (L) soils.
The inorganic groups are lean clay (CL), silt (ML), fat clay (CH) and elastic silt (MH); CL needs a plasticity index above 7 and ML one below 4.
Organic silts and clays (OL, OH) are told apart from inorganic ones by how their plasticity and liquid limit change on oven drying; highly organic soils are peat (PT).
Soils whose limits plot in the hatched zone near the chart's origin get the dual symbol CL-ML.

entries.text: Once at least half a soil passes the No. 200 sieve, grain size stops deciding its name. Such soils are classed as silts (M) or clays (C) by plotting plasticity index against liquid limit. The A-line splits clays from silts, and a liquid limit of 50% splits high (H) from low (L) plasticity. The inorganic groups are lean clay (CL), silt (ML), fat clay (CH) and elastic silt (MH). CL needs a plasticity index above 7, and ML one below 4. Organic silts and clays (OL, OH) are told apart by changes on oven drying.

entries.title: Clay activity: same clay content, different behavior

definition.text: The ratio of a soil's plasticity index to its clay-size fraction, used to judge how active its clay is.

facts.text: Clay with an activity below 0.75 is termed inactive, above 1.25 active, and in between normal.
Clay minerals differ greatly in their limits: montmorillonite has liquid limits of 100–900%, against 60–120% for illite and 30–110% for kaolinite.
In a table of example soils, a heavy clay with 72% clay had a liquid limit of 67 and a plasticity index of 40, while a well-graded loamy sand was non-plastic.

entries.text: Two soils with the same amount of clay can behave very differently, because {{ref:soil-chem-079}} differ. Clay activity is the ratio of a soil's plasticity index to its clay-size fraction, used to judge how active its clay is. Below 0.75 the clay is inactive, above 1.25 active, and in between normal. {{ref:soil-chem-093}} has liquid limits of 100–900%, against 60–120% for {{ref:soil-chem-094}} and 30–110% for {{ref:soil-chem-088}}. The ratio links clay as a size to clay as a mineral, the split explained in {{ref:soil-phys-054}}.

Montmorillonite, the clay that swells tenfold has liquid limits of 100–900%, against 60–120% for Illite, the potassium clay that will not swell and 30–110% for Kaolinite, the white clay of china and the tropics. The ratio links clay as a size to clay as a mineral, the split explained in Two meanings of clay: a size and a mineral.

entries.title: Shrinkage limit: the point where drying clay stops shrinking

definition.text: The water content below which further drying no longer makes a soil shrink.

facts.text: The shrinkage limit is used much less often than the liquid and plastic limits.
Reported shrinkage limits differ by clay mineral: 8.5–15% for montmorillonite, 15–17% for illite and 25–29% for kaolinite.

entries.text: A drying clay shrinks, but only up to a point. The shrinkage limit is the water content below which further drying no longer makes a soil shrink. It is used much less often than the liquid and plastic limits. Its value depends on the kind of clay. Reported shrinkage limits run 8.5–15% for {{ref:soil-chem-093}}, 15–17% for {{ref:soil-chem-094}} and 25–29% for {{ref:soil-chem-088}}. So the last of these clays stops shrinking while it still holds far more water than the first does.

entries.title: Sizing soil grains by the way they bend light

definition.text: An optical method that measures particle-size distribution from the way particles, dispersed in a liquid or as dry powder, bend light.

facts.text: The diffraction angle depends on particle size, so the pattern records the mix of sizes; it is analysed with Mie or Fraunhofer theory, Fraunhofer often being recommended for natural soils.
Fraunhofer theory treats only diffraction at the particle's edge and needs no optical data; Mie theory adds refraction, reflection and absorption but needs the material's complex refractive index.
The smaller the particle, the larger the scattering angle; with Mie theory the lower detection limit is thought to be around 10 nm.
Results are volume-weighted equivalent spherical diameters, summarised as the median D50, the D10 and D90, and the span, (D90 – D10)/D50.
It is fast and cost-effective, handles very small samples such as forensic ones, and built-in dispersion lets dry samples skip the preparation that sieving and sedimentation require.
With samples well dispersed, one technique covers the whole size range, including silt and clay, with no need to combine two methods.
Both theories assume spherical particles, so platy clay is sized by its plate cross-section and usually measured larger than by sedimentation analysis.
Compared with the traditional sieve-pipette method it is fast, reproducible and needs small samples, and it gave better precision.

entries.text: A pinch of soil from a crime scene can be sized with a beam of light. Laser diffraction particle sizing measures particle-size distribution from the way dispersed particles bend light. The angle depends on size, so the pattern records the whole mix, analyzed with Mie or Fraunhofer theory. It is fast and cost-effective, and one well-dispersed run covers the whole size range, silt and clay included. Both theories assume spheres, though. Flat clay plates are sized by their broad face and usually read larger than by sedimentation.

entries.title: Crumbs within crumbs: the aggregate hierarchy

definition.text: The idea that soil aggregates form in levels, larger and less dense aggregates being built from smaller, denser ones.

facts.text: Primary particles join into sub-microaggregates and microaggregates below 250 μm and macroaggregates above 250 μm.

Organic binders are grouped as transient (polysaccharides), temporary (fungal hyphae and roots) and persistent (resistant aromatic compounds held by polyvalent cations, and strongly adsorbed polymers).
Temporary binders stabilize macroaggregates, while transient and persistent binders stabilize microaggregates.
Organic matter's role is hard to pin down: only part of it binds aggregates, beyond a threshold more adds no stability, and in some soils it is not the main binder.

conflicts.text: Macroaggregates are put above 2000 μm, mesoaggregates at 20-250 μm and microaggregates at 2-20 μm.
conflicts.note: Same page, Biological Factors section; the Factors section puts the macroaggregate limit at 250 μm.

conflicts.text: Microaggregates are given as 20-250 μm.
conflicts.note: Soil formation page; conflicts with the 2-20 μm microaggregate class above.

entries.text: A soil crumb is usually built of smaller crumbs, which are built of smaller ones still. The aggregate hierarchy is the idea that aggregates form in levels, larger and looser ones made from smaller, denser ones. Particles join into microaggregates below 250 μm, and these into macroaggregates above 250 μm. Fungal hyphae and roots, the temporary binders, hold macroaggregates together. Transient long-chain sugars and persistent compounds hold microaggregates. Yet organic matter's role is hard to pin down, and in some soils it is not the main binder.

entries.title: Sieving and soaking: testing how tough crumbs are

definition.text: Tests of how well soil aggregates survive stresses like those from water, wind or machinery, made at different aggregate size scales.

facts.text: Wet methods are usually more relevant because they mimic water erosion; dry methods suit arid regions, where wind erosion dominates.
Wet sieving slowly wets 2-4 mm aggregates, runs the sieve nest in a wet sieving apparatus at 30 rotations per minute for about 10 minutes, and reports a mean weight diameter.
The dry method sieves 0.92-1.68 mm aggregates in a rotary cylinder and reports the percentage of aggregates larger than 0.42 mm.
Slaking tests score how well aggregates hold together when submerged in water; one version uses a smartphone app in the field.

entries.text: Soil crumbs are tested the way nature attacks them, with water or with wind. Arid regions, where wind erosion dominates, use a dry method that sieves 0.92-1.68 mm aggregates and reports the share above 0.42 mm.

entries.title: Slaking: when trapped air bursts soil crumbs

definition.text: The process by which earth materials, such as soil aggregates, disintegrate and crumble when exposed to moisture.

facts.text: Water entering aggregates displaces air from their pores, and aggregates with trapped air burst: a direct mechanical destruction of structure by water.
Slaking rises with the rate of wetting: the faster the wetting, the more slaking occurs.
On sloping or bare ground slaking often leads to erosion; re-vegetating bare soil and limiting disturbance on slopes prevent it.
Slaking can affect the B horizon too, becoming a problem once the A horizon is disturbed or eroded; calcium replacing sodium reduces slaking in sodic soils.

entries.text: Drop a dry crumb of soil into water, and the air trapped inside can blow it apart. That is slaking, the break-up of aggregates when entering water displaces air from pores and bursts aggregates holding trapped air. It is purely mechanical, one of the direct ways water destroys soil structure. In the field, slaking follows raindrop impact, so ground cover protects against both. Stable aggregates resist it, along with crusting and erosion. In {{ref:soil-chem-009}}, calcium that replaces sodium on particle surfaces eases slaking, dispersion and crusting alike.

entries.title: Soil resistivity: how soil resists electric current

definition.text: A measure of how strongly a soil resists the flow of an electric current.

facts.text: Resistivity affects how fast buried metal and concrete structures corrode.
Wetter soil or a higher electrolyte concentration lowers resistivity, raising conductivity and the rate of corrosion.
Values typically range from about 1 to 100000 Ω·m, the extremes being saline soils and dry soils over crystalline rocks.

entries.text: Soil carries electric current, and how easily it does so affects how fast buried metal and concrete corrode. Soil resistivity is a measure of how strongly a soil resists the flow of that current. Wetter soil, or soil with a higher electrolyte concentration, has lower resistivity. Current then flows more easily, and corrosion speeds up. Values typically range from about 1 to 100,000 Ω·m. Saline soils sit at the low end, and dry soils over crystalline rocks at the high end.

entries.title: Two numbers that grade a gravel or a sand
entries.article: Soil gradation#Calculating the coefficients of uniformity and curvature

definition.text: Two values, Cu and Cc, calculated from grain diameters on a soil's size-distribution curve and compared with published limits to grade a coarse soil.

facts.text: Cu, a crude shape parameter, is calculated from D60 and D10, the grain diameters at which 60% and 10% of the sample passes.
Cc, a shape parameter, combines D30, D10 and D60, the grain diameters at 30%, 10% and 60% passing.
Under the USCS, a gravel is well graded (GW) when Cu > 4 and 1 < Cc < 3; otherwise it is poorly graded (GP).
A sand is well graded (SW) when Cu ≥ 6 and 1 < Cc < 3; otherwise it is poorly graded (SP).

entries.text: Two numbers sort coarse soils into well graded and poorly graded. The coefficients of uniformity and curvature, Cu and Cc, come from grain diameters on a size-distribution curve. D60 and D10 are the diameters at which 60% and 10% of a sample passes. Cu, a crude shape parameter, uses D60 and D10; Cc adds D30 to the pair. A gravel with Cu above 4 and Cc between 1 and 3 is well graded, GW; otherwise it is GP. A sand needs Cu of 6 or more, with the same Cc band, to be SW; otherwise it is SP. The cutoffs belong to {{ref:soil-phys-036}}.

entries.title: Timing a water drop: measuring how much soil repels water

definition.text: Tests that rate how strongly a soil repels water, usually starting with the time one water drop takes to soak in.

facts.text: In the water drop penetration time test, soaking in under 5 seconds means not repellent, up to 1 minute slightly repellent, 1–10 minutes repellent, and over 10 minutes severely repellent.
A soil is judged hydrophobic when the contact angle between water and soil exceeds 90°.

The molarity of ethanol droplet test applies ethanol solutions of falling surface tension until one soaks in within 10 seconds; an index of 1 or less means non-repellent, 2.2 or more severely repellent.
Water entry pressure, linked to both the degree of repellency and pore size, is another indicator of infiltration.

entries.title: Specific surface area: why tiny grains do the most work

definition.text: The surface area of soil particles relative to their amount, defined as surface area per unit mass.

facts.text: Specific surface area, together with the particles' unbalanced electric charges, sets their role in soil fertility as measured by cation exchange capacity.
Sand has the least specific surface area and is least active, silt is intermediate, and clay is the most active.
Clay minerals form thin plates and typically have 10 to 1,000 square metres of surface per gram.
Clay's very high specific surface area and many negative charges give soil its high capacity to retain water and nutrients.
The water a soil holds at field capacity depends on the specific surface area of its particles.
Particles of one textural class share properties tied to surface area, such as moisture retention, but not those tied to composition, such as cation exchange capacity.
Much of a soil's reactivity relates to the surface area available, and surface area per unit weight rises as average particle size falls.
Table values: very coarse sand (2.00-1.00 mm) has 90 particles per gram and 11 cm2/g; fine sand (0.25-0.10 mm) 46,000 and 91 cm2/g; silt 5,776,000 and 454 cm2/g.

conflicts.text: Physical properties of soil describes specific surface area as the surface-area-to-volume ratio of soil particles.
conflicts.note: Soil mechanics defines it per unit mass (S:c2691e02484c), which the definition uses.

Surface area per unit weight rises as average particle size falls, so sand has the least and is least active, silt is intermediate and clay is the most active. The mineral crystals in clay form thin plates and typically have 10 to 1,000 square metres of surface per gram. In one table, very coarse sand (2.00-1.00 mm) has 90 particles per gram and 11 cm2/g, fine sand (0.25-0.10 mm) 46,000 and 91 cm2/g, and silt 5,776,000 and 454 cm2/g. entries.title: Soil as solid, liquid and gas

definition.text: Soil as a combination of solid, liquid and gas phases whose interaction determines how it behaves.

facts.text: The solid phase is mineral particles (rocks, gravel, sand, silt, clay) or organic matter, and ideally takes up about 50% of the soil volume.
The liquid phase is soil water plus dissolved nutrients, chemicals and gases, together forming the soil solution; both its quantity and its chemical composition matter.
The gaseous phase is soil air, commonly nitrogen, oxygen, water vapour and carbon dioxide; ideally about 25% of soil volume, but highly dynamic.
Mass-volume relationships among the three phases define porosity, bulk density and the shares of water and air in pore space.

sources.title: 1.4: Soil Physics - Geosciences LibreTexts (Digging into Canadian Soils)

entries.text: Soil is never just dirt; it is three things at once. It combines solid, liquid and gas phases, and their interaction determines how it behaves. The solid phase is mineral particles (rocks, gravel, sand, silt, clay) or organic matter, and ideally takes up about 50% of the volume. The liquid phase is soil water plus dissolved nutrients, chemicals and gases, together forming the soil solution; both its quantity and its chemical composition matter. The gaseous phase is soil air, commonly nitrogen, oxygen, water vapour and carbon dioxide. Ideally it is about 25% of volume, but it is highly dynamic. Mass-volume relationships among the three phases define porosity, {{ref:soil-phys-060}} and the shares of water and air in pore space.

entries.title: Sizing soil grains without measuring them

definition.text: The collective name for laboratory techniques that measure the size range or mean size of particles in a powder or liquid sample.

facts.text: Methods use light, ultrasound, electric fields, gravity or centrifugation, and most infer size from another measurement rather than measuring diameters directly.
Irregular particles are sized as an equivalent sphere: sieving gives a volume-based diameter, optical methods an area-based one.
Different methods are not expected to give identical results, so the method should match the use the data will be put to.
Sieving has long been the choice for soil texture, but laser diffraction is increasingly used because it is faster and highly reproducible.

entries.text: Most ways of sizing soil particles never measure a diameter directly. Particle size analysis is the collective name for laboratory techniques that find the size range or mean size of particles in a sample. They use light, ultrasound, electric fields, gravity or centrifugation, and most infer size from another measurement. Irregular grains are treated as equivalent spheres: sieving gives a volume-based diameter, optical methods an area-based one. Different methods are therefore not expected to agree, so the method should match the use the data will serve. Sieving has long been the choice for soil texture. Laser diffraction is gaining ground because it is faster and highly reproducible.

entries.title: Agrophysics: physics brought to the farm

definition.text: A science on the border of agronomy and physics that studies agroecosystems with the methods of the physical sciences.

facts.text: It is close to biophysics but restricted to the physics of the plants, animals, soil and atmosphere involved in farming.
It grew out of soil physics and first studied relations within the soil, then widened to crop properties and the quality and safety of food and raw farm produce.
Research centres include the Institute of Agrophysics of the Polish Academy of Sciences in Lublin and the Agrophysical Research Institute in St. Petersburg.
Soil science lists agrophysics among its related disciplines.

entries.title: Clods, the lumps that machines make

definition.text: A mass of soil formed artificially by mechanical disturbance such as cultivation, as opposed to a naturally formed ped.

facts.text: Clods result from tillage, excavation and heavy machinery used on wet soil; compaction gives hard clods instead of soft peds.
Tilling wetter or drier than the optimum water content produces large clods, and hardsetting soils give a cloddy surface when tilled.
Harrowing breaks up clods to create a tilth suitable for sowing.
Clods of 2 to 100 mm make up the second of the four classes of soil-surface roughness.

entries.text: Nature builds peds; people make clods. A clod is a mass of soil formed by mechanical disturbance such as cultivation, unlike the naturally formed ped. Plowing, excavation and heavy machinery on wet soil all produce them, and compaction gives hard clods where soft peds would be. Tilling wetter or drier than the best moisture raises large clods, and hardsetting soils turn cloddy when tilled. Harrowing breaks clods up into a tilth fit for sowing. Clods of 2 to 100 mm form the second of the four classes of {{ref:soil-water-141}}.

entries.title: The pipette method: sampling silt as it settles

definition.text: A laboratory sedimentation method that measures the proportions of coarse and fine silt in a sample from settling rates given by Stokes' law.

facts.text: Like the hydrometer, it is a sedimentation analysis widely used in soil engineering and geology to classify sediments.
It sizes the silt and clay finer than 60 μm that pass the bottom sieve of a sieve analysis.
Compared with the traditional sieve-pipette method, laser diffraction analysis gave better precision.

entries.text: Grains finer than 60 μm slip through the bottom sieve of a sieve analysis. The pipette method takes over from there. It is a laboratory settling method that measures the proportions of coarse and fine silt in a sample, using settling rates given by Stokes's law. Like the hydrometer, it is widely used in soil engineering and geology to classify sediments. It now has a rival. Compared with the traditional sieve-pipette method, laser diffraction analysis gave better precision.

entries.title: Porosity: how much of a soil is empty space

definition.text: The share of a material's total volume taken up by empty spaces, given as a fraction from 0 to 1 or as a percentage.

facts.text: In geology, hydrology and soil science it describes the void fraction of a porous medium such as rock or sediment, whose voids may hold air or water.
Written ϕ or n, it ranges from less than 0.005 in solid granite to more than 0.5 in peat and clay.
It can be calculated from bulk density and particle density; when the voids hold air, porosity is one minus bulk density divided by particle density.
Well-sorted materials are more porous than poorly sorted ones of similar size, in which small particles fill the gaps between larger ones.
A few fine grains lodged in the pores can sharply cut porosity and hydraulic conductivity while making up only a small share of the volume.
The porosity of a rock or sedimentary layer governs how much water or hydrocarbon it may hold.
Sediment porosity falls exponentially with burial depth as it compacts, a relationship described by the Athy (1930) equation.

entries.text: Solid granite is almost all rock, with less than 0.005 of its volume left empty. Peat and clay can be more than half empty space. That share is porosity: the fraction of a material's total volume taken up by voids, given from 0 to 1 or as a percentage. Geologists, hydrologists and soil scientists use it for any of the materials described in {{ref:soil-phys-172}}, such as rock or sediment, whose voids may hold air or water. It is written ϕ or n. Porosity can be worked out from two densities. When the voids hold air, it equals one minus a ratio of two densities. On top is the density of the whole soil, in {{ref:soil-phys-060}}; below is that of its solid grains alone, in {{ref:soil-phys-062}}. Sorting matters as much as grain size. A well-sorted material is more porous than a poorly sorted one of similar size, because in the mixed one small particles fill the gaps between larger ones. A few fine grains lodged in the pores can sharply cut porosity, and the ease of water flow, while making up only a small share of the volume. In rock and sedimentary layers, porosity governs how much water or hydrocarbon they may hold. It also falls with depth. As buried sediment compacts, its porosity drops exponentially, a pattern described by the Athy (1930) equation.

entries.title: Soil physics: the science of grains, water and air

definition.text: The study of the physical properties and processes of soil, covering its solid, liquid and gas phases.

facts.text: It draws on physics, physical chemistry, engineering and meteorology and applies them to practical problems in agriculture, ecology and engineering.
Its results are used for management and prediction in both natural and managed ecosystems.
The soil physical processes that shape crop response to drainage include aeration, structure, stability and temperature.
Franklin Hiram King has been called the father of soil physics in the United States; he studied water-holding capacity, aeration and the movement of water in soils.
Edgar Buckingham (1867–1940) worked out the theory of gas diffusion in soil and of water flow in the vadose zone.
Willard Gardner was the first to measure capillary potential with porous cups and manometers, and predicted the moisture distribution above a water table.
Lorenzo A. Richards described water transport in unsaturated soil and measured soil water potential with a tensiometer.
John R. Philip found an analytical solution for soil water transport, and Martinus van Genuchten developed water retention and hydraulic conductivity functions.

entries.text: How fast water sinks into a field, how air reaches a root, how warm the ground gets: these are questions for soil physics. It studies the physical properties and processes of soil across its solid, liquid and gas phases. The field borrows from physics, physical chemistry, engineering and meteorology, and turns them on practical problems in agriculture, ecology and engineering. Its results guide management and prediction in natural and managed ecosystems alike. F. H. King ({{ref:soil-hist-020}}), called the father of soil physics in the United States, studied how soils hold water, take in air and move water. Edgar Buckingham (1867–1940) worked out the theory of how gases diffuse through soil and how water flows in the unsaturated ground above the groundwater. Willard Gardner first measured capillary potential with porous cups and manometers. L. A. Richards ({{ref:soil-hist-023}}) described flow in unsaturated soil and measured how tightly soil holds its water with the instrument described in {{ref:soil-water-221}}. Later, John R. Philip found an analytical solution for soil water transport, and Martinus van Genuchten built functions for how soil holds and conducts water.

entries.title: Soil mechanics: how a mix of grains, water and air behaves

definition.text: The branch of soil physics and applied mechanics that describes how soils behave.

facts.text: Unlike fluid or solid mechanics, it deals with a mixed material of fluids, usually air and water, and particles such as clay, silt, sand and gravel, plus organic solids.
Together with rock mechanics it is the theoretical basis of geotechnical engineering and engineering geology.
It analyses deformation of, and fluid flow within, structures built on, made of or buried in soil, such as foundations, retaining walls, dams and pipelines.
Its principles are also used in agricultural, coastal and geophysical engineering and in hydrology.
Normal stresses are shared between pore fluid and particles, but neither gas nor liquid resists shear, so shear resistance comes from friction and interlocking of the particles.
Engineering classification tests use dried, sieved and remoulded samples, so they miss the effects of soil structure or fabric and of pore size and pore fluid distribution.

entries.text: A dam, a pipeline and a house foundation all rest on the same question: how will the soil behave? Soil mechanics is the branch of soil physics and applied mechanics that answers it. Unlike fluid or solid mechanics, it deals with a mixture: fluids, usually air and water, among particles of clay, silt, sand and gravel, plus organic solids. With rock mechanics it underpins engineering geology and the field traced in {{ref:soil-phys-167}}. It analyses how structures built on, made of or buried in soil deform, and how fluids flow inside them, from foundations and retaining walls to dams and pipelines. Agricultural, coastal and geophysical engineering and hydrology use its principles too. One idea runs through it. A load pressing down on soil is shared between the pore fluid and the particles. Neither gas nor liquid resists shear, though, so resistance to sliding comes from friction and interlocking of the grains. Standard classification tests miss part of the story. They use dried, sieved and remoulded samples, so the soil's structure and its pattern of pore sizes and fluids are lost.

entries.title: Bulk density: weighing soil with its holes included

definition.text: The mass of a soil or other particulate material divided by the whole volume it occupies, including the spaces between and within its particles.

facts.text: Unlike particle density, which excludes voids, bulk density depends on packing and changes with handling: a disturbed powder settles to a higher value.
In soil it depends mainly on the mineral make-up and the degree of compaction.
Quartz has a density of about 2.65 g/cm3, but the dry bulk density of a mineral soil is normally about half that, between 1.0 and 1.6 g/cm3.
Soils rich in organic carbon and some friable clays fall below 1.0 g/cm3, and peat soils range from 0.02 to 0.98 g/cm3.
Dry bulk density is inversely related to porosity: the more pore space a soil has, the lower its bulk density.
Measured at a standard moisture content, bulk density estimates compaction; a European Union study of the top 0-20 cm found croplands almost 1.5 times denser than woodlands.
A high value points either to compaction or to a mix of textures in which small particles fill the voids between coarse ones.
Humus lowers bulk density, and pedotransfer functions combine bulk density with particle size to estimate properties such as hydraulic conductivity.

conflicts.text: Most soils have a dry bulk density between 1.1 and 1.6 g/cm3.
conflicts.note: The Soil article gives 1.1 as the lower bound of the typical range; Bulk density (S:b0ea2daf5037) and Pore space in soil (S:886e31685869) give 1.0.

verification.title: Soil bulk density assessment in Europe
verification.evidence: In the 0–20 cm depth, croplands have 1.5 times higher bulk density (mean: 1.26 g cm−3) compared to woodlands (mean: 0.83 g cm−3).

entries.text: Quartz has a density of about 2.65 g/cm3, yet the dry bulk density of a mineral soil is normally about half that, between 1.0 and 1.6 g/cm3. Bulk density is the mass of a soil divided by the whole volume it occupies, counting the spaces between and within its particles. That last clause separates it from {{ref:soil-phys-062}}, which leaves the voids out. Because it counts the gaps, bulk density depends on packing and changes with handling: a disturbed powder settles to a higher value. In soil it depends mainly on the mineral make-up and on how compacted the soil is. Organic soils sit at the light end. Soils rich in organic carbon and some crumbly clays fall below 1.0 g/cm3, and peat soils range from 0.02 to 0.98 g/cm3. Dark, well-decomposed organic matter lowers it too. The rule is simple: the more pore space a soil has, the lower its dry bulk density. A high value points either to compaction or to a mix of textures in which small particles fill the voids between coarse ones. Measured at a standard moisture content, bulk density estimates compaction. A European Union study of the top 0-20 cm found croplands almost 1.5 times denser than woodlands. Simple formulas also combine bulk density with particle size to estimate properties such as how readily water flows through soil.

entries.title: The soil matrix, the solid frame around the pores

definition.text: The solid phase of a soil: the mineral particles and organic matter that make it up.

facts.text: A soil is made of the solid matrix, a pore space holding the soil atmosphere, and a liquid phase, the soil solution, holding water and dissolved substances.
Matrix particles are classed by size and by mineralogy; texture largely sets properties such as hydraulic conductivity and water potential, but mineralogy can strongly modify them.
Gravel, sand and silt usually inherit their minerals from the parent material; quartz is the most common because it resists chemical weathering.
Clay, with its high specific surface area and unbalanced negative charges, is the most active mineral component, so its mineralogy matters most.
Clay minerals are secondary minerals, precipitates whose make-up differs from their parent materials, and they keep forming as long as the soil exists.
Humus is the organic component of the matrix; on a dry weight basis its cation exchange capacity is many times that of clay.
Nutrients held in exchangeable form on clay colloids and organic matter in the matrix are an accessible reservoir of plant nutrients such as K, Ca, Mg, P and Zn.
Water moving down through the matrix can carry fine clay from the upper to the lower part of a soil, the process called lessivage.

entries.text: The soil matrix is the solid phase of a soil: the mineral particles and organic matter that make it up. Around it lie the pore space, holding the soil atmosphere, and the soil solution, holding water and dissolved substances. Matrix particles are classed by size and by mineral make-up. Texture largely sets how water moves and is held, but mineralogy can strongly modify both. Gravel, sand and silt usually inherit their minerals from the parent material, most often weathering-resistant quartz. Clay is the most active part, with a high specific surface area and unbalanced negative charges, so its mineralogy matters most. Its minerals are secondary, precipitates that keep forming as long as the soil exists. The organic part of the matrix, weight for weight, holds many times more exchangeable positive ions than clay. Nutrients held this way, such as K, Ca, Mg, P and Zn, form a ready reservoir for plants.

entries.title: Pore space, where soil keeps its water and air

definition.text: The part of a soil's volume not filled by its solid mineral and organic particles, which holds the soil's water and air.

facts.text: Total porosity is the pore volume divided by the total volume, often given in percent; in unsaturated soil the pores are shared by air and water.
Porosity depends on the soil's minerals and on sorting: a sandy soil is more porous than a silty sand, because silt fills the gaps between sand grains.
Pure sand resists compaction and raises porosity, but not when mixed with finer minerals that fill the voids between its grains.
Macropores and cracks largely control infiltration rates, preferential flow, hydraulic conductivity and evapotranspiration, and strongly affect gas exchange and soil respiration.
When water infiltrates, the largest cracks and pores fill first, mostly by gravity; smaller pores fill slowly by capillary forces and can trap air.
Hydraulic conductivity, the ease of water movement through pores, depends on permeability, compaction and degree of saturation and is calculated with Darcy's law.
Pore space is the habitat of roots, soil fauna and microbes, and growing roots and burrowing animals create networks of connected pores.
Microbial cells and the slime they produce can block soil pores, a process called bioclogging.

entries.text: Roots, burrowing animals and microbes all live in the gaps. Pore space is the part of a soil's volume not filled by solid mineral and organic particles, and it holds the soil's water and air. Total porosity is the pore volume divided by the total volume, often given in percent; in unsaturated soil, air and water share it. A sandy soil is more porous than a silty sand, because silt fills the gaps between sand grains. When water soaks in, the largest cracks and pores fill first, mostly by gravity. Smaller pores fill slowly by capillary forces and can trap air. Large pores and cracks largely control how fast water enters and moves. They also strongly affect gas exchange and the breathing of soil life. The ease of water movement through pores, {{ref:soil-water-193}}, depends on compaction and on how full the pores are. Roots and burrowing animals carve networks of connected pores. Microbial cells and their slime can also block pores, a process described in {{ref:soil-water-241}}.

entries.title: Soil compaction: squeezing the air out of the ground

definition.text: The densification of soil under applied stress as air is pushed out of the pores between its grains.

facts.text: When water rather than air is squeezed out, the process is consolidation; in soil science and agronomy compaction usually mixes the two and can be driven by suction as water evaporates.
It is normally caused by heavy machinery, but the passage of animal feet can also compact soil.
Compacted soils absorb less rainfall, so runoff and erosion increase.
Pressed-together grains leave little space for the air and water roots need, and burrowing animals find the denser soil hard to penetrate.
In one cotton field, tilled surface soil had a bulk density of 1.3 g/cm3 and 51% pore space, while wheel-trafficked inter-rows had 1.67 g/cm3 and 37%.
Recovery depends on climate, mineralogy and fauna; high shrink–swell soils such as Vertisols recover quickly where dry spells shrink and crack them.
Kaolinite clays, which do not crack as they dry, cannot recover unaided unless earthworms or other ground-dwelling animals live in them, as in the Cecil soil series.
Soil compaction is one of the factors that reduce groundwater recharge.

entries.text: In one cotton field, the tilled surface soil had a bulk density of 1.3 g/cm3 and 51% pore space. Between the rows, where wheels ran, it reached 1.67 g/cm3, and pore space fell to 37%. That is soil compaction: the densification of soil under applied stress as air is pushed out of the pores between its grains. When water rather than air is squeezed out, the process is consolidation, described in {{ref:soil-phys-110}}. In soil science and agronomy the word compaction usually covers both, and suction as water evaporates can drive it too. Heavy machinery is the usual cause, though the passage of animal feet can also compact soil. The damage follows from the lost pores. Pressed-together grains leave little room for the air and water roots need, and burrowing animals struggle to penetrate the denser soil. Compacted soil absorbs less rainfall, so runoff and erosion increase and less water recharges the groundwater. Recovery depends on climate, mineralogy and the animals living in the soil. Soils that shrink and swell strongly, such as those in {{ref:soil-class-106}}, recover quickly where dry spells shrink and crack them. Clays built of a mineral that does not crack as it dries, described in {{ref:soil-chem-088}}, cannot recover unaided. They need earthworms or other ground-dwelling animals living in them, as in the Cecil soils.

When water rather than air is squeezed out, the process is consolidation, described in Consolidation: the slow squeeze that sinks buildings. In soil science and agronomy the word compaction usually covers both, and suction as water evaporates can drive it too. Soils that shrink and swell strongly, such as those in Vertisols, the clay soils that plow themselves, recover quickly where dry spells shrink and crack them. Clays built of a mineral that does not crack as it dries, described in Kaolinite, the white clay of china and the tropics, cannot recover unaided. They need earthworms or other ground-dwelling animals living in them, as in the Cecil soils.

entries.title: The hidden damage under farm fields

definition.text: The rise in bulk density, or fall in porosity, of farmland soil under externally or internally applied loads, also called soil structure degradation.

facts.text: It can harm nearly all physical, chemical and biological properties and functions of soil, and with erosion it is called the costliest and most serious environmental problem of conventional agriculture.
Heavy machinery and poor management can compact the subsoil, forming impermeable layers that restrict water and nutrient cycles.
Unlike salinization or erosion it is mainly a hidden, sub-surface problem, so special identification methods are needed to locate and manage it.
On site it cuts crop growth, yield and quality; off site it adds runoff, erosion, greenhouse gas emissions, eutrophication, reduced groundwater recharge and biodiversity loss.
Plough-pans were linked to compaction before farming was mechanized, but modern farming techniques have raised the risk of harmful compaction.
In 1991 compaction was estimated to account for 4% (68.3 million hectares) of human-caused soil degradation worldwide.
In 2013 it was a major cause of degradation in Europe (about 33 million ha), Africa (18 million ha), Asia (10 million ha) and Australia (4 million ha).
In Europe about 32% of subsoils are highly and 18% moderately vulnerable to compaction.

entries.title: Pore water pressure, the push of water between grains

definition.text: The pressure of the groundwater held in the pores between the particles of a soil or rock.

facts.text: Below the water table it is measured with piezometers and is generally close to hydrostatic, rising linearly with depth where the water is not flowing.
The water table lies at the depth where the water pressure equals atmospheric pressure.
In the unsaturated, or vadose, zone it is set by capillarity and called tension, suction or matric pressure; tensiometers measure it through a porous ceramic cup in contact with the soil.
It is essential for finding the stress state of soil, because Terzaghi's effective stress is the total stress minus the pore water pressure.

Its components include hydrostatic pressure from the weight of overlying material, osmotic pressure from uneven ion concentrations, and adsorption pressure from water films that draw particles together.
ISO 11276:1995 sets out tensiometer methods for measuring it in unsaturated and saturated soil and defines it as the sum of matric and pneumatic pressures.
Excess pore water pressure can force blocks out at the base of river banks, and rising pore pressure on slopes helps burst the surface layer in frost boils.

entries.text: Water held between soil grains pushes back. Pore water pressure is the pressure of the groundwater in the pores between the particles of a soil or rock. Deep in saturated ground it is measured with piezometers. Where the water is not flowing it is close to hydrostatic, rising steadily with depth. The surface where it equals atmospheric pressure is the {{ref:soil-water-247}}. Above that level, capillarity sets the pressure, and it is called tension, suction or matric pressure. Instruments with a porous ceramic cup in contact with the soil measure it there, by methods set out in ISO 11276:1995. The pressure has several parts: the weight of overlying material, {{ref:soil-chem-216}} from uneven ion concentrations, and pressure from water films, held by {{ref:soil-chem-145}}, that draw grains together. It matters because the load carried by the grains, {{ref:soil-phys-100}}, is the total stress minus the pore water pressure. Too much of it can force blocks out at the base of river banks, and rising pressure on slopes helps burst the surface layer, as in {{ref:soil-phys-160}}.
