entries.title: The darcy, a unit for how easily fluids pass

definition.text: A unit of permeability, with the millidarcy as its thousandth, named after Henry Darcy.

facts.text: A medium of 1 darcy lets 1 cm³/s of a fluid with viscosity 1 cP pass through 1 cm² under a pressure gradient of 1 atm/cm.
1 darcy equals 9.869233×10−13 m², usually approximated as 1 μm².
Values run from as high as 100,000 darcys for gravel to under 0.01 microdarcys for granite; sand is about 1 darcy.
Not an SI unit, it is widely used in petroleum engineering and geology; in hydrology, 1 darcy corresponds to a water flux of 0.831 m/day under hydrostatic pressure at 20 °C.

entries.title: SMAP, NASA's watch on the planet's soil moisture

definition.text: A NASA satellite that measures soil moisture and its freeze-thaw state across the planet.

facts.text: It takes a global snapshot of soil moisture every 2 to 3 days, often enough to see the effect of single storms as well as seasonal change.
Launched on 31 January 2015 with a passive L-band radiometer and an active radar, it lost the radar to an amplifier failure that year and carries on with the radiometer alone.
It senses the top 5 cm of soil through moderate vegetation, and hydrologic models extend the readings to infer moisture in the root zone.
Its data improve drought monitoring, flood and landslide forecasts, weather prediction and famine early warning.

entries.title: The van Genuchten model: a soil's water curve in a few numbers

definition.text: An equation that describes the shape of a soil's water retention curve.

facts.text: Its parameter α relates to the inverse of the air-entry suction, and n, greater than 1, measures the pore-size distribution.
Its parameterization led to a model predicting how unsaturated hydraulic conductivity varies with saturation and pressure.
α and n come from field or laboratory tests such as the instantaneous profile method, fitted by non-linear least squares; Gaussian process regression on the residuals can improve the fit.
Alternative retention models include Brooks–Corey, Broadbridge–White and Rogers–Stallybrass–Clements.

entries.text: A whole {{ref:soil-water-175}} can be summed up in a few fitted numbers. The van Genuchten model is an equation that describes the shape of that curve. Both come from field or laboratory tests, such as the instantaneous profile method, fitted by non-linear least squares. The parameterization led to a model predicting how a soil's conductivity when not saturated ({{ref:soil-phys-225}}) varies with saturation and pressure. Alternatives include the Brooks–Corey, Broadbridge–White and Rogers–Stallybrass–Clements models.

entries.title: Adhesion: why water clings to soil

definition.text: Adhesion is the tendency of dissimilar particles or surfaces to cling to one another, whereas cohesion is that of like particles.

facts.text: Adhesion requires energy from chemical or physical linkages; the physical ones are reversible when enough energy is applied.
Proposed mechanisms are mechanical, chemical (ionic, covalent, hydrogen bonds), dispersive (van der Waals forces), electrostatic and diffusive.
In surface science adhesion almost always means dispersive adhesion; a low contact angle indicates higher adhesion per unit area.
Strength depends on the mechanisms present and contact area; liquids that wet a surface make larger contact.

In surface science it almost always means dispersive adhesion, and a low contact angle indicates higher adhesion per unit area. Strength depends on the mechanisms present and the contact area, and liquids that wet a surface make larger contact.

entries.title: Plinthite, the red clay that sets like stone

definition.text: An iron-rich, humus-poor mixture of clay with quartz and other minerals that forms as a redoximorphic feature in highly weathered soils.

facts.text: It forms in horizons saturated with water for part of the year, usually as dark red redox concretions in platy, polygonal or reticulate patterns.
Repeated wetting and drying, especially with heat from the sun, turns it irreversibly into ironstone hardpan or irregular aggregates; a single cycle does not.
It is firm near field capacity, hard below the permanent wilting point, and soft enough to cut with a spade when moist.
It marks Plinthosols, and though it can look like a mineral when hard, it is a pedogenic material.

entries.title: Surface tension: the skin on a liquid

definition.text: Surface tension is the energy per unit area that comes from a liquid having a surface, equivalently a force per unit length.

facts.text: Molecules inside a liquid are pulled equally in all directions, but surface molecules are pulled inward, so the surface contracts toward the smallest area.
Surface tension is a property of a liquid's interface with another medium, not of the liquid alone.
Surface tension falls as temperature rises and reaches zero at the critical temperature, so a stated value needs its temperature.
A curved liquid surface can balance a pressure difference across it, which is the basis of capillary effects.

entries.title: Capillary action: water that climbs without a pump

definition.text: Capillary action is a liquid flowing in a narrow space without help from external forces such as gravity.

facts.text: It arises from surface tension, caused by cohesion within the liquid, combined with adhesive forces between the liquid and the wall of a small enough tube or pore.
In a narrow tube water forms a concave meniscus; the contact length scales with the tube radius while the liquid weight scales with its square, so narrower tubes lift a liquid higher.
Jurin's law gives the rise height, which falls as tube radius increases: for water at 20 degrees C the rise is 0.7 mm in a 2 cm radius tube and 70 mm in a 0.2 mm radius tube.
In hydrology it describes attraction of water to soil particles; differences in soil matric potential drive it, moving water from wet to dry soil.
With mercury and glass the liquid's internal forces exceed those to the solid, giving a convex meniscus and a reversed capillary effect.
Where a high water table meets strong evaporation, capillary rise brings salts to the surface, and breaking capillary pores is used to stop it.

entries.title: Sorptivity: how readily a dry material drinks

definition.text: A measure of a porous medium's capacity to absorb or release liquid by capillarity, a term introduced by John Philip in 1957.

facts.text: It is widely used to characterize soils and porous building materials such as brick, stone and concrete.
Philip showed in 1969 that sorptivity can be found from horizontal infiltration, where flow is mostly capillary absorption, by relating cumulative infiltration to time.
Its SI unit is m·s−1/2; for vertical infiltration Philip's solution adds a second parameter, giving equations valid for short times.
Clapp and Hornberger derived average sorptivity values, with retention and saturated conductivity parameters, for different texture classes.

entries.title: Mariotte's bottle, a steady flow from a falling tank

definition.text: A device that delivers a constant rate of flow from a closed bottle or tank.

facts.text: It is named after Edme Mariotte (1620–1684), but the design was first reported by McCarthy (1934).
An air inlet keeps the pressure at its base atmospheric, so a siphon at that depth delivers water at a constant head however far the reservoir level falls.
Constant head simplifies measuring water movement in soil; the Guelph permeameter and single and double ring infiltrometers use the principle.
It is sensitive to leaks at the air inlet and cannot be refilled while running; electronic devices now give accurate control.

entries.title: The maze of large pores that steers water

definition.text: The linked system of a soil's macropores, irregular in shape, size and roughness, whose geometry shapes water movement, aeration and root growth.

facts.text: Higher connectivity usually means higher permeability, and links to the surface and to groundwater aid infiltration and recharge.
Connected pores may still not be continuous; dead-end pores block or slow water and air, while continuous pores improve aeration and room for roots.
Tortuosity, the ratio of actual path length to the straight distance between two points, measures resistance to flow: the more sinuous the path, the higher it is.

entries.text: A soil's macropores do not sit alone. They link into a network, irregular in shape, size and roughness, whose geometry shapes water movement, aeration and root growth. Dead-end pores block or slow water and air, while continuous pores improve aeration and give roots room. Tortuosity measures the winding: the ratio of a path's actual length to the straight distance between its two ends. The more sinuous the path, the higher the tortuosity and the resistance to flow.

entries.title: Hygroscopy: materials that draw water from the air

definition.text: Hygroscopy is the attracting and holding of water molecules from the surroundings by absorption or adsorption.

facts.text: Hygroscopic substances include many fertilizer chemicals and salts; the moisture held is usually proportional to relative humidity.
Deliquescent materials absorb enough water to dissolve into a solution, at a characteristic deliquescence relative humidity that depends on temperature and crystalline hydrate form.
Soil voids stay saturated with water vapour up to the point of maximal hygroscopicity, beyond which a vapour-pressure deficit develops in the pore space.

entries.title: Hydropedology, where soil science meets hydrology

definition.text: An emerging field joining soil science and hydrology that studies the interface between the pedosphere and the hydrosphere.

facts.text: Like hydrogeology, hydroclimatology and ecohydrology, it links hydrology with another of the Earth's spheres.
Soil hydrology and hydropedology are listed among the areas of practice of soil science.
The biomantle shows such roles: loosened by bioturbation, it speeds percolation through biopores and carries downslope throughflow above dense subsoil horizons.

entries.title: Ground that sheds rain though it counts as pervious

definition.text: Land usually classed as pervious that can still yield a substantial amount of surface runoff in small and large storms.

facts.text: It includes open water, wetlands, rock outcrops, barren ground and compacted soils.
Depending on conditions, it yields stormflow by infiltration-excess overland flow, saturation overland flow or direct precipitation.
Development compacts soils: Felton and Lull (1963) found a potential 80 percent cut in infiltration, and Taylor (1982) found construction cut infiltration rates by more than 77 percent.
Its effect on runoff matters more where total impervious area is low than in highly developed areas.

entries.title: Measuring how much of a landscape is sealed

definition.text: The share of an area covered by impervious surfaces, given as a fraction from zero to one or as a percentage.

facts.text: It is estimated from land-cover data in a GIS, land-use categories, percent developed area or population density; the US NLCD maps it in 30-metre pixels from 0 to 100 percent.
Percentage imperviousness (PIMP), an important factor in drainage, can be estimated as 6.4 times the square root of the number of dwellings per hectare.
PIMP is about 10% for woodland and 100% for dense commercial areas.
About 76 percent of the conterminous United States has less than 1 percent impervious cover.

entries.title: The continuity equation: what enters must go somewhere

definition.text: A continuity equation describes the transport of a quantity, and is a local form of a conservation law.

facts.text: It relates change of a quantity in a region to net flux through the boundary plus generation (sources) or removal (sinks) inside.
In fluid dynamics it says the rate at which mass enters a system equals the rate it leaves plus the mass accumulating within.

entries.title: A knowledge base that infers what was never measured

definition.text: A knowledge base, proposed by McBratney et al. (2002), that infers soil properties to fill digital soil databases.

facts.text: It infers unknown properties with minimal uncertainty through logically linked pedotransfer functions.
Its premise is that a soil's basic properties are enough to infer all its other physical and chemical properties.
It depends on reliable inputs, links between basic soil data and quantified uncertainty, and computes new properties from inferred values as well as inputs.
A working prototype was completed in 2007–2009 at the University of Sydney with a US partner.

entries.title: Hydraulic gradient, the slope that drives groundwater

definition.text: The change in hydraulic head between measurement points along a flow path.

facts.text: Its magnitude, i = dh/dl, is the head difference divided by the flow path length between two piezometers, a dimensionless ratio.
In groundwater it is also called the Darcy slope, because it sets the size of the Darcy flux.
As a vector it gives both the size and direction of groundwater flow, which runs down the gradient from high to low head.
Combined with Darcy's law and a hydraulic conductivity tensor, it gives the flux of water in three dimensions.

entries.title: Two rings to keep the flow straight down

definition.text: An infiltrometer with an inner ring and a larger outer ring around it, which keeps the flow from the inner ring one-dimensional.

entries.title: Counting slowed neutrons to find hidden water

definition.text: A device that measures the quantity of water in soil.

facts.text: A pellet of americium-241 and beryllium produces fast neutrons when alpha particles from the americium strike the beryllium nuclei.
The neutrons slow down on hitting hydrogen nuclei in the soil; counting the slow neutrons that return estimates the hydrogen, and so the water, present.
Read through an access tube installed in the soil, it is used in agriculture for highly accurate deep-soil readings.
Neutron probes can gauge soil water potential over a range of 0 to −1500 kPa.

facts.text: Water molecules are strongly polar, so they bond to each other and to charged surfaces such as soil minerals.
Clay is especially able to bond water molecules.
Bound water is much less mobile than the rest of soil water and strongly affects soil dielectric permittivity and freezing and thawing.

entries.title: Pressure head: pressure written as a height

definition.text: The height of a liquid column corresponding to the pressure the liquid exerts at its base, expressed as a length.

facts.text: Combined with elevation head it makes up hydraulic head.
Below the water table pressure head exceeds atmospheric pressure; the water table is where it equals atmospheric pressure.
Above the water table pressure head is negative and water partly filling the pores is under suction.
Because it is proportional to pressure for a given fluid, columns of water or mercury are used to measure pressure.

entries.title: The Hagen-Poiseuille equation for flow in a pipe

definition.text: The Hagen-Poiseuille equation gives the pressure drop for an incompressible Newtonian fluid in laminar flow through a long cylindrical pipe of constant cross section.

facts.text: It assumes laminar flow in a circular pipe much longer than its diameter, no acceleration, and an incompressible Newtonian fluid.

Above a threshold of velocity and pipe diameter flow becomes turbulent, giving larger pressure drops than the equation predicts; it also fails near the pipe entrance and for low viscosity or wide, short pipes.
It was derived experimentally by Poiseuille (1838) and Hagen, and justified theoretically by Stokes in 1845.

entries.title: The root zone, the soil that plants can reach

definition.text: The depth of soil from which plant roots draw water, often called the root zone.

facts.text: Water that moves below the root zone after heavy rain or irrigation is lost to plants and can take fertilizers and nutrients with it.
Irrigation scheduling aims to wet the whole root zone while keeping overwatering to a minimum.
Salts that build up in the root zone can be carried deeper, or into groundwater, by recharge.

entries.title: Sensing soil moisture through a circuit's frequency

definition.text: An instrument for measuring soil moisture in which the operating frequency of an oscillating circuit depends on the dielectric constant of the soil around it.

facts.text: Its types are capacitance probes and electrical impedance sensors.
Impedance sensors commonly feed a 100 MHz oscillator signal along a coaxial line into buried probe wires and measure the part reflected where impedance changes.
They are cheaper to build and respond faster than TDR, but the complex field around the probe means calibrating for each soil type, unless a high frequency is used.

entries.title: Horton overland flow: rain faster than the ground can drink

definition.text: Horton overland flow is water flowing across the land surface when rainfall exceeds both infiltration capacity and depression storage capacity.

facts.text: It is named for Robert E. Horton, the engineer who first studied it in detail, and is also called Hortonian or unsaturated overland flow.
The flow is shallow, sheetlike and fast, so it can erode soil extensively, especially on steep terrain and loose, flat farmland.
Impermeable paved surfaces reach it rapidly, and it is common on construction sites and unpaved roads where vegetation has been stripped.
It is also called Hortonian overland flow, after Robert E. Horton, or unsaturated overland flow.

entries.title: Wetting or drying: why soil water has a memory

definition.text: The dependence of a soil's water content at a given matric potential on whether the soil is wetting or drying, that is, on its saturation history.

facts.text: The matric potential–water content relationship is the basis of the water retention curve.
At a matric potential of 5 kPa, a fine sandy soil could hold anywhere between 8% and 25% volumetric water.
Some matric potential sensors show hysteresis within the sensor itself, yet as of 2002 usually only desorption curves were measured in calibration.

entries.text: The same soil at the same suction can hold very different amounts of water. At a matric potential of 5 kPa, a fine sandy soil could hold anywhere between 8% and 25% water by volume. The cause is water retention hysteresis: water content at a given matric potential depends on whether the soil is wetting or drying, that is, on its saturation history. The matric potential–water content relationship is the basis of the water retention curve, so one curve tells only part of the story. Some matric potential sensors show hysteresis themselves, yet as of 2002 calibrations usually measured only the drying curve.

entries.title: Capillary pressure: the smaller the pore, the greater the pull

definition.text: Capillary pressure is the pressure difference between two immiscible fluids in a thin tube or pore, arising from forces between the fluids and the solid walls.

facts.text: The Young-Laplace equation gives it as pc = 2 γ cos θ / r, with interfacial tension γ, wetting angle θ and effective radius r of the interface; the smaller the pore, the larger the pressure.
The wetting phase is the fluid that preferentially spreads across the walls; its wettability depends on surface tension and contact angle and can be changed by surface roughness or hydrophilicity.

In the porous plate method a water-saturated sample sits on a saturated plate in a gas chamber; gas pressure is raised, the gas pressure represents capillary pressure and the water expelled gives the saturation.
Beskow defined soil moisture tension as capillary pressure and soil water as capillary water, in his work on frost heave.

entries.title: Shortcuts: how water races down root and worm channels

definition.text: Rapid drainage of water under gravity along connected macropores, crevices, and root and worm channels in soil.

facts.text: Macropores and fractures strongly influence infiltration rates in many soils, along with preferential flow patterns and hydraulic conductivity.
Living or dead tree roots open preferential channels for rainwater that can raise infiltration rates up to 27 times.
Preferential paths speed drainage, but they also carry dissolved nutrients away quickly and leave water and chemicals unevenly spread in the soil.
Extreme forms in depressions speed the transport of contaminants toward groundwater.
Water that cannot enter strongly water-repellent patches finds preferential pathways that take it deeper into the profile.
Soil mixing by organisms and other disturbances creates preferential paths for soil gas and infiltrating water.
In soils with distinct macropores, preferential flow dominates measurements made with single- or double-ring infiltrometers under ponding.
Soil physics models often add preferential flow as dual-porosity or dual-permeability options, but these are generally bolted onto the Richards solution without rigorous physical grounding.

entries.title: Kozeny–Carman: permeability from grains and gaps

definition.text: A relation giving the pressure drop of a fluid flowing through a packed bed of solids, and from it the bed's permeability.

facts.text: Kozeny derived it in 1927 and Carman modified it in 1937 and 1956, modelling the bed as curving tubes with Poiseuille flow.
Permeability rises with particle diameter squared and with the cube of porosity, and falls with (1 − porosity) squared.
It is a special case of Darcy's law and holds only for creeping flow, with particle Reynolds numbers up to about 1.0.

entries.text: The Kozeny–Carman equation links how easily fluid passes through a packed bed of solids to the size of its grains and the space between them. It gives the pressure drop of the flowing fluid, and from it the bed's permeability. Kozeny derived it in 1927, and Carman modified it in 1937 and 1956. They modeled the bed as curving tubes carrying Poiseuille flow, smooth flow through a narrow pipe. Permeability rises with particle diameter squared and with the cube of porosity, and falls with (1 − porosity) squared. A special case of Darcy's law, it holds only for creeping flow, with particle Reynolds numbers up to about 1.0.

facts.text: Only part of the capillary water in a soil is available to plants.
Plant available water is held between field capacity and the permanent wilting point, in mesopores.

entries.title: The soil water relationship: calibrating a moisture sensor

definition.text: A soil water relationship is a graph of a sensor's measured value against soil water content, which acts as a calibration for one soil.

facts.text: Any soil moisture sensor reading must be interpreted through such a relationship.
Once calibrated, sensors quantify plant available water and show whether water flows by gravity, capillarity or osmotic potential.
At a given water potential, soil water content rises with clay content because clayey soils have higher porosity and hold more water.

entries.title: Groundwater recharge: how rain refills aquifers

definition.text: The downward movement of water from the surface to groundwater, also called deep drainage or deep percolation.

facts.text: Fed mainly by rain and snowmelt, and less by rivers and lakes, recharge is the main way water enters an aquifer.
It usually takes place in the vadose zone below plant roots and is often expressed as a flux to the water table.
Diffuse recharge is rain soaking through soil over large areas; focused recharge leaks from rivers, lakes, wetlands or depressions and grows more dominant as aridity increases.
Paving, development and logging can strip topsoil, reduce infiltration, increase runoff and so cut recharge.
Yet urban recharge can be up to ten times higher than rural, because leaking water-supply and sewage networks add water that rural areas lack.
For sustainable use, long-term abstraction from an aquifer should not exceed the rate at which it is recharged.
Recharge can flush salts that accumulate in the root zone into deeper layers or into groundwater.
Under climate change, fewer but more intense storms may raise recharge in many places, while harsher droughts may dry and compact soils and reduce infiltration.

entries.text: Most of the water in an aquifer arrived from above. Rain and snowmelt feed it mainly, rivers and lakes less. It usually takes place in unsaturated ground below plant roots and is often expressed as a flux to the water table. Diffuse recharge is rain soaking through soil over large areas. Focused recharge leaks from rivers, lakes, wetlands or depressions, and it grows more dominant as climates get drier. People push the balance both ways. Paving, development and logging can strip topsoil, reduce infiltration, increase runoff and so cut recharge. Yet urban recharge can be up to ten times higher than rural, because leaking water-supply and sewage networks add water that rural areas lack. Recharge can also flush salts that accumulate in the root zone into deeper layers or into groundwater. For sustainable use, long-term pumping from an aquifer should not exceed its recharge. Climate change may cut both ways too. Fewer but more intense storms may raise recharge in many places, while harsher droughts may dry and compact soils and reduce infiltration.

entries.title: Refilling aquifers on purpose

definition.text: Recharge engineered by people, routing rainwater or reclaimed water into the subsurface.

facts.text: Managed aquifer recharge methods include modifying streambed channels, bank filtration, water spreading and recharge wells.
A facility in Orange County, California, cleans and injects 100 million gallons per day, or 90 billion gallons per year.
In India, where farmers' over-pumping has depleted groundwater, the government in 2007 funded dug-well recharge projects in 100 districts of seven states.
Stormwater pollution collects in retention basins, and high water tables affect how detention ponds, retention ponds and rain gardens should be designed.

entries.title: Field capacity: the water a soil keeps after draining

definition.text: The water a soil still holds after excess water has drained away and downward movement has slowed.

facts.text: It is usually reached two to three days after rain or irrigation in pervious soils of uniform structure and texture.
By convention it is the water content held at −33 kPa (−0.33 bar) of suction, or −10 kPa for sandy soils, after work by Richards and Weaver.
At field capacity the smallest pores hold water and the largest hold air, the optimal condition for plant growth and microbial activity.
The water held depends on the specific surface area of the particles, so clay-rich and organic soils have higher field capacities.
It is measured by wetting a profile, covering it against evaporation and tracking water content; the point where macropore drainage stops is also called the drained upper limit.
The term came from Israelsen and West and from Veihmeyer and Hendrickson, improving on Lyman Briggs's moisture equivalent.
Veihmeyer and Hendrickson admitted it is not strictly a constant for a soil, but a practical measure of water-holding capacity.
Groundwater recharge is most likely when the water reaching a soil exceeds its field capacity.

entries.text: Two to three days after rain, a well-drained soil settles down. Field capacity is the water a soil still holds after excess water has drained away and downward movement has slowed. At this point the smallest pores hold water and the largest hold air, the best condition for plant growth and microbial activity. The water held depends on the particles' specific surface area, so clay-rich and organic soils have higher field capacities. The term came from Israelsen and West and from Veihmeyer and Hendrickson, improving on Lyman Briggs's {{ref:soil-water-245}}. Veihmeyer and Hendrickson admitted it is not strictly a constant, but a practical measure of water-holding capacity. When more water reaches a soil than its field capacity, groundwater recharge is most likely.

entries.title: Why low spots feed the water table

definition.text: Recharge in which rain falling fairly evenly over an area reaches groundwater mainly beneath surface depressions where runoff gathers.

facts.text: Rain spread evenly within the soil's field capacity barely percolates; pooled in low spots, the same volume can exceed field capacity and drain down to groundwater.
Water tables rise beneath such depressions, and the process can be very important in arid regions.
Deeper ponding forces water in faster, dislodging adsorbed contaminants and carrying them to the water table, so the quality of water in infiltration basins is a special concern.
In karst, focused flow can dissolve tunnels down to aquifers, an extreme form of preferential flow that speeds contaminant transport.

entries.text: The same rain can refill an aquifer or not, depending on where it pools. Spread evenly within a soil's field capacity, rain barely drains down. Gathered in low spots, the same volume can exceed field capacity and drain to groundwater. Water tables rise beneath them, and the process can matter greatly in arid regions. Deeper ponding forces water in faster and drives adsorbed contaminants down to the water table. In karst, focused flow can dissolve tunnels down to aquifers, an extreme form of preferential flow that speeds contaminant transport.

entries.title: Percolation: the slow trickle below the roots

definition.text: The downward drainage of water through a soil after the soil has absorbed it.

facts.text: Water that drains through macropores under gravity when it rains is called gravitational water; drainage stops at field capacity, when adhesion and cohesion hold the rest.
Once a soil is fully wetted, extra water percolates below the roots, carrying clay, humus, nutrients (mostly cations) and contaminants that may pollute groundwater.
Magnesium, sulfur and potassium leach most readily, nitrogen little unless nitrate fertilizer was recently applied, and phosphorus very little.
Deep percolation that reaches groundwater is groundwater recharge, and groundwater in turn feeds soil moisture through percolation.

Once a soil is fully wetted, extra water percolates below the roots. entries.title: Groundwater: the water held in the pores of the Earth

definition.text: Water held beneath the Earth's surface in the pore spaces of soil and rock and in rock fractures.

facts.text: About 30 percent of the world's readily available fresh water is groundwater.
In the technical sense it includes soil moisture, permafrost and immobile water in tight bedrock, not only water flowing in shallow aquifers.
Its natural input is infiltration that percolates down to the water table; its natural outputs are springs and seepage to the oceans.
It is a long-term store of the water cycle, with residence times from days to millennia.
In the Great Artesian Basin, groundwater travels about 1 metre per year and can be more than 1 million years old.
About 70% of extracted groundwater is used in agriculture.
Where salty water evapotranspires, salts are left behind; poor drainage in irrigation districts can raise water tables to the surface and cause soil salinity and waterlogging.
Pollution, often from improper waste disposal on land, forms plumes that spread by water movement and dispersion and is harder to clean up than surface water pollution.

It enters naturally as infiltration that percolates down to the water table, and leaves through springs and seepage to the oceans. It is a long-term store of the water cycle, with residence times from days to millennia. In the Great Artesian Basin it travels about 1 meter per year and can be more than 1 million years old. About 70% of extracted groundwater is used in agriculture, and that use carries risks. Where salty water evapotranspires, salts are left behind. Poor drainage in irrigation districts can raise water tables to the surface, causing soil salinity and waterlogging. Pollution, often from improper waste disposal on land, spreads in plumes and is harder to clean up than surface water pollution.

entries.title: Aquifers: not underground lakes but soaked rock

definition.text: An underground layer of permeable, porous or fractured rock, or of unconsolidated gravel, sand or silt, that holds and yields water.

facts.text: Aquitards are low-permeability beds of clay or non-porous rock that restrict flow between aquifers; a completely impermeable one is an aquiclude or aquifuge.
Aquifers occur from near the surface to deeper than 9,000 m; shallower ones are more often used for water supply and irrigation and more readily refilled by local rain.
Despite the image of underground rivers or lakes, most aquifers are porous rock saturated with water.
Recharge, water moving down from the surface to the groundwater, is the main way water enters an aquifer.
In porous aquifers groundwater seeps slowly between sand grains; 0.3 m a day counts as a high rate.
Porosity alone does not make a good aquifer: rocks such as the Deccan Traps basalts are highly porous but poorly permeable.
Karst aquifers form where carbonic acid widens fissures in limestone; their fast flow makes them far more sensitive to contamination than porous aquifers.
Overdrafting, land subsidence, salinization and pollution are the main environmental problems of pumping groundwater from aquifers.

entries.title: Hydrogeology: the geology of water underground

definition.text: The branch of geology dealing with the distribution and movement of groundwater in soil and rock, mainly in aquifers.

facts.text: It covers the laws of subsurface water movement, the water's interaction with the porous solid, and the transport of energy, chemicals and particles by flow.
Groundwater hydrology and geohydrology are near-synonyms, though hydrogeology is the usual term.
The type of aquifer decides what controls flow: storativity for confined aquifers, specific yield for unconfined ones.
Darcy's law, derived by Henry Darcy in 1856, is its basic constitutive equation for groundwater discharge.

entries.title: Spinning soil to gauge its water

definition.text: The percentage of water a soil retains against a centrifugal force 1000 times gravity, proposed in 1910 as a measure of field capacity for fine-textured soils.

facts.text: A saturated sample 1 cm thick is spun at 1000 times gravity for 30 min, and its gravimetric water content afterwards is the moisture equivalent.
Briggs and Shantz (1912) related it to texture: moisture equivalent = 0.02 sand + 0.22 silt + 1.05 clay.
Soil physics no longer uses the concept; field capacity has replaced it.

entries.title: Capped or open: confined and unconfined aquifers

definition.text: The division of aquifers by whether an impermeable layer lies directly above them (confined) or their upper boundary is the water table (unconfined).

facts.text: Confined aquifers are usually capped by clay, which may give some protection from surface contamination.
Confined aquifers store water by matrix expansion and water compressibility, with storativities far below 0.01 and as low as 10−5.
Unconfined aquifers release water by draining their pores, with specific yields above 0.01, or 1% of bulk volume.
A perched aquifer is a small body of groundwater held above the regional aquifer on a low-permeability layer such as clay.

entries.text: Aquifers are divided by what lies directly above them. A confined aquifer sits beneath an impermeable layer, usually clay, which may give some protection from surface contamination. An unconfined aquifer's upper boundary is the water table. Unconfined aquifers release water by draining their pores, with specific yields above 0.01, or 1% of bulk volume. Confined aquifers store water through expansion of the solid matrix and the compressibility of water, with storativities far below 0.01 and as low as 10−5. A perched aquifer is a small body of groundwater held above the regional aquifer on a low-permeability layer such as clay.

entries.title: The groundwater flow equation: diffusion underground

definition.text: The equation describing the movement of groundwater through a porous medium, known in mathematics as the diffusion equation.

facts.text: It is usually derived from Darcy's law combined with conservation of mass in a small control volume.
Fluid and matrix compressibility enter it; clay has a compressibility of 10−6 to 10−8 Pa−1 against 10−7 to 10−9 for sand.
The Theis and Thiem equations, its transient and steady-state solutions for flow to a well, are used in pumping tests.
The Hooghoudt equation applies it to subsurface drainage by pipes, tile drains or ditches.

entries.text: Mathematicians know it as the {{ref:soil-phys-241}}. The groundwater flow equation describes how groundwater moves through a porous medium. It is usually derived by combining Darcy's law with conservation of mass in a small control volume. The compressibility of both fluid and matrix enters it: clay's is 10−6 to 10−8 Pa−1, against 10−7 to 10−9 for sand. Its solutions do practical work. The Theis and Thiem equations, its transient and steady-state solutions for flow to a well, are used in pumping tests. The Hooghoudt equation applies it to drainage by pipes, tile drains or ditches.

entries.title: Subsurface flow: the slow road back to the surface

definition.text: The flow of water beneath the Earth's surface as part of the water cycle.

facts.text: Water that infiltrates wets the vadose zone and recharges aquifers, and the excess moves on as subsurface runoff.
Its movement is set mainly by the water gradient, the type of substrate and barriers to flow.
Flow in the soil can be unsaturated, but faster subsurface flow goes with local saturation.
It returns to the surface at lower elevations through springs, seeps, wells or streams, sometimes after thousands of years in an aquifer.

entries.text: Rain that soaks in has not left the water cycle. Subsurface flow is the movement of water beneath the Earth's surface. entries.title: The hidden costs of draining farmland
entries.article: Tile drainage#Social and ecological effects of tile drainage

definition.text: The effects of widespread tile drainage on wetlands, rivers and water quality.

facts.text: Draining wetlands caused population declines in hundreds of thousands of wetland species.
By moving water off the land faster, tile drainage delivers higher volumes to rivers, causing bank erosion and heavy sediment loads.
It can reduce erosion and phosphorus runoff, since soil filters water before it reaches streams, but its outflow tends to be very high in nitrogen.
Controlled drainage or constructed wetlands may work better than surface conservation practices on tile-drained land.

entries.text: Draining wetlands caused population declines in hundreds of thousands of wetland species. Widespread tile drainage changes rivers too. By moving water off the land faster, it delivers higher volumes downstream, causing bank erosion and heavy sediment loads. Its effect on water quality cuts both ways. Soil filters water before it reaches streams, so tiling can reduce erosion and phosphorus runoff. But its outflow tends to be very high in nitrogen. On tile-drained land, controlled drainage or built wetlands ({{ref:soil-water-260}}) may work better than surface conservation practices.

entries.title: Gravitational water: the part that drains away

definition.text: Gravitational water is the water that moves through the large soil pores and drains away under gravity.

facts.text: Gravitational water is the difference between the moisture content at saturation and at field capacity.
It drains from macropores too fast for plants to use.

entries.title: The vadose zone, between the surface and the water table

definition.text: The unsaturated zone between the land surface and the water table, where water in the pores is below atmospheric pressure.

facts.text: Its water is held by adhesion and capillary action; where the zone lies in soil, that water is called soil moisture.
Its pores hold air as well as water, and it excludes the still-saturated capillary fringe just above the water table.
It is absent where there are lakes and marshes but can be hundreds of metres thick in arid regions.
Water flow through it is often described by the Richards equation, which rests partly on Darcy's law.
It often controls water movement from the surface to aquifers, so it governs recharge and whether, where and how fast contaminants reach groundwater.
Unlike the aquifers below, it is not a ready source of drinking water, but it supplies water and nutrients to the biosphere and is heavily used for crops, building and waste disposal.
Its study spans soil physics and hydrology and matters for agriculture, contaminant transport and flood control.

entries.title: The capillary fringe: groundwater climbing into the soil

definition.text: The layer just above a water table into which groundwater rises by capillary action to fill the pores.

facts.text: Its base is saturated by tension, but this saturated part is shorter than the total capillary rise because pore sizes are mixed.
Small, uniform pores can keep soil saturated several feet above the water table, while large pores limit the saturated part to a few inches.
Above the saturated base, water content falls with height above the water table.
Definitions differ: solute-transport workers count only the tension-saturated base, while salinity, vapor-phase and bioremediation workers include the unsaturated part too.
Land whose surface lies within the capillary fringe of saline groundwater salinizes rapidly.
Where the water table meets soil it forms an oxic–anoxic zone, and oxygen from it feeds microbes that break down dissolved organic compounds.

entries.text: Groundwater does not stop at the water table. It climbs. The capillary fringe is the layer just above a water table into which groundwater rises by capillary action to fill the pores. Small, uniform pores can keep soil saturated several feet above the water table, while large pores limit the saturated part to a few inches. Because pore sizes are mixed, this tension-saturated base is shorter than the total capillary rise. Above it, water content falls with height. Definitions differ. Solute-transport workers count only the saturated base, while salinity and vapor-phase workers, and those in {{ref:soil-env-023}}, include the unsaturated part too. The fringe has consequences. Land whose surface lies within the capillary fringe of saline groundwater salinizes rapidly. Where the water table meets soil, it forms a boundary between oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor conditions, and oxygen there feeds microbes that break down dissolved organic compounds.

entries.title: The tensiometer, a gauge of how hard soil holds its water

definition.text: An instrument that measures the matric potential, or moisture tension, of water in unsaturated soil.

facts.text: It is a water-filled glass or plastic tube with a porous ceramic cup, topped by a vacuum gauge or by a rubber cap read with a needle instrument.
Buried and pumped to a partial vacuum, it gains vacuum as plants and evaporation dry the soil and loses it when the soil is rewetted.
Through the porous cup the water inside comes to balance with soil water, and the gauge then reads the soil's matric potential.
Irrigation managers use it to decide when to water and, with a water retention curve, how much.
Lorenzo A. Richards described its principles, construction and operation early in his career and kept improving the design.
ISO 11276:1995 sets out tensiometer methods for measuring pore water pressure in unsaturated and saturated soil.

entries.title: The Richards equation, a famously hard sum for moving water

definition.text: An equation describing the movement of water in unsaturated soils, published by Lorenzo A. Richards in 1931.

facts.text: It joins conservation of mass with the Darcy–Buckingham law for flow in variably saturated porous media, with a sink term that is usually root water uptake.
Although attributed to Richards, it was first introduced nine years earlier, in 1922, by Lewis Fry Richardson.
It is a quasilinear partial differential equation with analytical solutions only for particular conditions; existence and uniqueness of solutions were proved only in 1983, by Alt and Luckhaus.
Its mixed form has two unknowns, water content and pressure head, linked through the water retention curve.
It needs the soil's hydraulic properties: usually five van Genuchten retention parameters plus the saturated hydraulic conductivity.
It appears widely in environmental work because it describes flow in the vadose zone between the atmosphere and the aquifer.
Solving it numerically is among the hardest problems in earth science: solvers may fail to converge, and rain soaking into dry soil needs grid spacing under one cm near the surface.

entries.title: Tracking a wetting front as it sinks

definition.text: An equation for the speed at which water moves down through unsaturated soil under the combined pull of gravity and capillarity.

facts.text: It is a reworking of Richards' equation in which the unknown is the depth of a wetting front of a given water content as it moves with time.
Its advection-like term carries flow driven by gravity and the capillarity of the wetting front; its diffusion-like term, much like Fick's second law, reflects the shape of the front.
Dropping the diffusion-like term still gave over 99% accuracy in cumulative infiltration when checked against exact solutions of Richards' equation for idealized soils.
Solved by the method of lines, the advection-like term becomes three ordinary differential equations, for infiltrating water, falling slugs and capillary groundwater.

entries.text: The soil moisture velocity equation gives the speed at which water moves down through unsaturated soil under the combined pull of gravity and capillarity. Dropping the second term still gave over 99% accuracy in cumulative infiltration, checked against exact solutions for idealized soils. Solved by the method of lines, the advection-like term becomes three ordinary differential equations, for infiltrating water, falling slugs and capillary groundwater.

entries.title: Estimating the recharge no one can measure

definition.text: The methods used to estimate how much water reaches the water table, which no widely applicable method can measure directly and accurately.

facts.text: Recharge is hard to quantify because evaporation, transpiration and infiltration must first be measured or estimated to close the balance.
Common methods are chloride mass balance, soil physics methods, environmental and isotopic tracers, groundwater-level fluctuations, water balances and river baseflow.
Direct physical methods measure the water passing below the root zone; indirect ones infer recharge from soil physical parameters.
Numerical codes such as HYDRUS1D, UNSAT-H and SHAW use climate and soil data and some form of the Richards equation to model flow in the vadose zone.

entries.title: A sturdier way to simulate unsaturated flow
entries.article: Finite water-content vadose zone flow method

definition.text: A one-dimensional alternative to the numerical solution of Richards' equation for simulating water movement in unsaturated soils.

facts.text: It solves the advection-like term of the soil moisture velocity equation as three ordinary differential equations, for infiltrating water, falling slugs and capillary groundwater.
Being explicit, it is guaranteed to converge, cheap to solve and mass-conserving, and it handles sharp wetting fronts that Richards solvers struggle with.
It assumes soil homogeneous in layers and omits soil water diffusion, which barely affects flux accuracy; in practice it is so far limited to one dimension.
It works with any monotonic retention and conductivity relations, such as Brooks and Corey or van Genuchten–Mualem.

Being explicit, it is cheap to solve and mass-conserving, and it handles the sharp wetting fronts that Richards solvers struggle with. It assumes soil homogeneous in layers and omits {{ref:soil-phys-240}} of soil water, which barely affects flux accuracy. entries.title: The phreatic zone, where every pore is full

definition.text: The saturated zone below the water table, in which all pores and fractures are filled with water.

facts.text: It is the counterpart of the unsaturated vadose zone above the water table.
Its size and depth fluctuate with the seasons and with wet and dry periods.
Depending on particle packing and porosity, its boundary can be stable or form unstable fingering patterns known as Saffman–Taylor instability.
Deep-rooted phreatophytes draw much of their water from the phreatic zone or near it.

entries.title: Interflow: water that slips sideways through the soil

definition.text: Lateral movement of water through the unsaturated zone that returns to the surface or enters a stream.

facts.text: It occurs when infiltrated water meets hydraulic conductivity that decreases with depth and flows downslope.
Throughflow is the part of interflow that returns to the surface as overland flow before reaching a stream or groundwater.
If the subsurface saturates, interflow may exfiltrate as return flow and become overland flow.
Interflow and soil piping can erode gullies as well as surface runoff.

entries.title: Fingered flow: water falling in narrow fingers

definition.text: Uneven downward flow of water through unsaturated soil in narrow 'gravity fingers'.

facts.text: Soil moisture sources attribute gravity fingers to surface tension between water particles.
Fingering in the unsaturated zone is described as a Saffman–Taylor instability, arising mostly during drainage and leaving an unstable boundary between saturated and unsaturated soil.

entries.text: Water does not always sink through dry soil as an even front. In fingered flow it moves down through unsaturated soil unevenly, in narrow 'gravity fingers'. Soil moisture sources attribute the fingers to surface tension between water particles. The fingering is described as a Saffman–Taylor instability. It arises mostly during drainage and leaves an unstable boundary between saturated and unsaturated soil.

entries.title: Unsaturated conductivity: flow that depends on wetness

definition.text: The hydraulic conductivity of a soil that is not saturated, which depends on its water content.

facts.text: Its dependence on water content is a main complication in studying the vadose zone.
It enters the Richards equation as K(h) and the soil moisture velocity equation as K(θ).
Relations such as Brooks and Corey, Clapp and Hornberger and van Genuchten–Mualem describe it, with parameters from the water retention curve.
The Guelph permeameter measures it in the field using a Mariotte bottle to keep a constant head.

entries.title: The permanent wilting point, past which plants cannot recover

definition.text: The lowest amount of soil water a plant needs in order not to wilt.

facts.text: At or below it a plant wilts and cannot regain turgor even when kept in a saturated atmosphere for 12 hours.
By convention it is the water content at −1,500 kPa (−15 bar) of suction, as Lorenzo A. Richards proposed.
It roughly marks the boundary between available and unavailable water; there seeds will not germinate, and plants wilt and die unless adapted to recover.
Closing stomata can slow transpiration and delay wilting below the wilting point, especially in plants adapted to drought.
In 1912 Briggs and Shantz proposed the wilting coefficient, the water content at which plants first wilt beyond recovery without added water.
Veihmeyer and Hendrickson of UC Davis found it to be a constant of the soil, independent of environmental conditions.
Experiments by Richards and colleagues fixed today's accepted limits for plant growth: −1/3 bar at field capacity and −15 bar at the permanent wilting point.

entries.title: Available water: the share of soil water plants can use

definition.text: The amount of water a soil profile can store and make available to growing crops.

facts.text: It is also called available water content (AWC), profile available water (PAW) or total available water (TAW).
Frank Veihmeyer and Arthur Hendrickson defined readily available water as the difference between the water content at field capacity and at the permanent wilting point.
Plant-available water sits in pores of 0.1–75 μm; smaller cryptopores hold water too tightly for roots, and macropores are generally air-filled at field capacity.
Daniel Hillel argued that field capacity and wilting point were never clearly defined, lack a physical basis, and that water is never equally available across that range.
Lorenzo A. Richards called availability oversimplified: it depends both on roots absorbing water and on how readily soil water moves in to replace what they use.
Strongly alkaline, sodic soils have poor available water capacity, and thin rendzina soils have limited capacity.
Sepiolite clay can raise plant-available water in sandy soils.

entries.contested_note: Hillel and Richards criticised the field-capacity-to-wilting-point definition as poorly defined and oversimplified.
entries.text: Not all the water in a soil is water a plant can use. Available water capacity is the amount a soil profile can store and make available to growing crops. This water sits in pores of 0.1–75 μm. Smaller cryptopores hold water too tightly for roots, and macropores are generally air-filled at field capacity. The definition is disputed. Daniel Hillel argued that its two limits were never clearly defined and lack a physical basis. Water, he said, is never equally available across the range. Richards, profiled in {{ref:soil-hist-023}}, called it oversimplified, since availability also depends on how readily soil water moves in to replace what roots take. Strongly alkaline, sodium-rich soils hold little, as do thin soils of the kind in {{ref:soil-class-050}}, while the fibrous clay of {{ref:soil-chem-167}} can raise plant-available water in sandy soils.

entries.title: Deciding when to water, and for how long

definition.text: The process irrigation managers use to decide how often and for how long to water.

facts.text: The aim is to wet the whole root zone while minimizing overwatering and keeping water use efficiency high.
Replenishing depleted water before stress sets in avoids moisture stress.
Methods range from watching plants for wilting and judging soil by feel, through sensors in the root zone, to soil water balance calculations.
Root-zone sensors include tensiometers, capacitance sensors and neutron probes, the last used for accurate deep readings.
Scheduling has moved from calendar timers to smart controllers that adjust to weather-based evapotranspiration or to measured soil moisture.
Soil-based controllers either skip a timed cycle when the soil is wet or start watering only when moisture falls to a set threshold.
The EPA WaterSense programme estimates that up to 50% of landscape water is wasted by inefficient methods.
Good scheduling prevents root rot and drought stress, and daily soil moisture estimates cut the risk of runoff and erosion.

entries.title: Four benchmarks from soaked to bone-dry

definition.text: Four reference water contents routinely measured in soil science, saturation, field capacity, permanent wilting point and residual water, each tied to a suction.

facts.text: Saturated water content, θs, is at 0 kPa suction and typically 0.2–0.5 by volume, equivalent to effective porosity.
Field capacity, θfc, is at −33 kPa and typically 0.1–0.35, the moisture 2–3 days after rain or irrigation.
Permanent wilting point, θpwp, is at −1500 kPa and typically 0.01–0.25, the lowest moisture at which a plant wilts.
Residual water content, θr, is the water left at very high tension, typically 0.001–0.1.
Available water content is field capacity minus wilting point, ranging from 0.1 in gravel to 0.3 in peat.
Average values put sand's wilting point at 3.3% and field capacity at 9.1% by volume, against 27.2% and 39.6% for clay.
Available water peaks in silt loam at 19.7% by volume, against 5.8% in sand and 12.4% in clay.

entries.title: Agricultural drought, which can strike without a dry year

definition.text: A condition in which soil is too dry to sustain reliable plant growth.

facts.text: It is a particular focus of irrigation management and common in arid and semi-arid environments.
As soil dries, transpiration falls because water is held ever more tightly by suction; below the wilting point plants wilt and stop transpiring.
Agricultural or ecological droughts harm crop production or ecosystems generally.
It can arise without any fall in rainfall, when more irrigation, or soil conditions and erosion from poorly planned farming, leave crops short of water.

entries.text: A farm can suffer drought without any fall in rainfall. Agricultural drought is a condition in which soil is too dry to sustain reliable plant growth. It can arise when soil conditions and erosion from poorly planned farming leave crops short of water. As soil dries, transpiration falls, because suction holds the water ever more tightly. Below the permanent wilting point plants wilt and stop transpiring. Common in arid and semi-arid environments, it is a particular focus of irrigation management. Agricultural or ecological droughts harm crop production or ecosystems generally.

entries.title: How far to let soil dry before watering

definition.text: The percentage of available soil water that can be used up before plants become stressed.

facts.text: It is often set at 50% for standard crops, 30% for sensitive crops such as vegetables, and 60–70% for stress-tolerant plants such as established trees.
Soil moisture sensors can act as a thermostat, triggering irrigation only when moisture drops below the threshold.

entries.text: A vegetable crop can spare less of its water than an established tree. Management allowed depletion is the percentage of available soil water that can be used up before plants become stressed. Soil moisture sensors can then act as a thermostat, triggering irrigation only when moisture drops below the threshold.

entries.title: Hygroscopic water: the film that even dry soil keeps

definition.text: Hygroscopic water is the thin film of water held on soil particles between the hygroscopic coefficient and the oven-dry state.

facts.text: The hygroscopic coefficient is reached when the last micropore is drained and only films of water surround the particles.
Air-dry soil holds water at potentials of -3000 to -10,000 kPa, in equilibrium with pore air at about 98% relative humidity.
Soil dried at 105 degrees C to constant weight is oven dry, and the oven-dry weight is the reference for expressing water in mineral soils.
Unavailable water, held at the wilting point, is mostly hygroscopic water held too tightly in micropores for plants.

entries.title: Evapotranspiration, the soil's great return to the sky

definition.text: The combined movement of water from the Earth's surface, open water, ice, bare soil and plants, into the atmosphere by evaporation and transpiration.

facts.text: Evaporation moves water straight to the air from soil and water bodies; transpiration carries it from roots through the plant and out of the stomata as vapour.
Only 0.1% to 1% of the water a plant uses stays in it; most is lost through transpiration.
It is measured as millimetres of water over a set time, and returns on average three-fifths to three-quarters of land precipitation to the atmosphere.
It is controlled mainly by the water available in soil and water bodies, the energy in air and soil, and the atmosphere's capacity to take up moisture.
Drier soil means less evapotranspiration and a warmer soil surface; where potential evapotranspiration exceeds rainfall, soil dries out unless irrigated.
It is measured directly with a weighing lysimeter, or estimated from a catchment water balance, an energy balance or meteorological data.
Evapotranspiration is one of four main parts of the water balance at a point, with infiltration, deep leakage beyond roots and surface runoff.
Evapotranspiration can concentrate the salts in irrigation water to toxic levels.

entries.text: Of all the water a plant uses, only 0.1% to 1% stays inside it; transpiration carries off the rest. Evapotranspiration is the combined movement of water into the atmosphere from the Earth's surface, open water, ice, bare soil and plants. Evaporation moves water straight to the air from soil and water bodies. Transpiration carries it from the roots through the plant and out of the stomata as vapor. Together they return, on average, three-fifths to three-quarters of the precipitation that falls on land. Three things mainly control the flow: water available in soil and water bodies, the energy in air and soil, and the atmosphere's capacity to take up moisture. Drier soil means less evapotranspiration and a warmer soil surface. Where {{ref:soil-water-246}} exceeds rainfall, soil dries out unless irrigated. The flow is counted in millimeters of water over a set time. It is measured directly with a weighing {{ref:soil-water-248}}, or estimated from a catchment water balance, an energy balance or weather data. With infiltration, deep leakage beyond the roots and runoff, it is one of four main parts of the water balance at a point. It can also concentrate the salts in irrigation water to toxic levels.

entries.title: 500 kilograms of water for a kilogram of alfalfa
entries.article: Soil moisture#Consumptive use and water use efficiency

definition.text: A measure of water use efficiency: the water a plant transpires divided by the dry weight of the harvested plant.

facts.text: Transpiration ratios for crops range from 300 to 700.
Alfalfa may have a ratio of 500, so 500 kilograms of water produce one kilogram of dry alfalfa.

entries.text: Growing one kilogram of dry alfalfa may take 500 kilograms of water. That figure is alfalfa's transpiration ratio, a measure of water use efficiency: the water a plant transpires divided by the dry weight of the harvested plant. For crops, transpiration ratios range from 300 to 700.

entries.title: The water budget: every drop accounted for

definition.text: The principle that inflows to any water system equal its outflows plus the change in storage over a time interval.

facts.text: A system can be a soil column, a drainage basin, an irrigation area or a city; the balance is also called a water budget.
A general basin form is P = Q + ET + ΔS: precipitation equals streamflow plus evapotranspiration plus change in storage in soil or groundwater.
It rests on conservation of mass and assumes a closed system; water leaving to another basin must be accounted for.
Comparing budgets across areas quantifies how geology, soils, vegetation and land use affect the hydrologic cycle.
It is used in irrigation, runoff assessment, flood and pollution control and the design of subsurface drainage by pipes, tile drains, ditches or wells.
Monthly water balance models have been studied since the 1940s.

entries.text: A basin, a field or a city can keep a water budget. A water balance states that the inflows to any water system equal its outflows plus the change in storage over a time interval. The system can be a soil column, a drainage basin, an irrigation area or a city. For a basin, P = Q + ET + ΔS: precipitation equals streamflow plus evapotranspiration plus the change in storage in soil or {{ref:soil-phys-203}}. The balance rests on conservation of mass and assumes a closed system, so water leaving for another basin must be accounted for. Comparing budgets across areas shows how geology, soils, vegetation and the way land is used affect the water cycle. The balance guides irrigation, runoff assessment, flood and pollution control, and the design of subsurface drainage by pipes, tile drains, ditches or wells. Monthly water balance models have been studied since the 1940s.

entries.title: Ecohydrology, where water meets living systems

definition.text: An interdisciplinary field studying how water and ecological systems interact.

facts.text: It is a branch of hydrology with an ecological focus, covering both water bodies and land ecosystems such as forests and deserts.
Its research covers transpiration and plant water use, adaptation of organisms to water, vegetation effects on streams, and feedbacks between ecology, the soil carbon sponge and the water cycle.
A basic tool is the water balance at a point: water entering the soil equals water leaving plus the change in storage, through infiltration, evapotranspiration, deep leakage and runoff.
Where water is ample, as in rainforests, growth depends more on nutrients; in semi-arid savannas vegetation follows the water plants can draw from the soil.

entries.title: Lysimeters: soil in a can, sometimes on a scale

definition.text: A soil-filled container, usually a cylinder, used to study how water and dissolved substances move through soil.

facts.text: It can hold an undisturbed soil monolith or rebuilt layers, carry probes at several depths, and collect leachate through an opening at the bottom.
Weighing lysimeters sit on scales, so weight changes give evaporation, transpiration and drainage, and hence actual evapotranspiration.
Suction lysimeters draw soil water through a buried porous cup under vacuum, and drainage lysimeters collect water passing through the profile to study leaching.
Edward Lewis Sturtevant built the first lysimeter in the United States in 1875.

entries.title: Potential evapotranspiration: how much water the air demands

definition.text: The water a crop, soil or ecosystem would evaporate and transpire if water were not limited.

facts.text: It reflects the energy and wind available to move water vapour, the demand side of evapotranspiration, and is higher in summer, on clear or windy days and nearer the equator.
Actual evapotranspiration equals it when water is ample and can never exceed it.
Reference evapotranspiration (ET0) is calculated for a short-grass surface, most widely with the Penman–Monteith equation recommended by the FAO.
A crop coefficient and a stress coefficient convert reference evapotranspiration into actual crop evapotranspiration.

entries.text: Summer, clear skies, wind and nearness to the equator all raise the air's demand for water. entries.title: Agricultural hydrology: water budgets for farmland

definition.text: The study of the water balance components involved in agricultural water management, especially irrigation and drainage.

facts.text: It divides the soil profile into reservoirs: the surface, the unsaturated root zone with mainly vertical flow, a transition zone, and the aquifer with mainly horizontal flow.
For the root zone, infiltration plus capillary rise equals actual evapotranspiration plus percolation plus the change in storage.
Bordering zones can be combined, and over months or years storage terms are often negligible, giving steady-state balances.
Its water balances also underpin the salt balances of irrigated land and models such as SaltMod and SahysMod.

entries.text: A farm's soil can be treated as a stack of reservoirs. Agricultural hydrology studies the water balance components that matter for managing farm water, especially irrigation and drainage. It divides the soil profile into the surface, the unsaturated root zone with mainly vertical flow, a transition zone, and the aquifer with mainly horizontal flow. For the root zone, infiltration plus capillary rise equals actual evapotranspiration plus percolation plus the change in storage. Bordering zones can be combined. Over months or years storage terms are often negligible, giving steady-state balances. These water balances also underpin the salt balances of irrigated land and models such as SaltMod and the one in {{ref:soil-chem-040}}.

entries.title: Penman–Monteith: estimating evaporation from the weather

definition.text: An equation that estimates evapotranspiration from meteorological data in place of direct measurement.

facts.text: Penman published it in 1948 and Monteith revised it in 1965.
Its inputs include net irradiance, ground heat flux, vapor pressure deficit, air density and heat capacity, and atmospheric and stomatal conductance.
Stomatal conductance captures leaf area index, water stress and CO2, so the equation is sensitive to vegetation parameters.
The FAO recommends it, but errors against direct measurement can range from -9 to 40%.
In 1998 the FAO simplified it (FAO 56) to compute reference evapotranspiration in mm per day from radiation, temperature and wind at 2 m and vapor pressure deficit.
Stress coefficients cut the estimate for environmental stress, such as saturated soil starving roots of oxygen, dry soil causing wilt, and salinity.
GIS-linked hydrologic models such as SWAT estimate evapotranspiration with it.

entries.title: Keeping a checkbook for the water in soil

definition.text: An irrigation scheduling method, also called the checkbook method, that tracks the water in the soil like a bank account.

facts.text: Rain and irrigation are the deposits; evapotranspiration, the soil's evaporation plus the plants' transpiration, is the withdrawal.
Each day's depletion equals the previous depletion plus crop evapotranspiration, minus rain and irrigation.
Crop evapotranspiration is reference evapotranspiration, the loss from a standard grass surface, adjusted by a crop coefficient set out in FAO Paper 56.
Coefficients above 1 mark high water users such as corn, and below 1 drought-tolerant plants such as cactus; the method relies on accurate weather data.

entries.title: How much to irrigate, how much to drain

definition.text: Calculating how much water a field needs from irrigation, and must lose through drains or wells, from its water balances.

facts.text: With surface evaporation neglected and actual evapotranspiration set to potential, the topsoil balance gives Irr = Epo + Osu + Per − Rai − Cap.
Irrigation efficiency is the fraction of irrigation water the crop consumes, Epo/Irr.
Subsurface and well drainage requirements, from drain or well discharge in the balances, are central to designing agricultural drainage systems.

In the Netherlands, 720 mm of precipitation against 540 mm of evaporation gives a winter drainage requirement of 180 mm; shallow-rooted pastures need summer irrigation, deep-rooted wheat practically does not.

entries.title: Eddy covariance: catching vapor in the wind

definition.text: A micrometeorological technique that computes vertical turbulent fluxes of gases, heat and water vapour from high-frequency wind and concentration data.

facts.text: The flux is the covariance between fluctuations of vertical wind speed and of gas concentration, times mean air density.
It is used over natural ecosystems and agricultural fields to measure water loss and evapotranspiration, carbon dioxide and methane exchange.
The source area of the measured eddies, the flux footprint, changes with wind direction, stability and measurement height.
It assumes flat, uniform terrain and fully turbulent flow, and needs instruments sampling at 5 to 40 Hz.

entries.text: Swirling eddies of air carry water vapor, heat and gases up from a field. Eddy covariance measures those vertical turbulent fluxes from fast readings of wind and gas concentration. The flux is the covariance, a measure of how two quantities rise and fall together, between vertical wind speed and gas concentration, times mean air density. Instruments sample at 5 to 40 Hz. Over natural ecosystems and farm fields, the method measures water loss and evapotranspiration, and carbon dioxide and methane exchange. Its source area, the flux footprint, shifts with wind direction, stability and measurement height. It assumes flat, uniform terrain and fully turbulent flow.

entries.title: Priestley–Taylor: evaporation from radiation alone

definition.text: A simplified substitute for the Penman–Monteith equation that needs only radiation observations.

facts.text: It drops the aerodynamic terms and multiplies reference evapotranspiration by an empirical constant, α.
Observed evaporation over well-watered vegetation was 1.26 times the reference rate.
It assumes plants with abundant water; arid regions with high moisture stress are estimated to have higher α.

entries.title: ET0: the water use of an imaginary lawn

definition.text: The water a standard, well-watered grass surface would lose under current temperature, humidity, wind and solar radiation, written ET0.

facts.text: FAO 56 defines it for a hypothetical crop 0.12 m tall with a surface resistance of 70 s m-1 and an albedo of 0.23, actively growing and adequately watered.
The FAO derived the Penman–Monteith equation for modelling it.
Multiplying it by a crop coefficient gives the evapotranspiration of unstressed plants, ET = Kc × ET0; a stress coefficient converts it to actual crop evapotranspiration.
Weather-based irrigation controllers calculate it to set watering.

entries.text: Crop water use is measured against an imaginary patch of grass. Multiplying ET0 by {{ref:soil-phys-218}} gives the evapotranspiration of unstressed plants, ET = Kc × ET0. A stress coefficient then gives actual crop use. Weather-based irrigation controllers calculate it.

entries.title: Crop coefficients: from reference grass to real crop

definition.text: A plant property used to predict evapotranspiration, most simply the ratio of a crop's evapotranspiration to that of a reference crop, Kc.

facts.text: Kc varies through the season with growth stage, often following a trapezoidal or leaf area index curve.
Stress coefficients between 0 and 1, of which water stress (Kw) is the commonest, are multiplied in to reduce the estimate.
Kc can exceed 1 when the crop uses more water than the reference.
Irrigation scheduling multiplies ET0 by Kc to get the crop's actual water requirement, ETc.

entries.text: Watering plans, the subject of {{ref:soil-water-234}}, turn a weather figure into a crop's thirst with one multiplier. The crop coefficient, Kc, is most simply the ratio of a crop's evapotranspiration to that of a reference crop. Multiplying ET0 by Kc gives the crop's actual water requirement, ETc. Kc changes through the season with growth stage, often following a trapezoidal or leaf area index curve. It can exceed 1 when the crop uses more water than the reference. Stress coefficients between 0 and 1, most often for water stress (Kw), are multiplied in to reduce the estimate.

entries.title: A rye plant's 10,620 kilometers of root hairs

definition.text: The ways plants draw soil water into their roots, mainly by the pull of transpiration and partly by osmosis.

facts.text: Most soil water enters plants passively, pulled up the column of xylem sap from roots to leaves as water transpires, as the cohesion-tension theory describes.
Salts concentrated in roots create an osmotic gradient that pushes water in; osmotic uptake matters most when transpiration is low, at night or in high humidity.
The root endodermis and leaf stomata regulate the upward flow, which cavitation in the xylem can interrupt.
A winter rye plant grown four months in 0.0283 cubic metres of loam formed 620 km of roots and 10,620 km of root hairs, yet touched only 1.2% of the soil volume.
Because roots grow into new soil every day, the volume they explore, and the water they take up, grows greatly over a season.
Root architecture, the spatial layout of the root system, helps plants adapt to the soil's water and nutrient supply.
Grain sorghum held at 1300 kPa soil suction from seed-head emergence to seed set lost 34% of its production.
Some parts of a root system can also re-wet dry parts of the soil.

entries.title: Transpiration: how plants lift soil water into the air

definition.text: The movement of water through a plant and its evaporation from aerial parts such as leaves, stems and flowers.

facts.text: It is passive, costing the plant no energy, and also cools plants and drives the mass flow of mineral nutrients.
Only a small part of the water roots take up is used for growth; 97–99.5% is lost by transpiration and guttation.
Flow from soil to roots depends on the soil's hydraulic conductivity and the pressure gradient through the soil; flow up the plant is driven mainly by water potential differences.
When roots take up less water than leaves lose, stomata close, which slows nutrient uptake and limits photosynthesis and growth.
Soil temperature and moisture influence stomatal opening, and root uptake suffers in dry, very fertile or salty soils.
An acre of corn gives off about 3,000–4,000 U.S. gallons (11,000–15,000 liters) of water a day.
Isotope measurements show transpiration is the larger part of evapotranspiration, and that transpired water differs from groundwater and streams, so soil water is less well mixed than assumed.
It is measured with potometers, lysimeters, porometers, photosynthesis systems and sap flow sensors.

entries.title: One unbroken path from soil to sky

definition.text: The unbroken pathway along which water moves from the soil, through plants, into the atmosphere.

facts.text: Water potential is very low in the air and higher inside leaves, so water diffuses out through the stomata as vapour.
Water evaporating from leaf cells is replaced from the xylem, where cohesion and tension pull more water up from the roots.
Each discipline describes its own segment differently: soil physics by tension, physiology by diffusion pressure deficit, meteorology by vapour pressure or humidity.
The concept treats soil, plants, animals and air as one dynamic system, giving water in each part a water potential, which is the basis for modelling transport between them.

entries.text: Water can travel from soil into a root, up a stem and out of a leaf along one connected pathway. That pathway is the soil-plant-atmosphere continuum. Water potential is very low in the air and higher inside leaves, so water diffuses out through the stomata, the pores of the leaf, as vapor. Water lost from leaf cells is replaced from the xylem, the plant's water-carrying tissue, where cohesion and tension pull more up from the roots. Soil physics, physiology and meteorology each describe their own segment in different terms. The continuum treats soil, plants, animals and air as one dynamic system, giving water in each part a {{ref:soil-water-172}}. That shared measure is the basis for modelling transport between them.
entries.text_plain: Water can travel from soil into a root, up a stem and out of a leaf along one connected pathway. That pathway is the soil-plant-atmosphere continuum. Water potential is very low in the air and higher inside leaves, so water diffuses out through the stomata, the pores of the leaf, as vapor. Water lost from leaf cells is replaced from the xylem, the plant's water-carrying tissue, where cohesion and tension pull more up from the roots. Soil physics, physiology and meteorology each describe their own segment in different terms.
