That shared measure is the basis for modelling transport between them.

entries.title: Wilting: when a plant's cells lose their pressure

definition.text: The loss of rigidity of a plant's non-woody parts when turgor pressure in its cells falls towards zero for lack of water.

facts.text: It happens when the plant loses water faster than it absorbs it.
Soil causes include drought, high salinity drawing water from cells, and saturated soil that starves roots of oxygen so they cannot move water.
Plants may recover overnight as stomata close and evaporation falls, but permanent wilting kills the plant.
Wilting reduces water loss by exposing less leaf area but also curbs transpiration, reproduction and growth.

entries.title: Advection, the river that carries what it holds

definition.text: The transport of a substance or quantity by the bulk motion of a fluid.

facts.text: It needs currents in a fluid, so it cannot happen in rigid solids, and it excludes transport by molecular diffusion.
Ink dumped in a river moves downstream as a pulse by advection while also spreading by diffusion; the sum of the two is convection.
In groundwater, advection carries contaminants along the main direction of flow at the seepage velocity.
The advection equation is a first-order hyperbolic partial differential equation derived from the conservation law of the transported quantity.

entries.text: Dump ink into a river and it travels downstream as a pulse. The river's own current carries it, and that carrying has a name: advection, the transport of a substance or quantity by the bulk motion of a fluid. It needs currents, so it cannot happen in rigid solids. It also excludes the slow drift of molecules on their own, called {{ref:soil-phys-240}}. The ink does both at once, riding the current while it spreads, and the sum of the two is convection. Underground the same thing happens in {{ref:soil-phys-203}}. There advection carries contaminants along the main direction of flow at the seepage velocity, the speed at which water actually moves through the pores. Physicists write it as the advection equation, a first-order hyperbolic partial differential equation. It comes from a conservation law: whatever is transported is neither created nor lost along the way.

entries.title: How pollution travels with moving groundwater

definition.text: The movement of dissolved contaminants with moving groundwater, studied by contaminant hydrogeology.

facts.text: Contaminants may be man-made, such as petroleum products, nitrate or radionuclides, or natural, such as arsenic or salinity.
They move by three main mechanisms: advection at seepage velocity, diffusion from high to low concentration, and hydrodynamic dispersion.
Aquifer properties beyond the flow itself affect how dissolved contaminants move.
Diffusion and dispersion only spread a contaminant, while retardation by adsorption slows its average velocity.
Polluted groundwater forms a plume whose advancing edge can reach wells and springs; its movement is analysed with hydrological transport or groundwater models.
Diffusion, adsorption, precipitation and decay all influence pollutant transport.

entries.text: A spill on the surface can turn up years later in a distant well. Contaminant transport in groundwater is the movement of dissolved contaminants with the water flowing underground, and contaminant hydrogeology is the field that studies it, a branch of {{ref:soil-phys-208}}. Some contaminants are man-made, such as petroleum products, nitrate or radionuclides. Others are natural, such as arsenic or salinity. Three main mechanisms move them. {{ref:soil-phys-193}} carries them at seepage velocity. {{ref:soil-phys-240}} spreads them from high to low concentration. Dispersion, covered in {{ref:soil-phys-194}}, spreads them further still. Those two only spread a contaminant, though. Sticking to the soil, the process of {{ref:soil-chem-145}}, does something different: it slows the contaminant's average velocity. Precipitation and decay also change what arrives. So the properties of the {{ref:soil-phys-201}}, beyond the flow itself, shape where pollution goes. Polluted groundwater forms a plume, and its advancing edge can reach wells and springs. Hydrologists track it with transport and groundwater models.

entries.title: Why a contaminant plume spreads as it travels

definition.text: The spreading of dissolved contaminants away from the mean path of the groundwater carrying them, caused by small-scale heterogeneity and uneven velocities in the porous medium.

facts.text: Its strength is expressed by empirical dispersivities: longitudinal (αL) for solute ahead of or behind the mean flow, transverse (αT) for solute to the sides.
At the microscopic scale, water passing each soil particle must go left, right, up or down, so solute spreads around the mean path.
Over long distances, zones of higher and lower permeability give preferential paths that spread contaminants irregularly.
Dispersivity reflects details averaged away in a macroscopic model, such as thin gravel or clay beds in sand, so it is partly a measure of missing information.
It is therefore often claimed to depend on scale: dispersivity through 1 m3 of aquifer differs from that through 1 cm3 of the same material.
Salinity models need dispersivity as a soil input alongside water retention and unsaturated hydraulic conductivity.

entries.text: Water cannot flow straight through soil. At every grain it must go left, right, up or down, so dissolved substances fan out around their average path. Hydrodynamic dispersion is this spreading of dissolved contaminants away from the mean path of the groundwater carrying them. It comes from small-scale unevenness in the porous medium and uneven water speeds through its {{ref:soil-phys-063}}. Over long distances a second effect takes over. Zones of higher and lower permeability offer preferential paths, like the {{ref:soil-water-157}} met earlier, and spread contaminants irregularly. Hydrologists measure the strength of dispersion with empirical numbers called dispersivities. Longitudinal dispersivity, αL, covers solute running ahead of or behind the mean flow. Transverse dispersivity, αT, covers solute drifting to the sides. These numbers hide a surprise. They stand in for details a large-scale model averages away, such as thin gravel or clay beds in sand. entries.title: Retardation: why contaminants lag behind the water

definition.text: The slowing of a contaminant's average movement relative to groundwater because it adsorbs to the soil, measured by a retardation factor.

facts.text: The factor is analogous to the retardation factor of chromatography.
Adsorption holds the contaminant back until the amount set by the adsorption equilibrium has been adsorbed.
Less soluble contaminants can move hundreds or thousands of times slower than water, so only the more soluble species travel far.
The factor depends on the chemistry of both the contaminant and the aquifer.
Unlike diffusion and dispersion, which merely spread a contaminant, retardation changes its global average velocity, so it can be much slower than the water.
In chromatography the retardation factor R is the fraction of the substance in the mobile phase at equilibrium: the quantity in the mobile phase divided by the total quantity in the system.
In planar chromatography RF is the substance's travel distance over the solvent front's, always between 0 and 1 because nothing outruns the solvent; 2.5 cm over 5.0 cm gives 0.50.

entries.title: Molecular diffusion, fast over millimeters, slow over meters

definition.text: The random thermal movement of molecules that carries solutes from high to low concentration.

facts.text: Time to diffuse grows with the square of distance, so diffusion matters over small distances but spreads solutes slowly over large ones.
Its coefficient is small and often negligible, except where groundwater flows extremely slowly, as in clay aquitards.
Diffusion is a physical process, whereas dispersion is an empirical factor written in the same mathematical form.

entries.text: Double the distance and it takes four times as long. The random thermal movement of molecules ({{ref:soil-phys-243}}) carries solutes from high to low concentration in the {{ref:soil-found-079}}. Over small distances it matters, but it spreads solutes slowly over large ones. Its coefficient is small and often negligible, except where groundwater barely moves, as in clay aquitards. This drift is a real physical process. Dispersion is an empirical factor that merely shares its mathematical form.

entries.title: One equation for drifting and spreading

definition.text: A parabolic partial differential equation for a quantity moved by both diffusion and convection (advection).

facts.text: It is also called the advection–diffusion or scalar transport equation.
It follows from the continuity equation, with diffusive flux from Fick's first law, −D∇c, and advective flux vc.
A source or sink term R adds or removes the quantity, as when a chemical reaction creates or destroys a species.
For flow in porous media, the velocity in the equation is the superficial velocity.
Most soil water and solute models, such as SWAP, DrainMod-S, UnSatChem and Hydrus, couple the Richards equation with it to move salts by advection and dispersion.

entries.text: Most soil models describe salt on the move with one equation. entries.title: Dye tracing, following water with color

definition.text: A method of tracking flows by adding dye to a liquid as a tracer.

facts.text: It can be qualitative, showing a flow exists, or quantitative, measuring dye amounts with instruments such as fluorometers.
Fluorescein, first developed in 1871, and its sodium salt uranine remain among the best tracers, with rhodamine, pyranine and sulforhodamine B.
Organic matter, other chemicals, sunlight and acidic water affect dye performance.
Dye traces showed karst groundwater moving 0.8 to 11.3 km a day and that models assuming uniform porosity do not fit karst aquifers.

entries.title: The Péclet number: advection against diffusion

definition.text: A dimensionless number giving the ratio of advective to diffusive transport rate.

facts.text: For mass transfer, Pe = L u / D, with L a characteristic length, u flow velocity and D the diffusion coefficient; it equals the Reynolds number times the Schmidt number.
It can also be written as the ratio of diffusion time to advection time.
Where Pe is much greater than 1, advection predominates in mass transport because diffusion takes much longer.

entries.text: Two kinds of transport compete in any moving fluid, and the Péclet number says which one wins. It is a dimensionless number giving the ratio of advective to diffusive transport rate, the two processes of {{ref:soil-phys-193}} and {{ref:soil-phys-195}}. For mass transfer, Pe = L u / D, with L a characteristic length, u flow velocity and D the {{ref:soil-phys-240}} coefficient; it equals the Reynolds number times the Schmidt number. It can also be written as the ratio of that spreading time to advection time. Where Pe is much greater than 1, advection predominates in mass transport because it takes much longer.

entries.title: Vadose zone models: solute transport on a computer

definition.text: Computer models that simulate water flow and solute transport in unsaturated soil by solving the Richards equation numerically.

facts.text: Hydrus takes soil hydraulic parameters for the water retention and unsaturated conductivity functions, plus initial and boundary conditions.
Most such models, including SWAP, DrainMod-S, UnSatChem and Hydrus, join the Richards equation to a convection–diffusion equation for salts.
The one-dimensional HYDRUS1D program is available online and used to estimate groundwater recharge.

entries.title: Colloids, the hitchhikers that carry pollutants far

definition.text: Transport in which colloidal particles carry contaminants through surface water and groundwater.

facts.text: Colloids also move through surface soils and the ground depending on soil structure, compaction and particle size; the process drew real attention only in the 1980s.
Radionuclides, heavy metals and organic pollutants sorb easily onto suspended colloids, which may be inorganic (clays, iron oxy-hydroxides) or organic (humic and fulvic substances).
Colloids are suspected in long-range plutonium transport at the Nevada Nuclear Test Site.
Inorganic colloids barely move in compacted bentonite and deep clay, which ultrafilter them.

entries.text: Plutonium at the Nevada Nuclear Test Site may have traveled far on tiny passengers. In transport facilitated by {{ref:soil-chem-154}}, these particles carry contaminants through surface water and groundwater. Radionuclides, heavy metals and organic pollutants sorb easily onto them while they are suspended. These may be inorganic, such as clays and iron oxy-hydroxides, or organic, such as humic and fulvic substances. How far they move depends on soil structure, compaction and particle size. Compacted {{ref:soil-chem-100}} and deep clay ultrafilter them. The process drew real attention only in the 1980s.

entries.title: The breakthrough curve: watching a solute emerge from a column

definition.text: The course of a solute's concentration at the outlet of a column of porous material after a step change in inlet concentration.

facts.text: A fixed bed is purged with a carrier, then the adsorptive is added so that inlet concentration changes in a step, and the outlet concentration is monitored; chromatography instead uses pulses.
Integrating the area above the whole curve gives the material's maximum loading, and the time until the outlet reaches a threshold concentration gives its usable sorption capacity.
The curve's shape carries information on mass-transfer properties, which can be evaluated by fitting simplified models to the data.
The source page frames this in adsorption engineering; the soil-column version is not described in it.

entries.text: Feed a solute into one end of a column of porous material and measure what comes out of the other. Integrating the area above the whole curve gives the material's maximum loading, and the time until the outlet reaches a threshold concentration gives its usable capacity to take up the solute. entries.title: The hidden atmosphere between soil grains

definition.text: The gases filling the air spaces between soil particles, also called the soil atmosphere.

facts.text: The main soil gases are nitrogen, carbon dioxide and oxygen; nitric oxide, nitrous oxide, methane and ammonia also occur naturally.
Oxygen is critical because plant roots and soil organisms need it to respire.
Gas fills pores as water drains, evaporates or is taken up by roots, so soil air and soil water are often inversely related.
Microbes and roots consume oxygen and release carbon dioxide, so soil air holds less oxygen and more CO2 than the air above.
Soil organisms emit volatile compounds as metabolites, allelopathic agents and signals, making soil air a network of chemical cues.
Aerated soil is a net sink of methane, but oxygen-depleted soil at elevated temperatures produces it.
Soil is a net emitter of greenhouse gases, especially where permafrost thaws and degasses as the climate warms.
The familiar after-the-rain scent comes when infiltrating rain flushes out the soil atmosphere after a drought.

Soil organisms release volatile compounds as by-products of their metabolism, as chemicals that act on their neighbors and as signals. The result is a network of chemical cues. The soil's gas budget matters for climate too. Well-ventilated soil is a net sink of methane, yet oxygen-starved soil at higher temperatures produces it. Overall, soil is a net emitter of greenhouse gases, especially where {{ref:soil-env-129}} thaws and releases its gas as the climate warms.

entries.title: Greenhouse gases: the trace gases that warm the planet

definition.text: A gas in an atmosphere that absorbs the heat a planet radiates and so raises its surface temperature.

facts.text: Without greenhouse gases Earth's average surface temperature would be about -18 °C instead of the present 15 °C.

Nitrogen and oxygen, 99% of dry air, barely absorb infrared; carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide and other trace gases, under 0.1% of the atmosphere, absorb it because their molecules are asymmetric in charge.

Water vapour causes 41-67% of the greenhouse effect, but its short residence time of about nine days means human activity barely changes it globally; it amplifies warming through water vapour feedback.
Concentrations follow the balance of sources and sinks; the soil, oceans and vegetation are sinks, and about 0.55 of emitted CO2 is absorbed by land and ocean sinks in the first year.

Most human CO2 comes from fossil fuels, with additions from cement, fertiliser production and land-use change; agriculture is a major methane source, and rice paddies give 22% of agricultural methane and 11% of nitrous oxide.

A greenhouse gas is a gas in an atmosphere that absorbs the heat a planet radiates and so raises its surface temperature. Nitrogen and oxygen, 99% of dry air, barely absorb infrared. Carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide and other trace gases, under 0.1% of the atmosphere, absorb it because their molecules are asymmetric in charge. Water vapor causes 41-67% of the greenhouse effect, but its short residence time of about nine days means human activity barely changes it globally; it amplifies warming through water vapor feedback. Concentrations follow the balance of sources and sinks. Soil, oceans and vegetation are sinks, and about 0.55 of emitted CO2 is absorbed by land and ocean sinks in the first year. Most human CO2 comes from fossil fuels. Agriculture is a major methane source, with rice paddies giving 22% of agricultural methane and 11% of nitrous oxide.

entries.title: How warm the ground runs, and why it matters

definition.text: How warm or cold a soil is, set by the balance between the energy it absorbs and the energy it loses.

facts.text: Mean annual soil temperature ranges from −10 to 26 °C depending on the biome.
It regulates seed germination, the breaking of seed dormancy, plant and root growth and the availability of nutrients.
It varies by season, month and day, but the swings shrink with depth: upper layers follow air temperature while deeper layers fluctuate less.
Water content, soil colour, relief, cover and air temperature all affect it; paler soils with higher albedo stay cooler than dark ones.
Wet surface soil is typically 3 to 6 °C colder than dry surface soil, because water takes more energy to heat and to evaporate.
Drying or clear plastic mulch raises soil temperature; organic mulch slows warming and damps surface fluctuations.
Farming adapts to it by timing planting, applying anhydrous ammonia below 10 °C (50 °F) and protecting shallow-rooted crops from frost heaving.
Soil temperatures are rising worldwide with climate warming; the main threats concern permafrost thaw, carbon loss and ecosystem collapse.

entries.title: How oxygen finds its way into the ground

definition.text: The net movement of gas molecules through soil pores from higher to lower concentration, the main way soil air exchanges with the atmosphere.

facts.text: Gas molecules move constantly and collide in a random walk; diffusion is described numerically by Fick's law.
Oxygen diffuses in from the atmosphere and is consumed, while excess carbon dioxide, other gases and water vapour diffuse out.
Total porosity, pore connectivity, water content, air turbulence and temperature set the diffusion rate, rather than pore size.
The diffusion coefficient falls as soil is compacted, and platy structure also impedes gas flow.
In water-saturated soil, gas diffusion slows some 10,000 times because no open air passages remain.
Short of oxygen, anaerobic bacteria reduce nitrate to N2, N2O and NO gases, depleting soil nitrogen by denitrification.
Daily or seasonal changes in temperature and moisture alter soil gas and so the rate of soil respiration.
Thawing and rewetting of frozen or dry soils boost microbial activity and respiration, causing sudden fluxes of carbon dioxide and methane.

entries.text: Soil air is never still. Its gas molecules move constantly, colliding and bouncing in a random walk. Gas {{ref:soil-phys-240}} is the net movement of those molecules through soil pores from higher to lower concentration. It is the main way {{ref:soil-phys-146}} trades with the atmosphere, and Fick's law describes it in numbers. Oxygen diffuses in from the air above and is consumed below. Excess carbon dioxide, other gases and water vapor diffuse out. The rate depends on total porosity, how well the pores connect, water content, air turbulence and temperature. Pore size itself matters less. Compaction lowers its coefficient, the measure of how readily gas spreads, and a platy structure also blocks the flow. Water is the great obstacle. In saturated soil no open air passages remain, and it slows some 10,000 times. Short of oxygen, anaerobic bacteria, which live without free oxygen, reduce nitrate to N2, N2O and NO gases. This drains nitrogen from the soil. Daily and seasonal swings in temperature and moisture change the soil gas, and with it the pace of {{ref:soil-bio-033}}. When frozen soils thaw or dry soils are rewetted, microbes surge into activity. Sudden bursts of carbon dioxide and methane follow.

entries.title: Letting the soil breathe

definition.text: The exchange of gases between soil and atmosphere, and the means of improving it.

facts.text: Microbial activity and root respiration deplete oxygen and build up carbon dioxide in the soil, and lack of oxygen can hinder plant growth.
Aeration also allows water drainage and root growth; soil compaction is a common cause of poor aeration.
The pore network ventilates the soil, but it becomes blocked when water fills the pores.
Wind, atmospheric pressure, convection and diffusion all influence aeration rates.
Soil structure strongly affects the larger pores that control aeration, infiltration and drainage.
Waterlogging or compaction that limits aeration can cut nutrient uptake, and bacteria short of free oxygen take it from nitrate.
Liquid aeration applies solutions, commonly of ammonium lauryl sulfate, that break down dense particles and loosen compacted soil.
Liming improves soil structure and thus aeration, and digging megafauna improve it by disturbing soil horizons.

entries.text: Compaction is one of the commonest reasons a soil runs short of air. Soil aeration is the exchange of gases between soil and atmosphere, along with the ways of improving it. Below ground, microbial activity and root respiration use up oxygen and build up carbon dioxide. A lack of oxygen can then hold back plant growth. Good aeration also lets water drain and roots grow. The pore network ventilates the soil, and wind, atmospheric pressure, convection and {{ref:soil-phys-240}} all drive the exchange. Soil structure strongly shapes the larger pores that control aeration, infiltration and drainage. Those pores fail in two common ways: water fills them, or compaction crushes them. Either way, nutrient uptake can fall, and bacteria short of free oxygen take it from nitrate instead. Remedies range from chemistry to animals. Liquid aeration applies solutions, commonly of ammonium lauryl sulfate, that break down dense particles and loosen compacted soil. Adding lime improves soil structure and so aeration. Digging megafauna, large burrowing animals, help too by disturbing the soil's layers.

entries.title: Soil air: like the sky's, but rich in carbon dioxide

definition.text: The make-up of the soil atmosphere: similar to the air above, but richer in carbon dioxide and water vapour.

facts.text: A typical comparison gives soil air 79.2% nitrogen, 20.6% oxygen and 0.25% carbon dioxide, against 78.0%, 20.9% and 0.04% in the atmosphere.
In soil pores CO2 may reach 10 to 100 times the atmospheric 0.04%, possibly inhibiting root respiration; at extreme levels CO2 is toxic.
Carbon dioxide increases with depth because of decomposing organic matter and abundant roots.
Calcareous soils buffer CO2 through carbonates, while in acid soils respired CO2 accumulates in the pores.
Composition shifts daily and seasonally with chemical and biological processes, unlike the more uniform atmosphere.
Methane and nitrous oxide are minor but matter for greenhouse gas flux and human impacts on soils.
Temperature, atmospheric pressure, wind and rainfall are important controls on the soil atmosphere.

entries.title: How deep the winter reaches

definition.text: The depth to which groundwater in the soil is expected to freeze, also called frost depth or freezing depth.

facts.text: It depends on climate, the heat transfer properties of the soil and nearby materials, and nearby heat sources: snow cover and asphalt insulate, while homes warm the ground.
It deepens toward the poles; maximum frost depth in the contiguous United States ranges from 0 to 8 feet (2.4 m).
In Arctic and Antarctic locations freezing reaches year-round permafrost, and the term thaw depth is used instead.
The frost front is the shifting position of the frost line during seasonal freezing and thawing.
In the tropics, frost line can instead mean the elevation below which frost does not occur.
Building codes put foundations below frost depth because frost heaving can move them; water and sewer pipes are buried below it too.
Where shallow bedrock or utilities prevent deep trenching, pipes may instead be insulated or heated with heat tape.

entries.title: Why frozen ground rises: Stephen Taber's answer

definition.text: The upward swelling of soil in freezing weather as ice grows toward the surface from the freezing front.

facts.text: It needs frost-susceptible soil, a water supply from below such as a water table, and freezing temperatures penetrating the soil.
Water reaches the freezing front by capillary action and feeds growing ice lenses, which can lift soil 1 foot (0.30 m) or more.
Water expands only about 9% on freezing, too little to explain heave; by 1930 Stephen Taber had shown that water migrates to the freeze line.
Taber found that benzene, which contracts on freezing, also heaves, ruling out volume change as the main mechanism.
Differential heave cracks road surfaces, helping form springtime potholes, and damages building foundations.
Cold stores and ice rinks can freeze and heave the ground beneath them; non-susceptible fill, insulation or heating prevent it.
Needle ice is frost heaving at the start of the freezing season, before the freezing front has gone deep.

entries.text: Water expands only about 9% when it freezes, too little to explain how far frozen ground can rise. Frost heaving is the upward swelling of soil in freezing weather as ice grows toward the surface from the freezing front. It needs three things. The soil's fine pores must pull water upward ({{ref:soil-phys-155}}). Water must be supplied from below, as by a water table. And freezing temperatures must reach into the soil. Water climbs to the freezing front by capillary action. There it feeds growing layers of ice, described in {{ref:soil-phys-154}}, that can lift soil 1 foot (0.30 m) or more. By 1930 Stephen Taber had shown the real cause: water migrates to the freeze line. He also found that benzene, which contracts as it freezes, heaves too. That ruled out volume change as the main mechanism. The damage is familiar. Uneven heave cracks road surfaces, helping form springtime potholes, and it damages building foundations. Even cold stores and ice rinks can freeze and lift the ground beneath them. Fill that does not heave, insulation or heating prevents it. At the very start of the freezing season, before the freezing front has gone deep, the same process appears as {{ref:soil-phys-159}}.

entries.title: Needle ice: frost columns that heave seedlings from the ground

definition.text: Needle-shaped columns of ice that grow from groundwater at the soil surface, usually on cold nights.

facts.text: It forms when the soil is above 0 °C but the air at the surface is below 0 °C; water rises by capillary action and freezes onto the growing column.
Needles are typically a few centimetres long; 10 cm is the recorded maximum, though 15–20 cm specimens have been seen at Gerðuberg.
It needs ice segregation, in which supercooled water freezes onto existing ice in a porous medium, and it favours soils high in silt and organic matter.
It is frost heaving at the start of the freezing season, before there is any soil overburden to lift.
Growing needles lift soil particles and crusts that settle unevenly on melting, disturbing streambanks, aiding soil creep and shaping patterned ground.
It heaves seedlings out of the ground; they often die because they do not resettle or their roots dry out.
Other names include frost pillars, Kammeis, shimobashira and pipkrake, a Swedish term coined in 1907 by Henrik Hesselman.
Taber found that pore size controls the amount of frost heave and that a gradient of soil moisture tension drives water up toward the freezing front near the surface.

entries.title: The properties that steer heat through soil

definition.text: The properties that govern how energy, mostly heat, moves through soil by radiation, conduction and convection, a part of soil physics used in engineering, climatology and agriculture.

facts.text: The main ones are volumetric heat capacity (J·m−3·K−1) and thermal conductivity (W·m−1·K−1); they govern how energy is partitioned in the soil profile.
They change constantly with daily and seasonal cycles, so general statements about one site are hard to make.
Besides basic composition, they depend strongly on volumetric water content and the volume fractions of solids and air.
Soil moisture and thermal properties are so closely linked that they are often measured and reported together.
Surface temperature swings reach deeper layers at reduced rates and with a delay, sometimes called thermal lag.
Uses range from frost effects on construction, buried pipes and cables and the timing of planting to greenhouse gas studies, radioactive waste and locating buried land mines.

entries.text: Heat enters and leaves soil in three ways: radiation, conduction and convection. Soil thermal properties govern how that energy moves. They form a branch of soil physics used in engineering, climatology and agriculture. The two main ones measure how much heat a volume of soil stores, in J·m−3·K−1, and how well it passes heat along, in W·m−1·K−1. Each has its own entry later: {{ref:soil-phys-139}} and {{ref:soil-phys-141}}. Together they decide how energy is shared out through the soil profile. Basic composition matters, but water content and the volume fractions of solids and air matter strongly. Moisture and thermal properties are so closely linked that they are often measured and reported together. Both change constantly with daily and seasonal cycles, which makes general statements about any one site hard. Surface temperature swings reach deeper layers more slowly and with a delay, an effect explored in {{ref:soil-phys-142}}. The uses are broad. Engineers weigh frost effects on construction and on buried pipes and cables, and farmers time their planting. Others study greenhouse gases, store radioactive waste or search for buried land mines.

entries.title: Permafrost, ground frozen for ages

definition.text: Soil, rock or underwater sediment that stays continuously below 0 °C for two years or more.

facts.text: The oldest permafrost has been frozen for around 700,000 years; in practice it occurs where the mean annual temperature is 0 °C or below.
It underlies about 11% of the global land surface, around 18 million km2, including much of Alaska, Canada, Greenland and Siberia and high mountains such as the Tibetan Plateau.
Its thickness ranges from below a meter to greater than 1,500 m.
On land it usually lies beneath an active layer of soil that freezes and thaws with the seasons.
Dead biomass has built up in it over millennia without fully decomposing, which makes tundra soil a carbon sink.
As warming thaws it, decomposition restarts and releases carbon dioxide or methane, a climate change feedback.
Thawing ice-rich ground can suddenly exceed hydraulic saturation and shift or collapse, endangering buildings and infrastructure built on it.

conflicts.text: Permafrost base depth reaches 1,493 m in the northern Lena and Yana River basins in Siberia.
conflicts.note: The lead gives the deepest permafrost as greater than 1,500 m; the Classification section says it can exceed 1,400 m (S:cb45bb1e0218).

entries.text: The oldest permafrost has stayed frozen for around 700,000 years. Permafrost is soil, rock or underwater sediment that stays continuously below 0 °C for two years or more. In practice it occurs where the mean annual temperature is 0 °C or below. It underlies about 11% of the global land surface, around 18 million km2. That includes much of Alaska, Canada, Greenland and Siberia, and high mountains such as the Tibetan Plateau. Its thickness ranges from less than a meter to more than 1,500 m. On land it usually lies beneath soil that freezes and thaws with the seasons, the {{ref:soil-env-146}}. Over millennia, dead plant and animal remains have built up in it without fully breaking down. That makes tundra soil a store of carbon. Warming now threatens that store. As the frozen ground thaws, the remains begin to break down again, releasing carbon dioxide or methane, which feeds back into climate change. Thaw also weakens the ground itself. Ice-rich soil can suddenly exceed hydraulic saturation and shift or collapse, endangering the buildings and infrastructure on it.

entries.title: Ice lenses, the hidden engine of frost heave

definition.text: A body of ice that grows where moisture diffusing through soil or rock collects in one zone, usually parallel to the surface.

facts.text: Ice first gathers in small pores or cracks and keeps collecting, wedging the soil or rock apart.
Lenses grow several centimetres to several decimetres deep, and their growth is the dominant cause of soil displacement in frost heaving.
They grow by drawing water from groundwater below the freezing line through frost-susceptible soil with capillary pores.
Water in fine pores stays liquid below the bulk freezing point (the Gibbs–Thomson effect), so it can percolate toward the lens.
Rock fracture by ice segregation is a more effective weathering process than the freeze-thaw expansion proposed by older texts.
Arctic tundra favours deep lenses, because permafrost keeps the ground frozen at depth and stops meltwater draining.

entries.text: Most of the lift in frost heave comes from ice growing in hidden layers underground. An ice lens is a body of ice that forms where moisture moving through soil or rock collects in one zone, usually parallel to the surface. Ice first gathers in small pores or cracks. It keeps collecting there, wedging the soil or rock apart. Lenses grow several centimeters to several decimeters deep, and their growth is the dominant cause of soil displacement in frost heaving. They draw water from groundwater below the freezing line, through fine soils with capillary pores. The water can travel because water in fine pores stays liquid below the normal freezing point, the Gibbs–Thomson effect. The same process, the subject of {{ref:soil-phys-179}}, splits rock more effectively than the freeze-thaw expansion proposed by older texts. Arctic tundra favors deep lenses, because permafrost keeps the ground frozen at depth and stops meltwater draining away.

entries.title: Patterned ground: circles and stripes drawn by frost

definition.text: Distinct, often symmetrical geometric patterns formed by the deformation of ground material in periglacial regions.

facts.text: It occurs wherever soil freezing and thawing alternate, from the Arctic and Antarctica to the Australian Outback, the Atacama Desert and Mars.
Computer models of the past 20 years tie its formation to frost heaving of wet, fine-grained, porous soils.
Repeated freezing and thawing push larger stones up, and lateral forces pile them into clusters and stripes that smooth into polygons, circles and stripes.
Forms include polygons, circles a few centimetres to several metres across, steps, and stripes on slopes of 2° to 7°, each either sorted or unsorted.
Polygons form either in permafrost, as ice wedges, or in areas of seasonal frost.
It forms mostly within the active layer of permafrost.

entries.text: Stones sorted into neat circles and stripes can form with no human hand involved. Patterned ground is the distinct, often symmetrical geometric patterns formed when ground material deforms in periglacial regions, cold lands shaped by frost. It occurs wherever soil freezing and thawing alternate, from the Arctic and Antarctica to the Australian Outback, the Atacama Desert and Mars. Computer models of the past 20 years tie its formation to frost heaving of wet, fine-grained, porous soils. Repeated freezing and thawing push larger stones up. Sideways forces pile them into clusters and stripes that smooth into polygons, circles and stripes. Circles range from a few centimeters to several meters across, and stripes form on slopes of 2° to 7°. Steps occur too, and each form is either sorted or unsorted. Polygons form either in permafrost, as ice wedges, or in areas where the ground freezes and thaws each year ({{ref:soil-phys-185}}). Most of it forms in the seasonally thawing layer above permafrost, where the churning described in {{ref:soil-form-034}} also works.

entries.title: Mounds, pingos and polygons raised by frost
entries.article: Frost heaving#Landforms created by frost heaving

definition.text: Raised-ground features made by frost heaving in circles, polygons and stripes, called palsas in organic soils such as peat and lithalsas in mineral soils.

facts.text: Frost heaves occur in alpine regions even near the equator, as palsas on Mount Kenya show.
Pingos, up to 60 metres high, grow over hundreds of years in Arctic permafrost, fed by upwelling groundwater rather than capillary action.
Small earth hummocks formed by granular convection in seasonally frozen ground are called thúfur in Greenland and Iceland and pounus in Fennoscandia.
In May 2008 the Phoenix lander touched down on polygonal frost-heave ground on Mars and found ice a few centimetres below the surface.

entries.text: Frost heaving builds whole landscapes of mounds, on Earth and on Mars. Frost-heave landforms are raised-ground features arranged in circles, polygons and stripes. In organic soils such as {{ref:soil-class-070}} they are called {{ref:soil-water-266}}; in mineral soils, {{ref:soil-phys-161}}. They appear in alpine regions even near the equator, as such peat mounds on Mount Kenya show. {{ref:soil-env-170}} grow up to 60 meters high over hundreds of years in Arctic permafrost, fed by upwelling groundwater rather than capillary action. Small earth hummocks in seasonally frozen ground go by thúfur in Iceland and pounus in Fennoscandia. In May 2008 the Phoenix lander touched down on polygonal frost-heave ground on Mars and found ice a few centimeters down.

entries.title: Which soils heave, and which do not

definition.text: Soil whose pore sizes and particle surface area promote capillary flow, so that it can feed ice lenses and heave when it freezes.

facts.text: Silty and loamy soils, which contain fine particles, are typical frost-susceptible soils.
Many agencies class material as frost susceptible if 10 percent or more passes a 0.075 mm (No. 200) sieve or 3 percent or more a 0.02 mm (No. 635) sieve.
Dense clays, with low hydraulic conductivity, and clean sands and gravels, with pores too open for capillary flow, are not frost susceptible.
Standard tests rate pavement soils by comparing heave rate and thawed bearing ratio with an established classification.

entries.text: Frost-susceptible soil has pore sizes and particle surface area that promote capillary flow, so it can feed ice lenses and heave when it freezes. Silty and loamy soils, which contain fine particles, are the typical examples. Many agencies call a material frost susceptible if 10 percent or more passes a 0.075 mm (No. 200) sieve. Passing 3 percent or more through a 0.02 mm (No. 635) sieve also counts. Dense clays pass water too slowly. Clean sands and gravels have pores too open for capillary flow. For pavements, standard tests compare a soil's heave rate and thawed bearing ratio with an established classification.

entries.title: How soil grains travel through solid ice

definition.text: Thin films of liquid water that persist on ice below freezing and let fine soil particles migrate through ice toward warmer soil.

facts.text: Faraday reported the unfrozen premelted layer in 1860 and called the particle migration thermal regelation.
The film is thinner on a particle's cold side, so water keeps flowing from the warm side to the cold side and refreezing, moving the particle toward warmer soil.
A 10-nanometre film around a micrometre-sized particle can move it 10 micrometres a day in a thermal gradient as low as 1 °C m−1.
Regelation purifies growing ice lenses by repelling fine soil particles.

entries.text: A grain of soil can move through solid ice. The key is premelting: thin films of liquid water persist on ice below freezing. Faraday reported this unfrozen layer in 1860 and called the particle migration thermal regelation. The film is thinner on a particle's cold side. Water keeps flowing from the warm side to the cold side and refreezing, so the particle moves toward warmer soil. A 10-nanometer film around a micrometer-sized particle can move it 10 micrometers a day, in a thermal gradient as low as 1 °C m−1. The process purifies growing ice lenses by pushing fine particles away.

entries.title: Reading soil gas for oil and earthquakes

definition.text: The use of soil gases in research on microseepage, earthquakes and gas exchange between soil and atmosphere.

facts.text: Microseepage, the small release of hydrocarbons at the surface, is used to look for petroleum, assuming hydrocarbons migrate vertically.
Migration of soil gases, especially radon, is examined as a possible earthquake precursor.
Landfill waste, mining and petroleum contamination produce gases, including volatile organic compounds, that diffuse through soil.
Fluxes between soil gases and the air can be analysed by distance from the soil surface.

entries.title: Lithalsas, stony mounds lifted by ice

definition.text: A frost-raised mound in permafrost areas with mineral-rich soils, where a perennial ice lens has grown within the soil.

facts.text: The term sometimes also refers to palsas and pingos.
The stony heaved mounds on the Svalbard archipelago are an example.

entries.text: On the Svalbard archipelago, stony mounds have been heaved up out of the ground. They are lithalsas: frost-raised mounds in permafrost areas with mineral-rich soils, where a perennial ice lens, one that lasts year after year, has grown within the soil. A lithalsa is the mineral-soil counterpart of {{ref:soil-water-266}} among the frost-heave landforms. The term is sometimes also used for those peat mounds and for {{ref:soil-env-170}}.

entries.title: Albedo, how much sunlight a surface sends back

definition.text: The fraction of sunlight a surface reflects, on a scale from 0 (absorbs everything) to 1 (reflects everything).

facts.text: Typical albedos are 0.17 for bare soil, 0.40 for desert sand, 0.15 to 0.18 for deciduous forest and 0.80 for fresh snow.
Low-albedo surfaces look dark and absorb most radiation, while high-albedo surfaces such as snow look bright and reflect most of it.
When snow melts to reveal grass or soil, the darker surface lowers albedo and raises local temperature, causing more melting: a positive feedback.
Farming, deforestation and urbanization change the albedo of large areas.

entries.text: Fresh snow reflects 0.80 of the sunlight that strikes it; bare soil reflects 0.17. That fraction is albedo, measured from 0 for a surface that absorbs everything to 1 for one that reflects everything. Desert sand scores 0.40, deciduous forest 0.15 to 0.18. Dark, low-albedo surfaces absorb most radiation. When snow melts off grass or soil, the darker ground warms the area and speeds further melting, a positive feedback that touches {{ref:soil-phys-137}}. Farming, deforestation and urbanization change the albedo of large areas.

entries.title: Microclimate, the weather of a few meters

definition.text: Local conditions in the near-surface layer, covering the air just above a surface and the shallow soil and water below, that differ persistently from the surroundings.

facts.text: A microclimate spans a few metres to at most a few kilometres.
Soils that hold moisture damp temperature swings, while soils that dry easily have larger daily changes; clay-rich soils keep heat and moisture near the ground.
Slopes facing the Sun are warmer, while valley bottoms may frost sooner because cold air sinks.
Farmers manage microclimate with irrigation, shading, windbreaks and vegetation to buffer crops from heat and drought.

entries.text: A valley bottom can frost sooner than the slope above it, because cold air sinks. A microclimate is a set of local conditions near the surface that differs persistently from its surroundings. It covers the air just above and the shallow soil and water below. It spans a few meters to at most a few kilometers. Moist soils damp temperature swings, while soils that dry easily swing more each day, and clay-rich soils keep heat and moisture near the ground. Farmers shape microclimate with irrigation, shading, windbreaks and vegetation.

entries.title: Fick's laws: diffusion in two lines

definition.text: Two laws, posited by Adolf Fick in 1855, that describe diffusion: flux is proportional to the concentration gradient, and concentration changes with time as a result.

facts.text: The first law, J = −D dφ/dx, gives the diffusive flux J from the diffusion coefficient D and the concentration gradient; D has units of area per time.
The second law, ∂φ/∂t = D ∂²φ/∂x², has the same mathematical form as the heat equation.
Fick's law parallels Darcy's law for water flow and Fourier's law for heat, and is used to model transport in porous soils.
Diffusion through porous media may not follow Fick's laws and is then called non-Fickian.

Fick's law parallels Darcy's law for water and {{ref:soil-phys-182}}, and models transport in porous soils. Where porous media break these laws, diffusion is called non-Fickian.

entries.title: Diffusion: spreading over short distances

definition.text: The net movement of atoms, ions, molecules or energy from a region of higher concentration to one of lower concentration.

facts.text: Diffusion is driven by a gradient in chemical potential, and it differs from bulk flow, which moves a whole body of material down a pressure gradient.
By Fick's first law the diffusive flux is proportional to the negative concentration gradient, with the diffusion coefficient D as the constant.
In a porous medium the porosity must be counted in both the flux and accumulation terms; as porosity goes to zero, the molar flux for a given concentration gradient goes to zero.
Under normal conditions molecular diffusion dominates only over lengths from nanometres to millimetres; beyond that convection takes over.

entries.title: Partial pressure: each gas in a mixture on its own

definition.text: The pressure a single gas in a mixture would exert if it alone filled the whole volume at the same temperature.

facts.text: By Dalton's law, the total pressure of an ideal gas mixture is the sum of the partial pressures of its gases.
The partial pressure of a component equals its mole fraction times the total pressure, and its mole fraction equals its volume fraction.
Gases dissolve, diffuse and react according to their partial pressures, not their concentrations in a mixture or solution.
For non-ideal gases the concept generalises to fugacity.

entries.text: In a mixture of gases, each gas acts as if it were alone. entries.title: Spikes and cores: punching air into turf

definition.text: Mechanical aeration that punctures the soil with spikes or removes cores about 1 in × 2 in (25 mm × 51 mm) to improve gas exchange.

facts.text: Spike aerators use spikes up to a foot or more long and are sometimes used for drainage problems in turf.
Core aeration on turf reduces compaction and thatch, improves infiltration of water and nutrients and encourages deeper roots.
Lawn aerators range from walk-behind, ride-on and tractor-pulled machines to spiked shoes.

entries.title: Molecular diffusion: the restless motion that mixes gases and liquids

definition.text: The motion of atoms, molecules or other particles of a gas or liquid at temperatures above absolute zero, which spreads them from high to low concentration.

facts.text: The rate depends on temperature, fluid viscosity and particle size and mass; the result is gradual mixing until the distribution is uniform.
Once concentrations are equal, molecules keep moving in a dynamic equilibrium; chemical diffusion, which needs a gradient, is distinguished from self-diffusion, which does not.
For gases, Fick's law gives the diffusion rate as proportional to the concentration gradient, with a diffusivity that depends on temperature and pressure; it applies where there is no bulk motion.
Molecular diffusion is one of the slower mass-transport mechanisms.

entries.text: Above absolute zero, molecules never sit still. After that, molecules keep moving in a dynamic equilibrium. Chemical diffusion needs a gradient; self-diffusion does not. For gases, {{ref:soil-phys-181}} gives the rate as proportional to the concentration gradient, where there is no bulk motion. Molecular diffusion is one of the slower mass-transport mechanisms.

entries.title: Heat capacity: how much heat it takes to warm something

definition.text: The amount of heat that must be supplied to an object to raise its temperature by one unit.

facts.text: The SI unit is joule per kelvin; dividing by mass gives specific heat capacity, and dividing by volume gives volumetric heat capacity.
It varies with starting temperature and pressure, and changes sharply at phase transitions such as melting or vaporization.
The heat capacity of a heterogeneous object can usually be found by adding the capacities of its parts.

entries.title: Thermal conductivity: how readily a material passes heat

definition.text: A measure of a material's intrinsic ability to conduct heat locally, in watts per metre-kelvin.

facts.text: Conduction is energy transport by random molecular motion across a temperature gradient, without macroscopic flows; heat flows from high to low temperature.
Methods are steady-state, which wait for a steady temperature profile, or transient, which use the system as it approaches steady state.
A phase change can alter conductivity abruptly: ice at 0 °C conducts at 2.18 W/(m·K), liquid water at 0.56.
Without convection, air and other gases are good insulators, so insulating materials work by trapping many gas-filled pockets that block conduction.
Conductivity can differ with direction in some materials, for example wood conducts better along the grain than across it.

definition.text: A dimensionless measure of how much heat a greenhouse gas traps over a chosen period, as a multiple of the warming from the same mass of CO2.

entries.title: Why wet soil is slow to warm

definition.text: The energy needed to raise the temperature of soil by 1 °C, its specific heat.

facts.text: Pure water has a specific heat of about 1 calorie per gram and dry soil about 0.2, so wet soil lies between 0.2 and 1 (0.8 to 4.2 kJ per kilogram).

entries.title: Frost boils, mud circles that churn for centuries

definition.text: A small circular mound of fresh soil, also called a mud boil or mud circle, formed by frost action and cryoturbation.

facts.text: Typically 1 to 3 metres across, frost boils occur in periglacial or alpine areas with permafrost and are among the commonest features of patterned ground.
They are nonsorted circles with barren mineral-soil centres and vegetated, peaty ground between them.
Wetter silty or loamy centres grow more ice lenses and heave more than their surroundings, so over years soil is carried upward, a cycle that can take centuries.
In Svalbard, heave at frost boil centres was about 9.5 mm per day against about 1.6 mm per day at their margins.

entries.title: Linear aeration: grooves that feed the soil

definition.text: An aeration method that cuts grooves into soil or turf so that water and amendments penetrate and are retained in the right amounts.

facts.text: Organic amendments are spread on the surface, grooves are cut, and the grooves are closed again in the same pass, barely disturbing soil structure.
It can add humus, topsoil, compost, sand or clay as soil softeners where needed.
On lawns it relieves excess water and compaction in heavily used areas, with less surface disruption than coring.

entries.title: Ice segregation, the real force behind frost heave

definition.text: The growth of ice lenses where moisture moving through soil or rock collects in one zone, wedging the material apart.

facts.text: It needs a permeable soil or porous rock, temperatures at which ice and premelted water coexist, and a temperature gradient across the zone.
Where water is plentiful one lens thickens until the heat released by freezing slows it; where water is scarce, new lenses form below, giving multiple layers.
Under high overburden pressure or relatively warm surface temperatures no segregated ice forms and the surface does not deform.
Most frost heaving and bedrock fracture in cold regions comes from ice segregation rather than the expansion of freezing water.

entries.title: Seeing soil heat from the sky

definition.text: Detecting variations in soil thermal properties from satellites and aircraft, mainly with thermal infrared sensors.

facts.text: Reflected light shows only the topmost few molecular layers; thermal infrared reveals energy variations at shallow depths below the surface.
Thermal sensors pick up heat moving into and out of near-surface layers by conduction, convection and radiation.
Satellite microwave sensing also helps, since unlike thermal infrared it is not affected by cloud cover.

entries.title: Growing regions: where climate and soil favor a crop

entries.title: Seasonal frost, ground that freezes and thaws each year

definition.text: Ground that freezes each winter and thaws again, one of three kinds of frozen ground classed by how long they stay frozen, beside permafrost and pereletok.

facts.text: Repeated freezing and thawing in seasonally frozen areas pushes larger stones toward the surface, forming patterned ground such as polygons.
Cryogenic earth hummocks, formed by granular convection, appear in seasonally frozen ground as well as permafrost.
Rigid retaining-wall footings must sit below the seasonal frost depth.

facts.text: Typical values in W·m−1·K−1 are 8.8 for quartz, 0.57 for water, 0.25 for organic matter, 0.2–0.4 for dry soil and 1–3 for wet soil.

definition.text: A material's thermal conductivity divided by its density and specific heat capacity, measuring how fast heat spreads through it, in m2/s.

entries.title: Thermal effusivity, a material's resistance to temperature swings

definition.text: A material's ability to exchange heat with its surroundings, the square root of its thermal conductivity times its volumetric heat capacity.

facts.text: It measures thermal inertia: a material of low effusivity changes temperature a lot over a day, one of high effusivity much less.

In remote sensing, thermal inertia of a surface reflects particle size, rock abundance, bedrock outcrop and induration.
Diffusivity sets how fast a body reaches thermal equilibrium; effusivity sets how well it resists periodic temperature change.

entries.title: Needle probes that read soil heat in place
entries.article: Soil thermal properties#Single and dual heat probes

definition.text: In-situ measurement of soil thermal properties with needle probes that heat the soil and record its temperature response.

facts.text: A single probe heats continuously and senses how fast heat is conducted away, so it measures thermal conductivity only; IEEE 442-1981 and ASTM D 5334-08 cover it.
The dual-probe heat-pulse method uses two parallel needles a set distance apart, a heater and a sensor, and records the sensor's response to a heat pulse over time.
It measures thermal diffusivity and volumetric heat capacity, from which conductivity follows, so it gives all the main thermal properties.
Drawbacks are a small measured volume and sensitivity to probe-to-soil contact and heater-to-sensor spacing.

entries.title: Thermal lag: deep soil warms late and gently

definition.text: The damping and delay of temperature changes with depth in the ground, so that deeper soil reaches its highs and lows later and less sharply.

facts.text: About 50% of the Sun's heat is absorbed at the surface, where temperature swings with day and night, weather and season.
Below the surface the ground is warmer than the air in winter and cooler in summer.
Deep enough down, temperature stays constant year round at about the mean of summer and winter temperatures.
Sources vary on that depth: reported values include 5–6 m, 6 m, 15 m, 4.25 m for dry soil and 6.7 m for wet soil.

Deep enough down, temperature stays constant year round, at about the mean of summer and winter temperatures. Sources differ on that depth. Reported values include 5–6 m, 6 m and 15 m, and 4.25 m for dry soil against 6.7 m for wet soil.

entries.title: Banking summer sun in the ground for winter

definition.text: Using the ground as a long-term store of heat, carrying solar energy from summer to winter for ground source heat pumps.

facts.text: The thermal effusivity of soil lets the ground serve as underground thermal energy storage.
Design criteria for shallow-loop ground source heat pumps require an accurate in-situ thermal conductivity reading.
In earth-sheltered buildings the thermal mass and thermal lag of the earth keep the need for extra heating and cooling minimal.

entries.text: The ground can carry summer's solar energy into winter. Ground heat storage uses the earth as a long-term store of heat for ground source heat pumps. Design criteria for shallow-loop heat pumps require an accurate on-site reading of thermal conductivity. Earth-sheltered buildings draw on the same effect. The thermal mass and thermal lag of the surrounding earth keep their need for extra heating and cooling minimal.

entries.title: Ground source heat pumps, tapping the steady earth

definition.text: A heating and cooling system for buildings that moves heat to or from the ground, using the near-constant temperature of the earth through the seasons.

facts.text: In the top metre ground temperature follows sunlight and weather; down to about 8–20 m, depending on soil type, swings fade exponentially and lag the surface by about 6 months.
Annual temperature cycles penetrate about 18.0 m in wet clay and 14.5 m in wet sand, but only 6.5 m in dry clay and 4.5 m in dry sand.
Loops in wet ground work better than in dry ground, because water conducts and stores heat better than the solids of sand or soil.
Horizontal loops are laid in trenches deeper than the frost line; efficiency is typically a coefficient of performance of 3–6.

entries.text: A few meters down, the seasons blur. A ground source heat pump heats and cools buildings by moving heat to or from the ground, whose temperature stays nearly constant through the year. Down to about 8–20 m, surface swings fade exponentially and lag about 6 months behind, an example of {{ref:soil-phys-142}}. Annual cycles reach 18.0 m in wet clay but only 4.5 m in dry sand. Loops in wet ground work better, because water conducts and stores heat well. Horizontal loops lie below the frost line, and efficiency typically reaches a coefficient of performance of 3–6.

entries.title: Zeolites, the mineral sponges that swap ions

definition.text: A group of microporous, crystalline aluminosilicate minerals widely used as adsorbents and catalysts.

facts.text: Their negatively charged aluminium centres need accompanying cations, which can be exchanged, giving zeolites ion-exchange properties.
Over 40 naturally occurring frameworks are known among 253 identified by December 2018.
Altered volcanic glass has formed zeolite deposits.
Much material sold as zeolite is ground volcanic tuff holding little zeolite, used for building stone, aggregate, cement and soil conditioners.

entries.text: Some minerals behave like sponges built by a chemist. Zeolites are a group of crystalline minerals of the kind described in {{ref:soil-chem-223}}, a family of {{ref:soil-found-031}} riddled with microscopic pores. They are widely used to catch other substances on their surfaces and to speed up reactions as catalysts. Their frameworks carry negatively charged aluminium centres. Positive ions must sit beside them, and these can be swapped for others, so zeolites exchange ions. Over 40 natural frameworks are known among 253 identified by December 2018. Altered {{ref:soil-chem-200}} has formed zeolite deposits. Yet much material sold as zeolite is ground volcanic tuff holding little of it, used for building stone, aggregate, cement and products that improve soil.

entries.title: Bowen's reaction series: the order in which magma freezes

definition.text: The sequence in which common silicate minerals crystallize from a cooling basaltic magma, summarized by the petrologist Norman L. Bowen.

facts.text: Olivine and calcium plagioclase crystallize first, followed by pyroxene, amphibole, biotite, sodium plagioclase, orthoclase, muscovite and finally quartz.
It has a continuous branch of feldspars that grow more sodium-rich as temperature falls, and a discontinuous branch of mafic minerals.
Bowen derived it in the early 1900s by melting powdered rock and noting the minerals that formed at progressively cooler temperatures.
It explains why some minerals tend to occur together and others almost never do.
Because minerals are most stable near their conditions of formation, the series also ranks resistance to weathering at Earth's surface, with the last-formed most stable.

entries.text: Cool a basaltic magma slowly, and its minerals appear in a fixed order. The petrologist Norman L. Bowen worked out that order in the early 1900s. He melted powdered rock and noted which minerals formed as the temperature fell. Olivine and calcium plagioclase crystallize first. Pyroxene, amphibole and biotite follow, then sodium plagioclase, orthoclase, {{ref:soil-chem-226}} and finally quartz. This sequence of {{ref:soil-found-031}} is Bowen's reaction series. It has two branches. In the continuous branch, feldspars grow steadily richer in sodium as the melt cools. In the discontinuous branch, one mafic mineral, rich in iron and magnesium, gives way to the next. The order explains why some minerals tend to occur together in {{ref:soil-form-135}} and others almost never do. It also matters for soil. Minerals are most stable near the conditions where they formed, so the series ranks resistance to weathering at Earth's surface. Quartz, the last to form, lasts longest.

This sequence of Silicates: one building block, many ways to link it is Bowen's reaction series. It has two branches. In the continuous branch, feldspars grow steadily richer in sodium as the melt cools. In the discontinuous branch, one mafic mineral, rich in iron and magnesium, gives way to the next. The order explains why some minerals tend to occur together in Igneous rock, frozen from molten magma and others almost never do. It also matters for soil. Minerals are most stable near the conditions where they formed, so the series ranks resistance to weathering at Earth's surface. Quartz, the last to form, lasts longest.

entries.title: Goldich's ladder: which minerals weather first

definition.text: A ranking of how fast common igneous minerals weather at Earth's surface, with minerals formed at higher temperatures and pressures less stable than those formed at lower ones.

facts.text: S. S. Goldich derived it in 1938 after studying soil profiles and their parent rocks.
Mafic minerals, rich in iron and magnesium, are less stable than felsic, silica-rich ones; the order echoes Bowen's reaction series.
Apatite is the quickest common igneous mineral to weather and quartz the slowest, a difference that can span millions of years.
Quartz, least prone to weathering, is very common as a residual mineral in residual soils, while basaltic minerals weather relatively quickly.
It covers intrinsic mineral properties; extrinsic factors such as climate, through water-to-rock ratio, pH and alkalinity, also control weathering rate.
Mafic rocks weather to serpentine, Mg- and Ca-rich clays and iron oxides; felsic rocks to clays such as kaolinite, montmorillonite and illite.
It is applied to lithosequences, soils compared under similar weathering conditions so that differences reflect their parent minerals.
Experiments by White and Brantley (2003) found K-feldspar and plagioclase weather at similar rates, so the series may not hold for all weathering processes.

entries.text: Apatite and quartz can weather millions of years apart. S. S. Goldich ranked why in 1938, after studying soil profiles beside the rocks beneath them. His dissolution series orders common minerals of {{ref:soil-form-135}} by how fast they weather at Earth's surface. Minerals formed at higher temperatures and pressures are less stable, so the order echoes {{ref:soil-chem-186}}. Mafic minerals, rich in iron and magnesium, go faster than felsic, silica-rich ones. Apatite weathers quickest and quartz slowest. That is why quartz is so common as a leftover mineral in residual soils. Mafic rocks weather to serpentine, magnesium- and calcium-rich clays and oxides of iron; felsic rocks to clays such as {{ref:soil-chem-088}}. The series covers only a mineral's own properties. Climate also controls the rate, through the water-to-rock ratio, pH and {{ref:soil-chem-142}}. And White and Brantley (2003) found K-feldspar and plagioclase weathering at similar rates, so the series may not hold for every process.

entries.title: Volcanic glass, rock that froze before it could crystallize

definition.text: The amorphous, non-crystalline product of rapidly cooled magma.

facts.text: Lacking a crystal structure, it reacts easily with water and breaks down over time, forming new minerals.
Allophane forms by weathering of volcanic glass and feldspars, and devitrified glass in ash beds becomes bentonite clay.
Vitric Andosols, with limited soil formation, still contain much volcanic glass.
Soils with duripans are often found in volcanic areas and show evidence of ash or volcanic glass.

entries.text: When magma cools too fast for crystals to grow, it freezes as glass. Volcanic glass is this amorphous product, with no crystal structure at all. That disorder makes it reactive. Water attacks it easily, and over time it breaks down into new minerals. Its weathering, with that of feldspars, forms {{ref:soil-chem-097}}. Glass in ash beds that turns crystalline becomes {{ref:soil-chem-100}}. Some young volcanic soils, with limited soil formation, still contain much glass. Soils with {{ref:soil-form-027}} layers are often found in volcanic areas and show traces of ash or glass.
entries.text_plain: When magma cools too fast for crystals to grow, it freezes as glass. Volcanic glass is this amorphous product, with no crystal structure at all. That disorder makes it reactive. Water attacks it easily, and over time it breaks down into new minerals. Its weathering, with that of feldspars, forms Allophane, the shapeless clay of volcanic ash. Glass in ash beds that turns crystalline becomes Bentonite, the swelling clay that seals landfills. Some young volcanic soils, with limited soil formation, still contain much glass. Soils with Duripans, subsoil set as hard as concrete layers are often found in volcanic areas and show traces of ash or glass.

entries.title: Glauconite, the green mineral of slow seafloors

definition.text: A green iron potassium phyllosilicate of the mica group, very friable and with very low resistance to weathering.

facts.text: It forms in place in marine settings, commonly under low oxygen, and indicates continental shelf deposits laid down slowly.
As the main component of greensand it is a common potassium source in fertilizers and is used to adjust soil pH.
Greensand is low in potassium, so it pays to transport it only short distances to fields.
Konstantin Glinka's 1896 master's thesis dealt with glauconite's origin, composition and weathering.

entries.text: A green, crumbly mineral in a field can mark an ancient seabed. Glauconite is an iron potassium mineral among the {{ref:soil-found-033}}, a member of the {{ref:soil-chem-135}} group. It forms in place in the sea, commonly where oxygen is scarce, and indicates continental shelf deposits laid down slowly. It is very friable and has very low resistance to weathering. As the main component of greensand, it is a common potassium source in fertilizers and is used to adjust soil pH. Greensand is low in potassium, though, so it pays to haul it only short distances. In 1896, the master's thesis of {{ref:soil-hist-008}} dealt with its origin, composition and weathering.

entries.title: Jarosite, a store of slow-release acid

definition.text: A basic hydrous sulfate of potassium and ferric iron, KFe3(SO4)2(OH)6, formed by the oxidation of iron sulfides.

facts.text: It is common in acid mine drainage and acid sulfate soil environments.
When it forms from pyrite oxidation in clays, its potassium comes mainly from illite or K-feldspar.
With schwertmannite it holds retained acidity, releasing it slowly through hydrolysis of Fe3+ and Al3+; the WRB horizon suffix j marks their accumulation.
Rovers have found it on Mars, a sign of strongly oxidizing surface conditions.

entries.text: Rovers have found jarosite on Mars, a sign of strongly oxidizing surface conditions. On Earth it is a basic hydrous sulfate of potassium and ferric iron, KFe3(SO4)2(OH)6, one of the {{ref:soil-found-036}}. It forms when iron sulfides oxidize. It is common in drainage from mines and in strongly acid soils that form where sulfides oxidize. entries.title: Anatase: the short-lived form of titanium dioxide

definition.text: Anatase is a metastable tetragonal mineral form of titanium dioxide (TiO2).

facts.text: Rutile is the most common and stable of the TiO2 polymorphs; anatase is metastable at all temperatures and pressures but often forms first because of its lower surface energy.
It forms at relatively low temperatures, occurs in minor amounts in igneous and metamorphic rocks, and as microscopic crystals in sandstones, clays and slates.
Anatase converts to rutile between 550 and about 1000 degrees C, depending on impurities and sample morphology.
Compared with rutile it is softer (Mohs 5.5-6 vs 6-6.5), less dense (about 3.9 vs 4.2) and optically negative.

entries.text: Titanium dioxide comes in several forms, and anatase is the one that does not last. Anatase is a metastable tetragonal mineral form of titanium dioxide (TiO2), one of the oxide minerals of {{ref:soil-found-035}}. Rutile is the most common and stable polymorph. It converts to rutile between 550 and about 1000 degrees C, depending on impurities and sample morphology. It is also less dense than rutile, about 3.9 against 4.2.

entries.title: How layered silicate minerals differ in charge and surface area

definition.text: Phyllosilicates differ mainly in cation exchange capacity and reactive surface area, which depend on isomorphous substitution and whether the interlayer admits cations.

facts.text: Kaolinite has little substitution and does not expand, so CEC is 2-16 cmol(+) per kg and surface area is only external, 5-15 m2 per g.
Illite and chlorite have substantial substitution but a tightly bound K+ or hydroxide interlayer blocks expansion, so CEC is limited: 20-40 for illite and 10-40 for chlorite.
Smectite has intermediate substitution and admits interlayer cations, giving CEC 60-120 and internal surface of 570-660 m2 per g, and soils rich in it swell and shrink strongly.
Vermiculite has CEC of 100-150 but expands little because its charge, concentrated near the interlayer, binds cations tightly and restricts water entry.
Fe/Al oxyhydroxides have CEC near 0-3 but 200-500 m2 per g of surface; amorphous aluminosilicates range from 5 to 350 CEC.

entries.title: Quartz, the mineral that fills the sand

definition.text: Quartz (alpha-SiO2) is the most common mineral in Canadian soils and typically makes up most of the sand fraction.

facts.text: It is a framework silicate in which every silica tetrahedron shares all four oxygens, and it is essentially pure SiO2 needing no other bonding ions.
Strong Si-O covalent bonds make its solubility very low and its dissolution extremely slow, so quartz accumulates over time, for example in Ae horizons of Podzolic and Luvisolic soils.
It makes up about 40-60% of the sand fraction, a major part of the silt and a small part of the clay fraction.

entries.title: Secondary minerals: what weathering builds from the wreckage

definition.text: A secondary mineral is a by-product of chemical weathering, formed by partial alteration of a primary mineral or by precipitation from components dissolved from other minerals.

facts.text: Primary minerals form as the original molten crust cools, while secondary minerals form from their breakdown products.
In heavily weathered soils secondary minerals dominate, including iron and aluminium oxides from primary igneous silicates.
Most are hydrated aluminosilicates (phyllosilicates, or clay minerals) or Fe and Al oxyhydroxides, which are stable in soils.

Clay minerals are the most chemically reactive inorganic phases in soil; their amount and type influence porosity, swelling, compressibility, sorption and exchange capacity, and hydraulic conductivity.
In glaciated Canada most secondary minerals formed before the last glaciation and were redeposited, so little has formed since compared with the amount inherited.
Primary minerals form as the original molten crust cools and solidifies, while secondary minerals form from their breakdown products.

Most are hydrated minerals of aluminum and silicon (phyllosilicates, or the layered silicate minerals) or Fe and Al oxyhydroxides, which are stable in soils. Phyllosilicates are the most chemically reactive inorganic phases in soil; their amount and type influence porosity, swelling, compressibility, {{ref:soil-chem-068}} and exchange capacity, and hydraulic conductivity. In glaciated Canada most secondary minerals formed before the last glaciation and were redeposited, so little has formed since compared with the amount inherited.

entries.title: Reading a sample's elements from its X-rays

definition.text: Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) is an analytical technique for the elemental analysis of a sample by measuring X-rays it emits when excited by a beam.

facts.text: Each element has a unique set of emission peaks; an incident beam ejects an inner-shell electron and the X-ray released when an outer electron fills the hole has an energy characteristic of the element.
Excitation is by electron beam in electron microscopes (SEM, STEM) or by X-ray beam in XRF spectrometers.
Wavelength-dispersive spectroscopy has finer spectral resolution and avoids EDS artifacts such as false peaks.
Quantitative accuracy suffers from overlapping peaks (Ti K-beta with V K-alpha, Mn K-beta with Fe K-alpha) and X-ray absorption in the sample, so correction procedures are needed.
Newer silicon drift detectors work without liquid nitrogen cooling and give faster, higher-throughput analysis.

entries.text: Hit a sample with a beam and it answers in X-rays. Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy, or EDS, reads that answer to identify the elements present. The beam ejects an inner-shell electron, and when an outer electron fills the hole it releases an X-ray whose energy is characteristic of the element. The beam may be electrons in a microscope or X-rays in an XRF spectrometer. Overlapping peaks and absorption within the sample limit accuracy, so corrections are needed. Wavelength-dispersive spectroscopy resolves finer detail, and newer silicon drift detectors need no liquid nitrogen and work faster.

entries.title: Birnessite, the manganese mineral microbes make

definition.text: A hydrous manganese dioxide mineral, nominally MnO2·nH2O, the main manganese mineral at Earth's surface.

facts.text: It occurs as fine-grained, poorly crystalline aggregates in soils, sediments, rock coatings such as desert varnish and marine nodules.
Most natural birnessite is thought to be made by microorganisms, since biological oxidation of Mn(II) is faster than abiotic oxidation.
Vacancies in its layers are balanced by interlayer cations such as calcium, copper, zinc, lead and cadmium.
Manganese oxides can oxidize trivalent chromium in soils to hexavalent chromium.

entries.text: Microbes probably built most of the manganese mineral at Earth's surface. Birnessite, a hydrous manganese dioxide, nominally MnO2·nH2O, is the main one. It occurs as fine, poorly crystalline aggregates in soils, sediments, marine nodules and rock coatings such as desert varnish. Biological oxidation of Mn(II) is faster than the abiotic kind, which is why microorganisms are thought to make most of it. Its layers contain vacancies, balanced by interlayer cations such as calcium, copper, zinc, lead and cadmium. Manganese oxides like it, among the {{ref:soil-found-035}}, can oxidize trivalent chromium in soils to {{ref:soil-env-255}}.

entries.title: Schwertmannite, the orange crust of acid waters

definition.text: An iron oxyhydroxysulfate mineral, ideally Fe8O8(OH)6(SO4)·nH2O, usually seen as brownish-yellow crusts.

facts.text: It forms in iron-rich, acidic sulfate waters with a pH of 2 to 4.
It is commonly an orange precipitate in streams and lakes affected by acid mine drainage.
It is central to iron-sulfur geochemistry in the acid sulfate soils of coastal lowlands.
First described in 1994, it is named for the soil scientist Udo Schwertmann of the Technical University of Munich.

entries.text: Streams and lakes fouled by mine drainage are often coated with an orange precipitate. It is central to iron-sulfur geochemistry in the strongly acid, sulfur-rich soils of coastal lowlands. First described in 1994, it is named for the soil scientist Udo Schwertmann of the Technical University of Munich.

entries.title: Pedogenic carbonate, made in the soil itself

definition.text: Carbonate that forms in place within a soil, as opposed to carbonate inherited from the bedrock or parent material.

facts.text: Acid hydrolysis by dissolved carbon dioxide, called carbonation, can weather primary minerals into secondary carbonate minerals.
Horizon descriptions in the WRB and the FAO guidelines mark accumulated secondary carbonates with the suffix k.
Secondary carbonates define WRB groups: Calcisols accumulate them, Chernozems and Kastanozems have them, Phaeozems lack them within one metre.
Carbon isotopes in pedogenic carbonate nodules of paleosols are used to reconstruct past atmospheric carbon dioxide.
It can form during soil wetting and drying, which underlies proposed proxies for past seasonality.
