entries.text: Not all the carbonate in a soil came from its rock. Pedogenic carbonate forms in place within the soil, unlike carbonate inherited from bedrock or {{ref:soil-form-087}}. One route is carbonation, acid hydrolysis by dissolved carbon dioxide, described in {{ref:soil-found-060}}. It can weather primary minerals into secondary {{ref:soil-found-034}}. Carbonate can also form as a soil wets and dries, which underlies proposed clues to past seasonality. Horizon descriptions mark accumulated secondary carbonates with the suffix k. These carbonates also sort soils in the international classification: some soil groups are defined by accumulating them, others by lacking them within one meter. Ancient soils keep a record too. Carbon isotopes in carbonate nodules of {{ref:soil-form-072}} help reconstruct past atmospheric carbon dioxide.

entries.title: Soil mineralogy: where plant nutrients begin

definition.text: The study of the minerals in soil, one of the branches, with soil physics, chemistry and biology, through which soil processes are studied quantitatively.

facts.text: Most of the elements plants need come from the chemical breakdown of soil minerals.
As roots remove nutrients from the soil solution, weathering of soil minerals helps replenish them, along with ion exchange and decay of organic matter.
Soil colour is mainly influenced by soil mineralogy.
Gypsum, calcite, feldspar or quartz grains can be clay-sized without behaving like true clay minerals.
Soil minerals retain phosphorus, by adsorption onto iron and aluminium oxyhydroxides in acid soils and precipitation onto calcite in neutral to calcareous ones.
Organic matter binds to soil minerals: hydrophobic molecules partition onto them and stay longer in soil, and particulate organic matter adheres to them.
Weathering of soil minerals releases salts, which drainage flushes out or evaporation concentrates near the surface.
Advances in soil mineralogy, with the other soil sciences, have added new tools to the study of soil formation.

entries.title: Powder diffraction, a fingerprint for every crystal

definition.text: A technique that uses X-ray, neutron or electron diffraction on powdered or microcrystalline samples to characterize the structure of materials.

facts.text: Each crystalline solid gives a distinctive pattern; line positions, set by lattice spacings, and their intensities act as a fingerprint.
A mixture such as a soil sample shows several superposed patterns, from which the relative amounts of each phase can be found.
Diffraction occurs when radiation with a wavelength comparable to atomic spacings reflects off planes of atoms and interferes constructively.
Bragg's law, nλ = 2d sin θ, links the wavelength λ, the lattice spacing d and the glancing angle θ; the Braggs proposed it in 1913.
It has long been used to identify and classify minerals, and works on nearly any material for which a reference pattern exists.
The 2021 Powder Diffraction File held over 1,047,661 reference materials.
Its strengths are simple sample preparation and fast measurement; it mainly identifies phases rather than solving unknown structures.

entries.text: Every crystalline solid leaves its own fingerprint when struck by radiation. Powder diffraction reads it. The method aims X-rays, neutrons or electrons at powdered or microcrystalline samples. Diffraction happens when radiation of a wavelength comparable to atomic spacings reflects off planes of atoms and the reflections reinforce one another. Bragg's law, nλ = 2d sin θ, links the wavelength λ, the lattice spacing d and the glancing angle θ. The Braggs proposed it in 1913. Line positions, set by lattice spacings, and their intensities identify the solid. A soil sample is a mixture, so its patterns lie on top of one another, and from them the relative amount of each phase can be found. Preparation is simple and measurement fast. The method mainly identifies known phases rather than solving unknown structures, and the 2021 Powder Diffraction File held over 1,047,661 reference materials.

entries.title: X-ray fluorescence: making minerals glow with their elements

definition.text: The emission of characteristic X-rays from a material excited by high-energy X-rays or gamma rays, whose energies and intensities reveal which elements are present and in what amounts.

facts.text: It is a non-destructive technique for elemental analysis used in geochemistry, archaeology and forensic science, among other fields.
Minerals may be ground and pressed into a tablet or, for accurate work, dissolved in borate glass and cast into a bead.
In pressed mineral powders the finer minerals gather at the surface and mixtures cause absorption effects that depart from theory.
XRF tools are increasingly run with cone penetration test probes for in situ soil measurements.

entries.text: Hit a mineral with high-energy X-rays or gamma rays, and it answers with X-rays of its own. Their energies reveal which elements are present, and their intensities how much. This is X-ray fluorescence, a non-destructive method used in geochemistry, archaeology and forensic science. Minerals may be ground and pressed into a tablet or, for accurate work, dissolved in borate glass and cast into a bead. Pressed powders have pitfalls: finer minerals gather at the surface, and mixtures absorb in ways that depart from theory. XRF tools increasingly ride cone penetration test probes to measure soil in place.

entries.title: Electron probe microanalysis: chemistry from a speck

definition.text: A technique that bombards small volumes of a solid with an electron beam and reads the emitted X-rays to determine its chemical composition non-destructively.

facts.text: It shares its principle with the energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy of scanning electron microscopes, but uses a fixed beam and aims at analysis rather than imaging.
It is used mostly by mineralogists and petrologists, revealing chemical zoning from core to rim of a mineral grain that records its history.
Tephrochronology relies on geochemical fingerprinting of ash, usually with an electron microprobe.
Wavelength-dispersive analysis is limited for light elements such as hydrogen, lithium and beryllium.

entries.text: A single mineral grain can record its own history from core to rim. Electron probe microanalysis reads that record. It bombards small volumes of a solid with an electron beam and measures the emitted X-rays, much as {{ref:soil-chem-189}} does, without destroying the sample. Scanning electron microscopes share the principle, but the probe holds its beam fixed and aims at analysis rather than images. Mineralogists and petrologists use it to trace chemical zoning in grains. {{ref:soil-hist-135}}, which dates layers of volcanic ash, usually fingerprints ash with the probe. Light elements such as hydrogen, lithium and beryllium are hard to measure this way.

entries.title: Infrared spectra that reveal water in minerals

definition.text: A technique that records the infrared absorption or emission spectrum of a solid, liquid or gas over a wide range of wavelengths at once.

facts.text: A mathematical Fourier transform converts the raw data into the spectrum, which gives the method its name.
Geologists use it to quantify water and carbon dioxide in minerals and glasses.
Allophane, which lacks long-range order, is identified by its distinctive infrared spectrum and X-ray diffraction pattern.
Infrared spectroscopy is among the methods, with X-ray and electron diffraction, used to study clay minerals.

entries.text: Some minerals have no long-range order, yet still announce themselves. {{ref:soil-chem-097}} is one, identified by its distinctive infrared spectrum and its {{ref:soil-chem-228}} pattern. Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy records how a solid, liquid or gas absorbs or emits infrared light over a wide range of wavelengths at once. A mathematical Fourier transform converts the raw data into the spectrum, which gives the method its name. Geologists use it to quantify water and carbon dioxide in minerals and glasses. With that X-ray method and electron diffraction, infrared spectroscopy is a standard way to study clays.

entries.title: Variscite, the green aluminium phosphate

definition.text: Variscite is a relatively rare hydrated aluminium phosphate mineral, AlPO4·2H2O.

facts.text: It is a secondary mineral deposited directly from phosphate-bearing water that has reacted with aluminium-rich rocks in a near-surface environment.
It occurs as fine-grained masses in nodules, cavity fillings and crusts, often with veins of crandallite, a calcium aluminium phosphate.
Its green colour comes from small amounts of trivalent chromium.

entries.text: Variscite is a rare green mineral, a hydrated aluminium phosphate with the formula AlPO4·2H2O. It turns up as fine-grained masses in nodules, cavity fillings and crusts, often alongside veins of crandallite, a calcium aluminium phosphate. The green comes from small amounts of trivalent chromium.

entries.title: Why Canadian clays came from the ice

definition.text: Most phyllosilicates in Canadian soils are inherited from parent materials deposited by the continental glaciers rather than formed in place.

facts.text: Kaolinite, mica and chlorite come directly from the Canadian Shield, while others in the Interior Plains derive from degraded Cretaceous sediments.

Interior Plains clay is dominated by smectite, mica, chlorite and some kaolinite, whereas the older Devonian and Silurian sediments of the St. Lawrence Lowlands give mica, chlorite, vermiculite and kaolinite.
There is little evidence of alteration across regions, except in Podzolic and some Brunisolic and Gleysolic soils where inherited chlorite weathers to expandable phyllosilicates.

entries.title: Phosphate minerals and where soil phosphorus goes

definition.text: Phosphate forms over 300 minerals, of which the commonest pure primary ones are apatites, Ca5(PO4)3(F,Cl,OH).

facts.text: Soils typically hold 400-800 mg P per kg against a crustal average of 1050 mg per kg.
Fluor-, chlor- and hydroxyapatite are the end members; rock phosphate is mined for fertilizer.

Soil phosphate, from rocks or fertilizer, precipitates with Ca, Al and Fe: iron phosphates (vivianite, strengite) in wet sub-oxic soils, aluminium phosphate (variscite) in acidic soils, and calcium phosphates such as brushite in calcareous soils.
Brushite commonly precipitates in calcareous soil where fertilizer is banded at high concentration.

entries.title: Why some minerals vanish from soil faster than others

definition.text: Primary minerals are not chemically stable at the Earth's surface and weather and dissolve at different rates, releasing their elements.

facts.text: Minerals containing Na and K dissolve faster than those with Ca and Mg, which dissolve faster than those made of Si, Al and Fe.
Iron is soluble as Fe2+ under reducing conditions but forms insoluble Fe3+ oxyhydroxides, like rust, under oxidizing ones.
Carbonates precipitate under alkaline and dissolve under acid conditions; carbonic acid from atmospheric CO2 dissolves them, and alkaline deeper groundwater favours precipitation in C horizons.

entries.title: Calcite, dolomite and the carbonates in soil

definition.text: Soil carbonates are mostly calcite and dolomite inherited from sedimentary rock, with some secondary precipitates in subsurface horizons.

facts.text: Calcite is sparingly soluble, more so at low pH, and is not usually found where pH is below 6.0; it dissolves from the upper solum and is redeposited lower as secondary calcite nodules.
Dolomite also dissolves from the upper profile, supplying calcium to secondary calcite while magnesium is mostly leached or taken up by roots; aragonite is neither common nor stable.
Trona (Na2CO3) is highly soluble and found mostly in Solonetzic soils at pH about 9.5.
Carbonates keep base saturation, exchangeable Ca and Mg, and pH above 7 high, precipitate phosphate and metals, and stabilize clays and structure.

entries.title: Pyrite, sulfuric acid and gypsum in soil

definition.text: Sulfide minerals such as pyrite are absent from well-drained soils but may occur in poorly drained Gleysolic or Organic soils, tidal soils and mine wastes.

facts.text: Exposed pyrite oxidizes to iron and sulfuric acid (2FeS2 + 7O2 + 2H2O gives 2Fe2+ + 4H+ + 4SO4 2-), and oxidation of sulfides can push soil pH below 2.0.
Mining or excavation that exposes sulfides is mainly responsible for acid rock drainage.
Sulfate from sulfide oxidation or other sources forms gypsum, usually at high pH with soluble Ca present.

definition.text: Chemical extractions used in soil analysis to dissolve particular iron- and aluminium-bearing mineral phases selectively so they can be measured.

facts.text: Acid ammonium oxalate, at pH 3, extracts iron and aluminium from poorly crystalline minerals such as ferrihydrite, from iron(II) minerals such as magnetite, and from organic matter.
Dithionite with a complexing agent such as citric acid reduces iron(III) oxyhydroxides to soluble iron(II) and removes amorphous iron(III) phases.
Dithionite is a reducing agent with a reduction potential of −0.66 V at pH 7.

entries.title: Heavy minerals, the dense grains that betray a sand's origin

definition.text: A mineral denser than 2.9 g/cm3, usually one of the dense minor components of siliciclastic sediments.

facts.text: Common heavy minerals include zircon, tourmaline, rutile, garnet and magnetite, dense minerals that resist weathering.
The relative proportions of heavy minerals, a heavy mineral suite, help reveal the provenance of sediments.
Being minor constituents, they are separated for study in a dense liquid such as bromoform, in a funnel or centrifuge.
Deep weathering concentrates heavy minerals in residual accumulations.

sources.title: 3.1: Soil Mineralogy - Geosciences LibreTexts (Digging into Canadian Soils)

entries.text: A pinch of dense grains can reveal where a sediment came from. A heavy mineral is one denser than 2.9 g/cm3, usually a minor part of siliciclastic sediments, those built of silicate rock fragments that may harden into {{ref:soil-form-136}}. Zircon, tourmaline, rutile, garnet and magnetite are common examples, dense and resistant to weathering. Because they resist, deep weathering concentrates them in residual accumulations. Their relative proportions, a heavy mineral suite, help trace the provenance of sediments. Being scarce, they are separated for study in a dense liquid such as bromoform, in a funnel or centrifuge.

entries.title: Environmental magnetism: climate and fire written in iron

definition.text: The study of how climate, sediment transport, pollution and other environmental influences affect magnetic minerals, using their magnetic properties as proxies.

facts.text: The main magnetic minerals are iron oxides such as magnetite, maghemite and hematite, and iron sulfides such as greigite and pyrrhotite.
Magnetic susceptibility and remanence are used to estimate mineral size and composition; measurements are quick and non-invasive.
Susceptibility profiles of alternating loess and paleosols in north-central China mapped Quaternary monsoon variations.
Soil magnetism rises when goethite and ferrihydrite are converted to maghemite by heat.

entries.text: Magnetic minerals in soil keep a diary of climate, moving sediment, pollution and fire. Environmental magnetism reads it, using their magnetic properties as proxies. The main magnetic minerals are oxides of iron, among the {{ref:soil-found-035}}, such as magnetite, and iron sulfides such as greigite and pyrrhotite. Magnetic susceptibility and remanence estimate mineral size and composition, and the measurements are quick and non-invasive. Susceptibility profiles through alternating loess and {{ref:soil-form-072}} in north-central China mapped Quaternary monsoon variations. Heat leaves a mark too. It converts {{ref:soil-chem-104}} and {{ref:soil-chem-111}} into {{ref:soil-chem-166}}, raising soil magnetism.

entries.title: Strengite, the purple iron phosphate

definition.text: Strengite is a relatively rare orthorhombic iron phosphate mineral, FePO4·2H2O.

facts.text: It resembles variscite, is lavender, pink or purple, and is partly soluble, particularly at low pH and low oxidation-reduction potential.
It is named after the German mineralogist Johann August Streng.

entries.title: The chemistry hidden in a handful of soil

definition.text: The study of the chemical characteristics of soil.

facts.text: A soil's chemistry depends on its mineral composition, its organic matter and environmental factors.
J. Thomas Way, consulting chemist to the Royal Agricultural Society of England, ran many experiments on how soils exchange ions in the early 1870s and is considered the father of soil chemistry.
Until the late 1960s the field focused on reactions behind soil formation and plant growth; concern over pollution then shifted its emphasis toward environmental soil science.
Minerals, derived from the parent rock or regolith, make up about 90% of the total weight of soil.
Plants take part by exchanging nutrients with microorganisms and absorbing nutrients, which creates concentration gradients of cations and anions in the soil.
Plant nutrients follow their own biogeochemical cycles: nitrogen passes from a gas into nitrate and nitrite, while phosphorus moves in mineral form held in rock.
Agricultural soil science applies soil chemistry mainly to plant nutrients, soil fertility and fertilizer components.

entries.text: Nine-tenths of a soil's weight is rock-born. Minerals, derived from the parent rock or regolith, make up about 90% of the total weight of soil. Soil chemistry is the study of the chemical characteristics of soil, and those characteristics depend on three things: mineral composition, {{ref:soil-found-045}} and environmental factors. Plants take part too. They trade the elements they feed on with microorganisms, and they absorb them. That creates concentration gradients of cations and anions, the positively and negatively charged ions. Each of these elements follows its own cycle through rock, air, water and life. Nitrogen passes from a gas into nitrate and nitrite, while phosphorus moves in mineral form held in rock. The field has a founder. In the early 1870s J. Thomas Way, consulting chemist to the Royal Agricultural Society of England, ran many experiments on how soils exchange ions. He is considered the father of soil chemistry. Until the late 1960s the questions stayed close to the farm: the reactions behind soil formation and plant growth. On farms today the chemistry still serves plant feeding, the fertility of soil and the ingredients farmers spread to feed crops. Concern over pollution then shifted the field toward the environment, the turn traced in {{ref:soil-chem-077}}.

entries.title: Clay minerals, the sheet silicates born of water

definition.text: A hydrous aluminium phyllosilicate: a sheet-structured silicate that may also carry iron, magnesium, alkali metals and other cations.

facts.text: Clay minerals form in the presence of water, as common products of weathering, including weathering of feldspar, and of low-temperature hydrothermal alteration.
They are very common in soils and in fine-grained rocks such as shale, mudstone, siltstone, slate and phyllite.
Their structure rests on flat hexagonal sheets like those of the mica minerals.
Clay's ability to hold nutrient cations such as potassium and ammonium matters for soil fertility; cation exchange capacity comes mainly from charges on clay minerals and organic matter.
Clay minerals keep forming for as long as a soil exists, by inheritance, by neoformation or by transformation of earlier minerals.
Most soil clays are crystalline, but some are amorphous; a soil's clay is a mixture of types, with one often dominating according to soil type.
Only with X-ray diffraction in the 1930s did clay prove to be mainly sheet silicates formed as secondary minerals, not tiny grains of quartz, feldspar or mica.
Because they need water to form, clay minerals are rare in the Solar System, though they have been detected on Mars, Ceres and other bodies.

entries.title: Mica, the mineral that peels into thin elastic sheets

definition.text: A group of sheet silicate minerals whose crystals split easily into thin, elastic plates, a property called perfect basal cleavage.

facts.text: The mica group comprises 37 phyllosilicate minerals; muscovite and the biotite series are common examples.
Its TOT-c structure stacks layers of two tetrahedral sheets bonded to one octahedral sheet, held together only weakly by interlayer cations, hence the cleavage.
In most micas aluminium replaces one in four silicon ions, leaving each layer a negative charge that interlayer sodium, potassium or calcium ions neutralize.
Dioctahedral micas have a gibbsite-like aluminium sheet, while trioctahedral ones have a brucite-like sheet of magnesium or ferrous iron.
Very fine-grained, variable 'clay micas' include illite, which is short of potassium in the interlayer.
Mica is common in igneous and metamorphic rocks and occurs as small flakes in some sedimentary rocks.
Weathering of muscovite yields illite and, with feldspars, kaolin minerals such as dickite.

entries.text: Mica comes apart in thin plates that bend and spring back. That property, perfect basal cleavage, defines the group: sheet silicate minerals whose crystals split easily along flat planes. They belong to the {{ref:soil-found-033}}, and the group holds 37 of them. {{ref:soil-chem-226}} and the biotite series are common examples. Each layer is a sandwich, a pattern called TOT-c. Two tetrahedral sheets are bonded to one octahedral sheet between them. Only interlayer cations, positively charged ions, hold the layers together, and weakly, hence the cleavage. In most micas aluminium replaces one in four silicon ions. That swap leaves each layer with a negative charge, which interlayer sodium, potassium or calcium ions neutralize. Dioctahedral micas have a gibbsite-like aluminium sheet. Trioctahedral ones have a brucite-like sheet of magnesium or ferrous iron. Mica is common in igneous and metamorphic rocks and appears as small flakes in some sedimentary rocks. Very fine-grained, variable 'clay micas' include {{ref:soil-chem-094}}, which is short of potassium between its layers. Weathering turns that mineral into this clay and, together with feldspars, into kaolin minerals such as dickite.

entries.title: Goethite, the iron mineral in rust and yellow soils

definition.text: An iron(III) oxide-hydroxide mineral, the α form of FeO(OH), found in soils and other low-temperature settings such as sediment.

facts.text: It often forms by weathering of other iron-rich minerals, so it is a common soil component, concentrated in laterites, which consist of kaolinite, quartz, hematite and goethite.

Its formation turns ferrous into ferric iron: as iron-bearing minerals reach the soil's oxidation zone, iron(II) becomes iron(III) while the parent mineral's shape is kept, so goethite often forms pseudomorphs.
It is the main component of rust and of bog iron ore, which forms in swampy ground at the head of springs.
Goethite is yellowish to reddish to dark brown or black; soils rich in sesquioxides range from yellow to red according to their dominant iron oxides.
Clays rich in goethite hold phosphorus so tightly that plants cannot absorb it.
Heating converts goethite and ferrihydrite to maghemite, which raises soil magnetism.
Some bacteria produce goethite through their excretion processes.
Long used as the pigment brown ochre, it was first described in 1806 and named after Johann Wolfgang von Goethe.

entries.title: Diatomaceous earth, a powder of fossil shells

definition.text: A soft, siliceous sedimentary rock, also called diatomite or kieselgur, that crumbles into a fine white to off-white powder.

facts.text: It consists of the fossilized silica shells of diatoms accumulated in lake or marine sediments over millions of years, and is usually 80–90% silica.
Its particles are typically 10 to 200 μm, and its high porosity gives the powder a low density.
In FAO soil description, siliceous diatomaceous earth is one of the materials of limnic L layers, alongside coprogenous earth and marl.
Gardeners use it as a soil conditioner and bonsai medium because, like perlite and vermiculite, it holds water and nutrients yet drains freely and keeps the medium aerated.

entries.title: Colloids, particles too small to settle quietly

definition.text: A mixture in which microscopically small insoluble particles are dispersed throughout another substance.

facts.text: A colloid has a dispersed phase, the suspended particles, and a continuous phase, the medium they are suspended in.
IUPAC defines colloidal particles as having at least one dimension roughly between 1 nanometre and 1 micrometre, limits it says are not rigid.
Some colloids look translucent because their particles scatter light, the Tyndall effect.

Particles interact through excluded-volume repulsion, electrostatic attraction or repulsion, always-present short-range van der Waals attraction, steric repulsion from adsorbed polymers and depletion forces.
In soil, the colloidal fraction is tiny clay and humus particles under 1 μm across, whose positive or negative charges vary with soil pH.
Environmental colloids include inorganic particles such as clays, silicates and iron oxy-hydroxides, and organic ones such as humic and fulvic substances.
The study began with Francesco Selmi in 1845; Thomas Graham coined the word colloid in 1861.

entries.text: The most active particles in soil are less than 1 μm across. Mixed into water, particles this small form a colloid: a mixture in which microscopically small insoluble particles are dispersed through another substance. The suspended particles are the dispersed phase; the medium around them is the continuous phase. IUPAC puts colloidal particles roughly between 1 nanometer and 1 micrometer in at least one dimension, and says those limits are not rigid. Some colloids look translucent because their particles scatter light, the Tyndall effect. The particles push and pull through several forces, from electrostatic attraction or repulsion to always-present, short-range van der Waals attraction. In soil, the colloidal fraction is tiny particles of {{ref:soil-found-040}} and {{ref:soil-bio-089}} whose positive or negative charges vary with soil pH. Francesco Selmi began the study of colloids in 1845, and Thomas Graham coined the word in 1861.

entries.title: Hematite, the blood-red oxide of old soils

definition.text: A common iron oxide mineral, Fe2O3, widely found in rocks and soils.

facts.text: Clay-sized hematite forms as a secondary mineral during soil weathering and, with goethite and other iron oxides, gives many tropical, ancient or highly weathered soils their red colour.
It grows from ferrihydrite, a metastable precursor of both hematite and goethite.
Its name comes from the Greek for blood; red ochre is clay coloured by 20% to 70% unhydrated hematite.
Older ironstone crusts in Plinthosols contain more hematite and boehmite than plinthite does.

entries.title: Two kinds of sheet that build every clay

definition.text: The two kinds of sheet that build every clay mineral: one of corner-sharing silica tetrahedra, and one of small cations such as aluminium or magnesium each surrounded by six oxygens.

facts.text: In a tetrahedral sheet each tetrahedron shares three oxygens with its neighbours in a hexagonal array; the fourth, apical oxygen points the same way on every tetrahedron.
The apical oxygens also form one face of the octahedral sheet, and an extra oxygen above each hexagonal gap bonds to hydrogen as a hydroxyl group.
Kaolinite shows the naming: its T sheet holds silicon among four oxygens, its O sheet aluminium among six oxygens or hydroxyls.
Fitting the two sheets together corrugates the tetrahedral sheet and flattens the octahedral one.
Depending on composition, a layer is neutral or carries a net negative charge, balanced by interlayer cations such as Na+ or K+ or by a lone octahedral sheet.
A clay crystal is a stack of these layers separated by interlayers.

entries.text: Every clay mineral, however varied, is assembled from just two kinds of sheet. The tetrahedral sheet is made of corner-sharing silica tetrahedra. Each tetrahedron shares three oxygens with its neighbors in a hexagonal array. The fourth, apical oxygen points the same way on every tetrahedron. The octahedral sheet holds small cations such as aluminium or magnesium, each surrounded by six oxygens. The apical oxygens also form one face of the octahedral sheet, which locks the two together. An extra oxygen above each hexagonal gap bonds to hydrogen as a hydroxyl group. Fitting them together corrugates the tetrahedral sheet and flattens the octahedral one. The clay in {{ref:soil-chem-088}} shows the shorthand: its T sheet holds silicon among four oxygens, its O sheet aluminium among six oxygens or hydroxyls. Depending on composition, a finished layer is neutral or carries a net negative charge. Interlayer cations such as Na+ or K+ balance that charge, or a lone octahedral sheet does. A clay crystal is a stack of these layers separated by interlayers.

entries.title: One-to-one or two-to-one: how clay sheets stack

definition.text: The basic division of clay minerals by how their sheets stack: one tetrahedral and one octahedral sheet per layer in 1:1 clays, an octahedral sheet between two tetrahedral sheets in 2:1 clays.

facts.text: Kaolinite and serpentine are 1:1 clays; talc, vermiculite and montmorillonite are 2:1 clays.
1:1 layers are uncharged and held by hydrogen bonds; 2:1 layers carry a net negative charge and are bound by cations, as in illite and smectites, or by octahedral sheets, as in chlorites.
The main groups are kaolin (kaolinite, dickite, halloysite, nacrite), smectite (montmorillonite, nontronite, beidellite, saponite), illite and chlorite.
Palygorskite and sepiolite are 2:1 clays with long water channels inside their structure.
Mixed-layer clays interleave two types, randomly (R0) or in order; perfectly ordered R1 illite–smectite is called rectorite and chlorite–smectite corrensite.
In soils, the four main groups are usually given as kaolinite, montmorillonite–smectite, illite and chlorite.

entries.text: Clay mineralogists sort their subjects with two numbers. A 1:1 clay builds each layer from one tetrahedral and one octahedral sheet. A 2:1 clay places an octahedral sheet between two tetrahedral sheets. That difference decides how the layers hold together. 1:1 layers carry no charge and cling to each other by hydrogen bonds. 2:1 layers carry a net negative charge, so something positive must bind them. In some groups that is a scatter of cations; in others, a whole octahedral sheet. Four main groups result. The kaolin group, typified by {{ref:soil-chem-088}}, also holds dickite, {{ref:soil-chem-090}} and nacrite, all 1:1 clays like serpentine. The 2:1 groups are three. {{ref:soil-chem-091}} includes {{ref:soil-chem-093}}, nontronite, saponite and the clay of {{ref:soil-chem-152}}, and its layers are bound by cations. So are those of {{ref:soil-chem-094}}. {{ref:soil-chem-087}} is bound by octahedral sheets instead. Talc and {{ref:soil-chem-095}} are 2:1 clays too. Soil scientists usually give the same four groups for soils. Some clays break the pattern. {{ref:soil-chem-110}} and the clay of {{ref:soil-chem-167}} are 2:1 clays with long water channels inside their structure. Mixed-layer clays interleave two types, either randomly, coded R0, or in order. Perfectly ordered R1 mixes have their own names, such as rectorite and corrensite.
entries.text_plain: Clay mineralogists sort their subjects with two numbers. A 1:1 clay builds each layer from one tetrahedral and one octahedral sheet. A 2:1 clay places an octahedral sheet between two tetrahedral sheets. That difference decides how the layers hold together. 1:1 layers carry no charge and cling to each other by hydrogen bonds. 2:1 layers carry a net negative charge, so something positive must bind them. In some groups that is a scatter of cations; in others, a whole octahedral sheet. Four main groups result. The kaolin group, typified by Kaolinite, the white clay of china and the tropics, also holds dickite, Halloysite, the kaolinite-group clay that grows as tubes and nacrite, all 1:1 clays like serpentine. The 2:1 groups are three. Smectite, the swelling clay with an open interior includes Montmorillonite, the clay that swells tenfold, nontronite, saponite and the clay of Beidellite, a smectite charged in its silica sheet, and its layers are bound by cations. So are those of Illite, the potassium clay that will not swell. Chlorite, a green clay with no chlorine in it is bound by octahedral sheets instead. Talc and Vermiculite, the clay named for breeding worms are 2:1 clays too. Soil scientists usually give the same four groups for soils. Some clays break the pattern. Palygorskite, a clay of bristles instead of plates and the clay of Sepiolite, the fibrous clay of dry lands are 2:1 clays with long water channels inside their structure. Mixed-layer clays interleave two types, either randomly, coded R0, or in order. Perfectly ordered R1 mixes have their own names, such as rectorite and corrensite.

entries.title: Vermiculite, the clay named for breeding worms

definition.text: A hydrous 2:1 phyllosilicate clay mineral that expands greatly when heated.

facts.text: It forms by weathering or hydrothermal alteration of biotite or phlogopite: these micas lose the potassium between their sheets, which is replaced by magnesium and iron.
It is a limited-expansion clay with a medium shrink–swell capacity: hydrated magnesium holds its crystals loosely, so it swells, but less than montmorillonite.
Its cation exchange capacity of 100–150 meq/100 g is high, above that of smectite.
Heating makes it exfoliate, which gave it its name, from the Latin vermiculare, 'to breed worms'; it was first described in 1824 at Millbury, Massachusetts.
It occurs interlayered with chlorite, biotite and phlogopite, typically where felsic rocks meet mafic or ultramafic ones.
Pure vermiculite contains no asbestos, but ore from some deposits, notably the Libby mine in Montana, was contaminated, and some products contained asbestos until the early 1990s.

entries.title: Kaolinite, the white clay of china and the tropics

definition.text: A common 1:1 clay mineral with the composition Al2Si2O5(OH)4, also called kaolin.

facts.text: It is a soft, earthy, usually white mineral produced by chemical weathering of aluminium silicate minerals such as feldspar.
Each layer bonds a silica tetrahedral sheet to an aluminium octahedral sheet, and successive layers are held together by hydrogen bonds.
Its layers carry no net charge, so no large cations sit between them, which explains its low cation exchange capacity of 1–15 meq/100 g.
Tight hydrogen bonding keeps water from entering between the layers, so kaolinite does not swell and has a low shrink–swell capacity.
When moist, a film of water binds its plate-like crystals yet lets them slip, making the clay plastic; dried it is rigid but fragile, and plastic again when rewetted.
Kaolinite surfaces, like those of allophane and iron and aluminium oxides, often carry positive charges.
It abounds in soils formed by chemical weathering in hot, moist climates; soils whose clay is mostly kaolinite are called kaolisols in the INERA classification.
Rock rich in kaolinite is kaolin or china clay, an industrial raw material used above all for paper and ceramics.

entries.title: Illite, the potassium clay that will not swell

definition.text: A group of closely related, non-expanding 2:1 clay minerals, also called hydromica, structurally close to muscovite.

facts.text: Poorly hydrated potassium ions fill the space between its layers and bind them strongly, so illite does not swell.
Compared with muscovite it holds slightly more silicon, magnesium, iron and water and slightly less tetrahedral aluminium and interlayer potassium.
Its CEC, typically 20–30 meq/100 g, is lower than smectite's but higher than kaolinite's.
It forms by alteration of muscovite and feldspar in weathering and hydrothermal settings, and from smectite exposed to potassium-rich groundwater.
Illite is common in sediments, soils and argillaceous rocks, and its share of soil clay rises relative to kaolinite toward cooler climates.
Potassium bonds shrink its active surface, and how much it swells depends on how far potassium feldspar has weathered.
Its tiny crystals usually need X-ray diffraction or SEM-EDS to identify, and it is the only clay mineral containing potassium.
It was first described in 1937 from the Maquoketa shale of Calhoun County, Illinois, and named after the state.

entries.title: Gibbsite, what remains when silica is gone

definition.text: A mineral form of aluminium hydroxide, Al(OH)3.

facts.text: It is built of stacked sheets of linked octahedra, each an aluminium ion bonded to six hydroxide groups, with a third of the octahedral sites left empty.
Each sheet is electrically neutral, so no ions glue the sheets together; only weak residual bonds do, which makes gibbsite very soft and easily cleaved.
Identical aluminium hydroxide 'gibbsite layers' are sandwiched between silicate sheets in the illite, kaolinite and smectite clay groups.
Gibbsite forms by intense weathering of other clay minerals, and allophane alters to it where silica is removed.
It is among the less soluble oxides left when heavy rainfall leaches most silica from alumino-silica clays, as in the lateritic weathering profiles of tropical soils.
As one of the three main phases of bauxite, it is an important aluminium ore.
It is named after the American mineral collector George Gibbs (1776–1833).

entries.title: Bauxite, the rock behind the world's aluminium

definition.text: A sedimentary rock with a relatively high aluminium content, the world's main source of aluminium.

facts.text: It consists mostly of the aluminium minerals gibbsite, boehmite and diaspore, mixed with goethite, hematite, kaolinite and small amounts of anatase.
Lateritic bauxites, found mostly in the tropics, form by lateritization of silicate rocks such as granite, gneiss, basalt and shale; karst bauxites lie over limestone and dolomite.

Even more than iron-rich laterites, bauxite needs intense weathering and very good drainage, which dissolve kaolinite and precipitate gibbsite, almost the only aluminium hydroxide in lateritic bauxites.
Most deposits lie within 1 to 20 metres of the surface, so bauxite is usually strip mined, with little or no overburden.

entries.text: The world's aluminium comes mainly from one weathered rock. Bauxite is a sedimentary rock with a relatively high aluminium content. entries.title: What becomes of a pollutant once it reaches soil

definition.text: The part of soil chemistry that studies how contaminants are released into soil and what becomes of them there.

facts.text: Once a chemical reaches soil, adsorption and desorption, precipitation, polymerization, dissolution, hydrolysis, hydration, complexation and oxidation–reduction can raise or lower its toxicity.
Knowing these reactions helps predict a contaminant's fate and toxicity and design sound, cost-effective clean-up, though remediation engineers often disregard them.
Worry about pollution and ecological and health risks since the late 1960s turned soil chemistry from pedology and farming toward environmental soil science.

entries.text: A chemical spilled on soil does not simply sit there. Environmental soil chemistry studies how contaminants are released into soil and what becomes of them. Processes such as {{ref:soil-chem-145}}, {{ref:soil-chem-147}}, precipitation, polymerization, dissolution, hydrolysis, hydration, complexation and oxidation–reduction can each raise or lower a chemical's toxicity. Knowing these reactions helps predict a contaminant's fate and design sound, cost-effective clean-up, though clean-up engineers often disregard them. The field grew from worry, since the late 1960s, about pollution and its ecological and health risks.

entries.title: How soil chemists test a sample without spoiling it

definition.text: The laboratory techniques soil chemists use to study reactions in samples taken from undisturbed horizons, run with replicated treatments and controls.

facts.text: Air-drying samples at about 25 °C and sieving them to 2 mm markedly disrupts structure, microbial diversity and pH- and redox-related properties, so many chemists now keep samples field-moist at 4 °C.
In batch equilibration a solution of known ion content is shaken with soil, for example 25 mL with 5 g, then separated and analysed to give mg of ion per g of soil.
Column studies leach a solution through soil at a controlled rate to mimic rain, snowmelt and irrigation water passing through a field.
In situ surface spectroscopy, such as infrared, NMR, Mössbauer and X-ray methods, shows how ions bind to particle and colloid surfaces without disturbing the soil.

entries.text: Drying a soil sample changes the very chemistry under study. Air-drying at about 25 °C and sieving to 2 mm markedly disrupt structure, microbial life and properties tied to pH. Many chemists now keep samples, taken from undisturbed horizons, field-moist at 4 °C. In batch equilibration, a solution of known ion content is shaken with soil, say 25 mL with 5 g. The liquid is then analyzed for mg of ion per g of soil. Column studies leach a solution through soil at a controlled rate, mimicking rain and snowmelt. Surface spectroscopy, such as infrared or X-ray methods, shows how ions bind to particles without disturbing the soil.

entries.title: Soil colloids, the tiny particles that do the chemistry

definition.text: The microscopically small particles in soil, chiefly clay and humus, whose charged surfaces hold and exchange ions with the soil water.

facts.text: Colloidal particles have at least one dimension between about 1 nm and 1 μm.
High specific surface area and unbalanced negative charges make clay, a colloidal and usually crystalline phyllosilicate, the most active mineral part of soil.
Negative charges on colloids hold cations and positive charges hold anions, giving soil its cation and anion exchange capacities.
Exchange between colloids and soil water buffers soil pH, alters structure and purifies percolating water by adsorbing cations, useful and harmful.
Soil clays fall into layered alumino-silica clays, crystalline chain carbonates and sulfates, young amorphous clays, and old, highly leached sesquioxide clays.
Humus forms the organic colloids; on a dry-weight basis its CEC is many times that of clay.
Heat and heavy rain in tropical rainforests largely destroy clay and organic colloids, leaving only sesquioxide clays of low CEC.

entries.text: Most of a soil's chemistry happens on particles too small to see. Soil colloids, chiefly clay and the dark decayed material called {{ref:soil-bio-089}}, have at least one dimension between about 1 nm and 1 μm. Their charged surfaces hold ions and trade them with the soil water. Clay, a colloidal and usually crystalline phyllosilicate, is the most active mineral part of soil. It owes that to its high specific surface area and its unbalanced negative charges. Negative charges on colloids hold cations, and positive charges hold anions. Together they give soil its {{ref:soil-chem-046}} and {{ref:soil-chem-053}}. This exchange does quiet, constant work. It buffers soil pH, alters structure and purifies percolating water by adsorbing cations, both useful and harmful. Soil clays fall into four kinds: layered alumino-silica clays, crystalline chain carbonates and sulfates, young {{ref:soil-chem-099}}, and old, highly leached {{ref:soil-chem-106}}. The organic colloids are richer still: on a dry-weight basis their exchange capacity is many times that of clay. Climate can strip colloids away. In tropical rainforests, heat and heavy rain largely destroy clay and organic colloids, leaving only oxide clays that hold few cations.

entries.title: Van der Waals force, the weak pull that adds up

definition.text: A weak, distance-dependent attraction between atoms or molecules that is not a chemical bond.

facts.text: It arises from a transient shift in electron density that creates a short-lived charge, which a nearby atom is attracted to or repelled by.
The force is repulsive at very short range, zero at an equilibrium distance of 0.3 to 0.5 nm for single atoms, and attractive beyond it; past 1.0 nm it falls off roughly as the 7th power of distance.

It combines London dispersion forces, Debye forces between permanent and induced dipoles, and Keesom forces between permanent dipoles; induction and dispersion are always attractive, while the electrostatic part can attract or repel depending on orientation.
Strength rises with polarizability: pairwise energy is 0.06 kJ/mol between H atoms in H2 molecules, 0.44 kJ/mol between O atoms in O2, and 2.35 kJ/mol between xenon atoms.
The forces are additive, cannot be saturated and have no directional character, so many weak contacts can add up to strong attraction.

For very small particles such as fine dry powders, van der Waals attraction dominates over gravity and drag, so such powders are cohesive; free flow generally needs particles larger than about 250 micrometres.
In soils, organic contaminants can be held in organic matter by weak van der Waals interactions, and physisorption is the weak van der Waals form of adsorption.

entries.title: Chlorite, a green clay with no chlorine in it

definition.text: A chemically varied group of 2:1 clay minerals whose layers are bound by a positively charged hydrated magnesium sheet.

facts.text: Its 2:1 layers carry negative charge from aluminium replacing silicon and are bound by positively charged hydroxide (brucite) sheets, not by scattered cations as in vermiculite or mica.
With two silicon planes, one aluminium and one magnesium plane, it is described as a 2:2 clay.
Water is not adsorbed between its layers, so chlorite does not swell, and its CEC is low.
A common weathering product found widely in clay, it also forms in low-grade metamorphic rocks; the name is Greek for green, and it contains no chlorine.

entries.title: Ferrihydrite, iron oxide as a nanoparticle sponge

definition.text: A widespread, poorly crystalline hydrous iron(III) oxyhydroxide mineral that exists only as fine-grained nanoparticles.

facts.text: It forms in soils, waters, aquifers and mining areas, precipitating from oxygenated iron-rich water or through bacterial activity.
Its nanoporous particles give several hundred square metres of surface per gram, which adsorb arsenic, lead, phosphate and humic and fulvic acids.
Metastable, it is a precursor of hematite and goethite, though adsorbed impurities such as silica usually block that change in nature.
Under reducing conditions such as gley soils, often with microbial help, it can turn into green rust (fougerite), which brief contact with air oxidises back to ferrihydrite.

entries.text: A single gram of ferrihydrite offers several hundred square metres of surface. It forms in soils, waters, aquifers and mining areas, precipitating from oxygenated iron-rich water or through bacterial activity. Its nanoporous particles adsorb arsenic, lead, phosphate and the organic acids met in {{ref:soil-chem-059}} and {{ref:soil-chem-060}}. Ferrihydrite is metastable, a precursor of hematite and goethite, though adsorbed impurities such as silica usually block that change in nature. Under reducing conditions, as in gley soils and often with microbial help, it can turn into {{ref:soil-chem-170}}, here in the form covered in {{ref:soil-chem-109}}. Brief contact with air oxidizes it back to ferrihydrite.

entries.title: Did life begin on the surface of clay?
entries.article: Clay mineral#Clay and the origins of life

definition.text: The idea, proposed by Graham Cairns-Smith in 1985, that complex organic molecules arose on non-organic, replicating silicate crystal surfaces in water.

facts.text: Montmorillonite has been shown to catalyse the joining of nucleotides into RNA in water, and the formation of membranes from lipids.
In 1998 Hyman Hartman proposed that the first organisms were self-replicating iron-rich clays that fixed carbon dioxide into oxalic and other dicarboxylic acids.
Clay minerals form only where water is present, and many theories of abiogenesis involve them.

entries.text: The first living things may have had help from clay. In 1985 Graham Cairns-Smith proposed that complex organic molecules arose on non-organic, replicating silicate crystal surfaces in water. Clay minerals form only where water is present, and many theories of how life began involve them. Laboratory work lends weight to the idea: {{ref:soil-chem-093}} has been shown to catalyze the joining of nucleotides into RNA in water, and the formation of membranes from lipids. In 1998 Hyman Hartman went further. He proposed that the first organisms were self-replicating iron-rich clays that fixed carbon dioxide into oxalic and other dicarboxylic acids.

entries.title: Telling one clay from another in the laboratory
entries.article: Clay mineral#Tests which verify that clay minerals are present

definition.text: Laboratory tests that confirm and quantify clay minerals, using glycol adsorption, cation exchange capacity, X-ray diffraction, differential thermal analysis and chemical analysis.

facts.text: Clay minerals are usually too fine for ordinary optical study, so X-ray diffraction is the main tool, aided by electron diffraction, spectroscopy and SEM-EDS.
Once organic matter, carbonates, free oxides and non-clay minerals are measured, clay percentages are estimated from glycol adsorption, CEC, K2O and thermal data.
Illite is estimated from potassium oxide content, since it is the only clay mineral containing potassium.
Glycol adsorption measures how much ethylene glycol enters a clay's interlayer sites when it is exposed to the vapour at 60 °C for eight hours.

entries.title: Fougèrite, the green rust of waterlogged soils

definition.text: A naturally occurring green rust mineral, a layered double hydroxide of ferrous and ferric iron, described only relatively recently.

facts.text: It was first found in forest soils near Fougères, Brittany, and accepted as a mineral species by the International Mineralogical Association in 2002.
Its brucite-like layers hold Fe2+ and Fe3+, with loosely bound carbonate and water between them, and it forms clay-like hexagonal platelets under a micron across.
Green rust occurs as the mineral fougèrite in Gleysols.
Unstable in air, it oxidizes, dehydrates and loses carbonate, turning to ferrihydrite and finally to lepidocrocite or goethite.

entries.text: Fougèrite does not last long in air. It occurs as fougèrite in {{ref:soil-class-127}}. Exposed to air, it oxidizes, dehydrates and loses carbonate, turning to ferrihydrite and finally to goethite or the rust described in {{ref:soil-chem-164}}.

entries.title: Flocculation: how clay particles join and drift apart

facts.text: In colloid chemistry flocculation is when colloidal particles leave suspension as floc or flake; unlike precipitation they were first merely suspended in a stable dispersion.
The IUPAC definition is contact and adhesion that makes larger clusters; agglomeration of this kind is reversible, so the particles can be dispersed again.
In dispersed clay slurries, flocs form once agitation stops because negative face charges attract positive edge charges.
Flocculation of soil colloids is tied to freshwater quality: highly dispersible colloids make water turbid and adsorb nutrients that drive eutrophication.
The forces involved include van der Waals forces, electrostatic forces and hydrogen bonding.
It is the opposite of dispersion, in which particles are held apart; the balance between them is set mainly by soil pH, electrical conductivity and sodium content.
Clay plates flocculate when their slightly positive edges stick to the negative faces of other plates; sodium displacing polyvalent cations weakens this and deflocculates the clay.
Floccules become lasting aggregates only once cementing agents stabilize them.

entries.title: How water plants clear mud with coagulants

facts.text: Alum is the most common coagulant; gentle mixing then speeds particle collisions so destabilized particles enmesh in larger precipitates, depending on mixing shear, intensity, time and pH.
A jar test chooses the flocculant and dose by rapid mixing, slow mixing and sedimentation in beakers with paddle mixers.

Drinking-water treatment typically runs grates, coagulation, flocculation, sedimentation, granular filtration and disinfection; chitosan is an increasingly popular biodegradable flocculant that binds heavy metals and organic pollutants.

entries.title: Zeta potential, the voltage that keeps particles apart

definition.text: The electrical potential at the slipping plane around a dispersed particle, the boundary between fluid that moves with the particle and fluid that does not.

facts.text: It is usually given in millivolts and written ζ.
It differs from the Stern or surface potential of the double layer, but is often the only way to characterize double-layer properties.
It is a readily measured indicator of dispersion stability: colloids with high zeta potential, positive or negative, are electrically stabilized, while low values lead to coagulation or flocculation.
Magnitudes of 0 to 5 mV give rapid coagulation, 30 to 40 mV moderate stability, 40 to 60 mV good stability and over 61 mV excellent stability.
It is measured by applying an electric field: particles move toward the opposite electrode at a velocity proportional to their zeta potential, tracked by laser Doppler anemometry.
Electrophoresis is used for particles, streaming potential or current for porous bodies and flat surfaces.
The point of zero charge can be found where titration curves and pH–zeta potential curves intersect.

entries.text: A colloid's fate can hang on a few tens of millivolts. As a particle moves through liquid, a thin film of fluid travels with it. The boundary where that film ends and the still fluid begins is the slipping plane. The electrical potential there is the zeta potential, written ζ and usually given in millivolts. It is not the same as the potential at the particle's surface, but it is often the only way to characterize the charged layers around a {{ref:soil-chem-154}}. It is also a handy gauge of stability. Magnitudes of 0 to 5 mV give rapid coagulation, 30 to 40 mV moderate stability, 40 to 60 mV good stability and over 61 mV excellent stability. To measure it, an electric field is applied. Particles drift toward the opposite electrode at a velocity proportional to their zeta potential, tracked by laser Doppler anemometry. Where pH–zeta potential curves cross titration curves lies the {{ref:soil-chem-075}}.

entries.title: Allophane, the shapeless clay of volcanic ash

definition.text: An amorphous to poorly crystalline hydrous aluminium silicate clay mineraloid.

facts.text: It has only short-range order, so it is a mineraloid; it forms from weathering or hydrothermal alteration of volcanic glass and feldspars, typically at pH 5–7, with an Al:Si ratio usually of 2.
Electron micrographs show aggregates of hollow spherules about 3–5 nm across, built from curved alumina and silica layers.
It alters to halloysite where silica is added and to gibbsite where silica is removed.
With imogolite and ferrihydrite it is among the amorphous colloidal materials that define Andisols, soils formed in volcanic ash.

entries.contested_note: The source says allophane's structure has been debated, though it describes curved alumina and silica layers similar to clay minerals.
entries.text: Allophane never quite becomes a crystal. This hydrous aluminium silicate has only short-range order, so it counts as a mineraloid. It forms from weathering or hydrothermal alteration of volcanic glass and feldspars, typically at pH 5–7, with an Al:Si ratio usually of 2. Electron micrographs show hollow spherules about 3–5 nm across. Its structure has been debated; one account describes curved alumina and silica layers like those of clays. It alters to {{ref:soil-chem-090}} where silica is added and to gibbsite where silica is removed. It is among the amorphous materials that define the volcanic-ash soils of {{ref:soil-class-092}}.
entries.text_plain: Allophane never quite becomes a crystal. This hydrous aluminium silicate has only short-range order, so it counts as a mineraloid. It forms from weathering or hydrothermal alteration of volcanic glass and feldspars, typically at pH 5–7, with an Al:Si ratio usually of 2. Electron micrographs show hollow spherules about 3–5 nm across. Its structure has been debated; one account describes curved alumina and silica layers like those of clays. It alters to Halloysite, the kaolinite-group clay that grows as tubes where silica is added and to gibbsite where silica is removed. It is among the amorphous materials that define the volcanic-ash soils of Andisols, the young, fertile soils of volcanic ash.

entries.title: Imogolite, a clay built of nanotubes

definition.text: An aluminium silicate clay mineral, Al2SiO3(OH)4, made of a network of tiny nanotubes.

facts.text: It occurs in soils formed from volcanic ash; first described in 1962 in Kumamoto prefecture, Japan, it is named from imogo, a brownish-yellow soil derived from volcanic ash.
Its tubes are about 2 nm across outside and 1 nm inside, with walls of gibbsite sheets and orthosilicate groups.
It occurs together with allophane, quartz, cristobalite, gibbsite, vermiculite and limonite.
Where tephra is basic or the climate dry, allophane and imogolite develop and Andosols receive the Silandic qualifier.

entries.text: Some clay comes as tubes about 2 nm across. Imogolite, Al2SiO3(OH)4, is an aluminium silicate clay mineral made of a network of these nanotubes. Each tube is 1 nm wide inside, with walls of gibbsite sheets and orthosilicate groups. It was first described in 1962 in Kumamoto prefecture, Japan, and named from imogo, a brownish-yellow soil derived from volcanic ash. It occurs in such soils with allophane, quartz, cristobalite, gibbsite, vermiculite and the iron mixture of {{ref:soil-chem-165}}. Where tephra is basic or the climate dry, allophane and imogolite develop, and {{ref:soil-class-119}} receive the Silandic qualifier.

entries.title: Palygorskite, a clay of bristles instead of plates

definition.text: A fibrous magnesium aluminium clay mineral, also called attapulgite, with the formula (Mg,Al)2Si4O10(OH)·4(H2O).

facts.text: Unlike layered smectites it has a ribbon structure of continuous silica chains linked to magnesium–aluminium octahedral sheets, with long water channels inside.
It forms in shallow lake, river, marsh and soil settings, favoured by semi-arid conditions with high evaporation and alkaline water rich in magnesium and silica.
Its bristle-like crystals do not swell and have a high specific surface area of about 75 to 400 m²/g.
It is one type of fuller's earth, and in farming serves as a fertilizer carrier and a soil amendment that improves water retention, aeration and nutrient availability.

entries.text: Palygorskite grows as bristles rather than plates. Also called attapulgite, it is a fibrous magnesium aluminium clay mineral, (Mg,Al)2Si4O10(OH)·4(H2O). Unlike the layered clays of {{ref:soil-chem-091}}, it has a ribbon structure of continuous silica chains linked to magnesium–aluminium octahedral sheets. It forms in shallow lakes, rivers, waterlogged ground and soils, favored by semi-arid conditions and alkaline water rich in magnesium and silica. Its bristle-like crystals do not swell and have a high specific surface area of about 75 to 400 m²/g. It is one type of {{ref:soil-chem-102}}. Farmers use it to carry plant food and to improve water retention and aeration.

entries.title: Expanded vermiculite in the potting bench

definition.text: The use of heat-expanded vermiculite in potting mixes, seed raising and garden soils to hold water, air and nutrients for plants.

facts.text: Mixed with peat or composted pine bark, exfoliated vermiculite makes soilless growing media that speed root growth and hold air, fertilizer and moisture for release as plants need them.
Alone or mixed with soil or peat, it is used to germinate seeds with very little watering.
In heavy, sticky soils, mixing in vermiculite up to half the soil's volume creates air channels; in sandy soils it helps the soil hold water and air.
Agromineral practice uses vermiculites and zeolites to store moisture in soil, alongside perlite for aeration.

entries.title: Colloidal stability: why some suspensions never clear

definition.text: The ability of colloidal particles to stay suspended instead of clumping, which depends on the forces between them.

facts.text: A colloid stays stable while the attractive interaction energy between particles is below kT; above that, particles begin to clump.
Clumping is called aggregation, flocculation or coagulation; coagulation may mean permanent aggregation and flocculation a reversible one that forms a floc.
Aggregation leads to sedimentation or creaming, ending the suspension.
Particles are stabilized electrostatically, by the like charges of their double layers of counterions, or sterically, by adsorbed polymer or surfactant layers.
Adding salt shrinks the double layer, and shifting pH neutralizes surface charge; either removes the repulsion and lets van der Waals forces aggregate the particles.
When the zeta potential falls below about ±5 mV, rapid coagulation tends to follow.
Charged polymer flocculants bridge particles; negatively charged clay particles, for example, flocculate when a positively charged polymer is added.
Concentrated unstable suspensions form viscoelastic colloidal gels, such as bentonite, that flow under shear but hold their shape at rest.

entries.text: Whether a cloudy suspension stays cloudy comes down to a contest of forces. Colloidal stability is the ability of particles to stay suspended instead of clumping. A {{ref:soil-chem-154}} stays stable while the attraction between particles is below kT, the energy of thermal motion. Above that, they begin to clump: aggregation, flocculation or coagulation. Coagulation may mean permanent clumping, flocculation a reversible kind that forms a floc. The clumps settle out or cream to the top, ending the suspension. Particles are held apart electrostatically, by the like charges of their surrounding layers of counterions, or sterically, by adsorbed polymer or surfactant layers. Adding salt shrinks the charged layer, and shifting pH neutralizes surface charge. Either removes the repulsion and lets van der Waals forces win. When {{ref:soil-chem-160}} falls below about ±5 mV, rapid coagulation tends to follow. Charged polymers can also bridge particles: negatively charged clay flocculates when a positively charged polymer is added.

entries.title: Particle aggregation: how suspended grains clump and fall

definition.text: The sticking together of particles dispersed in a liquid into irregular flocs or agglomerates, which destabilizes a colloid.

facts.text: Also called coagulation or flocculation, it is triggered by adding salts or chemicals known as coagulants or flocculants, and can be reversible or irreversible.
Growing agglomerates settle out as sediment, or in concentrated suspensions link into a colloidal gel.
The reverse, peptization, hardly happens spontaneously but can occur under stirring or shear.
Added salt screens double-layer repulsion so van der Waals attraction dominates; the stability ratio W is near one in fast aggregation and very large in a stable suspension.
Each counter-ion charge has a critical coagulation concentration; because particles are often negative, multivalent metal cations are highly effective coagulants.
Polymers can protect particles by steric repulsion, or, when loosely adsorbed, bridge two particles in bridging flocculation.
Aggregation driven only by diffusion is perikinetic; aggregation sped up by shear such as stirring is orthokinetic.
Clusters are mass fractals: fast, diffusion-limited aggregation makes loose clusters (d ≈ 1.8), slow, reaction-limited aggregation compact ones (d ≈ 2.1).

entries.text: A stable suspension can be undone by a pinch of the right salt. Particle aggregation is the sticking together of dispersed particles into irregular flocs or agglomerates, which destabilizes a {{ref:soil-chem-154}}. It also goes by coagulation or flocculation. Salts or chemicals called coagulants or flocculants trigger it, and it can be reversible or irreversible. Growing agglomerates settle out as sediment. In concentrated suspensions they link instead into a colloidal gel. The reverse, {{ref:soil-chem-161}}, hardly happens on its own, though stirring or shear can drive it. Salt works by screening the repulsion of the charged layers around each particle, so van der Waals attraction dominates. Chemists track this with the stability ratio W. It is near one in fast aggregation and very large in a stable suspension. Each counter-ion charge has a critical coagulation concentration. Because particles are often negative, multivalent metal cations are highly effective coagulants. Polymers cut both ways. They can protect particles by steric repulsion, or, when loosely adsorbed, bridge two particles in bridging flocculation. The way particles meet matters too. Aggregation driven only by diffusion is perikinetic; aggregation sped up by shear, such as stirring, is orthokinetic. The clusters are mass fractals, shapes whose density changes with size. Fast, diffusion-limited aggregation builds loose clusters (d ≈ 1.8), and slow, reaction-limited aggregation compact ones (d ≈ 2.1). These outcomes follow from the balance described in {{ref:soil-chem-155}}.

It also goes by coagulation or flocculation. Salts or chemicals called coagulants or flocculants trigger it, and it can be reversible or irreversible. Growing agglomerates settle out as sediment. In concentrated suspensions they link instead into a colloidal gel. The reverse, Peptization: turning a precipitate back into a colloid, hardly happens on its own, though stirring or shear can drive it. Salt works by screening the repulsion of the charged layers around each particle, so van der Waals attraction dominates. Chemists track this with the stability ratio W. It is near one in fast aggregation and very large in a stable suspension. Each counter-ion charge has a critical coagulation concentration. Because particles are often negative, multivalent metal cations are highly effective coagulants. Polymers cut both ways. They can protect particles by steric repulsion, or, when loosely adsorbed, bridge two particles in bridging flocculation. The way particles meet matters too. Aggregation driven only by diffusion is perikinetic; aggregation sped up by shear, such as stirring, is orthokinetic. The clusters are mass fractals, shapes whose density changes with size. Fast, diffusion-limited aggregation builds loose clusters (d ≈ 1.8), and slow, reaction-limited aggregation compact ones (d ≈ 2.1). These outcomes follow from the balance described in Colloidal stability: why some suspensions never clear.

entries.title: Muscovite, the common mica

facts.text: Its TOT-c structure has tetrahedral-octahedral-tetrahedral layers bonded by potassium cations; strong bonds within layers and weak ones between them give perfect basal cleavage into thin elastic sheets.
It is the most common mica, found in granites, pegmatites, gneisses and schists, and as an alteration product of feldspar.
Biotite is almost always much darker, chlorite is green with inelastic sheets, and pyrophyllite and talc are softer and greasy.
Up to 10% of its potassium may be replaced by sodium, and phengite has more silicon than aluminium with Mg or Fe balancing charge.

definition.text: Muscovite, also called common mica or potash mica, is a hydrated phyllosilicate of aluminium and potassium, KAl2(AlSi3O10)(OH)2.

entries.title: X-ray diffraction and the crystal's hidden order

definition.text: The change in direction of X-ray beams by elastic scattering from the electrons around atoms, giving a diffraction pattern.

facts.text: A regular array of atoms scatters X-rays as secondary spherical waves that cancel in most directions but add up in a few specific ones; the Bragg model explains these as reflections from evenly spaced sheets in the crystal.
Scattering is set by electron density; the heavy nuclei contribute negligibly.

Laboratory sources are tubes whose electrons, accelerated through about 50 kV, hit a metal plate; copper is most common because it cools easily and gives strong K-alpha and K-beta lines. Synchrotrons are far brighter.
Where single crystals are unavailable, powder diffraction gives less detailed information; Max von Laue's 1912 observation of diffraction confirmed that X-rays are electromagnetic radiation.
Neutrons scatter from nuclei and so reveal light atoms such as hydrogen, which is nearly invisible to X-rays; electrons scatter 1000 or more times more strongly than X-rays.

entries.title: Dispersion: particles spread through another phase

facts.text: Dispersions are classed by particle size relative to the continuous phase, whether precipitation occurs and Brownian motion; particles big enough to sediment make suspensions, smaller ones colloids and solutions.

Dispersing a solid in a liquid separates agglomerated particles and creates a new interface; it is driven by molecular diffusion and convection, with convection dominating in turbulent flow and diffusion where there is little turbulence.
Above a critical concentration, which depends on particle size and interfacial tension, some liquid dispersions turn into gels or solids.

definition.text: A dispersion is a system in which particles of one material are distributed in a continuous phase of another.

entries.title: Growing kaolinite from dissolved silica and aluminium

definition.text: The crystallization of kaolinite from silica and aluminium in solution at ordinary temperature and pressure, as happens in soils.

facts.text: In soils, disordered amorphous material seems to turn into ordered kaolinite fairly quickly, at ambient temperature and pressure and without major environmental change.
Silica must arrive as single molecules in very dilute solution, and aluminium must be six-coordinated with oxygen, as in gibbsite.
In the reaction 2Al(OH)3 + 2H4SiO4 → Si2O5·Al2(OH)4 + 5H2O, five water molecules must be removed for each unit of kaolinite formed.
On basalt in Kivu, kaolinite formed only where wet and dry seasons alternate, not in perennially swampy ground; wetting–drying cycles also help allophane turn into kaolinite.

entries.text: Kaolinite can crystallize in soil at ordinary temperature and pressure, but only if its ingredients arrive the right way. Silica must come as single molecules in very dilute solution. entries.title: Aluminosilicates, the aluminium-silicon backbone of clays

facts.text: They occur as minerals, coal combustion products and synthetic materials, often zeolites, and matter technically as structural materials, catalysts and reagents.
Feldspar is a common tectosilicate aluminosilicate of potassium, sodium and calcium cations in a negatively charged network of silicon, aluminium and oxygen.
Soil alumino-silica clays are aluminosilicates with regular crystalline or quasi-crystalline structure, including montmorillonite, illite, vermiculite, chlorite and kaolinite.
Naturally occurring microporous, hydrous aluminosilicate minerals are zeolites; their Si/Al ratio varies, which tunes their properties.

entries.title: DLVO theory: attraction, repulsion and the barrier between

definition.text: A quantitative theory of colloid stability that sums van der Waals attraction and electrical double-layer repulsion between charged surfaces in a liquid.

facts.text: The total potential energy between two particles is the sum of attraction and repulsion; both grow as the particles approach.
The energy curve has a deep primary minimum at very close range, an energy barrier further out, and a shallow secondary minimum beyond it.
The barrier must exceed the thermal energy or particles aggregate; its height shows how stable the dispersion is.
Particles trapped in the primary minimum coagulate irreversibly, while those in the secondary minimum are held weakly and easily redispersed.
Derjaguin and Landau proposed it in 1941 and Verwey and Overbeek reached the same result independently in 1948.
It explained how dispersion stability depends on electrolyte ionic strength, which the earlier Levine–Dube theory could not.
Its electrostatic term uses κ, the inverse of the Debye–Hückel screening length, with κ² = 4πλB n for monovalent ions at concentration n.
Forces outside the theory also affect stability, and it cannot describe colloidal crystals forming in dilute, low-salt dispersions.

entries.text: Two charged particles in a liquid feel a pull and a push at once. DLVO theory adds them up. It sums van der Waals attraction and electrical double-layer repulsion to give a quantitative account of {{ref:soil-chem-155}}. Both forces grow as particles approach, and their sum traces a curve. A deep primary minimum lies at very close range, an energy barrier further out, and a shallow secondary minimum beyond it. The barrier's height shows how stable the dispersion is; if it does not exceed the thermal energy, particles aggregate. Particles trapped in the primary minimum coagulate for good, while those in the secondary minimum are held weakly and easily redispersed. Derjaguin and Landau proposed the theory in 1941, and Verwey and Overbeek reached it independently in 1948. Unlike the earlier Levine–Dube theory, it explained how stability depends on the {{ref:soil-chem-202}} of the electrolyte. Yet other forces matter too, and it cannot describe colloidal crystals forming in dilute, low-salt dispersions.

entries.title: Halloysite, the kaolinite-group clay that grows as tubes

definition.text: An aluminosilicate clay mineral of the kaolinite group, with the formula Al2Si2O5(OH)4.

facts.text: It occurs mainly in recently exposed volcanic soils but also forms from primary minerals in tropical soils; glassy basaltic rocks alter to it most readily.
It grows as nanotubes with walls 10–15 sheets thick, outer diameters of 50–60 nm and lengths of 0.5–10 μm.
Hydrated halloysite has a layer spacing of 1 nm and dehydrated meta-halloysite 0.7 nm; its CEC rises with hydration, from 5–10 to 40–50 meq/100 g.
Allophane alters to halloysite under resilicating conditions, and montmorillonite alters to its hydrated form, endellite, in acidic cave settings at pH 5 or lower.

entries.title: Amorphous clays, young minerals not yet in order

definition.text: Young mixtures of silica and alumina in soil that have not yet had time to form regular crystals.

facts.text: They are common in recent volcanic ash deposits such as tephra.
Most of their charge comes from hydroxyl groups that gain or lose a hydrogen ion as soil pH changes, so they buffer soil pH and can attract cations or anions.
Andisols are defined by high proportions of glass and amorphous colloidal materials, including allophane, imogolite and ferrihydrite.
Clays without plate-shaped minerals, such as allophanic clays, tend not to show a residual shear strength.

entries.title: Peptization: turning a precipitate back into a colloid

definition.text: Turning a settled precipitate back into a colloid by shaking it with a suitable electrolyte, a peptizing agent, so that the solid particles are suspended again.

facts.text: It is the reverse of flocculation and is also called deflocculation.
Concentrated salt compresses the electrical double layer, which collapses at high ionic strength, so particles coalesce into an easily filtered flocculent precipitate.
Washing such a precipitate with too much deionised water re-expands the double layer, repulsion returns and the precipitate peptizes.
Freshly precipitated aluminium or iron hydroxide is very hard to filter because its fine colloidal particles pass through paper filters.

entries.text: A settled precipitate can be coaxed back into suspension. Peptization does this by shaking the solid with a suitable electrolyte, a peptizing agent, until its particles form a {{ref:soil-chem-154}} again. It is the reverse of flocculation, also called deflocculation. Concentrated salt compresses the charged layer around each particle, which collapses in very salty solutions, so particles coalesce into an easily filtered precipitate. Wash it with too much deionized water and that layer re-expands, repulsion returns, and the precipitate peptizes. Freshly precipitated aluminium or iron hydroxide is very hard to filter, because its fine particles pass through paper.

entries.title: Sepiolite, the fibrous clay of dry lands

definition.text: A soft, white, fibrous magnesium silicate clay mineral, Mg4Si6O15(OH)2·6H2O, also known as meerschaum.

facts.text: The fibrous clays form a continuous series from sepiolite, the most magnesium-rich, to palygorskite; sepiolite has wider structural channels.
It occurs as a secondary mineral with serpentine and can precipitate in arid environments.
Soils of South Africa's arid west hold much sepiolite, grading inland to palygorskite; it raises plant-available water in sandy soils, but cemented layers hamper mining.
Sepiolite-cemented material is called sepiocrete, and soils rich in it may be termed sepiolitic or petrosepiolitic.

entries.title: Reading clay layers with X-rays

definition.text: Identifying clay minerals by passing X-rays through oriented samples and measuring the spacing of their stacked silicate layers.

facts.text: Ordered atoms in a crystal diffract an X-ray beam at particular angles and intensities, from which the structure is calculated; non-crystalline material can also be recognised.

Randomly oriented powders help little because clays share similar X and Y dimensions; the diagnostic Z dimension is the height of the T-O or T-O-T layer, so samples are oriented to boost basal (00l) reflections.
The Z spacing changes with substitution of the central cations in the sheets and with the presence and size of the interlayer cation.
Layer spacings come from Bragg's law written as l λ = 2d sin θ, so successive 00l peaks are evenly spaced.
Clays give broad peaks while well-crystallized minerals give sharp ones; some peaks broader than others suggest that several clays are present.
Patterns are compared with known samples, such as the Clay Mineral Society's reference collection, because calculated patterns rarely match experiment.
Clays are nearly always mixed with quartz, feldspars, zeolites or carbonates that give intense peaks, so samples are lightly crushed and sieved to remove the harder nonclays.
Of four common mounting methods, the glass slide is fastest but least accurate, while the centrifuged porous plate gives the best patterns, needs most skill, and lets exchangeable cations be swapped.
