entries.title: Hydrous oxides, porous metal compounds that grab other substances

definition.text: Inorganic compounds of a metal, hydroxide and weakly bound water.

facts.text: Examples include hydrous ferric oxide (HFO), hydrous aluminium oxide (HAO), hydrous cupric oxide and hydrous titanium oxide.
HFO and HAO precipitate in highly porous, poorly crystalline or amorphous forms that make good adsorbents, used for example in water treatment.
Oxidative weathering of rocks can produce HFO and HAO, giving iron and aluminium hydrous oxide clay soils.

entries.text: Hydrous oxides are inorganic compounds of a metal, hydroxide and weakly bound water. Examples include hydrous ferric oxide (HFO), hydrous aluminium oxide (HAO), hydrous cupric oxide and hydrous titanium oxide. Oxidative {{ref:soil-found-058}} of rocks can produce HFO and HAO, giving clay soils rich in iron and aluminium hydrous oxides.

entries.title: Iron oxides, the minerals that color and feed soils

definition.text: Compounds of iron and oxygen, together with the related ferric oxyhydroxides such as rust.

facts.text: They contain ferrous iron, ferric iron or both, and are often non-stoichiometric.
Only a few oxides matter at the Earth's surface, chiefly wüstite, magnetite and hematite; Fe2O3 occurs as hematite (α) and maghemite (γ) among other phases.
The oxyhydroxides include goethite (α-FeOOH), akaganéite (β), lepidocrocite (γ), feroxyhyte (δ), ferrihydrite and green rust.
Goethite and lepidocrocite are the commonest forms of iron(III) oxyhydroxide and the most important mineral carriers of iron in soils.
Iron(III) oxyhydroxide ranges from yellow through dark brown to black depending on hydration, particle size and shape, and crystal structure.
Bacteria such as Shewanella oneidensis and Geobacter species use iron oxides as terminal electron acceptors.
Iron(III) oxyhydroxide precipitates from iron(III) solutions at pH 6.5 to 8 and forms readily when iron(II) hydroxide meets air.
Iron oxide-hydroxide binds phosphate in aquarium water treatment, and its nanoparticles have been studied for removing lead from water.

entries.text: Rust is the most familiar of a large family. Iron oxides are compounds of iron and oxygen, together with related ferric oxyhydroxides such as rust. They hold ferrous iron, ferric iron or both, and are often non-stoichiometric, with no fixed ratio of elements. Only a few matter at Earth's surface, chiefly wüstite, magnetite and {{ref:soil-chem-112}}. Among the oxyhydroxides, {{ref:soil-chem-104}} and {{ref:soil-chem-164}} are the commonest and the most important mineral carriers of iron in soils. Others include akaganéite, feroxyhyte, {{ref:soil-chem-111}} and {{ref:soil-chem-170}}. Iron(III) oxyhydroxide ranges from yellow through dark brown to black, depending on hydration, particle size and shape, and crystal structure. It precipitates from iron(III) solutions at pH 6.5 to 8 and forms readily when iron(II) hydroxide meets air. Some bacteria, such as Shewanella oneidensis and Geobacter species, even breathe on these minerals, handing them the electrons left over from their metabolism.
entries.text_plain: Rust is the most familiar of a large family. Iron oxides are compounds of iron and oxygen, together with related ferric oxyhydroxides such as rust. They hold ferrous iron, ferric iron or both, and are often non-stoichiometric, with no fixed ratio of elements. Only a few matter at Earth's surface, chiefly wüstite, magnetite and Hematite, the blood-red oxide of old soils. Among the oxyhydroxides, Goethite, the iron mineral in rust and yellow soils and Lepidocrocite, the scaly red rust of wet places are the commonest and the most important mineral carriers of iron in soils. Others include akaganéite, feroxyhyte, Ferrihydrite, iron oxide as a nanoparticle sponge and Green rust, the iron mineral that fades in air. Iron(III) oxyhydroxide ranges from yellow through dark brown to black, depending on hydration, particle size and shape, and crystal structure. It precipitates from iron(III) solutions at pH 6.5 to 8 and forms readily when iron(II) hydroxide meets air. Some bacteria, such as Shewanella oneidensis and Geobacter species, even breathe on these minerals, handing them the electrons left over from their metabolism.

entries.title: Lepidocrocite, the scaly red rust of wet places

definition.text: An iron oxide-hydroxide mineral, γ-FeO(OH), also called esmeraldite or hydrohematite.

facts.text: Red to reddish brown, it forms when iron-bearing substances rust underwater and is common where primary iron minerals weather.
Its layers of iron(III) oxide octahedra, held by hydrogen bonds through hydroxide layers as in boehmite, are weakly bonded, giving its scaly habit.
In oxidizing conditions green rust generally turns into goethite and lepidocrocite.
First described in 1813 from Moravia, it takes its name from the Greek for scale and fibre.

entries.title: Maghemite, the magnetic mark of fire

definition.text: A ferrimagnetic iron oxide, γ-Fe2O3, with the formula of hematite but the spinel structure of magnetite.

facts.text: It forms by weathering or low-temperature oxidation of iron(II) spinels such as magnetite, or by dehydration of lepidocrocite and ferrihydrite.
It is a widespread brown or yellow pigment in sediments and soils, and also forms where bushfires have magnetised iron minerals.
Heating converts goethite and ferrihydrite to maghemite and raises soil magnetism; maghemite enrichment across a landscape points to fire.
A soil's magnetic susceptibility reflects magnetic iron oxides such as maghemite, a property geoarchaeologists measure.

entries.title: Limonite, the iron ore that is really a mixture

definition.text: An iron ore made of a variable mixture of hydrated iron(III) oxide-hydroxides.

facts.text: Once thought a single mineral, it is now a field term for a mixture including goethite, lepidocrocite, akaganeite and jarosite, whose exact makeup only X-ray diffraction can settle.
It forms by hydration of hematite and magnetite, oxidation of iron sulfides and weathering of iron-rich minerals, and is often the main iron component of lateritic soils.
Its name comes from Greek words for wet meadow or marshy lake, after its occurrence as bog iron ore.
Its yellowish-brown streak distinguishes it from hematite, with a red streak, and magnetite, with a black one.

entries.title: Measuring surface area: the answer depends on the ruler

definition.text: Determining a material's surface area per unit mass, most often by gas adsorption with the BET method.

facts.text: Results depend on the method: the probe molecule's size, the exposed crystal faces and the temperature all change the value obtained.
Calculating it from a particle size distribution needs an assumed particle shape and misses the particles' surface texture.
BET adsorption captures fine structure and deep texture, but results can differ markedly with the substance adsorbed.
Gas permeability through a powder bed is quick and simple but misses much deep surface texture; standards such as ISO 9277 govern measurement.

entries.title: Isomorphous substitution: how clays gain a fixed charge

definition.text: The replacement, while a clay forms, of cations in its crystal structure by others of lower valence, which leaves the clay a permanent negative charge.

facts.text: Al3+ may replace Si4+ in the silica sheet, and up to a quarter of the Al3+ in the alumina sheet may be replaced by Zn2+, Mg2+ or Fe2+.
Swapping Al(III) for Si(IV) turns a balanced +4/−4 site into +3/−4, a charge of −1; Mg2+ for Al3+ in the octahedral sheet gives +2/−3, also −1.
The excess negative charge must be balanced by cations in the interlayer, and it attracts water and positively charged cations, some useful to plants.
Substitutions in outer layers count for more than inner ones, since charge strength falls off with the square of the distance.
Montmorillonite's charge is mostly octahedral, from Mg replacing Al; beidellite's is mostly tetrahedral, from Al replacing Si.
Kaolinite has undergone almost no substitution, which is why its CEC is low.
This charge forms with the clay and does not change with time, unlike pH-dependent charge, which rises as pH rises.

entries.text: A clay's charge is set as the clay forms. While its crystals grow, some cations in the structure are replaced by others of lower valence, carrying less positive charge. This is isomorphous substitution, and it leaves the clay a lasting negative charge. The arithmetic is simple. In the silica sheet, Al3+ may replace Si4+. A site that balanced +4 against −4 now holds +3 against −4, a charge of −1. In the alumina sheet, up to a quarter of the Al3+ may give way to Zn2+, Mg2+ or Fe2+. Mg2+ in place of Al3+ gives +2/−3, again −1. Where the swap happens matters. {{ref:soil-chem-093}} carries its charge mostly in the octahedral sheet, from magnesium replacing aluminium. The clay of {{ref:soil-chem-152}} carries it mostly in the tetrahedral sheet, from aluminium replacing silicon. Substitutions in outer layers count for more than inner ones, since charge strength falls off with the square of the distance. Cations in the interlayer must balance the excess negative charge. It attracts water and positively charged ions, some of them useful to plants. Kaolinite has undergone almost no substitution, which is why its {{ref:soil-chem-046}} is low. This charge does not change with time. That sets it apart from the charge described in {{ref:soil-chem-049}}, which rises as pH rises.

entries.title: Smectite, the swelling clay with an open interior

definition.text: A group of swelling 2:1 clay minerals, mainly montmorillonite, that take water and cations between their layers.

facts.text: Smectite and montmorillonite name the same class of swelling clays, smectite being the usual term in Europe and montmorillonite in North America; industry calls them bentonite.
Each layer is two silica tetrahedral sheets cross-linked through an octahedral sheet of alumina or iron oxide.
The layers are not rigidly joined: the interlayer between them holds hydrated cations and water, and smectite swells as water and cations enter it reversibly.
Its layers are negatively charged by isomorphous substitution in both the tetrahedral and the octahedral sheets.
Because the interlayer is open to water and cations, smectites have the highest CEC of the clays common in soils; only vermiculite and some zeolites exceed it.
Smectites form by weathering of basalt, gabbro and silica-rich volcanic glass, and where hot water or seawater dissolves much of the silica from volcanic ash.
Soils with smectite clay expand when wet, and clay soils containing montmorillonite or smectite suffer alkalinity problems more than illite or kaolinite clay soils.

entries.text: Smectite clays swell because their layers are not rigidly joined. entries.title: Montmorillonite, the clay that swells tenfold

definition.text: A soft 2:1 clay mineral of the smectite group, with an alumina sheet between two silica sheets and a water content that varies.

facts.text: It is named after Montmorillon in France, where it was first described in 1847.
Its plate-shaped particles average about 1 μm across and 0.96 nm thick; resolving one takes about 25,000-fold electron-microscope magnification.
Its CEC comes from magnesium replacing aluminium in the central sheet, which leaves nearby oxygens negatively charged and able to attract cations.
Its crystals are loosely bound, so water enters between them and the clay can swell up to ten times its dry volume; it is a characteristic component of swelling soils.
Because its crystals are not bonded face to face, its whole surface is open to reactions, giving it a high CEC.
It occurs in soils that have had little leaching, hence in arid regions, often mixed with chlorite, muscovite, illite and kaolinite.
It is added to drought-prone soils to hold water, and its swelling suits it to drilling mud, earthen dams and levees.

entries.title: Bentonite, the swelling clay that seals landfills

definition.text: An absorbent swelling clay made mostly of montmorillonite, in either its sodium or its calcium form.

facts.text: Geologists use the name for a clay rock formed from volcanic ash, usually in seawater, as up to 40–50 wt.% of its silica dissolves away; industry uses it for any smectite-rich swelling clay.
It can absorb enough water to grow up to eight times in volume, and sodium bentonite swells far more than calcium bentonite.
Calcium bentonite can be turned into sodium bentonite by ion exchange, by mixing in 5–10% of a soluble sodium salt such as sodium carbonate.
Swelling makes sodium bentonite a self-sealing, low-permeability barrier: it lines landfills, and nearly sodium-saturated clay forms impermeable curtains in soil below dams.

entries.title: Fuller's earth, the clay that cleaned wool

definition.text: Any of various clays used as an absorbent, filter or bleaching agent.

facts.text: Products sold as fuller's earth are usually palygorskite (attapulgite) or bentonite; its clays commonly include montmorillonite, kaolinite and attapulgite.
In some places the name means calcium bentonite, altered volcanic ash made mostly of montmorillonite.
The name comes from fulling: fullers kneaded it with water into woollen cloth to absorb lanolin, oils and other greasy impurities.
Saturated by heavy rain it can become thixotropic, so hills, cliffs and slopes that contain it can be unstable.

entries.title: Swellers and collapsers: the cations between clay layers
entries.article: Smectite#Role of interlayer cations in the swelling process

definition.text: How the cations held between the layers of 2:1 clays govern how much the clay swells or shrinks as it gains or loses water.

facts.text: Na+ and Ca2+ are the main interlayer cations in smectites; sodium gives the most swelling, while calcium smectite swells much less but also shrinks less when dried.
How strongly each cation hydrates, and its hydrated radius, explain the swelling or shrinking of layered silicates.
Highly hydrated magnesium ions act as swellers, fully opening vermiculite's interlayer; poorly hydrated potassium ions act as collapsers, fully closing illite's.
Potassium replacing sodium collapses the interlayer, so smectite in contact with potassium-rich groundwater turns into non-swelling illite.
With sodium as its main exchangeable cation, montmorillonite can swell to several times its original volume.
Ammonium is fixed mainly between the layers of 2:1 clays such as illite, vermiculite or montmorillonite, along with ions of similar size and low hydration energy such as potassium.

With sodium as its main exchangeable cation, montmorillonite can swell to several times its original volume. Calcium smectite swells much less but also shrinks less when dried. Potassium replacing sodium collapses the interlayer, so smectite in contact with potassium-rich groundwater turns into non-swelling illite. Ammonium is caught the same way. It is fixed mainly between the layers of illite, vermiculite or montmorillonite, with potassium and other ions of similar size and low hydration energy. These cations help set a clay soil's {{ref:soil-phys-028}}.

entries.title: Clay that brought worn-out Thai fields back

definition.text: Adding bentonite clay to degraded farm soils to restore them, as farmers in northeast Thailand have done.

facts.text: In northeast Thailand, bentonite applied to degraded soils dramatically reversed the degradation and brought higher yields, better crop prices and greater returns.
Field trials by the International Water Management Institute and partners in 2002–2003 found that locally sourced bentonite raised yields of rain-fed forage sorghum.
Clay-using farmers had higher costs, but larger, better harvests let them invest and grow more than farmers who did not use clay.
Adding clays such as calcium bentonite to water-repellent soils gives them more surface area per unit volume and supports aggregation.

entries.title: From swelling clays to oxides: the weathering sequence

definition.text: The change in a soil's dominant clay minerals as weathering and leaching intensify, from 2:1 clays such as montmorillonite through kaolinite to iron and aluminium oxides.

facts.text: The clay that forms depends on the parent material and on the minerals in solution, so source rock and climate both matter.
Montmorillonite occurs in soils that have had little leaching, hence in arid regions, though depending on its origin it may occur in humid climates.
Where rainfall is high, acid soils lose more silica than alumina from their clays, leaving kaolinite; heavier weathering still produces sesquioxide clays.
Kaolinite abounds in soils of hot, moist climates; along gradients toward cooler climates illite increases, and toward drier ones smectite.
Acid weathering of feldspar-rich rock in warm climates yields kaolin, alkaline weathering yields illite, and intense weathering of other clay minerals yields gibbsite.
Because clay content tracks climate, the clays of buried ancient soils are used to infer past climates.

entries.text: A soil's clay records how hard it has been weathered. As weathering and leaching intensify, the dominant clay minerals change: from 2:1 clays such as montmorillonite, through kaolinite, to oxides of iron and aluminium. The starting point depends on the parent material and on the minerals in solution, so source rock and climate both matter. Montmorillonite occurs in soils that have had little leaching, hence in arid regions. Depending on its origin, it may also occur in humid climates. Where rainfall is high, acid soils lose more silica than alumina from their clays, leaving kaolinite. Heavier weathering still produces {{ref:soil-chem-106}}. Rock and chemistry steer the result as well. Acid weathering of feldspar-rich rock in warm climates yields kaolin, alkaline weathering yields illite, and intense weathering of other clay minerals yields gibbsite. Climate gradients show the same pattern. Kaolinite abounds in soils of hot, moist climates. Toward cooler climates illite increases, and toward drier ones smectite. Because clay content tracks climate, the clays of buried ancient soils are used to infer past climates.

entries.title: Sesquioxide clays, the last residue of deep weathering

definition.text: Old, highly leached soil clays made of oxides and hydroxides of iron, aluminium and titanium, left after heavy rainfall removes most of the silica from alumino-silica clays.

facts.text: They include hematite (Fe2O3), iron hydroxide (Fe(OH)3), gibbsite (Al(OH)3) and the manganese mineral birnessite, as seen in lateritic weathering profiles of tropical soils.
Forming them takes hundreds of thousands of years of leaching.
Their name comes from the Latin sesqui, 'one and one-half', for three parts oxygen to two of iron or aluminium, a ratio that does not hold for them all.
They are not sticky and do not swell; soils rich in them, such as lateritic soils, behave much like sand and pass water rapidly.
Their CEC is low, but as variable-charge minerals they can hold anions as well as cations.
They hold large amounts of phosphate, a sorption that humified organic matter partly inhibits; the more goethite they contain, the more phosphorus is locked away from plants.
Soils rich in them range from yellow to red according to which iron oxides dominate.
In tropical rainforests heavy rains wash the alumino-silicate clays out of the soil, leaving only sesquioxide clays of low CEC.

entries.title: Five stages of clay meeting water

definition.text: The umbrella term for the progressive interactions between clay minerals and water, described in five stages: hydration, dispersion, flocculation, deflocculation and aggregation.

facts.text: Dry clay packets sit in face-to-face stacks like a deck of playing cards; in water they first hydrate, absorbing water and swelling.
In dispersion, water pushes the platelets so far apart that they lose their attraction and spread through the water; once shearing stops, surface charges draw them back together in flocculation.
Deflocculation, or peptization, reverses flocculation: a chemical deflocculant covers the platelets' positive edge charges and greatly weakens their attraction.
Aggregation, driven by ionic or thermal conditions, alters the water layer around the platelets, strips deflocculant from their edges and lets them return to face-to-face stacking.

entries.text: Dry clay packets sit in face-to-face stacks like a deck of playing cards. Clay–water interaction names what happens next, in five stages. Once shearing stops, surface charges draw them back together in flocculation. Deflocculation, or peptization, reverses flocculation. A chemical deflocculant covers the platelets' positive edge charges and greatly weakens their attraction. Finally, in aggregation, ionic or thermal conditions alter the platelets' water layer, strip off the deflocculant and let them stack again.

entries.title: Layer charge, the negative pull of clay sheets

definition.text: The net negative charge on a clay mineral layer created when ions of lower charge, such as Al3+, replace Si4+, which interlayer cations balance.

facts.text: In nontronite usually more than 60% of the layer charge sits in the tetrahedral sheet, and it is generally balanced by Ca2+ or Mg2+.
Beidellite is defined by having more than 50% of its charge in the tetrahedral sheet.
In the manganese oxide birnessite, cations and water held between layers offset the layer charge, giving the mineral a cation-exchange capacity.
The presence and size of the charge-balancing interlayer cation changes the layer spacing measured by X-ray diffraction.

entries.text: Swap a silicon ion for an aluminium ion, and a clay layer gains a negative charge. Layer charge is the net negative charge created when ions of lower charge, such as Al3+, replace Si4+ through {{ref:soil-chem-085}}. Interlayer cations balance it. Where the charge sits defines minerals. In nontronite usually more than 60% lies in the tetrahedral sheet, generally balanced by Ca2+ or Mg2+, and {{ref:soil-chem-152}} is defined by more than 50% there. In the manganese oxide {{ref:soil-chem-195}}, cations and water between layers offset the charge, letting it exchange cations. The size of the balancing cation changes the layer spacing seen by X-ray diffraction.

entries.title: Beidellite, a smectite charged in its silica sheet

definition.text: A smectite clay mineral in which more than half of the layer charge comes from aluminium replacing silicon in the tetrahedral sheet.

facts.text: It is a dioctahedral smectite, grouped with montmorillonite and nontronite, whereas saponite is trioctahedral.
It is one of the clay minerals that give soils shrink–swell behaviour, along with smectite, montmorillonite, illite and vermiculite.

entries.title: The Schulze–Hardy rule: why aluminium salts clump clay best

definition.text: The rule that the critical coagulation concentration of an electrolyte varies as the inverse sixth power of the charge of its counter-ion.

facts.text: Critical coagulation concentrations fall steeply with counter-ion charge; for trivalent counter-ions they range from 0.03 to 0.5 × 10⁻³ mol/L.
The rule can be derived from DLVO theory.
Ions of the same charge still differ somewhat, reflecting particle properties or ion affinities for the surface.
Multivalent cations flocculate colloids more efficiently than monovalent ones: AlCl3 > CaCl2 > NaCl.

entries.text: Doubling an ion's charge does far more than double its power to clump colloids. The Schulze–Hardy rule says the critical coagulation concentration of an electrolyte varies as the inverse sixth power of its counter-ion's charge. For trivalent counter-ions it falls to 0.03 to 0.5 × 10⁻³ mol/L. So multivalent cations flocculate colloids far better than monovalent ones: AlCl3 beats CaCl2, which beats NaCl. The rule can be derived from {{ref:soil-chem-157}}. Ions of the same charge still differ somewhat, reflecting particle properties or how strongly ions favor the surface.

entries.title: Clay chemistry, from fertile fields to Mars

definition.text: The applied branch of chemistry that studies the structures, properties and reactions of clays and clay minerals.

facts.text: Clay minerals are built of nanometre-scale layers, carry fixed and exchangeable charges, adsorb and intercalate molecules and form stable colloidal dispersions.
Their cation exchange capacity balances the commonest soil cations (Na+, K+, NH4+, Ca2+, Mg2+) and controls pH, directly affecting soil fertility.
Interactions between clay minerals and soil organic substances help fix nutrients and decide whether pesticides and other contaminants are held or leached.
Clay minerals detected on Mars by the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter in 2009 were strong evidence that the planet once had water.

entries.text: In 2009, the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter spotted clay minerals on Mars, strong evidence that the planet once had water. They carry fixed and exchangeable charges, take molecules onto their surfaces and between their layers, and form stable colloidal dispersions. Their capacity to hold cations balances the commonest soil cations and controls pH, directly affecting how fertile a soil is. Their interactions with organic substances help fix nutrients and decide whether {{ref:soil-env-237}} and other contaminants are held or leached.

entries.title: Humic substances, the dark core of soil organic matter

definition.text: Dark, relatively decay-resistant organic compounds formed during the long-term decomposition and transformation of biomass residues.

facts.text: They make up most of the organic matter in soil, peat, coal and sediments, and much of the dissolved organic matter in lakes, rivers and sea water.
Humic substances account for 50 – 90% of the cation-exchange capacity of soils.
The term covers three fractions that differ in solubility: humic acid, fulvic acid and humin.
Their colour runs from bright yellow through light or dark brown to black; the name comes from the Latin humus, meaning 'soil, earth'.
They form by microbial breakdown of dead material such as lignin, cellulose and charcoal, yet how they form is among the least understood parts of humus chemistry.
Historic theories of their formation were Waksman's lignin theory (1932), the polyphenol theory and Maillard's sugar-amine condensation theory (1911).
Those from soil and peat, formed over hundreds to thousands of years, have higher molecular weights and more oxygen and nitrogen than those from coal and leonardite, formed over millions.

entries.title: Chelation: how molecules grip metals like a claw

definition.text: The bonding of a metal atom by a molecule that grips it at two or more points, forming a ring structure.

facts.text: The binding molecule, or ligand, is called a chelant, chelator, chelating agent or sequestering agent; it is usually, but not necessarily, organic.
The name comes from the Greek chēlē, 'claw', since the ligand holds the metal like a crab's claws; Morgan and Drew first used 'chelate' in 1920.
Most metal complexes in nature are bound in some kind of chelate ring, for example with a humic acid or a protein.
Metal chelates govern the mobilisation of metals in soil and their uptake and accumulation by plants and microorganisms.
Humus, a negatively charged colloid, raises a soil's cation-exchange capacity and so its ability to store nutrients by chelation.
Chelation is used in nutritional supplements, chelation therapy for toxic metals, MRI contrast agents, catalysts, water treatment and fertilizers.
Dechelation reverses it, recovering the chelating agent by acidifying the solution with a mineral acid to form a precipitate.

entries.text: A crab holds its prey with two pincers, and some molecules hold metal atoms the same way. Chelation is the bonding of a metal atom by a molecule that grips it at two or more points, closing a ring. The name comes from the Greek chēlē, 'claw', and Morgan and Drew first used the word 'chelate' in 1920. The gripping molecule, or ligand, is called a chelant, chelator, chelating agent or sequestering agent. It is usually organic, though it need not be. Most metal complexes in nature sit in some kind of chelate ring, held by a humic substance or a protein. In soil, these chelates govern how metals move. They also control how plants and microorganisms take up and store metals. As a negatively charged colloid, {{ref:soil-bio-089}} raises a soil's {{ref:soil-chem-046}} and so its ability to store nutrients by chelation. People use the same grip in nutritional supplements, chelation therapy for toxic metals, MRI contrast agents, catalysts, water treatment and fertilizers. The process can also run backward. In dechelation, acidifying the solution with a mineral acid forms a precipitate and recovers the chelating agent.

entries.title: Sorption: the many ways one substance sticks to another

definition.text: A physical and chemical process by which one substance becomes attached to another.

facts.text: It covers absorption of a substance into another of a different state, adsorption of ions and molecules onto the surface of another phase, and ion exchange.
Rates of adsorption and absorption of a dilute solute onto a surface can be calculated with Fick's laws of diffusion.
Much soil humus persists for over 100 years partly because it is tightly sorbed or complexed to clays, out of reach of microbes and enzymes.
Molybdenum sorption is strongest in acid soils, and liming often relieves molybdenum deficiency by decreasing it.
Aluminium sorbed onto exposed hydroxyl groups gives clay plate edges a slight positive charge, so they stick to the negative faces of other particles and flocculate.
In alkali soils, ammonium from urea, a strongly sorbing cation, exchanges with weakly sorbing Na+, releasing the sodium into water.

entries.title: Adsorption, the art of sticking to a surface

definition.text: The adhesion of atoms, ions or molecules from a gas, liquid or solution to a surface.

facts.text: It builds a film of adsorbate on the adsorbent and, unlike absorption, does not penetrate into the bulk of the material.
Sorption covers both adsorption and absorption; desorption is the reverse.
It arises from surface energy: atoms at a surface are not fully surrounded by their neighbours and can attract adsorbates.
Bonding is classed as physisorption, through weak van der Waals forces, or chemisorption, through covalent bonding; electrostatic attraction can also cause it.
Adsorption, ion exchange and chromatography are sorption processes that selectively move adsorbates from a fluid onto insoluble particles.
Physically adsorbed water on solids is removed by drying, while chemically adsorbed water may split into surface -H and -OH groups.
German physicist Heinrich Kayser coined the word in 1881.

entries.text: Every surface is a little unfinished. Atoms inside a solid are surrounded by neighbors, but those at the surface are not, and that leftover surface energy lets them attract other substances. The result is adsorption: the adhesion of atoms, ions or molecules from a gas, liquid or solution to a surface. It builds a film of adsorbate on the adsorbent. Unlike absorption, it does not penetrate into the bulk of the material. {{ref:soil-chem-068}} covers both, and {{ref:soil-chem-147}} is the reverse. The bonds vary in strength. Physisorption works through weak van der Waals forces; chemisorption through covalent bonds. Electrostatic attraction can also hold adsorbates. The difference shows with water. Physically adsorbed water on a solid is removed by drying, while chemically adsorbed water may split into surface -H and -OH groups. Adsorption, ion exchange and chromatography are all sorption processes. Each selectively moves substances from a fluid onto insoluble particles. entries.title: Variable charge: soil surfaces that shift with pH

definition.text: Surface charge on clay edges and organic matter that changes with the pH of the soil solution, because it comes from hydroxyl groups giving up hydrogen ions.

facts.text: The edges of clay sheets expose many acidic hydroxyl groups that lose their hydrogen at the pH of many soils, leaving negative charges.
Organic matter adds a large share of cation exchange through its many charged functional groups, and its CEC is highly pH-dependent.
Raising the pH, that is lowering the H+ concentration, increases the variable charge and so the cation-exchange capacity.
Hydrogens of humus hydroxyl groups can ionise into solution just as those of clay do, leaving an oxygen with a negative charge.

entries.text: Part of a soil's grip on nutrients turns up and down with acidity. Variable charge is surface charge on clay edges and {{ref:soil-found-045}} that changes with the pH of the soil water. Its many charged groups give it a large share of a soil's power to hold cations, positively charged ions, and that share depends heavily on pH. Raising the pH means fewer hydrogen ions in solution. More groups then lose their hydrogen, the variable charge grows, and so does the {{ref:soil-chem-046}}.

entries.title: Leonardite, the oxidized coal rich in humic acid

definition.text: A soft, waxy, black or brown mineraloid formed by the oxidation of lignite, which dissolves easily in alkaline solutions.

facts.text: It is a rich source of humic acid (up to 90%), used as a soil conditioner, in water treatment, in the remediation of polluted environments and as a drilling additive.
It occurs with near-surface lignite deposits; first described from North Dakota, it is named after A. G. Leonard, first director of the North Dakota Geological Survey.
It conditions soil either applied directly to the land or as a source of humic acid or potassium humate.
Added to contaminated ground, especially with compost, it reduces the uptake of metals by plants.

entries.title: Making humic substances in hours instead of years

definition.text: Humic-like substances produced by people, by composting lignin, adding biochar, or synthesising them industrially from organic feedstocks.

facts.text: Hydrothermal humification turns biomass into artificial humin, humic and fulvic acids at 180 °C–250 °C in an alkaline solution within minutes to hours, against years in nature.
Artificial humic acids have eased the effects of drought on soil microbial communities.
Oxidising lignite also yields humic substances, reversing coal formation; this 'mineral-derived fulvic acid' is widely used in China.
Synthesised humic substances were used to save a 160-year-old beech tree in Park Sanssouci, Potsdam, stressed by water scarcity and sandy soil.

entries.text: Nature needs years to make humic substances, and chemists can do it in hours. Artificial humic substances are humic-like materials made by people: by composting {{ref:soil-bio-116}}, adding {{ref:soil-fert-050}} or synthesizing them from organic feedstocks. Hydrothermal processing turns biomass in an alkaline solution at 180 °C–250 °C into all three humic fractions within minutes to hours. Oxidizing lignite does it too, reversing coal formation; China widely uses this 'mineral-derived' {{ref:soil-chem-060}}. Such products have eased drought's effects on soil microbes and helped save a 160-year-old beech tree in Park Sanssouci, Potsdam.

Artificial humic substances are humic-like materials made by people: by composting Lignin, the plant polymer that resists rot, adding Biochar, charcoal made to be buried or synthesizing them from organic feedstocks. Hydrothermal processing turns biomass in an alkaline solution at 180 °C–250 °C into all three humic fractions within minutes to hours. Oxidizing lignite does it too, reversing coal formation; China widely uses this 'mineral-derived' Fulvic acid, the humic fraction that always dissolves. Such products have eased drought's effects on soil microbes and helped save a 160-year-old beech tree in Park Sanssouci, Potsdam.

entries.title: Inside humic substances: thousands of molecules, no settled shape

definition.text: The make-up of humic substances: mixtures of many molecules built from aromatic, aliphatic and carbohydrate units that carry mainly carboxylic and phenolic groups.

facts.text: Carboxylic and phenolic groups give most of their surface charge and reactivity, protonating at a pK around 4 and around 8 respectively.
These groups let humic acids form complexes, often chelates, with Mg2+, Ca2+, Fe2+ and Fe3+, which regulates the bioavailability of metal ions.
Mass spectroscopy finds thousands of distinct components, and molecular weights are lower than once thought.
Their molecular structure is still debated: the traditional view sees large poly-condensates associated with clay, a newer one supramolecular associations of small molecules.

entries.contested_note: Sources disagree whether humic substances are large macromolecular poly-condensates or supramolecular associations of relatively small molecules.
entries.text: Mass spectroscopy finds thousands of distinct components in humic material. Humic substances mix many molecules built from aromatic, aliphatic and carbohydrate units, carrying mainly carboxylic and phenolic groups. They also bind Mg2+, Ca2+, Fe2+ and Fe3+, often as chelates, regulating how available those metals are. Molecular weights are lower than once thought. Researchers still disagree whether the molecules are large poly-condensates tied to clay or loose supramolecular associations of small ones.

entries.title: Does organic matter feed plants? A dispute since the 18th century

definition.text: The effects of humic substances and other soil organic matter on plant growth and soil fertility.

facts.text: Until Liebig showed that plants grow on inorganic compounds, humus was thought to feed plants directly; afterwards organic matter was valued only for the nutrients released as it broke down.
Soil scientists now at least recognise that humus affects fertility through the soil's water-holding capacity.
Plants may absorb soluble forms of humus, perhaps an essential route for taking up otherwise insoluble iron oxides.
Studies found humic acids increased plant growth even at low application rates, and humate added to soil raised root mass in creeping bentgrass turf.

entries.contested_note: The chemistry and function of organic matter in plant growth has been disputed since the 18th century, and direct uptake of humus is still not settled.
entries.text: People once believed plants fed directly on {{ref:soil-bio-089}}. Then Liebig showed that plants grow on inorganic compounds, and {{ref:soil-found-045}} came to be valued only for the nutrients it released as it broke down. Soil scientists now at least agree that it affects fertility by helping soil hold water. Its other effects on plants have been disputed since the 18th century. Plants may absorb soluble humic material, perhaps to take up iron, but this is not settled. Studies found humic products boosted growth even at low rates.

entries.title: Adsorption isotherms: counting what a surface holds

definition.text: A description of how much substance is adsorbed on a surface as a function of its pressure, or of its concentration in solution, at constant temperature.

facts.text: The quantity adsorbed is nearly always divided by the adsorbent's mass so materials can be compared.
Freundlich and Kuster published the first, purely empirical fit; Langmuir derived the first scientifically based isotherm.
The Langmuir model assumes equivalent sites holding one molecule each, an energetically uniform surface and at most a monolayer, assumptions seldom all true.
Choosing between Langmuir and Freundlich should rest on adsorption enthalpies, constant in Langmuir and falling with coverage in Freundlich, not on best fit.
The 1938 BET isotherm allows multilayers; Langmuir usually suits chemisorption, BET physisorption on non-microporous surfaces.
The monolayer capacity from a Langmuir fit can be used to calculate the adsorbent's surface area.
Linearized fits are no longer common practice now that nonlinear regression is fast.

conflicts.text: Langmuir presented his model in 1916.
conflicts.note: The Adsorption page dates Langmuir's isotherm to 1918 (S:3f112d1357dd); the Langmuir page says 1916.

entries.text: How much will a surface hold if the supply keeps rising? An adsorption isotherm answers. It describes how much substance is adsorbed as a function of its pressure, or its concentration in solution, at constant temperature. The amount is nearly always divided by the adsorbent's mass, so materials can be compared. Freundlich and Kuster published the first isotherm, a purely empirical fit. Langmuir derived the first scientifically based one. His model assumes equivalent sites holding one molecule each, a uniform surface and at most a single layer, assumptions seldom all true. The 1938 BET isotherm allows multiple layers. Langmuir usually suits chemisorption, BET physisorption on surfaces without tiny pores. Choosing between Langmuir and Freundlich should rest on adsorption enthalpies, not best fit: constant in Langmuir's model, falling with coverage in Freundlich's. A Langmuir fit also yields the monolayer capacity, from which surface area can be calculated.

entries.title: Desorption, letting go of a surface

definition.text: The release of adsorbed atoms or molecules from a surface into the surrounding fluid or vacuum; the reverse of adsorption.

facts.text: It happens when a molecule gains enough energy to overcome the activation barrier and binding energy holding it to the surface.
Heat, light, energetic particle beams or chemical reactions such as oxidation or reduction can drive it.
Thermal desorption is described by the Polanyi–Wigner equation, whose kinetic order links surface coverage to desorption rate.
As remediation, thermal desorption heats contaminated material to 90–560 °C to volatilize water and organic contaminants, which a gas treatment system then collects or destroys.

entries.text: Desorption is {{ref:soil-chem-145}} run backward: the release of adsorbed atoms or molecules from a surface into the surrounding fluid or vacuum. It happens when a molecule gains enough energy to overcome the barrier and binding energy holding it. Heat, light, energetic particle beams or reactions such as oxidation or reduction can supply it. The Polanyi–Wigner equation describes desorption driven by heat, linking surface coverage to desorption rate. The same idea cleans soil. As a cleanup method, {{ref:soil-env-230}} heats contaminated material to 90–560 °C, driving off water and organic contaminants for a gas treatment system to collect or destroy.

entries.title: Why two grips beat one: the chelate effect

definition.text: The greater affinity of a chelating ligand for a metal ion than of similar ligands that bind it at only one point.

facts.text: Bidentate ligands bind metal ions to form a chelate ring; as in organic chemistry, 5- and 6-membered rings predominate.
Cadmium holds ethylenediamine, which forms a five-membered ring, far more strongly than two methylamine ligands of about the same donor power.
The enthalpy changes of the two reactions are about equal, so the chelate effect is mainly an effect of entropy.

entries.text: A molecule that holds a metal at two points beats two molecules holding it at one point each. That is the chelate effect: a chelating ligand's greater affinity for a metal ion than similar ligands that bind it only once. Bidentate, or two-pronged, ligands close a chelate ring around the metal, and as in organic chemistry, 5- and 6-membered rings predominate. Cadmium holds ethylenediamine, which forms a five-membered ring, far more strongly than two methylamine ligands of about the same donor power. The enthalpy changes, the heat given off, of the two reactions are about equal. So the advantage comes mainly from entropy, the measure of disorder.

entries.title: Chelated fertilizers keep micronutrient metals in solution

definition.text: Fertilizers that supply micronutrient metals such as manganese, iron, zinc and copper as metal chelate compounds.

facts.text: Without a chelating agent, the phosphate salts in most fertilizers turn these metal ions into insoluble solids of no use to plants.
EDTA is the typical chelating agent that keeps the metals soluble; iron is often given as EDTA or EDDHA chelates.
Chelating a foliar-applied nutrient improves its absorption and movement in the plant and avoids losses to soil and groundwater.
Consumption of EDTA and NTA is declining (−6% annually) over toxicity and environmental concerns, as greener chelators such as EDDS and citrate gain ground.

entries.text: The phosphate salts in most fertilizers turn trace metal ions into insoluble solids of no use to plants. Chelated fertilizers avoid that trap by supplying manganese, iron, zinc and copper as metal chelates. EDTA is the typical chelating agent, and iron is often given as EDTA or EDDHA chelates. Sprayed on leaves, a chelated nutrient is absorbed and moved better, and less is lost to soil and groundwater. Use of EDTA and NTA is falling 6% a year over toxicity concerns, as greener EDDS and citrate gain ground.

entries.title: Living chelators: how microbes and roots fetch metals

definition.text: Molecules made by living things, such as proteins, polysaccharides, organic acids and microbial siderophores, that bind metal ions as chelates.

facts.text: Organic diacids such as malate, amino acids such as glutamic acid and histidine, and peptides such as phytochelatin are typical natural chelators.
Many microbes secrete water-soluble pigments called siderophores; Pseudomonas species release pyochelin and pyoverdine, which bind iron.
Chemical weathering is attributed to organic chelating agents, such as peptides and sugars, that extract metal ions from minerals and rocks.
Plant growth-promoting rhizobacteria produce siderophores that chelate iron and make it available to plant roots.

entries.text: Living things make their own claws for metal. Natural chelating agents are molecules made by organisms that bind metal ions as chelates: proteins, long-chain sugars, organic acids and microbial pigments. Malate, glutamic acid, histidine and the peptide phytochelatin are typical. Pseudomonas bacteria secrete the water-soluble pigments pyochelin and pyoverdine, which bind iron, and some root-dwelling bacteria use such pigments to hand iron to plants. Organic chelators such as peptides and sugars are even credited with chemical weathering, pulling metal ions out of rocks.

entries.title: Chemical equivalents: counting charge, not just atoms

definition.text: The amount of a substance that reacts with, or is equivalent to, a set amount, typically one mole, of another substance in a reaction.

facts.text: Formally, it is the amount that reacts with or supplies one mole of hydrogen ions in an acid–base reaction, or one mole of electrons in a redox reaction.
The number of equivalents of an ion equals its moles multiplied by its valence.
Thus 1 mmol of Na+ is 1 milliequivalent, but 1 mmol of Ca2+ is 2 milliequivalents.
It is an archaic quantity; small amounts are given in milliequivalents (meq), thousandths of an equivalent.

entries.text: A millimole of calcium does twice the work of a millimole of sodium. The chemical equivalent captures this. It is the amount of a substance that reacts with, or supplies, one mole of hydrogen ions in an acid–base reaction. In a {{ref:soil-chem-113}} reaction, it is one mole of electrons. The number of equivalents of an ion equals its moles times its valence. So 1 mmol of Na+ is 1 milliequivalent, but 1 mmol of Ca2+ is 2 milliequivalents. The quantity is archaic, yet small amounts are still given in milliequivalents (meq), thousandths of an equivalent.

entries.title: Point of zero charge, where a surface's sign flips

definition.text: The pH at which the net electrical charge on a particle's surface is zero.

facts.text: Below the point of zero charge a surface turns positive and adsorbs anions; above it, the surface is negative and adsorbs cations.
The idea came from studies of colloid flocculation; at this point particles have zero zeta potential and flocculate fastest.
It is usually found by acid–base titration of a colloid suspension while tracking pH and the particles' electrophoretic mobility.
It governs how readily a surface adsorbs harmful ions, and because soil pH sets mineral surface charges it also shifts emissions such as nitrous acid.

entries.text: At one pH, a charged soil surface carries no net charge at all. That pH is its point of zero charge. Below it the surface turns positive and adsorbs anions, negatively charged ions; above it, the surface turns negative and adsorbs cations. The idea came from studies of colloid flocculation, since particles at this point flocculate fastest. Chemists find it by titrating a colloid suspension with acid and base. It governs how readily a surface adsorbs harmful ions, and even shifts soil emissions of nitrous acid.

entries.title: Saline, sodic and saline-sodic: three ways soil goes salty

facts.text: Saline soils have EC above 4 dS/m but SAR below 13 and ESP below 15%, pH usually under 8.5, and flocculated colloids.
Sodic soils have EC below 4 dS/m but SAR above 13 and ESP above 15%, and pH usually above 8.5 from hydrolysis of Na2CO3.
Saline-sodic soils have EC above 4 dS/m, SAR above 13 and ESP above 15%; their pH is usually below 8.5 and they stay flocculated.
Hydrated Na+ between clay particles cancels the binding electrostatic forces and extra water layers push the particles apart, dispersing sodic soil; high pH also disperses organic matter.
Saline soils are aggregated with high infiltration so they leach easily, but dispersed sodic and saline-sodic soils infiltrate poorly and usually need gypsum.
Calcium replacing monovalent Na+ promotes aggregation and infiltration, and the displaced sodium and salts are leached; saline drainage may be diverted through subsurface drains.
Salt-tolerant crops such as barley or sunflower and trees can take up salts, but prevention is better than reclamation.

Natural sources include mineral weathering, atmospheric deposition, seawater intrusion, saline groundwater and natural brines; human sources include salty irrigation water, salty fertilizers, manure, biosolids, compost and road salt.

definition.text: Salt-affected soils are classed as saline, sodic or saline-sodic by total salt (EC) and sodium content (SAR, ESP).

entries.title: Fulvic acid, the humic fraction that always dissolves

definition.text: The fraction of humic substances that dissolves in water at any pH.

facts.text: It has more carboxylic groups and a lower average molecular weight than humic acid, and is more acidic.
Fulvic acids have a higher cation-exchange capacity, interact more strongly with fertilizers and form soluble chelates of trace metals.
Chelates of fulvic acid and metal ions in humus are strongly leached and redeposited, an important part of cheluviation.
Measured number-average molecular weights of aquatic fulvic acid are below 900.

entries.text: One fraction of humic substances dissolves in water at any pH, acid or alkaline. That fraction is fulvic acid. Compared with {{ref:soil-chem-059}}, it has more carboxylic groups, a lower average molecular weight and stronger acidity. Measured number-average molecular weights of fulvic acid from water are below 900. Fulvic acids hold more exchangeable cations, interact more strongly with fertilizers and form soluble chelates of trace metals. Those metal chelates are strongly leached and redeposited, an important part of cheluviation.
entries.text_plain: One fraction of humic substances dissolves in water at any pH, acid or alkaline. That fraction is fulvic acid. Compared with Humic acid, the fraction that strong acid leaves behind, it has more carboxylic groups, a lower average molecular weight and stronger acidity. Measured number-average molecular weights of fulvic acid from water are below 900. Fulvic acids hold more exchangeable cations, interact more strongly with fertilizers and form soluble chelates of trace metals. entries.title: Humic acid, the fraction that strong acid leaves behind

definition.text: The fraction of humic substances that dissolves in water at neutral and alkaline pH but not at acidic pH below 2.

facts.text: Extracted humic acid is a complex mixture of many acids with carboxyl and phenolate groups that behaves as a dibasic, or occasionally tribasic, acid.
Reported number-average molecular weights of soil humic acid are below 6000, though it is highly polydisperse.
Green manure lowers the pH of alkali soils by generating humic acid.
Its potassium salt, potassium humate, is extracted from leonardite and used mainly as a soil conditioner.

entries.text: Humic acid stays dissolved in neutral or alkaline water but not in strong acid. It is the fraction of humic substances that dissolves at neutral and alkaline pH but not below pH 2. It is a complex mixture of acids with carboxyl and phenolate groups that behaves as a dibasic acid, giving up two hydrogen ions, or occasionally three. Its number-average molecular weight is below 6000. {{ref:soil-fert-026}} lowers the pH of {{ref:soil-chem-019}} by generating humic acid. Its potassium salt, {{ref:soil-chem-074}}, comes from leonardite.

entries.title: Humate, the humic rock that is mined

definition.text: In economic geology, rock material rich in humic acids, such as weathered coal beds (leonardite), mudrock or pore material in sandstones.

facts.text: Humate has been mined from the Fruitland Formation of New Mexico as a soil amendment since the 1970s, with nearly 60,000 metric tons produced by 2016.
Humate deposits may also play an important role in forming uranium ore bodies.

entries.text: In New Mexico, soil amendment has been dug from the ground since the 1970s. The material is humate, which in economic geology means rock rich in humic acids. Weathered coal beds such as leonardite count, as do mudrock and the material filling pores in sandstone. The Fruitland Formation had produced nearly 60,000 metric tons of humate by 2016. Humate deposits may also play an important part in forming uranium ore bodies.

entries.title: When humic acid meets chlorine in drinking water
entries.article: Humic substance#Determination of humic acids in water samples

definition.text: Humic acid in water meant for drinking or industry, where it affects how well the water can be treated and disinfected.

facts.text: Humic and fulvic acids react with chlorination chemicals to form disinfection byproducts such as dihaloacetonitriles, which are toxic to humans.
Measuring it matters most for supplies drawn from upland peaty catchments in temperate climates.
Because exact measurement is cumbersome, its concentration is usually estimated from total or dissolved organic carbon.

entries.text: Water from peaty uplands brings a chemistry problem to the treatment plant. Humic and fulvic acids react with chlorination chemicals to form disinfection byproducts such as dihaloacetonitriles, which are toxic to humans. So humic acid in water meant for drinking or industry affects how well that water can be treated and disinfected. Measuring it matters most for supplies drawn from upland peaty catchments in temperate climates. Exact measurement is cumbersome, so its concentration is usually estimated from total or dissolved organic carbon.

entries.title: Splitting organic matter three ways with alkali and acid

definition.text: The laboratory separation of natural organic matter into humic acid, fulvic acid and humin by alkaline extraction and acidification.

facts.text: Soil is extracted with 0.1 M NaOH under nitrogen to prevent oxidation; the organic matter left unextracted is humin.
From natural waters, humic and fulvic acids are caught on a resin column after microfiltration and acidification to pH 2; humic acid is then precipitated at pH 1.
The International Humic Substances Society advocates standard methods, and commercial humic acid for soil amendment is made by these procedures.
The definition of humic substances is thus largely operational, rooted in alkaline extraction that goes back to Franz Karl Achard's treatment of peat with potassium hydroxide in 1786.

entries.text: In 1786 Franz Karl Achard treated {{ref:soil-class-070}} with potassium hydroxide, a strong alkali. Chemists still split natural organic material much the same way. Soil is extracted with 0.1 M NaOH under nitrogen to prevent oxidation, and the fraction left behind is {{ref:soil-bio-105}}. From natural waters, the acids are caught on a resin column at pH 2, and humic acid is then precipitated at pH 1. Commercial humic acid is made by these procedures. So humic substances are largely defined by the method used to extract them.
entries.text_plain: In 1786 Franz Karl Achard treated Peat, the half-rotted store of the world's soil carbon with potassium hydroxide, a strong alkali. Chemists still split natural organic material much the same way. Soil is extracted with 0.1 M NaOH under nitrogen to prevent oxidation, and the fraction left behind is Humin, the most stubborn part of soil organic matter. From natural waters, the acids are caught on a resin column at pH 2, and humic acid is then precipitated at pH 1. Commercial humic acid is made by these procedures. So humic substances are largely defined by the method used to extract them.

entries.title: Do humic substances exist, or does the lab make them?

definition.text: The dispute over whether humic substances exist in soil as distinct compounds or are products of the alkaline extraction used to isolate them.

facts.text: Alkaline extraction, used by soil chemists since the 18th century, led to the theory that a 'humification' process creates distinct humic acid, fulvic acid and humin.
Modern analysis of unprocessed mineral soil has not directly observed large humic molecules, which suggests extraction alters the organic matter.
Because humic and fulvic acids are defined by that separation, it is unclear whether the categories reflect the natural state of soil organic matter.
Some researchers argue that alkali extraction misrepresents humic substances because it uses highly alkaline extracts rather than water.
The humification theory persists, even in textbooks, and attempts to redefine humic substances have produced conflicting definitions that hamper communication.

entries.contested_note: Critics hold that humic substances are artefacts of alkaline extraction, while the humification concept persists in the field and in textbooks.
entries.text: Since the 18th century, soil chemists have pulled organic material out of soil with alkali. That alkaline extraction led to a theory: a process called {{ref:soil-bio-090}} creates distinct humic acid, fulvic acid and {{ref:soil-bio-105}}. Critics now ask whether these substances exist in soil at all, or are made by the extraction itself. Modern analysis of unprocessed mineral soil has not directly observed large humic molecules. That suggests extraction alters the material it is meant to reveal. Because humic and fulvic acids are defined by the separation, it is unclear whether the categories reflect the natural state of {{ref:soil-found-045}}. Some researchers argue that the method misrepresents humic substances because it uses highly alkaline extracts rather than water. Yet that theory persists, even in textbooks. Attempts to redefine humic substances have produced conflicting definitions, which hamper communication across the field. The question stays open: the old fractions may describe real soil, or they may be products of the flask.

entries.title: Potassium humate, humic acid in granules

definition.text: The potassium salt of humic acid, made by alkaline extraction of leonardite and used mainly as a soil conditioner.

facts.text: It is extracted in water with potassium hydroxide, sequestering agents and surfactants, using heat to raise humic acid solubility, and dried into granules that can be added to fertilizer.
Well-oxidised lignite (leonardite) is the best source: the less oxidised the coal, the less potassium humate it yields, and low-ash sources give the best quality.
It is used as a fertilizer additive to make nitrogen and phosphorus inputs more efficient.

entries.title: Permanent charge, locked into the clay crystal

definition.text: Negative charge built into a clay's crystal structure where lower-charged atoms replace higher-charged ones; it does not change with pH.

facts.text: Phyllosilicate clays are layered sheets of aluminium and silicon oxides; replacing, for example, Al3+ with Mg2+ leaves the structure with a net negative charge.
This isomorphous substitution happens while the clay forms and does not change with time.
No hydrogen ions are released, so the charge is independent of pH, unlike the variable charges of clay edges and humus.
Kaolinite has almost no isomorphous substitution and so a low CEC, while montmorillonite owes its CEC to magnesium substituting for aluminium.

entries.text: Some of a clay's charge is fixed the moment the clay forms. Permanent charge is negative charge built into a clay's crystal where atoms of lower charge replace atoms of higher charge. In layered clays of aluminum and silicon oxides, Mg2+ taking the place of Al3+ leaves a net negative charge. This isomorphous substitution never changes with time, and it releases no hydrogen ions, so the charge ignores pH. Kaolinite has almost no substitution and a low cation-holding power, while montmorillonite owes its power to magnesium replacing aluminum.

entries.title: Cation exchange: how soil trades nutrients with its water

definition.text: The attraction and release of positively charged ions by negatively charged sites on soil colloids, which swap them with ions in the soil water.

facts.text: It is one case of ion exchange, a reversible swap of like-charged ions between an insoluble solid and the surrounding solution; natural exchangers include zeolites, montmorillonite, clay and soil humus.
Exchange between colloids and soil water buffers soil pH, alters soil structure and cleans percolating water by adsorbing both useful and harmful cations.
Held cations keep a shell of water and form no direct chemical bond with the surface, so the hold is weak and other cations from solution displace them easily.
Cations differ in how strongly they are held: at equal amounts Al3+ replaces H+, which replaces Ca2+, then Mg2+, then K+ and NH4+, then Na+.
A cation added in large amounts, as in potash or lime, can displace the others by sheer numbers, an effect called the law of mass action.
As soil water turns more acidic, hydrogen ions take over exchange sites and push weakly held cations into solution, where plants can use them but they can also be leached.
Roots release H+ by making organic acids, lowering the pH next to the root and freeing cations from colloids for uptake.
Held cations resist being washed downward, which preserves soil fertility in areas of moderate rainfall and low temperatures.

entries.text: Calcium, potassium and ammonium do not simply wash through a good soil. They cling to it, loosely, and trade places with other ions in the soil water. That trading is cation exchange: negatively charged sites on soil colloids attract positively charged ions and swap them with ions in solution. It is one case of ion exchange, a reversible swap of like-charged ions between an insoluble solid and the surrounding solution. Natural exchangers include zeolites, montmorillonite, clay and {{ref:soil-found-045}}. The hold is weak. Held cations keep a shell of water and form no direct chemical bond with the surface, so other cations displace them easily. Some cations win more often than others: at equal amounts Al3+ replaces H+, which replaces Ca2+, then Mg2+, then K+ and NH4+, then Na+. Sheer numbers can also win. A cation added in large amounts, as in potash or lime, crowds out the rest, an effect called the law of mass action. As soil water turns more acidic, hydrogen ions take over exchange sites and push weakly held cations into solution. Plants can then use them, but they can also be leached away. Roots exploit this, making organic acids that release H+ and free cations next to the root. Exchange also buffers soil pH, alters soil structure and cleans percolating water by holding both useful and harmful cations. Because held cations resist washing downward, they preserve fertility where rainfall is moderate and temperatures are low.

entries.title: Cation-exchange capacity, the measure of a soil's nutrient store

definition.text: A measure of how many positively charged ions (cations) a soil can hold on the surfaces of its particles.

facts.text: Negative charges on soil particle surfaces bind cations but let them swap with other cations in the surrounding soil water.
It is the exchangeable positive charge per mass of soil, usually given in cmolc/kg; older texts use the equivalent me/100g or meq/100g.
Because it counts charge, a CEC of 10 cmolc/kg could hold 10 cmol of singly charged Na+ per kilogram of soil but only 5 cmol of doubly charged Ca2+.
Most of it comes from negative charges on clay minerals and soil organic matter, so CEC is usually highest near the surface, where organic matter is richest, and falls with depth.

CEC is used as a measure of soil fertility, showing how well a soil keeps nutrients such as K+, NH4+ and Ca2+ in plant-available form; it also shows its capacity to hold pollutant cations such as Pb2+.
Average CEC at pH 7 for US soils runs from 3.5 cmolc/kg in Ultisols through 18.7 in Mollisols and 35.6 in Vertisols to 128 in Histosols.
A soil's CEC depends on its parent material and the conditions it formed under; the same factors set its pH, which has a major influence on CEC.
Clay and humus are scarce in hot, wet climates because of fast leaching and decomposition, which explains the apparent infertility of tropical soils.

entries.text: A soil's store of calcium, potassium and ammonium has a ceiling, and electric charge sets it. Cation-exchange capacity, or CEC, measures how many positively charged ions a soil can hold on the surfaces of its particles. Negative charges on those surfaces bind the cations but let them swap with others in the surrounding soil water. CEC is the exchangeable positive charge per mass of soil, usually given in centimoles of charge per kilogram, cmolc/kg. Older texts use the equivalent me/100g or meq/100g. Because it counts charge, a CEC of 10 cmolc/kg could hold 10 cmol of singly charged Na+ per kilogram. It could hold only 5 cmol of doubly charged Ca2+. Most of the charge sits on clay minerals and {{ref:soil-found-045}}. So CEC is usually highest near the surface, where it is richest, and falls with depth. Soils differ enormously. Measured at pH 7, average CEC in US soils runs from 3.5 cmolc/kg in {{ref:soil-class-104}} through 18.7 in {{ref:soil-class-101}} and 35.6 in {{ref:soil-class-106}} to 128 in {{ref:soil-class-098}}. Parent material and the conditions of formation set a soil's CEC. The same factors set its pH, which has a major influence on CEC in turn. Hot, wet climates leach and decompose fast, leaving little clay or organic matter, which explains the apparent infertility of tropical soils. CEC therefore serves as a measure of fertility. It shows how well a soil keeps nutrients such as K+, NH4+ and Ca2+ within reach of plants. It also shows how much of a pollutant cation such as Pb2+ the soil can hold.

entries.title: Anion-exchange capacity, the smaller store for nitrate and phosphate

definition.text: A soil's ability to hold negatively charged ions, such as nitrate and phosphate, on positively charged surfaces and release them later by exchange.

facts.text: Kaolinite, allophane and iron and aluminium oxides often carry positive surface charges; amorphous and sesquioxide clays have the highest AEC, followed by iron oxides.
In most soils CEC far exceeds AEC, but the reverse can happen in highly weathered soils such as ferralsols (oxisols).
Anions are held with strength in the order H2PO4−, SO42−, NO3−, Cl−, and phosphates tend to stay on exchange sites.
Exchangeable anions amount to tenths to a few milliequivalents per 100 g of dry soil.
AEC falls as pH rises, because the extra hydroxyls displace anions from colloids into solution.
Colloids with low cation exchange capacity tend to have some anion exchange capacity; amorphous and sesquioxide clays have the most, followed by iron oxides.
Iron and aluminium hydroxide clays can swap their hydroxide anions for other anions, and phosphates tend to be held at anion exchange sites.
Anions are held with decreasing strength in the order phosphate (H2PO4−), sulfate, nitrate, chloride.

entries.text: In most soils, cation-exchange capacity far exceeds its mirror image. Anion-exchange capacity, or AEC, is a soil's ability to hold negatively charged ions, such as nitrate and phosphate, on positively charged surfaces and release them later by exchange. Kaolinite, allophane and iron and aluminum oxides often carry positive surface charges. Amorphous and sesquioxide clays have the highest AEC, followed by iron oxides, and colloids with low CEC tend to have some AEC. Iron and aluminum hydroxide clays can swap their own hydroxide anions for other anions. Anions are held with decreasing strength from phosphate (H2PO4−) to sulfate, nitrate and chloride, so phosphates tend to stay on exchange sites. Exchangeable anions amount to tenths to a few milliequivalents per 100 g of dry soil. In highly weathered soils such as ferralsols, or {{ref:soil-class-103}}, AEC can exceed CEC. AEC falls as pH rises, because the extra hydroxyls push anions off colloids into solution.

entries.title: Base saturation: how much of the exchange holds nutrients

definition.text: The percentage of a soil's cation-exchange capacity occupied by the base cations Ca2+, Mg2+, K+ and Na+.

facts.text: They are called base cations because they are non-acidic, not because they are bases in the usual chemical sense; hydronium, aluminium and iron are the acid-forming cations.
A soil with a CEC of 20 meq, 5 meq of it aluminium and hydronium, has a base saturation of 15 ÷ 20 × 100% = 75%.
It indexes how weathered a soil is and how available its exchangeable cation nutrients are to plants.
Base saturation rises almost in direct proportion to pH.
It is used to work out the lime requirement, which must count the acid cations held on colloids (exchangeable acidity), not only those in the soil water.
Soil classes turn on it: Alfisols have at least 35% base saturation, the more leached Ultisols less than 35%, and Mollisols more than 50%.

verification.evidence: For example, Mollisols are required to have 50 percent or more base saturation within specified depths.

entries.text: Take a soil with a CEC of 20 meq, 5 meq of it held by aluminum and hydronium. Its base saturation is 15 ÷ 20 × 100% = 75%. Base saturation is the percentage of the CEC occupied by the base cations Ca2+, Mg2+, K+ and Na+. They are called base cations because they are non-acidic, not because they are bases in the usual chemical sense. Hydronium, the hydrogen ion in water, together with aluminum and iron, makes up the acid-forming cations. Base saturation rises almost in direct proportion to pH. It indexes how weathered a soil is and how available its exchangeable cation nutrients are to plants. It also helps work out how much lime a soil needs. That sum must count the acid cations held on colloids, called exchangeable acidity, not only those in the soil water. Soil classes turn on it. {{ref:soil-class-090}} have at least 35% base saturation, the more leached {{ref:soil-class-104}} less than 35%, and {{ref:soil-class-101}} more than 50%.

entries.title: The diffuse double layer, a cloud of ions around every clay

definition.text: Two parallel layers of charge around a particle in a fluid: the surface charge itself and a loosely held diffuse layer of attracted ions that screens it.

facts.text: Exchangeable cations sit in the diffuse layer, held by electric attraction but kept moving by thermal motion, rather than bonding to the surface.
Double layers matter most where surface area is large relative to volume, as in colloids; clay platelets are always surrounded by one.
The layer thins as the electrolyte concentration rises, so adding salt to a suspension shrinks it and destabilises the colloid.
In alkali soils, abundant Na+ crowds into the double layer of clay particles and displaces Ca2+, raising the exchangeable sodium percentage.

entries.text: Clay platelets are never bare in soil water. Each is wrapped in a diffuse double layer: two parallel layers of charge, the surface charge itself and a loosely held layer of attracted ions that screens it. Exchangeable cations sit in that outer layer, held by electric attraction but kept moving by thermal motion rather than bonded to the surface. Double layers matter most where surface area is large relative to volume, as in colloids. Adding salt thins the layer and destabilizes the colloid. In {{ref:soil-chem-019}}, abundant Na+ crowds into the double layer of clay particles and displaces Ca2+, raising the {{ref:soil-chem-018}}.

entries.title: The base-cation saturation ratio and its 'ideal' soil

definition.text: A way of interpreting soil tests that balances soil cations to 'ideal' ratios, either between cations such as calcium and magnesium or as shares of the CEC.

facts.text: It contrasts with the sufficiency level of available nutrients (SLAN) used by most university laboratories, which only keeps each plant-available nutrient between deficiency and excess.
William Albrecht, working in Missouri from the late 1930s, set the ideal balance at H 10%, Ca 60 to 75%, Mg 10 to 20%, K 2 to 5%, Na 0.5 to 5.0% and other cations 5%.
F.E. Bear's 1945 bulletin with Prince and Malcolm proposed 65% Ca, 10% Mg, 5% K and 20% H; Neal Kinsey's later book with Charles Walters became the most influential BCSR work.
Reviews in 1916 and 1933 found no evidence that the Ca:Mg ratio affects growth, and later trials saw no yield difference across ratios so long as calcium dominated.
Much of the evidence for BCSR is explained by pH: Albrecht did not control it, and liming frees molybdenum, which legumes need to form root nodules.
A 3-year SARE trial found BCSR fertiliser cost $9.27 per acre more each year with no higher yield.
On low-CEC soils the method can leave crops short of a nutrient, because it sets ratios but no minimum amounts.

entries.contested_note: Supporters claim balanced cation ratios improve crop quality, livestock health and soil biology, while controlled studies find no benefit beyond what pH and deficiency correction explain.

Most university laboratories instead simply keep each nutrient between deficiency and excess. Supporters say balanced ratios improve crops, livestock and soil life, but controlled studies disagree. Trials saw no yield difference across ratios so long as calcium dominated. Albrecht did not control pH, and much of his evidence is explained by it. A 3-year SARE trial found BCSR fertilizer cost $9.27 per acre more each year with no higher yield.

entries.title: Measuring CEC by flooding the soil with one cation

definition.text: Finding a soil's CEC by displacing all its bound cations with a concentrated solution of another cation, then measuring the displaced cations or the added cation retained.

facts.text: Barium (Ba2+) and ammonium (NH4+) are frequently used as exchanger cations, though many other methods exist.
Because CEC depends on pH it is often measured in a buffer at a set pH; this potential CEC misstates the real value when the buffer's pH differs from the soil's.
Effective CEC, measured at the soil's own pH, is closer to the real value but makes comparing soils harder.
Applications of CaCO3 and CaSO4 can lead to an overestimate of CEC.

This potential CEC misstates the real value when the buffer's pH differs from the soil's. Effective CEC, measured at the soil's own pH, is closer to the real value but makes soils harder to compare. Applications of CaCO3 and CaSO4 can lead to an overestimate.

entries.title: Base-rich and base-poor ground

definition.text: The level of chemical bases, such as calcium, potassium or magnesium ions, in soil or water.

facts.text: Bases neutralise acids, so base-rich places are neutral or alkaline (pH>7), while acid ones are dominated by organic acids or by aluminium and hydrogen ions.
Ground over limestone and maritime settings is base-rich; ground over sandstone or granite, or fed directly by rainfall (ombrotrophic), is base-poor.
A higher CEC lets a soil hold more base cations, while sandy or low-organic soils have a lower CEC and leach more nutrients.
Base-richness shows no correlation with the availability of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.

entries.text: Ground over limestone is base-rich, and ground over granite is base-poor. Base-richness is the level of chemical bases, such as calcium, potassium or magnesium ions, in soil or water. A higher CEC lets a soil hold more base cations. Yet base-richness shows no correlation with available nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.

entries.title: Two ways to estimate a soil's CEC

facts.text: The sum-of-cations method adds up all the exchangeable cation quantities listed in a soil analysis to give the CEC.

The mineralogy method approximates CEC from the type and amount of each clay mineral; the manual uses 10 cmolc/kg for kaolinite, 100 for montmorillonite/smectite and 150 for vermiculite, though real colloids vary.
A soil with 10% kaolinite clay contributes 10 cmolc/kg clay times 10 kg clay per 100 kg soil, or 1.0 cmolc per kg of soil.

Colloids, below 0.002 mm, are called the active fraction because their charged surfaces are highly reactive; their small size gives large surface area per unit weight and their ionic structure a net charge.

definition.text: CEC can be estimated either by summing the exchangeable cations in a soil analysis or by weighting typical CEC values of the clay minerals present.

sources.title: 7.1: Introduction - Geosciences LibreTexts (Introduction to Soil Science Laboratory Manual (Schwyter and Vaughan))

Their small size gives large surface area per unit weight, and their ionic structure gives a net charge. See {{ref:soil-chem-046}} and {{ref:soil-chem-081}}.

entries.title: Thomas Way and the discovery of cation exchange

definition.text: The 19th-century finding, by Thomas Way and John Bennet Lawes at Rothamsted Experimental Station, that soils exchange cations.

facts.text: J. Thomas Way, consulting chemist to the Royal Agricultural Society in England, ran many experiments on how soils exchange ions and is considered the father of soil chemistry.
William Albrecht is sometimes credited with the discovery, but he may only have been the first to link cation exchange with colloidal clay particles.

entries.text: The finding that soils swap cations came from Rothamsted Experimental Station in the 19th century. William Albrecht is sometimes credited with the discovery. He may only have been the first to link cation exchange with colloidal clay particles.
