entries.title: Ionic strength: why a doubly charged ion counts fourfold

definition.text: A measure of the concentration of ions in a solution, weighted by their charge.

facts.text: Molar ionic strength is I = ½ Σ ci zi², summed over every ion, where c is molar concentration and z the ion's charge number.
For NaCl the ionic strength equals the concentration, but MgSO4, with doubly charged ions, gives four times as much; multivalent ions contribute strongly.
It can be molar or molal, so units should be stated; molality is preferred for non-ideal solutions.
Total electrolyte concentration affects dissociation constants and the solubility of salts.
The Debye length, which characterizes double-layer thickness, is inversely proportional to the square root of ionic strength; more or higher-valence counterions compress the double layer.
It plays a central role in Debye–Hückel theory of non-ideal ionic solutions.
Lewis and Randall introduced the concept in 1921 when describing activity coefficients of strong electrolytes.

entries.text: Dissolve magnesium sulfate in water and it counts for four times as much as the same concentration of table salt. The yardstick is ionic strength, a measure of the ions in a solution weighted by their charge. In molar form it is I = ½ Σ ci zi², summed over every ion, where c is molar concentration and z the ion's charge number. Squaring the charge makes multivalent ions weigh heavily: for NaCl the ionic strength equals the concentration, while MgSO4 gives four times as much. It can be molar or molal, so units should be stated, and molality is preferred for non-ideal solutions. In {{ref:soil-found-079}}, total electrolyte concentration shifts dissociation constants and the solubility of salts. It also sets the Debye length, the thickness scale of the charged double layer around a surface. That length is inversely proportional to the square root of ionic strength, so more or higher-valence counterions compress the layer. Lewis and Randall introduced the concept in 1921, while describing how strong electrolytes depart from ideal behavior.

entries.title: Activity coefficients: correcting for crowded ions

definition.text: A factor that corrects a substance's concentration for how far a mixture departs from ideal behaviour.

facts.text: Activity equals the activity coefficient times concentration; in an ideal electrolyte solution all coefficients equal one, which only very dilute solutions approach.
Activity coefficients matter especially in soil chemistry, where small volumes of water hold high concentrations of electrolytes.
Coefficients change with concentration because ions interact more as the electrolyte becomes more concentrated.
Cation and anion coefficients cannot be measured separately, so a mean activity coefficient, γ±, is used.
pH is defined from hydrogen ion activity, a definition IUPAC calls only notional because single-ion activities cannot be measured.
They can be calculated with the Debye–Hückel equation or extensions such as the Davies and Pitzer equations, or specific ion interaction theory.
For uncharged species such as dissolved CO2 the coefficient follows a salting-out model, log10 γ = bI, with b for CO2 0.11 at 10 °C.

entries.text: Soil water is crowded. Small volumes of it hold high concentrations of electrolytes, which is why activity coefficients matter so much in soil chemistry. An activity coefficient is a factor that corrects a substance's concentration for how far a mixture departs from ideal behavior. Activity equals the coefficient times concentration. In an ideal electrolyte solution every coefficient equals one, a state only very dilute solutions approach. As concentration rises, ions interact more and the coefficients change. Cation and anion values cannot be measured separately, so chemists use a mean activity coefficient, γ±. Even pH rests on this limit: it is defined from hydrogen ion activity, a definition IUPAC calls only notional. Coefficients come from the Debye–Hückel equation or its extensions, the Davies and Pitzer equations, or from specific ion interaction theory. Uncharged species such as dissolved CO2 follow a salting-out model, log10 γ = bI, with b for CO2 0.11 at 10 °C.

entries.title: Debye and Hückel explain why salt water misbehaves

definition.text: A theory by Peter Debye and Erich Hückel explaining why electrolyte solutions depart from ideal behaviour.

facts.text: A linearized Poisson–Boltzmann model, it predicts mean ionic activity coefficients accurately in dilute solution and underlies modern treatments.
Non-ideality arises mainly because unlike ions attract and like ions repel, so ions are not randomly distributed.
Each ion is pictured surrounded by a statistically averaged cloud of net opposite charge.
It assumes complete dissociation, spherical unpolarized ions and a solvent acting only as a medium of constant permittivity.
Its limiting law makes the logarithm of the mean activity coefficient proportional to the square root of ionic strength.
It fits measurements below about 10⁻³ mol/L, deviating at higher concentrations and with more highly charged ions.
The extended equation is accurate up to ionic strength 0.1; beyond that the Pitzer equations should be used.
Debye and Hückel published it in 1923 in Physikalische Zeitschrift.

entries.text: Unlike charges attract and like charges repel, and in a salt solution that simple rule spoils the arithmetic. Ions are not scattered at random, so the solution departs from ideal behavior. Debye–Hückel theory, published by Peter Debye and Erich Hückel in 1923 in Physikalische Zeitschrift, explains why. It pictures each ion surrounded by a statistically averaged cloud of net opposite charge. It assumes complete dissociation, spherical unpolarized ions and a solvent that acts only as a medium of constant permittivity. The result, a linearized Poisson–Boltzmann model, predicts mean ionic activity coefficients accurately in dilute solution. Its limiting law makes the logarithm of the mean activity coefficient proportional to the square root of {{ref:soil-chem-202}}. That law fits measurements below about 10⁻³ mol/L but drifts at higher concentrations and with more highly charged ions. The extended equation holds up to ionic strength 0.1; beyond that, the Pitzer equations should be used. The theory still underlies modern treatments.

entries.title: Inner sphere complexes: ions that bond straight to minerals

definition.text: A surface complex in which an ion binds directly to a mineral surface with no water molecules between them.

facts.text: Only ions with a high affinity for surface sites form them, including specifically adsorbed ions that bond covalently.
In outer sphere complexes water separates the ion from the surface; in inner sphere ones surface hydroxyl groups act as σ-donor ligands.
On oxide surfaces the metal ion acts as a Lewis acid and the ligand as a Lewis base; sorption of protonated ligands depends on pH.
They govern the transport and retention of trace elements in soil, where natural sorbents are often metal oxides.
Oxyanions such as sulfate can hinder the dissolution of iron and manganese oxides, slowing or preventing reductive dissolution.
Alkaline earth metals sorb less as their ion size increases, so they become more mobile during weathering.
In birnessite, cations such as Ca, Cu, Zn, Pb and Cd form inner-sphere complexes above and below vacancies in the oxide layers.
Through these interactions soil properties influence how nutrients and pollutants are retained or depleted.

entries.text: Some ions hover near a mineral surface; others grab it. In an inner sphere complex, an ion binds directly to the surface with no water molecules between them. In an outer sphere complex, water keeps the two apart. Only ions with a high affinity for surface sites form the inner kind, including specifically adsorbed ions that bond covalently. Surface hydroxyl groups act as electron-donating ligands. On oxide surfaces the metal ion is a Lewis acid, an electron-pair acceptor, and the ligand a Lewis base, an electron-pair donor. Sorption of protonated ligands therefore depends on pH. These complexes govern how {{ref:soil-fert-290}} move or stay put in soil, where natural sorbents are often metal oxides. Sulfate held this way can slow or prevent the dissolution of iron and manganese oxides. Alkaline earth metals sorb less as their ions get larger, so they grow more mobile during weathering. Through such bonds, soil properties decide whether nutrients and pollutants are retained or lost.

entries.title: Langmuir's model: one molecule per parking space

definition.text: A model of adsorption on a surface of identical sites, each holding at most one adsorbate molecule, with adsorption and desorption reversible.

facts.text: Binding is treated as a reaction between an adsorbate molecule and an empty site, with an equilibrium constant.
The isotherm is θ = K p / (1 + K p), where θ is the fraction of sites occupied.
At low pressure θ is about Kp; at high pressure θ approaches 1.
It assumes a flat homogeneous surface, immobile adsorbate, equal adsorption energy at every site, monolayer coverage and no interactions between adsorbed molecules.
It deviates in many cases because it ignores surface roughness, with its several site types, and interactions between adsorbates.
Its competitive form lets two species compete for the same sites, each site holding one or the other.
It nonetheless remains the first choice for most adsorption models.
Irving Langmuir presented it in 1916 and won the 1932 Nobel Prize for his surface chemistry.

conflicts.text: Irving Langmuir derived the first scientifically based adsorption isotherm in 1918.
conflicts.note: The Langmuir adsorption model page gives 1916 (S:404a89926886).

entries.text: Irving Langmuir won the 1932 Nobel Prize for his surface chemistry, and one idea from it still opens most adsorption studies. The Langmuir adsorption model pictures a surface of identical sites, each holding at most one molecule, with adsorption and its reverse, {{ref:soil-chem-147}}, both possible. Each binding is a reaction between a molecule and an empty site, with an equilibrium constant K. The fraction of occupied sites is θ = K p / (1 + K p). At low pressure θ is about Kp; at high pressure θ approaches 1 as the single layer fills. The model assumes a flat, uniform surface, immobile molecules, equal energy at every site and no interaction between neighbors. Real surfaces are rough, with several site types, and adsorbed molecules do interact, so it often deviates. A competitive form lets two species vie for the same sites. Langmuir presented it in 1916, and it remains the first choice for most adsorption models.

entries.title: Partition coefficients: how a compound splits between liquids

definition.text: The ratio of a compound's concentrations in two immiscible phases at equilibrium.

facts.text: Strictly, the partition coefficient covers only the un-ionized form, while the distribution coefficient covers all forms of the compound.
With water and a hydrophobic solvent such as octanol, it measures how hydrophilic or hydrophobic a substance is.
Hydrogeologists use the octanol–water coefficient Kow to predict how dissolved hydrophobic organic compounds migrate in soil and groundwater.
Partition coefficients can also be defined when one or both phases are solid.

entries.text: Shake a compound with water and octanol, and it divides itself between the two layers. The partition coefficient is the ratio of its concentrations in two immiscible phases at equilibrium. With water and octanol, it measures how water-loving or water-shunning a substance is. Hydrogeologists use this octanol–water coefficient, Kow, to predict how dissolved hydrophobic organic compounds migrate in soil and groundwater. Strictly it covers only the un-ionized form, while the distribution coefficient covers all forms. One or both phases can even be solid.

entries.title: Coprecipitation: solids that drag dissolved metals down

definition.text: The carrying down by a precipitate of substances that would normally stay dissolved under the same conditions.

facts.text: It works by inclusion in the crystal lattice, occlusion of adsorbed impurities trapped as the crystal grows, or adsorption onto the precipitate's surface.
Trace elements too dilute to precipitate alone are coprecipitated with a carrier of similar crystal structure.
It matters in acid mine drainage, radionuclide migration around waste repositories, heavy metal transport and wastewater treatment.
Constructed wetlands remove phosphorus by coprecipitation with iron, aluminium and calcium compounds, and iron coagulants remove arsenic from water the same way.

entries.text: A forming precipitate can carry down substances that would otherwise stay dissolved. That is coprecipitation. The captured material may sit inside the crystal lattice, be sealed in as the crystal grows, or cling to the precipitate's surface. {{ref:soil-fert-290}} too dilute to precipitate alone ride down with a carrier of similar crystal structure. The process matters in {{ref:soil-bio-059}}, in heavy metal transport, wastewater treatment and radionuclide migration around waste repositories. Wetlands built for treatment, the subject of {{ref:soil-water-260}}, remove phosphorus by coprecipitation with iron, aluminum and calcium compounds, and iron coagulants strip arsenic from water the same way.

entries.title: The Freundlich equation, a rule fitted to rough surfaces

definition.text: An empirical adsorption isotherm relating the amount adsorbed on a solid to the gas pressure or solute concentration.

facts.text: It is written x/m = K c^(1/n), where x/m is adsorbate mass per adsorbent mass and K and n are constants for a given pair at a given temperature.
In log form, log x/m = log K + (1/n) log c, a straight line.
Freundlich fitted it to adsorption of organic acids on coal from water.
Being empirical, it should give way to theoretically based isotherms such as Langmuir or BET when those fit.
It can also be derived from surface heterogeneity: high-energy sites fill first, then low-energy ones, so the heat of adsorption weakens with coverage.
A good fit makes a heterogeneous surface only likely, not proved; calorimetry can confirm it.
It fails at high pressure, where adsorption saturates.

conflicts.text: The first mathematical fit to an isotherm was published by Freundlich and Kuster in 1906.
conflicts.note: The Freundlich equation page dates Freundlich's expression to 1909 (S:c82536c45321) and his numerical work to 1907 (S:93f36f1632fc).

entries.text: Freundlich fitted his equation to organic acids adsorbing on coal from water, and it outlived that modest start. The Freundlich equation, dating from 1909, is an empirical adsorption isotherm. It links the amount adsorbed on a solid to the gas pressure or solute concentration. It reads x/m = K c^(1/n), where x/m is adsorbate mass per adsorbent mass and K and n are constants for a given pair at a given temperature. In log form, log x/m = log K + (1/n) log c, it becomes a straight line. It can also be derived from an uneven surface: high-energy sites fill first, then weaker ones, so the heat of adsorption falls as coverage grows. A good fit makes such a surface likely, not proved; calorimetry can confirm it. The equation fails at high pressure, where adsorption saturates. Being empirical, it should give way to theory-based isotherms such as Langmuir's or BET when those fit.

entries.title: X-ray absorption fine structure reveals an atom's neighbors

definition.text: Detailed structure in X-ray absorption spectra whose analysis reveals an atom's local structure and unoccupied electronic states.

facts.text: Spectra divide into the edge region, the XANES region spanning 50–100 eV around the threshold, and the EXAFS region; XAFS denotes XANES plus EXAFS.
EXAFS, from single scattering of the photoelectron by neighbouring atoms, gives local structure; XANES multiple-scattering peaks give its geometry.
Surface EXAFS reveals the coordination structure and chemical state of adsorbates.
XANES and EXAFS, with X-ray diffraction, are used to evaluate how microbes sorb and mineralize radionuclides in bioremediation.

entries.text: An X-ray absorption spectrum carries fine detail that maps the surroundings of a single kind of atom. This X-ray absorption fine structure divides into the edge, the XANES region spanning 50–100 eV around the threshold, and the EXAFS region; XAFS means the two together. EXAFS arises as the ejected photoelectron scatters once off neighboring atoms, giving local structure. Multiple-scattering peaks in XANES give its geometry. Surface EXAFS reveals the coordination and chemical state of adsorbed ions. With X-ray diffraction, both methods show how microbes sorb and mineralize radionuclides when they are used to clean up contamination, as in {{ref:soil-env-023}}.

entries.title: Chemical speciation: naming every form an element takes

definition.text: A calculation of the concentrations of all the chemical species present in a solution.

facts.text: Geochemical equilibrium models predict species distributions from measurements of bulk solution composition.
Such models are used to work out the ion speciation of plant nutrients in soil and of regulated metals in stored wastes.
Trace metals form complexes with hydroxide, carbonate and chloride, and their speciation changes between oxidized and reduced conditions.
Element toxicity varies with oxidation state, so food regulations require speciation of some elements.

entries.text: Knowing how much of a metal a solution holds says little about what form it takes. Chemical speciation is the calculation of the concentrations of all the chemical species present. Geochemical equilibrium models predict them from measurements of bulk solution composition, for plant nutrients in soil and for regulated metals in stored wastes. Trace metals form complexes with hydroxide, carbonate and chloride, and their speciation changes between oxidized and reduced conditions. An element's toxicity also depends on how oxidized it is, so food regulations require speciation of some elements.

entries.title: Geochemical models, from hand sums to reactive transport

definition.text: Using chemical thermodynamics, kinetics or both, usually by computer, to analyse the chemical reactions in geological systems, including low-temperature aqueous solutions near the Earth's surface.

facts.text: Models are built to understand natural water composition, contaminant mobility in groundwater and the ion speciation of plant nutrients in soil.
Garrels and Thompson first applied it in 1962, by hand, as an equilibrium model predicting species distributions, mineral saturation states and gas fugacities from bulk solution composition.
Coupling mass transfer to an equilibrium model gives a reaction path model; Helgeson's 1968 program first solved these, modelling processes such as weathering.
A model starts from a basis of aqueous species, minerals and gases, as many as the system's components, then solves mass action and mass balance equations for equilibrium.
A mineral's saturation index (log Q/K) is zero at equilibrium, positive when supersaturated and likely to precipitate, and negative when it tends to dissolve.
Reactions simulated include acid–base, aqueous complexation, dissolution and precipitation, redox, and sorption, ion exchange and surface complexation.
Coupling with hydrologic transport models gives reactive transport models of reactions along a flowpath.
Differences between thermodynamic databases can cause large uncertainties, which are seldom considered.

entries.text: In 1962 Garrels and Thompson built a geochemical model by hand. From a solution's bulk composition, they predicted its species, its saturation with each mineral and the fugacities of its gases. Geochemical modeling now does this mostly by computer, using thermodynamics, kinetics or both to analyze reactions in geological systems, including low-temperature waters near Earth's surface. A model starts from a basis of aqueous species, minerals and gases, as many as the system has components. It then solves mass action and mass balance equations for equilibrium. A mineral's saturation index, log Q/K, is zero at equilibrium, positive when the mineral is likely to precipitate and negative when it tends to dissolve. Helgeson's 1968 program added mass transfer, creating reaction path models of processes such as weathering. Linking to water-flow models gives reactive transport along a flowpath. Uses run from {{ref:soil-chem-211}} of plant nutrients to contaminant mobility in groundwater. One weakness is seldom considered: thermodynamic databases differ, causing large uncertainties.

entries.title: Redox: the electron trade behind rust and breath

definition.text: A chemical reaction in which the oxidation states of the reactants change; short for reduction–oxidation.

facts.text: Oxidation is a loss of electrons, or a rise in oxidation state; reduction is a gain of electrons, or a fall in oxidation state.
The two always happen together and cannot occur independently.
When iron rusts, the iron is oxidized to an oxide while oxygen is reduced by taking up the released electrons.
Respiration, photosynthesis, combustion and the corrosion of metals all run on redox chemistry.
In soils, sediments and water, redox gradients drive the biogeochemical cycling of elements.
Oxidation first meant reacting with oxygen, and reduction the weight lost when ore is heated to extract metal; both were later generalized to electron transfer.
The word redox first appeared in a 1928 article by Leonor Michaelis and Louis B. Flexner.

entries.text: A rusting nail and a breathing animal run the same kind of chemistry. Redox, short for reduction–oxidation, is any reaction in which the reactants' electron bookkeeping, set out in {{ref:soil-chem-178}}, changes. Oxidation is a loss of electrons, or a rise in that bookkeeping number. Reduction is a gain of electrons, or a fall in it. The two always happen together. Neither can occur on its own. When iron rusts, the iron is oxidized to an oxide, while oxygen is reduced by taking up the electrons the iron releases. The same trade powers respiration, {{ref:soil-hist-147}}, combustion and the corrosion of metals. The words are older than the idea of the electron. Oxidation first meant reacting with oxygen. Reduction meant the weight lost when ore is heated to extract its metal. Both were later widened to mean electron transfer. The word redox itself first appeared in a 1928 article by Leonor Michaelis and Louis B. Flexner. In soils, sediments and water, redox differs from place to place. Those differences drive the cycling of elements through living things and their surroundings, as {{ref:soil-chem-121}} shows.

entries.title: Electrons and protons, the two currencies of soil chemistry

definition.text: The electron-transfer reactions that underlie many soil processes and properties.

facts.text: Redox potential, expressed as Eh or as pe (the negative log of electron activity, like pH), is a master variable that, with pH, both controls and reflects soil reactions.
Soil chemical reactions involve some combination of proton and electron transfer.
Early theory grew out of flooded soils and paddy rice and shaped later work on redox thermodynamics and root growth.
Later work extended it to heavy metals, soil formation and morphology, organic compounds, wetland delineation, remediation and ways to characterize soil redox status.
Redox acts on soil development, and redoximorphic colour features give critical information for interpreting soils.
Soil microbes organize along electron transport chains, forming electrically conductive biofilms and networks of bacterial nanowires.
Understanding soil redox gradients matters for carbon sequestration, bioremediation, wetland delineation and soil-based microbial fuel cells.

entries.title: Redoximorphic features: colors that record wet and dry

definition.text: Colour patterns in soil from the loss or gain of pigment against the matrix colour, formed by oxidation and reduction of iron or manganese and their movement, or a matrix colour set by ferrous iron.

facts.text: A colour pattern counts as redoximorphic only once the processes that formed it are known or inferred.
Reducing conditions give disrupted colour with complex mottled patterns and points of colour concentration, whereas aerobic conditions give uniform or gradual changes.
As a wet soil dries and oxygen returns, reduced iron can re-oxidize locally into bright yellow-brown mottles.
They provide critical information for soil interpretation.
Classification uses them: Vertisols with aquic conditions and redoximorphic features are Aquerts, and the WRB suffix σ marks permanent saturation without them.
Eh, the voltage measured in a soil, expresses the potential for redoximorphic reactions to occur.
Fluctuating water levels cause alternating oxidation and reduction, producing mottling of red and yellow blotches mixed with gray.
Continuous strong reduction from long-term waterlogging gives gleyed conditions with dark gray to blue to black colors.

entries.title: Breathing and photosynthesis as electron transfers

definition.text: The redox reactions on which many essential life processes run, above all respiration and photosynthesis.

facts.text: Aerobic respiration oxidizes substrates such as glucose and reduces oxygen to water.
Photosynthesis reduces carbon dioxide to sugars and oxidizes water to oxygen; it complements respiration but is not simply its reverse.
Living things often store and release energy through redox reactions, relying on the cycling of NAD+ and NADH.

entries.title: Oxidizing agents, the electron takers

definition.text: A substance that oxidizes another by taking its electrons, and is itself reduced; also called an oxidant or electron acceptor.

facts.text: Oxidants usually contain elements in high oxidation states, such as permanganate, or are highly electronegative elements such as oxygen and chlorine.
Oxygen is the electron acceptor with the highest redox potential.
In oxidizing soils, oxygen accepts electrons and is reduced to water.

entries.title: Destroying pollution underground with strong oxidizers

definition.text: A remediation technique that injects strong chemical oxidizers into contaminated soil or groundwater to destroy contaminants where they lie.

facts.text: It treats many organic compounds, including some that resist natural breakdown, and works well on chlorinated solvents and gasoline compounds such as benzene and toluene.
Hydrogen peroxide was first used in 1985, on a formaldehyde spill in Springfield, Massachusetts.
Oxidants are delivered through direct-push rods or injection wells, or by soil mixing and hydraulic fracturing where permeability is low.
Success depends on site lithology, oxidant dose and residence time, competing oxidizable material and contact with the contaminant; rising carbon dioxide signals oxidation.
All the main oxidants are strong and pose serious hazards to the people handling them.

entries.text: In situ chemical oxidation injects strong oxidizers into contaminated soil or groundwater to destroy contaminants where they lie. Oxidants go in through rods or injection wells, or by soil mixing and hydraulic fracturing in tight ground. Success depends on the site's rocks, the dose, and real contact with the contaminant. Rising carbon dioxide signals that oxidation is working. Every main oxidant is hazardous to handle.

entries.title: Biofilters: letting microbes eat the pollution

definition.text: A pollution control technique in which a bioreactor holding living material captures pollutants and breaks them down biologically.

facts.text: Uses include treating wastewater, catching harmful chemicals or silt from surface runoff, and microbial oxidation of air pollutants.
Microorganisms attach to a bed of media such as sand, crushed rock or gravel and grow into a biofilm that degrades the pollutants.
Biofiltration was first introduced in England in 1893 as a trickling filter for wastewater.
Bioswales, constructed and natural wetlands and riparian zones work as biofilters; buildup of biomass can clog the media.

entries.text: Engineers have hired microbes to clean water since 1893, when England introduced the trickling filter for wastewater. A biofilter is a bioreactor holding living material that captures pollutants and breaks them down biologically. Microorganisms attach to a bed of sand, crushed rock or gravel and grow into a thin living film that degrades the pollutants. Biofilters treat wastewater, catch harmful chemicals or silt washed off the land, and oxidize air pollutants. {{ref:soil-water-092}}, wetlands and {{ref:soil-water-263}} work the same way. One drawback: buildup of biomass can clog the bed.

entries.title: Electron acceptors, the last stop for every electron

definition.text: A chemical species that takes up electrons transferred to it from another compound, and so acts as an oxidizing agent.

facts.text: Its electron-accepting power is measured by its redox potential.
In biology the terminal electron acceptor is the last compound to receive an electron in an electron transport chain, such as oxygen in aerobic respiration.
All organisms get energy by moving electrons from a donor to an acceptor, but the terminal acceptors they use vary widely.
The herbicide paraquat is toxic because it acts as a potent electron acceptor, taking electrons from photosynthesis and passing them to oxygen to form reactive oxygen species.

entries.text: All organisms get energy by moving electrons from a donor to an acceptor. An electron acceptor is a chemical species that takes up electrons transferred from another compound, so it is an oxidizing agent, described in {{ref:soil-chem-114}}. Its pull is measured by its redox potential. In biology, the terminal electron acceptor receives the last electron in a transport chain, such as oxygen in aerobic respiration, though organisms use many kinds. The weedkiller paraquat is a potent acceptor: it takes electrons from {{ref:soil-hist-147}} and passes them to oxygen, forming toxic reactive oxygen species.

entries.title: Oxidation states: bookkeeping for electrons

definition.text: The hypothetical charge an atom would carry if all its bonds were fully ionic, describing how far it has been oxidized.

facts.text: A rise in oxidation state is oxidation and a fall is reduction; the two always occur in pairs in redox reactions.
Pure elements have an oxidation state of zero, and oxidation numbers in a neutral molecule sum to zero.
Stock nomenclature writes it as a Roman numeral after the element, as in iron(III) oxide.
It can be an average fraction, such as 8/3 for iron in magnetite, Fe3O4.

entries.title: Reducing agents, the electron givers

definition.text: A substance that reduces another by giving it electrons, and is itself oxidized; also called a reductant or electron donor.

facts.text: Electropositive metals such as lithium, sodium, magnesium, iron, zinc and aluminium donate electrons readily and are good reducing agents.
A reducing equivalent is whatever transfers the equivalent of one electron, an electron or a hydrogen atom; the term is common in biochemistry.
Underground electron donors include organic matter, hydrogen, methane, reduced sulfur and iron compounds, and ammonium.
Organic matter is the main source of electrons in soil.

entries.title: Redox couples: splitting a reaction into halves

definition.text: A redox couple is a reducing species and its oxidized form, such as Fe2+/Fe3+; the oxidation and the reduction taken alone are each a half-reaction.

facts.text: In a redox reaction the reductant passes electrons to the oxidant, so the reductant is oxidized and the oxidant reduced.
The oxidizing and reducing agents in a given reaction form a redox pair.
In electrochemical reactions the two half-reactions happen at the same time but in different places.
The terms confuse many: the reagent that is oxidized is called the reducing agent, and the one reduced the oxidizing agent.

In electrochemical reactions the two halves happen at the same time but in different places.

entries.title: Standard electrode potential: ranking the electron takers

definition.text: The equilibrium voltage of a half-reaction under standard conditions, measured against a standard hydrogen electrode; also called its reduction potential.

facts.text: It measures how strongly an oxidizing agent tends to be reduced.
It is zero for hydrogen ions by definition, positive for stronger oxidants such as fluorine (+2.866 V) and negative for weaker ones such as zinc ions (−0.763 V).
A cell's potential is the cathode potential minus the anode potential.
Reduction potential is measured in volts or millivolts.

entries.title: Eh, the voltage that tells oxidizing soil from reducing soil

definition.text: The tendency of electrons to pass from an electron donor to an electron acceptor, measured in volts as Eh.

facts.text: Eh is zero for the standard hydrogen electrode couple; positive values mean an oxidizing environment that accepts electrons, negative values a reducing one that donates them.
It can be calculated from half-reactions with the Nernst equation.
Soil Eh generally ranges from −300 to +900 mV; cultivated soils typically sit between +300 and +500 mV.
Plants are generally held to tolerate +300 to +700 mV, and 300 mV separates aerobic from anaerobic conditions in wetland soils.
Eh is closely tied to pH, and higher redox potentials occur at lower pH.
Oxidation state of the species present, pH and the amount of oxygen together control a system's redox potential.
Aerated waters usually show positive potentials, while places short of air, such as submerged soils, swamps and marine sediments, are normally reducing with negative potentials.
Strict aerobes are generally active at positive Eh and strict anaerobes at negative Eh; facultative anaerobes work at negative Eh too when nitrate or sulfate is present.

entries.title: Redox gradients: oxidizing above, reducing below

definition.text: A series of redox reactions sorted according to redox potential.

facts.text: Redox gradients form in space and time from differences in microbial processes, chemical composition and oxidative potential.
They are driven by oxygen availability, soil hydrology, the chemical species present and microbial activity.
They are typical of waterlogged soils, wetlands, lakes, coastal marshes, contaminant plumes and marine sediments.
The Earth as a whole is oxidizing at the surface and increasingly reducing below it.
They are well understood at large scale, but micro-scale redox in heterogeneous settings needs more research and better measurement.

entries.title: Electron donors: the fuel behind natural cleanup

definition.text: A chemical species that transfers electrons to another compound, acting as a reducing agent that is itself oxidized.

facts.text: In biology, electron donors release electrons during respiration, releasing energy; microbes capture it as electrons pass along a transport chain to an acceptor.
Soil organic matter, petroleum hydrocarbons, less chlorinated solvents such as vinyl chloride and reduced inorganic compounds can all act as electron donors.
These reactions drive natural biodegradation of organic contaminants, a major part of monitored natural attenuation at contaminated sites.

entries.article: In situ chemical oxidation#Agents of Oxidization

definition.text: The strong oxidizers used in in situ chemical oxidation, most commonly permanganate, Fenton's reagent, persulfate and ozone.

facts.text: Fenton's reagent, hydrogen peroxide catalysed by iron, and potassium permanganate have been used longest and are still widely used.

Fenton's reagent makes hydroxyl radicals but needs lowered pH to keep iron dissolved, so whether field use is truly a Fenton reaction is disputed.
Ozone is about 12 times more soluble than oxygen and, being a gas, is injected from below so its bubbles rise through the contamination.

entries.title: The redox ladder: which electron acceptor goes first

definition.text: The order in which redox reactions take place, set by the free energy each redox pair yields.

facts.text: The most energetically favourable reaction sits at the top of the ladder and the least favourable at the bottom.
From oxidizing to reducing the usual sequence is aerobic respiration, denitrification, manganese reduction, iron reduction and sulfate reduction.
For anaerobic respiration the nitrate–nitrogen couple ranks just below oxygen, above manganese, iron, sulfate and finally carbon dioxide–methane.
As oxygen dwindles with depth in sediments, microbial respiration pathways stack in vertical layers.
Thermodynamics alone does not fix where microbes live; ecological and physiological factors also matter.

entries.text: Microbes spend their electron acceptors in a set order, best first. The redox ladder is that order, fixed by the free energy each redox pair yields. The most favorable reaction sits at the top, the least favorable at the bottom. From oxidizing to reducing, the usual sequence runs aerobic respiration, then nitrate reduction to nitrogen gas, then manganese, iron and sulfate reduction. For respiration without oxygen, the nitrate–nitrogen couple ranks just below oxygen, above manganese, iron, sulfate and, last of all, carbon dioxide to methane. In sediments, oxygen dwindles with depth, so these pathways stack in vertical layers. Yet thermodynamics alone does not decide where microbes live. Ecology and physiology matter too.

entries.title: Breathing without oxygen: anaerobic respiration

definition.text: Respiration that uses inorganic electron acceptors other than oxygen, such as nitrate, sulfate or sulfur, at the end of the electron transport chain.

facts.text: These acceptors have lower reduction potentials than oxygen, so less energy is released and it is less efficient than aerobic respiration; it differs from fermentation, which passes electrons to organic compounds.
Under a few millimetres of water, heterotrophic bacteria use up the soil's oxygen, forcing a switch to anaerobic respiration.
Even oxygenated soil holds oxygen-free micro-environments, because oxygen gas diffuses slowly.
Anaerobic processes such as denitrification, sulfate reduction and methanogenesis release nitrogen gas, hydrogen sulfide and methane; others change the oxidation state of iron and manganese.
Nitrate respiration (denitrification) is the main route returning fixed nitrogen to the air as N2; sulfate respiration makes hydrogen sulfide, the rotten-egg smell of coastal wetlands.
Aerobic respiration releases carbon dioxide, while anaerobic respiration releases methane.
Because decomposition is anaerobic, wetland soils store large amounts of organic carbon.
Martinus Beijerinck discovered bacterial sulfate reduction, a form of anaerobic respiration.

entries.title: How a flooded soil runs out of oxygen

definition.text: The shift of a saturated soil from oxidizing to reducing conditions as oxygen runs out and anaerobic microbes take over.

facts.text: Soil Eh depends largely on hydrology: flooding turns soil from oxic to anoxic, and draining and drying restore its starting Eh.
Small anoxic hotspots can develop inside soil pores even when the soil as a whole is not saturated.
Organic matter is the main source of electrons; decomposers consume oxygen as they break it down, lowering Eh.
Flooded above about 5 °C, soil loses its oxygen to microbes within a few days, and nitrate and ferric oxide are then reduced.
At high redox potential iron is deposited as ferric hematite; under low redox conditions ferrous iron builds up and decomposition slows.
Prolonged saturation can dissolve ferric iron minerals that hold phosphorus, releasing it to leaching.

entries.title: Methanogenesis: the last step of decay without air

definition.text: The formation of methane by microbes called methanogens, all of them archaea, as the final step in breaking down organic matter where oxygen is absent.

facts.text: In most freshwater wetlands sulfate is scarce, and methanogenesis takes over decomposition only once sulfate is used up.
In sediments, sulfate reducers take most of the hydrogen in upper layers, while methanogens dominate lower down where sulfate is depleted.
Methanogenic archaea in the anaerobic layers of peat combine carbon dioxide and hydrogen gas into methane and water.
Methanotrophs oxidize methane back to carbon dioxide; methane production is typically high in anoxic floodplain, lake and reservoir sediments.
Once every electron acceptor but carbon dioxide is used up, only methanogenesis and fermentation can proceed; without methanogenesis much carbon would pile up as fermentation products.
It is common in flooded rice fields and wetlands, natural methane sources, and needs microbes that prefer low oxygen.
Aerating such soils raises sulfate and nitrate, which cut methane production; in upland soils it is often confined to anoxic microsites inside aerobic bulk soil.
Methane's global warming potential is 25 times that of carbon dioxide, averaged over 100 years.

entries.title: Paddy fields: rice, flooding and methane

definition.text: A flooded field of arable land used to grow semiaquatic crops, above all rice and taro.

facts.text: Paddy farming, still the dominant way to grow rice, began in the Neolithic rice cultures of the Yangtze River basin.
Paddies are a major methane source, estimated at 50 to 100 million tonnes a year, about 10% of global methane emissions.
Draining paddies so the soil aerates interrupts methane production and can boost yield, while ammonium-based fertilizers raise emissions.
Long wet-field cultivation can turn paddy soils into Anthrosols, and early soil redox theory grew out of flooded paddy rice soils.

entries.text: Rice paddies release an estimated 50 to 100 million tonnes of methane a year, about 10% of global methane emissions. A paddy field is a flooded crop field used to grow semiaquatic crops, above all rice and taro. Paddy farming began in the Neolithic rice cultures of the Yangtze River basin and remains the dominant way to grow rice. Draining paddies so the soil aerates interrupts methane production and can boost yield. Ammonium-based fertilizers raise emissions. Early soil redox theory grew out of flooded paddy soils, and long wet-field cultivation can turn them into the human-made soils described in {{ref:soil-class-120}}.

entries.title: Microbes that breathe iron instead of oxygen

definition.text: Anaerobic respiration by bacteria and archaea that use a metal, rather than oxygen, as the terminal electron acceptor.

facts.text: Iron and manganese are the metals most used: Fe(III) is reduced to Fe(II) and Mn(IV) to Mn(II), and most Fe(III) reducers can also reduce Mn(IV).
Other metals and metalloids can serve too, including vanadium, chromium(VI), molybdenum, cobalt, palladium, gold and mercury.
It happens without oxygen, but the organisms include both strict anaerobes such as the Geobacteraceae and facultative anaerobes such as Shewanella.
In near-neutral soils and sediments iron is held in solid oxidized minerals, so these microbes reduce metals outside the cell, passing electrons out through membrane cytochromes c.
Some reduce minerals at a distance using electron shuttles; humic acids common in soils and sediments can act as such shuttles.
Many Fe(III) minerals can be reduced, including magnetite, hematite, goethite, lepidocrocite, ferrihydrite, smectite, illite and jarosite.
Secondary minerals such as magnetite, siderite, green rust and vivianite can form as by-products of the reduction.

entries.title: The hydrogen electrode that defines zero volts

definition.text: The reference redox electrode that sets the zero of the thermodynamic scale of oxidation–reduction potentials.

facts.text: Its standard electrode potential is declared to be zero volts at any temperature, though its absolute potential is estimated at 4.44 ± 0.02 V at 25 °C.
The potentials of all other electrodes are compared with it at the same temperature.
Soil redox potential, Eh, is the potential of a platinum electrode measured relative to the standard hydrogen electrode.
It is a theoretical ideal-solution standard, replacing the older normal hydrogen electrode of platinum in 1 N acid with bubbling hydrogen.

entries.text: Every redox potential is measured against one agreed zero. It is a theoretical ideal-solution standard. It replaced the older normal hydrogen electrode, platinum in 1 N acid with bubbling hydrogen.

entries.title: Obligate anaerobes, microbes poisoned by air

definition.text: Microorganisms that are killed by normal atmospheric concentrations of oxygen.

facts.text: Tolerance varies: some survive up to 8% oxygen, others lose viability above 0.5%; facultative anaerobes can use oxygen but survive without it.
Oxygen harms them through reactive oxygen species, which aerobes detoxify with enzymes that obligate anaerobes make in small amounts or not at all.
They gain energy by anaerobic respiration, using acceptors such as sulfate, nitrate, iron or manganese, or by fermentation, both yielding less ATP than aerobic respiration.
They live in oxygen-free places including deep soil sediments, landfills and still waters; some Mycobacterium, Streptomyces and Rhodococcus species are soil examples.

entries.text: For some microbes, ordinary air is lethal. Obligate anaerobes are microorganisms killed by normal atmospheric concentrations of oxygen. Oxygen harms them through reactive oxygen species, which aerobes detoxify with enzymes these microbes barely make. They respire sulfate, nitrate, iron or manganese, or ferment, both yielding less ATP than aerobic respiration. Facultative anaerobes, by contrast, use oxygen but survive without it. Obligate anaerobes inhabit deep soil sediments, landfills and still waters; some Mycobacterium and Rhodococcus species, and some of the bacteria in {{ref:soil-bio-225}}, live in soil.

entries.title: Methanogens, the methane makers of paddies and bogs

definition.text: Anaerobic archaea that produce methane as a by-product of their energy metabolism.

facts.text: Methanogenesis is their only biochemical pathway for making ATP, and all known methanogens belong to the domain Archaea.
They are common in oxygen-free settings such as wetlands, sediments, rice paddy soil, landfills, wastewater plants and animal guts.
Their oxygen sensitivity varies: methanogenesis is often detected in temporarily oxygenated rice paddy soil, and one wetland and soil species works in anoxic microsites within aerobic soil.
Methanogens grow at a redox potential below −0.3 V.

entries.title: Iron-oxidizing bacteria and their reddish-brown slime

definition.text: Chemotrophic bacteria that get their energy by oxidizing dissolved iron.

facts.text: They live where oxygen-free water meets an oxygenated setting, turning dissolved iron into an insoluble reddish-brown slime; they need at least 0.3 ppm dissolved oxygen.
Soil microbes feeding on dissolved organic matter, for example from landfill leachate or septic fields, can deoxygenate groundwater and so set the stage for them.
Bog iron ore deposits formed where such groundwater emerged and met atmospheric oxygen.
Some oxidize Fe(II) without oxygen by coupling it to nitrate reduction, a light-independent metabolism found in sediments including paddy soil.

entries.text: Bog iron ore deposits formed where oxygen-free groundwater emerged and met the air. Some species oxidize Fe(II) without oxygen by coupling it to nitrate reduction, a light-independent metabolism found in sediments including flooded rice soils.

entries.title: Green rust, the iron mineral that fades in air

definition.text: A family of green layered iron(II)–iron(III) hydroxides that hold another anion, such as carbonate, chloride or sulfate, between their layers.

facts.text: In nature it occurs as the mineral fougerite, and it is suspected in bluish-green soils formed under alternating redox conditions that turn ochre once exposed to air.
In oxidizing conditions it generally converts to the iron(III) oxyhydroxides goethite and lepidocrocite.
Iron-reducing bacteria such as Shewanella putrefaciens produce it when they reduce ferric oxyhydroxides while oxidizing organic matter, a process thought to occur in soil solutions and aquifers.
Sulfate green rust can reduce nitrate and nitrite to ammonium as its Fe2+ is oxidized to Fe3+.

entries.title: The manganese cycle, from bedrock to seafloor

definition.text: The biogeochemical cycle that moves manganese through the atmosphere, water, living things and rocks and soils.

facts.text: Manganese makes up about 0.1% of the Earth's crust and is cycled much like iron, but by distinct redox pathways.
Some bacteria oxidize manganese to insoluble oxides, while others reduce it to soluble Mn2+ in order to use it.
Weathering of regolith and dissolution of bedrock carry manganese into rivers and on to the ocean, where it can form minerals and be buried.
Mining, mineral processing and the burning of fossil fuels are altering the global cycle.
Over half the manganese in ridge soils near iron or steel plants in North America and Europe came from industrial waste and settled airborne particles.

entries.text: Manganese makes up only about 0.1% of the Earth's crust, yet it never sits still. The manganese cycle is the natural circuit, biological and geological, that moves it through the atmosphere, water, living things, rocks and soils. It is cycled much like iron, but by distinct redox pathways. Bacteria push it both ways. Some oxidize manganese to insoluble oxides, while others reduce it to soluble Mn2+ in order to use it. Weathering of regolith and dissolution of bedrock carry manganese into rivers. From there it travels to the ocean, where it can form minerals and be buried. People now tilt the cycle. Mining, mineral processing and the burning of fossil fuels are altering it globally. Near iron and steel plants in North America and Europe, over half the manganese in ridge soils came from industrial waste and settled airborne particles.

entries.title: Measuring Eh with a platinum electrode

definition.text: Determining Eh by sampling in the field and analysing in the lab, or by placing an electrode in the soil or water for in situ readings.

facts.text: Soil Eh is read with a platinum electrode relative to the standard hydrogen electrode.
Many samples give fine spatial but poor temporal resolution; fixed electrodes give continuous readings but poor spatial coverage.
Waters, soils and sediments can be highly heterogeneous, which complicates measurement.
Induced-polarization imaging can track redox at high spatial and temporal resolution, though its signal is not yet fully understood.

Many samples give fine detail across space but little over time. Fixed electrodes give continuous readings but cover little ground. Waters, soils and sediments can be highly patchy, which complicates both. Induced-polarization imaging can track redox finely in space and time, though its signal is not yet fully understood.

entries.title: Microbes that sharpen the gradients they live on

definition.text: The layered microbial communities that redox gradients support, and that in turn sharpen those gradients through their respiration.

facts.text: Microbes switch respiration processes, such as methanogenesis or sulfate reduction, to suit local conditions, amplifying the gradient.
Organic pollutants break down fastest at the oxic–anoxic interface, such as the groundwater capillary fringe, where electron donors and acceptors abound.
Cable bacteria, which oxidize sulfide, link zones short of electrons with zones holding a surplus.
Biofilms of metal- or sulfate-reducing bacteria create redox gradients on the micrometre scale.

entries.title: Redox layers in lakes, seas and their sediments

definition.text: The redox gradients that form in water columns and in the sediments beneath them.

facts.text: Oxic, suboxic and hypoxic water layers allow different redox reactions, and oxygen minimum zones add to the gradients.
In bottom sediments, gradients arise from differences in minerals, organic matter, structure and sorption.
Slow electron transport and varied pore sizes make bottom sediments highly heterogeneous.

entries.text: Water columns and the mud beneath them carry redox gradients of their own. Oxic, suboxic and hypoxic water layers, from well oxygenated to poorly oxygenated, each allow different redox reactions. Oxygen minimum zones add to the layering. In bottom sediments, gradients arise from differences in minerals, dead organic material, structure and sorption. Slow electron transport and varied pore sizes make these sediments highly patchy.

entries.title: Solubility equilibrium: dissolving and precipitating in balance

definition.text: The dynamic equilibrium between a solid compound and a solution of that compound, with dissolution and precipitation going on at equal rates.

facts.text: Each solubility equilibrium has a temperature-dependent solubility product that works like an equilibrium constant.
A solution at equilibrium with undissolved solid is saturated; one holding more solute than its solubility is supersaturated and can precipitate.
Strictly the constant is a quotient of activities, but it is usually converted to a quotient of concentrations.
Acid rain leaching aluminium from rocks and soil is dissolution with reaction: aluminosilicates react with the acid to give soluble Al3+.

entries.text: A crystal resting in its saturated solution looks still, but it is busy. In a solubility equilibrium, a solid compound and its solution exchange material, with dissolution and precipitation going on at equal rates. Each such equilibrium has a temperature-dependent solubility product, which works like an equilibrium constant. Strictly it is a quotient of activities, but it is usually converted to one of concentrations. A solution at equilibrium with undissolved solid is saturated; one holding more solute than its solubility is supersaturated and can precipitate. Acid rain leaching aluminum from soil is dissolution with reaction: aluminosilicates react with the acid to give soluble Al3+.

entries.title: How a solid appears out of solution

definition.text: The formation of a solid, the precipitate, from a liquid solution.

facts.text: Compounds precipitate when their concentration exceeds solubility, that is, when the solution is supersaturated; precipitation is faster from strongly supersaturated solutions.
Supersaturation can arise from temperature change, solvent evaporation or mixing of solvents.
Without enough attractive force to aggregate the particles, they stay suspended as a colloid instead of settling.
Ageing a fresh precipitate in its solution gives purer, larger recrystallized particles, through Ostwald ripening.

entries.title: Activity: the effective concentration of an ion

definition.text: A measure of the effective concentration of a species in a mixture, so that its chemical potential in a real solution depends on activity as it would on concentration in an ideal one.

facts.text: Activity is dimensionless; pure solids and liquids take a = 1, and it depends on temperature, pressure, composition and the chosen standard state.
Equilibrium constants should be defined by activities but are often defined by concentrations in practice.
The activity coefficient links activity to a measured concentration; near 1, the substance behaves almost ideally.

The activity of a single ion such as Ca2+ cannot be measured, since cations cannot be added without anions; the mean ionic coefficient is measurable and predicted by Debye-Hückel theory in dilute systems.
For water as solvent, water activity is the equilibrated relative humidity.

entries.title: Electron activity: redox measured like pH

definition.text: A dimensionless measure of redox potential, defined as the negative logarithm of electron activity by analogy with pH.

facts.text: Environmental chemists often use pe instead of Eh because it works directly on a logarithmic scale; at 25 °C, pe = Eh/0.05916 = 16.903 × Eh.
Environmental pe values run from −12 to +25, because beyond these water itself is reduced or oxidized.
Along with pH, Eh or pe is a master variable in soils that both controls and is governed by chemical and biological reactions.
Redox potential and pH together constrain the solubility of manganese in soils.

entries.title: Pourbaix diagrams: maps of what is stable in water

definition.text: A plot of the thermodynamically stable phases of an aqueous system against redox potential (Eh or pe) and pH.

facts.text: Lines mark the 50/50 boundaries between the predominant dissolved species or solid phases.
Like a phase diagram it assumes equilibrium and says nothing about reaction rates.
Water is stable only between two parallel lines, EH = −0.05916 pH and EH = 1.229 V − 0.05916 pH; outside them it is reduced to hydrogen or oxidized to oxygen.
The diagrams are used in corrosion, geochemistry and environmental science, and are named after the Belgian engineer Marcel Pourbaix (1904–1998).

entries.title: Manganese in soil, a nutrient steered by pH and pe

definition.text: The forms and redox behaviour of manganese in soils, where it is a micronutrient whose solubility is set by redox potential and pH.

facts.text: Manganese is a key soil micronutrient, acting as a catalyst in the oxygen-evolving complex of photosystem II.
Soil fungi oxidize soluble Mn2+ and may reprecipitate it as manganese oxides; much of the soil cycle is biological, though inorganic reactions also oxidize Mn.
As pH rises, manganese speciation becomes less sensitive to pe.
In acidic soils (pH 5) with high pe (above 8), manganese is mostly in reducible forms, and exchangeable and soluble Mn fall sharply as pe rises.

entries.title: Hydromorphic soils, shaped by standing water

definition.text: A soil formed under wetland conditions, waterlogged for long enough to shape its development.

facts.text: The 1938 USDA taxonomy listed hydromorphic soils as an intrazonal group, with gley soils, saturated and airless so their iron is reduced, as one sub-type.
Plinthosols form by the accumulation of iron under hydromorphic conditions.
Gypcretes can form in hydromorphic soils, among other settings.
Hydromorphic soils can have little plant-available zinc because of strong zinc sorption.

entries.text: Leave a soil waterlogged long enough and the water starts to shape it. A hydromorphic soil is one formed under such wetland conditions. The 1938 USDA taxonomy listed hydromorphic soils as an intrazonal group. One sub-type was the gley soils, saturated and airless, so that their iron is reduced. The soils described in {{ref:soil-class-137}} form by the accumulation of iron under hydromorphic conditions, and gypcretes can form in these soils, among other settings. Strong zinc sorption can leave hydromorphic soils with little plant-available zinc.

entries.title: Salt in the soil, and how it gathers

definition.text: The salt content of a soil; the process by which it increases is called salinization.

facts.text: The ions responsible for salinization are Na+, K+, Ca2+, Mg2+ and Cl−.
Salts come from mineral weathering, dust and precipitation; with enough rain they are leached away, but under intense evaporation they rise by capillarity and gather near the surface.
Salts accumulate naturally in dry regions, as in large parts of Australia.
Human causes include irrigation, road salt and disrupted drainage; after Egypt's Aswan High Dam was built in 1970, a persistently high water table salinized arable land.
Increasing aridity from human-induced global warming also adds to the salinization of waterlogged soils.
Salinity is an important land degradation problem: it harms plant growth and yield, damages roads, bricks, pipes and cables, and degrades water quality.
It can be reduced by leaching salts out with excess good-quality irrigation water, combined with water-table control and subsurface drainage.
Calcium counters salinity, easing effects such as reduced water uptake by plants.

entries.text: Egypt's Aswan High Dam was built in 1970. Afterward, a persistently high water table salinized farmland. Soil salinity is the salt content of a soil, and salinization is the process that raises it. A handful of ions do the work: sodium (Na+), potassium (K+), calcium (Ca2+), magnesium (Mg2+) and chloride (Cl−). Salts arrive through {{ref:soil-found-052}}, in dust and in precipitation. With enough rain they are leached away. Under intense evaporation they rise instead by capillarity and gather near the surface. That is why salts accumulate naturally in dry regions, as across large parts of Australia. People add to the load with irrigation, road salt and disrupted drainage. Growing dryness from human-induced global warming also adds to the salinization of waterlogged soils. Salinity seriously degrades land. It harms plant growth and yield, damages roads, bricks, pipes and cables, and degrades water quality. The usual cure is to leach salts out with extra good-quality irrigation water, combined with water-table control and drainage from below. Calcium helps as well, easing effects such as plants' reduced water uptake.

entries.title: How soils turn sour over time

definition.text: The build-up of hydrogen cations in a soil, which lowers its pH.

facts.text: It happens when a proton donor is added: an acid such as nitric, sulfuric or carbonic acid, or a compound such as aluminium sulfate that releases protons in the soil.
It also happens when base cations such as calcium, magnesium, potassium and sodium are leached from the soil.
It begins naturally as lichens and algae break down rock surfaces, and with time and weathering soils in natural ecosystems grow more acidic.
Soils start out acid and stay so when their parent materials are low in basic cations; acid rain, agriculture and pollution speed acidification up.
It leaves fewer available nutrients, more toxic elements and weaker biological functions such as nitrogen fixation.
Acidification helps alkaline soils but degrades land when it cuts crop productivity and biological activity and leaves soil more open to contamination and erosion.
It is most common in Southeast Asia, the Amazon Rainforest, Sub-Saharan Africa and the Eastern United States, each with its own causes.
Surface liming, less fertilizer and irrigation can prevent it.

entries.text: Acid soils begin with lichens and algae. As they break down bare rock surfaces, acidification starts, and with time and weathering soils in natural ecosystems grow more acidic. Soil acidification is the build-up of hydrogen cations in a soil, which lowers its pH. It follows two routes. One adds a proton donor: an acid such as nitric, sulfuric or carbonic acid, or a compound such as aluminium sulfate that releases protons in the soil. The other removes base cations such as calcium, magnesium, potassium and sodium by leaching. Soils on parent materials low in basic cations start out acid and stay that way. {{ref:soil-chem-002}}, agriculture and pollution speed the process up. The costs are real: fewer available nutrients, more toxic elements and weaker biological functions such as {{ref:soil-fert-100}}. Acidification is not always harmful, since it helps alkaline soils. It degrades land when it cuts crop productivity and biological activity and leaves soil more open to contamination and erosion. It is most common in Southeast Asia, the Amazon Rainforest, Sub-Saharan Africa and the Eastern United States, each with its own causes. Spreading lime on the surface, covered in {{ref:soil-fert-055}}, can prevent it, as can less fertilizer and irrigation.

entries.title: Acid rain and the soils it soaks through

definition.text: Rain or other precipitation that is unusually acidic, mainly from sulfuric and nitric acids formed from air pollutants, which acidifies the soils it falls on.

facts.text: Unpolluted rain is already acidic, around pH 5.0–5.5, from carbonic acid; acid rain is defined as below pH 5 and averages 4–5, with readings well below 2.4 reported in industrial areas.
Sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, from lightning, volcanoes or human emissions, are converted in the troposphere into sulfuric and nitric acids.
Fossil fuels are the largest human source of sulfuric gases and motor exhaust the largest of nitrogen oxides.
Hydrogen ions in acid rain exchange for calcium and magnesium on clay, leaching these base cations and mobilizing aluminium, which harms sensitive trees such as sugar maple.
Low pH kills sensitive soil microbes by denaturing their enzymes, collapsing functions such as decomposition and hurting plants that depend on microbes for nutrients.
Snow holds more nitric than sulfuric acid, so a spring meltwater pulse, up to 50% of annual precipitation, can sharply but briefly lower the pH of drainage water.
Soils buffer part of the acid: adsorbing sulfate releases OH−, and organic-rich forest floor horizons cut the H+ load reaching mineral horizons below.
Since the 1970s regulations such as the US Clean Air Act have cut sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide emissions, reducing acid rain, as improving pH in Ontario lakes showed.

entries.text: Even clean rain is sour. Atmospheric carbon dioxide forms carbonic acid, leaving natural rain at around pH 5.0–5.5. Acid rain and snow are more acidic still, and they acidify soil rapidly, mainly through sulfuric and nitric acids formed from air pollutants. Sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides come from lightning, volcanoes or human emissions, and react with water in the air to form those stronger acids. Fossil fuels are the largest human source of sulfuric gases, and motor exhaust the largest of nitrogen oxides. As acid rain flows through soil, it leaches calcium and other base cations, and aluminium and proton levels rise. This is {{ref:soil-chem-001}} on a fast clock. Snow brings its own hazard. It holds more nitric than sulfuric acid, so a spring meltwater pulse, up to 50% of annual precipitation, can sharply but briefly lower the pH of drainage water. That drop can release Al3+, which is toxic to fish, especially newly hatched fry. Soils buffer part of the acid. Adsorbing sulfate releases OH−, and organic-rich surface layers in forests cut the H+ load reaching the mineral horizons below. Prevention works. Cutting sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide emissions reduces acid rain and soil acidification, as improving water pH in Ontario lakes showed.

entries.title: How watering a field can salt it

definition.text: Salt build-up in irrigated soils, because nearly all water carries dissolved salts that stay behind in the root zone when plants use the water.

facts.text: Salinization occurs where evaporation concentrates dissolved salts in the root zone faster than drainage flushes them away.
Water applied beyond the plants' needs to carry salts away is called the leaching fraction.
Poor drainage and the use of saline water for irrigation greatly increase it.
In cities it often stems from watering gardens and recreation areas with salt-laden reclaimed water, combined with groundwater processes.
Good irrigation management prevents it by supplying enough drainage water to leach the added salts.
Even water with a low salt content of 0.3 g/L, applied at a modest 10,000 m3/ha a year, brings 3,000 kg of salt per hectare each year.
Most irrigation water is saltier and applied more heavily, so irrigated areas often receive more than 3,000 kg/ha of salt a year, some as much as 10,000 kg/ha.
Waterlogging is the secondary cause: irrigation efficiency is at most about 70%, so 30% or more of the water goes underground, raising water tables that block leaching.

entries.title: Flushing salt out to keep irrigated fields alive

definition.text: Controlling salinization to prevent soil degradation, and reclaiming soils that are already saline.

facts.text: Irrigation is the main human cause of salinization, since river water and groundwater carry salts that stay in the soil after the water evaporates.
The main method is to let 10–20% of the irrigation water leach the soil and leave through a drainage system.
Where salinity is stable, drainage water is normally 5 to 10 times saltier than the irrigation water, so salt export matches salt import.
When salinized soil is reclaimed, drainage water may at first be 50 times saltier than irrigation water; after one or two years a new, favourable equilibrium is reached.
About 62 million hectares, 20% of the world's irrigated land, is salt-affected, up from 45 million ha in the early 1990s.
In the Indo-Gangetic Plain, yield losses on salt-affected land could be 40% for wheat, 45% for rice, 48% for sugarcane and 63% for cotton.
Salinization normally affects 20% to 30% of the land in irrigation projects; depressions in undulating land degrade the most.
Salty drainage water can harm areas downstream, so drainage is best limited to wet seasons when possible.

entries.title: Sodic soils, where sodium rules the clay

definition.text: A soil in which sodium (Na+) predominates among the exchangeable and dissolved cations.

facts.text: Sodic soils may be acidic, neutral or alkaline in pH.
They tend to have very poor structure, which limits or prevents water infiltration and drainage; where clays are saturated with sodium the soil breaks down easily into fine particles that wash away.
They tend to form columnar peds near the surface.
They can accumulate boron and molybdenum in the root zone at levels toxic to plants.
Gypsum is the most common reclamation compound, and salt-tolerant organisms such as halophytes and halophilic rhizobacteria may help.
The term is used loosely, often interchangeably with alkali soil, defined as pH above 8.2, exchangeable sodium above 15% of CEC, or both.

entries.text: A soil can be acidic, neutral or alkaline and still be crippled by one element. A sodic soil is one in which sodium (Na+) predominates among the exchangeable and dissolved cations, the ions traded through {{ref:soil-chem-047}}. Sodic soils tend to have very poor structure, which limits or prevents water infiltration and drainage. Where clays are saturated with sodium, the soil breaks down easily into fine particles that wash away. Near the surface these soils tend to form columnar peds. They can also accumulate boron and molybdenum in the root zone at levels toxic to plants. Gypsum is the most common compound for reclaiming them. Salt-tolerant plants, the subject of {{ref:soil-chem-045}}, and salt-loving bacteria of the root zone may help. entries.text_plain: A soil can be acidic, neutral or alkaline and still be crippled by one element. A sodic soil is one in which sodium (Na+) predominates among the exchangeable and dissolved cations, the ions traded through Cation exchange: how soil trades nutrients with its water. Sodic soils tend to have very poor structure, which limits or prevents water infiltration and drainage. Where clays are saturated with sodium, the soil breaks down easily into fine particles that wash away. Near the surface these soils tend to form columnar peds. They can also accumulate boron and molybdenum in the root zone at levels toxic to plants. Gypsum is the most common compound for reclaiming them. Salt-tolerant plants, the subject of Halophytes, the plants that thrive on salt, and salt-loving bacteria of the root zone may help. The term is used loosely, often interchangeably with Alkali soils, clay ruined by sodium carbonate, defined as pH above 8.2, exchangeable sodium above 15% of the cation-exchange capacity, or both.

entries.title: How fertilizers make soil more acidic

definition.text: The lowering of soil pH by chemical fertilizers, above all ammonium-based nitrogen and sulfur fertilizers.

facts.text: Most nitrogen fertilizers acidify, ammonium-based ones such as ammonium sulfate, diammonium and monoammonium phosphate and ammonium nitrate most of all; urea and compost acidify less.
Nitrate sources with little or no ammonium, such as calcium, magnesium, potassium and sodium nitrate, do not acidify.
Elemental sulfur and iron sulfate can be highly acidifying, while potassium sulfate has no significant effect on pH.
Nitrification of ammonium releases hydrogen ions and nitric acid as byproducts, which keep acidifying the soil.
Monoculture with chemical fertilization often brings acidification and degradation; sugarcane monoculture raised acidity, lowered fertility and shifted soil microbes.
Generally 4-7 pounds of lime neutralize the acid from each pound of nitrogen applied; nitrate-only fertilizers such as calcium or potassium nitrate do not acidify and can slightly raise pH.
Most commercial nitrogen fertilizers are acid forming but many manures are not.

entries.title: Duricrust, the hard shell some dry soils wear

definition.text: A hard layer on or near the soil surface where soluble minerals have precipitated and hardened.

facts.text: Duricrusts range from a few millimeters or centimeters to several meters thick; the general term is not to be confused with duripan.
They form as mineral-bearing waters moving up, down or sideways by capillary action deposit soluble minerals, often helped by evaporation in arid settings.

Types are named by dominant mineral: ferricrete (laterite) iron sesquioxides, alcrete (bauxite) aluminium sesquioxides, silcrete silica, calcrete (caliche) calcium carbonate and gypcrete (gypcrust) gypsum.
In the per ascensum model, evaporation draws solutions up from a shallow water table to form thin crusts; in the per descensum model, downward-percolating solutions build thick ones.
Duricrust found at the Viking 2 and Phoenix landing sites on Mars, the latter confirmed water-based, may help show the planet once had more water.

entries.title: Acid sulfate soils, harmless until they meet air

definition.text: Soils, sediments or organic substrates such as peat, formed under waterlogged conditions, that contain iron sulfide minerals, mainly pyrite, or their oxidation products.

facts.text: Undisturbed below the water table they are benign, but when drained, excavated or exposed to air their sulfides react with oxygen to form sulfuric acid.
Drained, they can become extremely acidic (pH < 4), and the acid releases iron, aluminium and other metals and metalloids, particularly arsenic.
The acid and metals kill vegetation and fish, acidify groundwater and surface water, and degrade concrete and steel structures to the point of failure.
Those most prone formed within the last 10,000 years, after the last major sea level rise mixed seawater sulfate with land sediments rich in iron oxides and organic matter.
They are widespread around coasts; in Australia coastal acid sulfate soils cover an estimated 58,000 km2 beneath estuaries and floodplains.
Dredging and dewatering for canal, housing and marina developments often disturb them, and droughts can expose them too; some drained 100 years ago still release acid.
Potential acid sulfate soils, or cat-clays, are often left uncultivated or planted with rice to keep them wet, and subsurface drainage is normally not advisable.
The term was coined for the first International Symposium on Acid Sulfate Soils, held in 1972 at Wageningen.

entries.title: Dryland salinity: clear the trees, raise the salt

definition.text: Salinity in unirrigated landscapes: a rise in the salt of soil, water or the wider environment beyond normal levels, natural but greatly worsened by human activity.

facts.text: It results from groundwater recharge, movement and discharge; clearing deep-rooted plants lets excess water seep past the root zone and the water table rises.
Capillary action then brings salt to the surface; this happens when the water table is two to three metres down in clayey soils but less than a metre in sandy ones.
Clearing as little as 25% of a catchment can cause salinity, and in many Australian landscapes aquifer capacity is orders of magnitude below the altered recharge.
Native vegetation forms a 'soil sponge' of roots and soil up to 6 metres deep that keeps the water table low; shallow-rooted crops such as wheat thin it to 1 metre or less.
Salts accumulate where evaporation outpaces rainfall's replenishment of groundwater, as in arid environments.
Saline groundwater discharge cuts farm production, degrades natural environments and surface water, damages roads and leads to soil erosion.
Restoring the balance needs deep-rooted vegetation such as mallee eucalyptus or perennial grasses, or farming adapted to shallow saline groundwater.

entries.title: Australia's ancient salt, set loose by clearing

definition.text: Soil salinity and dryland salinity as problems degrading the environment of Australia.

facts.text: Most states are affected, above all south-west Western Australia, which holds around 70% of Australia's salt-affected land.
Australian soils naturally hold salt gathered over thousands of years from ocean winds, evaporated inland seas and weathered parent rocks.
Before British settlement in 1788 groundwater levels were in equilibrium, as deep-rooted native vegetation used groundwater year-round.
Land clearing replaced that vegetation with crops and pasture; rising groundwater then brings stored salt up, and evaporation leaves it in the soil.
By 1999 about 2.5 million hectares had become salinised since European farming began; 5.7 million hectares now have high potential, expected to reach 17 million by 2050.
Salt cuts plants' water uptake by osmosis, burns leaves through sodium and chloride and upsets nutrient balance; it also damages roads, buildings, pipes and cables.
In the Murray River valley irrigation has caused salinity, while near Werrimull in Victoria land clearing did.
Predictions for climate change are mixed: lower rainfall may reduce salinity, but heavier downpours may add excess water to aquifers.

entries.title: Pyrite, the fool's gold that turns to acid

definition.text: Iron sulfide, FeS2, the most common sulfide mineral, also known as fool's gold.

facts.text: It occurs in igneous, metamorphic and sedimentary rocks and is common in shale, where it precipitates from anoxic seawater, and in coal beds.
Exposed to oxygen and water it breaks down into iron oxyhydroxides and sulfuric acid, a reaction sped up by Acidithiobacillus bacteria.
Finely dispersed framboidal pyrite, formed by sulfate-reducing bacteria in clayey sediments, oxidizes faster.
Its oxidation causes acid mine drainage; limestone dust spread in coal mines neutralizes the acid and slows the oxidation.
