entries.title: Sodium adsorption ratio: a number for clay's stability

definition.text: An irrigation water quality index, calculated from sodium, calcium and magnesium concentrations, used in managing sodium-affected soils.

facts.text: It is also the standard diagnostic of a soil's sodicity hazard, measured on pore water extracted from the soil.
SAR = [Na+]/√([Ca2+]/2 + [Mg2+]/2), with concentrations in milliequivalents per litre.
Sodium and potassium disperse clay particles while calcium and magnesium flocculate them, so SAR shows whether clay aggregates will flocculate or disperse.
Years of irrigation with high-SAR water let sodium displace soil calcium and magnesium, ruining aggregate stability, structure and tilth and reducing infiltration and permeability.
Below an SAR of 3 there is no problem; above 9, fine-textured soils have severe problems, while sandy soils suffer less.
For irrigation the SAR should not be much above 20 and preferably below 10; after long exposure, a soil's ESP comes to roughly equal the water's SAR.
SAR addresses sodium only; the potassium adsorption ratio (PAR) and the cation ratio of structural stability (CROSS) extend it to other cations.

entries.title: Resistivity and conductivity: how well a material carries current

definition.text: Two intrinsic properties of a material that measure its ability to conduct electric current; each is the reciprocal of the other.

facts.text: Resistivity (ρ) has the SI unit ohm-metre; conductivity (σ) has the SI unit siemens per metre.
In a uniform conductor, resistance is proportional to length and inversely proportional to cross-sectional area, with resistivity as the constant of proportionality.
Resistivity and conductivity are intensive properties; resistance and conductance are the matching extensive properties of a specific object.
In electrolytes, current is carried by travelling ions. Resistivity varies tremendously with concentration: distilled water is almost an insulator, salt water a reasonable conductor.
A metal has high conductivity and low resistivity; an insulator such as glass has low conductivity and high resistivity.
Resistivity of metals generally rises with temperature, while that of intrinsic semiconductors falls.

entries.title: The hidden costs of watering dry land

definition.text: The changes irrigation makes to the quantity and quality of soil and water, and their effects on natural and social conditions in river basins and downstream.

facts.text: Direct effects include reduced downstream river flow, more evaporation in the irrigated area and a rising water table from increased groundwater recharge.
Slower but longer-lasting indirect effects include waterlogging, soil salination, ecological damage and socioeconomic impacts.
Deep percolation losses are commonly 40% to 60%, raising water tables; where tables are shallow, less water is applied, the soil is no longer leached and salinity develops.
Over-irrigation causes irrigation salinity through rising water tables, while under-irrigation also raises salinity by failing to flush out salts.
About one-third of irrigated land in the major irrigation countries is or soon will be badly salt-affected: estimates are 13% in Israel, 20% in Australia, 15% in China, 50% in Iraq and 30% in Egypt.
Irrigated land covers about 16% of the world's agricultural area but gives roughly 40% of total crop yield.
Pumping wells beyond recharge mines groundwater and can cause land subsidence and, on coasts, saltwater intrusion.
Stagnant water tables at the surface raise the incidence of water-borne diseases such as malaria and schistosomiasis.

entries.title: Measuring salt by the current soil water carries

definition.text: Determining soil salinity as the salt concentration of the soil solution in g/L, or as its electric conductivity (EC) in dS/m.

facts.text: The two units relate by about 5/3: y g/L corresponds to 5y/3 dS/m; seawater may hold 30 g/L (3%) with an EC of 50 dS/m.
The standard is the EC of an extract of a saturated soil paste, obtained by centrifugation and written ECe.
A 2:1 or 5:1 water:soil mixture is easier to measure, and ECe is about 4 times the EC of a 2:1 mixture.
Soils are saline when ECe > 4: slightly saline from 4 to 8, moderately saline from 8 to 16, and severely saline above 16.
Sensitive crops lose vigour already in slightly saline soils, most crops suffer in moderately saline ones, and only salt-resistant crops thrive in severely saline soils.

Soil salinity is measured on the same two scales: the salt concentration of the soil solution in g/L, or its electric conductivity (EC) in dS/m. The units relate by about 5/3, so y g/L corresponds to 5y/3 dS/m. The standard is the EC of an extract of a saturated soil paste, obtained by centrifugation and written ECe. A 2:1 or 5:1 water:soil mixture is easier to measure, and ECe is about 4 times the EC of a 2:1 mixture. Soils are saline when ECe exceeds 4. They are slightly saline from 4 to 8, moderately saline from 8 to 16, and severely saline above 16. Sensitive crops already lose vigor in slightly saline soils. Most crops suffer in moderately saline ones, and only salt-resistant crops thrive in severely saline soils.

entries.title: Rocks that leave acid soils behind

definition.text: Rocks and sediments whose weathering acidifies the soils formed on them, such as granite and sulfide-rich shale, coal and marine clay.

facts.text: Granites and allied igneous rocks are called 'acidic' because their abundant free quartz yields silicic acid on weathering; they are also low in calcium and magnesium.
Sulfide-rich shale and coal produce sulfuric acid, much stronger than silicic acid, when hydrated and oxidised; many coal soils are too acidic for vigorous plant growth.
Marine clays are often sulfide-rich and become very acidic if drained to an oxidising state.

entries.title: How roots and fallen needles acidify soil

definition.text: Acidification of soil by living things, as plant roots and decaying plant remains release protons and organic acids.

facts.text: Plant roots release protons and organic acids to chemically weather soil minerals.
Litter acidifies the O horizon more under conifers such as pine, spruce and fir, which return fewer base cations than deciduous trees, though such pH differences often preexisted the vegetation.
Calcium held in living biomass also strongly affects soil pH, by an amount that varies between species.

entries.title: What acid soil does to roots and life

definition.text: The harm acidification does to plants and soil organisms, from stunted roots to lost biological diversity.

facts.text: Plants develop smaller, less durable roots with damaged tips, reduced height, poorer germination and stunted growth overall.
It reduces microbial and macrofaunal diversity and is directly linked to declines in endangered plant species.
Leaching of base cations raises the availability of toxic ions such as aluminium, whose toxicity inhibits root growth.
Leaves yellowing between the veins can signal it, though alkaline or nutrient-poor soils cause the same symptom; at large scale it cuts agricultural productivity.

entries.title: Lime and careful habits against acid soil

definition.text: Ways of preventing or reversing soil acidification, chiefly lime, organic amendments and biochar, with careful fertilizer and irrigation management.

facts.text: Liming acidic soils under sugarcane, soybean and corn restored nutrients, raised pH, increased root biomass and improved plant health.
Liming deeper in the soil works better than surface liming but is costlier and harder.
Prevention includes less acidifying fertilizers, timing them to cut nitrate leaching, irrigating with acid-neutralising water and weighing basic nutrients against nitrogen removed in crops.
Sulfur fertilizers should be used only on responsive crops with a high rate of crop recovery.

entries.title: Calcareous soils, built on chalk and limestone

definition.text: Soil formed from or containing a high proportion of calcium carbonate, as calcite or aragonite.

facts.text: Calcareous soils are relatively alkaline because their parent material contains calcium carbonate, and the carbonate ion is a base.
They may have a calcic horizon of secondary carbonates, above 15% calcium carbonate equivalent and at least 5% more carbonate than the layer below.
Calcareous grassland grows on soils rich in calcium carbonate from underlying chalk or limestone.
Calcisols are common on calcareous parent materials in arid and semi-arid environments, and loess is often calcareous.
In such low-acidity soils, earthworms mix humus with the underlying mineral soil to form mull humus.

entries.title: Caliche, the rock that grows inside dry soils

definition.text: A soil accumulation of calcium carbonate at depth, where it precipitates and binds other materials such as gravel, sand, clay and silt.

facts.text: It occurs worldwide in aridisols and mollisols of arid and semiarid regions, such as central and western Australia, the Kalahari and the High Plains of the western United States.
Also called calcrete or kankar, it forms layers from a few inches to feet thick, sometimes called a K horizon.
It forms where annual precipitation is under 65 centimeters and mean annual temperature exceeds 5 °C; wetter climates leach the calcium away.
Root carbon dioxide in the A horizon, up to 15 times atmospheric levels, dissolves calcium carbonate as bicarbonate, which reverts to carbonate in the less active B horizon.
Its depth follows rainfall: about 25 centimeters down at 35 centimeters of rain a year, about 125 centimeters at 75, and gone above 100 centimeters.
Deposition takes several thousand years, and the calcium can arrive as aeolian dust even over calcium-poor bedrock.
Impermeable caliche blocks drainage and roots, and the basic soil it creates can cause iron deficiency that yellows the youngest leaves.
Caliches store significant carbon, mattering to the global carbon cycle, and calcretes in the geologic record preserve past climates.

entries.title: Osmotic pressure: why salty soil starves roots

definition.text: The minimum pressure that must be applied to a solution to stop its pure solvent flowing in across a semipermeable membrane.

facts.text: Osmosis happens when solutions of different solute concentration are separated by a selectively permeable membrane; solvent moves toward the higher-concentration side until osmotic equilibrium.
Van 't Hoff related osmotic pressure to solute concentration: Π = i c R T for low-concentration ideal solutions, so it is a colligative property.
In a hypotonic environment a cell takes in water; in plant cells the wall resists, creating turgor pressure that holds herbaceous plants upright and regulates stomata.
Reverse osmosis applies pressure above the osmotic pressure to purify water; ocean water is about 27 atm.

entries.title: Gypcrust, the gypsum armor of the driest lands

definition.text: A hardened soil layer made of around 95% gypsum (calcium sulfate).

facts.text: It is the arid-climate counterpart of calcrete, which cannot form in very arid climates.
Gypcrust horizons can be up to 5 m thick with 75–97% gypsum, mostly where annual rainfall averages under 250 mm, since gypsum is moderately soluble and leaches under higher rainfall.
It forms in three stages: crystallisation from surface brines or groundwater, transport and redeposition by wind or water, and alteration above or below the capillary fringe.
Gypsum cements are rarely as strong as calcretes or silcretes, though gypcrete has been used for road construction in the Sahara.

entries.title: Halophytes, the plants that thrive on salt

definition.text: A salt-tolerant plant that grows in soils or waters of high salinity, such as salt marshes, mangroves and saline semi-deserts.

facts.text: Perhaps only 2% of plant species are halophytes; most are glycophytes, which high salinity damages fairly easily.
By dissolved solids in irrigation water, beans and rice tolerate about 1–3 g/L, barley and date palm about 5 g/L, and Salicornia bigelovii grows well at 70 g/L.
Iversen (1936) grouped them by soil NaCl: oligo-halophytes at 0.01 to 0.1%, meso-halophytes at 0.1 to 1%, and euhalophytes above 1%.
Halophytes such as Suaeda salsa store salt ions taken from soil, so they can lower soil salinity enough for glycophytes to grow again.

entries.title: Drains that pull salt and water away

definition.text: Land drainage, usually by horizontal but also by vertical systems, that carries salty water away and lowers the water table.

facts.text: In many cases a seasonal average water table depth of 0.6 to 0.8 m is deep enough.
A fluctuating water table helps the soil breathe, expelling root carbon dioxide and drawing in oxygen.
A not-too-deep water table discourages over-irrigation, since crop yields would fall as the water table rose.
Where wet and dry seasons are marked, running drains only in the wet season, called controlled drainage, saves irrigation water.

entries.title: Leaching requirement: the water it takes to hold salt down

definition.text: The amount of water that must percolate through the root zone to keep soil salinity at a desired level, worked out from the salt balance.

facts.text: The water balance of the zone above the water table sets infiltration of rain and irrigation against evaporation, percolation to groundwater and capillary rise.
Leaching efficiency is often 0.7 to 0.8 but can be lower in poorly structured heavy clays; in Portugal's Leziria Grande polder it was only 0.15.
The desired soil salinity depends on the crop's tolerance to salt.
From it the irrigation and drainage needed for salinity control can be computed.

entries.title: Computer models that forecast salt in fields

definition.text: Computer models of water and salt movement in soil used to predict salinity under irrigation and drainage.

facts.text: Most, such as SWAP, DrainMod-S, UnSatChem and Hydrus, combine Richards' equation for unsaturated water flow with Fick's convection–diffusion equation for salts.
They need hard-to-measure soil properties, short time steps and daily or hourly data, and are hard to calibrate because field salinity varies greatly.
Simpler models such as SaltMod use monthly or seasonal water and salt balances for long-term predictions, and SahysMod adds spatial variation with groundwater.

entries.title: SahysMod, a salt forecaster for field engineers

definition.text: A computer program that predicts salinity of soil moisture, groundwater and drainage water, water table depth and drain discharge in irrigated land, mapping spatial variation with a network of polygons.

facts.text: Developed by the Institute for Land Reclamation and Improvement (ILRI), it was designed for field technicians, engineers and planners rather than specialised geohydrologists.
It computes groundwater levels and flows between polygons by numerically solving the Boussinesq equation.
It runs on seasonal inputs and outputs, with one to four seasons a year, and up to 240 internal and 120 external polygons.
Salt balances are computed for each soil reservoir separately, and farmers' responses to waterlogging and salinity can be built in.

entries.title: Sacrificing strips of land to save the rest
entries.article: Soil salinity control#Strip cropping: an alternative

definition.text: Irrigating alternate strips of land and leaving those between permanently fallow, so the fallow strips drain and absorb salt from the cropped ones.

facts.text: The irrigated strips have a higher water table that pushes groundwater toward the unirrigated strips, acting as subsurface drainage and allowing leaching.
In the dry, sacrificial strips groundwater rises by capillarity and evaporates, leaving its salts, so these strips salinize.
The sacrificial strips can carry livestock, salt-resistant grasses or deep-rooted salt-tolerant trees such as Casuarina, Eucalyptus or Atriplex, or be used for salt harvesting.

entries.text: One way to beat salt is to surrender some land to it. In strip cropping for salinity control, alternate strips are irrigated and those between are never planted. The irrigated strips have a higher water table, which pushes groundwater toward the unirrigated ones. That flow acts as subsurface drainage and lets the cropped strips leach. In the dry, sacrificial strips, groundwater rises by capillarity and evaporates, leaving its salts behind, so these strips salinize. They need not be wasted. They can carry livestock, salt-resistant grasses or deep-rooted salt-tolerant trees such as Casuarina, Eucalyptus or Atriplex, or be used for salt harvesting.

entries.title: Alkalinity, a stream's defense against acid

definition.text: The capacity of water to resist acidification, set by its buffer of weak acids and their conjugate bases.

facts.text: It is not the same as basicity, which is an absolute position on the pH scale.
It is measured by titrating with an acid such as HCl to an endpoint, and expressed in units such as meq/L or mg/L as CaCO3.
Alkalinity is low in freshwater on non-limestone terrain and is one of the best measures of a stream's sensitivity to acid inputs.
Acid rain from SOx and NOx emissions can change the alkalinity of streams and rivers over the long term.

entries.title: Chile's nitrate-rich caliche of the Atacama

definition.text: Vast deposits in Chile's Atacama Desert, also called caliche, of gypsum, sodium chloride, other salts and sand together with nitrate minerals (salitre).

facts.text: Salitre is sodium and potassium nitrate; the deposits average 7.5% sodium nitrate, with sodium sulfate, sodium chloride, borate, iodine and perchlorate.
Salitre earned Chile important export revenue until the early 1930s, when Europe began making nitrates industrially in large quantities.
Caliche is Chile's main iodine ore, and the country hosts over half the world's iodine reserves.
Its origin is unclear: an evaporated prehistoric inland sea and weathering of the Andes are both proposed.

entries.title: Framboids, the microscopic raspberries of pyrite

definition.text: A raspberry-like microscopic structure common in some sedimentary minerals, especially pyrite: a roughly spherical cluster of tiny crystals.

facts.text: Clusters average 5-20 μm across and are built of regular microcrystals around 0.5 μm in diameter; the name, first used by Rust in 1935, comes from French 'framboise', raspberry.
In acid sulfate soils, bacteria such as Desulfovibrio desulfuricans reduce sulfate to hydrogen sulfide, which reacts with ferrous iron to form fine, highly reactive framboidal pyrite.
Framboidal pyrite is common in coastal sediments such as marsh soils, estuarine sediments and beach sands; greigite is considered an essential precursor.
Once thought to be fossil bacterial colonies, framboids have since been made in the laboratory and found in places hostile to microbial life.

entries.title: Brønsted–Lowry: acids give protons, bases take them

definition.text: A theory of acids and bases in which an acid is a proton donor and a base is a proton acceptor.

facts.text: When an acid and a base react, the acid becomes its conjugate base and the base becomes its conjugate acid by exchanging a proton (H+).
The theory was proposed independently in 1923 by Brønsted in Denmark and Lowry in England, and it generalises the Arrhenius theory.
Acetic acid donates a proton to water and becomes acetate; water accepts it and becomes the hydronium ion. Unlike Arrhenius theory, an acid need not dissociate.
An acid is only an acid relative to a base. Water is amphoteric, acting as acid or base, and aluminium hydroxide also reacts with both OH− and H+.
Lewis theory, from the same year, defines a base as an electron-pair donor and an acid as an electron-pair acceptor, and explains the Brønsted–Lowry classification through electronic structure.
Metal aqua cations behave as acids in Brønsted–Lowry terms.

entries.title: Buffer solutions: why pH resists change

definition.text: A solution whose pH changes little on dilution or when a small amount of strong acid or base is added.

facts.text: A buffer resists pH change through the equilibrium between a weak acid HA and its conjugate base A−; added acid shifts the equilibrium toward HA (Le Chatelier's principle), so hydrogen ion concentration rises less than expected.
Added alkali likewise lowers hydrogen ion concentration by less than the amount expected.
The buffer region lies at pH = pKa ± 1, centred where [HA] = [A−]; once the acid is more than 95% deprotonated, pH rises rapidly.
Buffer capacity measures the strong acid or base needed to change the pH of a given volume by a given amount; it is highest when a large addition produces only a small pH change.
Capacity considers a macroscopic change of 1 pH unit, whereas the buffer index considers an infinitesimal change.
Polyprotic acids have several pKa values; when successive values differ by less than about 3 their ranges overlap, so citric acid buffers across pH 2.5 to 7.5.
A buffer can be made by mixing an acid with its conjugate base, such as acetic acid with sodium acetate, or by adding strong acid or base to a buffering agent.
Cation-exchange capacity is often measured with a buffer solution at a set pH, and fens keep a stable pH through bicarbonate buffering.

entries.title: Electrolytic conductivity, a quick read on salt

definition.text: A measure of how well a solution of ions conducts electricity, used to gauge how much dissolved salt it holds.

facts.text: Its SI unit is the siemens per metre (S/m).
Measuring it is a fast, cheap and reliable way to find a solution's ionic content, and it is often linked directly to total dissolved solids.
Typical drinking water runs 200–800 μS/cm, while sea water is about 50 mS/cm.

entries.title: How drained pyrite turns into sulfuric acid
entries.article: Acid sulfate soil#Generalised Pyrite Oxidation Reaction

definition.text: The oxidation of pyrite in drained soils to sulfuric acid and iron(III) hydroxide, which can make the soil extremely acidic.

facts.text: The overall reaction is 4FeS2 + 15O2 + 14H2O → 16H+ + 8SO42− + 4Fe(OH)3.
The orange iron(III) hydroxide precipitates and locks up the alkalinity, while the acidity stays active as sulfuric acid.
The acidity frees large amounts of Al3+ from clay minerals, harmful to vegetation, and leaves hydrogen clay, which is stable but poor in nutrients.
Other products include hydrogen sulfide, sulfur, hematite, goethite and iron sulfates such as jarosite, so these soils range from black and blue-gray to red, orange and yellow.

entries.title: Acid base accounting: balancing a soil's acid books

definition.text: The practice of quantifying the sources of acidity and alkalinity in acid sulfate soils so they can be managed.

facts.text: It is used, for example, to work out how much lime is needed to neutralise sulfidic material dug up or dredged.
Net acidity is potential sulfidic acidity plus titratable actual acidity plus retained acidity, minus the acid neutralising capacity, in mol H+ per tonne of dry soil.

Potential sulfidic acidity measures oxidisable reduced inorganic sulfur such as iron sulfides; the chromium reducible sulfur test measures it without interference from sulfate minerals or organic matter.
Samples oxidise rapidly in air, so they should be cooled below 4°C at once, and monosulfidic samples frozen.

entries.title: Keeping acid sulfate soils wet and safe

definition.text: Keeping acid sulfate soils wet, restoring their water table or neutralising their acid to prevent or repair acidification.

facts.text: On a Malaysian oil palm estate, yields fell from 17 tons of fresh fruit per ha in 1960 to 2 in 1965 after drainage was deepened in 1962, recovering after the water table was raised in 1966.
Aggressive drainage of potentially acid sulfate soils in the second half of the 20th century had disastrous results: barren land and clear, lifeless water.
Where soils cannot be kept wet, surface drainage in rainy periods removes acids formed in dry spells and can reclaim the soil in the long run.
When Australia's millennium drought exposed them, a bund, pumping and aerial limestone dosing were used to stop acidification of the Lower Lakes.

entries.title: Sulfidic and sulfuric: naming the danger in the mud
entries.article: Acid sulfate soil#Sulfidic and Sulfuric Material

definition.text: Diagnostic materials of acid sulfate soils: sulfidic material holds detectable inorganic sulfides, and sulfuric material has a pH below 4 from their oxidation.

facts.text: Sulfidic material holds at least 0.01% sulfidic sulfur in layers at least 30 mm thick, and is divided into hyposulfidic, hypersulfidic and monosulfidic classes.
Hypersulfidic material would fall below pH 4 if exposed to oxidising conditions and hyposulfidic would not, though its weathering still yields saline solutions with hazardous metals.
Coined mainly by Fanning, Rabenhorst and Fitzpatrick, the terms are diagnostic features in the Australian Soil Classification and the World Reference Base.
The term 'self-neutralising' acid sulfate soil is discouraged because it suggests the soil is not hazardous.

entries.title: Keeping water out of salty groundwater

definition.text: Reducing dryland salinity by cutting groundwater recharge through soils and vegetation, and coping with salt where groundwater discharges.

facts.text: Soils take up water by their field capacity and starting dryness, so the drier a soil enters winter, the more water it can store instead of leaking to groundwater.

Cutting recharge to pre-clearing levels is usually infeasible because too few profitable perennials can replace crops, so the aim is to minimise it with alley farming, perennials and winter–spring leaf cover.
In discharge areas salinity is managed with salt-tolerant plants or with engineering such as deep open drains, pumps and siphons.
Recharge is also the source of fresh groundwater, so its use must be traded off against salinity.

entries.title: Natural salt and the salt people make

definition.text: The division of salinity into primary salinity, which is natural, and secondary salinity, which human activity induces.

facts.text: Primary salinity occurs naturally in arid and saline settings such as salt lakes, marshes, pans and salt flats, left by past cycles of drainage, desiccation and sea winds.
Secondary salinity results directly from development, agriculture and irrigation, harming biodiversity and land productivity.
Secondary salinisation can make soils dispersive, so excess salt also needs managing at landscape scale.

entries.title: Saltwater intrusion: the sea creeping into aquifers

definition.text: The movement of saline water into freshwater aquifers, degrading groundwater quality.

facts.text: It occurs naturally in coastal aquifers: denser saline water pushes inland beneath the fresh water.
Pumping from coastal freshwater wells lowers the fresh groundwater's pressure and lets saltwater flow further inland.
Agricultural and drainage channels, sea level rise and storm surges also drive it.
Seawater intrusion into rivers can harm agriculture in upstream areas.

entries.title: Saline seeps, where salty groundwater surfaces

definition.text: A seep of saline water where alkali salt crystals form as the salty water reaches the surface and evaporates.

facts.text: Seeps form by capillary rise from a water table below the surface or where a water table flows out at the surface.
Saline discharge areas are called seeps where groundwater meets the soil surface, and scalds where water is lost by evaporation only.
They harm agriculture by reducing yields and restricting growth, yet host salt-adapted and often endemic organisms.

entries.title: Halotolerance: living with more salt than needed

definition.text: The ability of an organism to live in salt concentrations above those it needs for growth.

facts.text: Halotolerant bacteria, archaea and fungi live in saline waters and soils; unlike halophiles they do not need high salinity.
High salt in soil or water upsets ionic balance, impairing respiration and photosynthesis and slowing growth or killing sensitive plants.
Salinity places both osmotic and ionic stress on cells, which drives water out, so tolerant organisms retain water and sequester salt.
Halotolerant bacteria can remediate saline soil by lowering its sodium content and sodium adsorption ratio and by degrading toxic compounds.

entries.title: Maas–Hoffman: the yield line that bends under salt

definition.text: A mathematical model of how crop yield responds to soil salinity, drawn as a horizontal line that breaks into a downward slope.

facts.text: The breakpoint, or tolerance, is the salinity up to which yield is unaffected; beyond it yield falls.
Yield Y equals the maximum C below the breakpoint Pb and AX + B above it, where X is soil salinity, A the slope and B the regression constant.
Pb is found by regression and optimisation for the best fit, but a flat tail in the data can give a misleadingly low breakpoint.
An inverted form serves factors such as water table depth that cut yields only at low values.

entries.title: Road salt: winter safety that lingers in the soil

definition.text: The salt spread on roads and walkways to melt ice, and its build-up in roadside soils and waters.

facts.text: Sodium chloride is the most common form; calcium and magnesium chlorides are used too, especially in colder weather.
Millions of tons are applied to roads each year, making it one of the most widely used chemicals in urban infrastructure.
Chloride from road salt persists in soils, surface waters and groundwater, harming aquatic life, roadside vegetation and drinking water.
Salt build-up in roadside soils raises their salinity, hindering plant growth, killing sensitive species and adding to soil erosion.

entries.title: The Van Genuchten–Gupta curve of yield against salt

definition.text: An inverted S-curve relating crop yield to soil salinity.

facts.text: It is named after Martinus Theodore van Genuchten and Satyandra K. Gupta, from their work in the 1990s.
Yield is Y = Ym / (1 + (C/C50)^P), where Ym is maximum yield, C the soil salt concentration, C50 the concentration giving 50% yield and P a fitted exponent.
A logistic S-function or a cubic regression of yield on soil salt concentration can be used instead.

entries.title: Exchangeable sodium percentage and the swelling of clay

definition.text: The share of a soil's exchangeable cations, and so of its cation-exchange capacity, that is sodium, expressed as a percentage.

facts.text: Calculated as sodium divided by total cations times 100, it is a key indicator of dispersive soils.
High sodium makes wet particles repel one another, so soils with a high ESP lose structure as their aggregates disperse.
Clay with an ESP above 16 in contact with non-saline water has an expanded double layer, so the soil swells and disperses.
Applying gypsum lowers ESP by displacing sodium with calcium.
Clays with an ESP near 100%, almost fully sodium-saturated, are called bentonite and are used to make impermeable curtains below dams.

entries.title: Alkali soils, clay ruined by sodium carbonate

definition.text: A clay soil with a high pH, generally above 8.5, often with poor structure and low infiltration capacity.

facts.text: Its poor properties come mainly from sodium carbonate, which makes the soil swell and hard to settle; such soils are also called alkaline sodic soils.
Alkali soils often have a hard calcareous layer 0.5 to 1 metre beneath the surface.
Alkalinity comes from sodium carbonate and bicarbonate, released by weathering of soil minerals or brought in by irrigation and flood water.
Na2CO3 is about 78000 times more soluble than CaCO3, so it can push pH above 8.5, the most calcium carbonate in equilibrium with dissolved carbon dioxide allows.
As Ca2+ precipitates, clays take up Na+ and their ESP rises; above an ESP of 16 they swell and disperse, crusting and compacting the topsoil and cutting infiltration.
Alkalinity is worse in clay soils, especially swelling montmorillonite or smectite clays, and alkaline soils are in principle not saline, since alkalinity worsens as salinity falls.
Rainwater stagnates and evaporates on the surface, so farming is mostly limited to crops tolerant of waterlogging, such as rice.
Irrigation with softened water, its calcium and magnesium replaced by sodium, dissolves organic matter and disperses clay, giving the structure typical of alkali soils.

entries.title: How people make soils alkaline

definition.text: Soil alkalinity caused by people, mainly through sodium salts and lime that reach soil in irrigation water, effluent and industrial emissions.

facts.text: Fly ash from coal-fired boilers contains calcium oxide, which dissolves to slaked lime, Ca(OH)2, and is carried by runoff into rivers and irrigation systems.
Lime softening precipitates Ca2+ and Mg2+ from water and converts its sodium bicarbonate into sodium carbonate.
Sodium from industrial and household salts enters surface water and groundwater; global sodium chloride consumption was 280 million tons in 2020.
Sodium salt loads are worst downstream in intensively cultivated river basins, where salts concentrate in the water left after transpiration and evaporation.

entries.title: Farming fish on land too salty for crops
entries.article: Alkali soil#Remediation and utilization via aquaculture

definition.text: Using fish and seafood farming on saline-alkali land to leach salts, add organic matter and put non-arable land to use.

facts.text: Research and experiments in China and elsewhere since the 1990s have combined agriculture and aquaculture on alkali land with considerable success.
Farmed species include shrimps, crabs, shellfish and fish such as sea bass and grouper, raised in inland saline-alkali water.
China's Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs recommends it as an economically viable and environmentally beneficial way to use saline-alkali land.

entries.title: Residual sodium carbonate: rating water's alkali threat

definition.text: An index of the alkalinity hazard that irrigation water or soil water poses to soil.

facts.text: It judges irrigation water for clay soils with a high cation-exchange capacity, where sodium high relative to calcium and magnesium makes clay swell or disperse and infiltration collapse.
RSC = (HCO3− + CO32−) − (Ca2+ + Mg2+) in meq/L; for irrigation it should not be much above 1 and preferably below 0.5.
Unlike saline water, high-RSC water does not raise osmotic pressure against root uptake, but irrigating clay soils with it creates fallow alkali soils.
Soda ash from weathered basalt, lime from burnt calcareous coal, and industrial soda ash raise river water RSC, often making lower reaches unfit for irrigation.

entries.title: Gypsum, the calcium cure for sodium-sick soils

definition.text: Gypsum (calcium sulfate) applied to soil as a fertilizer and amendment, supplying calcium and sulfur without generally changing soil pH.

facts.text: It is used to reclaim saline and sodic soils regardless of pH, lowering the exchangeable sodium percentage.
In sodic and acidic soils it turns soluble sodium metaborate into less soluble calcium metaborate and reduces aluminium and boron toxicity.
It also improves soil structure, water absorption and aeration.
In the late 18th and early 19th centuries Nova Scotia gypsum, called plaster, was a sought-after fertilizer for US wheat fields.

entries.title: Reclaiming alkali soils with calcium, acid and drains

definition.text: Improving alkali soils by supplying calcium or acidifying material to replace or neutralise excess sodium, and leaching the sodium away.

facts.text: Gypsum supplies Ca2+ to replace sodium on the exchange complex and turns sodium carbonate into neutral sodium sulphate.
Enough natural or artificial subsurface drainage is needed for rain or irrigation water to leach the excess sodium.
Acidifying minerals such as pyrite, alum or aluminium sulfate, calcium chloride, calcium nitrate and spent acids can also be used.
Soils with solid CaCO3 can be reclaimed with grass, compost and other organic waste that adds acidifying material and releases CO2 to dissolve calcium.
Efforts usually target the top 10 cm, and treatments need repeating in about 5 years as amendments leach or decompose.
Halophytes such as glasswort, saltwort or barilla absorb sodium carbonate into their tissues, a form of phytoremediation; their ash yields soda.
Saline soils are mostly also sodic but keep good structure, so leaching does not usually turn them into alkali soils and they mostly need no gypsum.

entries.title: Critical loads: how much acid rain a landscape can bear

definition.text: A quantitative estimate of pollutant exposure below which significant harm to specified sensitive parts of the environment does not occur, as far as is known.

facts.text: Work has centred on sulfur and nitrogen deposition, both of which can acidify soils and surface waters.
As acidifying agents they can strip calcium from soil and release toxic aluminium, harming plants and animals.
Deposition above the critical load is an exceedance, putting the biota at greater risk of ecological harm.

In Europe a sensitive element is tied to a chemical criterion, such as the soil base cation to aluminium ratio with a limit of Bc/Al = 1, and a mass balance model gives the deposition that reaches it.
Today a two-dimensional critical load function is often calculated, with nitrogen deposition on one axis and sulfur deposition on the other.
It is a steady-state concept that says nothing about how long effects take to appear; target load functions add a time dimension.
Empirical critical loads come from observed ecosystem responses, while steady-state mass balance ones come from models that can include soil chemistry and mineral weathering rates.

entries.title: Biosaline agriculture: farming land too salty for crops

definition.text: Growing plants with saline groundwater or on saline soil, using salt-tolerant plants to farm land too salty for ordinary crops.

facts.text: Halophytes are its cornerstone, used for food and forage, restoring salty land, medicine and biofuel.
Irrigating with high-salinity water eases pressure on scarce fresh water, especially in arid and semi-arid regions with brackish or saline sources.
Soil salinization affects an estimated one billion hectares worldwide, with another one million hectares added each year.
Salinity affects one quarter of global arable land and is projected to double by 2050.
Repeated cycles of halophyte growth can restore degraded soil and water; the plants also accumulate heavy metals from soils and groundwater.
Salinity troubles date back to Mesopotamia, where widespread soil salinization from poor irrigation helped bring the civilizations down, from 2400 BC to 1700 BC.
The field was formalized in the late 1990s, with the International Center for Biosaline Agriculture founded in 1996.

entries.title: How organic matter adds to a soil's CEC

definition.text: Well-humified organic matter and clay minerals together supply a soil's cation exchange capacity, and the organic share can be estimated from pH and organic matter content.

facts.text: A soil's total CEC is the sum of the CEC due to organic matter and that due to clays; in fine soils with medium to high-CEC clays most of it is clay-based.
In sandy loams with little clay, and in southeastern US and tropical soils with low-CEC clays, organic matter may supply most of the CEC.
CEC is expressed as milliequivalents of negative charge per 100 g of soil.
Rule of thumb: for every pH unit above 4.5, organic matter gives 1 me of CEC per 100 g of soil for each percent of organic matter; at pH 6 and 3% organic matter this is 4.5 me/100 g.

entries.title: Managing salty soil where the groundwater is deep

definition.text: Where saline soils have no shallow salty groundwater, salinity is handled by keeping soil moist, growing tolerant crops and leaching.

facts.text: Keeping soil continually moist, as with low-salt drip irrigation plus mulch, stops salt concentrating as the soil dries.
Tolerant plants include barley, bermuda grass, oak, rosemary and willow, but only washing salt below the root zone removes it.
Poorly draining subsoil may need drainage tiles, which discharge salty water that can harm downstream water.
Seawater flooding after storm surges can make soils sodic, treated by gypsum, or lime where the soil is naturally acidic.

entries.title: Copper deficiency in high-pH and organic soils

definition.text: Copper is sometimes deficient in high-pH soils and in organic soils.

facts.text: It can also be deficient in organic soils with 10-20% or more organic matter; tomatoes, lettuce, beets, onions and spinach have relatively high copper needs.
Copper sulfate and copper chelates correct a deficiency.
Most soil sulfur is in organic matter, so maintaining organic matter usually supplies enough; deficiency is likelier on acidic sandy soils and cold, dry spring soils with slow mineralization.
Deficiency is spreading in places as sulfur air pollution from coal falls, while Great Plains irrigation water may supply enough sulfur.

entries.title: Reserve acidity: the acid hiding on soil solids

definition.text: Reserve acidity is the acid held on soil solids, mostly on organic matter and as aluminum, which dwarfs the acid in the soil water.

facts.text: Almost all of a soil's acid sits in reserve on the solids; only an extremely small amount is active in the soil water.
Neutralizing only the acid in the water would need a few handfuls of lime per acre, but raising pH takes tons per acre.
As H+ is removed from organic matter new CEC sites appear; as soils acidify, H+ takes over CEC sites and cuts their hold on calcium, magnesium, potassium and ammonium.
Alfalfa, from semiarid high-pH regions, needs pH 6.5-6.8 or higher; most states recommend about 6.8 only for the most sensitive crops and 6.2-6.5 for many clovers.

entries.title: Manganese toxicity, when acid soil poisons plants

definition.text: Poisoning of plants by manganese that becomes soluble at low soil pH.

facts.text: With aluminium toxicity it is a serious problem in Alisols, whose low pH makes normally insoluble metals soluble enough to poison intolerant plants.
It may occur in strongly acidic horizons, especially when they are waterlogged.
Liming with finely ground limestone or dolomite to bring acid soil near neutral reduces aluminium and manganese toxicity.

entries.title: Efflorescence: salt crusts on the surface

definition.text: The migration of a salt to the surface of a porous material, where it forms a coating.

facts.text: Water dissolves a salt held inside, carries it to the surface and evaporates, leaving a salt coating. It occurs in natural and built environments.
In primary efflorescence the water is the invader and the salt was already inside; in secondary efflorescence salt from outside is carried in solution into the material.
Salt crystals can clog pores and destroy the material through internal water pressure, as in the spalling of brick.

entries.title: The crowded underworld that keeps soil alive

definition.text: The study of the activity and ecology of the microbes and animals that live in soil.

facts.text: Soil life, also called soil biota or edaphon, covers every organism that spends a significant part of its life cycle in the soil profile or at the soil-litter interface.
Soil organisms include bacteria, fungi, protozoa, nematodes, earthworms and arthropods, along with some snakes and burrowing mammals such as gophers, moles and prairie dogs.
Soil is home to circa 59% of the world's biodiversity.
By decomposing organic matter, soil organisms release nutrients for plants and strongly shape soil fertility, plant growth, soil structure and carbon storage.
Soil life powers nutrient cycles: without it, organic material would pile up as undecayed litter, with no humus and no nutrients available to plants.
Nutrients held in the bodies of soil organisms are kept from leaching away, nitrogen and phosphorus in particular.
Microbial exudates help maintain soil structure, and earthworms mix the soil through bioturbation.
It is a relatively new science with much still unknown; the discovery of glomalin in 1996 showed that basic questions about soil biogeochemical cycles remained open.

entries.title: Soil microbiology and the 33,000 species on a beet root

definition.text: The study of the microorganisms in soil, what they do and how they affect soil properties.

facts.text: Soil microorganisms are grouped as bacteria (including cyanobacteria and actinomycetes), archaea, fungi, algae, slime molds and protozoa.
The first cyanobacteria, which arose two to four billion years ago, fixed carbon and nitrogen, releasing oxygen into the air and nitrogen into the soil.
Microbial diversity in soil depends on pH, texture, organic matter content, plant community and contaminants such as heavy metals.
In 2011 more than 33,000 bacterial and archaeal species were detected on sugar beet roots.
Microbes make soil nutrients more available to plants, produce growth hormones, stimulate plant immunity and trigger or dampen plant stress responses.
A more diverse soil microbiome generally brings fewer plant diseases and higher crop yields.
Soil microbes communicate through soluble metabolites, volatile organic compounds and extracellular polysaccharides, and exchange metabolites that support one another's growth.
Cover crops raise soil microbial activity, improving nitrogen availability, crop nitrogen uptake and yields.

entries.title: Biomineralization: life that builds with stone

definition.text: The process by which living organisms produce or retain inorganic minerals, often hardening or stiffening their tissues.

facts.text: It is extremely widespread: every major lineage of the biosphere has mineral-forming members, and over 60 different minerals have been identified in organisms.
Most biominerals are silicates, carbonates or phosphates: silica in algae, diatoms and sponges, carbonates in invertebrates, and calcium phosphates and carbonates in vertebrates.
The most common are calcium phosphate and carbonate salts, used with organic polymers such as collagen and chitin to give bones and shells their structural support.
Bacteria take part in copper, iron and gold deposits; microorganisms can precipitate metals from solution and can also catalyse the dissolution of minerals.
It plays global roles in shaping the planet, in biogeochemical cycles and as a carbon sink.
Bicarbonate released by weathering and carried through soil to the sea is biomineralized there into carbonate minerals for shells and skeletons.
Microbes can clean uranium-contaminated groundwater by releasing phosphate, which precipitates uranium phosphate minerals and so reduces the uranium's mobility.
The first evidence of biomineralization dates to some 750 million years ago, and organisms have made mineralized skeletons for the past 550 million years.

entries.text: Every major lineage of living things has members that make minerals. Biomineralization is the process by which organisms produce or retain inorganic minerals, often to harden or stiffen their tissues. Over 60 different minerals have been identified in organisms. Most are silicates, carbonates or phosphates. Algae, diatoms and sponges build with silica, invertebrates with carbonates, and vertebrates with calcium phosphates and carbonates. Calcium phosphate and carbonate salts are the most common. Paired with organic polymers such as collagen and chitin, they give bones and shells their structural support. Microbes work on a geological scale. Bacteria take part in forming copper, iron and gold deposits, and microorganisms can both precipitate metals from solution and catalyze the dissolution of minerals. Soil sits inside a planetary loop. Bicarbonate released by weathering travels through soil to the sea, where it is turned into carbonate minerals for shells and skeletons. That makes biomineralization a store that locks carbon away, and a force in {{ref:soil-fert-140}}. It can even clean up pollution. Microbes that release phosphate precipitate uranium phosphate minerals in contaminated groundwater, so the uranium moves less. The first evidence of biomineralization dates to some 750 million years ago, and organisms have made mineralized skeletons for the past 550 million years.

entries.title: Why ecologists treat soil as an ecosystem

definition.text: The study of how soil organisms interact with one another and with their environment.

facts.text: This branch of ecology is especially concerned with nutrient cycling, soil aggregate formation and soil biodiversity.
Because soil is so complex and internally connected, soil ecologists regard it as an ecosystem.
Soil is a heterogeneous mix of minerals and organic matter whose variations in structure, nutrients, moisture, temperature and pH support different organisms.
Moisture is a major limiting factor: soil organisms constantly face dehydration, and microbial communities shift through cycles of drying and rewetting.
Soil temperature fluctuates less with depth and governs microbial and enzyme activity, mineralization and decomposition.
Most soil organisms are aerobic: microbes grow in air-filled micropores, while larger animals need macropores or water films to move about.
Patchy soil properties across the landscape, and changes between horizons, make soil communities patchy and stratified with depth.
Soil organisms remain underrepresented in studies and models of soil processes, partly from assuming that much below-ground diversity is ecologically redundant.

entries.title: Five hundred sheep beneath a football pitch

definition.text: The relationship between soil and the variety of life, and the aspects of soil that can be managed with that variety in mind.

facts.text: Soil is a habitat chiefly for microbes such as bacteria and fungi, but also for microfauna (protozoa, nematodes), mesofauna (microarthropods, enchytraeids) and macrofauna (earthworms, termites, millipedes).
The primary role of soil biota is to recycle organic matter that comes from the above-ground, plant-based food web.
In turn, biological activity is a primary factor in the physical and chemical formation of soil.
Natural and agricultural vegetation boundaries closely follow soil boundaries, even at continental and global scales.
Microbial exudates are now accepted as dominating the aggregation of soil particles and the protection of carbon from further breakdown.
The organisms beneath a football pitch are estimated to equal the size of 500 sheep.
Soil health depends on soil biodiversity and can be improved by keeping living covers on the soil and adding carbon-containing amendments.
Management matters: crop rotation, crop diversification, legume intercrops and organic inputs correlate with higher soil diversity.

entries.title: Burning a sample to measure its organic carbon

definition.text: An analytical measure of the concentration of organic carbon in a sample.

facts.text: Total carbon is the organic carbon plus the inorganic carbon, such as that in carbonate minerals; analysers measure only total carbon, so the inorganic part is subtracted or first driven off with acid.

The sample's carbon is oxidized to carbon dioxide, for example by combustion at 1000 up to 1200 °C or on a catalyst at 680 up to 950 °C, and most modern analysers read the gas by non-dispersive infrared.
Soil organic matter content can be calculated from it; in the UK, guideline values for pollutants such as phenol and toluene depend on that content.
It also serves as a non-specific indicator of water quality and is the first chemical analysis made on potential petroleum source rock.

entries.title: Oligotrophs, the slow specialists of scarcity

definition.text: An organism able to live where nutrients are available only at very low levels.

facts.text: The word joins the Greek oligos ('few') and trophikos ('feeding'); oligotrophs are contrasted with copiotrophs, which prefer nutrient-rich environments.
They grow slowly, have low metabolic rates and generally live at low population densities.

'Oligotrophic' describes land and water with very low concentrations of nitrates, iron, phosphates and carbon sources, such as deep ocean sediments, caves, polar ice, aquifers, deep subsurface soil and leached soils.
They survive scarcity by switching on genes during low-nutrient periods, but excess nutrients overwhelm their metabolism, and their enzymes struggle in rich conditions.
Lichens, with their extremely low metabolic rate, and the cave-dwelling olm are examples of oligotrophic organisms.
Elevated carbon dioxide would speed plant and microbial growth, slow the soil carbon cycle and favour oligotrophs, which are slower-growing and more resource-efficient than copiotrophs.

entries.title: Why so many animals choose life underground

definition.text: The animals that live in soil for their whole life or at least as larvae; about 30% of arthropods live in soil.

facts.text: Soil shelters animals from swings in temperature and moisture and from predators, supplies food all year and offers a safe place to lay eggs.
By increasing body size, soil fauna are classed as microfauna (20 μm to 200 μm), mesofauna (200 μm to 2 mm), macrofauna (2 mm to 2 cm) and megafauna (more than 2 cm).
Size sets an animal's place in the soil food web: bigger species eat smaller ones or modify their environment.
Many are adapted to life underground: smaller, blind, unpigmented, legless or short-legged, and often reproducing asexually.
They are tightly linked with microbes, which feed them and help digest tough compounds, while the animals' guts, faeces and cavities house microbes, disperse them and regulate their numbers.
Soil may have been a crucible for the evolution of land invertebrates, a step between aquatic and aerial life.
Animals must be extracted, expelled, trapped or hand-sorted and named by specialists, which slowed soil zoology; DNA barcoding now yields full species lists, cryptic species included.
Whether and how fertilizers affect soil animals is still debated; organic fertilizers raised soil fauna abundance while mineral fertilizers did not.

entries.contested_note: Sources say it is still debated whether and how fertilizers affect soil animals.
entries.text: About 30% of all arthropods live in soil. Soil animals are those that spend their whole life there, or at least their larval stage. The soil shelters them from swings in temperature and moisture and from predators. It supplies food all year and a safe place to lay eggs. By body size they fall into four classes: 20 μm to 200 μm, 200 μm to 2 mm, 2 mm to 2 cm, and more than 2 cm. Size sets an animal's place in the {{ref:soil-bio-025}}, since bigger species eat smaller ones or reshape their surroundings. Many bear the marks of underground life. They tend to be smaller, blind, unpigmented, legless or short-legged, and often reproduce asexually. They are tightly bound to microbes, which feed them and help digest tough compounds. In return, the animals' guts, feces and cavities house microbes, spread them and regulate their numbers. Soil may even have been a crucible for the evolution of land invertebrates, a step between life in water and life in air. Studying them is slow. Each animal must be extracted, expelled, trapped or hand-sorted, then named by a specialist. DNA barcoding now yields full species lists, cryptic species included. One question stays open: researchers still debate whether and how fertilizers affect soil animals. In the sources, {{ref:soil-fert-010}} raised soil animal numbers while mineral fertilizers did not.

entries.title: The earthworm, which Darwin ranked among history's great movers

definition.text: A soil-dwelling invertebrate of the phylum Annelida; the name covers the largest members of the Oligochaeta.

facts.text: Found mostly in moist, compost-rich soil, earthworms eat detritus along with protozoa, nematodes, bacteria, fungi and algae, and rank among nature's most important detritivores.
Adults range from 10 mm long to 3 m, but the typical Lumbricus terrestris grows to about 360 mm.
They move by waves of muscle contraction anchored by bristles called setae, and breathe through their moist skin, having no special respiratory organs.
Populations depend on soil temperature, moisture, pH, salts, aeration and texture; most favour neutral to slightly acidic soils, and their activity can shift pH to suit them.
Their activity aerates and mixes soil, favours nutrient mineralization and uptake by plants, and links organic matter to soil minerals.
They are indicators of soil health: healthy soil holds more earthworms, and their gut microbes reveal the condition of the soil.
Nitrogen fertilizers create acidity fatal to worms and pesticides kill them; at least three species are listed as extinct and many more endangered.
In 1881 Charles Darwin wrote that few other animals had played so important a part in the history of the world.

entries.title: Detritivores, the shredders that keep litter from piling up

definition.text: A heterotroph that gets its nutrients by eating detritus: decomposing plant and animal parts and faeces.

facts.text: Detritivores swallow discrete lumps of matter, unlike decomposers such as bacteria and fungi, which absorb food at a molecular scale; the two terms are often confused.
Typical soil detritivores include millipedes, springtails, woodlice, slugs and many worms.
They carry out the first stage of remineralization by fragmenting dead plant matter, letting decomposers complete the second.
Plant litter does not pile up in nature because of them, even though cellulose, lignin and xylan decay much more slowly than other organic molecules.
Together with decomposers they return carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, calcium and potassium to the soil for plants to use.
Detritus feeders mainly digest the protein-rich microbes growing on detritus and excrete the detritus itself little changed.
Moist soil increases their feeding and excretion; in deserts they shelter in burrows and are the main clearers of plant litter.
In the Carboniferous, fungi and bacteria could not yet digest lignin, so dead plant tissue piled up and later became fossil fuels.

entries.text: Dead leaves and stems do not pile up in nature, and detritivores are the reason. A detritivore is a heterotroph, an organism that must eat to get its carbon, that feeds on {{ref:soil-bio-112}}: decomposing plant and animal parts and feces. It swallows discrete lumps of matter. Decomposers such as bacteria and fungi instead absorb their food at a molecular scale, and the two terms are often confused. Typical soil detritivores include millipedes, {{ref:soil-bio-085}}, woodlice, slugs and many worms. They do the first stage of returning dead matter to mineral form, fragmenting plant remains so decomposers can complete the second. Together the two groups return carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, calcium and potassium to the soil for plants. They keep litter moving even though cellulose, xylan and other woody compounds decay much more slowly than other organic molecules. Oddly, these feeders mainly digest the protein-rich microbes growing on dead matter and excrete the dead matter itself little changed. Moist soil increases their feeding. In deserts they shelter in burrows and are the main clearers of fallen plant matter. The past shows a world without full decay. In the Carboniferous, fungi and bacteria could not yet digest {{ref:soil-bio-116}}, so dead plant tissue piled up and later became fossil fuels.

entries.title: The soil food web, a digestive system for the land

definition.text: The community of organisms living all or part of their lives in the soil, viewed as the network of feeding links that passes energy among them.

facts.text: Unlike a food chain, which follows one linear energy pathway, a food web shows all the potential pathways.
Plants are the producers, using sunlight to make plant material from carbon dioxide and minerals; their roots exude acids, sugars and enzymes that feed the web underground.
Its members range from bacteria, algae, fungi and protozoa to nematodes and microarthropods, and on to earthworms, insects and small vertebrates.
Decomposers such as bacteria and fungi break dead plant and animal material into simple nutrients; all soil organic matter is processed through the web as in a digestive system.
It keeps manure, plant residues and pesticides out of water, holds nitrogen back from groundwater, fixes nitrogen and raises infiltration.
Soil organisms also prey on crop pests and feed animals above ground.
Once thought simple, soil food webs proved to have common omnivory and long, complex chains that still resist drying, freezing and fumigation.
Litter transformers, mutualists and ecosystem engineers strongly affect their communities in ways food webs do not capture.

entries.title: Soil respiration: the ground breathes out carbon

definition.text: The production of carbon dioxide by respiring roots, rhizosphere microbes and soil fauna below ground.

facts.text: It is a key ecosystem process that returns soil carbon to the air as CO2: carbon fixed by photosynthesis is respired by roots or by the heterotrophs that consume plant material.
Temperature, moisture, nutrient content and oxygen make rates vary enormously; oxygen gradients in aggregates create anoxic microsites where anaerobic metabolism dominates.
Researchers estimate that soil respiration releases 77 Pg of carbon a year, more than human sources such as fossil fuel burning.
Global soils hold up to 3150 Pg of carbon, more than four times the atmosphere, so a small change in soil respiration can upset the balance of atmospheric CO2.
Litter decomposition, a major part of it, releases CO2 while immobilizing or mineralizing nutrients, so respiration rates track microbial turnover and nitrogen mineralization.
Tillage usually increases soil respiration, depleting soil organic matter.
Between 1989 and 2008 soil respiration increased by about 0.1% per year.
It forms a positive feedback with climate: warming raises respiration and so CO2; a 2 °C rise is estimated to add 10 Pg of carbon a year from soils.

conflicts.text: In 2008 the global total of CO2 released by soil respiration was roughly 98 billion tonnes.

entries.title: Litter dwellers, soil eaters and deep diggers

definition.text: The grouping of earthworms by where they live and feed: epigeic, endogeic and anecic.

facts.text: Epigeic worms live in leaf litter or compost at the soil-litter interface, do not burrow and eat decomposing organic matter; Eisenia fetida is one.
Endogeic worms live in topsoil or subsoil, eat soil and make horizontal burrows in the upper 10–30 cm.
Anecic worms ('reaching up'), such as Lumbricus terrestris, build permanent deep vertical burrows and come up to gather leaves, mixing surface organic matter into mineral soil.
Epigeic Eisenia species suit vermicomposting because they eat fresh organic matter without burrowing and tolerate the heat of compost heaps.
Healthy soil holds a larger number and biomass of earthworms, especially endogeic and anecic species.

entries.text: Not all earthworms live the same life. Ecologists group them by where they live and feed into three categories: epigeic, endogeic and anecic. Epigeic worms live in leaf litter or compost where litter meets soil. They do not burrow, and they eat decaying plant and animal matter; Eisenia fetida is one. Because they eat fresh waste without burrowing and tolerate the heat of compost heaps, epigeic Eisenia species suit {{ref:soil-bio-044}}. Endogeic worms live in topsoil or subsoil. They eat soil itself and dig horizontal burrows in the upper 10–30 cm. Anecic worms, whose name means 'reaching up', include the common earthworm. They build permanent, deep vertical burrows and come up to gather leaves. In doing so they mix surface plant matter into the mineral soil below. The categories help in judging land. Healthy soil holds a larger number and biomass of earthworms, especially endogeic and anecic species.

entries.title: How earthworms turn leaf fall into fertile soil

definition.text: The biological, chemical and physical ways earthworm activity improves soil for plants, by fragmenting, mixing, grinding and digesting plant debris.

facts.text: Anecic worms pull leaf fall and manure into their burrows, shred it and mix it with soil, turning it into humus; casts can hold 40 percent more humus than the top 230 mm of soil.
Grit in the gizzard grinds swallowed particles, sand grains up to 1.3 mm included, into a paste whose large surface favours microbes and enzymes.
Casts are richer in carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus than the bulk soil, with nutrients in plant-available form; where humus is plentiful, one worm may produce over 4.5 kilograms of casts a year.
Burrows keep soil structured, aerated and drained, and earthworms speed the formation of water-stable macroaggregates.
Darwin estimated up to 53,000 worms per acre of arable land; newer figures run from 250,000 per acre on poor soil to 1,750,000 per acre on rich farmland.
Richly organic topsoil averages 500 earthworms per square metre, weighing up to 400 g/m2.
Whether worms hasten the loss of organic matter as CO2 or preserve it as humus was long debated; a consensus now credits them with carbon sequestration, as most is stabilized deep with clay.
Their greenhouse gas emissions, direct or through soil microbes, are not fully quantified but likely add to global warming.

entries.title: Petrichor, the smell of rain on dry ground

definition.text: The earthy scent often noticed when rain falls on dry soil or rock.

facts.text: Isabel Joy Bear and Richard Grenfell Thomas introduced the term in a 1964 Nature paper for what had been called 'argillaceous odour', from the Greek petra (rock) and ichor, the fluid in the gods' veins.

It is a mixture of volatiles: oils from plant matter build up on mineral surfaces in dry spells and are pushed out of rock and soil pores by moisture, joined by microbial geosmin and 2-methylisoborneol.
The scent offers a glimpse of the soil atmosphere: after a drought, infiltrating rainwater flushes the soil air out.
Pliny the Elder noted the pleasant smell of earth when rain follows drought and took it as a sign of fertile soil.
In 1891 Marcellin Berthelot and G. André steam-distilled an odorous substance from soil but could not identify it.
In 1965 Bear and Thomas reported that small amounts of the oily extracts delay seed germination and early plant growth.
High-speed filming at MIT in 2015 showed raindrops on porous surfaces trap air bubbles that burst as aerosols, and light or moderate rain made more aerosols than heavy rain.
A 2026 study in dryland soils reaching into the Negev Desert found 58 volatile organic compounds released on rewetting, which may feed atmospheric ozone and secondary aerosol formation.

entries.title: Soil enzymes, the chemical tools of decay

definition.text: Enzymes in soil, released mainly by microbes, that break down organic matter and free nutrients for plants.

facts.text: Fungi, bacteria and archaea excrete them, and plant roots produce some; they decompose soil organic matter into humus, releasing nutrients plants need.
They catalyse the breakdown of compounds such as cellulose, lignin, starch and urea, making them prominent agents of the carbon and nitrogen cycles.
They may be intracellular, cell-associated or free, and microbes use them to degrade large molecules left by dead plants and animals.
Bound to clay and humic colloids, they are protected from rapid breakdown but less active: a trade-off between protection and activity.
Their distribution is highly patchy, varying at millimetre scale with nutrients, microbes and roots, and also from single trees to whole catchments.
Fertilizers may include urease inhibitors to delay the release of nutrients over a longer period.
Enzyme activity was higher with manure than with inorganic fertilizer, though other studies found a mix of mineral and organic fertilizers better still.
Their activity both stabilizes and degrades soil structure, and they play a decisive role in maintaining soil health.

entries.text: Microbes face a problem of scale: much of their food comes as large molecules left by dead plants and animals. Soil enzymes solve it. Released mainly by microbes, they break down {{ref:soil-found-045}} and free nutrients for plants. Fungi, bacteria and archaea excrete them, and plant roots produce some. They speed the breakdown of compounds such as cellulose, starch and {{ref:soil-fert-021}}, which makes them prominent agents in the cycling of carbon and nitrogen. Some work inside cells, some stay attached to cells, and some float free. Enzymes bound to clay and humic particles are protected from rapid breakdown but are less active, a trade-off between protection and activity. Their spread is highly patchy, varying at the millimeter scale with nutrients, microbes and roots, and from single trees to whole catchments. Farming steers them. Some fertilizers include {{ref:soil-fert-085}}, which hold back the enzyme that breaks down that compound so nutrients are released over a longer period. Enzyme activity was higher with manure than with inorganic fertilizer, though other studies found a mix of mineral and organic inputs better still. entries.title: Billions in a teaspoon: the bacteria of the soil

definition.text: The single-celled prokaryotic organisms of the soil, its most numerous inhabitants.

facts.text: A 'teaspoon' of productive soil holds 100 million to 3 billion bacteria, and up to 10 billion culturable cells live in each gram of soil in and around plant roots.
They live in soil water, including the moisture film around particles, where some swim with flagella, and multiply fast by binary fission when conditions suit.
Most beneficial soil bacteria are aerobic and most active in moist but unsaturated soil of neutral pH with plenty of food; anaerobic bacteria tend to putrefy dead organic matter.
Away from roots, most bulk-soil bacteria rest as drought-resistant colonies in a polysaccharide matrix coated with clay platelets, until root exudates or earthworm mucus reach them.
Hostile conditions send them dormant: Gram-positive Bacillus and Clostridium form spores, and Gram-negative bacteria enter a nonculturable resting stage.
Bacteria carry out key steps of the nitrogen cycle: nitrogen fixation, nitrification by chemolithotrophs such as Nitrosomonas, and denitrification in oxygen-free conditions.
Their biochemistry is versatile: Pseudomonas can metabolize a wide range of chemicals, while Nitrobacter gets its energy only by oxidizing nitrite to nitrate.
Soil archaea, also prokaryotes, are still poorly known but may matter in nitrification and methanogenesis; some bacteria colonize minerals and speed their weathering.

entries.title: Geosmin, the earthy molecule noses catch in traces

definition.text: A chemical with a distinct earthy or musty smell, made by bacteria common in soil and water.

facts.text: The name joins the Greek geō- ('earth') and osmē ('smell'); Nancy N. Gerber and Hubert A. Lechevalier coined it in 1965 after isolating it from actinomycete cultures, and Gerber worked out its structure in 1968.
It is a secondary metabolite of cyanobacteria such as Anabaena, Phormidium and Planktothrix and of actinomycetes, mainly Streptomyces.
It gives beetroot its earthy taste and contributes to petrichor, the smell of rain after dry weather or of disturbed soil.
People smell it at very low levels, from 0.006 to 0.01 micrograms per litre of water; the natural (−) form, with a mean threshold of 9.5 ng/L against 78 ng/L, is about eight times more potent.
With 2-methylisoborneol it is the main biological cause of muddy tastes in drinking water and farmed fish worldwide; it is nontoxic to humans and breaks down in acid.
It attracts springtails, which feed on Streptomyces and spread its spores, and repels the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans.
Standard water treatment cannot remove it, so suppliers need combined methods such as advanced oxidation.

conflicts.text: Humans detect geosmin at concentrations as low as anywhere from 400 parts per trillion to 5 parts per trillion.
conflicts.note: A wider and partly higher range than the lead's 0.006–0.01 micrograms per litre; Petrichor (S:9e9ddb7c941c) notes measured thresholds vary with experimental conditions.

entries.title: Seven hundred kilometers of fungal thread in a gram of soil

definition.text: The yeasts, moulds and other fungi of the soil, which lack chlorophyll and spread through the soil as threads called mycelium, feeding on organic matter.

facts.text: A gram of garden soil can hold around one million fungi and around 700 km of fungal hyphae.
Fungi may be outnumbered by bacteria in cell counts but can contribute greater biomass and respiration in some soils.
As chemo-heterotrophs they need organic substrates for carbon; their mycelium breaks fresh remains down into humus and carbon dioxide.
For humus formation the key fungi are saprotrophs, which turn dead matter into mineral forms such as nitrate, ammonium and phosphate that plants can use.
Dead matter is colonised by a succession of species: sugar and starch users first, then those able to break down cellulose and lignin.
Many are parasites that cause plant disease, while others are beneficial symbionts such as mycorrhizae; fungi also aid aggregation and feed larger soil organisms.
Compared with bacteria, fungi fare relatively well in acidic soils and in dry soils, which hold more of the oxygen they need.
Fruiting bodies such as mushrooms release spores that spread by wind, water and fungus-eating animals and can lie dormant for years.

entries.title: Actinomycetes: the branching bacteria behind earthy smell

definition.text: Soil bacteria of the phylum Actinomycetota (formerly Actinobacteria), Gram-positive and rich in guanine and cytosine, many of which grow fungus-like branching mycelia.

facts.text: They decompose the organic matter of dead organisms so plants can take it up anew, and build humus by breaking down cellulose, lignin and arthropod chitin.
Fungi play a similar role, but actinomycetota are much smaller and likely fill a different niche; the order name Actinomycetales recalls that they were long thought to be fungi.

The phylum is one of the dominant bacterial groups and includes Streptomyces, one of the largest bacterial genera; Streptomyces and its relatives are major contributors to the biological buffering of soils.
Some, such as Frankia, live symbiotically with plant roots, fixing nitrogen in exchange for some of the plant's sugars.
Their volatile metabolites give healthy soil its sweet, earthy smell.
They need plenty of air and a pH between 6.0 and 7.5, but tolerate dry conditions better than most bacteria and fungi.
They yield many antibiotics, among them streptomycin, neomycin, erythromycin and tetracycline, and agricultural compounds such as insecticides, herbicides, fungicides and plant growth promoters.
They break large lignin molecules into smaller pieces; lignin is hard for most organisms to break down and often shields cellulose from decomposition.

entries.title: Lumbricus terrestris, the nightcrawler that remakes forest soils

definition.text: A large, reddish earthworm, known as the common earthworm, lob worm or nightcrawler, thought to be native to Western Europe and now spread around the world.

facts.text: Generally 110–200 millimetres long and 7–10 millimetres across, with around 120–170 segments, it is the largest naturally occurring earthworm through much of Europe.
A deep-burrowing anecic worm, it builds vertical burrows, pulls surface litter down into the mineral soil and leaves casts of mixed organic and mineral material on the surface.
Where it has invaded podzols it has erased their banded profile of litter, pale E and coloured B horizons, leaving thin litter and a dark, worm-mixed Ap horizon over the B.
It is invasive in the north central United States, thriving in fence rows and woodlots and reducing native plant and tree regrowth, though it fares poorly in tilled fields.

entries.title: Vermicomposting: putting worms to work on waste

definition.text: Feeding organic waste to earthworms to turn it into vermicompost.

facts.text: It usually uses the brandling worm Eisenia fetida or Eisenia andrei, which live in manure heaps rather than soil; in the tropics the African nightcrawler and Indian blue are used.
Vermicompost, also called worm castings or worm humus, is the end product of earthworms breaking down organic matter.
Earthworms fed partly composted material excrete castings that make nitrogen, calcium, phosphorus and magnesium available to plants.
Added to soil, ideally as a surface mulch, the humified material improves moisture and nutrient availability and benefits soil microbes.

entries.title: Ecosystem engineers, the builders of soil habitat

definition.text: Species that create, significantly modify, maintain or destroy a habitat; in soil, chiefly burrowing animals such as earthworms, ants and termites, and fungi.

facts.text: They are defined by their ability to modify resources for other organisms, not by being eaten, which sets them apart from keystone species.
Allogenic engineers change materials mechanically, as burrowers do; autogenic engineers create habitat with their own bodies, as Sphagnum moss builds peatlands.
Earthworms, ants and termites mix the soil as they burrow, strongly affecting soil formation and organic matter dynamics while building granular structure.
Ant and termite nests change the soil chemically and physically, enriching it in carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus and mixing particles from different depths.
Burrowing mammals such as moles, gophers and prairie dogs turn soil, spread mycorrhizal fungi and open underground corridors used by arthropods, birds, small mammals and reptiles.
Fungi are engineers too: by linking distant patches and moving nutrients between them, even redistributing carbon between trees, they control nutrient cycles.
Where earthworm activity is poor, enchytraeids take on the role, digging galleries in which they deposit their faeces.
Earthworms are particularly sensitive to many contaminants, and the loss of such engineers brings dramatic changes in humus forms.

entries.contested_note: Some ecologists treat the term as a buzzword, arguing that it implies intent or that every species would qualify.
