entries.title: Bioturbation: how burrowers stir the earth

definition.text: The reworking of soils and sediments by animals or plants, through burrowing and the swallowing and excreting of grains.

facts.text: Bioturbation profoundly affects the environment and is thought to be a primary driver of biodiversity.
Walruses, salmon and pocket gophers are conspicuous bioturbators, but small invertebrates such as earthworms, polychaetes, shrimps and midge larvae dominate.
It differs from bioirrigation, the mixing of water and solutes in sediments, which is one of its effects.
Burrowers carry oxygen into reduced layers, changing microbial metabolism and speeding organic matter decomposition, and their burrows shelter other species.
Darwin began its formal study in the 1800s: chalk spread on a field lay 18 centimeters deep after 30 years, a burial rate of 6 millimeters per year he credited to earthworms.
Nathaniel Shaler added ants and trees in 1891, Rudolf Richter coined the term in 1952, and it has been widely used in soil and geomorphology literature since the 1980s.
Since its onset around 539 million years ago it has changed ocean chemistry, and it is thought to have been a co-factor of the Cambrian Explosion.
When pollution harms soil engineers such as earthworms, termites and ants, bioturbation falls and the humus form shifts toward mor.

entries.title: Symbiosis, the long partnership of unlike organisms

definition.text: Any close and long-term biological interaction between two organisms of different species.

facts.text: Heinrich Anton de Bary defined it in 1879 as 'the living together of unlike organisms'; the word is sometimes kept for mutualism, where both partners benefit.
Symbiosis can be obligate or facultative, and an ectosymbiont lives on its partner while an endosymbiont lives inside its tissues.
Examples include rhizobia in legume root nodules and nitrogen-fixing Frankia in alder root nodules.
Antagonism is shown by black walnut, whose secreted juglone destroys many herbaceous plants within its root zone.

An ectosymbiont lives on its partner, while an endosymbiont lives inside its tissues. {{ref:soil-bio-178}} in the roots of legumes are one example; nitrogen-fixing {{ref:soil-bio-200}} in alder roots is another. Not every link is friendly. Black walnut secretes juglone, which destroys many herbaceous plants within its root zone.

entries.title: Fungi: the threads that decompose and partner

definition.text: Fungi are a kingdom of mostly hypha-forming organisms that, with bacteria, are the major decomposers on land.

facts.text: Most fungi grow as thread-like hyphae 2 to 10 micrometres across and up to several centimetres long, which extend at their tips and branch; their high surface-to-volume ratio suits nutrient extraction and invading substrates.
Fungi are more closely related to animals than to plants, though they were once classed as plants for their immobile lifestyle.
Along with bacteria they are the major decomposers in most terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems, so they are central to biogeochemical cycles and food webs.
Over 90% of plant species form mycorrhizal relationships with fungi and depend on them for survival; the symbiosis dates back at least 400 million years.
Lichens pair a fungus with photosynthetic algae or cyanobacteria, and some ants cultivate fungi for food and nest structure.
Many fungi are plant parasites, such as the rice blast fungus and those causing Dutch elm disease and chestnut blight.

As of 2019 nine major lineages are recognised, including Chytridiomycota, Glomeromycota, Ascomycota and Basidiomycota; the last two form the species-rich Dikarya, with all mushrooms and most plant pathogens.

entries.title: Farming with microbes: promise and pitfalls

definition.text: Using and managing soil microorganisms to make nutrients available to crops, spur their growth and protect them from disease.

facts.text: Healthy soil life can supply nutrients such as nitrogen and protect crops against pests and diseases while reducing the need for water and other inputs.
Fertilizer and pesticide used without offsetting their effects can destroy the rhizobiome, the microbial ecosystem around roots.
Almost all registered microbial products are biopesticides, now about 10% of the global pesticide market.
Long-marketed examples are Trichoderma fungi that suppress pathogenic fungi and the caterpillar killer Bacillus thuringiensis.
Many strains that looked promising in the lab fail in the field because of soil, climate and ecosystem effects.
Introduced populations can fade, as Bacillus subtilis does for lack of a defensible niche; using several collaborating strains helps.
Rules demanding safety evidence have led many products to call themselves 'biostimulants' rather than 'biopesticides'.
Excess fertilizer can suppress mycorrhizae, phosphorus in particular above a threshold, and turn symbiotic bacteria into competitors.

entries.text: Healthy soil life can supply crops with nutrients such as nitrogen and protect them against pests and diseases, while reducing the need for water and other inputs. Using and managing soil microorganisms toward those ends is the agricultural use of soil microbes. The partnership is fragile. Fertilizer and pesticide used without offsetting their effects can destroy the rhizobiome, the microbial ecosystem around roots. Excess fertilizer, phosphorus above a threshold in particular, can suppress the fungi that partner with roots and turn symbiotic bacteria into competitors. Almost all registered microbial products are biopesticides, now about 10% of the global pesticide market. Long-marketed examples include Trichoderma fungi, which suppress disease-causing fungi, and the caterpillar killer Bacillus thuringiensis. The field is hard going. Many strains that look promising in the lab fail outdoors because of soil, climate and ecosystem effects. Rules demanding safety evidence have even led many products to call themselves by the label discussed in {{ref:soil-fert-205}} rather than 'biopesticides'.

entries.title: Microbial inoculants: bottled helpers for crops

definition.text: An agricultural amendment, also called a soil inoculant or bioinoculant, that uses beneficial rhizosphere or endophytic microbes to promote plant health.

facts.text: Many of the microbes form mutualistic partnerships with the crop; besides improving nutrition they can promote growth by stimulating plant hormone production.

Bacterial inoculants, called plant growth promoting rhizobacteria, include nitrogen fixers and phosphate solubilisers; Rhizobium, which fixes nitrogen in legume root nodules, is the most commonly applied.
Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi are used to supply phosphorus: in one reduced-fertilization greenhouse, AM fungi with rhizobacteria gave the tomato yields of 100% fertility at 70% fertility.
Inoculants can induce systemic acquired resistance in crops, shown so far against powdery mildew, take-all, leaf spot and root rot.
Mixing strains raises plant nutrient uptake from soil and fertilizer, and several strains together raise nitrogenase activity even when only one fixes nitrogen.
Inoculants often change the existing soil microbial community.

Research in 2024 suggests as few as one in nine commercial products are beneficial; with commercial products mycorrhizal colonization was under 10%, though an estimated 836 million USD is spent on inoculants each year.
They are not widely used in industrial agriculture because large-scale application is not yet economically viable.

entries.title: Gophers, worms and fallen trees: how soil gets stirred

definition.text: The mixing and moving of soil by burrowing animals and by plant roots, which matters for soil production, burial, organic matter content and downslope transport.

facts.text: Plants and animals disturb the upper soil and bring weathered rock, saprolite, up from depth to the surface.
Tree roots add organic matter and leave voids when they rot, and uprooted trees throw up mounds and can invert sections of soil.
Burrows of earthworms and small mammals carry air and water and change particle-size distribution with depth, porosity and nutrient content.
Detritus-eating burrowers build the organic-rich topsoil called the soil biomantle and so help form soil horizons.
Pocket gophers may produce soil on a scale equal to abiotic processes; their mounds bring little-weathered rock to the surface, speeding soil formation, and are easily eroded downslope.
Mounds bury vegetation that decays into nutrient hotspots, and burrows, even backfilled, lower soil density.

entries.title: Sorting bacteria by how they eat and breathe

definition.text: The grouping of bacteria by their source of energy, the electron donors they use and their source of carbon.

facts.text: Phototrophs get their energy from light by photosynthesis, while chemotrophs get it by oxidizing chemical compounds.
Bacteria that take electrons from inorganic compounds such as hydrogen, carbon monoxide or ammonia are lithotrophs; those that use organic compounds are organotrophs.
Heterotrophs take their carbon from organic compounds, while autotrophs such as cyanobacteria and some purple bacteria fix carbon dioxide.
Aerobes use oxygen as the final electron acceptor and anaerobes use nitrate, sulfate or carbon dioxide; facultative anaerobes switch between fermentation and different acceptors as conditions change.

Heterotrophs take their carbon from organic compounds, while autotrophs such as cyanobacteria and some purple bacteria fix carbon dioxide. Aerobes use oxygen as the final electron acceptor, and anaerobes use nitrate, sulfate or carbon dioxide. Facultative anaerobes switch between fermentation and different acceptors as conditions change.

entries.title: Lithotrophs, the microbes that eat rock

definition.text: An organism that takes the electrons it needs for building its cells or making energy from an inorganic substance, usually of mineral origin, rather than from organic matter.

facts.text: The name joins the Greek lithos (rock) and troph (consumer), so lithotrophs are 'eaters of rock'; Lwoff and collaborators suggested the term in 1946.
In the broad sense lithotrophs include light-using photolithotrophs such as plants, but chemolithotrophs are exclusively microorganisms, all in the domains Bacteria and Archaea.
The opposite strategy is the organotroph, which gets its reducing agents by breaking down organic compounds.

Lithoautotrophs take their carbon from carbon dioxide in the air as plants do; lithoheterotrophs cannot fix carbon dioxide and must consume organic compounds, and only a few bacteria are fully lithoheterotrophic.
Many lithotrophs are mixotrophs, taking up organic material to supplement the carbon they fix from carbon dioxide.
They live in deep terrestrial subsurfaces, soils, mines and rock-dwelling endolith communities, and take part in soil formation and the cycling of carbon, nitrogen and other elements.
In the iron cycle they can use iron either as an electron donor, turning Fe(II) into Fe(III), or as an electron acceptor, turning Fe(III) into Fe(II).
The last universal common ancestor of life is thought to have been a chemolithotroph.

Many lithotrophs are mixotrophs, topping up the carbon they fix with organic material. They live in the deep subsurface, soils, mines and endolith communities inside rock. There they take part in soil formation and the cycling of carbon, nitrogen and other elements. In the cycling of iron they can use it both ways: as an electron donor, turning Fe(II) into Fe(III), or as an electron acceptor, turning Fe(III) into Fe(II).

entries.title: Bacteria that turn loose soil into stone

definition.text: A biogeochemical process in which microbes cause calcium carbonate to precipitate within the soil matrix.

facts.text: The main microbes that can induce it are photosynthetic cyanobacteria and microalgae, sulfate-reducing bacteria and some species involved in the nitrogen cycle.

Bacteria can trigger it by urea hydrolysis, denitrification, sulfate production or iron reduction; autotrophic pathways deplete carbon dioxide, while heterotrophic ones run through the nitrogen and sulfur cycles.

In ureolysis, microbial urease splits urea into ammonium and carbonate; the hydroxide ions formed raise the pH and shift bicarbonate to carbonate, which precipitates with calcium as calcium carbonate crystals.
A first layer of calcite makes bacteria cling more strongly to the soil surface, so further calcite layers build up.
Calcium carbonate can precipitate as calcite, aragonite or vaterite, in that order of usual stability; such biological precipitation goes back to the Precambrian.
Proposed uses include repairing cracks in concrete and preventing its corrosion, biogrout, and sequestering radionuclides and heavy metals.
Contaminant metals and radionuclides are trapped by co-precipitation into the calcite lattice, and chelation with the precipitate reduces the availability of lead in soil.

entries.text: Bacteria can glue sand grains together with crystals of their own making. Bacteria can trigger it by breaking down {{ref:soil-fert-021}}, by {{ref:soil-fert-108}}, by sulfate production or by iron reduction. Autotrophic pathways use up carbon dioxide, while heterotrophic ones run through the cycling of nitrogen and sulfur. The first route, ureolysis, shows the chemistry step by step. A microbial enzyme, the subject of {{ref:soil-fert-224}}, splits this nitrogen compound into ammonium and carbonate. Hydroxide ions formed along the way raise the pH and shift bicarbonate to carbonate. That carbonate meets calcium and drops out as calcium carbonate crystals. The process feeds itself. The carbonate can form as calcite, aragonite or vaterite, in that order of usual stability. Such biological precipitation goes back to the Precambrian. They are trapped by co-precipitation into the calcite lattice, and binding to the precipitate makes lead in soil less available. Its use to strengthen sand is {{ref:soil-bio-068}}.

entries.title: Chemolithotrophy: making a living from minerals in the dark

definition.text: A way of living in which a cell gets its energy by oxidizing reduced inorganic compounds, such as ammonia, sulfur, ferrous iron or hydrogen.

facts.text: The oxidation is coupled to ATP synthesis: electrons taken from the inorganic donor are passed into respiratory chains that make ATP.
Most chemolithotrophs are chemolithoautotrophs that fix carbon dioxide, usually through the Calvin cycle, an energetically expensive pathway.
The group includes sulfur oxidizers, iron oxidizers, hydrogen oxidizers and nitrifying bacteria: Nitrosomonas oxidizes ammonia to nitrite and Nitrobacter oxidizes nitrite to nitrate.
Oxygen is the usual electron acceptor of the best-documented forms, but nitrate and other organic and inorganic acceptors are also used, and the list of anaerobic chemolithotrophs is growing.
Energy yields differ by substrate: oxidizing hydrogen sulfide to sulfur gives 50 kcal/mol (210 kJ/mol), while oxidizing sulfur to sulfate gives 150 kcal/mol (627 kJ/mol).
On low-energy substrates such as ferrous iron, cells must process large amounts of material for a little energy, which keeps them from thriving in many places.
Because chemosynthesis needs no sunlight, chemolithotrophs can build organic matter in the dark, and some thrive above 110 degrees Celsius or below pH 2.
Sergei Winogradsky first characterized this metabolism, discovering the first known form of lithotrophy while working with Beggiatoa in 1887.

entries.text: Some microbes build living matter in total darkness, from nothing but minerals and gases. {{ref:soil-hist-013}} first characterized their metabolism, chemolithotrophy. In 1887, working with the bacterium Beggiatoa, he discovered the first known form of lithotrophy. In chemolithotrophy a cell gets its energy by oxidizing reduced inorganic compounds such as ammonia, sulfur, ferrous iron or hydrogen. The oxidation is coupled to making ATP, the cell's energy carrier. Electrons taken from the inorganic donor pass into respiratory chains that make ATP. Most chemolithotrophs also fix carbon dioxide, usually through {{ref:soil-hist-149}}, an energetically expensive pathway. The group includes sulfur oxidizers, iron oxidizers, hydrogen oxidizers and the bacteria that turn ammonia into nitrite and nitrite into nitrate. Oxygen is the usual electron acceptor in the best-documented forms. Nitrate and other acceptors are also used, and the list of chemolithotrophs that live without oxygen is growing. Energy yields depend on the fuel. Oxidizing hydrogen sulfide to sulfur gives 50 kcal/mol (210 kJ/mol), while oxidizing sulfur to sulfate gives 150 kcal/mol (627 kJ/mol). On low-energy fuels such as ferrous iron, cells must process large amounts of material for a little energy, which keeps them from thriving in many places. Because this kind of chemosynthesis needs no sunlight, chemolithotrophs can build living material in the dark. Some thrive above 110 degrees Celsius or below pH 2.

entries.title: What acid, salt and the plow do to soil life

definition.text: Soil changes that reduce the variety of soil life, such as acidification, salinisation, sodicity, structure decline and erosion, many of them driven by how soil is managed.

facts.text: In Dutch soils below pH 5, biodiversity fell as pH fell, in grasslands and heathlands alike.
Acidification cuts the numbers of most macrofauna, earthworms included, harms rhizobium survival and may slow decomposition and nitrogen fixation.
At low salinity microbes are active and soil respiration is high; as salinity rises, microbes have less available water and respire less.
Prolonged high sodium leaves soil cement-like, holding and passing less water and decomposing organic matter more slowly.
Erosion strips topsoil, organic matter and nutrients and breaks down structure, making it a major threat to soil biodiversity.
Constant tillage redistributes soil organic matter, degrading structure and altering populations of organisms such as earthworms.
Chloride from potassium chloride fertilizer raises salinity and is biocidal, harming the growth, survival and reproduction of soil organisms, nitrifiers included.

entries.title: Hyphae, the threads that fungi grow by

definition.text: A long, branching filament of a fungus, oomycete or actinobacterium; in most fungi hyphae are the main mode of growth and together form a mycelium.

facts.text: A hypha is one or more cells inside a tubular wall, usually of chitin, divided in most fungi by perforated cross-walls called septa.
Hyphae average 4–6 μm across and grow at their tips.
Arbuscular mycorrhizal hyphae alone are estimated to extend about 110 quadrillion kilometres through Earth's topsoils.
Specialised forms include arbuscules that exchange nutrients with plant cells and mycelial cords that move nutrients over long distances.

entries.title: Mycelium, the hidden body of a fungus

definition.text: The root-like body of a fungus, a mass of branching, thread-like hyphae.

facts.text: Mycelial colonies grow in and on soil, from colonies too small to see to one Armillaria spanning thousands of acres.
It feeds in two stages: hyphae secrete enzymes that break polymers into small units such as monomers, which are then absorbed.
Mycelia decompose plant material, add to the organic fraction of soil and release carbon dioxide as they grow.
Mycelial networks make up 20-30% of soil biomass, though traditional biomass measures fail to detect them.
Mycorrhizal mycelium helps most plants take up water and nutrients and by some estimates receives well over 10% of the host's photosynthetic output.
Mycelium is an important food for many soil invertebrates.
Fungi break down lignin in compost, which many other composting microbes cannot.
Fungi can degrade soil contaminants such as petroleum products and some pesticides (mycoremediation), and mycelium spread on logging roads binds disturbed soil.

entries.title: Thatch, the spongy mat that builds up under lawns

definition.text: In lawn care, a layer of organic matter that builds up around the base of the grass plants.

facts.text: It is a mix of living and dead crowns, stolons, rhizomes and roots, about 25% of it lignin, which resists decay; grass clippings add little because soil microbes break them down easily.
It builds up when acid soils cannot support enough decomposers, when insecticides cut earthworm activity and so bioturbation, or when excess nitrogen fertilizer spurs growth and acidifies the soil.
A thin layer insulates against swings in temperature and moisture, but too much causes root problems and mowing difficulties and is removed with a dethatcher.

entries.text: In lawn care, thatch is a layer of plant material that builds up around the base of the grass plants. It mixes living and dead crowns, stolons, rhizomes and roots. Excess nitrogen fertilizer adds to it by spurring growth and acidifying the soil. A thin layer insulates against swings in temperature and moisture. Too much causes root problems and mowing difficulties, and is removed with a dethatcher.

entries.title: Soil-borne pathogens, the enemies waiting below the crop

definition.text: A disease-causing agent that lives both in soil and in a plant host and tends to infect healthy plants grown in that soil.

facts.text: Common examples are Fusarium, Pythium, Rhizoctonia, Phytophthora, Verticillium, Rhizopus, Thielaviopsis and nematodes such as Meloidogyne.
Fungi are among them, although other soil fungi are beneficial plant partners such as mycorrhizae.
Their propagules can be stirred to germinate by plant exudates in the laimosphere and start the hypocotyl and stem rots that cause damping-off.
Monoculture and chemical fertilization often bring soil-borne diseases along with acidification and degradation, lowering productivity.
Fallowing disrupts them by temporarily removing their hosts, and soil solarization heats the soil until many are killed or greatly weakened.
Disease-suppressive soils inhibit them, mycorrhizal plants often resist them, and compost teas have a suppressive effect on soil-borne diseases.
Hydroponics, which grows roots in substrates instead of soil, eliminates soil-borne diseases and pests.

entries.text: Some of a plant's worst enemies wait in the ground beneath it. A soil-borne pathogen is a disease-causing agent that lives both in soil and in a plant host, and it tends to infect healthy plants grown in that soil. Common examples are Fusarium, Pythium, Rhizoctonia, Phytophthora, Verticillium, Rhizopus, Thielaviopsis and roundworms such as Meloidogyne. Many are fungi, even though other soil fungi are helpful partners of plants. Their propagules are the spores and fragments that spread them. Chemicals released by plants can stir them to germinate in the soil around a seedling's lower stem. They then start the stem rots that cause damping-off, the collapse of young seedlings. Monoculture and chemical fertilization often bring these diseases, along with acidification and degradation that lower productivity. Growers have several defenses. Fallowing disrupts pathogens by removing their hosts for a while. Heating the soil with sunlight, {{ref:soil-agri-034}}, kills or badly weakens many. Disease-suppressive soils inhibit them, and teas brewed from {{ref:soil-fert-028}} suppress them too. Growing roots in substrates instead of soil, as {{ref:soil-fert-167}} does, eliminates soil-borne diseases and pests altogether.

entries.title: Macrofauna, the soil animals big enough to see

definition.text: Soil and litter invertebrates between 2 mm and 2 cm, such as earthworms, termites, ants, millipedes, woodlice, beetles, slugs and snails.

facts.text: Earthworms, termites, ants, some millipedes and some insect larvae make pore spaces and so change soil structure.
Diets differ: millipedes, woodlice and some earthworms eat leaf litter, lower termites eat wood, endogeic earthworms and higher termites eat humus, and centipedes and spiders hunt prey.
Shredding plant remains and waking dormant bacteria in the soil they swallow speeds decomposition: the 'Sleeping Beauty' paradigm, with the earthworm as 'Prince Charming'.
Saprophagous macrofauna need enzymes from gut microbes to digest wood or soil organic matter; in lower termites, symbiotic flagellates help digest lignocellulose.
Food ground in earthworm gizzards or chewed by termites leaves pasty faeces that harden into stable earthworm casts and termite mounds.
Abundant in fertile soils, they are typical of mull humus, with many trophic niches and more complex food webs.
Needing much calcium and nitrogen, they depend on plants with fast-decaying litter, and by speeding nutrient cycling they favour such plants: a positive above- and below-ground feedback.

entries.title: Termites, the engineers of tropical soils

definition.text: Eusocial insects that eat decaying plant material, mostly wood, leaf litter and soil humus.

facts.text: They are important decomposers in subtropical and tropical regions, and their recycling of wood and plant matter is of considerable ecological importance.
Many species are ecosystem engineers that change soil hydrology, decomposition, nutrient cycling and plant growth, and so the biodiversity around their large mounds.
Primarily detritivores, they eat dead plants at any stage of decay; higher termites also eat faeces, humus, grass, leaves and roots.
Of 3,014 classified species, 754 live in Africa, where mounds are islands of soil fertility in savannas; the northern Kruger National Park alone has about 1.1 million active mounds.
Nests are subterranean, epigeal (mounds) or arboreal; most termites build underground colonies, using soil for subterranean nests and mounds.
Around 330 species of the Macrotermitinae farm Termitomyces fungi on their faecal pellets in fungus cones inside the nest.
Termite diversity and abundance fall with disturbance, such as loss of trees and soil cover and trampling by cattle and goats.

entries.title: Mesofauna, the mites and jumpers of the pore spaces

definition.text: Soil and litter invertebrates between 0.2 mm and 2 mm, chiefly microarthropods such as mites and springtails, and potworms (enchytraeids).

facts.text: They feed on plant remains, microbes, lichens, spores, pollen and other animals, and their heavy consumption of litter and microbes gives them an important part in the carbon cycle.
Microarthropods cannot reshape soil and must use the existing macropores, which makes them very sensitive to compaction; enchytraeids instead dig galleries.
By eating fungal hyphae and spores they help regulate fungal communities, mycorrhizal fungi included, both spreading and severing them.
Springtails, with high reproductive rates and large populations, are prey for predatory mites, pseudoscorpions and macrofauna, making them pivotal in soil food webs.
They eat and break down the faeces of larger animals, such as earthworm casts.
Their community make-up reflects environmental differences, so mesofauna are good bioindicators of soil quality.
Being sensitive to environmental hazards, they are likely to be harmed by climate change, land use change and agricultural intensification.

entries.title: Springtails, the tiny jumpers that graze on fungi

definition.text: Springtails (class Collembola) are tiny six-legged arthropods, no longer counted as insects, that live in moist soil and leaf litter almost everywhere on Earth.

facts.text: More than 9,000 species are known; they are omnivorous, free-living and prefer moist conditions.
They do not decompose organic matter directly but speed decomposition by fragmenting it and by controlling and spreading soil microbial communities.
They mostly eat fungal hyphae and spores, but also plant material, pollen, animal remains and bacteria; geosmin from Streptomyces attracts some species, which eat and spread its spores.
Estimates reach 100,000 individuals per square metre; temperate deciduous woodland litter typically holds 30 to 40 species, and the tropics may exceed 100.
Species assemblages change with depth from canopy to litter to deeper soil horizons, and across landscapes with soil acidity, moisture and light; as a group they are highly sensitive to drying out.
They are prey for mesostigmatan mites and soil centipedes, and escape by jumping with a spring-like furcula, which is hard to do inside soil.

Folsomia candida is used in standardized toxicity and avoidance tests for soil pollution; unlike earthworms, springtails are very sensitive to herbicides, and they serve as bioindicators of soil quality.
In lawns and turfgrass they act as 'thatch busters', helping decompose the thatch layer between the green vegetation and the soil surface.

entries.title: Potworms, the earthworms' small white cousins

definition.text: Enchytraeids are a family of small, earthworm-like oligochaete worms; the terrestrial species, called potworms, live in highly organic soils.

facts.text: Over 700 species are described; most are whitish or transparent worms a few millimetres long that eat decaying organic matter and its microbes, aiding decomposition and nutrient cycling.
Like earthworms they are ecosystem engineers, shaping soil structure by creating aggregates of various sizes.
They feed on earthworm casts and turn them into fluffy masses of their own faeces, which make up the bulk of the OH horizon of moder humus.
Less sensitive than earthworms to farming intensification, they replace them in soils with heavy pesticide use and serve in standard ecotoxicity tests (ISO 16387).

Like earthworms, they are ecosystem engineers, shaping soil structure by building aggregates of various sizes. They feed on earthworm casts and turn them into fluffy masses of their own feces. Those masses make up the bulk of the OH horizon in the moder type of {{ref:soil-bio-095}}. They are less sensitive than earthworms to farming intensification. So they replace earthworms in soils with heavy pesticide use and serve in standard ecotoxicity tests (ISO 16387).

entries.title: Slime molds and myxobacteria, single cells that act as one

definition.text: Soil microorganisms whose single cells join into syncytia (slime molds, which are eukaryotes) or swarms (myxobacteria, which are prokaryotes).

facts.text: These collective organisms glide in a coordinated way when foraging, a behaviour still largely unexplored.
Both groups form spores in fruiting bodies, often iridescent and conspicuous.
Slime molds make complex nutritional decisions with no coordination centre, as a single vast multinucleate cell.

entries.text: A slime mold makes complex decisions about food with no coordinating center at all. Slime molds and myxobacteria are soil microorganisms whose single cells band together. Slime molds, which are eukaryotes, cells with a nucleus, merge into syncytia: one vast cell with many nuclei. Myxobacteria, which are prokaryotes, gather into swarms. Both glide in a coordinated way while foraging, a behavior still largely unexplored. Both also form spores in fruiting bodies, which are often iridescent and conspicuous.

entries.title: Soil algae, sunlight harvesters at the surface

definition.text: Photosynthetic microorganisms that live at or near the soil surface and make their own carbon from light.

facts.text: Needing light, they are spread wherever sunlight and moderate moisture reach, not far below the surface.
Below the surface they can live given steady temperature and moisture, feeding heterotrophically on easy carbon sources such as glucose.
Soil algae divide into green Chlorophyceae and golden-brown diatoms, coloured by the carotenoid fucoxanthin.
Chlorella vulgaris has been shown to promote plant growth together with rhizosphere bacteria.

entries.text: Soil algae are photosynthetic microorganisms that live at or near the soil surface and make their own carbon compounds from light. Needing light, they spread wherever sunlight and moderate moisture reach, but not far below the surface. Deeper down, some live on given steady temperature and moisture, taking in ready-made carbon such as glucose. Soil algae divide into green Chlorophyceae and golden-brown diatoms, which owe their color to the carotenoid pigment fucoxanthin. One alga, Chlorella vulgaris, has been shown to promote plant growth together with bacteria around roots.

entries.title: Phages, the viruses that prey on soil bacteria

definition.text: Viruses that infect soil bacteria, among the most abundant yet least studied members of soil microbial communities.

facts.text: Phage richness varies with season, soil moisture, location and plant growth, and rises with bacterial abundance.
Soil phages may be lytic, killing the host to release virions, lysogenic, joining the host genome, or chronic, releasing virions without killing it.
By killing hosts, lytic phages affect bacterial cycling of carbon, nitrogen, sulfur and phosphorus; phages are also a major agent of horizontal gene transfer.
Phages can open plants to disease: phage ΦGP100 kills Pseudomonas fluorescens, which produces antifungals.

entries.text: Viruses that infect soil bacteria, called bacteriophages or phages, are among the most abundant yet least studied members of soil microbial communities. Their richness varies with season, soil moisture, location and plant growth, and rises with the number of bacteria. Soil phages follow three strategies. Lytic phages kill the host to release new virus particles. Lysogenic phages join the host's genome. Chronic phages release particles without killing it. By killing hosts, lytic phages affect how bacteria cycle carbon, nitrogen, sulfur and phosphorus. Phages are also a major route by which genes move between bacteria. They can even open plants to disease: phage ΦGP100 kills Pseudomonas fluorescens, a bacterium that produces antifungal compounds.

entries.title: The soil's single-celled grazers

definition.text: Single-celled eukaryotes of the soil, grouped as flagellates, amoebae and ciliates.

facts.text: Most eat bacteria; others eat bacteria and fungi, fungi alone, or particles of humus.
Flagellates are the smallest; heterotrophic flagellates may occasionally number several million per gram of soil.
Naked amoebae move through water-filled pores and films, while testate amoebae shelter in shells against drying and serve as indicators of past climates.
Ciliates, the largest, move by many short beating cilia.

entries.text: Heterotrophic flagellates may occasionally number several million in a gram of soil. They are the smallest of these grazers, single-celled eukaryotes grouped as flagellates, amoebae and ciliates. Most of them eat bacteria. Others eat bacteria and fungi, fungi alone, or particles of decayed plant and animal matter. Naked amoebae move through water-filled pores and films. {{ref:soil-bio-195}} shelter in shells against drying out, and they serve as indicators of past climates. Ciliates, the largest, move by many short beating cilia.
entries.text_plain: Heterotrophic flagellates may occasionally number several million in a gram of soil. Testate amoebae, single cells that carry a shell shelter in shells against drying out, and they serve as indicators of past climates. Ciliates, the largest, move by many short beating cilia.

entries.title: Protozoa: single cells that eat bacteria

definition.text: Protozoa are single-celled eukaryotes, free-living or parasitic, that feed on organic matter such as other microorganisms or debris.

facts.text: The name is now used loosely for heterotrophic single-celled protists, since Protozoa as a taxon is not monophyletic; classic examples are Amoeba, Paramecium and Euglena.
They range from about 1 micrometre to several millimetres, and are flagellates, ciliates or amoebae according to how they move.
All need a moist habitat, but many survive dry spells as resting cysts; they are common in soils and mosses.
All are heterotrophs, engulfing prey by phagocytosis or taking up dissolved matter by osmotrophy, and some are mixotrophs hosting symbiotic algae.
Most reproduce asexually by binary or multiple fission; sexual exchange is generally decoupled from reproduction.
In the microbial food web they are the most important bacterivores and mobilise nutrients, passing bacterial and algal production on and solubilising nutrients in microbial biomass.
Termite gut flagellates help their host digest wood by breaking down complex sugars.

entries.title: The microbial loop: how predators free nutrients for roots

definition.text: The pathway by which bacteria take up dissolved organic carbon and pass it back up the food web; in soil it concerns soil carbon and the nutrients freed when protozoa and nematodes eat root-fed bacteria.

facts.text: Farooq Azam, Tom Fenchel and others coined the term in 1983 for the role of bacteria in marine carbon and nutrient cycles; 'microbial food web' is now often used instead.
Roots exploring new soil prime quiescent bacteria, which naked amoebae then eat, freeing mineral nitrogen for root hairs to absorb.
Predation by amoebae and free-living nematodes raises the mineralization rate, which in turn stimulates root growth; Clarholm's hypothesis of this loop is hard to verify experimentally.
Bacteria-eating protozoa release the nutrients locked in microbial biomass in a form plants can use.

The microbial carbon pump model has plants add carbon through root exudates and litter; microbes then either respire it to the atmosphere or store it in the stable pool as dead microbial biomass (necromass).

Microbes transform plant carbon outside the cell with extracellular enzymes and inside it through biomass turnover; the balance of CO2-releasing and carbon-building pathways sets net carbon retention.
Fresh plant carbon can prime microbes to decompose existing soil organic carbon faster than models expect.
Most of the soil microbiome is uncultivated, which leaves its contribution to soil carbon cycling uncertain and hampers climate models of carbon flux.

entries.text: Farooq Azam, Tom Fenchel and others coined the term microbial loop in 1983 for the role of bacteria in marine carbon and nutrient cycles. It names the pathway by which bacteria take up dissolved organic carbon and pass it back up the food web. 'Microbial food web' is now often used instead. In soil, the loop concerns carbon and the nutrients freed when protozoa and {{ref:soil-bio-193}} eat bacteria fed by roots. It runs like this. Roots pushing into new soil prime resting bacteria, which naked amoebae then eat. That frees mineral nitrogen for root hairs to absorb. Predation by amoebae and free-living roundworms raises the rate at which nutrients are released, which in turn stimulates root growth. This loop is Clarholm's hypothesis, and it is hard to verify by experiment. Bacteria-eating protozoa release the nutrients locked in microbial bodies in a form plants can use. A related idea, the model in {{ref:soil-bio-266}}, has plants add carbon through {{ref:soil-bio-142}} and litter. Microbes then either respire it to the atmosphere or store it in a stable pool as dead microbial matter, called necromass. They transform plant carbon outside the cell with enzymes and inside it as their populations grow and die. The balance between pathways that release CO2 and those that build carbon sets how much carbon the soil keeps. Fresh plant carbon can also prime microbes to break down carbon already stored in {{ref:soil-found-045}} faster than models expect. Much remains unknown. Most of the soil microbiome has never been cultivated, which leaves its part in carbon cycling uncertain and hampers climate models of carbon flux.

entries.title: Soil microfauna, the animals that live in water films

definition.text: The smallest soil animals, 20 μm to 200 μm in size: protozoa and tiny multicellular animals such as nematodes, rotifers and tardigrades.

facts.text: They move through mesopores (30–75 μm) and macropores (>75 μm) and mostly live in the water films around aggregates and roots, eating microbes or other microfauna.
Grazing rejuvenates microbial colonies, and microfauna excrete nutrients such as ammonium in a form plants can use.
Tied to pore water, they are sensitive to drying, but cryptobiotic stages such as cysts, dauer larvae and tardigrade tuns wait out bad times and revive within a few hours.
Unlike most soil invertebrates they may not suffer critically from climate warming, but they are highly sensitive to acid rain.
Nematodes and protozoa, abundant in soil, shape rhizosphere functions; root-feeding nematodes alter the soil's organic carbon.
Protozoa release phosphorus and nitrogen by dissolving organic material, and their grazing keeps bacterial populations decomposing efficiently, improving fertility.
Selective grazing changes the diversity of rhizosphere microbes and speeds their turnover.

entries.text: A tardigrade dried out in soil can wait as a shrunken tun and revive within a few hours. Tardigrades belong to the soil microfauna, the smallest soil animals at 20 μm to 200 μm. The group includes protozoa, {{ref:soil-bio-193}} and rotifers. They move through mesopores (30–75 μm) and macropores (>75 μm) and mostly live in the water films around aggregates and roots. There they eat microbes or one another. Their grazing rejuvenates microbial colonies, and they excrete nutrients such as ammonium in a form plants can use. Tied to pore water, they are sensitive to drying. Cysts, dauer larvae and tuns are their survival stages. Unlike most soil invertebrates, they may not suffer critically from climate warming, but they are highly sensitive to acid rain.

entries.title: Nematodes, the most numerous animals on Earth

definition.text: Roundworms or eelworms, the animal phylum Nematoda, most of them free-living microbe feeders but many parasitic.

facts.text: Earth's topsoil holds about 4.4 × 10^20 nematodes, roughly 60 billion per person, with the highest densities in tundra and boreal forests.
Often exceeding a million individuals per square metre, they make up about 80% of all individual animals on Earth.
About 90% of soil nematodes live in the top 15 cm of soil.
They do not decompose organic matter but feed on living material; eating up to 5,000 bacteria per minute, they regulate bacterial numbers and community composition.
Through nitrogen mineralization they can play an important role in the nitrogen cycle.
Nematophagous fungi prey on them, trapping them with lassos or adhesive structures or releasing toxins on contact.
Species are hard to tell apart, so estimates of their number run from over 25,000 to close to one million.
The soil-dwelling Caenorhabditis elegans is a major model organism, and a Panagrolaimus kolymaensis was revived after 46,000 years in Siberian permafrost.

entries.text: Earth's topsoil holds about 4.4 × 10^20 nematodes, roughly 60 billion for every person. Nematodes are roundworms, or eelworms, the animal phylum Nematoda. Most live freely and feed on microbes, but many are parasites. They often exceed a million individuals per square meter, and they make up about 80% of all individual animals on Earth. Densities peak in tundra and boreal forests. About 90% of soil nematodes live in the top 15 cm. They do not break down dead material. They eat living things instead, up to 5,000 bacteria per minute, and so regulate bacterial numbers and the mix of bacterial kinds. By releasing nitrogen in mineral form, they can play an important part in the movement of nitrogen through soil. They are prey too: the fungi of {{ref:soil-bio-215}} trap them with lassos or sticky structures, or release toxins on contact. Species are hard to tell apart, so estimates of their number run from over 25,000 to close to one million. The soil-dwelling Caenorhabditis elegans is a major model organism. In 2023 a Panagrolaimus kolymaensis was revived after 46,000 years in Siberian permafrost.

entries.title: Entomopathogenic nematodes, worms that hunt insects

definition.text: Nematodes (thread worms) that infect and kill only insects, living as parasites inside their hosts.

facts.text: They attack insects living in the soil, such as the larvae of moths, butterflies, flies and beetles, and adult beetles, grasshoppers and crickets.

An infective juvenile enters an insect and releases gut bacteria, Xenorhabdus or Photorhabdus, that kill it within 24–48 hours; after about a week hundreds of thousands of new juveniles leave the cadaver.

Ambushers such as Steinernema carpocapsae wait at the surface and infect surface insects, while cruisers such as Heterorhabditis bacteriophora hunt deeper, so tillage cut the first's numbers but left the second's unchanged.

Steinernematids and heterorhabditids are used in biological pest control: together they cut plum curculio populations by as much as 70–90% in northeastern American orchards, though they fail against foliage pests because UV light and drying harm them.

entries.title: When burrowers scramble the archaeologist's layers

definition.text: The disturbance of archaeological layers by burrowing organisms, which blurs the order in which deposits were laid down.

facts.text: Archaeologists date finds relatively by stratigraphy, in which the topmost layer is the youngest.
By moving material up, down and sideways, bioturbation confuses the archaeological record and makes relative dating harder.
It is studied by archaeologists alongside geologists and biologists.

entries.text: Archaeologists date finds relatively by stratigraphy: in a stack of deposits, the topmost layer is the youngest. Burrowing organisms break that rule. By moving material up, down and sideways, bioturbation blurs the order in which deposits were laid down, confusing the archaeological record and making relative dating harder. Archaeologists study it alongside geologists and biologists.

entries.title: When a living thing makes a crystal, is it a mineral?

definition.text: The dispute over whether crystalline substances made by living things should count as minerals.

facts.text: The geological definition of a mineral normally excludes compounds found only in living beings, yet calcite is often biogenic and organisms make hydroxylapatite, which also occurs in rocks.
The International Mineralogical Association, the recognized standard body, accepted 5,650 official mineral species out of 5,862 proposed or traditional ones as of December 2020.

Lowenstam (1981) noted that organisms form some minerals that cannot form inorganically; Skinner (2005) counts any element or compound, amorphous or crystalline, formed through biogeochemical processes as a mineral.
Mineral-forming microorganisms live on nearly every rock, soil and particle surface, down to at least 1,600 metres below the sea floor.

entries.contested_note: Geologists and mineralogists disagree over the International Mineralogical Association's decision to exclude biogenic crystalline substances from the list of minerals.

entries.title: Geomycology: fungi that build and break minerals

definition.text: The study of the part fungi play in geological processes, including forming, transforming and dissolving minerals.

facts.text: Fungi deposit minerals on an organic matrix, such as a protein, that offers a nucleation site; proteins they secrete control the size and shape of the carbonate minerals they precipitate.
Using organic phosphorus, fungi can precipitate uranium-bearing phosphate minerals and gather them in their mycelium; species such as Aspergillus niger and Paecilomyces javanicus tolerate uranium.
Fungi also break minerals down, mainly strains that produce oxalic acid: Aspergillus niger, Serpula himantioides and Trametes versicolor corrode apatite and galena.

entries.text: Fungi quietly do geology. Geomycology is the study of the part fungi play in geological processes, including forming, transforming and dissolving minerals. Using organic phosphorus, fungi can even precipitate uranium-bearing phosphate minerals and gather them in their mycelium. Aspergillus niger and Paecilomyces javanicus tolerate uranium. Fungi also break minerals down, joining in {{ref:soil-found-052}}. The main culprits are strains that produce oxalic acid: Aspergillus niger, Serpula himantioides and Trametes versicolor corrode apatite and galena.

entries.title: Three degrees of control in living mineral-making

definition.text: A scheme that sorts mineral formation by living things according to how much the organism controls it: biomineralization proper, organomineralization and inorganic mineralization.

facts.text: In biologically controlled mineralization the cells of one organism fully control the crystals' shape, growth, composition and location, as in mollusc and brachiopod shells.

In biologically induced mineralization microbial metabolism creates chemical conditions that favour mineral growth on an organic matrix the microbes secrete, as in stromatolites and other microbial mats.
In biologically influenced mineralization abiotic processes such as evaporation or degassing set the chemistry, while a microbial organic matrix still shapes the crystals.
The terms have no standardized definitions and their use varies widely; this scheme follows a 2009 framework by Dupraz and colleagues.

entries.text: Living things build minerals with very different degrees of control. One scheme, following a 2009 framework by Dupraz and colleagues, sorts {{ref:soil-bio-063}} into three kinds. In the biologically controlled kind, the cells of one organism fully control the crystals' shape, growth, composition and location. Mollusc and brachiopod shells are built this way. In the biologically induced kind, the metabolic activity of microbes, covered in {{ref:soil-bio-208}}, creates chemical conditions that favor mineral growth on an organic matrix the microbes secrete. Stromatolites and other microbial mats form like this. In the biologically influenced kind, abiotic processes such as evaporation or degassing set the chemistry, while a microbial organic matrix still shapes the crystals. The terms have no standardized definitions, and their use varies widely.
entries.text_plain: Living things build minerals with very different degrees of control. In the biologically controlled kind, the cells of one organism fully control the crystals' shape, growth, composition and location. Mollusc and brachiopod shells are built this way. In the biologically induced kind, the metabolic activity of microbes, covered in How microbes make a living, from fermenting to eating methane, creates chemical conditions that favor mineral growth on an organic matrix the microbes secrete. Stromatolites and other microbial mats form like this. In the biologically influenced kind, abiotic processes such as evaporation or degassing set the chemistry, while a microbial organic matrix still shapes the crystals. The terms have no standardized definitions, and their use varies widely.

entries.title: Dwarf forests, where poor soil grows miniature trees

definition.text: An uncommon ecosystem of miniature trees, also called elfin or pygmy forest, home to small animals such as rodents and lizards.

facts.text: Dwarf forests usually grow at high elevations where the air is humid but the soil is poor; the two main types are coastal temperate and montane tropical.
Tropical montane elfin forests have small trees, 5–8 m tall, with shallow roots and abundant epiphytes; high winds largely set their stature.
At 6,834 hectares, the pygmy forest of Mount Hamiguitan in the Philippines is the largest known dwarf forest in the country and possibly the world.

entries.title: Worm casts, the soil that has passed through a worm

definition.text: A small pile, coil or pellet of soil or sand that burrowing worms expel at the surface.

facts.text: Worms swallow soil with its organic matter and microbes; digestion breaks up mineral particles and partly decomposes organic matter, and the rest is pushed out through the burrow.
On lawns and grasslands, earthworm casts are taken as a sign of biologically active, healthy soil.
Casts often hold more plant-available nutrients than the surrounding soil and build stable soil aggregates.
On beaches and tidal flats, burrowing polychaete worms leave coiled, spaghetti-like casts.

entries.title: Oribatid mites, the slow-living shredders of forest litter

definition.text: Oribatid mites, also called moss or beetle mites, are a group of slow-living mites that are the most prevalent arthropods in forest soils.

facts.text: They measure 0.2 to 1.4 millimetres; about 12,000 species are described, and estimates of the total run from 60,000 to 120,000.
They are essential for breaking down organic detritus and distributing fungi, feeding on living and dead plant and fungal material, lichens and carrion; none is parasitic.
Like earthworms they speed the breakdown of organic material, but unlike many earthworms they do not mix it with mineral matter; some mine conifer needles from inside.
They have low metabolic rates, slow development and low fecundity, taking months to two years to mature in temperate forest soils, and are densest in forests with thick organic layers.

entries.title: Heat, water and nitrogen set the pace of soil breathing

definition.text: The non-living factors, chiefly temperature, soil moisture and nitrogen, that set how fast soil carbon is respired to CO2.

facts.text: Respiration rises exponentially with temperature to a maximum, then falls to zero as enzymes fail; root respiration starts to shut down above 35 °C.
Cryophiles work best below 20 °C, mesophiles between 20 and 40 °C and thermophiles above 40 °C, so mixed communities respire over a broad range.
Respiration is low when dry, peaks at intermediate moisture and falls when water shuts out oxygen.
Nitrogen costs roots energy: taking in nitrate costs 0.4 units of CO2 and reducing it 2 units; nitrogen-rich litter also decomposes faster.

entries.title: Putting a lid on the soil to measure its breath

definition.text: Field and laboratory techniques for measuring how fast CO2 leaves the soil and where it comes from.

facts.text: Closed chambers sealed over the soil derive the flux from CO2 build-up over a few minutes (F=bV/A); longer runs underestimate it as CO2 is stored in the soil.
Open systems pump fresh air through the chamber and read the flux at equilibrium; portable survey systems move between soil collars to capture variation from place to place.
Basal respiration is measured with nothing added; substrate-induced respiration adds nutrients and sugars.
Stable carbon isotopes separate sources: swapping C3 and C4 crops, or spraying C4 cane sugar, tells old from new carbon and microbial from root respiration.

entries.title: How a changing planet is changing soil's breath

definition.text: How rising CO2, warming, changing rainfall and nitrogen fertilization are altering soil respiration around the planet.

facts.text: Free air CO2 enrichment (FACE) studies show elevated CO2 raises soil respiration through more roots and microbial activity, by up to 40.6% in sweetgum and poplar forests.
Warming may hit hardest in the Arctic, where thawing permafrost turns aerobic and its large carbon stores are respired much faster.
Dry soils burst into respiration after rain and slow as they dry, so more frequent, intense rain should raise respiration sharply in arid lands.
Nitrogen fertilization since the Green Revolution boosts plant growth, root respiration and root biomass, and with them soil respiration.

entries.title: Roots, microbes and animals: who breathes out soil CO2
entries.article: Soil respiration#Sources of carbon dioxide in soil

definition.text: The organisms and pathways that produce the CO2 leaving soil: roots, rhizosphere microbes, decomposers and soil animals.

facts.text: Root respiration accounts for approximately half of all soil respiration, though values range from 10 to 90% with plant type and conditions.
Up to 20% of photosynthetic carbon enters the soil as root exudates, decomposed mainly by bacteria; mycorrhizal fungi also respire sugars the plant gives them.
The CO2 comes from the TCA cycle of cellular respiration and also from fermentation, which works without oxygen, as in the oxygen-poor rhizosphere.
Soil animals add to it by grazing bacteria and fungi and by fragmenting litter, exposing more surface to microbes.

entries.text: Roughly half the CO2 rising from soil comes from roots. Root respiration accounts for approximately half of {{ref:soil-bio-033}}, though values range from 10 to 90% with plant type and conditions. The rest comes from the organisms around them. Up to 20% of the carbon a plant captures in {{ref:soil-hist-147}} leaks into the soil from roots, and bacteria decompose most of it. Fungi partnered with roots also respire sugars the plant gives them. Most of the CO2 comes from the TCA cycle of cellular respiration. Fermentation, which works without oxygen, adds more in the oxygen-poor soil right around roots. Soil animals contribute by grazing bacteria and fungi and by fragmenting litter, which exposes more surface to microbes.

entries.title: Light or chemicals, rock or food: how life gets fed

definition.text: The division of organisms by the sources of energy, electrons and carbon they need to live, grow and reproduce.

facts.text: Energy comes from light (phototrophs) or chemical compounds (chemotrophs); electrons from organic donors (organotrophs) or inorganic ones (lithotrophs); carbon from organic compounds (heterotrophs) or carbon dioxide (autotrophs).
Names combine one term from each source: a chemoorganoheterotroph, for example, takes its carbon from organic substrates and its energy from breaking down an organic compound.
Aerobic respiration, anaerobic respiration and fermentation describe the electron acceptor used and do not define a nutritional group.
Organotrophs are often also heterotrophs, and lithotrophs are often also autotrophs that use carbon dioxide.
Plants count as lithotrophs because they use water as the electron donor of photosynthesis; cyanobacteria, algae and land plants are photolithoautotrophs.
Decomposers are chemoorganoheterotrophs that take carbon and electrons from dead organic matter; all animals, fungi and protozoa and some bacteria are chemoheterotrophs.
Plants and some bacteria can switch between phototrophy and chemotrophy depending on the light available.

entries.text: Every living thing must answer three questions: where do its energy, its electrons and its carbon come from? The answers sort life into primary nutritional groups. Energy comes from light, for phototrophs, or from chemical compounds, for {{ref:soil-bio-205}}. Electrons come from organic donors, as in {{ref:soil-bio-206}}, or from inorganic ones, for lithotrophs. Carbon comes from organic compounds, for heterotrophs, or from carbon dioxide, for autotrophs. A name combines one term from each pair. A chemoorganoheterotroph, for example, takes its carbon from organic substrates and its energy from breaking down an organic compound. The pairs often travel together. Organisms that draw electrons from organic matter are often heterotrophs too, and lithotrophs are often autotrophs that use carbon dioxide. Plants count as lithotrophs because water is the electron donor of their {{ref:soil-hist-147}}. Cyanobacteria, algae and land plants are therefore photolithoautotrophs. Decomposers are chemoorganoheterotrophs, taking carbon and electrons from dead organic matter. All animals, fungi and protozoa, and some bacteria, are chemoheterotrophs. The labels are not always fixed: plants and some bacteria can switch between phototrophy and chemotrophy depending on the light. One distinction is easy to confuse. Aerobic respiration, anaerobic respiration and fermentation describe the electron acceptor used, the substance that finally takes the electrons, and do not define a nutritional group.

entries.title: Millipedes, slow shredders of the forest floor

definition.text: Arthropods of the class Diplopoda, with two pairs of jointed legs on most body segments.

facts.text: Most are slow-moving detritivores of forest floors that eat decaying leaves and dead wood; some eat fungi or suck plant fluids.
Individual species are estimated to consume 1 to 11 percent of all leaf litter, depending on species and region.
Litter is fragmented in the gut and excreted as pellets of leaf fragments, algae, fungi and bacteria, which helps microbes decompose it further.
Burrowing that mixes organic with mineral matter makes them soil ecosystem engineers, especially where earthworms are absent or scarce, as in some tropical forests.

entries.title: Acid mine drainage, sulfuric acid brewed by microbes

definition.text: The acid runoff made when lithotrophic microbes in mining areas oxidize pyrite and other reduced sulfur minerals to sulfate.

facts.text: The acidophilic bacterium Acidithiobacillus ferrooxidans, for example, uses iron sulfide to generate sulfuric acid, which can drain from the mine with runoff.
It drives the pH of groundwater and streams down to 2–3, changes their chemistry and may endanger plant and animal populations downstream.
The same kind of activity runs on a much smaller scale in nature: in soil and talus, on glacier beds, on stone buildings and monuments, and in the deep subsurface.

entries.text: Streams below some mines run at pH 2–3. It changes the chemistry of groundwater and streams and may endanger plant and animal populations downstream. This is {{ref:soil-bio-057}} on an industrial scale. The same activity runs far more modestly in nature: in soil and talus, on glacier beds, on stone buildings and monuments, and in the deep subsurface.

entries.title: How microbes living on bare rock start a soil

definition.text: The part that rock-colonizing lithotrophs, cyanobacteria above all, play in starting soil formation on bare rock.

facts.text: Cyanobacteria are nitrogen-fixing photolithotrophs: they use energy from sunlight and inorganic nutrients from rock as reductants.
This lets them grow on native, nutrient-poor rock and leave behind organic matter that other organisms can then colonize.
Colonization can start the decomposition of organic compounds, a primary factor in soil genesis, and the mechanism is thought to have helped shape the early biological Earth.
Lithoautotrophs take part in weathering bedrock into soil and in cycling sulfur, potassium and other elements, freeing nutrients that sustain life.

entries.title: Soil zoology, the science of animals underfoot

definition.text: The study of animals that live wholly or partly in the soil, also called pedozoology.

facts.text: Mercury Ghilarov developed the field in Russia in the 1940s.
Ghilarov noted that the smaller soil organisms are, the more numerous they are, and suggested soil may have been the transitional environment between aquatic and terrestrial life.
The term was apparently first used in English at a 1955 conference of soil zoologists at the University of Nottingham.
Studying interactions among soil animals can help farmers cut chemical use through integrated pest management.

entries.title: Does life underground follow the map of life above?

definition.text: The unsettled question of how life in soil is distributed over the globe and whether it follows the same drivers as life above ground.

facts.text: A survey of 17,516 18S rRNA gene sequences from 20 phyla of soil animals suggested that below-ground animal diversity may be inversely related to above-ground diversity.
Soil biodiversity lacks the clear latitudinal gradients of plants; in 2007 salinity, not temperature or pH, was found to be the main global determinant of bacterial diversity.
A 2014 global study found fungal richness unrelated to plant diversity and better explained by climate, then soil and spatial factors.
Some studies find that losing soil organisms reduces many ecosystem functions; others find above-ground plant diversity a better predictor of multifunctionality.

entries.contested_note: Studies disagree on whether soil biodiversity mirrors above-ground diversity and how strongly it drives ecosystem functioning.

entries.title: Microbial hotspots, the crowded corners of soil

definition.text: Small sites in soil, rich in resources such as moisture or nutrients, where microorganisms are concentrated.

facts.text: Examples are the rhizosphere and the detritusphere, where organic matter accumulates.
There, decaying root litter and root exudates regulate the supply of carbon and nitrogen and so steer microbial processes.
Root tips are hotspots of cellulase and chitinase activity.
The spatial separation of microbes, shaped by labile carbon, temperature and moisture, affects how they interact and how the soil ecosystem functions.

entries.text: Soil microbes do not spread evenly. They crowd into hotspots, small sites rich in resources such as moisture or nutrients. One is the soil around roots. Another is the detritusphere, where dead organic material accumulates. In both, decaying root litter and compounds released by roots regulate the supply of carbon and nitrogen and so steer microbial processes. Root tips are hotspots of cellulase and chitinase, enzymes that break down plant and fungal materials. Between hotspots, microbes are separated in space. That separation, shaped by easily used carbon, temperature and moisture, affects how they interact and how the soil ecosystem works.

entries.title: Counting soil life by reading its DNA

definition.text: Ways of counting and identifying soil organisms, increasingly by extracting DNA directly from the soil.

facts.text: Most soil microbes have never been cultured and remain undescribed, so the diversity of soil life is hard to measure.
Next-generation sequencing and DNA extracted directly from the soil matrix are opening soil diversity to study.
Omics approaches such as metagenomics, metatranscriptomics and proteomics are advancing fast for microbes; metaphenomics has been proposed to add environmental constraints.
A 2020 FAO report found major gaps in knowledge about biodiversity in soils.

entries.text_plain: Most soil microbes have never been cultured and remain undescribed, so measuring the diversity of soil life is hard. The answer, increasingly, is to read DNA instead of growing cells. Next-generation sequencing of DNA extracted directly from the soil is opening Five hundred sheep beneath a football pitch to study. Omics approaches for microbes are advancing fast. One method, described in Metagenomics: reading the DNA of a whole soil, reads the genes of a whole community, metatranscriptomics its active genes and proteomics its proteins. Metaphenomics has been proposed to add environmental constraints. Much remains unknown. A 2020 FAO report found major gaps in knowledge about biodiversity in soils.

entries.title: Chemotrophs, life powered by chemistry instead of light

definition.text: An organism that gets its energy by oxidizing electron donors from its surroundings, in contrast to phototrophs, which use light.

facts.text: The donors may be organic (chemoorganotrophs) or inorganic (chemolithotrophs), and chemotrophs may be either autotrophic or heterotrophic.

Chemoautotrophs build all their organic compounds from carbon dioxide using energy from substances such as hydrogen sulfide, sulfur, ferrous iron, hydrogen or ammonia; nitrifiers, methanogens and sulfur oxidizers are among them.
Chemoheterotrophs cannot fix carbon into their own organic compounds; most animals and fungi are chemoheterotrophs.

Methanogens take over the last step of organic matter breakdown only once richer electron acceptors such as oxygen, nitrate and sulfate are used up; thawing frozen soils is expected to raise their methane output.

entries.title: Ammonia fungi, which fruit where nitrogen floods the soil

definition.text: Fungi whose fruiting bodies develop quickly and germinate readily when ammonia or other nitrogen-rich material makes the soil alkaline.

facts.text: They appear naturally after decomposition events such as animal excretion or death, and heavy additions of ammonia or urea create the conditions they thrive in until the soil reverts.
Most live in temperate forests on well-rotted wood, plant debris or dung, and they are most active in the O horizon, then the A and B horizons.
Adding ammonia or urea raises the pH of soil litter to 8–10, which interrupts nutrient recycling; soil ammonia takes up to 2 years to return to its earlier level, helped by late-phase fungi.
They help maintain the nitrogen cycle, and some are predators: Laccaria bicolor catches and kills springtails.

entries.title: How a few earthworm species hitched rides around the world

definition.text: The spread of a few earthworm species, carried by people, into regions where they are not native.

facts.text: Of around 7,000 earthworm species, only about 150 are widely distributed: the peregrine or cosmopolitan earthworms.
Of the 308 earthworm taxa in the United States and Canada, 70 (23%) are introduced species.
In podzols, invading earthworms can erase the banded profile, mixing the organic, E and upper B horizons into a single dark Ap horizon.
Surface-dwelling earthworms speed up carbon cycling and have been spread by humans into many new regions.
Peregrine earthworms spread through intentional and accidental transport of plants and soil, helped by growing trade, and can carry viruses and spores of plant pathogens.
Jumping worms, pheretimoid earthworms of Amynthas, Metaphire and Pheretima native to Australia and East Asia, commonly harm the places they invade.
In the UK the invasive New Zealand flatworm feeds on earthworms, and other earthworm populations declined after it appeared.
No known method removes earthworms from soil; buying heat-treated compost and removing shrubs such as buckthorn, whose litter worms favour, slow or reduce them.

entries.title: How invading earthworms are eating North America's forest floor

definition.text: The spread of introduced, mostly European and Asian earthworms into North American forests, especially northern forests that have lacked native worms since the last ice age.

facts.text: Most northern forests lost their native earthworms to the Wisconsin glaciation, so a deep detritus layer is typical and many native plants rely on it.
Invading worms break up the organic layer by burrowing, eating litter and leaving casts, mixing nutrients beyond the reach of shallow roots, where they may be leached.
Effects include a thinner organic layer, more mineralization, higher bulk density and faster decomposition; podzols lose their banded E horizons.
Invasions reduce plant diversity, seedlings and mycorrhizal associations, while invasive plants such as buckthorn and garlic mustard increase.
European worms arrived in soil with settlers from the 18th century, likely in the root balls of imported plants; recreation, bait and construction now spread them.
Sandy, saline or acidic soils and high C:N litter resist invasion, while high pH and low C:N favour it.
Asian jumping worms of Amynthas and Metaphire grow and breed faster and live at higher densities than European species, stripping the forest floor of organic matter.
Worms cannot be removed from soil, so control aims to slow spread: fewer bait releases, regulated soil movement and heat-treated compost or mulch.

entries.title: Sporosarcina pasteurii, the bacterium that turns sand to stone

definition.text: Sporosarcina pasteurii is a gram-positive, soil-borne bacterium that precipitates calcite and solidifies sand given calcium and urea.

facts.text: It is a rod-shaped endospore former, 0.5 to 1.2 micrometres wide and 1.3 to 4.0 micrometres long, an alkaliphile growing at pH 9 to 10 and surviving up to pH 11.2.
It is a heterotrophic facultative anaerobe needing urea and ammonium, secreting urease to hydrolyse urea for nitrogen, carbon and energy.
Carbonate ions from urea hydrolysis react with calcium to precipitate calcium carbonate that cements sand grains; it is non-pathogenic and makes much urease, so it is a common MICP organism.
It is proposed for self-healing concrete and other bio-cement uses.

entries.title: Bottom-up control: feed the base and the web swells

definition.text: Control of a food web from its base, where the biomass, abundance or diversity of higher levels depends on resources from lower levels.

facts.text: Correlations in abundance or biomass between consumers and their resources are evidence of bottom-up control.
On land, the biomass of herbivores and detritivores rises with primary productivity.
More productivity means more leaf litter, more bacteria and fungi, more nematodes that eat them and more mites and predatory nematodes: the whole web swells.

entries.text: Feed the base of a food web and the whole web grows. In bottom-up control, the biomass, abundance or diversity of higher levels depends on resources from lower levels. The evidence is correlation: consumers rise and fall with their resources. On land, the biomass of herbivores and detritivores rises with primary productivity, the rate at which plants make new growth. In the {{ref:soil-bio-025}} the chain is easy to follow. More productivity means more leaf litter, then more bacteria and fungi, more {{ref:soil-bio-193}} that eat them, and more mites and predatory roundworms. The whole web swells.

entries.title: The external rumen: animals that let microbes cook their food
entries.article: Soil food web#Interactions not included in food webs

definition.text: A partnership in which litter-eating animals such as isopods let microbes enrich their faecal pellets outside the body, then eat the pellets again.

facts.text: Isopods and other litter transformers excrete pellets that are moister and richer in nutrients than the surrounding soil, which bacteria and fungi then colonise.
On nutrient-poor litter the microbes enrich the food, and isopods kept from eating their own faeces can die.
Fungi play a similar role for wood-eaters, enriching nutritionally scarce dead wood so xylophages can develop and speed wood decay.
Such mutualisms and habitat changes are not captured by standard food webs, which emphasise competition and predation.

entries.title: Funnels, cores and lamps: getting animals out of soil

definition.text: Techniques for separating organisms from soil samples so they can be counted and identified.

facts.text: Samples are often taken with a metal core; large animals such as earthworms are picked out by hand, which is impossible for nematodes and small arthropods.
A dry Berlese funnel drives microarthropods down away from light and heat into a collecting vial; a wet Baermann funnel collects nematodes, which sink because they cannot swim.
Microbes are characterized by their respiration, by genetic profiling of extracted cell components, or by biomass estimated before and after fumigation.

entries.title: Do soil predators rule the web from the top?

definition.text: Control of a food web from above, where consumers at higher levels set the abundance, diversity or biomass of lower levels.

facts.text: In a trophic cascade, predators affect organisms at least two links down; whether cascades matter on land is actively debated, and in soil they occur in bacterial and fungal channels but may be infrequent.
Omnivory, dormancy and the spatial separation of predator and prey all damp top-down effects in soil.
Soil food webs are donor controlled: decomposers cannot change how fast litter falls, which limits top-down effects.
Added predators or parasites can still matter: an entomopathogenic nematode that kills root-eating ghost moth caterpillars protected bush lupine, the principle behind biological control.

entries.contested_note: The importance of trophic cascades and top-down control on land, and whether cascades occur in soil, is actively debated.

entries.title: Why tangled soil food webs hold together
entries.article: Soil food web#Stability of food webs

definition.text: How well soil food webs resist and recover from disturbance, and why their complexity seems to help.

facts.text: May's models, with randomly linked community matrices, predicted that complexity destabilizes food webs, and soil webs were long thought simple; the random matrices drew much criticism.
Soil food webs did not fit those predictions: long, complex, omnivorous chains resisted drying, freezing and fumigation.
Many weak interactions, donor control, the buffering of soil structure and dormancy in organisms such as bacteria all promote stability.
Nitrogen-containing fertilizers reduce stability because they acidify soil.

entries.title: Three ways to draw who eats whom in soil
entries.article: Soil food web#Types of food webs

definition.text: The three ways of drawing a food web: topological webs, flow webs and interaction webs.

facts.text: Topological webs, the earliest kind, map which organisms eat which without numbers; the first, in 1912, covered predators and parasites of the cotton boll weevil.
How many species are lumped into functional groups varies by author, which hampers standardized comparisons.
Interaction webs show how one group influences another: each link has a positive effect on the consumer and a negative one on the resource, and these can cause indirect effects.
Community matrix models describe every link with differential equations, using Lotka–Volterra equations and data on biomass and feeding rate to calculate interaction strengths.

entries.text: In 1912, a food web traced the predators and parasites of the cotton boll weevil. It was the first topological web, the earliest of three ways to draw a food web. Each link has a positive effect on the consumer and a negative one on the resource, and these links can cause indirect effects. Community matrix models describe every link with differential equations. They use Lotka–Volterra equations and data on biomass and feeding rate to calculate interaction strengths. Comparisons stay difficult, because authors lump different numbers of species into functional groups.

entries.title: Flow webs put numbers on soil's feeding links

definition.text: Food webs that add numbers to the feeding links, tracing how much carbon or other nutrients move from producers to consumers.

facts.text: Hunt et al. (1987) published the first soil flow web, for the shortgrass prairie of Colorado, estimating nitrogen transfer and mineralization rates for a range of soil organisms.
Building one starts from a topological web; each functional group's biomass is then calculated, usually in kg carbon/hectare, assuming populations are at equilibrium to derive feeding rates.
Flow webs revealed three main energy channels: the bacterial and fungal channels carry the largest flow, the root-herbivory channel much less.
Bacteria and fungi are now widely recognized as critical to decomposing carbon and nitrogen in both cycles.

entries.title: Plant-parasitic nematodes, the hidden thieves of crops

definition.text: Pest nematodes that attack crop plants, chiefly their roots, or spread plant viruses between them.

facts.text: They take about 10% of crops worldwide each year; major genera include Meloidogyne (root-knot), Globodera and Heterodera (cyst) and Pratylenchus (lesion) nematodes.
Root-knot nematodes leave visible galls on roots that help diagnose them in the field, and species such as Xiphinema index carry plant viruses.
Controls include rotation with resistant crops, marigold cover crops and antagonistic fungi and bacteria; Brassica juncea green manure cut densities 13- to 14-fold in CSIRO plots.
Soil steaming kills nematodes before planting but removes harmful and beneficial soil fauna alike.
