entries.title: Microbial ecology: studying microbes beyond medicine

definition.text: The study of how microorganisms interact with their environment, also called environmental microbiology.

facts.text: Martinus Beijerinck invented the enrichment culture, and Sergei Winogradsky, studying microbes outside medicine, discovered chemosynthesis.
Lorenz Hiltner recognised the bacteria responsible for denitrification, nitrification and nitrogen fixation.
Microbes drive the nitrogen, phosphorus, sulfur and carbon cycles, making nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium available in soil.

entries.title: The microbiome, a community with an address

definition.text: The community of microorganisms usually found living together in a given habitat.

facts.text: The term was first defined in 1988 by Whipps and colleagues, who studied rhizosphere microorganisms, as a characteristic community in a well-defined habitat with distinct physico-chemical properties.
Relic DNA can make up to 40% of the DNA sequenced from soil.
Synthetic nitrogen fertiliser may barely change soil microbiome composition but drastically reduces the connectivity of its network.
TerraGenome, a reference soil metagenome project, began in 2008.

entries.title: Metagenomics: reading the DNA of a whole soil

definition.text: The study of all the genetic material from all organisms in an environment, revealing their composition, diversity and functional potential.

facts.text: It profiles microbial communities without culturing species, and early environmental gene studies showed that cultivation had missed most microbial diversity.
Unlike amplicon sequencing (metabarcoding) of marker genes such as 16S rRNA, which shows which taxa are present, metagenomics sequences all DNA and also recovers enzymes and pathways.
Norman Pace proposed cloning DNA directly from environmental samples in 1985, and his group first reported doing so in 1991.
One gram of soil holds about 10^9–10^10 microbial cells, about one gigabase of sequence, and soil communities are among the most complex known.
Functional metagenomics explores plant–microbe interactions and the roles of uncultivated or rare community members in nutrient cycling and plant growth.
Because sampling is uncontrolled, the most abundant organisms dominate shotgun sequence data.
Long-read sequencing of soils in industrial zones showed that chronic heavy metal contamination restructures the soil microbial community.
The 16S rRNA gene identifies bacteria and archaea, and 18S rRNA or ITS identifies fungi; more similar sequences are taken to mean closer evolutionary relatedness.

entries.title: Living on almost nothing in deep and frozen soils

definition.text: Soils, such as farmed and frozen soils, in which microbes have very few nutrients to live on.

facts.text: Nutrients thin out with depth because surface microbes quickly consume what decomposes from plant and animal debris, and their metabolic wastes build up toxic chemicals lower down.
Water and oxygen diffuse less easily as depth increases; aggregates, pores and extracellular enzymes help water, oxygen and nutrients move into the soil.
Frozen polar soils are dominated by Actinomycetota, Pseudomonadota, Acidobacteriota and Cyanobacteria; Actinomycetota keep their enzymes working across a wide range of low temperatures.
The bacterium Collimonas lives in such soils by digesting chitin from fungi and by weathering rocks and minerals for electron sources.

entries.title: How plants thrive on the poorest soils

definition.text: The ways plants of oligotrophic soils take up nutrients more efficiently, use less of them and store them.

facts.text: Uptake improves through root adaptations such as nitrogen-fixing root nodules, mycorrhizae and cluster roots.
Plants grow very slowly and use abundant ions for turgor while saving scarce nutrients for building tissue; many store nutrients, in trunk tissue for example, and remobilize them when demand rises.
On the ancient sandplains and lateritic soils of southern Western Australia, most plants rely on cluster roots for phosphorus and sulfur, yet the vegetation is highly diverse.
White-sand soils of the Rio Negro basin in northern Amazonia, with pH below 5.0, carry low-diversity, extremely fragile forests and savannahs.

entries.title: The drilosphere, soil remade by earthworms

definition.text: The part of the soil shaped by earthworm secretions, burrowing and casts: soil that has passed through their gut or lines their burrows.

facts.text: The burrow lining averages 2 mm thick but can reach about 8 mm around the burrows of litter-feeding earthworms.
It is generally richer in nitrogen, phosphorus and humified organic matter than the surrounding soil, probably because earthworms prefer to eat leaf and root litter.
In one soil it held 40 per cent of the aerobic and 13 per cent of the anaerobic nitrogen-fixing bacteria, and 16 per cent of the denitrifiers.
Through it earthworms steer soil microbial communities and with them organic matter and nutrient dynamics.

entries.title: Fungal biocontrol: fungi that fight crop disease

definition.text: Fungi can protect crops by competing with pathogens or by parasitising them.

facts.text: About 300 species of fungi and fungus-like organisms, in 13 classes and 113 genera, are used as biocontrol agents against plant fungal diseases.
Organisms that parasitise fungi are called mycoparasitic.
Fungi may also compete with pathogenic bacteria or fungi for nutrients and space, by the competitive exclusion principle.

entries.title: How fungi reproduce and spread

definition.text: Fungi reproduce asexually, sexually or both, and spread mainly by spores.

facts.text: Asexual reproduction uses vegetative spores (conidia) or mycelial fragmentation, in which pieces of mycelium each grow into a separate mycelium.
An estimated third of fungi use more than one method, with a sexual teleomorph stage and an asexual anamorph stage.
Spores of most studied species travel by wind; dry, hydrophobic spores are readily scattered by raindrops.

entries.title: Geomicrobiology: microbes that make and break minerals

definition.text: The field between geology and microbiology that studies the role of microbes in geological and geochemical processes and the effects of minerals and metals on microbes.

facts.text: Its interactions take place in rocks, minerals, soils and sediments, the atmosphere and the hydrosphere, where microbes drive biogeochemical cycles, precipitate and dissolve minerals and concentrate metals.
Some bacteria gain energy by reducing dissolved metal ions, and as a side effect concentrate the metals into what can become ore deposits.
In soil, microbes transform mineral and metal speciation, toxicity and mobility, and immobilise and detoxify metals, radionuclides, sulfur and phosphorus.
Cr(VI) is mobile and toxic while Cr(III) is less toxic and precipitates in soils above pH 6, so microbial reduction of Cr(VI) is a low-cost bioremediation technique.
Sulfate-reducing bacteria precipitate metals as sulfides and add bicarbonate alkalinity that neutralises acid mine drainage.
Applications include bioremediation, mining, climate change mitigation and drinking water supply.

entries.title: Moles, gophers and badgers: the giants that dig soil

definition.text: Soil animals over 2 cm long, mostly burrowing vertebrates, that dig nests and galleries and throw earth up into mounds.

facts.text: They include fossorial mammals such as moles, pocket gophers, voles and badgers, plus burrowing birds, reptiles, amphibians, large earthworms and big arthropods; they are most common in arid areas.
Most dig without eating soil, but stirring the horizons improves nutrient availability, infiltration, aeration, mycorrhizal inoculation and seed germination.
Burrows create nutrient-rich patches and raise porosity and infiltration, reducing runoff on slopes.
Often treated as pests, their loss from whole landscapes has been called an ecological catastrophe, especially in dry lands where they are keystone species for soil health.

entries.title: Testate amoebae, single cells that carry a shell

definition.text: Single-celled amoeboid protists partly enclosed in a shell, or test, with an opening through which their pseudopodia emerge.

facts.text: The test is either made by the cell itself, organic, siliceous or calcareous, or glued together from sediment particles it collects.
They live in most fresh waters, mires and soils; in soil the shell protects them from drying, and they may stay encysted until conditions improve.
Their tough tests survive after death, and some species respond to temperature, pH and conductivity, so they serve as bioindicators and paleoclimate proxies.
Sampled with pollen and plant remains in soil horizons, they can reveal climate or land-use changes during soil formation.

entries.title: Streptomyces, the bacteria that make soil smell like soil

definition.text: The largest genus of actinomycete bacteria, found mainly in soil and decaying vegetation.

facts.text: Most produce spores and give soil its earthy odour by releasing the volatile compound geosmin.
They are filamentous, Gram-positive bacteria with branched hyphae 0.5–2.0 μm across, forming a substrate mycelium that scavenges organic compounds.
Streptomycetes produce over two-thirds of the clinically useful natural antibiotics; streptomycin is named after the genus.
Several species are plant pathogens, causing scab of potatoes and soft rot of sweet potatoes.

entries.title: Copiotrophs, the microbes that live for the feast

definition.text: An organism found in environments rich in nutrients, especially carbon.

facts.text: Copiotrophs are the opposite of oligotrophs and grow at organic substrate levels up to 100 times higher.

Soil bacterial phyla can be sorted into copiotrophic and oligotrophic groups; soils rich in organic carbon favour copiotrophs, key players in the soil carbon cycle when plants exude simple compounds such as sugars.
They live a 'feast-and-famine' life: motile and chemotactic, they rush to nutrients and use them fast, but survive poorly once supplies run out, when oligotrophs outcompete them.
They grow fast, carrying up to fifteen ribosomal RNA operons against one in oligotrophs, but use carbon less efficiently.

entries.title: Azotobacter, the nitrogen fixer that works alone

definition.text: A genus of aerobic, free-living soil bacteria that fix atmospheric nitrogen and release it into the soil as ammonium.

facts.text: They are common in neutral and weakly basic soils but not acid soils, and can survive in dry soil as cysts for up to 24 years.
Unlike Rhizobium they fix nitrogen without a plant partner, and fixation stops when ammonium or nitrate is available.
They shield oxygen-sensitive nitrogenase by speeding up their metabolism; besides the molybdenum-iron enzyme they have a vanadium nitrogenase that fixes nitrogen down to 5 °C.
Martinus Beijerinck described the genus in 1901; Azotobacter is used in nitrogen biofertilizers such as azotobacterin and makes plant hormones such as auxins.

entries.title: Bacterivores, the grazers of the microbial world

definition.text: An organism that gets its energy and nutrients mainly or entirely by eating bacteria.

facts.text: The term is used mostly for free-living microscopic heterotrophs such as nematodes, amoebae and other protozoa, though some larger invertebrates, certain arthropods among them, also eat bacteria.
Many are generalist predators of any bacteria, but not all bacteria are easily digested; spores of some species, such as Clostridium perfringens, are never eaten.
Springtails and many protozoa are listed among bacterivores.
Bacterivores contaminating environmental samples hinder the growing of bacteria for study; cycloheximide can suppress them but also inhibits some anaerobic prokaryotes.

Cycloheximide can suppress them but also inhibits some anaerobic prokaryotes.

entries.title: Fungivory: the many creatures that eat fungi

definition.text: Fungivory or mycophagy is the eating of fungi; organisms that eat nothing else are called fungivores.

facts.text: Fungus eaters include birds, mammals, insects, plants, amoebae, snails and slugs, nematodes, bacteria and other fungi.

Mycoparasitic Trichoderma fungi detect other fungi, bind to their hyphae and digest their cell walls with enzymes such as chitinases; they have protected crops from pathogens such as Rhizoctonia solani.
Bacterial mycophagy, a term coined in 2005, is bacteria growing at the expense of living fungal hyphae; most of what is known concerns bacteria and fungi in soil and around plants.
Beetles, ants and termites each evolved fungus farming 40 to 60 million years ago; about 330 termite species cultivate Termitomyces fungi in their nests.

entries.title: Fossorial animals, the diggers that remake soil

definition.text: Animals adapted to digging that live mainly, though not only, underground.

facts.text: Examples include moles, badgers, naked mole-rats, armadillos and wombats, and among invertebrates many clams, beetles, wasps, bees and spiders.
Small burrowers such as ants, termites and earthworms move so much soil that the global total matches the global rate of tectonic uplift.
Burrowing changes soil composition, structure and vegetation, usually shifting plant species and raising plant diversity.
Mounds and bare soils with burrowers hold more ammonium and nitrate and show greater nitrification potential than vegetated soils, mainly because the grass cover is removed.

entries.title: Termite mounds, earthen towers built by insects

definition.text: Termite nests that protrude above the soil surface, built of earth and mud and stronger than underground nests.

facts.text: Macrotermes builds some of the largest mounds, 8 to 9 metres high with chimneys, pinnacles and ridges; the largest recorded measured 12.8 metres.
Being rich in clay, mounds in areas of torrential, continuous rain risk erosion.
Compass termites build wedge-shaped mounds aligned north–south, which warms them quickly in the morning but avoids midday overheating.
Mounds shelter birds, lizards, snakes and scorpions, and 54 ant species are known to live in Nasutitermes mounds.

entries.title: The fungal loop that links desert plants and crusts

definition.text: The idea that, in arid ecosystems, soil fungi link the activity of plants and biological soil crusts, which respond to different amounts of soil moisture.

facts.text: It proposes that carbon and nutrients stay cycling in living pools rather than being leached or lost to the air between rain pulses.
Fungi can work at higher temperatures and lower water potentials than bacteria, so they likely drive nutrient cycling in hot, dry ecosystems.
Crusts wake after small rains; fungi hold their nutrients until larger rains activate plants, which then pass carbon back to their fungal partners.
Direct tests remain rare, but one isotope study found nitrogen moving up to 100 cm per day in both directions between plants and crust.

entries.title: The detrital food web, where most food ends up

definition.text: A food web in which dead plant and animal matter is broken down by decomposers such as bacteria and fungi and passes to detritivores and then carnivores.

facts.text: Detritus is any non-living organic matter: leaf litter, dead wood, carrion, dead microbes and faeces among others.
Most of an ecosystem's primary production is not eaten but recycled through detritus into useful nutrients.
It links to the grazing web: mushrooms from decomposers feed deer, squirrels and mice, and robins eat earthworms that consume decaying leaves.
Basal species of food webs include saprophytic detritivores such as the decomposer community of soil, whose role Raymond Lindeman emphasised.

entries.text: Most of what an ecosystem's plants produce is never eaten. Instead it is recycled through {{ref:soil-bio-112}}, the dead remains of living things, into useful nutrients. In a detrital food web, decomposers such as bacteria and fungi break it down, and it passes to detritivores and then to carnivores. Raymond Lindeman emphasized the soil's decomposer community among the basal species of food webs. This web links to the grazing web. entries.title: Organotrophs, which take their electrons from food

definition.text: An organism that obtains hydrogen or electrons from organic substrates.

facts.text: The term classifies microorganisms by how they obtain electrons for respiration; Lwoff and collaborators suggested it in 1946.
Many organotrophs, such as animals and many bacteria, are also heterotrophs, and organotrophs can be aerobic or anaerobic.
Its counterpart is the lithotroph, which obtains its electrons from inorganic substrates.

entries.title: How microbes make a living, from fermenting to eating methane

definition.text: The means by which a microbe obtains the energy and nutrients, such as carbon, that it needs to live and reproduce.

facts.text: A microbe's metabolic properties largely decide its ecological niche and can make it responsible for biogeochemical cycles.
Metabolisms are sorted by carbon source (autotrophic, heterotrophic or mixotrophic), source of reducing equivalents (lithotrophic or organotrophic) and energy source (phototrophic or chemotrophic).
Nitrifying, sulfur-oxidizing and iron-oxidizing bacteria are chemolithoautotrophs; most bacteria, Bacillus and the Actinomycetota among them, are chemoorganoheterotrophs.
Fermenters use organic carbon instead of oxygen as the terminal electron acceptor; facultative anaerobes respire with oxygen when it is present and switch to fermentation when it is not.
Many facultative anaerobes denitrify because nitrate, like oxygen, has a high reduction potential; nitrate is reduced stepwise through nitrite, nitric oxide and nitrous oxide to dinitrogen.
Methanotrophs oxidize methane step by step to carbon dioxide; because the process needs oxygen, all conventional methanotrophs are obligate aerobes.
Ammonia and nitrite oxidation yield so little energy that nitrifiers grow very slowly; in 2015 the genus Nitrospira was shown to carry out complete nitrification (comammox).

entries.title: Saprotrophic bacteria, which digest the dead from outside

definition.text: Mostly soil-dwelling bacteria that feed on dead organic matter, digesting it outside the cell with enzymes and absorbing the products.

facts.text: Alongside saprotrophic fungi and water molds they drive decomposition and nutrient cycling, feeding higher trophic levels.
Bacteria outcompete fungi for easily available substrates, but their higher nitrogen demand and inability to move nutrients make them less efficient decomposers in forest soils.
Their community make-up and growth rates are used as signals of soil health, since growth responds quickly to environmental change.
Some are pathogens spread through contact with excrement, such as Escherichia coli; others ferment cellulose in the rumen of cows.

entries.text: Many soil bacteria digest their food before they eat it. Saprotrophic bacteria, mostly soil-dwelling, feed on dead organic material. They release enzymes that digest it outside the cell, then absorb the products. Alongside saprotrophic fungi and water molds, they drive the breakdown of dead matter and the cycling of nutrients, and they feed higher trophic levels. Bacteria outcompete fungi for easily available food. In forest soils, though, their higher nitrogen demand and inability to move nutrients make them less efficient at breaking litter down. Their community make-up and growth rates signal the soil's condition, since growth responds quickly to change. Some are pathogens spread through contact with excrement, such as Escherichia coli. Others ferment cellulose in the rumen of cows.

entries.title: The Mendocino staircase, where old soil grows pygmy pines

definition.text: A flight of uplifted marine terraces on the northern California coast, each about 100,000 years older than the one below and carrying its own soils, microbes, plants and animals.

facts.text: Plant succession repeated on each terrace eventually forms a very acid, nutrient-poor podzol, the Blacklock series, with a clay or iron hardpan beneath.
Pygmy forest soils are low in macro- and micronutrients and high in exchangeable aluminium, and the iron hardpan blocks deep roots and internal drainage.
Pines there are rarely more than three or four feet high, with inch-thick trunks holding 80 or more growth rings, while the same species grows many dozens of feet high on younger soils nearby.

Hans Jenny studied the pygmy forest on a 500,000-year-old terrace, and the sequence shows one soil passing through several successive steady states; the site became the Pygmy Forest National Natural Landmark in 1974.

entries.title: Biocementation: bacteria that keep sand from liquefying

definition.text: The use of microbially induced calcium carbonate precipitation as a cementing technique to strengthen sand that might otherwise liquefy.

facts.text: Treated sand gains shear strength, compressive strength, stiffness and liquefaction resistance because grains are bonded and the soil becomes denser; triaxial tests on bio-cemented Ottawa sand showed shear strength rising by a factor of 1.8.

Strength comes mostly from point-to-point contacts between carbonate crystals and sand grains, so trickling solution from the surface, which forms crystals at grain bridges, gives more strength per amount of calcite.
It could be a cheap, green alternative to chemical grouting, whose synthetic additives are costly and, except for sodium silicate, toxic.

Bacteria cannot pass pore throats smaller than about 0.4 μm, so the method suits soils with few fines (USCS GW, GP, SW, SP, ML and organic soils); enriching native ureolytic bacteria in place can help.

entries.title: Humus: the dark, stable core of soil organic matter

definition.text: Humus is the stable, dark, amorphous fraction of soil organic matter left after most added residues have decomposed, bound to clays and oxides that shield it from microbes.

facts.text: It has low bulk density (0.05 to 0.25 g per cubic centimetre), high porosity and water holding capacity, and a cation exchange capacity above 200 cmol(+) per kilogram.
Its approximate composition is 50% carbon, 35% oxygen, 8% hydrogen, 5% nitrogen and 2% sulfur.
It commonly supplies 20 to 30% or more of a soil's cation exchange capacity, buffers pH and binds peds into aggregates.
Arable soils average 2 to 3% humus, with a range from under 1% to over 12%.
Holding the normal humus level needs 1000 to 5000 kg per hectare of organic material a year, since added material does not permanently raise it.
Cultivated soils lose humus by decomposition at 1 to 2% per year; rotations with grasses and legumes, conservation tillage and residue management help sustain it.

entries.title: From residue to humus: how microbes recycle organic matter

definition.text: Microbes oxidise soil organic matter partly to carbon dioxide, water and energy, leaving humus, new microbial cells and inorganic plant nutrients.

facts.text: Fresh residues first decompose rapidly, releasing carbon dioxide, water and energy and small amounts of inorganic nitrogen, phosphorus and sulfur.
The microbes' most important function is recycling organic carbon to CO2, which keeps photosynthesis going.
Microbial oxidation turns nutrients from unavailable organic forms into plant-available inorganic ones, so organic matter acts as a slow-release fertilizer that buffers nutrient supply.
Soil with 1% organic matter holds up to 45 million kilocalories per acre-furrow-slice, equivalent to about 6 tons of coal.
Microbes use only a small share of the energy for new cells; making one pound of soil organic matter may destroy 10 to 20 pounds of residues.
Fresh residues accelerate decomposition of humified material already in the soil.
Added organic matter improves tilth and structure, raises cation exchange and water holding capacity and aeration, and reduces erosion.

entries.title: The order in which fungi follow a flood of ammonia

definition.text: The order in which ammonia fungi fruit after ammonia or urea reaches forest soil, divided into early-phase and late-phase groups.

facts.text: Anamorphic fungi come first, tolerating pH above 8; once they bring the pH to 7, cup fungi (Ascomycota) develop, and at pH 6 small basidiomycetes follow.
Early-phase fungi fruit 20 to 200 days after urea is applied, in alkaline to neutral soils rich in ammonium-nitrogen, and usually run only one cycle.
Late-phase agarics with larger fruiting bodies develop once the pH is 3.5–6.0, typically 2–3 years after application, and gradually turn soil ammonium into nitrate-nitrogen.
Late-phase fungi are larger and more numerous, can recur over several cycles, and are mostly biotrophic, with few saprobic species.

entries.text: When ammonia or {{ref:soil-fert-021}} reaches forest soil, {{ref:soil-bio-071}} fruit in a set order as the pH falls. Anamorphic fungi come first, tolerating pH above 8. Once they bring the pH to 7, cup fungi (Ascomycota) develop, and at pH 6 small basidiomycetes follow. These early-phase fungi fruit 20 to 200 days after application, in alkaline to neutral soils rich in ammonium-nitrogen. They usually run only one cycle. Late-phase agarics, with larger fruiting bodies, develop once the pH is 3.5–6.0, typically 2–3 years after application. They gradually turn soil ammonium into nitrate-nitrogen. Late-phase fungi are larger and more numerous and can recur over several cycles. Most are biotrophic, living off living partners, and few feed on dead matter.

entries.title: Microarthropods, tiny animals that travel by pore

definition.text: A size group of small arthropods, usually one to several millimetres long, that live mostly in soil.

facts.text: They include springtails, soil mites such as Oribatida and Mesostigmata, small centipedes, small insects and their larvae, and small crustaceans.
They can move only through existing soil pores and are most common in fallen leaves, litter and the upper soil layers.
They speed the decomposition of organic matter and help form soil structure.
Very sensitive to changes in ecosystems, their communities serve as bioindicators for environmental assessment.

entries.title: Soil mites, eight-legged recyclers of leaf litter

definition.text: Mites are small eight-legged arachnids, and many species live in soil as decomposers.

facts.text: Soil mites span a range of taxa; Oribatida and Prostigmata are more numerous in soil than Mesostigmata and have more soil-dwelling species.
They live in organic debris of all kinds and are extremely numerous in leaf litter.
After a disturbance such as agriculture most mites recolonise soil within a few months, whereas Oribatida take several years.
Most are beneficial, helping decompose organic material as part of the carbon cycle; some Laelapidae are used to control fungus gnats and soil pests.

entries.title: Nematophagous fungi, the soil's worm hunters

definition.text: Carnivorous fungi specialised in trapping and digesting nematodes; more than 700 species are known.

facts.text: They catch prey with adhesive hyphae, knobs or nets, or with hyphal loops that tighten on contact; others stun nematodes with toxins or infect them or their eggs as parasites.
Nematode trappers are concentrated in the upper soil, pastures and leaf litter, mostly in nitrogen-deficient habitats.
Arthrobotrys oligospora builds its costly snares only when it detects nematode pheromones such as ascarosides.
Some are studied for biological control: Purpureocillium lilacinum attacks the root-knot nematode Meloidogyne incognita, though field results have been mixed.

entries.title: Counting the living with membrane fats

definition.text: A technique that uses the fatty acids of membrane phospholipids as chemical markers to estimate the living microbial biomass and community make-up of soil and water.

facts.text: Phospholipids break down rapidly when organisms die, so the phospholipid content of a sample is taken to come from living cells.
Saponifying the phospholipids releases their fatty acids, whose composition is compared with that of known organisms.
D.C. White pioneered the method in the early to mid 1980s, after a 1965 article proposed using molecules made by organisms as biomarkers.
It became widely used for soil because it measures the dominant microbes sensitively and reproducibly without cultivation, which is costly and biased.
Lipids are extracted from dried soil with a chloroform–methanol–phosphate buffer and the fatty acids analysed as methyl esters by gas chromatography.
The same PLFAs occur in many life forms, including plant roots, fungi and bacteria, so assigning them to specific microbial groups needs care.
Archaeal lipids are ether-linked rather than ester-linked, so routine preparation misses archaea.
Extraction is long and cumbersome, though a 96-well plate procedure raised throughput 4-to-5 fold.

entries.title: The enzymatic latch that holds decay in check

definition.text: The control of decomposition in peat by phenol oxidases: by breaking down phenolics that inhibit hydrolase enzymes, they release decay, so limits on the microbes limit decomposition.

facts.text: Saprotrophic bacteria release microbial extracellular enzymes (MEEs) to break down soil organic matter when their energy and nutrient needs are unmet, so MEEs indicate nutrient availability.
Phenol oxidases can also degrade or detoxify aromatic pollutants into carbon sources.
β-glucosidase releases sugars that give microbes energy and labile carbon.
Acid and alkaline phosphatases indicate the potential for phosphorus mineralization in soil.

entries.title: How fast soil bacteria grow and replace themselves

definition.text: How fast soil bacteria produce new biomass and replace their populations, a measure that responds quickly to changing conditions.

facts.text: Under normal conditions bacterial biomass production stays fairly steady, growth being balanced by predation and other deaths.
Leucine or thymidine incorporation suggests turnover in days to weeks at around 20 °C, while other studies estimate 107–160 days at 25 °C, a gap put down to methods and temperature.
Root exudates make the rhizosphere a special case, with turnover estimated at just 12–19 hours, shorter on younger roots.
Growth rises with soil moisture, and added glucose boosts it at low concentrations but inhibits it at very high ones.

entries.title: What controls the number of microbes in soil

definition.text: Soil organisms are under 0.5% of dry soil mass, and their numbers depend on temperature, moisture, pH, nutrients, energy supply and oxygen.

facts.text: Decay organisms work best at about 20 to 40 degrees C; temperatures outside that range slow most soil organisms.
Too much water cuts the numbers and kinds of organisms through poor aeration, yet at low moisture soil organisms do better than higher plants.
Fungi, bacteria and actinomycetes vary with pH; below pH 6.0 fungi become the dominant microorganisms.
Adding organisms to a soil is usually ineffective because the community is already vast; changing the crop alters populations more.

entries.title: How healthy soil holds pests in check

definition.text: Diverse soil organisms keep checks and balances that stop disease organisms and parasites from becoming major plant problems.

facts.text: Only a small number of bacteria, fungi, insects and nematodes might harm plants in a given year, and their impact is reduced in more diverse soil.
Some fungi kill nematodes or insects, some produce antibiotics, and protozoa, springtails and mites eat disease-causing fungi and bacteria.
Trichoderma and Pseudomonas fluorescens colonize roots and protect them; Bacillus thuringiensis toxin is sold as a biological control agent.
Suppression is thought to arise from competition for nutrients, antagonistic substances or direct parasitism, and some beneficial organisms induce plant immune defenses.

entries.title: Roots as soil engineers

definition.text: Plant roots influence soil as much as soil influences roots, shaping aggregates and feeding soil organisms.

facts.text: Root pressure brings particles closer, small roots bind them, and root hairs add soil contact for water and nutrient access and help form aggregates.
Roots exude compounds that feed organisms in the surrounding zone; corn sends about 20 percent of photosynthesis sugars to roots early to mid-season.
Mucigel, a sticky layer around roots, gives close contact between microorganisms, soil minerals and the plant.
Roots add organic matter that may decompose more slowly than surface residues; in grasses the living tissue below ground can exceed that above.
Roots do not grow well in compact, nutrient- or water-poor, high-pathogen or extreme-pH soil.

entries.title: The Winogradsky column: a jar of sediment as an ecosystem

definition.text: A simple stratified microbial ecosystem built from sediment in a container, showing different microbial metabolisms.

facts.text: Columns are set up as a control and with added carbon (cellulose), sulfur (egg yolk calcium sulfate) or both, then form oxygen and sulfide gradients.
Purple and green sulfur bacteria use sulfide to support photosynthesis, and green sulfur bacteria tolerate higher sulfide than purple.
He developed it, and discovered chemosynthesis, in his early efforts to understand microbes outside the medical context.
It remains an important demonstration of chemoautotrophy and microbial ecology in microbiology lectures around the world.

entries.title: Free-living bacteria that fix nitrogen

definition.text: Some free-living soil bacteria take nitrogen gas from the air and turn it into a form plants can use to make amino acids and proteins.

facts.text: Plants and animals cannot use nitrogen gas or nitrogen locked in organic molecules; it must be converted to ammonium and nitrate, a bacterial process called nitrogen mineralization.
Azospirillum and Azotobacter are free-living fixers; Azospirillum attaches to root surfaces and makes substances that help plants tolerate stress.
They add only modest nitrogen, but it matters in natural systems where nutrient cycling is efficient.
Rhizobia in legume root nodules receive sugars from the plant and supply usable nitrogen; an alfalfa stand may fix hundreds of pounds per acre a year, peas about 30 to 50.

entries.title: Soil organisms span ten orders of magnitude

definition.text: Soil organisms span nearly ten orders of magnitude in size, from sub-micrometre bacteria to vertebrates and kilometre-long fungal threads.

facts.text: The smallest soil bacterium is about 0.5 micrometres across, soil-dwelling amphibians and mammals are about 10 cm long, roots run 0.1 to 10 m, and some forest fungi form mycelia of 1 km or more.

Traditional groups are microflora, macroflora (roots), microfauna, mesofauna (0.1 to 2 mm metazoans) and macrofauna (over 2 mm), but the scheme confuses: fungi are called microflora yet are macroscopic and heterotrophic.
A colony of Armillaria ostoyae in an Oregon Douglas fir forest covers several square kilometres and may be the largest organism by area.

Archaea were widely recognized as distinct from bacteria only in the early 1990s; DNA analysis shows them as different from bacteria as from plants or animals, in Woese's three domains Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya.

entries.title: Soil insects and arthropods

definition.text: Soil insects such as termites, springtails, ants, fly larvae and beetles are often secondary and tertiary consumers.

facts.text: Springtails eat fungi and animal remains and are prey for predacious mites; many beetles eat other soil animals, and dung beetles bury manure balls.
Millipedes are primary consumers of plant residues, centipedes eat other organisms, mites eat fungi, other mites, insect eggs or residues, and spiders hold insect pests down.
Termites eat wood and also decomposed organic residues in soil.

entries.title: The Birch effect: a burst of breath when rain hits dry soil

definition.text: The influence of soil moisture on the cycling of carbon in soil.

facts.text: Respiration in dry soil usually bursts to a very high level after rainfall, then declines as the soil dries.
Sudden wetting can burst bacterial cells; the released contents feed other bacteria and briefly boost respiration.
Soil microbial communities shift in diversity and composition through drying and rewetting cycles.

entries.text: When rain falls on dry soil, its respiration usually bursts to a very high level, then declines as the soil dries. This is the Birch effect, the influence of soil moisture on the cycling of carbon in soil. Sudden wetting can burst bacterial cells. Their released contents feed other bacteria and briefly boost {{ref:soil-bio-033}}. Through repeated drying and rewetting, microbial communities shift in diversity and composition.

entries.title: Is every microbe everywhere? Mapping microbial life

definition.text: The study of where microorganisms live, at what abundance and why, across space and time.

facts.text: In 1934 Lourens Baas Becking concluded that 'everything is everywhere, but the environment selects', an idea later challenged by clear geographic patterns in microbial life.
The field grew with cheaper, higher-throughput DNA sequencing that allows global analyses of microbial data.
Unlike most larger organisms, global topsoil microbiomes are more diverse in temperate zones than in the tropics.
Soil bacterial patterns are usually linked to soil pH, which may stand in for the climatic water balance that controls carbon inputs and the connectivity of water-filled habitats.

entries.contested_note: Geographic patterns in microbes dispute the Baas Becking view that microbes are everywhere and only the environment selects.

entries.title: Biofilms, the slime cities where soil bacteria live

definition.text: A community of microorganisms whose cells stick to each other, and often to a surface, inside a self-made slime of extracellular polymeric substances (EPS).

facts.text: The EPS matrix combines polysaccharides, proteins, lipids and DNA, and can hold many times its dry weight in water.
Called 'cities for microbes', biofilms let residents share nutrients and shelter them; cells inside differ physiologically from free-floating (planktonic) cells of the same organism.
The matrix keeps extracellular enzymes close to the cells, working as an external digestion system, and carries chemical signals and gene exchange.
In soil and on plant surfaces most bacteria live bound in biofilms; soils with more clay minerals hold more bacteria as biofilms on clay surfaces.
Root biofilms of plant growth-promoting bacteria such as Bacillus, Pseudomonas and Azospirillum can prime plants' systemic resistance to pathogens.
Biofilms help cycle nitrogen, phosphorus, carbon and oxygen; their internal gradients let nitrifiers work near the surface while anoxic microbes deeper inside denitrify.
Microbial activity in the matrix can precipitate calcium carbonate, a form of biomineralization.
In soil, biofilms can cause bioclogging; in sewage works and slow sand filters they are used to strip pollutants from water.

entries.title: Extracellular polymeric substances, the glue of microbial life

definition.text: High-molecular-weight natural polymers that microorganisms secrete into their surroundings.

facts.text: They are mostly polysaccharides and proteins, with DNA, lipids and humic substances, and make up 50% to 90% of a biofilm's total organic matter.
They hold biofilms together and protect the microbes inside from harsh conditions, mechanical removal and antimicrobials.
Exopolysaccharides help nitrogen-fixing bacteria attach to plant roots and soil particles, which matters for colonizing roots and the rhizosphere.
Together with microbial cells, EPS can block soil pores in bioclogging, lowering hydraulic conductivity.
EPS make sediment more stable by changing its cohesion, permeability and erosion, and they affect the precipitation of minerals, especially carbonates.
They adsorb metal cations such as copper, lead, nickel and cadmium, which helps in bioremediation of heavy metals.
EPS from the bacterium Zoogloea and the fungus Aspergillus niger remove polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons from contaminated soils, using enzymes that degrade them.

entries.text: Between 50% and 90% of the organic material in a biofilm is the slime its microbes secrete. They are mostly long sugar chains and proteins, with DNA, lipids and humic compounds. They hold biofilms together and protect the microbes inside from harsh conditions, mechanical removal and antimicrobials. Sugar-polymer slimes help nitrogen-fixing bacteria attach to plant roots and soil particles, so the bacteria can colonize roots and the soil around them. EPS also shape the soil itself. Together with microbial cells they can block soil pores in bioclogging, lowering hydraulic conductivity. They make sediment more stable by changing its cohesion, permeability and erosion, and they affect the precipitation of minerals, especially carbonates. They adsorb metal cations such as copper, lead, nickel and cadmium, which helps clean up heavy metals. EPS from the bacterium Zoogloea and the fungus Aspergillus niger even remove {{ref:soil-env-199}} from contaminated soils, using enzymes that degrade them.

entries.title: Five stages from a lone cell to a biofilm

definition.text: The microbial developmental process by which a biofilm forms, summarized in five major stages.

facts.text: It starts with reversible attachment of free-floating cells to a surface, held first by weak van der Waals forces and hydrophobic effects.
Attachment becomes irreversible as cells anchor with structures such as pili and further cells aggregate.
Stages three and four are maturation, with cell clusters embedded in matrix growing into micro-colonies.
The fifth stage, dispersal, releases cells that colonize new surfaces.

entries.text: A {{ref:soil-bio-050}} grows up in five major stages. It starts with reversible attachment. Free-floating cells settle on a surface, held at first by weak van der Waals forces and hydrophobic effects. In stage two, attachment becomes irreversible as cells anchor with structures such as pili and more cells gather. Stages three and four are maturation, as cell clusters embedded in the matrix grow into micro-colonies. The fifth stage, dispersal, releases cells that go on to colonize new surfaces.

entries.title: Roots, the hidden half that anchors and feeds a plant

definition.text: The plant organ, usually below the soil surface, that anchors the plant and takes in water and dissolved nutrients.

facts.text: Roots anchor the plant, absorb water and dissolved minerals and conduct them to the shoot; they also store reserves, make growth regulators and support symbiotic nutrient uptake.
Root epidermal cells and root hairs take up soil water and dissolved ions, which then move to the shoot through the xylem.
A root system's depth and spread decide which soil horizons the plant can draw water and nutrients from.
The root cap helps a new root push through soil; its cells are sloughed off as the root deepens, leaving a slimy, lubricating surface.
The roots of most vascular plants form mycorrhizae with certain fungi, and many other organisms, bacteria among them, live closely with roots.
Grass roots hold soil together and reduce erosion, and the decay of old roots of perennial rangeland grasses adds organic matter and releases nutrients.
Fossil roots, mostly infilled voids left where roots rotted, go back to the late Silurian, about 430 million years ago, and are easily confused with animal burrows.

events.date_text: late Silurian, about 430 million years ago

entries.text: Roots left their mark in rock long before any animal walked on land. Fossil roots go back to the late Silurian, about 430 million years ago. Most are voids that filled in after the roots rotted, and they are easily confused with animal burrows. A root is the plant organ, usually below the soil surface, that anchors the plant and takes in water and dissolved nutrients. Its skin cells, the epidermis, and their fine outgrowths, described in {{ref:soil-bio-140}}, take up soil water and dissolved ions. These then travel to the shoot through the xylem, the plant's water-conducting tissue. Roots also store reserves and make growth regulators. A cap of cells guards each growing tip and helps the new root push through soil. As the root deepens, the cap sheds cells and leaves a slimy, lubricating surface. The depth and spread of a root system decide which soil horizons the plant can draw water and nutrients from. Roots rarely work alone. Most vascular plants partner with certain fungi, described in {{ref:soil-bio-157}}, and bacteria and many other organisms live close to roots too. On rangeland, grass roots hold soil together and reduce erosion. When the old roots of perennial grasses decay, they add organic matter and release nutrients.

entries.title: The legume family and its nitrogen-making guests

definition.text: The legume or pea family of flowering plants, about 19,000 species, including soybean, beans, pea, chickpea and alfalfa.

facts.text: Many legumes host rhizobia in root nodules, which take nitrogen gas from the air and turn it into a form the plant can use.
Nodule formation is common throughout the family, though rarer in the Caesalpinioideae, and some species in every subfamily do not nodulate.
Rhizobia are host-specific, but one plant can host several kinds: Acacia senegal nodules can hold seven rhizobial species from three genera.
Because of their nodules, legumes are used in crop rotations, and green-manure crops are commonly legumes.

entries.text: About 19,000 species of flowering plants share one underground talent. The legume or pea family, Fabaceae, includes soybean, beans, pea, chickpea and alfalfa. Many legumes host bacteria, described in {{ref:soil-bio-178}}, in small swellings on their roots. These guests take nitrogen gas from the air and turn it into a form the plant can use. The swellings are common across the family, though rarer in the Caesalpinioideae, and some species in every subfamily lack them. One plant can host several kinds: those of Acacia senegal can hold seven bacterial species from three genera. That talent is why farmers rotate crops with legumes and why green-manure crops are commonly legumes.

entries.title: Taproots, the single deep anchor

definition.text: A large, central, dominant root, usually straight, thick and tapering, from which smaller roots branch sideways.

facts.text: Dicots start with a taproot grown from the seed's radicle; it may last the plant's life but is more often replaced by a fibrous root system.
Soil shapes taproots: deep, rich soils favour vertical taproots in many oaks, while clay soils promote several taproots.
Many taproots are storage organs, as in carrot, radish and turnip.
Taprooted plants are hard to transplant, and deep-rooted weeds such as dandelion resprout unless the taproot is cut several centimetres below ground.

entries.text: Snap a dandelion off at ground level and it simply grows back. Its taproot survives below: a large, central, dominant root, usually straight, thick and tapering, with smaller roots branching sideways. Unless that root is cut several centimeters down, the weed resprouts. Dicots, plants with two seed leaves, start life with a taproot grown from the seed's first root, the radicle. It may last the plant's life but is more often replaced by {{ref:soil-bio-138}}. Soil shapes it. Deep, rich soils favor vertical taproots in many oaks, while clay soils promote several. Carrot, radish and turnip are taproots built for storage.

entries.title: Fibrous roots, the dense mat near the surface

definition.text: A root system of many thin, similar-sized roots growing from the stem base and forming a dense mat near the soil surface, the opposite of a taproot system.

facts.text: It is universal in monocots and ferns, with grasses such as wheat and rice as typical examples; in many species the network is mostly adventitious roots from the stem base.
It arises when the embryonic root dies back while the plant is young, leaving a mass of fine roots with no distinct taproot.
Fibrous roots bind soil, take up surface nutrients quickly and control erosion; forage crops cover the whole field and anchor its top layer of soil.
Most trees switch from a taproot to a wide fibrous system within a few years; a mature tree 30–50 m tall spreads roots as far as its height or more, with well over 95% in the top 50 cm.
Root mats of meadow grasses may help immobilise radioactive materials in soil.

entries.title: How roots feel their way through the soil

definition.text: The ways roots sense their surroundings, such as gravity, light, physical barriers and soil conditions, and steer their growth in response.

facts.text: Gravitropism, worked through auxin pathways, sends roots downward from germination, and different root types hold different set angles of growth.
Air, mineral nutrients and water steer root growth, and roots turn away from dry or otherwise poor soil.
Roots searching for nutrients can sense and avoid compacted soil through the diffusion of the gas ethylene.
Roots can tell their own roots from other plants' roots in the same soil, and over time they can crack foundations, snap water lines and lift sidewalks.

entries.text: Roots are not blind diggers. They sense gravity, light, physical barriers and soil conditions, and they steer their growth in response. Gravitropism, growth guided by gravity and worked through auxin, one of the {{ref:soil-bio-245}}, sends roots downward from germination. Each root type holds its own set angle. Air, nutrients and water pull roots toward them, and roots turn away from dry or otherwise poor soil. Roots hunting for nutrients can sense compacted soil through the diffusion of ethylene gas, and avoid it. They can even tell their own roots from other plants' roots in the same soil. Given years, roots crack foundations, snap water lines and lift sidewalks.

entries.title: Root system architecture, the shape of the hidden half

definition.text: The spatial layout of a plant's whole root system: how its roots branch, spread and angle through the soil.

facts.text: Architecture depends on the plant species, the soil's composition and the nutrients available, and it secures water, nutrients and anchorage.
It is described by branching pattern (herringbone, dichotomous or radial), link length between branches, link radius and root angle.
Outside influences include gravity, light, water and oxygen, and the supply or lack of nitrogen, phosphorus, sulphur, aluminium and sodium chloride.
A root system that developed in dry soil may work less well when the soil floods.

entries.text: Two plants in one field can lay out their roots in entirely different shapes. Root system architecture is that layout: how a plant's whole root system branches, spreads and angles through the soil. It is described by branching pattern (herringbone, dichotomous or radial) and by link length between branches, link radius and root angle. The species, the soil's composition and the nutrients on offer all shape it. So do gravity, light, water and oxygen, and the supply or lack of nitrogen, phosphorus, sulfur, aluminum and sodium chloride. A system built in dry soil may work less well when the soil floods.

entries.title: How deep roots go, and what stops them

definition.text: How a plant's roots are spread down through the soil, which depends on the plant's form, where and when water and nutrients are available, and the soil's physical properties.

facts.text: Most roots of most plants lie fairly close to the surface, where nutrients are more available and aeration is better.
Rock, compacted soil close below the surface or anaerobic conditions can physically limit rooting depth.
The deepest roots are generally found in deserts and temperate coniferous forests, the shallowest in tundra, boreal forest and temperate grasslands.
In continuous permafrost, roots cannot go below the active layer, so plants must be shallow-rooted and trees are limited to specialists such as larch.
Some roots grow as deep as the tree is tall; the deepest living root observed, at least 60 metres (200 ft) down, turned up in an open-pit mine in Arizona.

entries.title: Roots that breathe, pull, prop and store

definition.text: Root forms adapted to tasks beyond anchorage and uptake, such as aerial, prop, buttress, storage, contractile and cluster roots.

facts.text: Cluster or proteoid roots are dense clusters of rootlets of limited growth that form under low phosphate or low iron, notably in the Proteaceae.
Aerating roots, or pneumatophores, rise above ground or water so that mangroves and other plants can exchange gases where soil oxygen is limited.
Root nodules, found in virtually all legumes, house nitrogen-fixing soil bacteria; coralloid roots near the soil surface house nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria.
Contractile roots pull bulbs, corms and some taproots deeper into the soil by expanding radially and contracting lengthwise.

entries.text: Not every root just anchors and drinks. Specialized roots take on other tasks; they include aerial, prop, buttress, storage and contractile roots, and the tufts described in {{ref:soil-bio-191}}. Those tufts of short rootlets form when phosphate or iron runs low, notably in the Proteaceae. Mangroves raise aerating roots, or {{ref:soil-bio-199}}, above ground or water to exchange gases where soil oxygen is limited. Contractile roots expand sideways and shorten lengthwise, pulling bulbs, corms and some taproots deeper. Swellings in virtually all legumes, described in {{ref:soil-bio-179}}, house nitrogen-fixing bacteria. Coralloid roots near the surface house nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria.

Specialized roots take on other tasks; they include aerial, prop, buttress, storage and contractile roots, and the tufts described in Cluster roots, phosphorus miners of poor soils. Those tufts of short rootlets form when phosphate or iron runs low, notably in the Proteaceae. Mangroves raise aerating roots, or Pneumatophores, roots that rise to breathe, above ground or water to exchange gases where soil oxygen is limited. Contractile roots expand sideways and shorten lengthwise, pulling bulbs, corms and some taproots deeper. Swellings in virtually all legumes, described in Root nodules, the pink factories of fixed nitrogen, house nitrogen-fixing bacteria. Coralloid roots near the surface house nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria.

entries.title: Root hairs, where most of the water comes in

definition.text: A thin outgrowth of a single epidermal cell near the root tip that collects water and mineral nutrients from the soil.

facts.text: Root hairs raise the root's surface area relative to its volume, and most of a root's water uptake passes through them.
They are 15–17 micrometres across and 80–1,500 micrometres long, and their length lets them reach in between soil particles.
They grow only in the zone of maturation, perhaps because older hairs are sheared off as the root elongates through the soil.
Root hair cells secrete malic and citric acids, which solubilise minerals by changing their oxidation state so that the ions are easier to absorb.
They are the main interface with mycorrhizal fungi; ectomycorrhizal fungi colonise root hairs first, then build a Hartig net in the outer root cortex.
In legumes, root hairs curl around rhizobia so that an infection thread can grow into dividing cortical cells and form a nodule.
Transplanting or repotting can strip off many root hairs and make the plant wilt.

entries.title: Plant hormones, the tiny signals that steer roots

definition.text: Signal molecules produced within plants in extremely low concentrations that control growth and development.

facts.text: Every plant cell can make hormones, and they are not nutrients but chemicals that in small amounts steer cell growth and differentiation.
Fungi and bacteria make very similar chemicals that also affect plant growth, though in microbes they act as secondary metabolites.
Auxins promote root initiation and lateral and adventitious root growth; synthetic auxins such as IBA and NAA are sold as rooting powders for cuttings.
When roots run short of water a signal triggers ABA formation; roots release ABA to the leaves, where it closes the stomata.
When a growing root hits an obstacle underground, ethylene production surges and halts cell elongation.
Strigolactones exuded into soil promote the growth of symbiotic arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi.
Went and Thimann coined the term phytohormone in their 1937 book.

entries.title: Roots that move water from wet soil to dry

definition.text: The passive movement of water by plant roots from moist soil to dry soil.

facts.text: It happens in plants rooted in both wet and dry soil, especially those with taproots reaching the water table and lateral roots near the surface.
In drought, groundwater is drawn up the taproot and released from the laterals into the dry surface soil; under flooding, roots move water the other way.
Xylem links from taproot to laterals let wet or dry conditions at the laterals set up a pressure gradient, much like transpirational pull.
Once described as roots releasing water and nutrients into soil mostly at night ('hydraulic lift'), it is now seen as two-way movement helped by mycorrhizal networks.
Hydraulic lift is regulated by the root endodermis and leaf stomata and can be broken by cavitation in the xylem.
Roots doing this smooth out differences in soil moisture, which affects crop irrigation and helps seedlings establish.
It is traced with deuterium, sap flow and soil moisture measurements, and efforts are under way to add it to land-surface models.

entries.text: During a drought, a deep-rooted plant can draw up groundwater and release it into parched topsoil. Hydraulic redistribution is this passive movement of water by roots from moist soil to dry soil. It happens in plants rooted in both wet and dry soil. It is strongest in those with taproots reaching the water table and side roots near the surface. In drought, water rises up the taproot and seeps from the laterals into the dry surface soil. Under flooding, roots move water the other way. The xylem, the plant's water-conducting tissue, links taproot to laterals. Wet or dry soil around the laterals then sets up a pressure gradient, much like transpirational pull, the tug of water evaporating from leaves. It was once described as hydraulic lift: roots releasing water and nutrients into soil, mostly at night. Researchers now see two-way movement, helped by fungal networks described in {{ref:soil-bio-164}}. Hydraulic lift is regulated by the root endodermis, an inner sheath of root cells, and by stomata, the pores in leaves. Cavitation, air breaking the water column in the xylem, can stop it. By smoothing out differences in soil moisture, the process affects crop irrigation and helps seedlings establish. Scientists trace it with deuterium, a heavy form of hydrogen, and with sap flow and soil moisture measurements. Efforts are under way to add it to land-surface models.

entries.title: Mutualism, the partnerships where both sides win

definition.text: An ecological interaction between two or more species in which each gains a net benefit.

facts.text: About 80% of land plant species rely on mycorrhizal fungi for inorganic compounds and trace elements, a 'biological barter' of plant carbohydrates for minerals.
Rhizobia fix nitrogen for legumes in return for carbohydrates; in Three Sisters farming, beans fix nitrogen in the soil for the corn they climb.
Mutualism with mycorrhizal fungi is linked to the colonisation of land by plants.
Plant lineages in nutrient-rich environments have abandoned mycorrhizal mutualism many times, and mutualistic fungi can turn parasitic on weak or dying plants.

entries.title: Root exudates, the food roots give away

definition.text: The organic compounds, such as sugars, amino acids, proteins, enzymes and DNA, that plant roots release into the surrounding soil.

facts.text: Exudates help protect roots against bacterial and fungal infection, help them penetrate the soil and can create a microclimate that benefits the plant.
Root exudation supports microbial activity, and exudates are a source of soil carbon.
Exudates such as organic acids change the chemistry and biological communities of the rhizosphere relative to the bulk soil.
Different plant species release different exudates and so recruit different microbial communities from the bulk soil into their rhizosphere.
Root and microbial exudates can extract phosphorus from apatite, the most common mineral source of soil phosphorus.
Exudates called strigolactones, together with soil phosphorus, control how arbuscular mycorrhizal hyphae grow through the soil.
Roughly 5% of a plant's photosynthetically fixed carbon is estimated to pass into soil as root exudates, though it is hard to quantify.
Arabidopsis seedlings grow more lateral roots in exudates of non-kin than of kin, which may let plants spend less on competition among relatives.

entries.text: Roots leak food into the soil on purpose. Root exudates are the organic compounds, such as sugars, amino acids, proteins, enzymes and DNA, that roots release into the surrounding soil. They help protect roots against bacterial and fungal infection and help them push through the soil. They can also create a microclimate that benefits the plant. Exudates feed microbial activity and add carbon to the soil. Organic acids among them change the chemistry and the living communities right next to the root, compared with soil farther away. Each plant species releases its own mix and so recruits its own microbes from the surrounding soil. Root and microbial exudates can even extract phosphorus from apatite, the most common mineral source of soil phosphorus. One group, described in {{ref:soil-bio-172}}, works with soil phosphorus to steer how fungal threads grow through the soil.

entries.title: The rhizosphere, the crowded zone around every root

definition.text: The narrow zone of soil directly influenced by root secretions and by the microorganisms that live with the roots.

facts.text: The German plant physiologist Lorenz Hiltner coined the term in 1904 for a zone around roots whose microbes are partly controlled by chemicals the roots release.
Microbes in its pores feed on sloughed-off root cells (rhizodeposition) and on the proteins and sugars that roots release (root exudates).
Up to 10 billion culturable bacterial cells inhabit each gram of soil in and around roots, making the rhizosphere a hotspot of microbial diversity.
Roots may exude 20–40% of their photosynthetically fixed carbon as sugars and organic acids.
Much of the nutrient cycling plants need, and disease suppression by antibiotics, happens right beside roots because of exudates and microbial products.
Organic acids and sugars there affect how microbes shuttle phosphorus, nitrogen, potassium and water to the root, and how much iron is available.
Root respiration and exudation can create anoxic microsites next to roots, and in acid soils the pH is raised close to roots.
The rhizoplane is the root surface itself together with the soil particles closely bound to it.

entries.text: Each gram of soil in and around roots can hold up to 10 billion bacterial cells that grow in culture. In 1904 a German plant physiologist, the subject of {{ref:soil-hist-075}}, named this crowded zone the rhizosphere. He meant soil around roots whose microbes are partly controlled by chemicals the roots release. Today it is defined as the narrow zone of soil directly influenced by root secretions and by the microorganisms living with the roots. The roots pay generously for their company. They may exude 20–40% of the carbon they fix by {{ref:soil-hist-147}} as sugars and organic acids. Microbes in the zone's pores feed on these root exudates and on sloughed-off root cells, a process described in {{ref:soil-bio-148}}. The result is a hotspot of microbial diversity. Much of the nutrient cycling plants need happens right beside roots, and so does disease suppression by microbial antibiotics. Organic acids and sugars affect how microbes shuttle phosphorus, nitrogen, potassium and water to the root, and how much iron is available. Root respiration and exudation can create pockets without oxygen next to roots. In acid soils, the pH rises close to roots. At the very center lies the rhizoplane: the root surface itself, with the soil particles closely bound to it.

entries.title: Mycorrhiza, the ancient pact between root and fungus

definition.text: A symbiosis between a fungus and a plant in which fungal hyphae and plant roots interconnect and form an interface at the level of cells.

facts.text: The plant gives the fungus sugars or lipids made by photosynthesis; the fungus gives the plant water and soil nutrients such as phosphorus, nitrogen and zinc.
The fungus colonises root tissue either inside the cells, as in arbuscular mycorrhizas, or between them, as in ectomycorrhizas.
The association is normally mutualistic, but in some species or circumstances it can be parasitic.
Mycorrhizas occur in 92% of plant families studied (80% of species), but some families, such as Brassicaceae and Chenopodiaceae, cannot form them.
In some ecosystems up to 80% of plant nitrogen and 90% of plant phosphorus comes through mycorrhizal fungi, and plants may give them about 20–40% of their carbon.
The plant's need for phosphorus is a strong trigger: arbuscular fungi are recruited when the plant senses phosphorus starvation, and nitrogen starvation also plays a part.
Mycorrhizae emerged as early as 450–500 million years ago, and proto-mycorrhizal fungi may have been key to plants colonising land.

entries.text: In some ecosystems up to 80% of plant nitrogen and 90% of plant phosphorus reaches the plant through fungi. A mycorrhiza is the partnership behind those numbers. It is a symbiosis in which fungal hyphae, the fungus's fine threads, interconnect with plant roots and meet them at the level of single cells. The plant pays the fungus in sugars or lipids made by {{ref:soil-hist-147}}, perhaps 20–40% of its carbon. The fungus returns water and soil nutrients such as phosphorus, nitrogen and zinc. Some fungi colonize root tissue inside the cells, as in {{ref:soil-bio-166}}. Others grow between the cells, as in {{ref:soil-bio-173}}. The partnership occurs in 92% of plant families studied, covering 80% of species. Some families, such as Brassicaceae and Chenopodiaceae, cannot form it at all. A plant short of phosphorus is quick to recruit fungi, and nitrogen starvation also plays a part. The deal is normally mutualistic, good for both sides, but in some species or circumstances it turns parasitic. It is also ancient. Mycorrhizae emerged as early as 450–500 million years ago, and early fungal partners may have been key to plants colonizing land.

entries.title: The root microbiome, the company a root keeps

definition.text: The changing community of microorganisms, mainly bacteria, fungi and archaea, that lives with plant roots.

facts.text: The communities inside the root, in the rhizosphere and in bulk soil differ from one another, though some species overlap.
Beneficial members include nitrogen-fixing bacteria, growth-promoting microbes, mycorrhizal fungi, protozoa and biocontrol organisms; harmful ones include some bacteria, fungi and nematodes.
Root symbionts live on carbon-rich products of the host plant's photosynthesis.
Mycorrhizal fungi extend far into the bulk soil, widening the root system's reach and surface area.
Microbes cover only part of the root surface, about 10% of three-week-old root segments and about 37% of three-month-old roots, though before the 1970s most was thought covered.
Methanogens and ammonia-oxidizing archaea are common root microbes, especially in anaerobic soils and wetlands.
Plants recruit selectively: in finger millet only about 8% of the core microbiota was consistently shared between soil and plant.

entries.text: Before the 1970s, most scientists thought microbes blanketed the whole root surface. In fact they cover about 10% of three-week-old root segments and about 37% of three-month-old roots. The root microbiome is the changing community of microorganisms, mainly bacteria, fungi and archaea, that lives with plant roots. The communities inside the root, in the rhizosphere and in bulk soil differ, though some species overlap. Helpful members include nitrogen-fixing bacteria, growth-promoting microbes, mycorrhizal fungi, protozoa and organisms that fight disease. Some bacteria, fungi and nematodes do harm. Root partners live on carbon-rich products of the host's {{ref:soil-hist-147}}. Mycorrhizal fungi stretch far into the bulk soil, widening the root system's reach. Archaea that make methane or oxidize ammonia are common, especially in wetlands and other soils without oxygen. Plants also pick their company: in finger millet, only about 8% of the core microbiota was consistently shared between soil and plant.

entries.title: Bulk soil, the quiet ground beyond the roots

definition.text: The soil outside the rhizosphere, not penetrated by plant roots.

facts.text: Natural organic compounds are much scarcer in bulk soil than in the rhizosphere.
Microbes are more varied in bulk soil but more abundant in the rhizosphere, and bulk-soil organisms are generally smaller than the same species near roots.
Bulk soil tends to have smaller pores and more moisture at a given matric potential than the rhizosphere, which affects which microbes survive there.
Away from roots most bacteria are quiescent, in mucilaginous colonies glued with clay particles that protect them from drying out and from protozoa and nematodes.
Its chemical properties include organic matter, organic carbon, nutrient content, cation-exchange capacity, free ions, pH and base saturation.
Bulk-soil respiration responds to temperature swings, and added nutrients or warming can strongly change its microbes, especially in sandy soils.

entries.title: Sugar for minerals: how the mycorrhizal trade works

definition.text: The trade in which a mycorrhizal fungus gets carbohydrates from its host and in return improves the plant's uptake of water and minerals.

facts.text: Sugars such as glucose and sucrose move from their source, usually the leaves, to the roots and on to the fungus.
Most mycorrhizal hyphae are far finer than the smallest root or root hair, so they explore soil that roots cannot reach and add absorbing surface.
Fungi may secrete organic acids that dissolve or chelate ions, or release ions from minerals by ion exchange.
Hyphae reach phosphate and iron that roots alone cannot, including nutrients immobilised in clay-rich or strongly basic soils.
Some mycorrhizal fungi decay organic matter directly; in some nutrient-poor forests their hyphae take phosphate straight from leaf litter, bypassing soil uptake.
Inga alley cropping, proposed as an alternative to slash-and-burn, relies on mycorrhizae in Inga roots to stop rain washing phosphorus out of the soil.
Mycorrhizae help most in nutrient-poor soils, but in boreal forests fungi have been found hoarding nitrogen in times of scarcity, so the trade may be more than simply mutualistic.

entries.text: Most mycorrhizal hyphae are far finer than the smallest root or root hair. That fineness is the fungus's whole advantage. Sugars such as glucose and sucrose travel from their source, usually the leaves, down to the roots and on to the fungus. In some nutrient-poor forests their hyphae take phosphate straight from leaf litter, bypassing the soil. Farmers can lean on the trade. {{ref:soil-agri-134}} with Inga, proposed as an alternative to slash-and-burn, relies on the fungi in Inga roots to stop rain washing phosphorus out of the soil. The trade helps most in nutrient-poor soils. Yet in boreal forests the fungi have been found hoarding nitrogen in times of scarcity, so the deal may be more than simply mutualistic.

entries.title: Fungal partners as bodyguards against stress
entries.article: Mycorrhiza#Disease, drought and salinity resistance and its correlation to mycorrhizae

definition.text: The protection mycorrhizal fungi give plants against soil-borne disease, drought, salt and toxic metals.

facts.text: Mycorrhizal plants are often more resistant to soil-borne pathogens, and mycorrhizas secrete enzymes toxic to soil organisms such as nematodes.
Forming the association primes the plant's immune system, so its defence responses are stronger.
Mycorrhizal fungi were correlated with soil water level, not aggregate stability, and can make plants more resistant to drought.
Salinity can harm the fungi, yet many reports show mycorrhizal plants growing better under salt stress.
Fungi protect plants rooted in acidic, contaminated or metal-rich soils; pines inoculated with Pisolithus tinctorius tolerated contaminated sites well.
Zinc-tolerant Suillus bovinus protected Scots pine, probably by binding the metal in its external mycelium without blocking useful exchange.

entries.title: Inside the cell or around it: the kinds of mycorrhiza

definition.text: The grouping of mycorrhizas by how the fungus colonises the root, with the main split between ectomycorrhizas and endomycorrhizas.

facts.text: Ectomycorrhizal hyphae do not enter individual root cells, whereas endomycorrhizal hyphae pass through the cell wall up to the cell membrane.
Arbuscular, ericoid, arbutoid, monotropoid and orchid mycorrhizas all count as endomycorrhizae.
The mycorrhizal lifestyle evolved independently many times: arbuscular fungi form a single phylum, while other mycorrhizal fungi converged on similar ways of life.
Fungal endophytes live harmlessly inside plants but lack the structures mycorrhizal fungi use to bring in nutrients from outside the plant.
Mucoromycotina 'fine root endophytes' were long mistaken for arbuscular fungi; they seem able to live without a host and prefer wet, acidic soils.
In monotropoid mycorrhizas, found in Monotropoideae and some orchids, the plant takes its carbon from the fungus, making the association parasitic.

entries.text: The first question about any mycorrhiza is how far the fungus gets into the root. Mycorrhizal types group these partnerships by how the fungus colonizes the root. The main split runs between {{ref:soil-bio-173}} and endomycorrhizas. In the first kind, the hyphae never enter individual root cells. In endomycorrhizas they pass through the cell wall, up to the cell membrane. The endomycorrhizas include the types described in {{ref:soil-bio-166}}, {{ref:soil-bio-176}} and {{ref:soil-bio-186}}, along with arbutoid and monotropoid forms. The lifestyle evolved independently many times. The fungi of the first of those endomycorrhizal types form a single phylum, while other mycorrhizal fungi converged on similar ways of life. Not every fungus inside a root is a partner of this kind. Fungal {{ref:soil-bio-202}} live harmlessly inside plants but lack the structures mycorrhizal fungi use to bring in nutrients from outside. Mucoromycotina fungi of this kind, living in the roots described in {{ref:soil-bio-242}}, were long mistaken for partners of the first type. They seem able to live without a host and prefer wet, acidic soils. In monotropoid mycorrhizas, found in Monotropoideae and some orchids, the flow runs backward. The plant takes its carbon from the fungus, making the association parasitic.

entries.title: Arbuscular mycorrhiza, the most widespread plant partnership

definition.text: A type of mycorrhiza in which the fungus enters the cortical cells of a plant's roots and forms tree-like arbuscules inside them.

facts.text: Arbuscules are the sites where phosphorus, carbon, water and other nutrients are exchanged; balloon-like vesicles often store reserves.
It is formed by fungi of the Glomeromycotina and some Mucoromycotina, and helps plants capture phosphorus, sulphur, nitrogen and micronutrients from the soil.
It is the most widespread plant symbiosis known, found in 80% of vascular plant families and about 80% of plant species, on every continent except Antarctica.
The fungi are obligate symbionts with little ability to live on dead matter, and up to 20% of the host plant's carbon may pass to them.
Earth's topsoils hold an estimated 110 quadrillion kilometres of arbuscular fungal hyphae, about 40% of it in wild grasslands, with a biomass of about 300 megatons of carbon.
These fungi are most frequent on mineral soils and vital on nutrient-poor volcanic soils and sand dunes, but colonisation is lower in very arid or nutrient-rich soils.
Their extraradical hyphae and the soil protein glomalin improve soil aggregate stability.
Members of the mustard family, such as cabbage, cauliflower and canola, do not form arbuscular mycorrhizas.

entries.title: Ectomycorrhiza, the fungal sheath of forest trees

definition.text: A mycorrhiza in which the fungus sheathes the root tip and grows between the root's outer cells without entering them.

facts.text: Its fungi, mostly Basidiomycota and Ascomycota, form a mantle up to 40 μm thick and a Hartig net between epidermal and cortical cells, with hyphae reaching several centimetres into the soil.
It forms on about 2% of plant species, mostly woody plants of families such as birch, beech, willow, pine and rose, but these dominate their ecosystems and much plant biomass.
Nitrogen is scarce in most ecosystems and locked in hard-to-break-down organic matter; the fungi reach further than roots and extract nitrogen from the organic layer.
The fungi are estimated to receive about 15% of the host's food and in return supply up to 86% of its nitrogen needs.
With heavy fertiliser nitrogen plants divert resources from the fungi; in one study species fell from over 30 at low-nitrogen sites to 9 at high-nitrogen sites.
Ectomycorrhizas are usually sampled in surface horizons, where roots are densest, but occur on tree roots at least 4 m deep.
Many European ectomycorrhizal fungi have declined because of poorer tree vitality, forest conversion, pollution and acidification of forest soils.
Laccaria bicolor lures and kills springtails for nitrogen; eastern white pine inoculated with it got up to 25% of its nitrogen from springtails.

entries.title: Glomeromycota, the fungi behind most root partnerships

definition.text: A group of fungi, with about 230 described species, whose members form arbuscular mycorrhizas with plant roots.

facts.text: Its arbuscular species live in soils worldwide, partnering the roots of most plant species (over 80%), and also occur in wetlands including salt marshes.
Most evidence shows they depend on land plants for carbon and energy, and this biotrophic habit long hindered growing them in the laboratory.
They reproduce asexually by spores 80–500 μm across; new colonisation depends on the inoculum in the soil, and colonisation rate tracks spore density.
A metatranscriptomic survey of arid land found 5.4% of fungal rRNA reads were Glomeromycota, suggesting earlier PCR-based studies had underestimated their abundance.

conflicts.text: Mycorrhiza says 244 species of Glomeromycota have been identified from spore differences, and genetic studies suggest 300–1600 may exist.
conflicts.note: Against about 230 described species on Glomeromycota.
