entries.title: Suberin, the cork that guards roots and bark

definition.text: A lipophilic, complex polyester biopolymer of plants, made of long-chain fatty acids and glycerol.

facts.text: Interlinked with cutin and lignin, it forms a protective barrier in plant cell walls whose main job is to block the movement of water and solutes.
In roots it lines the endodermis as the Casparian strip, forcing water through living cells so the plant can select which solutes pass on.
It is a major constituent of cork, named after the cork oak, Quercus suber, and may protect bark from microbial degradation.
Its aliphatic part shares upstream biosynthesis with cutin, and its aromatic part with lignin.

entries.text: Cork takes its name from the cork oak, Quercus suber, and so does suberin, its major constituent. Suberin is a fatty, water-repelling polyester of plants, built from long-chain fatty acids and glycerol. Interlinked with {{ref:soil-bio-233}} and lignin, it forms a barrier in cell walls that blocks water and dissolved substances. In roots it lines the endodermis as the Casparian strip. Water must then pass through living cells, so the plant chooses which solutes go on. In bark it may hold off microbial decay.

Suberin is a fatty, water-repelling polyester of plants, built from long-chain fatty acids and glycerol. Interlinked with Cutin, the waterproof skin of leaves and stems and lignin, it forms a barrier in cell walls that blocks water and dissolved substances. In roots it lines the endodermis as the Casparian strip. Water must then pass through living cells, so the plant chooses which solutes go on. In bark it may hold off microbial decay.

entries.title: Litter quality: why some leaves rot faster

definition.text: The chemical make-up of fallen plant material, such as its nutrient, lignin and tannin content, which governs how fast it decomposes and which humus form develops.

facts.text: Litter with high nutrient concentrations decomposes faster, slowing as those nutrients fall.
Plants on mull drop easily decomposed, low C:N litter that releases nutrients and encourages bioturbation.
Low pH, low nutrients and high lignin, tannin or terpene contents make the needle and heath litter of mor slow to decompose.
Deciduous 'improving' litter goes with mull, while coniferous 'acidifying' or 'recalcitrant' litter goes with moder or even mor.
Tannins protect plants from insects and infection and lower soil pH; high tannin content can lock nitrogen into resistant tannin-protein complexes.
A positive feedback links them: higher litter quality speeds decomposition, nutrient cycling and plant growth.

entries.title: Microbial necromass, the dead that build soil carbon

definition.text: The dead biomass of soil microbes, left as cells die and their remains enter the soil organic matter.

facts.text: Microbes cycle soil carbon so extensively that their necromass can make up 30 to 80% of the carbon in soil.
In the microbial carbon pump model, carbon that microbes take up is either respired to the atmosphere or enters the stable carbon pool as necromass.
Necromass is one of the primary materials of humification, alongside plant detritus, excreta of soil organisms and black carbon from past fires.
Pollutants metabolised or immobilised in soil organisms' biomass and necromass become incorporated into stable humus.

entries.text: Much of the carbon in soil was once inside a microbe. Microbes cycle the carbon in soil so thoroughly that their necromass, the dead biomass left as cells die, can make up 30 to 80% of it. The remains join {{ref:soil-found-045}} as the cells break apart. One model, the {{ref:soil-bio-266}}, gives carbon taken up by microbes two fates. It is either respired to the atmosphere or locked into a stable store as necromass. Necromass is one of the primary raw materials of humification, the slow making of humus. It joins plant detritus, the excreta of soil organisms and black carbon from past fires. Pollutants follow the same route. Once metabolized or immobilized in living or dead biomass, they become part of stable humus.

entries.title: The soil continuum model and the case against humus

definition.text: The view that soil organic matter is a continuum of progressively decomposing organic compounds rather than a set of distinct, persistent humic substances.

facts.text: Because the boundary between humus and other soil organic matter is ambiguous, some authors contest the terms humus, humic substances and humification and propose the Soil Continuum Model.
Its supporters say the evidence does not support the formation of large, persistent humic molecules in soils.
Critics of the humic-substance concept argue that the alkali extracts used to isolate it do not give a fair picture of soil organic matter.
Others hold that humus has distinct properties, mostly from its richness in functional groups, which justify keeping it as a specific term.
The humification theory persists in the field and in textbooks, and attempts to redefine humic substances have produced many conflicting definitions.

entries.contested_note: Soil scientists disagree on whether humus and humic substances exist as distinct materials or are artefacts of extraction within a continuum of decomposing organic matter.
entries.text: Some soil scientists doubt that humus, as textbooks describe it, exists at all. The soil continuum model holds that soil organic matter is a continuum of progressively decomposing compounds, not a set of distinct, persistent humic substances. Its starting point is a blurry line. The boundary between humus and other soil organic matter is ambiguous, so some authors contest the terms humus, humic substances and humification. Supporters say the evidence does not show large, persistent humic molecules forming in soils. Critics of the humic-substance concept add that the alkali extracts used to isolate it misrepresent soil organic matter. Others push back. They hold that humus has distinct properties, mostly from its richness in functional groups, the reactive clusters of atoms on its molecules. Those properties, they argue, justify keeping the term. The humification theory persists in the field and in textbooks. Attempts to redefine humic substances have produced many conflicting definitions. The question stays open: soil scientists still disagree on whether humus and humic substances are distinct materials or artifacts of extraction.

entries.title: Rethinking what soil organic matter is
entries.article: History of soil science#Soil organic matter

facts.text: Historically stability was blamed on humic substances formed from inputs and extracted with strong base and acid, interpreted as large stable macromolecules.
From the late 1990s high-resolution chemistry showed soil organic matter is recognizable plant and animal biomolecules at varying degradation stages that can associate like larger molecules.

A newer paradigm holds that molecular structure alone does not explain persistence; microbial carbon-use efficiency matters, and labile molecules taken up by microbes may form most stable organic matter.
Flaws in the established paradigm showed in 1999, when soil models could not account for the large charcoal component of Chernozems.

entries.contested_note: The humification theory still appears in textbooks while some researchers argue it is wrong.

entries.title: The soil organic matter balance

definition.text: The amount of organic matter in a soil is the net result of all additions and losses over the years.

facts.text: If additions exceed losses it rises, as in natural soil formation; if losses exceed additions it falls, as generally when soils enter crop production; if equal it holds steady.
Residue additions raise it, while faster decomposition or erosion deplete it; tillage, rotation and manuring all strongly affect it.

entries.title: What cropping costs a soil's organic matter

definition.text: Converting grassland or forest to cropland sharply cuts soil organic matter through less residue returned, plowing-accelerated mineralization and erosion.

facts.text: Cash grain systems export 55-60% of organic matter even with residue retention.
Loss is rapid in early years because active organic matter is plentiful; later the rate slows as mainly stable material remains.
A Vermont clay soil lost 20% of its organic matter in five years of silage corn after decades of sod, and many Midwest soils lost 50% within 40 years of cropping.
Deep tall-grass prairie soils kept their productivity long because they began with unusually high organic matter and nutrient reserves.
In Canada, converting native land to cropland cost about 25% of the carbon in the top 30 cm, about 1 Pg of emissions from 19th-century grassland soils; most loss came in the first twenty years.

Increased decomposition, not erosion, is typically the main culprit, as tillage breaks aggregates and exposes organic matter; the loss is mostly the light fraction of partly decomposed young residues.
Residue removal, erosion, and sometimes fire used to clear land added to the loss.

entries.title: How management shifts the living soil

definition.text: The weight of living organisms in soil differs with vegetation and cropping system.

facts.text: Fungi outweigh bacteria in forest soils, roughly equal them in grasslands, and weigh less than bacteria in routinely tilled soils.
Compaction removes large pores first; a 1 mm pore is large, root tips are about 0.1 mm wide, and fewer earthworms, beetles, mites and springtails survive in compacted soil.
Organisms are more abundant and diverse under complex rotations with diverse residues, cover crops, manures and composts, but frequent cultivation depletes their food.

entries.title: How much organic matter is enough

definition.text: There are few accepted guidelines for adequate organic matter, and the right level depends strongly on texture and erosion risk.

facts.text: Two percent is very good for a sandy soil but marks severe depletion in a clay soil.
Fine mineral particles can saturate with organic matter: a soil with 20% silt and clay can store at most about 3.6% organic matter, and one with 80% about 6.1%, excluding particulate organic matter.
Total organic matter changes slowly, but an active-fraction test is more sensitive and gives an early sign of improvement.
Sloping, erodible or already eroded soils need more organic input than level land.

entries.title: Why farmed soils hold less organic matter than pasture

definition.text: Cropping systems differ in how much plant biomass and carbon they return, so natural soils hold more organic matter than farmed ones and systems differ from each other.

facts.text: Cash grain farms sell 55-60% of aboveground biomass and replace nutrients with fertilizer but not carbon, while dairy farms return most biomass as manure and organic vegetable farms import compost or manure.
In a New York study organic matter averaged 2.7% in conventional vegetable, 2.9% in annual grain, 3.4% in dairy, 3.9% in mixed vegetable and 4.5% in pasture soils.
Water-stable aggregate share rose with organic matter and no tillage, from 27% in conventional vegetable soils to 70% in no-till pasture.

entries.title: Five groups of soil health practices

definition.text: Practices to improve soil health should grow healthy plants, suppress pests or increase beneficial organisms while reducing environmental impact.

facts.text: They group into minimizing disturbance, keeping soil covered, maximizing biodiversity, managing water, and maintaining pH and nutrients without excessive loss.
Organic matter practices come first for long-term sustainability, since each has multiple benefits; good physical condition and nutrient management need additional practices.

entries.title: What organic matter practices do for nutrients

definition.text: Organic matter practices bring nutrients and help manage them, but specific nutrient practices are still needed.

facts.text: A legume cover crop adds active organic matter, cuts erosion and supplies nitrogen to the next crop; cover and deep-rooted crops cycle nitrate, potassium, calcium and magnesium that might leach.
Importing manure or compost adds nutrients and can overload soil if applied routinely every year; testing manure, timing nutrients, liming and soil tests are separate practices.

entries.title: How a crop rotation raises or drains organic matter

definition.text: Soil organic matter rises and falls through a rotation; perennial forages build it while annual row crops under plowing deplete it.

facts.text: Hay and pasture crops add much root biomass and leave soil undisturbed; sod crops also cut erosion and residue decomposition.
Residues returned vary by crop and harvest: corn grain leaves more than soybean, wheat or silage harvest.
Cover crops protect bare soil and add organic material, in amounts set by cover type and biomass before termination.

entries.title: How erosion strips organic matter and yield

definition.text: Erosion strips organic-matter-rich topsoil, lowering organic matter, water storage and yields.

facts.text: Agricultural practice greatly speeds water, wind and tillage erosion; US erosion costs about $1 billion a year in available nutrients.
Yields fall 5-10% under moderate erosion and 10-20% or more under severe erosion.
On Corwin soil, organic matter fell from 3.03% to 1.86% and available water capacity from 12.9% to 6.6% between slight and severe erosion.

entries.title: Manure and other amendments from off the field

definition.text: Applying manures or other organic residues from off the field helps maintain or increase soil organic matter.

facts.text: A Vermont study found 20-30 tons per acre of wet dairy manure were needed yearly to maintain organic matter under continuous silage corn.
Manure type, storage and handling, and surface application versus incorporation change effects on organic matter and nutrients.
Synthetic nitrogen raises yields and residue, but is often applied up to 50% above plant need.

Synthetic nitrogen raises yields and residue, but it is often applied up to 50% above what the plants need.

entries.title: Should crop residues be burned as fuel?
entries.article: doc>geo.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Soil_Science/Building_Soils_for_Better_Crops_-_Ecological_Management_for_Healthy_Soils_4e_(Magdoff_and_van_Es)/09%3A_Managing_for_High-Quality_Soils_and_Focusing_on_Organic_Matter_Management/9.02%3A_Organic_Matter_Management#Using Organic Materials > Crop Residues: Fuel Versus Soil Organic Matter

definition.text: Using crop residues as biofuel feedstock could starve soil of organic inputs that maintain its quality.

facts.text: Most aboveground corn residue must return to soil: an estimated 2-5 tons of corn residue are needed to keep favourable properties.

A long-term New York study found modest cornstalk removal caused limited extra deterioration under no-till, yet routine removal calls for caution, most of all on cash grain fields with conventional tillage and no manure or compost.
Hans Jenny argued in 1980 against indiscriminate conversion of biomass and organic wastes to fuels, because the humus capital deserves to be maintained.

entries.contested_note: Residue use as fuel is weighed against its value for soil organic matter, with limited evidence on how much removal is tolerable.

entries.title: Why farms with animals keep more organic matter

definition.text: Animal-based farms maintain soil organic matter more easily because manure recycles carbon and nutrients from farm-grown feed.

facts.text: Integrating crops and livestock can start an upward spiral: manure improves soil, crops produce more residue and feed, and more animals mean more manure.
Pasture, hay and haylage give an economic use for perennial forages in rotation, and manure can be obtained by trading hay with neighbours.

entries.title: How much organic material it takes to gain 1 percent
entries.article: doc>geo.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Soil_Science/Building_Soils_for_Better_Crops_-_Ecological_Management_for_Healthy_Soils_4e_(Magdoff_and_van_Es)/03%3A_Amount_of_Organic_Matter_in_Soils/3.09%3A_The_Dynamics_of_Raising_and_Maintaining_Soil_Organic_Matter_Levels#Starting Point > How Much Organic Material is Needed to Increase Soil Organic Matter by 1%?

definition.text: Raising soil organic matter by 1% takes a very large addition of organic material because most of it is consumed by decomposers.

facts.text: The top 6 inches of soil weigh about 2 million pounds, so 1% organic matter is 20,000 pounds.
If 80% is lost and 20% ends up as stable organic matter, roughly 100,000 pounds (50 tons) of dry organic material is needed for each 1% gain.

entries.title: Forests, farmland and soil carbon
entries.article: doc>geo.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Soil_Science/Digging_into_Canadian_Soils%3A_An_Introduction_to_Soil_Science/01%3A_Digging_In/1.03%3A_Soil_Organic_Matter#HOW CAN WE MANAGE SOIL ORGANIC MATTER? > Land Management

definition.text: Deforestation typically lowers soil carbon, while afforestation may partly restore the original levels.

facts.text: Boreal reforestation gains carbon more slowly than other climates because trees grow slowly, and previous land use and disturbance type control the rate.
Afforested farmland gains more soil carbon than pasture or grassland, and mine-disturbed soils also gain a lot.
Where suited, deciduous trees raise soil carbon faster than conifers and over time store more in the mineral soil than in the forest floor.

entries.title: Where organic matter sits in aggregates

definition.text: Organic matter lies outside aggregates as roots, organisms and residue, and inside them where it is adsorbed on clay and small silt or trapped in small aggregates.

facts.text: Organic matter inside very small aggregates is out of reach of microorganisms and enzymes, and it also helps bind mineral particles.
Larger aggregates are held mainly by fungal hyphae and their secretions, other microbial products, and roots; tiny pores inside them can shelter microbes from predators.
The more clay and silt a soil has, the more organic matter it needs for stable aggregates: for over half water-stable aggregates, a 50% clay soil may need twice the organic matter of a 10% clay soil.

entries.title: When carbonates fool a carbon test

definition.text: Carbonates in soil decompose to CO2 during combustion-based analysis, inflating the estimate of organic carbon.

facts.text: The problem arises on limestone-derived soils, including surface soils where tillage erosion has exposed carbonate-rich horizons.
Three approaches separate carbonate carbon from organic carbon: heat treatment, acid treatment and wet oxidation.

entries.title: Why wet and low places collect organic matter
entries.article: doc>geo.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Soil_Science/Building_Soils_for_Better_Crops_-_Ecological_Management_for_Healthy_Soils_4e_(Magdoff_and_van_Es)/03%3A_Amount_of_Organic_Matter_in_Soils/3.02%3A_Natural_Factors#Soil Drainage and Position in the Landscape

definition.text: Poor aeration slows decomposition, so organic matter accumulates in wet soils and low landscape positions.

facts.text: Lignin does not decompose at all in anaerobic conditions; very long wetness produces peat or muck soils with over 20% organic matter.
Draining organic soils makes the organic matter decompose rapidly and the surface sink; some Florida homes now stand on posts above a lowered surface.
Depressions and floodplains collect runoff, sediment and organic matter and accumulate more, while steep slopes and knolls stay low because topsoil keeps eroding.

entries.title: Measuring carbon and nitrogen by burning the soil
entries.article: doc>geo.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Soil_Science/Digging_into_Canadian_Soils%3A_An_Introduction_to_Soil_Science/01%3A_Digging_In/1.03%3A_Soil_Organic_Matter#HOW DO WE MEASURE SOIL ORGANIC MATTER? > Dry Combustion

definition.text: Dry combustion burns a ground soil sample in oxygen and measures the CO2 and nitrogen released to give total carbon and nitrogen together.

facts.text: Samples under 250 μm are burned at about 1250°C in oxygen; copper at 600°C reduces nitrogen oxides to N2, and a gas chromatograph separates CO2 from N2 for detection.
To get organic carbon, carbonates are removed by acid, measured by neutralization, or avoided by burning at 860°C, which decomposes only organic carbon.

entries.title: Why some organic matter lasts and some vanishes
entries.article: doc>geo.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Soil_Science/Digging_into_Canadian_Soils%3A_An_Introduction_to_Soil_Science/01%3A_Digging_In/1.03%3A_Soil_Organic_Matter#WHERE DOES SOIL ORGANIC MATTER COME FROM AND WHY DOES IT PERSIST? > Degradation of Carbon Inputs

definition.text: Under aerobic conditions microbes respire organic inputs to carbon dioxide and water, using oxygen as electron acceptor, and the rate depends on input chemistry.

facts.text: Cellulose breaks into simple sugars that are readily degraded, whereas lignin, a network of aromatic components, is hard to break down and mainly degraded by fungi.
More complex organic matter needs more chemical energy and oxygen to degrade, one reason it persists longer.
Fresh plant residue can fuel microbial activity that degrades stored carbon (priming), or it can add to stored carbon, depending on input quality, microbes, oxygen, water and time.
Respiration is much slower without oxygen, so conversion of plant carbon takes longer in anaerobic soils.

entries.title: Why roots build more soil organic matter than shoots
entries.article: doc>geo.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Soil_Science/Building_Soils_for_Better_Crops_-_Ecological_Management_for_Healthy_Soils_4e_(Magdoff_and_van_Es)/03%3A_Amount_of_Organic_Matter_in_Soils/3.02%3A_Natural_Factors#Acidic Soil Conditions > Root Versus Aboveground Residue Contribution to Soil Organic Matter

definition.text: Roots add a larger share of their weight to persistent soil organic matter than aboveground residues do.

facts.text: Roots are well distributed, in close contact with soil, and often richer in slowly decomposing lignin than aboveground parts.

In an oat experiment one-third of surface residue remained after a year but 42% of root organic matter did; for hairy vetch, 13% of aboveground carbon and nearly 50% of root carbon remained after five months.
Root residue contributed much more to particulate organic matter than aboveground residue.
Roots are probably the most effective way to raise soil organic matter: they decompose more slowly, add more to stable organic matter, and need no incorporation to reach depth.

entries.title: How organic matter shapes the water cycle

definition.text: Organic matter helps water infiltrate into soil and be stored there, which shapes local to global water cycles.

facts.text: Soils rich in organic matter with good tilth let rainwater infiltrate quickly and store more water; the water may serve plants or percolate to recharge groundwater.
When organic matter is depleted, soil accepts and stores less water, so runoff and erosion rise and plants and groundwater recharge get less.

entries.title: Converting organic matter to carbon, and its weakness
entries.article: doc>geo.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Soil_Science/Digging_into_Canadian_Soils%3A_An_Introduction_to_Soil_Science/01%3A_Digging_In/1.03%3A_Soil_Organic_Matter#HOW DO WE MEASURE SOIL ORGANIC MATTER? > Soil Organic Matter vs Soil Organic Carbon and the Conversion Issue

definition.text: Soil organic carbon and soil organic matter are different quantities, though they are routinely converted by assuming carbon is 58% of organic matter mass (factor 1.72).

facts.text: The 58% figure comes from Waksman and Stevens (1930), who urged caution; organic matter also holds hydrogen (about 4%) and oxygen (about 30%) that vary with decomposition state.
Reviews of many studies find actual factors are usually higher than 1.72, meaning carbon is a smaller share of organic matter.
The best approach is separate direct analyses; otherwise state what was analyzed and how values were converted.

entries.title: Why clay soils hold more organic matter than sand

definition.text: Fine-textured soils naturally hold more organic matter than sands or sandy loams.

facts.text: Organic matter is under 1% in sands, 2-3% in loams and 4% to over 5% in clays.
Strong bonds between organic matter and clay or fine silt protect molecules from microbes and enzymes, and tiny aggregates shield organic matter inside them.
Smaller pores and less oxygen in fine soils further limit decomposition.

entries.title: Why grassland soils are richer than forest soils

definition.text: Soils formed under grassland hold more organic matter, distributed deeper, than soils formed under forest.

facts.text: Grassland roots are deep, extensive and turn over quickly, and slow grass fires add biochar that resists degradation; this helps explain why former grassland soils are highly productive.
In forests litter piles on the surface, where organic layers often exceed 50% organic matter, but the mineral layers beneath usually contain less than 2%.
About 25-40% of a perennial wheatgrass root system dies back each year, adding much more organic matter than annual wheat.

Slow grass fires also add Biochar, charcoal made to be buried that resists degradation. This helps explain why former grassland soils are highly productive. Forests do it differently. definition.text: The Walkley-Black method oxidizes organic carbon with chromate, heated by added sulfuric acid, and titrates leftover chromate to get carbon.

facts.text: It was once the standard method but oxidizes carbon incompletely, so a correction factor that varies with soil type is needed and biases results.
Carbon present as charcoal may be missed, underestimating total soil carbon.

entries.title: Saprophagy: the animals that eat the dead

definition.text: Feeding on decomposing dead plant or animal biomass; organisms that do so are saprophages.

facts.text: Necrophages consume dead animal biomass and thanatophages dead plant biomass; animals feeding only on dead wood are sapro-xylophagous.
In fallen plant litter, decomposition is largely carried out by saprophagous soil invertebrates.
Saprophagous macrofauna that digest wood or soil organic matter rely on enzymes of symbiotic gut microflora.
As saprophagous fauna and microbes digest organic matter, its C/N falls because carbon is released as carbon dioxide.

entries.text: Fallen leaves are taken apart largely by small animals of the soil. They are saprophages, organisms that feed on decomposing dead plants or animals, and their habit is saprophagy. Specialists have their own names: necrophages eat dead animals, thanatophages dead plants, and sapro-xylophagous animals dead wood alone. Larger saprophages that digest wood or soil organic matter rely on enzymes from microbes living in their guts. As these animals and microbes digest litter, carbon leaves as carbon dioxide. The remaining material's C/N therefore falls, feeding {{ref:soil-bio-115}} onward.

entries.title: White-rot fungi, the lignin breakers

definition.text: Wood- and litter-decaying fungi that break down lignin, one of the main precursors of humus.

facts.text: Lignin decomposes very slowly, mainly through white rot fungi and actinomycetes, while brown rot fungi decompose cellulose and hemicellulose and leave lignin behind.
Leaves or needles colonized by white-rot fungi may be bleached in the litter layer.
By cutting the lignin and tannin content of residues, white-rot fungi and bacteria make them more palatable to earthworms, helping form mull.

entries.title: Exoenzymes: digesting food before eating it

definition.text: An enzyme that a cell secretes and that works outside it, most often to break down large molecules.

facts.text: Breaking macromolecules into small pieces lets their constituents pass through the cell membrane and be used inside the cell.
Bacteria and fungi digest nutrients in their surroundings this way; once inside, the nutrients are processed with help from endoenzymes.
In soil they target carbohydrates (cellulases), lignin (oxidases), organic phosphates (phosphatases), amino sugar polymers (chitinases) and proteins (proteases).
Grouped as hydrolases, lyases, oxidoreductases and transferases, they control soil enzyme activity by degrading biopolymers.
Fungi used in bioremediation secrete oxidative exoenzymes, such as laccases, from their growing hyphal tips.
Cell-free microbial exoenzymes can also clean up pollution, but they are often less robust and hard to introduce into soil.
The word 'exoenzyme' entered English in 1908; pepsin and trypsin were probably the first known.

entries.title: How fungi spend energy to dismantle litter

definition.text: The secretion by fungi of enzymes that break down complex organic matter outside the cell; most such enzymes in leaf litter and soil come from fungi.

facts.text: Making and secreting enzymes is energy-intensive, so evolution favours limiting production.
Some exoenzymes are made constitutively at low levels and boosted when their substrate is plentiful, while glucose represses cellulase production.
Soil pH, temperature, moisture and litter type and quality alter enzyme expression and activity, and fertilizer and tillage shift it through the profile.
In decaying litter, cellulose and other labile substrates go first; lignin is depolymerised later as oxidative enzyme activity rises.
Cellulose is cut by hydrolytic endoglucanases, cellobiohydrolase and β-glucosidase; lignin by phenol oxidases, peroxidases and laccases.
Lignin peroxidase and manganese peroxidase are the hallmark of basidiomycetes and are used to gauge their activity.
Enzyme activity serves as an indicator of soil quality.

entries.title: Amplicons, copied DNA that names the microbes

definition.text: A piece of DNA that is the source or product of amplification or replication.

facts.text: Amplicons are made artificially by the polymerase or ligase chain reaction, so the term is used interchangeably with 'PCR product'.
Bacteria and archaea can be classified by comparing amplicons of the highly conserved 16S rRNA gene with known sequences.
Fungi are classified the same way from the 18S rRNA gene and the ITS1 region.
In amplicon sequencing, counts of identical taxa give their relative abundance in the sample.

Counting identical taxa gives their relative abundance.

entries.title: Metabarcoding: a census of a whole sample

definition.text: DNA or RNA barcoding done so that many taxa in one sample are identified at once.

facts.text: Unlike barcoding, it aims at the species composition of a sample, passing through DNA extraction, PCR amplification, sequencing and data analysis.
Soil can be a bulk sample of collected organisms or a source of environmental DNA taken without separating the organisms.
Soil contains inhibitors, so special techniques are needed to isolate its DNA.
There is not yet consensus on the best experimental design and bioinformatics criteria.

entries.title: Lignin peroxidase, a fungal tool for tough wood

definition.text: A heme-containing peroxidase enzyme, one of the ligninases, that uses hydrogen peroxide to cleave lignin-like compounds.

facts.text: Lignin resists biodegradation so strongly that only higher fungi and some bacteria can break it down, by oxidation.
Fungi such as Phanerochaete chrysosporium produce it to degrade lignin.
It works with veratryl alcohol, a secondary metabolite of white-rot fungi that acts as its cofactor.
Despite twenty years of study, its mechanism is not yet fully elucidated.

entries.title: Michaelis–Menten: how fast an enzyme can work

definition.text: The simplest model of enzyme kinetics, for reactions that turn one substrate into one product.

facts.text: Its equation gives the rate as v = Va/(Km + a), where V (Vmax) is the limiting rate at saturating substrate concentration.
The Michaelis constant Km is the substrate concentration at which the rate is half of V.
Michaelis and Menten published the theory in 1913, building on Victor Henri's 1902 equation.
Copiotrophic microbes have a higher Michaelis–Menten constant than oligotrophs.

entries.text: Add more food and an enzyme speeds up, but only to a limit. Michaelis–Menten kinetics, the simplest model of enzyme speed, captures this for one substrate turning into one product. Its equation is v = Va/(Km + a), where a is substrate concentration. V, or Vmax, is the limiting rate when substrate saturates the enzyme. Km, the Michaelis constant, is the concentration giving half that rate. Michaelis and Menten published it in 1913, building on Victor Henri's 1902 equation. Copiotrophic microbes have a higher Km than oligotrophs.

entries.title: Manganese peroxidase, a metal messenger against lignin

definition.text: A heme peroxidase enzyme that uses hydrogen peroxide to oxidise manganese(II) to manganese(III).

facts.text: White-rot fungi secrete it to degrade lignin; discovered in Phanerochaete chrysosporium in 1985, it seems unique to Basidiomycota.
Unstable Mn(III) is released as a chelate with a carboxylic acid, most commonly oxalate.
The Mn(III) oxidises phenolic compounds in lignin directly and can cleave alkyl–aryl bonds.
Rising extracellular Mn(II) and hydrogen peroxide up-regulate it, and lignin also induces it.

entries.title: Amino sugars, the nitrogen-carrying sugars of chitin

definition.text: A sugar molecule in which a hydroxyl group has been replaced by an amine group.

facts.text: More than 60 are known; one of the most abundant, N-acetyl-D-glucosamine, is the main component of chitin.
Soil microbes break down amino sugar polymers with chitinases.
Decomposing plant material yields simpler forms, including sugars and amino sugars, that become microbial biomass or humic assemblages.

entries.title: The acid enzyme that unlocks bound phosphorus

definition.text: An enzyme that frees attached phosphate groups from other molecules, working best at acidic pH.

facts.text: It hydrolyses a phosphate monoester with water to give an alcohol and phosphate, at an optimum pH below 7.
Soil microorganisms use phosphatase enzymes to reach organically bound phosphate.
Assays of phosphatase activity can reveal the biological demand for phosphate in a soil.
Some roots, especially cluster roots, exude carboxylates with acid phosphatase activity that mobilise phosphorus in nutrient-poor soils.

entries.text: Much soil phosphorus is bound inside organic molecules, out of reach. An acid-working enzyme frees it. This enzyme strips attached phosphate groups from other molecules, working best at an acidic {{ref:soil-found-014}} below 7. It uses water to split a phosphate monoester into an alcohol and phosphate. Soil microorganisms rely on it to reach organically bound phosphate. Some roots, especially cluster roots, exude carboxylates with this activity to mobilize phosphorus in poor soils. Measuring its activity reveals how much a soil's life is demanding phosphate.

entries.title: Microbial biomass, the living fraction of soil

definition.text: The living microbes of soil and their metabolites, a few percent of soil organic matter with a short residence time.

facts.text: Temperate grassland soils have held 1–2 t/ha of bacterial and 2–5 t/ha of fungal biomass.
Microbial biomass can be estimated by weighing soil before and after fumigation.
Microbes compete with plants for inorganic nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium, tying them up in their biomass: immobilization.
Microbial biomass is a reservoir of stored soil carbon, one way soil microbes sequester carbon.
Soil microbial biomass averages a C:N:P ratio of 60:7:1 worldwide.
Tillage can immediately cut microbial biomass carbon and nitrogen, while cover crops raised microbial biomass carbon by roughly 20% in a meta-analysis.
Microbial biomass and activity are standard measures of soil health.

entries.text: A hectare of temperate grassland has held 1–2 t of bacteria and 2–5 t of fungi. That living mass, with its metabolites, is microbial biomass. The biomass also stores carbon, one way microbes sequester it. Worldwide it averages a C:N:P ratio of 60:7:1. Farming moves it quickly. Microbial biomass and activity are standard measures of soil health.

entries.title: Ecological stoichiometry: life as a balance of elements

definition.text: The study of how the balance of energy and elements affects living systems, and how organisms affect that balance.

facts.text: Like chemical stoichiometry it rests on mass balance, an idea traced to Liebig, Lotka and Redfield.
A mismatch between what organisms need and what their food holds is an elemental imbalance: termites have tissue C:N of about 5 but eat wood of 300–1000.
Plants have weak stoichiometric homeostasis and vary widely in composition, while animals keep close to a fixed composition.
It has been applied to nutrient recycling, resource competition, animal growth and nutrient limitation in whole ecosystems.
A 2007 study found global average C:N:P ratios of 186:13:1 in soil and 60:7:1 in soil microbial biomass.
The growth rate hypothesis holds that phosphorus demand rises during active growth, to build P-rich nucleic acids.

entries.title: Isotope-ratio mass spectrometry: weighing atoms by type

definition.text: Mass spectrometry that measures the relative abundance of isotopes in a sample, used for stable-isotope and radiogenic-isotope studies.

facts.text: Stable-isotope analysis measures variations from mass-dependent fractionation, while radiogenic analysis measures decay products and underpins most long-lived radiometric dating.

Magnetic sector instruments are preferred over quadrupoles because they allow multiple-collector analysis and give good peak shapes; ions are accelerated, bent by mass-to-charge ratio and counted in Faraday cups.
Light elements such as H, C and O are measured as pure gases from combustion, GC or chemical trapping against standards; carbon uses VPDB and oxygen uses V-SMOW.
Thermal ionization MS suits low-ionization elements like Sr and Pb, while MC-ICP-MS reaches elements such as Hf-W and Lu-Hf that TIMS cannot; quadrupole ICP-MS precision is only about 1%.

entries.title: Stable-isotope probing: following labeled food

definition.text: A microbial ecology technique that traces nutrient uptake by microorganisms by feeding them substrate enriched in a heavy stable isotope.

facts.text: Biomarkers carrying the heavy isotope are separated from unlabelled ones by isopycnic centrifugation.
With 13CO2, labelled DNA is spun out and sequenced to show which organisms use freshly made photosynthate; 18O-water shows which are actively growing.
13C is used most often; 15N gives a weaker DNA density shift because DNA holds fewer nitrogen atoms.
Because the density shift is predictable, quantitative SIP (qSIP) can estimate how much isotope was incorporated.

entries.text: Feed microbes a heavier version of their food, and the eaters reveal themselves. Stable-isotope probing traces uptake with substrate enriched in a heavy stable isotope. Isopycnic centrifugation then sorts labeled biomarkers from unlabeled ones by density. With 13CO2, heavy DNA is spun out and sequenced to show who uses fresh photosynthate. 18O-water shows who is actively growing. 13C is used most; 15N shifts DNA density less, because DNA holds fewer nitrogen atoms. Quantitative SIP, or qSIP, uses the predictable shift to estimate how much isotope went in.

entries.title: β-Glucosidase, the last cut in cellulose breakdown

definition.text: An enzyme that hydrolyses terminal β-D-glucosyl residues, releasing glucose.

facts.text: Together with cellulases (endoglucanases) and cellobiosidases it is needed to consume cellulose, a polymer of β-1,4-linked glucose.
It finishes cellulose breakdown by splitting cellobiose into glucose; removing cellobiose also relieves its inhibition of other cellulose enzymes.
Both white- and brown-rot fungi secrete it, and it can also cleave xylose, mannose and galactose.
Soil and litter assays track cellulose degradation through cellobiohydrolase and β-glucosidase activity on pNP or MUF substrates.

This enzyme removes terminal glucose units, splitting cellobiose into glucose. Clearing cellobiose also lifts its brake on the other cellulose enzymes. White- and brown-rot fungi both secrete it, and it can also cleave xylose, mannose and galactose. definition.text: Laboratory methods that estimate enzyme activity in soil or litter by mixing samples with buffers and a substrate.

facts.text: Hydrolytic enzymes are measured colorimetrically with p-nitrophenol-linked substrates or fluorometrically with 4-methylumbelliferone-linked ones.
Phenol oxidase is measured by oxidation of L-DOPA, pyrogallol or ABTS; peroxidase is the difference when the same assay is rerun with hydrogen peroxide added.
Results depend on sample transport and storage, assay pH, substrate concentration, temperature and sample preparation.
Assays mostly reveal exo-acting enzymes that cut from chain ends; molecular methods now count enzyme-coding genes to link enzymes with their producers.

entries.title: Accelerator mass spectrometry for very rare isotopes

definition.text: An isotope-ratio technique for isotopes at extremely low levels, which accelerates negative ions through a mega-volt potential.

facts.text: Charge exchange removes interfering species and energy-loss detectors separate ions of the same mass-to-charge ratio, allowing isotope ratios above 10^12.
It extended 14C dating to about 60,000 years BP and is about 10^6 times more sensitive than conventional IRMS.

entries.text: Some isotopes are so rare that ordinary instruments cannot count them. Accelerator mass spectrometry is an isotope-ratio technique for such extremely low levels, and it accelerates negative ions through a mega-volt potential. Charge exchange removes interfering species, and energy-loss detectors separate ions of the same mass-to-charge ratio. This allows isotope ratios above 10^12. It extended 14C dating to about 60,000 years BP and is about 10^6 times more sensitive than conventional IRMS. It builds on {{ref:soil-bio-324}}.

entries.title: Isotope dilution: measuring by adding a known spike

definition.text: A method of measuring the quantity of a substance by adding a known amount of an isotopically enriched form of it to the sample.

facts.text: The enriched standard dilutes the sample's isotopic composition; the method works from signal ratios, not intensities, and is an internal standardisation method, giving it very high metrological standing.
It is almost always paired with mass spectrometry, is used by national metrology institutes to certify reference materials, and helps when analyte recovery is low.
In gas chromatography it can cut uncertainty from 5% to 1%; isotope dilution mass spectrometry measures ratios to better than 0.25%.
Double (reverse) dilution first calibrates the enriched spike against a natural-composition standard, because spikes come in small amounts of questionable purity.
The principle is analogous to mark-and-recapture population estimates in ecology.

entries.title: Carbon use efficiency: growth versus upkeep

definition.text: A measure of how much of the carbon a microbe takes up goes into biomass rather than into maintenance energy.

facts.text: Copiotrophs tend to have lower carbon use efficiency than oligotrophs, so they make less protein per gram of oxygen consumed.
In soil, the balance between catabolism that releases carbon as CO2 and anabolism that builds stable carbon compounds controls net carbon retention.

entries.text: A microbe can spend carbon on growing or on staying alive. Microbial carbon use efficiency measures how much of its carbon intake goes into biomass rather than maintenance energy. Copiotrophs tend to score lower than oligotrophs, making less protein per gram of oxygen consumed. In soil, two flows decide the result. Catabolism releases carbon as CO2, as in {{ref:soil-bio-033}}. Anabolism builds stable carbon compounds. Their balance controls how much carbon the soil keeps.

entries.title: The microbial carbon pump: making carbon hard to eat

definition.text: A process in which microorganisms turn dissolved organic carbon into refractory forms that resist further microbial degradation.

facts.text: In the ocean it can lock carbon away for centuries to millennia, unlike the biological pump, which relies on sinking particles.
A conceptual model of the same name describes how soil microorganisms transform and stabilise soil organic matter.
In it, microbial carbon is either respired to the atmosphere or enters the stable pool as microbial necromass.
Under ocean warming, extra carbon is converted to CO2 rather than used to build new microbial biomass.

entries.title: Q10: how much warmth speeds up life

definition.text: A unitless measure of temperature sensitivity: the factor by which a reaction rate changes for a 10 °C rise.

facts.text: It assumes rates depend exponentially on temperature, with Q10 = (R2/R1)^(10 °C/(T2−T1)), and applies to processes such as respiration and photosynthesis.
For most biological systems Q10 is about 2 to 3: rates double or triple with every 10 °C.
Environmental scientists often take 0 °C or 10 °C as the reference temperature.
The idea is thought to come from van 't Hoff's work in the late 19th century.

entries.text: Warm most living systems by 10 °C and their chemistry runs two to three times faster. That factor is Q10, the temperature coefficient: a unitless measure of how much a rate changes with a 10 °C rise. entries.title: The resistome: soil's ancient store of drug resistance

definition.text: All the antibiotic resistance genes in communities of pathogenic and non-pathogenic bacteria.

facts.text: Soil metagenomes from urban, agricultural and forest sites showed spore-forming soil bacteria resistant to most major antibiotics.
In soil, resistance genes sit on mobile genetic elements, making soil and water communities reservoirs from which resistance can pass to pathogens.
Sequencing has shown resistance genes exchanged between soil bacteria and clinical pathogens, some matching exactly across five antibiotic classes.
Sequences from ancient permafrost show antibiotic resistance existed millennia before human-made antibiotics.

entries.title: Putting the world's soils in order

definition.text: The systematic grouping of soils by their distinguishing characteristics and by criteria that guide how they are used.

facts.text: Classification systems group soils by measurable traits such as texture, structure, mineral composition and the way the soil formed.
Soil science, engineering and environmental management all classify soils, to evaluate soil properties and decide on suitable land use.
Soil can be classified as a material, as geotechnical engineers do when judging foundations and building material, or as a resource.
Classification is old: inscriptions at the temple of Horus at Edfu record a soil classification used to choose temple sites, and ancient Greek scholars devised several.
Major modern systems include USDA soil taxonomy, the World Reference Base and engineering systems that judge soil stability and performance.
Standardized systems let soils be compared across regions and applications.
Knowledge of where soils occur has grown dramatically; SoilGrids maps soils worldwide at 1.00–0.25 km resolution from soil profiles and environmental data.
It remains a dynamic subject, with change in the structure of systems, the definitions of classes and their use in the field.

entries.title: World Reference Base: one name for a soil everywhere
entries.article: World Reference Base for Soil Resources

definition.text: An international soil classification system for naming soils and building soil-map legends, edited by a working group of the International Union of Soil Sciences.

facts.text: It grew out of the FAO soil classification and the IUSS's International Reference Base project; its first edition appeared at the 1998 World Congress of Soil Science in Montpellier.
In 1998 the ISSS endorsed it as its correlation system and it replaced the FAO classification as the international system; USDA soil taxonomy also became a correlation system in 2014.
Further editions followed in 2006, 2014 (updated 2015) and 2022; the current fourth edition is open access under a Creative Commons licence.
It has two levels: 32 Reference Soil Groups, each refined by adding qualifiers, of which there are 202.
Classes rest mainly on soil morphology, from field and laboratory data, as an expression of pedogenesis; soil climate counts only as a soil-forming factor, not as a soil characteristic.
Its two levels resemble the French Référentiel pédologique, whereas USDA soil taxonomy is strongly hierarchical with six levels.
It is not meant to replace national systems, which may be more detailed for their own areas; the European Union uses it.
Group and qualifier names are capitalized and always given in English, so a soil carries the same name all over the world.

entries.title: Soil type, the word many systems avoid

definition.text: A taxonomic unit of soil science: all soils that share a defined set of properties.

facts.text: In hierarchical systems soil types usually sit at a higher or intermediate level; they can be split into subtypes and combined into higher categories.
In the first U.S. classification (Whitney, 1909), by contrast, the soil type was the lowest level and the mapping unit.

Systems differ in what defines a type: German soil systematics uses mainly pedogenic features, WRB and USDA soil taxonomy add inherited parent-material traits, and the Australian Soil Classification ignores origin.
Horizons are a convenient basis, but some young soils lack clear horizons, so types may rest on whole-profile properties, as WRB defines Arenosols by sand content.
Many soils are shaped by human activity, and many systems define soil types to reflect it.
Because the term is so general, many systems avoid it: USDA soil taxonomy names six levels from order to series, and WRB calls its first level the Reference Soil Group.
In U.S. soil survey, 'soil type' was the original name of the soil phase, which records surface texture, slope, stoniness, saltiness and erosion.

entries.text: Few terms in soil science are so common, or so slippery. A soil type is a taxonomic unit: all the soils that share a defined set of properties. In hierarchical systems it usually sits at a higher or intermediate level, split into subtypes and combined into higher categories. The first U.S. classification, by Whitney in 1909, did the reverse: there the soil type was the lowest level and the mapping unit. Systems also disagree on what defines a type. German soil systematics uses mainly features made by soil formation. The WRB and {{ref:soil-class-006}} add traits inherited from the parent material, and the {{ref:soil-class-022}} ignores origin. Horizons make a convenient basis, but some young soils lack clear ones, so types may rest on whole-profile properties. The WRB, for instance, defines one group by sand content alone. Many systems also define types that reflect human activity. Because the word is so general, many systems avoid it. In early U.S. mapping, 'soil type' was the original name of the {{ref:soil-agri-220}}, which records surface texture, slope, stoniness, saltiness and erosion.

entries.title: USDA soil taxonomy: six levels from order to series

definition.text: The soil classification of the U.S. Department of Agriculture and the National Cooperative Soil Survey, which sorts soils by their properties into six levels from order to series.

facts.text: Its levels, from most general to most specific, are order, suborder, great group, subgroup, family and series.
The United States recognizes 12 orders, 47 suborders, about 185 great groups, about 1,000 subgroups, about 4,500 families and more than 14,000 series.
It uses quantitatively measurable properties: depth, moisture, temperature, texture, structure, cation exchange capacity, base saturation, clay mineralogy, organic matter and salt content.
Guy Donald Smith, director of USDA soil survey investigations, originally developed it as a substantial revision of the strictly natural 1938 system.
Work began by 1945; a series of 'approximations' followed, the 7th in 1960, and the taxonomy appeared in 1975 with 10 orders and in 1999, revised, with 12.
It is a hierarchical hybrid of natural and objective criteria, designed to guide land use and soil management, and supplies the core criteria for U.S. soil map units.
Order names end in -sol, and the criteria for orders reflect major differences in how soils formed.

The lab manual describes Soil Taxonomy as a quantitative hierarchy of six categories running from 12 broad orders to more than 23,000 series, and says it helps carry management research between similar soils worldwide.

conflicts.text: More than 14,000 soil series are recognised in the United States.

entries.title: The FAO map legend that became a world system

definition.text: A supra-national soil classification developed by the FAO, generalizing how soils form from the interaction of the main soil-forming factors.

facts.text: It began as the legend of the FAO–UNESCO Soil Map of the World, published 1971–1981 in 10 volumes at 1:5 million; Rudi Dudal led the 1974 legend.
It gathered ideas from national systems, among them the diagnostic horizons of the USDA's 1960 '7th approximation'.
Its 106 soil units were mapped as associations named for the dominant unit, with soil phases, three texture classes and three slope classes.
Simple and broad, it was the first truly international system, fitting most soils from field descriptions, and meant for continental rather than local maps.
The 1988 Revised Legend had 153 soil units in 28 major soil groupings and underlies the Harmonized World Soil Database.
United Nations projects applied it and many countries adapted it; many of its names are known widely with similar meanings.
The World Reference Base replaced it in 1998.
In the 1974 legend, Leptosols on calcareous rock were called Rendzinas and those on acid rock Rankers.

entries.text: The first truly international soil classification began life as the key to a map. The FAO soil classification, developed by the {{ref:soil-env-372}}, is a supra-national system that generalizes how soils form from the interaction of the main soil-forming factors. It started as the legend of the FAO–UNESCO map of the world's soils, published from 1971 to 1981 in 10 volumes at a scale of 1:5 million. Rudi Dudal led the 1974 legend. It gathered ideas from national systems, among them the diagnostic horizons of the USDA's 1960 '7th approximation'. Its 106 soil units were mapped as associations named for the dominant unit, with phases marking local land features, three texture classes and three slope classes. Simple and broad, it fitted most soils from field descriptions alone. It was meant for continental maps, not local ones. The 1988 Revised Legend had 153 soil units in 28 major soil groupings, and it still underlies the Harmonized World Soil Database. United Nations projects applied the system, and many countries adapted it. Many of its names are known widely, with similar meanings. In the 1974 legend, thin soils on calcareous rock were called {{ref:soil-class-050}} and those on acid rock were called {{ref:soil-class-040}}. The WRB replaced it in 1998.

It gathered ideas from national systems, among them the diagnostic horizons of the USDA's 1960 '7th approximation'. Its 106 soil units were mapped as associations named for the dominant unit, with phases marking local land features, three texture classes and three slope classes. Simple and broad, it fitted most soils from field descriptions alone. It was meant for continental maps, not local ones. The 1988 Revised Legend had 153 soil units in 28 major soil groupings, and it still underlies the Harmonized World Soil Database. United Nations projects applied the system, and many countries adapted it. Many of its names are known widely, with similar meanings. In the 1974 legend, thin soils on calcareous rock were called Rendzina, the thin dark soil on limestone and those on acid rock were called Rankers: a thin topsoil straight on rock. The WRB replaced it in 1998.

entries.title: Canada's system, built for cool-climate soils

definition.text: Canada's national soil classification, closer to the U.S. system than any other but designed to cover only Canadian soils.

facts.text: Introduced in 1955, it was designed to separate soils formed by pedogenic processes in cool climates; earlier Canadian work had used U.S.-like systems.
Its five levels are order, great group, subgroup, family and series: it drops the suborder, and separates Solonetzic and Gleysolic soils at order level.
Ten orders sit at the top; 31 great groups subdivide them by properties reflecting differences in soil-forming processes.
Its unit is the pedon, a 3-dimensional body commonly 1 metre across and 1 to 2 metres deep, classified with a key using horizon thickness, Munsell colour and pH.
Subgroups follow horizon sequence and often intergrade to other orders; families add parent material and soil climate, as in 'Orthic Gray Luvisol, clayey, mixed, cold, subhumid'.
A series name such as Breton implies all the properties of its order, great group, subgroup and family, supporting many judgements of land suitability.
Class limits are arbitrary, since nature has few sharp breaks in the soil continuum, and the system changes as mapping and research add knowledge.
Recent research proposes adding a Leptosolic order for soils that are shallow or over bedrock.

entries.text: Canada classifies its soils with a system closer to the U.S. one than any other, yet built to cover only Canadian soils. Introduced in 1955, it was designed to separate soils formed by soil-forming processes in cool climates. Earlier Canadian work had used U.S.-like systems. It has five levels: order, great group, subgroup, family and series. It drops the suborder, and it separates sodium-affected and waterlogged soils at the order level, as the {{ref:soil-class-029}} and the {{ref:soil-class-028}}. Ten orders sit at the top. Below them, 31 great groups reflect differences in how the soils formed. The unit classified is the pedon, a 3-dimensional body of soil commonly 1 meter across and 1 to 2 meters deep. A key sorts it using horizon thickness, Munsell color and pH. Subgroups follow the sequence of horizons and often intergrade toward other orders. Families add parent material and the climate of the soil. A series name such as Breton implies all the properties of its order, great group, subgroup and family, which supports many judgments of land suitability. Class limits are arbitrary, since nature has few sharp breaks in the soil continuum. The system changes as mapping and research add knowledge, and recent research proposes a new order for soils that are shallow or over bedrock.

entries.title: Australia's fifteen orders for an old, weathered land

definition.text: The general-purpose, hierarchical system currently used to describe and classify soils in Australia.

facts.text: It has five levels, from most general to most specific: order, suborder, great group, subgroup and family.
Ray Isbell, a retired CSIRO soil scientist, developed it and first published it in 1996; later editions came in 2002, 2010 and March 2021.
It superseded the Factual Key (1960) and the Handbook of Australian Soils (1968); since Isbell's death in 2001 the National Committee on Soil and Terrain has led its updates.
Its fifteen orders run from Anthroposols, Arenosols and Calcarosols to Sodosols, Tenosols and Vertosols, many reflecting the arid, strongly weathered Australian continent.
In seven orders, suborders name the dominant colour of the upper B2 horizon (Red, Brown, Yellow, Grey or Black), giving names such as Red Kurosol.
Other orders have their own suborders: Hydrosols, for instance, split into Intertidal, Supratidal, Salic, Redoxic and other Hydrosols.
It defines soil types without asking whether their properties result from soil formation.
Some equivalents: Histosols are Organosols, and Podzols are Podosols.

entries.text: Australia's soils needed names of their own, many of them shaped by an arid, strongly weathered continent. The Australian Soil Classification is the general-purpose, hierarchical system now used to describe and classify them. It has five levels: order, suborder, great group, subgroup and family. Ray Isbell, a retired CSIRO soil scientist, developed it and first published it in 1996. Later editions came in 2002, 2010 and March 2021. It superseded the Factual Key of 1960 and the {{ref:soil-class-046}} of 1968. Since Isbell's death in 2001, the National Committee on Soil and Terrain has led its updates. Its fifteen orders run from {{ref:soil-class-044}} and Calcarosols to Sodosols, Tenosols and Vertosols. In seven orders, suborders name the dominant color of the upper B2 horizon: Red, Brown, Yellow, Grey or Black. One of those orders is {{ref:soil-found-070}}, so a soil there takes a color and an order as its name. Other orders have their own suborders. Hydrosols, for instance, split into Intertidal, Supratidal, Salic, Redoxic and other Hydrosols. The system defines soil types without asking whether their properties result from soil formation. Some names translate directly: soils called {{ref:soil-class-098}} elsewhere are Organosols here, and the {{ref:soil-class-138}} becomes the Podosol.
entries.text_plain: Australia's soils needed names of their own, many of them shaped by an arid, strongly weathered continent. The Australian Soil Classification is the general-purpose, hierarchical system now used to describe and classify them. It has five levels: order, suborder, great group, subgroup and family. Ray Isbell, a retired CSIRO soil scientist, developed it and first published it in 1996. Later editions came in 2002, 2010 and March 2021. It superseded the Factual Key of 1960 and the The Handbook of Australian Soils of 1968. Since Isbell's death in 2001, the National Committee on Soil and Terrain has led its updates. Its fifteen orders run from Anthroposols, soils that people built or remade and Calcarosols to Sodosols, Tenosols and Vertosols. In seven orders, suborders name the dominant color of the upper B2 horizon: Red, Brown, Yellow, Grey or Black. One of those orders is Kurosols: a light topsoil over acid clay, so a soil there takes a color and an order as its name. Other orders have their own suborders. Hydrosols, for instance, split into Intertidal, Supratidal, Salic, Redoxic and other Hydrosols. The system defines soil types without asking whether their properties result from soil formation. Some names translate directly: soils called Histosols, soils built from organic matter elsewhere are Organosols here, and the Podzol, the ash-grey soil beneath northern forests becomes the Podosol.

entries.title: How engineers classify soil to build on it

definition.text: The grouping of soils by the engineering properties that matter when they support foundations or serve as building material.

facts.text: Modern engineering systems are built to move easily from field observations to basic predictions of how a soil will behave.
The Unified Soil Classification System is the most common in North America; it and the fuller engineering description are standardized in ASTM D 2487.
Europe's ISO 14688 closely resembles the USCS but codes soils differently and adds an intermediate-plasticity class for silts and clays.
In the United States the AASHTO system rates soils and aggregates for pavement construction, and the Modified Burmister system works like the USCS but codes more properties.
Moderately organic soils are treated as subdivisions of silts and clays, told apart by how their plasticity and Atterberg limits change on drying.
A full geotechnical description adds colour, in-situ moisture and strength, and more material detail than the USCS code carries.

entries.text: To an engineer, soil is a material to build on or to build with. Engineering soil classification groups soils by the properties that matter when they support foundations or serve as building material. Modern systems are designed to move easily from field observations to basic predictions of how a soil will behave. In North America the most common is the Unified Soil Classification System, or USCS. It and the fuller engineering description are standardized in ASTM D 2487. Europe's standard, {{ref:soil-class-152}}, closely resembles the USCS but codes soils differently. It also adds an intermediate-plasticity class for silts and clays. In the United States, the {{ref:soil-class-036}} rates soils and aggregates for pavement construction. The Modified Burmister system works like the USCS but codes more properties. Moderately organic soils count as subdivisions of silts and clays. They are told apart by how their plasticity and Atterberg limits change on drying. A full geotechnical description goes further than any code. It adds color, moisture and strength in place, and more detail about the material than the USCS code carries.

entries.title: Natural classes and technical classes

definition.text: The contrast between natural systems, which group soils by intrinsic properties, behaviour or genesis, and technical systems, which group them by fitness for a particular use.

facts.text: Experience shows that natural classes, based on morphology, behaviour or genesis, can be interpreted for many different uses.
Some natural systems, such as the French Référentiel pédologique, rest on presumed soil genesis.
USDA soil taxonomy and the World Reference Base use morphology and laboratory tests as criteria for their hierarchical classes.
Differing ideas of pedogenesis, and of which morphological features matter for land use, shape each system's approach.
In U.S. soil survey, map units classed by soil taxonomy are also sorted into technical classes such as Land Capability Classes, hydric soil and prime farmland.
Numerical classification, or ordination, groups soil individuals by multivariate statistics such as cluster analysis, producing natural groupings without any inference about genesis.

entries.text: A soil can be classified for what it is, or for what it is good for. Natural systems group soils by their intrinsic properties, behavior or genesis. Technical systems group them by fitness for a particular use. Experience shows that natural classes can be interpreted for many different uses. Some natural systems, such as the French {{ref:soil-class-035}}, rest on presumed soil genesis. USDA soil taxonomy and the WRB use morphology and laboratory tests as the criteria for their hierarchical classes. Each system's approach reflects its own ideas of how soils form and of which features matter for {{ref:soil-agri-221}}. In U.S. soil mapping the two kinds meet. Map units classed by soil taxonomy are also sorted into technical classes such as Land Capability Classes, {{ref:soil-water-119}} and {{ref:soil-agri-088}}. A third route is numerical classification, or ordination. It groups soil individuals by multivariate statistics such as cluster analysis, producing natural groups without any inference about genesis.

entries.title: Moisture regimes: how wet a soil stays all year

definition.text: A class describing how wet a soil stays through the year, defined by the groundwater table and the water available to plants.

facts.text: A soil's moisture regime, often reflecting climate, is a major control on the productivity of land ecosystems, farms included.
Moisture regime names modify soil names at the suborder level of USDA soil taxonomy.
Aquic soils are saturated and almost free of oxygen long enough to show gleying and mottling; they are common in wetlands.
Udic soils stay moist enough for plants year-round in most years and are common in humid regions.
Ustic soils lie between udic and aridic: moisture is usually available in the growing season, but severe droughts occur; they are common in semi-arid regions.
Aridic soils are dry for at least half the growing season and moist for less than 90 consecutive days, as in deserts.
Xeric soils belong to Mediterranean-type climates, with cool, moist winters and long summer droughts.

entries.text: A desert soil may stay moist for less than 90 consecutive days; a waterlogged soil may sit saturated and almost airless. A soil moisture regime is a class describing how wet a soil stays through the year, defined by the groundwater table and the water available to plants. It often reflects climate, and it is a major control on the productivity of land ecosystems, farms included. In USDA soil taxonomy, regime names modify soil names at the suborder level. Aquic soils are saturated and almost free of oxygen long enough to show gleying and mottling; they are common in {{ref:soil-water-124}} areas. At the other end, aridic soils are dry for at least half the growing season and moist for less than 90 consecutive days, as in deserts. Soils of the {{ref:soil-found-101}} stay moist enough for plants year-round in most years and are common in humid regions. Between that regime and aridic soils lies the {{ref:soil-class-041}} regime. There moisture is usually available in the growing season, but severe droughts occur; such soils are common in semi-arid regions. Xeric soils belong to Mediterranean-type climates, with cool, moist winters and long summer droughts.

entries.title: The 1938 U.S. system and its three orders

definition.text: The earlier U.S. soil classification, which divided soils into three orders according to their dominant soil-forming factors.

facts.text: It grew from Curtis Marbut's scheme, begun in 1920, which became the 1935 system and, modified, was published in the 1938 Yearbook of Agriculture, Soils and Men.
Zonal soils reflected climate and vegetation; intrazonal soils reflected a local factor of relief or parent material strong enough to override them.
At the top level soils were split into carbonate-rich pedocals of drier climates and pedalfers rich in aluminium and iron; 'alfer' later became the root of Alfisol.
It was a strictly natural system, and after 1938 classifying soil series under it met with mixed success; work on a replacement began by 1945.

entries.text: Before modern soil taxonomy, the United States sorted soils by what had made them. The 1938 system divided soils into three orders according to their dominant soil-forming factors. Its {{ref:soil-class-015}} order reflected climate and vegetation. Its {{ref:soil-class-013}} order reflected a local factor of relief or parent material strong enough to override them. At the top level, soils were split into carbonate-rich pedocals of drier climates and the {{ref:soil-class-042}} group, rich in aluminum and iron. Its root 'alfer' later became part of a modern order name, {{ref:soil-class-090}}. The 1938 scheme was a strictly natural system, and after 1938 classifying individual series under it met with mixed success. Work on a replacement began by 1945.

entries.title: OSHA soil types: keeping trench walls standing

definition.text: A U.S. workplace-safety scheme that sorts soils by strength so that excavations and trenches can be protected against collapse.

facts.text: It uses three soil types plus stable rock, based mainly on strength but also on other factors that affect the stability of cut slopes.

Type A soils are cohesive and plastic, with unconfined compressive strength above 1.5 tsf (144 kPa); Type B lie between 0.5 tsf (48 kPa) and 1.5 tsf; Type C fall below 0.5 tsf or are granular or seeping.
The lateral earth pressure each type induces rises from 25 psf per foot of depth for Type A to 45 for Type B and 80 for Type C.
Each type dictates how the excavation is cut or protected by sloping, shoring or shielding; the scheme guides construction safety, not the study of soil formation.

entries.title: The diagnostic toolkit behind every WRB name
entries.article: World Reference Base for Soil Resources#Architecture

definition.text: The diagnostic horizons, diagnostic properties and diagnostic materials on which the WRB bases its classification.

facts.text: Diagnostic horizons are typical products of soil formation with a minimum thickness, so they form a recognizable layer in the soil.
Diagnostic properties are typical results of soil-forming processes or reflect particular conditions of soil formation.
Diagnostic materials influence or indicate soil formation; they may be inherited from the parent material or produced by soil formation.
Each diagnostic has a name, such as argic horizon, stagnic properties or fluvic material.
Organic carbon sets one boundary: mineral material has less than 20% soil organic carbon, organic material 20% or more.
Diagnostic horizons entered the international system from the 1960 '7th approximation' of USDA soil taxonomy, by way of the FAO legend.
Only the diagnostic criteria decide whether a diagnostic is present in a soil.

entries.title: The 32 Reference Soil Groups, in the order of the key
entries.article: World Reference Base for Soil Resources#List of the Reference Soil Groups according to WRB 2022

definition.text: The 32 top-level classes of the World Reference Base, each with a two-letter code, listed in the order of its key.

facts.text: The key opens with Histosols, with thick organic layers, then soils under strong human influence: long and intensively farmed Anthrosols and artefact-rich Technosols.
Groups that limit root growth are Cryosols (permafrost), Leptosols (thin or stony), Solonetz (sodium-rich clayey subsoil), Vertisols (shrink–swell clays) and Solonchaks (soluble salts).
Groups set apart by iron and aluminium chemistry are Gleysols, Andosols, Podzols, Plinthosols, Planosols, Stagnosols, Nitisols and Ferralsols.
Chernozems, Kastanozems, Phaeozems and Umbrisols have organic-rich mineral topsoils; Durisols, Gypsisols and Calcisols accumulate secondary silica, gypsum or carbonates.
Clay-enriched subsoils mark Retisols and four groups split by clay activity and by whether exchangeable aluminium exceeds base cations: Acrisols, Lixisols, Alisols and Luvisols.
The key ends with little-differentiated soils: Cambisols (moderately developed), Fluvisols (stratified sediments), Arenosols (very sandy) and Regosols (no significant development).
Group names are plural in map legends and singular everywhere else.

entries.text: The WRB sorts the world's soils into just 32 top-level classes, and it always lists them in the same order. These are the Reference Soil Groups, each with a two-letter code, arranged as the key runs. The key opens with {{ref:soil-class-098}}, soils with thick organic layers. Then come soils under strong human influence: the long and intensively farmed {{ref:soil-class-120}} and the artefact-rich {{ref:soil-class-145}}. Next are groups that limit root growth, with permafrost, thin or stony ground, a sodium-rich clayey subsoil, shrink–swell clays or soluble salts. Eight groups are set apart by iron and aluminum chemistry, among them the {{ref:soil-class-127}} and the {{ref:soil-class-138}}. Four have organic-rich mineral topsoils, led by the {{ref:soil-class-123}}. Three more accumulate secondary silica, gypsum or carbonates. Clay-enriched subsoils mark five groups, split by clay activity and by whether exchangeable aluminum exceeds base cations. The key ends with little-differentiated soils: moderately developed, built of stratified sediments, very sandy, or with no significant development at all. Group names are plural in map legends and singular everywhere else.

Then come soils under strong human influence: the long and intensively farmed Anthrosols, soils remade by centuries of farming and the artefact-rich Technosols, the soils of cities, mines and dumps. Eight groups are set apart by iron and aluminum chemistry, among them the Gleysols, soils stained by groundwater and the Podzol, the ash-grey soil beneath northern forests. Four have organic-rich mineral topsoils, led by the Chernozem, the black earth of the steppes. Three more accumulate secondary silica, gypsum or carbonates. Clay-enriched subsoils mark five groups, split by clay activity and by whether exchangeable aluminum exceeds base cations. The key ends with little-differentiated soils: moderately developed, built of stratified sediments, very sandy, or with no significant development at all. Group names are plural in map legends and singular everywhere else.

entries.title: What a vineyard asks of its soil

definition.text: The soils in which grapevines grow, whose make-up is one of the most important considerations in planting a vineyard.

facts.text: Soil anchors the vine's roots and governs drainage and the minerals and nutrients the vine receives.
The ideal is thin topsoil and subsoil that hold enough water yet drain well, so roots are not waterlogged; soil that stores or reflects heat also affects ripening.
Growers name soils by rock or texture: limestone-based Kimmeridgian soil is the principal type of the Loire Valley, Champagne and Burgundy.
Sandy soils drain well but hold water poorly, and the phylloxera louse does not thrive in them.

entries.title: Temperature regimes, measured 50 cm down

definition.text: A class of soil temperature, set by mean annual and seasonal temperatures at 50 cm depth, used to classify soils in USDA soil taxonomy.

facts.text: Regimes such as frigid, mesic and thermic classify soils at lower levels, while the cryic regime separates some higher-level groups.
They rest on mean annual soil temperature, mean summer temperature and the summer–winter difference at 50 cm; mean annual soil temperature is normally taken as mean annual air temperature plus 2 °C.
Classes run from pergelic (about −8 to −4 °C) through subgelic, frigid (about 0 to 8 °C), mesic (8 to 15 °C) and thermic (15 to 22 °C) to hyperthermic (22 °C or higher).
Where mean summer and winter temperatures differ by less than 6 °C, the prefix 'iso' is added to the class name.

entries.title: Suborders and great groups: the second and third rungs

definition.text: The second and third levels of USDA soil taxonomy: suborders split each order by properties tied to soil moisture and temperature, and great groups split suborders by the kind and sequence of horizons.

facts.text: Forty-seven suborders and about 185 great groups are recognized in the United States.
Great groups are told apart by horizons marked by clay, iron, humus or hardpans, and by features such as self-mixing shrink–swell clays, temperature and large amounts of salts.
Soil moisture regime names act as modifiers at the suborder level.
For example, the suborder Xeralfs contains the great group Durixeralfs, whose subgroup Abruptic Durixeralfs includes the San Joaquin series.

entries.title: Typic, intergrade, extragrade: the subgroup level

definition.text: The fourth level of USDA soil taxonomy, which divides each great group into typic, intergrade and extragrade subgroups.

facts.text: A typic subgroup carries the basic, typical concept of its great group.
An intergrade subgroup has properties grading toward another great group, suborder or order, but not expressed strongly enough to place it there.
Extragrade subgroups have aberrant properties that keep them out of any other class.
About 1,000 subgroups are defined in the United States.
