entries.title: Soil families: grouping soils by how they behave

definition.text: The fifth level of USDA soil taxonomy: a group of soils within a subgroup sharing the physical and chemical properties that govern their response to farming and engineering.

facts.text: Families are distinguished by texture, mineralogy, pH, permeability, structure, consistency, precipitation pattern and soil temperature, and sometimes by the percentages of silt, sand and coarse fragments.
About 4,500 families are recognized in the United States, and each may contain several soil series.
A family name stacks descriptors on the subgroup: 'fine-loamy, mixed, superactive, calcareous, Typic Torrifluvents' belongs to suborder Fluvents and includes the Jocity series.

entries.title: Soil series: named for a town, mapped across states

definition.text: The lowest level of USDA soil taxonomy, grouping pedons with similar pedogenesis, soil chemistry and physical properties.

facts.text: A series groups pedons whose horizons match in colour, texture, structure, pH, consistency, composition and arrangement in the profile, so the soils perform alike for land use.
The concept dates from 1903, when series were meant as soils alike in origin, from the same kind of rock or sediment, but differing in texture.
Series are named after a town or landmark near where they were first recognized, such as Haugan, Montana, though a series such as Hagerstown can range across several states.
More than 14,000 series are recognized in the United States; they are the most homogeneous classes in the taxonomy.
A series may be a taxonomic unit, the conceptual core of a class, or a mapping unit outlining similar soils on the land; the two need not fully coincide.
Map units carry the name of their dominant series: in Greenbrier County, West Virginia, unit LhE is 80% Lily series, the rest Dekalb, Berks and less stony soils.

entries.title: State soils, official emblems like flowers and birds

definition.text: A soil that a U.S. state has chosen as having special significance to it.

facts.text: Every state has selected one, and twenty have been established by law, giving them the same standing as official state flowers and birds.
Representative soils have also been chosen for Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands.
Examples include San Joaquin in California (1997), Drummer in Illinois (2001) and Port Silt Loam in Oklahoma (1987).
The Cecil soil, which runs from Virginia to Alabama, is the state soil of North Carolina.

entries.title: Udic soils: moist enough, most years

definition.text: The soil moisture regime of humid climates, where stored moisture plus rainfall roughly equals or exceeds evapotranspiration.

facts.text: Water moves down through the soil at some time in most years.
In USDA soil taxonomy, udic soils are moist enough year-round in most years to meet plant needs; the ustic regime lies between udic and aridic.
Suborders such as udalfs (Alfisols), udepts (Inceptisols) and udolls (Mollisols) have a udic moisture regime.

entries.title: AASHTO groups: rating the soil beneath a road

definition.text: An American highway-engineering system that classifies soils and soil–aggregate mixtures for road construction.

facts.text: Hogentogler and Terzaghi first developed it in 1929, and it has been revised several times since.
Soils with 35% or less passing the 0.075 mm (No. 200) sieve are granular materials; those with more than 35% are silt–clay materials.
Groups run from A-1 to A-7, set by sieve results and by the liquid limit and plasticity index of the fraction passing 0.425 mm (No. 40).
As road subgrade, granular materials rate excellent to good and silt–clay materials fair to poor.

entries.title: Naming a soil the WRB way, one qualifier at a time
entries.article: World Reference Base for Soil Resources#Naming a soil

definition.text: The WRB procedure that keys a soil out to a Reference Soil Group and then adds every qualifier that applies to it.

facts.text: The key asks, in a fixed sequence, whether given diagnostics occur in given depth ranges, plus traits such as clay content; the soil goes to the first group whose criteria it meets.
Principal qualifiers precede the group name, the highest-ranked closest to it, with Haplic used if none applies; supplementary qualifiers follow in brackets.
Specifiers such as Epi- (0 to 50 cm) and Endo- (below 50 cm) turn qualifiers into depth-related subqualifiers, such as Epiarenic.
In the worked example, a loess soil with clay migration becomes an Amphialbic Endostagnic Luvisol, followed by supplementary qualifiers such as Anosiltic, Endoloamic and Aric.

entries.title: How map scale sets the length of a WRB name
entries.article: World Reference Base for Soil Resources#Creating map legends with the WRB

definition.text: The WRB rules for naming the units of a soil map, where the number of qualifiers used depends on the map's scale.

facts.text: Three map scale levels use the Reference Soil Group alone, the group plus its first applying principal qualifier, or the group plus the first two.
A map unit names an association of soils: dominant soils cover at least 50%, codominant 25 to 50% and associated 5 to 25%; smaller shares are ignored.
Matching scale levels to actual map scales is difficult because the choice depends on how uniform the landscape is.
Only the third and later editions can build map legends; the second edition could only name soils.

entries.title: The argillic horizon, where washed-down clay collects

definition.text: The USDA soil taxonomy term for a subsurface horizon enriched in clay.

facts.text: Clay accumulates mainly by illuviation, the downward washing of existing clay, with some clay formed in place.
It is a diagnostic subsurface horizon used to define higher categories: Alfisols and Ultisols require it, Histosols and Entisols never have it, and other orders vary.
An argillic horizon needs at least 1.2 times the clay of any overlying eluvial horizon and usually shows clay films or bridges visible by eye or hand lens.
A 2014 study by James Bockheim found argillic horizons in 44% of U.S. soil series.
It is the starting point for kandic horizons, dominated by low-CEC 1:1 clays, and natric horizons, rich in exchangeable sodium; fragipans commonly form within it.
The WRB equivalent is the argic horizon, from the same Latin root argilla; it needs at least 8% clay and a texture class other than sand.
Buried paleo-argillic horizons, as in the Wounded Moose paleosol of the Yukon, show that the climate was once hot and wet enough to form them.

entries.title: Rankers: a thin topsoil straight on rock

definition.text: A soil developed over non-calcareous material, usually rock.

facts.text: It is often called an A/C soil, because its topsoil, the A horizon, sits directly on unaltered parent material, the C horizon.
Some classifications group it as lithomorphic, together with the rendzina, the similar soil over calcareous material.

entries.title: Ustic soils: water, but not always enough

definition.text: A soil moisture regime in which water is present but limited at times when conditions suit plant growth, intermediate between aridic and udic.

facts.text: The name comes from Latin ustus, 'burnt'; the regime is common in semi-arid and sub-humid climates.
Averaged over the year, stored moisture plus rainfall is less than the water lost by evapotranspiration.
Ustic soils suit drought-tolerant crops; maize there generally needs supplemental irrigation, which udic soils do not require.
The long dry season gives a wide harvest window: farmers in Brazil's Cerrado harvest grain at a leisurely pace.

entries.title: Poland's soil system and its three-part description

definition.text: The system used to describe, classify and organize knowledge about the soils of Poland.

facts.text: The Soil Science Society of Poland published editions in 1956, 1959, 1974, 1989, 2011 and 2019; early ones followed Dokuchaev's natural criteria, the 2011 edition quantitatively defined diagnostic horizons, materials and properties.
Each soil is described three ways: its type, from genesis and diagnostic horizons; its kind, the geological origin of the bedrock; and its texture class.
Soil type is the basic unit, and types are grouped into orders by the presence or absence of diagnostic horizons and properties.
It borrows much from USDA soil taxonomy (1999) and the WRB (2006) and gives equivalents: its rusty soils, sandy soils with rusty horizons, match WRB Arenosols and USDA Psamments.

entries.title: Miami, Indiana's state soil on glacial till

definition.text: A soil series of the Wisconsin Till Plains that is the state soil of Indiana.

facts.text: It formed in up to 18 inches (46 cm) of loess or silty material over calcareous loamy till, under native hardwood forest.
Some 794,994 acres (3,217 km2) are mapped in Indiana; the fertile, gently sloping soils grow corn, soybeans and winter wheat and help rank the state in farm output.
USDA soil taxonomy classifies it as fine-loamy, mixed, active, mesic Oxyaquic Hapludalfs, an Alfisol.
It is an old series: by 1906 the Miami series already held 16 soil types from glaciated regions.

entries.title: Pedalfers, the iron-and-aluminum soils of 1938

definition.text: In the 1938 U.S. classification, a major group of soils rich in aluminium and iron, in which sesquioxides increase relative to silica as the soil forms.

facts.text: Pedalfers were a subdivision of the zonal order; together with the carbonate-rich pedocals they formed the top level of Marbut's classification.
They began at about the udic border, and lateritic soils were one of their three subdivisions.
The term is no longer used in U.S. soil classification but survives in college geology texts, and its 'alf' lives on in the name Alfisol.

Its 'alf' lives on in the name of the order in {{ref:soil-class-090}}.

entries.title: Brunisolic soils, Canada's in-between order
entries.article: Canadian system of soil classification#Brunisolic Order

definition.text: The Canadian order for soils with developed B horizons that meet the requirements of none of the other orders.

facts.text: Many have brownish B horizons without the clay build-up of Luvisolic soils or the amorphous material of Podzolic soils, and some evolve into one or the other.
Brunisolic soils cover almost 790,000 km2 (8.6%) of Canada, in all regions south of the permafrost zone.
Four great groups follow the A horizon and acidity: Melanic Brunisols have an Ah at least 10 cm thick and pH above 5.5, Sombric a thick Ah below pH 5.5; Eutric and Dystric lack a thick Ah.

entries.text: Almost 790,000 square kilometers of Canada, 8.6% of the country, is covered by soils that fit no other order. entries.title: Canadian Organic soils: the peatland order
entries.article: Canadian system of soil classification#Organic Order

definition.text: The Canadian order of soils made mostly of organic matter, over 30% by weight in the upper half metre, without permafrost near the surface.

facts.text: They are the main soils of peatlands such as swamps, bogs and fens, mostly built from plants of waterlogged ground, though some come from lake deposits or forest litter on rainy, rocky slopes.
Organic soils cover almost 374,000 km2 (4.1%) of Canada, with large areas in Manitoba, Ontario and northern Alberta.

Four great groups follow decomposition: little-decomposed soils with over 40% fibre, mostly from Sphagnum, as Fibrisols; others with 10–40% or up to 10% fibre; and thick forest-litter soils over rock.
Wetland soils with an O horizon at least 40 cm thick are Organic; with less than 40 cm or none they are Gleysolic.

entries.title: Chernozemic soils of Canada's southern grasslands
entries.article: Canadian system of soil classification#Chernozemic Order

definition.text: The Canadian order of grassland soils whose A horizon is darkened by organic matter, mostly from decaying grass roots.

facts.text: The A horizon is neutral to slightly acid and rich in bases such as calcium; the C horizon usually holds lime and may hold gypsum.
With mean annual soil temperatures above 0 °C, they cover more than 4% of Canada and dominate the grassy southern Interior Plains.
Four great groups follow surface colour and dryness: Brown soils in the driest areas, Dark Brown, thick-topped Black soils under tall grass, and transitional Dark Gray soils.

entries.title: Cryosolic soils, frozen beneath 40% of Canada
entries.article: Canadian system of soil classification#Cryosolic Order

definition.text: The Canadian order of soils with permafrost within 1 metre of the surface, or 2 metres if strongly churned by frost.

facts.text: Because permafrost blocks roots and water, the seasonally thawed active layer above it can turn saturated and semifluid in spring.
Disturbing the boreal forest or tundra cover melts ground ice, which can make soil slump and disrupt roads, pipelines and buildings.
Cryosolic soils cover about 3,672,000 km2 (about 40%) of Canada and dominate much of Yukon, the Northwest Territories and Nunavut.
Defined in 1973 after Mackenzie Valley surveys, the order has three great groups: Turbic Cryosols, mixed by cryoturbation; Static Cryosols, on sandy or gravelly material; and peaty Organic Cryosols.

entries.title: Gleysolic soils: gray ground where water lingers
entries.article: Canadian system of soil classification#Gleysolic Order

definition.text: The Canadian order of soils that are periodically or permanently saturated with water and depleted of oxygen.

facts.text: When flooding comes with soil warmer than about 5 °C, microbes use up the oxygen within days and nitrate and ferric oxide are reduced.
Losing ferric oxide turns the soil grey; when it dries, reoxidized iron forms yellow-brown mottles, so poor drainage and drab grey colour identify these soils.
Gleysolic soils cover about 117,000 km2 (1.3%) of Canada, in depressions and level areas of subhumid and humid climates.
Its three great groups are Humic Gleysols, with a dark organic A horizon, Gleysols without one, and Luvic Gleysols, with a clay-enriched B horizon.

Three great groups are defined: the Humic group, with a dark organic A horizon; a plain group, without one; and the Luvic group, with a clay-enriched B horizon.

entries.title: Luvisolic soils, where clay moves down under forest
entries.article: Canadian system of soil classification#Luvisolic Order

definition.text: The Canadian order of soils with a leached Ae horizon above a Bt horizon in which the washed-down clay has been deposited.

facts.text: They typically form under forest in subhumid to humid climates where the parent material holds appreciable clay; in saline or calcareous material, salts and carbonates leach before the clay moves.
Luvisolic soils cover about 809,000 km2 (8.8%) of Canada, largely in the central to northern Interior Plains.
Two great groups split by soil temperature: Gray Brown Luvisols, at 8 °C or more, in the Great Lakes–St Lawrence Lowlands, and Gray Luvisols of the boreal Interior Plains.

entries.text: Under forest, clay can leave one layer of a soil and settle in the next. The Luvisolic order holds Canadian soils with a leached Ae horizon above a Bt horizon, where the washed-down clay has been deposited. They typically form under forest, in subhumid to humid climates where the parent material holds appreciable clay. In saline or calcareous material, salts and carbonates leach out before the clay moves. Luvisolic soils cover about 809,000 square kilometers, 8.8% of Canada, largely in the central to northern Interior Plains. Two great groups split by soil temperature. The Gray Brown group, at 8 °C or more, lies in the Great Lakes–St Lawrence Lowlands; the Gray group belongs to the boreal Interior Plains.

entries.title: Podzolic soils under Canada's conifers
entries.article: Canadian system of soil classification#Podzolic Order

definition.text: The Canadian order of acid soils whose B horizon accumulates amorphous humified organic matter bound to aluminium and iron.

facts.text: They form mostly in sandy materials under forest or shrubs in cold, humid climates.
Percolating water leaches bases; organic acids from litter free iron and aluminium, and the complexes become insoluble and settle in the B horizon once metals reach a critical proportion.
Podzolic soils occupy 14.3% of Canada, in the Appalachian Uplands and Canadian Shield and in British Columbia, usually under coniferous forest.
Great groups follow the B horizon: Humic Podzols are low in iron, Ferro-Humic Podzols hold at least 5% organic carbon, and Humo-Ferric Podzols, the commonest, less than 5%.

entries.text: Organic acids from forest litter can free iron and aluminum and carry them down through a soil. The Humic group is low in iron, the Ferro-Humic group holds at least 5% organic carbon, and the Humo-Ferric group, the commonest, holds less than 5%.

entries.title: Regosolic soils, too young for layers
entries.article: Canadian system of soil classification#Regosolic Order

definition.text: The Canadian order of weakly developed soils whose properties are essentially those of their parent material.

facts.text: They support plants but have not been stable long enough to develop well-differentiated horizons.
The name joins Greek rhēgos, 'blanket', with Latin solum, 'soil'; Regosolic soils cover about 0.8% of Canada.
Two great groups are defined: Regosols, made essentially of C horizons, and Humic Regosols, with an Ah horizon at least 10 cm thick.

entries.title: Solonetzic soils, rock-hard when dry, sticky when wet
entries.article: Canadian system of soil classification#Solonetzic Order

definition.text: The Canadian order of soils whose B horizon is very hard when dry and swells into a sticky, compact mass when wet, because of sodium.

facts.text: They usually develop in saline parent materials in semiarid and subhumid regions.
Sodium ions make the clay disperse and swell on wetting, closing large pores and stopping water flow.
Solonetzic soils cover almost 73,000 km2 (0.7%) of Canada, mostly in southern Alberta.
As leaching moves salts and sodium downward, soils develop from saline parent material to Solonetz, Solodized Solonetz and Solod; resalinization can reverse this.

entries.text: Some Canadian subsoils are very hard when dry and swell into a sticky, compact mass when wet. Sodium is the reason. Its ions make the clay disperse and swell on wetting, closing large pores and stopping water flow. Soils with such a B horizon form the Solonetzic order, which usually develops in saline parent materials of semiarid and subhumid regions. It covers almost 73,000 square kilometers, 0.7% of Canada, mostly in southern Alberta. As leaching moves salts and sodium downward, the soil develops from saline parent material through two sodium-rich stages to a final, leached stage called Solod. Resalinization can reverse the sequence.

entries.title: Vertisolic soils, churned by their own clay
entries.article: Canadian system of soil classification#Vertisolic Order

definition.text: The Canadian order of clay-rich soils that shrink and swell markedly as they dry and wet.

facts.text: Shrinking and swelling cut shiny slickensides in the subsoil, mix former surface material downward and prevent or scramble subsurface horizons.
They form mainly in clayey materials of the semiarid to subhumid Interior Plains and cover less than 1% of Canada.
Recognized in the 1990s after studies of Great Plains pedons, the order has two great groups, Vertisol and Humic Vertisol, told apart by the darkness of the A horizon.

entries.text: Some clay soils turn themselves over. In the Vertisolic order, clay-rich soils shrink and swell markedly as they dry and wet. The movement cuts shiny slickensides in the subsoil, mixes former surface material downward, and prevents or scrambles subsurface horizons. These soils form mainly in clayey materials of the semiarid to subhumid Interior Plains and cover less than 1% of Canada. The order was recognized in the 1990s, after studies of Great Plains pedons. Its two great groups are told apart by the darkness of the A horizon, the darker one being humic.

entries.title: Anthroposols, soils that people built or remade

definition.text: A soil profoundly modified or constructed by people, with one or more natural horizons altered, removed or replaced.

facts.text: Anthroposols occur on industrial, commercial, urban and resource-extraction sites and along transport, fuel and power corridors.
Human-made soils were long left out of classification systems because criteria built for natural soils often do not apply to them.
A proposed Canadian order requires a disturbed D horizon at least 10 cm thick or removed natural horizons, with great groups set by artefacts or organic carbon; ordinary tillage does not qualify.
The WRB splits such soils into Anthrosols, long cultivated, and Technosols, holding industrial products and artefacts; Australia's system also has an Anthroposol order.

entries.title: Kurosols: a light topsoil over acid clay

definition.text: One of the fifteen soil orders of the Australian Soil Classification: soils with a sharp texture contrast between a lighter surface and a strongly acidic, clay-rich subsoil.

facts.text: What sets kurosols apart from other texture-contrast orders is the upper B horizon: strongly acidic in kurosols, sodic in sodosols, and neither in chromosols.
The strongly acidic subsoil generally has a pH below 5.5 measured in water.
They are widespread in higher-rainfall, strongly leached and weathered landscapes of eastern and southern Australia.
The dense clay subsoil and acidity can restrict roots and water and cause aluminium and manganese toxicity; lime corrects surface acidity, but deep acidity is hard to fix.

entries.title: France's Référentiel pédologique

definition.text: The French soil reference system, a natural classification based on presumed soil genesis.

facts.text: Like the WRB, it has two hierarchical levels; versions appeared in 1992, 1995 and 2008.
Its reference soil types, relevant to European soils, carry names such as Brunisol, Calcarisol, Colluviosol, Fluviosol, Podzosol and Reductisol, refined by terms such as humic or typic.

entries.title: Working through the Keys to Soil Taxonomy

facts.text: The first order whose criteria the soil meets is chosen, and the same process runs through suborder, great group and subgroup; family and series use other criteria in the Keys.

Suborders rest on soil moisture regimes and diagnostic features, great groups on how strongly diagnostic horizons are expressed, and subgroups on properties transitional to other orders, suborders and great groups.
The family name combines terms such as particle size class, mineralogy of the control section, soil temperature regime, CEC and depth.

entries.title: Greyzem, the grey earth of the FAO system

definition.text: A soil group of the FAO soil classification, named from English 'grey' and Russian zemlja, 'earth'.

facts.text: The name refers to uncoated silt and quartz grains in its organic-rich layers; it forms in decalcified loose deposits such as wind-blown, river and lake sediments and glacial till.
With Chernozems, Kastanozems and Phaeozems it forms a set of steppe and prairie soils with a mollic horizon, where organic matter accumulates faster than leaching removes it.
One of the original 26 FAO groups, it remained among the 28 of the 1988 revision, with two units: gleyic and haplic greyzems.
It correlates most closely with Dark Grey Chernozems in Canada and with Albolls and Boralfic Boroll subgroups in USDA soil taxonomy.

entries.title: Describing a soil profile, step by step

facts.text: The steps are: observe the landscape setting, examine morphology to separate horizons, describe each horizon in detail, assign horizon designations, then classify the soil by its morphology and horizonation.

In the Harney silt loam example the Ap horizon is 0 to 9 in, dark grayish brown (Munsell 10YR 4/2), silt loam, with moderate medium granular structure, very friable, many fine roots and slightly acid.
Formative elements give each level a connotation, and the bolded syllable of each order name appears in the names of its suborders and lower levels.
In the Clarion-Nicollet-Webster-Glencoe catena, the wetter the drainage class the more the 'aqu' element appears, because Soil Taxonomy prioritizes management concerns such as a shallow water table.

definition.text: A soil profile description records each horizon's depth, color, texture, structure, consistence, roots, pH and boundary so that one soil can be told from another.

entries.title: Canadian soil classification, level by level

facts.text: Orders reflect the overall soil environment and dominant soil-forming process; great groups reflect differences in the strength of those processes or a major added process.

Subgroups differ by closeness to the central (Orthic) concept, transition toward another order and special features; families group series of one subgroup with similar management and engineering response but are seldom used in Canada.

facts.text: A soil must be saturated for at least a few days a year to count as aquic.
Aquerts are Vertisols with aquic conditions for some time in most years and redoximorphic features; high clay slows permeability, favouring such conditions.
Many Histosols show aquic conditions or artificial drainage.

entries.title: The aridic regime, where soil stays dry

definition.text: The soil moisture regime of arid and semi-arid climates, in which soil is dry for at least half the growing season and moist for less than 90 consecutive days.

facts.text: Its control section, at 50 cm depth, is judged against soil temperatures above 5 °C and 8 °C in counting dry and moist days.
Aridisols must have an aridic moisture regime.
It is also called torric: Torripsamments are Psamments with an aridic or torric regime.
The ustic regime is wetter than the aridic and drier than the udic.

entries.title: ISO 14688, the engineer's international soil yardstick

definition.text: The international standard that sets basic principles for identifying and classifying soils for engineering purposes.

facts.text: ISO 14688-1 covers natural soils in situ, similar man-made materials in situ and soils redeposited by people.
It grades clay as particles smaller than 2 μm, and sand as fine, medium and coarse with limits at 0.063, 0.2, 0.63 and 2.0 mm.
Gravel is graded fine, medium and coarse with limits at 2, 6.3, 20 and 63 mm.
It closely resembles the Unified Soil Classification System but codes soils differently and adds an intermediate-plasticity class for silts and clays.

entries.title: Zonal soils, shaped by regional climate

definition.text: In the 1938 U.S. system, the order of soils whose character reflects the regional climate and vegetation.

facts.text: Pedocals and pedalfers were both subdivisions of the zonal order.

Fertile, carbon-rich dark earths of North America and Eurasia were long explained as zonal soils of dry continental climates under steppe or prairie, before past human activity was recognized as a driver.

entries.text: In the 1938 U.S. system, a zonal soil was one whose character reflects the regional climate and vegetation. Both pedocals and pedalfers were subdivisions of this order. The idea long shaped how soils were explained. Fertile, carbon-rich dark soils of North America and Eurasia were long read as zonal soils of dry continental climates under steppe or prairie. Only later was past human activity recognized as a driver of them.

entries.title: Azonal soils, never given time to mature

definition.text: Immature soils that never get time to develop because their material keeps sliding downslope or is buried by fresh deposits.

facts.text: On mountain slopes such as the Himalayas, fine weathered material constantly slides downhill, leaving no time for soil to form.
On river flood plains new alluvium arrives every year, so the soils stay immature even though the farmland is fertile.
Gleysols are called azonal soils that occur in nearly all climates, and Canada's system calls Anthroposols azonal soils highly modified or built by people.

entries.text: On Himalayan slopes, fine weathered material slides downhill so constantly that soil has no time to form. Such places hold azonal soils: immature soils that never develop because their material keeps sliding downslope or is buried by fresh deposits. River flood plains are the other classic case. New alluvium arrives every year, so the soils stay immature even though the farmland is fertile. The label is also given to the {{ref:soil-class-127}} group, found in nearly all climates. Canada's system calls Anthroposols azonal soils, highly modified or built by people.

entries.title: Intrazonal soils, ruled by local conditions

definition.text: Soils whose profiles reflect a dominant local factor of relief or parent material more than the zonal effects of climate and vegetation.

facts.text: Calcimorphic soils develop from limestone and include thin rendzinas, with limited available water, and deep red terra rossa soils of wetter climates.
Hydromorphic soils form in wetlands: gley soils, whose waterlogged, airless pores reduce iron and turn them grey-blue with red flecks, and peat soils, where plant remains never fully break down.
Halomorphic soils form through salinization.

entries.text: Limestone or waterlogged ground can outweigh the regional climate in shaping a soil. Intrazonal soils are those whose profiles reflect a dominant local factor of relief or parent material more than the zonal effects of climate and vegetation. Calcimorphic soils develop from limestone. They include the thin {{ref:soil-class-050}}, with limited available water, and the deep red {{ref:soil-class-051}} of wetter climates. Hydromorphic soils form in waterlogged ground. In gley soils, waterlogged, airless pores reduce iron and turn the soil grey-blue with red flecks. In soils of {{ref:soil-class-070}}, plant remains never fully break down. Halomorphic soils form through salinization.
entries.text_plain: Limestone or waterlogged ground can outweigh the regional climate in shaping a soil. Intrazonal soils are those whose profiles reflect a dominant local factor of relief or parent material more than the zonal effects of climate and vegetation. Calcimorphic soils develop from limestone. They include the thin Rendzina, the thin dark soil on limestone, with limited available water, and the deep red Terra rossa, the red soil of Mediterranean karst of wetter climates. Hydromorphic soils form in waterlogged ground. In gley soils, waterlogged, airless pores reduce iron and turn the soil grey-blue with red flecks. In soils of Peat, the half-rotted store of the world's soil carbon, plant remains never fully break down. Halomorphic soils form through salinization.

entries.title: Twelve names ending in -sol: the USDA soil orders

definition.text: The twelve top-level classes of USDA soil taxonomy, whose criteria reflect major differences in how soils formed.

facts.text: Order names end in -sol: Alfisols, Andisols, Aridisols, Entisols, Gelisols, Histosols, Inceptisols, Mollisols, Oxisols, Spodosols, Ultisols and Vertisols.
Each order reflects distinct soil-forming processes and characteristics such as climate, vegetation and mineral composition.
In order of increasing development they run Entisols, Inceptisols, Aridisols, Mollisols, Alfisols, Spodosols, Ultisols and Oxisols; Histosols and Vertisols can appear at any stage.
Many orders hinge on diagnostic horizons: Alfisols and Ultisols need an argillic or kandic horizon, Mollisols a mollic epipedon, Oxisols an oxic horizon and Spodosols a spodic horizon.
By share of global ice-free land, Entisols lead with 16.3%, then Aridisols (12.7%), Inceptisols (9.9%) and Alfisols (9.6%); Andisols are smallest at 0.7%.
In the United States, Mollisols cover the most ice-free land (22.4%), followed by Alfisols (14.5%), while Oxisols cover less than 0.01%.
Mountain soils, a mixture of orders or soil-free 'Rugged Mountains', make up the remaining 11.6% of ice-free land.
The 1975 taxonomy recognized 10 orders; the 1999 second edition recognized 12.

entries.title: Mollisols, the deep dark soils of the grasslands

definition.text: A USDA soil order of soils with a deep, dark surface horizon rich in organic matter and nutrients, called the mollic epipedon.

facts.text: The mollic epipedon, typically 60 to 80 cm deep, builds up from long-term additions of organic matter from roots and usually has a soft, granular structure.
Mollisols must have base saturation above 50% and are common in grasslands.
They form in savannas and mountain valleys, as in Central Asia and the North American Great Plains, landscapes long shaped by fire and by ants and earthworms churning the soil.
As the world's most agriculturally productive order they are among the most economically important; a 2003 estimate found only 14 to 26 percent of grasslands still relatively natural.
They cover about 7% of global ice-free land but 22.4% of the United States, more than any other order there.
In the WRB, Mollisols split into Chernozems, Kastanozems and Phaeozems; shallow ones may be Leptosols, many Aquolls are Gleysols and natric ones Solonetz.
Soils with a mollic epipedon key out elsewhere when other traits dominate: as Vertisols where shrink–swell clays rule, as Andisols where andic properties take precedence.
Their development is tied to the cooling and drying of global climate in the Oligocene, Miocene and Pliocene; fossils are confidently known from the Eocene.

entries.text: No soil order grows more food than this one. Mollisols are the world's most agriculturally productive order, and among the most economically important. Their mark is a deep, dark surface horizon rich in organic matter and nutrients, called the mollic epipedon. It is typically 60 to 80 cm deep and usually has a soft, granular structure. It builds up slowly, from long-term additions of organic matter by roots. Mollisols must also have base saturation above 50%. They are common in grasslands, and they form in savannas and mountain valleys, as in Central Asia and the North American Great Plains. Fire long shaped those landscapes, while ants and earthworms churned the soil. The order covers about 7% of the world's ice-free land but 22.4% of the United States, more than any other order there. Little of its native grassland survives: a 2003 estimate found only 14 to 26 percent still relatively natural. A dark topsoil alone does not settle the name. Where shrink–swell clays rule, the soil keys out as a {{ref:soil-class-106}}. Where volcanic-ash traits take precedence, it becomes an {{ref:soil-class-092}}. In the WRB, Mollisols split into three groups, among them {{ref:soil-class-123}}. Their rise is tied to the cooling and drying of global climate in the Oligocene, Miocene and Pliocene. Fossil Mollisols are confidently known from the Eocene.

entries.title: Vertisols, the clay soils that plow themselves

definition.text: A soil rich in expansive clays that crack deeply when dry and swell when wet; an order in USDA soil taxonomy and a WRB Reference Soil Group.

facts.text: They need more than 30% clay to 50 cm and usually have a mollic epipedon; they form in clay-rich material, often from basic rocks such as basalt, in seasonally humid or erratic climates.
Alternate shrinking and swelling makes the soil plough itself (argillipedoturbation), giving some a very deep A horizon and no B horizon and heaving subsoil up as gilgai.
Colours range from grey or red to deep black: 'black earths' in Australia, 'black gumbo' in East Texas, 'black cotton' soils in East Africa.
Found between 50°N and 45°S, they dominate eastern Australia, India's Deccan Plateau, parts of Sudan, Ethiopia and Kenya and the lower Paraná, covering 2.4% of global ice-free land.
Natural vegetation is grassland, savanna or grassy woodland, because the heavy, unstable soil makes it hard for trees to grow.
Very hard when dry and sticky when wet, they are hard to farm without irrigation, but near-impermeability when saturated suits rice; most are grazed by cattle or sheep.
Shrink–swell damages buildings and roads but lets the soil recover quickly from compaction; Australians prize them as among the few soils not acutely short of phosphorus.
The WRB's diagnostic vertic horizon has at least 30% clay, shrink–swell cracks and wedge-shaped aggregates or slickensides; Australia calls these soils Vertosols.

entries.title: Alfisols, fertile soils with a clay-rich subsoil

definition.text: A USDA soil order of moderately leached soils with a clay-enriched subsoil and relatively high native fertility.

facts.text: They form in semi-arid to humid areas, typically under hardwood forest, and must have an argillic, natric or kandic horizon.
The name comes from 'alf', for aluminium (Al) and iron (Fe), a root inherited from the old pedalfer group.
By definition they have at least 35% base saturation, so calcium, magnesium and potassium are relatively abundant; the more leached Ultisols fall below 35%.

Productive and abundant, they are among the most important orders for food and fibre, though Australian and African Alfisols lack nitrogen and phosphorus and monsoonal ones acidify under heavy cultivation.
They cover about one-tenth of the ice-free land (9.6% globally, 14.5% of the U.S.) and dominate areas such as the Ohio River basin, the Baltic region and Sudan.
In eastern North America, Alfisols occur in glaciated areas, while Ultisols lie south of the limit of maximum glaciation.
Suborders follow wetness and climate: oxygen-depleted Aqualfs, cold Cryalfs, humid Udalfs, semiarid Ustalfs and Mediterranean Xeralfs.
In the WRB most Alfisols are Luvisols or Lixisols, some Retisols or Nitisols; Aqualfs are mainly Stagnosols or Planosols, and natric Alfisols Solonetz.

entries.title: Andisols, the young, fertile soils of volcanic ash

definition.text: A USDA soil order of soils formed in volcanic ash, rich in glass and in amorphous colloids such as allophane, imogolite and ferrihydrite.

facts.text: They must have andic properties: abundant poorly crystalline iron and aluminium minerals, high phosphorus, low bulk density and high organic matter.
Being generally young, they are usually very fertile, except where phosphorus is easily fixed, as sometimes happens in the tropics.

They support intensive use: wet rice on Java feeds some of the world's densest populations, others grow fruit, maize, tea, coffee or tobacco, and Pacific Northwest Andisols carry very productive forests.
They cover about 1% of global ice-free land, mostly around the Pacific Ring of Fire, from Chile and Mexico to Japan, Java and New Zealand's North Island.
Suborders are wet Aquands, very cold Gelands, very dry Torrands, semiarid Ustands, dry-summer Xerands and young, glassy, coarse Vitrands.
In the WRB they are known as Andosols, though some WRB Histosols are Andisols and some Andosols are Inceptisols.
Fossil Andisols occur far from present-day volcanoes, some dated to the Mesoproterozoic, 1.5 billion years ago.

entries.title: Histosols, soils built from organic matter

definition.text: A soil, in both the WRB and USDA soil taxonomy, made primarily of organic materials.

facts.text: It has 40 cm or more of organic soil material starting within 40 cm of the surface; organic material means at least 12% organic carbon in Soil Taxonomy or 20% in the WRB.
Its materials are muck (sapric), mucky peat (hemic) or peat (fibric), and Soil Taxonomy's suborders Saprists, Hemists and Fibrists follow them, alongside drier Folists and submerged Wassists.
Histosols form wherever organic matter accumulates faster than it is destroyed, usually because poor drainage prevents aerobic decay; with enough time, coal forms.
With Gelisols they store large quantities of organic carbon, which makes them ecologically very important.
They have very low bulk density, and many are acidic and short of major nutrients, especially rain-fed raised bogs cut off from groundwater.
Hard to cultivate, drained Histosols on young glacial land can make good dairy or beef pasture, but dried organic matter can blow away as powder and heavy structures subside.
Most lie in Canada, Scandinavia, the West Siberian Plain, Sumatra, Borneo and New Guinea; they cover 1.2% of global ice-free land.
Known as peat or muck in many countries and as Organosols in Australia, they appear as fossils with the first extensive land vegetation in the Devonian.

Most lie in Canada, Scandinavia, the West Siberian Plain, Sumatra, Borneo and New Guinea, and they cover 1.2% of the world's ice-free land. Australia calls them Organosols. As fossils they appear with the first extensive land vegetation, in the Devonian.

entries.title: Aridisols, the slow-forming soils of the deserts

definition.text: A USDA soil order of dry soils of arid and semi-arid climates, also called desert soils.

facts.text: Water deficiency is the defining trait: they have an aridic moisture regime, with fewer than 90 consecutive moist days in the growing season, and are not leached.
They also need enough age to show subsoil weathering, including some diagnostic subsurface horizon; an ochric epipedon is common.
Named from Latin aridus, 'dry', they dominate deserts and xeric shrublands, about one-third of Earth's land surface, and cover 12.7% of global ice-free land.
Sparse vegetation leaves them very low in organic matter, and soil formation is slow.
Limited leaching leaves subsurface horizons of deposited clay, sodium, calcium carbonate, gypsum or salts, sometimes cemented, as in caliche or duripans.
Many have well-developed Bt horizons from clay moved in past wetter periods, and salt build-up at the surface can cause salinization.
In the WRB most Aridisols are Calcisols, Gypsisols, Durisols or Solonchaks.

entries.title: Ultisols, the red clay soils at the end of weathering

definition.text: A USDA soil order of strongly weathered, acid mineral soils, commonly known as red clay soils.

facts.text: They hold no calcareous material, under 10% weatherable minerals in the top layer and under 35% base saturation throughout, and must have an argillic or kandic horizon.
The name comes from 'ultimate': they were seen as the end product of continuous weathering in a humid climate without renewal by glaciation.
Iron oxide colours them from purplish-red to pale yellowish-orange; they are typically quite acidic, often below pH 5, and kaolinite is often the main clay.
Short of calcium and potassium, they need lime and fertilizer for settled farming and are more easily exhausted than Alfisols or Mollisols; organic-rich Humults are relatively fertile.
Kaolinite gives good bearing capacity and no shrink–swell, so well-drained Ultisols such as the Cecil series suit urban development.
They dominate the Southern United States, southeastern China and Southeast Asia, and cover 8.5% of global ice-free land.
Taking hundreds of thousands of years to form, they stop sharply at the limit of maximum Pleistocene glaciation in North America.
In the WRB most are Acrisols or Alisols, some Retisols or Nitisols; Acrisols match the Humult, Udult and Ustult suborders.

entries.title: Oxisols, the most weathered soils on Earth

definition.text: A USDA soil order of very highly weathered soils rich in iron and aluminium oxides, best known from tropical rainforest within 25 degrees of the Equator.

facts.text: They show the most profile development of any order and must have an oxic horizon within 150 cm; at all depths they hold no more than 10% weatherable minerals and have low cation exchange capacity.
Iron(III) and aluminium oxides and hydroxides make them always red or yellowish, alongside quartz and kaolin; the name comes from 'oxide'.
Weathering, humification and mixing by animals form them; rain acidified by forest litter leaches the minerals, so plants depend on nutrients from decaying litter.
Low CEC and strong phosphorus fixation on iron and aluminium oxides make permanent cropping hard, but regions able to afford lime and fertilizer farm them intensively, as with Brazilian soybeans.
Today they occur almost only in tropical South America and Africa, mostly on stable cratons; they cover 7.6% of global ice-free land but under 0.01% of the U.S.
Suborders are wet Aquox, continuously humid Perox, humid Udox, semiarid Ustox and arid Torrox, which are always paleosols from wetter times, mainly in Southern Africa.
In the WRB they are mainly Ferralsols, some Plinthosols or Nitisols, and some were once classed as laterite soils.
Fossil Oxisols date from the first free oxygen in the atmosphere, about 2,200 million years ago, and in warm periods such as the Mesozoic they reached North America and Europe.

entries.title: Entisols, soils that have barely begun

definition.text: A USDA soil order of soils with no profile development beyond an A horizon and no diagnostic horizons, little changed from their parent material.

facts.text: They are the most common order, covering about 16% of global ice-free land (16.3% in the order table) and 12.2% of the U.S.
Development is held back by unweatherable parent material, erosion, repeated deposition by floods, wind or slope processes, shallow bedrock, or toxic materials such as serpentine or mine spoil.
They are common on river and beach sediments and volcanic ash, and some are just an A horizon on bedrock.
Suborders are Aquents, saturated soils of riverbanks and mudflats; Fluvents, alluvium renewed by floods; shallow Orthents; sandy Psamments; and Wassents, under water over 21 hours a day.
So varied are they that their suborders match different WRB groups: Psamments Arenosols, Fluvents Fluvisols, many Orthents Regosols or Leptosols, Wassents Gleysols.
In Australia most Entisols are called Rudosols or Tenosols.
Most fossil soils from before land plants spread in the Silurian are Entisols, but unlike other orders they reveal little about past climate.

conflicts.text: The order list in USDA soil taxonomy says Entisols are 18% of soils worldwide.
conflicts.note: Same measure (share of ice-free land, S:0da82a5078bb); the order table gives 16.3% (S:4fe0f587ba75) and the Entisol page about 16% (S:022a0f35abfe).

entries.text: The most common soil order on Earth is the one that has done the least. Entisols show no profile development beyond an A horizon and have no diagnostic horizons, so they are little changed from their parent material. entries.title: Inceptisols, young soils just starting a subsoil

definition.text: A USDA soil order of young soils with little to moderate development and weathering, more developed than Entisols.

facts.text: A B horizon has begun to form, but there is no diagnostic subsurface horizon of another order; soils that fit no other order may default to Inceptisols.
Profiles vary widely but usually have an ochric or umbric epipedon over a cambic horizon; some have histic or plaggen epipedons, calcic horizons, duripans or fragipans.
They occur everywhere except extremes such as deserts and permafrost: on mountains, sand dunes, fresh coastal and river deposits and late Pleistocene glacial drift.
They develop on eroded landscapes that, if stable, would have supported more developed Alfisols.
Suborders follow temperature, moisture, saturation and epipedon: wet Aquepts, human-made Anthrepts, cold Gelepts and Cryepts, humid Udepts, semiarid Ustepts and dry-summer Xerepts.
Many crops grow on them, but Ustepts and Xerepts may need irrigation and Aquepts drainage, except those with a sulfuric horizon, where draining can produce sulfuric acid.
They cover 9.9% of global and 9.1% of U.S. ice-free land.

entries.title: Gelisols, soils over permanently frozen ground

definition.text: A USDA soil order of very cold climates, defined by permafrost within two metres of the surface.

facts.text: The order table requires permafrost within 100 cm, or cryoturbation within 100 cm plus permafrost within 200 cm.
The name comes from Latin gelare, 'to freeze', after the cryoturbation caused by alternate freezing and thawing.
Organic matter builds up on top, so most are black or dark brown over a shallow mineral layer; calcium and potassium leach easily above the permafrost, limiting fertility.
Permafrost greatly restricts engineering use, as large structures subside when the frozen ground thaws.
They lie chiefly in Siberia, Alaska and Canada, with smaller areas in the Andes, Tibet, northern Scandinavia and ice-free Greenland and Antarctica, covering 8.6% of global ice-free land.
Slow decomposition makes them an important sink for carbon dioxide.
Gelisols key out before Histosols in soil taxonomy, so organic permafrost soils are Histels there but Cryic Histosols in the WRB, where most Gelisols are Cryosols.
Fossil Gelisols are known from Precambrian ice ages 900 million years ago.

conflicts.text: The order list in USDA soil taxonomy defines Gelisols by permafrost within two metres, or gelic materials and permafrost within one metre.
conflicts.note: The order table (S:1aed59a2ba65) puts the depths the other way round: permafrost within 100 cm, or cryoturbation within 100 cm plus permafrost within 200 cm; the Gelisol page (S:1c6d2a9e2aed) gives permafrost within two metres.

entries.title: Psamments, sandy soils that hold almost nothing

definition.text: A USDA suborder of Entisols made of unconsolidated sand, found in shifting dunes or in very coarse parent material weathered for millions of years.

facts.text: A Psamment has no distinct horizons and must be loamy sand or coarser all the way through.
Psamments cover 3.4% of the global land mass, abundant in the deserts of Africa and Australia, on old landforms of eastern South America and in Florida and Nebraska's Sand Hills.
Their poorly graded, constantly mixed sand gives them very low water-holding capacity.

Being highly siliceous, they are extremely low in nutrients, especially phosphorus, and highly acidic except in very arid climates; young glacial Psamments of northern Europe are somewhat more fertile.
Their vegetation is often remarkably well adapted, as in the species-rich Fynbos of South Africa's Cape and the Kwongan of Western Australia.
Few are farmed: fertilizing is costly, yields stay below other soils of the region, and the sand erodes very easily.
USDA soil taxonomy divides them by temperature and moisture regime into Cryopsamments, Torripsamments, Ustipsamments and Xeropsamments, plus Quartzipsamments with over 90 percent resistant minerals.
In the WRB most Psamments are Arenosols, but those of river, lake or marine origin are Fluvisols.

verification.source: USDA NRCS Keys to Soil Taxonomy
verification.evidence: Other Psamments that have, in the 0.02 to 2.0 mm fraction within the particle-size control section, a total of more than 90 percent (by weighted average) resistant minerals.

Quartzipsamments, with over 90 percent resistant minerals, form a fifth group. In the WRB most are Arenosols, but those of river, lake or marine origin belong with Fluvisols, the young layered soils of floodplains.

entries.title: Paleopedology, reading the soils of lost worlds

definition.text: The study of soils of past geological eras, from the recent Quaternary back to the earliest periods of Earth's history.

facts.text: It can be seen as a branch of soil science or of paleontology, since its methods combine the two.
It began with observations in Scotland around 1795 of cliff soils that seemed to be remains of a former land surface.
Interest grew once soils were tied to climate: Hilgard related them in the United States in 1892, and by the 1920s Glinka had found Russian soils that were relics of warmer climates.
Fossil soils lie under sediment or volcanic ash, in steep cliffs beneath younger soils, or where younger soil has eroded away, as in the Badlands of South Dakota.
Buried soils lose their vegetation and organic matter, but the shape and size of root traces still reveal the kind of vegetation they carried.
Chemical analysis centres on lime content, but X-ray diffraction, developed since the 1960s, now lets paleosols be placed in the 12 soil orders.
Many Precambrian soils fit no modern order and are grouped as 'green clays', coloured by unoxidized minerals that formed before free oxygen.
It sheds light on ancient ecosystems and on how life moved onto land in the Paleozoic, and it feeds the emerging field of astropedology.

entries.title: Orthents, skeletal soils of steep slopes

definition.text: A USDA suborder of Entisols that lack horizon development because of steep slopes or parent materials with no lasting weatherable minerals.

facts.text: Typically exceedingly shallow, they are also called skeletal soils, or lithosols in the FAO classification; any former soil has been removed or truncated.
Most lie on very steep mountain slopes, where erosion strips material too fast for deep soil to form; in Australia and parts of Africa they occur on flat land whose rock has no weatherable minerals.
Shallow, steep and erosion-prone, they are unfit for arable farming and carry only low stocking rates, but are important wildlife habitat.
Many belong to WRB Regosols or Leptosols, and they can mark extremely ancient landscapes with minimal soil formation, as in Australia today.

entries.title: What fossil soils reveal about the history of land

definition.text: The fossil record of soils, made up chiefly of paleosols buried by flood sediments or volcanic deposits, or preserved at geological unconformities.

facts.text: After burial, organic matter decays, iron oxidizes from Fe2+ to Fe3+ and hydrous ferric oxides dry out, which makes fossil soils harder to recognize.
Telltale signs are downward-branching root traces, gradual alteration below a sharp former land surface, and crack patterns like peds and cutans.
Most fossil soils fit the twelve USDA orders, usually identified by X-ray diffraction; only some very old soils with a grey-green horizon formed without oxygen do not.
With little or no ozone layer, Precambrian soils eroded fast, and most are undeveloped Entisols or Inceptisols; Vertisols and Aridisols run continuously from the Paleoproterozoic.
Outside ice ages Oxisols have dominated the record, because new soil formation needs the glaciation and mountain building that come with cooler times.
Land plants brought new orders: Histosols in the Devonian, Alfisols and Ultisols in the late Devonian and early Carboniferous, while Mollisols spread only from the Miocene as grasslands evolved.
Gelisol fossils are confined to times of extensive continental glaciation, the earliest 900 million years ago in the Neoproterozoic.
Unlike fossil plants and animals, very few fossil soils are of extinct types, which makes them useful for reading past ecosystems.

entries.title: Sapric material, organic matter rotted past recognition

definition.text: Organic soil material, as in a Histosol, so thoroughly decomposed that plant parts and even faecal matter can no longer be identified.

facts.text: The WRB defines sapric material as having less than one-sixth of its volume as recognizable plant tissue within 100 cm; USDA soil taxonomy uses a fibre content below one-sixth.
Muck is sapric soil that is naturally waterlogged or artificially drained; the USDA NRCS definition requires saturation for more than 30 cumulative days in normal years.
Canada places muck soils in its Organic order, with at least 30% organic matter and a depth of at least 40 cm.
Sapric soils are deep, dark and friable, often underlain by marl or marly clay.

entries.title: Seven Mollisol suborders, sorted by water and warmth

definition.text: The seven suborders of Mollisols, set mainly by soil moisture and temperature regimes.

facts.text: Albolls and Aquolls are wet soils with an aquic moisture regime; Albolls also have an eluvial horizon.
Cryolls have a frigid or cryic temperature regime, and Gelolls a mean annual soil temperature below 0 °C.
Udolls, Ustolls and Xerolls carry the udic, ustic and xeric moisture regimes of humid, subhumid and Mediterranean climates.
Mollisol-like permafrost soils of Tibet and the Andean altiplano, called Molliturbels or Mollorthels, are not acidic and make the best grazing land in those cold climates.

entries.title: Six Vertisol suborders, timed by their cracks

definition.text: The six USDA suborders of Vertisols, set by wetness, temperature and how long their cracks stay open.

facts.text: Aquerts have aquic conditions and redoximorphic features; slow permeability brings ponding, and reduced manganese may help darken the profile.
Cryerts, with a cryic regime, are most extensive in the Canadian Prairies; Xererts, with cracks open in summer and closed in winter, in the eastern Mediterranean and California.
Usterts, with cracks open at least 90 cumulative days a year, are the most extensive suborder worldwide, though Torrerts are the most extensive in Australia.
Uderts, with cracks open less than 90 days a year and sometimes only in droughts, are rare, mostly in Uruguay and eastern Argentina.

entries.title: Alfisols, the oldest forest soils

definition.text: The record of Alfisol paleosols, which reaches back to woodland and early forest soils of the Late Devonian.

facts.text: Probably owing to their fertility, Alfisols are the oldest forest soils; the oldest lie in the Aztec Siltstone of Victoria Land, Antarctica, with fossil wood and spores of Archaeopteris-Callixylon trees.
Large woody roots pipe water and clay downward and leave material in the subsoil as they decay, the likely reason argillic horizons, Alfisols and forests go together.
All tetrapod bones and tracks from Late Devonian and Mississippian paleosols of New York and Pennsylvania occur in Aridisols and Alfisols.
Trace fossils such as the nest cells of ground-nesting bees (Celliforma) and termite nests also occur in Alfisols, as well as in Aridisols and Oxisols.

entries.title: Turning red clay Ultisols into garden soil

definition.text: Managing the low organic matter and low pH of red clay Ultisols so that garden plants can grow.

facts.text: Amendments are generally needed every year, guided by soil tests, and lime raises the typically low pH.
Gardeners aim for about 45% mineral, 5% organic matter and 50% pore space; North Carolina Ultisol is roughly 82% mineral, 2% organic matter and 16% pore space.
Mulch makes the soil more porous, and 2 to 3 inches of compost and manure mixed to a shovel's depth add organic matter, best in the fall so microbes release nutrients in time.
Some gardeners skip amending by using raised beds or Hügelkultur, or grow native plants adapted to damp, poorly drained soils.

entries.title: Five ways to be an Ultisol

definition.text: The five suborders of Ultisols in USDA soil taxonomy, set by wetness, organic matter and climate.

facts.text: Aquults have a water table at or near the surface for much of the year; Udults are Ultisols of humid climates.
Ustults are Ultisols of semiarid and subhumid climates; Xerults are temperate ones with arid summers and moist winters.
Humults are well-drained and rich in organic matter, which makes them relatively fertile, as in the Olympic series.
Great groups build on the suborder name: the Cecil series is Typic Kanhapludults, the Bama series Typic Paleudults.

entries.text: Not all {{ref:soil-class-104}} soils behave alike. {{ref:soil-class-006}} splits them into five suborders by wetness, organic matter and climate. Aquults have a water table at or near the surface for much of the year. Udults belong to humid climates and Ustults to semiarid and subhumid ones. Xerults are temperate, with arid summers and moist winters. Humults stand apart: well drained and rich in organic matter, they are relatively fertile, as in the Olympic series. Each suborder seeds longer names below it. The Cecil series is a Typic Kanhapludult, the Bama series a Typic Paleudult.

USDA soil taxonomy: six levels from order to series splits them into five suborders by wetness, organic matter and climate. Aquults have a water table at or near the surface for much of the year. Udults belong to humid climates and Ustults to semiarid and subhumid ones. Xerults are temperate, with arid summers and moist winters. Humults stand apart: well drained and rich in organic matter, they are relatively fertile, as in the Olympic series. Each suborder seeds longer names below it. The Cecil series is a Typic Kanhapludult, the Bama series a Typic Paleudult.

entries.title: More than 20,000 kinds of soil in one country

definition.text: The varied soils of the United States, classified in USDA soil taxonomy down to the series, each a unique kind of soil.

facts.text: Over 20,000 soil series have been identified, and soil maps cover more than 95 percent of U.S. counties, served online through Web Soil Survey.
Estimated shares of U.S. land, territories included, put Mollisols first at 21.5%, then Alfisols (14%), Entisols (12.3%), Inceptisols (9.7%) and Ultisols (9.2%); Oxisols cover 0.02%.
Mollisols lie mostly on the Great Plains, Aridisols in the dry West, Gelisols only in Alaska, Ultisols in warm humid regions, and Spodosols under cool conifer forest and in Florida.
Federal authority for U.S. soil survey dates from the Agricultural Appropriations Act of 1896; today the National Cooperative Soil Survey, led by the NRCS, carries it out.

entries.title: Histels, Turbels and Orthels: the three Gelisol suborders

definition.text: The three suborders of Gelisols: organic Histels, frost-churned Turbels and little-churned Orthels.

facts.text: Histels resemble Histosols but have permafrost within two metres and 80% or more organic material in the top 50 cm; they dominate subarctic and low-arctic permafrost regions.
Turbels show cryoturbation through more than a third of the active layer, with broken horizons, involutions, patterned ground and ice or sand wedges; they lie mainly in continuous permafrost.
Orthels show little cryoturbation, affecting less than a third of the active layer, and occur mainly in discontinuous permafrost and alpine areas.
Cryoturbation is much stronger on exposed sites, where Turbels dominate, than in sheltered valleys.

entries.title: Finding the starting material of a fossil soil

definition.text: Estimating the vanished parent material of a fossil soil from nearby materials, to measure how much soil formation took place.

facts.text: Soils start much like their parent material and lose its features over time, so a baseline is needed to judge how far formation went.
Comparing soils formed under similar conditions on different parent materials, or lithosequences, shows what role the parent material played.
Estimates rest on four assumptions: the proxy material is fresh, it was uniform through the profile, at least one constituent survived weathering, and volume change tracks thickness and density.
No constituent is fully immune to weathering: quartz is fairly stable above pH 9, alumina between pH 4.5 and 8, and lead and zirconium over wider ranges.

entries.title: Soil climate, the weather inside the pores

definition.text: The moisture, temperature and other climatic conditions within a soil's pores, a special kind of microclimate.

facts.text: In well-drained soils it is a subdued version of the regional climate; in waterlogged soils it depends more on local groundwater than on the atmosphere.
Classifying soils by climate data has been challenged by classifying them on observable features; the WRB counts soil climate only as a soil-forming factor.
Climate-sensitive soil features allow a broad reading of past climate from paleosols, though soils record climate less precisely than instruments.
Estimates of soil climate are now entering soil classification, models of soil formation and soil biology.

entries.title: Burrows, dung and roots: trace fossils in old soils

definition.text: Footprints, burrows, coprolites and root traces preserved in fossil soils as evidence of the activity of past organisms.

facts.text: Trace fossils rarely identify a species, but unlike body fossils they usually stay where the organism lived, so they record its behaviour, as with the shallow burrows of solitary bees.
Root-trace patterns and horizon sequences reveal the plant formation, such as forest, woodland or grassland, even when the species cannot be named.
Paleosols can themselves be seen as trace fossils of whole ancient ecosystems.

entries.title: Muck farming, vegetables from drained swamps

definition.text: Farming drained swamp soils of sapric organic matter, or muck, mostly for vegetables.

facts.text: Muck grows specialty crops such as onions, carrots, celery and potatoes, and matters to farming in New York, Ohio, Illinois, Indiana, Michigan, Wisconsin and Florida.

Torrey Farms' muckland at Elba, New York, is thought to be the world's largest continuous section; the Black Dirt Region's 26,000 acres (10,400 ha) are the largest U.S. concentration outside the Everglades.
Because draining wetlands destroys habitat, muck farming is controversial, and U.S. environmental regulations make new muckland unlikely.
The light soil needs windbreaks, can burn underground for months, and oxidizes away each year, growing shallower and releasing carbon dioxide.

entries.title: Calcids, desert soils cemented with carbonate

definition.text: A suborder of Aridisols in USDA soil taxonomy that has accumulated high levels of residual or dust-fall calcium carbonate.

facts.text: Calcids have a calcic, hypercalcic or petrocalcic horizon whose top lies within 1.0 m of the surface.
Their parent materials are rich in carbonate or received it as dust, and rainfall has been too low to remove it or move it deep.
Most are rangeland or wildlife habitat, some irrigated cropland, where micronutrient deficiency is normal.
Great groups include Salicalcids, Gypsicalcids, Petrocalcids, Hypercalcids and Haplocalcids.

entries.text: Too little rain falls on a Calcid to wash its lime away. This suborder of {{ref:soil-class-093}} has piled up high levels of calcium carbonate, either left from carbonate-rich parent material or delivered as dust. Rainfall has been too low to remove it or carry it deep. The result is a {{ref:soil-form-121}}, a hypercalcic horizon or a {{ref:soil-form-029}} whose top lies within 1.0 m of the surface. Most Calcids serve as rangeland or wildlife habitat. Where they are irrigated for crops, micronutrient deficiency is normal. Great groups include Salicalcids, Gypsicalcids, Petrocalcids, Hypercalcids and Haplocalcids.

entries.title: Spodosols, acid soils of the cool conifer forests

definition.text: A USDA soil order of acid soils with a spodic horizon, where organic matter complexed with iron and aluminium has accumulated after leaching from the layer above.

facts.text: They must have a spodic horizon within 2 m of the surface and lack andic properties; most also have a bleached albic horizon.
Their B horizon holds illuviated aluminium with organic matter, and often iron.
Typical of coniferous and boreal forests in cool, moist climates such as southeastern Alaska and the Great Lakes, they are also Florida's most prominent order.
They cover 2.6% of global and 3.3% of U.S. ice-free land.
They correspond to the Podzols of Russia and northern and central Europe and to Canada's Podzolic soils; Australia calls them Podosols.
Spodosols are known only from the Carboniferous onward, though less acidic look-alikes from the Mesozoic and Tertiary may be an extinct suborder.

entries.title: Podzol, the ash-grey soil beneath northern forests

definition.text: An acid soil with an organic topsoil over a bleached, ash-grey leached layer and an iron-, aluminium- or humus-enriched subsoil; the typical soil of boreal and coniferous forests.

facts.text: Podzols, also called podosols, spodosols or espodossolos, also typify eucalypt forests and heathlands of southern Australia.
The name is Russian for 'under-ash', given by Dokuchaev in 1875 after peasants who ploughed up what looked like a layer of ash on first breaking such soils.
Under 5 to 10 cm of decomposing litter lies an E horizon, usually 4 to 8 cm thick and poor in iron and aluminium oxides and humus, over a red or red-brown podzolic B horizon.
Podzolization makes them: dissolved organic matter, iron and aluminium form chelates that percolating water carries from the E to the B horizon, sometimes cementing a hardpan called ortstein.
They form mostly on quartz-rich sands, sandstone or debris of magmatic rock under high rainfall, in cool humid climates where slow decay lets acid mor layers build up.
Most are poor farmland, sandy, short of water and nutrients, acidic, phosphate-deficient and aluminium-toxic; grazing suits them best, though limed and fertilised loamy types can crop well.
Podzols cover about 4,850,000 square kilometres, mostly in temperate and boreal zones of the Northern Hemisphere.
USDA and Chinese taxonomy call them Spodosols; Canada matches them with its Podzolic order, Australia uses Podosols and Brazil Espodossolos.

entries.text: Peasants breaking such soils for the first time ploughed up what looked like a layer of ash. Dokuchaev named the soil for it in 1875: podzol is Russian for 'under-ash'. A Podzol is an acid soil with an organic topsoil over a bleached, ash-grey leached layer and a subsoil enriched in iron, aluminum or humus. It is the typical soil of boreal and coniferous forests, and of the eucalypt forests and heathlands of southern Australia too. Under 5 to 10 cm of decomposing litter lies an E horizon, usually 4 to 8 cm thick and poor in iron and aluminum oxides and humus. Below it sits a red or red-brown podzolic B horizon. {{ref:soil-form-061}} builds this profile. Dissolved organic matter binds iron and aluminum into chelates, and percolating water carries them from the E to the B horizon. Sometimes they cement a hardpan called ortstein. Podzols form mostly on quartz-rich sands, sandstone or debris of magmatic rock under high rainfall. In cool humid climates decay is slow, so acid layers of litter called mor build up. Most Podzols make poor farmland: sandy, short of water and nutrients, acidic, low in phosphate and toxic with aluminum. Grazing suits them best, though limed and fertilized loamy types can crop well. They cover about 4,850,000 square kilometers, mostly in the temperate and boreal Northern Hemisphere. Other systems give them other names. USDA and Chinese taxonomy say Spodosols, Canada has its Podzolic order, Australia uses Podosols and Brazil Espodossolos.

entries.title: Chernozem, the black earth of the steppes

definition.text: A black soil, also called black earth or regur, with 4% to 16% humus and plenty of phosphorus and ammonia compounds; a WRB reference soil group.

facts.text: The name joins the Russian words for 'black' and 'earth'.
In the WRB key a Chernozem has a very dark, well-structured topsoil and secondary carbonates.
Chernozem is very fertile and holds much moisture, but long cropping still needs fertiliser because its humus, and with it its nutrients, steadily declines.
Dokuchaev studied the steppe soils of Poltava in 1883 and that year published Russian Chernozem, the first description of the soil in European Russia.
Chernozem covers about 230 million hectares in two belts: the Eurasian Steppe, and the Canadian Prairies south through the Great Plains to Kansas.
Its dark layer ranges from a few centimetres to 1.5 metres (60 inches) thick in Ukraine and the Red River Valley.
In the WRB the USDA Mollisols split into Chernozems, Kastanozems and Phaeozems, which together match Canada's Chernozemic order.
Ukraine banned farmland sales from 1992 to 2020, but trucked-away soil could be sold, feeding a black market put at about US$900 million a year in 2011.

entries.title: Solonchak, where salt builds up in the soil

definition.text: A WRB reference soil group of pale or grey, poorly drained soils of arid to subhumid lands with high concentrations of soluble salts.

facts.text: The word is Russian for 'salt marsh', from sol, 'salt'.
Most USDA Aridisols fall into the WRB's Calcisols, Gypsisols, Durisols and Solonchaks.
Many Calcisols lie next to Solonchaks that are really salt-affected Calcisols.
Solonetz zones are associated with Gleysols, Solonchaks and Kastanozems.
Irrigation with saline groundwater has caused catastrophic salinisation and Solonchak formation, as in Central Asia.

entries.text: Solonchak is Russian for 'salt marsh', from sol, 'salt'. In the WRB it names a group of pale or grey, poorly drained soils of arid to subhumid lands that hold high concentrations of soluble salts. Its neighbors say a lot about it. Many lime-rich soils, the {{ref:soil-class-121}}, lie next to Solonchaks that are really salt-affected members of that same group. Solonchaks also turn up beside {{ref:soil-class-143}} soils, along with {{ref:soil-class-127}} and {{ref:soil-class-130}}. Crossing to the U.S. system shows the same family resemblance. Most USDA Aridisols fall into just four WRB groups: Solonchaks, the lime-rich soils above, and the soils rich in gypsum or silica described in {{ref:soil-class-129}} and {{ref:soil-class-125}}. People can make Solonchaks too. Irrigation with saline groundwater has caused catastrophic salinization and Solonchak formation, as in Central Asia. Water meant to grow crops left salt behind instead.

entries.title: Solonetz, the soil with a sodium-laden subsoil

definition.text: A WRB reference soil group with a clay-enriched subsoil high in exchangeable sodium, the natric horizon, within the upper 100 cm.

facts.text: The natric horizon, named from Latin natrium, 'sodium', has more clay than the layer above and over 15% exchangeable sodium.
The name comes from Russian sol, 'salt'; the Ukrainian folk word solontsi means salty soil, and many Ukrainian villages bear it.
Solonetz zones go with Gleysols, Solonchaks and Kastanozems.
In USDA soil taxonomy Solonetz are sodium-rich Alfisols; Alfisols and Mollisols with a natric horizon key out as Solonetz.
In Canada such soils develop from saline parent material to Solonetz, Solodized Solonetz and Solod as leaching removes salts, until the sodic B horizon may disintegrate.
Solonetz is one of the Russian soil terms, with chernozem, podzol and gley, that Dokuchaev's work brought into international use.

entries.text: Many Ukrainian villages carry the folk word solontsi, meaning salty soil. The WRB name Solonetz comes from the same Russian root, sol, 'salt'. A Solonetz has a clay-enriched subsoil high in exchangeable sodium within the upper 100 cm. That layer is the natric horizon, named from Latin natrium, 'sodium'. It holds more clay than the layer above, and over 15% of its exchange sites carry sodium, a share measured as the {{ref:soil-chem-018}}. Solonetz zones go with Solonchaks, {{ref:soil-class-127}} and {{ref:soil-class-130}}. In USDA soil taxonomy Solonetz are sodium-rich Alfisols, and any Alfisol or Mollisol with a natric horizon keys out as Solonetz. Canada's soils show how such a soil ages. Starting from saline parent material, it develops into Solonetz, then Solodized Solonetz, then Solod, as leaching removes the salts. In the end the sodic B horizon may disintegrate. The name has deep roots in the science. Solonetz is one of the Russian soil terms, with chernozem, podzol and gley, that Dokuchaev's work brought into international use.

entries.title: Anthrosols, soils remade by centuries of farming

definition.text: A WRB reference soil group of soils formed or heavily changed by long-term human use, such as irrigation, added organic waste or paddy-field cultivation.

facts.text: Anthrosols can form from any parent soil and are common where people have farmed for centuries.
In north-western Europe they commonly have plaggic or terric horizons built up with manure, together covering some 500,000 hectares.
Telltale signs include high phosphate from bones, tissue or excrement, dark colour, high pH from added wood ash, and buried tools or waste.
Qualifiers record the cause: plaggic (long manuring), irragric (flood or surface irrigation), hortic (deep cultivation and kitchen waste), anthraquic (man-made water management such as terracing).
Archaeologists use Anthrosols, spotted by eye or even from satellite images, to find sites of long-term habitation.
Rich in minerals and decayed organic matter, Anthrosols are good for farming, and well-managed ones act as a carbon sink.
Similar soils go by many national names, among them plaggen soils, paddy soils, terra preta, Agrozems in Russia and Anthroposols in Australia and Canada.

entries.contested_note: Because Anthrosols vary so widely in composition and structure, there is debate over whether they should be an independent soil group.

entries.text: Some soils carry a human signature. Anthrosols are soils formed or heavily changed by long-term human use, such as irrigation, added organic waste or paddy-field cultivation. They can form from any parent soil and are common where people have farmed for centuries. The clues are distinctive: high phosphate from bones, tissue or excrement, dark color, high pH from added wood ash, and buried tools or waste. A qualifier in the name records the cause. Plaggic means long manuring, irragric flooding or watering over the surface, hortic deep cultivation and kitchen waste, and anthraquic man-made water management such as terracing. In north-western Europe they commonly have plaggic or terric horizons built up with manure, together covering some 500,000 hectares. Rich in minerals and decayed organic matter, Anthrosols are good for farming, and well-managed ones store carbon. Archaeologists use them too. Spotted by eye or even from satellite images, they mark sites of long-term habitation. Similar soils carry many national names, among them {{ref:soil-class-149}}, paddy soils, the Amazon's {{ref:soil-class-053}}, Agrozems in Russia and Anthroposols in Australia and Canada. That variety raises a real question. Because Anthrosols differ so widely in composition and structure, soil scientists debate whether they should be an independent soil group at all.
