They can form from any parent soil and are common where people have farmed for centuries. The clues are distinctive: high phosphate from bones, tissue or excrement, dark color, high pH from added wood ash, and buried tools or waste. A qualifier in the name records the cause. Plaggic means long manuring, irragric flooding or watering over the surface, hortic deep cultivation and kitchen waste, and anthraquic man-made water management such as terracing. In north-western Europe they commonly have plaggic or terric horizons built up with manure, together covering some 500,000 hectares. Rich in minerals and decayed organic matter, Anthrosols are good for farming, and well-managed ones store carbon. Archaeologists use them too. Spotted by eye or even from satellite images, they mark sites of long-term habitation. Similar soils carry many national names, among them Plaggen soils, built one sod at a time, paddy soils, the Amazon's Terra preta, the black soil people made in the Amazon, Agrozems in Russia and Anthroposols in Australia and Canada. That variety raises a real question. Because Anthrosols differ so widely in composition and structure, soil scientists debate whether they should be an independent soil group at all.

entries.title: Aridity, the drying of the land

definition.text: The condition of regions with low annual precipitation, high temperatures and little available water.

facts.text: Arid areas make up about 43% of the world's land and tend to have degraded soils.
Where aridity falls depends mainly on the general circulation of the atmosphere, which shifts with climate change; land-use change can also raise the demand on soil water.
A December 2024 UNCCD report found that over three-quarters of Earth's land has become permanently drier in recent decades, and a quarter of people live in expanding drylands.
Desertification is a gradual rise in soil aridity, and warming-driven aridity also adds to the salinisation of waterlogged soils.

entries.title: Gleysols, soils stained by groundwater

definition.text: A WRB reference soil group of soils saturated by groundwater long enough, unless drained, to develop gleyic colours: grey or blue inside, rusty at ped surfaces.

facts.text: They are also called meadow soils, groundwater soils or Gleyzems, and match the Aqu- suborders of USDA Entisols, Inceptisols and Mollisols.
In the WRB, redox features from rising groundwater make a Gleysol, while those from stagnant surface water make a Stagnosol or Planosol.
Gleysols form in many unconsolidated sediments, mostly river, marine and lake deposits, in depressions and low positions with shallow groundwater.
They cover an estimated 720 million hectares, occur in nearly all climates, and are most extensive in northern Russia, Siberia, Canada, Alaska, China and Bangladesh.
About 200 million hectares lie in the tropics, mainly in the Amazon, equatorial Africa and the coastal swamps of Southeast Asia.
Drained Gleysols are used for arable crops, dairy farming and horticulture, and in the tropics and subtropics they are widely planted with rice.
Green rust, a layered iron(II)-iron(III) hydroxide, occurs in them as the mineral fougerite.

entries.title: Fluvisols, the young layered soils of floodplains

definition.text: A WRB reference soil group of genetically young, stratified soils in river, lake or marine sediments.

facts.text: Fluvisols occur on alluvial plains, river fans, valleys and tidal marshes on every continent and in every climate zone.
They show clear layering and weak horizons, and under natural conditions flood from time to time.
They correspond to the fluvents and fluvaquents of USDA soil taxonomy.
People recognised their natural fertility, and dry living sites on river levees, in prehistoric times.
Many dryland crops grow on them with water control, and paddy rice is widespread on irrigated and drained tropical Fluvisols.
Coastal Fluvisols with sulphidic material are acid sulfate soils, limited by low pH, toxic aluminium and salt; strongly saline tidal land is best left under mangroves.
Large areas lie along the Amazon, the Ganges plain and Lake Chad, and in deltas such as the Mekong, Mississippi and Nile.

entries.title: Acrisols, weathered tropical soils ruled by aluminum

definition.text: A WRB reference soil group of strongly weathered soils with low-activity clays, in which exchangeable aluminium exceeds the exchangeable base cations.

facts.text: Acrisols are linked to humid tropical and subtropical climates, such as Brazil's, and often carry forest.
In USDA soil taxonomy they match the Humult, Udult and Ustult suborders of the Ultisols, plus Oxisols with a kandic horizon and some Alfisols.
Most Ultisols are classed in the WRB as either Acrisols or Alisols.
Low fertility and toxic aluminium limit farming, so many Acrisols are used for forestry, low-intensity pasture or protected areas.
Where climate allows, tea, rubber, oil palm, coffee and sugar cane can be grown on them.
Infertile Acrisols make up most of the 'common soil' that surrounds the Amazon's fertile terra preta patches.

entries.title: Leptosols, thin soils from the tropics to the peaks

definition.text: A WRB reference soil group of very shallow soils over continuous rock, or deeper soils packed with gravel and stones.

facts.text: Leptosols cover about 1.7 billion hectares, from the tropics to polar regions and from sea level to the highest peaks.
They are widespread in mountains, notably in Asia, South America, northern Canada and Alaska, and in the Saharan and Arabian deserts.
Elsewhere they occur on hard rock or where erosion has kept pace with soil formation or stripped the topsoil.
Lithic Leptosols, less than 10 cm deep, in mountain regions are the most extensive Leptosols on Earth.
The 1974 FAO legend called Leptosols on limestone Rendzinas and those on acid rock Rankers; in the WRB a rendzina may key out as a Leptosol, Chernozem, Kastanozem or Phaeozem.
They hold little water, so are poor for rainfed farming, though some suit tree crops or extensive grazing.
Many USDA orthents, and shallow or gravelly Mollisols, belong to the Leptosols.

entries.title: Cambisols, soils just beginning to change

definition.text: A WRB reference soil group of moderately developed soils at the beginning of soil formation, shown by weak brownish colouring or structure in the profile.

facts.text: Cambisols form in medium- and fine-textured material from many rock types, mostly in alluvial, colluvial and wind-blown deposits.
Most make good, intensively used farmland, and temperate Cambisols are among the most productive soils on earth.
They cover an estimated 15 million square kilometres worldwide.
They are widespread in temperate and boreal lands glaciated in the Pleistocene, where parent material is young and soil formation is slow.
In the tropics they are less common, appearing mainly where active erosion keeps soils young.
The weakly leached brown earths of Europe are Cambisols in the WRB; Poland's brown forest soils correspond to Cambisols and to USDA Udepts.

entries.title: Luvisols, fertile soils with clay washed downward

definition.text: A WRB reference soil group with a clay-enriched subsoil of high-activity clays, in which base cations equal or exceed exchangeable aluminium.

facts.text: Their defining feature is an argic horizon, a subsurface layer with more clay than the material above, formed as water washes clay downward.
The clays are little weathered, high-activity 2:1 types, giving high cation exchange capacity and high base saturation.
Where uneroded, a paler, clay-depleted eluvial horizon lies above the argic horizon.
Luvisols cover 500–600 million hectares, mainly in temperate zones, form on many parent materials, and are generally fertile and widely farmed.
In Mediterranean regions hematite colours them red as Chromic Luvisols; such duplex soils with strong wet-dry seasons are called calcic and chromic luvisols.
In USDA soil taxonomy most are Alfisols; Canada's system also has Luvisols, whose clay-enriched Bt horizon forms mainly by lessivage.

entries.title: Technosols, the soils of cities, mines and dumps

definition.text: A WRB reference soil group of soils whose properties and formation are dominated by their technical, human-made origin.

facts.text: A Technosol holds a significant amount of artefacts, has a geotechnical liner, or is sealed by technic hard material unlike natural rock.
They include soils of landfills, sludge, cinders, mine spoil and ash, pavements with their underlying material, and constructed soils; merely transported natural soil does not count.
Often called urban or mine soils, they occur near cities, roads, mines, dumps, oil spills and fly-ash deposits, usually in small patches.
A Technosol can differentiate A and O horizons at more than one centimetre per year.
They are more likely than other soils to be contaminated, and many must be handled with care because of toxic industrial substances.
Some are made on purpose to cover wastes such as mine tailings, as at Andacollo in Chile.
They are closely related to Anthrosols, soils created by long-term measures to raise fertility for farming.

entries.title: Calcisols, dryland soils rich in lime

definition.text: A WRB reference soil group of soils with a substantial secondary accumulation of lime (calcium carbonate).

facts.text: Calcisols are common on calcareous parent materials and widespread in arid and semi-arid lands; they were formerly called Desert soils and Takyrs.
They develop mostly in alluvial, colluvial and wind-blown deposits of base-rich weathering material, on level to hilly land.
Natural vegetation is sparse: drought-adapted shrubs and trees and short-lived grasses.
Dryness, stoniness or a shallow petrocalcic horizon limit farming, but irrigated, drained and fertilised Calcisols can be highly productive.
Many occur alongside Solonchaks that are in fact salt-affected Calcisols.
Their total area may be some 10 million square kilometres, almost all in the arid and semi-arid subtropics.
Most USDA Aridisols fall into the Calcisols, Gypsisols, Durisols and Solonchaks of the WRB.

entries.title: Regosols, the leftover group for barely formed soils

definition.text: A WRB reference soil group of very weakly developed mineral soils in unconsolidated material, with no significant profile development.

facts.text: Regosols are a leftover group for soils that fit no other; weakly developed soils that qualify as Leptosols, Arenosols or Fluvisols are excluded.
Their profiles stay minimal because they are young or form slowly, and they are extensive in eroding lands, especially arid and semi-arid areas and mountains.
They cover about 260 million hectares, mainly in arid areas of the mid-western United States, northern Africa, the Near East and Australia.
They match USDA Entisols and Australian Rudosols; most are lightly grazed, some are irrigated intensively, and mountain Regosols are best left under forest.

entries.text: Regosols are what remains when a soil fits no other group. They are very weakly developed mineral soils in unconsolidated material, with no significant profile development. They match USDA Entisols and Australian Rudosols. Most are lightly grazed, some are irrigated intensively, and mountain Regosols are best left under forest.

entries.title: Alisols, acid soils with active clays

definition.text: A WRB reference soil group of acidic soils with high-activity clays, in which exchangeable aluminium exceeds the exchangeable base cations.

facts.text: Alisols have a clay-enriched argic horizon with a high cation exchange capacity, but low base saturation in the subsoil.
Their clays are far more active than those of Lixisols, Acrisols and Ferralsols, and they tend to lie on younger or more geologically active terrain.
They occur in tropical and humid subtropical climates and also in temperate regions.
Farming them needs lime and fertiliser, they erode easily, and at their low pH aluminium and manganese dissolve and can poison intolerant plants.

entries.text: Alisols pair lively clays with acid conditions. In these soils the clays are high-activity, yet exchangeable aluminum exceeds the exchangeable base cations. Their clay-enriched argic horizon has a high cation exchange capacity but low base saturation in the subsoil. Their clays are far more active than those of {{ref:soil-class-132}}, Acrisols and Ferralsols, and they tend to lie on younger or more geologically active terrain. They occur in tropical and humid subtropical climates and also in temperate regions. Farming them needs lime and fertilizer, and they erode easily. At their low pH, aluminum and manganese dissolve and can poison intolerant plants.

entries.title: Andosols, the dark soils of volcanic ash

definition.text: A WRB reference soil group of soils formed in volcanic ash and other tephra, rich in allophane or in complexes of aluminium and organic matter.

facts.text: The name comes from Japanese an, 'dark', and do, 'soil'; it is a synonym of kuroboku.
Andosols develop in glass-rich parent material: while much volcanic glass remains they are called Vitric, and as the glass weathers they gain andic properties.
Acidic tephra in humid climates yields aluminium-organic complexes (Aluandic Andosols); basic tephra or dry climates yield allophane and imogolite (Silandic Andosols).
Both kinds hold much ferrihydrite and have a bulk density of 0.9 kg/dm3 or less.
Andosols cover about 1–2% of Earth's ice-free land, mostly around the Pacific Ring of Fire, from Chile and Mexico to Japan, Java and New Zealand.
Silandic Andosols are very fertile unless phosphorus is fixed; wet rice on Java's Andosols feeds some of the world's densest populations.
In USDA soil taxonomy many Andosols are Andisols, though some fall in the Inceptisols.
Fossil Andosols far from today's volcanoes have been dated as far back as the Precambrian, 1.5 billion years ago.

While much volcanic glass remains they are called Vitric, and as the glass weathers they gain andic properties. The path depends on the ash and the climate. Andosols cover about 1–2% of Earth's ice-free land, mostly around the Pacific Ring of Fire, from Chile and Mexico to Japan, Java and New Zealand. In USDA soil taxonomy many are Andisols, though some fall in the Inceptisols. The type is also very old. Fossil Andosols far from today's volcanoes have been dated as far back as the Precambrian, 1.5 billion years ago.

entries.title: Stagnosols, soils waterlogged from above

definition.text: A WRB reference soil group with strong mottling caused by redox processes under stagnating surface water, without a marked texture change.

facts.text: Periodically wet, they are mottled in topsoil and subsoil, sometimes with concretions or a fully bleached albic topsoil; many national systems call them pseudogley.
They cover 150–200 million hectares, mostly on flat to gently sloping land in humid temperate West and Central Europe, North America, south-east Australia and Argentina.
Water stagnating above a dense subsoil starves roots of oxygen, and unlike Gleysols they often need deep loosening or ploughing, not just drains; once drained they can be fertile.
Many are Aqualfs, Aquults, Aquents, Aquepts or Aquolls in USDA soil taxonomy.

entries.text: Stagnosols get wet from the top down. Surface water stagnates in them, and the redox processes it drives leave strong mottling, without a marked change in texture. Periodically wet, they are mottled in topsoil and subsoil, sometimes with concretions or a fully bleached albic topsoil. Many national systems call them pseudogley. They cover 150–200 million hectares, mostly on flat to gently sloping land in humid temperate West and Central Europe, North America, south-east Australia and Argentina. Water stagnating above a dense subsoil starves roots of oxygen. Unlike Gleysols they often need deep loosening or ploughing, not just drains, and once drained they can be fertile. Many are Aqualfs, Aquults, Aquents, Aquepts or Aquolls in USDA soil taxonomy.

entries.title: Planosols, sandy topsoil on a clay floor

definition.text: A WRB reference soil group with a pale, coarse-textured topsoil showing periodic water stagnation that abruptly overlies a dense, slowly permeable, much more clayey subsoil.

facts.text: The abrupt texture change comes from layered deposits or from clay destruction and removal; water perched above it creates temporary reducing conditions and a stagnic colour pattern.
The 1938 US classification used the name Planosols; USDA soil taxonomy now puts most in the Albaqualfs, Albaquults and Argialbolls.
They cover about 130 million hectares of seasonally waterlogged flats in subtropical and temperate regions with marked wet and dry seasons.
Oxygen shortage when wet, dense subsoil and sometimes toxic aluminium hamper roots, so most are grazed and yields stay modest, though Southeast Asia grows paddy rice on them.

entries.text: A Planosol changes abruptly from one layer to the next. A pale, coarse-textured topsoil sits directly on a dense, slowly permeable, much more clayey subsoil. The sharp break comes from layered deposits, or from clay being destroyed and removed. Water perches above it, creating temporary reducing conditions and a stagnic color pattern. Planosols cover about 130 million hectares of seasonally waterlogged flats in subtropical and temperate regions with marked wet and dry seasons. Oxygen shortage when wet, the dense subsoil and sometimes toxic aluminum hamper roots. Most are grazed and yields stay modest, though Southeast Asia grows paddy rice on them. The 1938 US classification already used the name; USDA soil taxonomy now puts most in the Albaqualfs, Albaquults and Argialbolls.

entries.title: Phaeozems, dark prairie soils without lime

definition.text: A WRB reference soil group of dark soils with a high base status but no secondary carbonates within one metre of the surface.

facts.text: Most Phaeozems match the Udolls, a suborder of the Mollisols in USDA soil taxonomy.
They form on loess and glacial till under humid and sub-humid tall-grass steppe, with extensive areas in the United States, Argentina and China.
They typically hold about 5% organic matter and have a pH of 5–7.
They are farmed intensively for wheat, soybean and cotton and as improved cattle pasture.

entries.text: Phaeozems are dark soils with a high base status, much like Chernozems, but with no secondary carbonates within one meter of the surface. They form on loess and glacial till under humid and sub-humid tall-grass steppe. Extensive areas lie in the United States, Argentina and China. They typically hold about 5% organic matter and have a pH of 5–7. Farmers use them intensively for wheat, soybean and cotton and as improved cattle pasture. Most Phaeozems match the Udolls, a suborder of the Mollisols in USDA soil taxonomy.

entries.title: Kastanozems, the chestnut soils of dry grasslands

definition.text: A WRB reference soil group, also called chestnut soil, with a dark, humus-rich topsoil and secondary carbonates.

facts.text: Kastanozems are paler than Chernozems and relate to the Mollisols of USDA soil taxonomy.
Native grassland gave them a brown surface layer within the first metre, a high level of exchangeable calcium and secondary carbonates starting within 70 cm of the mineral surface.
They occupy relatively dry zones receiving 200 to 450 mm of rain a year.
The name comes from the Russian and Latin words for chestnut, after the colour of its husk.

entries.title: Lixisols, weathered tropical soils that keep their bases

definition.text: A WRB reference soil group of soils with a subsurface build-up of low-activity clays and high base saturation, where base cations equal or exceed exchangeable aluminium.

facts.text: Lixisols develop under intense tropical weathering in subhumid to semi-arid climates.
Most USDA Alfisols are Luvisols or Lixisols in the WRB.
With Acrisols they are the FAO groups of tropical climates with clay-enriched layers, and in Amazonia they are among the natural soils too poor in minerals to resupply nutrients.

entries.text: Lixisols are hard-weathered tropical soils that still keep their bases. They develop under intense tropical weathering in subhumid to semi-arid climates. Low-activity clays build up below the surface, and base saturation stays high: base cations equal or exceed exchangeable aluminum. With Acrisols they are the FAO groups of tropical climates with clay-enriched layers. In Amazonia they are among the natural soils too poor in minerals to resupply nutrients. Most USDA Alfisols are Luvisols or Lixisols in the WRB.

entries.title: Plaggen soils, built one sod at a time

definition.text: A deep, humus-rich anthropogenic soil, or plaggic Anthrosol, built up on poor podzols of north-west Europe from the Middle Ages by plaggen farming.

facts.text: Farmers cut sods of heath or grass with roots and humus, used them as bedding for cattle or sheep, then spread the slurry-soaked bedding on fields in spring as manure.
Centuries of this built fertile soil 40 cm to over 1.50 m deep, against about 30 cm for modern arable soils, raising fields with sharp edges called Plaggenesche in Germany or Es in Dutch.
The practice ended around 1900 with the arrival of fertilisers, though Orkney had such soils by the 12th to 13th centuries and parts of Shetland kept the method until the 1960s.
Maori farmers in New Zealand used plaggen-like practices to improve drainage for kumara.

entries.text: Farmers in north-west Europe built their own soil, one sod at a time, from the Middle Ages on. They cut sods of shrubland or grass with roots and humus, and used them as bedding for cattle or sheep. In spring they spread the slurry-soaked bedding on their fields as manure. Centuries of this turned poor Podzols into plaggen soil, a deep, humus-rich plaggic Anthrosol 40 cm to over 1.50 m deep. Modern arable soils reach about 30 cm. The fields rose with sharp edges, called Plaggenesche in Germany or Es in Dutch. The practice ended around 1900 with the arrival of fertilizers. Orkney had such soils by the 12th to 13th centuries, and parts of Shetland kept the method until the 1960s. Far away, Maori farmers in New Zealand used plaggen-like practices to improve drainage for kumara.

entries.title: Nitisols, deep red soils with shiny clods

definition.text: A WRB reference soil group of deep, red, well-drained tropical soils with at least 30% clay and a strong polyhedral or blocky structure.

facts.text: The clay-rich layer extends as deep as 150 cm, and its blocky aggregates show shiny pressure faces, shaped by iron oxides and high water content.
Nitisols form from fine material weathered from intermediate to basic rock; kaolinite, halloysite and iron oxides dominate, and they fix phosphorus.
They occur in the tropics and subtropics, extensively in the highlands of Ethiopia, Kenya, the DR Congo and Cameroon.
They correlate with kandic Alfisols, Ultisols and Inceptisols of USDA soil taxonomy.

entries.title: Umbrisols, dark topsoils poor in bases

definition.text: A WRB reference soil group with a dark, organic-rich mineral topsoil of low base saturation.

facts.text: Umbrisols are the low-base counterpart of Chernozems, Kastanozems and Phaeozems, and develop in weathered siliceous rock.
They cover about 100 million hectares, above the tree line in the Andes, Himalaya and Central Asia, and lower down in cleared northern and western Europe and on North America's Pacific seaboard.
Slopes and wet, cool climate restrict most to extensive grazing improved by better grasses and liming, and many erode easily; in New Zealand they became productive sheep and dairy land.
USDA soil taxonomy places such soils in great groups of Entisols and Inceptisols, and British brown podzolic soils are Umbrisols in the WRB.

entries.title: Retisols, where pale soil reaches down in a net

definition.text: A WRB reference soil group in which a pale, clay-poor eluvial horizon tongues in a net-like pattern into the darker, clay-rich argic horizon below.

facts.text: The interfingering is called retic properties, from Latin rete, 'net'.
Retisols entered the WRB in its third edition in 2014, absorbing the more narrowly defined Albeluvisols of 1998 and 2006; they resemble the FAO's Podzoluvisols.
They occur mainly in former periglacial areas of the last glaciation in Europe and North America, along a belt from Belgium to Russia, rarely over large areas.
Water drains through the clay-poor tongues while the dense, nutrient-richer clay parts are often too dry and hard to root; earthworms avoid them and most are forest or pasture.

entries.text: In a Retisol, pale soil reaches down into the darker layer below in a net-like pattern. The pale part is a clay-poor eluvial horizon; the dark part is the clay-rich argic horizon. They occur mainly in former periglacial areas of the last glaciation in Europe and North America, along a belt from Belgium to Russia, though rarely over large areas. Water drains through the clay-poor tongues. The dense, nutrient-richer clay parts are often too dry and hard for roots, and earthworms avoid them. Most Retisols are forest or pasture.

entries.title: The Black Dirt Region, onion country on drained muck

definition.text: A drained former marsh in Orange County, New York, and Sussex County, New Jersey, named for its dark, extremely fertile sapric muck soil.

facts.text: The muck formed on an ancient glacial lake bed, enriched by decades of Wallkill River floods; its 26,000 acres (10,400 ha) are the largest such tract in the US outside the Everglades.
Early settlers avoided the flood-prone land; a drainage canal was dug in 1835, and Polish and Volga German immigrants used to similar soils began farming it.
Its black dirt onions averaged 30,000 lb/acre (3.4 kg/m2) by the late 20th century; farmers now also grow vegetables, sod, hemp and cannabis.
The muck is poor ground for building, so development of the farmland is considered unlikely.

entries.title: Plinthosols, soils that can harden into ironstone

definition.text: A WRB reference soil group defined by plinthite, petroplinthite or pisoliths, iron-oxide concretions, in a plinthic horizon starting within 50 cm of the surface.

facts.text: They form in wet-dry tropics where water tables rise and fall: saturated soil reduces and mobilises iron, which on drying precipitates as ferric oxides in mottled patterns.
Plinthite, a red clay-rich material rich in iron oxides, sometimes over 80%, hardens irreversibly into ironstone with repeated wetting and drying.
Fertility is low; bottomlands waterlog, shallow areas suffer drought, and shallow petroplinthite often leaves only grazing, though cocoa and cashew are grown in places.
Soils with plinthite cover about 60 million hectares; soft plinthite dominates the humid Amazon and Congo basins, while hardened caps cover drier Sudano-Sahelian landforms.

entries.title: Gypsisols, gypsum soils of the driest lands

definition.text: A WRB reference soil group of soils with a substantial secondary accumulation of gypsum (CaSO4·2H2O).

facts.text: Gypsisols are confined to the driest arid lands, probably about 100 million hectares in all, around Mesopotamia, central Asia, the Libyan and Namib deserts, Australia and the south-western United States.
They are Gypsids in USDA soil taxonomy and Desert soils in the Russian classification.
Calcium sulphate, with or without carbonates, collects in and below the B horizon of soils formed in alluvial, colluvial and wind-blown deposits.
Deep Gypsisols near water can grow many crops, but a shallow petrogypsic horizon cuts yields, and gypsum dissolving in irrigation water makes the land subside unevenly, so canals must be lined.

entries.title: Why chernozem is black: an open question

definition.text: The competing explanations, offered since 1763, for how chernozem's thick black topsoil formed.

facts.text: Early ideas ranged from decaying plants and animals (Lomonosov, 1763) and weathered Jurassic marine shales (Murchison, 1840) to marine sediments (1851) and decomposed steppe grasses (Ruprecht, 1866).
No single reconstruction of past climate explains the geochemical variation of central European chernozems; evidence of human-made pyrogenic carbon led to a burning theory (Schmidt, 1999).
Chernozem has the highest magnetic susceptibility of the major soil types; heat turns goethite and ferrihydrite into maghemite, pointing to fire, likely set by early humans.
Humification alone can darken soils, so 'chernozem' may cover black soils that look alike but formed in different ways.

entries.contested_note: Sources propose humus build-up under steppe grass, marine sediments and prehistoric burning, and no single explanation fits all chernozems.
entries.text: How chernozem got its thick black topsoil has been argued since 1763. That year Lomonosov pointed to decaying plants and animals. Murchison proposed weathered Jurassic marine shales in 1840, others marine sediments in 1851, and Ruprecht decomposed steppe grasses in 1866. The puzzle is still open. No single reconstruction of past climate explains the geochemical variation of central European chernozems. Evidence of human-made pyrogenic carbon, carbon formed by burning, led to a burning theory from Schmidt in 1999. Chernozem has the highest magnetic susceptibility of the major soil types. Heat turns goethite and ferrihydrite into maghemite, which points to fire, likely set by early humans. Yet humification alone can darken soils. So 'chernozem' may cover black soils that look alike but formed in different ways, and no single explanation yet fits them all.

entries.title: Durisols, dryland soils cemented by silica

definition.text: A WRB reference soil group of free-draining dryland soils whose grains are cemented by secondary silica in the upper metre, as nodules or as a continuous hardpan.

facts.text: The name comes from Latin durus, 'hard'; the cemented layer is called a duripan, hardpan in Australia or dorbank in South Africa.
Durisols form mainly in alluvial and colluvial deposits on plains, terraces and gentle piedmont slopes in arid, semi-arid and Mediterranean regions; erosion often exposes the hard layer.
Most are fit only for extensive grazing; crops need irrigation.
Large areas occur in Australia, South Africa, Namibia and the south-western United States, but as a new group they are rarely mapped and their extent is unknown.

entries.title: Five groups with clay-rich subsoils, and how to tell them apart
entries.article: Retisol#Relationships with other Reference Soil Groups

definition.text: The five WRB reference soil groups that must have an argic, clay-enriched subsoil horizon: Retisols, Acrisols, Lixisols, Alisols and Luvisols.

facts.text: Only Retisols have retic properties; the other four are separated by the cation exchange capacity per kg of clay in the argic horizon and by the subsoil's effective base saturation.
Acrisols have low-activity clays with more exchangeable aluminium than base cations; Lixisols have low-activity clays with base cations at least equal to aluminium.
Alisols have high-activity clays dominated by aluminium; Luvisols have high-activity clays with base cations at least equal to aluminium.
A soil with an argic horizon and retic properties dominated by stagnant water is classed instead as a Retic Stagnosol.
Most USDA Alfisols become Luvisols or Lixisols, and most Ultisols become Acrisols or Alisols.

entries.text: Five WRB groups must have an argic horizon, a clay-enriched subsoil: Retisols, Acrisols, Lixisols, Alisols and Luvisols. The key sorts them with a few measurements. Retisols stand apart first, as the only group with retic properties. The other four are separated by the cation exchange capacity per kg of clay in the argic horizon, and by the effective base saturation of the subsoil. Low-activity clays with more exchangeable aluminum than base cations make an Acrisol. Low-activity clays with base cations at least equal to aluminum make a Lixisol. High-activity clays dominated by aluminum make an Alisol. High-activity clays with base cations at least equal to aluminum make a Luvisol. One exception guards the edge. A soil with an argic horizon and retic properties dominated by stagnant water is classed instead as a Retic Stagnosol. The groups also map onto the U.S. system. Most USDA Alfisols become Luvisols or Lixisols, and most Ultisols become Acrisols or Alisols.

entries.title: Albeluvisols, a soil group retired in 2014

definition.text: A former WRB reference soil group (1998 and 2006 editions): soils with a thin dark topsoil over a bleached albic horizon that tongues into a clay-enriched Bt horizon.

facts.text: The third edition of the WRB in 2014 replaced them with the more broadly defined Retisols.
They correlate with the Glossaqualfs, Glossocryalfs and Glossudalfs of USDA soil taxonomy.
They formed in glacial till, lake and river deposits or loess on plains under coniferous or mixed forest, and cover an estimated 320 million hectares, mostly on former Pleistocene permafrost.
Acidity, few nutrients and tillage and drainage problems limit farming, so those of the northern taiga are almost all forest.

entries.title: Peat, the half-rotted store of the world's soil carbon

definition.text: An accumulation of partially decayed vegetation or organic matter, found in peatlands, bogs, mires, moors and muskegs.

facts.text: Sphagnum, or peat moss, is one of its commonest components, though many other plants contribute.
Peat forms in wetlands where flooding or stagnant water cuts off oxygen and slows decomposition; soils made mainly of peat are Histosols.
There are about 4 trillion cubic metres of peat in the world.
Peat stores up to 550 Gt of carbon, 42% of all soil carbon and more than all other vegetation including forests, while covering just 3% of the land surface.
Peat is renewable in principle, but it regrows only about 1 mm a year, and in only 30–40% of peatlands, far slower than industrial extraction.
Over geological time peat is often the first step toward coal, especially low-grade lignite.
Centuries of burning and draining peat have released much CO2, contributing to human-caused climate change.
Engineers treat highly organic peat soil as a problem: it consolidates poorly and makes an unstable foundation for roads or buildings.

conflicts.text: Joosten and Clarke say peatlands hold one third of the world's soil carbon.
conflicts.note: Differs from the 42% of all soil carbon given in the Peat lead.

conflicts.text: PEATMAP puts global peatland coverage at 4.23 million km², about 2.84% of the world land area.

Engineers see a different problem. Highly organic peat consolidates poorly, so it makes an unstable foundation for roads and buildings.

entries.title: Draining peat lets ancient carbon escape

definition.text: The draining of peat soils, often through canals, for agriculture, forestry and peat extraction.

facts.text: Drainage exposes organic carbon, built up underwater over thousands of years, to the air, where it decomposes to CO2.
About 12% of current peatlands have been drained and damaged; as of 2022 they emit an estimated 4% of human-made greenhouse gases, not counting fires.
Draining peat also destroys the habitat of many species.
The Netherlands, largely peat 2,500 years ago, has lost peatland to drainage-driven compaction, oxidation and excavation, leaving about 2,733 km², 10% of its land.
England's peatlands store 584 million tonnes of carbon but emit around 11 million tonnes of CO2 a year through degradation and draining.

About 2,500 years ago the country was largely peat. Compaction, oxidation and digging, all driven by drainage, have left about 2,733 km², 10% of its land. Draining peat also destroys the habitat of many species.

entries.title: Peat fires that smoulder underground for years

definition.text: Fires in peat deposits, which smoulder underground for long periods and are not put out by light rain.

facts.text: Peat's high carbon content lets it burn when dry; once ignited, for example by a wildfire reaching below the surface, it smoulders.
Smouldering fires can creep undetected through underground peat for months, years or even centuries.
Bogs naturally burn and depend on wildfires to stop woody plants lowering the water table and shading out bog plants.
In 1997 peat and forest fires in Indonesia released between 0.81 and 2.57 gigatonnes of carbon, equal to 13–40% of carbon from global fossil fuel burning.
A 2010 heat wave of up to 40 °C ignited peat in Central Russia, and in June 2019 Arctic peat fires emitted 50 megatonnes of CO2.
Climate change makes peat fires much more likely than before.

entries.text: A fire in peat can outlast the season, the year, even the century. Peat fires burn in peat deposits and smoulder underground for long periods, and light rain does not put them out. Peat's high carbon content lets it burn once dry. A wildfire reaching below the surface can ignite it. Then it smoulders, creeping undetected through the ground for months, years or even centuries. Fire is not wholly foreign to peat bogs. Bogs burn naturally and depend on wildfires to stop woody plants from lowering the water table and shading out bog plants. The damage comes at scale. In 1997 peat and forest fires in Indonesia released between 0.81 and 2.57 gigatonnes of carbon, equal to 13–40% of the carbon from global fossil fuel burning. A 2010 heat wave of up to 40 °C ignited peat in Central Russia. In June 2019 Arctic peat fires emitted 50 megatonnes of CO2. Climate change now makes such fires much more likely than before.

entries.title: How stalled decay builds a bog

definition.text: The build-up of peat where plant material fails to decay fully under acidic, oxygen-poor, waterlogged conditions.

facts.text: Peat is made mainly of wetland vegetation, principally bog plants such as mosses, sedges and shrubs.
Accumulating peat holds water, slowly making conditions wetter so the wetland expands.
Sphagnum promotes its own habitat: it secretes tannins that preserve organic material, and its water-holding hyaline cells keep the bog constantly wet.
Most modern peat bogs formed 12,000 years ago at high latitudes, after the glaciers retreated at the end of the last ice age.
Peat usually accumulates at about a millimetre a year, so boreal peatlands take thousands of years to reach their average depth of 1.5 to 2.3 m.
Northern peatlands hold an estimated 415 gigatonnes of carbon, tropical peatlands 50 Gt and South American ones 15 Gt.

entries.text: Peat is what happens when rot stalls. Most of the material comes from bog plants such as mosses, sedges and shrubs. The process feeds itself. Accumulating peat holds water, so conditions slowly grow wetter and the bog spreads. Sphagnum is especially good at this. It secretes tannins that preserve organic material, and its water-holding hyaline cells keep the bog constantly wet. Boreal peat bogs therefore take thousands of years to reach their average depth of 1.5 to 2.3 m. The result is a vast store of carbon: an estimated 415 gigatonnes in the north, 50 Gt in the tropics and 15 Gt in South America.

entries.title: Serpentine soil, where heavy metals rule

definition.text: An uncommon soil formed from weathered ultramafic rock, such as peridotite and serpentinite, that contains minerals of the serpentine group.

facts.text: Its minerals include antigorite, lizardite and chrysotile, or white asbestos; the ultramafic parent rocks contain more than 70% iron or magnesium minerals.
Steep, rocky, erosion-prone serpentine terrain keeps the soils shallow, and with sparse vegetation they run hot and dry.
Often reddish, brown or grey from high iron and little organic matter, it has a low calcium-to-magnesium ratio and little nitrogen, phosphorus or potassium.
It carries high concentrations of heavy metals, including chromium, iron, cobalt and nickel, and is generally poor for agriculture.
Serpentinite forms when olivine-rich peridotite reacts with water, mostly in oceanic crust near mid-ocean ridges; its chrysotile asbestos makes dust from crushed rock a health hazard.
Serpentine soils occur worldwide, partly mirroring ophiolites, from the Balkans, Cyprus and the Alps to Cuba and New Caledonia; most North American ones are in California.
Adding gypsum or other soluble calcium improves the calcium-to-magnesium ratio, so amended soils can support crops and pasture.
Plants adapted to its heavy metals have been used in phytoremediation to remove metals from polluted soil.

entries.text: Some soils are poisoned by their own bedrock. Its minerals belong to the serpentine group: antigorite, lizardite and chrysotile, or white asbestos. Serpentinite forms when olivine-rich peridotite reacts with water, mostly in oceanic crust near mid-ocean ridges. They hold little organic matter, nitrogen, phosphorus or potassium, and too little calcium for their magnesium. High chromium, iron, cobalt and nickel make them poor for farming. Adding gypsum or other soluble calcium fixes the ratio enough for crops and pasture. These soils occur from the Balkans, Cyprus and the Alps to Cuba and New Caledonia, and most North American ones are in California. Dust from the crushed rock carries asbestos, a health hazard.

entries.title: Charcoal, wood baked without air

definition.text: A lightweight black carbon residue made by strongly heating wood or other plant and animal material in minimal oxygen, driving off water and volatile compounds.

facts.text: In traditional charcoal burning, a kiln or conical pile burns part of its own wood under limited oxygen to char the rest; modern retorts are more efficient.
Research on Amazonian terra preta revived charcoal's use in horticulture, both to improve soils and to sequester carbon.
Biochar is a form of charcoal, sometimes modified, intended for organic uses such as adding to soil.
Large-scale charcoal production has long driven deforestation, particularly in Central Europe.

entries.text: Charcoal is what remains when wood or other plant and animal material is strongly heated with little oxygen. Modern retorts do the job more efficiently. Large-scale production has long driven deforestation, particularly in Central Europe. entries.title: Terra preta, the black soil people made in the Amazon

definition.text: A very dark, fertile, human-made soil (an anthrosol) of the Amazon Basin, also called Amazonian dark earth.

facts.text: Its black colour comes from weathered charcoal; it was made by adding charcoal, bones, broken pottery, compost and manure to poor Amazonian soil.
The charcoal from slash-and-char farming stays in the soil for thousands of years, binding minerals and nutrients, so terra preta resists leaching.
Pre-Columbian farming communities created it between 450 BCE and 950 CE; it can reach 2 m deep and is reported to regenerate at 1 cm a year.
It is surrounded by infertile terra comum, mainly Acrisols, Ferralsols and Arenosols; cleared Amazon soils lose their nutrients to rain or flooding within a short time.
The WRB calls it Pretic Anthrosol; most terra preta began as Ferralsol, and its A horizon holds more than 13–14% organic matter.
Estimates of its extent run from 0.1–0.3% of low forested Amazonia, or 6,300 to 18,900 square kilometres, to 10% or more; plots average 20 hectares.
It holds on average three times the organic matter of surrounding soils, up to 150 g/kg, and phosphorus reaches 200–400 mg/kg.
Lighter, brownish terra mulata, the farmed land around settlements, is more fertile than surrounding soils but less fertile than terra preta.

conflicts.text: Model-based predictions put terra preta at 3.2% of the forest.
conflicts.note: A third estimate of the same extent, between the 0.1–0.3% and 10% figures.

verification.title: Abundant and Stable Char Residues in Soils: Implications for Soil Fertility and Carbon Sequestration
verification.evidence: (Mollisols) contain char (generated by presettlement fires) that is structurally comparable to char in the Terra Preta soils and much more abundant than previously thought (~40-50% of organic C).
verification.note: the paper's 40-50% is char's share of organic carbon in Mollisols; the entry gives terra preta's extent and organic matter content

entries.text: Clear a patch of Amazon forest and rain or flooding soon strips the soil of its nutrients. Yet scattered through the basin lie patches of soil that stay dark and fertile. This is terra preta, a human-made {{ref:soil-class-120}}. Pre-Columbian farming communities created it between 450 BCE and 950 CE. They added charcoal, bones, broken pottery, {{ref:soil-fert-028}} and {{ref:soil-fert-023}} to poor Amazonian soil. Weathered charcoal gives the black color. Charcoal from {{ref:soil-fert-087}} stays in the soil for thousands of years, binding minerals and nutrients, so terra preta resists leaching. It holds on average three times the organic matter of the soils around it, up to 150 g/kg, and phosphorus reaches 200–400 mg/kg. Its A horizon holds more than 13–14% organic matter, and the soil can reach 2 m deep. It is reported to regenerate at 1 cm a year. The WRB calls it Pretic Anthrosol, and most began as Ferralsol. Around it lies infertile terra comum, mainly Acrisols, Ferralsols and Arenosols. Lighter, brownish terra mulata, the farmed land around settlements, falls in between for fertility. Its extent is uncertain. Estimates run from 0.1–0.3% of low forested Amazonia, or 6,300 to 18,900 square kilometers, to 10% or more, and model-based predictions put it at 3.2% of the forest. Plots average 20 hectares.

entries.title: Brown earth, the easy farmland of temperate lands

definition.text: A well-drained, fertile type of soil found mainly in humid temperate climates.

facts.text: Brown earths lie mostly between 35° and 55° north, with the largest expanses in western and central Europe, Russia, eastern North America and eastern Asia; they cover 45% of England and Wales.
They form where rainfall is moderate, usually below 76 cm a year, and have a pH between 5.0 and 6.5.
The brownish A horizon, over 20 cm deep, is mull humus mixed into mineral matter by soil organisms and roots, so its boundary with the B horizon can be blurred.
The lighter B horizon is weathered parent material, often weakly illuviated; limited leaching moves only the more soluble bases down the profile.
Their rich colour comes from iron compounds, mainly complex oxides that are reddish-brown like rust, and the B horizon lacks the grey colours and mottles of gley soils.
Permeable and easy to work for most of the year, brown earths are valued for farming, and much of the deciduous woodland on them has been cleared.
The WRB calls the weakly leached brown earths Cambisols; German and Austrian taxonomy calls them Braunerde, and Polish classification maps them to Inceptisols in USDA Soil Taxonomy.
More strongly leached soils of continental eastern Europe, mapped as Luvisols, are called argillic brown earths in British and French systems for their clay-enriched horizon at depth.

entries.title: Peat archives, a diary kept in layers

definition.text: The record of past vegetation, pollen, spores, animals and archaeological remains preserved layer by layer in a peat profile.

facts.text: Because peat builds up over thousands of years, preserved pollen and plant remains let scientists reconstruct past vegetation, climate and land use.
The peatland scientist Harry Godwin coined the phrase in 1981.
Peat records are compared with modern bogs to gauge human effects on the mercury cycle, dated with methods such as the vertical distribution of lead-210.
Acidic, tanning water and the antibiotic sphagnan preserve bog bodies almost perfectly, such as Denmark's Tollund Man, who lived in the 4th century BC.

entries.title: Burning peat for heat, power and whisky

definition.text: Dried peat burned for heat and power, traditionally cut by hand and left to dry in the sun.

facts.text: In Ireland and Scotland peat was stacked to dry and used for cooking and home heating, a tradition traced back to the Roman period.
Ireland's state-owned Bord na Móna milled peat for power stations and sold peat briquettes for domestic heating.
In 1929 over 40% of the Soviet Union's electricity came from peat, falling to 1% by 1980.
Some Scotch whisky distilleries, such as those on Islay, dry malted barley over peat fires.

entries.title: Peat hags, the overhanging banks of eroding bogs

definition.text: A form of erosion at the sides of gullies cut into peat, leaving overhanging banks of peat and vegetation.

facts.text: Hags form when flowing water cuts down into the peat or when fire or overgrazing exposes its surface.
Exposed peat then erodes further under wind, water and livestock.
Hags are too steep and unstable for plants to establish, so they keep eroding unless restored.

entries.text: In damaged peat the ground can break into steep banks capped by an overhanging lip of plants. These are peat hags, a form of erosion at the sides of gullies cut into peat. The banks are too steep and unstable for plants to take hold, so they keep eroding unless restored.

entries.title: Gardening without peat

definition.text: The use of peat as a raw material for gardening and horticulture, now being restricted in some places.

facts.text: Kew Gardens has discouraged peat as a soil additive since 2003, and the Royal Horticultural Society promotes peat-free gardening.
Bark- and coir-based peat-free potting mixes are rising in the UK, while peat is still used in other European countries, Canada and parts of the US.
In 1999 the UK set its horticulture industry a target of 90% peat-free by 2010; Chile has forbidden peat extraction since April 2024.
Peat grow cups have about 4.5 times the carbon footprint of single-use plastic cups.

entries.title: Fibric, hemic, sapric: grading peat by decay

definition.text: The division of peat material into fibric, hemic and sapric kinds by how far it has decomposed.

facts.text: Fibric peat is the least decomposed and consists of intact fibre; hemic peat is partly decomposed and sapric peat the most decomposed.
Phragmites peat, made of reed grass and other grasses, is denser than many other kinds of peat.

entries.title: Frozen peat and the carbon it guards

definition.text: Permanently frozen peat ground, which makes up around half the area of northern peatlands.

facts.text: Permafrost peatlands are about a tenth of all permafrost area and hold about a tenth of permafrost carbon, 185 ± 66 Gt.
Dry peat insulates well, with a thermal conductivity of around 0.25 W m−1 K−1, shielding permafrost from thaw and forming palsas and peat plateaus.
Thaw tends to raise methane emissions while only slightly increasing CO2 uptake, adding to the permafrost carbon feedback.
Under 2 °C of global warming, 0.7 million km² of peatland permafrost could thaw.

entries.text: Around half the area of northern peat bogs is frozen year-round. This peatland permafrost covers about a tenth of all permafrost area and holds about a tenth of permafrost carbon, 185 ± 66 Gt. Thaw tends to raise methane emissions while only slightly increasing CO2 uptake, so it adds to the warming feedback from thawing permafrost carbon. Under 2 °C of global warming, 0.7 million km² of peatland permafrost could thaw.

entries.title: Rewetting a peatland back to life

definition.text: Repairing damaged peatlands, usually by blocking drainage channels so they rewet and native vegetation recovers.

facts.text: Rewetting limits carbon release in the short term, and new vegetation later supplies the litter that restarts peat formation.
Active reintroduction of peatland plants re-establishes typical communities within 5 years, supporting the return of animals, insects and birds.
Pools in restoration projects raise biodiversity by adding microhabitats.
The Convention on Biological Diversity names peatlands as key ecosystems to protect, and wetlands are also protected under the 1971 Ramsar Convention.

entries.title: Rendzina, the thin dark soil on limestone

definition.text: A shallow, humus-rich soil formed on carbonate-rich, or occasionally sulfate-rich, parent rock, recognized in British, German and some obsolete classifications.

facts.text: Limestone is by far the commonest parent rock, but rendzinas also form on dolomite, gypsum, marble, chalk and marl, typically on slopes in karst and mountain landscapes.
Water carrying dissolved carbon dioxide dissolves the carbonate and leaches it away, leaving the upper soil enriched in insoluble clay minerals.
Biological activity builds humus in the surface soil, where clay protects it from further decay; together clay and humus give dark colours and crumb structure.
Rendzinas in Wales have a simple A–C profile: dark calcareous topsoil directly over shattered limestone.
Typical pH is 5 to 8 with high base saturation; calcium and magnesium are plentiful but potassium is often low, so nutrient imbalances are common.
Rendzinas are a transitory stage: losing their carbonate turns them into another soil type, unless erosion keeps removing soil and holds them in place.
Shallowness hinders tillage and limits water storage, and slopes raise the erosion risk, so rendzina areas often keep semi-natural vegetation.
The WRB places rendzinas among Leptosols, Chernozems, Kastanozems or Phaeozems; the 1974 FAO world soil map called Leptosols on calcareous rock Rendzinas.

entries.text: On limestone slopes the soil can be little more than a dark skin over broken rock. Rendzina is a shallow, humus-rich soil formed on carbonate-rich, or occasionally sulfate-rich, parent rock, recognized in British, German and some older classifications. Limestone is by far the commonest base, but rendzinas also form on dolomite, gypsum, marble, chalk and {{ref:soil-fert-079}}, typically on slopes in karst and mountain landscapes. Water carrying dissolved carbon dioxide dissolves the carbonate and carries it away. Insoluble clay minerals stay behind in the upper soil. There, organisms build humus, and the clay protects it from further decay; together they give dark colors and crumb structure. In Wales the profile is simply dark calcareous topsoil straight onto shattered limestone. Calcium and magnesium are plentiful, but potassium is often low. Rendzinas are a passing stage. Once they lose their carbonate they become another soil, unless erosion keeps stripping soil away. Shallow and sloping, they store little water, so they often keep semi-natural vegetation.

entries.title: Terra rossa, the red soil of Mediterranean karst

definition.text: A well-drained, reddish, clayey to silty soil of neutral pH, typical of the Mediterranean region.

facts.text: Its red colour comes from hematite forming in preference to goethite.
It covers limestone and dolomite bedrock in karst regions as a discontinuous layer from a few centimetres to several metres thick.
The karstic rock beneath gives it high internal drainage and neutral pH, surprisingly good drainage for a clay-rich soil.
Its drainage makes it popular for wine, in regions such as La Mancha in Spain and Coonawarra and the Barossa Valley in Australia.
As red Mediterranean soil, the class is formally superseded by systems such as the FAO's but still in common use, and as of 1997 it remained in Israel's and Italy's national classifications.
Its equivalents are chromic Luvisols on the UNESCO/FAO world map and rhodustalfs in USDA soil taxonomy.
Red Mediterranean soils developed fastest from the Miocene to the Late Pleistocene, during large climate fluctuations.
The 1938 USDA taxonomy described terra rossa as deep red soils of higher rainfall than rendzina.

entries.title: Dark earth, the soil left by centuries of settlement

definition.text: A dark, organic-rich layer up to 1 m thick that, in geology and archaeology, marks long-lasting human settlement.

facts.text: Charcoal in its organic matter gives the dark colour, and it may hold fragments of pottery, tile, animal bone and other artefacts.
It is read as soil enriched with sooty remains of thatch from chimneyless houses and other waste, and in some areas it seems to add fertility.
Archaeologists first called London's dark earth 'black earth', renaming it to avoid confusion with chernozem, whose colour is traditionally attributed to humus rather than soot.
Soot was used on purpose: Hebridean farmers spread old thatch from black houses on their fields each spring, and Achill Island farmers spread the sods of smoke huts.
In England it covers many areas built up in the Roman period, especially Londinium, between deposits dated to the 2nd–5th centuries and the 9th century.
Archaeologists debate whether London's dark earth records Roman refuse disposal or gardening or formed only after abandonment; French findings tie it to a switch from stone to timber and straw.
For at least 700 years West African farmers have enriched rainforest soils around their towns with compost of kitchen, animal, farm and fire waste, making a signature dark earth.
In Sweden, dark earth covers 40 hectares at Uppåkra and 7 hectares at the Viking town of Birka.

entries.title: Why Amazonian charcoal still feeds the soil

definition.text: The low-temperature charcoal, a form of pyrogenic or black carbon, that indigenous farmers added to poor soils to make terra preta.

facts.text: Some terra preta holds up to 9% black carbon against 0.5% in surrounding soils, and other measurements found carbon 70 times higher than in nearby Ferralsols.
Poly-condensed aromatic groups keep the charcoal stable against microbial breakdown for thousands of years.
Slow oxidation of the charcoal creates carboxylic groups that raise the soil's cation exchange capacity.
Its porous structure retains organic matter, water and dissolved nutrients, as well as pollutants such as pesticides.
Fresh charcoal must first be charged with nutrients, for example by soaking two to four weeks in a liquid nutrient, or it briefly depletes available nutrients.
Low-temperature charcoal carries an inner layer of condensates that bacteria consume; charring at high temperature burns it off and adds little fertility.
The earthworm Pontoscolex corethrurus eats charcoal and mixes it, finely ground, into the mineral soil.

entries.title: Tropical peat, built from fallen trees

definition.text: A histosol of tropical latitudes, found in South East Asia, Africa and Central and South America.

facts.text: It forms mostly from dead trees rather than the sphagnum typical of temperate peat.
Its organic matter content usually exceeds 75%, with a low dry bulk density.
Tropical peatlands cover about 380,000 km², roughly 0.25% of Earth's land, yet hold 50,000–70,000 million tonnes of carbon, about 3% of global soil carbon.
About 46% of tropical peat area is in South America, though the world's largest tropical peatland is in the Democratic Republic of Congo.
Peat swamp forests yield timber, bark, resins and latex and shelter endangered species such as the orangutan.
Once the forest is cleared and the peat drained, surface peat oxidises and loses carbon rapidly as CO2, and the sinking surface causes local flooding.
Plantations, logging and fire are shrinking the carbon store; Indonesia's burning peat bogs contain more than 50 billion tonnes of carbon.
Leaving these emissions out underestimates the rise in atmospheric greenhouse gases and human-induced climate change.

entries.title: Red soil, the iron-stained clay of warm lands

definition.text: A reddish, clay-rich soil that typically develops in warm, temperate and humid climates and makes up about 13% of Earth's soil.

facts.text: Thin, highly leached organic and organic-mineral layers rest on a red layer of alluvium; the soil usually comes from weathered ancient crystalline and metamorphic rock.
High iron content gives colours from reddish brown to reddish yellow; Ultisols, Alfisols and Oxisols count as red soil once they develop this colour.
No single composition defines red soils, and one type may be infertile in one region but nutrient-rich in another.
Heavy leaching leaves them acidic and low in water-holding capacity, nutrients and humus; nitrogen is often deficient, and phosphorus and potassium run short after repeated harvests.
Liming raises their pH so acid-intolerant crops can thrive, though it can stimulate microbes that deplete organic matter and harm soil structure.
Organic manure, suitable tillage and crop rotation raise their organic matter, fertility and water retention.
They make up much farmland in tropical, subtropical and Mediterranean zones: about 102 million hectares in China and about 350,000 km², 10.6% of the country, in India.
India's red soils, nicknamed the omnibus group, formed on Precambrian granites, gneisses and quartzites; they are thin and poor in the uplands but deep, fertile loams on the lower plains.

entries.title: Brown podzolic soils, halfway between two kinds

definition.text: A class of the British soil classification, grouped with the podzolic soils but intermediate between podzols and brown earths.

facts.text: They form on hilly land in western Europe where more than about 900 mm of precipitation exceeds evapotranspiration for much of the year, so the profile is leached.
Their dark surface horizon holds more than 5% organic carbon, and unploughed examples may carry a mor humus layer.
Unlike true podzols they have no continuous E horizon: soil creeping downslope keeps supplying iron and aluminium oxides, which build up as a distinctive orange-brown B horizon.
The WRB calls them Umbrisols; they are common in Ireland, Scotland, Wales (about 20% of the country) and western England, and occur in the Appalachians.

entries.title: Bay mud, the soft floor of estuaries

definition.text: Thick deposits of soft, water-saturated, unconsolidated silty clay on the floors of certain estuaries, mostly in temperate regions shaped by glacial cycles.

facts.text: With low shear strength, high compressibility and low permeability, and a typical bulk density of about 1.3 g/cm³, it is hazardous to build on in seismic areas such as San Francisco Bay.
It forms from alluvial clay, silt and sand washed in by tributary streams and, in glacial periods, from a separate layer of silt, sand and organic detritus.
Heavy buildings need deep foundations on stiffer layers below the mud, and even then the surrounding ground settles over time, damaging utility connections.
Exposed at low tide it forms mudflats, feeding grounds for shorebirds and a substrate for eelgrass, cordgrass and pickleweed.

entries.title: Who made terra preta, and how

definition.text: The question of how Amazonian dark earths came to exist: made on purpose, built up from settlement refuse, or improved from naturally fertile patches.

facts.text: Early theories traced them to ashfall from Andean volcanoes or to sedimentation in ancient lakes or ponds.
Charcoal- and pottery-rich soil builds up by accident near dwellings, and many terra preta soils are now thought to have formed under kitchen middens as well as being made deliberately.
Recent research suggests terra preta may be natural, with pre-Columbian people using and improving scattered patches of existing fertility.
Variation among the dark earths leaves unclear whether all were made on purpose or whether the lightest are by-products of habitation.

entries.contested_note: Sources differ on whether terra preta was made deliberately, accumulated as refuse, or began as naturally fertile soil that people improved.

Many patches probably formed under kitchen refuse heaps, the kind described in {{ref:soil-hist-102}}. Recent research suggests terra preta may even be natural, with pre-Columbian people using and improving scattered patches of existing fertility. The soils vary so much that it remains unclear whether all were made deliberately, or whether the lightest are by-products of daily life.

entries.title: Recreating Amazonian dark soil

definition.text: A fertilizer made from materials meant to replicate those of terra preta, such as crushed clay, blood and bone meal, manure and biochar.

facts.text: Being particulate, it can move down the soil profile and add fertility and carbon to existing peds and aggregates.
Poor tropical soils can be enriched to terra preta nova by adding charcoal and condensed smoke.
It might sequester carbon while reversing declining soil fertility and desertification, but whether this works at large scale is unproven.
Terra preta sanitation pairs lactic-acid treatment in urine-diverting dry toilets with vermicomposting as an alternative sanitation option.

entries.text: Synthetic terra preta is a {{ref:soil-fert-001}} made from materials meant to copy those of the original: crushed clay, blood and ground bone, animal dung and charcoal made for soil. Because it is particulate, it can move down the soil profile and add fertility and carbon to existing peds and aggregates. Poor tropical soils can also be enriched to terra preta nova by adding charcoal and condensed smoke. It might lock away carbon while reversing declining fertility and the spread of desert, but whether this works at large scale is unproven. A related idea, terra preta sanitation, pairs lactic-acid treatment in urine-diverting dry toilets with worms that break down the waste.

entries.title: Brickearth, the wind-blown silt of southern England

definition.text: A superficial deposit of homogeneous loam or silt, first named in southern England, that is periglacial wind-blown loess.

facts.text: It was laid down in the Pleistocene, when wind picked up fine sediment from glacial outwash in cold, dry periods and dropped it where the wind slackened.
It lies in discontinuous spreads up to a metre deep across southern England and South Wales, with commercial deposits about 2 to 4 m thick in Kent, Hertfordshire and Hampshire.
Its name comes from brick-making: it needs little or no added material to make stock bricks, which harden at lower temperatures than clay bricks.
It gives rich, fertile farmland, but it collapses rapidly when saturated and makes a poor foundation for buildings.

It gives rich farmland, but it collapses rapidly when saturated and makes a poor foundation.

entries.title: Fill dirt, the earth used to raise the ground

definition.text: Earthy material used to fill a depression or hole, build mounds or otherwise artificially change the level of land.

facts.text: It is usually subsoil and underlying parent material, with little organic matter or biological activity, and may include sand, rocks and stones.
Fill should be as free of organic matter as possible, since decomposing organic matter leaves voids that make the fill settle and can damage structures on it.
Common uses are building up highway shoulders and raising low construction sites against flooding; Kansai International Airport stands on a new fill island of about five square kilometres.
Most fill is mined from commercial sand and gravel pits and must meet the gradation specifications set by the project's geotechnical engineer.

entries.title: Stagnogley, the waterlogged soil over a dense layer

definition.text: A non-alluvial, non-calcareous loamy or clayey soil with a dense, impervious subsurface horizon, classed among the gleyic soils.

facts.text: Continual waterlogging bleaches the topsoil; it often forms on sandy material over dense subsoil in cool, moist climates.
Nutrient-poor, often highly acidic and poorly aerated, it suits woodland such as English oak rather than crops.
Where saturated all year it becomes bog stagnogley and eventually bog, as in the missen of the Black Forest.
Related to the pseudogleys, stagnogleys occur in perhumid climates and on steep slopes, in Germany's Central Uplands and on the Midvale Ridge in the UK.

Related to the pseudogleys, stagnogleys occur in very humid climates and on steep slopes, in Germany's Central Uplands and on the Midvale Ridge in the UK.

Continual waterlogging bleaches its topsoil, and it often forms on sandy material over dense subsoil in cool, moist climates. Nutrient-poor, often highly acidic and poorly aerated, it suits woodland such as English oak better than crops. Where it stays saturated all year it becomes bog stagnogley and eventually bog, as in the missen of the Black Forest. Related to the pseudogleys, stagnogleys occur in very humid climates and on steep slopes, in Germany's Central Uplands and on the Midvale Ridge in the UK.

entries.title: Subaqueous soil, soil beneath the water

definition.text: Soil formed in sediment of shallow, permanently flooded environments, or in any area under water too deep for rooted plants to grow.

facts.text: Shallow-water sediments undergo soil-forming processes, can support rooted plants such as eelgrass, and meet Soil Taxonomy's definition of soil, opening a new frontier for soil survey.
Submerged soils formed on land and were later flooded by rising water tables, beaver dams or sea level rise; subaqueous soils formed under a continuous water column, as in an estuary.
Proposals to treat submersed sediments as soil date from the mid-1800s, but the US concept arose only in the early 1990s, pioneered by George Demas in Maryland's Chesapeake Bay.
Demas saw that these areas supported rooted plants and had formed horizons; later study showed additions, losses and transformations of energy and matter.
Soil survey inventories use an arbitrary water depth limit of 2.5 m, which some states have extended to 5 m.
Treating them as soils rather than sediments lets scientists study linked horizons across the underwater landscape, aiding management of shallow-water habitats and seagrass restoration.
Under submergence, as in rice fields, wetlands, estuaries and flood plains, nitrogen dynamics differ from those of aerated soils.

entries.title: Calcareous grassland, the grazed turf of chalk downs

definition.text: A grassland ecosystem on thin, basic soils such as those of chalk and limestone downland, also called alkaline grassland.

facts.text: Large areas occur in northwestern Europe, especially on Salisbury Plain and the North and South Downs of England; machair is a variant on calcium-rich shell sand.
Its plants are short, hardy grasses and herbs such as clover, held at a plagioclimax by sheep or cattle grazing.
It is an important habitat for insects, particularly butterflies and ants.
Its lichen communities, favoured by stable flints and nutrient-poor soil, have declined since the mid-20th century through reduced grazing, nitrogen deposition and habitat loss.

entries.title: Blue goo, the clay that slides off California hills

definition.text: A sticky, plastic, bluish-grey clay soil formed from highly weathered serpentinite mélange.

facts.text: Its colour comes from gleying under anaerobic conditions; a greyer variant is called grey goo.
It weathers from the Franciscan Complex, a mélange of greenstones, cherts, basalts, shales, sandstones, schists and serpentinites sheared between the Pacific and North American plates.
Its clay holds much water and drains poorly; saturated, it slips, especially in shallow soils under heavy rain, feeding landslides on the Northern California coast.
It has been found only in the Trinidad and Orick regions of Humboldt County, California.

entries.title: Takir, the bare clay flats of Central Asia

definition.text: A smooth, bare clay flat in the deserts of Central Asia, similar to a salt flat; the Turkic name means 'smooth, even, or bare'.

facts.text: A takir forms in a shallow depression of heavy clay soil that floods after seasonal rains.
As the water evaporates, a dried, fissured crust forms on the surface, often colonised by filamentous cyanobacteria.
Similar flats are called playas or salt flats in the southwestern United States and sabkha in Arab countries.
Calcisols were formerly known internationally as Desert soils and Takyrs.

entries.title: Serpentine barrens, grassland where forest should be

definition.text: Grassland or savanna on serpentine outcrops where the climate would otherwise support forest, found as an ecoregion in parts of the United States.

facts.text: Barrens are most likely where ultramafic rock never received richer sediment carried by water, glaciers or wind, such as loess, sand or volcanic ash.
They occur on altered ultramafic ophiolites in small, scattered areas of the Appalachians and the Coast Ranges of California, Oregon and Washington.
Grazing serpentine land carries metal risks: one study found toxic nickel in the kidneys of 20% of grazing animals and toxic copper in the livers of 32%.
Fire suppression turned Pennsylvania's Rock Springs barren from grassland to forest, while controlled burns since 1995 have restored sparse species at Buck Creek, North Carolina.

entries.title: The tough, rare plants of serpentine soils

definition.text: The distinctive flora of serpentine soils, marked by poor productivity, high endemism and tolerance of drought, heavy metals and scarce nutrients.

facts.text: Plants often have a stunted habit and dull, waxy grey-green leaves that help retain water and reflect sunlight.
Low calcium-to-magnesium ratios limit root growth and nutrient uptake, and heavy metals stunt growth and cause chlorosis; plants respond with deep roots, metal exclusion or storage, and tolerance.
In California 45% of serpentine-associated taxa are rare or endangered, and 10% of the state's plants are serpentine endemics.
Serpentine tolerance has evolved many times, and patchy, isolated habitats limit gene flow while promoting speciation.

entries.title: Duplex soils, sand over clay in Australia

definition.text: An Australian term for a soil with a sharp contrast in texture between its horizons, also called a texture contrast soil.

facts.text: In Northcote's Factual Key, the B horizon is at least one and a half texture classes finer than the A horizon, with a clear to sharp change within 0.1 m.
Topsoils range from coarse sand to clay loam and subsoils from light to heavy clay; some have a bleached A2 horizon.
Northcote used colour to separate brown, red and yellow duplex soils; the Australian Soil Classification spreads them among Podosols, Sodosols, Chromosols and Kurosols.
Similar soils in strongly seasonal climates such as the Mediterranean are called calcic and chromic Luvisols.

entries.title: Where terra rossa came from: three rival answers

definition.text: The long-running dispute among geologists, geomorphologists and soil scientists over what terra rossa formed from and how it relates to the carbonate rock beneath it.

facts.text: One group holds that terra rossa formed from the insoluble sediment and chert concentrated as the underlying carbonate rocks dissolved.
Another argues that residue alone cannot explain it: the soil is polygenetic, with parent material that includes volcanic ash, non-carbonate and wind-blown sediment depending on location.
A third group proposes that terra rossa formed by metasomatic replacement.

entries.contested_note: Researchers disagree whether terra rossa is the insoluble residue of limestone, a polygenetic soil with exotic sediment, or a product of metasomatic replacement.
entries.text: What is terra rossa made of? Geologists, geomorphologists and soil scientists have long argued over its origin and its link to the carbonate rock beneath, and they still disagree. One group holds that it is insoluble residue: sediment and chert left concentrated as the underlying carbonate rocks dissolved. Another says residue alone cannot explain it. In this view the soil is polygenetic, formed by more than one process, with parent material that includes volcanic ash and non-carbonate or wind-blown sediment, depending on location. A third group proposes metasomatic replacement, the chemical swapping of one rock's minerals for others.

entries.title: Constructed soil, built to bring dead ground back

definition.text: A mixture of organic and mineral materials, often including repurposed organic waste, designed to approximate natural soil and grow plants.

facts.text: Constructed soils reclaim degraded land without usable topsoil, such as mines, landfills and industrial or urban sites, and are classed as Technosols.
They are preferred to imported topsoil, since harvesting topsoil degrades a second site and usually costs more.
Layers thinner than about 45 cm tend to be uniform topsoil mixes; thicker ones can mimic natural horizons, using cheaper material for subsoil and a sand or gravel drainage layer.
Abrupt changes in texture and bulk density between layers govern lateral versus vertical water flow and perched water.
They combine a mineral fraction that sets texture, an organic fraction supplying nutrients and a slowly decomposing carbon source such as wood chips or biochar.
Topsoil organic matter should not exceed 15% by weight, or the soil settles and waterlogs, and a C:N near 20:1 gives a sustained release of nutrients.
They usually omit living organisms and lack stable structure, relying on biotic processes and pedogenesis to start as the site revegetates.
They must meet regulatory limits for pathogens, harmful trace elements, salinity and pH.

entries.title: Latosol, the deep red soil of the rainforest

definition.text: A tropical rainforest soil, also called tropical red earth, with a relatively high content of iron and aluminium oxides.

facts.text: Latosols are usually classed as Oxisols in USDA soil taxonomy or Ferralsols in the WRB.
Red or yellowish-red throughout from iron oxides, they lack the distinct horizons of a podzol and often reach 20–30 m deep, against 1–2 m for podzols.
A thin but very fertile humus layer from the forest above overlies an infertile layer stripped by rapid leaching under high rainfall.
Fertility depends wholly on the rainforest: once it is felled and the humus is no longer replaced, the nutrients leach away quickly.

entries.title: Gumbo, the clay that turns to sticky mud

definition.text: A soil dominated by very fine clay particles, often with small amounts of sand or organic material.

facts.text: Gumbo holds water exceptionally well, but rain turns it into a sticky mud that is hard to work with large farm machinery.
No-till farming on gumbo appears strongly correlated with higher yields than traditional tillage.

entries.title: Mesotrophic soil, the middle rank of fertility

definition.text: A soil of moderate inherent fertility, between eutrophic and oligotrophic soils.

facts.text: Base status, an indicator of fertility, relates the major nutrient cations (calcium, magnesium, potassium and sodium) to the soil's clay percentage.
It is commonly expressed in hundredths of a mole of cations per kilogram of clay, cmol(+) kg−1 clay.
