entries.title: Losing nitrogen even when the books balance

definition.text: Nutrients can be lost by leaching and runoff even when farm imports and exports are about balanced.

facts.text: In high-yielding corn, roughly 150–160 lb N applied matches the 160 lb in the grain, but much of the applied N is tied up in organic matter or lost by leaching or denitrification.
Corn needs large amounts of nitrate daily during its two-month growth spurt; pollution arises when fertilizer, manure and decomposing organic matter together supply far more than the crop needs.
Leftover nitrate after harvest can leach into groundwater in fall, winter or early spring, at roughly 30–70 pounds per acre depending on precipitation, and some may become nitrous oxide.
Losses are reduced by predicting crop needs from all N sources, timing application close to crop demand, and planting a quick-establishing cover crop.

entries.title: Grain trade as a nutrient pipeline

definition.text: Traded grain and oilseed crops carry carbon and nutrients between regions, leaving deficiencies in exporting soils and excesses in importing ones.

facts.text: The biggest transfers are corn and soybeans shipped from the Americas to East Asia, Europe and the Middle East, driven by demand for animal protein and oils.
The United States, Brazil and Argentina supply almost 90% of soybean and 75% of corn exports, and South America has met demand by converting grassland, savannah and rainforest to crops.
Exporting regions show less healthy breadbasket soils that have lost organic matter, while importing countries accumulate nutrients on livestock farms and see hypoxia in nearby seas.
Trade can also help: importing U.S. wheat raises selenium intake in Europe.

entries.title: Nitrogen-15 tracing: following one heavy atom

definition.text: A technique that uses the heavy stable isotope nitrogen-15 to follow and measure conversions within the nitrogen cycle.

facts.text: It separates simultaneous soil processes, such as ammonium being made by mineralisation while being oxidised and assimilated, which bulk concentrations alone cannot explain.
Natural-abundance methods express 15N as delta values relative to air and need no disturbance; the 15N site preference within nitrous oxide helps tell nitrification from denitrification.
Enrichment methods add 15N-labelled ammonium or nitrate, allowing precise rate calculations, though the added nitrogen can itself bias natural transformations.
Rates of simultaneous transformations are solved numerically, for example with the Ntrace model, based on a Markov chain Monte Carlo simulation.

entries.title: Fertilizer, the material behind up to half of every harvest

definition.text: Any natural or synthetic material applied to soil or to plant tissues to supply plant nutrients.

facts.text: Fertilizers can be distinguished from liming materials and other soil amendments that supply no nutrients.
Modern fertilization centres on three macronutrients, nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium, occasionally with supplements such as rock flour for micronutrients.
Fertilizers boost plant growth mainly by supplying nutrients; some also act by improving the soil's water-holding capacity and aeration.
Before synthetic products, fertility came from compost, animal and human manure, mined minerals, crop rotations and by-products such as fish waste or bloodmeal.
Application rates depend on the crop and on soil fertility, usually measured by a soil test; legumes fix their own nitrogen and generally need no nitrogen fertilizer.
Conservative estimates attribute 30 to 50% of crop yields to natural or synthetic commercial fertilizers.
Agriculture used 190 million tonnes of inorganic fertilizer nutrients in 2023, of which 112 million tonnes (58%) was nitrogen.
Excessive use can pollute water through nutrient runoff and eutrophication, and some mined fertilizers add heavy metals to soil.

entries.title: Compost, waste turned back into living soil

definition.text: A mixture of decomposed organic materials used as plant fertilizer and to improve the soil's physical, chemical and biological properties.

facts.text: It is made by decomposing plant and food waste, recycled organic materials and manure, and is rich in nutrients and organisms such as bacteria, protozoa, nematodes and fungi.
Compost feeds crops, conditions the soil, raises its humus or humic acid content, and adds microbes that suppress pathogens and soil-borne diseases.
It adds organic matter to the soil and increases both its nutrient content and the biodiversity of its microbes.
Compost improves fertility in gardens, horticulture, urban agriculture and organic farming, reducing dependence on chemical fertilizers.
Food and other compostables make up about 20% of landfill waste; composting them avoids the methane released when they decay without oxygen in landfills.
Compost is also used for land and stream reclamation, wetland construction and landfill cover, and composting in biopiles and windrows is a bioremediation technique.
Alkaline soils containing solid calcium carbonate can be reclaimed by working in compost and other acidifying organic materials.
Composting dates back at least to the early Roman Empire, described by Cato the Elder in 160 BCE; the first industrial composting station opened in Wels, Austria, in 1921.

entries.title: Soil conditioners loosen, feed and rebalance the ground

definition.text: A material added to soil to improve its physical qualities, usually its fertility and sometimes its mechanics.

facts.text: Soil conditioners are usually seen as a subset of soil amendments, a broader category that also takes in many fertilizers and non-organic materials.
Examples include biochar, bone meal, compost, manure, straw, peat, vermiculite, sulfur, lime, water-absorbing polymers, biosolids and rock flour.
Their most common use is loosening soil that has become compacted, since compaction hampers root uptake of water and nutrients.
Many add nutrients such as carbon, nitrogen, calcium, magnesium and phosphorus, and amendments can greatly raise cation-exchange capacity.
Organic material can greatly improve water retention in sandy soils, and conditioners can adjust pH for particular plants or make very acid or alkaline soils usable.
Soil testing should come before application to show which conditioner suits the soil.
Over-application can harm plants through excess salts, nitrogen and metals, and surplus nutrients can run off into waterways.
In construction, soil conditioning is also called soil stabilization.

entries.title: Mulch, a blanket laid over the soil

definition.text: A layer of material applied to the surface of soil.

facts.text: It is used to conserve soil moisture, improve soil fertility and health, suppress weeds, regulate soil temperature and improve appearance.
Mulch is usually organic but not always; it may be permanent, like plastic sheeting, or temporary, like bark chips.
Layers are normally 5 centimetres (2 in) or more deep.
Early in the season mulch warms soil by keeping heat otherwise lost at night, allowing earlier sowing; later it stabilizes soil temperature and moisture.
It cuts evaporation, but can also intercept light rain, and overly thick layers can reduce oxygen in the soil.
Mulches of manure and compost are worked into the soil naturally by worms and other organisms.
Mulch is also laid to prevent soil erosion on slopes.
Materials are chosen for availability, cost, appearance, effect on soil chemistry and pH, durability, decomposition rate and freedom from weed seeds and pathogens.

entries.title: Biochar, charcoal made to be buried

definition.text: A form of charcoal, sometimes modified, made by heating biomass with little oxygen and intended for use in soil.

facts.text: It is the light, black residue of carbon and ash left after biomass is pyrolysed; it is sterile when made and gains life only after contact with soil organisms.
In soils it is used mainly to improve aeration and fertility, cut greenhouse gas emissions and nutrient leaching, reduce acidity and perhaps raise the water content of coarse soils.
Applied in excess, or made from a feedstock unsuited to the soil, it can harm soil organisms, reduce available water, alter pH and raise salinity.
Its refractory stability lets it persist in soils for thousands of years, the basis of biochar carbon removal.
Pre-Columbian Amazonians made it by smouldering farm waste under soil in pits or trenches, though whether they meant to improve the soil is unknown; settlers called the result terra preta.
The word is a late-20th-century coinage joining the Greek bios, life, with char.
Beyond soils it serves slash-and-char farming, animal feed, concrete mixes and water treatment, where it removes heavy metals, dyes and organic pollutants.

Beyond soils, biochar goes into animal feed, concrete mixes and water treatment, where it removes heavy metals, dyes and organic pollutants.

Biochar is a form of Charcoal, wood baked without air, sometimes modified, made by heating biomass with little oxygen. What remains after this pyrolysis is a light, black residue of carbon and ash. It is sterile when made and comes alive only after soil organisms reach it. Farmers add it mainly to improve aeration and fertility, cut greenhouse gas emissions and nutrient leaching, and reduce acidity. It may also raise the water content of coarse soils. Too much, or a feedstock unsuited to the soil, can harm soil organisms, reduce available water, alter pH and raise salinity. The word, joining the Greek bios, life, with char, dates from the late 20th century, but the practice is older. Pre-Columbian Amazonians smoldered farm waste under soil in pits or trenches, and settlers called the result terra preta. Whether those farmers meant to improve the soil is unknown. Beyond soils, biochar goes into animal feed, concrete mixes and water treatment, where it removes heavy metals, dyes and organic pollutants.

entries.title: The hidden bill for feeding the world's crops

definition.text: The direct and indirect harm that producing and using fertilizers does to water, soil, air and ecosystems.

facts.text: Direct effects include runoff that causes ocean dead zones and contaminates waterways, degradation of the soil microbiome and accumulation of toxic compounds.
The IPCC Special Report on Climate Change and Land names fertilizer production and associated land use among the drivers of global warming.
Indirect impacts include nitrogen-crop-pest cascades, fracking for Haber process gas, and biodiversity loss and soil loss tied to industrial agriculture.
Most synthetic fertilizer depends on fossil fuel, with methane supplying hydrogen for ammonia; solar energy, waste treatment and electrolysis are proposed alternatives.
Excessive organic amendments such as pig slurry can also contaminate aquifers and eutrophy the waters they feed.
Policy responses favour sustainable or regenerative farming with less synthetic fertilizer, better soil management and more organic fertilizer.
Practices such as reduced tillage and buffer strips can lessen these effects.

entries.title: Feeding the crop when it is hungry

definition.text: Matching when and how much fertilizer is applied to crop needs, weather and the type of farming.

facts.text: Timing applications to peak nutrient demand is essential for yield and quality; uptake peaks from early to mid-season, so fertilizing near seeding works well.
For fall-planted grains such as winter wheat, autumn nitrogen followed by spring topdressing is likely the best combination.
Soluble fertilizers such as ammonium nitrate are not applied during heavy rain, which would carry most of it away and pollute the aquifer.
Conservation agriculture and smallholdings cut mineral fertilizer to the crop's strict needs, sometimes to none.
After harvest, a fast-growing, nitrogen-hungry catch crop such as white mustard can take up leftover nitrate before it reaches groundwater, then be buried to form humus.

entries.title: Nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium: the big three of fertilizer

definition.text: The nutrients fertilizers supply in varying proportions: chiefly nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium (NPK), plus micronutrients.

facts.text: Nitrogen supports leaf and stem growth; phosphorus root, flower, seed and fruit development; potassium strong stems, water movement, flowering and fruiting.
Nutrients are not applied as pure elements; fertilizers are made of compounds that contain them.
Macronutrients make up 0.15% to 6.0% of plant dry matter, and plants take up more than they need (luxury consumption) when overfertilized.
Nitrogen is the most important fertilizer element, being part of proteins, DNA and chlorophyll; atmospheric nitrogen is abundant but in a form plants cannot use.
Plants obtain nitrogen through weathering of nitrogen-bearing rocks and through fixation by some free-living and symbiotic bacteria, notably in legume roots.
Phosphate is needed for DNA, the energy carrier ATP and the phospholipids of cell membranes.
Calcium, long thought a luxury, is now considered essential for keeping plant cell walls and membranes intact.

entries.text: Three letters, NPK, sum up most of what fertilizers deliver: nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium. Fertilizers supply these in varying proportions, along with micronutrients. entries.title: Sorting fertilizers by nutrient count and origin

definition.text: The grouping of fertilizers by how many nutrients they supply, straight or multinutrient, and by origin, inorganic or organic.

facts.text: Straight fertilizers supply a single nutrient such as N, P or K; multinutrient or complex fertilizers supply two or more.
Inorganic fertilizers exclude carbon-bearing materials except urea and are also called synthetic, because chemical treatments are needed to make them.
Organic fertilizers are usually recycled plant- or animal-derived matter such as compost or manure.
NP fertilizers such as monoammonium phosphate (11% N, 48% P2O5) and diammonium phosphate (18% N, 46% P2O5) supply both nitrogen and phosphorus.
NPK fertilizers supply all three main nutrients: compound NPKs bind them chemically, while blends are physical mixtures of single-nutrient fertilizers.
Solubility varies: more than 90% of a typical superphosphate dissolves in water, against about 85% of MAP and DAP.

Compound NPKs bind the nutrients chemically, while blends are physical mixtures of single-nutrient fertilizers. The second scale is origin. Inorganic fertilizers exclude carbon-bearing materials, except {{ref:soil-fert-021}}. They are also called synthetic, because chemical treatments are needed to make them. The other class, covered in {{ref:soil-fert-010}}, is usually recycled plant- or animal-derived matter such as compost or animal dung. Solubility also differs between products. More than 90% of a typical {{ref:soil-fert-094}} dissolves in water, against about 85% of MAP and DAP.

entries.title: Nitrogen fertilizer, pulled from the air by industry

definition.text: Fertilizers that supply nitrogen, made from ammonia produced by the Haber–Bosch process.

facts.text: In this energy-intensive process natural gas usually supplies the hydrogen and the air supplies the nitrogen.
The ammonia is the feedstock for other nitrogen fertilizers such as ammonium nitrate and urea; nitrates are also made from it by the Ostwald process.
Common straight nitrogen fertilizers include ammonium nitrate with 34-35% nitrogen and calcium ammonium nitrate, a limestone or dolomite blend with 24-28% nitrogen.
Sodium nitrate (Chilean saltpeter) from the Atacama Desert was one of the original nitrogen fertilizers, used from 1830, and is still mined.
About a third of annual global food production uses Haber–Bosch ammonia, supporting nearly half the world's population.
Nitrogen fertilizer was used at about 110 million tons of nitrogen a year in 2012.
Only part of the nitrogen applied becomes plant matter; the rest accumulates in the soil or is lost as runoff.
In soil, bacteria such as Nitrosomonas oxidize ammonia to nitrite and Nitrobacter oxidizes nitrite to nitrate, which is highly soluble and easily leached.

entries.title: Urea, from urine and the laboratory to the field

definition.text: A simple organic nitrogen compound, CO(NH2)2, found in mammal urine and widely used as a nitrogen fertilizer.

facts.text: More than 90% of the world's industrial urea is used as a nitrogen-release fertilizer.
With 45-46% nitrogen it has the highest nitrogen content of common solid nitrogen fertilizers, so it is cheap to transport per unit of nitrogen, and it is non-explosive.
Soil bacteria with the enzyme urease convert it to ammonium, which roots take up; in some soils bacteria then oxidize the ammonium to nitrate.
Because nitrogen lost to air and runoff is wasteful and harmful, urea is coated in inert sealants or converted to urea-formaldehyde compounds that release nitrogen slowly.
Biuret, the most common impurity in synthetic urea, impairs plant growth.
Where it is cheap, urea is used to reduce soil alkalinity: ammonium from its hydrolysis displaces sodium from the soil's exchange sites.
Urea runoff from fertilized land may help make algal blooms toxic.
In 1828 Friedrich Wöhler made urea from inorganic starting materials, contradicting the doctrine of vitalism.

entries.title: Leachate, the liquid that carries a material away

definition.text: Any liquid that passes through a material and carries away dissolved or suspended components of it.

facts.text: In environmental science the term means a liquid carrying harmful substances that can enter the environment, most often from landfills.
Composting sites produce leachate in wet periods, as rain makes decomposed matter flow off as runoff.
Stockpiled coal and mine wastes yield leachate when sulfide minerals exposed to air form sulfuric acid, often rich in metals.
Acidic leachate flushed from acid sulfate soils can harm groundwater and surface waters, with effects that may persist or peak after dry spells.

entries.title: Agricultural lime, crushed rock against acid soil

definition.text: A soil additive of pulverized limestone or chalk whose main active component is calcium carbonate.

facts.text: Unlike quicklime and slaked lime, ground limestone needs no burning in a kiln, only milling; all these limes are used to supply a base that corrects acidity.
It raises the pH of acid soils, supplies calcium, improves water penetration and improves plant uptake of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.
Lime is not a fertilizer, though it can be used together with fertilizers.
Soils become acid through leaching under high rainfall, removal of minerals by crops, and reactions of modern chemical fertilizers in the soil.
Dolomitic lime has similar effects while supplying magnesium as well as calcium.
A soil test is the best way to tell whether a soil is acidic or short of calcium or magnesium.
Fields were once usually limed with burnt lime, because affordable fine milling of stone only developed after the mid-19th century.
Other amendments that raise soil pH include wood ash, burnt lime, magnesium oxide, basic slag, silicate rock dust and oyster shells.

entries.title: Liming: calcium against the aluminum in acid soil

definition.text: Adding calcium- and magnesium-rich materials such as marl, chalk, limestone, burnt lime or hydrated lime to soil.

facts.text: In acid soils these materials act as a base and neutralize acidity, often improving plant growth and soil bacterial activity, though oversupply can harm plants.
Most acid soils are saturated with aluminium rather than hydrogen ions, and their acidity generally comes from aluminium hydrolysis.
Sandy, heavily leached or strongly acid mineral soils are low in calcium and need liming, which can also offset the poor cation-exchange capacity that lets potassium leach.
Raising the pH by liming frequently relieves molybdenum deficiency by decreasing molybdenum sorption.
A German forestry study comparing stands two and twenty years after liming found it promoted nitrate leaching and lowered phosphorus in some leaves.
Modern liming was preceded by marling, the spreading of raw chalk and lime debris, with evidence dating to the 1200s in the British Isles.

entries.text: Most acid soils are saturated not with hydrogen ions but with aluminum, and their acidity generally comes from aluminum hydrolysis. entries.title: Carbon farming: putting the air's carbon back in the field

definition.text: A set of farming methods that aim to store carbon in soil and biomass, for a net removal of carbon from the atmosphere.

facts.text: Methods include changing tillage and grazing, using organic mulch or compost, working with biochar and terra preta, and changing crop types; forestry adds reforestation and bamboo.
Converting forest, grassland or savanna to cropland cuts soil organic carbon by about 30–40%, largely because harvests remove carbon-bearing plant material.
The loss can be countered by adding carbon, for example by leaving harvest residues, applying manure or rotating perennial crops with their larger root biomass.
More soil organic matter aids plant growth, improves water retention and reduces fertilizer use.
Gains are reversible: disturbance or intensive tillage turns soil into a greenhouse gas source, and after several decades soils saturate and stop absorbing carbon.
Plowing splits aggregates so microbes consume their organic compounds, briefly lifting yield before the lost structure reduces water holding and erosion resistance.
It costs more than conventional farming, US$3–130 per tonne of CO2 sequestered depending on region, and some countries subsidize it.
By 2016 carbon farming variants covered hundreds of millions of hectares of the nearly 5 billion hectares of world farmland.

entries.contested_note: Many researchers dispute the soil-carbon benefits claimed for managed grazing, and the effect of added soil carbon on yields is not settled.

Farmers change how they plow, graze and choose crops, spread compost or plant-based mulch, and work with biochar and terra preta. Leaving harvest residues, applying manure or rotating in deep-rooted perennial crops all add carbon back. The gains are reversible. Some claims remain disputed: many researchers question the carbon benefits claimed for {{ref:soil-env-090}}, and the effect of added carbon on yields is not settled.

entries.title: Perlite, volcanic glass that swells in the heat

definition.text: An amorphous volcanic glass, usually formed by hydration of obsidian, that expands greatly when heated.

facts.text: At 850–900 °C its trapped water vaporizes, expanding it to 7–16 times its original volume as a brilliant white material.
As a soil amendment it is highly permeable, holds little water and helps prevent compaction; alone it serves for hydroponics and rooting cuttings.
In potting mixes perlite and vermiculite improve aeration and water retention, and cacti and succulents need a large share of perlite or sand for drainage.

entries.title: Using finished compost on fields and in beds

definition.text: The use of finished compost on fields, in beds and in growing mixes to add organic matter and nutrients.

facts.text: On open fields compost is broadcast in a very thin layer, about 6 mm (0.24 in), and worked in before planting; 25 mm (0.98 in) or more is used to rebuild poor soils or control erosion.
Added to soil, coir or peat, it improves tilth and supplies humus and nutrients; tilled in, it raises organic matter and overall fertility.
It is rarely used alone but mixed with sand, grit, bark, vermiculite, perlite or clay granules; blends of 20–30% compost are common for transplanting seedlings.
Seeding directly into compost is not advised: it dries fast, immature compost may hold germination-inhibiting phytotoxins, and undecomposed lignin may tie up nitrogen.
Compost ready for use is dark brown or black with an earthy smell.
Compost can increase plant immunity to diseases and pests.

Finished compost supplies little readily available nitrogen, since composting converts much N to stable organic forms while P and K availability is unchanged; it still releases other nutrients slowly and raises organic matter.

Annual high rates set by nitrogen need overload soil with phosphorus and potassium, and salts may build up under high tunnels and greenhouses, so soil tests should guide a switch to legume cover crops.

entries.title: Inside a compost heap: carbon, nitrogen, air and water

definition.text: The aerobic decomposition of organic solid wastes into a humus-like material, compost.

facts.text: Composting organisms need four ingredients: carbon for energy, whose oxidation gives heat; nitrogen to grow; oxygen to oxidize the carbon; and enough water without waterlogging.
Aerobic bacteria need oxygen above 5%, so heaps are turned to keep up oxygen and the right moisture.
Bacteria and fungi turn the inputs into heat, carbon dioxide and ammonium ions, and the materials become humus over months.
Composting is most efficient at a carbon-to-nitrogen ratio of about 25:1; above 30 the mix is nitrogen-starved, and below 15 it tends to lose nitrogen as ammonia.
Green waste such as grass, leaves and food scraps supplies nitrogen and brown waste such as stalks, paper and wood chips carbon; fresh grass is about 15:1, dry autumn leaves about 50:1.
Balancing air and water keeps the heap at 130–160 °F (54–71 °C) until the materials are broken down.
On farms, manure is the usual nitrogen source and bedding such as straw or sawdust the carbon source; poultry manure needs blending with high-carbon materials and wet pig manure with straw.

entries.title: What heavy fertilizing does to life underground

definition.text: The changes heavy fertilizer use brings to soil organisms, from root symbioses to soil animals and microbes.

facts.text: High fertilizer levels, especially beyond plant needs, can break down the symbiosis between plant roots and mycorrhizal fungi.
Organic and organic–mineral fertilizers increase soil fauna abundance while mineral fertilizers do not, and chemical fertilizers boost microbial growth without changing diversity.
Acid stress combined with high nitrogen, rare before industrial agriculture, weakens links between aboveground and belowground parts of agroecosystems.
Nitrogen deposition is turning Sphagnum bogs from carbon sinks into carbon sources by stimulating decomposers.

entries.contested_note: Whether and how fertilizers affect soil animals is still debated, with group-specific responses masking overall effects.

Nitrogen deposition is even turning Sphagnum bogs from stores of carbon into sources of it, by stimulating decomposers. entries.title: The climate cost of nitrogen fertilizer

definition.text: The carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide released in making and using nitrogen fertilizer, estimated at around 5% of human greenhouse gas emissions.

facts.text: About one third of these emissions comes from production and two thirds from fertilizer use.
Soil bacteria convert nitrate to nitrous oxide, the third most important greenhouse gas, 296 times stronger per ton than carbon dioxide and a contributor to ozone depletion.
Human nitrous oxide emissions, mostly from fertilizer, were estimated at 700 million tons of CO2 equivalent between 2007 and 2016.
Ammonium-based fertilizers increase methane emissions from crop fields, notably rice paddies.

entries.title: Micronutrient fertilizers: tiny doses, outsized effects

definition.text: Fertilizers that supply elements plants need only in tiny amounts, typically boron, zinc, molybdenum, iron and manganese.

facts.text: Micronutrients occur in plant tissue at 0.15 to 400 ppm, less than 0.04% of dry matter, yet as enzyme co-factors their impact far exceeds their concentration.
They are supplied as water-soluble salts; iron is often given as a chelate such as EDTA or EDDHA, since at moderate pH and phosphate it turns insoluble.
Needs depend on plant and setting: sugar beets need boron and legumes cobalt, while heat or drought makes boron less available.
Zinc deficiency is common in soils worldwide, affecting both plants and people, and zinc fertilizers are widely used against it.

entries.title: Granules or solutions: the two forms of fertilizer

definition.text: The two physical forms in which fertilizers reach crops: granules, powders or prills, or water-based solutions.

facts.text: About 90% of fertilizers are applied as solids, most commonly urea, diammonium phosphate and potassium chloride.
Liquid fertilizers are solutions of ammonia, ammonium nitrate or urea; they act faster and cover more evenly, while granules are cheaper to ship, store and apply.
Adding fertilizer to irrigation water is called fertigation, used mostly on high-value crops such as vegetables, turf, fruit trees and ornamentals.
Fertigation places nutrients where the water goes and allows small doses, reducing fertilizer use and leaching.

entries.title: Why foods hold fewer trace minerals than they used to

definition.text: The question of why concentrations of micronutrients such as iron, zinc, copper and magnesium in many foods have fallen over the last 50–60 years.

facts.text: Intensive farming with synthetic fertilizers is often blamed, and organic farming is often proposed as the remedy.
Higher NPK-driven yields dilute other nutrients, but much of the decline is attributed to higher-yielding crop varieties with lower mineral concentrations.
Fertilizers more often cure trace deficiencies: zinc, copper, manganese, iron and molybdenum shortages found in Western Australia in the 1940s and 1950s are now corrected routinely.

entries.contested_note: Synthetic fertilizers are often blamed for falling micronutrient levels in food, but the source attributes most of the decline to higher-yielding crop varieties.

entries.title: Biofertilizers: living microbes as plant food

definition.text: A substance containing living microorganisms that colonize the rhizosphere or plant interior and promote growth by increasing the supply or availability of nutrients.

facts.text: Biofertilizers add nutrients through nitrogen fixation and phosphorus solubilization and stimulate growth through growth-promoting substances.
Their microorganisms restore the soil's natural nutrient cycle and build soil organic matter.
Plant-growth-promoting rhizobacteria and mycorrhizae increase nitrogen fixation, make inorganic phosphorus soluble, raise mineral bioavailability and produce hormones such as auxins and gibberellin.
They can reduce the use of synthetic fertilizers and pesticides but cannot yet replace them.
Reported yield increases reach about 10–40%, through nitrogen fixation and higher protein, amino acid and vitamin content.
They also suppress plant pathogens, protect against drought and other stresses, and detoxify pollutants below ground.
Effects vary between and even within environments, and are most marked in drier climates.
Compost, compost tea and vermicompost-based inoculants are also used as biofertilizers.

entries.title: Rock flour, ground stone that feeds the soil

definition.text: Fine, silt-sized rock particles made by glaciers grinding bedrock, or by artificial grinding to a similar size.

facts.text: Although clay-sized, the particles are ground quartz and feldspar rather than clay minerals; carried far by wind they form loess.
As rock dust it is used in organic farming as a soil conditioner supplying micronutrients; basalt and granite are richest, while limestone is often deficient.
A 2022 study found basalt dust raised available phosphorus, potassium, calcium and magnesium within months; in forests rock flour slowly raises soil pH and buffering.
Nutrient-poor soils may need 10 to 50 tonnes per hectare; the German miller Julius Hensel reported success with stonemeal in the 1890s.

entries.title: Marl, the clay-and-carbonate earth of lakes and fens

definition.text: An earthy material rich in carbonate minerals, clay and silt, which becomes marlstone when hardened into rock.

facts.text: Marls typically contain 35–65% clay and 65–35% carbonate, mostly calcite.
It forms in marine or fresh water, often through algae; marl lakes in recently glaciated areas and very rich fens deposit it from calcium-rich water.
It is used as a soil conditioner and to neutralize acid soil, adding calcium, improving structure and making other nutrients more available.
Because its carbonate is mostly calcium carbonate, marled crops may show magnesium deficiency unless magnesium is also supplied.

entries.title: Vermicompost, compost made by worms

definition.text: The product of composting with worms: a mix of decomposing food or plant waste, bedding and worm castings (vermicast).

facts.text: Red wigglers (Eisenia fetida or E. andrei) are the usual worms; composting worms are surface-dwelling epigeic species, while burrowing anecic Lumbricus species adapt poorly to shallow bins.
Worm castings hold fewer contaminants and more concentrated nutrients than the original materials.
It treats organic wastes faster than conventional composting, and vermicomposted manure has lower salinity and a more neutral pH.
It is richer in many nutrients than other composts, and the worm mucus coating castings slows nutrient release and keeps nutrients from washing away.
Microbial activity in worm castings is 10 to 20 times higher than in the soil and organic matter the worm eats.
Redworms feed fastest at 15–25 °C, survive 10 °C and may be harmed above 30 °C; bin moisture must stay above 50%, ideally 70–80%.
It can be mixed into soil or steeped as worm tea; the leachate draining from bins is different, uncomposted and may carry pathogens.
Worms also treat sewage: vermifiltration cleans wastewater or blackwater, and vermicomposting follows urine-diverting dry toilets in terra preta sanitation.

entries.title: Controlled-release fertilizer feeds crops slowly on purpose

definition.text: A granulated fertilizer that releases its nutrients into the soil gradually, over a controlled period.

facts.text: It is also called controlled-availability, delayed-release, metered-release or slow-acting fertilizer, and usually supplies nitrogen.
Conventional fertilizers dissolve and disperse; controlled-release ones are not water-soluble, so their nutrients reach the soil more slowly.
Release rate is set by low solubility in soil moisture, the breakdown of pellet coatings, and conversion of the chemicals into ammonia or another usable nutrient.
Most slow-release types are urea derivatives: urea-formaldehyde, first made in 1936 and sold from 1955, and IBDU slowly convert to urea in the soil.
Coated types wrap ordinary fertilizer in sulfur or plastic; sulfur-coated urea releases as soil microbes degrade the sealant and through cracks, typically over 6 to 16 weeks in turf.
On average 16% of conventional nitrogen fertilizer is lost as ammonia, nitrous oxide or nitrogen gas or in runoff, so slower release aims at more efficient use.
Controlled release protects crops from fertilizer burn, needs fewer applications and less fertilizer, and in most cases improves yield by more than 10%.
It can reduce nitrogen pollution behind eutrophication and nitrous oxide emissions, which arise when microbes act on ammonia faster than plants absorb it.

entries.title: Biochar in the field: big promise, uneven results

definition.text: Mixing biochar into or spreading it on soil to raise fertility, hold water and nutrients and store carbon over the medium to long term.

facts.text: Benefits are greatest in degraded tropical and nutrient-poor soils and smaller in temperate regions.
Its pores and high specific surface area make it hygroscopic, so it keeps water and dissolved nutrients in the upper soil and lowers fertilizer needs.

entries.title: Biochar carbon removal: locking carbon underground

definition.text: Carbon sequestration by turning biomass into biochar, whose stable carbon then stays locked in soil or other materials.

facts.text: Making biochar releases CO2, up to 50% of the biomass, but the carbon that remains is stable and can stay in the ground for hundreds to thousands of years.
The World Bank says biochar keeps 10–70% (about 50% on average) of the original biomass carbon and slows its decomposition by one or two orders of magnitude.
Removal also counts when high-quality biochar goes into construction materials such as concrete and tar, not only into soils.
Charcoal-rich black spots in Belgian arable soils, left by kilns before 1870, showed lower respiration and slower carbon turnover.
Biochar can also store carbon indirectly by raising crop yields while possibly slowing carbon mineralization.
A 2021 review put potential removal at 1.6–3.2 billion tonnes of CO2 a year; economically feasible estimates are roughly 0.3–1.8 Gt CO2 a year at carbon prices below US$100 a tonne.
Actual deployment is small: production is on the order of a few hundred thousand tonnes a year, giving well under 1 Mt CO2 of certified removal annually.
A 2018 study doubted enough biomass exists for significant sequestration, and some authors warn that inflated expectations could bring a boom and bust.

entries.contested_note: Sources disagree on how much carbon biochar can realistically remove: technical estimates reach billions of tonnes a year, while others doubt the biomass supply and warn of a boom and bust.

entries.title: The crew that turns waste into compost

definition.text: The chemical decomposers, such as bacteria and fungi, and physical decomposers, such as worms and insects, that break down compost.

facts.text: Bacteria are the most abundant and important, excreting plant-available nitrogen, phosphorus and magnesium; mesophilic or thermophilic kinds dominate depending on the phase.
Actinomycetota break down tough paper, bark, lignin and cellulose and give compost its earthy smell; fungi decompose woody material that bacteria cannot.
Earthworms eat partly composted material and excrete castings that make nitrogen, calcium, phosphorus and magnesium available, while their tunnels improve aeration and drainage.
Thermophilic bacteria, inactive between −5 and 25 °C yet present throughout soil, activate once mesophiles warm the heap and thrive at 40–60 °C.

entries.text: Bacteria do most of the work in a compost heap. They are the most abundant of the compost organisms, which range from chemical decomposers such as bacteria and fungi to physical ones such as worms and insects. Bacteria excrete plant-available nitrogen, phosphorus and magnesium. Moderate-temperature mesophilic or heat-loving thermophilic kinds dominate depending on the phase. Thermophiles, inactive between −5 and 25 °C, wake once mesophiles warm the heap and thrive at 40–60 °C. Actinomycetota break down tough paper, bark, lignin and cellulose, and fungi handle woody material bacteria cannot. Earthworms eat partly composted material, and their castings free nitrogen, calcium, phosphorus and magnesium.

entries.title: Compost tea, a brew of microbes for crops

definition.text: A liquid of fermented water extracts leached from composted materials, applied to crops.

facts.text: It is usually made by adding compost to water at 1:4–1:10 and stirring occasionally to release microbes, either with or without aeration.
Field studies show benefits from added organic matter, nutrient availability and microbial activity, and suppression of plant pathogens and soil-borne diseases.
Aerated tea brews faster with more microbes; non-aerated tea is cheaper, but studies conflict on its phytotoxicity and pathogen risks, and added nutrients can regrow E. coli and Salmonella.
Compost extracts are unbrewed, unfermented extracts in any solvent; aerated compost teas suppress pathogens more effectively than extracts.

entries.contested_note: Sources report debate over the benefits of aerating compost tea and conflicting studies on the risks of non-aerated tea.

entries.title: Composting at industrial scale

definition.text: Large-scale composting methods, chiefly in-vessel, aerated static-pile and windrow composting.

facts.text: In-vessel composting confines material in tanks or bunkers where airflow and temperature are controlled as in a bioreactor; it treats sewage biosolids, food waste and municipal organics.
In-vessel systems sanitize pathogens so the waste can be reclaimed as a soil amendment, while limiting odours, runoff and emissions.
Aerated static piles are kept aerobic by forcing air through perforated pipes instead of turning; roofs reduce leachate.
Windrow composting piles manure, crop residues and other wastes in long rows; such large operations can get hot enough to kill beneficial microbes while pasteurizing the waste.

entries.text: Large-scale composting relies on three main methods. In-vessel composting confines material in tanks or bunkers where airflow and temperature are controlled, as in a bioreactor. Aerated static piles stay aerobic by forcing air through perforated pipes instead of turning, and roofs reduce leachate. Windrow composting piles manure, leftover crop material and other wastes in long rows. Such large operations can get hot enough to kill beneficial microbes while pasteurizing the waste.

entries.title: The rise and fall of a compost heap's temperature

definition.text: The sequence of temperature stages that composting passes through under ideal conditions, from mesophilic to thermophilic to cooling and maturation.

facts.text: In the first, mesophilic phase, microorganisms decompose the material at moderate temperatures.
As the heap warms, thermophilic bacteria take over at 50 to 60 °C (122 to 140 °F).
As high-energy compounds run out the temperature falls through a cooling and a maturation phase, and mesophilic bacteria cure the compost, making it more bioavailable to plants.
Semicomposting, of volumes too small for full composting, never reaches a thermophilic stage.

entries.title: Hot compost in weeks, cold compost in a year
entries.article: Compost#Hot and cold composting – impact on timing

definition.text: Two ways of composting that differ in pile size and temperature, and so in how long they take.

facts.text: Composting time depends on the volume of material, the particle size of the inputs, and how much it is mixed and aerated.
In hot composting, the usual method of municipal and farm operations, large piles reach high temperatures and stay thermophilic for days or weeks.
The Berkeley method finishes compost in 18 days from at least 1 cubic metre of material, turned every two days after the first four, with C:N held at 30:1 or less.
Cold composting in piles under 1 cubic metre, such as most home heaps, can take up to a year; it needs no turning, but parts may go anaerobic.

entries.title: How a compost heap's heat kills germs

definition.text: The killing of pathogens and weed seeds by the heat of composting, and the suppression of plant pathogens by finished compost.

facts.text: Stabilized compost that has reached 50–70 °C poses very little risk, since these temperatures kill pathogens and even make oocysts unviable.
The temperature that kills a pathogen depends on the organism, how long the heat lasts (seconds to weeks) and pH.

Compost teas and extracts inhibit crop pathogens such as Fusarium oxysporum, Rhizoctonia and Pythium, and compost supplies biocontrol agents such as Bacillus subtilis; sterilizing compost weakens this effect.
Compost that has not passed 50 °C should be turned wearing a respirator and gloves, against diseases such as aspergillosis, farmer's lung, Legionnaires' disease and tetanus.

entries.title: How urea's nitrogen escapes into the air

definition.text: The loss of fertilizer nitrogen to the air as ammonia gas when urea breaks down at the soil surface.

facts.text: The enzyme urease hydrolyses urea to unstable carbamic acid, which breaks down without enzymes into ammonia and carbon dioxide.
The ammonia escapes unless it reacts with water to form ammonium, which plants can use and ammonia cannot.
The reaction makes hydroxide, raising pH near each urea particle to around 9.0, which increases volatilization and makes the zone toxic for several hours.
Without enough moisture, up to thirty percent of the available nitrogen can be lost to the air within seventy-two hours of application.
Losses rise with temperature, pH and drying soil; urea hydrolysed completely within two days on soils of pH about 8.2 or more but took twice as long at pH 5.2.
Surface residues and organic-rich soils carry more urease and so lose more, while about 0.1 inch of rain soon after application moves urea into the soil.
Incorporating or injecting urea reduces losses, because good soil contact buffers pH and slows ammonia formation.
Urea makes up more than fifty percent of the world's nitrogen fertilizers, so these losses matter for yields and costs.

entries.title: Fertilizer burn: when plant food parches a plant

definition.text: Damage to a plant caused by too much fertilizer, the wrong type of fertilizer, or too little water applied with it.

facts.text: Excess salt, nitrogen or ammonia impairs photosynthesis and respiration, causing visible burns.
When salts outside the root exceed those inside, water stops entering and may even leave the roots, so the plant responds as in drought.
Early signs are white salt marks and crusts around the roots; later the leaves brown and die, root growth stops and roots may rot.
Dry, overheated plants are most susceptible; salt burns are treated by heavy watering to wash the salts away, or by cleaning the roots and repotting.

entries.title: Potash, named for ashes soaked in a pot

definition.text: Fertilizers that supply potassium, made from potash, a mixture of potassium minerals.

facts.text: Potassium is the third major crop nutrient after nitrogen and phosphorus, and about 90% of potash goes to fertilizer.
The main potassium straight fertilizer is muriate of potash, 95–99% potassium chloride; others are potassium sulfate, carbonate or nitrate.
Potassium content is reported as K2O equivalent for comparison, though plants do not take up K2O and the fertilizers contain none.
The name comes from pot ash: plant or wood ashes soaked in water in a pot, the main way potash was made before the industrial era.
Potash ores are natural mixtures of sylvite (potassium chloride) and halite; mined ore is processed to separate KCl into a high-analysis potassium fertilizer.
World production exceeded 71.9 million tonnes in 2021, Canada producing most; China, the United States, Brazil and India are the largest consumers.
Potash improves the water retention, yield, nutrient value, taste, colour, texture and disease resistance of food crops.
Manure and glauconite (greensand) are low-potassium sources that pay to transport only short distances.

entries.title: Raised beds: soil that nobody walks on

definition.text: Gardening in soil raised above ground level and usually enclosed in a frame.

facts.text: The soil is usually enriched with compost, and crops are planted so close that their touching leaves suppress weeds and conserve moisture.
Because no one walks on the beds, the soil is not compacted and roots grow easily; beds also extend the season and avoid poor native soil.
Built along contour lines on slopes, they help control erosion and conserve water and nutrients.
Gardeners on heavy red clay Ultisols use raised beds or Hügelkultur to avoid amending the soil.

entries.title: Hügelkultur, a garden bed built on rotting wood

definition.text: A horticultural technique in which a mound of decaying wood and other compostable plant matter is planted as a raised bed.

facts.text: Advocates claim it improves fertility, water retention and soil warming; the term was first published in a 1962 German gardening booklet by Herrman Andrä.
Wood has one of the highest carbon-to-nitrogen ratios, so its decay may tie up soil nitrogen at first, lowering fertility for perhaps one to two years.
Peer-reviewed studies are few; a student thesis found hügel mounds held almost twice as much water as flat control plots.
Critics say it lacks genuine scientific principles and runs counter to soil building by litterfall, since in nature wood decays at the surface.

entries.contested_note: Permaculture advocates promote it on personal experience, while critics say it lacks a scientific basis and peer-reviewed evidence is scarce.

entries.title: Foliar feeding: fertilizer through the leaves

definition.text: Feeding plants by applying liquid fertilizer directly to their leaves.

facts.text: Leaves absorb nutrients through their stomata and epidermis.
In the 1950s H. B. Tukey and S. H. Wittwer at Michigan State traced radioactive phosphorus and potassium sprayed on leaves moving about one foot per hour through the plant.
It avoids leaching losses and helps most with phosphorus, zinc and iron, which soils fix or hold in poorly available forms.
It is best done in early morning or late evening below 24 °C (75 °F), since heat closes leaf pores in some species.

entries.title: Water-hoarding polymers that promised more than they gave

definition.text: Polymers such as polyacrylamides and polymethacrylates that absorb several hundred times their own weight in water, tested as soil conditioners.

facts.text: The first synthetic soil conditioners appeared in the 1950s, chiefly hydrolysed polyacrylonitrile.
Trials in agriculture, horticulture and landscaping from the 1960s stalled when the polymers proved phytotoxic from residual acrylamide monomer.
Even after monomer levels fell below toxic levels, few studies show these polymers improving plant quality or survival.
Such materials are judged on cost-effectiveness, how long they raise soil moisture, and their effects on microbes, nutrient levels and plant survival.

entries.title: Polyacrylamide, a synthetic binder for heavy clay

definition.text: Synthetic polyacrylamide polymers added to soil to improve its structure and how it handles water.

facts.text: Introduced in the 1950s as linear soil conditioners, they were presented at a 1951 symposium on improving soil structure.
Water-soluble forms increase pore space and infiltration in clay soils, make soil friable and let it dry and be worked sooner after rain.
Cross-linked forms hold water strongly and are used in horticulture, agriculture and some potting soils.
On construction sites they are used for erosion control to protect the water quality of nearby streams.

entries.title: Organic fertilizers: plant food from living things

definition.text: Fertilizers of biological origin, derived from living or formerly living materials.

facts.text: They include animal wastes, crop wastes, seaweed, compost and treated sewage sludge (biosolids), plus slaughter by-products such as bloodmeal, bone meal and feather meal.
The term also covers packaged products meeting organic farming rules, which limit or avoid synthetic fertilizers and pesticides.
Sewage sludge may be unacceptable in organic farming because of residual contaminants and public perception.
Most hold less-concentrated nutrients that are harder to quantify, but they can offer soil-building advantages.
Compost and similar materials can raise nutrient availability by improving cation-exchange capacity or by boosting microorganisms that free nutrients.
Peat, the most used packaged organic amendment, improves aeration and moisture but adds no nutrients, so it is an amendment rather than a fertilizer.
Fresh sawdust can draw down soil nitrogen as wood-decay fungi colonize it, a property that can also capture excess mineral nitrogen.
Their nutrient content, solubility and release rates are typically much lower than mineral fertilizers', which can make them slow-release and lessen the risk of over-fertilization.

entries.title: Manure, the oldest way to feed a field

definition.text: Organic matter, mostly animal feces, used as organic fertilizer in agriculture.

facts.text: Most manure is animal feces; compost and green manure are the other two main classes used in soil management today.
Manures build fertility by adding organic matter and nutrients such as nitrogen that feed soil bacteria and fungi, which in turn feed the rest of the soil food web.
Egyptians, Romans, Babylonians and early Germans are all recorded using manure or minerals to make farms more productive.
The term artificial manure, once in wide use, meant what are now called artificial fertilizers.
Adding manure, like compost or mulch, can change a soil's carbon-to-nitrogen ratio.
Long manuring leaves a mark in the profile: anthrosols of northwestern Europe often have plaggic or terric horizons, covering some 500,000 hectares.
Manure is also composted, bagged and sold as a soil amendment.

entries.title: Green manure, a crop grown to be plowed under

definition.text: A crop grown specifically to be worked into the soil while still green.

facts.text: Its biomass is ploughed or disced in, as with ordinary manure, mainly to add organic matter to the soil.
Green manuring often uses legumes such as clover and vetch, whose root-nodule bacteria fix atmospheric nitrogen, a natural fertilizer for the next crop, in organic and conventional farming alike.
Depending on the species, 45 to 224 kg/ha (40 to 200 lb/acre) of nitrogen is released, and usually 40-60% of the crop's nitrogen becomes available to the next crop.
As it decays it also releases phosphorus, potassium and sulfur, and deep-rooted species bring up nutrients shallower crops cannot reach.
Added organic matter and microbial mycelium and sticky substances improve aggregation, infiltration, water retention and aeration, and its roots can penetrate compacted soil.
While growing it suppresses weeds, helps control erosion, feeds pollinators, shelters beneficial insects and can reduce some pests and diseases.
Green manure also lowers the pH of alkali soils by generating humic acid.
Greek farmers ploughed beans into the soil by about 300 BC and the Romans used faba beans and lupines; colonists took the practice to North America.

entries.title: Animal manure, from farmyard straw to liquid slurry

definition.text: Manure made from livestock dung and urine, handled either as farmyard manure mixed with bedding or as liquid slurry.

facts.text: Farmyard manure includes straw bedding that has soaked up feces and urine; slurry is the liquid form from intensive units using concrete or slats instead of straw.
Manures from horses, cattle, pigs, sheep, poultry and other animals, and guano from seabirds and bats, differ in quality and need different application rates.
Sheep manure is high in nitrogen and potash and pig manure relatively low in both; cattle manure supplies nitrogen and organic carbon, and chicken litter is rich in nitrogen and phosphate.
Animal manure improves soil aggregation so the soil holds more water and nutrients, and it stimulates microbes that improve the supply of trace minerals.
Poultry droppings harm plants when fresh but become valuable fertilizer after composting.
Horse manure can carry grass and weed seeds, because horses do not digest seeds as cattle do.
Strong-smelling slurries, such as those from intensive pig farms, are usually injected into the soil to limit odour; pig and cattle manure is normally spread with a manure spreader.

entries.title: Bone meal, the slow phosphorus of ground bones

definition.text: Ground animal bones and slaughterhouse waste, used as a livestock supplement and as a slow-release organic fertilizer.

facts.text: It supplies phosphorus and calcium with little nitrogen; its N-P-K rating is typically 3–15–0, with about 12% calcium.
Being insoluble in water, it must be broken down by soil acidity or microbial acids, releasing nutrients only in acidic soils (pH < 7.0) over 1 to 4 months.
Liebig suggested dissolving bones in sulphuric acid around 1840, and the process was first used in Britain in 1841.
Before that, farmers on nutrient-depleted soils crushed bones collected from battlefields such as Waterloo and Austerlitz.

entries.title: Seaweed, a fertilizer from the shore

definition.text: Organic fertilizer made from seaweed and used to raise soil fertility and plant growth.

facts.text: Brown seaweeds are used most; seaweed may be laid as mulch, composted, dried and powdered, or made into liquid extracts.
It supplies macro- and micronutrients, humic acids and plant hormones, and can raise crop tolerance of low moisture, high salinity and freezing.
As a soil conditioner its humic acid and soluble alginates help clay soils short of organic matter gain better texture, aeration and water retention.
Heavy metals accumulated by seaweed may pass into crops, one of several challenges alongside the spread of diseases and invasive species.

entries.title: Guano, the seabird dung that fed the world

definition.text: The accumulated excrement of seabirds or bats, used as fertilizer.

facts.text: It is rich in nitrogen, phosphate and potassium; seabird and bat guano both exceed 40% organic matter, and bat guano may hold up to 6% available P2O5.
The word comes from Quechua, and Andean people may have used seabird guano from Peru's coastal islands as a soil amendment for as long as 5,000 years.
After Alexander von Humboldt studied it in 1802 and Humphry Davy praised Peruvian guano, it became popular in Europe in the 19th century.
The 19th-century seabird guano trade played a pivotal role in the rise of modern input-intensive farming.
European guano was poorer because high rainfall and humidity leached its potency.
Demand fell rapidly after 1910 with the Haber–Bosch process, but organic food has revived it in the 21st century.
Unsustainable seabird guano mining has destroyed habitat and killed millions of seabirds, and harvesting bat guano can drive bats from their roosts.

entries.title: What can go wrong with animal manure

definition.text: The health and environmental risks of animal manure, from pathogens and nitrogen losses to drug residues taken up by crops.

facts.text: Any manure can carry pathogens or food-spoilage organisms, spread by flies, rodents and other vectors, that threaten food safety.
Under intensive land use manure is applied less precisely than mineral fertilizer, so its nitrogen is used poorly, and it can emit the greenhouse gas nitrous oxide.
In 2007 a University of Minnesota study found corn, lettuce and potatoes taking up antibiotics from soils spread with manure containing these drugs.
Organic farming standards require non-organic manure to be rotted or composted first, to break down drug residues and kill pathogenic bacteria.

entries.title: Manure management: handling a useful hazard

definition.text: The capture, storage, treatment and use of animal manure in an environmentally sustainable way.

facts.text: Manure can be liquid, slurry or solid, and includes bedding and urine as well as feces.
A part of nutrient management, it aims to spread manure on fields in amounts that enrich soil without polluting water.
Stored manure gives off hydrogen sulfide, methane, ammonia and carbon dioxide, peaking when it is agitated for pumping; in confined spaces the gases can kill.
Hydrogen sulfide deadens smell at about 100 to 150 ppm, and 500 to 700 ppm can kill within 30 to 60 minutes.
About 33% of global ammonia emissions in 2018 could be attributed to manure.
Over-application can acidify soil and build up heavy metals, together reducing fertility.
Runoff and leaching carry nutrients, pathogens, antibiotics, hormones and heavy metals from manured fields to water, driving eutrophication.
Mitigating practices include anaerobic digestion to biogas and digestate, composting, separating solids from liquids, and vegetated buffer strips.

entries.title: Living mulch, a groundcover that grows with the crop

definition.text: Low groundcover plants grown under a main crop to slow weeds and give the other benefits of mulch.

facts.text: They are usually fast-growing plants that keep growing with the crop, whereas cover crops are worked into the soil or killed.
They may eventually need to be killed mechanically or chemically to stop them competing with the main crop.
Clovers can fix nitrogen, and creeping comfrey can gather nutrients from the subsoil.

entries.title: Organic mulch and the hidden cost of straw and sawdust

definition.text: Mulch of plant or animal residues, such as leaves, straw, bark, wood chips or manure, which decays over time.

facts.text: Straw, peat, sawdust and wood products can briefly slow plant growth because their wide carbon-to-nitrogen ratio lets decomposing microbes draw nitrogen from the soil.
Organic mulches can mat into a barrier to water and air, and vertically applied ones can wick water up and dry the soil.
Fully composted material is used to avoid phytotoxicity, and seed-free material to avoid bringing in weeds.
Peat moss can form a crust that water cannot soak into once wetted and dried, and it lowers surface pH, suiting acid-loving plants.

entries.title: Plastic mulch, the film over millions of acres

definition.text: Thin plastic sheeting laid over soil, with crops growing through slits or holes in it.

facts.text: It dominates large-scale vegetable growing, covering millions of acres worldwide each year.
Because it is impermeable, drip tape is usually laid underneath; black and clear films capture sunlight and warm the soil.
Polyethylene mulch must be removed at the end of the season, or it breaks into fragments that pollute the soil with ketones and aldehydes.
Biodegradable films of plant starches or sugars are broken down by soil microorganisms into water and carbon dioxide and can be tilled in.

entries.title: Sour mulch, when a pile smells of vinegar

definition.text: Organic mulch that has turned anaerobic and smells of vinegar, ammonia, sulfur or silage.

facts.text: It develops when nitrogen-rich material is not turned often enough and forms pockets of intense decomposition.
The anaerobic process makes small amounts of phytotoxic compounds, which can linger for a while after the material is aerated again.
Low-growing and newly planted plants suffer most, and some seeds may fail to germinate.

entries.title: How biochar is made: heat without flame

definition.text: Biochar is made mainly by pyrolysis, the heating of biomass without oxygen so that it decomposes instead of burning.

facts.text: Pyrolysis yields a solid (biochar), a liquid (bio-oil) and a gas (syngas); temperature, heating rate and residence time set the yield and can favour energy or char.
Gasifiers, which run through oxidation, drying, pyrolysis and reduction, make most biochar sold in the United States; their pyrolysis zone runs at 250–550 °C.

Smallholders make it without equipment by lighting crop-waste piles from the top and quenching the embers with soil or water, the top-down or conservation burn, which gives far less smoke than open burning.
Hydrothermal carbonization also yields a carbon-rich solid, but because the process differs the product is called hydrochar rather than biochar.

entries.title: Slash-and-char: clearing land without losing its carbon

definition.text: An alternative to slash-and-burn in which cleared vegetation is charred instead of burned, leaving biochar for the soil.

facts.text: Slash-and-burn leaves only 3% of the organic carbon in the soil, whereas slash-and-char can keep up to 50% in a highly stable form.
Shifting from slash-and-burn to slash-and-char could sequester an estimated 0.22–0.42 Gt of carbon a year.
Slash-and-burn soils soon lose their nutrients and are abandoned, whereas biochar-enriched soils can sustain cropping indefinitely.
The char, mixed with crop residues, food waste or manure and buried, can form terra preta, itself a product of Amazonian slash-and-char farming.

entries.title: What sets one biochar apart from another

definition.text: The physical and chemical makeup of a biochar, set by its feedstock and production method, which explains how it performs in a given use.

facts.text: Properties are grouped by proximate and elemental composition, pH and porosity; the International Biochar Initiative publishes standard evaluation methods.
Hydrogen-to-carbon and oxygen-to-carbon ratios track polarity and aromaticity, and both fall during carbonization as hydrogen- and oxygen-bearing groups are driven off.
Pyrolysis at 450–550 °C leaves amorphous carbon; hotter runs progressively convert it into turbostratic graphene sheets.
Higher production temperatures raise conductivity, aromaticity and intrinsic recalcitrance, which governs how long the carbon lasts.

entries.title: Night soil, the town's waste carted to the fields

definition.text: A historical euphemism for human excreta collected, usually at night, from cesspools, privies, pail closets and pit latrines.

facts.text: It came from sanitation without sewers or septic tanks, collected undiluted by water, and was sometimes carted out of town and sold as fertilizer.
Using unprocessed feces as fertilizer is risky: parasitic worm infections such as ascariasis are linked to night soil use because the eggs pass from person to person in feces.
Proper fecal sludge management, such as composting, reduces these risks, and human excreta can be safely turned into compost.
Ancient Athens channelled its sewage to the Cephissus valley as fertilizer, Edo's compost merchants sold feces to farmers, and Aztec chinampas were built of mud and human waste.

entries.title: Closing the loop: human excreta as fertilizer

definition.text: The use of treated human excreta for the plant nutrients, organic matter and energy it contains, most often as fertilizer and soil conditioner.

facts.text: Reuse in agriculture 'closes the loop' between sanitation and farming and is central to ecological sanitation.
Excreta-derived fertilizers include urine, dried feces, composted feces, fecal sludge, sewage and sewage sludge, each with different fertilizing properties.
Treatments such as urine diversion and drying of feces, composting, and sewage or fecal sludge treatment remove pathogens to varying degrees and reduce water content.
In Africa the nutrients theoretically recoverable from excreta match all current fertilizer use, offering smallholders an alternative to often unaffordable chemical fertilizer.
Unlike mined phosphate fertilizers, which can carry cadmium and uranium into the food chain, excreta-based fertilizers generally lack these heavy metals.
Their nutrients are bound in organic compounds or adsorbed on humic acids, so they release slowly and leach less readily than mineral fertilizers.
Like other nitrogen fertilizers they can cause nitrate leaching, while pharmaceutical residues in excreta degrade better in soil than in water.
Excreta and sewage nutrients have been used in farming for centuries, but often in unregulated and unsafe ways in developing countries.

entries.contested_note: The source says debate is ongoing about whether reuse of excreta is cost-effective.

entries.title: Biosolids: sewage sludge returned to the land

definition.text: Treated sewage sludge: solid organic matter recovered from sewage treatment and used as fertilizer or soil conditioner.

facts.text: Farmers began using sewage sludge in the 1920s, and research confirms biosolids hold nutrients similar to those in animal manures.
They can supply nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, sulfur and micronutrients, and are 60–65% organic matter that stimulates soil microbes.
Treated biosolids, in cake, granule, pellet or liquid form, are spread and worked into the soil or injected directly.
Biosolids can contain synthetic organic compounds, radionuclides and heavy metals; PFAS from spread biosolids has contaminated farm soils, groundwater, animals and crops.
Their use is controversial in some countries because of heavy metals and persistent pharmaceutical pollutants, and some places ban them on farmland.
Applying sewage sludge has been shown to raise soil available phosphorus and soil salinity.
One study found that high-temperature pyrolysis of biosolids into biochar reduced PFAS below detectable limits.
Treatment routes include anaerobic and aerobic digestion, composting, alkaline treatment that holds lime-mixed sludge above pH 12, heat drying and dewatering.

entries.title: Humanure, compost made from people

definition.text: Human excreta used as a nutrient-rich input to composting.

facts.text: In soil it builds organic matter and healthy microbial communities; feces supply nitrogen, urine phosphorus, and both are a good source of potassium.
Feces can carry bacteria, viruses and parasitic worms, but proper fermentation kills pathogens and parasite eggs within two weeks to six months, depending on climate.
Urine added to compost raises its temperature, helping destroy pathogens and seeds, and unlike feces it does not attract flies or carry worm eggs.
The term was coined by organic farmer Joseph Jenkins.

entries.title: The composting toilet: sawdust instead of a flush

definition.text: A dry toilet that treats human waste by composting, turning it into a compost-like material.

facts.text: Most use no flush water; a carbon additive such as sawdust, coir or peat moss is added after each use, making air pockets, improving the C:N ratio and reducing odour.
Most rely on mesophilic composting; long retention or a secondary composting step kills more pathogens and gives a humus-like product that can enrich soil where rules allow.
Nutrients in composting-toilet compost are more plant-available than in dried feces from urine-diverting dry toilets.
Using composting-toilet compost in one's own garden is regarded as safe, though legal restrictions may apply because pathogens can survive.

entries.text: Most composting toilets use no flush water at all. They are dry toilets that treat human waste by composting it into a compost-like material. Its nutrients are more available to plants than those in dried feces from urine-diverting dry toilets. Using it in one's own garden is regarded as safe, though because pathogens can survive, legal restrictions may apply.

entries.title: Urine, the nitrogen-rich share of human waste

definition.text: The use of human urine, rich in nitrogen (mostly as urea) and potassium, as a crop fertilizer.

facts.text: Urine carries about 70% of the nitrogen and more than half the potassium in sewage while making up less than 1% of its volume.
Design values are 4 kg nitrogen, 0.36 kg phosphorus and 1.0 kg potassium per person per year, about 7:1.5:2.2 as N:P2O5:K2O, varying with diet.
Its nitrogen content rises with the protein in the diet.
It is applied diluted, 1:5 for container crops or 1:8 for general use, because undiluted urine can burn leaves or roots, especially in dry soil.
Its fertilizing effect is comparable to commercial nitrogen fertilizers, and it holds far less lead, mercury and cadmium than sewage sludge.
Limits are excess nitrogen and salts such as sodium chloride; over-application can cause excess ammonia, acidity or other phytotoxicity.
In storage its urea is quickly hydrolyzed to ammonia; delivering it through perforated hoses about 10 cm below the surface cuts odour, volatilization and pathogen transfer.
Health risks are generally regarded as negligible, especially when urine is dispersed in soil rather than on edible plant parts.

entries.title: Azolla, the floating fern that feeds rice

definition.text: A genus of seven small floating aquatic ferns, the mosquito ferns, that host a nitrogen-fixing cyanobacterium.

facts.text: Its partner, the cyanobacterium Anabaena azollae, fixes atmospheric nitrogen and passes directly from one plant generation to the next.
It can double its biomass in 1.9 days and yield 8–10 tonnes of fresh matter per hectare in Asian paddy fields.
Planted in flooded rice paddies, it covers the water and suppresses weeds, then releases nitrogen to the rice as it dies; it is widely used as a biofertilizer in southeast Asia.
Rice farmers used it as a biofertilizer 1500 years ago; the earliest known written record is Jia Sixie's Qimin Yaoshu of 554 CE.

entries.title: IBDU, urea that dissolves slowly

definition.text: An organic compound derived from urea (IBDU) that acts as a controlled-release nitrogen fertilizer.

facts.text: Unlike urea, IBDU is not water-soluble, and its low solubility limits how fast it hydrolyses to fast-acting urea.
It is made by condensing isobutyraldehyde with two equivalents of urea, and releases nitrogen by the reverse reaction once dissolved.
Related urea-based slow-release materials include crotonylidene diurea and urea-formaldehyde products such as ureaform.

entries.text: Urea dissolves at once and acts fast. Isobutylidenediurea, or IBDU, does neither. This organic compound derived from urea is not water-soluble, and its low solubility limits how fast it hydrolyzes, splitting back into fast-acting urea. It is made by condensing isobutyraldehyde with two equivalents of urea. Once dissolved, it releases nitrogen by the reverse reaction, which makes it a controlled-release nitrogen fertilizer. Related urea-based slow-release materials include crotonylidene diurea and urea-formaldehyde products such as ureaform.
entries.text_plain: Urea dissolves at once and acts fast. Isobutylidenediurea, or IBDU, does neither. This organic compound derived from urea is not water-soluble, and its low solubility limits how fast it hydrolyzes, splitting back into fast-acting urea. It is made by condensing isobutyraldehyde with two equivalents of urea. Once dissolved, it releases nitrogen by the reverse reaction, which makes it a controlled-release nitrogen fertilizer. Related urea-based slow-release materials include crotonylidene diurea and urea-formaldehyde products such as ureaform.

entries.title: Bokashi: pickling food waste for the soil

definition.text: An anaerobic, fermentation-based composting method that turns food waste and other organic matter into a soil amendment using specialized bran.

facts.text: Waste inoculated with yeast, photosynthetic bacteria and lactic acid bacteria ferments for a few weeks in an airtight vessel and is preserved by lactic acid, much like silage.
Mixed into soil, the lactate-rich preserve is eaten by soil life, mainly bacteria, within a few weeks, and earthworm action gives the soil a vermicompost-like texture.
Unlike aerobic compost it barely heats, loses little carbon as carbon dioxide and almost no nitrogen as nitrous oxide or ammonia, and lowers the risk of nutrient leaching.
It began in Korea; Teruo Higa's commercial 'EM' (Effective Microorganisms) method of 1982 became the best known form.

entries.contested_note: Nobody disputes that EM starts the fermentation, but other claims, such as direct soil inoculation and whether benefits come from particular microbes, are robustly contested.

entries.title: Digestate, what remains after biogas is made

definition.text: The material left after anaerobic digestion of a biodegradable feedstock, the other main product besides biogas.

facts.text: Feedstocks include sewage sludge, livestock manure, energy crops such as maize, food and municipal waste, crop residues and industrial wastes, and they set its chemistry.
Acidogenic digestate is fibrous solid matter rich in lignin and cellulose that holds moisture well.
Methanogenic digestate is a liquid sludge high in ammonium and potassium.
The liquid fraction is up to 90% of the volume, with 2–6% dry matter and most soluble N and K; the solid fraction keeps most of the phosphorus.
Ammonia is usually 60–80% of its total nitrogen, up to 99% from kitchen food waste, and it carries more phosphorus and potassium than compost.
Its main use is as a soil conditioner: the solid part adds organic matter and water retention, the liquid part nutrients, and it can protect soil from erosion.
It is not technically compost, which forms aerobically and breaks down lignin and cellulose further.
Quality is judged on heavy metals, nutrients, pathogens and physical contaminants; in the UK, digestate meeting PAS110 ceases to be waste and can be sold as bio-fertiliser.

entries.title: Feces as fertilizer: nutrients plus carbon

definition.text: The use of treated human feces, dried, composted or as fecal sludge, to fertilize crops and add organic carbon to soil.

facts.text: By Swedish default values an adult excretes 0.55 kg nitrogen, 0.18 kg phosphorus and 0.36 kg potassium in feces a year, giving wet feces an NPK% of 1.1:0.8:0.9.
Post-treated dried feces from urine-diverting dry toilets raise crop yields through their nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium and improve soil fertility through organic carbon.
Urine can hold up to 90% of the nitrogen, 50% of the phosphorus and 70% of the potassium in human excreta.
Fecal sludge from pit latrines, septic tanks and dry toilets can be made fit for farm use by dewatering, drying, composting, pelletizing or anaerobic digestion.

entries.title: The multiple barrier approach to safe reuse
entries.article: Reuse of human excreta#Multiple barrier concept for safe use in agriculture

definition.text: A series of treatment steps and other precautions that together prevent pathogens spreading when excreta are reused in farming.

facts.text: World Health Organization guidelines of 2006 on safe reuse of wastewater, excreta and greywater rest on this concept.
Barriers include choice of crop, farming and application methods and farmer education; how much treatment is needed depends on which other barriers are used.
Temperatures above 50 °C, as in thermophilic composting or digestion, or pH above 10, from ammonia or lime treatment, inactivate most pathogens.
Helminth eggs, among the hardest pathogens to destroy, serve as indicator organisms in reuse schemes.

entries.text: Reusing excreta safely depends on a series of barriers rather than any single step. World Health Organization guidelines of 2006 on safe reuse of wastewater, excreta and greywater rest on this multiple barrier approach. Treatment is one barrier. Others include the choice of crop, farming and application methods, and farmer education. How much treatment is needed depends on which other barriers are in use. Temperatures above 50 °C, as in thermophilic composting or digestion, inactivate most pathogens. So does a pH above 10, from ammonia or lime treatment. Helminth eggs, the eggs of parasitic worms, are among the hardest pathogens to destroy, so reuse schemes use them as indicator organisms.

entries.title: Lime requirement: how much lime an acid soil needs

definition.text: The amount of lime needed to neutralize an acid soil, which soil-testing laboratories work out from the soil's base saturation.

facts.text: How far a given dose raises pH depends on the soil's buffer capacity, which is generally related to its cation-exchange capacity.
Lime must neutralize the acid-forming ions held on soil colloids, not just those in the soil water, or they will restore the original pH.
Low-CEC soils show a sharper pH rise but lose the added bases faster to leaching, so they return to acidity sooner unless limed again.
Over-liming is most likely on low-CEC soils such as sands that lack organic matter and clay to buffer them.

entries.text: The acid-forming ions held on soil colloids, the finest charged particles, must be neutralized along with those in the soil water, or they will restore the original pH. The lime requirement is the dose that does this, worked out by soil-testing laboratories from the soil's base saturation.
