entries.title: Does liming add or remove soil carbon?

definition.text: The net change in soil organic carbon after liming, the outcome of three processes pulling in different directions.

facts.text: Better growing conditions raise yields, returning more organic matter to the soil as dying roots and crop residue.
A more favourable pH briefly stimulates soil biological activity, speeding mineralization and turnover of organic matter.
Improved structure protects organic carbon from mineralization, as calcium-driven flocculation builds more stable aggregates.

entries.text: Liming changes the organic carbon stored in soil through three processes that pull in different directions. First, better growing conditions raise yields, so more organic matter returns to the soil as dying roots and crop leftovers. Second, a more favorable pH briefly stimulates soil biological activity, speeding mineralization and the turnover of organic matter, which works against storage. Third, calcium drives flocculation, building more stable aggregates, and that better structure protects organic carbon from mineralization. The net change is the balance of all three.

entries.title: Structure liming, lime that firms up clay

definition.text: Liming aimed at improving aggregate stability in clay soils, usually with calcium oxide or hydroxide mixed with calcium carbonate.

facts.text: It can reduce losses of clay and nutrients from soil aggregates.
High calcium concentrations and ionic strength in the soil solution enhance flocculation of clay minerals, forming more stable aggregates.

entries.text: Structure liming aims at the crumbs of a clay soil. It usually uses calcium oxide or hydroxide mixed with calcium carbonate, to improve aggregate stability. The lime brings high calcium concentrations and high ionic strength, a high total of dissolved ions, to the soil solution. Both enhance flocculation of clay minerals, which then form more stable aggregates. Firmer aggregates can reduce losses of clay and nutrients from the soil.

entries.title: Marling, one of farming's oldest soil fixes

definition.text: Spreading marl, or raw chalk and lime debris, on fields to improve the soil, one of the oldest soil amendments in agriculture.

facts.text: Marl was used sporadically in Britain from prehistoric times, and Pliny the Elder mentioned its use in the 1st century.
Wider use from the 16th century contributed to the early modern agricultural revolution; in 18th-century Lancashire almost every field had its marl pit.
Lime and imported mineral fertilizers gradually replaced marl early in the 19th century.
By the late 19th century New Jersey mined marl industrially, grading it and publishing detailed chemical analyses.

entries.title: How farm lime misleads archaeologists
entries.article: Agricultural lime#Effect on prehistoric mobility studies

definition.text: The distortion that agricultural lime introduces into strontium-based studies of where prehistoric people lived.

facts.text: The effect is significant in areas with calcium-poor soils.
In Denmark's Karup River catchment, more than half the strontium came from runoff of agricultural lime rather than the natural environment.
Comparing remains with lime-contaminated burial sites has led researchers to wrongly conclude that some prehistoric people came from far away.

entries.title: Calcium carbonate equivalent: rating a lime's strength

definition.text: A rating that compares a liming material's neutralizing power with that of pure calcium carbonate.

facts.text: Limestones containing dolomite can rate above 100 percent, because magnesium carbonate is lighter than calcium carbonate.
Soil acids are weak, so lime must be finely ground: particles over 8 mesh are of little value, 8–60 mesh somewhat effective, and finer than 60 mesh fully effective.
The effective calcium carbonate equivalent (ECCE) combines CCE with fineness; commercial aglime typically ranges from 45 to 110 percent.
Marl application rates are adjusted for its lower calcium carbonate content using the calcium carbonate equivalent.

entries.text: Some limestone outperforms pure calcium carbonate at its own job. Particles over 8 mesh are of little value, 8–60 mesh somewhat effective, and anything finer than 60 mesh fully effective. The effective calcium carbonate equivalent (ECCE) combines CCE with fineness; commercial aglime typically ranges from 45 to 110 percent. Marl, with less calcium carbonate, is spread at rates adjusted by its CCE.

entries.title: The lime that turned Brazil's cerrado into farmland

definition.text: The large-scale liming that turned Brazil's acidic, nutrient-poor cerrado into farmland from the 1960s on.

facts.text: Before the 1960s the inland cerrado was considered unfit for farming because its soil was too acidic and poor in nutrients.
Brazil spread 14–16 million tonnes of lime a year in the late 1990s, rising to 25 million tonnes in 2003 and 2004, about five tonnes per hectare.
The result helped make Brazil the world's second-biggest soybean exporter.

entries.title: One dose of compost that stored carbon for years
entries.article: Carbon farming#Using organic mulch and compost

definition.text: Spreading compost over the soil surface without tilling so that it stores carbon in a stable form.

facts.text: A 2013 study found a single compost application significantly and durably raised grassland carbon storage by 25–70%.
Forage output rose 78% at a drier valley site and 42% at a wetter coastal site, with no significant rise in methane or nitrous oxide emissions.
Composting is not an NRCS-approved technique, and commercial compost supplies are too limited to cover large areas.

entries.title: Can grazing cattle build soil carbon?

definition.text: The dispute over whether rotating livestock through small paddocks builds carbon in grassland soils.

facts.text: Rotating herds lets paddocks rest and favours deep-rooted perennials over shallow-rooted annual grasses that die once grazed.
Only a small amount of carbon may be stored in grassland soils through root exudates and manure, while ruminants also emit methane.
Many researchers argue the approach cannot deliver the benefits claimed, and studies find that excluding livestock from semi-arid grasslands can recover vegetation and soil carbon.

entries.contested_note: Advocates credit rotational grazing with building soil carbon, but many researchers dispute the claimed benefits and find livestock exclusion can do more.

Some studies find that simply excluding livestock from semi-arid grasslands recovers both vegetation and the carbon in the soil. The question remains open.

entries.title: How green manure feeds the next crop

definition.text: The breakdown of incorporated green manure by heterotrophic bacteria into nutrients available to the following crop.

facts.text: Warmth and moisture drive the process, as in composting, and the decaying matter gives off carbon dioxide and weak acids that free nutrients from insoluble minerals.
On soils rich in calcium minerals, green manure can raise the phosphate content.
The plant's carbon-to-nitrogen ratio, which varies with species and age, must be below 30:1 or decomposing bacteria will deplete soil nitrogen and starve the crop.
Working green manure in too short a time before planting can cause nitrogen immobilization, leaving too little for the next crop.

entries.title: Wood ash, a liming agent from the fireplace

definition.text: The powdery residue left when wood burns, made up largely of calcium compounds.

facts.text: As a fertilizer it supplies potassium and calcium carbonate, which acts as a liming agent to neutralise acid soils.
It typically holds 7–33% calcium, 3–10% potassium, 1–2% magnesium and 0.3–1.4% phosphorus; calcium carbonate may be 25% or even 45% of its weight.
Burning wood leaves about 6–10% ash on average; hotter fires leave less and drive off potassium, sulfur and boron.
It also carries trace heavy metals, such as lead at 2–500 ppm and cadmium at 0.18–60 ppm.

entries.title: The microbes inside a biofertilizer

definition.text: The organisms used in biofertilizers, longest among them the nitrogen fixers Rhizobium, Azotobacter, Azospirillum and blue-green algae.

facts.text: Rhizobium inoculant is used for legumes, Azotobacter for crops such as wheat, maize, cotton and potato, and Azospirillum mainly for sorghum, millets, maize, sugarcane and wheat.
Nitrogen-fixing blue-green algae such as Nostoc and Anabaena inoculate paddy crops; Anabaena with the water fern Azolla can add up to 60 kg/ha of nitrogen per season.
Other organisms used include Bacillus and Bradyrhizobium bacteria, Trichoderma fungi and Gigaspora mycorrhizal fungi.
Seaweeds rich in potassium, phosphorus and trace elements are widely used in coastal districts in place of manure.

entries.title: The salt index: how hard a fertilizer pulls on water

definition.text: A measure of how much a fertilizer raises the osmotic pressure of water, compared with sodium nitrate set at 100.

facts.text: Fertilizers with a salt index above 20 are not recommended for particularly sensitive crops.
Potassium chloride has a salt index of 116.2, urea 74.4 and diammonium phosphate 29.2.
Using too much fertilizer, or one with too high a salt index, builds up salts in the soil and causes burns.

entries.title: Coated urea: a shell that slows the nitrogen

definition.text: Controlled-release fertilizers made of urea prills coated in less-soluble materials such as sulfur or polymers.

facts.text: The coatings release urea gradually, lowering the risk of fertilizer burn and allowing less frequent applications.
Sulfur-coated urea, 32% to 41% nitrogen and developed by the Tennessee Valley Authority, releases once water enters cracks in the coating; a wax seal slows it further until microbes degrade it.
Polymer-coated urea releases nitrogen more precisely, with release delayable for 10 months, but costs more than sulfur-coated urea.
Combination products coat urea with sulfur and then polymer, a cheaper route to precise release.

entries.title: Urease inhibitors: buying time for urea

definition.text: Additives that block the urease enzyme so that urea fertilizer stays in its non-volatile form for longer.

facts.text: Most studies find they reduce nitrogen losses when fertilizer must be applied in poor field conditions.
They give rain time to carry urea into the soil, so hydrolysis happens below the surface and less nitrogen escapes.
They also shrink the zones of high pH around untreated urea, and help most in high-residue conservation tillage.
NBPT, a common inhibitor sold as an enhanced efficiency fertilizer, is mixed with urea at about 0.5% by weight.

entries.title: Stabilized nitrogen: slowing fertilizer down in the soil

definition.text: Chemicals added to nitrogen fertilizers to slow their conversion in the soil and so make them more efficient.

facts.text: Nitrification inhibitors, also called nitrogen stabilizers, suppress the biological oxidation of ammonia into nitrate, an anion more prone to leaching.

entries.title: Reading the three numbers on a fertilizer bag

definition.text: A label of three numbers giving a fertilizer's content of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.

facts.text: The numbers, separated by dashes as in 10-10-10, give the percentages of nitrogen, P2O5 and K2O.
Fertilizers contain no actual P2O5 or K2O; the oxides are a conventional shorthand for their phosphorus and potassium.
UK rules allow the elemental phosphorus and potassium values in parentheses after the standard figures, as in 15-30-15 (15-13-13).
Australia uses an N-P-K-S system that adds a fourth number for sulfur and gives elemental values for all nutrients.

entries.title: Ammonium nitrate, stable nitrogen with a dangerous edge

definition.text: A salt of ammonium and nitrate ions that is an important nitrogen fertilizer, with an NPK rating of 34-0-0.

facts.text: It is less concentrated than urea (46-0-0) but more stable, and does not rapidly lose nitrogen to the atmosphere.
It is made by reacting ammonia from the Haber process with nitric acid.
Natural deposits in Chile's Atacama Desert were mined until the Haber–Bosch process made nitrate mining obsolete.
It forms explosive mixtures with fuels, so it is a greater security risk than urea, which is not an oxidizer.

entries.title: UAN, the nitrogen fertilizer that stays liquid

definition.text: A liquid fertilizer made of urea and ammonium nitrate dissolved in water.

facts.text: The mixture has a very low critical relative humidity (18% at 30 °C), so it can only be used as a liquid.
Together the two salts are far more soluble than either alone, giving a stable solution with 32% total nitrogen.
The commonest grade, UAN 32, is 45% ammonium nitrate, 35% urea and only 20% water; UAN 28, UAN 30 and UAN 18 also exist.
The solutions corrode mild steel, and mixed with calcium nitrate solutions they form a precipitate that can plug nozzles.

entries.title: Management intensive grazing: many paddocks, short stays

definition.text: A grazing system that rotates animals through many paddocks and does not regraze one until its plants have regrown.

facts.text: Continuous or rarely rotated pastures produce poorly because repeated grazing of early regrowth depletes root reserves and weakens plants.
Rotation cycles run from about a week or 10 days up to 6-8 weeks depending on season and weather; dairy cows may get a fresh paddock after every milking.

Harvesting and fertilizing need little equipment or labour, and electric fencing makes new paddocks quick to set up; intensively managed pasture often lowers production cost despite the animals' foraging energy.

Well-managed pasture combines perennial forage, no tillage and regular manure; New York soil health scores for organic matter, active carbon, respiration, water capacity and aggregate stability were far higher under pasture.
Stocking is about 100,000 pounds of animals per acre for 8-12 hours, used to suppress or kill poor plant species and let hooves help reseed more productive ones.
Where animals roam large rangeland by day and are stocked densely at night, the carbon, nutrients and seeds they gather are excreted into the small area, boosting fertility and revegetation.
Grazing crop residue after grain harvest cuts feed costs and improves nutrient and carbon cycling; cattle grazing corn residue in winter on the Great Plains raised soil health and yields.
Swath grazing leaves annual crops such as barley and triticale cut in swaths for beef cattle, which improves forage access under deep snow.

entries.title: When farms specialize, the nutrient cycle breaks

definition.text: Specialized crop-only and animal-only farms break the nutrient cycle, causing nutrient excess on one and depletion on the other.

facts.text: Animal operations such as CAFOs often import feed from afar, so supplying crop farms need large fertilizer amounts to replace the exported nutrients.
Manure piling up relative to the land base can be applied beyond crop needs, polluting ground and surface water, and stored manure can contaminate surface water directly.
Animals excrete most of the nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium in their feed, so animal-product farms export few nutrients, whereas annual grain and vegetable farms export many.

Annual-only farms have little reason to grow perennial forages; growing only one or two annuals complicates weed control, forgoes multi-year grass and legume soil health, favours pests and demands much nitrogen fertilizer.
Integrating livestock can make a farm more sustainable but more complex, and done wrongly can add environmental problems.

entries.title: Nitrogen and phosphorus: two nutrients, opposite habits

definition.text: Nitrogen and phosphorus behave very differently in soils, which shapes how each is supplied, lost and managed.

facts.text: Nitrogen comes mainly from decomposing organic matter and can be added biologically by legumes, but no biological process adds phosphorus, which also comes from soil minerals.
Nitrate, the main form plants absorb, is very mobile, whereas phosphorus movement is very limited and its available form is a small dissolved amount, mainly H2PO4- and HPO4 2-.
Most N loss is nitrate leaching, denitrification or ammonia volatilization; leaching dominates in sandy soils and denitrification in heavy loams and clays.
Phosphorus is lost mainly in runoff and eroded sediment, but low losses have a high effect per unit on water quality because P often limits freshwater algae.
P leaching matters in artificially drained fields: after years of excess manure or compost, P-saturated sandy soils leak P, and liquid manure can flow through wormholes and cracks to drain lines.
Cover crops store nitrogen that would otherwise leach, and mobilize P through mycorrhizae and store it for the next crop.
Excess N pollutes water with nitrate, raises nitrous oxide from denitrification, wastes energy in manufacture, speeds loss of soil organic matter and is linked to more insect damage.
Making, hauling and applying N fertilizer is about 30 percent of the energy used to grow corn.

entries.title: Composting: what it gains and when to skip it

definition.text: Composted material is less bulky than the feedstock, so it is cheaper to transport and nicer to handle.

facts.text: The pile shrinks by 30-60 percent as carbon dioxide and water escape; heat kills many weed seeds and pathogens, odors and flies decline, and compost has about half the bulk and weight of manure.
Composting removes the nitrogen drawdown that follows adding sawdust or straw to soil, reduces nutrient solubility and stream pollution, and helps lower antibiotic levels in manure.
Compost stores easily for application when conditions are right, and lets farms with excess manure move nutrients to fields, gardens and landscapes that need them.

Direct addition of residues can be better: fresh residues stimulate more aggregate-binding gums, supply more readily available nutrients and cost less labour and energy; composting suits hard-to-handle, unsafe or odorous feedstocks, long hauls, pathogen concerns or good markets.

entries.title: Managing nitrogen and phosphorus: count, test, time, place, cover

definition.text: Nitrogen and phosphorus need similar management strategies even though they behave differently in soil: count all sources, test, time and place applications, and keep soil covered.

facts.text: Take all nutrient sources into account, using soil, manure and compost tests, crop residue N, and the 4R principles of right rate, time, place and source, plus conservation practices.
Place fertilizer below the surface, split N applications where leaching or denitrification threaten, and apply when leaching and runoff threats are minimal.

Cover crops with minimal or no tillage improve structure, cut leaching, runoff and denitrification, and store N and P in organic form between cash crops; reduced tillage also keeps mycorrhizal networks intact for P.
Sod-type forage crops in rotation reduce nitrate leaching and P runoff, and grass cover crops such as cereal rye capture leftover nitrate.
Time N close to crop uptake; holding most fertilizer until a PSNT, sensor or model shows need lets sidedress N be applied only if wanted.

entries.title: Tending a compost pile: air, moisture and heat

definition.text: Building and tending a compost pile so that air, moisture and heat stay in the range where composting microbes work well.

facts.text: Oxygen moves into a pile while carbon dioxide, moisture and heat rise out, so it must pass air yet hold heat; bulking agents such as chips or chopped straw keep fine material open.
Settled piles are about 3-5 feet tall and 6-10 feet across at the base, wider in winter to hold warmth; sites must be accessible yet away from watercourses, wells, flood plains and homes.
Ideal moisture is about 40-60 percent, like a wrung-out sponge; at 35 percent or less ammonia escapes as gas and molds replace beneficial organisms.
Temperature is the main monitor: the most efficient range is 104-140 degrees F (40-60 C), though piles reach 170 F, and overheating kills beneficial organisms too.

Turning creates a new hot center, since lower sides barely compost; farm compost may need only one or two turns, and a pile heating uniformly needs none, while too much turning dries the pile and loses nitrogen and organic matter.

entries.title: How much manure nitrogen a crop can use

definition.text: The share of the nitrogen in applied manure that a crop can use, which is hard to predict because nitrogen is the most dynamic nutrient.

facts.text: Phosphorus, potassium and most other manure nutrients stay in the soil and can be judged by soil testing, whereas manure nitrogen is easily lost with rain.
University and government guidelines give nitrogen availability factors, the fertilizer-N equivalent per pound of manure N; they suit planning but are imprecise because they ignore weather.
Spring applications use manure nitrogen better than fall or winter ones, since wet northeastern winters cause losses; the type of manure matters only modestly.
Prompt incorporation matters a great deal because much ammonia is lost from manure left on the surface, especially poultry and swine manure with more ammonium and urea than ruminant manure.
In the Penn State table, spring poultry manure incorporated immediately has a factor of 0.75 but only 0.15 if incorporated after more than 7 days or never.

A cover crop conserves fall and winter manure nitrogen by taking it up and returning it when terminated; analysis separating ammonia-N from organic N, and credits for earlier applications, refine the estimate.
Follow-up checks such as the pre-sidedress soil nitrate test, simulation models, remote imagery and crop sensors allow in-season correction of nitrogen.

entries.title: Biostimulants, neither fertilizer nor pesticide

definition.text: A substance, microbial culture or mixture used to promote crop growth that is neither a pesticide nor a fertilizer.

facts.text: A proposed standard definition calls it a biological product that improves productivity through emergent properties of its constituents, not merely through known nutrients, growth regulators or protective compounds.

Recognised constituents include humic substances, amino acids, inorganic salts, seaweed extracts and chitin derivatives; biological agents include growth-promoting rhizobacteria, non-pathogenic fungi and arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi.
Endophytic biostimulants from registered microbial strains have improved nutrient use efficiency and abiotic stress tolerance under field conditions.
With no agreed definition, as of 2016 no country had a specific regulatory framework for them; some treat them under fertilizer law.

entries.text: Some products help crops grow without being fertilizer or pesticide. These biostimulants are substances, microbial cultures or mixtures used to promote crop growth. Ingredients include humic substances, amino acids, seaweed extracts and chitin derivatives. Living agents include growth-promoting rhizobacteria and arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi. Registered endophytic strains, microbes living inside plants, have improved nutrient use efficiency and stress tolerance in the field. With no agreed definition, as of 2016 no country had a specific regulatory framework for them.

entries.title: The Guano Age, when bird droppings ran a treasury

definition.text: The 19th-century era of large-scale guano export, from Humboldt's investigations at Callao in 1802 to the War of the Pacific.

facts.text: From 1840 Peru made guano an exclusive state resource, and its royalties became the country's largest source of revenue.
By 1846, 462,057 tonnes had been shipped from Ichaboe Island off Namibia to Britain; the biggest markets in 1840–1879 were Britain, the Low Countries, Germany and the United States.
Peru's exports peaked above 700,000 tonnes in 1870 despite the near exhaustion of the Chincha Islands; afterwards Chile saltpetre eclipsed guano.
The US Guano Islands Act of 1856 let citizens claim unclaimed islands holding guano, and nearly 100 islands were annexed.

entries.title: Fixed versus adaptive nitrogen recommendations
entries.article: doc>geo.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Soil_Science/Building_Soils_for_Better_Crops_-_Ecological_Management_for_Healthy_Soils_4e_(Magdoff_and_van_Es)/19%3A_Management_of_Nitrogen_and_Phosphorus/19.02%3A_Management_of_N_and_P#Fixed and Adaptive Methods for Estimating Crop N Needs

definition.text: Methods to estimate crop N needs fall into fixed approaches, which ignore season-to-season weather, and adaptive approaches, which adjust with field data, sensors or models.

facts.text: The mass-balance approach, the most common, takes N uptake for a yield goal minus credits from soil organic matter, preceding crops and amendments, but yield and optimum N rate are only weakly related in humid regions.
Fixed methods suit drier climates but are very imprecise in humid ones.
Pre-plant nitrate and labile N tests, measured early in the season, work better in drier climates such as the Great Plains but cannot include seasonal weather.
Leaf chlorophyll meters and satellite, aerial, drone or tractor sensors assess canopy N status to guide sidedress N, and simulation models use radar rainfall and soil databases.

In humid regions yield and optimum N rate are only weakly related, so fixed methods suit drier climates but are very imprecise in humid ones. entries.title: Why this year's weather changes the nitrogen a crop needs

definition.text: Available soil nitrogen depends on recent weather, so crop need for supplemental N fertilizer shifts from year to year.

facts.text: Mineral N rises in spring but falls in a wet spring as leaching and denitrification exceed conversion to mineral forms; a drier spring leaves more.
Mineralization, leaching and denitrification vary with organic matter, amendments, soil temperature (warmer means more mineralization) and wetness (saturated warm soils lose much N).

Seedlings take up little N at first, then rapidly, so an unusually wet spring may need extra sidedress N; Minnesota corn trials 2015-2019 gained an average of 11 bushels an acre in a quarter of cases from sidedress N.
Dry years lower yields and N need, but a drought at pollination cannot be foreseen at sidedress time.
Soil tests work well for P because plant-available P is strongly adsorbed, whereas N tests cannot give all answers.

entries.title: How regular manure builds up phosphorus and potassium

definition.text: The accumulation of phosphorus and potassium in soil when manure is applied regularly at rates set by crop nitrogen need.

facts.text: Manure nutrient ratios are roughly equal to crop needs, about 2:1 nitrogen to phosphorus, so buildup is not caused by an unbalanced manure; it arises from nitrogen losses that force high rates.
Conserving nitrogen through timing, injection or incorporation lowers the manure rate needed, cutting P and K accumulation and the fertilizer N needed where P limits manure rates.

Erosion of P-rich topsoil carries sediment and phosphorus to streams and lakes; remedies include moving manure to other fields, soil conservation to trap sediment, and rotation crops like alfalfa that draw phosphorus down.
After many years the soil test P and K can reach excessive levels; all solutions need lower fertilizer P and P-containing amendments.
Remedies are exporting manure and using N fertilizer or legumes, spreading manure more evenly across fields, rotating to alfalfa, or sending manure to a neighbor or composting facility.

entries.title: Managing soils overloaded with phosphorus

definition.text: High-P soils result from excessive P fertilizer or, more often, heavy manure use, and they need managing to limit phosphorus loss to water.

facts.text: They are common on livestock farms with limited land and imported feed, where feed nutrients exceed those exported in animal products, and where manure or compost applied to meet N adds extra P.

Risk depends on context: sites near critical water with slope, fine texture, poor structure or poor drainage need aggressive measures, while flat, grass-bordered vegetable or urban plots pose far less risk.

First cut P in animal diets (a survey found US dairy herds fed about 25% more P than NRC advice), then stop extra P by spreading manure on more land, swapping fields, or using legume covers and forages for N.
Do not use a high-P source such as compost to supply N, since P builds up over the long term.
Reduce runoff and erosion with reduced tillage, contour strips, cover crops, grassed waterways and buffers; tile drainage can still carry P, especially after heavy liquid manure.
Soil-test P falls slowly once imports stop, so test every two to three years; a one-time tillage can redistribute P built up at the surface of no-till soil, followed by starter P and injected manure.
A survey found the average US dairy herd was fed about 25 percent more P than the National Research Council recommends.
The extra supplemental P can cost thousands of dollars for a 100-cow herd and ends up as a potential pollutant.

entries.title: Composts that help plants fight disease

definition.text: Composts can suppress root and leaf diseases of plants, according to research by Harry Hoitink and coworkers at Ohio State University.

facts.text: Plants become healthier because microorganisms produce plant hormones and chelates that make micronutrients more available, so they resist infection better.
Beneficial organisms compete with pathogens for nutrients, consume them or produce antibiotics, and springtails and mites devour pathogen propagules.
Composts rich in biodegradable organic matter support microbes that induce systemic resistance in plants against root and leaf diseases.

Composts rich in available nitrogen can stimulate phytophthora root rot, fusarium wilt and fire blight; applying them months ahead, leaching salts or blending with low-nitrogen compost lowers the risk.

entries.title: Liquid manure, from slurry pit to vegetable field

definition.text: A mixture of animal waste and organic matter, sometimes thinned with water, used as farm fertilizer.

facts.text: It can be aged in a slurry pit to concentrate it, and it was developed in the 20th century as an alternative to fermented manure.
Like solid manure it is rich in nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium that come from the animals' feed.
Powerful post-war tractors could haul heavy tanks, letting farmers spread liquid manure evenly near plant roots.

Concentrated animal feeding operations supply most liquid manure spread on US vegetable fields, a route for E. coli O157:H7; runoff from such operations contaminated wells in the fatal Walkerton outbreak.

entries.text: Post-war tractors changed how farms handle dung. Powerful enough to haul heavy tanks, they let farmers spread liquid manure evenly near plant roots. entries.title: Landfill leachate, the liquid that seeps from waste

definition.text: Contaminated liquid formed when rain or other water percolates through landfill waste, which can pollute groundwater if not managed.

facts.text: Its composition varies with the landfill's age and waste type; it carries dissolved and suspended matter, and decomposition adds organic acids, aldehydes, alcohols and simple sugars.
Risks are cut by siting landfills on impermeable ground or lining them with geomembranes or engineered clay; bentonite is used to line landfill bases.
In a 2012 New York survey, all double-lined landfill cells leaked less than 500 litres per hectare per day.
Granular laterite in constructed wetlands has removed phosphorus and heavy metals from landfill leachate.

entries.text: Rain falling on a landfill does not simply vanish. It percolates through the waste and emerges as landfill leachate, a contaminated liquid that can pollute groundwater if not managed. Its makeup varies with the landfill's age and waste type. It carries dissolved and suspended matter, and decomposition adds organic acids, aldehydes, alcohols and simple sugars. Siting landfills on impermeable ground, or lining them with geomembranes or engineered clay, cuts the risk; bentonite is used to line landfill bases. In a 2012 New York survey, all double-lined landfill cells leaked less than 500 liters per hectare per day. Granular laterite in purpose-built treatment beds has removed phosphorus and heavy metals from leachate.

entries.title: From ancient dung to factory nitrogen

definition.text: The development of fertilizer use from ancient manuring and minerals to the synthetic fertilizer industry that grew from the 19th century.

facts.text: Early farmers may have manured crops as long as 8,000 years ago; Egyptians, Romans, Babylonians and early Germans are recorded using minerals or manure.
Andean farmers used guano for at least 1,500 years before 19th-century Europe and the USA imported it in quantity from Peru and Chile.
Justus von Liebig, often called the father of the fertilizer industry, attacked Thaer's humus theory and stressed ammonia and then inorganic minerals in plant nutrition.
John Bennet Lawes began testing manures on potted plants in 1837 and in 1842 patented a manure of phosphates treated with sulfuric acid, founding the artificial manure industry.
Lawes and Joseph Henry Gilbert founded the Rothamsted station, which still studies how inorganic and organic fertilizers affect crop yields.
Industrial nitrogen fertilizer began with processes such as Birkeland–Eyde, which fixed atmospheric nitrogen into nitric acid; the Haber and Ostwald processes rose in the 1910s and 1920s.
Nitrogen fertilizer use grew 800% between 1961 and 2019, a crucial part of the Green Revolution's productivity gains.
Phosphate fertilizer use rose from 9 million tonnes a year in 1960 to 40 million tonnes in 2000.

entries.title: Turning an NPK label into real phosphorus and potassium
entries.article: Labeling of fertilizer#Converting nutrient analysis to composition

definition.text: Calculating a fertilizer's elemental phosphorus and potassium from the P2O5 and K2O values on its NPK label.

facts.text: P2O5 is 43.6% phosphorus by weight, so elemental phosphorus is 0.436 times the P value; K2O is 83% potassium, so elemental potassium is 0.83 times the K value.
The N value already gives elemental nitrogen by weight and needs no conversion.
An 18-51-20 fertilizer thus holds 18% nitrogen, 22% phosphorus and 17% potassium.
Pure potassium chloride, 52% potassium, would be labelled 0-0-63; sylvite, which contains other compounds, is usually labelled 0-0-60.

entries.text: A bag labeled 18-51-20 does not hold 51% phosphorus. Labels give phosphorus as P2O5 and potassium as K2O, so a simple calculation recovers the elements. P2O5 is 43.6% phosphorus by weight, so elemental phosphorus is 0.436 times the P value. K2O is 83% potassium, so elemental potassium is 0.83 times the K value. The N value already gives elemental nitrogen and needs no conversion. That 18-51-20 fertilizer thus holds 18% nitrogen, 22% phosphorus and 17% potassium. Pure potassium chloride, 52% potassium, would read 0-0-63; sylvite, which contains other compounds, usually reads 0-0-60.

entries.title: Ecological sanitation: closing the loop from toilet to field

definition.text: An approach to sanitation that aims to reuse human excreta safely in agriculture, closing the nutrient loop between sanitation and farming.

facts.text: It is an approach rather than a technology; urine-diverting dry toilets are its most common technology but not the only one.
Agricultural trials around the world show measurable benefits from treated excreta, especially urine, as fertilizer and soil conditioner.
It also answers a possible phosphorus shortage: one review suggested phosphate collected from urine could meet 22% of total demand.
How well its treatments destroy pathogens is still debated, though WHO reuse guidelines with a multiple barrier concept give a common framework.

entries.title: Manure as an asset, not waste

definition.text: Farm manure has considerable economic value as a source of nutrients and soil organic matter.

facts.text: After cheap fertilizer arrived post-war, manure came to be seen as waste to dispose of; it is better spread widely than concentrated in a few places.
U.S. manure from 100 million cattle, 120 million hogs and 9 billion chickens holds about 23 million tons of nitrogen.

Nutrients in manure from a 100-cow dairy may exceed $20,000 a year, a 100-sow farrow-to-finish operation about $16,000, a 20,000-bird broiler operation about $6,000; soil organic matter benefits may double the value.

entries.title: What manure contains

definition.text: A high share of nutrients in feeds passes through animals into their manure, where it is available for recycling on cropland.

facts.text: Over 70% of nitrogen, 60% of phosphorus and 80% of potassium fed may be excreted as manure.
Manure also holds calcium, magnesium, sulfur and micronutrients; zinc deficiency is rare on soils regularly receiving manure.
Analyses vary widely by feed, supplements, bedding and storage, so manure should be analysed routinely; average liquid dairy manure holds about 25 pounds N per 1,000 gallons but may be 10 or 40.
About 10 tons of dairy solid manure or 4,000 gallons liquid supply 100 pounds N; poultry needs about 4 tons or 1,500 gallons.
Poultry manure is significantly higher in nitrogen and phosphorus than other types.

entries.title: Composting in pits and closed vessels

definition.text: Composting in pits or closed vessels instead of open piles, for dry climates or small, controlled operations.

facts.text: Small farmers in developing countries, especially in dry and hot climates, dig compost pits; covering them with soil keeps animals out and retains moisture.
Home composters use vessels for easier turning, better temperature and moisture control and rodent exclusion, but vessels are generally not economical at commercial scale.

entries.title: Two kinds of crop-livestock farm

definition.text: Integrated crop-livestock farms grow all or nearly all of their animal feed and come in two general types.

facts.text: One type mainly sells animal products and matches animal numbers to the land's carrying capacity, such as grass-fed beef, pastured hogs or dairy growing its own grain and forage.
The other is the diversified farm that raises all its feed but sells a range of crops and animal products.
Multiple products protect against seasonal failure and price swings.
Crops feed animals and manure returns to the soil, giving a continuous supply of organic materials; perennial forages cut erosion and keep or raise soil organic matter.

entries.title: Solid, semi-solid or liquid: how dairy manure is handled

definition.text: The type of barn on a dairy farm frequently determines how manure is handled, as solid, semi-solid or liquid.

facts.text: Dairy manure with bedding at around 20% dry matter or more is spread as solid; liquid manure from free-stall barns is 2-12% dry matter; 12-20% is semi-solid, as with pasture cow manure.

Composting stabilizes nutrients, though considerable ammonium is lost, and gives less, more pleasant material to spread; separating liquid from solids lets solids compost without added material and eases transport.
Compost barns stir the bedded pack twice daily to 8-10 inches and clear it in spring or fall; vermicomposting uses worms to turn dairy manure into castings.
Industrial hog farms use slatted floors over pits and hold liquid manure in ponds for spring and fall spreading; small hoop-house hog systems use bedding.

entries.title: Maximum return to nitrogen for corn
entries.article: doc>geo.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Soil_Science/Building_Soils_for_Better_Crops_-_Ecological_Management_for_Healthy_Soils_4e_(Magdoff_and_van_Es)/19%3A_Management_of_Nitrogen_and_Phosphorus/19.02%3A_Management_of_N_and_P#Fixed and Adaptive Methods for Estimating Crop N Needs

definition.text: A fixed nitrogen recommendation method, used for corn, based on the rate with the largest average net return over many field trials.

facts.text: It draws on extensive field trials, model fitting and economics, and recommendations vary with grain and fertilizer prices.
Because it generalizes over large areas and many seasons, it ignores soil and weather effects and is imprecise for an individual field.

entries.title: How much nitrogen compost really supplies

definition.text: The higher the percent nitrogen in compost or another organic amendment, the larger the share of that N that becomes available to plants.

facts.text: An amendment with about 2 percent N or less (high C:N) supplies little to no available N, at about 5 percent N roughly 40 percent is available, and at 10-15 percent N 70 percent or more is available.
Fertilizer should supplement what soil organic matter, manure, compost and rotation or cover crops supply; organic farmers try to meet all demands from these sources.

entries.title: The pre-sidedress nitrate test
entries.article: doc>geo.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Soil_Science/Building_Soils_for_Better_Crops_-_Ecological_Management_for_Healthy_Soils_4e_(Magdoff_and_van_Es)/19%3A_Management_of_Nitrogen_and_Phosphorus/19.02%3A_Management_of_N_and_P#Fixed and Adaptive Methods for Estimating Crop N Needs

definition.text: A soil test of nitrate in the top 0-12 inches in late spring that guides sidedress or topdress nitrogen.

facts.text: It implicitly captures early-season weather and is especially good at identifying sites that need no more N fertilizer.
It needs special sampling in a short late-spring window and is sensitive to timing and early-spring mineralization; in the US Midwest it is called the late spring nitrate test.
It was the first approach to address dynamic N processes, giving more precise recommendations and cutting unnecessary N applications.

entries.title: Dung patches: uneven fertility on pasture

definition.text: Animals on pasture drop excrement on the surface, making small concentrated nutrient spots between which soil is poorer.

facts.text: Some ammonium and urea is lost to the air as the pies dry, and dense vegetation keeps runoff low and N leaching less of a concern.
Because the patches are unevenly spread, nitrate leaching can still occur on intensively managed, fertilized dairy pasture.

entries.title: When a herd outgrows its land

definition.text: Purchased feed brings nutrients onto a livestock farm that stay as manure, so a farm whose herd exceeds its land base accumulates them.

facts.text: Integrated crop-livestock farms that grow most of their feed keep nutrient imports and exports near balance.

Farms with animal numbers beyond their land's feed output risk nutrient buildup and groundwater and surface water pollution; options are sharing manure with neighbours, composting and selling it, or drying to ease transport.

entries.title: The Phosphorus Index: scoring the risk of runoff

definition.text: A tool for assessing the risk of phosphorus moving from agricultural fields to surface water.

facts.text: It combines source factors such as soil test P, total soil P and the rate, method and timing of P application.
It also counts transport factors: sediment delivery, field position in the watershed, conservation practices, precipitation, runoff and tile drainage.
A nutrient planner uses it to rate P movement risk as low, medium or high and to suggest mitigation.

entries.title: Three forms of nitrogen in manure

definition.text: Manure nitrogen occurs as ammonium, urea (soluble and quickly converted to ammonium) and solid organic N.

facts.text: Ammonium and urea are readily available but are lost as ammonia gas when left on a drying surface, with significant losses within hours.
Some manures have half to three-quarters of N in readily available form, others 20% or less; reports give ammonium and total N, the difference being mostly organic N.
Cattle manure is fairly balanced between available and organic N, while swine manure N is mostly ammonium or urea.

entries.title: How much manure to spread

definition.text: Manure is usually applied at rates judged to supply the current crop's nitrogen.

facts.text: Common dairy rates are 10-30 tons solid or 4,000-11,000 gallons liquid per acre, supplying about 50-150 pounds available N; small grains need 10-15 tons, corn 20-30 tons.
Higher rates may build organic matter but risk nitrate buildup in leafy crops, nitrate leaching, salt damage and excess soil phosphorus.
Where soil P is far above optimum, apply by crop P need and export part of the manure.
Manure on legumes is discouraged because the legume then fixes less N, though it can suit intensive animal farms with excess N.
Manure P and K availability resembles fertilizer; 20 tons of dairy manure give about 30-50 pounds phosphate and 180-200 pounds potash.

entries.title: Why corn wastes so much nitrogen

entries.title: Counting the nitrogen last year's crop left behind

definition.text: Nitrogen fertilizer decisions should subtract the N supplied by manure, decomposing sods and legume or cover crops.

facts.text: Example credits (pounds per acre): corn 0; soybeans 0-40; 2-year clover 70; 3-year alfalfa 70 (20-60% legume) or 120 (>60%); crimson clover, winter peas and excellent hairy vetch 110.
Credits are the N available to the crop, not the total in residue; sandy soils get less, and cover crop growth stage and amount matter strongly.
High-yielding legume covers such as hairy vetch and crimson clover can supply most or all of the N for the next crop; many labs do not ask about cover crops.

definition.text: Broadcast fertilizer covers 500-800 acres in eight hours against about 200 for injection, but in no-till it risks nitrogen and phosphorus losses.

facts.text: After intense storms, surface urea on no-till soil can wash into wormholes and deep into the subsoil, so N should not be broadcast and left on the surface; residue urease speeds urea conversion to ammonia gas.

entries.title: Curing: the last stage of compost

definition.text: The one to three month stage after hot composting, in which the pile cools and finishes its decomposition.

facts.text: Curing starts once temperatures drop to about 105 degrees F and no longer rebound after turning; a pile that reheats is not finished, and Solvita measures CO2 loss to judge maturity.
It further breaks down resistant chemicals and large particles, brings pH toward neutral, converts ammonium to nitrate, leaches soluble salts and lets common soil organisms colonize.
Moisture should stay at or below about 50 percent, and the early curing processes are thought to give compost some of its disease-suppressing quality.

entries.title: Turning manure into biogas

definition.text: Anaerobic digesters process manure on large livestock farms to make biogas, mostly methane.

facts.text: The gas fuels on-farm heat and electricity or off-farm vehicles, and digesters can cut greenhouse gas emissions, odors and pathogens.
They are a major capital investment and may not pay without subsidies, energy, carbon credits, tipping fees and coproducts.
They separate liquid and solids but generally do not change total nutrient content, so excess nutrients and runoff remain.

entries.title: Why manures differ in what they add to organic matter

definition.text: Equal amounts of different manures affect soil organic matter differently, depending on how much solid is returned.

facts.text: Dairy and beef manures hold undigested forage and bedding rich in lignin, so they influence organic matter far more than unbedded poultry or swine manure.
Sand bedding and separating solids return less organic material to fields, whereas a bedded pack is high in solids.
With corn silage under conventional tillage, 20 to 30 tons of solid dairy manure per acre yearly maintain organic matter; less is needed if more residue returns.
20 tons of manure holds about 5,200 pounds of solids; mixed into the top 6 inches it would raise organic matter about 0.3%, but if 75% decomposes the net gain is 0.065%.
New York samples of 300 fields showed dairy-crop fields receiving manure averaged 0.5% higher organic matter than cash grain fields.

entries.title: What years of manure do to a soil

definition.text: Manure application causes biological, chemical and physical soil changes.

facts.text: In an 11-year Vermont continuous corn silage experiment, 20 tons of dairy manure yearly kept organic matter and CEC levels and close to the original pH, offsetting a monoculture's low residue return.
Dairy and poultry manures have a liming effect and counteract acidification.
Manured plots were better aggregated and less dense; organic matter was 5.2% originally, 4.3% unmanured and 5.2% at 30 tons, with pore space 44% versus 47%.
Liquid manure supplying the same N would not have raised organic matter, CEC and pore space nearly as much.

entries.title: What manure loses while it waits

definition.text: Storing manure lets farmers apply it at the best time for the crop, cutting runoff, leaching and gaseous losses, but storage itself loses nutrients.

facts.text: In one study, dairy manure in uncovered piles lost over a year 3% of solids, 10% of nitrogen, 3% of phosphorus and 20% of potassium.
Covered piles and bottom-loading liquid systems with a surface crust conserve nutrients better; poultry manure may lose 50% of its nitrogen as ammonia unless protected.
Potassium is soluble, so a stack that lets water drain may lose much of it, since it sits mostly in the liquid portion.

entries.title: How surface manure loses its nitrogen to the air

definition.text: Ammonium and urea in manure left on the soil surface turn to ammonia gas as they dry and are lost to the air.

facts.text: About half of dairy manure N comes from urine urea, which converts to the ammonium that is almost all of its readily available N.
Surface-left dairy manure loses about 25% of its N after one day and 45% after four days, around 70% of the readily available N.
Half an inch of rain soon after application leaches ammonium in; incorporating the manure in spring helps, and fall injection of liquid manure greatly reduces loss compared with broadcasting.
Surface manure also risks nutrient runoff to surface waters.

entries.title: Timing manure to the crop

definition.text: Manure is best applied near the time the crop needs nutrients.

facts.text: For annual crops apply in one dose just before tillage so it is incorporated fast; injection close to planting cuts runoff and erosion risk.

Fall application in humid climates lets ammonium convert to nitrate that leaches or denitrifies; a three-year New York study found about twice the N leaching from fall as from spring liquid manure on corn silage.
Grass hay, constantly N deficient, does best with about 50-75 pounds available N in early spring and after each harvest; wet early-spring soils risk compaction.
Spreading on frozen or snow-covered ground is legal in most states but poor practice; injection into a shallow 2-4 inch frozen layer avoids runoff.

entries.title: Polyhalite, four nutrients from deep under Yorkshire

definition.text: An evaporite mineral, a hydrated sulfate of potassium, calcium and magnesium, used as fertilizer.

facts.text: It supplies four nutrients and is low in chloride: 48% SO3, 14% K2O, 6% MgO and 17% CaO.
As a soil amendment it can improve drainage and fertility and help reduce soil acidity.
The only polyhalite mined comes from a 260-million-year-old layer more than 1,000 m below North Yorkshire, worked at Boulby Mine since 2010.

entries.title: Nutrient budgeting, keeping the books on a farm's soil

definition.text: A comparison of all the nutrients applied to a farm's soil with all those removed from the land.

facts.text: Inputs include fertilizer, rainfall, brought-in supplements and spread effluent; outputs include sold stock, crops and products such as milk, meat and wool, plus nitrate leaching, volatilization and phosphate runoff.
A surplus, with inputs above outputs, builds up nutrients and the risk of loss; a deficit depletes reserves and risks deficiencies and lower yields.

Less exact than a financial statement, a budget draws on yield history, past applications, average removal coefficients and nutrients in irrigation water, and is a best management practice in the 4R strategy.
In turf, sensors and variable-rate application put fertilizer only where uptake potential is highest, shrinking the surplus and leaching into urban watersheds.

entries.title: Fertilizer placement: broadcast or banded with the seed

definition.text: Where fertilizer is put relative to the crop, such as broadcast over the field or banded with the seed, a choice that can strongly affect how efficiently crops take it up.

facts.text: Broadcast applications of urea beyond what plants use cause nitrous oxide emissions and water pollution.
Because hydrolysing urea creates a toxic high-ammonia zone, urea fertilizers should not be applied or banded with seed at more than 10–20 kg/ha, depending on the crop.
Fertigation places nutrients wherever the irrigation water goes.

entries.title: Phosphate fertilizers, from rock to soluble salt

definition.text: Fertilizers that supply phosphorus, extracted from phosphate rock whose main minerals are fluorapatite and hydroxyapatite.

facts.text: Acid treatment turns the rock's minerals into water-soluble phosphate salts; this use is the main reason so much sulfuric acid is made.
The main straight phosphate fertilizers are superphosphates: single superphosphate has 14–18% P2O5 plus phosphogypsum, triple superphosphate 44–48% P2O5 and no gypsum.
Billions of kilograms of phosphate rock are mined each year, but the remaining ore is shrinking in size and quality, making future supply a critical issue.
Each ton of phosphoric acid made from phosphate rock leaves five tons of phosphogypsum, an impure radioactive waste; 100 to 280 million tons are produced yearly.
A maize crop yielding 6–9 tonnes of grain per hectare needs 31–50 kg of phosphate fertilizer, and soybeans about half, 20–25 kg per hectare.
Phosphate, normally a limiting nutrient, is the main contributor to eutrophication, since high concentrations promote the growth of cyanobacteria and algae.

entries.title: The cadmium, fluoride and uranium in some fertilizers

definition.text: Contaminants such as cadmium, fluoride, uranium and other heavy metals that some fertilizers, especially phosphate and slag-based ones, add to soils.

facts.text: Cadmium varies widely: monoammonium phosphate can hold from 0.14 to 50.9 mg/kg, and phosphate rock up to 188 mg/kg.
Continued use of high-cadmium fertilizer can contaminate soils and plants, so producers now choose phosphate rock by its cadmium content.
Phosphate rock is rich in fluoride, so phosphate fertilizers have raised soil fluoride; plants take up little, so the greater concern is livestock that eat contaminated soil.
Uranium-238 runs from 7 to 100 pCi/g in phosphate rock and 1 to 67 pCi/g in phosphate fertilizers; heavy use can raise levels in soils and drainage water several-fold.
The added health risk from radionuclides in food is very small, less than 0.05 mSv/y.
Steel slag, recycled as an amendment for its calcium, magnesium and trace elements, can carry arsenic, cadmium, chromium and nickel, though it helps immobilize lead.
Mixing biochar into steel slag makes a good amendment for immobilizing heavy metals in farm soils.

Some fertilizers, especially phosphate and slag-based ones, add such contaminants to soils: cadmium, fluoride, uranium and other heavy metals. Continued use of high-cadmium fertilizer can contaminate soils and plants, so producers now choose phosphate rock by its cadmium content. Phosphate rock is rich in fluoride too, and phosphate fertilizers have raised soil fluoride. Plants take up little, so the greater concern is livestock that eat contaminated soil. entries.title: How fertilizer reaches rivers, lakes and wells

definition.text: The movement of nitrogen and phosphorus from fertilized land into surface water with rain and snowmelt, and into groundwater by leaching.

facts.text: Agricultural runoff is a major contributor to freshwater eutrophication, mainly through phosphate, which feeds algae and cyanobacteria whose decay uses up oxygen.
Nitrogen-rich runoff is the primary cause of serious oxygen depletion in coastal zones, lakes and rivers, and coastal dead zones are increasing.
Much of the nitrogen that plants do not take up, whether from synthetic or natural fertilizer, turns into easily leached nitrate; groundwater above 10 mg/L can cause blue baby syndrome.
Even where eutrophication can be reversed, decades and much soil management may pass before natural denitrification clears accumulated groundwater nitrate.

entries.text: Coastal dead zones are increasing, and nitrogen-rich water draining off farmland is the primary cause of serious oxygen depletion in coastal zones, lakes and rivers. Rain and snowmelt carry nitrogen and phosphorus off fertilized land into surface water, and leaching carries them down into groundwater. In fresh water the main culprit is phosphate. It feeds algae and cyanobacteria whose decay uses up the oxygen, the process of {{ref:soil-env-020}}, and farm drainage is a major contributor. Much of the nitrogen that plants do not take up, becomes easily leached nitrate. Groundwater above 10 mg/L can cause blue baby syndrome. Even where this can be reversed, decades of careful land care may pass before natural denitrification clears the accumulated nitrate.

entries.title: Phosphorite, the rock behind phosphate fertilizer

definition.text: Phosphate rock: a non-detrital sedimentary rock rich in phosphate minerals.

facts.text: Its grade ranges from 4% to 20% P2O5, against under 0.2% phosphorus in average sedimentary rock.
Fertilizer industry rock must be beneficiated, by washing, flotation and similar steps, to at least 28% P2O5, and most marketed grades reach 30% or more.
The phosphate is mostly fluorapatite in very fine masses, with hydroxyapatite often derived from bones and teeth.
Phosphorites form mostly in shallow marine settings, most commonly where strong upwelling brings deep phosphate-rich water to the coast.
About 90% of rock phosphate goes to fertilizer and animal feed supplements.
Mined rock is made into wet-process phosphoric acid, which with more rock gives triple superphosphate, or with ammonia gives ammonium phosphates.
World economic reserves were 70 gigatonnes in 2018, but high-grade ore is declining.
Beneficiated rock is sold as an 'organic' phosphate source, and an FAO report finds direct application can be more sustainable in certain soils and countries.

entries.title: Superphosphate, the first chemical manure

definition.text: A chemical phosphate fertilizer made by treating phosphate-rich material, first bones and later phosphate rock, with acid.

facts.text: First made in the 1840s from bones and sulfuric acid, it was then made from phosphate coprolites and later from phosphorite.
John Bennet Lawes patented his 'super phosphate of lime' and in 1842 began making it from fossil coprolites on an industrial scale, the world's first chemical manure.
Much of its phosphate is soluble and immediately available, giving plants a quick boost, and it is relatively cheap, so it is widely used in developing regions.
In soil, phosphate readily binds to clays, aluminium and iron salts or organic ligands, becoming largely unavailable to plants.
Single superphosphate comes from phosphate rock and sulfuric acid; triple superphosphate, mainly monocalcium phosphate, from rock and phosphoric acid; double superphosphate mixes both.
Typical fertilizer-grade triple superphosphate contains 45% P2O5 equivalent and single superphosphate 20%.
Continuous use can acidify soils, especially poorly buffered ones.
Its soluble phosphate, and phosphate bound to fine sediments, washes into rivers, where it is lost to farming and feeds eutrophication.

conflicts.text: Single superphosphate consists of 14–18% P2O5.
conflicts.note: Fertilizer page gives 14–18% for single superphosphate; Superphosphate page gives a typical 20% P2O5 equivalent.

entries.title: Peak phosphorus: will the rock run out?

definition.text: The potential shortage of economically mineable phosphorus, a limited resource used up by fertilizer production.

facts.text: A shortage of mined phosphorus would threaten worldwide food security.
The term arose from the limited occurrence of rock phosphate; one estimate puts the US peak in 1988 and the world peak in 1989.
Phosphorus recovered from excreta, for example as struvite from urine or from sludge treatment liquids, is an alternative to mined phosphate ore.
Using less fertilizer, as when mycorrhizal inoculants allow lower rates, helps prolong finite phosphorus reserves.

conflicts.text: Peak phosphorus will occur within the next few hundred years, or perhaps earlier.
conflicts.note: Sustainable agriculture puts the world peak in the future; Soil fertility (S:2da45bb19b64) estimates it already occurred in 1989.

entries.text: Phosphorus for fertilizer comes from a limited resource, and a shortage of mined phosphorus would threaten food security worldwide. And using less fertilizer, as when mycorrhizal inoculants allow lower rates, helps prolong the finite reserves.

entries.title: Phosphate-rich organic manure: compost that unlocks rock

definition.text: An organic fertilizer made by co-composting rock phosphate, used as an alternative to diammonium phosphate and single superphosphate.

facts.text: It is made by co-composting very finely ground (80% finer than 54 microns) high-grade rock phosphate of 32% ± 2% P2O5; the finer the rock, the better it works.
Rock phosphate holds its phosphorus as insoluble tricalcium phosphate; microbial organic acids slowly dissolve it, and the organic matter stops other ions locking phosphorus into insoluble forms.
Phosphorus dissolves best between pH 5.5 and 7: aluminium, iron and manganese hold pH below 5.5, and magnesium and calcium keep it above 7, both blocking release.
It may add phosphorus more efficiently than chemical fertilizers and feeds a second crop as well as the first; acidic waste solids from biogas plants can be used to make it.

entries.title: Diammonium phosphate and its delayed acid twist

definition.text: A water-soluble ammonium phosphate salt, (NH4)2HPO4, made by reacting ammonia with phosphoric acid and used as fertilizer.

facts.text: Its typical NPK rating is 18-46-0: 18% nitrogen, 46% P2O5 and no K2O.
It raises soil pH at first, but over the long term the ground becomes more acidic than before as its ammonium is nitrified.
Its solution averages pH 7.5–8, and it is incompatible with alkaline chemicals, which turn its ammonium into ammonia.
It slowly loses ammonia in air and breaks down to ammonia and monoammonium phosphate at around 70 °C.

entries.title: Struvite, the mineral that clogs pipes and feeds crops

definition.text: Magnesium ammonium phosphate, a phosphate mineral with formula NH4MgPO4·6H2O.

facts.text: It forms in alkaline conditions from equal molar amounts of magnesium, ammonium and phosphate, and dissolves readily in acid but only sparingly in neutral or alkaline water.
It scales pipes and pumps in wastewater plants, especially after anaerobic digesters release ammonium and phosphate.
Recovering phosphorus from manure and municipal wastewater as struvite for fertilizer appears promising.
First described as a fertilizer in 1857, it supplies phosphorus, nitrogen and magnesium, and can be made from urine by raising pH and adding magnesium.

entries.title: Phosphogypsum, the radioactive leftover of fertilizer acid

definition.text: The calcium sulfate hydrate, mainly gypsum, left as a by-product when phosphoric acid for fertilizer is made from phosphate rock.

facts.text: About five tons form per ton of phosphoric acid, an estimated 100 to 280 million tonnes a year worldwide.
Uranium at 5–10 ppm, thorium and their daughter nuclides make it weakly radioactive, so most is stored indefinitely; up to 15% of production is used, partly as a soil amendment.
In 1990 the US EPA banned most uses of phosphogypsum with more than 10 picocuries of radium-226 per gram.
It can pollute through phosphorus that drives eutrophication, toxic heavy metals and radioactivity, and its contents leach into groundwater and soil.

entries.contested_note: Long-term storage of phosphogypsum is called controversial, and the EPA approved its use in roads in 2020 over environmentalists' objections, then withdrew the rule in 2021.

entries.title: The water cycle, a sun-driven loop through the soil

definition.text: The continuous movement of water, changing form as it goes, between reservoirs on, above and below the Earth's surface.

facts.text: Its fluxes are evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation, sublimation, infiltration, surface runoff and subsurface flow, all powered by energy from the sun.
Rain reaching land either flows over the ground as surface runoff or soaks in by infiltration, becoming soil moisture or groundwater.
Shallow infiltrated water may seep back to streams or be taken up and transpired by plants; deeper water recharges aquifers, where it can stay for thousands of years.
Evapotranspiration combines water transpired by plants with water evaporated from the soil.
About 505,000 km3 (121,000 cu mi) of water falls as precipitation each year, 398,000 km3 (95,000 cu mi) of it over the oceans.
Flowing water reshapes the land through weathering, erosion and deposition, and runoff carries almost all eroded sediment and phosphorus from land to water bodies.
A global study of stable water isotopes found that not all soil moisture is equally available for groundwater recharge or plant transpiration.

entries.title: Surface runoff: rain that cannot soak in

definition.text: The unconfined flow of water over the ground surface, as opposed to flow in stream channels; also called overland flow.

facts.text: It forms when rain, stormwater or meltwater cannot soak in fast enough, because the soil is saturated or rain arrives faster than the soil absorbs it.
Impervious areas such as roofs and pavement are a common cause, since water cannot soak into the ground there.
It is a major part of the water cycle and the primary agent of soil erosion by water.
The land area whose runoff drains to a common point is called a drainage basin.
Soil storage absorbs light showers; on ancient Australian and southern African soils, dense proteoid root networks can prevent runoff even in heavy rain.
Runoff carries soil particles about 0.001 to 1.0 mm across; larger ones settle quickly, while small ones stay suspended over long distances.
It is a nonpoint source of pollution, carrying petroleum, pesticides and fertilizers; agricultural runoff drives nutrient pollution and eutrophication downstream.
In towns it is a primary cause of urban flooding, from street flooding to damp and mould in basements.

entries.title: Subsidence: when the ground itself sinks

definition.text: The downward vertical movement of the Earth's surface, caused by natural processes or by human activity.

facts.text: It involves little or no horizontal movement, which sets it apart from slope movements.
Causes include groundwater dissolving carbonate rock, gradual compaction of sediments, mining, pumping of groundwater or petroleum, and tectonic warping of the crust.
Pumping of groundwater or petroleum has lowered the ground by as much as 9 meters (30 ft) in many places, at costs of hundreds of millions of US dollars.
In karst, a weakened cave roof can collapse and drop rock and earth into the void, forming sinkholes that may be many hundreds of meters deep.
The weight of high buildings can press down the soil beneath them, a problem already felt in New York City, the San Francisco Bay Area and Lagos.
Lowered ground raises flood risk, especially on river flood plains and deltas, and uneven settlement can tilt or crack buildings.

entries.title: Stormwater and the dirty first flush

definition.text: Water that comes from precipitation, including heavy rain and meltwater from hail and snow.

facts.text: It may infiltrate and become groundwater, pond in depressions, evaporate or run off; most runoff reaches streams and other water bodies untreated.
In forests the soil absorbs much stormwater, and plants reduce it further by improving infiltration, intercepting rain and taking up water through their roots.
Impervious surfaces and compacted soil let less rain infiltrate, so more runoff forms, raising stream discharge and causing erosion and flooding.
Because the water is flushed away during storms, little of it recharges groundwater or feeds stream baseflow in dry weather.
Runoff carries trash, sediment, nutrients, bacteria, pesticides, metals and petroleum byproducts; the first flush of a storm is usually the most concentrated.
Phosphorus dissolved from fertilizers or bound to sediment from construction and farm runoff feeds algae and toxic cyanobacteria blooms in lakes.
Treatment facilities are usually designed with Stokes' law to settle particles larger than 40 micron and to hold water back against downstream flooding.

entries.text: In a forest, much of a storm soaks into the soil. In a city, much of it races to the nearest stream. Stormwater is water from precipitation, including heavy rain and meltwater from hail and snow. It may infiltrate and become groundwater, pond in hollows, evaporate or run off as {{ref:soil-water-019}}. Forest plants help the soil absorb it: they improve infiltration, intercept rain and take up water through their roots. Impervious surfaces and compacted soil do the opposite. More water runs off, streams swell, and erosion and flooding follow. Because storms flush the water away, little is left to recharge groundwater or feed streams in dry weather. Most runoff reaches streams untreated, carrying trash, sediment, nutrients, bacteria, pesticides, metals and petroleum byproducts. The first flush of a storm is usually the most concentrated. Phosphorus from fertilizers, or bound to sediment from building sites and farms, feeds algae and toxic cyanobacteria blooms in lakes. Treatment facilities usually rely on Stokes' law to settle particles larger than 40 microns, and they hold water back against downstream flooding.

entries.title: Runoff, from hillslope to river channel

definition.text: The flow of water across the land, a major part of the water cycle.

facts.text: Water flowing over land before it reaches a watercourse is surface runoff or overland flow; once in a watercourse it is streamflow, or channel runoff.
Surface runoff forms when water cannot infiltrate fast enough, because the soil is saturated, rain arrives faster than it can be absorbed, or surfaces are impervious.
Channel flow comes from hillslope runoff, groundwater flowing out of the ground and pipe discharges; it is measured with stream gauges or estimated by the Manning equation.
Floods occur when the volume of water exceeds a channel's capacity; a record of flow over time is called a hydrograph.

entries.text: Water moving across the land changes its name along the way. Runoff is the flow of water across the land, a major part of the water cycle. Before it reaches a watercourse it is surface runoff, or overland flow; once inside one it is streamflow, or channel runoff. Channel flow is fed by hillslope runoff, groundwater flowing out of the ground and discharges from pipes. Hydrologists measure it with stream gauges or estimate it with the Manning equation. A record of flow over time is a hydrograph. When the volume of water exceeds what a channel can hold, the result is a flood.

entries.title: Straw, the half of the harvest left behind

definition.text: The dry stalks of cereal plants left after the grain and chaff have been removed, an agricultural byproduct.

facts.text: It makes up about half the yield by weight of cereal crops such as barley, oats, rice, rye and wheat.

Straw bales are sometimes used to control sediment on construction sites, but they often protect water quality poorly and need much upkeep, so the US EPA prefers silt fences, fiber rolls or geotextiles.
It is also spread as ground cover after wildfires, used in in-stream check dams, and makes an excellent mulch.
Mixed with clay-rich subsoil and water it binds earth building materials such as cob and adobe.

entries.text: About half the weight of a cereal crop is not grain at all. Straw is the dry stalks of cereals such as barley, oats, rice, rye and wheat, left after the grain and chaff are removed. entries.title: Retention basins, ponds that hold back the storm

definition.text: An artificial pond with a permanent pool of water and vegetation around its edge, built to manage stormwater runoff.

facts.text: It differs from a detention basin, or dry pond, which holds water only for a while, and from an infiltration basin, which sends stormwater to groundwater through permeable soils.
Impervious urban surfaces rush rain into drains; the pond contains the surge and releases it slowly, reducing flooding downstream.
It also traps suspended sediment, often abundant in stormwater from construction and road sanding, while its plants take up soluble nutrients.
It can stand in for the natural absorption of a forest lost to development, and serves for erosion control and groundwater recharge.

entries.text: City pavement rushes rain into the drains; a retention basin slows it down. It is an artificial pond with a permanent pool of water and plants around its edge, built to manage {{ref:soil-water-081}}. An infiltration basin sends stormwater down to groundwater through permeable soil.

entries.title: Bioswales, planted channels that clean runoff

definition.text: A channel built to gather and carry stormwater runoff while removing debris and pollution from it.

facts.text: It is a vegetated, mulched or xeriscaped drainage course with gently sloping sides of less than 6%, built on soil with no more than 5% clay.
It is designed to keep water in the swale as long as safely possible: plants catch and settle pollutants, which then decompose or are broken down by soil bacteria.
It slows runoff, recharges groundwater and reduces flooding and erosion, and suits places with much impervious surface that must handle a storm's first flush.
In permaculture, swales are used to harvest water.

entries.text: A bioswale is a channel that gathers and carries stormwater runoff while removing debris and pollution from it. A bioswale slows runoff, recharges groundwater and reduces flooding and erosion. It suits places with much impervious surface that must handle a storm's first flush. entries.title: Land development and the soil it seals away

definition.text: The alteration of a landscape, for example turning natural land over to farming or housing, or dividing it into building lots.

facts.text: Conversion to building land brings road building, topsoil abrasion, soil compaction, chemical change from soil stabilization, impervious surfaces and polluted runoff.
Construction seals much of the soil off from rainfall and the nutrient cycle, so the soil under buildings and roads is in effect consumed and made infertile.
New farmland usually comes from forest, savanna or grassland cleared by assarting or slash-and-burn; reclaiming wasteland or sealed ground is rarer for lack of fertile soil.
Economic land improvement can mean ecological degradation, such as salinization from saline irrigation water, or erosion and desertification after drainage.

entries.text: Soil under a road or a building is, in effect, used up. It seals the soil off from rainfall and the nutrient cycle, leaving it infertile. New farmland usually comes from forest, savanna or grassland cleared by assarting, the grubbing up of woodland, or by slash-and-burn. Reclaiming wasteland or sealed ground is rarer, for lack of fertile soil. Profitable improvement can still degrade land, through salt buildup from saline irrigation water or erosion after drainage.

entries.title: How clearing and building rewire the local water cycle
entries.article: Water cycle#Land cover and land use changes

definition.text: The local and regional changes to the water cycle that follow changes in land use and land cover.

facts.text: Urbanization, farm expansion and deforestation can increase soil compaction and impervious cover, lowering soil infiltration capacity and raising surface runoff.
Locally, deforestation reduces soil moisture, evaporation, rainfall and snowfall.
Stormwater drains lower runoff rates and raise groundwater recharge, while leaking sewers add recharge but can contaminate groundwater.

entries.title: Four ways to limit the damage runoff does

definition.text: Measures that limit the harm done by surface runoff: land-use controls, erosion controls, flood control and controls on chemical use.

facts.text: Land-use codes encourage narrow sidewalks and pavers set in earth to let as much water as possible infiltrate in towns.
Since the 1960s some governments have required builders to use erosion and sediment controls such as straw bales, silt fences and limits on bare graded ground.
Flood control uses holding ponds (detention basins) to buffer peak flows and energy dissipators to slow channel flow.
Chemical controls include double containment of underground tanks, fewer allowed pesticides and stricter rules for fertilizers and herbicides.

entries.text: Runoff mitigation covers the measures that limit the harm done by surface runoff. They fall into four groups. Land-use codes encourage narrow sidewalks and pavers set in earth, so that as much water as possible soaks into town ground. Controls on erosion and sediment have been required of builders by some governments since the 1960s, among them straw bales, {{ref:soil-water-093}} and limits on bare graded ground. Flood control uses holding ponds, or detention basins, to buffer peak flows, and energy dissipators to slow water in channels. Chemical controls include double containment of underground tanks, fewer approved pesticides and stricter rules for fertilizers and weedkillers.

entries.title: When the soil is already full: Dunne runoff

definition.text: Runoff produced at once when rain keeps falling on soil that is already saturated and whose surface hollows are full.

facts.text: It is also called saturated overland flow or Dunne runoff.
Moisture left from earlier rain (antecedent soil moisture) sets how soon soil saturates: the wetter it starts, the sooner runoff begins.
Saturated soils absorb less rain, so a given volume of rainfall produces more runoff and more erosion.

entries.text: Soil that is already soaked cannot take in more rain. Saturation-excess overland flow is runoff produced at once when rain keeps falling on saturated soil whose surface hollows are full. It is also called saturated overland flow or Dunne runoff. Its timing depends on the {{ref:soil-water-155}} left from earlier rain, known as antecedent soil moisture. The wetter the soil starts, the sooner runoff begins. Because saturated soil absorbs less rain, the same volume of rainfall produces more runoff and more erosion.
