entries.title: Throughflow, water that slips back out of the hillside

definition.text: Water that soaks into a hillside upslope, flows sideways through the soil and seeps back out near a channel; also called throughflow.

facts.text: On its way, runoff shrinks as some water evapotranspires, some is held in small surface hollows and some infiltrates.
The water that remains ends up in a river, lake, estuary or ocean.

entries.text: Not all runoff travels on the surface. Subsurface return flow, also called throughflow, is water that soaks into a hillside upslope, moves sideways through the soil and seeps back out near a channel. Along the way the flow shrinks. Some water returns to the air by evapotranspiration, some is held in small surface hollows and some infiltrates. Whatever remains ends up in a river, lake, estuary or ocean.

entries.title: Urban runoff, from rooftops to storm drains

definition.text: Surface runoff from rain, landscape irrigation and car washing created by urbanization.

facts.text: Roads, parking lots, sidewalks and roofs carry polluted stormwater to storm drains instead of letting it percolate through soil.
Less water reaches groundwater, so the water table falls and droughts worsen, while more water left on the surface causes flooding.
Most municipal storm sewer systems discharge the stormwater untreated into streams, rivers and bays, where erosion and siltation can be major problems.

entries.text: In a city, rain lands mostly on surfaces that shed it. Urban runoff is surface runoff from rain, landscape irrigation and car washing, created by urbanization. entries.title: Ground that sinks and rises with the seasons

definition.text: The sinking of the ground as clay-rich soils dry and shrink with the seasons, and its rise again when they rewet.

facts.text: Clay's very small particles make clay-rich soils sensitive to changes in moisture content.
Foundations above the depth reached by seasonal drying move with the soil, which can crack buildings with tapering cracks.
Growing trees dry the soil cumulatively; when a tree declines or is felled the soil heaves, rising and spreading for up to 25 years as the deficit reverses.

entries.text: A felled tree can make the ground rise for up to 25 years. Seasonal subsidence and heave is the sinking of the ground as clay-rich soils dry and shrink with the seasons, and its rise again when they rewet. Clay's very small particles make such soils sensitive to changes in moisture, the behavior described in {{ref:soil-phys-028}}. Foundations above the depth reached by seasonal drying move with the soil, which can crack buildings with tapering cracks. Growing trees dry the soil cumulatively. When a tree declines or is felled, that deficit reverses, and the soil heaves, rising and spreading.

entries.title: Managing stormwater for quantity and quality

definition.text: The control of both the quantity and the quality of stormwater.

facts.text: Its best management practices include engineered devices such as retention ponds and routine practices such as street sweeping.
Technical aims include controlling flooding and erosion and building retention basins, filter vaults and vortex separators that remove coarse solids.
Nature-based options such as ponds, swales and constructed wetlands work alongside pipes and concrete channels and can also give habitat.
Passive treatment uses gravity flow through ditches and pipes, with gel flocculants, jute fibre filters and silt retention mats to settle sediment.

entries.text: A street sweeper and a planted swale belong to the same toolkit. Stormwater management is the control of both the quantity and the quality of stormwater. Its best management practices range from engineered devices, such as {{ref:soil-water-090}}, to routine chores such as street sweeping. Its technical aims include controlling flooding and erosion. Engineers build retention basins, filter vaults and vortex separators that remove coarse solids. Nature-based options, such as ponds, swales and {{ref:soil-water-260}}, work alongside pipes and concrete channels and can also give wildlife habitat. Passive treatment lets gravity carry water through ditches and pipes, with gel flocculants, jute fiber filters and silt retention mats to settle the sediment.

entries.title: How city stormwater opens sinkholes in karst

definition.text: Sinkhole collapses caused when urban stormwater drains down through karst ground and carries soil and rock fragments away.

facts.text: In undisturbed karst, soil and rock fragments choke the openings and limit their growth, and the drainage stays balanced with most storms.
Urban karst areas lack surface streams, so extra runoff from roofs and streets moves down through the ground; once flow can move soil and rock, openings grow fast.
Under a roof of competent limestone there is often no surface warning before an opening collapses, so planners are advised to avoid karst for new development.

entries.text: Undisturbed karst keeps a quiet balance with the rain. Soil and rock fragments choke the openings in the rock and limit their growth, and the drainage keeps pace with most storms. Cities upset that balance. Urban karst areas lack surface streams, so extra runoff from roofs and streets moves down through the ground. Once the flow can carry soil and rock, the openings grow fast. The result is a stormwater sinkhole, a collapse caused when urban stormwater drains through karst and carries soil and rock fragments away, a sudden form of {{ref:soil-water-084}}. Under a roof of competent limestone there is often no surface warning before an opening collapses. Planners are advised to avoid karst for new development.

entries.title: Turning a rainstorm into a predicted flood curve

definition.text: A model of how rainfall on a drainage basin is converted into runoff.

facts.text: It turns a rainfall event, entered as a hyetograph, into a surface runoff hydrograph, and must be calibrated before use.
The linear reservoir model is well known but of limited use; a non-linear reservoir applies more widely, but only where rain falls roughly evenly over the catchment.
Large study areas are split into sub-catchments whose hydrographs are combined by flood routing.

entries.text: Hydrologists need to know how much water a storm will send downstream, and when. A rainfall-runoff model describes how rainfall on a drainage basin is converted into {{ref:soil-water-086}}. It takes a rainfall event, entered as a hyetograph, a record of rainfall over time, and turns it into a surface runoff hydrograph. Every such model must be calibrated before use. The linear reservoir model is well known but of limited use. A non-linear reservoir applies more widely, but only where rain falls roughly evenly over the catchment. Large study areas are split into sub-catchments, whose hydrographs are combined by flood routing.

entries.title: Models that follow water and everything it carries

definition.text: A mathematical model that simulates the flow of rivers, streams, groundwater or drainage fronts and calculates water quality.

facts.text: These models came into use in the 1960s and 1970s, when environmental laws demanded water-quality forecasts and computing power became widely available.
Physically based models represent surface runoff, subsurface flow, evapotranspiration and channel flow; stochastic models link inputs such as rainfall to outputs such as runoff statistically.
Their surface runoff element lets them assess sediment, fertilizer, pesticide and other chemical contaminants.
Robert E. Horton's work on surface runoff, joined to quantitative treatment of erosion, laid the groundwork for modern chemical transport hydrology.

Horton's work on surface runoff, joined to quantitative treatment of erosion.

entries.title: The ion cloud that decides whether clay holds together

definition.text: The cloud of balancing cations that surrounds every negatively charged clay platelet, whose thickness depends on the salinity of the water.

facts.text: Clay particles carry permanent and pH-dependent negative charges, balanced by cations such as Na+ held on their surfaces, in interlayers or in pore water.
In salty water the double layer is compressed, so the platelets flocculate into stable aggregates; adding salt to a suspension likewise thins the layer.
When rain leaches salt out of uplifted marine clay, the layer expands and stronger repulsion disperses the platelets (peptization), destabilising the clay.
Adding salt back compresses the layer again, and quick clay rapidly regains its strength.

entries.text: Salt can decide whether a clay stands firm. Clay platelets carry permanent and pH-dependent negative charges, as {{ref:soil-chem-079}} describes, balanced by cations such as Na+ on their surfaces, in interlayers or in the pore water. The electrical double layer is that cloud of balancing cations around each platelet, and its thickness depends on the water's salinity. In salty water the layer is compressed, so the platelets flocculate into stable aggregates. When rain leaches salt out of uplifted clay laid down in the sea, the layer expands. Stronger repulsion then disperses the platelets, called peptization, and the clay is destabilized. Adding salt back compresses the layer again, and {{ref:soil-water-071}} rapidly regains its strength.

entries.title: Four letters that rank soils by runoff

definition.text: One of four classes, A to D, into which the NRCS sorts soils by how readily they take in water, used to choose a runoff curve number.

facts.text: Group A, mostly deep well-drained sands and gravels, has a final infiltration rate above 0.30 in (7.6 mm) per hour and low runoff potential.
Group B infiltrates at 0.15–0.30 in (3.8–7.6 mm) per hour; group C, often with an impeding layer or fine texture, at 0.05–0.15 in (1.3–3.8 mm).
Group D, with high runoff potential, covers swelling clays, soils with a permanent high water table or a claypan near the surface, and shallow soils over impervious material.
The group is picked from measured infiltration rates, a soil survey such as the NRCS Web Soil Survey, or a soil professional's judgement.

entries.title: The curve number, one figure for a storm's runoff

definition.text: An empirical number, CN, used in hydrology to predict direct runoff or infiltration from rainfall excess.

facts.text: It was developed by the USDA Soil Conservation Service, now the Natural Resources Conservation Service, from runoff measured on small catchments and hillslope plots.
A curve number depends on the area's hydrologic soil group, land use, treatment and hydrologic condition.
CN ranges from 30 to 100: lower numbers mean more permeable soil and low runoff potential, higher numbers more runoff.
No runoff starts until the initial abstraction, such as infiltration and interception, is met; it was long taken as 0.2 S, but 0.05 S may suit urban watersheds better.
The method works storm by storm and should not be applied to a single annual rainfall total.
Curve numbers are adjusted for antecedent moisture: dry (AMC I), average (AMC II) and moist (AMC III).
It is widely used as an efficient way to estimate approximate direct runoff from a rainfall event.

entries.title: Soil erosion and the 75 billion tons lost each year

definition.text: The wearing away of the upper layer of soil, a form of soil degradation.

facts.text: It is driven by erosive agents: water, ice, snow, wind, plants such as uprooted trees, and animals including humans.
Following those agents, it is divided into water, glacial, snow, wind (aeolian), zoogenic and human-caused erosion such as tillage erosion.
It can go on slowly and almost unnoticed, or so fast that it causes a serious loss of topsoil.
Human activities have raised the rate of erosion worldwide by about 28 times the natural rate.
On-site, accelerated erosion lowers farm productivity and can collapse ecosystems by stripping nutrient-rich upper layers, sometimes ending in desertification.
Off-site, it silts waterways, feeds eutrophication of water bodies and damages roads and houses with sediment.
Water and wind erosion together account for about 84% of the world's degraded land.
About 75 billion tons of soil are eroded from the land each year; one global model puts the loss to water alone at almost 36 billion tons.

entries.title: How rain and runoff carry soil away

definition.text: The removal of soil by rainfall and by the surface runoff it produces.

facts.text: Runoff begins when the soil is saturated or when rain falls faster than water can infiltrate.
Runoff with enough flow energy carries loosened soil particles down the slope as sediment.
Rain and runoff cause four main types of erosion, in rising severity: splash, sheet, rill and gully erosion.
Concentrated runoff cuts small channels called rills; if runoff keeps deepening them, they may grow into gullies.
Water erosion removes soil mainly from the middle and lower parts of a slope rather than from hilltops.
A global model estimates that almost 36 billion tons of soil are lost to water every year.
Raindrops bombard aggregates and detach small particles that are easily transported, by splash or by water running downhill, to a low area where they are deposited.
Sheet and rill erosion cause most soil erosion; a gully is a rill too deep for tillage equipment to smooth.

entries.title: Rainfall erosivity, the striking power of rain

definition.text: The power of rainfall to cause soil erosion, set mainly by how much rain falls and how intensely.

facts.text: The amount and intensity of precipitation is the main climatic control on water erosion, especially when the soil surface lacks plant cover.
Larger, faster raindrops have more kinetic energy and displace soil particles further than small, slow ones.
In places such as the Midwestern United States and the Amazon, rainfall intensity is the main determinant of erosivity.
In western Europe, erosion follows low-intensity stratiform rain on already saturated soil, so total rainfall matters more than intensity.
Rainfall erosivity is the R factor of the Universal Soil Loss Equation.
The Global Rainfall Erosivity Database (GloREDa) covers 3,625 stations in 63 countries and was used to map erosivity worldwide at about 1 km resolution.

entries.title: Wind erosion and the bouncing grain

definition.text: Erosion by wind, which lifts and carries away loose particles (deflation) and wears down surfaces with windborne grains (abrasion).

facts.text: It is a major landscape-shaping force, especially in arid and semi-arid regions.
It drives land degradation, desertification, harmful airborne dust and crop damage, above all where deforestation, urbanization and farming have raised it above natural rates.
Deflation moves particles by surface creep (rolling or sliding), saltation (short bouncing hops) and suspension (fine particles lifted and carried far).
Saltation does most of the work (50–70%), followed by suspension (30–40%) and surface creep (5–25%).
Silty soils such as loess are the most affected, because silt particles detach and travel easily.
It needs strong winds and is worst in drought; on the Great Plains, wind erosion losses can be up to 6100 times greater in drought years than wet years.
Tillage worsens it by drying and breaking up the soil, and clearing trees from fields gives the wind long, open runs.
Vegetation shelters soil from the wind, and windbreaks of trees and shrubs along field edges significantly reduce wind erosion.

entries.text: In a drought year on the Great Plains, wind erosion losses can be up to 6100 times greater than in a wet year. Wind erosion is erosion by wind, and it works in two ways. {{ref:soil-water-030}} lifts and carries away loose particles. Abrasion wears down surfaces with windborne grains. It is a major force shaping landscapes, especially in arid and semi-arid regions. That lifting moves particles in three ways. Surface creep rolls or slides them. {{ref:soil-water-251}} sends them in short, bouncing hops. Suspension lifts fine particles and carries them far. The hopping does most of the work, 50 to 70%, followed by suspension at 30 to 40% and surface creep at 5 to 25%. Silty soils such as loess suffer most, because silt particles detach and travel easily. Wind erosion needs strong winds and is worst in drought. It is worsened by {{ref:soil-agri-095}}, which dries and breaks up the soil, and clearing trees from fields gives the wind long, open runs. Where deforestation, urbanization and farming have raised it above natural rates, it drives the decline of land, the spread of desert, harmful airborne dust and crop damage. Plants shelter the soil. Rows of trees and shrubs along field edges significantly reduce wind erosion, as {{ref:soil-agri-061}} explains.

entries.title: Erosion control, from terraces to riprap

definition.text: The practice of preventing or controlling wind and water erosion in farming, land development, coastal areas, river banks and construction.

facts.text: Effective controls manage surface runoff and help prevent water pollution, soil loss, habitat loss and property damage.
Many controls are physical barriers of vegetation or rock that absorb some of the energy of the wind or water.
Methods include crop rotation, conservation tillage, contour ploughing, cover crops, hydroseeding, riparian buffers, strip farming and windbreaks.
Terracing is an extremely effective control, practised around the world for thousands of years.
Mixed cropping and crop rotation reduce erosion, crop residues soften raindrop impact under conservation tillage, and forages' fibrous roots anchor the topsoil.
Agroforestry, mixing crops with trees, is efficient against erosion, especially in rainy tropical climates and on severely degraded land.
On construction sites, erosion controls are combined with sediment controls such as sediment basins and silt fences; in towns they are part of stormwater programmes.
Bank erosion is natural, but where people want to hold a river in place, they line its banks with riprap or gabions.

entries.text: One of the best defenses against erosion is thousands of years old: {{ref:soil-agri-073}}, practiced around the world and still extremely effective. Erosion control is the practice of preventing or controlling wind and water erosion in farming, land development, coastal areas, river banks and construction. Good controls manage surface runoff and help prevent water pollution, soil loss, habitat loss and property damage. Many are physical barriers of vegetation or rock that absorb some of the energy of the wind or water. On farms, the methods include {{ref:soil-agri-004}}, {{ref:soil-agri-099}}, {{ref:soil-agri-123}} and {{ref:soil-agri-066}}, along with hydroseeding, streamside buffers, alternating crop strips and rows of sheltering trees. Crop leftovers on the surface soften raindrop impact, and the fibrous roots of forage crops anchor the topsoil. Mixing crops with trees works well, especially in rainy tropical climates and on severely degraded land. On construction sites, erosion controls are paired with controls on sediment such as {{ref:soil-water-099}} and {{ref:soil-water-093}}. In towns, they are part of stormwater programs. Bank erosion is natural, but where people want to hold a river in place, they line its banks with riprap or gabions.

Good controls manage surface runoff and help prevent water pollution, soil loss, habitat loss and property damage. On farms, the methods include Crop rotation: a different crop each season, Conservation tillage: leave the residue, keep the soil, Contour plowing: furrows that run across the slope and Cover crops: plants grown to protect, not to sell, along with hydroseeding, streamside buffers, alternating crop strips and rows of sheltering trees. On construction sites, erosion controls are paired with controls on sediment such as Sediment basins: settling ponds for building sites and Silt fences: cheap, simple and often failing. In towns, they are part of stormwater programs. Bank erosion is natural, but where people want to hold a river in place, they line its banks with riprap or gabions.

entries.title: Dust, the soil that travels on the wind

definition.text: Fine particles of solid matter; on Earth, mostly particles in the air from soil lifted by wind, volcanic eruptions and pollution.

facts.text: Dust that stays suspended in the atmosphere for a long time is considered an aerosol.
Windborne dust comes mainly from saltation in dry regions, where strong winds strip mostly silt-sized material up to 1/16 mm across.
Grazing, ploughing, vehicles and other human activity further destabilize dust source areas.
Dust-producing surfaces cover about one-third of the global land area, roughly 13 billion hectares.
Saharan dust reaches the Caribbean and the Amazon basin, about 132 million tons crossing the Atlantic each year, and can affect temperatures and rainfall.
Soil dust from wind erosion is a major source of air pollution and often carries toxic chemicals such as pesticides or petroleum fuels.
Dust from erosion suppresses rainfall, and dust events have been linked to declining coral reef health in the Caribbean and Florida since the 1970s.
Dust poses a health risk to children, older people and people with respiratory diseases.

entries.title: Why plant cover is the best shield against erosion

definition.text: The protection that living plants and the litter they leave give the soil against wind and water erosion.

facts.text: Vegetation makes the soil more permeable to rain, which reduces runoff, and shelters it from the wind.
Plant roots bind the soil and interweave into a solid mass that resists both water and wind erosion.
Removing vegetation increases the rate of surface erosion.
In forests, the litter and humus of the forest floor absorb raindrop impact and let water percolate slowly; the floor, more than the canopy, prevents surface erosion.
Raindrops regain terminal velocity within about 8 metres, so drops falling from a tall canopy can still strike the ground at full speed.
Increasing vegetative cover is the most effective known way to prevent both wind and water erosion.

The forest floor does. Its litter and humus absorb the impact of the drops and let water percolate slowly. More than the canopy, the floor prevents surface erosion. Vegetation cover and erosion names this protection that living plants and their litter give the soil against wind and water. Their roots bind the soil and interweave into a solid mass that resists both water and wind erosion. Remove the vegetation and surface erosion speeds up. Increasing plant cover is the most effective known way to prevent both wind and water erosion.

entries.title: How farming speeds erosion beyond repair

definition.text: The acceleration of soil erosion by farming practices that loosen, bare or compact the soil.

facts.text: Unsustainable farming raises erosion one to two orders of magnitude above the natural rate, far beyond what soil formation can replace.
Tillage, which breaks soil into finer particles, is a primary cause; mechanized deep ploughing makes far more soil available for water to carry off.
Monocropping, farming steep slopes, row crops, surface irrigation, and pesticides and fertilizers that kill soil-binding organisms also raise erosion.
Heavy grazing strips plant cover and severely compacts soil, both of which increase erosion.
Erosion is size-selective: the finer eroded fraction loses more total phosphorus than the soil as a whole.
At farm sites in the Appalachian Mountains, intensive practices have caused erosion up to 100 times the natural regional rate.
Growing potatoes carries a higher erosion risk than growing cereals or oilseed crops.
Over a third of the U.S. Corn Belt has lost its topsoil entirely; switching to no-till would cut erosion from U.S. fields by more than 70 percent.

entries.text_plain: Over a third of the U.S. Corn Belt has lost its topsoil entirely. Unsustainable farming raises erosion one to two orders of magnitude above the natural rate, far beyond what soil formation can replace. Agriculture and soil erosion names this speeding up. The culprits are practices that loosen, bare or compact the soil. Tillage: why farmers dig, and why digging less won, which breaks soil into finer particles, is a primary cause. Mechanized deep plowing makes far more soil available for water to carry off. Growing one crop year after year, farming steep slopes, row crops and irrigation that runs water over the surface all add to the loss. So do pesticides and fertilizers that kill soil-binding organisms. Heavy grazing strips plant cover and severely compacts the soil. At farm sites in the Appalachian Mountains, intensive practices have driven erosion up to 100 times the natural regional rate. Potatoes carry a higher erosion risk than cereals or oilseed crops. Erosion is also selective by size: the finer eroded fraction loses more total phosphorus than the soil as a whole. Switching U.S. fields to No-till farming: growing crops without turning the soil would cut their erosion by more than 70 percent.

entries.title: Erodibility, or why some soils give way more easily

definition.text: The inherent lack of resistance of a soil or rock to erosion.

facts.text: A highly erodible material loses more material for the same amount of work done by erosive processes.
Soil erodibility is a lumped value for how a soil profile responds each year to detachment and transport by raindrops and surface flow.
In the Universal Soil Loss Equation it is the K factor, estimated from silt and very fine sand content, clay content, organic matter, structure and permeability.
Clay-rich soils resist erosion better than sandy or silty ones because clay binds particles together.
Organic matter makes soil more resistant by coagulating colloids into a stronger, more stable structure; long cultivation depletes it and raises erodibility.
Wet or compacted soils absorb less rain, so more water runs off and erodes.
Stone cover protects against erosion, which matters greatly in Mediterranean countries.
For channels and dams, erodibility in a shear stress model can be measured with a hole erosion test or a jet erosion test.

entries.title: Warmer climate, heavier rain, faster soil loss

definition.text: The expected rise in soil erosion as warming brings heavier rainfall and alters vegetation, litter, soil moisture and frozen ground.

facts.text: Warmer temperatures are expected to intensify the water cycle, with more extreme rainfall and so more erosion unless measures are taken.
Studies by Pruski and Nearing suggest about a 1.7% change in soil erosion for each 1% change in total precipitation.
Early 21st-century studies predicted rainfall erosivity rising by 17% in the United States, 18% in Europe and 30 to 66% globally.
Other routes include shifts in plant canopy and litter, loss of soil organic matter, winter snow turning to erosive rain and thawing permafrost.

entries.title: What happens to forest soil when the trees go

definition.text: The rise in soil erosion that follows removal of forest cover and its protective forest floor.

facts.text: Deforestation exposes mineral soil by removing litter and humus, removes the roots that bind soil, and compacts it under logging machinery.
After fire or logging, erosion stays low as long as the forest floor remains intact, but severe fires followed by heavy rain cause much more erosion.
Slash-and-burn clearing of tropical forest is one of the largest contributors to erosive soil loss worldwide.
In Brazilian studies, runoff and soil loss fell to forest-like levels after 4–5 years of regrowth, and a 15-year fallow restored the original soil.

entries.contested_note: Sources call it a debate whether slash-and-burn with forest regrowth or permanent pasture and cash crops after logging does more lasting damage to tropical soils.

entries.title: Steeper and longer slopes, faster soil loss

definition.text: The influence of a slope's steepness and length on how fast runoff flows and how much soil it erodes.

facts.text: Topography sets the speed of surface runoff, and that speed sets how erosive the runoff is.
Longer, steeper slopes, especially poorly vegetated ones, erode much faster in heavy rain than short, gentle ones.
Steep terrain is also more prone to mudslides, landslides and other gravity-driven erosion.
The Universal Soil Loss Equation represents slope length and steepness with its L and S factors.

entries.title: Splash erosion, the first blow of the raindrop

definition.text: Erosion caused when falling raindrops strike bare soil and knock particles loose.

facts.text: A falling raindrop makes a small crater in the soil and throws out soil particles, which then move off with surface runoff.
It is usually seen as the first and least severe stage of water erosion, followed by sheet, rill and gully erosion.
On level ground without wind, ejected particles can travel up to 0.6 m vertically and 1.5 m horizontally.
Larger, faster raindrops carry more kinetic energy and throw particles further; plant cover and crop residues soften the impact.

entries.text: A single raindrop can fling soil particles up to 1.5 meters. Splash erosion is the erosion caused when falling raindrops strike bare soil and knock particles loose. Each drop makes a small crater and throws soil out of it. The loosened particles then move off with surface runoff. On level ground without wind, they can travel up to 0.6 meters vertically and 1.5 meters horizontally. Larger, faster drops carry more kinetic energy and throw particles further. Plant cover and crop leftovers soften the impact. Splash is usually seen as the first and least severe stage of water erosion, followed by {{ref:soil-water-005}}, {{ref:soil-water-025}} and {{ref:soil-water-027}}.

entries.title: Building cities, speeding erosion

definition.text: The increase in erosion and polluted runoff caused by construction, roads and paved urban land.

facts.text: Construction strips vegetation, alters drainage and compacts soil; asphalt and concrete then increase surface runoff and surface wind speeds.
Sediment in runoff from urban areas, especially roads, is often heavily contaminated with fuel, oil and other chemicals.
The extra runoff changes how much water flows through nearby watersheds and how fast, fills them with polluted sediment and greatly increases bank erosion.

entries.title: Rills, the first scratches of an erosion problem

definition.text: Erosion in rills, shallow channels no more than a few centimetres deep cut into soil by flowing surface water.

facts.text: Smaller incised channels are microrills and larger ones are gullies.
Hillslope runoff cuts rills into unprotected soil, as on farmland left bare, after deforestation or during construction.
Rills are easy to see when first cut, so they are often the first sign of an erosion problem.
Flow in rills is typically a few centimetres deep or less, so its hydraulics differ greatly from flow in streams and rivers.
Rill flow may carry nearly ten times as much as interrill areas, and in moderate rain can move rock fragments up to 9 cm across.
Tractors compact soil so water runs over it, and wheel tracks channel that water into rills.
Without soil conservation, rills can grow into gullies or, in semi-arid regions, badlands; under good management contour tilling repairs them.

entries.text: The first sign that a field is losing soil is often a set of tiny channels. Rills are shallow channels, no more than a few centimeters deep, cut into soil by flowing surface water, and rill erosion is the erosion that happens in them. Smaller incised channels are microrills. Larger ones are the subject of {{ref:soil-water-027}}. Hillslope runoff cuts rills into unprotected soil, as on farmland left bare, after deforestation or during construction. Rills are easy to see when first cut, so they often give the first warning of an erosion problem. Tractors help start them. They compact the soil so that water runs over it, and their wheel tracks channel the water into rills. Flow in a rill is typically a few centimeters deep or less, so its hydraulics differ greatly from flow in streams and rivers. It is still strong. Rill flow may carry nearly ten times as much as the interrill areas between rills. In moderate rain it can move rock fragments up to 9 cm across. Without conservation measures, rills can grow into those larger channels or, in semi-arid regions, into the bare, carved ground of {{ref:soil-water-269}}. Under good management, contour tilling repairs them.

entries.title: Gullies, the scars a neglected rill can become

definition.text: Erosion that cuts gullies, steep-sided channels formed in soil by running water, mass movement or both, usually on hillsides or in floodplains.

facts.text: Gullies are metres to tens of metres deep and wide, have a distinct headscarp and lengthen by headward erosion at a knickpoint.
They carry intermittent flow after intense or long rain or snowmelt, and often begin where a rill has been neglected and kept growing.
Hillslope cultivation, clearing, overgrazing and tracks worn by livestock or vehicles start or speed up gullying.
Processes include incision and bank erosion by flow, collapse of gully walls, groundwater seepage and collapse of soil pipes in dispersive soils.
Gullies cut farm productivity and supply sediment that chokes downstream waters; losses are greatest in unstable, dispersive soils.
The Universal Soil Loss Equation cannot simulate gullies, though they can supply 10–80% of total erosion on cultivated and grazed land.
On Madagascar's high central plateau, gully furrows commonly exceed 50 metres deep and 1 kilometre wide.

entries.text: On Madagascar's high central plateau, gully furrows commonly exceed 50 meters deep and 1 kilometer wide. Gully erosion cuts gullies: steep-sided channels formed in soil by running water, mass movement or both, usually on hillsides or on low ground that rivers flood. Most are meters to tens of meters deep and wide. Each has a distinct headscarp, the steep wall at its head, and lengthens by uphill cutting ({{ref:soil-water-278}}) at a knickpoint, a sudden step in its bed. Gullies carry water only intermittently, after intense or long rain or snowmelt. Many begin where a rill was neglected and kept growing. Hillslope cultivation, clearing, heavy grazing and tracks worn by livestock or vehicles start or speed up gullying. Inside a gully, flowing water cuts down and erodes the banks, walls collapse and groundwater seeps out. In dispersive soils, buried soil pipes collapse as well. Gullies cut farm productivity and supply sediment that chokes downstream waters. Losses are greatest in unstable, dispersive soils. They can supply 10 to 80% of total erosion on cultivated and grazed land, yet the {{ref:soil-water-041}} cannot simulate them.

entries.title: The Universal Soil Loss Equation, six factors multiplied

definition.text: A widely used empirical model (USLE) that estimates long-term average annual soil loss from water erosion as the product of six factors.

facts.text: It multiplies rainfall erosivity (R), soil erodibility (K), slope length and steepness (L and S), cover and management (C) and support practices (P).
It was built in the U.S. from erosion plot and rainfall simulator experiments, using data the USDA Soil Conservation Service collected from the 1930s.
The unit plot standard has LS = 1 (a 9% slope 22.1 m long), bare fallow, up-and-down-slope tillage and no conservation practice.
K can be read from a nomograph using particle size, organic matter, structure and permeability, and LS from a slope chart; C and P must come from plot data.
It is the most commonly used soil loss model and the main one used by U.S. agencies, and helped implement the multibillion-dollar U.S. conservation program.
Though plot-based, it is often applied to watersheds, continents and the globe, and it cannot simulate gully erosion.
Revised (RUSLE) and Modified (MUSLE) versions remain in use, and newer models such as G2 still build on it.

entries.title: Predicting erosion, and why the forecasts often miss

definition.text: Using data and models to predict where, and how fast, erosion may happen in the future.

facts.text: There are dozens of models; some treat long-term natural erosion within landscape evolution, while many quantify human-accelerated soil erosion.
Most predict average annual soil loss from a plot, field or catchment under different land management.
Most consider only water erosion; few predict wind erosion, and models of tillage or gully erosion are rare.
Process-based models solve equations for detachment, transport and deposition, while empirical models relate soil loss statistically to environmental and management factors.
No model is fully process-based yet; research favours process-based models, but the empirical USLE remains the standard for conservation planning.
Two widely used North American models are the Revised Universal Soil Loss Equation (RUSLE) and the Water Erosion Prediction Project model (WEPP).
Predicted and observed erosion rates often differ widely, so models remain better research tools than regulatory instruments unless calibrated locally.
Erosion models are non-linear, which makes it hard or impossible to scale predictions from small plots up to large areas.

entries.title: Riparian buffers, green strips that guard a stream

definition.text: A vegetated strip beside a stream, usually forested, that shades it and partly shields it from the effects of neighbouring land use.

facts.text: It intercepts sediment, nutrients, pesticides and other materials in surface runoff and reduces pollutants in shallow subsurface flow.
It stabilises the stream bank, so eroding banks take less farmland out of production and less silt reaches downstream lakes and reservoirs.
A typical buffer is 50 feet (15 m) wide on each side, in three zones: native grasses that first slow runoff, shrubs, and fast-growing trees that shade the water and hold the bank.
A nine-year University of Georgia study found buffers removed at least 60% of the nitrogen and at least 65% of the phosphorus from fertilizer in runoff.

entries.title: Geotextiles, fabrics that hold the soil in place

definition.text: A permeable fabric laid with soil to separate, filter, reinforce, protect or drain it.

facts.text: Geotextiles are usually polypropylene or polyester, either woven or felt-like nonwoven, and belong to the wider family of geosynthetics.
They were first meant to replace granular soil filters; in the 1950s R.J. Barrett used them behind seawalls and under erosion control blocks and riprap.
They are used in silt fences and bank protection, as matting that steadies flow in channels and swales, and to let plants grow on steep slopes.
Coir geotextiles are popular for erosion control and slope stabilization; they last about 3 to 5 years and break down into humus.

Most are polypropylene or polyester, either woven or felt-like nonwoven, and they belong to the wider family of geosynthetics. They go into Silt fences: cheap, simple and often failing and bank protection. As matting, they steady flow in channels and swales and let plants grow on steep slopes. Geotextiles of coconut fiber, Coir: the coconut husk that stands in for peat, are popular for erosion control and for steadying slopes. They last about 3 to 5 years and then break down into humus.

entries.title: Soil loss tolerance: how much erosion is too much

definition.text: The maximum average yearly soil loss, in tons per acre per year, that still lets a soil sustain current production economically and indefinitely; also called the T value.

facts.text: T values range from 1 to 5 tons per acre per year.
It is calculated with the formula T=υQρC+R(1−C).
Devised by the US Soil Conservation Service, it rests on the minimum rate of loss that would deplete organic matter and harm crop productivity.
In 1961–1962 US soil groups were given T values of 2 to 6 tons per acre per year, later adjusted to 1 to 5; conservation management adopted it from the mid-1960s.
In 2007, 99 million acres, 28% of US cropland, were eroding faster than T, down from 169 million acres, 40% of cropland, in 1982.
Critics note that T values vary across space, may not hold where soluble carbonates abound, as in karst, and should be weighed against actual soil loss.
For soil deeper than 5 feet, T is 5 tons per acre per year (11 metric tons per hectare), about 0.03 inch of depth a year, or 1 inch in 33 years.
T is lower for shallow soils: with rooting depth under 10 inches it equals 0.006 inch a year, or 1 inch in 167 years.

entries.contested_note: The T value's validity is questioned because it varies across space and may not apply in carbonate-rich karst regions.

entries.title: Mineral dust, the soil that travels by sky

definition.text: An atmospheric aerosol of suspended soil minerals, mainly oxides and carbonates.

facts.text: It is mostly the crustal oxides SiO2, Al2O3, FeO, Fe2O3 and CaO and the carbonates CaCO3 and MgCO3.
Global emissions are estimated at 1000 to 5000 million tons a year, mostly from deserts; about a quarter may come from human desertification and land-use change.
The Sahara is the largest source, at 60 to 200 million tons a year, and its dust feeds nutrients to the Amazon rainforest and Mediterranean phytoplankton.
Spring dust from the Gobi, called Asian dust, harms visibility and health but is thought to enrich soils with trace minerals; farming pressure and desertification worsened it after 1950.
Soil moisture, vegetation cover, wind speed and soil type control dust emissions.
North American dust deposition has risen sharply since the early 1800s, with a 60% increase in the 1800s from accelerating land disturbance.
Modern observations link drought to more dust, but lake-sediment records of megadroughts show both increases and no change in deposition.

entries.contested_note: Modern observations tie drought to higher dust levels, while paleo records of megadroughts disagree on whether deposition rose.

entries.title: The jet erosion test, scouring soil to measure it

definition.text: A geotechnical test, done in the field or the laboratory, that measures a soil's resistance to erosion with a jet of water.

facts.text: A turbulent jet strikes the soil at constant hydraulic head; where its shear stress exceeds the soil's critical value it scours a hole, whose depth is measured over time.
Fitting the erosion rate gives erodibility and critical shear stress, used in designing vegetated channels, road embankments, dams, levees and spillways.
Its jet erosion index, which correlates with erodibility, typically ranges from 0 to 0.03.
As of 2017 no method for soil erodibility was universally accepted, and depending on the fitting method, erodibility for a given critical stress can vary up to 100 times.

entries.contested_note: The test's underlying assumptions have been criticised, and other erosion tests can give inconsistent erodibility values.

entries.title: Dust control, from water trucks to paved lots

definition.text: The suppression of airborne solid particles smaller than 500 micrometres.

facts.text: Environmental agencies such as the US EPA require facilities that generate fugitive dust to minimize it; new urban housing developments are the most frequent violators.
Construction and demolition sites are sprayed with water, and dust is kept from being tracked onto nearby roads.
Unpaved lots and dirt roads are paved or gravelled, or stabilized with water, vegetable oil, calcium chloride or other suppressants.
Benefits include fewer allergic reactions, pneumonia and asthma attacks, and better visibility and road safety.

entries.title: Tillage erosion, when the plow moves the hill

definition.text: Soil erosion in cultivated fields caused by the movement of soil during tillage.

facts.text: Growing evidence shows it is a major erosion process on farmland, surpassing water and wind erosion in many fields, especially on sloping and hilly land.
The pale, eroded hilltops often blamed on water erosion are actually caused by tillage erosion, which strips organic-rich topsoil from convex spots.
Its rate depends on tillage erosivity, set by the implement's design, speed and depth, and on landscape erodibility, set by slope shape and soil properties.
It arises from changes in tillage translocation (soil moved by tillage) across a field, which grows with slope gradient and curvature.
Soil is lost from hilltops and field-boundary downslopes and piles up in hollows and against boundaries, building tillage banks and terraces.
As topsoil thins, tillage mixes poorer subsoil into the plough layer and spreads it across the field, cutting crop productivity for a long time.
Soil degraded by tillage erosion likely becomes more erodible by water and wind.
It is reduced by lighter tillage (fewer, slower, shallower passes, smaller implements), contour tillage, ploughing furrows upslope and moving soil back to eroded hilltops.

entries.title: Grassed waterways, green lines down the valley floor

definition.text: A strip of native grassland 2 to 48 meters (6.6 to 157.5 feet) wide, laid along the lowest line of a cultivated dry valley to control erosion.

facts.text: Storm runoff from cropland concentrates along the valley line, where it can cut rills and gullies that speed its transfer and worsen damage downstream.
The grass raises soil cohesion and roughness, prevents rills and gullies, slows runoff and lets it soak back in during long winter rains.
It cannot reinfiltrate runoff from heavy spring and summer storms, so earthen dams across it may be added to hold the flow back for a while.
Vegetative filter strips are different: narrower, only a few metres wide, and placed along rivers or along or within fields.

entries.title: Revegetation, putting plants back on bare ground

definition.text: The replanting and rebuilding of the soil of disturbed land.

facts.text: It may happen naturally through plant colonisation and succession, or be carried out to repair damage from wildfire, mining, floods or other causes.
Erosion prevention is usually the main reason: it holds soil, helps it absorb water in heavy rain and sharply reduces turbidity in nearby waters.
Early practice simply applied seed and fertilizer, usually grasses or clover, whose fibrous roots give short-term erosion control on slopes.
Mine reclamation may need soil to be amended, replaced or created, and mycorrhizal fungi are important to success, since most woody plants need them.

entries.title: Bringing back the tallgrass prairie

definition.text: The work of restoring prairie destroyed by industrial, agricultural, commercial or residential development to its earlier state.

facts.text: Settlers plowed up the tallgrass prairie, and by 1849 most prairie grass species had given way to crops, leaving soil without the grasses' extensive fibrous roots.
Restoration helps conserve topsoil, which is exposed to wind and rain erosion once prairie is plowed under.
Prairie grasses take carbon from the air by photosynthesis and store it in the soil, making prairie soil useful for carbon sequestration.
In Europe, former cropland is restored by spontaneous succession, sowing seed mixtures, transferring plant material, and removing and transferring topsoil.

entries.title: WEPP, the physics-based heir to the USLE

definition.text: The Water Erosion Prediction Project model, a physically based erosion simulation built on hydrology, plant science, hydraulics and erosion mechanics.

facts.text: An interagency team developed it to replace the Universal Soil Loss Equation; released publicly in 1995, it is widely used in the United States and elsewhere.
It takes climate, topography, soil and management inputs and returns the water balance, soil detachment and deposition along the slope, sediment delivery and vegetation growth.
It runs for single storms or continuously, on hillslopes, roads and small parcels, or on whole watersheds of linked hillslopes, channels and impoundments.
Its sediment output falls into five size classes, primary clay, silt and sand and small and large aggregates, so selective transport and enrichment of fines can be calculated.

entries.title: The tipping point where a rill is born

definition.text: The start of a rill, when the shear stress of runoff exceeds the soil's shear strength and water begins to tear particles loose.

facts.text: Sandy and loamy soils are especially prone to rills, while dense clays resist them.
Slope steepness mainly controls rill formation and depth; slope length and soil permeability set how many rills form.
Each soil has a threshold slope below which rills cannot form; on many non-cohesive slopes it is about 2 degrees, at a shear velocity of 3 to 3.5 cm/s.
Up to 37% of erosion in rilled areas may come from collapse of rill sidewalls undercut and weakened by water.

entries.title: Sheet erosion, the thin film that strips a field

definition.text: The even erosion of soil or other material across a wide area by a thin, unchannelled layer of flowing water.

facts.text: It works in two steps: rainsplash loosens small particles, then a thin, uniform sheet flow carries them a short distance.
Each event moves material only a short way, but frequent repetition makes up for the small change per episode.
It is common on freshly ploughed fields and bare, unconsolidated ground; one rainstorm can remove up to a hundred tons of fine particles per acre.
On an uneven hillslope, sheet erosion may give way to erosion in small channels called rills, which can merge into gullies.

entries.title: The P factor, credit for conservation practices
entries.article: Universal Soil Loss Equation#Description of USLE

definition.text: The P factor of the Universal Soil Loss Equation, a soil loss ratio expressing how much conservation practices reduce erosion.

facts.text: It is hard to determine because regional maps of conservation practices are usually lacking, so it is often estimated from land use and slope.
Field boundaries such as stone walls, hedgerows, earth banks and lynchets effectively prevented or reduced erosion in pre-industrial farming.
A European P-factor model was built from a survey recording stone walls and grass margins, and landscape archaeology mapping can fill gaps in the data.

entries.title: Rainfall simulators, storms on demand

definition.text: A device used in soil science and hydrology to study how soil reacts to rainfall.

facts.text: Natural rain cannot be reproduced on demand, so simulated rain speeds the study of erosion, surface runoff and leaching.
The first, in the 1930s, were sprinkling cans or pipes with holes; 1960s nozzles matched raindrop size, impact speed and evenness, and 1980s valves varied the intensity.
In the early 1990s simulators were used in the US Water Erosion Prediction Project to update the universal soil loss equation.
On bare soil, drop size and terminal velocity must be simulated accurately because they control splash erosion.

entries.title: Steadying burned slopes before the rains come

definition.text: Treatments that steady burned slopes by offsetting fire's damage to vegetation and soil, to cut the risk of damaging runoff and erosion downhill.

facts.text: Fire burns canopy, litter, fine roots and soil organic compounds, leaving soil less protected, more water-repellent and less stable.
Heavy rain after a fire can bring catastrophic floods and debris flows; after the Thomas Fire in California, those of 2018 killed 20 people and destroyed 300 houses.
Seeding and mulching cover the soil, surfactants and flocculants counter water repellency and lost aggregation, and contour log or straw barriers shorten the slope length.
Risk peaks in the first year, so work must be quick; in the USA seeding fell from 75% of treated burned areas in the 1970s and 1980s to 30% in the 2000s.

entries.title: Measuring how far the plow drags a field

definition.text: Ways of quantifying tillage erosion, either by tracking soil moved by tillage or by measuring where soil is lost and gained.

facts.text: Translocation is measured by mixing point or bulk tracers into plots and comparing their positions before and after tillage.
Soil loss and gain show up as changes in surface elevation, compared against an uneroded fence line or hedgerow or surveyed with RTK GPS or photogrammetry.
Changes in soil organic matter can also indicate loss, but many other factors affect it, so the method is unreliable.
Since the 1980s, radioisotopes such as Cs-137 and Pb-210 have given much more accurate soil erosion estimates.

entries.text: A few buried tracers can reveal how far cultivation drags a field downhill. Tillage erosion measurement covers two approaches: tracking the soil that cultivation moves, or measuring where soil is lost and gained. These are compared against an uneroded fence line or hedgerow, or surveyed with RTK GPS or photogrammetry. Changes in soil organic matter can also signal loss, but so many other factors affect it that the method is unreliable. Since the 1980s, radioisotopes such as Cs-137 and Pb-210 have given much more accurate erosion estimates.

entries.title: Computer models of soil on the move

definition.text: Computer models that simulate how tillage moves soil along a hillslope or across a field.

facts.text: One-dimensional hillslope models such as TEP and TillERI use slope length, gradient and the erosivity of the tillage operation to give erosion rates and risk.
WaTEM calculates both water and tillage erosion on a digital elevation model, treating tillage redistribution as diffusion in the steepest-slope direction.
Field-scale models such as SORET and TillEM add the direction of tillage, moving soil both parallel and perpendicular to it.

entries.text: Tillage erosion models are computer models that simulate how cultivation moves soil along a hillslope or across a field. Field-scale models such as SORET and TillEM add the direction of cultivation, moving soil both parallel and perpendicular to it.

entries.title: The erosion index and highly erodible land

definition.text: Potential erosion from all sources except gullies divided by the soil's T value, the erosion rate above which long-term productivity may suffer; also called the erodibility index.

facts.text: It is used for U.S. conservation compliance and the Conservation Reserve Program, which requires land to have an index above 8.
In the United States, farmers cultivating highly erodible land often must follow a conservation plan to qualify for agricultural assistance.

entries.text: The erosion index, also called the erodibility index, compares how fast a soil could erode with how fast it can afford to. It is potential erosion from all sources except gullies, divided by the soil's T value, the erosion rate above which long-term productivity may suffer. It is used for U.S. conservation compliance and for the Conservation Reserve Program, which requires land to have an index above 8. In the United States, farmers cultivating highly erodible land often must follow a conservation plan to qualify for agricultural assistance.

entries.title: RUSLE, the soil loss equation revised

definition.text: A revised form of the Universal Soil Loss Equation, known as RUSLE, still used to estimate soil erosion.

facts.text: RUSLE and the WEPP model are two of the most widely used soil erosion models in North America.
Various techniques have emerged to compute its five factors.
Its support practice (P) factor is often estimated from land use and slope gradient, lower values meaning better erosion control.
Much of the literature on erosion of mined land focuses on fitting or improving RUSLE parameters.

entries.text: An equation first built for farm fields is still among North America's busiest erosion tools. The Revised Universal Soil Loss Equation, or RUSLE, is an updated form of {{ref:soil-water-041}}. With the WEPP model, it is one of the two most widely used erosion models on the continent. Various techniques now compute its five factors. The support practice factor, P, is often estimated from {{ref:soil-agri-221}} and slope gradient, and a lower value means better erosion control. Much research on eroding mined land focuses on fitting or improving its parameters.

entries.title: Predicting how much a field loses to wind

definition.text: A model that estimates a field's potential average annual soil loss to wind, used to design wind erosion control.

facts.text: It is written E = f(I, K, C, L, V): soil erodibility, ridge roughness, a climatic factor, the unsheltered distance across the field and the equivalent vegetative cover.
Soil starts moving above a critical wind speed, and the erosion rate follows the cube of the friction velocity.
Friction velocity is calculated from wind speed at a measured height using the von Kármán constant, about 0.4, in line with the logarithmic wind profile.
Wind records mostly come from airports and military bases, often only since the Second World War, which limits erosion research.

entries.text: Wind moves soil in bursts. Grains sit still until the wind passes a critical speed. Then the erosion rate climbs with the cube of the friction velocity, a measure of the wind's drag on the ground. The wind erosion equation estimates a field's potential average annual soil loss to wind as E = f(I, K, C, L, V). The five inputs are soil erodibility, ridge roughness, a climatic factor, the unsheltered distance across the field and the equivalent vegetative cover. Friction velocity is calculated from measured wind speed using the von Kármán constant, about 0.4. Most wind records come from airports and military bases, often only since the Second World War.

entries.title: Sediment, loose grains on their way somewhere

definition.text: Solid material made of loose particles that is carried to a new place and deposited there.

facts.text: It is produced by weathering and erosion and moved by wind, water, ice or gravity.
Water (fluvial processes) moves it most often: beach sands and river deposits are fluvial, dunes and loess are windblown, and moraines and till are carried by ice.
Buried sand and silt can be lithified into sedimentary rocks such as sandstone and siltstone.
Sediment is classified by grain size, shape and composition; size is measured on the log base 2 phi scale, from colloid to boulder.
Because clay names both a size range and a group of minerals, the term is ambiguous for sediment.
Seas and lakes accumulate terrigenous sediment from land, mostly supplied by rivers, along with sediment formed in the water, often from organisms.
Lake bed sediments that have not yet hardened into rock record past climates.

Seas and lakes accumulate terrigenous sediment, washed from land mostly by rivers, along with sediment formed in the water, often by organisms. Lake bed sediments that have not yet hardened into rock hold a record of past climates.

entries.title: Erosion, the great mover of the Earth's surface

definition.text: The removal of soil, rock or dissolved material from one place on the Earth's surface by processes such as flowing water or wind, and its transport to another place where it is deposited.

facts.text: Erosion differs from weathering, which involves no movement of material.
Removing material as clastic sediment is physical or mechanical erosion; removing it by dissolution is chemical erosion.
Eroded sediment or solutes may travel only a few millimetres or for thousands of kilometres.
Agents include rainfall, river flow, waves, glaciers, flooding, wind, groundwater and mass movements such as landslides and debris flows.
Physical erosion is usually fastest on steep slopes, and its rate also responds to rainfall, storminess, wind speed, wave fetch and temperature.
Transport of eroded material ends in deposition, when it arrives and settles at a new location.
Where erosion outpaces soil formation it destroys the soil; slower erosion can still prevent soil features that need time to develop.
Inceptisols form on eroded landscapes that, if stable, would have developed into Alfisols.

entries.text: Eroded material may travel only a few millimeters, or for thousands of kilometers. Erosion is the removal of soil, rock or dissolved material from one place on the Earth's surface, by processes such as flowing water or wind. The material is carried to another place and deposited there. Movement is what sets it apart from weathering, which moves nothing. Removing material as clastic sediment, made of broken fragments, is physical or mechanical erosion. Removing it by dissolution is {{ref:soil-water-008}}. The agents are many: rainfall, river flow, waves, glaciers, flooding, wind, groundwater, and mass movements such as {{ref:soil-water-057}} and {{ref:soil-water-252}}. Physical erosion is usually fastest on steep slopes. Its rate also responds to rainfall, storminess, wind speed, wave fetch and temperature. The journey ends in deposition, when the material arrives and settles at a new location. For soil, the balance matters. Where erosion outpaces soil formation, it destroys the soil. Slower erosion can still prevent soil features that need time to develop. Inceptisols form on eroded landscapes that, if stable, would have developed into Alfisols.

entries.title: Aeolian processes: how wind moves the land

definition.text: The erosion, transport and deposition of sediment by wind at or near the Earth's surface.

facts.text: Wind is most effective where vegetation is sparse, soil moisture is lacking and loose sediment is plentiful.
Worldwide, water erodes more than wind, but wind erosion is important in arid and semi-arid regions such as deserts.
Aeolian deposits also occur outside dry climates, along shorelines and on glacial outwash; much of North America and Europe is underlain by Pleistocene windblown sand and loess.
Wind sorts sand from silt and clay, so it builds separate sandy deposits (ergs) and silty ones (loess), with loess laid down further from the source.
Collisions between windborne grains (attrition) round and frost sand grains and are a major source of dust 2–5 microns across.
Wind carries minerals from the Sahara to the Amazon basin, and Saharan dust has formed red clay soils in southern Europe.
The name comes from Aeolus, the Greek god who kept the winds.

entries.text: Wind carries minerals from the Sahara all the way to the Amazon basin, and Saharan dust has built red clay soils in southern Europe. That long haul is the work of aeolian processes: the erosion, transport and deposition of sediment by wind at or near the Earth's surface. The name comes from Aeolus, the Greek god who kept the winds. Worldwide, water erodes more than wind does. Yet wind matters greatly in arid and semi-arid regions such as deserts. It works best where plants are sparse, the soil is dry and loose {{ref:soil-water-046}} lies ready. Wind is also a sorter. It separates sand from silt and clay, heaping sand into sandy deposits called ergs and laying silty loess farther from the source. Grains colliding in the air chip at one another, a process called attrition. It rounds and frosts sand grains and is a major source of dust 2–5 microns across. Wind deposits are not confined to dry lands. They also form along shorelines and on glacial outwash, and much of North America and Europe rests on windblown sand and loess from the Pleistocene.

entries.title: Sediment control: keeping a building site's soil at home

definition.text: A practice or device that keeps eroded soil on a construction site so it does not wash off and pollute nearby waters.

facts.text: Sediment controls are usually paired with erosion controls, which prevent erosion in the first place and so reduce the need for them.
They are mostly temporary, though some also serve for stormwater management.
Common controls include silt fences, sediment basins and traps, fiber rolls, straw bale and sand bag barriers, storm drain inlet protection and turbidity curtains.
All U.S. states require erosion and sediment controls on construction sites above a set size; federal rules apply from 1 acre (0.40 ha).
Controls must be installed before land clearing and grading begin and maintained through the whole disturbance phase.
Montgomery County, Maryland, began the first local government sediment control program in 1965, followed by a Maryland statewide program in 1970.

entries.text: In 1965 Montgomery County, Maryland, began the first local government program to keep construction soil out of its waters. Maryland followed with a statewide program in 1970. Sediment control is any practice or device that holds eroded soil on a construction site so it does not wash off and pollute nearby waters. It usually works alongside {{ref:soil-water-050}}, which stops soil moving in the first place and so lightens the load on sediment controls. The common tools include fabric fences, settling ponds and traps, rolls of fiber, straw bale and sand bag barriers, storm drain inlet protection and turbidity curtains. Most are temporary, though some also serve for stormwater management. Every U.S. state requires these controls on construction sites above a set size, and federal rules apply from 1 acre (0.40 ha). They must go in before clearing and grading begin and stay maintained until the disturbance ends.

entries.title: When eroded soil becomes the river's pollutant

definition.text: The harm done to rivers, lakes, coasts and their life by excess sediment washed in from eroding soil.

facts.text: Soil erosion, especially from farmland, is considered the leading global cause of diffuse water pollution.
Sediments are pollutants in their own right and also carry attached pesticides and heavy metals; eroded soil also carries fertilizers into rivers, causing eutrophication.
Silt smothers fish spawning beds by filling gaps between gravel, cuts food supply and clogs gills; plant, algal and invertebrate diversity declines.
The Yellow River carries over 1.6 billion tons of sediment to the ocean each year, mostly from water erosion on the Loess Plateau.
On Madagascar's central plateau, gullies called lavakas may supply 84% of river sediment, turning rivers dark red-brown and killing fish.
Watershed development near coral reefs is a primary cause of sediment stress, as sediment smothers and abrades corals and feeds algal blooms.
Removing an estimated 135 million m3 of sediment from water erosion likely costs over 2.3 billion euros a year in the EU and UK.

entries.text: Each year the Yellow River carries over 1.6 billion tons of sediment to the ocean, most of it washed off the Loess Plateau by water erosion. Near coral reefs, sediment from watershed development smothers and scrapes the corals and feeds algal blooms. entries.title: Mass wasting: when gravity alone moves the ground

definition.text: The movement of rock or soil down slopes under the force of gravity; also called mass movement.

facts.text: Unlike other erosion, the moving debris is not carried along in a medium such as water, wind or ice.
Types include creep, solifluction, rockfalls, debris flows and landslides, acting over seconds to hundreds of years.
Water usually aids it without being a transporting medium; with more water, landslides grade into debris avalanches, earthflows, mudflows and finally sheetfloods.
Movements are broadly creeps or landslides, and subsidence is sometimes counted as a form of mass wasting.
It is often the first stage in moving weathered material in mountains, carrying it down to where streams and glaciers can pick it up.
Weak, unconsolidated material, steep slopes, freeze-thaw or heavy rain, and undercutting by excavation or erosion all promote it.
Slow creep deforms roads and breaks pipelines, while rapid landslides can be deadly.
It is mitigated by slope stabilization, walls, catchment dams for rockfall and debris flows, afforestation and better drainage of source areas.

entries.text: Some soil leaves a hillside with no river, wind or ice to carry it. Mass wasting, also called mass movement, is the movement of rock or soil down slopes under the force of gravity. Unlike other erosion, the moving debris travels in no medium at all. Water usually aids it without being the carrier. With more water, a sliding mass grows ever more fluid, grading through flows of debris and mud and finally into sheetfloods. The forms range from slow creep of the soil to sudden rockfalls, acting over seconds to hundreds of years. Broadly, movements are either creeps or slides, described in {{ref:soil-water-055}} and {{ref:soil-water-057}}, and subsidence is sometimes counted as well. In mountains it is often the first stage in moving weathered material, carrying it down to where streams and glaciers can pick it up. Weak, unconsolidated material, steep slopes, freeze-thaw, heavy rain and undercutting by digging or erosion all promote it. Speed decides the damage. Slow creep deforms roads and breaks pipelines, while rapid slides can be deadly. Walls, catchment dams for rockfall and debris, tree planting, better drainage of source areas and {{ref:soil-water-065}} all reduce the threat.

entries.title: Soil creep: the slope that moves while no one watches

definition.text: The slow downward movement of soil and rock on a gentle slope; also called soil creep.

facts.text: Creep looks continuous but is the sum of many tiny, separate movements driven by gravity; the steeper the slope, the faster the creep.
Friction holds slope material in place; as a slope steepens, the part of gravity pressing into it shrinks, so friction falls.
A little water gives soil cohesion, like damp sand in a sandcastle, but saturation fills the pores and creates a slip plane.
Clay that swells when wet pushes soil downhill and settles at the new position as it dries; freeze-thaw and heating-cooling cycles move soil the same way.
Objects ride along: old churchyard headstones lean and sit metres from where they were set, and trees grow curved and fences tilt.
Plant roots bind loose material and draw off excess water, though they add weight; bare slopes are more likely to move.
Creep deforms roads and breaks pipelines, so engineers drive pilings deep enough to keep it from undermining foundations.
Modelled as diffusion of regolith, linear on gentle slopes and non-linear on steep ones, creep rounds ridges over long timescales.

entries.text: In old churchyards, headstones lean and sit metres from where they were set. The ground beneath them has been moving. Downhill creep, or soil creep, is the slow downward movement of soil and rock on a gentle slope. It looks continuous but is the sum of many tiny, separate movements driven by gravity, and the steeper the slope, the faster it goes. Friction holds slope material in place. As a slope steepens, less of gravity's pull presses into it, so friction falls. Water cuts both ways. A little gives soil cohesion, like damp sand in a sandcastle, but saturation fills the pores and creates a slip plane. Clay that swells when wet pushes soil downhill and settles at its new position as it dries. Freeze-thaw and heating-cooling cycles ratchet soil down the same way. Trees grow curved and fences tilt as the soil carries them along. Plant roots bind loose material and draw off excess water, though they add weight, so bare slopes are more likely to move. Creep deforms roads and breaks pipelines, so engineers drive pilings deep enough to keep it from undermining foundations. Modelled as a slow diffusion of {{ref:soil-form-097}}, creep rounds off ridges over long timescales.

entries.title: Slope stability: the balance between strength and stress

definition.text: The ability of a soil or rock slope to withstand movement; the opposite condition is slope instability or slope failure.

facts.text: It is studied in soil mechanics, geotechnical engineering and engineering geology, to explain failures and to prevent, slow or stop slope movement.
Stability is set by the ratio of available shear strength to acting shear stress, expressed as a safety factor along a potential sliding surface.
A slope is globally stable if the safety factor exceeds 1 along every potential sliding surface from top to toe; the smallest value represents the whole slope.
Safety factors between about 1 and 1.3 mark marginally stable slopes that need monitoring or stabilization.
Triggers include intense rain, snowmelt, saturation, earthquakes, internal erosion (piping), toe erosion, loading by buildings and cutting for roads.
After heavy rain, pore water pressure on the slip surface reduces effective normal stress and friction, while the added groundwater increases soil weight.
Failures in pure clay are often close to circular, while slab-shaped slips strip a layer of soil off the underlying bedrock.
Some moisture can steady a slope, but saturation acts as a lubricant; fine clay and silt soils hold more water than sandy ones.

entries.title: Landslides: when a slope's strength gives way

definition.text: Any of several forms of mass wasting with relatively rapid ground movement, such as rockfalls, mudflows, slope failures and debris flows.

facts.text: Landslides happen on steep and gentle slopes alike, from mountains to coastal cliffs and under water.
Gravity drives them: a slope fails when the shear strength of its material falls, the shear stress on it rises, or both.
Many are set off by a specific event such as heavy rain, an earthquake or a road cut, though the trigger is not always identifiable.
Natural causes include wetting and rising pore water pressure, loss of vegetation and soil structure after wildfire, undercutting by rivers or waves, weathering and earthquake shaking.
Deforestation, cultivation, construction, earthworks and removing deep-rooted plants that bind colluvium to bedrock all aggravate them.
Land degradation weakens the hold of vegetation on soil and, with extreme rainfall, makes erosion and landslides more frequent.
Saturated slope material can become a debris flow or mudflow that carries off trees, houses and cars and blocks rivers.
Landslides under water or into water can generate tsunamis.

entries.text: A landslide can strike a mountain, a coastal cliff, a gentle slope or the seafloor. A slope fails when the shear strength of its material falls, the shear stress on it rises, or both, the balance set out in {{ref:soil-water-064}}. Many slides follow a specific event such as heavy rain, an earthquake or a road cut, though the trigger is not always identifiable. Natural causes include wetting and rising pore water pressure, undercutting by rivers or waves, weathering and earthquake shaking. Wildfire adds another, by destroying vegetation and soil structure. People aggravate slides through deforestation, cultivation, construction and earthworks. Removing deep-rooted plants that bind loose slope debris to bedrock does the same. Degraded land loosens the grip of plants on soil, and with extreme rainfall it makes erosion and landslides more frequent. Saturated material can turn into a flowing mass that carries off trees, houses and cars and blocks rivers. Landslides under water or into water can generate tsunamis.

entries.title: Reading a sand grain's travels from its shape

definition.text: The description of sediment particles by three parameters: overall form (sphericity), roundness of corners and surface texture.

facts.text: Form is spherical, platy or rodlike, measured from the lengths of a grain's long, intermediate and short axes using formulas such as Krumbein's or Sneed and Folk's.
Roundness runs from very angular to very rounded and is usually judged against comparison charts rather than calculated.
Surface pits, fractures and scratches, studied mostly on quartz grains with an electron microscope, reveal a grain's transport history.
Frosted grains are particularly characteristic of windblown sediment.

entries.text: A frosted sand grain is a strong hint that the wind once carried it. entries.title: Sediment transport: how water, wind and ice move the pieces

definition.text: The movement of solid particles, from clay to boulders, by gravity together with the water, air or ice in which they are carried.

facts.text: Its study is mostly used to predict whether erosion or deposition will happen, how much, and over what time and distance.
Stronger flows raise lift and drag on a particle, while larger or denser particles tend to fall out of the flow.
Water moves larger particles than air because it is denser and more viscous; rivers usually carry sand and gravel, and big floods move cobbles and boulders.
Fluvial transport shapes ripples, dunes, floodplains and river patterns, and moves sediment by eroding and depositing on the bed.
Wind moves fine sediment, building dune fields and soils from airborne dust; glaciers carry a wide range of sizes and deposit them in moraines.
Changes in flow power cause erosion or deposition, locally behind boulders and inside meanders, and regionally after dam building or removal or base level change.
On hillslopes, soil creep, tree throw, burrowing animals and landslides move regolith downslope; as slopes near the angle of repose, erosion rates rise steeply.
When human activity raises the suspended load enough to fill channels, the problem is called siltation.

entries.text: Every grain on a riverbed, from clay to boulder, waits for a flow strong enough to move it. Sediment transport is the movement of solid particles by gravity together with the water, air or ice that carries them. Its study mostly serves prediction: whether erosion or deposition will happen, how much, and over what time and distance. The physics is a contest. Stronger flows raise the lift and drag on a particle, while larger or denser particles tend to fall out. Water moves bigger grains than air because it is denser and more viscous. Rivers usually carry sand and gravel, and big floods shift cobbles and boulders. Moving water shapes ripples, river patterns and the flat ground beside channels by eroding and depositing on its bed. Wind moves fine sediment and builds soils from airborne dust, while glaciers carry a wide range of sizes and drop them in moraines. Changes in flow power decide where material is lost or gained. Locally that happens behind boulders and inside meanders, and regionally after a dam is built or removed. On hillslopes, soil creep, falling trees, burrowing animals and landslides move {{ref:soil-form-097}} downslope, and erosion rates climb steeply as slopes near the angle of repose. When human activity loads a river with enough fine material to fill its channels, the problem is called siltation.

entries.title: How much eroded soil actually reaches the river
entries.article: Sediment#Erosion and agricultural sediment delivery to rivers

definition.text: The fraction of gross erosion on a catchment (interrill, rill, gully and stream erosion) expected to reach the river outlet.

facts.text: Sediment transfer and deposition can be modelled with sediment distribution models such as WaTEM/SEDEM.
WaTEM/SEDEM estimates put the sediment delivery ratio in Europe at about 15%.
Sediment reaching river basins brings management and siltation costs.

entries.text: In Europe, only about 15% of eroded soil is expected to reach a river outlet. That share is the sediment delivery ratio: the fraction of gross erosion on a catchment, counting interrill, rill, gully and stream erosion, that arrives at the outlet. The rest is deposited along the way. Sediment distribution models such as WaTEM/SEDEM simulate where material is moved and where it settles, and the European figure comes from them. The share that does arrive still brings management and siltation costs to river basins.
