entries.title: Chemical erosion: landscapes carried off in solution

definition.text: The loss of material from a landscape in dissolved form, as solutes.

facts.text: It contrasts with physical erosion, which removes rock or soil as solid particles of sediment.
It is usually calculated from the dissolved load carried by streams.
Sinkholes and other karst features are an extreme example of chemical erosion.
Anders Rapp pioneered its study in work on Kärkevagge published in 1960.

entries.text: A sinkhole is erosion with no solid debris to show for it. Chemical erosion is the loss of material from a landscape in dissolved form, as solutes. Physical erosion, by contrast, removes rock or soil as solid particles of sediment. Because the material leaves in solution, chemical erosion is usually calculated from the dissolved load that streams carry. Sinkholes and other karst features are its extreme example. Anders Rapp pioneered its study in work on Kärkevagge, published in 1960.

entries.title: Coastal erosion: waves against the shore

definition.text: The wearing away of shorelines, mainly by currents and waves, with changes in sea level also playing a part.

facts.text: Waves erode by hydraulic action, pounding, abrasion (corrasion), corrosion of rock such as limestone by carbonic acid, and attrition of the carried load.
Abrasion, in which waves hurl their sediment load at cliffs, is the most effective and rapid form of shoreline erosion.
Longshore drift moves sediment along the coast; erosion occurs where less sediment arrives from upcurrent than is carried away.
Sea-level rise caused by climate change has greatly increased coastal erosion rates.

entries.text: A wave's most effective weapon is the sediment it carries. Coastal erosion is the wearing away of shorelines, mainly by currents and waves, with changes in sea level also playing a part. Waves work by hydraulic action, pounding, corrosion of rock such as limestone by carbonic acid, and attrition of their own load. Abrasion, also covered in {{ref:soil-water-271}}, in which waves hurl sediment at cliffs, is the fastest and most effective. Longshore drift moves sediment along the coast, and erosion occurs where less arrives from upcurrent than is carried away. Sea-level rise caused by climate change has greatly increased coastal erosion rates.

entries.title: Glacial erosion: ice that sandpapers whole valleys

definition.text: Erosion by moving glacier ice, mainly through abrasion, plucking and ice thrusting.

facts.text: In abrasion, debris frozen in the base of the ice scrapes, polishes and gouges the bed like sandpaper on wood; in plucking, the glacier breaks off pieces of bedrock.
In ice thrusting, a glacier frozen to its bed carries large sheets of frozen sediment forward as it surges.
Glaciers carve U-shaped valleys, a steady shape estimated to take about 100,000 years to form.
Glacial erosion and meltwater leave landforms such as moraines, drumlins, ground moraine (till), kames and glacial erratics.

entries.title: How rivers cut their valleys down and out

definition.text: Erosion by water flowing continuously along a linear channel, which deepens valleys and wears away river banks.

facts.text: Stream erosion cuts both downward, deepening the valley, and headward into the hillside, creating head cuts and steep banks.
Early on, erosion is mostly vertical and makes V-shaped valleys; once a base level is reached it turns lateral, widening the floor into a floodplain.
Most stream erosion happens during floods, and pebbles and boulders carried by the water also abrade the bed, a process called traction.
Bank erosion wears away a river's banks, as distinct from scour of its bed; heavier runoff from built-up land sharply increases it.

entries.text: Most of a river's erosion happens during floods. River and stream erosion is the work of water flowing continuously along a channel, deepening valleys and wearing away banks. It cuts downward and also headward into the hillside, leaving head cuts and steep banks. Early on it works mostly downward, carving V-shaped valleys. Once the stream reaches a base level, erosion turns sideways and widens the valley floor. Pebbles and boulders dragged along the bed abrade it, a process called traction. Bank erosion, distinct from scour of the bed, rises sharply with heavier runoff from built-up land.

entries.title: Six ways a slope can fail

definition.text: A scheme sorting landslides into six types of movement (fall, topple, slide, spread, flow and slope deformation), each found in both rock and soil.

facts.text: David Varnes proposed a tighter classification in 1978; it was revised by Cruden and Varnes in 1996 and most recently by Hungr, Leroueil and Picarelli in 2014.
Falls are blocks in free fall, topples rotate away from a vertical face, and slides move as an intact body over planar or spoon-shaped (rotational) shear surfaces.
Spreads crack and extend sideways, flows move fluidised dry or wet material, and slope deformations are slow, distributed movements.
Soil classes include clay and silt rotational slides, sensitive clay spreads, debris flows, mud flows, earthflows and soil creep.
Moving material is called rock, earth or debris; earth has less than 20% by weight of particles over 2 mm, debris more.
Narrower definitions restrict landslides to slumps and translational slides that do not involve fluidisation, excluding falls, topples, lateral spreads and mass flows.
Typical slope angles are 45–90 degrees for falls and topples, 20–45 degrees for translational slides and 20–40 degrees for rotational slides.
Classifying a landslide by its activity and movement velocity matters most for judging future hazard.

entries.title: Solifluction: soil that creeps over frozen ground

definition.text: Gradual downslope mass movement of soil linked to freezing and thawing.

facts.text: Johan Gunnar Andersson coined the term in 1906 for water-saturated debris moving in periglacial regions; such slow movements were later tied to freeze-thaw instead.
It is typical of arctic and alpine climates, where soil thawed and saturated in summer creeps down moderate, sparsely vegetated slopes over permafrost.
It is slow but widespread across mountains and periglacial lowlands, and because it needs cold, humid conditions it is used to infer past climates.
It builds tongue-shaped lobes and sheets; its deposits are poorly stratified diamicton, sometimes with buried organic soils.

entries.title: Internal erosion: the hidden threat inside dams

definition.text: The formation of voids inside a soil as seeping water removes material.

facts.text: It happens when seepage through the pores and cracks of a dam or its foundation exerts enough hydraulic force to detach particles and carry them out.
It causes about half of embankment dam failures and is the second most common cause of levee failure.
It may show little outward sign, often only a sand boil that can be hidden under water, and a dam may breach within hours of the evidence becoming obvious.
Piping is its progressive growth, eroding back from the downstream exit until a continuous pipe discharges water.
Four types are recognised: concentrated leak through a crack, backward erosion from the exit point, suffusion of fines through coarse pores, and contact erosion along a fine–coarse interface.
Suffusion affects widely or gap-graded cohesionless soils, termed internally unstable, where fines pass between coarse grains that carry most of the effective stress.
Filters coarser and more permeable than the soil trap eroded particles but pass seepage; they must be internally stable, non-cohesive, free-draining and strong.
The critical shear stress that starts concentrated leak erosion can be estimated with the hole erosion test or the jet erosion test.

entries.title: Quick clay: solid ground that turns to liquid

definition.text: A highly sensitive glaciomarine clay, also called Leda or Champlain Sea clay, that can change from a solid into a watery fluid when disturbed.

facts.text: Once remolded, quick clay keeps far less strength than it had on first loading, because its clay particle structure is highly unstable.
It consists of very fine silt and clay-sized particles from glacial grinding, first laid down in the sea.
It is found only in lands near the North Pole glaciated in the Pleistocene: Russia, Canada, Norway, Sweden, Finland and Alaska.
In Canada it is tied mainly to the Pleistocene Champlain Sea, in the Ottawa Valley, the St. Lawrence Valley and the Saguenay River region.
Sudden liquefaction, set off by earthquake vibrations or massive rainfall, causes its landslides; in Canada alone it is linked to more than 250 mapped landslides.
Liquefaction usually affects sandy or non-plastic silty soils; quick clay is one of the rare cases in clay.
It is a particular challenge for civil engineering, and known deposits are now commonly tested before any major development.

entries.text: Some clay stands as firm ground until a shock turns it into a watery fluid. Quick clay, also called Leda or Champlain Sea clay, is a highly sensitive glaciomarine clay. It consists of very fine silt and clay-sized particles ground up by glaciers and first laid down in the sea. Its particle structure is highly unstable, so once remolded it keeps far less strength than it had on first loading. It is found only in lands near the North Pole glaciated in the Pleistocene: Russia, Canada, Norway, Sweden, Finland and Alaska. In Canada it lies mainly in the Ottawa Valley, the St. Lawrence Valley and the Saguenay River region. Earthquake vibrations or massive rainfall can liquefy it suddenly and set off landslides. In Canada alone, quick clay it is linked to more than 250 mapped landslides. Liquefaction, described in {{ref:soil-phys-116}}, usually affects sandy or non-plastic silty soils, so quick clay is one of the rare cases in clay. Known deposits are now commonly tested before any major development.

entries.title: Debris flows: rivers of rock and mud

definition.text: A water-laden mass of soil and broken rock that flows down mountainsides, funnels into channels and leaves thick muddy deposits on valley floors.

facts.text: Its bulk density is about 2000 kilograms per cubic meter, like other landslides, yet high pore-fluid pressure liquefies the sediment so it flows almost like water.
Sediment fills more than about 40 to 50% of its volume; floods with about 10 to 40% solids are hyperconcentrated floods, and true mudflows are mostly finer than sand.
It needs slopes steeper than about 25 degrees, plenty of loose sediment, soil or weathered rock, and enough water to almost fully saturate it.
Triggers include intense rain or snowmelt, dam-break or glacial outburst floods and landslides, and debris flows become more frequent after forest and brush fires.
Flows in steep channels often exceed 10 m/s (36 km/h), and flows of up to about 100,000 cubic meters are common in mountains.
A boulder-rich head is followed by a liquefied body of finer sediment; deposits are poorly sorted lobes with boulder levees that build alluvial fans.
Debris flows killed more than 20,000 people at Armero, Colombia, in 1985 and tens of thousands in Vargas State, Venezuela, in 1999.
Debris basins can catch them, but they are a costly last resort that needs yearly maintenance.

entries.title: Where moving sediment finally comes to rest

definition.text: The geological process by which sediment, soil and rock are added to a landform or landmass.

facts.text: Wind, ice, water and gravity carry weathered material and drop it in layers when the flow loses enough kinetic energy.
Deposition starts when the forces moving sediment can no longer overcome gravity and friction, an idea known as the null point hypothesis.
Large grains in bed load or suspended load come to rest when bed shear stress and turbulence fall too low; suspended grains may travel some way as they fall through the water.
Fine silt and clay particles settle individually by Stokes' law, but in seawater they flocculate, bonding electrically into flocs.
Deposition can also build sediment from organic or chemical matter, as with chalk from plankton skeletons and coal from plant material laid down without oxygen.

entries.text: Everything that erosion carries away must eventually land somewhere. Deposition is the geological process by which sediment, soil and rock are added to a landform or landmass. Wind, ice, water and gravity all carry weathered material, and they drop it in layers when the flow loses enough kinetic energy. The tipping point has a name, the null point hypothesis: deposition begins when the forces moving sediment can no longer overcome gravity and friction. Grain size shapes how this plays out. Large grains come to rest when the water's drag on the bed and its turbulence fall too low. Grains held up in the water may still drift some way as they sink. Fine silt and clay particles settle one by one, following {{ref:soil-phys-188}}. In seawater, though, they flocculate, bonding electrically into clumps called flocs that sink together. Deposition is not only about broken rock. It can build sediment from organic or chemical matter too. Chalk forms from the skeletons of plankton, and coal from plant material laid down without oxygen.

entries.title: Three ways the wind moves grains

definition.text: The movement of sediment by wind through suspension, saltation (skipping) and creep (rolling or sliding).

facts.text: Grains start moving at the fluid threshold wind speed; impacts then keep transport going until wind falls below the lower impact threshold, a hysteresis.
Turbulence holds fine particles in suspension, letting wind separate grains under 0.05 mm from coarser ones and carry them far.
Saltation matters most for grains up to 2 mm; landing grains launch others and push heavier ones forward as creep, up to 25% of grain movement in deserts.
Vegetation suppresses aeolian transport: a plant cover of as little as 15% stops most sand movement.

entries.text: Wind moves sediment in three ways: suspension, short skipping hops described in {{ref:soil-water-251}}, and creep, a rolling or sliding along the ground. Grains start moving at the fluid threshold wind speed, and impacts keep them moving until the wind drops below a lower threshold, a lag called hysteresis. Turbulence lets wind carry grains under 0.05 mm far from coarser ones. Hops matter most for grains up to 2 mm, and landing grains shove heavier ones along as creep, up to 25% of grain movement in deserts. A plant cover of just 15% stops most sand movement.

entries.title: Deflation: wind that scoops out the desert

definition.text: The lifting and removal of loose surface material by turbulent wind.

facts.text: It works through surface creep, saltation and suspension, with saltation likely accounting for 50–70% of it.
Most deflation zones are floored by desert pavement, a sheet of rock fragments left behind once fines are removed, which shields the material below.
Deflation hollows called blowouts range from dimples 0.3 m deep to Mongolian hollows 8 km across and 60 to 100 m deep.

entries.text: Some hollows scoured by wind in Mongolia are 8 km across and 60 to 100 m deep. Deflation is the lifting and removal of loose surface material by turbulent wind. It works through surface creep, suspension and grains bouncing along in short hops, and the hops likely account for 50–70% of it. The hollows it digs, called blowouts, range from dimples 0.3 m deep to those Mongolian giants. Once the fines are gone, a sheet of rock fragments is left behind, the {{ref:soil-water-253}} that floors most deflation zones and shields the material below.

entries.title: Sand dunes: hills the wind builds

definition.text: A mound or ridge of sediment heaped up by the wind, independent of any obstacle.

facts.text: Dunes have a gentle windward slope and a steep downwind avalanche slope called the slipface.
Transverse dunes such as crescent-shaped barchans form under one prevailing wind; linear dunes run for tens of kilometres; star dunes have more than two slipfaces.
Vegetated parabolic dunes are crescents whose ends point upwind, formed where plant patches meet active sand such as blowouts.
Ralph Bagnold named the barchan and the linear seif dune; John Tilton Hack added vegetation-shaped parabolic dunes in 1941.

entries.title: Wind abrasion: sandblasting that mattered less than thought

definition.text: The wearing of rock and landforms by wind-driven grains, also called corrasion.

facts.text: Once thought a major cause of desert erosion, it was judged much less important by the mid-20th century; features like mushroom rocks are now credited to other processes.
Wind usually lifts sand only a short way: most stays within 50 cm of the surface and practically none rises above 2 m.
Yardangs, rock ridges up to tens of metres high streamlined by desert winds, are widely attributed to abrasion and form mostly in soft material such as silt.
Polished or faceted stones called ventifacts are rare, needing abundant sand, strong winds and no vegetation.

entries.title: A warming climate can raise or lower landslide risk

definition.text: The effects of changing temperature, rainfall and evapotranspiration on where, how often and how strongly landslides occur.

facts.text: The effects vary strongly between areas, can raise or lower landslide activity, and must be studied regionally.
Warming can reduce landslides where higher evapotranspiration dries soils and growth of vegetation is stimulated.
It increases them through faster snowmelt and rain on snow, permafrost thaw that removes the cohesion of interstitial ice at high elevation, and glacier retreat.
More extreme rainfall focuses infiltration and increases runoff events that may trigger debris flows.

entries.text: Climate change does not push landslides in one direction. Shifts in temperature, rainfall and {{ref:soil-water-161}} change where, how often and how strongly slides occur. The effects vary so much between areas that they must be studied regionally. Warming can reduce landslides where faster evaporation dries soils and plant growth is stimulated. It increases them through faster snowmelt, rain on snow and glacier retreat. At high elevation, thawing frozen ground loses the cohesion its interstitial ice once gave. More extreme rainfall also focuses infiltration and increases runoff events that may trigger debris flows.

entries.title: Mapping where the next landslide will strike

definition.text: Analysing the factors behind past landslides to map where future ones are likely, to reduce losses and guide land-use planning.

facts.text: Factors used are usually grouped into geomorphology, geology, land use and land cover, and hydrogeology.
Geographic information systems handle the many layered factors, and before-and-after aerial photos and satellite images record landslide distribution and triggers.
Prediction assumes that future landslides will occur under the same conditions as past ones.
Hazard maps should show past events and clearly mark probable locations of future ones.

entries.text: Landslide hazard mapping rests on one assumption: future slides will happen under the same conditions as past ones. Analysts study the factors behind earlier landslides, usually grouped as {{ref:soil-water-295}}, geology, {{ref:soil-agri-221}} and land cover, and hydrogeology. Mapping software, the subject of {{ref:soil-agri-165}}, handles the many layered factors. Aerial photos and satellite images taken before and after events record where slides happened and what set them off. A good hazard map shows past events and clearly marks probable future sites, so planners can reduce losses.

entries.title: Watching slopes move to warn of landslides

definition.text: Tracking slope movement to judge danger, issue timely alerts and plan protective measures.

facts.text: Remote sensing uses InSAR for precise, large-scale displacement, repeated LiDAR point clouds, optical satellite imagery and drones.
Ground-based methods include GPS, topographic surveys of marked targets and ground-based radar.
Geotechnical instruments include piezometers for pore water pressure, borehole inclinometers, extensometers across cracks and tiltmeters.

entries.title: Shallow slides and deep-seated slides

definition.text: Landslides grouped by the depth of their sliding surface: within the soil mantle or weathered bedrock (shallow), or well below tree rooting depth (deep-seated).

facts.text: Shallow slides reach from a few decimetres to some metres deep; debris slides and debris flows are usually shallow.
They often occur where permeable soil lies over less permeable soil, which traps water, builds pressure and lets the saturated topsoil slide.
Deep-seated slides involve deep regolith, weathered rock or bedrock, often move along faults or bedding planes, and show concave head scarps and steep toes.
Deep-seated landslides shape landscapes over geological time and supply sediment that strongly alters stream courses.

They often move along faults or bedding planes, leaving concave head scarps and steep toes. Over geological time they shape landscapes and feed sediment that strongly alters stream courses.

entries.title: Silt fences: cheap, simple and often failing

definition.text: A temporary fabric fence used on construction sites to keep sediment carried by stormwater runoff out of nearby waters.

facts.text: Geotextile fabric is stretched between stakes along a contour, its lower edge buried in the soil, so that runoff pools behind it and sediment settles out.
Fine particles soon clog the fabric; no sediment-retention device filters stormwater for long.
It is widely used for its low cost and simple design, but field tests show generally poor results, often from bad placement, installation or maintenance.
Static slicing, which pushes the fabric into a slot cut by a blade and then compacts the soil, has proved the most effective installation method since 1998.

entries.title: Dust storms: when dry ground takes to the sky

definition.text: A storm in which strong wind blows loose sand and dirt off dry ground, common in arid and semi-arid regions; also called a sandstorm.

facts.text: By one definition, it is a wind storm carrying enough dust to cut visibility below 1 kilometre.
Saltating sand grains strike the ground and break off finer dust, which then travels in suspension.
Drought, wind, wildfire and poor farming and grazing cause them; intensive tillage in dryland farming and bare ground without crops or cover crops are especially risky.
Gusts come from thunderstorm outflows or from dry cold fronts, the type common in the Dust Bowl years.
They remove soil from drylands, preferentially taking organic matter and the light, nutrient-rich particles, and their abrasion damages young crops.
Saharan dust storms have increased about 10-fold since the 1950s, causing topsoil loss in Niger, Chad, northern Nigeria and Burkina Faso.
Inhaled dust can cause dust pneumonia, and prolonged exposure can cause silicosis.
Deposited dust can help: rainforests of Central and South America gain mineral nutrients from the Sahara, and ancient dust deposits form fertile loess.

entries.title: The Dust Bowl: when the Great Plains blew away

definition.text: A decade of severe dust storms and drought, 1930–1940, that badly damaged the farming and ecology of the High Plains and North American prairies.

facts.text: It hit hardest in western Kansas, the Oklahoma and Texas panhandles, southeast Colorado and northeast New Mexico; its drought and erosion affected 100 million acres (400,000 km2).
It combined natural causes, above all severe drought, with human ones: settlers destroyed the topsoil by not using dryland farming methods that prevent wind erosion.
Deep plowing of the virgin prairie had removed the native deep-rooted grasses that held soil and moisture through droughts and high winds.
Cotton farmers left fields bare in winter, when High Plains winds are strongest, and burned the stubble, stripping the soil of organic matter and surface cover.
Drought came in three waves, 1934, 1936 and 1939–1940; it dried the topsoil to a powder, and failed crops left plowed fields open to the wind.
Black blizzards of dust reached the East Coast; a two-day storm in May 1934 dropped 12 million pounds (5,400 tonnes) of dust on Chicago.
In many regions more than 75% of the topsoil had blown away by the end of the 1930s.
A key result was the government's greatly expanded role in land management and soil conservation.

entries.title: How Washington fought the Dust Bowl

definition.text: The US federal programmes of the 1930s that answered the Dust Bowl with soil conservation, tree planting and farm relief.

facts.text: The Soil Erosion Service was set up in August 1933 under Hugh Hammond Bennett; moved to the Department of Agriculture in 1935, it became the Soil Conservation Service, now the NRCS.
The Civilian Conservation Corps planted the Great Plains Shelterbelt, over 200 million trees from Canada to Abilene, Texas, to break the wind and hold soil and water.
Farmers were taught crop rotation, strip farming, contour plowing and terracing, and from 1937 were paid a dollar an acre to adopt soil-conserving methods.
By 1938 the conservation effort had cut the amount of blowing soil by 65%.

entries.title: The Dust Bowl's long shadow on farm values

definition.text: The lasting fall in farmland value and population that followed the Dust Bowl's loss of topsoil.

facts.text: By 1940, relative to low-erosion counties, farmland value per acre had fallen 28% in high-erosion counties and 17% in medium-erosion counties.
In highly eroded areas less than 25% of the original agricultural losses were ever recovered.
Thinner topsoil favoured a shift from wheat to livestock and hay, but farmers were slow to switch, partly because bank failures cut off credit.
The economy adjusted mainly through population decline in the more eroded counties, both in the 1930s and through the 1950s.

entries.title: Earthflows: slow rivers of saturated clay and silt

definition.text: A viscous downslope flow of water-saturated fine-grained material moving under gravity.

facts.text: It is a mass movement between downhill creep and mudflow: slower than a mudflow, and covered with solid material carried along by the flow.
Clay, fine sand, silt and fine pyroclastic material are prone to it; once saturated with enough water they begin to flow.
Higher water content means faster flow, so an earthflow may take minutes or years to move and can cover a few square meters or several hectares.
Draining slopes is one of the best defences; slopes undercut by rivers or construction, or made of wet clay and silt, are most at risk.

entries.title: Denudation, the slow lowering of the land

definition.text: The sum of processes by which moving water, ice, wind and waves wear down the Earth's surface, lowering its elevation and relief.

facts.text: Erosion moves soil and rock from place to place, whereas denudation is the total of erosion and other processes that lower the surface.
It combines mechanical, biological and chemical weathering, erosion and mass wasting, and removes both solid particles and dissolved material.
Its rate depends on human activity, living organisms, climate, rock type, topography and tectonic activity.
Tectonic uplift, volcanoes and earthquakes expose crust to weathering and erosion; as denudation lightens the crust, it allows further uplift.
Denudation rates are usually much lower than uplift rates, and average mountain-building rates can be eight times the maximum average denudation.
Hutton and Playfair's idea that landscapes are worn down to near sea level gave rise to planation theories such as Davis's peneplanation cycle, which faded after 1964.

entries.title: Sedimentation: when falling grains finally stop

definition.text: The settling of suspended particles out of a fluid until they come to rest against a barrier.

facts.text: Settling is the fall of particles through the liquid; sedimentation is its end result.
Type 1 particles such as sand settle singly at constant velocity, type 2 particles flocculate so their settling velocity changes, and above 1000 mg/L type 3 particles settle together as a zone.
Geological rates range from under 3 millimetres per thousand years for deep-sea sediment to several metres per thousand years in parts of major deltas.
Sedimentation-enhancing strategies restore water and sediment exchange between rivers and delta plains so that subsiding deltas can keep their elevation.

entries.text: Settling is the fall of particles through a liquid; sedimentation is where that fall ends, with the particles at rest against a barrier. How they fall depends on the particle. Sand grains, called type 1, settle singly at constant velocity. Type 2 particles flocculate, so their settling speed changes as they clump. Above 1000 mg/L, type 3 particles settle together as a zone. Deep-sea sediment builds up at under 3 millimetres per thousand years; parts of major deltas gain several metres. Restoring the exchange of water and sediment between rivers and delta plains helps sinking deltas keep their height.

entries.title: Siltation, when eroded soil chokes the water

definition.text: Water pollution by fine silt and clay particles, both as raised suspended sediment and as unwanted fine deposits on the bottom.

facts.text: It is most often caused by soil erosion or by sediment spilled during dredging and dumping.
In rural areas the source is usually soil degraded by intensive or poor farming, especially fine-grained soils such as loess; in towns it is construction sites stripped of vegetation.
Because erosion at the source may be a fraction of a millimetre a year, sediment is measured in transport: concentration times discharge, so 50 mg/L at 30 m3/s gives 1.5 kg/s.
Suspended sediment disrupts filter-feeding organisms and deposits bury them; as little as 1 mm of accumulation may kill coral polyps.
Hard-bottom communities and mussel and oyster banks are more sensitive than sand and mud bottoms.
The first defence is keeping land covered to prevent erosion, the second is trapping sediment before it reaches streams; construction sites use short exposure times and silt screens.
Silt also fills navigation and irrigation channels, where dredging is often the only remedy once it has settled.

entries.title: River bank failure: when the bank gives way

definition.text: The sudden mass wasting of a stream bank, when gravity on its rock and soil exceeds the cohesive and adhesive forces holding them together.

facts.text: All streams erode their banks by friction, shearing and solution; floods, helicoidal flow on the outside of bends and downcutting rills and gullies speed this up.
Extra weight near the edge, soil saturation from rain, irrigation or septic systems, groundwater undermining and loss of deep-rooted vegetation can all set off failure.
The toe zone, between ordinary and low water level, is most exposed to erosion; most banks are layered, with cohesionless soils interbedded with cohesive ones.
Failure may be hydraulic, geotechnical, tectonic or gravitational; cohesive soils fail on rotational or planar surfaces, non-cohesive soils by avalanching.

entries.text: Every stream eats at its banks by friction, shearing and solution. Extra weight near the edge, saturation from rain, watering of crops or septic systems, groundwater undermining and loss of deep-rooted plants can all set off a collapse. The toe zone, between ordinary and low water level, is most exposed. Cohesive soils fail on rotational or planar surfaces; non-cohesive ones avalanche.

entries.title: Sediment basins: settling ponds for building sites

definition.text: A temporary pond on a construction site that captures soil washed off in rain storms and protects the water quality of nearby waters.

facts.text: Sediment-laden runoff settles in the pond before the water is discharged.
Basins suit construction sites of 5 acres (20,000 m2) or more; smaller sites use sediment traps, small embankments along low ground or above storm drain inlets.
After earthmoving ends, a basin may be cleaned out and kept as a permanent detention or retention basin for stormwater.

entries.title: Mudflows: liquefied slopes on the run

definition.text: A fast-moving flow of debris and soil that has been liquefied by added water; also called a mudslide.

facts.text: Mudflows move at three to five metres per second; their clay makes them more fluid than debris flows, so they travel farther over gentler slopes.
They contain at least 50% silt- and clay-sized material and up to 30% water.
Many begin as slides triggered by heavy rain, snowmelt or groundwater and turn into flows as they take up water.
Whether mud starts to flow depends on its grain size, water content and the slope.

entries.title: Gelifluction: spring meltwater sets topsoil flowing

definition.text: The downslope movement of waterlogged topsoil driven by seasonal freezing and thawing, closely related to solifluction.

facts.text: It is prominent in periglacial regions with snow for six to eight months a year, where spring melt releases half a year's precipitation within a couple of days.
The waterlogged topsoil flows like a liquid, so gelifluction can occur on slopes of less than half a degree.
It forms tongue-shaped lobes on slopes of 10° to 20° and terrace-like benches on gentler ones; lobes have risers of up to 5 metres (16 ft) and treads of up to 50 metres (160 ft).

entries.text: In some periglacial regions, spring melt releases half a year's precipitation within a couple of days. It is a close relative of {{ref:soil-water-056}}, prominent where snow lies six to eight months a year. The soaked topsoil flows like a liquid, so gelifluction can occur on slopes of less than half a degree. On slopes of 10° to 20° it builds tongue-shaped lobes, with risers up to 5 metres (16 ft) and treads up to 50 metres (160 ft). Gentler slopes get terrace-like benches.

entries.title: Fiber rolls: straw tubes that catch a slope's soil

definition.text: A temporary tube of straw, coconut fibre or similar material laid on construction slopes to control erosion and trap sediment.

facts.text: Rolls are laid along contours in shallow trenches 2 to 4 inches (5 to 10 cm) deep and staked down, with more rows on steeper slopes and one at the slope's base.
They slow surface runoff without channelling it, letting water through while sediment stays uphill; properly installed, they trap sediment better than straw bales.
They should not be used on very steep land prone to mudslides, landslides or creep, and rolls that are poorly staked can be carried off by high flows.

entries.title: Clearing muddy runoff with flocculants

definition.text: Systems that clear sediment-laden construction runoff by adding flocculants and then filtering or settling the water.

facts.text: Active systems pump the water and dose it with natural polymers, synthetic polymers or inorganic flocculants to cut total suspended solids before discharge.
Cationic flocculants such as chitosan can cause hypoxia in fish, so anionic flocculants are best practice in open systems.
Passive systems use gravity flow through ditches with self-dosing gel flocculants, jute filters and sedimentation ponds, needing no power and little skill.
Stormwater management facilities are usually designed with Stokes' law to remove particles larger than 40 microns.

entries.text: Sediment treatment systems clean muddy construction runoff by adding flocculants, chemicals that make fine particles clump, then filtering or settling the water. entries.title: How rivers carve, carry and build with sediment

definition.text: The movement of sediment by rivers and streams, with the erosion, deposition and landforms it creates.

facts.text: Flowing water exerts shear stress on the bed and lowers it where the bed is weak or loose; carried sediment abrades the bed while the fragments themselves are worn smaller and rounder by attrition.
Sediment travels as bed load, suspended load or dissolved material.
Where flow is fast more particles are picked up than dropped, and where it is slow the dropped particles build floodplains of alluvium.
The Rouse number, settling velocity over upward velocity, sets a grain's mode: above 2.5 bed load, 0.8 to 2.5 suspended load, below 0.8 wash load.
Water moves larger sediment than air because it is denser and more viscous; floods can carry cobbles and boulders.
The Mississippi is estimated to carry 406 million tons of sediment to the sea each year, the Yellow River 796 million tons and the Po 67 million tons.
Sediment motion builds ripples, dunes and antidunes, which preserved in rock record the direction and strength of past flows.

entries.text: Each year the Yellow River is estimated to deliver 796 million tons of sediment to the sea. The Mississippi carries 406 million tons and the Po 67 million. Fluvial sediment processes are the movement of sediment by rivers and streams, with the erosion, deposition and landforms they create. Flowing water drags on its bed and lowers it where the bed is weak or loose. The sediment it carries scrapes the bed, while the fragments themselves grind smaller and rounder, a wearing called attrition. Sediment travels in three ways: rolling along the bed as bed load, held up in the flow as {{ref:soil-water-286}}, or dissolved. A single ratio, the Rouse number, sorts the grains. It compares a grain's settling velocity with the water's upward velocity. Above 2.5 a grain moves as bed load, between 0.8 and 2.5 held up in the flow, and below 0.8 as wash load, the finest fraction. Water moves bigger grains than air does because it is denser and more viscous, and floods can roll cobbles and boulders. Where flow is fast, the river picks up more than it drops. Where it is slow, dropped particles build {{ref:soil-water-264}} of {{ref:soil-form-112}}. The moving bed shapes ripples, dunes and antidunes, which preserved in rock record the direction and strength of ancient flows.

entries.title: Saltation: grains that travel in hops

definition.text: A mode of transport in which wind or water lifts loose grains from a bed and carries them in short hops back to the surface.

facts.text: At low flow speeds grains only roll along the surface as creep; above the fluid threshold, drag and lift raise them into roughly ballistic arcs.
Landing grains splash others into motion, and in air this saltation bombardment makes most of the dust in dust storms.
Particles of about 70 micrometres or less in air are held up by turbulence and travel in suspension instead.
It moves pebbles in rivers, sand over deserts, soil blowing off fields and drifting snow; fences with holes slow it, and sand piles up on their lee side.

Particles of about 70 micrometres or less ride the turbulence in suspension instead. Fences with holes slow saltation, piling sand on their lee side.

entries.title: The hole erosion test: drilling a leak to measure it

definition.text: A geotechnical laboratory test of a soil's resistance to erosion, used above all for internal erosion in embankment dams.

facts.text: A small hole, typically 6 mm, is drilled through a soil sample compacted in a mould, and water forced through it erodes and widens the hole while the flow is measured.
Plotting erosion rate against hydraulic shear stress gives the critical shear stress at which a leak starts to erode, and the erodibility that sets how fast erosion then proceeds.
A modified version adds a pitot-static tube to measure total head; it gives much smaller critical shear stresses, closer to other tests such as the jet erosion test.

entries.text: The hole erosion test measures how well a soil resists erosion, above all for {{ref:soil-water-100}} in embankment dams. Plotting erosion rate against hydraulic shear stress gives two values. One is the critical shear stress at which a leak starts to erode. The other is the erodibility, which sets how fast erosion then proceeds. A modified version adds a pitot-static tube to measure total head. It gives much smaller critical shear stresses, closer to the jet erosion test.

It gives much smaller critical shear stresses, closer to the jet erosion test.

entries.title: Healing a gully by taming its water

definition.text: Altering water flow through a gully to reduce scouring, let sediment build up and allow plants to return.

facts.text: Good land management prevents gullies: vegetation along drainage lines, evenly spread runoff, high soil organic matter and no over-cultivation.
Drop structures, pipe structures, grass chutes and rock chutes carry water safely down to the gully floor.
Sediment settling on flatter stretches lets vegetation re-establish, and damaged areas should be fenced off until restoration is complete.
Evidence on how well gully controls work is scattered, and terrain, climate and landscape can make them fail.

entries.title: Marine clay: soft sediment from the sea floor

definition.text: Marine clays are fine-grained sedimentary deposits made mostly of clay minerals that build up in coastal environments.

facts.text: They derive from weathered continental rocks carried to the ocean, where they settle and consolidate on the seabed.
They commonly contain illite, smectite, kaolinite and chlorite, plus varying silt, organic matter and biogenic material.
Saline deposition shapes their structure and bonding, often giving high natural water content and low permeability.
They are highly sensitive: their fragile internal structure can lose much of its strength when disturbed.
Seawater's excess ions make deposited clay flocculate into a loose, open structure; once dried by falling sea level it admits water easily.
Marine clay lying over peat may mark a marine flooding surface, reflecting landward coastal shift during relative sea-level rise.

entries.title: Trees on a slope: anchor or burden

definition.text: The two-way link between slopes and the plants growing on them, which can either strengthen or weaken a slope.

facts.text: The relationship depends on the soil type, the rainfall regime, the plant species, the slope aspect and the steepness of the slope.
Plants act on slopes in four main ways: wind throw, removal of water, the added mass of the vegetation (surcharge) and mechanical reinforcement by roots.
Wind throw topples a tree and exposes its root plate and the soil beneath; it matters for a single tree, less for a stand, where inner trees are sheltered.
Plant mass matters only where large trees grow: a tree 30–50m tall may load a slope with roughly 100–150 kN/m2.
Large trees at the toe of a slope prone to rotational failure could raise its factor of safety by 10%; planted at the top they could lower it by 10%.
Felling large trees at a slope's toe removes both their drying effect and their load, and in clay soils the resulting suction can draw in water and soften the soil.
Judging how plants alter a slope rests on knowing its underlying stability as a function of soil type, age, horizon development and compaction.

entries.title: Calculating whether a slope will hold

definition.text: Static or dynamic, analytical or empirical methods for evaluating the stability of natural slopes and of dams, embankments and excavations in soil and rock.

facts.text: It is used to design safe embankments, road cuts, open-pit mines, excavations and landfills.
It needs site data on soil and rock properties, slope geometry, groundwater and discontinuities; water pressure in pores and fractures lowers material strength.
Limit equilibrium is the most common and simplest method, but complex failures such as progressive creep or liquefaction need numerical modelling.
Simple 2-D circular analysis is widely used, but finding the most probable slip plane is a primary difficulty, and real failures in mixed soils are not always circular.

entries.title: Engineering slopes that stay put

definition.text: Engineering work on slopes that raises their stability and lessens the effect of landslides.

facts.text: Methods are classed as geometric (reshaping the slope), hydrogeological (lowering groundwater or drying the material) and chemical or mechanical (raising shear strength, anchors, nails, piles).
Vegetation is a widely used bioengineering method where landslides are shallow: roots reinforce the upper soil, and interception and transpiration dry it.
Slopes are also stabilized by flattening, piles or retaining walls, grouting, and consolidation by surcharging or electro-osmosis.
Installing drainage paths significantly improves stability by reducing destabilizing forces.

entries.text: Draining water out of a slope significantly improves its stability by reducing the forces that push it toward failure. entries.title: Reading the marks gravity leaves on slopes

definition.text: The deposits and landforms left by mass wasting, usually subtle but occasionally spectacular.

facts.text: Soil creep shows itself in curved tree trunks and tilted fences and poles, and freeze-thaw creep builds small steps called terracettes.
Solifluction leaves lobed or sheet-like deposits whose rock fragments point perpendicular to the deposit's contours.
Rockfall builds talus slopes at the foot of cliffs, and landslides leave scarps and step-like terraces.
Debris flows leave long, narrow tracks of very poorly sorted material, often with levees, and build much of the upper slopes of alluvial fans.

entries.text: Most traces of mass wasting are subtle, but a few are spectacular. Soil creep shows in curved tree trunks and tilted fences and poles, and freeze-thaw creep builds small steps on hillsides. Solifluction leaves lobed or sheet-like deposits whose rock fragments point perpendicular to the deposit's contours. Rockfall piles talus slopes at the foot of cliffs, and landslides leave scarps and step-like benches. Debris flows leave long, narrow tracks of very poorly sorted material, often with levees, and build much of the upper slopes of the sediment cones described in {{ref:soil-water-293}}.

entries.title: Baer–Babinet law: blaming Earth's spin for lopsided rivers

definition.text: The idea that the Earth's rotation influences how rivers form, making them erode one bank more than the other.

facts.text: It holds that rivers erode mostly their right banks in the Northern Hemisphere and their left banks in the Southern Hemisphere.
Jacques Babinet proposed it in 1859 from the Coriolis force, and Karl Ernst von Baer gave a fuller explanation in 1860.
The Coriolis force is orders of magnitude weaker than local flow forces in a channel, so the effect is unlikely to matter in any one river; Einstein explained the true causes in 1926.

entries.contested_note: The page presents it as a hypothesis whose Coriolis mechanism is too weak to matter in a given river.
entries.text: In 1859 Jacques Babinet proposed that the Earth's rotation makes rivers erode one bank more than the other. Karl Ernst von Baer gave a fuller explanation in 1860. Their Baer–Babinet law holds that rivers wear mostly their right banks in the Northern Hemisphere and their left banks in the Southern. The proposed cause was the Coriolis force. It is best treated as a hypothesis with too weak a mechanism. The Coriolis force is orders of magnitude weaker than local flow forces in a channel, so it is unlikely to matter in any one river. Einstein explained the true causes in 1926.

entries.title: Soil sloughing: the shallow slip that can grow

definition.text: The falling of soil off banks and slopes when it loses cohesion.

facts.text: It is shallow, involving the uppermost soil layers, and has the same causes as landslides, very wet soil above all; left unchecked it can end in massive bank or slope failure.
Rising water content weakens shear strength and so cohesion; active pore water pressure can cut shear strength by up to 60%.
Bare soils slough more readily than vegetated ones because roots hold the surface, so clearing vegetation from banks and slopes raises the risk.
Loss of root strength after harvesting can lower the safety factor so far that a moderate storm brings slope failure.

Clearing banks therefore raises the risk, and lost root strength after harvesting can lower the safety factor so far that a moderate storm brings failure. Left unchecked, sloughing can end in massive bank or slope failure.

entries.title: Rivers that melt their way through frozen banks

definition.text: The combined mechanical and thermal erosion of ice-rich soils and sediments by an unfrozen river or stream.

facts.text: Strong flow thaws the frozen bank, and the thawed material is removed where hydraulic forces can cut into it; banks may collapse, often along ice wedges.
Melting ice inside a porous material weakens it, leaving it easy to break up and carry away.
On the Lena, spring floods break river ice up to 2 m thick, discharge rises about tenfold within days, and the banks retreat about 40 m per year.
Cold-room experiments show that water temperature, ice temperature and discharge drive thermal erosion, while high ice content in the soil slows it.

entries.title: A buried cable that feels a slope shift

definition.text: The use of time-domain reflectometry to watch for slope movement at highway cuts, rail beds and open-pit mines.

facts.text: A coaxial cable set in a vertical borehole with brittle grout deforms sharply when the ground moves, showing up as a peak in the reflection trace.
Once insensitive to small movements and dependent on people reading traces, it was improved by Farrington and Sargand (2004), whose numerical-derivative method gives earlier warning.
Timing infiltration with probes in different layers helps judge how well best management practices cut stormwater runoff.

entries.title: Suspended load: sediment carried by turbulence

definition.text: The part of a flow's sediment that is lifted off the bed and held up in the fluid by turbulence.

facts.text: It is mostly fine sand, silt and clay, though stronger flows carry coarser sand low in the water column.
It forms the middle layer of fluvial transport, between bed load below and the finest wash load above, and a particle can shift between them as flow speed changes.
Grains are fully suspended at Rouse numbers of 0.8 to 1.2 and half suspended at 1.2 to 2.5; above 2.5 they move as bed load.
Suspended load needs flow velocity to stay up and is deposited when the flow slows.

entries.text: Muddy river water owes its color to grains that never touch the bottom. Suspended load is the part of a flow's sediment lifted off the bed and held up by turbulence. It is mostly fine sand, silt and clay, though strong flows carry coarser sand low in the water. It forms the middle layer of transport, between bed load below and the finest wash load above, described in {{ref:soil-water-249}}. Grains are fully suspended at Rouse numbers of 0.8 to 1.2 and half suspended at 1.2 to 2.5. When the flow slows, the load drops out.

entries.title: Bed load and suspended load: two ways a river carries

definition.text: The two main ways a flow carries sediment: rolling and sliding along the bed as bed load, or held up in the water as suspended load.

facts.text: Bed load rolls, slides and hops along the bed at a small fraction of the flow speed and is usually thought to be 5–10% of a stream's total sediment load.
Suspended load moves at a large fraction of the mean flow speed; wash load, fine material from upstream, moves with the stream and is spread almost evenly through the water.
The Rouse number, set by a grain's settling velocity against turbulent upward velocity, decides its mode: above 7.5 it stays put, below 0.8 it travels as wash load.
Small particles settle more slowly than heavy ones, which governs how far downstream they travel; Stokes' law gives the settling velocity of small grains.

entries.text: A stream's bed load, the sediment that rolls, slides and hops along the bottom, is usually thought to be only 5–10% of its total load. It moves at a small fraction of the flow speed. Small grains settle more slowly and so travel farther downstream.

entries.title: The Hjulström curve: a classic graph now retired

definition.text: A graph, drawn by Filip Hjulström in 1935, of the flow velocity needed to erode, transport or deposit sediment of each grain size.

facts.text: It uses logarithmic axes, and Åke Sundborg later added separate movement thresholds for several water depths.
It now has mainly historical value: it ignores water depth and does not show that slowing flow causes deposition and speeding flow causes erosion.
The dimensionless Shields diagram, based on shear stress, is now accepted for the start of sediment motion in rivers.

entries.title: Stream power, the energy a river spends

definition.text: The energy that flowing water in a river or stream expends on its bed and banks, first derived by R. A. Bagnold in the 1960s.

facts.text: It is the product of water density, gravitational acceleration, discharge and slope: Ω = ρgQS, in watts per unit length of channel.
Unit stream power divides by channel width, allowing rivers of different widths to be compared and giving a better estimate of sediment carrying capacity.
Critical unit stream power is the power needed to move a grain of given size, and it sets a river's competence, the largest grain it can move.
Several studies found that rivers shift from stable to actively reshaping themselves at a unit stream power of 30 to 35 W m−2.
It is used widely in landscape evolution and river incision models, and to design bridges and culverts that avoid starting erosion.

entries.text: A river is a machine that spends energy on its own bed and banks. In the 1960s R. A. Bagnold put a number on that energy, now called stream power. It is the product of water density, gravitational acceleration, discharge and slope, Ω = ρgQS, in watts per unit length of channel. Dividing by channel width gives unit stream power. That lets rivers of different widths be compared and better estimates how much sediment a river can carry. Critical unit stream power is the power needed to move a grain of a given size, and it sets a river's competence, the largest grain it can shift. Several studies found a threshold at 30 to 35 W m−2, where rivers switch from stable to actively reshaping themselves. Engineers use stream power to design bridges and culverts that will not start erosion, and modelers use it to simulate how rivers cut down and landscapes evolve.

entries.title: Fech fech: desert powder that swallows vehicles

definition.text: A very fine powder formed by the erosion of clay-limestone terrain, found mostly in deserts.

facts.text: It forms a surface horizon of pulverised, weakly cohesive soil protected under a thin crust.
It derives from ancient lake muds or certain argillaceous rocks and is one of the desert surfaces that produce dust.
Invisible from the surface, it can collapse under a vehicle and trap it in a quicksand-like mass; it makes part of Egypt's Qattara Depression impassable to most vehicles.

entries.title: Bank erosion: how rivers eat their sides

definition.text: The wearing away of the banks of a stream or river, as distinct from scour of its bed.

facts.text: Its two main mechanisms are fluvial erosion, the direct removal of particles by flowing water, and mass failure, when a bank's weight exceeds the soil's strength; undercutting by the first sets up the second.
Groundwater flowing out of a bank can cause seepage erosion, which when concentrated is called piping.
Vegetated banks generally erode more slowly because roots strengthen the soil, though heavy trees can load the bank top and reduce stability.
Rates are measured with erosion pins driven into the bank, repeated cross-section surveys, or aerial and satellite images compared over time.

entries.text: Rivers wear away their banks as well as their beds, and bank erosion works in two linked steps. Flowing water removes particles directly, an action called fluvial erosion. Undercutting then sets up mass failure, when a bank's weight exceeds the soil's strength and it gives way. Groundwater seeping out of a bank can also erode it, a process called piping when concentrated. Roots usually slow bank erosion, though heavy trees can overload the bank top. Erosion pins, repeated surveys and aerial or satellite images track the rates.

entries.title: Desert pavement: a stone floor of disputed origin

definition.text: A desert surface covered with closely packed, interlocking pebble- and cobble-sized rock fragments.

facts.text: A common explanation is that wind and occasional rain remove sand and dust, leaving larger stones; once formed, the pavement shields the ground from further erosion.
Fine particles collect beneath the stones as a vesicular A horizon, labelled Av.
A newer idea is that windblown dust settles between and under the stones, building soil beneath them; helium-3 dating in the Mojave Desert in 1995 found the rocks older than the soil below.
It is used as a sign of aridity and of the relative age of a surface, since older surfaces carry better-developed pavements.

entries.contested_note: Geologists debate how desert pavements form and how old they are; deflation, clay shrink–swell and dust accretion are all proposed.
entries.text: Some desert ground is tiled with closely packed, interlocking pebbles and cobbles. This is desert pavement, and geologists still debate how it forms and how old it is. A newer idea runs the other way: windblown dust settles between and under the stones, building soil beneath them. In 1995, helium-3 dating in the Mojave Desert found the rocks older than the soil below. Once formed, a pavement shields the ground, and older surfaces carry better-developed pavements, so it signals aridity and relative age.

entries.title: Why rock masses fail along their cracks

definition.text: The shear strength along a discontinuity, such as a joint, in a soil or rock mass, which strongly shapes how the mass behaves.

facts.text: It is often far lower than the strength of the intact blocks between discontinuities, and many natural and man-made slopes fail because of it.
It depends on the discontinuity's persistence, surface roughness, infill, fluid pressure, solution and cementation, and on whether it has moved before.
Weak discontinuities make deformation plastic rather than elastic, which can cause larger, permanent settlement of foundations.
Real discontinuities cannot be calculated analytically, so their strength comes from laboratory or field tests, such as the direct shear test, or from empirical characterisation.

entries.text: Many natural and man-made slopes fail not through solid rock but along its joints. The shear strength along a discontinuity, such as a joint, is often far lower than that of the intact blocks between. It depends on how far the discontinuity extends, its roughness, infill, fluid pressure, solution and cementation, and whether it has moved before. Weak discontinuities make a mass deform plastically rather than elastically, which can bring larger, permanent settlement of foundations. Real discontinuities cannot be calculated analytically. Their strength comes from laboratory or field tests, such as the direct shear test, or from empirical characterisation.

entries.title: How the last glaciation built a clay that can liquefy

definition.text: The sequence by which glacial rock flour, laid down loosely in the sea and later raised above it, became a weak and water-rich clay.

facts.text: At the height of the last glaciation, about 20,000 years ago, ice pressed the land down and the sea, reaching far inland, received the ground-up rock.
Loose settling of silt and clay in seawater gave an unusual flocculation: a strongly bonded soil skeleton glued by mobile sea-salt ions.
Post-glacial rebound then lifted the clay above the sea, and soft rainwater and snowmelt weakened its ionic glue, leaving a loose skeleton holding much water.
A normal topsoil cover absorbs ordinary stresses, but a large earthquake, extra load near a slope or saturating rain can disturb the clay and start liquefaction.

entries.title: Quick clay slides that eat their way inland

definition.text: Landslides in quick clay, which are retrogressive: they usually start at water and work their way upslope.

facts.text: They usually advance at slow walking speed, but deep quick clay on slopes can collapse much faster or slide in large chunks, and slides have reached kilometres inland.
Because topsoil hides the clay, vulnerable sites are usually found only by soil testing, so settlements and roads were often built on them.
A slide at Verdal, Norway, in 1893 killed 116 people; at Rissa in 1978 about 33 hectares of farmland liquefied and flowed into a lake within a few hours.
Engineering precautions include lightweight polystyrene fill, vertical wick drains and groundwater cutoff walls that keep water out of the clay.

entries.title: Legacy sediment: the buried record of human erosion

definition.text: Bodies of sediment laid down as a result of human activity since the Neolithic.

facts.text: It comes from land clearance, logging, mining, road building and urban growth, and from river engineering such as dams.
In the eastern US, soil eroded from uplands from the late 17th to the late 19th centuries buried valley floors and piled up behind low-head mill dams.
Human-caused soil erosion has raised river sediment transport by 2.3 (± 0.6) billion metric tons a year, yet reservoirs cut delivery to the coasts by 1.4 (± 0.3) billion metric tons a year.
Fine sediment can carry trace metals, nutrients, PAHs, PCBs and pesticides, and heavy metals may stay toxic in river sediment for decades to centuries.

entries.title: Armoring river banks with rock, wire and willow

definition.text: The structural and vegetative measures used to keep river banks from eroding and failing.

facts.text: Common options are lime stabilization, retaining walls, riprap, sheet piling, deep vegetation, windrows and trenches, sacks and blocks, gabions, soil-cement, and keeping structures back from the bank.
Riprap, rock laid to resist erosion, is expensive and can fail but covers large areas; gabions, stone-filled wire boxes, suit steep banks where flow is too fast for riprap.
Trees add deep, dense roots; shrubs and fascines of willow or cottonwood cuttings staked in trenches root and hold the soil, the most labour-intensive but cheapest method.
On steep banks trees may fail to stabilise the toe, and their own weight can bring the bank down.

entries.text: The cheapest way to hold a river bank is also the most laborious: willow or cottonwood cuttings staked in trenches, left to root and grip the soil. Trees add deep, dense roots, but on steep banks they may fail to hold the toe, and their weight can bring the bank down.

entries.title: Headward erosion, a stream cutting uphill

definition.text: Erosion at the head of a stream channel that moves its origin upslope, lengthening the stream, valley or gully and enlarging its drainage basin.

facts.text: Once a stream starts cutting back, the steep gradient at its head speeds the erosion.
Water collecting in channels gains speed and erosive power, cutting into and extending the heads of gullies.
Given time, a stream can break into a neighbouring watershed and capture its drainage, as the Shenandoah River did to Potomac tributaries.
It produces dendritic patterns on uniform bedrock, trellis patterns on alternating weak and strong rock, and rectangular patterns on jointed rock.

entries.text: Some streams grow backward. Headward erosion cuts away the head of a channel, moving its origin upslope and lengthening the stream, valley or gully. Water gathering in channels gains speed and erosive power, and the steep gradient at the head speeds the cutting further. Given time, a stream can break into a neighboring watershed and capture its drainage, as the Shenandoah River did to Potomac tributaries. The rock decides the pattern: branching on uniform bedrock, trellis-like on alternating weak and strong rock, and rectangular on jointed rock.

entries.title: Aggradation, when rivers raise the land

definition.text: The rise in land elevation, usually in a river system, as sediment is deposited; also called alluviation.

facts.text: It happens where more sediment is supplied than the river can carry; the Exner equation describes the balance between sediment in transport and sediment in the bed.
Typical settings are lowland alluvial rivers, deltas and alluvial fans, which often subside slowly enough to offset the rising surface.
A drier climate can trigger it: suppressed plant growth weakens soil binding, so more sediment enters rivers just as their flow drops and they choke with sediment.
Land use, volcanic eruptions, earthquakes and faulting can also cause it; reduced aggradation was reported in 2009 to be raising flood risk in many deltas.

entries.text: Give a river more sediment than it can carry and it starts building the ground up. Aggradation, also called alluviation, is that rise in land elevation as sediment is deposited. The Exner equation describes the balance between sediment in transport and sediment in the bed. Lowland rivers, deltas and {{ref:soil-water-293}} are typical settings, and their slow sinking often offsets the rise. A drier climate can trigger it: sparse plants bind less soil, so more sediment enters rivers just as their flow drops. A 2009 report found reduced aggradation raising flood risk in many deltas.

entries.title: Entrainment, the moment a grain lifts off

definition.text: The incorporation of surface sediment into a moving fluid such as air, water or ice, as part of erosion.

facts.text: Each grain size has a flow velocity, the entrainment velocity, at which grains begin to move.
Once moving, grains keep travelling below that velocity because friction with the bed is reduced, and settle only when the flow slows further, as the Hjulström curve shows.

entries.text: Every grain on a riverbed waits for a certain speed. Entrainment is the incorporation of surface sediment into a moving fluid such as air, water or ice, and it starts erosion. Each grain size has its own entrainment velocity, the flow speed at which those grains begin to move. Once moving, grains keep traveling even below that speed, because friction with the bed drops. They settle only when the flow slows further, as {{ref:soil-water-250}} shows.

entries.title: Shear velocity, drag measured as speed

definition.text: A shear stress rewritten in units of velocity, also called friction velocity.

facts.text: It is used to describe dispersion of particles and contaminants, the velocity profile near a flow's boundary, and sediment transport in channels.
It scales well with bedload transport, and in most rivers it is between 5% and 10% of the mean flow velocity.
Near the ground, the log wind profile lets friction velocity be found from wind speeds measured at two heights.
The zero-plane displacement, where wind speed falls to zero among trees or buildings, is roughly 2/3 to 3/4 of obstacle height.

entries.text: Engineers often express the drag of a flow on its boundary as a speed. Shear velocity, also called friction velocity, is shear stress rewritten in units of velocity. It describes how particles and contaminants spread, how flow speed changes near a boundary, and how channels move sediment. It scales well with bedload transport, and in most rivers it is 5% to 10% of the mean flow velocity. Over land, the log wind profile gives it from wind speeds at two heights. Among trees or buildings, wind falls to zero at about 2/3 to 3/4 of obstacle height.

entries.title: Badlands, where clay and rare storms carve bare ground

definition.text: Dry terrain in which soft sedimentary rocks and clay-rich soils have been deeply eroded into steep, bare ground.

facts.text: They have steep slopes, little vegetation and almost no regolith, with drainage densities of 48 to 464 kilometres of channel per square kilometre.
They form where an impermeable but easily eroded surface, sparse vegetation and rare heavy rains combine; runoff that cannot soak into the clay cuts dense networks of gullies.
The badlands of Badlands National Park erode at roughly 25 millimetres a year, and bentonite clay raises erodibility further.
Overgrazing, acid rain or acid mine drainage that strips vegetation can create anthropogenic badlands, as poor farming did at the Cheltenham Badlands in Ontario.

entries.title: Clocking how fast a landscape wears down

definition.text: The estimation of how fast a landscape is being lowered, usually expressed in centimetres or inches per 1000 years.

facts.text: The commonest method converts suspended, bed and dissolved loads at a gauging station to a volume and divides it by the watershed area upstream.
Cosmogenic isotopes, mostly 10Be and 26Al, are used because their concentration in sediment leaving a basin is inversely related to how fast the basin erodes.
Stream load can vary by up to a factor of five between successive years, and rates often assume uniform erosion.
The stream power law, E = KA^m S^n, relates erosion rate to an erodibility constant, drainage area and channel gradient.

entries.text: A landscape's lowering is slow enough to be quoted in centimetres per 1000 years. The commonest method starts at a river gauging station. Its suspended, bed and dissolved loads are converted to a volume and divided by the watershed area upstream. Cosmogenic isotopes, mostly 10Be and 26Al, offer a check: their concentration in sediment leaving a basin falls as erosion speeds up. The stream power law, E = KA^m S^n, ties erosion rate to erodibility, drainage area and channel gradient.

entries.title: The Shields parameter: when a grain starts to move

definition.text: A dimensionless number used to calculate when sediment begins to move in a fluid flow.

facts.text: Developed by Albert F. Shields, it is a non-dimensional shear stress, θ = τ / ((ρs − ρ) g D), with τ the shear stress, ρs and ρ the sediment and fluid densities and D the grain diameter.
It is proportional to the ratio of the fluid force on a particle to the particle's weight.
The critical Shields number marks the onset of motion; shear stress belongs to the current, critical shear stress to the sediment.
The Shields diagram, using critical shear stress and Reynolds number, is considered more precise than the Hjulström curve for estimating suspended load.

entries.text: Albert F. Shields gave engineers a single number for the moment a sediment bed starts to move. The Shields parameter is a dimensionless shear stress, θ = τ / ((ρs − ρ) g D). Here τ is the shear stress, ρs and ρ the densities of sediment and fluid, and D the grain diameter. In effect it compares the fluid's push on a particle with the particle's weight. Motion starts at the critical Shields number. Shear stress belongs to the current, critical shear stress to the sediment. The Shields diagram is considered more precise than {{ref:soil-water-250}} for estimating suspended load.

entries.title: Corrasion, rock scoured by what water carries

definition.text: Mechanical erosion of the land surface by material dragged across it by running water, waves, glaciers, wind or downslope movement.

facts.text: Rock on a river or sea bed is worn away by the impact and grinding of moving particles, and the result on the rock is called abrasion.
It differs from corrosion, which is the chemical and solvent action of water on soluble rock.
Lateral corrasion widens a river by sideways erosion, while vertical corrasion deepens its valley.

entries.text: Running water alone barely scratches rock; the grit it carries does the cutting. Corrasion is mechanical erosion of the land by material dragged across it by running water, waves, glaciers, wind or downslope movement. On a river or sea bed, moving particles strike and grind the rock, and the wear they leave is called abrasion. Corrosion is different: the chemical, dissolving action of water on soluble rock. Lateral corrasion widens a river by cutting sideways, while vertical corrasion deepens its valley.

entries.title: Why clay clumps where rivers meet the sea

definition.text: Flocculation is the process by which fine particles in water clump together into flocs.

facts.text: Fine silt and clay stay suspended longer than sand, and small, negatively charged clay particles can resist settling and stay suspended, producing turbidity.
In estuaries, changing physicochemical conditions from river to sea trigger flocculation and siltation, a main cause of harbour dredging.
Organic matter plays a major role by adhering to marine clay particles.
The exchange cations on the particles (sodium, potassium, calcium) set their arrangement and properties.

entries.title: Building on marine clay

definition.text: Building on marine clay is a geotechnical challenge because the soil is open, sensitive and weak under load.

facts.text: Marine clays are sensitive to weathering, which affects support under loads and limits bearing capacity and service life; pavements over them lose durability and cost more over their life.
Quick clays are very unstable: when saturated they liquefy and flow, causing mass wasting.
Ground improvement techniques can handle the problems; marine clay can be stabilized by mixing with cement and fly ash in set proportions.
Marine clays serve as low-permeability landfill liners and adsorb contaminants, and have long been used for heat-resistant ceramics.

entries.title: How roots stitch soil to the ground below
entries.article: Vegetation and slope stability#Mechanical reinforcement of roots

definition.text: The strengthening of soil by roots that grow across potential failure planes, act as piles and limit surface erosion.

facts.text: Roots crossing a potential failure plane raise shear strength by binding particles and anchor unstable surface soil to deeper stable layers or bedrock.
In the root reinforcement model, a root stretched across a slip plane develops a tensile force that passes to the soil through cohesion and friction.
Root strength generally extends only to about 1 m (3.3 ft), while most slope failures occur at 1.2–1.5 m (3.9–4.9 ft) depth.
Fine roots of shrubs and grasses hold the surface soil against sheet wash and overland flow, with a cohesion likened to geosynthetic mesh, mostly in the top 1 m.

entries.text: Root strength generally reaches only about 1 m (3.3 ft) down, yet most slope failures occur at 1.2–1.5 m (3.9–4.9 ft). Near the surface, fine roots of shrubs and grasses hold soil against sheet wash and overland flow, like a mesh.

entries.title: How hard a root holds before it lets go
entries.article: Vegetation and slope stability#Tensile root strength contribution and pull out resistance

definition.text: The force a root resists before being pulled out of the ground, usually only a little less than its laboratory tensile strength.

facts.text: Laboratory tests on many species and root diameters put tensile root strength at about 5–60 MN/m2.
Unbranched roots fail in tension and slip out with little resistance; branched roots hold a high force that declines as branches fail, or break in stepped stages.
Thicker roots resist pull-out more than thinner ones, and roots tend to fail at weak points such as branching points, nodes or damage.
A root strengthens a slope only with enough embedment and adhesion in the soil; for engineering, in situ pull-out tests measure its contribution.

entries.text: A root resists being pulled out of the ground with a force only a little less than its laboratory tensile strength. Tests on many species and root diameters put that strength at about 5–60 MN/m2. Thicker roots resist more than thinner ones. Unbranched roots fail in tension and slip out with little resistance. Branched roots hold a high force that declines as branches fail, or they break in stepped stages, often at weak points such as branching points, nodes or damage. entries.title: Thirsty plants that help hold slopes
entries.article: Vegetation and slope stability#Removal of water

definition.text: The stabilising of slopes by plants that draw water out of the soil and transpire it, lowering soil pore water pressure.

facts.text: Lower pore water pressure offsets the strength a soil loses on wetting; the effect shows as drier soil around trees.
Plants transpire little in wet weather, so the strength gain fades when storms saturate a slope, though transpiration still makes failure after heavy rain less likely.
Studies in Malaysia linked high root length density to low soil water content, higher shear strength, lower permeability and fewer slope failures.
Plants can deepen desiccation cracks in dry weather, letting water reach a slip plane, but shading by their foliage limits the drying and cracking.

entries.text: The soil around trees is drier, and drier soil is stronger. Plants draw water out of the soil and transpire it, lowering pore water pressure and offsetting the strength soil loses when wet. The help fades in storms, because plants transpire little in wet weather. Even so, transpiration still makes failure after heavy rain less likely. Dry weather brings a catch: plants can deepen desiccation cracks that let water reach a slip plane. Shade from their foliage limits that drying and cracking.

entries.title: Causes and triggers: why slopes fail when they do

definition.text: The distinction between the conditions that make a slope vulnerable to failure (causes) and the single event that finally sets it moving (trigger).

facts.text: A landslide can have many causes but only one trigger, which is usually easy to identify afterwards but hard to predict beforehand.
Causes are grouped as geological (weathered or jointed material), morphological (slope angle, erosion, vegetation change), physical and human (deforestation, excavation, mining).
Following Terzaghi, internal causes weaken the material's resistance to shear stress, while external causes increase the shear stress.
Earthquakes trigger slides by shaking and by raising pore water pressure; topographic amplification makes ground accelerations strongest at slope crests.

entries.title: Rain, the trigger behind most landslides

definition.text: Landslides set off by heavy or prolonged rain, the main trigger in most cases.

facts.text: Of 210 damaging landslide events worldwide in the year to September 2003, over 90% were triggered by heavy rainfall.
Rain raises pore water pressure, which buoys the slope material and reduces its resistance to movement; groundwater flow can add a downslope push.
Water can also destabilise slopes by fluidising old debris into debris flows, removing suction in silty soils, undercutting the toe and causing soil piping.
Caine's 1980 worldwide threshold, I = 14.82 D^-0.39 (intensity in mm per hour, duration in hours), applies over 10 minutes to 10 days.

entries.title: Sediment yield, a river's report on its watershed

definition.text: The quantity of sediment per unit area of a watershed that a river removes over a period of time.

facts.text: Monitoring it shows ecologists the health of river ecosystems, the rate of erosion and the effects of human activity.
Switching from grains to potatoes in late 19th-century Poland raised sediment yields so much that meandering rivers became braided.
Dams, reservoirs and sediment detention basins upstream reduce it.
WEPP watershed runs link hillslopes, channels and impoundments to predict sediment yield from a whole catchment.
