entries.title: Salinity classes: matching salty soils to crops

definition.text: Bernstein's grouping of soils by the electrical conductivity of a saturated soil-paste extract (ECe), matched to the crops each class can still grow well.

facts.text: Soil salinity is most often expressed as ECe in decisiemens per metre, formerly millimhos per centimetre.
Bernstein's classes: ECe 0–2 non-saline; 2–4 slightly saline, sensitive crops lose yield; 4–8 moderately saline; 8–16 saline, only tolerant crops yield normally; above 16, only very tolerant crops.
Soil salinity control uses different bounds: saline only above ECe 4, slightly saline from 4 to 8, moderately saline from 8 to 16, severely saline above 16.
Schleiff ranks crop tolerance in 2 dS/m steps, from very sensitive below 2 to very tolerant above 10, narrower than the 4 dS/m steps in Richards' 1954 USDA handbook.

entries.title: Crops that tolerate seawater

definition.text: The ability of a crop to withstand the high salinity of irrigation with seawater or a mix of fresh water and seawater.

facts.text: Demonstration farms show some crops can grow on seawater; Dutch trials found that certain varieties of potato, carrot, red onion, white cabbage and broccoli thrive under salt-water irrigation.
Salt Farm Texel tests crops on 56 plots of 160 m2 at seven salt levels, from EC 2 to 35 dS/m, made by mixing fresh water with seawater of about 50 dS/m.
Thresholds there varied widely even within one crop: potato ranged from 1.9 dS/m for the variety Met to 4.1 dS/m for Mignonne.

entries.title: Old rotations and the corn-soybean rotation

definition.text: Rotations should suit each farm's soil, climate, resources and economics, so only historic examples can guide.

facts.text: A five- to seven-year rotation on northern Midwest and Northeast mixed farms put nitrogen-hungry corn after pasture, grain only two of five to seven years, and oats as a nurse crop when hay was seeded; it roughly maintained organic matter.
Cheap pesticides and fertilizer, feedlots, export markets and price-support programs narrowed production to corn and soybeans.
The corn-soybean rotation beats monoculture but brings erosion, nitrate and herbicide pollution, organic matter loss and sometimes more insects; soybeans leave minimal residue.

entries.title: Crop diversification in time and space

definition.text: Cropping systems can be diversified over time, across the farm landscape, or with perennials, trees and livestock.

facts.text: Diversity over time comes from cover crops and rotations; spatial diversity from different crops in different fields or strips; a staggered rotation gives both.
Perennials add diversity with less frequent rotations, for example dairy farmers growing alfalfa three to four years before corn; agroforestry and integrated livestock add further dimensions.
An ecological principle behind this is that diversity contributes to stability and productivity.

entries.title: Designing a crop rotation: the main rules

definition.text: A set of guidelines for designing a new crop rotation.

facts.text: Follow a legume forage with a high-nitrogen crop such as corn, and grow oats, barley and wheat less in the second or third year after the sod.

Grow the same annual crop only one year and avoid closely related species in sequence, since pests and diseases are shared; western corn rootworm populations have lately emerged that survive corn-soybean alternation.
Plant nonhost grains for root-knot nematodes for a few years before a susceptible crop such as carrots or lettuce.
Small grains suppress weeds, row crops allow cultivation, and mowed or grazed sods control annual weeds; use longer perennial periods on sloping, erosive land.
Deep-rooted crops such as alfalfa, safflower or sunflower scavenge subsoil nutrients and water, and their root channels aid infiltration.

In limited-rainfall regions, water use is critical: hay and sunflowers may leave too little moisture; under 25% of rain during the 14-month fallow in the Central High Plains reaches the next wheat crop.

entries.title: Active rooting period: how long roots live in a rotation

definition.text: The active rooting period is the percent of a rotation during which living roots are present.

facts.text: It runs from 32% for corn-soybeans to 57% for soybean-wheat and 76% for a three-year soybean-wheat-corn rotation.
Adding winter wheat to a corn-soybean alternation greatly lengthens it, because winter annuals, perennials and cover crops extend the growing period beyond summer annuals.
Longer living cover decreases erosion, nitrate loss and groundwater contamination.
Dry beans-winter wheat with a cover crop reached 92% with three species.

entries.title: What diversified rotations cost and save in labor

definition.text: Diversified rotations spread labor and reduce exposure to price swings, but add equipment and management demands.

facts.text: Forage hay and early-harvested crops spread labor over the season, easing management by family labor and giving steadier income.
Costs include more equipment and labor conflicts, such as cultivating corn at the same time as harvesting hay.
Integrated livestock with multi-species grazing need less specialized equipment, harvest and spread manure themselves, and diversify income.

entries.title: How rotations protect water and cut nitrous oxide

definition.text: Diversified rotations offer benefits over very simple ones, including better water quality and lower nitrous oxide loss.

facts.text: In South Dakota, a four-year corn-field pea-winter wheat-soybean rotation beat corn-soybean with higher soybean yield, more soil organic matter and less nitrous oxide lost.

Spring-planted annuals leave soil without roots for much of the year, so nitrate can leach, a problem accentuated by tile drainage in the Midwest and Northeast; bare wetter soil also runs off and erodes more.
Perennial forages and winter grains protect water; cover crops help similarly but do not substitute for a good rotation, and the combination gives the greatest improvement.

entries.text: In South Dakota, a four-year rotation of corn, field pea, winter wheat and soybean beat corn-soybean. It gave higher soybean yield, more soil organic matter and less nitrous oxide lost. Bare wetter soil also runs off and erodes more. Perennial forages and winter grains protect water. Cover crops help similarly but do not substitute for a good rotation, and the combination gives the greatest improvement.

entries.title: When cover crops cause trouble

definition.text: Cover crops can cause serious problems if not managed carefully.

facts.text: They can deplete soil moisture, become weeds, compete with an intercropped cash crop for water, light and nutrients, and cost seed and establishment.
In dry areas and on sands, late killing of a winter cover may cause moisture deficiency; in warm humid no-till climates longer growth means less wet soil at planting and more residue.
Cover crops raise infiltration through macropores and water-holding capacity through organic matter, and residue slows runoff.

sources.title: 10.4: Cover Crop Management - Geosciences LibreTexts (Building Soils for Better Crops, 4th ed. (Magdoff and van Es))

entries.text: A cover crop is not free. It can deplete soil moisture, become a weed, compete with an intercropped cash crop for water, light and nutrients, and cost money for seed and establishment. In dry areas and on sands, late killing of a winter cover may cause moisture deficiency. In warm humid no-till climates, longer growth means less wet soil at planting and more residue. The benefits are real too: cover crops raise infiltration through macropores and water-holding capacity through organic matter, and residue slows runoff. Careful management decides which side wins.

entries.title: Cover crop mixtures: pairing a grass with a legume

definition.text: Mixtures of cover crop species offer combined benefits, the most common being a grass with a legume.

facts.text: Mixed stands usually suppress weeds better than a single species, and legumes with small grains offset the nitrogen decline when grains mature.
In the mid-Atlantic, a rye-hairy vetch mix manages nitrogen: rye is stimulated when much nitrate remains, reducing leaching, while vetch competes better and fixes more when little is available.
Erect rye supports vetch, and vetch held up by rye is killed more easily by close mowing, which may replace herbicide in no-till.

entries.title: When to plant a cover crop

definition.text: A cover crop can be planted for a whole growing season, after the cash crop harvest, or interseeded into a growing cash crop.

facts.text: A full-season high-biomass mix builds the most organic matter and suits infertile or eroded soils and organic transition, but no income crop grows that year.
Most farmers sow after harvest, avoiding competition with the main crop; seed can be no-till drilled for better stands, and tillage before seeding should be avoided.
The choice depends on the goal, cash crops, season length and climate.

entries.title: Ending a cover crop: termination methods

definition.text: Cover crops are killed or drastically weakened before or during soil preparation for the next cash crop.

facts.text: Methods include mowing after flowering, herbicide with no-till, plowing in, mow-roll-crimp with no-till planting in one pass, and winter injury.
Waiting a week or two lets residue decompose, easing nitrogen immobilization, allelopathy, damping-off, cutworm and wireworm problems, and a better seedbed.
A sudex cover crop is especially allelopathic, so tomatoes, broccoli and lettuce should wait six to eight weeks.

entries.title: Choosing cover crops to limit nematodes

definition.text: Cover crop choice can limit nematode damage, because species differ in host status.

facts.text: Grain crops are nonhosts of root-knot nematode (M. hapla), so growing grains reduces numbers; very bad infestations may need two full grain seasons.
Root-lesion nematode (P. penetrans) infects most crops; a legume such as hairy vetch will stimulate it, while sudangrass, sorghum-sudan, ryegrass and pearl millet reportedly cut numbers.
Suppression comes from poor host status, stimulated microbial antagonists and toxic products released on decomposition; brassicas and pearl millet also biofumigate.

sources.title: 10.4: Cover Crop Management - Geosciences LibreTexts (Building Soils for Better Crops, 4th ed. (Magdoff and van Es))

entries.text: Whether a cover crop helps or harms depends on how well nematodes can feed on it. Grain crops are nonhosts of the root-knot nematode (M. hapla), so growing grains reduces numbers, though very bad infestations may need two full grain seasons. The root-lesion nematode (P. penetrans) infects most crops. A legume such as hairy vetch will stimulate it, while sudangrass, sorghum-sudan, ryegrass and pearl millet reportedly cut numbers. Suppression comes from poor host status, stimulated microbial antagonists and toxic products released on decomposition. Brassicas and pearl millet also biofumigate. For the pests themselves, see {{ref:soil-bio-194}}.

entries.title: Planting green into a living cover crop

definition.text: Planting green is seeding a cash crop directly into a still-living cover crop and terminating the cover soon after.

facts.text: Older advice left a week or two between killing the cover and planting, which remains best in a dry spring.
The cover is usually sprayed shortly after planting, or suppressed mechanically with a rolling stalk chopper or a cereal-rye roller-crimper ahead of a no-till planter.
It has worked for soybeans, corn and cotton but is not recommended for most direct-seeded vegetables.

entries.title: Buckwheat, the fast frost-sensitive cover

definition.text: Buckwheat is a frost-sensitive summer annual cover crop that completes its life cycle quickly.

facts.text: It takes about six weeks from planting in warm soil to early flowering, can exceed 2 feet in a month, and grows better than many cover crops on low-fertility soils but tolerates compaction poorly.
It competes well with weeds and has been reported to suppress root pathogens including Thielaviopsis and Rhizoctonia.
Its seeds do not persist for years but it can reseed as a volunteer weed, so mow, roll or till it before seeds develop.

entries.title: Groundcovers in orchards and vineyards

definition.text: In orchards and vineyards, groundcover or floor management with perennial cover crops can improve soil health and crop quality.

facts.text: The cover should not overly compete with the main crop and should persist with little maintenance while giving erosion and weed control, tolerating shade, traffic and drought.
It acts as a living mulch; Dutch white clover gives modest nitrogen, and low-growing fescues with dense fine roots need minimal mowing.
In vineyards covers are sometimes kept away from the vines but used to compete with them and curb excess vegetative growth.

entries.text: Between the rows of an orchard or vineyard, a perennial groundcover can improve soil health and crop quality. The ideal cover does not overly compete with the main crop and persists with little maintenance. It gives erosion and weed control and tolerates shade, traffic and drought. In vineyards covers are sometimes kept away from the vines but used to compete with them and curb excess vegetative growth.

entries.title: Rotation as a tool against plant disease

definition.text: Carefully chosen rotations, especially alternating grains and broadleaf plants, help control plant diseases and nematodes.

facts.text: Some diseases need only a one-year break; others need several years of nonhost crops to cut inoculum.
Pulse crops seem to stimulate beneficial organisms and reduce cereal root disease; a multiyear broadleaf break lowers common root rot of wheat and barley.
Rotation is hard for wide-host-range pathogens, seed-borne disease and windborne wheat leaf rust, which need other tactics.

entries.text: Some diseases need only a one-year break from their host; others need several years of nonhost crops to cut inoculum. That is why careful rotations, especially alternating grains and broadleaf plants, help control plant diseases and nematodes (see {{ref:soil-agri-004}}). Pulse crops seem to stimulate beneficial organisms and reduce cereal root disease, and a multiyear broadleaf break lowers common root rot of wheat and barley. Rotation has limits. It is hard for wide-host-range pathogens, seed-borne disease and windborne wheat leaf rust, which need other tactics.

entries.title: Faidherbia albida, the dry-season shade tree

definition.text: Faidherbia albida is a tropical legume tree of seasonally dry climates used in silvopasture and alley cropping.

facts.text: Its feathery leaves give a light canopy for corn or pasture, and it has a deep taproot.
It carries foliage in the dry season when forage is scarce, blooms for bees at the dry season's end, and gives pods for livestock and wood for fuel.

entries.title: Forest farming under the canopy

definition.text: Forest farming grows understory crops within an established natural or timber forest, without separate growing zones.

facts.text: Shade is desired; examples are ginseng, mushrooms, elderberries, rhododendrons and moss, many quite profitable.

entries.title: Silvopasture: trees and grazing together

definition.text: Silvopasture integrates trees and grazing livestock on the same land.

facts.text: It gives forest products and forage, so both short- and long-term income.
Partial shade helps cool-season grasses in heat in temperate climates, and keeps animals cool in hot ones.
It still needs agronomic care such as forage selection, fertilization and rotational grazing, and can stabilize landslide-prone slopes.

entries.title: Agroecosystems: the ecosystems people farm

definition.text: An ecological system that people manage and shape in order to farm.

facts.text: System properties studied in agroecosystems include productivity, stability, sustainability and equitability.
Harper's 1974 concept of agroecosystems, perhaps inspired by Tansley's process ecology of the 1930s, is considered the foundation of modern agroecology.
Erosion can irreparably reduce an agroecosystem's productive capacity, and cover crops are often grown for that reason alone.

entries.title: Agroecology: ecology applied to farming

definition.text: An academic discipline that studies ecological processes as they apply to agricultural production systems.

facts.text: The term can mean a science, a movement or a farming practice, and it is not tied to any single method such as organic, regenerative, integrated or industrial farming.
It is multidisciplinary, using sciences to study soil properties and plant-insect interactions and social sciences to study farming's effects on rural communities.
Ecosystem agroecology treats farms as integrated ecological systems, analysing their energy flows, nutrient cycles and the interactions between living and non-living components.
As a set of practices it harnesses ecological processes, biodiversity, nutrient recycling, agroforestry, intercropping and composting.
Biodynamic farming, organic agriculture and China's Green Food are the three certified forms; organics is the most widely practised, in 188 countries.
Wezel et al. date the first use of the term to 1928, by Basil Bensin; Tischler's 1965 book Agrarökologie may be the first titled 'agroecology'.
Researchers in agronomy, environmental science and related fields debate heatedly which model of agriculture or agroecology policy should support; the UN is perhaps its most prominent backer.

entries.contested_note: Researchers disagree over which model of agriculture or agroecology public policy should support.

conflicts.text: Dalgaard et al. credit the German zoologist Friederichs with first using the name, in 1930.
conflicts.note: Wezel et al. instead give 1928 and Basil Bensin for the first use of the term.

entries.text: Basil Bensin used the word agroecology in 1928, according to Wezel and colleagues; another account credits the German zoologist Friederichs. Agroecology is an academic discipline that studies ecological processes as they apply to agricultural production systems. Tischler's 1965 book Agrarökologie may be the first with the word in its title. Today the term can mean a science, a movement or a farming practice, and it is not tied to any single method, whether organic, regenerative, integrated or industrial. It draws on the sciences to study soil properties and plant-insect interactions, and on the social sciences to study farming's effects on rural communities. Ecosystem agroecology treats farms as integrated ecological systems, analysing their energy flows and nutrient cycles. As practice, it harnesses biodiversity, nutrient recycling, {{ref:soil-agri-140}}, intercropping and composting. Its certified forms are biodynamic farming, organic agriculture and China's Green Food. Its politics are unsettled. Researchers debate heatedly which model of agriculture policy should support, and the UN is perhaps agroecology's most prominent backer.

entries.title: When a field grows tired of its crop

definition.text: A decline in soil fertility and crop yield, often after long-term monoculture, marked by a shift in harmful and beneficial soil microbes.

facts.text: In 1832 the Swiss botanist De Candolle suggested that exudates from crop plants caused soil sickness.
In aged tea plantations, polyphenols building up in the soil shift microbial communities and contribute to soil sickness.

entries.title: Tillage: why farmers dig, and why digging less won

definition.text: The preparation of soil for farming by mechanically agitating it, for example by digging, stirring or overturning it.

facts.text: Hand methods include shovelling, picking, mattock work, hoeing and raking; animal-drawn or machine work includes ploughing, rototilling, rolling, harrowing and cultivating.
Deeper, more thorough tillage is called primary and shallower, more selective tillage secondary; harrowing and rototilling often combine the two in one pass.
In farming, cultivation overlaps with tillage, but it can also mean shallow, selective secondary tillage of row crops that kills weeds while sparing the crop.
Tillage kills weeds by uprooting them or burying their leaves, which keeps them from competing with the crop and from setting seed.
In 1731 Jethro Tull argued that soil had to be pulverized into a fine powder for plants to feed on it, and that land could never be tilled too much.
Scientific observation has shown the opposite: tillage robs soil of the structure that lets roots, water and nutrients in, speeds erosion and compacts the soil.
Tilling the prairie topsoil of the American Midwest helped cause the Dust Bowl; in 2019 erosion in the United States still took an estimated 3 trillion pounds of soil.
Modern agricultural science has greatly reduced tillage: with herbicides, crops tolerant of packed soil and direct-seeding equipment, crops can be grown for years without it.

entries.title: The plough, from human muscle to the tractor

definition.text: A farm tool for loosening or turning over soil before sowing seed or planting.

facts.text: Ploughing chiefly turns over the uppermost soil, bringing fresh nutrients to the surface and burying weeds and crop remains to decay; the trenches it cuts are furrows.
Ploughing and cultivating even out the upper 12 to 25 centimetres (5 to 10 in) of soil, where most plant feeder roots grow.
A ploughed field is normally left to dry and then harrowed before planting.
Ploughs were first pulled by people, then by oxen, horses and mules, then by steam engines, and from the early 20th century by tractors.
The earliest ploughs had no wheels, a type the Romans called an aratrum; Celtic peoples first used wheeled ploughs in the Roman era.
A Sumerian poem from the 3rd millennium BC stages a debate between the hoe and the plough over which is better.
In 1837 John Deere began making polished steel ploughs strong enough to farm US soils, such as tough Midwest prairie, once thought unsuitable.
Where soil damage and erosion threaten, the traditional plough has given way to shallower ploughing or other conservation tillage.

entries.title: Arable land, the share of farmland that can take a plough

definition.text: Land that can be ploughed and used to grow crops.

facts.text: In FAO statistics it means land under temporary crops, temporary meadows, market and kitchen gardens, and land fallow for less than five years; land abandoned by shifting cultivation is excluded.
The statistics record actual, not potential, use; Eurostat defines it as land ploughed or tilled regularly, generally under crop rotation.
In 2013 the world had 1.407 billion hectares of arable land out of 4.924 billion hectares used for agriculture.
Agricultural land that is not arable includes meadows and pastures and permanent crops such as orchards, vineyards and coffee plantations.
Land may be unfit for cultivation through lack of freshwater, stoniness, steepness, adverse climate, undrainable wetness or excess salts; clay content is a major factor in arability.
Such land can still be productive: about 59 percent of US non-federal pasture and unforested rangeland cannot be cultivated but is valuable for grazing.
Arable land is lost every year to desertification and human-induced erosion, and improper irrigation concentrates salts in the root zone.
Climate change may add arable land by thawing frozen ground.

entries.title: What tillage gives a soil, and what it takes away

definition.text: The consequences of tilling for a soil: it loosens and aerates the topsoil for planting, but it also degrades structure, speeds erosion and compacts the soil.

facts.text: Benefits include loosening and aerating the A horizon, mixing residue, humus and nutrients evenly into the soil, and destroying weeds mechanically.
Autumn tillage lets frost crumble the exposed soil over winter, giving a smooth surface for spring planting.
Tillage can reduce slugs, cutworms, armyworms and other pests drawn to old residues, and crop diseases harboured in surface residues.
Drying the soil before seeding appears both as a benefit, in wetter climates, and as a drawback.
Tilled soil loses nutrients and water-storing ability, and its infiltration rate falls, so more water runs off and erodes it.
Tillage breaks the cohesion between particles and destroys aggregates, and it reduces organic matter and soil life such as microbes, earthworms and ants.
It disrupts the hyphal network of arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, lowering the soil's capacity to infect new roots.
Other harms are compaction into a tillage pan, chemical runoff and eutrophication of waters fed by nutrient runoff.

It also cuts slugs, cutworms, armyworms and crop diseases that shelter in old surface residues. Drying the soil before seeding counts as a benefit in wetter climates, but also as a drawback. The debits run longer. Tillage breaks the cohesion between particles and destroys aggregates, the basis of soil structure. It reduces organic matter and soil life such as microbes, earthworms and ants. It tears the hyphal network of arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, so the soil can infect fewer new roots. Tilled soil loses nutrients and water-storing ability, and its infiltration rate falls, so more water runs off and erodes it. Compaction into a dense layer, {{ref:soil-agri-101}}, chemical runoff and the over-enrichment of waters fed by nutrient runoff complete the list.

entries.title: Primary and secondary tillage: rough first, fine second

definition.text: The division of tillage into deeper, more thorough primary operations and shallower, often more selective secondary ones.

facts.text: Primary tillage, such as ploughing, loosens the soil and mixes in fertilizer or plant material, leaving a rough surface.
It usually follows the last harvest, when soil is wet enough to plough but still gives traction, and aims for soft soil to a reasonable depth, buried residues, killed weeds and aeration.
Secondary tillage is any later operation: it works in fertilizer, reduces soil to a finer tilth, levels the surface, shapes rows and controls weeds.
Its smoother surface finish is what many crops need for a good seedbed.
Seedbed tools include harrows, dibbles, hoes, shovels, rotary tillers, subsoilers, ridge- or bed-forming tillers, rollers and cultivators.
Weed control by tillage usually uses cultivators or hoes that disturb only the top few centimetres of soil around the crop plants.

entries.title: The harrow, which smooths what the plough leaves rough

definition.text: A farm implement for surface tillage, used after ploughing to break up and smooth the soil surface.

facts.text: Harrowing breaks up clods to give a tilth suitable for planting seeds; coarser harrowing can also remove weeds and cover seed after sowing.
Ploughs cut the upper 12 to 25 centimetres of soil and leave furrows, and cultivators disturb only narrow tracks between rows, whereas harrows disturb the whole surface.
The four general types are disc harrows, tine harrows (including spring-tooth, drag and spike harrows), chain harrows and chain-disk harrows.
Farmers commonly run a disk harrow first to slice the large clods left by the mouldboard plough, then a spring-tooth harrow, leaving a smooth field with powdery surface soil.
Chain harrows do light work such as levelling the tilth or covering seed, while disc harrows do heavy work such as breaking up sod after ploughing.
Where harrowing leaves a very fine tilth, or the soil is light enough to blow away, a roller is often added as the last implement.
A power harrow's tines spin on vertical axes, so unlike a rotary tiller it does not invert soil layers or slice the subsurface in a way that can form a hardpan.
In China the rake had developed into the harrow by the end of the Han dynasty, when the flat pa and the vertical chao were both known.

entries.title: Contour plowing: furrows that run across the slope

definition.text: Ploughing or planting across a slope along its elevation contour lines, also called contour farming.

facts.text: The level furrows run across the slope rather than down it, forming water breaks that reduce rills and gullies in heavy rain and give water time to soak in.
It also helps prevent tillage erosion, the movement of soil by tilling itself.
It reduces fertilizer loss, power use, time and machine wear while raising yields; demonstrations showed row-crop gains of up to 50% under ideal conditions, with 5 to 10% common.
The Phoenicians developed contour farming and spread it around the Mediterranean, but the Romans preferred straight furrows, which became standard.
The US Soil Conservation Service, set up in 1935 during the Dust Bowl, promoted it; by 1938 such techniques had cut soil loss by 65% despite continuing drought.
It works only on slopes of 2% to 10% and below a certain rainfall; steeper or wetter land adds strip cropping, and terraces and cover crops make it more effective.
In the similar practice of contour bunding, stones are placed along the contours of slopes.

conflicts.text: Contour plowing can increase crop yields by 10 to 50 percent.

entries.title: Crop residue, the leftovers that guard the soil

definition.text: The stalks, stubble, leaves and other plant material left in a field after harvest.

facts.text: Farmers once treated residue as trash, but keeping more than 50% of it on the surface benefits soil health, nutrient cycling, erosion control and microbial activity.
Surface residue softens the impact of raindrops that break up soil particles, reducing splash and sheet erosion.
Covering the surface, it cuts evaporation, lowers surface soil temperature and reduces wind effects.
Decaying residue opens routes for water to soak in quickly, reducing the need for supplemental irrigation.
Residue cover defines tillage systems: under 15% for intensive, 15 to 30% for reduced and at least 30% for conservation tillage.
Leaving residues to decay returns their stored potassium to the soil.
Its nutrients are released slowly: by the next year cereal straw releases about 10 to 15 per cent of its nutrients and pea residue about 35 percent.
Residue with over 1.5 per cent nitrogen releases it quickly, but below 1.2 per cent microbes decomposing it immobilize soil nitrogen.

entries.title: Conservation tillage: leave the residue, keep the soil

definition.text: A group of practices that reduce tillage and leave at least 30% of crop residue, or at least 1,000 lb/ac (1,100 kg/ha) of small grain residue, on the surface during the critical erosion period.

facts.text: The residue slows water movement and softens raindrop impact on soil particles, so less soil erodes.
Fewer passes over the field save fuel and labour and reduce soil compaction; it also benefits predatory arthropods that can help control pests.
Its forms include no-till, strip-till, mulch-till, ridge-till and rotational tillage, in which soil is tilled every two years or less often.
It is used on over 370 million acres, mostly in South America, Oceania and North America, and in most years since 1997 it has covered more US cropland than intensive or reduced tillage.
By 2014 more than 75% of cropland on the Canadian Prairies had adopted conservation tillage.
Researchers found a nearly 60 percent reduction in runoff losses under conservation tillage, which also guards the surface against crusting.
Less exposed dark soil means slower warming in spring, which delays planting of the next corn crop.
Equipment designed to cut water erosion may not reduce tillage erosion.

entries.title: No-till farming: growing crops without turning the soil

definition.text: A way of growing crops or pasture without disturbing the soil by tillage, also called zero tillage or direct drilling.

facts.text: It cuts tillage-caused erosion, especially on sandy, dry, sloping soils; the top inch of no-till soil holds more aggregates and is two to seven times less vulnerable than ploughed soil.
Surface residue helps rain and irrigation water infiltrate and limits evaporation; each tillage pass loses around 0.85 to 1.9 cm of water to evaporation.
Crops are sown into a herbicide-killed cover crop (sod seeding), through the previous crop's residue (direct seeding), or onto the bare surface (surface seeding).
No-till means never tilling a field; like strip tillage it is a form of conservation tillage, but the two terms are not equivalent.
Organized opposition to ploughing began in the 1940s with Edward H. Faulkner's Plowman's Folly, but trials spread only after post-war herbicides such as paraquat.
Land under no-till grew from about 45 million ha in 1999 to 72 million ha in 2003 and 111 million ha in 2009; in 2014 South America held 47% of it.
Light-coloured residue absorbs less solar energy than bare soil, so no-till soil warms and dries more slowly in spring, which may delay planting.
Nitrogen immobilized in decomposing residue often reduces yields and calls for more fertilizer, but after a transition (4–5 years in Kansas) soil organic matter may build up.

entries.title: Readying a cleared forest for new trees

definition.text: Any of the treatments applied to a forest site to ready it for seeding or planting.

facts.text: It aims to ease regeneration by improving access, reducing or rearranging slash, and ameliorating poor forest floor, soil or vegetation conditions.
In Ontario around 1970 the most widely used technique was mechanical scarification with bulldozer-mounted blades, rakes, V-ploughs or teeth, or tractor-drawn scarifiers.
In a British Columbia disk-trenching trial, trees on south-, east- and west-facing microsites had larger tenth-year stem volumes than north-facing or untreated ones.
Choosing the planting spot mattered more overall than the orientation of the trench.

entries.title: Intensive tillage, the old conventional way

definition.text: Tillage that leaves less than 15% crop residue cover, or less than 500 pounds per acre (560 kg/ha) of small grain residue, on the soil.

facts.text: It often involves several passes with implements such as a mouldboard, disk or chisel plough, then a finisher with a harrow, rolling basket and cutter to prepare the seedbed.
It is often called conventional tillage, but in the United States conservation tillage is now more widely used, so the label is often inappropriate.
Conventional tillage means the operations standard for a place and crop, which tend to bury residues; it is the baseline for costing erosion control practices.
Faster travel with disks and chisel ploughs, and steeper disk angles, bury more residue and so make tillage more intensive.

entries.title: Burning logging slash, and what the fire does to the soil

definition.text: Broadcast or prescribed burning of logging slash on cleared forest sites to prepare them for planting or seeding.

facts.text: Burning raises soil pH, by as much as 2 units, a 100-fold change, and the increase persisted more than a year in central British Columbia.
The higher pH may explain copper and iron deficiencies in white spruce foliage on burned clearcuts.
Phosphorus availability rose after one burn and was still higher 21 months later, but in another study it fell below pre-burn levels within 9 months; nitrogen is lost.
Burns are patchy: in one 140-ha slash burn only 4% burned severely, 47% lightly and 49% not at all.

entries.title: Does no-till really store carbon in the soil?

definition.text: The dispute over whether no-till farming really increases the organic carbon stored in soil.

facts.text: Many studies report more soil organic carbon under no-till, but others find the effect absent in some systems, depending on factors such as climate and topsoil carbon content.
Some question whether measured gains are real or artefacts of flawed testing methods or other factors.
A 2014 study found the no-till subsurface layer often loses more soil organic carbon over time than the surface gains, and called for a uniform definition of sequestration.
A 2020 study found no-till combined with cover cropping stores more carbon than either practice alone.
Critics add that no-till may increase herbicide use, diminishing or eliminating its carbon benefits.
No-till cuts emissions of nitrous oxide, a gas 300 times stronger than CO2 that lasts 120 years, by 40–70% depending on rotation.
The cooling from no-till croplands' higher albedo is similar in magnitude to other biogeochemical carbon sequestration processes.

entries.title: The mouldboard plough, which turns the soil upside down

definition.text: A plough whose curved mould board lifts the slice of soil cut by the share and turns it over into the previous furrow.

facts.text: The coulter cuts down into the soil and the share cuts horizontally, freeing a strip of sod that rolls over and lands upside down.
General-purpose mould boards turn the slice gently for ploughing up to 200 mm deep; digger boards shatter it at 300 mm or more; semi-digger boards work at about 250 mm.
The heavy iron mouldboard plough was invented in Han China in the 1st and 2nd centuries and later spread to the Netherlands.
It greatly cut the time needed to prepare a field, and its ridges and furrows form channels that drain the soil.
Ploughing to 20 cm aerates the soil and works in residues, manure, lime and fertiliser, speeding mineralisation and cutting nitrogen loss by denitrification.
It raises numbers of soil-eating endogeic earthworms but deters vertical-burrowing anecic ones.
It leaves little surface residue against wind and water erosion, and over-ploughing can form a hardpan.
Being hard to turn, it changed fields from mostly square plots into long rectangular strips, hence the furlong.

entries.title: Controlling weeds when the plough stays out

definition.text: Controlling weeds without tillage, using herbicides, cover crops, mowing or crimping in place of cultivation.

facts.text: Herbicides such as glyphosate replace tillage for seedbed preparation, so no-till uses more herbicide than conventional tillage.
Residue left on the surface can bring different, greater or more frequent disease and weed problems than tilled fields.
Weed-suppressing cover crops add organic residue but must be killed, typically by crimping at flowering, and the crop is planted through the remaining mulch.
Herbicides are not strictly necessary, as natural farming and permaculture show; winter cover crops, soil solarization and burning are alternatives.

entries.title: The three-field system: crops two years in three

definition.text: A crop rotation in which a field grows one set of crops in the first year, a different set in the second and lies fallow in the third.

facts.text: An estate's arable land was split into three fields: one sown in autumn with winter wheat or rye, one with peas, lentils or beans, and one left fallow.
Legumes fixed nitrogen that cereals depleted, and livestock grazing the weedy fallow fertilized it with their excrement.
Each field was cropped two years in three, against half the land lying fallow under the older two-field system.
First used in China in the Eastern Zhou period, it spread in Europe from the 9th to the 11th century alongside the moldboard plough, though summer-dry Mediterranean lands suited it less.

entries.title: Keyline design: steering runoff so it soaks in

definition.text: P. A. Yeomans' system of planning farm landscapes around the natural flow of water to make the best use of their water resources.

facts.text: The keyline is the contour through the keypoint, where a valley floor suddenly steepens; cultivating parallel to it drifts runoff away from the valley centre.
Ordinary contour ploughing drifts off contour too, sending runoff off ridges into valleys; keyline cultivation delays runoff concentration and gives water more time to infiltrate.
Its Keyline Scale of Permanence orders farm elements from landshape and water supply through roads and structures to fences.
Philipp Gerhardt's Seepage Line System replaces fixed keylines with custom contour ditches, and trials in Germany show it reduces surface runoff.

entries.title: Setting the stubble alight

definition.text: Deliberately setting fire to the straw stubble left after harvesting grains such as rice and wheat.

facts.text: It clears fields quickly and cheaply, helps combat pests and weeds, and can reduce nitrogen tie-up.
It wastes nutrients, and prolonged burning kills beneficial soil microflora and fauna, reducing organic matter and upsetting the carbon–nitrogen balance.
Its smoke spreads particulate pollution, linked to lung cancer, respiratory infections and harm to people with chronic lung disease.
It is illegal in India and Pakistan but weakly enforced, and has effectively been banned in the United Kingdom since 1993.
Spraying an enzyme that decomposes stubble into fertiliser improves the soil and avoids air pollution.
Residues can go into particle board or biofuel, though removing them can still cause erosion and nutrient loss.

entries.title: The ard, an ox-drawn scratch plough

definition.text: The early animal-drawn scratch plough, which drags a share through the topsoil to cut a shallow furrow.

facts.text: Domesticated oxen in Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley, perhaps as early as the 6th millennium BC, supplied the draft power that made the ard possible.
A ploughed field from about 2800 BCE has been found at Kalibangan, India.
Because it left undisturbed strips between furrows, fields were cross-ploughed both ways, which tended to form squarish Celtic fields.
It suits loamy or sandy soils renewed by floods, as in the Nile Delta and Fertile Crescent, and struggled in northern Europe's heavy soils.

entries.title: The chisel plough, which loosens deep and leaves the cover

definition.text: A plough for deep tillage that loosens and aerates soil while leaving crop residue on the surface.

facts.text: Unlike most ploughs it does not invert the soil, which suits no-till and low-till farming; some consider it more sustainable than the mouldboard plough.
It can reduce the effects of compaction and help break up plough pans and hardpans.
It is essentially a heavy-duty field cultivator working 15 cm to 46 cm deep, needing 10 to 20 horsepower (7.5 to 14.9 kW) per shank.
Cultivator teeth work near the surface, mainly against weeds, whereas chisel shanks work deep, so cultivating needs far less power per shank.

entries.title: The heavy plough that made farming communal

definition.text: A wheeled plough heavy enough to carry a large metal-faced mould board and so to work the heavy soils of northern Europe.

facts.text: By the Han period Chinese ploughshares were wholly cast iron, the earliest known heavy iron mould-board ploughs.
Adoption of the carruca heavy plough in Europe accompanied the three-field system in the later 8th and early 9th centuries, raising yields per unit of land.
Pulling it took four to eight oxen, more than one peasant household had, so it made farming communal and helped the manorial system rise.
Heavy ploughs raised food production, coinciding with a marked rise in world population in the second millennium AD.

entries.title: Hoe cultivation, where farming began

definition.text: Turning soil with hand-held digging sticks and hoes, the way soil was worked when agriculture began.

facts.text: Hoes were used in very fertile areas such as the Nile banks, renewed by the annual flood, to cut furrows for seeds.
Digging sticks, hoes and mattocks arose in many places, and hoe cultivation must have been common wherever farming was practised.
Hoe farming is the traditional tillage of tropical and subtropical regions with stony soils, steep slopes, root crops and widely spaced coarse grains.

entries.title: The mole plough, which drains a field from below

definition.text: A deep plough with a torpedo-shaped tip that leaves a drainage channel underground, or breaks up deep impermeable layers, without digging trenches.

facts.text: Its bullet-shaped share forms a tunnel about 75 mm (3.0 in) across, and an expander presses the soil outward into a long-lasting channel.
Mole drains lie up to 950 mm (37 in) deep at an angle to pipe drains, into which their water seeps and runs to a ditch.
A simple field test: if a pencil pushed through a hand-compacted, tennis-ball-sized sample from moling depth leaves the ball unsplit, the subsoil suits mole ploughing.
Heavy land needs draining to bring its water content down to a level efficient for plant growth.

entries.title: The cultivator, which stirs the soil around the crop

definition.text: A farm implement for secondary tillage, either a frame with teeth dragged through the soil or a machine with rotating disks or teeth such as a rotary tiller.

facts.text: Cultivators stir and pulverize soil before planting to aerate it and prepare a smooth, loose seedbed, or after crop emergence to kill weeds.
Unlike a harrow, which disturbs the whole soil surface, a cultivator disturbs soil in careful patterns that spare the crop plants.
Toothed cultivators resemble chisel ploughs, but their teeth work near the surface against weeds, while chisel shanks work deep to break hardened layers.
Field cultivators prepare the seedbed, bury residue to help warm the soil, control weeds and mix the soil so the crop has enough water and nutrients.

entries.title: Vertical tillage, a method without a settled definition

definition.text: A set of tillage principles that, like conservation agriculture, aims to improve soil health, raise infiltration and reduce erosion and compaction.

facts.text: It avoids inverting the soil and keeps residue on the surface, using small forward-facing discs that slice residue for faster decomposition.
It often adds a deep ripping tool to break hard pans and compaction left by traditional implements and heavy machinery such as combine harvesters.
Proponents class it with no-till and conservation agriculture; detractors say its vigorous soil movement excludes it, which matters for US payments that promote no-till.
What counts as vertical tillage varies considerably, even among its proponents.

entries.title: The moisture at which soil crumbles best

definition.text: The soil moisture content at which tillage breaks the soil into the largest number of small aggregates.

facts.text: Tilling wetter or drier than the optimum damages structure by producing large clods and raises the readily dispersible clay content.
It can be related to the water content at the lower plastic limit; for several soils the optimum equals 0.9 times the plastic limit.
That link has limits: the plastic limit is measured on moulded rather than undisturbed soil, and many sandy soils have no plastic limit.
Many clay soils drain so slowly that they stay wetter than the plastic limit unless plant roots draw the water out; friability, the tendency to crumble, peaks at the plastic limit.

entries.title: Angled discs that slice and lift

definition.text: A harrow whose cutting edges are rows of concave metal discs set at an angle, used to till soil and chop weeds or crop residue.

facts.text: Because the discs are concave and offset from the direction of travel, they repeatedly slice the ground and loosen and lift the soil they cut.
Heavy primary disc harrows of 120 to 454 kg per disc break virgin land and work residue into the topsoil, speeding its decay; lighter secondary ones break clods into a seedbed.
It is the preferred way to work agricultural lime and gypsum into soil, reaching a 50/50 mix that reduces topsoil acid saturation.
Since lime does not move in the soil, this poses a critical challenge for zero-till farming.

entries.title: The seedbed, a seed's first home in the soil

definition.text: The local soil environment into which seeds are planted.

facts.text: Seedbed soil needs to be loose and smooth, without large lumps, so seeds can be planted easily at the depth that germinates them best.
On farms it is usually prepared by secondary tillage with harrows and cultivators, perhaps after primary tillage with mouldboard or chisel ploughs; no-till skips this step.
Preparation breaks up compacted soil so air and water can enter and seedlings can penetrate; smaller seeds need a finer soil structure.
Organic matter such as compost or peat may be added to improve the seedbed's soil structure.

entries.title: Ploughing below half a metre

definition.text: Ploughing deeper than 50 cm, compared with ordinary ploughing that rarely goes below 20 cm.

facts.text: Its purpose is to change the soil's water retention over the long term.
In a 35-year test, deep-ploughed plots averaged 3,138 kg of grain per hectare a year, 10% more than the 2,858 kg from unploughed plots.
In soils such as Podzols it can break up a hardpan and help release nutrients, and it is sometimes recommended before planting vineyards.
Farming is moving away from ploughing, especially deep ploughing, to save topsoil and organic matter, though a 35-year study found no-ploughing does not conserve ground moisture.

entries.title: Minimum tillage: only as much as the crop needs

definition.text: A soil conservation system that keeps soil manipulation to the minimum a crop needs, without turning the soil over.

facts.text: Primary tillage is avoided entirely, and secondary tillage is practised only to a small extent.
It includes minimum furrowing, organic fertilizer, biological pest control and minimal use of chemicals.
Some minimum or low-till methods mix tilled and untilled approaches, for example shallow disc harrowing without ploughing, or strip tillage.

entries.text: Minimum tillage avoids primary tillage entirely. This system for conserving soil keeps manipulation to the minimum a crop needs, without turning the soil over. Secondary tillage is practiced only to a small extent. The system also includes minimum furrowing, organic fertilizer, {{ref:soil-agri-217}} and minimal use of chemicals. Some minimum or low-till methods mix tilled and untilled approaches, for example shallow disc harrowing without ploughing, or {{ref:soil-agri-120}}.

Some minimum or low-till methods mix tilled and untilled approaches, for example shallow disc harrowing without ploughing, or Strip-till: tilling only where the seed will go.

entries.title: Strip-till: tilling only where the seed will go

definition.text: A minimum-tillage conservation system that tills only the narrow strip of soil that will hold the seed row, leaving the soil between rows untilled.

facts.text: It combines the soil drying and warming of conventional tillage with the soil protection of no-till.
Each strip-tilled row is usually about eight to ten inches wide.
Also called zone tillage, it breaks up plough pans under the row, helps warm the soil, prepares a seedbed and improves internal drainage.
Breaking the crust lets air in and speeds organic matter decay, yet a two-year study found no change in soil organic carbon or extractable phosphorus.
Fertilizer can be placed directly in the seed row during strip-tilling, cutting the amount needed and putting it closer to the roots.
Combined implements can cut field trips to two or even one, saving time and fuel and reducing compaction.
It conserves more moisture than intensive tillage, though sometimes less than no-till, and erosion is light by comparison with intensive tillage.
At a low-phosphorus site strip-till yielded 43.5 bushels/acre (2,925.5 kg/ha) against 41.5 bu/a (2,791 kg/ha) under no-till; yields match intensive tillage without its cost.

conflicts.text: Zone tillage produces a tilled strip approximately five inches wide.

entries.text_plain: Each tilled row is usually only about eight to ten inches wide. Strip-till is a minimum-tillage conservation system that tills just the narrow strip of soil that will hold the seed row, leaving the soil between rows untilled. It combines the soil drying and warming of conventional tillage with the soil protection of no-till. Also called zone tillage, it breaks up compacted layers under the row, prepares a seedbed and improves internal drainage. Breaking the crust lets air in and speeds organic matter decay, yet a two-year study found no change in organic carbon or extractable phosphorus. Fertilizer can be placed directly in the seed row during strip-tilling, so less is needed and it sits closer to the roots. Combined implements can cut field trips to two or even one, saving time and fuel and reducing compaction. Strip-till conserves more moisture than intensive tillage, though sometimes less than no-till, and its erosion is light by comparison with intensive tillage. At one low-phosphorus site it yielded 43.5 bushels/acre (2,925.5 kg/ha) against 41.5 bu/a (2,791 kg/ha) under no-till. Its yields match intensive tillage without the cost.

entries.title: Leaving the stubble standing

definition.text: Leaving stubble or crop residue in place on the land as a surface cover during a fallow period.

facts.text: It can prevent soil erosion by wind or water and conserve soil moisture.

entries.text: The simplest cover for a resting field is the last crop's leftovers. Stubble mulching leaves stubble or {{ref:soil-agri-129}} in place on the surface during a {{ref:soil-agri-044}} period, a kind of {{ref:soil-fert-066}} the field grows for itself. That cover can keep wind and water from carrying soil away, and it conserves soil moisture until the next crop goes in.

entries.title: Controlled traffic farming: wheels stay in their lanes

definition.text: A management system that confines all machinery loads to the smallest possible area of permanent traffic lanes, to limit soil damage from heavy or repeated passes.

facts.text: Random traffic compacts about 75% of a field in one season and all of it by the second, while a proper system cuts tracking to 15%, always in the same place.
It needs matched implement widths and wheel track widths, and machines kept in the same lanes every year, most easily with RTK satellite guidance and auto-steer accurate to about ± 2 cm.
Untracked soil gains porosity, infiltration and drainage, with less erosion and waterlogging and better rooting; most adopters till little or not at all because structure no longer needs repair.
Compacted soils can take more than 5 years to recover; drawbacks of the system are a high initial investment and the need for GPS guidance and adapted machines.

entries.title: Tilling everything, burying only part

definition.text: A seeding method in which the whole soil surface is tilled and crop residue mixed in, while some residue stays on the surface.

facts.text: It is done with a wide variety of cultivators and counts as conservation tillage in the United States.

entries.text: Mulch tillage is a compromise between turning the soil and protecting it. The whole surface is tilled and {{ref:soil-agri-129}} is mixed in, but some residue stays on top as a {{ref:soil-fert-066}}. Farmers do it with a wide variety of cultivators. In the United States it counts as {{ref:soil-agri-099}}.

entries.title: Working out residue cover after tillage passes

definition.text: Estimating the share of the soil surface still covered by crop residue after a sequence of tillage operations by multiplying each tool's remaining fraction.

facts.text: Each pass of a tillage tool buries some residue, so surface cover shrinks; when passes follow one another, remaining cover is estimated by multiplication.
Example: 80% cover after corn, then chisel (70%), tandem disk (45%), field cultivator and planter (75%) leaves about 19%; dropping the disk leaves 42%.
After corn or cereals a moldboard plough leaves 0-10% residue, twisted-point chisel 50-70%, tandem finishing disk 30-60%, field cultivator 60-90% and a row-crop planter 85-95%.
Speed, depth and soil moisture affect the amounts, and cover also depends on surface roughness and soil loosening.

entries.title: A short history of tillage

definition.text: How tillage began with small-grain farmers and spread, from the ard and animal traction to the moldboard plough and powerful tractors.

facts.text: Tillage began with small-grain farmers of the Fertile Crescent, Europe and North Africa to make a fine, clean seedbed, give the crop a head start on weeds and stimulate mineralization of nutrients.
Centuries of this system caused excessive erosion, organic matter loss and nutrient depletion, especially around the Mediterranean.
Jethro Tull's 1731 book promoted row seeding with a seed drill and intensive tillage; he believed pulverized soil particles fed plants and grew wheat 13 years without manure by mining soil nutrients.
Pre-Columbian American farmers used no full-field tillage, instead direct seeding with planting sticks or hoeing small hills, and intercropped corn, beans and squash.

entries.title: Frost tillage: working soil as it freezes

definition.text: Tilling soil after frost has entered it but before it has penetrated more than about 2 inches (5 cm).

facts.text: Water moves up to the freezing front and the soil beneath dries; the frozen layer supports equipment, so compaction is reduced.
The rough surface favours water infiltration and prevents runoff; livestock farms can use it to incorporate or inject manure in winter.
Recent research in Nebraska and Australia indicates occasional tillage does not harm soil health; purposes include weed or insect control, incorporating immobile amendments and compaction relief.
It should be rare (once every 5-10 years) with tools that leave residue, because any tillage can destroy structure built by years of no-till.

entries.title: The plough pan, a hard floor made by tillage

definition.text: A compacted layer of soil created by tillage, also called a tillage pan.

facts.text: Over-ploughing can form a hardpan, which farmers usually break with a subsoiler that slices through the hardened layer deep below the surface.
Chisel ploughs and zone tillage are used to break up plough pans.
Continued cultivation and traffic create compacted, impermeable layers within the soil profile.

entries.text: Tillage that loosens the surface can harden the soil beneath it. A plough pan, also called a tillage pan, is a compacted layer of soil created by tillage. Continued cultivation and traffic create compacted, impermeable layers within the soil profile. Chisel ploughs and zone tillage are also used to break up plough pans.

entries.title: Subsoiling: breaking hard layers below the plough's reach

definition.text: Deep tillage with a subsoiler, an implement whose heavy shanks loosen and break up soil below the depth reached by ploughs, harrows or rototillers.

facts.text: Most tillage tools work the top 15–20 cm (6–8 in), while a subsoiler loosens soil to twice that depth, usually 45–75 cm (18–30 in) or more.
Angled wings on the shanks lift and shatter the hardpan that builds up through compaction, improving the growth of crops wherever compaction is a problem.
After subsoiling, roots reach deeper moisture and nutrients in hot, dry seasons, and in wet weather water drains through the shattered zones, so crops are less likely to drown.
It is slow and power-hungry: pulling one point through hard soil takes 60 to 100 horsepower (45 to 75 kW), and shanks should reach 2.5–5 cm (1–2 in) below the deepest compacted layer.
A subsoiler is not a mole plough, which cuts underground drainage channels.
The para-plough is a primary tillage implement that loosens compacted layers 3 to 4 dm (12 to 16 inches) deep without inverting soil, keeping surface residue high.
In-row subsoiling counts among the conservation tillage practices.
On poorly drained land deep tillage may substitute for costlier tile drainage, and subsoiling may be needed where a clay-enriched lower horizon becomes too compacted.

entries.title: Ridge tillage: seedbeds on raised ridges

definition.text: A conservation tillage system that builds ridges or beds for the seed zone and keeps fixed traffic lanes.

facts.text: It is one of the conservation tillage practices, with no-till, in-row subsoiling and strip-till, that aim to keep 30% or more of the surface under crop residue.
Ridges allow the seed zone to dry and warm faster, give some weed control and reduce saturation after heavy rain; fixed travel lanes reduce overall compaction.
Poorly drained fields benefit greatly from ridging or bedding because the sensitive seedling root zone stays aerobic when wet; controlled-traffic lanes greatly reduce compaction.

entries.title: Keeping topsoil in place and fertile

definition.text: Preventing the loss of topsoil to erosion, and the loss of fertility through overuse, acidification, salinization or chemical contamination.

facts.text: Its techniques include crop rotation, cover crops, conservation tillage and planted windbreaks, which affect both erosion and fertility.
Deforestation typically brings large-scale erosion, loss of soil nutrients and sometimes total desertification.
Farmers have practised soil conservation for millennia; the ancient Phoenicians ploughed on the contour on slopes of two to ten percent.
Government involvement in land management and soil conservation expanded greatly after the Dust Bowl, beginning in Franklin D. Roosevelt's first 100 days in 1933.
In Europe, the Common Agricultural Policy promotes reduced tillage, winter cover crops, plant residues and grass margins for soil conservation.
Salinity, left when irrigation water evaporates or rises from shallow saline water tables, is estimated to affect about one third of the earth's arable land.
Each one percent increase in soil organic matter helps soil hold 20,000 gallons more water per acre.
Solving erosion also needs political and economic action, since how land is valued is a governance hurdle that cultural change can shift.

entries.text: Farmers have practiced soil conservation for millennia. The ancient Phoenicians already plowed along the contour on slopes of two to ten percent. Soil conservation means preventing two kinds of loss. One is topsoil carried away by erosion. The other is fertility worn down by overuse, {{ref:soil-chem-001}}, salinization or chemical contamination. The stakes can be total. Deforestation typically brings large-scale erosion and lost nutrients, and sometimes complete {{ref:soil-env-072}}. Salinity alone is estimated to affect about one third of the earth's arable land. It is left behind when irrigation water evaporates, or when it rises from shallow saline water tables. The techniques include crop rotation, {{ref:soil-agri-066}}, conservation tillage and rows of trees planted against the wind, and each works on erosion and fertility together. Organic matter pays off in water: each one percent increase in soil organic matter helps soil hold 20,000 gallons more water per acre. Governments joined in on a large scale after the Dust Bowl, starting in Franklin D. Roosevelt's first 100 days in 1933. In Europe, the Common Agricultural Policy promotes reduced tillage, crops kept over winter to cover the soil, plant residues and grass margins. Yet erosion is not only a farming problem. How land is valued is a governance hurdle, so solving erosion also takes political and economic action, and cultural change can shift it.

entries.title: Cover crops: plants grown to protect, not to sell

definition.text: A crop planted to cover the soil rather than to be harvested.

facts.text: Cover crops help manage erosion, fertility, soil quality, water, weeds, pests, diseases, biodiversity and wildlife in an agroecosystem.
They are often sown off-season after the cash crop is harvested and grown over winter, and they act as nurse crops that help the main crop survive.
Often grown solely against erosion, they protect the surface, scatter raindrop energy, slow overland flow and raise infiltration, while their roots anchor soil and add porosity.
They increase microbial activity, which improves nitrogen availability, nitrogen uptake by the following crop and yields.
A meta-analysis of 102 field studies found saturated hydraulic conductivity up about 106% and topsoil organic carbon and nitrogen up about 10% and 20%.
Microbial biomass carbon rose about 20% and particulate organic carbon nearly 50% compared with bare or fallow ground.
Trade-offs exist: cover crops may reduce water for the next crop or leave yields unchanged, especially in semi-arid regions or with poorly timed termination.
They are killed before the cash crop by mowing, tilling, discing, rolling or herbicide.

entries.text: Some crops are never meant for market. A cover crop is planted to cover the soil rather than to be harvested. Farmers often sow it off-season, after the cash crop comes in, and let it grow over winter. Often its only job is to fight erosion. Its leaves shield the surface and scatter the energy of falling raindrops. It slows water flowing over the ground and lets more of it soak in, while its roots anchor the soil and open new pores. Below ground it stirs up microbial activity, which makes more nitrogen available to the next crop and can lift yields. A meta-analysis of 102 field studies measured these effects against bare or fallow ground. Saturated hydraulic conductivity, the ease with which water flows through soaked soil, rose about 106%. Topsoil organic carbon rose about 10% and nitrogen about 20%. Microbial biomass carbon climbed about 20%, and particulate organic carbon nearly 50%. The benefits come with trade-offs. A cover crop may use water the next crop needs, or leave yields unchanged, especially in semi-arid regions or when it is killed at the wrong time. Before the cash crop goes in, farmers end it by mowing, tilling, discing, rolling or spraying herbicide. In all, cover crops touch erosion, fertility, soil quality, water, weeds, pests, diseases, biodiversity and wildlife. They also act as nurse crops that help the main crop survive.

entries.title: Terraces: staircases carved into hillsides

definition.text: A flat surface cut into a hill or mountainside for growing crops, usually built as a series of steps like a staircase.

facts.text: Terraced fields reduce both erosion and surface runoff and can hold irrigated crops such as rice.
Each terrace is itself protected from erosion by other soil barriers, and terracing is more common on small farms.
Terraced paddies are used for rice, wheat and barley across much of Asia, the Mediterranean Basin, Africa and South America.
Terraces in the Yemen Highlands date from the start of the Bronze Age in the 3rd millennium BC, and Levant terrace farming from as early as the 4th millennium BCE.
Andean terraces, or andenes, were developed by the Wari and others before 1000 AD to use shallow soil efficiently and irrigate crops, and were later adopted by the Inca.
Luminescence dating shows a major burst of Mediterranean terrace building in the later Middle Ages, around AD 1100–1600.
Long-term soil moisture management by terracing or irrigation can create anthraquic Anthrosols.
Scholars lack consensus on when the ancient terraces of the Jerusalem Mountains were built, with proposals ranging from the Bronze Age to the Roman and Byzantine periods.

entries.contested_note: Scholars disagree on the construction dates of the Jerusalem Mountains terraces, and luminescence dates may reflect later modification.

entries.title: Soil management: keeping fields productive for decades

definition.text: Applying operations, practices and treatments to protect soil and improve its performance, such as its fertility or mechanical behaviour.

facts.text: It takes in soil conservation, soil amendment and optimal soil health, and both conventional and organic farms need it to stay productive over decades.
Organic farming relies on soil health for almost all of its fertility and pest control, so it stresses soil management.
Controlling traffic on the soil surface reduces compaction, which can cut aeration and water infiltration.
Cover crops keep soil anchored and covered off-season, and rotations alternate high- and low-residue crops to keep plant material on the surface against erosion.
Conventional tillage disturbs soil most deeply; reduced-tillage and no-till keep residues on the surface for erosion protection and water retention.
Fertilizers add nitrogen, phosphorus, sulfur and potassium but often acidify soils, potassium fertilizer excepted.
Adding organic matter to the surface can raise soil carbon and the abundance and diversity of soil microbes.
Project Drawdown names improved nutrient management, conservation agriculture and regenerative agriculture as soil management steps for climate change mitigation.

entries.title: Windbreaks: rows of trees that hold the soil down

definition.text: One or more rows of trees or shrubs, also called a shelterbelt, planted to shelter land from the wind and protect soil from erosion.

facts.text: Shelterbelts are rows of trees set perpendicular to the prevailing wind, while woodlots are more extensive areas of woodland.
Evergreens protect all year, but deciduous trees may be enough if they are in leaf while the soil is bare.
Besides sharply reducing wind erosion, windbreaks improve the microclimate for crops, shelter beneficial birds, sequester carbon and improve the landscape.
They reduce evapotranspiration as well as erosion, and with woodlots they are used to fix the soil against desertification.
Farmers plant them to cut wind erosion of loess, and very light soils need them in dry weather.
Windbreaks also separate fields and protect them from pesticide spray drift.
Behind a windbreak the wind is slowest at about 3 to 5 times its height downwind, then recovers.
Farmers also use windbreaks to hold snow on fields, where it supplies water when it melts in spring.

entries.title: Agroforestry: farming with the forest as a model

definition.text: A land use system that integrates trees with crops or pasture.

facts.text: It is managed to optimize interactions among the plants and animals, using the forest as a model, which makes it applied agroecology.
The term was coined in 1973 by forester John Bene, though the practices are millennia old.
In 2025, 91 countries and areas reported 55.4 million hectares under agroforestry, most of it in Asia.
Groundcover protects depleted soil from erosion, and trees slow runoff and evaporation so more water infiltrates.
Nitrogen-fixing plants such as legumes can restore soil nitrogen fertility.
It can increase carbon stocks in soil and woody biomass.
The USDA lists five temperate practices: alley cropping, forest farming, riparian forest buffers, silvopasture and windbreaks.
Honduras's Quesungual system replaced slash-and-burn hillside farming, whose exposed soil washed away, by keeping nitrogen-fixing trees that cut erosion and hold moisture.

entries.title: Strip farming: alternating bands that act as dams

definition.text: Farming a field divided into long, narrow strips that alternate in a crop rotation, also called strip cropping.

facts.text: It is used where a slope is too steep, or no other method can prevent soil erosion.
Strips of close-sown hay, wheat or forage, serving mainly as cover crops, alternate with strips of row crops such as corn, soybeans, cotton or sugar beets.
Laid out along the approximate contour, the sod strips act as natural dams that slow water and hold back soil from the cultivated strips.
Strip width depends chiefly on average wind speed and slope gradient; strips are usually 25 feet (7.6 m) to 75 feet (23 m) wide, and 50 feet (15 m) suits most machinery.
In dry farming on the Great Plains and Canadian Prairies, fallow and cropped strips run at right angles to the prevailing wind to limit wind erosion of bare fields.
Contour strip cropping, used mainly on gentle slopes, makes the protective strips wider than the row-crop strips so they intercept runoff.
In strip intercropping the strips are narrower and contiguous, which suits machinery and lets neighbouring crops benefit from each other.
In the Midwestern United States, prairie strips of native plants serve as contour buffers and edge-of-field filters that build soil health and curb erosion.

entries.title: Soil stabilization: engineering weak ground for roads

definition.text: Any physical, chemical, mechanical or biological method, alone or combined, of altering a natural soil to meet an engineering purpose.

facts.text: It raises the bearing capacity, tensile strength and overall performance of unstable subsoils, sands and waste materials, chiefly to strengthen roads.
Traditional binders for a road base are bitumen, tar emulsions, asphalt, cement and lime, along with fly ash, cement kiln dust and tree resins.
Bitumen is not environmentally friendly and turns brittle when dry, and Portland cement is often expensive.
Newer stabilizers include enzymes, surfactants, synthetic and bio-polymers, fibre reinforcement and chloride salts; some make hydrophobic layers that keep out water and frost.
Many so-called green products work like soap powder, only lubricating and realigning soil without binding it, while many new approaches rely on clay's binding properties.
The Deep Mixing Method injects through a small probe to strengthen weak or loose soil strata and repair sinkholes.
Adding materials to stabilize a soil can also limit its ability to shrink and swell.

entries.text: A road is only as strong as the ground beneath it. Soil stabilization is any physical, chemical, mechanical or biological method, alone or combined, of altering a natural soil to meet an engineering purpose. Bitumen is not environmentally friendly and turns brittle when dry, and Portland cement is often expensive. Newer stabilizers include enzymes, surfactants, synthetic and bio-polymers, fiber reinforcement and chloride salts. Some form water-repelling layers that keep out water and frost. The Deep Mixing Method injects through a small probe to strengthen weak or loose soil strata and repair sinkholes. Adding stabilizing materials can also limit a soil's ability to shrink and swell.

entries.title: Green manures: cover crops that feed the soil

definition.text: Growing cover crops, often legumes, to raise soil fertility, chiefly by supplying or conserving nitrogen.

facts.text: Fertility-building cover crops are called green manures; they are often ploughed under before maturity.
Leguminous cover crops, nodulated by bacteria such as Bradyrhizobium that fix atmospheric nitrogen into ammonium, can often supply all the nitrogen a crop needs.
This ability to stand in for chemical nitrogen fertilizer is called fertilizer replacement value.
Some scientists see biological nitrogen fixation, mainly through cover crops, as the only alternative to fossil-fuel-dependent industrial nitrogen fixation for future food production.
Nitrogen fertilizer lost to waterways causes eutrophication, as in the Gulf of Mexico's summer dead zone of over 22,000 square kilometres.
In Nigeria the velvet bean cover crop increased soil phosphorus availability after rock phosphate was applied.

entries.text: Some cover crops are grown not to guard the soil but to feed it. Fertility-building cover crops are called green manures, and they are often plowed under before they mature. A leguminous cover crop can often supply all the nitrogen a crop needs. This ability to stand in for chemical nitrogen fertilizer is called fertilizer replacement value. It matters beyond the farm. Nitrogen fertilizer lost to waterways causes {{ref:soil-env-020}}, as in the Gulf of Mexico's summer dead zone of over 22,000 square kilometers. Some scientists see biological nitrogen fixation, mainly through cover crops, as the only alternative to fossil-fuel-dependent industrial nitrogen fixation for future food production. Other nutrients can benefit too. In Nigeria, a velvet bean cover crop increased soil phosphorus availability after rock phosphate was applied.

entries.title: Conservation agriculture: disturb little, cover always

definition.text: A farming system, as defined by the FAO, that prevents loss of arable land and regenerates degraded land through minimal soil disturbance, permanent soil cover and diverse plant species.

facts.text: Soil cover comes from mulch or cover crops, and disturbance is minimized by eliminating or greatly reducing ploughing, as in no-till farming.
By cutting ploughing it encourages earthworms and the formation of a mull-like agricultural humus form called agri-mull.
Mineral fertilizer use is reduced to the strict requirements of the crop and is sometimes unnecessary.
With regenerative and organic agriculture it is grouped as sustainable agriculture, an alternative to industrialized conventional farming.
Tillage, once thought to raise fertility through mineralization, is now seen to destroy organic matter and cause erosion and crusting.
The mulch layer slows runoff and softens raindrop impact, and keeps soil moisture and temperature higher than yearly tillage.
Producers can save 30% to 40% of time and labour with no-till.
Benefits can take many years, new planters or drills cost money, and in developing countries the residues it needs are traditionally fed to livestock.

entries.text: Tillage was once thought to raise fertility. It is now seen to destroy organic matter and cause erosion and crusting. Conservation agriculture is one response. The FAO defines it as a farming system that prevents loss of arable land and regenerates degraded land. It rests on minimal soil disturbance, permanent soil cover and diverse plant species. Plowing is eliminated or greatly reduced, as in no-till farming, and mulch or cover crops keep the ground covered. The mulch slows runoff, softens raindrop impact, and keeps soil moister and warmer than yearly tillage would. With less plowing, earthworms thrive and a mull-like agricultural humus form called agri-mull develops. Mineral fertilizer is cut to the crop's strict requirements and is sometimes unnecessary. No-till can save producers 30% to 40% of their time and labor. The drawbacks are real. Benefits can take many years, new planters or drills cost money, and in developing countries the residues it needs are traditionally fed to livestock. With regenerative and organic agriculture, it counts as sustainable agriculture.

entries.title: Fewer pesticides, healthier soil
entries.article: Soil conservation#Reducing the use of pesticides

definition.text: Cutting pesticide use to protect soil, since pesticides can contaminate soil, nearby vegetation and water for a long time.

facts.text: Pesticides affect soil structure and its biotic and abiotic composition.

Alternatives include irradiation, cultivation methods, biological controls such as pheromones and microbial pesticides, genetic engineering and disrupting insect breeding; composted yard waste has also controlled pests.
Differentiated taxation schemes are among the options studied for reducing pesticide use.

entries.text: Pesticides do not vanish after spraying. They can contaminate soil, nearby vegetation and water for a long time, and they affect soil structure and its living and nonliving makeup. Cutting their use is one way to protect soil. Alternatives include irradiation, cultivation methods, biological controls such as pheromones and microbial pesticides, genetic engineering and disrupting insect breeding. Composted yard waste has also controlled pests. Researchers have studied policy tools too, among them differentiated taxation schemes.
