entries.title: Soil-conservation farming and its critics

definition.text: Farming that combines no-till, green manures and other soil-enhancing practices to protect and rebuild the soil.

facts.text: Its advocates say it can revive damaged soil, minimize erosion, remove the need for nitrogen fertilizer or fungicide and protect crops in drought or flood, at lower labour and cost.
No-till and cover crops act as sinks for nitrogen and other nutrients, which raises soil organic matter.
Repeated ploughing degrades soil and kills its beneficial fungi and earthworms, and damaged soil may need several seasons to recover.
Critics call no-till and related methods impractical and costly, cite advantages of conventional tillage in some settings, and say no-till complicates pest control and residue management.

entries.contested_note: Critics dispute that no-till and related conservation farming methods are practical and affordable for many growers.

entries.title: How farm soils can warm or cool the climate

definition.text: The effect of how soils are managed on greenhouse gases: management can emit nitrous oxide and carbon, or store carbon dioxide as soil organic carbon.

facts.text: Fertilizer use, irrigation and tillage contribute to nitrous oxide emissions, and soil management accounts for over half of the agriculture sector's emissions.
Using biochar may cut nitrous oxide emissions from soils by an average of 54%.
Converting natural land to farmland releases carbon, and how much carbon a soil can store depends on climate, land-use history and management.
Cropland could sequester 0.5–1.2 Pg C/year and grazing and pasture land 0.3–0.7 Pg C/year.
Sequestration rises with more biomass inputs, smaller losses of soil organic carbon and a longer mean residence time of that carbon.
No-till, residue mulching, cover cropping and crop rotation significantly enhance soil carbon sequestration and are more common in organic than conventional farming.

entries.text: Farm soil can work on either side of the climate ledger. Management can emit nitrous oxide and carbon, or store carbon dioxide in the soil, described in {{ref:soil-env-108}}. Using biochar may cut nitrous oxide emissions from soils by an average of 54%. Converting natural land to farmland releases carbon. Storage rises with more biomass inputs, smaller losses of that stored carbon and a longer mean residence time for that carbon. No-till, residue mulching, cover cropping and crop rotation significantly enhance carbon storage in soil. All four are more common in organic than in conventional farming.

entries.title: Lynchets: the stepped hillsides of ancient Britain

definition.text: An earth terrace on a hillside, typical of the ancient field systems of the British Isles.

facts.text: Lynchets often run in vertical rows, called strip lynchets, mostly in southern Britain near Iron Age forts and older earthworks.
The traditional theory is that long ploughing makes soil slip downslope, building a positive lynchet where the surface rises and a negative lynchet where it drops.
The size, spacing and number of rows show that many were man-made, most likely dug to make the most of land for farming.
The word is the diminutive of lynch, an old term for an agricultural terrace.

entries.title: How cover crops steer rain into the ground

definition.text: The ways cover crops change how water enters, moves through and leaves a field's soil.

facts.text: By curbing erosion they reduce the rate and amount of water draining off fields, a risk to waterways downstream.
Their biomass shields the surface from rain, and their roots open pores that let water filter down instead of running off.
Greater infiltration can improve soil water storage and aquifer recharge.
Where water is scarce, cover crops used as mulch shade and cool the surface, reducing evaporation.

entries.title: Cover crops that trap pests and fight disease

definition.text: Using cover crops to break pest and disease cycles, lure pests away as trap crops and attract their natural enemies.

facts.text: Mustards and other Brassicaceae suppress fungal diseases with toxic chemicals released as their glucosinolates break down.
Nematode-resistant white mustard and radish trap nematodes that enter their roots but cannot reproduce there, cutting populations by 70–99%.
Grasses, legumes and brassicas also raise soil organic matter and microbial activity, making cash crops more resilient to insect pests and pathogens.
Findings on cover crops and predator–pest dynamics are mixed, so effects depend on the cover crop type and management.

Grasses, legumes and brassicas also raise soil organic matter and microbial activity, making cash crops more resilient to insect pests and pathogens. Findings on predators and pests are mixed, though, so effects depend on the cover crop and its management.

entries.title: Smothering weeds with a cover crop

definition.text: The control of weeds by cover crops, through competition while they grow and smothering or chemical inhibition after they die.

facts.text: A cover crop flattened on the surface forms a nearly impenetrable mat that blocks light, cutting weed germination; this is the smother effect.
Some cover crops release compounds that inhibit other plants, called allelopathy; examples include rye, hairy vetch, red clover, sorghum-sudangrass and mustards.
After termination, yellow sweetclover residues held weeds 75–97% below levels in fallow systems.
Rye cover crop residues used as mulch gave 80% to 95% control of early-season broadleaf weeds.

entries.title: Biological pest control with living enemies

definition.text: A method of controlling animal pests, weeds or plant and animal pathogens by using other organisms.

facts.text: It relies on predation, parasitism and herbivory with active human management, and can be a component of integrated pest management.
Three strategies exist: importation of a pest's natural enemy to a new place, augmentation by releasing more of the enemies already there, and conservation of existing natural enemies.
Conservation can be simple and cheap: nectar-producing plants on rice field borders cut pest densities 10- or even 100-fold, so farmers sprayed 70% less insecticide and yields rose 5%.

Bacillus thuringiensis, a soil-dwelling bacterium, is the most widely applied bacterial control agent, used against moth, butterfly, beetle and fly pests; it infects through the gut, so it works poorly on sucking insects.
Imported enemies can have side effects: some early introductions became serious pests themselves, and controls can attack native non-target species.

entries.title: Contour trenches that catch the rain

definition.text: Digging continuous trenches along the contour of a slope to conserve water and soil and raise crop yields, an easily applied technique in arid sub-Saharan areas.

facts.text: The trench catches water flowing downhill so it soaks into the soil, and crops between trenches draw on this subsoil reserve during the drier growing season.
Rainwater no longer runs straight off the hill, crops suffer less from later water shortage, and fertile particles are not lost to water and wind erosion.
Trench spacing follows the slope, its size suits local climate and soil, it must hold all the water, and its upslope side is protected with grass, shrubs or fabric.
It is one of the techniques used to reverse desertification.

entries.title: A green border between field and stream

definition.text: A strip of land kept under permanent vegetation, mostly on farmland, to protect soil, water and air quality.

facts.text: By slowing surface runoff, buffer strips trap sediment and filter out nutrients and pesticides before they reach surface waters.
Roots of the planted vegetation bind soil particles, reducing wind erosion and stabilizing stream banks against erosion and landslides.
Vegetation ranges from grass alone to mixes of grass, trees and shrubs; more diverse strips give more protection from nutrient and pesticide flow.
Governments often pay for buffer strips because they cut nitrogen losses to water and soil loss by wind erosion.
Soil drainage is the first criterion for siting grasses: poor drainage causes ponding, high drainage is droughty, and medium drainage suits planting best.
The NRCS finds contour strip cropping most effective on slopes of 4 to 8%.

entries.title: The 1936 law that paid farmers to save soil
entries.article: Soil Conservation and Domestic Allotment Act of 1936

definition.text: A US federal law of 1936 that let the government pay farmers to cut production in order to conserve soil and prevent erosion.

facts.text: It was passed after the Supreme Court declared the Agricultural Adjustment Act unconstitutional.
It amended and renamed the Soil Conservation Act of 1935 to preserve soil fertility and reduce exploitation and unprofitable use of national soil resources.
Landlords now had to share the government payments with the sharecroppers and tenants who worked their land.
It directed soil conservation on the Dust Bowl's high plains, educating farmers and planting trees and native grass.

entries.title: Terracettes: the catsteps of steep pastures

definition.text: A landform of roughly parallel, step-like ridges on a steep hillside.

facts.text: These small, irregular steps are common on steep pastures, where soil creep or surface erosion is worsened by trampling sheep or cattle; they are also called catsteps or cattle terracing.
One explanation is that saturated soil swells and then shrinks as it dries, so particles creep slowly downhill; freeze–thaw and heating–cooling cycles can do the same.

Darwin (1904) thought grazing animals made them, but some end abruptly at rock faces or soil changes, livestock trails cut across others, and geomorphologists doubt animals alone could form such regular steps.

entries.contested_note: Sources dispute whether grazing animals or soil processes such as creep and solifluction mainly form terracettes.

entries.title: The Great Plains Shelterbelt: 220 million trees against dust

definition.text: A US project, begun in 1934, to plant windbreaks across the Great Plains states.

facts.text: Franklin D. Roosevelt started it in response to the Dust Bowl's dust storms; the Forest Service expected trees around farms to cut wind speed and evaporation of soil moisture.
By 1942, 30,233 shelterbelts held 220 million trees over 18,600 square miles (48,000 km2), in a 100-mile wide zone from North Dakota's Canadian border to the Brazos River in Texas.
Farmers were paid to plant and tend native trees such as red cedar and green ash along fence rows; the first tree, an Austrian pine, went into an Oklahoma farm in 1935.
Because a long-term project was ineligible for emergency relief funds, Roosevelt moved it to the Works Progress Administration, helped by the Forest Service and Civilian Conservation Corps.
By 2010 many of the shelterbelts were old and declining, and federal grants funded their renovation in Kansas, North Dakota, South Dakota and Nebraska.

entries.title: Check dams: small barriers that slow the flow

definition.text: A small, sometimes temporary dam built across a swale, ditch or waterway to counter erosion by slowing the water.

facts.text: It flattens the channel gradient, slowing the flow, which induces infiltration and reduces erosion; it is not mainly a sediment trap.
Coarse and medium sediment settles behind it while finer grains pass through.
In arid areas check dams are built to increase groundwater recharge.
They are made of rocks, gravel, logs, hay bales or sandbags and are usually less than 2 to 3 feet high.

entries.title: Catch crops: grabbing leftover nitrogen between harvests

definition.text: A fast-growing crop, a type of cover crop, grown between two successive main crops.

facts.text: It takes up surplus nitrogen left from the previous crop, keeping it from loss by leaching, denitrification or volatilization; catch crops are usually fast-growing cereals.
The nitrogen it holds returns to the soil when it is worked in as green manure or decomposes.
Its residue roughens the surface against splash and runoff, and decaying roots leave biopores that increase infiltration.
Sowing date, harvest date and tillage decide its benefit; sowing later than recommended reduces its nitrogen uptake.

entries.title: Magnesium chloride: a salty answer to road dust

definition.text: Spreading magnesium chloride on unpaved roads and dusty sites, where its moisture-absorbing nature keeps fine particles from becoming airborne.

facts.text: It absorbs water from air at 32% relative humidity, keeping the surface damp and binding gravel and clay particles to the road.
It works better in humid than in arid climates, and its chief benefit is lower maintenance costs for gravel roads.
Its use is controversial: advocates cite cleaner air and safer roads, but the dissolved salts reach groundwater and surface water, where chloride above 250 mg/L is regulated.
Salts accumulating in roadside soils harm plants by raising the osmotic pressure of the soil solution, altering mineral nutrition and building toxic ion levels.

entries.title: Geogrids and geocells: holding soil grains in place

definition.text: Strengthening a soil layer by confining the movement of its particles, for example with geogrids or three-dimensional geocells.

facts.text: Geogrids confine aggregate by interlocking with it, while geocells confine it by the hoop stress of their cell walls.
On Swedish forest roads, geocell-reinforced sections markedly raised bearing capacity and reduced permanent deformation under repeated traffic.
Locally sourced infill in geocells may perform as well as or better than imported crushed aggregate.
Better drainage, for instance with stone mattresses, also stabilizes roads by removing excess pore water and spreading loads.

entries.title: Structures or soil building: two ways to control erosion

definition.text: Runoff and erosion control methods fall into structural measures, which are engineered works, and agronomic practices, which change soil and crop management.

facts.text: Structures such as terraces, diversion ditches and drop structures need an up-front investment; agronomic practices include reduced tillage, cover cropping and vegetating critical areas.
Structures mainly contain runoff and sediment after erosion has started, while agronomic measures prevent erosion by lowering runoff potential.
Structures cost more to build and maintain and tend to be less effective, so soil-building agronomic practices are the first choice and structures mostly complement them.
Agronomic measures also improve soil health and productivity, and advances in conservation tillage machinery have shifted practice away from structures.
Erosion reduction works either by reducing the shear forces of water and wind or by keeping soil in a condition where it cannot easily erode.

entries.title: Erosion's damage beyond the farm

definition.text: Soil carried off fields harms places beyond the farm, as sediment fills streams, rivers, reservoirs and estuaries or blowing dust reaches towns.

facts.text: Sediment is the number one contaminant of most waters worldwide and often carries nutrients, pesticides and other chemicals.
Off-site costs to fisheries, recreation and industry can exceed the lost farm productivity, so soil loss below T may be tolerable for yields but not for water and air quality.
Clay-rich soils are especially troublesome: particles suspended as colloids in runoff do not settle in ponds or filter strips and travel far with nutrients and pesticides.
Clay and silt suspended in the air also travel long distances and can cause respiratory problems.

entries.title: Prairie strips: a tenth of a field that guards the rest

definition.text: Strips of native perennial vegetation placed within row-crop fields to protect soil and water and support biodiversity.

facts.text: Setting aside 10% of a corn field can reduce sediment movement by 95%, and cut runoff losses of phosphorus and nitrogen by 90% and 85%.
Native prairie plants stabilize soil and concentrate more organic carbon in it than corn and soybean.
They are placed as contour buffers and edge-of-field filters, often on hard-to-farm areas.
They supported twice as many aphid-eating insects as soybean fields.

entries.title: Principles of erosion control

facts.text: Keep soil covered: water and wind erosion occur almost exclusively on exposed soil, and live plants protect best and stimulate soil health.
Use practices that increase aggregation and infiltration, and do not disturb soil unless it is well covered; loosening cuts runoff only briefly before the soil settles.

Focus control on high-risk spots where runoff concentrates, using inexpensive biological measures such as grass in waterways and filter strips, and on critical periods such as after winter fallow or after the dry season.
Erodible fields that are not profitable may be better taken out of production under conservation reserve or set-aside payments.

entries.title: Reduced tillage as the top erosion fix

facts.text: Moving to tillage that leaves more surface cover and less disturbance is described as the single most effective way to reduce erosion, and it generally pays better than conventional tillage.
A rougher surface without secondary passes and packers prevents aggregate dispersion and surface sealing, cutting runoff and erosion.
In an Ohio four-year test, conventional-till corn runoff averaged about 7 inches of water a year against under 0.1 inch for no-till.

Less tillage also reduces tillage erosion, which moves soil downhill and exposes subsoil on upslopes; if tillage is needed to ease compaction, use low-disturbance tools such as zone builders or strip tillers.

entries.title: Rain gardens that clean the runoff

definition.text: Removing sediment and contaminants from stormwater runoff by passing it through planted soil, where plants and microbes hold and break down pollutants.

facts.text: A bioretention area typically has a sand bed, a layered filter-media soil and plants on top; stored water seeps into the underlying soils over a period of days.
Pollutants are treated by filtration, adsorption, chemical transformation and biological degradation; clay in the planting soil supplies adsorption sites for hydrocarbons, heavy metals and nutrients.
Loamy sand sites suit it best, since the dug soil can be reused; clay content above 25 percent or slopes above 20 percent may rule it out.
In laboratory tests cells removed 94%, 88%, 95% and over 95% of zinc, copper, lead and cadmium, but their capacity is finite, so the media eventually needs replacing.

entries.title: Grass bands across the hillside

definition.text: Strips of perennial vegetation alternating with wider cultivated strips of cropland across a slope.

facts.text: They work best when runoff arrives evenly as sheet flow, and are well suited to trapping pesticides and reducing rill erosion.
They need to be at least 15 feet (4.6 m) wide and can often serve as a cheap substitute for terraces.
Vegetative barriers are a narrower version: rows of hardy native perennial grasses or shrubs that reduce wind and water erosion and trap sediment.

entries.text: Contour buffer strips alternate bands of perennial vegetation with wider strips of crops across a slope, following the logic of {{ref:soil-agri-123}}. They work best when runoff arrives evenly as a sheet, and they excel at trapping pest-killing chemicals and curbing the small channels water cuts into fields. Each band must be at least 15 feet (4.6 m) wide, and the strips often stand in cheaply for terraces. Vegetative barriers are a narrower version: rows of hardy native perennial grasses or shrubs that slow wind and water and trap sediment.

entries.title: The last line before the water

definition.text: A band of grass or other permanent vegetation at a field's edge that shields riparian areas from sediment, pesticides, pathogens and nutrients in runoff.

facts.text: Filter strips matter for protecting stream banks and water quality, and work best when other practices steer water toward them.
Once mainly agricultural, they are now common in urban areas where water quality is a growing concern.
Field borders, strips of perennial vegetation on cropland edges, reduce wind and water erosion but only help with runoff that flows across them.

entries.title: How farming speeds up natural erosion

definition.text: Erosion is a natural geological process, but farming greatly accelerates it, especially where soil is bare.

facts.text: Natural erosion goes on all the time; Sahara dust carried about 3,000 miles to South America is thought to be a major phosphorus source for the Amazon basin.
Erosion is worst when soil has no living plants, roots or residue mulch, and tillage that breaks aggregates lowers infiltration and worsens runoff.

Intense or prolonged rain drives water erosion and landslides, while drought and strong winds drive wind erosion; soils with poor aggregation, especially silts, are more susceptible, as soil erodibility ratings reflect.

entries.title: Diversion ditches: sending runoff aside

facts.text: A diversion ditch is a channel or swale built across a slope to carry water to a waterway or pond.

Its purpose is to channel water away from upslope areas so runoff does not accumulate and concentrate downslope, scouring and forming gullies; a narrow filter strip on the upslope edge removes sediment.

entries.title: Controlling landslides on farmed slopes

facts.text: Landslides are hard to control, so unstable steep slopes are best left in forest.
Where steep slopes are farmed, wide-spaced trees let roots stabilize soil while leaving light for pasture or crops, as in a New Zealand poplar experiment.
Horizontal drains can dewater critical zones and prevent supersaturation in long rains, but they are costly and mainly used in urban areas and along roads.

entries.title: Wind erosion control on farmland

facts.text: Most water-erosion controls also curb wind erosion: reduced tillage or no-till, cover crops and perennial rotation crops.
A rougher surface increases turbulence near the ground and lowers wind shear, so tilled fields without cover are best left rough-tilled.
Tree shelterbelts planted perpendicular to the prevailing wind reduce evaporative demand and also serve as ecological corridors that raise biodiversity.

entries.title: Cover crops as a shield against winter erosion

facts.text: Cover crops can be grown in erosion-prone seasons such as winter and early spring; roots bind soil, residues maintain aggregation, and leaves absorb raindrop energy so less crusting occurs.
They protect best when cut and mulched or rolled and crimped near maturity rather than incorporated, when they are somewhat lignified and C:N ratios are not high enough to immobilize nutrients.
Cover cropping, mulching and no-till together, called conservation agriculture, virtually eliminate runoff and erosion and spread rapidly in temperate South America.

entries.text: Winter and early spring leave many fields bare just when rain and wind erode them. Cover crops fill that gap. They protect best when cut and mulched, or rolled and crimped, near maturity rather than worked in. At that stage they are somewhat lignified and their C:N ratios are not high enough to immobilize nutrients. Combined with mulching and no-till, they form conservation agriculture, which virtually eliminates runoff and erosion and has spread rapidly in temperate South America.

entries.title: How organic materials hold soil in place

facts.text: More soil organic matter gives better aggregation and less surface sealing, so more water infiltrates instead of running off and carrying soil away.
Regular compost or manure additions stimulate earthworm activity and give larger, more stable aggregates; manure injection in zone-till or no-till limits disturbance, runoff and odor.

entries.title: Sod in the rotation: perennial crops against erosion

facts.text: Grass and legume forages hold a cover on most of the soil all year and their roots hold soil; rotated with row crops they keep erosion and runoff lower during the row-crop phase.
In strip cropping, strips of sod and row crop lie across the slope so sod filters erosion from the row crop; each crop is grown two to five years on a strip, then rotated.
Washington research found winter wheat erosion near 4 tons per acre a year with a sod crop in the rotation versus about 15 tons without.
Permanent sod as hay or pasture suits easily eroded steep soils, though slumping and landslides may concern on extremely steep slopes.

entries.title: Surface residue cover and erosion
entries.article: doc>geo.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Soil_Science/Building_Soils_for_Better_Crops_-_Ecological_Management_for_Healthy_Soils_4e_(Magdoff_and_van_Es)/14%3A_Reducing_Runoff_and_Erosion/14.04%3A_Addressing_Runoff_and_Erosion#Significance of Plant Residues and Competing Uses

facts.text: Surface residues intercept raindrops and slow runoff; a moldboard plow may leave under 5% cover, chisel or disk systems over 30%, and continuous no-till 90% or more.
Full soil cover virtually eliminates runoff and erosion on most agricultural land, and even 30% cover cuts erosion by 70%.
Permanently removing large amounts of residue for fuel or building material harms soil health and resistance to erosion, especially when no manure is returned.

entries.title: Why rare storms do most of the erosion damage

definition.text: Most erosion damage comes from rare extreme weather events, so its risk is easy to underestimate.

facts.text: About one-third of the water erosion damage in a field over 30 years commonly comes from a single extreme rainfall event.
The 1930s Dust Bowl wind erosion followed a decade of extremely dry years.

entries.title: A grass hedge that builds its own terrace

definition.text: A soil and water conservation system built on hedgerows of the vetiver grass.

facts.text: Planted across a slope, vetiver forms a dense barrier that slows and spreads runoff; sediment built up behind the hedge gradually forms a lasting terrace.
Its roots can reach 3–4 m deep in the first year, and it tolerates roughly pH 3 to pH 11 and most heavy metals.
A good hedge can cut rainfall runoff by as much as 70% and sediment by as much as 90%.
It is used in more than 100 countries, for erosion and sediment control, slope stabilization and phytoremediation.

entries.title: Soil survey: putting an area's soils on the map

definition.text: The process of classifying the soil types and other soil properties of an area and recording them geographically; also called soil mapping.

facts.text: Soil surveys apply soil science and draw heavily on geomorphology, theories of soil formation, physical geography and patterns of vegetation and land use.
Primary data come from field sampling and remote sensing, mainly aerial photography, with LiDAR and other digital techniques steadily gaining ground.
Surveyors once carried paper air photos, topographic maps and mapping keys; many now carry a rugged tablet with GPS, digital imagery, LiDAR and soil geodatabases.
In the United States the National Cooperative Soil Survey once published surveys as books for each county; paper surveys could take years to publish.
Surveys are now published on the web through the NRCS Web Soil Survey, where users build custom surveys and changes go live in moments.
A county survey typically holds a general soil map, a detailed map of indexed soil series, a section on soil use and management, and tables of land-use suitability.
NRCS has soil maps and data online for more than 95 percent of US counties.
In the second half of the 20th century soil mapping meant field survey and drawing soil-type boundaries on maps at scales that varied by country and purpose.

entries.title: The soil map, from hand-drawn polygons to predicted grids

definition.text: A geographical representation of the soil types, or of soil properties such as pH, texture, organic matter or horizon depth, across an area.

facts.text: A soil map is usually the product of a soil survey, and traditional maps show only the general distribution of soils alongside the survey report.
Soil maps are used mostly for land evaluation, spatial planning, agricultural extension and environmental protection.
Many new maps come from digital soil mapping; they show more detail but are not necessarily more accurate, and statistical maps can include an estimate of model uncertainty.
Map types include hand-drawn polygon maps of soil types, predicted or simulated 2D or 3D soil-property maps, and predicted soil-class maps.
Maps of primary attributes show what was described or measured in the field; maps of secondary, inferred attributes show properties for a use, such as production capacity or degradation.
Farmers in precision agriculture use soil maps to adjust field inputs.

entries.title: Prime farmland: the best soils, and the cities on them

definition.text: A US Department of Agriculture designation for land with the best combination of physical and chemical characteristics for producing food, feed, forage, fibre and oilseed crops, and available for those uses.

facts.text: Prime farmland has the soil quality, growing season and moisture supply to give economically sustained high yields under acceptable farming methods, including water management.
It generally has a dependable water supply, a favourable temperature and growing season, acceptable acidity or alkalinity, acceptable salt and sodium content, and few or no rocks.
It is not excessively erodible or long saturated with water, and either rarely floods or is protected from flooding.

Because many cities grew up in rich farming areas, prime farmland is also well suited to housing, and the designation helps growth management use zoning, conservation easements and green belts to keep it.

Complementary USDA designations are farmland of statewide importance, farmland of local importance and unique farmland, the last used for specific high-value crops such as nuts, olives, cranberries and citrus.
State and local agencies set the criteria for the statewide and local categories in cooperation with the USDA.
Preserving prime farmland soils is hard when they occupy less than 60% of an area, so a universal demarcation method joining science and policy is needed.

entries.text: Many cities grew up in rich farming country, so the best land for crops is often well suited to houses too. The US Department of Agriculture (USDA) calls the best of it prime farmland. This land has the best combination of physical and chemical characteristics for producing food, feed, forage, fiber and oilseed crops, and it is still available for those uses. Its soil quality, growing season and moisture supply give economically sustained high yields under acceptable farming methods, including water management. It generally has a dependable water supply and a favorable temperature and growing season. Its acidity or alkalinity is acceptable, as is its salt and sodium content, and it has few or no rocks. It is not excessively erodible or long saturated with water. It either rarely floods or is protected from flooding. The designation helps growth management keep such land farmed, through zoning, conservation easements and green belts. Three USDA designations complement it: farmland of statewide importance, farmland of local importance and unique farmland. Unique farmland is used for specific high-value crops such as nuts, olives, cranberries and citrus. State and local agencies set the criteria for the statewide and local categories in cooperation with the USDA. Preserving prime soils is hard where they cover less than 60% of an area. A universal way to mark them out, joining science and policy, is still needed.

entries.title: Land use: what people do with a parcel

definition.text: A description of what people do on a parcel of land, covering the benefits taken from it and the management actions applied.

facts.text: The IPCC groups land use into forest land, cropland, grassland, wetlands, settlements and other lands, and defines it as the total of arrangements, activities and inputs applied to a parcel.
The FAO defines land use as the products and benefits obtained from land together with the management actions people carry out to obtain them.
Land use and management practices strongly affect water, soil, nutrients, plants and animals; poor choices contribute to soil erosion, soil degradation, land degradation and desertification.
Arable land was about 10.7% of the land surface in 2015, with 1.3% permanent cropland; early-1990s figures were 13% arable, 26% pasture and 32% forest and woodland.
Governments plan and regulate land use through zoning and other ordinances to avoid land-use conflicts; an urban growth boundary is one such tool.

entries.title: Reading the land from orbit

definition.text: Gathering information about an object or area from a distance, usually with sensors on satellites or aircraft, instead of measuring it on site.

facts.text: It is active when the sensor emits a signal and detects its reflection, and passive when it detects reflected sunlight.
Soil moisture, surface water storage, precipitation and evapotranspiration can all be measured by remote sensing at various resolutions and accuracies.
Land cover and land use maps from thematic mapping can detect deforestation and track the health of crops and native plants.
Agricultural and environmental statistics usually combine classified satellite images with ground-truth data from a field sample.
Interferometric synthetic aperture radar produces precise digital elevation models of large areas of terrain.

entries.title: Germany's soil value, scored from 0 to 100

definition.text: Germany's comparative rating of soil quality (Bodenwertzahl), scored from soil sampling data on a scale from 0 (very low) to 100 (very high).

facts.text: For arable land it combines field assessments of soil type, soil development and parent material, and expresses the relative net income the soil alone would yield under proper management.
Heavy to clayey loams score 31–50, loams partly covered with loess 51–70 and loams with a loess cover 71–90.
Adjusting the soil value for terrain, climate and location gives the field value, or Ackerzahl.

It began with the Reich Soil Assessment under the 1934 Soil Assessment Act, which set a Magdeburg Börde farm at 100 as the basis for farm tax ratings; a record 102.8 was later measured near Hildesheim.

entries.title: Maps that answer questions

definition.text: Integrated computer hardware and software that store, manage, analyse, edit and display geographic data.

facts.text: A GIS relates otherwise unrelated information by using location as the key index variable.
The first, the Canada Geographic Information System, handled the Canada Land Inventory, which mapped soils, agriculture, forestry and land use at 1:50,000 to judge rural land capability.
GIS data typically represent features such as roads, land use, elevation and waterways; masses such as the soil types of an area are represented less directly.
Survey data can be entered directly into a GIS from digital survey instruments by coordinate geometry.

entries.title: Digital soil mapping hands the pen to computers

definition.text: The computer-assisted production of digital maps of soil types and soil properties, also called predictive soil mapping.

facts.text: The Working Group on Digital Soil Mapping defines it as building geographically referenced soil databases at a set resolution from field and laboratory observations linked to environmental data by quantitative relationships.
It is distinct from traditional soil mapping, in which field soil scientists draw soil boundaries by hand, though hand-drawn maps can also be digitised.
It relies on GPS, field scanners and remote sensing, together with geostatistical interpolation, GIS, digital elevation models and data mining.
Semi-automated methods lower costs, and its products are routinely assessed for accuracy and uncertainty and are easier to update as new data arrive.
It tries to overcome traditional maps that often only delineate soil classes, give no basis for modelling changing soil conditions and are inflexible for quantitative studies of soil function.
Examples include EU maps of texture and bulk density from about 20,000 LUCAS topsoil samples, and ISRIC's global SoilGrids maps at 250 m resolution built with machine learning.

entries.title: Reading a soil survey for farms, buildings and gardens

definition.text: The use of soil survey information to predict the potentials and limitations of soils for particular uses, such as crops, building or gardens.

facts.text: Farmers and ranchers use it to judge whether a soil suits crops or livestock and what management it needs; architects and engineers use soil engineering properties to judge sites for construction.
Survey data must be interpreted before planners can use them, and the resulting predictions guide land use and management on areas from small tracts to several million acres.
These predictions must be weighed with economic, social and environmental considerations before they become valid land-use recommendations.
Published US surveys include land-use suitability tables based on Natural Resources Conservation Service standards.

entries.title: The ground surface as a grid of heights

definition.text: A computer representation of elevation data that depicts terrain, or the objects on top of it.

facts.text: A digital terrain model shows the bare ground surface, while a digital surface model may include tree canopy and buildings; the terms are not used consistently.
DEMs are usually built from remote sensing, such as photogrammetry, lidar or radar interferometry, but can also come from land surveying.
Terrain models are needed for drainage modelling and land-use studies, and DEMs are widely used in geographic information systems.
Uses include extracting terrain parameters for geomorphology and modelling soil wetness with depth-to-water indexes.

entries.title: The European Soil Database, one grid for a continent

definition.text: The only harmonized soil database in Europe, the source of many other soil data, information and services.

facts.text: Its v2 Raster Library holds public-domain grids with 1 km x 1 km cells, aligned with the INSPIRE reference grid, for many soil parameters.
Parameters include texture, parent material, WRB soil type, soil depth, mineralogy, cation exchange capacity and available water capacity.
It is based on experts' knowledge, and the European Commission's LUCAS topsoil survey adds sampled soil data across the European Union.
Combined with land cover, climate and topography data, it gives the most homogeneous data on the organic carbon content of European soils.

facts.text: It records soil types and their distribution, soil characteristics and properties, and the limits, risks and suitability of soils for various uses.
It is the dataset in which the NRCS maintains its soil information.
Its survey data reach users through Web Soil Survey, which the NRCS runs as the single authoritative source of US soil survey information.

entries.title: Pedometrics: measuring soil with mathematics

definition.text: The application of mathematical and statistical methods to the study of the distribution and genesis of soils.

facts.text: The name joins the Greek pedos, 'soil', and metron, 'measurement'.
It tackles soil problems clouded by deterministic or random variation, vagueness and lack of knowledge, using simulation models built on chaos theory, statistical distributions or fuzzy logic.
It is a sub-discipline of pedology focused on quantitative techniques, especially for mapping soil properties.
Its advance is tied to better remote and close-range sensing and to wavelets, fuzzy sets and data mining.

entries.title: Pedometric mapping turns soil into continuous grids

definition.text: Data-driven production of soil property and soil class maps by statistical methods, also called statistical soil mapping.

facts.text: It predicts soil variables at unsampled places and estimates the uncertainty of each prediction by statistical inference, largely through geostatistics.
Its practical aim is to predict how a soil-plant ecosystem will respond to management, producing maps for environmental models and decisions.
Traditional survey infers soil bodies from mental models and draws them by hand, which is subjective and hard to test for accuracy without extra sampling.
Pedometric outputs come from rigorous statistical computing, so they are reproducible.
It leans on detailed covariate layers such as elevation-model derivatives, remote sensing imagery and climate, land cover and geology data.
Traditional mapping targets soil types as discrete bodies on polygon maps; pedometric mapping targets measured properties as continuous grids with prediction-error maps.
Unlike digital soil mapping, it relies strictly on geostatistics and does not delineate discrete soil types.
Its workflow runs from data screening and covariate preparation through model fitting, spatial prediction and cross-validation to visualisation.

entries.title: Matheron's three-part model of soil variation

definition.text: A model that splits a soil variable at any place into a deterministic trend, a spatially autocorrelated random part and leftover noise: Z(s) = m(s) + ε′(s) + ε″.

facts.text: French mathematician Georges Matheron introduced it, and it has proven the best unbiased linear predictor for spatial data.
Regression-kriging, also called universal kriging, uses it to make soil predictions or simulations.
For soils the deterministic part is often modelled from Hans Jenny's soil-forming factors of climate, organisms, relief, parent material and time, the CLORPT model.

entries.text: Every soil measurement hides three parts. The universal model of soil variation writes a soil variable as Z(s) = m(s) + ε′(s) + ε″. French mathematician Georges Matheron introduced the model, and it has proven the best unbiased linear predictor for spatial data. The method of {{ref:soil-meth-004}} uses it to predict or simulate soils; this variant of {{ref:soil-meth-003}} is also called its universal form. The trend is often modeled from the classic soil-forming factors: climate, organisms, relief, parent material and time, the CLORPT model.

entries.title: Land use change and its carbon cost

definition.text: The change from one land-use category to another, mostly driven by human activity.

facts.text: Land-use change and fossil fuel use are the major human sources of carbon dioxide, a dominant greenhouse gas.
Deforestation, the permanent conversion of forest to other uses, has historically been a primary driver, and global forest cover has fallen by 35% since agriculture began.
Urban areas cover just 3% of the Earth's surface, yet their growth shifts demand onto rural land and can take over adjacent cropland.
Scientists track land change with satellite imagery, aircraft imagery, field observations and modelling, and use land change models to simulate possible futures for planning.

entries.title: Erosion seen from the air

definition.text: Taking photographs of landscapes and surface features from aircraft or other airborne platforms.

facts.text: Vertical aerial photographs underpin photogrammetric surveys, the usual basis of topographic maps, and are used in land-use planning.
Photogrammetry, mapping from aerial photographs, was pioneered commercially in the 1930s.
One of Fairchild's first government contracts was an aerial survey of New Mexico to study soil erosion.
Stereoscopic pairs of aerial photographs have often been used by terrain analysts to make topographic maps.

entries.title: Is this land fit for that use

definition.text: An FAO method of land evaluation that appraises and groups areas of land by their fitness for a defined use.

facts.text: Land can be assessed in its present condition or after improvements.
It has four categories of decreasing generality: orders (kinds of suitability), classes (degrees), subclasses (kinds of limitation) and units (minor management differences).
There are two orders: S, land whose sustained use yields benefits justifying the inputs without unacceptable damage, and N, land whose qualities seem to rule that use out.
Land may be Not Suitable because the use is impracticable, would cause severe degradation such as cultivating steep slopes, or, most often, would not repay its costs.
Climate change shifts land suitability for many crops, usually toward higher latitudes and altitudes.

entries.text: Cultivating a steep slope may be possible, yet still a bad idea. Land suitability classification is the FAO method of land evaluation for answering that question. It appraises and groups land by its fitness for one defined use, drawing on {{ref:soil-agri-083}}. Land can be judged as it is now or after improvements. The scheme has four levels of decreasing generality. Orders give the kind of suitability, classes the degree, subclasses the kind of limitation, and units the minor differences in management. There are just two orders. S marks land whose sustained use yields benefits that justify the inputs without unacceptable damage. N marks land whose qualities seem to rule that use out. Land falls into N for three reasons. The use may be impracticable, or it may cause severe degradation, as cultivating steep slopes would. Most often, it simply would not repay its costs. The answers are not fixed. Climate change shifts suitability for many crops, usually toward higher latitudes and altitudes.

entries.title: The Storie index, where one zero sinks the score

definition.text: A soil rating method based on the soil characteristics that govern a land's potential use and productive capacity.

facts.text: R. Earl Storie developed it at the University of California, Berkeley, in the 1930s for land valuation, independent of other physical or economic factors.
It rates soil depth and texture, permeability, chemical characteristics, drainage and runoff, and climate where climate is not uniform.
The index multiplies these ratings, so a zero in any one makes the whole result zero.
Its ratings are subjective; O'Geen and colleagues updated the method in 2008 to reduce this.

entries.title: What land could do, not what it does

definition.text: A map showing the potential uses, usually for farming, of each unit of land.

facts.text: The commonest indicators are five physical factors: rock type, soil type, slope, erosion degree and type, and vegetation.
It differs from a land use map, which shows how land is actually used now.
In the United States the Soil Conservation Service developed the Land Capability System in 1951, and soil survey standards keep data consistent with it.

entries.title: Judging a forest site by its tallest trees

definition.text: A forestry measure of a site's potential for tree growth, given as the height of dominant and co-dominant trees at a base age.

facts.text: Base ages such as 25, 50 and 100 years are used; a 50-year-old red oak 70 feet (21 m) tall gives a site index of 70.
Site index is specific to each tree species.
It can be found from tree height, from understory indicator plants, or from soil maps.
In the United States the NRCS measured site index on surveyed soils and tabulated soils against site indexes for important species.
Indirect estimates use dominant species, lesser vegetation, and topographic, climatic and edaphic factors.
Despite shortcomings, it has been the most widely used way of estimating site productivity in North America.

entries.title: Soil phases: dividing a series by how it is used

definition.text: A subdivision of a soil series made when slope, erosion, stoniness or another feature changes how the soil can be used.

facts.text: Series vary so much in slope, erosion, stones or similar features that management advice could not be given if each were shown as one unit, so they are divided into soil phases.
The phase name gives the surface feature that most affects management; Vina loam 0 to 2 percent slopes and Vina gravelly loam 2 to 9 percent slopes are two of four phases of the Vina series.
The area inside each continuous line on a soil map is the delineation of a map unit.
A map unit includes the soil phase and all inclusions.

entries.title: Reconnaissance surveys for poor land

definition.text: A small-scale soil survey of low-value land that identifies regions dominated by soil associations rather than delineating individual soils.

facts.text: Large expanses of land with little direct agricultural or forest value are often too poor to justify the cost of a detailed survey, so they are mapped at small scale.
A reconnaissance survey shows soil associations, in contrast to the detailed map in which specific soils are delineated.

entries.title: Web Soil Survey: soil maps on demand

definition.text: An online service run by the USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service that gives access to soil data from the National Cooperative Soil Survey.

facts.text: US soil surveys are no longer printed as books; they are published on Web Soil Survey, where users can build a custom soil survey.
It holds everything in the old county reports plus extra tools, and can be updated as needed, whereas new surveys of the same county took 30 to 60 years.
A user picks an area of interest anywhere in the United States where survey data exist; the Soil Map tab then shows the area's component soil map units, and a report can be saved as a PDF.
The Soil Data Explorer gives properties for each map unit, such as depth to water table, surface texture, bulk density, pH and depth to a restrictive layer, along with suitability ratings for uses.
Ratings cover uses such as dwellings with basements, local roads and streets, vegetative productivity and wastewater disposal by irrigation, each with reasons for the rating.
It is one recognized basis, alongside measured infiltration rates, for choosing the hydrologic soil group of a site.

entries.title: From highly suitable to never suitable

definition.text: The numbered degrees of suitability within each FAO land suitability order, in decreasing order of suitability.

facts.text: The number of Suitable classes is not fixed but should be kept minimal, probably never more than five.

Not Suitable land normally has two classes: N1, limitations that might be overcome in time but not at acceptable cost now, and N2, limitations ruling out any sustained use.

entries.title: Soil information systems hold the whole inventory

entries.title: Turning height and age into a site index

definition.text: Graphs or equations that convert a stand's measured dominant height and age into its site index.

facts.text: Height comes from a dominant or co-dominant site tree measured with a clinometer, laser hypsometer or releskop; age from an increment borer or planting records.
On a curve, a 60-foot (18 m) tree in a 50-year-old stand is read where age 50 on the x-axis meets 60 feet on the y-axis; the nearest line gives the site index.
One equation is lnS = lnHd − b1(A⁻¹ − Ai⁻¹), where S is site index, Hd dominant height, A stand age and Ai index age.
For planted white spruce, curves cannot be reliably extended below about 15 years because early growth is hard to predict.

entries.title: Gas chromatography, sorting compounds as vapor

definition.text: Chromatography that separates and analyses compounds that can be vaporized without decomposing.

facts.text: It is used to measure chemicals in soil, air or water, including soil gases.
The Dumas nitrogen method ends with a gas chromatography column that separates nitrogen from carbon dioxide and water.

entries.title: Burning soil to learn what it is made of

definition.text: Analysis of a material such as soil for its elemental, and sometimes isotopic, composition.

facts.text: The commonest form, CHNS analysis, is done by combustion analysis, burning the sample and measuring the oxidized products.
CHN analyzers use the Dumas method's flash combustion and detect the resulting gases by thermal conductivity or infrared.
In the Dumas method a sample is burned at 800–900 °C in oxygen, and gas chromatography separates the released nitrogen for a thermal conductivity detector.
Dumas analysis takes a few minutes per measurement, against an hour or more for Kjeldahl, and uses no toxic chemicals or catalysts.

entries.text: One quick way to learn what a soil contains is to set it on fire. Elemental analysis measures the elemental, and sometimes isotopic, composition of a material such as soil. CHN analyzers borrow the flash combustion of the Dumas method. A sample burns at 800–900 °C in oxygen, {{ref:soil-meth-029}} separates the released nitrogen, and a thermal conductivity or infrared detector reads it. Each Dumas measurement takes a few minutes and uses no toxic chemicals or catalysts. The older {{ref:soil-meth-020}} takes an hour or more.

entries.title: Reading a soil's elements in the glow of a plasma
entries.article: Inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectroscopy

definition.text: An analytical technique (ICP-AES or ICP-OES) that detects chemical elements from the light emitted by atoms and ions excited in an argon plasma.

facts.text: The plasma runs at 6000 to 10,000 K, and the intensity emitted at each element's wavelengths is proportional to its concentration.
A pump feeds the sample to a nebulizer, which sprays it as a mist directly into the plasma.
Detector arrays read all wavelengths at once, so every element the unit can sense is analysed simultaneously and quickly.
Concentrations come from comparing line intensities with calibration curves of known standards.
It is fast becoming the method of choice for nutrient levels in agricultural soils, used to calculate the fertiliser needed for yield and quality.
It is often used for trace elements in soil, and so in forensics to trace the origin of soil found at crime scenes.
It has largely replaced older methods such as gravimetric analysis for routine multi-element trace analysis.

entries.text: Inside the instrument burns a plasma of argon at 6000 to 10,000 K. Inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectroscopy, shortened to ICP-AES or ICP-OES, uses that heat to excite atoms and ions until they emit light. Each element shines at its own wavelengths, and the intensity there is proportional to its concentration. A pump feeds the sample to a nebulizer, which sprays it as a mist directly into the plasma. Detector arrays read all the wavelengths at once, so every element the unit can sense is analysed together, and quickly. Comparing line intensities with calibration curves of known standards gives the concentrations. The method has largely replaced older ones such as gravimetric analysis for routine trace work on many elements. It is fast becoming the method of choice for nutrient levels in farm soils. In a {{ref:soil-fert-187}}, those levels set the fertilizer a crop needs for yield and quality. Its skill with trace elements even helps forensic scientists trace the origin of soil found at crime scenes.

entries.title: ICP-MS, counting ions down to parts per quadrillion

definition.text: Mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) that ionizes a sample in an inductively coupled plasma and counts the resulting ions to detect metals and some non-metals at very low concentrations.

facts.text: It is faster, more precise and more sensitive than atomic absorption, and it scans all elements at once rather than one at a time.
It covers atomic masses 7 to 250 (Li to U) over a dynamic range from 1 part per quadrillion to 100 ppm, and distinguishes isotopes.
Environmental uses run from water testing to analysis of soil and other materials.
Measuring Fe2+ and Fe3+ in ancient rocks with ICP-MS or X-ray fluorescence reveals the redox potential of ancient soils.

entries.title: Atomic absorption: metals caught by the light they absorb

definition.text: An elemental analysis method that measures the concentration of metals in a sample from the light their atoms absorb.

facts.text: Metals are vaporized in a flame; each absorbs at its own wavelengths, and the absorbed radiation is proportional to the density of its atoms.
Soil extracts from batch equilibration are commonly analysed by atomic absorption, among other methods.
Flame AAS works in the mg/L range; graphite-furnace AAS is 2–3 orders of magnitude more sensitive.
Its modern form was developed in the 1950s by Alan Walsh's team at CSIRO in Melbourne; it is used from agriculture to medicine.

entries.title: Loss on ignition: weighing what the furnace takes away

definition.text: A test that strongly heats a soil or mineral sample at a set temperature until its mass stops changing, so the weight lost measures the volatile components driven off.

facts.text: A few grams go into a tared, pre-ignited crucible, are weighed, heated in a temperature-controlled furnace for a set time, cooled in a dry, CO2-free atmosphere and weighed again.
The furnace temperature is chosen for the component sought; the mass lost equals the mass of that component.
A sample left overnight in a drying oven at 100 °C loses all its water, giving the dry weight and so the original water content.
It is typically used to estimate water content, carbon, organic matter and volatile compounds; in minerals the loss is mostly combined water and carbon dioxide from carbonates.
Weighing samples taken down a profile before and after burning off their organic content gives organic content at each depth.
A sudden rise in organic content down a profile, with other indicators, is strong evidence for a buried soil surface not visible to the eye.
Monitoring mass continuously as the temperature changes is a variant called thermogravimetry.

entries.text: A furnace and a balance are all this test needs. In a loss-on-ignition test, a soil or mineral sample is heated strongly at a set temperature until its mass stops changing. The weight lost measures the volatile components driven off. A few grams go into a crucible weighed empty and already fired. They are weighed, heated in a temperature-controlled furnace for a set time, cooled in a dry, CO2-free atmosphere and weighed again. Left overnight in a drying oven at 100 °C, a sample loses all its water, which gives its dry weight and so its original water content. The test typically estimates water, carbon, {{ref:soil-found-045}} and volatile compounds. Samples burned down a profile show the organic content at each depth. A sudden rise down the profile, with other clues, is strong evidence of a buried soil surface invisible to the eye. Weighing continuously as the temperature changes is a variant called thermogravimetry.
entries.text_plain: A furnace and a balance are all this test needs. In a loss-on-ignition test, a soil or mineral sample is heated strongly at a set temperature until its mass stops changing. The weight lost measures the volatile components driven off. A few grams go into a crucible weighed empty and already fired. They are weighed, heated in a temperature-controlled furnace for a set time, cooled in a dry, CO2-free atmosphere and weighed again. Left overnight in a drying oven at 100 °C, a sample loses all its water, which gives its dry weight and so its original water content. The test typically estimates water, carbon, Soil organic matter: the small fraction that shapes everything and volatile compounds. Samples burned down a profile show the organic content at each depth. A sudden rise down the profile, with other clues, is strong evidence of a buried soil surface invisible to the eye. Weighing continuously as the temperature changes is a variant called thermogravimetry.

entries.title: The Kjeldahl method: nitrogen from a flask of boiling acid

definition.text: A wet-chemistry method that measures the organic nitrogen plus ammonia and ammonium in a sample.

facts.text: The sample is digested in concentrated sulfuric acid at 360–410 °C, which oxidizes the organic matter and holds the reduced nitrogen as ammonium sulfate.
Sodium hydroxide then turns the ammonium into ammonia gas, which is distilled into a standard acid and measured by titration.
Without modification it misses other inorganic nitrogen such as nitrate.
Total Kjeldahl nitrogen (TKN) is the sum of organic, ammonia and ammonium nitrogen in analyses of soil, water and waste water.
Besides foods, it is used to assay soils, waste waters and fertilizers.
Catalysts such as selenium, Hg2SO4 or CuSO4 speed digestion, and Na2SO4 or K2SO4 raises the acid's boiling point.
Its hot concentrated acid and testing time of an hour or more compare poorly with the faster Dumas method.

entries.title: Soil test calibration: what a number really means

definition.text: The multi-year matching of a soil test value to crop yield response, which is what makes the test value meaningful.

facts.text: Soil tests estimate a few nutrients from a small sample meant to represent many acres, so they are not 100% accurate.
Researchers apply different nutrient levels (always including zero) to plots on many fields over several years and compare yields to learn what a test level means.
A new test cannot be called useful until it has been correlated with plant response on varied soils and weather, and small-plot results must be validated on commercial farms.

A low test may fail to raise yield if it is poorly calibrated for that soil or if drainage or compaction harms the crop; extra nutrients on a high-testing soil occasionally help when weather reduces availability.

entries.title: Taking a soil sample that represents the field

definition.text: Collecting a representative composite of soil cores from a field so a laboratory can evaluate fertility.

facts.text: Samples for general fertility are usually taken in fall or spring before the season, analysed for pH, lime requirement, P, K, Ca and Mg; repeat at the same season and with the same lab for comparable years.
Take cores from at least 15-20 random spots per field or zone, whatever its size; one sample should represent no more than 10-20 acres, or 1-5 acres for precision zone or grid management.
Sample between rows, avoid old fence rows and dead furrows, and sample problem areas separately, since nutrient levels vary with crop history and topography.
Sample cultivated fields to plow depth, permanent pasture to 3 or 4 inches, and no-till fields twice: 6 inches for lime and fertilizer advice and 2 inches to monitor surface acidity.
Mix the cores in a clean container, remove roots and stones and air dry; sample fields at least every three years.

entries.title: Which phosphorus test? It depends on the region

definition.text: Regional chemical extractions used to estimate plant-available phosphorus, with different numeric ranges for each extractant.

facts.text: The extractant varies by region: Olsen and AB-DTPA in arid and semiarid western areas, Mehlich 3 or Bray 1 in the humid Midwest and East, Mehlich 1 in the Southeast and mid-Atlantic, Morgan in the Northeast.
Bray 1 is used for acidic soils and Olsen for alkaline soils in Washington and Oregon.
Ranges for the optimum category in ppm P: Olsen 11-16, Bray 1 25-45, Mehlich 1 20-40, Mehlich 3 30-50; in calcareous soil the Olsen optimum is higher, with over 25 ppm for zero P fertilizer.

A soil high in P by one test is generally high by another, though the numbers differ; low and medium levels mean likely yield gain from P, while high levels raise the potential for P pollution in runoff.
Tests capture P from recent manure and from soil minerals, but active organic matter from residues or manure may supply more P than the test shows.

entries.title: Ion chromatography, sorting ions by their grip

definition.text: Chromatography that separates ions and ionizable molecules by their affinity for an ion exchanger.

facts.text: Anion-exchange columns carry a positive stationary phase that holds anions; cation-exchange columns a negative one that holds cations.
It is a popular method for anions and complexes in environmental problems and is one of the methods used to analyse soil extracts.
Its origins trace to Thompson and Way, who treated clays with fertilizer salts and found ammonia retained and calcium released.

entries.title: Sample preparation before the instrument

definition.text: The treatment a sample receives before analysis so that it is in a form the instrument can measure.

facts.text: It matters because techniques are often unresponsive to the analyte in its in-situ form, or results are distorted by interfering species.
Steps can include crushing and dissolution, acid or alkali digestion, extraction, clean-up and pre-concentration.
It may also involve pulverizing, filtering, dilution, masking, sub-sampling or treatment with a chelating agent such as EDTA.

entries.title: Certified reference materials: a lab's yardstick

definition.text: Controls or standards of known composition used to check the quality and traceability of measurements, validate methods and calibrate instruments.

facts.text: Most analytical instruments are comparative, so they need a sample of known composition for accurate calibration.
A certified material differs from a laboratory reagent in its certificate: it gives the value, its uncertainty and a statement of metrological traceability.
Accreditation under ISO/IEC 17025 requires traceability to certified reference materials where possible, and they are preferred where available.
ILAC lists five types: pure substances, standard solutions and gas mixtures, matrix materials, physico-chemical materials, and reference objects.
Natural matrix materials are made by homogenizing a natural sample to a fine powder, since natural materials are rarely homogeneous at the gram scale, then measuring each analyte.
Producers test homogeneity on 10-30 randomly chosen units with two or three subsamples each, and test stability by real-time or accelerated storage studies.

entries.title: From test value to advice: the interpretation categories

definition.text: Labs sort each test value into categories from very low to excessive, each tied to the probability that adding the nutrient will raise yield.

facts.text: Categories run very low, low, optimum, high and excessive, with probability of response falling from very high to very low.
For the pre-sidedress nitrate test on corn 6-12 inches tall sampled to 1 foot, nitrate-N of 11-22 ppm is low, 23-28 optimum and over 35 excessive.
Ranges depend on the extractant: for Mehlich 3 in North Carolina, P is optimum at 26-50 ppm.
Reports adapt advice using the manure and previous crop information supplied; legume cover crop N is usually not credited and manure decided on later is missed.

entries.title: Reading odd soil test results

definition.text: Odd soil test values that usually trace to management history or to using the wrong extractant for the soil.

facts.text: Very high phosphorus comes from years of heavy poultry or other manure; very high pH with high calcium relative to K and Mg points to lime-stabilized sewage sludge.
High salt in humid regions can come from large poultry manure doses in high tunnels where rain cannot leach salts, or from deicing salt beside a road.
Acid extractants (Morgan, Mehlich 1 or 3) dissolve free limestone and give too much calcium, and on alkaline calcareous soils (pH above 7) they extract little P because the soil neutralizes the acid.
Many labs report the CEC the soil would have at pH 7 or higher, whereas the textbook estimates current CEC by summing the exchangeable bases.

entries.title: Sensing a crop's nitrogen from the field to orbit

definition.text: In-season technologies that assess a crop's nitrogen status to guide fertilizer rates.

facts.text: Chlorophyll meters estimate leaf chlorophyll as an N indicator; they need field visits and adequate leaf sampling and are mainly used for final cereal applications.
Canopy reflectance sensors read near-infrared and red or red-edge light; mounted on equipment they adjust N on the go, usually with a high-N reference strip for calibration.
Satellite, aircraft or drone imagery uses the same bands at 10-30 m resolution; satellites are limited by cloud cover and aircraft and drones are more expensive.
Computer models simulate field N dynamics daily and are cheap and scalable, but involve no direct field observation.

entries.title: Grid sampling for site-specific rates

definition.text: Sampling a large field on a grid and analysing each point separately to guide site-specific nutrient and lime rates.

facts.text: The general recommendation is 2.5- to 5-acre grids, especially where manure and fertilizer rates varied; some areas use one-acre grids.
Unaligned grids are advised: points are shifted randomly off the regular grid so that a past applicator malfunction is not unknowingly sampled in a line.
Each grid point still needs 10-15 cores within about 30 feet.
Grid testing is expensive, so do it once per rotation, when lime may be needed, or every five to eight years; fertility patterns often do not follow soil survey maps.

entries.title: Testing the soil in a high tunnel

definition.text: High tunnel soils need adjusted tests because very high yields demand much more nutrient and rain does not leach salts.

facts.text: Tunnel tomatoes reaching the equivalent of 60-80 tons per acre need roughly 200-300 lb N, 300-400 lb P2O5 and 700-900 lb K2O per acre.
Recommendations from routine field soil tests must be adjusted upward, and a saturated media extract measures water-soluble nutrients including nitrate-N and ammonium-N plus total salinity.

entries.title: Fine earth: the part of soil 2 mm and smaller

definition.text: The part of a soil made of particles 2 mm across or smaller.

facts.text: In the WRB the whole soil comprises the fine earth plus coarse fragments, artefacts, cemented parts and dead plant residues of any size.
Many WRB horizon criteria are stated as percentages by volume related to the fine earth, such as the share of rock structure in an A or B horizon.
Where feldspars weather slowly in cool climates on granite, sand comes to dominate the fine-earth fraction.
A loam can lose its desirable qualities when clay is dispersed throughout its fine-earth fraction.

entries.title: Ion-selective electrodes turn one ion into a voltage

definition.text: A membrane-based potentiometric sensor that converts the activity of a specific ion in solution into an electrical potential.

facts.text: Its voltage depends on the logarithm of the ion's activity, following the Nernst equation, and is read against a reference electrode.
The pH glass electrode is a very common type.
Ion-specific electrodes are among the methods used to analyse soil extracts, and their use extends to environmental science and agriculture.
Readings drift with temperature and time, so frequent recalibration against standards is needed, ideally before and after each sample.

An ion-selective electrode is a membrane sensor that converts the activity of one specific ion in solution into an electrical potential. The pH glass electrode is a very common type. The voltage is read against a reference electrode, and it depends on the logarithm of the ion's activity, following the Nernst equation. These electrodes are among the methods used to analyse soil extracts, and they serve environmental science and agriculture. They have one weakness. Readings drift with temperature and time, so they need frequent recalibration against standards, ideally before and after each sample.

entries.title: Ammonium acetate, the cation that evicts the others

definition.text: The use of ammonium acetate solution in soil analysis to displace exchangeable cations, for measuring CEC and available potassium.

facts.text: The ammonium ion acts as a replacement cation, displacing potassium from exchange sites.
Ammonium is one of the cations frequently used to displace a soil's bound cations when measuring CEC.
A pure ammonium acetate solution has a pH of about 7, but it buffers only around pH 4.75 and 9.25, not at pH 7.

entries.title: Phosphorus turns blue: the molybdenum test
entries.article: Molybdenum blue#Colorimetric determination of P, As, Si and Ge

definition.text: A colorimetric test in which phosphate forms a blue molybdenum complex whose depth of colour is proportional to phosphorus concentration.

facts.text: Phosphate is mixed with an acid molybdate solution and the complex is reduced, for example by ascorbic acid, to the blue form.
However phosphorus is brought from soil into solution, it is usually detected this way, with a colorimeter in the lab or detector sticks and a colour chart in the field.
Comparable amounts of arsenate spoil the test, since arsenate behaves much like phosphate.
Soil phosphate mapped on archaeological plans shows former activity areas and helps prospect for sites.

entries.text: Phosphate can be made to turn a solution blue, and the depth of blue tells how much is there. The color's depth is proportional to the phosphorus concentration. However phosphorus leaves the soil for solution, it is usually detected this way. Labs use a colorimeter; field workers use detector sticks and a color chart. Comparable amounts of arsenate spoil the test, since arsenate behaves much like phosphate. Mapped on archaeological plans, soil phosphate shows former activity areas and helps prospect for sites.

entries.title: Soil micromorphology, the profile under the microscope

definition.text: The description, measurement and interpretation of soil features too small to see with the unaided eye.

facts.text: Work may begin in the field with a 10x hand lens, but much more is seen in thin sections under a petrographic polarizing microscope.
A recognized technique for some 50 years, it spread from pedogenic and paleosol studies to the soils and sediments of archaeological sites.
Micromorphologists have characterized humus-form horizons on thin soil sections.

entries.title: The soil thin section, a slice thin enough for light

definition.text: A slice of rock, mineral or soil ground to about 30 μm and mounted on glass for study under a polarizing microscope.

facts.text: Soil micromorphology describes far more in thin sections viewed with a petrographic polarizing light microscope than a 10x hand lens can show.
Between crossed polarizing filters the minerals' optical properties alter the colour and intensity of light, so most rock-forming minerals can be identified.
Thickness is checked with the Michel-Lévy interference colour chart, usually with quartz as the gauge.
Thin sections reveal the relation of a material's components to one another, features often invisible in a hand specimen.
Paleosols are identified partly from thin sections: at least 60% recognizable pyroclastic fragments marks an Andisol paleosol.
Humus-form horizons have been characterized on thin soil sections by micromorphologists.

entries.title: Digital image analysis: teaching computers to read pictures

definition.text: Image analysis extracts meaningful information from images, mainly digital ones, by digital image processing.

facts.text: Computers are indispensable for large data and quantitative extraction, but human vision still cannot be replaced in many applications.
Object-based analysis groups pixels into homogeneous objects by segmentation and then classifies them; over-segmentation is often preferred when classifying high-resolution images.
It is applied in metallography, for instance to determine the mineral content of a rock sample.

entries.title: Polarized light microscopy and birefringent minerals

definition.text: Polarized light microscopy covers optical microscopy techniques that illuminate a sample with polarized light, most useful on birefringent samples.

facts.text: A polarizing plate converts natural light into polarized light, and birefringent samples interact strongly with it, giving contrast against the background.
It is used extensively in optical mineralogy, the basis of identifying minerals in thin sections.
More complex variants include differential interference contrast and interference reflection microscopy.

entries.title: X-ray microtomography: a 3D look without cutting

definition.text: X-ray microtomography uses X-rays to make cross-sections of an object at micrometre pixel size and rebuild a 3D model without destroying the sample.

facts.text: Also called micro-CT, it is computed tomography in which the sample rotates while source and detector stay still, or the source and detector rotate around the specimen.
Cone-beam systems use a 2D detector to record projection images from which cross-sections are reconstructed.
Stacking slices builds a volume of voxels that can be viewed in any plane, and segmentation separates structures that have similar density.
In geology it is used to analyze micropores in reservoir rocks.

entries.title: Spatial analysis: studying things by where they are

definition.text: Spatial analysis is any of the formal techniques that study entities using their topological, geometric or geographic properties.

facts.text: It spans many methods, especially spatial statistics, and covers spatial interpolation, spatial regression and spatial autocorrelation statistics such as Moran's I and Geary's C.
Geographic information systems capture, store, manipulate and analyse spatial data, with map overlay a basic vector operation.
Common errors include the ecological fallacy (drawing conclusions about individuals from aggregate data) and the locational fallacy (a poor spatial characterisation of the elements).
Spatial sampling picks limited locations to measure phenomena that show dependency and heterogeneity; basic schemes are random, clustered and systematic.

entries.title: Landsat: fifty years of Earth from orbit

definition.text: The Landsat program is the longest-running enterprise that has acquired satellite imagery of Earth.

facts.text: The first satellite launched on 23 July 1972 as the Earth Resources Technology Satellite and was renamed Landsat 1 in 1975; Landsat 9 launched on 27 September 2021.
Landsat 7 data has eight spectral bands with spatial resolutions from 15 to 60 m and a temporal resolution of 16 days; a scene is about 185 km by 185 km.

Instruments progressed from the Multispectral Scanner (Landsat 1-5) to the Thematic Mapper, the Enhanced Thematic Mapper Plus (Landsat 7) and, on Landsat 8, the Operational Land Imager plus a Thermal Infrared Sensor.
Landsat gives one of the longest uninterrupted remote-sensing time series, from 1972 to the present, and is widely used for land-cover determination.

entries.title: Geomorphometry, measuring the shape of the land

definition.text: The science of measuring the shape of the land surface and the effects of that shape on human and natural processes.

facts.text: It extracts surface parameters and objects such as watersheds, stream networks and landforms from digital elevation models.
These parameters improve the mapping and modelling of soils, and serve precision agriculture and soil-landscape modelling.
Thanks largely to the Shuttle Radar Topography Mission and lidar, elevation models now cover almost all of Earth at 100 m resolution or better.
Slope, how steep the surface is, and aspect, the direction the slope faces, are its most basic derivatives.
Slope is computed from a raster model by discrete derivatives; the Horn method uses a cell and its eight neighbours.
Because water flows downhill, surface derivatives can predict surface stream flow.
Its ideas go back to Brisson (1808) and Gauss (1827), but it grew mainly with GIS and elevation data sets from the 1970s.
