entries.title: Ground-penetrating radar, echoes from buried layers

definition.text: A geophysical method that images the subsurface with radar pulses, recording reflections from buried boundaries.

facts.text: It uses radio waves usually between 10 MHz and 2.6 GHz, reflected where materials of different permittivity meet.
It can reach up to 15 m in dry sandy soils but only a few centimetres in moist or clay-rich soils; higher frequencies trade penetration for resolution.
Clay soils and salt-contaminated soils limit it most, and rocky soils scatter the signal.
It is used to study soils and bedrock, and cross-borehole radar assesses the presence and amount of soil water.

entries.text: Radar can see into the ground, but how far depends on the soil. Ground-penetrating radar sends radio waves, usually between 10 MHz and 2.6 GHz, and records their reflections from buried boundaries, such as the edge of a {{ref:soil-found-001}}. Reflections occur where materials of different permittivity, an electrical property, meet. In dry sandy soils it reaches up to 15 m; in moist or clay-rich soils, only a few centimeters. It is used to study soils and bedrock, and cross-borehole radar assesses the presence and amount of soil water.

entries.title: The scorpan model: clorpt made digital

definition.text: The scorpan model, proposed by McBratney and colleagues in 2003, extends Jenny's clorpt model so that soil-environment relationships can be applied digitally.

facts.text: It keeps climate, organisms, relief, parent material and age, and adds s (intrinsic soil properties captured by remote and proximal sensors) and n (spatial coordinates or position relative to a geographic phenomenon).
A quantitative function f links individual scorpan factors, or a combination, to the soil property or class being predicted.
Its strength is flexibility: it combines existing soil surveys with remote sensing, elevation, climate, land use and geology data, all as raster layers re-projected to one projection and resolution.

Relief (usually from a digital elevation model) is the most used factor in digital soil mapping, soil is second, and climate one of the least used, partly because topography proxies for local climate.
Age is rarely used because soil age is hard to put into a GIS-friendly form; the position factor can use sample coordinates or distance to a feature.
Pedometrics applies mathematical and statistical methods to the distribution and genesis of soils; DSM techniques date from the 1970s, and technology made them practical products since the 2000s.
A map needs three ingredients: environmental layers representing scorpan factors, geo-referenced soil data, and a model relating soil to environment to predict at unsampled locations.
It is usually supervised learning: sample locations are intersected with the environmental layers to build a training set, a fitted classification or regression function is then applied to all cells.

entries.title: Electromagnetic induction: a field from a changing field

definition.text: Electromagnetic induction is the production of an electromotive force across a conductor in a changing magnetic field.

facts.text: Faraday published its discovery in 1831 and Joseph Henry found it independently in 1832; Maxwell later described it mathematically.
Faraday's law says the induced emf in a closed circuit equals the rate of change of enclosed magnetic flux, and Lenz's law says the induced current opposes the change that produced it.
A changing current in one wire induces an emf in a second wire within reach of its magnetic field, which is the principle of the transformer.
Conductors in changing magnetic fields develop circular eddy currents in planes perpendicular to the field.

entries.title: Electrical resistivity tomography, imaging soil with current

definition.text: A geophysical technique that images subsurface structure from electrical resistivity measured with electrodes at the surface or in boreholes.

facts.text: Current is passed between two outer electrodes in a line of four, voltage is read between the inner two, and a geometric factor converts the result to apparent resistivity.
Wetter soil is less resistive, dry and saturated soil can differ by orders of magnitude, and clays conduct through charged particle surfaces as well as pore water.

entries.title: Conventional soil mapping and its limits

definition.text: Conventional soil mapping is the surveyor-led production of soil maps from field inspections, building on Jenny's soil-forming factors and national taxonomic systems.

facts.text: The steps are objectives, background compilation and initial legend, then soil inspections, field mapping and correlation, and finally map production and a report.
Soils are represented as a profile, a 1-3 m wide pedon, a polypedon of connected similar pedons, or a map unit, the polygon mapped by surveyors.
Choropleth maps assume each map unit is homogeneous, yet units contain inclusions of minor soils too small to map, and real soil change is often a fuzzy gradation rather than a sharp boundary.
Raising map-unit purity raises cost exponentially, and maps made for different objectives leave mismatched boundaries and inconsistent series names across counties and provinces.
Legacy maps still hold decades of surveyor knowledge and serve as training data for digital soil maps.

entries.title: Judging a digital soil map: accuracy assessment

definition.text: Accuracy assessment measures how far a digital soil map's predicted values differ from observed ones, using an independent validation dataset.

facts.text: Categorical predictions use overall accuracy (share correctly predicted) and Cohen's kappa, which corrects for chance agreement; both range from 0 to 1.
Continuous predictions use mean square error, root mean square error (in the soil variable's units), R2 and Lin's concordance correlation coefficient; lower MSE or RMSE means a more accurate model.
R2 is not accuracy because it ignores bias from systematic over- or underprediction; the concordance coefficient, which measures fit to the 45-degree line, is more appropriate.

entries.title: Where digital soil map uncertainty comes from

definition.text: Digital soil map uncertainty is the error that accumulates in a predicted soil map, which should be estimated as carefully as it is validated.

facts.text: It comes from three sources: the measured soil property, the environmental predictors, and the predictive model.
Property errors arise from laboratory methods, pedotransfer functions and GPS location accuracy; predictor errors from DEM vertical error, sensor error and polygon boundaries and scale.
Model structure matters because linear, non-linear and hybrid models (such as model trees) capture different soil-environment relationships.
International standards such as GlobalSoilMap require a 90% prediction interval map with 5% and 95% limits; a wider interval means higher uncertainty, and this applies only to continuous variables.

entries.title: Spatial scale: how big is the space?

definition.text: Spatial scale describes or categorises the size of a space, or the extent at which a phenomenon or process occurs.

facts.text: A common geography and meteorology scheme runs from micro (1 m to 1 km, local) through meso (1 to 100 km, regional) and macro (100 to 10,000 km, continental) to mega (global) and giga (superglobal).
These divisions are somewhat arbitrary and shift by context, so meso and macro must be adjusted accordingly.

entries.title: Multispectral imaging: a few bands beyond sight

definition.text: Imaging that captures data in a small number of separate wavelength bands, typically 3 to 15, including bands beyond visible light.

facts.text: Hyperspectral imaging differs by using often hundreds of contiguous bands.
A single multispectral image can show water depth, vegetation cover and soil moisture content.
Mid-infrared bands at 1550–1750 nm image vegetation and soil moisture, and far-infrared bands at 2080–2350 nm image soil, silicates and clays.
Surface and subsurface soil differ spectrally; disturbed soil emits more at 8.5 to 9.5 micrometres, which helps detect buried land mines.

entries.title: Hyperspectral imaging, a full spectrum in every pixel

definition.text: Imaging that records a full, finely resolved spectrum across many continuous bands for each pixel, to identify materials or detect processes.

facts.text: Materials leave characteristic spectral signatures that allow them to be identified.
Sensors on aircraft, satellites or drones are used to investigate plants and soils remotely, assessing ground cover and soil chemistry.
In farming it is being used to detect the nutrient and water status of wheat and heavy-metal stress in plants.
Although often treated as a surface technique, it can probe beneath the surface, to a depth set by the spectral range and the sample.

entries.title: NDVI: reading plant health in red and near-infrared light

definition.text: A widely used remote-sensing measure of the health and density of vegetation, calculated from the red and near-infrared bands.

facts.text: Values run from -1 to 1: near zero means little or no vegetation, negative values mean water or non-land, and high values mean dense healthy vegetation.
Chlorophyll strongly absorbs visible light from 400 to 700 nm, while leaf cell structure strongly reflects near-infrared from 700 to 1100 nm.
Bare soils give small positive values of about 0.1 to 0.2, and because wet soil darkens, soil moisture changes can shift the index without any change in vegetation.
Alternatives such as the soil-adjusted vegetation index and the enhanced vegetation index correct for soil background effects.

entries.title: The modifiable areal unit problem

definition.text: The modifiable areal unit problem (MAUP) is a source of statistical bias that arises when point-based measures are aggregated into areal units.

facts.text: Summary values depend on both the shape and the scale of the aggregation unit, so results differ between, say, state and county boundaries.
The scale effect changes results between aggregation levels (correlation generally rises as unit size rises); the zoning effect changes them when data are regrouped at the same scale.
Gehlke and Biehl first recognised it in 1934 and Openshaw described it in detail in 1984; it is closely related to ecological fallacy.
Aggregation can hide a strong correlation or create a spurious one, so sensitivity analysis with several areal units is recommended to estimate the uncertainty of coefficients.

entries.title: Why no two spots in a field are alike

definition.text: The way a quantity measured at different places takes different values from place to place.

facts.text: It can be described with spatial descriptive statistics such as the range.
Variability is not uncertainty: a perfectly known field still varies, and uncertainty depends on sampling as well as on the amount of variability.
Geostatistics has been used to study how pesticide sorption and degradation vary across a field.
Geostatistical descriptions carry their own uncertainty, since variograms can be uncertain and interpolation methods differ.
Precision agriculture studies variability within fields, such as how terrain and soil properties affect crop growth and water distribution.
Urban landscapes and golf courses show high spatial variability in soil composition, unlike uniform farm fields.

entries.title: Geostatistics, from ore mines to farm fields

definition.text: A branch of statistics that deals with spatial or spatio-temporal data sets.

facts.text: It was first developed to predict the distribution of ore grades in mines and is now applied in soil science and in agriculture, especially precision farming.
Simpler interpolators such as inverse distance weighting came first; geostatistics goes further by treating values at unsampled places as correlated random variables.
A model of spatial continuity, often a parametric variogram, describes how strongly nearby values constrain the value at an unsampled point.
Using one spatial model across a whole area assumes stationarity, the same statistical properties everywhere; several methods relax that assumption.
It serves two goals: estimating the most likely value at each place, or simulating many alternative maps, called realizations, that together give probabilistic forecasts.
Bayesian inference plays a growing part, implementing kriging through a Gaussian process that is updated with Bayes' theorem.

entries.title: The variogram: how difference grows with distance

definition.text: A graph or function describing how much pairs of observations differ according to the distance separating them, the key tool of geostatistics.

facts.text: Matheron defined the semivariogram in 1963 as half the average squared difference between values a distance h apart, the value being, for example, the iron content of soil.
Samples taken far apart vary more than samples taken close together.
Since nobody can sample everywhere, an empirical variogram is built from the squared differences between every pair of sample points, such as soil samples.
It is summarized by the nugget, a jump at the origin; the sill, its limit at large distances; and the range, where it nears the sill, often taken as 95% of it.
An empirical variogram is not guaranteed to be valid, so a model is fitted to it, most often linear, spherical, Gaussian or exponential.
The fitted variogram model sets the weights used in kriging.
Usage is muddled: some authors call the semivariogram a variogram, and the word semivariance can mislead.

entries.title: Filling the gaps between sample points

definition.text: Estimating the values of a quantity at arbitrary places from values known at a set of points, when the variables are spatial coordinates.

facts.text: Geostatistics uses it to build digital elevation models from spot heights or survey depths.
Methods for scattered points include nearest-neighbour and natural-neighbour schemes, inverse distance weighting, kriging variants and thin-plate or other splines.
Gridding converts irregularly spaced data into a regular grid.
GIS software produces interpolated surfaces with methods such as inverse distance weighting, kriging, splines and trend surfaces.

entries.title: Kriging, the best guess between boreholes

definition.text: A geostatistical interpolation method that predicts a value at an unsampled point as a weighted average of nearby known values, based on a model of their covariance.

facts.text: Georges Matheron set out its theory in 1960, building on Danie Krige's thesis estimating gold grades from a few boreholes in South Africa's Witwatersrand.
Under suitable assumptions it gives the best linear unbiased prediction (BLUP) at unsampled locations.
Ordinary kriging chooses weights that minimize the mean squared error, with the weights summing to 1 so the estimate is unbiased.
Its estimation variance grows as samples lie farther from the target point and depends on the sampling layout, not on the sample values.
Only one realization of the random function is ever observed, so kriging must assume some degree of stationarity to infer its statistics.
Variants include simple kriging with a known mean, ordinary kriging with an unknown local mean, universal kriging with a trend, indicator kriging and co-kriging of related variables.
Its basic form is computationally heavy, but approximations scale it to larger problems.

entries.title: Regression-kriging: letting terrain and satellites guide the map

definition.text: A spatial prediction technique that regresses the target variable on auxiliary variables, such as terrain and remote-sensing layers, and then kriges the regression residuals.

facts.text: It is mathematically equivalent to universal kriging and kriging with external drift.
It implements Matheron's 1969 universal model of spatial variation, in which deterministic and stochastic parts of variation are modelled separately.
The trend is fitted by ordinary or generalized least squares, then the residuals are interpolated by kriging and added back.
Pure regression and pure kriging are special cases: with no spatial autocorrelation it reduces to multiple regression, and with no useful covariates to ordinary kriging.
It is used to map the spatial distribution of soil properties, provided covariate layers exist that correlate significantly with the property.
Covariates keep multiplying: near-global topography at about 90 m from the 2000 Shuttle Radar Topography Mission, and MODIS images at 250 m.
Odeh and colleagues named it regression-kriging in 1995; Minasny and McBratney call it the empirical BLUP.
Minasny and McBratney found that more, better data matter more than more sophisticated statistics.

entries.text: Part of a soil property's pattern follows the landscape, and part behaves like chance. Regression-kriging models the two separately, as Matheron's 1969 {{ref:soil-agri-093}} proposed. It first regresses the target variable on auxiliary layers, such as terrain from {{ref:soil-meth-008}} and remote-sensing images, fitting the trend by ordinary or generalized least squares. The leftover residuals are interpolated by {{ref:soil-meth-003}} and added back. The method is mathematically equivalent to universal kriging and kriging with external drift. With no spatial autocorrelation it reduces to multiple regression; with no useful covariates, to ordinary kriging. Odeh and colleagues named it in 1995, and Minasny and McBratney call it the empirical BLUP. It maps soil properties wherever covariate layers correlate significantly with the property. Those layers keep multiplying, from near-global topography at about 90 m from the 2000 Shuttle Radar Topography Mission to MODIS images at 250 m. Yet Minasny and McBratney found that more, better data matter more than more sophisticated statistics.
entries.text_plain: Part of a soil property's pattern follows the landscape, and part behaves like chance. Regression-kriging models the two separately, as Matheron's 1969 Matheron's three-part model of soil variation proposed. It first regresses the target variable on auxiliary layers, such as terrain from Geomorphometry, measuring the shape of the land and remote-sensing images, fitting the trend by ordinary or generalized least squares. The leftover residuals are interpolated by Kriging, the best guess between boreholes and added back. The method is mathematically equivalent to universal kriging and kriging with external drift. Those layers keep multiplying, from near-global topography at about 90 m from the 2000 Shuttle Radar Topography Mission to MODIS images at 250 m. entries.title: Inverse distance weighting, a freshman's fix

definition.text: A deterministic interpolation method that estimates unknown values as a weighted average of known points, each weighted by the inverse of its distance.

facts.text: Donald Shepard, a Harvard freshman, published the method in 1968 while overhauling the interpolation in the SYMAP mapping program.
Shepard tested exponents of distance and settled near -2, close to the gravity model.
It was among the simpler interpolators known before geostatistics.
In Slovenia's Idrija area, it was used in GIS to turn soil samples into a raster map of mercury concentration.

entries.title: Random forest: many trees voting

definition.text: Random forest is an ensemble learning method for classification and regression that builds many decision trees during training.

facts.text: Classification returns the class chosen by most trees; regression returns the average of the trees' predictions, which corrects decision trees' habit of overfitting.

Each tree is trained on a bootstrap sample drawn with replacement (bagging), and each split considers only a random subset of features, which decorrelates trees when a few features are very strong predictors.
Tin Kam Ho created the first algorithm in 1995; Breiman and Cutler extended it.
Variable importance can be ranked by permutation: permute a feature in the out-of-bag samples and see how much the error rises, or by mean decrease in impurity.
The cost of higher accuracy than a single tree is lost interpretability.

entries.title: Why nearby soil samples are not independent
entries.article: Spatial analysis#Fundamental issues > Spatial dependence > Spatial auto-correlation

definition.text: Spatial dependency is the co-variation of properties across geographic space, so characteristics at nearby locations appear correlated, positively or negatively.

facts.text: It produces the spatial autocorrelation problem, which violates standard statistical techniques that assume independent observations.

Dependence means one location can predict another, so observations are not needed at both; heterogeneity means the relation changes across space, so an observed dependence cannot be trusted beyond a possibly small region.
Classic statistics include Moran's I, Geary's C and Getis's G.

entries.text: Two soil samples taken a meter apart usually tell you more about each other than two taken kilometers apart. That is spatial autocorrelation: properties at nearby places vary together, positively or negatively, a core idea in {{ref:soil-meth-045}}. It creates a problem, because standard statistics assume independent observations, and nearby samples are not. Dependence also helps, since one location can predict another and you need not sample both. Heterogeneity limits that help: if the relation changes across space, a dependence cannot be trusted beyond a possibly small region. Moran's I, Geary's C and Getis's G are the classic statistics for measuring it.

entries.title: Stratified sampling: sampling each group on its own

definition.text: Stratified sampling samples a population that can be partitioned into subpopulations by sampling each stratum independently.

facts.text: Strata must be collectively exhaustive and mutually exclusive, so every element falls in exactly one; sampling inside each, for example by simple random sampling, improves precision by reducing sampling error.
Proportionate allocation samples each stratum in proportion to its size; optimum allocation takes larger samples where variability is greatest, and Neyman allocation is one such strategy.
It gives a smaller estimation error when within-strata standard deviation is lower than the overall one, and it ensures enough samples from strata of interest.
Combining sub-strata to reach adequate numbers can cause Simpson's paradox, in which trends disappear or reverse.

entries.text: A field with a sandy ridge and a clay hollow is really two populations. Stratified sampling treats them that way. It partitions a population into subpopulations, called strata, and samples each stratum independently, for example by simple random sampling. The strata must be collectively exhaustive and mutually exclusive, so every element falls in exactly one. Done well, it reduces sampling error and improves precision. The estimation error is smaller when the standard deviation within strata is lower than the overall one, and the method ensures enough samples from strata of interest. Proportionate allocation samples each stratum in proportion to its size. Optimum allocation takes larger samples where variability is greatest, and Neyman allocation is one such strategy. One trap remains: combining sub-strata to reach adequate numbers can cause Simpson's paradox, in which trends disappear or reverse.

entries.title: Compositional data: when only the ratios matter

definition.text: Compositional data are quantitative descriptions of the parts of some whole, conveying relative information.

facts.text: They are represented as points on a simplex; proportions, percentages and ppm all count as compositional data.
Closure divides each part by the total, so only the ratios between components carry information and scaling by any positive constant changes nothing.
John Aitchison defined compositional data as proportions of some whole in 1982.
Three-part compositions are plotted on a ternary (barycentric) triangle showing the ratios of the three variables as a position.
Examples include molar concentrations in chemistry and mineral fractions of a rock in geology.

entries.title: Log-ratio transformations for compositional data

definition.text: Log-ratio transformations map compositions from the simplex into real space so ordinary statistics can be applied.

facts.text: The additive log ratio (alr) takes logs of ratios to one arbitrarily chosen component; it is common in chemistry (pH) and multinomial logistic regression but is not an isometry.
The centred log ratio (clr) is an isomorphism and isometry, but it forces a linear dependency so the covariance matrix is singular.
The isometric log ratio (ilr) gives orthonormal coordinates in D-1 dimensions, built by Gram-Schmidt, singular-value decomposition or a bifurcating tree.
The article argues that noise distorts compositions asymmetrically, so ilr can create artifacts in real data.

entries.text: Ordinary statistics break down on compositions, so analysts translate them first. The isometric log ratio gives orthonormal coordinates in D-1 dimensions, built by Gram-Schmidt, singular-value decomposition or a bifurcating tree. A caution applies: the article argues that noise distorts compositions asymmetrically, so the isometric version can create artifacts in real data.

entries.article: doc>geo.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Soil_Science/Digging_into_Canadian_Soils%3A_An_Introduction_to_Soil_Science/03%3A_Digging_Deeper/3.04%3A_Digital_Soil_Mapping#CONVENTIONAL SOIL MAPPING > Table 17.1. Soil survey intensity level guidelines adapted from Mapping Systems Working Group (1981)

definition.text: Survey intensity levels grade how densely a conventional soil survey is checked in the field.

facts.text: Level 1, very detailed, needs one inspection per polygon with foot traverses under 0.5 km apart, published at 1:5,000 at series level.
Level 2, detailed, inspects over 90% of polygons with traverses 2 km apart at 1:20,000; level 3, reconnaissance, inspects 60-80% with traverses 4 km apart at 1:50,000.

entries.title: Sampling design: the odds behind every sample

definition.text: A sampling design specifies for every possible sample its probability of being drawn.

facts.text: It is written as a function P(S) giving the probability of drawing sample S; Bernoulli sampling is one example.
Designing a sample means defining the population, sampling frame and sampling unit, the margin of error to achieve, and how to balance sampling and non-sampling error.

entries.text: A sample is only as good as the rule that produced it. A sampling design specifies, for every possible sample, its probability of being drawn. It is written as a function P(S) giving the probability of drawing sample S, and Bernoulli sampling is one example. Designing a sample means defining the population, the sampling frame and the sampling unit. It also means choosing the margin of error to achieve and deciding how to balance sampling and non-sampling error.

entries.title: Choosing where to sample for a digital soil map

definition.text: Sampling design for digital soil mapping selects sites representative of the geographic area and of the soil-forming factors (covariates) being modelled.

facts.text: Geometric designs include grid, simple random, stratified random, transect, cluster and nested sampling; grid sampling places points at the centre of evenly spaced cells, and stratified random applies random sampling within strata.
Cluster sampling groups sites closely to cope with rough terrain, and nested sampling quantifies variability at different distances.

Feature-space designs use covariate values: fuzzy k-means sampling minimises distance in covariate space, and conditioned Latin hypercube sampling (Minasny and McBratney, 2006) samples all covariates with one sample per stratum.
An optimal design covers both geographic and feature space.

entries.title: The topographic wetness index: where hillslopes stay wet

definition.text: A steady-state wetness index, computed from slope and upslope contributing area, that quantifies topographic control on hydrological processes.

facts.text: It combines the upslope area draining through a point per unit contour length with the local slope in radians.
Beven and Kirkby developed it within the TOPMODEL runoff model; it was designed for hillslope catenas and is not meaningful on flat ground.
It correlates highly with soil attributes such as horizon depth, silt percentage, organic matter content and phosphorus.
Areas with similar values become saturated under similar moisture conditions.

entries.text: Where a hillside gets soggy can be read from two quantities. The topographic wetness index combines the upslope area draining through a point, per unit contour length, with the local slope in radians, a basic product of {{ref:soil-meth-008}}. This steady-state index quantifies how topography controls hydrological processes. Areas with similar values become saturated under similar moisture conditions. Beven and Kirkby developed it within the TOPMODEL runoff model. It correlates highly with soil attributes such as horizon depth, silt percentage, organic matter content and phosphorus. It was designed for a hillslope {{ref:soil-form-054}}, and it is not meaningful on flat ground.

entries.title: Fuzzy clustering: points that belong to several groups

definition.text: Fuzzy clustering, also called soft clustering, is a form of clustering in which each data point can belong to more than one cluster.

facts.text: In hard clustering each point belongs to exactly one cluster, while fuzzy clustering gives each point a membership grade for every cluster; points at a cluster's edge have lower grades.
Fuzzy c-means, developed by Dunn in 1973 and improved by Bezdek in 1981, alternates computing membership-weighted centroids with updating each point's coefficients until they converge.
A parameter m controls fuzziness: larger m gives fuzzier clusters, m near 1 reduces to k-means, and m is commonly set to 2 without other knowledge.
Like k-means, it finds only a local minimum that depends on the initial weights.

entries.text: Soils rarely fall neatly into one class, and fuzzy clustering admits it. Also called soft clustering, it lets each data point belong to more than one cluster. entries.title: Mapping the soils of the Moon and Mars from orbit

definition.text: The use of orbiting gamma-ray spectrometers to map the elements of planetary surfaces, especially the Moon and Mars.

facts.text: Cosmic rays strike nuclei in the soil, releasing neutrons and exciting nuclei that then emit gamma rays of characteristic energy.
The energy of each emission line identifies an element and its intensity gives the concentration; about 20 elements can be measured.
Neutron detectors sense hydrogen in the upper metre of the surface, revealing water ice; Mars Odyssey carried one with two neutron detectors.
Mapping from orbit fails for bodies with thick atmospheres such as Earth and Venus.

entries.title: Latin hypercube sampling: one point per slice

definition.text: Latin hypercube sampling (LHS) is a statistical method for generating a near-random sample of parameter values from a multidimensional distribution.

facts.text: The range of each variable is split into M equally probable intervals and M points are placed so each interval of every variable holds exactly one point, like non-attacking rooks on a chess board.
It needs no more samples for more variables, and samples can be taken in sequence while remembering which cells were already used.
Unlike plain random sampling, the number of points must be chosen beforehand, but every subspace is then sampled with equal density.

entries.title: Uncertainty quantification: how sure is the model?

definition.text: Uncertainty quantification is the science of quantitatively characterising and estimating uncertainties in computational and real-world applications.

facts.text: It tries to determine how likely outcomes are when some aspects of a system are not exactly known.

Forward propagation pushes input uncertainty through a model to get the output's mean and variance, reliability or full distribution; inverse quantification estimates the discrepancy between model and experiment and unknown parameters.
Forward methods include Monte Carlo simulation, surrogate models, local and functional expansions and first/second-order reliability methods.
Inverse problems are harder and face dimensionality and identifiability issues, since different parameter and discrepancy combinations can give the same prediction.

entries.title: Near-infrared spectroscopy, a quick scan for soil tests

definition.text: A spectroscopic method using the near-infrared part of the spectrum, from 780 nm to 2500 nm.

facts.text: It rests on weak overtone and combination vibrations, so light penetrates deep into a sample and bulk material can be probed with little preparation.
Its broad, overlapping bands require multivariate calibration, such as principal components or partial least squares, built on carefully chosen calibration samples.
Karl Norris at the USDA pioneered it for agricultural products in the 1980s; it is valued as accurate, rapid, non-destructive and inexpensive.
Soil-testing laboratories may use near-infrared scanning.

entries.title: Chemometrics: mining chemical measurements for answers

definition.text: Chemometrics is the science of extracting information from chemical systems by data-driven means.

facts.text: It draws on multivariate statistics, applied mathematics and computer science to solve problems in chemistry, biology, medicine and engineering.
Svante Wold coined the term in a 1971 grant application, and the field emerged in the 1970s as computers came into scientific use.
Infrared and UV/visible spectra contain thousands of measurements per sample, but strong low-rank structure lets principal components analysis and partial least squares model them compactly.
Chemometric models are usually judged by root mean squared error of prediction, and model selection relies on resampling such as bootstrap, permutation and cross-validation.

entries.title: Partial least squares regression

definition.text: Partial least squares (PLS) regression is a reduced-rank method that projects both predictors and responses into new spaces to find the relation between them.

facts.text: It looks for the direction in predictor space that explains maximum variance in response space, modelling the covariance structure of two matrices with latent variables.
It suits data with more variables than observations or with multicollinearity among predictors, where standard regression fails unless regularised.
Herman Wold introduced it, with his son Svante Wold, first in the social sciences; it is now most widely used in chemometrics.
Components are extracted iteratively by finding directions of maximal covariance and regressing on the scores; PLS1 handles a single response vector and PLS-DA a categorical one.

entries.title: Multivariate calibration: turning spectra into soil properties

definition.text: Multivariate calibration builds models that predict a property of interest from measured responses such as spectra.

facts.text: A training set pairs reference values (for example analyte concentration) with the measured spectra; partial least squares or principal component regression then relates response to property.
Methods are classed as classical, which optimally describe the measured responses, or inverse, which need less physical knowledge and usually predict better in mean-squared-error terms.
It lets fast, cheap, non-destructive measurements estimate properties that would otherwise need slow or costly analysis, even under heavy interference from other analytes.
Broad, non-selective near-infrared spectra can still predict properties when paired with carefully developed calibration, because selectivity comes partly from the mathematics.

entries.title: The carbon cycle: one element circling through soil, sea and sky

definition.text: The part of Earth's biogeochemical cycles in which carbon moves among living things, soils, rocks, water and the atmosphere.

facts.text: Carbon is the main component of biological compounds and also a major part of many rocks, such as limestone.
The cycle is usually divided into reservoirs, or carbon pools: the atmosphere, the terrestrial biosphere (including soils), the ocean, sediments and Earth's interior.
Carbon passes between these pools through chemical, physical, geological and biological processes; the ocean holds the largest active pool near Earth's surface.
Photosynthesis is the main route by which carbon dioxide leaves the atmosphere and enters land and ocean life.
Without human influence the natural flows between atmosphere, ocean, land ecosystems and sediments are fairly balanced, so carbon levels would stay roughly stable.
Humans have disturbed the cycle for centuries by changing land use and by mining and burning coal, petroleum and gas.
By 2020 atmospheric carbon dioxide had risen nearly 52% above pre-industrial levels, causing global warming.
Land and ocean sinks each currently take up about one-quarter of human carbon emissions every year.

entries.title: Soil carbon, a store three times the atmosphere's

definition.text: The solid carbon stored in soils, both as organic matter from plants, animals and microbes and as inorganic carbonate minerals.

facts.text: Soil carbon underpins water holding capacity, nutrient retention and soil structure.
Soils hold about 2,700 Gt of carbon, 1550 GtC organic and 950 GtC inorganic, roughly three times the carbon in the atmosphere.
Peat and wetlands hold a further 150 GtC and surface plant litter 50 GtC.
Photosynthesis, respiration and decomposition are the main processes setting how much carbon is stored on land.
About 60 GtC a year accumulates in soil, and an equivalent 60 GtC a year is respired from soil back to the atmosphere.
As a carbon sink in the global cycle, soil carbon matters for climate change mitigation, and data on it feed global climate models.
Human activities have caused a massive loss of soil organic carbon, but people could also deliberately return carbon to the soil.
Global data on soil organic carbon are inconsistent, with some regions far better covered than others.

entries.title: Carbon sinks: places that take in more than they give

definition.text: A natural or artificial process that removes a greenhouse gas, or a substance that forms one, from the atmosphere, taking up more carbon than it releases.

facts.text: Sinks are an important part of the natural carbon cycle.
Globally the two most important sinks are vegetation and the ocean, and soil is an important carbon store.
Natural sinks include soil, a carbon store and active sink; land plants during growing seasons; and the ocean through its solubility and biological pumps.
Artificial sinks store carbon in building materials or deep underground, but no major artificial system yet removes carbon from the atmosphere at large scale.
For greenhouse gases other than CO2 a sink need not store the gas; nitrous oxide, for example, can be reduced to harmless N2.
Deforestation and industrial agriculture have depleted natural sinks, and this land-use change is one cause of climate change.
For climate change mitigation, keeping and enhancing natural sinks, mainly soils and forests, is important.

entries.text: During the growing season, land plants pull more carbon from the air than they release. That makes them a carbon sink. A sink is a natural or artificial process that removes a greenhouse gas, or a substance that forms one, from the atmosphere. It takes up more carbon than it releases. Sinks are an important part of the natural carbon cycle. Globally the two most important are vegetation and the ocean, which absorbs carbon through its solubility and biological pumps. Soil is both an important carbon store and an active sink. Artificial sinks lock carbon in building materials or deep underground. No major artificial system yet removes carbon from the atmosphere at large scale. For gases other than CO2, a sink need not store anything. Nitrous oxide, for example, can be reduced to harmless nitrogen gas, N2. Deforestation and industrial agriculture have depleted natural sinks, and this land-use change is one cause of climate change. Keeping and enhancing natural sinks, mainly soils and forests, is therefore important for slowing it.

entries.title: Climate change mitigation: cutting the gases that warm the planet

definition.text: Action to limit the greenhouse gases in the atmosphere that cause climate change, also called decarbonisation.

facts.text: Mitigation actions include conserving energy and replacing fossil fuels with clean energy sources.
An important measure is preserving and enhancing carbon sinks, managing them so they remove more CO2 and store it durably; scientists also call this carbon sequestration.
The 2022 IPCC report calls land-based options AFOLU mitigation options, with an economic potential of 4.2 to 7.4 GtCO2-eq per year.
Almost 20% of greenhouse gas emissions come from agriculture and forestry; cutting nitrogen fertilizer use could avoid nitrous oxide equal to 2.77 - 11.48 gigatons of CO2 from 2020 to 2050.

entries.title: Carbon sequestration: putting carbon away

definition.text: The storing of carbon in a carbon pool, which limits climate change by reducing carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.

facts.text: Its two main types are biological sequestration (biosequestration) and geological sequestration.
Biological sequestration captures CO2 by living processes such as photosynthesis, and land-use and farming changes that speed it up are called carbon farming.
It is sometimes confused with carbon capture and storage, which separates CO2 from industrial sources and stores it underground or under the sea bed.
Biological stores may be temporary: wildfire, disease, economic pressure and politics can release their carbon again.
Mineral sequestration locks carbon in insoluble carbonate salts for thousands to millions of years.
Converting natural or semi-natural land to cropland cuts soil organic carbon by about 30-40%, and soil carbon keeps changing until a new equilibrium is reached.
Leaving residues, using manure and adding perennial crops, with their larger below-ground biomass, raise carbon input to soil.
About 70% of soil organic carbon outside permafrost lies deeper within the upper metre, stabilized by mineral-organic associations.

entries.title: Soil carbon and climate: a two-way street
entries.article: Soil carbon#Soil carbon and climate change

definition.text: The two-way link between climate and soil carbon: climate change alters soils and their carbon, and soil carbon losses or gains alter the climate.

facts.text: Changing temperature and moisture alter soil formation, so climate change is likely to affect fertility, salinity, moisture, temperature, organic carbon and aggregation.
Plant uptake fixes carbon dioxide in soil, building a pool of around 1500 Pg in the first few metres, 20-40% of it lasting more than 100 years.
Forest soils are a large carbon pool, and deforestation releases carbon from it that may markedly raise greenhouse gases in the atmosphere.
Soil microbes break down soil carbon, and changes in their activity as temperatures rise could contribute to climate change.
In polar regions melting permafrost can expose land to more plant growth and carbon uptake, while in the tropics warmer soils lose aggregation and quality.
Researchers are looking for ways that farming and other human interventions can restore carbon to soils.

entries.title: How a warming climate makes farming harder
entries.article: Effects of climate change on agriculture

definition.text: The many ways a changing climate alters farming, most of them making it harder for agriculture to provide global food security.

facts.text: Climate change is likely to worsen farming's environmental impacts by lowering productivity, weakening agrochemicals and increasing soil erosion and pests.
Drought, heat waves and flooding lower crop yields; one study linked 1°C of warming to a 3 to 7% fall in global yields of major staple crops.
Effects on land include coastal farmland lost to sea level rise, new arable land as frozen ground thaws, more erosion and changes in soil fertility and growing seasons.
CO2 fertilization offsets a small part of the harm but lowers essential micronutrients in crops and does little for C4 crops like maize.
The future extent of soil erosion and groundwater depletion are among the main uncertainties.
Adaptation can come through management practices, agricultural innovation, institutional change and climate-smart agriculture.

entries.title: Carbon locked in minerals: soil's carbonate store

definition.text: Carbon held in soil as minerals, mainly carbonates, formed by weathering of parent material or by soil minerals reacting with atmospheric CO2.

facts.text: In arid and semi-arid environments most soil carbon is inorganic, as carbonates such as calcite and dolomite.
Carbonates can come from the bedrock or parent material, or form in place in the soil as pedogenic carbonate.
Inorganic carbon makes up about 950 GtC of the world's soil carbon, roughly a third of the total.
The reactions are reversible: when carbonate meets hydrogen ions from acids, as in soils, it forms water and releases CO2 back to the air.

entries.text: In arid and semi-arid lands, most soil carbon is not organic at all. It is soil inorganic carbon: carbon held as minerals, mainly carbonates such as calcite and dolomite. It arises from the weathering of parent material, or from soil minerals reacting with CO2 from the air. Worldwide, inorganic carbon makes up about 950 GtC, roughly a third of all soil carbon. The store can be undone. The reactions are reversible: when carbonate meets hydrogen ions from acids, as it does in soils, it forms water and releases CO2 back to the air.

entries.title: Soil organic carbon, built from roots, leaves and dead microbes

definition.text: The carbon held in soil organic matter, which is about 50% carbon by dry weight.

facts.text: In humid environments most soil carbon is organic.
Its main source is dead plant material added as roots, fallen leaves and crop residue; animal bodies and excreta add more.
Plants supply 5–20% of the carbon they fix by photosynthesis to the soil as root exudates feeding rhizosphere organisms such as mycorrhizal fungi.
Cellulose, starches, proteins and lipids break down fast, while lignin, humus, aggregate-bound organic matter and charcoal resist change and persist long.
Microbes cycle soil carbon so thoroughly that their dead remains, microbial necromass, can make up 30 to 80% of soil carbon.
Most upland topsoils hold 0.5% to 3.0% organic carbon; below 0.5% is mostly limited to deserts, and above 12–18% soils are classed as organic soils.
Organic carbon builds up where waterlogging slows decomposition so additions outpace losses, as in swamps, bogs and marshes.
Fire-derived charcoal and black carbon occur in most soils, typically supplying 5–50% of organic carbon and more than 50% in mollisols, chernozems and terra preta.

entries.title: Managing soil carbon: stop the losses, build the stock

definition.text: Choosing land and farm practices to avoid losses of soil organic carbon and to build it up.

facts.text: Exchange of carbon between soils and the atmosphere is a significant part of the global carbon cycle, and humans and farming now affect it most.
Land-use change such as deforestation has caused substantial soil carbon losses, though exact amounts are hard to measure.
Fire strips soil cover and causes immediate and continuing losses of soil organic carbon.
Tillage and drainage expose organic matter to oxygen; peatlands in the Netherlands, East Anglia, Florida and the California Delta have subsided severely as a result.
Grazing that leaves soil bare, through too long or too short recovery periods, also loses soil carbon.
Farmers are discouraged from stubble burning and over-cultivation and encouraged to work in organic material such as manure.
Raising soil carbon is not simple, because soil organisms consume and release carbon and become more active when nitrogen fertilizer is added.

Past losses mean farmed soils can store more carbon; reducing tillage intensity and summer fallow cuts losses, while manure, biochar, cover crops, residue retention, perennials and good fertilization raise inputs.

entries.title: Carbon in the deep freeze: the permafrost carbon cycle

definition.text: The Arctic part of the global carbon cycle, in which carbon moves from permafrost soils to plants, microbes and the air and back into frozen soil by burial.

facts.text: Carbon returns to permafrost soils through burial and sedimentation by cryogenic processes, while some passes to the ocean and the wider global cycle.
It includes exchanges of carbon dioxide and methane with the air and transfers to water as dissolved and particulate organic and inorganic carbon.
Permafrost-affected soils cover nearly 9% of Earth's land yet store between 25 and 50% of the soil organic carbon.
Because permafrost responds slowly to climate, it keeps carbon out of the air for long periods; radiocarbon dating shows much of it is thousands of years old.
This large reservoir was often neglected in early carbon estimates and climate models, but research on it has grown enormously since the 2000s.
Microbial respiration is the main route by which old permafrost carbon re-enters the air, its rate set by soil temperature, moisture, nutrients and oxygen.
Iron oxides can hold back microbial respiration, and iron and aluminum can adsorb freed carbon before it escapes, especially in the sandy layers often over permafrost.
Despite the large stores, the whole pool is unlikely to mobilize, because much permafrost will stay frozen even as thaw deepens.

entries.title: Pingos, hills with a heart of ice

definition.text: An ice-cored hill, 3–70 m high and 30–1,000 m across, that grows only in permafrost.

facts.text: Pingos are typically conical periglacial landforms; more than 11,000 exist, the most, 1,350, on the Tuktoyaktuk peninsula.

Closed-system pingos form in continuous permafrost as an infilled lake freezes and squeezes trapped water upward; open-system pingos are fed by artesian groundwater, often in thin discontinuous permafrost.
They grow a couple of centimetres a year, and when their ice core melts they collapse into depressions that show permafrost once existed.
John Franklin first described one in 1825; in 1938 Alf Erling Porsild borrowed the Inuvialuit word, meaning conical hill, for scientific use.

entries.title: The active layer, the ground that thaws each summer

definition.text: The top layer of soil in permafrost regions that thaws each summer and freezes again in autumn.

facts.text: Soil temperature is steadier at depth than at the surface, so seasonal heating and cooling fade with depth.
In winter a frost front forms in the soil, and in spring and summer the soil thaws from the top down.
Where summer heat cannot thaw the soil completely, permafrost forms; the year-round frozen soil below the active layer is the inactive layer.
The boundary between the active layer and permafrost is sometimes called the permafrost table.
Water cannot drain below the active layer, so permafrost lands tend to be very poorly drained and boggy.
In 2018 it averaged ~145 centimetres in the Northern Hemisphere, under 50 centimetres in northeastern Siberia, Alaska and Greenland and over 600 centimetres in southern Norway and Mongolia.
Roots cannot grow below the active layer, so continuous permafrost restricts trees to shallow-rooted species such as larch.

entries.title: Why soils hold more carbon than plants and air combined

definition.text: The role of soils as a short- to long-term carbon store holding more carbon than all land vegetation and the atmosphere combined.

facts.text: Plant litter and other biomass, charcoal included, build up as soil organic matter that weathering and microbes then break down.
Tougher compounds such as cellulose, hemicellulose, lignin, waxes and terpenoids are retained together as humus.
Organic matter accumulates in cold regions such as the boreal forests of North America and the Russian taiga.
In tropical and subtropical climates litter and humus are oxidized fast and leached by rain, so slash-and-burn fields stay fertile only two to three years.
Grasslands store organic matter mainly in fibrous root mats, helped by cool, semi-arid to arid climates; natural grass fires also leave stable biochar in the soil.
Since the 1850s much of the world's grassland has been tilled into cropland, rapidly oxidizing large amounts of soil organic carbon.
Intensive farming has severely depleted the organic carbon of many agricultural soils worldwide.
Methods that markedly raise soil carbon storage, such as no-till, residue mulching, cover cropping and crop rotation, are called carbon farming.

entries.title: Soil carbon sequestration: drawing carbon down into the ground

definition.text: Drawing carbon dioxide from the air into soil, where plants fix it as organic carbon; it is a major soil property and an ecosystem service.

facts.text: There are many measures to raise soil carbon, which makes it hard to measure and account for, but they carry fewer trade-offs than BECCS or afforestation.
Protecting healthy soils and restoring the soil carbon sponge could remove 7.6 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide a year, more than annual US emissions.
Farming can deplete soil carbon, but conservation farming can protect it and repair the damage over time.
Methods include cover crops, no-till farming, residue mulching and crop rotation.
Best practices for European soils are converting arable land to grassland, straw incorporation, reduced tillage, ley cropping and cover crops.
Trees exude more carbon below ground than they capture above it, helping build a soil carbon sponge.
Biochar retains half the carbon of the biomass it is made from and can endure in soil for thousands of years.
Rattan Lal's 2004 Science paper on soil carbon sequestration was the first to report that restoring soil organic matter both improves soil health and reduces atmospheric CO2.

entries.text: In 2004 Science published a paper on soil carbon sequestration by the scientist profiled in {{ref:soil-hist-026}}. It was the first to report that restoring soil organic matter does two jobs at once. It improves soil health, and it reduces atmospheric CO2. Soil carbon sequestration is that process: drawing carbon dioxide from the air into soil, where plants fix it as organic carbon. It is both a major soil property and an ecosystem service. Farming can deplete soil carbon, but conservation farming can protect it and repair the damage over time. Methods include cover crops, no-till farming, residue mulching and crop rotation. For European soils the best practices are converting arable land to grassland, straw incorporation, reduced tillage, ley cropping and cover crops. Trees exude more carbon below ground than they capture above it, helping build a carbon-rich soil described in {{ref:soil-env-119}}. Biochar retains half the carbon of the biomass it is made from and can endure in soil for thousands of years. The potential is large. Protecting healthy soils and restoring that sponge could remove 7.6 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide a year, more than annual US emissions. The many measures make soil carbon hard to measure and account for. Yet they carry fewer trade-offs than afforestation or BECCS, bioenergy with carbon capture and storage.

entries.title: When warming soils breathe out more carbon

definition.text: The release of carbon from soils in response to global warming, which in turn adds to warming.

facts.text: Soils hold roughly two to three times as much carbon as the atmosphere, which makes the feedback crucial for future climate.
Faster soil respiration is the main cause; measurements imply 4 °C of warming raises annual soil respiration by up to 37%.
Global soil respiration rose by about 0.1% a year between 1989 and 2008, most likely because warming sped up decomposition of soil organic matter.
A warming experiment at Harvard, run since 1991, suggests the top metre of soils could release about 190 petagrams of carbon by 2100.
A 2018 study found climate-driven soil carbon losses already occurring across many ecosystems, with a detectable global trend.
Observations of thawing permafrost suggest a linear, chronic release of greenhouse gases as warming continues.
Global decomposition models poorly represent soil animals such as insects and worms and their interactions with microbes.

entries.title: Permafrost thaw: the frozen ground is shrinking

definition.text: The warming and thawing of permafrost under climate change, seen as a thickening active layer and shrinking frozen ground.

facts.text: Permafrost warmed globally by about 0.3 °C between 2007 and 2016, more in the continuous zone than the discontinuous zone.
Warming reached up to 3 °C in parts of Northern Alaska from the early 1980s to mid-2000s, and up to 2 °C in the Russian European North from 1970 to 2020.
Average active layer thickness rose from ~127 centimetres to ~145 centimetres between 2000 and 2018, about ~0.65 centimetres a year.
In Yukon the continuous permafrost zone may have moved 100 kilometres poleward since 1899, though accurate records span only 30 years.
Model projections, process understanding and paleoclimate evidence make it virtually certain that permafrost will keep shrinking as climate warms.
The volume of permafrost in the upper 3 m is expected to fall by about 25% per 1 °C of global warming.

entries.title: Continuous to isolated: grading permafrost by coverage

definition.text: The division of permafrost regions by how much of the land is underlain by permafrost: continuous, discontinuous, sporadic and isolated.

facts.text: In the continuous zone 90%–100% of land is underlain by permafrost, in the discontinuous zone 50%–90%, and in the sporadic zone 10%–50%; isolated patches cover 10% or less.
About 15% of the Northern Hemisphere's ice-free land is directly underlain by permafrost, but 22% lies within a permafrost zone.
Permafrost usually forms wherever mean annual air temperature is below freezing, except in humid boreal forests where snow insulates the ground.
Where the mean annual soil surface temperature is between −5 and 0 °C, permafrost usually stays discontinuous, forming only in sheltered spots.
Below −5 °C slope aspect can never thaw it, and a continuous permafrost zone (CPZ) forms.
Soil scientists abbreviate the sporadic zone SPZ and the extensive discontinuous zone DPZ.

entries.text: About 15% of the Northern Hemisphere's ice-free land sits directly on permafrost, yet 22% lies within a permafrost zone. The difference comes from how the zones work. Permafrost zones divide frozen regions by how much of the land is underlain by permafrost. In the continuous zone 90%–100% is, in the discontinuous zone 50%–90%, and in the sporadic zone 10%–50%. Isolated patches cover 10% or less. Soil scientists abbreviate the continuous zone CPZ, the extensive discontinuous zone DPZ and the sporadic zone SPZ. Temperature sets the pattern. Permafrost usually forms wherever mean annual air temperature is below freezing. Humid boreal forests are the exception, because snow insulates the ground there. Where the mean annual soil surface temperature lies between −5 and 0 °C, permafrost usually stays discontinuous, forming only in sheltered spots. Below −5 °C, not even a slope's aspect, the direction it faces, can thaw it, and a continuous zone forms.

entries.title: Two speeds of the carbon cycle

definition.text: The split of the carbon cycle into a fast biological cycle that turns over in years and a slow geological cycle that takes millions of years.

facts.text: The fast cycle runs through living things, moving carbon between the atmosphere, land and marine ecosystems, soils and seafloor sediments.
It includes annual cycles driven by photosynthesis and decadal cycles of vegetation growth and decomposition.
The slow cycle runs through rocks: weathering returns carbon to the atmosphere by degassing and to the ocean by rivers, over spans of millions of years.
Between 10 and 100 million tonnes of carbon move around the slow cycle in a given year.

entries.title: What extra soil carbon does for a whole catchment

definition.text: The wider benefits to soil and catchment health that come from raising soil carbon, beyond its role as a carbon sink.

facts.text: More stable aggregates resist erosion and sedimentation, and soils that keep their strength when wet are less prone to mass movement.
Nutrients and sediment stay in the soil instead of leaching or washing into waterways.
Greater water holding capacity cuts overland flow and keeps water available to plants.
The benefits are hard to quantify because natural resource systems are complex and soil health is open to interpretation.

entries.title: Counting the carbon: how countries track soil stocks
entries.article: Soil carbon#Measuring data on soil organic carbon

definition.text: Estimating soil organic carbon stocks and their changes by field survey and modelling, as climate reporting requires.

facts.text: Under the UN climate convention, countries report changes in five carbon pools, soil carbon among them, following IPCC good practice guidance.
Tanzania, with the FAO, runs a forest soil carbon monitoring programme that combines survey and modelling methods.
For Europe, the European Soil Database gives the most consistent organic carbon data, and one model puts the topsoil stock of EU farmland at 17.63 Gt.
Carbon in Australian farm soils, typically 1.6–4.6% today, may once have been twice as high.

entries.title: How organic carbon keeps a soil working
entries.article: Soil carbon#Soil organic carbon and soil function

definition.text: The way organic carbon sustains a soil's ability to provide services, a capacity known as soil health.

facts.text: Carbon benchmarks used to judge soil health include CO2 release, humus levels and microbial metabolic activity.
In sandy soils bulk density falls as organic carbon rises, and bulk density is needed to calculate organic carbon stocks.
Organic carbon raises cation exchange capacity in sandy soils, accounting for up to 76% of its variation in one study.
Organic carbon rises with silt and clay content and is highest in the clay fraction, as fine particles bind decomposing matter into protective aggregates.

entries.text: In one study of sandy soils, organic carbon accounted for up to 76% of the variation in cation exchange capacity, the soil's power to hold nutrient ions. That is one of many services organic carbon sustains. Together they add up to soil health, a soil's capacity to provide services. Carbon benchmarks used to judge it include CO2 release, humus levels and microbial metabolic activity. In sandy soils, bulk density falls as organic carbon rises, and bulk density is needed to calculate carbon stocks. Organic carbon also rises with silt and clay content and is highest in the clay fraction, where fine particles bind decomposing matter into protective aggregates.

entries.title: Feedbacks that speed up or slow down warming

definition.text: Natural processes that change how much the planet warms for a given amount of greenhouse gas emissions; positive feedbacks amplify warming and negative ones damp it.

facts.text: Calling a feedback positive or negative does not mean it is good or bad.
The sum of feedbacks is negative but becoming less so, so warming will accelerate if emissions continue at current levels.
Physical feedbacks include less reflective snow and ice and more water vapour; biological ones mostly involve how fast plants take up CO2 in the carbon cycle.
The carbon cycle absorbs more than half of yearly CO2 emissions into plants and the ocean, but that share will fall as sinks saturate and drought and wildfire increase.
Methane from land, especially wetlands, and nitrous oxide from land and oceans are a known positive feedback.
Carbon cycle feedbacks are uncertain, and permafrost thaw releases CO2 and methane in ways that are hard to model.
The IPCC estimates permafrost could release the equivalent of 14-175 billion tonnes of CO2 per 1 °C of warming.

entries.text: The IPCC estimates that permafrost could release the equivalent of 14-175 billion tonnes of CO2 per 1 °C of warming. Releases like that are climate change feedbacks: natural processes that change how much the planet warms for a given amount of greenhouse gas emissions. Positive feedbacks amplify warming, and negative ones damp it. The labels do not mean good or bad. Physical feedbacks include less reflective snow and ice and more water vapour. Biological ones mostly involve how fast plants take up CO2. The carbon cycle absorbs more than half of yearly CO2 emissions into plants and the ocean. That share will fall as sinks saturate and drought and wildfire increase. Methane from land, especially wetlands, and nitrous oxide from land and oceans are a known positive feedback. The sum of all feedbacks is negative but becoming less so, so warming will accelerate if emissions continue at current levels. The carbon side remains uncertain, and permafrost thaw releases CO2 and methane in ways that are hard to model.

entries.title: Methane, the gas behind a third of near-term heating

definition.text: The release of methane, a potent greenhouse gas, to the atmosphere from human activities and natural sources such as wetlands.

facts.text: Rising methane emissions cause up to one-third of near-term global heating; in 2019 about 60% came from human activities and 40% from natural sources.
Most natural emissions come from methanogens producing methane in warm, moist soils and in animal guts.
Wetlands supply about three-quarters of the enduring natural sources of methane.
Plant agriculture contributes about 15% of human emissions, with rice the largest single source: waterlogged paddies act like wetlands, emitting about 30 of 400 million tonnes in 2022.
Converting forests to farmland adds soil nitrogen, which inhibits methane oxidation, and changing the water table shifts a soil between methane source and sink.

entries.text: Rising methane emissions cause up to one-third of the global heating expected in the near term. Methane emissions are the release of this potent greenhouse gas to the air, from human activities and from natural sources such as wetlands. In 2019 about 60% came from people and 40% from nature. Most natural methane is made by methanogens, microbes that produce it in warm, moist soils and in animal guts, the process described in {{ref:soil-chem-129}}. Wetlands supply about three-quarters of the enduring natural sources. Farming copies them. Plant agriculture contributes about 15% of human emissions, and rice is the largest single source. Waterlogged paddies behave like wetlands: in 2022 they emitted about 30 million of 400 million tonnes. Land use shifts the balance too. Converting forests to farmland adds nitrogen to the soil, and that nitrogen inhibits methane oxidation, the microbial breakdown of methane. Moving the water table up or down can switch a soil between methane source and methane sink, a theme taken up in {{ref:soil-env-283}}.

entries.title: Carbon pools, the Earth's carbon reservoirs

definition.text: Any reservoir in the Earth system where carbon resides in some chemical form for a period of time.

facts.text: Carbon pool is the overarching term: pools include the atmosphere, oceans, soil, plants and fossil fuels, and a carbon sink is one type of pool.
Pools and sinks both matter for understanding the carbon cycle, but they mean slightly different things.
Related terms are reservoir, sequestration, source and uptake.

entries.text: The atmosphere, the oceans, soil, plants and fossil fuels share one label: each is a carbon pool. The two words mean slightly different things, and both matter for understanding the carbon cycle. Related terms are reservoir, sequestration, source and uptake.

entries.title: Carbon on land, above and below ground

definition.text: The carbon held on land, in all living and dead land organisms and in soils.

facts.text: About 500 gigatons of carbon are stored above ground in plants and other organisms, while soil holds approximately 1,500 gigatons.
Most land carbon is organic, but about a third of soil carbon is held in inorganic forms such as calcium carbonate.
Because land uptake depends on living things, it follows daily and seasonal cycles that show up in the Keeling curve of CO2 measurements.
Carbon leaves the land pool by burning or respiration, by export to the ocean in rivers, or stays sequestered in soils as inert carbon.
Soil carbon can stay put for up to thousands of years before erosion washes it into rivers or soil respiration releases it.
How long soil holds carbon depends on local climate, so it changes as the climate changes.
Forests hold 86% of the planet's land above-ground carbon, and forest soils hold 73% of its soil carbon.
About half of gross primary production is respired straight back by plants; of the rest, part goes to fires and heterotrophic respiration and part becomes slower-cycling soil organic carbon.

entries.title: Clearing forests, releasing carbon

definition.text: The release of land carbon to the atmosphere when people clear or convert vegetation, chiefly by turning forest into farmland or towns.

facts.text: Since the invention of agriculture, people have shifted the carbon cycle over centuries by changing the mix of vegetation on land.
Cropland and urban land store comparatively little carbon, so replacing forest with them leaves more carbon in the atmosphere.
Land-use change has also cut biodiversity, lowering ecosystems' resilience and their ability to remove carbon from the air.
The effect can be reversed, deliberately or naturally, by reforestation.

entries.text: Replace a forest with cropland or a town, and carbon once stored on land ends up in the atmosphere. Cropland and urban land store comparatively little carbon. That release, chiefly from turning forest into farmland or towns, is the carbon cost of land-use change. Since the invention of agriculture, people have shifted the carbon cycle over centuries by changing the mix of vegetation on land. The change has also cut biodiversity, lowering ecosystems' resilience and their ability to remove carbon from the air. Reforestation, deliberate or natural, can reverse the effect.

entries.title: Frozen ground on the high mountains

definition.text: Permafrost found at high elevations, in mountains cold enough to keep the ground frozen year after year.

facts.text: Extensive alpine permafrost generally needs a mean annual air temperature of −3 °C, though some mountains hold it at −1 °C.
It is hard to study, and systematic research began only in the 1970s; in 2009 permafrost was even found on Mount Kilimanjaro.
Regional estimates collected in 2014 put its global extent at 3,560,000 km2, with the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau the largest area at 1,300,000 km2.
Subsurface alpine permafrost can lie beneath warmer soil that supports vegetation.

entries.title: Building on frozen ground without thawing it

definition.text: Engineering methods for building on permafrost without thawing the frozen ground that supports the structure.

facts.text: Heat from a building or pipeline can thaw the soil, and as ice turns to water the ground loses its ability to support the structure.
Norilsk and Yakutsk, both in Russia, are the only two large cities built on continuous permafrost.
Wood pile foundations, pioneered by Mikhail Kim in Norilsk, should reach 15 metres, where the temperature stays at about −5 °C all year.
Other methods are gravel pads 1–2 m thick and ammonia heat pipes, as in the supports of the Trans-Alaska Pipeline.

entries.title: From a blocked well in Yakutsk to a world science

definition.text: The development of permafrost science from early Siberian reports to modern international collaboration.

facts.text: One of the earliest reports dates to 1684, when permafrost stopped well digging in Yakutsk; until the mid-20th century most of the literature was in Russian.
Karl Ernst von Baer, often called the founder of scientific permafrost research, published from 1838 and wrote the first permafrost textbook in 1843.
Siemon William Muller's 1943 report coined the English word permafrost from permanently frozen ground, translating the Russian vechnaia merzlota.
The First International Conference on Permafrost met at Purdue University in November 1963, and the International Permafrost Association was created in 1983.

entries.title: Massive ground ice, frozen soil that is mostly ice

definition.text: Permafrost so rich in ice that ice exceeds 250 percent of the dry soil by mass.

facts.text: Massive icy beds are at least 2 m thick and 10 m across, and range from icy mud to pure ice.
Of the four kinds of ground ice, pore ice, ice wedges, buried surface ice and intrasedimental ice, only the last two grow large enough to count as massive.
Segregational ice, the main intrasedimental type, forms as water migrates to the freezing front, mostly in silts of low salinity.
Forming it in the top 2.5 m takes 1–1000 years in clay, 10–10,000 years in peat and 1,000–1,000,000 years in silt.

entries.title: Yedoma, Ice Age permafrost packed with carbon

definition.text: Ice-rich, organic-rich permafrost of Pleistocene age, about 2% carbon by mass with 50–90% ice by volume.

facts.text: It covers more than one million square kilometers from northeast Siberia to Alaska and Canada, in many places tens of meters thick.
It forms in poorly drained, severely cold lowlands with ice wedge polygons, sparse vegetation, intense periglacial weathering and nearby sediment sources.
It may hold about 210 to 500 Gt of carbon, a multiple of yearly fossil fuel emissions.
Thawing yedoma is a significant methane source, about 4 Tg of CH4 per year.
At the end of the last ice age, thawing yedoma and its thermokarst lakes may have produced 33 to 87% of the high-latitude rise in atmospheric methane.

verification.title: Deep Yedoma permafrost: A synthesis of depositional characteristics and carbon vulnerability
verification.evidence: Based on incubation experiments, up to 10% of the Yedoma carbon is considered especially decomposable and may be released upon thaw.
verification.note: the paper's 10% is the readily decomposable share of Yedoma carbon; the entry gives Yedoma's share of deglacial methane rise (33-87%)

entries.text: Yedoma covers more than one million square kilometers from northeast Siberia to Alaska and Canada, in many places tens of meters thick. It is ice-rich, organic-rich permafrost of Pleistocene age, about 2% carbon by mass and 50–90% ice by volume. It forms in poorly drained, severely cold lowlands with ice wedge polygons, sparse vegetation, intense periglacial weathering and nearby sources of sediment. Yedoma may hold about 210 to 500 Gt of carbon, a multiple of yearly fossil fuel emissions. As it thaws it becomes a significant methane source, about 4 Tg of CH4 a year. It has done this before. At the end of the last ice age, thawing yedoma and its thaw lakes may have caused 33 to 87% of the high-latitude rise in atmospheric methane.

entries.title: How deep permafrost goes, and how slowly

definition.text: The depth at which Earth's geothermal heat balances the mean surface temperature at 0 °C, marking the bottom of permafrost.

facts.text: Base depth ranges from less than a meter to 1,493 m in the northern Lena and Yana River basins of Siberia.
Permafrost forms much more slowly after the first few metres: at Prudhoe Bay it reaches 4.44 m after 1 year but 687.7 m only after 775,000 years.
The deep permafrost at Prudhoe Bay, Alaska, took over half a million years to form, spanning several Pleistocene glacial cycles.
Permafrost in soil conducts heat less well than in bedrock, so it is less affected by the geothermal gradient.

entries.title: Polygons, slumps and mounds: the shapes of frozen ground

definition.text: The surface features built by freezing, cracking and thawing of permafrost ground.

facts.text: Thermal contraction cracks that become ice wedges, and solifluction downslope, create polygons, rings, steps and other patterned ground.
Melting ground ice in ice-rich permafrost starts thermokarst landforms: thermokarst lakes, thaw slumps, thermal-erosion gullies and active layer detachments.
Meltwater trapped over deep permafrost in Arctic bogs freezes into ice lenses that push the ground up into mounds.
These grow into palsas, peat mounds 15–150 m long but under 6 m tall, and larger pingos, 3–70 m high and up to 1,000 m across.

entries.title: Thawing ground under Arctic towns and roads

definition.text: The threat that thawing permafrost poses to settlements, roads, pipelines and buildings built on frozen ground.

facts.text: As of 2021, 1162 settlements with about 5 million people sit on Arctic permafrost, and the permafrost below 42% of them is expected to thaw by 2050.
By 2050 nearly 70% of infrastructure in permafrost areas could be at high risk, including 30–50% of critical infrastructure, at costs of tens of billions of dollars.
In Alaska alone, damages by 2100 would reach $4.6 billion under the high-emission RCP8.5 scenario.
The Qinghai–Tibet Plateau is warming at twice the global rate, 40% of its permafrost is already warm, and around 30% of its roads are damaged.

entries.title: Toxic waste and mercury waiting in the ice

definition.text: Toxic waste and natural mercury held in frozen ground that thaw could release into the environment.

facts.text: For much of the 20th century permafrost was thought to preserve buried material indefinitely, so it became a popular site for hazardous waste disposal.
About 4500 industrial facilities handle hazardous chemicals in Arctic permafrost areas, and 13,000 to 20,000 heavily contaminated sites, 70% in Russia, are trapped in it.
An estimated 800,000 tons of mercury are frozen in permafrost soil; around 70% is taken up by vegetation after thaw.
Under RCP8.5, enough mercury would reach the Yukon River basin by 2050 to make its fish unsafe to eat under EPA guidelines.

entries.title: Ice Age life waiting in the frozen ground

definition.text: The survival of ancient microbes and plant tissue in frozen ground, and their possible revival when permafrost thaws.

facts.text: Dormant bacteria and inactive viruses have raised concerns that thaw could free unknown pathogens of humans, livestock or crops.

In 2012 Russian researchers revived Silene stenophylla from 30,000-year-old tissue in an Ice Age squirrel burrow, the oldest plant tissue ever revived.
