entries.title: Subsea permafrost, the Ice Age land the sea drowned

definition.text: Permafrost beneath the seabed of polar continental shelves, on land exposed during the Last Glacial Maximum and since flooded.

facts.text: It formed on land during the last Ice Age, when sea levels were low, and has slowly declined since being submerged under warmer, saltier conditions.
Today it covers an estimated 2 million km2, about a fifth of the land permafrost domain and 30–50% less than at the Last Glacial Maximum.
It holds around 560 GtC in organic matter and 45 GtC as methane, releasing 18 and 38 MtC a year in a millennial-scale response to post-glacial warming.
Under RCP 8.5 it could release 43 GtC by 2100 and 190 GtC by 2300, though human-driven effects will show only after hundreds or thousands of years.

entries.title: Drunken trees and sliding slopes on thawing ground

definition.text: The weakening and movement of ground as its permafrost ice thaws and drains.

facts.text: As meltwater drains or evaporates, soil structure weakens and can turn viscous; trees tilting at random, so-called drunken trees, are a visible sign.
Warming has increased slope disturbances on permafrost, sharply raising sediment loads in rivers, and thaw can also drain and dry northern wetlands.
In high mountains thaw reduces slope stability by building pore-water pressure, leading to slope failure and rockfalls such as the 1987 Val Pola landslide.
Thaw also forms frozen debris lobes, slow landslides of soil, rock, trees and ice; 43 were identified in Alaska's southern Brooks Range by December 2021.

entries.title: Methanotrophs, the microbes that eat methane

definition.text: Bacteria or archaea that use methane as their source of carbon and energy.

facts.text: They live in wetlands, soils, marshes, rice paddies and landfills, mostly near methane sources, though some oxidize atmospheric methane.
By cutting the methane that reaches the atmosphere, they play a significant role in the global methane budget.
Aerobic methanotrophs combine oxygen and methane to form formaldehyde, built into organic compounds, and carbon dioxide; the first step uses methane monooxygenase enzymes.
Type I methanotrophs tend to dominate cold, oxygen-poor, methane-rich settings; Type II are more stress-tolerant and dominate methane-limited and acidic ones.
In anoxic soils, rice paddies and sediments, some methanotrophs oxidize methane using nitrate, nitrite, iron, sulfate or manganese instead of oxygen.

entries.text: Some microbes make their living from the very gas that methanogens release. Methanotrophs are bacteria or archaea that use methane as their source of both carbon and energy. They live in wetlands, soils, marshes, rice paddies and landfills, mostly close to methane sources, though some oxidize methane straight from the atmosphere. By cutting the methane that reaches the air, they play a significant part in the global methane budget. Aerobic methanotrophs combine oxygen with methane. Enzymes called methane monooxygenases perform the first step. The products are formaldehyde, which is built into organic compounds, and carbon dioxide. Two groups divide the territory. Type I methanotrophs tend to dominate cold, oxygen-poor, methane-rich settings. Type II are more stress-tolerant and dominate methane-limited and acidic ones. In anoxic soils, rice paddies and sediments, some methanotrophs oxidize methane with nitrate, nitrite, iron, sulfate or manganese instead of oxygen.

entries.title: The root fungi that hold much of the soil's carbon
entries.article: Mycorrhizal fungi and soil carbon storage

definition.text: The part that root-associated mycorrhizal fungi play in building, keeping and losing the soil carbon pool.

facts.text: Mycorrhizal fungi live symbiotically with the roots of almost all plants and are emerging as important to maintaining soil carbon, alongside plants, decomposers and minerals.
Plants send an estimated 5 to 20% of their carbon uptake to these fungi, whose biomass can rival that of fine roots in some ecosystems.
On forested islands in Sweden, mycorrhizal fungi hold 50 to 70 percent of the carbon stored in leaf litter and soil.
Their biomass turns over quickly and in some ecosystems is the main route by which living carbon enters the soil carbon pool.
Arbuscular and ectomycorrhizal fungi are phylogenetically distinct and often act in very different ways, so evidence is weighed separately for each.
Their effect on fine root decay is equivocal: ectomycorrhizal colonization speeds it in some ecosystems but slows it in Pinus edulis roots.

entries.title: Rewetting wetlands to keep their carbon locked away

definition.text: Restoring wetlands and peatlands so that they keep sequestering carbon and storing water.

facts.text: It has moderate to great mitigation potential on limited land, with low trade-offs and costs; wetlands store about 45 million tonnes of carbon a year.
Some wetlands are significant sources of methane, and some also emit nitrous oxide.
Peatland covers just 3% of the land surface but stores up to 550 gigatonnes of carbon, 42% of all soil carbon.

entries.title: The greenhouse gases that rise from farms and fields

definition.text: The greenhouse gases released by farming, including from agricultural soils and from clearing land for crops.

facts.text: Agriculture, forestry and land use contribute between 13% and 21% of global greenhouse gas emissions.
Direct emissions come from rice and livestock farming, and indirect ones from converting forests and other land to farmland.
Nitrous oxide and methane make up over half of direct agricultural greenhouse gas emissions.
Emissions from farm soils depend on soil type, climate and management; conservation tillage, precision agriculture, better water use and biochar can cut them and store soil carbon.
Deforestation, rice methane, cattle methane and fertilizer nitrous oxide together make up 54% of methane emissions, about 80% of nitrous oxide emissions and nearly all land-use CO2.
Making and using nitrogen fertilizer gives about 5% of human greenhouse emissions, two thirds of it during use, as soil bacteria turn nitrate into nitrous oxide.
Long-flooded rice soils cannot take in oxygen, so organic matter ferments to methane; better water management, such as wetting and drying, can cut this by up to 90%.
Reduced tillage, returning crop residues to the soil and more cover crops can lower farm carbon dioxide emissions.

entries.title: How a warming climate wears down soil fertility
entries.article: Effects of climate change on agriculture#Erosion and soil fertility

definition.text: The decline in soil quality expected as warming brings heavier rain and faster decay of soil organic matter.

facts.text: A more vigorous water cycle with extreme rainfall makes erosion, soil degradation and compaction more likely; erosion can strip up to 22% of soil carbon in 50 years.
Warmer soils decompose organic matter faster, lowering soil organic carbon and the soil's ability to hold nutrients and water.
Soil microbe populations could rise 40–150%, and warmth would favour certain bacteria, shifting community composition.
Elevated carbon dioxide would speed plant and microbial growth, slowing the soil carbon cycle and favouring slow-growing, efficient oligotrophs over copiotrophs.

entries.text_plain: Erosion can strip up to 22% of soil carbon in 50 years, and a warmer world gives it more chances. A more vigorous water cycle brings extreme rainfall, making erosion, compaction and a general decline of the soil more likely. Warmth works below ground too. Warmer soils decompose organic matter faster, lowering soil organic carbon and with it the soil's hold on nutrients and water. Soil microbe populations could rise 40–150%, and warmth would favor certain bacteria, shifting the community's makeup. Extra carbon dioxide would speed plant and microbial growth and slow the soil carbon cycle. It would favor slow-growing, efficient microbes called oligotrophs over copiotrophs, which thrive where food is plentiful.

entries.title: Rising seas and the rice fields at the shoreline
entries.article: Effects of climate change on agriculture#Agricultural land loss from sea level rise

definition.text: The loss of low-lying farmland to flooding, erosion and salt as sea levels rise.

facts.text: Erosion, shoreline submergence and a saltier water table would affect farming mainly by inundating low-lying land, especially in South East Asia.
Bangladesh, India and Vietnam face major rice losses; a one-metre rise would cover several square kilometres of Vietnam's rice paddies.
Sea level rise also drives saltwater into freshwater wells, which become unusable once saltwater exceeds 2–3%.

entries.title: New farmland in the thawing far north
entries.article: Effects of climate change on agriculture#Thawing of potentially arable land

definition.text: The prospect that climate change will open new farmland as frozen ground in the far north thaws.

facts.text: A 2005 study reported that Siberia had warmed by three degrees Celsius on average since 1960, much more than the rest of the world.
A 2025 study of Arctic Western Siberia projects more permafrost thaw by 2100 and a northward shift of the permafrost zone's southern boundary.
Reports on Russian agriculture expect farmland to extend northward but warn of possible productivity losses and greater drought risk.
The Arctic is expected to gain opportunities for agriculture and forestry.

entries.title: Climate tipping points
entries.article: Tipping points in the climate system

definition.text: A critical threshold that, when crossed, leads to large, accelerating and often irreversible changes in the climate system.

facts.text: A small disturbance can cause a disproportionately large change, and self-reinforcing feedbacks can make the change irreversible on a human timescale.
Thawing permafrost releasing methane and melting ice sheets lowering albedo are examples; crossing one threshold can trigger another in cascading tipping points.

Three types are bifurcation-induced, noise-induced and rate-induced tipping; only bifurcation-induced tipping shows early warning signals such as critical slowing down, rising autocorrelation and variance.
Early IPCC assessments held tipping points likely only at about 4 degC or more of warming above preindustrial.

entries.title: How thaw lets ancient Arctic carbon escape
entries.article: Permafrost carbon cycle#Carbon release from the permafrost

definition.text: The escape of long-stored carbon from thawing permafrost soils to the atmosphere as microbes decompose it.

facts.text: Arctic warming deepens the active layer, exposing carbon stored for decades to millennia to microbial processes that release it into the air.
Warming also intensifies the Arctic water cycle, and more warm rain deepens thaw further.
How much is released depends on thaw depth, the carbon content of thawed soil, physical change and microbial and plant activity.
Once thawed, ground will not return to permafrost for centuries even if warming reverses.
A 1993 study found the tundra had been a carbon sink until the late 1970s but had since become a net carbon source.
The 2019 Arctic Report Card estimated net release of 0.3 to 0.6 Pg C a year, winter emissions exceeding growing-season uptake by vegetation.
A 2022 study of atmospheric records from 1980 to 2017 challenged this, finding permafrost regions had been gaining carbon on net.
Methane lasts under 12 years in the air but warms around 80 times more than CO2 over 20 years, so the gas released matters as much as the carbon amount.

entries.contested_note: Studies disagree on whether permafrost regions are already a net carbon source: the 2019 Arctic Report Card estimated a net release, while a 2022 study of atmospheric records found a net gain.

conflicts.text: Methane's global warming potential is about 28 times larger than that of CO2 over a 100-year period.
conflicts.note: Permafrost page; this page gives between 28 and 40 times over 100 years (S:07938da4807f).

entries.text: Some Arctic carbon has sat frozen for decades, some for millennia. Warming is setting it loose. As the Arctic heats up, the active layer, the soil that thaws each summer, grows deeper. That exposes long-stored carbon to microbes, whose decomposition releases it into the air. Warming also intensifies the Arctic water cycle, and more warm rain deepens the thaw further. The amount that escapes depends on four things. They are how deep the thaw goes, the carbon content of the thawed soil, physical changes to the ground, and the activity of microbes and plants. The change lasts. Once thawed, ground will not return to permafrost for centuries, even if warming reverses. Whether the region already gives off more than it takes in is contested. A 1993 study found the tundra had been a carbon sink until the late 1970s and a net carbon source since. The 2019 Arctic Report Card estimated a net release of 0.3 to 0.6 Pg C a year. Winter emissions, it found, exceeded what vegetation takes up in the growing season. But a 2022 study of atmospheric records from 1980 to 2017 found permafrost regions had been gaining carbon on net. The form of the carbon matters too. Methane lasts under 12 years in the air but warms around 80 times more than CO2 over 20 years. So which gas escapes matters as much as how much carbon.

entries.title: The permafrost carbon feedback: thaw that feeds itself

definition.text: The warming caused when thawing permafrost releases its stored carbon as carbon dioxide and methane, which in turn drives more thaw.

facts.text: Northern circumpolar permafrost holds organic matter equal to 1400–1650 billion tons of carbon, about twice the carbon in the atmosphere.
Most of it, ~1,035 billion tons, lies in near-surface permafrost no deeper than 3 metres, but only a fraction is expected to reach the atmosphere.
Even under the RCP8.5 scenario of over 4 °C warming, about 5% to 15% of permafrost carbon is expected to be lost over decades and centuries.
Aerobic respiration releases CO2 and anaerobic respiration methane; methane will be a small share of the carbon yet cause 40–70% of the 21st-century warming from thaw.
Arctic greening will offset some emissions, but very unlikely all of them, while more Arctic wildfires can speed permafrost carbon release.
The IPCC Sixth Assessment Report estimates releases equal to 14–175 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide per 1 °C of warming.
There is widespread agreement that permafrost emissions will be smaller than human emissions and too small to cause runaway warming.
Gradual thaw would add around 0.09 °C by 2100 if warming is held to 2 °C; abrupt collapse near 4 °C of warming could add 0.2–0.4 °C.

entries.contested_note: Whether permafrost thaw is a global tipping point is debated: thaw is self-perpetuating locally, but in aggregate it proceeds gradually with warming.

entries.title: Counting the carbon locked in frozen soils

definition.text: The amount of organic carbon held in permafrost-region soils and deposits, more than twice the carbon in the atmosphere.

facts.text: Soil organic carbon in the northern circumpolar permafrost region is estimated at around 1,460–1,600 Pg; with the Tibetan Plateau, Northern Hemisphere permafrost holds around 1832 Gt.
By depth, the top 0–30 cm holds about 200 Pg, the top 0–100 cm about 500 Pg and the top 0–300 cm about 1024 Pg of organic carbon.
These estimates more than doubled the carbon previously known in permafrost soils.
Yedoma (400 Pg) and Arctic deltaic deposits (240 Pg) add more carbon, generally deeper than the 3 m of traditional studies.
In 2003 Tarnocai and colleagues estimated carbon stocks in cryosols, soils with permafrost within two meters of the surface, from the Northern and Mid Latitudes Soil Database.

entries.title: Thermokarst, the hollow land left by melting ground ice

definition.text: Irregular terrain of marshy hollows and small hummocks formed when ice-rich permafrost thaws.

facts.text: It occurs in Arctic areas and on a smaller scale in mountains such as the Himalayas and Swiss Alps; the name comes from its resemblance to limestone karst.
Thermokarst lakes form in thaw depressions in permafrost with over 30% ice by volume, and tend to form and drain in a cycle.
Thaw lakes warm the ground beneath them, so permafrost below is shallower and a talik is present under deep enough lakes.
Forming thaw lakes is a positive feedback, releasing methane, nitrous oxide and carbon dioxide from thawing permafrost.

entries.text: When ice-rich permafrost thaws, the ground sags into a jumble of marshy hollows and small hummocks. This terrain is called thermokarst, a name that comes from its resemblance to karst, the pitted landscape of dissolving limestone. It occurs across Arctic areas and, on a smaller scale, in mountains such as the Himalayas and the Swiss Alps. Where permafrost holds over 30% ice by volume, thaw depressions fill with water and become thermokarst lakes. These lakes tend to form and drain in a cycle. Each one warms the ground beneath it, so the permafrost below is shallower, and unfrozen ground ({{ref:soil-env-150}}) lies under lakes that are deep enough. The lakes also feed the warming. As permafrost thaws around them it releases methane, nitrous oxide and carbon dioxide, a positive feedback that drives more thaw.

entries.title: Taliks, the ground that never freezes in permafrost country

definition.text: A zone of ground that stays unfrozen all year within a permafrost area.

facts.text: In continuous permafrost, taliks often lie under shallow thermokarst lakes and rivers whose deep water does not freeze in winter.
They are classed as closed, open or through, depending on whether permafrost surrounds them, they open at the top, or they also connect to unfrozen ground below the permafrost.
One study suggests open taliks are more widespread in fault zones and near large rivers.

entries.text: Even in permafrost country, some ground stays soft all winter. A talik is a zone that remains unfrozen all year within a permafrost area. In continuous permafrost, taliks often lie under shallow lakes in thaw hollows, described in {{ref:soil-env-153}}, and under rivers whose deep water does not freeze in winter. Taliks come in three kinds. A closed talik is surrounded by permafrost. An open talik opens at the top. A through talik also connects to unfrozen ground below the permafrost. One study suggests open taliks are more widespread in fault zones and near large rivers.

entries.title: The soil carbon sponge that drinks the rain

definition.text: Porous, well-aggregated, healthy soil that absorbs and holds water well.

facts.text: The Australian scientist Walter Jehne set out the idea in his 2017 paper Regenerate Earth, linking soil carbon to a restored water cycle that could cool the planet.
A soil carbon sponge is much lighter, about 1 gram/cc, than the parent mineral soil at 2.6–3.5 grams/cc.
Bare soils, heavy cultivation, fertilizers, biocides and irrigation speed oxidation of soil carbon and shrink the sponge; fire and flooding also harm it.
Afforestation, reforestation and cover cropping build the sponge, which also serves as a carbon sink.

entries.text: Healthy topsoil weighs about 1 gram/cc. The parent mineral soil beneath it weighs 2.6–3.5 grams/cc. The light, porous, well-aggregated layer is what the Australian scientist Walter Jehne called a soil carbon sponge: soil that soaks up water and holds it well. In his 2017 paper Regenerate Earth he linked soil carbon to a restored water cycle that could cool the planet. Bare soil, heavy cultivation, fertilizers, biocides and irrigation speed the oxidation of its carbon and shrink the sponge. Fire and flooding harm it too. Afforestation, reforestation and cover cropping build it back, and the growing sponge also serves as a carbon sink.

entries.title: Thaw depth, how far summer reaches into frozen soil

definition.text: The level down to which soil has warmed to zero degrees Celsius at a given moment, separating thawed soil from frozen soil below.

facts.text: The active layer thickness is the maximum thaw depth over two years.
Maximum air temperature is the main control: the active layer is only 10 cm on Ellesmere Island, about 2.5 m at Yakutsk and 5 meters at Yellowknife.
Coarse sandy or gravelly parent material conducts heat better, giving active layers up to five times deeper than in loam- or clay-rich material.
Vegetation and soil organic matter alter bulk density and so thermal conductivity; thaw depth matters for both ecology and construction.

entries.text: On Ellesmere Island summer thaws the ground only 10 cm deep. At Yakutsk it reaches about 2.5 m, and at Yellowknife 5 meters. Thaw depth is the level down to which soil has warmed to zero degrees Celsius at a given moment, with frozen soil below. Its maximum over two years is the active layer thickness. Maximum air temperature is the main control, but the ground matters too. Coarse sandy or gravelly parent material conducts heat better, giving active layers up to five times deeper than in loam- or clay-rich material. Vegetation and soil organic matter change bulk density and so thermal conductivity, how well soil carries heat. Thaw depth matters for both ecology and construction.

entries.title: Permafrost that grows upward as the ground builds up

definition.text: Growth of permafrost upward as new material is deposited on a site under freezing conditions.

facts.text: It is an efficient mode of growth compared with heterogenetic growth, in which cold penetrates previously unfrozen ground of uniform composition.
The new material comes from river sediment, debris fallen from hillsides, wind-blown material and lake-bottom deposits.
It is one of the two main processes that store carbon in permafrost, burying organic and mineral soil as the permafrost surface rises.
Ice wedges growing upward into permafrost cracks can count as syngenetic; studies draw on the permafrost tunnel near Fairbanks, Alaska.

entries.text: Frozen ground does not only thaw. It can also grow upward. When new material piles onto a site under freezing conditions, the frozen ground rises to take it in. This syngenetic growth is efficient compared with heterogenetic growth, in which cold works down into unfrozen ground of uniform composition. The new layers come from river sediment, debris fallen from hillsides, wind-blown material and lake-bottom deposits. As the surface rises it buries organic and mineral soil, making this one of the two main ways permafrost stores carbon. Ice wedges growing upward into permafrost cracks can count as syngenetic too. Studies draw on the permafrost tunnel near Fairbanks, Alaska.

entries.title: Carbon dioxide, the main gas from thawing permafrost

definition.text: The carbon dioxide released by aerobic microbial respiration in thawed permafrost soils, the bulk of permafrost emissions.

facts.text: Most permafrost soils are oxic, so carbon dioxide makes up the overwhelming majority of permafrost and Arctic emissions.
Early 2020s studies show soil microbes respire mostly modern carbon in the growing season but live on ancient carbon in winter.
Plants on thawed ground root deeper, grow larger and take up more carbon, generally the main counteracting feedback.
Wildfires on thawed land burn off the insulating organic mat, warming the soil and deepening the active layer.

entries.contested_note: Researchers debate whether rising permafrost emissions come mainly from ancient frozen carbon or from faster respiration of modern plant litter in warmer soils.
entries.text: Most permafrost soils hold oxygen, so their microbes breathe out carbon dioxide. That gas makes up the overwhelming majority of permafrost and Arctic emissions. Studies from the early 2020s add a twist. In the growing season soil microbes respire mostly modern carbon, but in winter they live on ancient carbon. Researchers debate whether rising emissions come mainly from that old frozen carbon or from faster respiration of fresh plant litter in warmer soils. Plants push back. On thawed ground they root deeper, grow larger and take up more carbon, generally the main counteracting feedback. Wildfires push the other way, burning off the insulating organic mat, warming the soil and deepening the active layer.

entries.title: Two ways plant carbon ends up frozen underground

definition.text: The two processes, syngenetic permafrost growth and cryoturbation, that carry plant-derived carbon down into permafrost for storage.

facts.text: Permafrost makes no carbon itself; organic carbon from plants must enter the soil and then be incorporated into the frozen ground.
In syngenetic growth the surface rises by wind or river sediment or peat, up to 0.5mm/yr for peat and 0.7mm/yr for sediment, burying carbon into permafrost.
Cryoturbation, mixing by freeze–thaw cycles and most often frost heaving, moves surface carbon down until it is incorporated into permafrost.
Storage rates increase when cryoturbation and sediment deposition act together.

entries.title: Methane from waterlogged thaw and Arctic lakes

definition.text: The methane produced by anaerobic microbes in waterlogged thawed permafrost, especially under thermokarst lakes.

facts.text: Methanogenesis needs thoroughly anaerobic conditions, so it centres on Arctic lakes, where 2022 observations show at least half of the methane made reaches the air.
A 2015 review found anaerobic sites emitted 75–85% less than aerobic ones, but a 2018 incubation study found methane matched CO2 once methanogens were established.
A 2017 paper found that less than 10% of methane from thawing peatlands came from old, thawed carbon, the rest from decomposition of modern carbon.
Peatland methane from thaw starts high, at 82 milligrams per square meter per day, then falls nearly threefold as the permafrost bog matures.

entries.contested_note: The sources call the rate and trajectory of methane production in thawed permafrost a matter of continuing scientific debate.

entries.title: Arctic methane and a feedback still taking shape

definition.text: Methane released in the Arctic, mainly from thawing permafrost, melting sea ice, clathrate breakdown and the melting Greenland ice sheet, which adds to atmospheric methane.

facts.text: It is a positive climate feedback: thaw exposes organic material to methanogenesis, and methane is a powerful greenhouse gas.
Permafrost holds almost twice as much carbon as the atmosphere, with about 20 Gt of permafrost-associated methane trapped in clathrates.
A 2024 assessment put Arctic-Boreal land emissions at about 48.7 Tg of methane a year, with marine sources adding about 4.9 Tg.
Methanogenesis needs fully anaerobic conditions; a 2015 review found anaerobic thaw sites emitted 75-85% less in total than aerobic ones.
A 2018 seven-year incubation found methane production matched CO2 once methanogenic microbes became established at anaerobic sites.
Thermokarst lakes are frequent methane sources, and at least half the methane made in them reaches the atmosphere.
Radiocarbon dating suggests 0.2 to 2.5 Pg of permafrost carbon was released as methane and CO2 over the last 60 years.
No evidence ties the Arctic to the methane rise since about 2018, which points to tropical wetlands, but its role will very likely grow.

entries.title: Putting numbers on permafrost's future emissions

definition.text: Projections of the total greenhouse gases that thawing permafrost will release over this century and beyond.

facts.text: Preliminary 2011 analyses put permafrost emissions at around 15% of human emissions, but could not account for abrupt thaw.
A 2020 study found northern permafrost peatlands, 3.7 of the 18 million km2, would cause ~1% of human radiative forcing by 2100 and become net carbon sinks within 200 years.
A 2021 estimate including abrupt thaw gave 150–200 billion tonnes of CO2 equivalent by 2100 at 1.5 °C of warming, 220–300 at 2 °C and 400–500 above 4 °C.
A 2022 assessment found abrupt thaw adds 50% to gradual rates, 14 billion tons of CO2 equivalent by 2100 per degree of warming.

entries.title: Counting the carbon that land use adds and removes
entries.article: Land use, land-use change, and forestry

definition.text: The greenhouse gas inventory sector covering emissions and removals that result from human land use, land-use change and forestry.

facts.text: LULUCF activities can add carbon dioxide to or remove it from the atmosphere through their effects on the carbon cycle, but are difficult to measure.
The IPCC estimates land-use change, such as turning forest into farmland, adds a net 1.6 ± 0.8 Gt of carbon a year, against 6.3 ± 0.6 Gt from fossil fuels and cement.
Updated assessments put LULUCF emissions at 1.1 ± 0.7 Gt C (4.1 ± 2.6 Gt CO2) a year over 2014–2023.
Under Kyoto, accounting is mandatory for afforestation, reforestation and deforestation, and voluntary for forest, cropland and grazing land management.
Land-use change also alters albedo and evapotranspiration; a 2021 study found it affected 17% of land in 1960–2019.

entries.text: Clearing a forest for farmland releases carbon that no smokestack ever emitted. Greenhouse gas inventories record it in a sector called land use, land-use change and forestry, or LULUCF. It covers the emissions and removals that result from how people use land, change its use and manage forests. These activities can add carbon dioxide to the atmosphere or take it out, through their effects on the carbon cycle, but they are hard to measure. The IPCC estimates that land-use change, such as turning forest into farmland, adds a net 1.6 ± 0.8 Gt of carbon a year. Fossil fuels and cement add 6.3 ± 0.6 Gt. Updated assessments put LULUCF emissions at 1.1 ± 0.7 Gt of carbon, or 4.1 ± 2.6 Gt of carbon dioxide, a year over 2014–2023. Under the Kyoto rules the activities fall into two classes. Accounting is mandatory for afforestation, reforestation and {{ref:soil-env-269}}. It is voluntary for managing forests, cropland and grazing land. Carbon is not the whole story. Land-use change also alters albedo and evapotranspiration, and a 2021 study found it had affected 17% of land between 1960 and 2019.

entries.title: Abrupt thaw, when frozen hillsides collapse in days

definition.text: Rapid thaw by hillside collapse (retrogressive thaw slumps) and thermokarst lake formation, which can expose deep soil to microbes within days.

facts.text: After a 2020 Siberian heatwave, thaw slumps on the northern Taymyr Peninsula rose 17-fold, from 82 to 1404, and soil carbon mobilization 28-fold.
Abrupt thaw adds between 60 and 100 gigatonnes of carbon by 2300, raising emissions by ~125–190% over gradual thaw alone.
It often raises the share of methane over carbon dioxide, a major source of uncertainty in projections of permafrost methane.
Climate models long focused on gradual thaw because abrupt thaw is hard to model.
In 2019, three permafrost sites expected to stay frozen for 70 more years under the intermediate RCP4.5 pathway had already thawed abruptly.
Methane from peatlands after thaw starts high, 82 milligrams per square metre per day, but falls nearly threefold as the bog matures.

entries.text: In 2020 a heatwave struck Siberia. Afterward, thaw slumps on the northern Taymyr Peninsula rose 17-fold, from 82 to 1404, and the soil carbon they mobilized rose 28-fold. This is abrupt permafrost thaw. Hillsides collapse in retrogressive thaw slumps, and thermokarst lakes form, exposing deep soil to microbes within days. Climate models long focused on gradual thaw, because the abrupt kind is hard to model. Some sites have not waited for the models. In 2019, three permafrost sites expected to stay frozen for 70 more years under the intermediate RCP4.5 pathway had already thawed abruptly. The stakes are large. Abrupt thaw adds between 60 and 100 gigatonnes of carbon by 2300, raising emissions by ~125–190% over gradual thaw alone. It often raises methane's share relative to carbon dioxide, a major source of uncertainty in projections of permafrost methane. In peatlands, methane after thaw starts high, 82 milligrams per square metre per day, but falls nearly threefold as the bog matures.

entries.title: Black carbon, the charcoal hidden in soil

definition.text: Fire-derived carbon, from vegetation fires or deposited from the air, held in soil as charcoal particles and soot.

facts.text: Black carbon typically makes up 1 to 6%, and up to 60%, of the organic carbon stored in soils.
In tropical soils it serves as a reservoir of nutrients, and soils without much black carbon are significantly less fertile.
Terra preta soils of central Amazonia, rich in black carbon, average three times more soil organic matter than surrounding soils.
Slash-and-burn adds black carbon to soil, but slash-and-char would avoid high emissions of CO2 and volatile black carbon.

conflicts.text: Soil organic carbon is typically 5–50% derived from char, with levels above 50% in mollisol, chernozem and terra preta soils.

entries.title: Pereletok, the frost that outlasts a summer

definition.text: A layer of frozen ground that stays frozen through several summers but eventually thaws.

facts.text: The Russian word means that which survives over the summer; it is also called intergelisol.
Frozen ground is sometimes split into permafrost, pereletok and seasonally frozen ground by how long it stays frozen.
Pereletok can be seen as part of the active layer that stays frozen after an unusually cool summer or cold winter.
The line between pereletok and permafrost is not universally defined and is hard to draw in the field.

entries.title: How soils form in the thin layer that thaws
entries.article: Active layer#Soil formation in the active layer

definition.text: The cold-climate soil-forming processes, dominated by frost churning, that act in the seasonally thawed layer above permafrost.

facts.text: Cryoturbation dominates and tends to make the active layer uniform in composition.
Yet soils vary markedly with parent rock, because weathering is so slow in the very cold climate.
Slow decomposition makes gelisols, the permafrost soils, an important sink for carbon dioxide.
This stored carbon means permafrost thaw may accelerate global warming, especially if the carbon predates the recent glacial maxima.

entries.text: Above permafrost, the ground churns itself. Cryoturbation, mixing by freezing and thawing, dominates soil formation in the active layer and tends to make it uniform. Yet these soils still vary markedly with their parent rock, because weathering is so slow in the very cold climate. Decay is slow too. That makes gelisols, the permafrost soils, an important sink for carbon dioxide. The same stored carbon is a hazard. Permafrost thaw may accelerate global warming, especially if the carbon predates the recent glacial maxima.

entries.title: The compost bomb, a proposed runaway in peat

definition.text: A proposed tipping point at which warming triggers runaway, explosive releases of soil carbon from peatlands.

facts.text: It was identified in a 2011 study, whose authors noted a unique stable soil carbon equilibrium for any fixed atmospheric temperature.
Climate models do not account for the heat released by microbes as they decompose organic matter.
Peatlands are predicted to shift from carbon sink to source this century, yet they are still left out of the main Earth system models.

entries.text: Microbes release heat as they decompose organic matter, yet climate models do not account for it. A 2011 study identified a possible consequence, the compost-bomb instability. It is a proposed tipping point at which warming triggers runaway, explosive releases of soil carbon from peatlands. The authors noted that for any fixed atmospheric temperature, soil carbon has a unique stable equilibrium. Peatlands are predicted to shift from carbon sink to source this century. Even so, they are still left out of the main Earth system models.

entries.title: Carbon cycle feedbacks, mostly on the side of cooling

definition.text: The positive and negative climate feedbacks that come from Earth's carbon cycle, mostly negative so far.

facts.text: Land and ocean sinks absorb around half of current emissions; the fraction could rise to three-quarters if emissions fall, or drop to one-third by 2100 if they rise.
If emissions stay very high after the 21st century, land ecosystems would become a net carbon source.
Through CO2 fertilization, more CO2 raises plant productivity, and plants lose less water through their stomata.
Chemical weathering removes CO2 over the geological long term and is increasing with current warming.

entries.text: So far, Earth's carbon cycle has mostly worked against warming. Land and ocean sinks absorb around half of current emissions. That fraction could rise to three-quarters if emissions fall, or drop to one-third by 2100 if they rise. Through CO2 fertilization, more carbon dioxide raises plant productivity, and plants lose less water through their stomata, the pores in their leaves. Over the geological long term, chemical weathering removes CO2, and current warming is increasing it.

entries.title: How long biochar keeps its carbon locked away

definition.text: How long the carbon locked in biochar stays stored before returning to the atmosphere, the key measure of its durability as carbon removal.

facts.text: Multi-pool models give biochar in soil a centennial to millennial turnover, depending on feedstock, production conditions, application rate and site.
Biochar made above 600 °C resembles the stable coal maceral inertinite; under certain conditions 97% of its organic carbon is highly refractory.
For biochar made at 350–800 °C the labile carbon fraction falls from about 16% to 1%, and incubation experiments have mostly measured the decay of that fraction.
Some studies report sub-centennial turnover, but re-analysis finds the common two-pool decay model badly parameterised, so permanence is generally underestimated.

entries.contested_note: Some studies report biochar turnover within a century, while re-analyses argue that the decay models behind those estimates are flawed and permanence is underestimated.
entries.text: Biochar counts as carbon removal only if the carbon stays put. Its permanence is how long that carbon remains stored before returning to the atmosphere. Multi-pool models give biochar in soil a turnover of centuries to millennia, depending on feedstock, production conditions, application rate and site. Biochar made above 600 °C resembles inertinite, a stable component of coal. Under certain conditions 97% of its organic carbon is highly refractory, meaning it resists decay. The question is not settled. Some studies report turnover within a century. Re-analyses argue that the common two-pool decay model behind them is badly parameterised, so permanence is generally underestimated. Part of the trouble is what gets measured. Incubation experiments have mostly tracked the labile, easily decayed fraction, which falls from about 16% to 1% across production temperatures of 350–800 °C.

entries.title: Selling biochar's stored carbon as credits

definition.text: Certified credits sold for carbon dioxide removed by producing biochar and storing it durably, traded on voluntary carbon markets.

facts.text: Because abatement costs are high, biochar credits trade at prices an order of magnitude above credits from emission reductions.
In 2024 biochar projects made up 86% of the volume of carbon dioxide removal purchases.
Standards such as the European Biochar Certificate list permissible feedstocks, and certified suppliers must be carbon net-negative.

entries.title: How weathering rock pulls carbon from the sky
entries.article: Enhanced weathering#Natural mineral weathering and ocean acidification

definition.text: The natural removal of atmospheric CO2 when carbonic acid in rain and groundwater dissolves silicate and carbonate minerals.

facts.text: For silicate weathering, theory gives 1 mol of CO2 sequestered for each mol of Ca2+ or Mg2+ released, though natural ratios vary with temperature and CO2 pressure.
Carbonate weathering followed by carbonate precipitation sequesters no net CO2.
Dissolved bicarbonate travels through soil and groundwater to the ocean, where organisms build carbonate shells; over geological time this is thought to stabilize climate.
The reactions reverse when carbonate meets acids, as in soils; liming acid soils neutralizes hydrogen ions but releases CO2 from the limestone.

Liming acid soil neutralizes hydrogen ions but releases CO2 from the limestone.

entries.title: Enhanced weathering: crushed rock as a carbon trap

definition.text: A carbon dioxide removal method that speeds up natural weathering by spreading finely ground silicate rock, such as basalt, so that it reacts with water and air.

facts.text: Through carbonic acid it removes CO2 from the atmosphere and stores it permanently in solid carbonate minerals or as ocean alkalinity.
Methods are land-based, such as in-situ carbonation of silicates, or ocean-based; ultramafic rock could store hundreds to thousands of years' worth of CO2 emissions.
Mine tailings and alkaline industrial wastes such as steel slag or biomass ash could serve first, though more basalt mining might eventually be needed.
Mixing crushed silicate rock into soil can benefit plant health as well as carbon sequestration when calcium or magnesium is present.
In July 2020 a group of scientists judged that spreading finely crushed basalt on fields has potential for national carbon dioxide removal.
A 2020 analysis put its cost on cropland at US$80–180 per tonne of CO2, comparable to BECCS (US$100–200) and direct air capture (US$100–300).
It could remove 2–4 Gt of CO2 per year, with cost estimates in the US$50–200 per tonne range.

entries.title: Mineral carbonation, turning rock and CO2 into stone

definition.text: The deliberate dissolution and carbonation of silicate minerals to lock CO2 into carbonate.

facts.text: It was first proposed by Seifritz in 1990 and developed by Lackner and colleagues and the Albany Research Center.
Early work reacted crushed silicates at about 180 °C and 15 MPa of CO2 in reactors; in-situ methods inject CO2 into silicate rock formations instead.
Research has mostly targeted CO2 from flue gas, but with CO2 taken from the air it could serve as geoengineering.
Soil remineralization with crushed rock contributes to the same enhanced weathering process.

entries.text: In 1990 Seifritz proposed locking carbon dioxide into rock on purpose. Mineral carbonation dissolves silicate minerals and turns them into carbonate, which holds the CO2. Lackner and colleagues and the Albany Research Center developed the idea. Early work reacted crushed silicates in reactors at about 180 °C and 15 MPa of CO2. In-situ methods instead inject CO2 into silicate rock formations. Research has mostly targeted CO2 from flue gas, the exhaust of furnaces and boilers. Using CO2 taken from the air instead, it could serve as geoengineering. Soil remineralization with crushed rock contributes to the same process of enhanced weathering.

entries.title: Spreading rock dust on land and the questions it raises

definition.text: Enhanced weathering done on land by spreading crushed silicate minerals over the ground surface.

facts.text: How fast the rock dissolves depends on its reactive surface area, the pH and buffer capacity of the receiving soil and soil biological activity, though rates remain uncertain.
Weathering slows as the soil solution saturates, so some argue low rainfall limits it, while others say new minerals or plant uptake keep weathering going.
The energy needed to grind the rock depends on how quickly it dissolves.
A 2012 study found a wide range of possible costs, mostly because dissolution rates are uncertain.

entries.title: The unfrozen gap that warming opens above permafrost

definition.text: An unfrozen layer that forms between the seasonally frozen surface and the permafrost when summer-thawed ground fails to refreeze in winter.

facts.text: Unlike ordinary taliks, which are usually tied to water bodies, it results from climate warming.
Warming produces it in moderately cold regions; colder regions just thaw deeper in summer, and warm, shallow permafrost simply disappears.
With rising air temperature or snow depth the talik thickens until the deep permafrost vanishes.
This type of talik has recently been observed in Russia.

entries.text: Sometimes ground that thaws in summer fails to refreeze in winter. An unfrozen layer then opens between the seasonally frozen surface and the permafrost below: a supra-permafrost talik. Ordinary taliks are usually tied to lakes and rivers, but this one results from climate warming. It forms in moderately cold regions. Colder regions simply thaw deeper in summer, and warm, shallow permafrost just disappears. As air temperature or snow depth rises, the talik thickens until the deep permafrost vanishes. This type of talik has recently been observed in Russia.

entries.title: How root fungi build crumbs that guard carbon
entries.article: Mycorrhizal fungi and soil carbon storage#Effects on soil aggregation

definition.text: The way mycorrhizal fungi help bind soil into aggregates that physically shield organic carbon from microbial decay.

facts.text: Because aggregates protect organic carbon from soil microbes, more aggregate formation can mean more soil carbon storage.
Much evidence shows arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi increase aggregate formation, possibly through the protein glomalin.
Even if glomalin itself decays readily, it may still store carbon by promoting aggregates that protect other organic matter.
Ectomycorrhizal fungi have only anecdotal links to aggregation in sand bags, with no evidence yet that they aid aggregates in field soils.

entries.title: When root fungi starve the decomposers
entries.article: Mycorrhizal fungi and soil carbon storage#Inhibition of decomposition

definition.text: The slowing of soil carbon decomposition when ectomycorrhizal fungi compete with free-living decomposers for nutrients or water.

facts.text: The first report, in 1971, came from Pinus radiata plantations in New Zealand, where excluding roots and their fungi led to net carbon loss.
Several later studies found ectomycorrhizal fungi reduce decomposer activity and so increase soil carbon storage.
A theoretical model shows that fungal access to organic nitrogen should slow decomposition by leaving decomposers nutrient-limited.
Koide and Wu (2003) argued that competition for soil water may matter more than competition for nutrients.

entries.title: When root fungi feed the decomposers instead
entries.article: Mycorrhizal fungi and soil carbon storage#Stimulation of decomposition (priming)

definition.text: The speeding-up of soil carbon decomposition when mycorrhizal fungi feed free-living decomposers with easily used carbon compounds.

facts.text: Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi have been shown to increase soil carbon decomposition in nutrient-rich patches.
Since they are thought to lack the enzymes to do this themselves, they are believed to stimulate decomposers by exuding labile energy substrates.
Lab experiments show soils with arbuscular fungi lose more carbon than soils without them, and the gap widens under elevated CO2.
Evidence for ectomycorrhizal priming is inconclusive: field data suggest faster carbon loss, but lab tests show root exudation falls as ectomycorrhizal colonization rises.

entries.title: Do tough fungal tissues keep carbon in the soil
entries.article: Mycorrhizal fungi and soil carbon storage#Recalcitrance of mycorrhizal tissues

definition.text: The idea that how slowly mycorrhizal fungal tissue decays helps set how long its carbon stays in soil.

facts.text: Glomalin, made only by arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, accumulates in some soils and may be a substantial share of their carbon.
Later experiments found arbuscular fungi cause net soil carbon losses, and proteomics showed most glomalin-extracted proteins are not mycorrhizal, so its role is likely overestimated.
Chitin was thought to slow decay of ectomycorrhizal tissue, but Fernandez and Koide (2012) found it does not decompose more slowly than other compounds.

entries.contested_note: Whether glomalin adds much to soil carbon is disputed: early work reported large stores, while later experiments and protein analyses suggest the contribution is overestimated.

entries.title: Letting rice paddies dry out to cut methane

definition.text: A controlled, intermittent irrigation method for lowland rice in which fields are allowed to dry for a few days before being re-flooded, instead of being kept under standing water.

facts.text: In 'safe' AWD a perforated tube shows the water table; when it falls 15 cm below the soil surface the field is re-flooded to 5 cm, and it stays flooded at flowering.

Letting the water drop below the surface periodically ends the anaerobic conditions that produce methane; seasonal CH4 emissions fell by up to 85%, and the 2006 IPCC methodology assumes an average 48% cut.
It saves about 38% of water without harming yields, and periodic soil drying lowers arsenic and cadmium in the grain.
Its main drawback is higher nitrous oxide emissions; it suits areas where soils can be drained in 5-day intervals, mainly in the dry season.

entries.text: Rice need not stand in water all season. Alternate wetting and drying, or AWD, lets lowland rice fields dry for a few days before they are flooded again. AWD also saves about 38% of water without harming yields, and drying lowers arsenic and cadmium in the grain. The main drawback is higher nitrous oxide emissions. It suits areas where soils can be drained in 5-day intervals, mainly in the dry season.

entries.title: Compost bomb instability in peatlands
entries.article: Tipping points in the climate system#Mathematical theory > Rate-induced tipping

definition.text: Rate-induced tipping in peatlands that can cause an explosive release of soil carbon to the atmosphere.

facts.text: Rate-induced tipping occurs when an environmental change is faster than the force restoring the system to its stable state.
In peatlands, after years of relative stability, it can produce an explosive release of soil carbon, sometimes called compost bomb instability.

entries.title: Permafrost thaw and its tipping dynamics
entries.article: Tipping points in the climate system#Tipping points in the cryosphere > Permafrost thaw

definition.text: Permafrost thaw releases CO2 and methane as microbes decompose newly unfrozen organic matter, a self-reinforcing feedback that is not expected to cause a global tipping point.

facts.text: Permafrost holds nearly twice as much carbon as the atmosphere.

Most thaw is gradual over centuries, but ice-rich permafrost can thaw abruptly, slumping or forming thermokarst lakes over years to decades, with self-sustaining local dynamics that could raise greenhouse gas emissions by around 40%.

entries.title: Three escape routes for wetland methane
entries.article: Greenhouse gas emissions from wetlands#Pathways of methane emission

definition.text: The three routes by which methane made in wetland soils reaches the air: molecular diffusion, transport through plant aerenchyma, and ebullition.

facts.text: The water table marks the boundary between anaerobic methane production below and aerobic methane consumption above; a low water table forces methane past methanotrophs.
Diffusion is slow through peat full of undecayed organic matter, and matters more in drier, loosely packed soils, since methane moves faster through soil than water.
Aerenchyma, porous tissue in some plants, lets methane shunt straight from the roots to the air, bypassing oxidation.
In ebullition, methane builds up in soil pockets until the pressure bursts, releasing it too fast for methanotrophs to consume it; piezometers detect these pockets.

entries.text: Methane made in a wetland soil still has to get out, and it has three routes. The water table marks the boundary. Below it, in soil without oxygen, methane is produced; above it, in aerated soil, methanotrophs consume it. A low water table forces rising methane past these microbes. The first route is molecular diffusion. It is slow through peat full of undecayed organic matter and matters more in drier, loosely packed soils, since methane moves faster through soil than through water. The second runs through aerenchyma, porous tissue in some plants. It shunts methane straight from the roots to the air, bypassing oxidation. The third is ebullition, or bubbling. Methane builds up in soil pockets until the pressure bursts them, releasing it too fast for methanotrophs to consume. Piezometers detect these pockets.

entries.title: What decides how much wetland methane escapes
entries.article: Greenhouse gas emissions from wetlands#Controlling factors

definition.text: The factors, chiefly water table, temperature, substrate and ecosystem production, that set how much wetland methane reaches the atmosphere.

facts.text: Net flux depends mainly on how much methane made by methanogens reaches the surface before methanotrophs oxidize it.
Large methane fluxes have followed drought-driven drops in the water table; with water at or above the surface, ebullition and plant transport dominate.
Soil temperature sets microbial production and consumption rates, and with the water table drives seasonal cycles.
Soils rich in acetate or hydrogen and CO2 favour methane production; steady cellulose and a soil pH of about 6.0 are optimal.

entries.text: A wetland's methane output is a race between makers and eaters. Net flux depends mainly on how much methane made by methanogens reaches the surface before methanotrophs oxidize it. Four controls set the result: water table, temperature, substrate and ecosystem production. Large fluxes have followed drought-driven drops in the water table. With water at or above the surface, bubbling and transport through plants dominate. Soil temperature sets how fast microbes produce and consume methane, and with the water table it drives seasonal cycles. Substrate matters too. Soils rich in acetate, or in hydrogen and carbon dioxide, favor production, and a steady supply of cellulose and a soil pH of about 6.0 are optimal.

entries.title: Draining a wetland can cut methane, or raise it
entries.article: Greenhouse gas emissions from wetlands#Human development of wetlands

definition.text: The mixed effect on methane emissions of draining wetlands for development, housing and farming.

facts.text: Lowering the water table increases methane consumption by soil methanotrophs and can turn a wetland from a methane source into a sink.
Drainage ditches that stay saturated, especially when drains are too close together, become warm wet mini-wetlands that emit much methane.

entries.text: Wetlands are drained for development, housing and farming, and the effect on methane is mixed. Lowering the water table increases methane consumption by soil methanotrophs. That can turn a wetland from a methane source into a sink. The drains themselves can undo the gain. Ditches that stay saturated, especially when drains sit too close together, become warm, wet mini-wetlands that emit much methane.

entries.title: Wetland nitrous oxide, flowing both ways
entries.article: Greenhouse gas emissions from wetlands#Nitrous oxide fluxes

definition.text: The exchange of nitrous oxide between wetland soils and the air, which can run in either direction.

facts.text: Nitrous oxide has a global warming potential 300 times that of CO2 and is the leading ozone-depleting emission of the 21st century.
Excess nutrients, mostly from human sources, raise wetland soil N2O fluxes through denitrification and nitrification.
Measured fluxes range from 0.14 to 23.83 μmol N2O m−2 h−1 in mangroves of Shenzhen and Hong Kong, and negative fluxes, caused by soil consumption, are common.

entries.text: Nitrous oxide has a global warming potential 300 times that of carbon dioxide. It is also the leading ozone-depleting emission of the 21st century. Wetland soils exchange it with the air in either direction. Excess nutrients, mostly from human sources, raise the outward flux through denitrification and nitrification. In mangroves of Shenzhen and Hong Kong, measured fluxes ranged from 0.14 to 23.83 micromoles of nitrous oxide per square meter per hour. Negative fluxes are common as well: the soil consumes the gas instead of releasing it.

entries.title: Computer models that put soil into the climate

definition.text: Computer models that represent the land surface, including vegetation, soil and terrain, within simulations of climate and the carbon and water cycles.

facts.text: A land surface model combining vegetation cover, soil type and terrain with rainfall data estimates how much water soaks into the ground and how much becomes streamflow.
Earth system models extend climate models to include the biosphere and land use change.
They predict a wide range of future land and ocean carbon uptake even under identical emission scenarios.
Peatlands are still omitted from the main Earth system models, although their carbon balance is expected to shift from sink to source this century.

entries.text: Climate forecasts need a ground floor. Land surface models represent vegetation, soil and terrain inside simulations of climate and the carbon and water cycles. Such a model combines vegetation cover, soil type and terrain with rainfall data. It then estimates how much water soaks into the ground and how much becomes streamflow. Earth system models go further, extending climate models to include the biosphere and land use change. Even under identical emission scenarios, they predict a wide range of future carbon uptake by land and ocean. One gap stands out. The main Earth system models still omit peatlands, although peatland carbon balance is expected to shift from sink to source this century.

entries.title: Soils that swallow methane

definition.text: The consumption of methane, including atmospheric methane, by methanotrophic microbes in soils, which makes soils a natural methane sink.

facts.text: Converting forests and natural land to farmland raises soil nitrogen, which inhibits methane oxidation by methanotrophs.
Changing the water table directly shifts a soil between acting as a methane source or sink.
Lowering a wetland's water table increases soil methanotroph consumption and can turn it into a methane sink.
Nutrient-supplemented landfill cover soils can act as small methane sinks as abundant methanotrophs consume methane.

entries.text: Soil can soak up methane as well as release it. Methanotrophic microbes in soils consume methane, including methane from the atmosphere, which makes soils a natural methane sink. Land use can weaken that sink. Converting forests and natural land to farmland raises soil nitrogen, which inhibits methane oxidation by methanotrophs. Water decides the balance most directly. Changing the water table shifts a soil between methane source and sink, and lowering a wetland's water table can make it a sink. Even landfills can help: nutrient-supplemented cover soils, rich in methanotrophs, can act as small methane sinks.

entries.title: Rewetting drained peatlands by blocking the drains

definition.text: Returning a drained peatland to its original waterlogged state so peat-forming vegetation recovers and peat can accumulate again.

facts.text: It keeps the soil moist and slows drainage by blocking and filling canals and digging deep wells.
Peat dams are built from stable, impermeable, erosion-resistant unoxidized peat dug from the channel bottom.
Plastic dams of interlocking piling can hold deep pools but work only on peat, not on mineral soil.

entries.text: A drained peatland heals by getting wet again. Peatland rewetting returns the land to its original waterlogged state, so peat-forming vegetation recovers and peat can accumulate once more. Workers keep the soil moist and slow drainage by blocking and filling canals and digging deep wells. Peat itself makes good dams. Unoxidized peat dug from the channel bottom is stable, impermeable and resistant to erosion. Plastic dams of interlocking piling can hold deep pools, but they work only on peat, not on mineral soil.

entries.title: Paludiculture: farming a peatland that stays wet

definition.text: Rewetting drained peatlands while continuing to farm them with crops suited to wet conditions.

facts.text: Raising the water table restores the peatland ecosystem that stores large amounts of carbon, so the land serves as both carbon sink and farmland.
Possible crops include berries, herbs, timber and biomass for biofuel.
Degraded farmed peatlands are often nutrient-rich; paludiculture can remove the excess nutrients over time, a cheaper alternative to stripping the topsoil.

entries.text: Rewetting a peatland need not end farming on it. Raising the water table restores a peatland ecosystem that stores large amounts of carbon. The same land then serves as both carbon sink and farmland. It can also fix an old problem. Degraded farmed peatlands are often nutrient-rich, and paludiculture can remove the excess nutrients over time, a cheaper alternative to stripping the topsoil.

entries.title: The Cuvette Centrale peatland in the Congo Basin
entries.article: Tipping points in the climate system#Tipping points in terrestrial systems > Vulnerable stores of tropical peat carbon: Cuvette Centrale peatland

definition.text: A Congo Basin peatland found in 2017 that is the most vulnerable store of tropical peat carbon in the world.

facts.text: It holds about 30 petagrams of carbon, 28% of all tropical peat carbon, equal to all trees in the other 96% of the Congo Basin even though it covers only 4%.
Burning all of it would release the equivalent of three years of all anthropogenic CO2 emissions.
Only 8% of this peat carbon lies within existing protected areas, while 26% is open to logging, mining or palm oil.
Its climate is already drier than other tropical peatlands, and conditions 7,500 to 2,000 years ago were dry enough to release substantial peat, so it could become a climate tipping point.

entries.text:
Found in 2017, the Cuvette Centrale in the Congo Basin is the most vulnerable store of tropical peat carbon in the world, a kind of soil described in {{ref:soil-class-081}}.

Its size is striking. It holds about 30 petagrams of carbon, 28% of all tropical peat carbon. That equals all the trees in the other 96% of the Congo Basin, even though the peatland covers only 4%. Burning all of it would release the equivalent of three years of all anthropogenic CO2 emissions.

Protection is thin. Only 8% of this peat carbon lies within existing protected areas, while 26% is open to logging, mining or palm oil.

The climate adds to the risk. It is already drier than that of other tropical peatlands, and conditions 7,500 to 2,000 years ago were dry enough to release substantial peat. For that reason the Cuvette Centrale could become a climate tipping point, of the kind described in {{ref:soil-env-322}}.

entries.title: Soil degradation: when a stable soil starts to slide

definition.text: A regressive change in which a stable soil loses its equilibrium; more broadly, any disturbance to a soil judged harmful or undesirable.

facts.text: Degradation, also called pedolysis, departs from natural soil evolution: climax vegetation is replaced by secondary plant communities, which changes the amount and makeup of humus.
Degradation is directly tied to human activity, whereas its companion process, retrogression, is driven mainly by soil erosion.
Soil erosion is the main factor in soil degradation, acting through water erosion, wind erosion, chemical degradation and physical degradation.
Roads add impermeable surfaces that cause runoff and soil loss; overgrazing, monoculture, row cropping, tillage, crop removal and land-use conversion speed up erosion.
Soils naturally reach high productivity and then decline as mineral nutrients are removed, so older soils are more vulnerable to induced degradation.
Globally, the quality of 33% of pastureland, 25% of arable land and 23% of forests has deteriorated over the last 30 years; 3.2 billion people depend on this land.
Erosion, compaction, lowered fertility and contamination remain serious concerns for agricultural soils.

entries.text: Over the last 30 years, the quality of 33% of the world's pastureland has deteriorated. So has that of 25% of its arable land and 23% of its forests, and 3.2 billion people depend on this land. Soil degradation is the name for that slide. Strictly, it is a regressive change in which a stable soil loses its equilibrium. More broadly, it is any disturbance to a soil judged harmful or undesirable. Degradation, also called pedolysis, departs from the natural course of soil formation. Secondary plant communities replace the mature vegetation, and the amount and makeup of humus change with them. Degradation is tied directly to human activity, while its companion process, {{ref:soil-env-059}}, is driven mainly by erosion. Erosion is still the main factor, acting through water erosion, wind erosion, and chemical and physical decline. Roads add impermeable surfaces that shed runoff and soil. Grazing too many animals, monoculture, row cropping, tillage, crop removal and land-use conversion all speed erosion. Age matters too. Soils naturally climb to high productivity and then decline as mineral nutrients are removed, so older soils are more vulnerable to damage people cause. On farms, erosion, compaction, lowered fertility and contamination remain serious concerns.

entries.title: Land degradation: when land loses its power to provide

definition.text: A process in which land becomes less healthy and productive through human activities or natural conditions.

facts.text: The 2005 Millennium Ecosystem Assessment defined it as the reduction or loss of the biological or economic productivity of drylands.
The FAO describes it as a persistent decline in land's ability to sustain ecosystem functions and services, driven by deforestation, overgrazing and unsustainable farming.
Human activities, above all unsustainable land management, are usually the main cause; natural hazards are excluded, though people can indirectly affect floods and wildfires.
It reduces agricultural productivity, causes biodiversity loss and can reduce food security and water security.
It can weaken the land's natural capacity to store and filter water, leading to water scarcity.
Its impacts range from subtle productivity losses to the complete abandonment of farmland.
What one group sees as degradation another may see as an opportunity: a steep, rainy slope worries scientists about erosion but may promise farmers high yields.
In 2007 up to 40% of the world's agricultural land was estimated to be seriously degraded, and the UN estimated the global economy could lose $23 trillion by 2050.

entries.title: Deforestation and the soil left behind

definition.text: The clearing of a forest or stand of trees and conversion of the land to non-forest uses such as farms, ranches or towns.

facts.text: Forests now cover about 31% of Earth's land, one-third less than before agriculture spread, with half that loss in the last century.
Agriculture is by far the main direct cause: in 2025 nearly 90% of global deforestation came from cropland expansion and pasture creation.
Topsoil often erodes once forests are cleared, raising sediment in rivers; tree roots bind soil, so cleared slopes become more prone to landslides.
Clearing alters soil microbial communities and reduces soil properties such as hydraulic conductivity, with sandier soils hit harder than clayey ones.
In an Amazon simulation, surface and soil temperatures rose by 1 to 3 °C after clearing, and changed soil properties could turn the soil into a carbon source.
Repeated slash-and-burn with shortened fallows leaves less vegetation and lower soil biomass on burned land.

entries.text: Forests now cover about 31% of Earth's land, one-third less than before agriculture spread. Half of that loss came in the last century. Deforestation is the clearing of a forest or stand of trees and the conversion of the land to non-forest uses such as farms, ranches or towns. Agriculture is by far the main direct cause. In 2025 nearly 90% of global deforestation came from cropland expansion and the creation of pasture. The soil feels the change quickly. Topsoil often erodes once the trees are gone, and rivers carry more sediment. Tree roots bind soil, so cleared slopes become more prone to landslides. Clearing also alters soil microbial communities and reduces soil properties such as hydraulic conductivity, and sandier soils suffer more than clayey ones. In a simulation of the Amazon, surface and soil temperatures rose by 1 to 3 °C after clearing. The changed soil properties could even turn the soil into a carbon source. Repeated slash-and-burn with shortened fallows, the rest periods between crops, leaves less vegetation and lower soil biomass on burned land.

entries.title: What drives land degradation, near and far

definition.text: The many interrelated human and natural drivers of land degradation, both proximate and underlying.

facts.text: Proximate drivers are biophysical factors and unsustainable land management; underlying drivers are social, economic and institutional.
Land degradation is largely tied to agriculture, deforestation and climate change; clearcutting and overlogging are among the land-clearance causes.
More than 1 660 Mha, over 10 percent of the world's land area, has been degraded by unsustainable land use and management, more than 60% of it on cropland and pasture.
Leaving soil bare after harvest and deep plowing deplete nutrients; areas under conventional tillage degrade 5-10 times faster than no-till areas.
Monocultures, overgrazing beyond the livestock carrying capacity and inappropriate irrigation also degrade land.
Soil pollution from littering, urbanization, mining, oil spills, pesticides, herbicides, fertilizers and animal waste adds to the damage.
High population density is not always linked to degradation; it is people's practices that degrade a landscape.

entries.title: How much of Earth's land is wearing out

definition.text: How much of the world's land is degraded and how many people live on it, as estimated by the UN, the IPCC and others.

facts.text: The IPCC's 2019 Special Report on Climate Change and Land put about a quarter of Earth's ice-free land under human-induced degradation (medium confidence).
Erosion from farm fields runs 11 to 20 times (no-tillage) to more than 100 times (conventional tillage) faster than soil forms.
In 2014 the UN estimated that around 30% of land was degraded, with around 3.2 billion people living in the degrading areas.
About 120,000 km2 of productive land, roughly the size of Greece, is degraded every year, through exploitation without planning for long-term sustainability.
In 2024 the UN claimed that 75% of soils are degraded to some extent; the share might rise to 90% by 2050 if current trends continue.
In 2025 around 1.7 billion people lived where degradation causes sizeable crop yield losses, nearly 1 billion of them in middle-income countries.
Eastern and Southern Asia hold the largest affected populations, combining a large accumulated degradation debt with high population densities.
In 2021 two-thirds of Africa's productive land was claimed to be severely affected by land degradation.

entries.title: The bill for degraded land: harvests, water and lives

definition.text: The harm degraded land and soil cause: lost productivity, food insecurity, water pollution, biodiversity loss, natural hazards and economic costs.

facts.text: Results include lower crop yields, less diverse ecosystems, more vulnerability to floods and droughts, people losing their homes, less food and economic problems.
Productive capacity declines temporarily or permanently, seen as lost biomass, lost actual or potential productivity, or changed vegetation cover and soil nutrients.
Slight degradation cuts yield potential by 10% and moderate degradation by 10–50%; severely degraded soils have lost more than 50% of their potential.
Most severely degraded soils are in developing countries; in Africa yield reduction is 2–40%, an average loss of 8.2% for the continent.
Eroded soil carries nitrogen, phosphorus, farm chemicals and pollutants such as heavy metals into surface water, raising turbidity and risking eutrophication.
Degradation can disturb soil microbes, remove climax vegetation and shrink animal habitat, leading to biodiversity loss; floods degrade soil and degraded soil causes floods.
Degradation sharpens competition for farmland: all except 3 internal conflicts in African states in the 1990s are linked to such competition.
Land degradation is estimated to cost US$44 billion a year, while the annual loss of 76 billion tons of soil costs the world about US$400 billion a year.

Degradation disturbs soil microbes, removes mature vegetation and shrinks animal habitat, so biodiversity falls. Floods degrade soil, and degraded soil causes floods. Scarce farmland breeds conflict: all except 3 internal conflicts in African states in the 1990s are linked to competition for it.

entries.title: Sustainable land management: keeping land in working order

definition.text: Managing land in ways that prevent and reverse its degradation while conserving soil and water.

facts.text: Actions to halt land degradation fall broadly into prevention, mitigation and restoration.
It raises soil moisture and infiltration while cutting runoff, erosion and flood discharge, which supports water security.
Reversing just 10% of human-induced cropland degradation could feed an additional 154 million people a year; restoring abandoned cropland could feed between 292 and 476 million.
Because degradation also harms pastures and wider ecosystem services, restoring land requires collective action to provide these public goods.
Regenerative agriculture aims to reverse degradation through continuous ground cover, minimal soil disturbance, diverse crop rotations and rotational grazing.
Public awareness, education and outreach help people and communities adopt sustainable practices and act as stewards of the land.

entries.title: Soil sealing: burying living ground under asphalt

definition.text: The loss of soil resources when land is covered over for housing, roads or other construction.

facts.text: Topsoil is covered or replaced by asphalt and cement and the layers below are compacted, a mostly irreversible loss of soil ecosystem services.
Sealed land is a serious form of land take; together they cause complete loss of the soil's biological, physical and chemical functions.
Sealed surfaces hinder infiltration and increase surface runoff, and sealing for underground construction alters water movement and weakens the soil's ability to purify water.
Heat-absorbing concrete and asphalt without cooling vegetation create urban heat islands.
Fertile farmland converted to buildings no longer produces food; countries with fast-growing populations and economies are losing notable areas of farmland this way.
Sealing fragments habitats and causes soil biodiversity loss, worsened by falling soil carbon, nitrogen and respiration.
It removes urban green spaces that offer cultural benefits such as recreation, learning and a sense of belonging.
Sealing is assessed with raindrop impact tests in the field and laboratory and with indices such as the NDVI and the Normalized Difference Built-up Index.

entries.text: Pave a field and its soil stops working almost for good. Soil sealing is the loss of soil resources when land is covered over for housing, roads or other construction. Topsoil is covered or replaced by asphalt and cement, and the layers below are compacted. The loss of the soil's ecosystem services is mostly irreversible. Sealing is a serious form of land take, and together they destroy the soil's biological, physical and chemical functions completely. Water suffers first. Sealed ground becomes the kind of surface described in {{ref:soil-water-231}}: it hinders infiltration and increases surface runoff. Sealing for underground construction also alters water movement and weakens the soil's ability to purify water. Heat-absorbing concrete and asphalt, with no vegetation to cool them, create urban heat islands. Fertile farmland under buildings no longer produces food, and countries with fast-growing populations and economies are losing notable areas this way. Sealing fragments habitats and causes soil biodiversity loss, made worse by falling soil carbon, nitrogen and respiration. It also removes urban green spaces that offer recreation, learning and a sense of belonging. Researchers assess sealing with raindrop impact tests in the field and laboratory, and with indices such as the NDVI and the Normalized Difference Built-up Index.
entries.text_plain: Pave a field and its soil stops working almost for good. Soil sealing is the loss of soil resources when land is covered over for housing, roads or other construction. Topsoil is covered or replaced by asphalt and cement, and the layers below are compacted. The loss of the soil's ecosystem services is mostly irreversible. Sealing is a serious form of land take, and together they destroy the soil's biological, physical and chemical functions completely. Water suffers first. Sealed ground becomes the kind of surface described in Impervious surfaces: when the city seals the soil: it hinders infiltration and increases surface runoff. Sealing for underground construction also alters water movement and weakens the soil's ability to purify water. entries.title: Land consumption: open country that never comes back

definition.text: The conversion of land with healthy soil and intact habitats into industrial farmland, roads and especially urban settlements.

facts.text: The European Environment Agency names three land-consuming activities: expansion of built-up area, the extent of land exploited for farming, forestry and other uses, and over-intensive exploitation of farm and forest land.
Because these activities are virtually irreversible, the term land loss is also used; erosion and desertification also cause land loss, mostly traceable to people.
From 1990 to 2000 the U.S. consumed 1.4 million hectares of open space, and Germany consumes more than 70 hectares every day.
Land take in 21 EU countries is estimated at about 1.2 million hectares over 1990–2006.
A region's land footprint, the area needed at home and abroad for what it consumes, can far exceed its own land; Europe depends most on such imported land.
Its effects include habitat loss, loss or contamination of topsoil, compaction that eradicates soil life, and impervious surfaces that disrupt water and biogeochemical cycles.
The land economy still lacks environmental full-cost accounting for the long-term costs of environmental degradation.
