entries.title: Overgrazing: when herds eat faster than grass grows

definition.text: Grazing in which animals eat grass faster than it can grow back, as when pastures are stocked above the livestock carrying capacity.

facts.text: It is thought to be the principal cause of grassland degradation and is a farming activity that causes desertification.
Urbanization leaves less farmland, so farmers pack small plots densely with animals and must gather much grass for long alpine winters.
Rapid eating and constant trampling stop grass regrowing, and the suppressed sward invites rats and insects that further inhibit growth.
It is a main cause of shrub and bush encroachment in grasslands and savannas.
Overgrazing is among the improper farming practices that accelerate soil erosion and degrade land.
Continued overuse leaves soils so poor that only drought-tolerant and early successional plants can grow.
A meta-analysis of 148 studies found most ecosystem functions decline as grazing intensity rises, and aridity weakens the benefits of light grazing.
Hardin's 1968 Tragedy of the Commons used overgrazing as its example, though English common land was historically protected by stinting, a cap on each commoner's animals.

entries.text: Overgrazing is thought to be the principal cause of grassland decline, and it is one of the farming activities that cause desertification. entries.title: Drylands: where evaporation spends nearly every drop

definition.text: Zones defined by scarce water, where precipitation is balanced by evaporation and plant evapotranspiration; UNEP counts tropical and temperate areas with an aridity index below 0.65.

facts.text: Drylands fall into four sub-types: dry sub-humid, semi-arid, arid and hyper-arid lands; the UNCCD leaves hyper-arid zones out of its definition.
They cover 41.3% of Earth's land surface, including 66% of Africa, 40% of Asia, 24% of Europe and 15% of Latin America, and are home to more than 2 billion people.
Drylands include 45% of the world's agricultural land and are among the ecosystems most vulnerable to climate and land-use change.
72% of drylands lie in developing countries, and almost all hyper-arid land does.
Unlike more humid biomes, drylands redistribute water mostly through above-ground runoff.
Arid lands make up about 10% of the world's land; hyper-arid lands cover about 8% and get irregular rain barely above 100 mm.
From 1982 to 2015, 12.6% of the world's drylands degraded because of human-caused climate change, and about 7.6% of global land has shifted to drier conditions.
Pressure to farm marginal drylands brings overgrazing, land exhaustion and overdrafting of groundwater to many poorer countries.

entries.title: Desertification: fertile land turned to desert

definition.text: The gradual degradation of fertile land into arid desert through a combination of natural processes and human activities.

facts.text: Its immediate cause is the loss of most vegetation, driven alone or together by drought, climatic shifts, acid rain, tillage, overgrazing and deforestation for fuel or building materials.
In many environments the rate of erosion and runoff falls exponentially as vegetation cover increases.
Unprotected dry topsoil blows away or washes off in flash floods, leaving infertile lower layers that bake in the sun into an unproductive hardpan.
Some 10–20% of drylands are estimated to be degraded, 6 to 12 million square kilometres are affected, and a billion people are threatened by further desertification.
The most affected areas are the Sahel in Africa, the Gobi Desert and Mongolia in Asia, and parts of South America.
Its effects include sand and dust storms, food insecurity and poverty, and it is recognized as a major threat to biodiversity.
Remedies include improving soil quality, greening deserts, managing grazing, and reforestation and afforestation.
Wind erosion, especially when people raise it far above natural rates, is a major source of desertification, and erosion can end in desertification.

entries.title: The UN treaty built to fight desertification
entries.article: United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification

definition.text: An international convention (UNCCD) to combat desertification and ease the effects of drought through national action programmes backed by international cooperation.

facts.text: The only convention stemming directly from the Rio Conference's Agenda 21, it was adopted in Paris on 17 June 1994 and entered into force in December 1996.
It is the only internationally legally binding framework on desertification, built on participation, partnership and decentralization.
It has 197 parties, including all 193 UN member states and the European Union; Canada withdrew in 2013 and rejoined in 2017.
The Conference of the Parties, of all ratifying governments, is its supreme decision-making body; its sessions were annual from 1997 to 2001 and are biennial since.
A Committee on Science and Technology, with a Group of Experts, sets research priorities and reviews data on the natural and human causes of desertification.
National Action Programmes, developed with local communities, set out the practical steps against desertification in specific ecosystems and are its key instruments.
Its 2018–2030 Strategic Framework, adopted in 2017, aims to restore affected ecosystems, support land degradation neutrality, improve living conditions and strengthen drought resilience.
At COP16 in Riyadh in December 2024, more than US$12 billion was pledged against desertification, land degradation and drought.

entries.contested_note: Sources report debate over how effective the 2006 International Year of Deserts and Desertification, declared to publicise the Convention, was in practice.

entries.title: How land is stripped bare and turned to desert

definition.text: The natural and human factors that strip land of most of its vegetation and turn it into desert.

facts.text: Overgrazing lets livestock feed on land for long periods without replanting grass, leaving it bare to harden in the sun and lose nutrients to the wind.
Overcultivation and monocropping drain soil nutrients; depleted soil loses organic matter and its ability to hold moisture, then hardens and cracks.
Intensive farming to maximize yields needs more fertilizer, pesticides and machinery, and continuous use rapidly depletes soil nutrients.
Population growth turns once-acceptable practices into unsustainable overgrazing, over-farming and deforestation.
The Sahara owes its existence to natural changes in solar insolation from Earth's orbital precession, which alter the West African Monsoon and trigger vegetation and dust feedbacks.
Regional studies find soil health, human activities and weather all contribute, in different balances: in Shaanxi, meteorological factors work against desertification while the soil worsens it.

entries.title: A warming world grows its drylands

definition.text: The role of a warming climate in expanding the world's drylands and driving desertification.

facts.text: Drylands are expected to grow from 38% of the continents in the late 20th century to 50% or 56% by the end of the century under RCP 4.5 and RCP 8.5.
Most of the expansion is expected in southwest North America, the northern fringe of Africa, southern Africa and Australia.
A 2020 attribution study found 6% of the world's drylands underwent desertification between 1982 and 2015, driven by unsustainable land use compounded by human-caused climate change.
Despite average global greening, human-caused climate change has degraded 12.6% (5.43 million km2) of drylands, affecting 213 million people, 93% of them in developing economies.
Research is complex because no single metric captures every aspect of desertification.

entries.title: Do people make deserts? A long-running dispute

definition.text: The dispute over how far local human overexploitation, rather than natural climate variability, drives desertification.

facts.text: Early studies named overgrazing, the overconsumption of vegetation by livestock, as one of the most common causes of desertification.
Sahel drought is now thought to stem mainly from rainfall variability set by sea surface temperatures, which are driven by natural variability, sulphate aerosols and greenhouse gases.
Changing ocean temperatures and lower sulfate emissions have re-greened the Sahel, leading some scholars to call agriculture-induced vegetation loss a minor factor.
Overgrazing by local cattle may have partly driven the mid-Holocene change of the Sahara from savanna to desert.
Studies of critical regions confirm that human activities and soil health join meteorological factors as main contributors to desertification.

entries.contested_note: Sources call the role of local overexploitation in recent desertification controversial, and some scholars treat agriculture-induced vegetation loss as a minor factor.

Overgrazing by local cattle may have partly driven the mid-Holocene change of the Sahara from savanna to desert. Meanwhile, studies of critical regions confirm that human activities and soil health join meteorological factors as main contributors. The weight of each remains disputed.

entries.title: Why halting desertification is harder than it looks

definition.text: Techniques and countermeasures that mitigate or reverse desertification.

facts.text: One barrier is that sustainable practices can cost individual farmers more than they gain, even when they benefit society and the environment.
Lack of political will and of funding for land reclamation and anti-desertification programmes also holds progress back.
Some countries have biodiversity action plans to protect endangered flora and fauna from desertification.
The FAO launched its Drylands Restoration Initiative in 2012 and in 2015 published global guidelines for restoring degraded dryland forests and landscapes.
UN Sustainable Development Goal 15 adds global advocacy for combating desertification and restoring affected land.

entries.title: Greening the desert, one kind of desert at a time

definition.text: Reclaiming deserts and desertified land, with methods matched to each kind of desert.

facts.text: Salt flats in Saudi Arabia's Rub' al Khali are among the most promising sites for seawater agriculture, which needs no freshwater and little energy.
Farmer-managed natural regeneration has reclaimed some 30,000 square kilometers of degraded land in Niger.
Ethiopia's Humbo Assisted Regeneration Project uses these techniques with money from the World Bank's BioCarbon Fund, which backs carbon sequestration in forests and farmland.
Large tree-planting belts are the best-known approach: China's Green Wall and the African Union's Great Green Wall along the Sahara.

entries.title: Fixing, watering and feeding desert soils

definition.text: Techniques that supply water to dryland soils and fix and enrich them to halt desertification.

facts.text: Shelter belts, woodlots and windbreaks of trees and bushes fix the soil, reducing erosion and evapotranspiration; sand fences control drifting sand.
Short of water, clay soils can consolidate instead of staying porous; techniques such as zaï or tillage then still allow crops to be planted.
Contour trenching digs 150 m long, 1 m deep trenches along the contour, edged with stone walls, so water cannot flow and cause erosion.
Plants restore fertility, chiefly nitrogen-fixing legumes, succulents such as Opuntia, and food crops and trees such as grains, barley, beans and dates.
Nitrogen-rich fertilizer also restores fertility, but its cost deters smallholders, so India, Zambia and Malawi subsidize it.
Research centres are inoculating arid-zone trees with mycorrhizal fungi, which greatly enlarge the root surface that gathers nutrients.
Bioengineering soil microbes, especially photosynthesizers, has been modelled as a way to strengthen the cooperative loops between microbes and vegetation in drylands.

entries.title: Climate change and degraded land feed each other
entries.article: Land degradation#Climate change and land degradation

definition.text: The worsening of land degradation by climate change, especially in low-lying coasts, river deltas, drylands and permafrost areas.

facts.text: From 1961 to 2013 the area of drylands in drought grew by more than 1% a year.
In 2015 about 500,000,000 people lived in areas that had undergone desertification during the 1980s–2000s, and they are severely affected by climate change.
Some 74% of the world's poor are reported to be directly affected by land degradation.
Sea-level rise can flood river deltas and low islands with seawater, raising salinity until farming becomes impossible in very low-lying areas.
The 2022 IPCC report found degradation responding more directly to climate change, with all types of erosion and soil organic matter decline increasing.
Degraded land also releases greenhouse gases, which worsens climate change.
Heavy rainfall and extreme weather make erosion, soil degradation and compaction more likely.

entries.title: From bare rock to climax: a soil grows up

definition.text: The steady balance that a soil and its vegetation reach after evolving together, the highest development its environment can produce.

facts.text: Bare rock is colonized first by lichens and mosses, then by herbs, shrubs and forest, while a humus-bearing A horizon and then mineral B horizons form.
Some ecologists call the balanced stage the climax, others the natural potential; succession is the evolution toward it.
Soil evolution cycles last from tens to thousands of years for quickly evolving soils with only an A horizon to more than a million years for slowly developing ones.
The regional climate and its biome set the general course, while parent rock and local drainage explain specialized associations such as peat bogs.

entries.text: On bare rock, lichens and mosses arrive first, then herbs, shrubs and finally forest. Beneath them a humus-bearing A horizon forms, then mineral B horizons. This evolution is succession, and its endpoint is a steady balance between soil and vegetation, the highest development the environment can produce. Some ecologists call it the climax, others the natural potential. The journey takes tens to thousands of years for fast soils with only an A horizon, and more than a million years for slow ones. Regional climate and biome set the general course, while parent rock and local drainage explain specialized cases such as peat bogs.

entries.title: Soil retrogression: sliding back toward bare rock
entries.article: Soil retrogression and degradation#Perturbations of the balance of a soil

definition.text: The reversion of a soil toward pioneer conditions, mainly through erosion of its upper horizons after its vegetation is destroyed.

facts.text: A soil at its climax tends to stay stable: vegetation supplies humus, moves material upward and shields the ground from water and wind, while roots bind its particles.
After a disturbance, secondary succession usually takes over, and it runs much faster than primary succession because a soil already exists.
When vegetation is destroyed on a large scale, by an avalanche or by people, erosion strips the upper horizons; retrogression can be partial or total, leaving bare rock.
Clearing a sloping site exposed to violent rains can destroy its soil completely.

Clearing, excessive cutting, forest grazing and litter raking replace climax vegetation, as when broadleaf forest gives way to moorland or pine plantations; retrogression often stems from very old practices.
Cycles of succession and regression follow each other over short intervals under human action or over long intervals under climatic change.

entries.text: A soil at its climax tends to stay stable. Its vegetation supplies humus, moves material upward and shields the ground from water and wind, while roots bind the particles together. Destroy that cover on a large scale, by an avalanche or by people, and erosion strips away the upper horizons. This reversion toward pioneer conditions is soil retrogression. It can be partial, or total, leaving bare rock. Clearing a sloping site exposed to violent rains can destroy its soil completely. People often drive it more slowly. Clearing, excessive cutting, forest grazing and litter raking replace the climax vegetation, as when broadleaf forest gives way to moorland or pine plantations. Many such cases stem from very old practices. Recovery is possible. After a disturbance, secondary succession usually takes over, and it runs much faster than primary succession because a soil already exists. Succession and regression can follow each other over short intervals under human action, or over long ones as the climate changes.

entries.title: Rebuilding a degraded soil with a dose of clay
entries.article: Soil retrogression and degradation#Soil enhancement, rebuilding, and regeneration

definition.text: Practices that counter erosion and rebuild a degraded soil, chiefly by improving its structure, adding organic matter and limiting runoff.

facts.text: Such techniques can never fully restore a soil, with its fauna and flora, that took more than a thousand years to build.
On low-clay soils in northern Thailand, one application of 200 kg of bentonite per rai (6.26 rai = 1 hectare) helped retain water and nutrients and raised yields by an average of 73%.
A 2008 survey of 250 farmers in northeast Thailand found output 18% higher among clay users, and some had switched to vegetables, which need more fertile soil.
Bentonite applied to degraded sandy soils also reduced the risk of crop failure in drought years.

entries.text: No technique can fully restore a soil, with its fauna and flora, that took more than a thousand years to build. On degraded sandy soils, bentonite also cut the risk of crop failure in drought years.

entries.title: Solar panels that help desert soil recover

definition.text: Pairing solar panels with planted vegetation in deserts to support ecosystem function even where rain is scarce.

facts.text: A 2025 study in the Kubuqi Desert, which gets around 300 mm of rain a year, found microbial counts, soil quality and nutrients improved most under integrated agrivoltaic systems.
Panel shade cut soil temperature and evaporation, the panels acted as windbreaks that stopped sand burying plants, and with the vegetation they created a better microclimate.
A 2 GW project in Inner Mongolia plans to apply this at scale to restore vegetation, stabilize dunes and weaken dust storms.

entries.title: More than 100 ways to define desertification

definition.text: The competing formal definitions of desertification, of which more than 100 existed by 2005.

facts.text: The UNCCD defines it as land degradation in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid regions resulting from factors including climatic variations and human activities.
That definition ties desertification to land use and land management and highlights its economic, social and environmental implications.
The original idea that desertification meant the physical expansion of deserts has been rejected as the concept evolved.
Sub-groupings such as 'man-made desert' and 'non-pattern desert' are also disputed.

entries.title: Desertification raises the dust

definition.text: Storms of wind-blown sand and dust that become more frequent as desertification leaves more loose material for the wind to pick up.

facts.text: Global annual dust emissions rose 25% between the late nineteenth century and the present day.
Middle Eastern dust storms are becoming more frequent and intense as long-term rainfall decline lowers soil moisture and plant cover.
Dust storms contribute to respiratory disorders such as pneumonia and asthma, pollute open water and can halt most transport.
Airborne dust scatters sunlight and warms the atmosphere, shortening cloud lifetimes and reducing rainfall, which can worsen desertification.

entries.title: Drylands feed the world, and they are shrinking

definition.text: The threat desertification poses to global food security by shrinking the land that can be farmed sustainably.

facts.text: 44% of agricultural land is in drylands, and it supplies 60% of the world's food production.
Food demand keeps growing with population while desertification removes sustainable farmland, so demand may soon exceed supply.
Climate change, land degradation and population growth have worsened violent herder–farmer conflicts in Nigeria, Sudan, Mali and other Sahel countries.

The squeeze has already turned violent. Climate change, land degradation and population growth have worsened herder–farmer conflicts in Nigeria, Sudan, Mali and other Sahel countries.

entries.title: Desertification and the road from farm to slum

definition.text: The deepening poverty of dryland communities as desertification lowers land productivity and pushes people off the land.

facts.text: Investors avoid low-potential arid zones, and without infrastructure, markets and suitable techniques most such zones are excluded from development.
When rural land can no longer support its population, people migrate to cities, particularly in Africa, creating unemployment and slums.
Environmental refugees in sub-Saharan Africa are projected to rise from 14 million in 2010 to nearly 200 million by 2050.
In Mongolia, where the land is 90% fragile dryland, many herders migrate to the city for work.

entries.title: South America's spreading dry ground

definition.text: Desertification across South America, where 25% of the land is drylands and over 68% has suffered soil erosion from deforestation and overgrazing.

facts.text: Between 27 and 43% of the land in Bolivia, Chile, Ecuador and Peru is at risk of desertification.
In Argentina, Mexico and Paraguay more than half the land is degraded by desertification and cannot be farmed.
Rural Mexico loses about 1,000 km2 of land a year to desertification, and drought in Central America has driven unemployment, food insecurity and migration.

entries.title: The Gobi, Earth's fastest-growing desert

definition.text: The spread of the Gobi Desert across northern China and southern Mongolia, the fastest-expanding desert on Earth.

facts.text: The Gobi turns over 3,600 km2 of grassland into wasteland each year, and large sand dunes are forming only 70 km from Beijing.
About 13% of Mongolia's desertification is put down to natural factors and the rest mainly to overgrazing and erosion of cultivated soils; over 70% of its land is degraded.
From 1940 to 2015 Mongolia's mean air temperature rose by 2.24 °C while precipitation fell by 7%, making conditions more arid.
A shift from sheep to goats to meet cashmere export demand has degraded grazing land, because goats eat roots and flowers.

entries.text: Each year the Gobi turns over 3,600 km2 of grassland into wasteland, and large sand dunes are forming only 70 km from Beijing. The rest comes mainly from too many grazing animals and erosion of cultivated soils, and over 70% of the country's land is degraded. Cashmere exports added pressure: herds shifted from sheep to goats, which eat roots and flowers and so degrade grazing land.

entries.title: The Sahel, where the Sahara's edge keeps moving

definition.text: Desertification in Africa's Sahel, a hot dry belt with 100–600 mm of rain a year, where climate change and human activity combine.

facts.text: The Sahel has lost approximately 650,000 km2 of productive agricultural land over the past 50 years.
The Sahara has swung between wet grassland and dry desert every 20,000 years, linked to a roughly 40,000-year cycle in Earth's axial tilt between 22° and 24.5°.
Since 1900 the Sahara has reportedly expanded 250 km southward along a 6,000 km west–east front.
Lake Chad has shrunk by over 90% since 1987 through irrigation withdrawals and lower rainfall, displacing millions of people.

entries.title: Deserts that came and went long before people

definition.text: The long natural history of deserts, which grew and shrank mostly independently of people, and the later study of human-driven land deterioration.

facts.text: Paleodeserts are large sand seas now stabilized by vegetation, some reaching beyond the present margins of core deserts such as the Sahara.
Centuries ago, severe land deterioration in arid regions centred on three densely populated areas: the Mediterranean, the Mesopotamian Valley and China's Loess Plateau.
The earliest known discussion followed the French colonization of West Africa, when the Comité d'Etudes commissioned a study of the prehistoric spread of the Sahara.
The modern study of desertification emerged from research on the 1980s drought in the Sahel.

entries.title: Managed grazing and its contested carbon promise

definition.text: Grazing that moves herds through many small fenced paddocks every day or two, mimicking natural grazers so the grass can regrow.

facts.text: Restored grasslands store atmospheric CO2 as plant material, whereas confined grazing livestock keep grass growth low.
Proponents claim wider use could raise soil carbon across the world's 3.5 billion hectares of agricultural grassland and offset nearly 12 years of CO2 emissions.
Many researchers dispute these claims, saying it neither reverses desertification nor offsets its emissions.

entries.title: Farmland bears most of the damage

definition.text: The degradation of agricultural land, shaped by farmers' local choices and by global drivers such as trade, climate change and demographic change.

facts.text: By 2025 unsustainable farming had degraded 996 Mha of agricultural land, over 60% of all human-induced land degradation.
In high-income countries, heavy fertilizer use masks severe per-hectare losses but brings diminishing returns and can worsen degradation through acidification, nutrient imbalances and pollution.
Sub-Saharan Africa shows low degradation-induced yield losses mainly because limited access to inputs, machinery, credit and markets dominates its yield gaps.
In 2025, 47 million stunted children under five lived where stunting overlaps significant yield losses from degradation; Southern Asia and sub-Saharan Africa combine degraded land with high poverty.

entries.title: How fragile is a landscape? Sensitivity and resilience

definition.text: Two measures that together describe how vulnerable a landscape is to degradation.

facts.text: Sensitivity is the degree to which a land system changes under natural forces, human intervention or both.
Resilience is a landscape's ability to absorb change without altering the balance of species in its community, and to return to its original state afterwards.
Land-use management can raise or lower resilience; degraded land is less resilient, so shocks can drive it into further degradation.

entries.text: A landscape that bends is not the same as one that breaks. Two measures together describe how vulnerable land is to degradation. Land-use management can raise or lower resilience. Degraded land is less resilient, so a shock can drive it into further degradation.

entries.title: The many faces of land degradation

definition.text: The forms land degradation takes, from long-known erosion and physical, chemical and biological decline to newer forms such as pollution and land loss.

facts.text: Types known for centuries are water, wind and mechanical erosion and physical, chemical and biological degradation.
Four types have emerged in the last 50 years: pollution, loss of arable land to construction and expansion, artificial radioactivity, and land-use limits from armed conflict.
More than 36 types can be assessed, all caused or worsened by people, among them erosion, contamination, acidification, sheet erosion, silting, aridification, salinization and urbanization.

entries.text: More than 36 types of land degradation can be assessed, and people cause or worsen every one of them. The full list includes contamination, acidification, sheet erosion, silting, aridification, salinization and urbanization.

entries.title: Grassland degradation: brown patches that spread for decades

definition.text: A biotic disturbance, also called vegetation or steppe degradation, in which grass struggles to grow or disappears from land through overgrazing, burrowing small mammals or climate change.

facts.text: Since the 1970s it has affected alpine meadows and grasslands, notably in the Philippines and in China's Tibetan and Inner Mongolian region, where 2,460 km2 is degraded each year.
It takes years or decades: dead brown patches appear first and, if untreated, spread over many acres, and restoration is just as slow.
Warming speeds evaporation and both heavy rain and drought hinder grass, but some scientists dismiss climate change as an insignificant cause.
Roads, herders' settlements with their animals, monocropping of converted grassland, deforestation and medicinal plant gathering also degrade grassland.
Less arable land and lower harvests push farmers onto smaller plots that are more easily overgrazed and exhausted, and livestock numbers fall.
On the Tibetan Plateau 15–20% of species are now endangered, and carbon and nitrogen losses cost $8,033/ha and $13,315/ha respectively.
With fewer plants to anchor the soil, erosion and dust storms increase, and more carbon and nitrogen may escape to the atmosphere.
In northern China, grassland degradation affects 400 million people a year, with 54 billion yuan of annual economic loss.

entries.contested_note: Most sources link grassland degradation to climate change, but some scientists dismiss it as an insignificant cause.

entries.title: When native shrubs crowd out the grass

definition.text: The spread and thickening of native woody plants, bushes and shrubs at the expense of grasses and forbs.

facts.text: Encroachers are native to the ecosystem, unlike introduced invasive species; they count as encroachers when they outcompete other native species.
It occurs mainly in grasslands, savannas and woodlands on all continents, about 500 million hectares, and can turn open grassland into closed woodland.
Rates reach 1 percent per decade in the Eurasian steppes, 10-20 percent in North America, 8 percent in South America, 2.4 percent in Africa and 1 percent in Australia.
It has occurred at unparalleled rates since the mid-19th century and is classed as a type of grassland degradation.
It is often treated as land degradation that harms biodiversity, groundwater recharge, carbon storage and grazing capacity, but some argue it is natural succession.
In arid lands it has been called 'green desertification', though grass between the canopies can survive, whereas desertification leaves bare soil without organic matter.
Soil quality declines under encroachment in arid and semi-arid regions but often improves in Mediterranean and very humid climates, with more topsoil carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus.
In North America, each 1 percent increase in woody cover cuts carrying capacity by 0.6 to 1.6 cattle per 100 hectares.

entries.contested_note: Sources treat it both as a symptom of land degradation and as a form of natural succession, with context-dependent impacts.

entries.title: China's Great Green Wall against the Gobi

definition.text: China's Great Green Wall: planted windbreak forest strips (shelterbelts), begun in 1978, meant to hold back the Gobi Desert and supply timber.

facts.text: It is planned to finish around 2050 as a barrier about 4,828 km long and up to 1,448 km wide, covering around 88 million acres of forest.
It set out to raise northern China's forest cover from 5 to 15 percent; 29.7% of China had been desertified by 2000, driven by water use, mining, excess farming and wood cutting.
The Gobi grew by 10,000 square kilometres a year in the 1980s but was shrinking by more than 2,000 square kilometres a year in 2022.
By 2009 China's planted forest covered more than 500,000 square kilometres, the largest artificial forest in the world.
In 2024 China finished a 3,000 km green belt around the Taklamakan Desert; desert cover fell from 27.2% to 26.8% over a decade.
Reforestation raised evapotranspiration more than rainfall, and the forests dry the soil more than farmland; dense exotic plantings on the Loess Plateau may worsen water shortages.
A 2023 study found only a fifth of surviving forests became forest stands within 10 years and a tenth were alive after 40.
Monoculture planting left trees open to disease: in 2000 one billion poplars in Ningxia were lost to a single disease.

entries.contested_note: Reports credit it with reversing the Gobi's spread, while critics question tree survival, water use and whether it addresses the causes of desertification.

conflicts.text: Proposed in the late 1970s, the project is not predicted to end until 2055.
conflicts.note: The article says around 2050 (S:4ead0968645c).

conflicts.text: Desert land has shrunk by an annual average of 1,980 square km.
conflicts.note: The article gives more than 2,000 km2 a year in 2022 (S:15cb9069db7b); different periods.

entries.title: Africa's Great Green Wall, from tree line to mosaic

definition.text: An African Union project adopted in 2007, first conceived as a belt of trees across the Sahel from Djibouti to Dakar to combat desertification and hold back the Sahara.

facts.text: The wall was to be 15 km wide and 7,775 km long, but it grew into a mosaic of water harvesting, protected greenery and improved indigenous land use.
Its goal is to restore 100 million hectares of degraded land, capture 250 million tonnes of carbon dioxide and create 10 million jobs by 2030.
It aims to help the ground retain seasonal rainfall, supporting land rehabilitation and future farming.
In the 1950s Richard St. Barbe Baker proposed a 'Green front', a 50-kilometre-deep tree buffer against the expanding desert.
A 2020 UNCCD report found only 4% of the planned area covered; about 18 million hectares were restored by 2023 and about 30 million by 2024.
Nigeria has restored 4.9 million hectares of degraded land and Ethiopia has reclaimed 15 million hectares.
Critics point to the colonial origins of the term 'desertification', mostly European funding, and top-down strategies that push sedentarization.
Little monitoring has been done, and by 2023 the project faced a risk of collapse from terrorist threats, lack of political leadership and too little funding.

entries.contested_note: Progress figures differ widely, and critics question the project's colonial framing, funding and top-down design.

conflicts.text: The project combats desertification in 20 countries.
conflicts.note: S:a66c1b5b0f81 says 22 countries.

conflicts.text: The wall is 8,000 km wide.
conflicts.note: The article gives 7,775 km long and 15 km wide (S:b84586aca331); 'wide' here probably means long.

conflicts.text: The project has restored 36 million hectares of land.
conflicts.note: The article gives about 30 million hectares as of 2024 (S:027ae82e42f2).

conflicts.text: As of 2022, over 56 000 ha of degraded lands have been restored.
conflicts.note: Far below the 18 million ha for 2023 (S:b1cf864b62a2); may count a narrower set of projects.

entries.title: Farmer-managed natural regeneration and the underground forest

definition.text: A low-cost land restoration technique in which farmers regrow and manage trees and shrubs from living stumps, roots and seeds.

facts.text: Australian agricultural economist Tony Rinaudo developed it in West Africa in the 1980s, adapting the centuries-old practices of coppicing and pollarding.
Seemingly bare fields hold an 'underground forest' of living stumps; each can send up 10 to 30 stems, of which the tallest and straightest are kept.
Trees kept among crops and pastures raise yields, soil fertility, organic matter and soil moisture, and reduce wind damage and soil erosion.
Pruned residue mulches fields, raising soil water retention and cutting evaporation.
Trials and long-running programs suggest it can at least double crop yields on low-fertility soils.
Faidherbia albida, the 'fertiliser tree', fixes nitrogen, and its leaf fall adds nutrients and organic matter to the soil.
By 2004 it was practised on over five million hectares, half of Niger's farmland, after nurseries and tree planting had largely failed.
From the 1930s until 1993, Niger's forestry laws took tree ownership out of people's hands, a major obstacle later eased by property-law changes.

conflicts.text: The method has enabled farmers to regenerate some 30,000 square kilometers in Niger.
conflicts.note: FMNR page gives over five million hectares (50,000 km2) by 2004 (S:7755ee15e2f4).

entries.title: Rangeland management, a lesson of the Dust Bowl

definition.text: The science and practice of conserving and sustainably managing rangelands, manipulating their components to yield the best mix of goods and services over time.

facts.text: It developed in the United States in response to rangeland deterioration from overgrazing and misuse of arid lands, shown by the Dust Bowl.
Historically it focused on managing grazing and the proper use of range vegetation for livestock.
Today it seeks to protect and enhance soils, riparian zones, watersheds and vegetation while sustaining products such as meat, water, wood and fibre.
Its scope has widened to the ecosystem services rangelands provide, and growing degradation, such as woody plant encroachment, makes rehabilitation part of the work.
Rangelands are highly vulnerable to climate change: heatwaves, droughts and floods are expected to alter ecological states and cut forage production.
Range science draws on animal science, plant ecology, soil science, wildlife management, climatology and anthropology.

entries.text: The Dust Bowl showed what overgrazing and misuse of arid land could do, and rangeland management grew up in the United States in response. It is the science and practice of conserving rangelands and managing them sustainably, adjusting their parts to yield the best mix of goods and services over time. At first it focused on grazing and the proper use of range vegetation by livestock. Today it aims to protect and enhance soils, riparian zones, watersheds and vegetation while still producing meat, water, wood and fiber. Its scope has widened to the benefits described in {{ref:soil-env-285}}. Growing degradation, such as woody plant encroachment, makes rehabilitation part of the job. Climate adds pressure: heatwaves, droughts and floods are expected to alter rangelands' ecological states and cut forage production. The field draws on animal science, plant ecology, soil science, wildlife management, climatology and anthropology.

entries.title: Measuring dryness with the aridity index

definition.text: A numerical indicator of how dry the climate is at a given place.

facts.text: Aridity is permanent, whereas drought is temporary.
UNEP's 1992 index compares average annual precipitation with potential evapotranspiration in the same units, so it rises as conditions get wetter.
Its classes are hyperarid (below 0.05, 7.5% of land), arid (0.05-0.20, 12.1%), semi-arid (0.20-0.50, 17.7%) and dry subhumid (0.50-0.65, 9.9%).
One of the first indices, by Köppen and Geiger, set an annual rainfall threshold that depends on mean annual temperature and the season the rain falls in.

entries.title: Soil unsealing: prying the pavement off

definition.text: Removing asphalt, cement and other human-made covers so that a sealed soil can again perform its natural functions.

facts.text: Because sealing losses are mostly irreversible, unsealing is very difficult, and research on it is very limited.
Urban, barren or old dumping soils can become parks, green roofs and gardens, but only after thorough decontamination.
Under the 'no net land take' principle used in the Walloon Region and Germany, sealed surfaces are removed to offset new urban projects.
A Palermo field trial found vegetated de-sealing stabilised infiltration and raised microbial activity over eighteen months, while crushed asphalt kept higher permeability but less plant cover.

entries.title: Restoring drylands, one island of plants at a time

definition.text: Work to return degraded drylands to their former function, or to manage them so they degrade no further.

facts.text: It is especially hard because rain is rare and variable, temperatures are high, soils are infertile and invasive species spread.
Restoration islands are small, well-placed plantings that spread into neighbouring ground, suiting patchy dryland vegetation and reducing soil erosion.
Soil fauna improve soil structure, nutrient cycling and infiltration; they can be helped with endemic species, nucleation sites and mulching to keep the soil moist.
Rangelands cover about 25% of drylands, and their restoration counts as a climate mitigation option because of its carbon sequestration potential.

entries.text: Rangelands cover about 25% of drylands, and restoring them counts as a climate mitigation option because of their potential to sequester carbon. entries.title: How compaction stunts roots

definition.text: Compaction removes large pores and raises penetration resistance, restricting roots and the organisms that live in soil.

facts.text: Large pores between aggregates are lost first, which hurts fine and medium soils most because they depend on those pores for infiltration, percolation and air exchange; coarse soils suffer less.

Compacted soil hardens as it dries because many small pores hold water under high suction; penetration resistance of a good soil stays below the 300 psi (2 MPa) level at which root growth ceases, while compacted soil quickly exceeds it.
Growing roots need pores wider than about 0.1 mm, the size of most root tips; without them roots stay short and thick with few fine roots or root hairs and are poor at taking up water and nutrients.

Roots meeting a mechanical barrier send a hormonal signal that slows shoot growth, an effect hard to separate from drought; subsoil compaction also limits deep rooting, raising drought losses in rain-fed farming.
Earthworms and insects need large pores and aerobic microbes need air exchange, so compacted soils hold fewer of them, though they return quickly once better practices are adopted.

entries.title: Bush control: thinning shrubs, not erasing them

definition.text: Action to manage the density and composition of bushes and shrubs in an area, also called brush management.

facts.text: Encroaching native woody plants are to be thinned, not eradicated, because they still provide functions such as animal habitat.
Measures are preventive (suitable stocking rates and rotational grazing), responsive (bush thinning) or maintenance (keeping the thinned density).
Prevention is thought cheaper than treatment, and control works best early in encroachment, at around 3% shrub cover.
Encroached grassland can be a stable state that will not recover without intervention, and chemical control can lose more carbon than mechanical thinning.

entries.title: Why shrubs are winning against grass

definition.text: Local land-use drivers such as overgrazing, fire suppression and the loss of wild herbivores, together with global drivers such as rising CO2, that favour woody plants over grasses.

facts.text: By the two-layer theory, grasses use topsoil moisture and woody plants subsoil moisture, so overgrazing grass lets more water reach the subsoil for woody plants.
Coarse-textured soils promote woody growth while fine-textured soils limit it, and moisture and nutrients make downslope and cooler slopes more prone.
Woody plants with the C3 photosynthetic pathway thrive under high CO2, unlike C4 grasses.
When rainfall intensity rises, deep soil water usually increases, which benefits bushes more than grasses.

entries.title: More wood, but not necessarily more carbon

definition.text: The change in ecosystem carbon when woody plants invade grassland: a sink if only above-ground biomass is counted, but uncertain once grass and soil organic carbon losses are included.

facts.text: Several studies find above-ground carbon gains entirely offset by below-ground losses.
Soil organic carbon tends to rise under encroachment in dry ecosystems and fall in mesic ones; in tropical savanna soils most of it comes from grass.
A meta-analysis of 142 studies found changes in soil organic carbon (0-50 cm) from -50 to 300 percent, with gains under leguminous shrubs and on sandy soils.
Rooting depth increases with encroachment, on average by 38 cm and up to 65 cm.

entries.title: Thirsty bushes and the rain that never reaches the soil
entries.article: Woody plant encroachment#Groundwater recharge and soil moisture

definition.text: The link between woody encroachment and reduced groundwater recharge, because bushes use far more rainwater than grasses and alter streamflow.

facts.text: Denser canopies raise transpiration and evaporation of soil moisture, and enhanced soil porosity can speed soil drought.
In South Africa about 44% of rainfall is caught by woody canopies and evaporated, and up to 10% less rain enters the soil.
In arid and semi-arid lands encroachment reduces stream flows, while woody plant control can improve the connectivity of water resources.

entries.title: Shallow compaction of the plow layer

definition.text: Compaction of the surface or plow layer, found to some degree in all intensively worked agricultural soils.

facts.text: It results from lost aggregation, typically caused by erosion, low organic matter and the weight of field equipment; the first two cut the supply of sticky binding materials.

Soil wetter than its plastic limit is smeared into a dense mass by tillage or traffic, seen as shiny cloddy furrows and deep ruts, while friable soil below the plastic limit crumbles and resists compaction.
Sandy soils turn from plastic to friable quickly as they drain, whereas loams and clays need longer drying; frozen soil is also resistant to compaction.

Rain on unprotected soil disperses wet aggregates into a thin dense layer that seals the surface and hardens into a crust, which cuts infiltration and can block seedling emergence; residue cover and strong aggregation reduce it.
A compacted soil tills up cloddy and needs extra secondary tillage and packing, which breaks aggregates and burns organic matter, so compaction recurs in a vicious cycle.

entries.title: Subsoil compaction and the plow pan

definition.text: Compaction deeper in the soil, often called a plow pan, though it has causes beyond plowing.

facts.text: Subsoil compacts easily because it is usually wetter, denser, higher in clay, lower in organic matter and less aggregated than topsoil, and regular tillage does not loosen it.
Being buried, it is invisible unless you dig or push a rod into the soil.

A surface load spreads through the soil in a cone, so pressure falls with depth; light loads do little at depth but heavy manure spreaders or combines compact deeply, and wet soil carries the force deeper.
Plows and disks press down on the layer below, and tractor wheels in an open furrow press directly on the soil under the plow layer; such pans may persist for many years after a field goes no-till.
In a ball test, a handful from the lower plow layer that molds and sticks is too wet to work, while one that crumbles is dry enough for tillage or heavy traffic.
Soils with roughly equal sand, silt and clay and non-swelling 1:1 clays are prone to dense subsoils: when aggregates weaken from organic matter loss, silt and clay wash down into subsoil pores.
Tropical oxisols with strongly aggregated clay can disperse when limed, because the raised pH lets clay particles wash into lower pores.

entries.title: Light, moderate, high: grading grassland decline

definition.text: The three sequential stages of grassland degradation: light, moderate and high.

facts.text: Lightly degraded grassland has patches of dead or missing grass scattered across the land.
In moderately degraded grassland, dead patches grow in size and number, plant and animal diversity clearly falls, and pests such as rats and insects damage soil and plants.
Highly degraded grassland is a vast expanse of dead grass, neither arable nor fit for livestock, with very low diversity and a few poisonous plants.
Severely degraded grassland is called heitutan, or black beach or black-soil-land: bare, unusable black soil extending 10–15 cm below ground level.

entries.text: At its worst, grassland becomes heitutan, 'black beach' or black-soil-land: bare, unusable black soil extending 10–15 cm below ground level. Before that, grassland degradation passes through three stages. Lightly degraded grassland has scattered patches of dead or missing grass. In moderately degraded grassland the patches grow in size and number, plant and animal diversity clearly falls, and pests such as rats and insects damage soil and plants. Highly degraded grassland is a vast expanse of dead grass, fit for neither crops nor livestock, with very low diversity and a few poisonous plants.

entries.title: Matching the cure to the damage on grassland

definition.text: Restoring degraded grassland with methods matched to how severely it is degraded.

facts.text: Success needs recognition in policy, standard indicators of degradation, scientific innovation, knowledge transfer and data sharing, and early action makes it easier.
Lightly degraded land can be fenced from grazing, fertilized or weeded; grazing may continue at lower, monitored intensity, for example by rotating fields seasonally.
Moderately degraded land needs reseeding and rodent control; active brush control can restore areas invaded by woody plants.
Highly degraded land with 30% or more plant cover gets semi-artificial grassland; worse heitutan land needs artificial grassland with weed and rodent control, plowing, seeding and fertilizing.

entries.title: Burrowing small mammals: culprits or bystanders?

definition.text: Damage to grassland blamed on growing populations of burrowing small mammals such as marmots, voles, pikas and zokors.

facts.text: Burrowing and gnawing encourage soil erosion and make it hard for plants to root, leaving grass patchy.
Others argue that burrowing recycles soil nutrients and that the population rise simply follows increased grazing.
Rodent control, by shooting, sterilizing or low-toxicity poison such as Botulin toxin C, aims to manage populations rather than wipe them out.

entries.contested_note: Sources disagree on whether burrowing mammals cause grassland degradation or merely follow heavier grazing.

entries.title: The non-limiting water range

facts.text: The optimum water range for plant growth is the least-limiting water range; in a well-structured soil it runs from field capacity on the wet end to the wilting point on the dry end.
In severely compacted soil the range is much narrower: at field capacity it is still too wet because it lacks large pores, and good aeration needs at least 20% of pore space air filled.
On the dry end, growth in compacted soil is commonly limited by hardness rather than lack of available water.
John Letey introduced it in 1985 to refine available water capacity; da Silva, Kay and Perfect refined it in 1994 as the least limiting water range (LLWR).

entries.title: When farmers give up the land

definition.text: The giving up of farmed land, after which, for example, woody plants may re-establish on it.

facts.text: Threshold effects of land degradation may lead to abandonment in areas with a long history of intensive farming.
Abandonment can lead to woody plant encroachment as trees and shrubs re-establish on former farmland.
Farmland values in parts of southern Europe are projected to fall by more than 80% by 2100 under climate change, which could cause abandonment.

entries.title: Land degradation neutrality: a target for 2030

definition.text: A policy goal, set in UN Sustainable Development Goal 15, of restoring degraded land and soil so that the world becomes land degradation-neutral by 2030.

facts.text: Target 15.3 reads: by 2030, combat desertification, restore degraded land and soil, including land hit by desertification, drought and floods, and strive for a land degradation-neutral world.
The Land Degradation Neutrality Fund, launched at UNCCD COP 13 in 2017, invests in projects with environmental, socio-economic and financial returns.
The Fund was initially capitalized at US$100 million and is expected to grow to US$300 million; the European Investment Bank agreed to invest up to $45 million.
Supporting land degradation neutrality is one objective of the UNCCD's 2018–2030 Strategic Framework.

entries.title: Rain gardens, where city runoff sinks in and gets cleaned

definition.text: A designed planted site, also called a bioretention facility, that lets runoff from roofs, roads and other hard urban surfaces soak into the soil and be cleaned.

facts.text: Plants and natural or engineered soil hold stormwater, delay infiltration, and filter and remediate pollutants carried by urban runoff.
Deep roots open extra channels for infiltration, maintain soil permeability and sustain the microbes that break down pollutants and remove nitrogen.
Water is cleaned by settling, filtration, assimilation, adsorption to roots, soil particles and organic matter, and microbial decomposition.
Typical removal is about 80% of suspended solids and 50–60% of heavy metals; a 2025 meta-analysis found loads of nitrogen and phosphorus cut by about 55% and 62%.
They restore groundwater recharge and cut stormwater volumes, but may not reduce pollution unless remediation materials are built into the filter layers.

entries.text: Every roof and road sends rain racing toward the drains, carrying pollutants with it. A rain garden, also called a bioretention facility, is a designed planted site that lets this runoff soak into the soil and be cleaned. Plants and natural or engineered soil hold the stormwater, delay its infiltration, and filter and remediate its pollutants. Deep roots open extra channels for water and keep the soil permeable. They also sustain the microbes that break down pollutants and remove nitrogen. The cleaning works by settling, filtration, assimilation, adsorption to roots, soil particles and organic matter, and microbial decomposition. A typical garden removes about 80% of suspended solids and 50–60% of heavy metals. A 2025 meta-analysis found nitrogen and phosphorus loads cut by about 55% and 62%. Rain gardens restore groundwater recharge and cut stormwater volumes. Unless remediation materials are built into the filter layers, though, they may not reduce pollution.

A rain garden, also called a bioretention facility, is a designed planted site that lets this runoff soak into the soil and be cleaned. Plants and natural or engineered soil hold the stormwater, delay its infiltration, and filter and remediate its pollutants. Deep roots open extra channels for water and keep the soil permeable. They also sustain the microbes that break down pollutants and remove nitrogen. The cleaning works by settling, filtration, assimilation, adsorption to roots, soil particles and organic matter, and microbial decomposition. A typical garden removes about 80% of suspended solids and 50–60% of heavy metals. A 2025 meta-analysis found nitrogen and phosphorus loads cut by about 55% and 62%. Rain gardens restore groundwater recharge and cut stormwater volumes. Unless remediation materials are built into the filter layers, though, they may not reduce pollution.

entries.title: Assessing an urban site before sampling

definition.text: Assessing an urban site starts with researching its past use before any soil is sampled.

facts.text: Land-use history comes from owners, old aerial photos, maps, permits and tax records, plus a visit to look for sources such as peeling lead paint or a nearby highway; green-space or residential histories usually mean fewer problems than industrial ones.
There are no federal contaminant limits in the US for gardens; the EPA recommends testing for pH, organic matter, nutrients, micronutrients and metals including lead.

Samples may be needed per contaminant and at different depths (metals near the surface, solvents deeper), and because distribution is unpredictable many locations and suspect spots near old buildings, bare patches or drains need separate sampling.
Lead rarely harms plants, but copper, zinc and nickel can be phytotoxic at high concentrations.
A full assessment also considers slope, drainage and buried utility lines.

entries.title: Urban soil contamination and who it harms

definition.text: Contamination is much more prevalent in urban soils than agricultural ones, lead being the most common contaminant.

facts.text: Lead is widespread because of its long use in gasoline (banned in the US since 1989) and paint (banned for residential use since 1978); other contaminants include petroleum products and legacy pesticides such as lead arsenate and copper sulfate.
Of special concern are former industrial sites, roadsides, recent construction sites, waste disposal sites and junkyards; contaminants can also arrive by atmospheric deposition.
People are exposed by ingesting soil, breathing dust and volatiles, eating crops, and through skin; risk is greatest on bare soil and for children.
Plants absorb little lead, especially at neutral pH, so dirty hands, dust and unwashed produce are the larger exposure; lead can accumulate in roots, so root crops should be avoided.
Solvents such as trichloroethylene move readily to groundwater, some pesticides persist for years, and petroleum products tend to stay near the surface where they can be scraped off.
Road salt (sodium chloride) causes sodic conditions, aggregate breakdown and compaction.

entries.title: Urban soil: stripped, squeezed and contaminated

definition.text: Soil in cities and towns, often stripped of its topsoil, compacted and contaminated by human activity.

facts.text: Urban soil holds more heavy metals, especially lead, copper and nickel, and has a lower pH than comparable soil in the wild.
With the topsoil typically stripped away, it has low aeration, porosity and drainage; compaction and contamination limit root growth and tree health.
Contamination persists in cities with a history of industry, leaded gasoline or lead-based house paint.
The Polish soil classification's 'urban soils' type corresponds to Urbic, Mollic or Ecranic Technosols in the WRB.
Urban soil management is interdisciplinary, aiming to protect soil biodiversity, cut industrial pollution and make soils more resilient to construction compaction.
In a Palermo trial, de-sealing long-sealed urban soils and revegetating them stabilised infiltration and raised microbial activity within eighteen months.
Construction rather than farm machinery is the usual cause of urban compaction: jobs on tight schedules ignore the risk of working wet soil, and topsoil is stripped or fill added.
Disturbed urban soils are low in organic matter and biological activity, and construction debris such as concrete often raises the pH because concrete contains lime.

entries.title: Reconditioning degraded urban soil

definition.text: Reconditioning improves degraded urban soil with physical, chemical and biological practices, generally applied in that order.

facts.text: Removing contaminated soil by excavation is expensive and regulated; if contamination is modest or shallow, scraping the surface and replacing it with good topsoil is more feasible.
Tillage or subsoiling can dilute a thin contaminated layer into deeper soil and relieve compaction; where compaction is the main problem, amelioration in place is better than removal.
Phosphorus binds lead and makes it less dangerous over time; lime or dolomite can stabilize pH.
Compost and other organic amendments raise organic matter, improve structure and biology, dilute toxic compounds and bind some contaminants, but the compost itself must be free of contaminants.
Mulch suppresses weeds, reduces erosion and splash, and acts as a barrier to contact with contaminated soil.

entries.title: Spoil tips and the disaster at Aberfan

definition.text: A pile of spoil, the waste earth material removed during mining or large excavations.

facts.text: Spoil may be ordinary soil and rock or heavily contaminated with chemical waste; clean spoil can be used for land reclamation.
Tips trap solar heat, hindering plant establishment and encouraging erosion and unstable slopes; they also cause acid rock drainage and leach noxious chemicals into groundwater.
In 1966 a tip at Aberfan, Wales, built over a spring and saturated by heavy rain, collapsed onto a school, killing 144 people.
Regreening uses geotextiles to control erosion while the site is resoiled and seeded; old tips may later shelter rare plants, though without nearby seed sources invasive species dominate.

entries.title: Growing trees in cramped city soil

definition.text: The care and management of single trees and tree populations in towns and cities to improve the urban environment.

facts.text: Trees aid stormwater management by intercepting rain in the canopy and slowing, filtering and returning water to the air through their roots.
Street trees face limited soil volume, high soil compaction and harsh microclimates, so they grow and survive less well than trees elsewhere.
Species are chosen for tolerance of alkaline and compacted soils, low soil volume, de-icing salts and drought; healthy large trees need about 1,000 cubic feet of soil.
Urban forests support services such as nutrient cycling and soil formation.

entries.title: The engineered soil inside a rain garden

definition.text: The engineered growing soil, or substrate, through which a rain garden filters collected water.

facts.text: A typical mix is 60% sand, 20% compost and 20% topsoil; more compost improves filtering, while more sand improves infiltration but may retain fewer nutrients.
The sandy mix must not be blended with less sandy surrounding soil, since clay settles between sand grains into a concrete-like, poorly draining mass.
Where native soil drains too slowly, such as Type D soils, it should be replaced and an underdrain installed.
A five-year USGS study found rain gardens in urban clay soils worked without underdrains or soil replacement if pre-installation infiltration was at least 0.25 in/hour.

entries.title: Protecting topsoil on a construction site

definition.text: Good construction practice limits traffic and protects topsoil to avoid lasting compaction and mixing of soil layers.

facts.text: Digging for pipes or drains mixes fertile topsoil with subsoil, leaving poor soil at the surface; compaction matters little under pavement but long-term where land is revegetated.
Controlled traffic lanes, metal plates or geotextile under gravel, and avoiding work on wet soil limit compaction.
Strip and stockpile topsoil separately, refill subsoil first and loosen it with rippers, then replace topsoil without further compaction.

entries.title: Soil mixes for containers and green roofs

definition.text: Pots, planters and green roofs need clean, light soil mixes with excellent drainage and high water- and nutrient-holding capacity.

facts.text: Rooftop mixes must be light enough not to overload the roof yet heavy enough to anchor plants against wind and water.
Mixes combine heat-treated vermiculite and perlite with organic materials such as peat moss, compost or biochar; they are low in density but cost more than ordinary soil.

entries.title: Gap-graded soil: pavement that lets roots breathe

definition.text: Gap-graded soil contains only certain particle sizes, with some sizes left out deliberately to guarantee pore space.

facts.text: Street trees face a dilemma: pavement needs a compacted substrate to bear loads, while roots need a healthy rooting environment, and trees often die early from constricted roots, salt, heat and moisture stress.
Large uniform stones form a load-bearing skeleton while the large pores, partly filled with high-quality soil, let roots grow under the pavement.
Golf greens use similar gap-graded sand to support foot traffic while keeping turf healthy.

entries.title: Remediating soil in urban green spaces

entries.title: Saving dug-up topsoil in a stockpile

Before re-use, stockpiled soil may be tested for contamination.

entries.title: Rebuilding soil faster than it is lost

definition.text: Creating new soil and restoring soil health by minimizing topsoil loss, retaining more carbon than is lost, boosting biodiversity and keeping water and nutrient cycles working.

facts.text: It is a form of ecological regeneration within restoration ecology, reforming degraded soil through biological, chemical or physical processes.
Its benefits include carbon sequestration against climate change, lower erosion risk and greater overall soil resilience.
Healthy soil is a mix of living organisms, organic matter and inorganic material, with air and water typically making up half its volume.
Plants trade carbohydrates for nutrients released by rhizosphere microbes, a symbiosis that maintains mostly fungal living biomass and raises soil carbon.
For optimal plant growth a carbon to nitrogen ratio of 20–30:1 must be maintained.
Soil biodiversity creates competitive pressure that shrinks the niche open to disease and parasitic organisms.
Organic carbon content is one of the most predictable ways to tell whether a soil has degraded.
Reducing or halting tillage raises topsoil carbon concentrations, allowing the soil to regenerate.

entries.text: Soil can be made, not only spent. Soil regeneration is the creation of new soil and the restoration of soil health. It means keeping topsoil loss low, holding more carbon than escapes, boosting biodiversity and keeping water and nutrient cycles working. It is a form of ecological regeneration within restoration ecology, reforming degraded soil through biological, chemical or physical processes. Healthy soil mixes living organisms, organic matter and mineral material, and air and water typically fill half its volume. Plants trade carbohydrates for nutrients released by microbes in the rhizosphere. That bargain keeps the living biomass mostly fungal and raises soil carbon. Carbon is also the best gauge, since organic carbon content is one of the most predictable signs of a degraded soil. Reducing or halting tillage raises topsoil carbon and lets the soil recover. For optimal plant growth, the carbon to nitrogen ratio must stay at 20–30:1. A diverse soil life also crowds out disease, because competition shrinks the niche open to parasites. The rewards are carbon stored against climate change, less erosion and a sturdier soil overall.

Healthy soil mixes living organisms, organic matter and mineral material, and air and water typically fill half its volume. Plants trade carbohydrates for nutrients released by microbes in the rhizosphere. That bargain keeps the living biomass mostly fungal and raises soil carbon. Carbon is also the best gauge, since organic carbon content is one of the most predictable signs of a degraded soil. Reducing or halting tillage raises topsoil carbon and lets the soil recover. For optimal plant growth, the carbon to nitrogen ratio must stay at 20–30:1. A diverse soil life also crowds out disease, because competition shrinks the niche open to parasites. The rewards are carbon stored against climate change, less erosion and a sturdier soil overall.

entries.title: Testing a soil's health, not just its nutrients

definition.text: Assessing soil health by measuring the ecosystem services a soil provides against benchmarks, combining physical, chemical and biological analyses.

facts.text: Benchmarks used include CO2 release, humus levels, microbial activity and available calcium.
Testing is spreading in the United States, Australia and South Africa; Cornell University has had a Soil Health Test since 2006, and Woods End Laboratories a soil quality package since 1985.
Both combine aggregate stability, mineral balance and CO2 respiration analyses, now considered hallmarks of soil health testing.
Other labs add biological factors to routine chemical nutrient tests, notably a soil respiration test called the CO2-Burst.
Many labs and scientists resist new biological tests because fertility metrics rest on crop-response models that do not exist for soil health; critics say novel tests may miss management changes.
Over the past 40 years US soils may have lost up to 75% of their carbon (humus), though how much is debatable; critics say old testing models have failed.
Older models stressed maximum yield, while nutrient pollution of US surface and groundwater grew, reported in the early 2000s as the worst since the 1970s.
In practice soil health testing tends to be confined largely to agronomic objectives.

entries.title: Ecosystem services, the work nature does for people

definition.text: The many benefits that people derive from ecosystems, such as clean water, food, decomposition of wastes and flood control.

facts.text: The UN Millennium Ecosystem Assessment popularized four categories: provisioning, regulating, supporting and cultural services.
Supporting services, such as nutrient cycling, primary production and soil formation, make possible others such as food supply, flood regulation and water purification.
Regulating services include waste decomposition and detoxification, and erosion regulation affects people indirectly through environmental conditions.

New York City restored its Catskill watershed, where soil absorption and filtration, roots and soil microbes brought water back to standard, for $1–1.5 billion instead of a $6–8 billion filtration plant.
Evaluations of ecosystem services may assign them an economic value.

entries.title: Soil science beyond the farm gate

definition.text: The study of how humans interact with the pedosphere and with key parts of the biosphere, lithosphere, hydrosphere and atmosphere.

facts.text: It is one of the general subfields of edaphology, alongside agricultural soil science, and studies human interaction with the pedosphere beyond crop production.

Its topics include surface water quality, vadose zone functions, septic drain fields, wastewater land treatment, stormwater, erosion control, contamination and remediation, wetland restoration, soil degradation and nutrient management.
It also covers movement of viruses and bacteria in soil, bioremediation, microbes engineered to degrade pollutants, land use, global warming, acid rain and anthropogenic soils such as terra preta.
Much of the research in environmental soil science is done with models.
Soil chemistry's emphasis has shifted toward environmental soil science, whose knowledge is key to predicting the fate of contaminants in soil.

entries.text: Soil science does not stop at the edge of the field. Environmental soil science studies how people interact with the pedosphere and with the living world, rock, water and air around it. It is one of the general subfields of edaphology, alongside agricultural soil science, and looks beyond crop production. Its topics run from surface water quality, stormwater and erosion control to {{ref:soil-env-195}}, wastewater land treatment and wetland restoration. It covers polluted ground and its cleanup, soil degradation and nutrient management. It tracks viruses and bacteria moving through soil, and {{ref:soil-env-023}}, the use of microbes to break down pollutants. Land use, global warming and acid rain belong to it too, as do human-made soils such as terra preta. Much of its research relies on models. Soil chemistry itself has shifted toward this field, because its knowledge is key to predicting where contaminants in soil end up.

entries.title: Healthy for whom? The many meanings of soil health

definition.text: The differing ways users define soil health, understood as a soil's condition at a defined place and scale against benchmarks of healthy functioning.

facts.text: Because users weigh a soil's functions differently, the term only makes sense in the context of the user's aims and the boundary of the soil in question.
Ecological landscape assessment and agronomic objectives give potentially conflicting interpretations, each claiming its own criteria; a soil can function well ecologically yet not serve crops.

Benchmarks differ with a soil's inherited qualities and geography; generically, a healthy soil absorbs and cycles well, sheds clean runoff, keeps carbon and productivity near climatic limits and leaks few nutrients.
Unlike soil quality, soil health is not applied to a purpose such as preparing a roadbed.

entries.title: Measuring how far farmed soil falls short

definition.text: A concept, introduced by Maharjan and colleagues in 2020, that uses native land in a region as the benchmark for measuring how far managed soils fall short in health.

facts.text: Soil's importance for food security, agro-ecosystems, the environment and human life has shifted research strongly toward soil health.
Without site- or region-specific benchmarks, research on how different agronomic management affects soil health had been limited.

entries.text: How healthy should a farmed soil be? In 2020 Maharjan and colleagues proposed an answer: compare it with native land in the same region. The soil health gap is the shortfall between managed soils and that local benchmark. The idea filled a hole. Without site- or region-specific benchmarks, research on how different farm management affects soil health had been limited. Meanwhile, soil's importance for food security, farm ecosystems, the environment and human life had pushed research strongly toward soil health.

entries.title: Soil health and soil quality: two overlapping ideas

definition.text: The relation between two overlapping terms: soil quality, a soil's fitness for a given purpose, and soil health, a holistic view of soil as a self-sustaining living system.

facts.text: Soil health has largely replaced the older term soil quality, though the two still overlap considerably.
Soil quality meant fitness for a use, such as quality of soil for maize production or for roadbed preparation.
The phrase soil health comes from European organic or biological farming movements, well before soil quality became a discipline around 1990.
Swiss soil biologist Otto Buess's 1978 essay 'The Health of Soil and Plants' largely defines the field even today.

entries.title: Permaculture: designing farms on nature's model

definition.text: An approach to land management and settlement design that copies arrangements seen in flourishing natural ecosystems.

facts.text: Bill Mollison and David Holmgren coined the term in 1978; its three ethics and Holmgren's twelve design principles are widely cited.
Common practices include Hügelkultur (burying wood to hold soil water), sheet mulching, no-till gardening, keyline design and vermicomposting.
It has been largely isolated from science and criticised as pseudo-scientific or poorly defined.
Some 21st-century studies support claims that it improves soil quality and biodiversity; a 2024 review said it strongly enhances carbon stocks and soil quality.

entries.contested_note: Critics call it pseudo-scientific and ill-defined, while recent studies report gains in soil quality and carbon.

entries.title: Judging soil quality by what can be measured

definition.text: The chemical, physical and biological measurements used to judge soil quality, since soil function itself cannot easily be measured directly.

facts.text: Physical indicators measure texture, bulk density, porosity, water content at saturation, aggregate stability and penetration resistance, showing infiltration and water available to plants.
Chemical indicators include pH and nutrient levels; a typical soil test evaluates only chemical properties.
Biological indicators reflect organisms such as earthworms, millipedes, centipedes, ants and spiders, which regulate soil structure, degrade contaminants and cycle nutrients.
Soil quality can be evaluated with the Soil Management Assessment Framework, and in Germany agricultural soil quality is rated on the soil value scale (Bodenwertzahl).
Very few monitoring systems give near real-time indicator data, and almost all of them report only at research level.

entries.text: Soil function itself is hard to measure directly, so scientists measure stand-ins. These soil quality indicators fall into three groups. Together they show infiltration and the water available to plants. Chemical indicators include soil pH and nutrient levels, and a typical soil test checks only these. Biological indicators reflect organisms such as earthworms, millipedes, centipedes, ants and spiders, which regulate structure, break down contaminants and cycle nutrients. The Soil Management Assessment Framework pulls such readings together, and Germany rates farm soil on its soil value scale, the Bodenwertzahl. Very few monitoring systems give near real-time indicator data, and almost all report only at research level.

entries.title: Four ways a soil wears out

definition.text: The four general ways soil declines in condition under poor management: erosion, and physical, chemical and biological degradation.

facts.text: Erosion displaces soil by water runoff or wind, typically from bare fields; physical degradation changes structure so water and air cannot enter, as in compaction by large vehicles.
Chemical degradation includes contamination with heavy metals or hydrocarbons, acidification, salinization, nutrient leaching and toxins from mining and waste management.
Biological degradation is a loss of biological activity, as when fertilizer buildup inhibits nitrogen-fixing microbes, bringing biodiversity loss, greenhouse gas emissions and less carbon storage.
One third of the globe's land has degraded soil, with around 500 million hectares degraded in the tropics and subtropics.
Excessive tillage, especially ploughing, leaves soil open to wind erosion, and farm vehicles compact it, reducing its permeability to air and water.
Chemical fertilizer suppresses nitrogen-fixing microbes and raises nitrous oxide emissions; replacing lost fertility with more fertilizer creates a positive feedback loop.
Overgrazing removes plant roots, reducing organic content and the symbiosis between plants and the soil microbiome.
Urban construction compacts and seals soils, intensifying storm runoff and erosion, and cities concentrate pollutants that leach into soils.

entries.text: One third of the globe's land has degraded soil, with around 500 million hectares degraded in the tropics and subtropics alone. Poor management wears soil down in four general ways. The first is erosion, in which water runoff or wind carries soil away, typically from bare fields. Excessive tillage, especially ploughing, leaves soil open to the wind. The second is physical degradation, a change in structure that keeps water and air out. Heavy farm vehicles cause it through compaction. Urban construction compacts and seals soil too, which intensifies storm runoff and erosion. The third is chemical degradation: heavy metals or hydrocarbons, acidification, salinization, nutrient leaching, and toxins from mining and waste management. Cities concentrate pollutants that leach into their soils. The fourth is biological degradation, a loss of biological activity. Chemical fertilizer is one cause. It suppresses nitrogen-fixing microbes and raises nitrous oxide emissions. As fertility falls, more fertilizer goes on, a positive feedback loop. Overgrazing strips away plant roots, and with them organic matter and the partnership between plants and soil microbes. The toll includes lost biodiversity, more greenhouse gas emissions and less carbon storage.
