entries.title: Geogenic contamination: when the rocks poison the water

definition.text: Groundwater contamination that arises naturally from geological processes rather than human activity.

facts.text: Arsenic and fluoride are the most widespread geogenic contaminants; salinity, iron, manganese, uranium, radon and chromium matter more locally.
High fluoride usually reflects fluoride minerals such as fluorite and a lack of calcium in the aquifer; above 1.5 mg/L it can cause dental fluorosis.
WHO tests found 20% of 25,000 Bangladesh boreholes above 50 μg/L arsenic.

entries.title: How soil filters germs from latrine seepage

definition.text: The die-off and adsorption of pathogens in liquid leaching from pit latrines and septic tanks as it passes through the unsaturated soil to groundwater.

facts.text: Removal depends mostly on travel time to the well; most, but not all, pathogens die within 50 days underground.
It varies with soil type, aquifer type and distance, and long heavy rain can wash the unsaturated zone and open fast pathways.
Biological activity, and so pathogen attenuation, is greatest in the topsoil layers.
A general guideline puts a pit's base at least 2 m above groundwater and 30 m horizontally from a water source.

entries.text: Soil is a slow but real germ filter. Liquid leaching from pit latrines and septic tanks loses pathogens as it trickles through the unsaturated soil, as they die off or stick to grains. Travel time to the well matters most. Most, but not all, pathogens die within 50 days underground. Soil type, aquifer type and distance change the result, and long heavy rain can flush the zone and open fast pathways. The topsoil, the most biologically active layer, removes the most. A general guideline sets a pit's base at least 2 m above groundwater and 30 m from a water source.

entries.title: Neutralizing acid mine drainage

definition.text: The neutralization of acidic mine outflow and removal of its dissolved metals, using limestone, lime, calcium silicate, ion exchange, wetlands or sulfide precipitation.

facts.text: Crushed limestone is the cheapest neutralizer, but its grains become armored with gypsum and an iron–aluminium hydroxysulfate film that stops calcite from dissolving.
In lime treatment, a lime slurry raises the water to about pH 9, where most toxic metals precipitate and settle out as sludge.
Constructed wetlands are cheap: sediment bacteria reduce sulfate to sulfide, which binds and precipitates heavy metals, though they handle only limited metal loads.
Sulfate-reducing bacteria can also be used in reactors, yielding bicarbonate that neutralizes acidity and hydrogen sulfide that precipitates metals.

entries.text: Treating {{ref:soil-bio-059}} means neutralizing its acid and stripping out dissolved metals. Crushed limestone is the cheapest neutralizer, but its grains get armored with gypsum and an iron–aluminium film that stops them dissolving. Lime slurry instead raises the water to about pH 9, where most toxic metals settle out as sludge. Constructed wetlands are cheap. Their sediment bacteria turn sulfate into sulfide, which binds and drops heavy metals, though only limited loads. Sulfate-reducing bacteria in reactors also yield bicarbonate, which neutralizes acid.

entries.title: Yellow boy, the orange stain of mine water

definition.text: The yellow-orange iron(III) hydroxide that precipitates when the pH of acid mine drainage rises above 3.

facts.text: Iron oxides, oxyhydroxides and sulfates such as jarosite can also form; all of them discolor water and smother streambed life.
Precipitation releases more hydrogen ions, lowering pH further, and very rich deposits can be recovered for pigments.

entries.text: Streams below old mines often run a lurid yellow-orange. The color is yellow boy, the iron(III) hydroxide that settles out when the pH of {{ref:soil-bio-059}} rises above 3. Other iron compounds, including oxyhydroxides and sulfates such as jarosite, can form too. All of them discolor water and smother life on the streambed. Their formation releases more hydrogen ions, which lowers the pH further. Very rich deposits can even be recovered as pigment.

entries.title: Thermal desorption: baking pollutants out of soil

definition.text: A remediation technology that heats contaminated soil or other solids so that contaminants volatilize and can be separated, then collected or destroyed.

facts.text: A system has two main parts, the desorber and the offgas treatment system, and it is not incineration.
It was used at 69 US Superfund sites through FY2000 and is regarded as a permanent remedy at competitive cost, unlike stabilization, which leaves contaminants on site.
Common desorbers are indirect- and direct-fired rotary cylinders and heated screws; indirect rotary units reach about 1,000 °F with carbon steel shells.
Removing 500 mg/kg of organics from 20,000 tons of soil yields under 3,000 US gallons of liquid, less than one tank truck.

entries.title: LNAPLs: pollutants that float on the water table

definition.text: A hydrocarbon groundwater contaminant that does not dissolve in water and is less dense than it, so it forms a separate floating phase.

facts.text: Once it infiltrates the ground, an LNAPL stops at the water table because it is buoyant; benzene, toluene and xylene are examples.
Because they float on the water table, LNAPLs are easier and cheaper to locate and remove than DNAPLs.

entries.text: Some pollutants float. A light non-aqueous phase liquid, or LNAPL, is a hydrocarbon that does not dissolve in water and is lighter than it. Benzene, toluene and xylene are examples. Once an LNAPL soaks into the ground, it stops at the {{ref:soil-water-247}} and spreads there as a separate layer. That buoyancy is good news. Sitting on top, LNAPLs are easier and cheaper to find and remove than {{ref:soil-env-220}}, which sink.

entries.title: Biosorption: dead cells that grab metals

definition.text: A passive physicochemical process by which certain biomass concentrates and binds contaminants such as heavy metals onto its cell structure.

facts.text: Unlike bioaccumulation, which needs a living, respiring organism, biosorption needs no energy and depends on equilibrium and the sorbent's cell-surface composition.
Because metals are only bound to the cell surface, biosorption is reversible, and in one test dead Bacillus sphaericus cells took up 13–20% more chromium than living ones.
Its performance depends strongly on pH, biomass concentration and interactions between different metal ions.
Cheap wastes such as eggshells, peat, fungi, seaweed and crab shells can remove toxic metal ions from water, and biosorbents cost about a tenth as much as ion-exchange resins.

entries.title: Five ways to deal with metal-polluted soil

definition.text: The cleanup of soils contaminated by heavy metals through isolation, immobilization, toxicity reduction, physical separation or extraction.

facts.text: Isolation quarantines soil with caps, membranes or buried barriers, while immobilization alters the soil to hinder metal movement.
Toxicity reduction oxidizes or reduces metal ions chemically or biologically into less toxic or mobile forms.
Extraction uses chemicals, high-temperature volatilization or electrolysis, on or off site; the choice depends on the contaminant and site.

entries.text: Metals never break down, so cleanup must move them, trap them or change them. The remediation of metal-contaminated soil has five broad routes. Isolation quarantines the soil with caps, membranes or buried barriers. Immobilization alters the soil itself so metals cannot travel. Toxicity reduction oxidizes or reduces metal ions, chemically or biologically, into less toxic or less mobile forms. Physical separation sorts them out of the soil, and extraction pulls them out with chemicals, high-temperature volatilization or electrolysis, on or off site. The contaminant and the site decide which fits.

entries.title: Pesticide leaching: the slow trip to groundwater

definition.text: The movement of dissolved pesticides through the soil to sites beyond their target, a major source of groundwater pollution.

facts.text: Leaching depends on the soil, the pesticide, and rainfall and irrigation.
It is worst for water-soluble pesticides with weak soil adsorption, on sandy soils, and when heavy watering follows soon after application.
Mixing areas, machinery-washing sites and disposal areas are sources as well as treated fields.

entries.text: A pesticide that dissolves can travel far beyond the field it was meant for. Pesticide leaching is that movement of dissolved pesticides down through the soil, a major source of groundwater pollution. Three things decide it: the soil, the pesticide, and the rainfall and irrigation. It is worst for water-soluble pesticides that cling weakly to soil, on sandy soils, and when heavy watering follows soon after spraying. Treated fields are not the only source. Mixing areas, machinery-washing sites and disposal areas leak too.

entries.title: Soil reclamation: rebuilding ground after disturbance

definition.text: The part of land reclamation that rebuilds soil on a disturbed site, usually after infrastructure removal, recontouring and contaminant cleanup and before revegetation.

facts.text: Land reclamation converts disturbed or damaged land to its former or another productive use and covers soils, hydrology, flora and fauna; soil reclamation and soil remediation are components of it.
The goals depend on the end land use: regulatory requirements are stricter for agricultural land and land people will occupy than for industrial land, and the end use may mean a different ecosystem.
Stripped soil is normally replaced in its natural horizon sequence; careful placement limits horizon mixing, and compaction on replacement can be eased by tillage.
Damage is reduced by working under frozen or dry conditions, and soil quality is kept if stockpiles are held only briefly.
Bare reclaimed soil is exposed to wind and water erosion, so contouring, amendments, erosion control blankets, mulch and bioengineering such as live staking are used.
Soils rich in swelling smectite clays are often very fertile: the smectite-rich paddy soils of Thailand's Central Plains are among the world's most productive.
On low-clay soils in Thailand, adding bentonite clay once at 200 kilograms per rai (1,300 kg/ha) raised yields by an average of 73% in field trials.
Soils too high in clay or salts can be balanced with gypsum, washed river sand and organic matter; sandy, nutrient-poor soils benefit from compost or ramial chipped wood.

entries.title: Amendments that make reclaimed soil fit for use

definition.text: Materials added to a reclamation soil to correct chemical, physical or biological properties that do not meet the end land use.

facts.text: Lack of organic matter is common and is fixed with animal manure, straw, or forest floor (LFH) material from a cleared area; lack of nutrients is fixed with commercial nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium fertilizer blended for the site.
Waste materials are widely used, which also keeps them out of landfills; raw sewage supplies nutrients and organic matter but may carry salts, metals and disease organisms.
Biosolids, sewage sludges treated to lower pathogen risk, are widely used amendments; others include calcium sources, paper mill waste, industrial sludge, biochar and wood ash.
Each amendment has properties that suit a soil need and usually a drawback to balance, and many jurisdictions regulate waste use.
Micro-topography such as mounds, furrows, depressions, rocks and mulches gives micro sites for plants and microbes and reduces erosion.

Each has properties that suit a soil need and usually a drawback to balance, and many jurisdictions regulate waste use. Micro-topography such as mounds, furrows, depressions, rocks and mulches gives micro sites for plants and microbes and reduces erosion.

entries.title: Cadmium poisoning: a metal that stays for decades

definition.text: Poisoning by cadmium, a naturally occurring toxic metal met in industry, in plant soils and in tobacco smoke.

facts.text: Some phosphate fertilizers contain up to 100 mg/kg cadmium, which can build up in soil.
Chronic exposure softens and weakens bones and irreversibly damages the kidneys, which can shrink by up to 30 percent.
Daily dietary intake is about 8 to 30 μg in Europe and the US but 59 to 113 μg in parts of Japan, where people ate rice irrigated with contaminated water.
Cadmium in bone has a biological half-life of about 30 years.

entries.title: Bioslurping: sipping oil off the water table

definition.text: A technique combining bioventing with vacuum pumping of floating free product (LNAPL) to recover it from groundwater and soil and bioremediate the soil.

facts.text: A slurp tube reaching into the free-product layer draws up liquid and soil gas together, lifting oil off the water table and capillary fringe.
Air drawn into the unsaturated zone drives aerobic biodegradation of the hydrocarbons.

entries.text: Bioslurping works like a straw dipped into floating fuel. It combines {{ref:soil-env-024}} with vacuum pumping of free product, the LNAPL floating on groundwater. A slurp tube reaching into the fuel layer draws up liquid and soil gas together. It lifts oil off the water table and the capillary fringe, the damp band just above it. Meanwhile air pulled into the unsaturated zone feeds microbes that break down the remaining hydrocarbons aerobically.

entries.title: Dual-phase extraction: one well for water and vapor

definition.text: A high-vacuum technology, also called multi-phase extraction, that removes both contaminated groundwater and soil vapor through one well.

facts.text: Pumping depresses the water table, exposing the often highly contaminated capillary fringe, whose contaminants are then removed by vapor extraction.
Treating the capillary fringe can shorten cleanup time at a site.

entries.text: The dirtiest layer at a spill is often the thin damp band just above the water table, the capillary fringe. Dual-phase vacuum extraction, also called multi-phase extraction, reaches it with a high vacuum. A single well removes both contaminated groundwater and soil vapor. Pumping lowers the water table and exposes the fringe. {{ref:soil-env-045}} then draws its contaminants out. Treating that layer can shorten the cleanup of a site.
entries.text_plain: The dirtiest layer at a spill is often the thin damp band just above the water table, the capillary fringe. Pumping lowers the water table and exposes the fringe. Soil vapor extraction: vacuuming pollution out of the ground then draws its contaminants out. Treating that layer can shorten the cleanup of a site.

entries.title: Rhizofiltration: roots that strain metals from water

definition.text: Phytoremediation that filters contaminated groundwater, surface water or wastewater through a mass of roots to remove toxic substances or excess nutrients.

facts.text: Like phytoextraction it traps contaminants, mainly heavy metals, in harvestable biomass, but it treats water while phytoextraction treats soil.
Plants are usually raised in a greenhouse first, then planted at the site or fed contaminated water brought to them off site.
In one study sunflower roots cut uranium levels by nearly 95% in 24 hours; removing radionuclides with sunflowers was estimated at $2 to $6 per thousand gallons treated.
Contaminants below rooting depth are missed, reaching regulatory levels can take years, and harvested plants threaten health unless non-fodder crops are used.

entries.title: Pneumatic fracturing: cracking the ground to clean it

definition.text: A remediation method that injects gas into contaminated ground at a pressure above that of the gases already there, cracking the subsurface.

facts.text: The fractures spread like a spider web, so pumps can draw contaminated water out through the cracks.
Substrates can also be injected through the cracks to speed remediation of soil and groundwater.

entries.text: Tight ground keeps its pollution. Pneumatic fracturing breaks it open by injecting gas at a pressure above that of the gases already present. The fractures spread like a spider web. Pumps can then draw contaminated water out through the cracks. The same cracks carry injected substrates that speed the cleanup of soil and groundwater.

entries.title: Total petroleum hydrocarbons: one number for crude oil

definition.text: A measure of the total amount of the mixture of hydrocarbons found in crude oil present at a site.

facts.text: Crude oil holds several hundred such compounds, too many to measure separately when testing for contamination.
TPH is the sum of volatile petroleum hydrocarbons (gasoline-range, C6–C10) and extractable petroleum hydrocarbons; diesel-range organics span C10–C28.
Its constituents include hexane, benzene, toluene, xylenes, naphthalene and fluorene.

entries.text: Crude oil holds several hundred hydrocarbon compounds, far too many to measure one by one at a spill. Total petroleum hydrocarbon, or TPH, solves this by measuring them all as a single total. It adds the volatile, gasoline-range compounds, with six to ten carbon atoms (C6–C10), to the extractable ones. Diesel-range organics span C10–C28. The mix includes hexane, benzene, toluene, xylenes, naphthalene and fluorene.

entries.title: Electrical resistance heating: boiling pollutants out

definition.text: An intensive in situ remediation method that passes alternating current through soil and groundwater between buried electrodes, heating them until contaminants evaporate.

facts.text: The soil's resistance to current generates heat until water boils at depth; the steam then strips out volatile contaminants, which a vapor recovery system captures and treats at the surface.
It works best on volatile organic compounds such as perchloroethylene and trichloroethylene; less volatile ones such as diesel need more energy.
Current travels mainly through the thin water film on grains, so ERH works in any soil type and in sedimentary bedrock, but cannot dry the ground out.
Electrodes are typically 15 to 20 feet apart with run times under a year; peat or high organic carbon raises the energy needed by adsorbing VOCs.

entries.text: Electrical resistance heating turns the ground into a kettle. Alternating current runs between buried electrodes, and the soil's resistance heats it until water boils at depth. The steam strips out volatile contaminants, which a vapor recovery system captures and treats at the surface. It works best on volatile compounds such as perchloroethylene and trichloroethylene; diesel needs more energy. Current flows through the thin water film on grains, so it works in any soil and in sedimentary bedrock. Electrodes typically sit 15 to 20 feet apart, and runs last under a year.

entries.title: Microbial biodegradation: putting microbes to work on pollution

definition.text: The harnessing of microbes' natural ability to degrade, transform or accumulate pollutants such as oil, PCBs, PAHs, pharmaceuticals, radionuclides and metals.

facts.text: Hydrocarbons and halogenated compounds were long doubted to break down without oxygen, until anaerobic hydrocarbon-degrading and reductively dehalogenating bacteria were isolated.
Bioavailability, the amount of a pollutant physically accessible to microbes, is a key factor in efficient biodegradation.
Most soil clays, kaolinite excepted, slowed bacterial degradation of 2-picoline by adsorbing the substrate.
Hydrocarbon-degrading bacteria remove a considerable share of the petroleum entering marine systems.

entries.text: For years, scientists doubted that hydrocarbons and halogenated compounds could break down without oxygen. Then bacteria that do exactly that were isolated. Microbial biodegradation harnesses microbes' natural ability to degrade, transform or accumulate pollutants, from oil, PCBs and PAHs to pharmaceuticals, radionuclides and metals. Bioavailability, the share of a pollutant microbes can physically reach, is key. In one study, most soil clays, kaolinite excepted, slowed bacterial breakdown of 2-picoline by adsorbing it. At sea, hydrocarbon-degrading bacteria remove a considerable share of the petroleum that enters.

entries.title: Ecotoxicity tests: how hazard gets a number

definition.text: Standardized acute and chronic toxicity tests on terrestrial and aquatic organisms, including earthworms, used to rate a chemical's ecological hazard.

facts.text: LC50 is the concentration that kills 50% of test organisms within the test period, which can last up to 96 hours.
EC50 is the concentration causing an adverse effect in 50% of organisms, and NOEC is the highest dose with no statistically significant effect.
Acute toxicity below 1 part per million places a substance in Class I, 1–10 ppm in Class II and 10–100 ppm in Class III.

entries.text: How toxic is a chemical to an earthworm? Ecotoxicity testing answers with standardized acute and chronic tests on soil and aquatic organisms, including {{ref:soil-bio-040}}. LC50 is the concentration that kills 50% of test organisms within the test, which can last up to 96 hours. EC50 is the concentration causing an adverse effect in 50% of them. NOEC is the highest dose with no statistically significant effect. Acute toxicity below 1 part per million puts a substance in Class I, 1–10 ppm in Class II and 10–100 ppm in Class III.

entries.title: Breakdown products that outlive the pesticide

definition.text: The compounds a pesticide breaks down into, which may keep or even exceed the parent's harmful activity.

facts.text: Being smaller and more polar than their parents, they reach groundwater and surface water more readily.
Europe classes metabolites as nonrelevant, groundwater-relevant (likely above 0.1 μg/liter with parent-like toxicity) or ecotoxicologically relevant.
Tolerating up to 10 μg/liter of nonrelevant metabolites in groundwater is politically contentious: some see no proven health risk, others a breach of the precautionary principle.

entries.contested_note: Whether a 10 μg/liter limit for nonrelevant metabolites in European groundwater is acceptable is disputed.
entries.text: A pesticide's breakdown is not always the end of the story. Its transformation products can keep, or even exceed, the parent's harmful activity. Smaller and more polar than the parent, they reach groundwater and surface water more readily. Europe sorts these metabolites as nonrelevant, groundwater-relevant or ecotoxicologically relevant. A metabolite is groundwater-relevant when it is likely above 0.1 μg/liter and as toxic as its parent. Allowing up to 10 μg/liter of nonrelevant metabolites in groundwater is disputed. Some see no proven health risk; others see a breach of the precautionary principle.

entries.title: How soil microbes eat spilled oil

definition.text: The breakdown of petroleum hydrocarbons by native soil microbes that use them for energy and carbon.

facts.text: Up to twenty percent of soil microbial populations can metabolize hydrocarbons, mainly aerobically, to carbon dioxide and water.
Long-chain aliphatics degrade most readily; short-chained, branched and quaternary ones less so.
Aromatic compounds with two or three rings degrade at effective rates, but those with four or more resist and are broken down only by cometabolism.
Porous, carbon-rich biochar traps PAHs and gives microbes good conditions to degrade them.

entries.text: Up to twenty percent of soil microbes can live on petroleum. Hydrocarbon biodegradation in soil is their breakdown of these compounds for energy and carbon, mostly with oxygen, ending in carbon dioxide and water. Structure decides speed. Long straight chains degrade most readily; short, branched and quaternary ones less so. Ring compounds with two or three rings break down at useful rates. Those with four or more resist, yielding only to cometabolism, breakdown alongside another food. Porous, carbon-rich biochar traps {{ref:soil-env-199}} and gives microbes good conditions to degrade them.

entries.title: The Raymond process: feeding microbes in a loop

definition.text: An accelerated in situ bioremediation method, developed by Richard Raymond, that adds nutrients and electron acceptors to contaminated groundwater.

facts.text: Groundwater is pumped up downstream, infused with nutrients and oxygen, and re-injected upstream in a loop.
Oxygen can be supplied through injection wells or galleries, or as ozone, half of which decomposes to oxygen within twenty minutes.

entries.text: Richard Raymond devised a way to speed up {{ref:soil-env-262}} by feeding the microbes underground. Groundwater is pumped up downstream of the contamination, infused with nutrients and oxygen, and re-injected upstream. The loop repeats. The oxygen serves as the {{ref:soil-chem-176}} the microbes need. It can arrive through injection wells or galleries, or as ozone, half of which turns to oxygen within twenty minutes.
entries.text_plain: Richard Raymond devised a way to speed up In situ bioremediation: cleaning soil where it lies by feeding the microbes underground. Groundwater is pumped up downstream of the contamination, infused with nutrients and oxygen, and re-injected upstream. The loop repeats. The oxygen serves as the Electron acceptors, the last stop for every electron the microbes need. It can arrive through injection wells or galleries, or as ozone, half of which turns to oxygen within twenty minutes.

entries.title: Organic and inorganic soil contaminants

definition.text: Soil contaminants are grouped as organic (pesticides, solvents, industrial products) and inorganic (metals, salts, nutrients, radionuclides).

facts.text: The most common organic contaminants at Canadian contaminated sites are petroleum hydrocarbons, including crude oil, fuels and lubricating oils; dioxins, furans and PAHs are also organic.

Inorganic contaminants include heavy and trace metals, metalloids, acids and bases, excess nutrients and salts, and radionuclides, from sources such as mine wastes, firing ranges, fly ash and battery disposal.
Some inorganics help soil ecosystems at background levels: copper, molybdenum, cobalt and zinc are plant micronutrients but contaminants at high concentrations.
Chloride from de-icing or spills can build up and raise electrical conductivity; excess nitrogen, phosphorus and sulphur from misplaced livestock waste can also be contaminants.

entries.title: Matching the cleanup method to the contaminant
entries.article: doc>geo.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Soil_Science/Digging_into_Canadian_Soils%3A_An_Introduction_to_Soil_Science/03%3A_Digging_Deeper/3.03%3A_Soil_Reclamation_and_Remediation_of_Disturbed_Lands#SOIL REMEDIATION > Properties of Soils and Contaminants Relevant to Remediation

definition.text: Choosing a remediation method depends on the contaminant, the site and soil properties.

facts.text: Petroleum hydrocarbons differ in molecular weight, solubility, volatility and density; larger compounds are less volatile and less soluble, and gasoline is lighter and more volatile than lubricating oil.
Large insoluble hydrocarbons sorb strongly to soil organic matter and are hard to degrade or remove, especially in fine-textured soils where aggregates trap them and air and water move poorly.
Metals are spread among soil components depending on texture, mineralogy, pH, exchange capacity, organic matter and aeration, so remediation must consider each chemical form.
Treatments are biological, chemical or physical, often combined, and applied ex situ (excavated, treated on or off site) or in situ (treated in place).

entries.title: Vitrification: melting soil into glass
entries.article: doc>geo.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Soil_Science/Digging_into_Canadian_Soils%3A_An_Introduction_to_Soil_Science/03%3A_Digging_Deeper/3.03%3A_Soil_Reclamation_and_Remediation_of_Disturbed_Lands#SOIL REMEDIATION > Table 16.2. Common remediation strategies for contaminated soils

definition.text: Heating soil to 1400 to 2000 °C so its silica melts into stable glass and crystalline solids.

facts.text: Heat may come from electrodes and electrical resistance or from plasma arc technology.
Organic contaminants are volatilized, trapped and treated or destroyed, while inorganic contaminants, including radionuclides, are encased.
Ex situ incineration heats soil to 870 to 1370 °C to destroy organic contaminants.

entries.title: Soil washing and flushing
entries.article: doc>geo.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Soil_Science/Digging_into_Canadian_Soils%3A_An_Introduction_to_Soil_Science/03%3A_Digging_Deeper/3.03%3A_Soil_Reclamation_and_Remediation_of_Disturbed_Lands#SOIL REMEDIATION > Table 16.2. Common remediation strategies for contaminated soils

definition.text: An ex situ treatment that may separate silt and clay fines from coarse material to cut the soil mass needing treatment.

facts.text: Contaminants cling to the fines, so removing them reduces total mass and volume to treat.

In situ soil flushing instead treats the contaminated zone with a solution (water, acid, base, chelating agent, co-solvent or surfactant) and brings mobilized contaminants to the surface for disposal, treatment or recirculation.

entries.text: Contaminants tend to cling to the smallest particles. Soil washing, an ex situ treatment, may separate the silt and clay fines from the coarse material. Because the contaminants cling to the fines, removing them reduces the total mass and volume that needs treatment. In situ soil flushing works differently. It treats the contaminated zone with a solution of water, acid, base, chelating agent, co-solvent or surfactant. It then brings the mobilized contaminants to the surface for disposal, treatment or recirculation.

entries.title: Breaking down PCBs takes two teams of microbes

definition.text: The use of microorganisms, working in sequence, to degrade polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) at contaminated sites.

facts.text: PCBs are stable, poorly soluble persistent organic pollutants once used as dielectric fluids and coolants; natural degradation takes 3 to 37 years depending on chlorination.
Anaerobic bacteria first dechlorinate PCBs by using them as electron acceptors; aerobic microbes then break the products down through the biphenyl pathway.
PCBs bind tightly to soil, and higher organic carbon and clay content further lower their availability to microbes.
PCBs are toxic to bacteria above 1000 mg/kg, degradation slows sharply below 50 mg/kg, and it gets harder the more chlorines a molecule carries.

entries.text: PCBs, once used as dielectric fluids and coolants, are stable, poorly soluble {{ref:soil-env-198}}. Natural degradation takes 3 to 37 years, depending on how chlorinated they are. The job is hard: PCBs bind tightly to soil, especially soil rich in organic carbon and clay. They are toxic to bacteria above 1000 mg/kg, and breakdown slows sharply below 50 mg/kg.

entries.title: Geochemical background: what counts as normal

definition.text: The natural levels of elements and other substances in soil, water and air, set by processes such as weathering, against which contamination is judged.

facts.text: Typical background levels in soil do not exceed about 100 mg/kg for arsenic, lead and nickel, 2 mg/kg for cadmium, 150 mg/kg for copper and 300 mg/kg for zinc.
Chromium background in soil is under 500 mg/kg, and selenium does not exceed 1 mg/kg.
Establishing baseline or background levels of naturally occurring harmful materials in soil, water, air and food is a stated priority of medical geology.
Remediation emission results are compared with natural background levels in the area as well as with zoning standards.

entries.text: To call soil contaminated, you first need to know what is natural there. Geochemical background is the natural level of elements and other substances in soil, water and air, set by processes such as {{ref:soil-found-052}}. Typical soils hold no more than about 100 mg/kg of arsenic, lead and nickel, 2 mg/kg of cadmium, 150 mg/kg of copper and 300 mg/kg of zinc. Chromium stays under 500 mg/kg and selenium under 1 mg/kg. Remediation results are compared with these local levels as well as zoning standards, and {{ref:soil-env-287}} makes setting them a priority.

entries.title: Emerging contaminants: pollutants the rules have not caught

definition.text: Pollutants found in environmental monitoring that may harm ecosystems or health and are usually not yet regulated.

facts.text: They include pharmaceuticals, personal care products, industrial byproducts and agricultural chemicals, which often escape detection and treatment and persist.
Agricultural runoff after rain or irrigation carries pesticides and pharmaceuticals from soil into rivers, lakes and groundwater.
Water treatment must not simply move them into sludge, since sludge spread on land is another route into the environment.
Explosives such as TNT are major contaminants of groundwater and soils.

entries.title: Living cleanup crews for radioactive soil

definition.text: The use of bacteria, plants and fungi to catalyze reactions that decontaminate soil, water and sediment affected by radionuclides.

facts.text: Conventional cleanup by excavation and long-distance transport can have estimated costs exceeding a trillion dollars in the US.
The organisms change radionuclides' solubility, bioavailability and mobility to speed their stabilization.
The commonest natural radionuclides in soils are radium-226, radon-222, thorium-232, uranium-238 and potassium-40.
Some fungi can use ionizing radiation as energy, and oyster mushrooms can bioremediate plutonium-239 and americium-241.

entries.title: Bioreduction: bacteria that pin uranium in place

definition.text: The enzymatic reduction of radionuclides by bacteria to lower oxidation states, changing their solubility, mobility and radiotoxicity.

facts.text: Anaerobes use the radioisotope as the terminal electron acceptor, for example reducing soluble uranium(VI) to insoluble uranium(IV).
Sulfate-reducing and metal-reducing bacteria also reduce radionuclides indirectly through the metabolites they excrete.
Siderophores and other bacterial chelators can instead raise radionuclide solubility and bioavailability.

entries.text: Bacteria can turn dissolved uranium into a solid. In bioreduction, their enzymes reduce radionuclides to lower oxidation states, changing their solubility, mobility and radiotoxicity. Anaerobes use the radioisotope as the final electron acceptor, reducing soluble uranium(VI) to insoluble uranium(IV). Sulfate-reducing and metal-reducing bacteria also act indirectly, through the metabolites they excrete. Microbes can work the other way too. Siderophores and other bacterial chelators raise radionuclide solubility and availability.

entries.title: Plants that pull radioactivity from soil

definition.text: The removal of radionuclides from soil by plants that carry them from the roots into their shoots.

facts.text: It leaves soil structure and fertility largely intact and suits large areas of low-level contamination, but needs fast, large biomass production.
It works for caesium-137, strontium-90, technetium-99, plutonium-240 and americium-241, among others.
In the Chernobyl zone, mustard greens removed up to 22% of average caesium activity in one growing season.

entries.title: Sustainable remediation: a cleanup should not do more harm

definition.text: An approach to cleaning up contaminated land that weighs a remedy's environmental, economic and social effects and seeks to minimize the footprint of the cleanup itself.

facts.text: Footprint analysis covers five core elements: energy, air and atmosphere, materials and waste, land and ecosystem, and water.
There are estimated to be more than 450,000 brownfield sites in the US alone needing significant reinvestment.
Pump-and-treat and dig-and-haul can sometimes have lasting side effects worse than the contamination they address.
Some newer in situ techniques have cut life-cycle greenhouse gas emissions by 50 to 80 percent compared with traditional methods.

entries.title: Vapor intrusion: pollution that seeps indoors

definition.text: The migration of volatile chemicals, usually VOCs, from contaminated soil or groundwater into the indoor air of buildings above or nearby.

facts.text: VOCs diffuse through porous soil in the vadose zone to beneath buildings, then enter through foundation cracks by advection and diffusion, driven by the building's stack effect.
Pipes, storm drains and elevator shafts act as preferential pathways into buildings.
Indoor exposure can cause headaches and raise the risk of some cancers, and some vapors pose an explosion hazard.
Mitigation includes sub-slab depressurization with a fan and over-pressurizing the building.

entries.text: Contaminated groundwater can poison the air inside a house. Vapor intrusion is the migration of volatile chemicals, usually VOCs, from soil or groundwater into buildings above or nearby. The vapors diffuse up through the porous {{ref:soil-water-230}} and enter through foundation cracks, drawn in by the building's stack effect. Pipes, storm drains and elevator shafts offer easy paths. Indoors they can cause headaches, raise the risk of some cancers and even threaten explosion. Fixes include a fan that depressurizes the space under the slab, or over-pressurizing the building.

entries.title: Geophagia, the ancient habit of eating earth

definition.text: The deliberate eating of earth or earth-like substances such as clay, chalk or termite-mound soil, by animals and people.

facts.text: It is documented in over 100 primate species, where it protects against parasites, supplies minerals and helps neutralize toxic compounds in leaves.
In humans it is most often reported in children and pregnant women and is classed as a form of pica.
The oldest evidence comes from Kalambo Falls, where calcium-rich white clay lay alongside Homo habilis bones.
Kaolin is sold for eating in Cameroon markets and eaten by pregnant women against nausea, despite possibly dangerous arsenic and lead levels.
Clay minerals may protect the stomach against toxins, parasites and pathogens, and many soils supply calcium, iron and zinc.
Faecally contaminated soil can pass on helminth eggs such as Ascaris, which survive in soil for years, as well as tetanus and lead poisoning.
Bentonite and kaolin are sold as digestive aids, and attapulgite clay is an active ingredient in anti-diarrhoeal medicines.

entries.title: Itai-itai disease, the poisoned rice of the Jinzū River

definition.text: The mass cadmium poisoning in Toyama Prefecture, Japan, from about 1912, named for the severe spine and joint pain it caused.

facts.text: Mines upstream released cadmium into the Jinzū River from 1910 to 1945; cadmium accompanies zinc because the ore sphalerite is almost always paired with greenockite.
Residents irrigated rice with the river water; the highly soluble cadmium contaminated paddies and rice, raising body burdens.
Cadmium accumulated in the kidneys, and kidney damage disrupted calcium balance, causing the bone pain and deformities.
Cadmium was suspected only in 1955, and the 1961 investigation tied it to the Kamioka mine, 55 years after the first reports.
It is one of the Four Big Pollution Diseases of Japan, and the mining company was successfully sued.

entries.text: For 55 years, people along Japan's Jinzū River fell ill without knowing why. Itai-itai disease was a mass cadmium poisoning in Toyama Prefecture, beginning around 1912 and named for the severe spine and joint pain it caused. It is the best-known case of the illness in {{ref:soil-env-256}}. Mines upstream released cadmium into the river from 1910 to 1945. The metal travels with zinc, because the zinc ore sphalerite is almost always paired with greenockite. Residents irrigated their rice with the river water. The highly soluble cadmium soaked into paddies and grain, and body burdens rose. It built up in the kidneys, and damaged kidneys upset the body's calcium balance, bringing bone pain and deformities. Cadmium was suspected only in 1955. A 1961 investigation tied it to the Kamioka mine, 55 years after the first reports. It became one of the Four Big Pollution Diseases of Japan, and the mining company was successfully sued.

entries.title: Valley fever, the illness that rides on dust

definition.text: Valley fever: a fungal disease of mammals caused by inhaling spores of the soil fungi Coccidioides immitis or C. posadasii.

facts.text: The fungus grows as a mycelium in soils of the southwestern US, northern Mexico and parts of Central and South America.
Rain starts its growth; in long dry spells its hyphae break into light arthroconidia that construction, farming, dust storms or earthquakes lift into the air.
A 1977 windstorm near Arvin, California, caused several hundred cases hundreds of miles from the endemic area.
Incidence rises after wet winters that follow drought, and one model projects the endemic region could more than double in area by 2100 under high warming.
Dust control such as planting grass and wetting soil is advised, and NIOSH counts it an occupational hazard in farming, construction, archaeology and mining.
Dogs, which dig and sniff at the ground, are exposed earlier than people and serve as sentinels.

entries.title: Medical geology: when the ground decides who falls ill

definition.text: The interdisciplinary science of how natural geological factors affect the health of people and animals.

facts.text: It covers exposure to or deficiency of trace elements and minerals, mineral dusts, volcanic emissions, radionuclides, microbes and pathogens.
Its two stated priorities are the bioavailability of trace elements and baseline background levels of harmful natural materials in soil, water, air and food.
People who live off the land face either impoverished soils that cause mineral-imbalance diseases, as in Maputaland, or an excess of elements causing toxicity, as in India and Bangladesh.
Iodine deficiency is one of the biggest geochemical diseases; humus and clay in soil trap iodine and make it hard for people to obtain.
Regional problems include fluoride in Africa and India, arsenic in Argentina, Chile and Taiwan, selenium in parts of the US, Venezuela and China, and nitrate in farm areas.
Paracelsus's dictum that the dose makes the poison sums up the field, whose goal is the right balance of element intake.
Hippocrates and Aristotle first linked disease to the earth's elements; the modern field was established in 1990 by the International Union of Geological Sciences.

entries.text: Hippocrates and Aristotle were the first to link disease to the elements of the earth. Medical geology is the modern form of that idea: the interdisciplinary science of how natural geological factors affect the health of people and animals. The International Union of Geological Sciences established the field in 1990. It covers exposure to, or deficiency of, trace elements and {{ref:soil-found-029}}, along with mineral dusts, volcanic emissions, radionuclides, microbes and pathogens. Two priorities lead the work. One is the bioavailability of trace elements, the share the body can actually absorb. The other is the baseline background level of harmful natural materials in soil, water, air and food. People who live off the land meet both extremes. In Maputaland, impoverished soils cause diseases of mineral imbalance. In India and Bangladesh, an excess of elements causes toxicity. A shortage of iodine is among the biggest geochemical diseases, partly because humus and clay in soil trap iodine and keep it from people. Other problems are regional. Fluoride troubles Africa and India, and arsenic troubles Argentina, Chile and Taiwan. Selenium is a problem in parts of the US, Venezuela and China, and nitrate in farm areas. Paracelsus summed up the field in one dictum: the dose makes the poison. Its goal is the right balance of element intake.

entries.title: Iodine, the element missing from inland mountains

definition.text: A lack of the essential dietary trace element iodine, which the thyroid hormones need.

facts.text: It is common in remote inland and especially mountainous areas, where food grows in iodine-poor soil and no marine foods are eaten.
It causes goitre, and in the womb a syndrome of developmental delay; it is a preventable cause of intellectual disability.
Natural deficiency affects about two billion people, particularly in the Western Pacific, South-East Asia and Africa; goitre affected 187 million in 2010.
Adding small amounts of iodine to table salt, at a cost of only a few cents a ton, is the main prevention.
Selenium deficiency is among its risk factors.

entries.text: About two billion people get too little iodine simply because of where their food grows. Iodine deficiency is a lack of this essential dietary trace element, which the thyroid hormones need. It is common in remote inland and especially mountainous areas. There, food grows in iodine-poor soil and nobody eats marine foods. The burden falls particularly on the Western Pacific, South-East Asia and Africa. The lack causes goitre, a swelling of the thyroid gland, which affected 187 million people in 2010. In the womb it causes a syndrome of developmental delay, making it a preventable cause of intellectual disability. The main prevention is cheap. Adding small amounts of iodine to table salt costs only a few cents a ton. A shortage of selenium, described in {{ref:soil-env-296}}, is among its risk factors.

entries.title: Selenium: when the soil runs short, so does the body

definition.text: A shortage of selenium, a critical nutrient, below the levels an organism requires.

facts.text: People who depend on food grown in selenium-deficient soil are at risk.
Croplands and diets are low in selenium in regions of China, Europe, Russia and New Zealand, and loss of selenium from croplands under climate change is predicted to raise prevalence.
Combined with Coxsackievirus it causes Keshan disease, and with iodine deficiency it contributes to Kashin-Beck disease of cartilage.
Finland adds selenium salts to chemical fertilizers to raise soil selenium.
In livestock it causes white muscle disease, to which ruminants are especially prone because they absorb less selenium, particularly from forage.
Adult intake recommendations are 55 μg/day in the US and 70 μg/day from the European Food Safety Authority.

entries.title: Prions, the infectious proteins that cling to clay

definition.text: A misfolded protein that makes normal copies of the same protein misfold, causing fatal, transmissible neurodegenerative diseases.

facts.text: Prions contain no DNA or RNA and cause diseases such as scrapie, chronic wasting disease, BSE and Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease.
Shed from carcasses and body fluids, they may linger in soil by binding to clay and other minerals.

Unbound prions degrade over time, but soil-bound ones stay stable or increase, so prions likely accumulate in the environment; repeated wetting and drying may reduce their infectivity, depending on soil type.
Hamsters fed grass grown where a deer with chronic wasting disease was buried became ill, showing plants can carry prions.

entries.text: A prion carries no DNA or RNA, yet it spreads disease. Repeated wetting and drying may reduce their infectivity, depending on soil type. Hamsters fed grass grown where an infected deer was buried became ill, so plants can carry prions.

entries.title: Melioidosis, the soil bacterium called a time bomb

definition.text: An infectious disease caused by the soil-dwelling bacterium Burkholderia pseudomallei, caught by contact with contaminated soil or water.

facts.text: The bacterium is most abundant 10 to 90 cm deep in soil and also lives in ponds, streams and rice paddies.
It survives more than 16 years in nutrient-poor settings such as desert soil, and tolerates pH 4.5 for 70 days.
It enters through wounds, inhalation or ingestion; it is endemic in Southeast Asia and northern Australia, and cases rise with heavy rain and storms.
A 2016 model estimated about 165,000 infections and 89,000 deaths a year; diabetes is a major risk factor.
Latent infections earned it the name 'Vietnam Time Bomb' after soldiers fell ill years after deployment.
Prevention includes protective gear for handling soil or water and avoiding direct contact with them; there is no approved vaccine.

entries.text: Soldiers came home from Vietnam apparently healthy and fell ill years later. Those latent infections earned melioidosis the name 'Vietnam Time Bomb'. The bacterium is most abundant 10 to 90 cm deep in soil and also lives in ponds, streams and rice paddies. It is hardy. It survives more than 16 years in nutrient-poor settings such as desert soil, and tolerates pH 4.5 for 70 days. It enters the body through wounds, inhalation or ingestion. The disease is endemic in Southeast Asia and northern Australia, and cases rise with heavy rain and storms. A 2016 model estimated about 165,000 infections and 89,000 deaths a year. Diabetes is a major risk factor. There is no approved vaccine, so prevention means protective gear and avoiding direct contact with soil and water.

entries.title: Roundworms in the soil, the commonest human parasites

definition.text: Infection with roundworms spread through soil contaminated with human faeces: ascariasis, hookworm and whipworm.

facts.text: It is the most common human parasitic disease, with about two billion people infected and four billion at risk.
Eggs passed in faeces mature into infective larvae in soil and are swallowed on unwashed produce or hands; hookworm larvae instead hatch and penetrate the skin.
Its main causes are open defecation, lack of hand washing and walking barefoot on contaminated soil, so it is commonest in warm, moist, poorly sanitized regions.
Hookworm is the leading cause of anaemia and protein deficiency in developing nations, affecting an estimated 740 million people.
Deworming reduces worm burdens, but reinfection follows continued exposure; improved water, sanitation and hygiene lower the odds of infection.

entries.text: About two billion people carry worms picked up from soil, and four billion are at risk. Soil-transmitted helminthiasis is infection with roundworms spread through soil contaminated with human faeces. It takes three forms: ascariasis, hookworm and whipworm. Together they make the most common human parasitic disease. The worms are nematodes, the animals of {{ref:soil-bio-193}}. Eggs passed in faeces mature into infective larvae in the soil, and people swallow them on unwashed produce or hands. Hookworm larvae work differently: they hatch and penetrate the skin. Open defecation, lack of hand washing and walking barefoot on contaminated soil are the main causes. So the disease is commonest in warm, moist, poorly sanitized regions. Hookworm affects an estimated 740 million people and is the leading cause of anaemia and protein deficiency in developing nations. Deworming reduces worm burdens, but reinfection follows continued exposure. Improved water, sanitation and hygiene lower the odds of infection.

entries.title: Keshan disease, a heart illness written in the soil

definition.text: A congestive cardiomyopathy caused by dietary selenium deficiency together with a mutated strain of Coxsackievirus, named after Keshan County in China.

facts.text: It was found across a belt from northeast to southwest China, all due to selenium-deficient soil, and peaked in 1960–1970, killing thousands.
Selenium deficiency appears to let a more virulent viral strain dominate.
Selenium supplementation over decades reduced it, and some patients use Astragalus, a herb that accumulates selenium from soil.
Vegetables such as garlic, onions and broccoli are good selenium sources only if their soil contains it.

entries.title: One Health: people, animals and soil as one system

definition.text: An integrated approach that seeks to balance and optimize the health of people, animals, plants and ecosystems together.

facts.text: It arose from the spread of zoonotic diseases and awareness that human and animal health and ecological change are interdependent.
Antimicrobial resistance is treated as a One Health issue: misuse in medicine, veterinary care and farming selects resistant organisms, and wastewater, soil and runoff spread them.
It is backed by the FAO, WHO, the World Organisation for Animal Health and UNEP.

entries.title: Podoconiosis, red clay that swells the legs

definition.text: A disease of the lymphatic vessels of the lower legs, also called nonfilarial elephantiasis, caused by long-term barefoot contact with irritant soils.

facts.text: It is the second most common cause of tropical lymphoedema after lymphatic filariasis, causing disfiguring leg swelling.
It occurs in genetically susceptible people in contact with red clay soils formed over alkaline volcanic bedrock in highlands with about 1500 mm of rain at 1500 m altitude.
Affected areas are enriched in kaolinite and gibbsite; smectite, mica, quartz and iron oxides are also suspects, but no single culprit is proven.
Soil particles penetrate the feet, are taken up by macrophages and collect in lymph nodes, causing chronic inflammation, fibrosis and blockage.
Ernest Price showed silicon, aluminium and other soil metals inside macrophages in patients' lymph nodes.
An estimated 4 million people are affected, 1.5 million in Ethiopia; wearing shoes and using floor coverings prevent it.

entries.title: Why parrots flock to eat one layer of clay

definition.text: The eating of clay-rich soil by birds, notably South American parrots at clay licks.

facts.text: Parrots on the Manu River eat from one specific soil layer, ignoring layers a metre above or below it.
Preferred soils are rich in smectite, kaolin and mica and have far higher cation-exchange capacity, so they bind toxins from seeds that become positively charged in the stomach.
Consumed soils are consistently higher in sodium, and geophagy increases with distance from the ocean, making sodium the likely main driver.

entries.title: Cattle and sheep that eat soil with every bite

definition.text: The swallowing of soil by grazing animals such as cattle and sheep, pressed onto pasture plants by their hooves.

Soil supplies grazers with iron, manganese, zinc, cobalt, copper, selenium and iodine that herbage lacks, but can wear down sheep's incisors.

entries.title: Chronic wasting disease and the ground that spreads it

definition.text: A fatal transmissible spongiform encephalopathy caused by prions that naturally affects deer, elk, moose and their relatives.

facts.text: Prions shed by infected animals are transmitted by eating grass growing in contaminated soil, and stay infectious in the environment for years.
They bind so tightly to soil particles that the ground may be a major route of transmission for grazing deer.
Prions mixed with clay infected deer through the nose, and they were shown by 2006 to bind to sandy quartz clay minerals.
After a Quebec outbreak, inspectors ordered 25 cm of soil decontaminated in parts of the farm.

entries.title: Mycobacterium vaccae, the soil microbe that calmed mice

definition.text: A nonpathogenic bacterium of the Mycobacteriaceae that lives naturally in soil.

facts.text: It was first isolated in Uganda, where locals said a muddy substance could cure ailments; its name comes from cow dung, where the first strain was cultured.
Heat-killed cells injected into mice raised serotonin and lowered anxiety, and mice fed live cells ran a maze twice as fast with less anxiety.
Killed-cell vaccines are being studied for asthma, depression, psoriasis, eczema and tuberculosis.

entries.title: Replacing the poisoned paddies of the Jinzū River

facts.text: Japan's 1970 agricultural soil contamination law stopped planting for restoration where soil held 1 ppm cadmium or more; by 1977, 1,500 hectares were designated.

By 1996 cadmium in the farmland had returned to a background level of 0.1 ppb.

entries.title: Biofortification: breeding nutrients into the crop itself

definition.text: Breeding crops, conventionally or by genetic engineering, so that they contain more nutrients as they grow.

facts.text: It targets micronutrient deficiencies such as vitamin A, zinc and iron in low- and middle-income countries, reaching the rural poor who rarely get fortified foods.
Beta-carotene sweet potatoes cut vitamin A deficiency in Mozambican children by 24%, and iron- and zinc-rich pearl millet improved iron status in India.
Researchers are developing bread grain biofortified with selenium to raise low selenium levels in British grains.
Critics warn it may further simplify diets and urge it be part of wider food diversification.

entries.title: The hygiene hypothesis and the microbes that may tune immunity

definition.text: The idea that early-childhood exposure to certain microorganisms protects against allergies by properly tuning the immune system.

facts.text: Later versions, such as Graham Rook's 2003 'old friends' hypothesis, focus on microbes that co-evolved with humans rather than recent crowd infections.
Rook's candidates include ambient species sharing human environments, and most mammalian evolution took place in mud and rotting vegetation.
Much evidence supports it, yet many scientists still reject it, and it struggles to explain allergies in less affluent regions.
It is not about personal cleanliness: poor hygiene raises infection risk without lowering allergy risk.

entries.title: Photosynthesis: how light becomes the food that feeds soil

definition.text: The biological process by which plants, algae and cyanobacteria convert light energy into chemical energy stored in organic compounds.

facts.text: Usually it means oxygenic photosynthesis, which splits water and releases oxygen; the stored carbohydrates are later used in cellular respiration.
In plants, chlorophyll in chloroplasts absorbs red and blue light; light reactions make NADPH and ATP, and the Calvin cycle then builds sugars from atmospheric CO2.
It maintains atmospheric oxygen and supplies most biological energy; global photosynthesis captures about 130 terawatts and fixes 100-115 billion tons of carbon into biomass yearly.
Plants convert light with efficiency usually 3-6%, ranging from 0.1% to 8% with light, temperature and CO2.
Photosynthesis was discovered in 1779 by Jan Ingenhousz, who showed that plants need light, not just soil and water.

entries.title: Reading the clocks hidden inside rocks and soil

definition.text: The science of finding the age of rocks, fossils and sediments from signatures held in the materials themselves.

facts.text: Absolute ages come from radioactive isotopes, while relative ages come from tools such as paleomagnetism and stable isotope ratios.
Combining several dating indicators, including fossil-based ones, makes the recovered age more precise.
Radiometric dating measures how far an isotope of known half-life has decayed; slowly decaying isotopes reach further back but give less exact ages in years.
Radiocarbon dating suits organic samples younger than about 60,000 years, uranium–lead dating samples older than about 1 million years.
Uranium–thorium dating covers a few years to about 700,000 years and is used on speleothems, corals, carbonates and fossil bones.
Marker horizons are layers so distinctive that their age-equivalence across different sites is certain; dated volcanic ash layers are one example.
Incremental methods such as dendrochronology and lichenometry build year-by-year chronologies.
Amino acid dating is cheap but cannot give numerical ages without calibration from other methods at the same site.

Uranium–thorium dating spans a few years to about 700,000 years, on speleothems, the mineral deposits of caves, and on corals, carbonates and fossil bones. Relative ages come from paleomagnetism and stable isotope ratios. Marker horizons, such as dated volcanic ash layers, are so distinctive that their age-equivalence across sites is certain. Incremental methods such as dendrochronology, tree-ring dating, and lichenometry build year-by-year chronologies. Amino acid dating is cheap, but gives no numbers without calibration from other methods at the same site. Combining several indicators, fossils among them, sharpens any age.

entries.title: Radiocarbon dating and the clock that starts at death

definition.text: A method of finding the age of material containing organic carbon from how much of its radioactive carbon-14 is left.

facts.text: Cosmic rays striking atmospheric nitrogen constantly make carbon-14, which enters plants through photosynthesis and animals through the plants they eat.
When an organism dies it stops exchanging carbon and its carbon-14 decays, so older samples hold less of it.
Carbon-14's half-life is about 5,730 years, so reliable dates reach back to roughly 50,000 years ago.
Willard Libby developed the method at the University of Chicago in the late 1940s and received the 1960 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it.
Dates must be corrected for fractionation and reservoir effects, and are complicated by fossil-fuel burning and 1950s–1960s nuclear tests.
Accelerator mass spectrometry counts every carbon-14 atom rather than only decays, so it works on samples as small as single seeds.
Contamination with 1% modern carbon makes a 17,000-year-old sample look 600 years younger; 1% old carbon makes any sample look about 80 years older.
Its impact on archaeology was so great that histories of the field call it the 'radiocarbon revolution'.

entries.title: Palynology, the science of pollen that refuses to dissolve

definition.text: The study of acid-resistant microscopic organic remains, such as pollen and spores, found in sediments and sedimentary rocks.

facts.text: Palynomorphs, 5 to 500 micrometres across, include pollen, spores, dinoflagellate cysts, fungi and plant tissue.
They are extracted from soils, rocks and sediment cores by ultrasonic treatment, wet sieving and acid digestion that remove the mineral fraction.
Potassium hydroxide removes humic substances, hydrofluoric acid digests silicate minerals, and acetolysis dissolves the cellulose that hampers work on peat.
Quantitative pollen analysis began with Lennart von Post, whose 1916 Kristiania lecture spread the method.
Grains of each taxon are counted under the microscope to make a pollen diagram, with depth on the y-axis and abundance on the x-axis.
Records from peat or lake sediments reconstruct past vegetation and climate and reveal human effects such as logging and land use.
It is applied in geology, archaeology, pedology and physical geography, including relative dating of strata through biostratigraphy.

entries.text: Pollen is tough enough to survive acid baths that dissolve rock minerals. Analysts count each taxon's grains under the microscope and draw a pollen diagram, with depth on the y-axis and abundance on the x-axis. Quantitative pollen analysis began with Lennart von Post, whose 1916 lecture in Kristiania spread the method. Analysts count each taxon's grains under the microscope and draw a pollen diagram, with depth on the y-axis and abundance on the x-axis. Records from peat or lake sediments reconstruct past vegetation and climate. They also reveal human effects such as logging and land use. Geologists, archaeologists, pedologists and physical geographers all use it, including for dating strata relative to one another.

entries.title: Luminescence dating: when a grain last saw the sun

definition.text: A group of methods that find how long ago mineral grains were last exposed to sunlight or strong heating.

facts.text: Natural radiation from cosmic rays and traces of potassium, uranium, thorium and rubidium builds up trapped charge in buried quartz or feldspar grains.
Stimulating the grains with light or heat releases a luminescence signal whose intensity reflects how long they were buried.
The methods assume grains were 'bleached' when buried; 1–100 s of daylight resets quartz, as usually happens in dunes, loess and some water-laid deposits.
Age equals the equivalent dose in grays divided by the environmental dose rate, typically 0.5–5 Gy per 1000 years.
Quartz OSL ages typically span 100 to 350,000 years BP, with uncertainties of 5–10% of the age; feldspar IRSL may reach a million years.
Unlike radiocarbon dating it needs no organic material and avoids errors from old, carbon-14-deficient carbon.
At Lake Ulaan in Mongolia, wind-blown carbon from nearby soils and old carbonate rocks made radiocarbon dates up to 5800 years too old, while OSL was unaffected.
Thermoluminescence was first used to date unheated sediments in 1965, and optical dating with OSL was developed in 1984.

entries.title: Cosmogenic nuclides, atoms forged by rays from space

definition.text: A rare isotope created when a high-energy cosmic ray strikes an atom's nucleus in the Solar System and knocks out protons and neutrons.

facts.text: They form within rocks and soil, in the atmosphere, and in meteoroids.
Useful ones are absent from the host material when it forms, so their build-up records later exposure.
Beryllium-10 (half-life 1,387,000 years) dates exposure of rocks, soils and ice cores; aluminium-26 and chlorine-36 date rocks and sediment.
In rock most of the cosmic-ray flux is absorbed within the first metre, where new nuclides form.
Spallation dominates in the top 0 to 60 cm, muon capture a few metres down, and neutron capture depends on snow, soil moisture and trace elements.
Air pressure changes nuclide production in minerals by a factor of 30 between sea level and the top of a 5 km mountain.

entries.text: Earth's surface sits under a constant, invisible bombardment. When a high-energy cosmic ray strikes an atom's nucleus and knocks out protons and neutrons, it can leave a rare isotope: a cosmogenic nuclide. These form within rocks and soil, in the atmosphere and in meteoroids. The useful ones are absent from the host material when it forms. Their build-up therefore records how long it has been exposed since. Beryllium-10, with a half-life of 1,387,000 years, dates the exposure of rocks, soils and ice cores. Aluminum-26 and chlorine-36 date rocks and sediment. Rock absorbs most of the cosmic-ray flux within its first meter, and that is where new nuclides form. Spallation, the chipping of nuclei by direct hits, dominates in the top 0 to 60 cm. Muon capture takes over a few meters down. Neutron capture depends on snow, soil moisture and trace elements. Altitude matters too: air pressure changes production in minerals by a factor of 30 between sea level and the top of a 5 km mountain.

entries.title: When photosynthesis began, and how it changed the air

definition.text: Photosynthesis began early in Earth's history, probably as anoxygenic forms using hydrogen or sulfur rather than water.

facts.text: Possible filamentous photosynthetic fossils are 3.4 billion years old, and thylakoid membranes are preserved in 1.75-billion-year-old cherts.

Using water as electron source evolved once, in a common ancestor of living cyanobacteria at least 2450-2320 million years ago; their oxygen oxygenated Earth, an event sometimes called the oxygen catastrophe.

definition.text: Photosynthesis is limited by light, leaf area for capturing light, CO2 supply to chloroplasts, water and temperature.

facts.text: Shading by other plants is a major limitation, and sugar production rises with CO2 concentration until another factor limits it.

entries.title: Light reactions: capturing sunlight as ATP and NADPH

definition.text: The first stage of photosynthesis, in which chlorophyll absorbs light, electrons flow down a transport chain, and ATP and NADPH are made.

facts.text: An electron passes through pheophytin and an electron transport chain to reduce NADP to NADPH, while a proton gradient drives ATP synthase.
Chlorophyll regains its lost electron when water is split by photolysis, releasing oxygen; the reactions occur in the thylakoid membranes of chloroplasts.
Not all wavelengths work: in green plants the action spectrum peaks in violet-blue and red light, while red algae use blue-green light to grow deeper.

entries.title: Photorespiration: when RuBisCO grabs the wrong molecule
entries.article: Photosynthesis#Factors > Carbon dioxide levels and photorespiration

definition.text: When CO2 is low, RuBisCO binds oxygen instead, a wasteful process that uses energy and makes no sugar.

facts.text: The oxygen reaction yields phosphoglycolate, which the Calvin cycle cannot use, and glycolate, which is toxic at high concentration and inhibits photosynthesis.
Salvaging glycolate is energetically expensive: only 75% of its carbon returns to the cycle, and ammonia is lost, so nitrogen leaves the plant.
In hot, dry conditions closed stomata drop CO2 and raise oxygen, increasing photorespiration.

entries.title: C4 and CAM: two ways to dodge photorespiration
entries.article: Photosynthesis#Light-independent reactions > Carbon concentrating mechanisms > On land

definition.text: Some plants raise CO2 concentration at RuBisCO using PEP carboxylase, in C4 plants by separating steps in space and in CAM plants by separating them in time.

facts.text: C4 plants fix CO2 in mesophyll cells into oxaloacetate, then release it in bundle sheath cells where RuBisCO sits away from the oxygen-producing light reactions, cutting photorespiration.
C4 plants outproduce C3 plants in high light and temperature and include maize, sorghum, sugarcane and millet; over 90% of plants are C3 and about 3% C4, yet C4 evolved in over sixty lineages.
CAM plants such as cacti and succulents fix CO2 at night with open stomata, storing it as malic acid and releasing it by day; about 16,000 species use it.

entries.title: δ13C, the carbon signature plants leave in soil

definition.text: A normalized ratio of the stable carbon isotopes carbon-13 and carbon-12, reported in parts per thousand (per mille, ‰).

facts.text: It compares a sample's 13C/12C ratio with that of an established reference standard, expressed per mille.
The original standard, a Cretaceous belemnite fossil (PDB), ran out and was replaced by standards such as VPDB.
Organisms take up light carbon-12 preferentially and have δ13C of about −25‰, depending on their metabolic pathway.
C4 plants have δ13C of −16 to −10‰ and C3 plants −33 to −24‰, so the rise of C4 grasses can be traced through time.
It separates carbon dioxide from ecosystem respiration from that of burned fossil fuels, the basis of the Suess effect.
Carbon isotopes in pedogenic carbonate nodules of paleosols are used to reconstruct past atmospheric carbon dioxide.
On the Loess Plateau, δ13C of pedogenic carbonate rose by 5% over the Late Miocene and Pliocene, indicating drying.

entries.text: Plants stamp their soil with a signature of how they photosynthesize. δ13C is a normalized ratio of the stable carbon isotopes carbon-13 and carbon-12. In a paleosol, carbon isotopes in pedogenic carbonate nodules reconstruct past atmospheric carbon dioxide. On the Loess Plateau, the δ13C of such carbonate rose by 5% over the Late Miocene and Pliocene, a sign of drying.

entries.title: Optically stimulated luminescence: grains that glow on cue

definition.text: A method of measuring the radiation dose a mineral has absorbed from the light it emits when stimulated, used to date sediments.

facts.text: Radiation traps electrons at impurities and defects in quartz and feldspar; light frees them, and they emit light when they recombine at luminescence centres.
Grains, usually coarse 100–200 μm or fine 4–11 μm, must be extracted from the sample without exposure to light.
It dates minerals rather than organic material, such as the deposition of wind-blown and river sediments.
Developed in 1984 by David J. Huntley and colleagues, it is now most often done by single-aliquot regeneration (SAR).

entries.title: Tephrochronology: volcanic ash as a time marker

definition.text: Dating and correlating sequences and events by their position between layers of volcanic ash (tephra) of known date.

facts.text: Each eruption leaves a tephra horizon with a unique chemical fingerprint, which becomes a time marker once the eruption is dated.
Ash falls almost instantly over wide areas, linking distant sequences into one 'age-equivalent' chronology and checking other dating methods.
Fingerprinting uses the electron microprobe and laser-ablation ICP-MS on single shards, though basaltic tephra chemistry can alter over time.
Since the late 1990s, invisible 'cryptotephra' layers have been extracted from archives such as peat, lake sediment and loess.

entries.title: Thermoluminescence dating and the reset of heat

definition.text: Dating by the accumulated radiation dose of the time since crystalline material was last heated, as in lava or ceramics, or exposed to sunlight, as in sediments.

facts.text: Heating or sunlight empties the electron traps to zero; afterwards the surrounding radiation steadily refills them.
The dose measured by heating is divided by the yearly dose rate, found from uranium, thorium and potassium contents plus cosmic rays, to give the age.
The annual dose a buried object receives from the surrounding soil affects accuracy, so it is ideally measured at the find spot over a long period.
It is used where radiocarbon dating is not possible, such as for sediments; heated objects must have gone above 500 °C.

entries.text: Heating a pot in a kiln, or melting rock into lava, sets a clock to zero. entries.title: Radiocarbon calibration: turning lab numbers into calendar dates

definition.text: The use of a calibration curve of past atmospheric carbon-14 to convert a sample's radiocarbon measurement into an estimated calendar age.

facts.text: Calibration is needed because atmospheric carbon-14 has varied significantly, breaking the simple decay equation's assumption of a constant level.
Tree-ring sequences gave the first calibration data, and Hans Suess published the first calibration curve in 1967.
The IntCal curves, first published in 1998 and updated to 2020, have separate northern (IntCal20), southern (SHCal20) and marine (MARINE20) versions.
Uncalibrated 'conventional radiocarbon ages' still use the Libby half-life of 5568 years, agreed in 1962 for consistency with early papers.

entries.title: Why soil and peat are hard to radiocarbon date

definition.text: Radiocarbon dating of the organic matter in soils and peat, which is hard to do reliably because younger humic acid tends to contaminate it.

facts.text: For soil it is better to sieve out fragments of organic origin and date them with methods that tolerate small samples.
Of peat's humic acid, humins and fulvic acid, the humins give the most reliable date because they are insoluble in alkali and less contaminated.
Old carbon from limestone or groundwater can give apparent ages of thousands of years, and humus can do the same or, if younger, lower the apparent age.
Radiocarbon dating of soil organic carbon and lake methane showed 0.2 to 2.5 Pg of permafrost carbon released over the last 60 years.

entries.title: Surface exposure dating: how long a rock has seen the sky

definition.text: A set of techniques for estimating how long a rock has been exposed at or near Earth's surface.

facts.text: It dates glacial advances and retreats, erosion history, lava flows, rock slides and fault scarps, and works best for exposures of 10³ to 10⁶ years.
Measuring cosmogenic nuclide concentrations, with cosmic-ray flux and half-life, gives exposure time, burial time or how fast a drainage basin erodes.
Beryllium-10 and aluminium-26 form from quartz's oxygen and silicon; their ratio dates burial below the production depth, typically 2–10 meters.
Production rates are calibrated on samples dated by radiocarbon or luminescence, and the nuclides are measured by accelerator mass spectrometry.

entries.text: A boulder left by a retreating glacier starts collecting cosmic-ray atoms once exposed. Surface exposure dating estimates how long a rock has been at or near Earth's surface. It dates glacial advances and retreats, erosion history, lava flows, rock slides and fault scarps. It works best for exposures of 10³ to 10⁶ years. Measured concentrations of cosmogenic nuclides, with the cosmic-ray flux and their half-lives, give exposure time, burial time or how fast a drainage basin erodes. Beryllium-10 and aluminum-26 form from the oxygen and silicon in quartz. Their ratio dates burial below the production depth, typically 2–10 meters. Rates are calibrated on samples dated by radiocarbon or luminescence; accelerator mass spectrometry measures the nuclides.

entries.title: Beryllium-10, a rain-borne tracer of soil

definition.text: The use of beryllium-10, a cosmogenic isotope with a half-life of 1.387 million years formed in the atmosphere, to trace soil formation and erosion.

facts.text: Beryllium dissolves below about pH 5.5, so rain carries it down, and it drops out of solution as the water turns more alkaline.
It therefore accumulates at the soil surface, where its long half-life does not limit its residence time.
It has been used to study soil erosion, soil formation from regolith, the development of lateritic soils and the age of ice cores.
Short-lived beryllium-7, with a half-life of 53.22 days, shows that sediments are fresh, less than about 3–4 months old.

entries.title: The bomb pulse, a nuclear-age spike in carbon-14

definition.text: The sudden rise of carbon-14 in Earth's atmosphere caused by above-ground nuclear tests from 1945 until the 1963 Limited Test Ban Treaty.

facts.text: The tests almost doubled the relative concentration of carbon-14 in the atmosphere.
Since the 1963 ban the relative concentration has fallen by about 4% a year, which lets scientists date recent tissues and deaths.
The pulse has been used to test atmospheric transport models and to study carbon movement between the atmosphere and oceanic or terrestrial sinks.
It will die out around 2030 if no more nuclear weapons are detonated above ground.

entries.title: Lead-210 dating, a century of soil movement

definition.text: The use of lead-210, a radioactive isotope in the uranium-238 decay chain with a half-life of 22.20 years, to date recent sediments and trace soil movement.

facts.text: Excess lead-210 from atmospheric fallout of radon-222 decay products builds up in surface soils.
Its activity profile with depth reconstructs soil redistribution over the past century, giving erosion and deposition rates and testing conservation practices.
Because its deposition is continuous and global, it complements the medium-term record from human-made radionuclides such as caesium-137.
It suits sedimentation chronologies on time scales shorter than 100 years.

entries.title: Rhizoliths, the fossil ghosts of roots

definition.text: An organosedimentary structure formed by plant roots in soils or fossil soils (paleosols).

facts.text: Rhizoliths include root moulds, casts, tubules, petrifactions and rhizocretions.
They help identify paleosols, but only in post-Silurian beds, since plants with extensive roots did not flourish before then.
Roots that secrete bicarbonate rather than hydrogen ions raise the surrounding pH, which may trigger calcium carbonate to precipitate as rhizocretions.
Rhizohaloes are grey reduced zones with reddish rims around decayed roots; rhizolith mineralogy shows how waterlogged a paleosol was.

entries.text: Roots rot away, but the shapes they leave in soil can outlast them. A rhizolith is an organosedimentary structure formed by plant roots in soils or paleosols.
