Rhizolith mineralogy shows how waterlogged a paleosol was. They help identify paleosols, but only in post-Silurian beds, since plants with extensive roots did not flourish before then.

entries.title: Marine isotope stages: numbering ice ages

definition.text: Alternating warm and cool periods of Earth's climate deduced from oxygen isotope data in deep-sea cores.

facts.text: Counting back from the present (MIS 1), even-numbered stages have high oxygen-18 and are cold glacials, while odd-numbered stages are warm interglacials.
The scale grew from Emiliani's 1950s work on Urey's prediction that calcite's oxygen-18 ratio varies with water temperature; Shackleton showed in 1967 that ice-sheet volume was the main cause.
The record matches Milankovitch orbital cycles, which helped that theory win acceptance, and is the standard for correlating Quaternary climate records.
Over 100 stages are identified; MIS 5e (about 123 kya) is the Last Interglacial, MIS 5d to 2 is the Last Glacial Period, and the list reaches MIS 104 at 2.614 million years ago.

entries.title: Clumped isotopes: a thermometer inside carbonate

definition.text: Clumped isotopes are heavy isotopes bonded to other heavy isotopes within a molecule such as carbonate; their abundance depends on temperature.

facts.text: The carbonate clumped-isotope thermometer uses the temperature dependence of 13C-18O bonding in the carbonate lattice, with more clumping as temperature falls, reported as Δ47.
Unlike conventional δ18O analysis it does not need the water's δ18O, so it gives temperature and lets source-water δ18O be reconstructed.
Carbonate is reacted with phosphoric acid to release CO2, which is purified and analyzed by mass spectrometry at precision near 10^-5.
Uses include past lake and seawater temperatures, paleoaltimetry such as Andes uplift, and extinct animal body temperatures.
The signal is subtle (-0.0005%/°C) and the key isotopologue is about 60 ppm, so analyses take 2-3 hours and need large, uncontaminated samples.

entries.title: When roots first broke rock into soil

definition.text: The rapid spread and diversification of land plants and fungi between 428 and 359 million years ago, in the Silurian and Devonian periods.

facts.text: Earlier non-vascular plants lacked the deep roots needed to break solid rock into regolith and soil.
Plant roots eroded rock and created a water-holding, mineral- and organic-rich soil layer, the pedosphere.
Roots and their microbial partners formed the rhizosphere, speeding weathering and releasing phosphates, calcium and magnesium, as pedogenic carbonates show.
Enhanced silicate weathering is thought to have cut atmospheric CO2 from around 6300 to 2100 ppmv, though another hypothesis says plants slowed weathering.

entries.contested_note: Sources disagree whether early land plants increased silicate weathering or instead lowered CO2 mainly through organic carbon burial in wetlands.
entries.text: Earlier non-vascular plants lacked the deep roots needed to break solid rock into regolith and soil. The Silurian-Devonian Terrestrial Revolution was the rapid spread and diversification of land plants and fungi between 428 and 359 million years ago. The new roots eroded rock and built the pedosphere, a water-holding layer rich in minerals and organic matter. With their microbial partners they formed the rhizosphere, which sped weathering and released phosphates, calcium and magnesium, as pedogenic carbonates show. Enhanced silicate weathering is thought to have cut atmospheric CO2 from around 6300 to 2100 ppmv. Researchers still disagree, though. Another view holds that plants slowed weathering and lowered CO2 mainly by burying organic carbon in wetlands.

entries.title: Taphonomy: the journey from death to fossil

definition.text: The study of how organisms decay and become fossilized or preserved.

facts.text: The Soviet scientist Ivan Efremov introduced the term in 1940 for the passage of remains from the biosphere to the lithosphere.
Its processes fall into biostratinomy, between death and burial, and diagenesis, after burial.
In archaeology it considers effects such as burning, rodent disturbance, gnaw marks and soil pH.
Archaeologists observe these transformation processes to understand their impact on archaeological material at real sites.

entries.text: Between death and discovery, every bone and shell goes through a long series of changes. Taphonomy is the study of how organisms decay and become fossilized or preserved. Archaeologists observe these processes at real sites to judge how they alter what survives.

entries.title: Geoarchaeology: reading a site as a landscape

definition.text: A multidisciplinary field that applies the theories and techniques of the geosciences to archaeology.

facts.text: It draws on geomorphology, sedimentology, pedology, stratigraphy and geochronology to interpret the sediments, soils and landforms of sites.
Its three aims are to place sites in time, to understand the natural processes that create them, and to reconstruct their landscapes.
It studies natural processes that affect buried sites and artefacts after deposition.
Its stratigraphic principles go back to Nicolas Steno in 1669 and James Hutton in 1788; it became a subfield of archaeology in the 1970s–1980s.
Monolith sampling hammers narrow metal tins into a section in overlapping sequence to collect a site's complete profile for laboratory study.
A soil sample's particle-size distribution may show the conditions under which its layer was deposited.

entries.text: An archaeological site is also a piece of ground, shaped by sediments, soils and landforms. entries.title: Environmental DNA, the genetic traces left in soil

definition.text: DNA collected from environmental samples such as soil, sediment, water, snow or air rather than from an individual organism.

facts.text: Sequencing it reveals which species are present in an ecosystem, including microscopic ones not otherwise detectable.
Many microbes cannot be cultured in the laboratory, so their genetic make-up is accessible only through eDNA.
Extracellular DNA can reach 2 μg/L in soil and 88 μg/L in natural waters.
It was first applied to terrestrial sediments, yielding DNA of extinct and living animals and plants, known as sedimentary ancient DNA or 'dirtDNA'.

entries.title: Soil marks: buried features that show through as color

definition.text: A difference in soil colour caused by archaeological features beneath it.

facts.text: A ploughed-out earthwork leaves hard, dry bank material and damper ditch material, or a feature may cut through topsoil to expose chalk.
They usually show in ploughed or harrowed fields before crops grow.
Black or red soil can show organic or burnt deposits, indicating whether fire was used.
They can reveal former river channels or slightly raised dry ground on floodplains that attracted settlement.

entries.title: Middens, the rubbish heaps that keep the past

definition.text: An old dump for domestic waste.

facts.text: Middens may hold animal bones, human excrement, plant material, mollusc shells, potsherds and stone tools.
Damp, anaerobic conditions in a midden can preserve organic remains.
Shell middens are alkaline from calcium carbonate, which slows decay by soil acidity and preserves organic material.
Sediment laid down by wind, water and animal digging forms a matrix that yields seasonal and climatic information.

entries.title: The law of superposition: oldest at the bottom

definition.text: The principle that in undeformed layered sequences the oldest layers lie at the bottom and newer material stacks on top.

facts.text: Nicolas Steno first proposed it in 1669, and William 'Strata' Smith popularized it in English to make the first geologic map of Britain.
Archaeological layers can form by undercutting earlier ones, so applying superposition at sites needs interpretation.
Animals, vegetation and limestone crystallization can disrupt the original layering.

entries.text: In a stack of undisturbed layers, the bottom one came first. At archaeological sites, layers can form by undercutting earlier ones, so applying the law needs interpretation.

entries.title: Stratigraphy: putting a site's events in order

definition.text: The study of a site's sequence of superimposed units, or contexts, to learn when and how its deposits formed.

facts.text: Contexts are single events that leave discrete traces: deposits such as a ditch's back-fill, structures such as walls, or 'cuts' that remove earlier material.
Stratigraphic relationships give the order in which contexts formed: a ditch must be cut before it is back-filled.
A Harris matrix represents a site's formation in space and time.
Two long-accepted principles: lower units are older than upper ones, and a layer is no older than the most recent artefact in it.
E.C. Harris added the principles of original horizontality, lateral continuity and stratigraphic succession.
A context sealed between two dated layers must date between them.
Older 'residual' finds and later 'intrusive' finds can enter a context, so dating rests on its latest evidence.

entries.title: Forensic geology, from Sherlock Holmes to the courtroom

definition.text: The study of earth materials as evidence to answer questions raised by the legal system.

facts.text: Its main use today is trace evidence: soil and sediment particles can link a suspect to a crime or crime scene.
Trace evidence rests on Edmond Locard's exchange principle, that every contact leaves a trace.
In 1891 Hans Gross used microscopic analysis of soil from a suspect's shoes to link him to a crime scene.
Ray Murray dates the field's idea to Arthur Conan Doyle, whose Sherlock Holmes could tell where someone had been from clays on their shoes.
Murray and John Tedrow published the book Forensic Geology in 1975.
Ground-penetrating radar is used mainly to find buried bodies, narrowing the search area and cutting excavation time.

entries.title: Matching a muddy shoe to a crime scene

definition.text: The comparison of a questioned soil sample of unknown origin with control samples, such as soil from the crime scene, to find similarities or differences.

facts.text: Colour is one of the most important properties; it is matched to the Munsell soil chart, though colour perception differs between people.
Spectrophotometry using CIELAB coordinates gives objective numerical colour values to avoid errors of human perception.
Particle-size distribution is among the most discriminating properties, measured by microscope, laser diffraction or dry or wet sieving.
pH can point to elements such as P, Zn, B, Cu and Fe and to lime requirement.
Because soils differ over very short distances, the questioned sample is examined first to choose where to sample at the scene.
A lump of soil is kept whole to preserve its layers, and ground samples are taken from different horizons varying in colour, minerals and texture.
Samples are dried before collection, or refrigerated if damp, so microbial activity does not change their composition.

entries.title: Celtic fields, small prehistoric plots with a misleading name

definition.text: An old name for traces of prehistoric field systems in north-west Europe.

facts.text: The fields have nothing to do with Celtic culture; O. G. S. Crawford gave them the name.
They date from the Early Bronze Age (c. 1800 BC) to the early medieval period and survive as earthworks or soil marks.
Plots were rarely more than 2,000 m², small enough for one person or household to cultivate.
Lynchets at their upper and lower ends are evidence of early ploughing.

entries.title: Ridge and furrow, the ripples of medieval ploughing

definition.text: A pattern of ridges and troughs left by a ploughing system used in medieval Europe, typical of the open-field system.

facts.text: Non-reversible ploughs turned soil toward the centre of the same strip each year, gradually building a ridge with a furrow between strips.
Ridges drained wet soils into the furrows; only some well-drained soils were left flat.
Surviving ridges stand up to 24 inches (61 cm), but in use they were over 6 feet (1.8 m) in places.
The pattern survives where land became grassland and was never ploughed again; reversible ploughs erased it elsewhere.

entries.title: Forensic palynology: pollen as a witness

definition.text: The use of pollen, spores and other palynomorphs to prove or disprove a link between objects, people and places in criminal and civil cases.

facts.text: Regions, and even parts of one garden, have distinctive pollen assemblages, and pollen can also show the season it was picked up.
Pollen in soil, clothing, hair and rock is hard for a suspect to remove because it adheres so well.
In a 2023 Argentine case, soil in the suspect's car and shoe soles matched the palynomorph composition of the coast where the body was found.
A Bolivian study built a forensic database of pollen assemblages in high-altitude, non-seasonal soils.

entries.title: Forensic archaeology: finding graves through the soil

definition.text: The branch of forensic anthropology that uses archaeological methods in legal cases, such as finding overlooked graves and processing mass graves.

facts.text: Differences in the soil help forensic archaeologists locate grave sites.
Burying a body leaves a small mound of soil from the grave fill.
Loose soil and nutrients from the decomposing body encourage different plant growth from the surroundings.
Grave sites typically have looser, darker, more organic soil than the area around them.

entries.title: Geotaphonomy: how a burial changes the ground

definition.text: The study of how a decomposing body and its burial affect the surrounding environment.

facts.text: It examines how the soil was disturbed, how the pH around the body changed, and whether plant growth sped up or slowed.
It also covers tool marks from digging the grave and changes to land and drainage from adding an unnatural mass.
Forensic taphonomy as a whole studies post-mortem changes to remains caused by soil, water, plants, insects and animals.
William M. Bass created the first body farm to study decomposition in conditions such as partial or full burial.

entries.title: Magnetic susceptibility: fire's lasting mark in soil

definition.text: Measurement of how readily a material becomes magnetised in an external magnetic field, used on soils and sediments.

facts.text: A soil's susceptibility reflects magnetic iron oxides such as maghemite, not its total iron content.
Burning and microbial activity form magnetic iron, as in topsoils and some anaerobic deposits.
It finds hearths and burning residues and tells reddening by fire from reddening by natural processes such as gleying.
It can also identify buried soils and soil material redeposited in peat or lake sediments.

It can identify buried soils, too, and soil material redeposited in peat or lake sediments.

entries.title: Geophysical survey: mapping a site without digging

definition.text: Ground-based physical sensing techniques used to image or map buried archaeological features.

facts.text: Instruments detect buried features whose physical properties contrast measurably with their surroundings, without digging or damage.
Most sites lie within the top metre, and targets may be as faint as organic staining from decayed wooden posts.
The usual instruments are magnetometers, electrical resistance meters, ground-penetrating radar and electromagnetic conductivity meters.
A stone foundation resists electric current, while organic midden deposits conduct it more easily than surrounding soils.
Magnetometers respond strongly to brick and burned soil and can pick up subtle anomalies from disturbed soils or decayed organic matter.
Radar works best in uniform sandy soils; conductive clays and silts weaken the signal and rocky sediments scatter it.
Ploughed fields are a source of magnetic noise, while old tracks can show through differential compaction in magnetic soils.
The approach was pioneered in Britain in the 1940s and 1950s.

entries.title: Soil phosphate survey: the chemical footprint of people
entries.article: Geoarchaeology#Phosphate and Orthophosphate Content with Spectrophotometry

definition.text: Measuring and mapping phosphate in soil, which comes from people, their animals, rubbish and bones, to find former activity areas and sites.

facts.text: One hundred people excrete about 62 kg of phosphate a year, with about as much again from their rubbish.
Most of it is quickly fixed on soil clay and can persist for thousands of years, so human activity soon makes large differences.
The human body holds about 650 g of phosphate, raising levels at burial sites.
Phosphorus is detected by the molybdate blue reaction, whose colour depth is proportional to concentration.

entries.title: Cropmarks: buried walls drawn in growing grain

definition.text: A pattern in growing crops, visible from the air or high ground, that reveals buried archaeological, natural or recent features.

facts.text: Cropmarks come from differential growth, and soil conditions are a key factor.
A buried wall diverts water and displaces fertile soil, stunting crops, while an organic-rich ditch fill holds water and boosts growth.
They show only seasonally and may need very wet or dry years; droughts make them appear even in hardy grass.
Thermal imaging can show crop marks at any growth stage, because water loss depends on water available to roots.

entries.title: Raised fields: farming on mounds above the water

definition.text: A large cultivated mound, usually bounded by water-filled ditches, used to control moisture, frost damage and flooding.

facts.text: Raised fields were used by Pre-Hispanic cultures of Latin America, for example in the Llanos de Moxos of lowland Bolivia.
The Tiwanaku culture used them near Lake Titicaca, where the technique is called Waru Waru.
The Maya farmed raised fields at Pulltrouser Swamp in Belize, and the Aztecs built chinampas on Lake Texcoco.

entries.title: World Congress of Soil Science, every four years

definition.text: The International Union of Soil Sciences' conference, held every four years apart from a break for World War II.

facts.text: A congress advances soil science and its application and handles the society's business; only members may attend.
The 1st congress met in Washington, DC, in 1927 and the 2nd in Leningrad in 1930.
About 2000 members have attended each congress since the 15th, in Acapulco, Mexico.
Editions of the World Reference Base were launched at congresses: the first at Montpellier in 1998 and the fourth at Glasgow in 2022.
Until 2014 the IUSS President was named by the national society hosting the next congress.
The 23rd congress met in Nanjing, China, in 2026; the 24th is planned for Toronto in 2030.

entries.title: Darwin's last book: the earthworm as a force of nature
entries.article: The Formation of Vegetable Mould Through the Action of Worms

definition.text: Charles Darwin's 1881 book on earthworms, their habits and their part in forming and moving the soil.

facts.text: It was Darwin's last scientific book, published in October 1881, shortly before his death.
It was the first significant work on soil bioturbation, though the term itself entered the soil and geomorphic literature only a hundred years later.
It carried Darwin's recurring theme that gradual changes over long periods can have large and sometimes surprising consequences.
Darwin calculated that there were 53,767 earthworms per acre.
He concluded that worms matter through their part in decomposing rock, slowly denuding the land, preserving archaeological remains and improving soil for plant growth.
Darwin found worms drag leaves into their burrows by the most efficient end and show complex, flexible behaviour despite rudimentary sense organs.
It sold thousands of copies in its first few weeks.

entries.title: From a nutrient ledger to a science of soil

definition.text: How ideas about soil developed, starting from concepts built on Justus von Liebig's chemistry and refined by agricultural scientists in laboratories, greenhouses and small field plots.

facts.text: Early agricultural chemists held a balance-sheet theory: soil was a more or less static store of plant nutrients that crops used and that could be replaced.
These early workers rarely looked at soil below the depth of normal tillage.
Early geologists accepted the balance-sheet theory and described soil as disintegrated rock, such as granite, sandstone or glacial till, modified by weathering and shaped into landforms.
Many early soil surveyors were geologists, because only they had the field methods needed; they saw soils mainly as weathering products of geologic formations.
Surveys published before 1910 were strongly shaped by geological ideas, and those of 1910 to 1920 added refinements but stayed fundamentally geological.
The balance-sheet theory ruled the laboratory and the geological concept ruled field work; both were taught in many classrooms until the late 1920s.
Broader concepts came from Eugene W. Hilgard and George Nelson Coffey in the United States and from Russian soil scientists, but the data behind them came from soil survey field work.
The balance-sheet idea keeps some value today, though understanding soils goes well beyond removing nutrients in crops and returning them as manure, lime and fertilizer.

entries.title: The World Soil Museum, a gallery of soil profiles

definition.text: A museum in Wageningen, the Netherlands, that displays soil profile monoliths representing the world's major soil types.

facts.text: It is managed by ISRIC, an independent science-based foundation, on the campus of Wageningen University and Research Centre.
It began as the International Soil Museum at the request of UNESCO and the International Society of Soil Science, to support the FAO-UNESCO Soil Map of the World.
Some 80 monoliths are on display, with a much larger collection of some 1000 from over 70 countries kept in its repository.
Each monolith comes with site information, a horizon-by-horizon profile description and data on chemical and physical properties.
It shows examples of the 32 WRB Reference Soil Groups, a section on Dutch soils and soils much changed by long human use.

entries.title: 2015, the year the world was asked to notice soil

definition.text: The year 2015, declared by the United Nations General Assembly on 20 December 2013 to raise worldwide awareness of soils.

facts.text: It aimed to show the importance of soils for food security, agriculture, climate change mitigation, poverty alleviation and sustainable development.
The FAO implemented it within the Global Soil Partnership, which planned a website, logo and activities while organizations worldwide held local events.
In the United States the USDA held a kick-off event and the Natural Resources Conservation Service marked it with monthly themes.
It closed at FAO headquarters on 4 December 2015, and the IUSS then proclaimed 2015–2024 the International Decade of Soils to continue its work.

entries.title: Agricultural chemistry, the science behind the fertilizer bag

definition.text: The chemistry, especially organic chemistry and biochemistry, of agriculture.

facts.text: It often aims to preserve or raise soil fertility so as to keep or improve crop yields and crop quality.
Soil analysis looks at the mineral matter, which makes up most of the mass of dry soil, and at organic matter, including humic and fulvic acids.
Time-honoured organic fertilizers have largely given way to chemicals from mined phosphate rock and the Haber-Bosch process, which greatly raised crop production.
Its pesticides raise yields but can contaminate ground and water and harm species they were not aimed at.

entries.title: From word pictures to measurements: building Soil Taxonomy

definition.text: The move from the qualitative soil classifications of Marbut and of 1938 to the quantitative Soil Taxonomy built under Guy D. Smith.

facts.text: The classes of Marbut's system and the 1938 USDA system were described qualitatively, not in terms that different scientists could apply consistently.
Neither system linked its higher, genetically defined classes to the soil series used in US soil mapping.
A 1949 modification of the 1938 system fixed some flaws but showed that its concepts and principles needed reappraisal.
More than 15 years of work under Guy D. Smith produced a new system, made official for the US National Cooperative Soil Survey in 1965 and published in 1975 as Soil Taxonomy.
The Smith system was adopted in the United States and by many other nations for their own classification.

entries.title: When Russian scientists made soil a natural body

definition.text: The school led by V. V. Dokuchaev and N. M. Sibirtsev from 1870, which treated soils as independent natural bodies with their own properties.

facts.text: Before it, soil was seen as a product of physical and chemical changes in rock, a dead substrate from which plants take mineral nutrients.
Its workers saw each soil's unique properties as the result of a unique combination of climate, living matter, parent material, relief and time.
Instead of inferring properties from rocks or climate, they read the combined effect of all these factors in the soil's own morphology.
Requiring all soil properties to be considered together as one integrated natural body made a science of soil possible; the ideas are called revolutionary.
Americans learned of the work through K. D. Glinka's 1914 textbook in German and especially C. F. Marbut's English translation of 1927.
Some enthusiasts thought soil study could ignore geology and agricultural chemistry, but the new concept in fact made those sciences more useful.
Soil morphology gave a firm basis for grouping observations, experiments and experience into principles that predict how soils behave.

entries.text: For a long time, soil counted as dead ground. It was seen as a product of physical and chemical changes in rock, a substrate from which plants take mineral nutrients. From 1870 a Russian school led by {{ref:soil-hist-001}} and N. M. Sibirtsev saw it differently. Soils, they held, are independent natural bodies with properties of their own. Each soil's unique properties come from a unique combination of climate, living matter, parent material, relief and time. Instead of inferring those properties from rocks or climate, they read the combined effect in the soil's own morphology, its visible form and layers. Considering all properties together, as one natural body, made a science of soil possible. The ideas are called revolutionary. Some enthusiasts thought soil study could now ignore geology and agricultural chemistry. In fact the new concept made those sciences more useful. Morphology gave a firm basis for turning observations, experiments and experience into principles that predict how soils behave.

entries.title: Putting the soil profile first, in America

definition.text: The American adaptation of the Russian soil concept, led by C. F. Marbut, which put the individual soil profile ahead of external soil features and surface geology.

facts.text: Focusing on profiles made early soil scientists overlook how much soils vary even within a small area, which seriously reduced the value of their maps.
Emphasis on genetic profiles was so strong that material without one, such as recent alluvium, seemed not to be soil, and rock weathering was sharply separated from soil formation.
Marbut insisted that classification rest on morphology, not on theories of soil genesis, which he saw as ephemeral and dynamic.
His 1935 classification relied on a "normal soil", formed in equilibrium on a landscape where downward erosion keeps pace with soil formation.
After 1930, studies moved from single pits to trenches or series of pits, and soils were described by ranges of properties around a central concept instead of one typical profile.
In the 1930s soil formation was explained by loosely conceived regional processes such as podzolization, laterization and calcification.

entries.title: Park Grass, a hay field watched since 1856

definition.text: A long-term field study at Rothamsted set up to test how fertilizers and manures affect hay yields.

facts.text: Begun in 1856 at Rothamsted Research in Hertfordshire and monitored ever since, it is one of the longest-running experiments in modern science.
Its treatments changed the plant make-up and ecology of the 28,000 m² field, making it a resource for studying natural selection and biodiversity.
It showed how plant species richness, biomass and pH are related, and that ordinary field trials probably underestimate long-term threats such as soil acidification.
Its archive of soil and hay samples has been used to track atmospheric pollution, including nuclear fallout.

entries.title: Germany's soil society, founded in Berlin in 1926

definition.text: Germany's non-profit society of soil science experts and others interested in the field, the Deutsche Bodenkundliche Gesellschaft (DBG).

facts.text: It was founded in Berlin in 1926 as a section of the International Soil Science Society and re-formed in Wiesbaden after the Second World War.

Its journal is the Journal of Plant Nutrition and Soil Science, published with the German Society of Plant Nutrition.

entries.title: How earthworms slowly bury stones and ruins
entries.article: The Formation of Vegetable Mould Through the Action of Worms#Summary

definition.text: The slow sinking of surface objects, from stones to Roman ruins, as earthworms bring up earth from below and leave it as castings.

facts.text: Darwin estimated the earth brought up by worms from the burial rate of surface objects and by weighing castings produced over set times.
He spread broken chalk on a pasture near Down House in December 1842; it ended up buried 18 centimetres deep, a rate of 6 millimetres per year.
He found Stonehenge's outer stones partly buried and studied Roman ruins such as Abinger and Silchester, concluding that worms, dust and soil wash had buried them.
Rain and wind move castings downslope, while worms' humic acids and the stones they swallow help break down rock.

conflicts.text: Darwin's chalk experiment ran 29 years.
conflicts.note: Bioturbation § Research history (S:982a010f571d) says the chalk was excavated 30 years after it was laid; probably rounding.

entries.title: Darwin's first worm paper, read in 1837
entries.article: The Formation of Vegetable Mould Through the Action of Worms#Paper "On the Formation of Mould"

definition.text: Darwin's 1837 paper to the Geological Society of London on the role of earthworms in forming soil.

facts.text: At Maer Hall his uncle Josiah Wedgwood showed him ground where lime and cinders spread years before lay beneath a layer of loam, and suggested earthworms were the cause.
Darwin read the paper on 1 November 1837; William Buckland backed its publication as "a new Geological Power" but rejected Darwin's idea that chalkland formed the same way.
It appeared in the society's Proceedings in 1838 and, with a woodcut, in its Transactions in 1840.

entries.title: World Soil Day, every 5 December
entries.article: International Year of Soils#World Soil Day

definition.text: An annual day, 5 December, that celebrates the importance of soil in people's lives.

facts.text: The International Union of Soil Sciences proposed 5 December as World Soil Day in 2002.
The UN General Assembly designated the day in December 2013, when it also declared 2015 the International Year of Soils.
The Soil Science Society of America and the American Society of Agronomy invite the public to keep celebrating it every year.
The FAO runs the #WorldSoilDay hashtag and campaigns such as "Stop soil erosion, Save our future", with activities for students, farmers, teachers and others.

entries.title: The world's first soil museum, in Saint Petersburg
entries.article: V.V. Dokuchaev Central Museum of Soil

definition.text: A soil museum in Saint Petersburg, founded in 1902 by Vasily Dokuchaev.

facts.text: Dokuchaev, commonly called the father of soil science, began his large collection of soil samples in 1880.
It opened in 1904, a year after his death, as the first museum of soil science in the world.
It holds about 330 soil monoliths from the Arctic to New Zealand, and expeditions bring new ones every year.

entries.title: OPAL Soil Centre and its earthworm survey

facts.text: It ran the OPAL Soil and Earthworm Survey, launched in March 2009, in which the public collected habitat and soil information and counted and identified earthworms.

Its aims include community-level information on soil quality and biodiversity, and research on pollution sources and pathways in soil.

entries.title: Central Soil Salinity Research Institute

definition.text: An autonomous Indian institute under the Indian Council of Agricultural Research for research on salt-affected soils.

facts.text: It began at Hisar in 1969 after an Indo-American team's water management recommendations and moved to Karnal that year.
Four divisions cover soil and crop management, irrigation and drainage engineering (groundwater recharge and subsurface drainage of waterlogged saline soils), crop improvement and social science.
Crop improvement breeds saline- and alkali-tolerant rice, wheat and mustard, and the institute coordinates the national project on managing salt-affected soils and using saline water.

entries.title: Indian Institute of Soil Science

definition.text: An autonomous Indian research institute under the Indian Council of Agricultural Research, set up for advanced research in soil science.

facts.text: Founded in 1988 at Bhopal, it covers coordinated projects on soil test crop response (17 centres), micronutrients and biofertilizers (11 centres each).

It has six divisions, among them soil physics, soil chemistry and fertility, soil biology and environmental soil science, and trains in soil testing, nutrient and water efficiency, carbon sequestration and soil quality assessment.

Its mandate covers research on soil physical, chemical and biological processes and environment-friendly management technologies; a long-term fertilizer experiments project studies fertilizer effects on productivity and soil quality.

definition.text: Field experiments run for decades, some for more than 100 years, to test the sustainability of farming practices from yield trends.

facts.text: Examples include the Park Grass Experiment at Rothamsted, the Morrow Plots (1876), Sanborn Field (1888), the Magruder Plots (1892) and Auburn's Old Rotation (1896).
Rothamsted showed grain yields can be sustained for almost 150 years in wheat and barley monocultures given organic or inorganic fertilizer every year.
Even so, there is abundant evidence that crop rotation and organic inputs are often beneficial.
The Haughley Experiment ran organic farming without outside nutrients; whether its yield decline came from soil nutrient depletion is disputed.
Nitrogen released from soil organic matter can hide a legume nitrogen shortfall for a decade or more, so short trials cannot prove sustainability.
The Old Rotation showed legume nitrogen ploughed in as green manure can balance nitrogen removed by harvests over the long term.
In 2017 Rothamsted began the Large Scale Rotation Experiment to study regenerative approaches such as no-till and crop rotation.

entries.title: Bioturbation: a word from 1952 for an idea from Darwin

definition.text: The study of how burrowing and mixing by living things shapes soil, from Darwin's earthworm work to its re-evaluation by soil geomorphologists from the 1980s.

facts.text: Darwin first recognized the importance of bioturbation for soil processes and geomorphology, devoting his last scientific book to it.
In 1891 geologist Nathaniel Shaler extended Darwin's idea to soil disturbance by ants and trees.
Rudolf Richter coined the term bioturbation in 1952 for sediment structures made by living organisms; since the 1980s it has been widely used in soil and geomorphology.
There is now ample evidence for Darwin's conclusions, and in many areas burrowing biota are major agents of soil formation.

entries.title: Soil formation becomes a measurable science

definition.text: The shift, from about 1940, to treating soil formation as many interrelated physical, chemical and biological processes open to quantitative study.

facts.text: Hans Jenny's 1941 book Factors of Soil Formation: A System of Quantitative Pedology summarized many basic principles of modern soil science up to that date.
Since 1940 time has gained much more weight among the soil-forming factors, with geomorphology used to find how long material has undergone soil formation.
Advances in soil chemistry, physics, mineralogy and biology added new tools for studying soil formation.
Attention moved from gross attributes of the whole soil to the co-varying detail of its parts, down to grain-to-grain relationships.

entries.title: Soil surveys move beyond the farm

definition.text: The broadening of soil survey after 1950 from farming, ranching and forestry to information on how soils affect nonfarm uses.

facts.text: Before 1950 soil surveys served mainly farming, ranching and forestry.
Some states saw their value for highway planning by the late 1920s and put soil interpretations in highway engineers' manuals in the 1930s and 1940s.
Nonfarm uses of soil grew rapidly in the 1950s and 1960s, creating a great need for information on soils' effects on them.
This had an immense impact on soil survey, especially during the 1960s.

entries.text: Soil surveys were once made almost entirely for farmers, ranchers and foresters. That held until about 1950. Then nonfarm uses of soil grew rapidly in the 1950s and 1960s. That created a great need for information on how soils affect those uses. The impact on soil survey was immense, especially during the 1960s.

entries.title: Broadbalk, a wheat field sown every year since 1843

definition.text: A long-running field experiment at Rothamsted Research, sown with winter wheat every year since 1843.

facts.text: It is one of the classical field experiments begun by Lawes and Gilbert that remain in place as a resource for agricultural and environmental research.
Its continuous wheat showed take-all disease building up to a peak in the 3rd to 5th crop, then declining and restoring yields to 80 to 90% of early levels.

entries.title: Humus theory, the belief that plants eat rot

definition.text: The once-prevalent view that decayed plant matter, humus, was plants' main source of carbon.

facts.text: Fertilizers were believed to work by breaking humus down so plants could absorb it more easily.
Albrecht Thaer, a German agronomist, supported it and dismissed Humphry Davy's idea of atmospheric carbon.
The theory set out in Thaer's Principles of Agriculture (1809–12) was still accepted between 1800 and 1860.
Justus von Liebig argued against it.

entries.title: The Soil Map of the World, ten volumes long

definition.text: The world soil map published by FAO and UNESCO from 1971 to 1981 in 10 volumes at a scale of 1:5 million.

facts.text: The FAO soil classification was first developed as the map's legend and then applied by United Nations projects.
A Revised Legend of the Soil Map of the World followed in 1988.
The 3,230,000 km² of saline land worldwide has been mapped by region from it.
The World Soil Museum was created in 1996 at the request of UNESCO and the International Society of Soil Science to support it.

entries.title: The Virgin Lands campaign and the eroded steppe

definition.text: Nikita Khrushchev's 1953 plan to boost Soviet farm output by ploughing new land in southern Western Siberia and northern Kazakhstan.

facts.text: After early success output fell considerably, and severe soil erosion made it an environmental disaster for the Kazakh steppe.
The region got only 200 to 350 mm of rain a year, mostly at harvest, and its soils had high salt content.
Strong winds blew snow off the fields in winter and caused soil erosion in spring.
Monoculture, with grain on 83% of cropland in 1958–1959, depleted the soil of nutrients.

entries.text: A plan to feed the Soviet Union became an environmental disaster for the Kazakh steppe. In 1953 Nikita Khrushchev launched the Virgin Lands campaign to boost farm output by ploughing new land in southern Western Siberia and northern Kazakhstan. After early success, output fell considerably. The region got only 200 to 350 mm of rain a year, mostly at harvest, and its soils had high salt content. Strong winds blew snow off the fields in winter and caused soil erosion in spring. Monoculture, with grain on 83% of cropland in 1958–1959, depleted the soil of nutrients. Severe erosion followed.

entries.title: Vasily Dokuchaev, who saw soil as a natural body

definition.text: Russian geologist and geographer (1846–1903) credited with laying the foundations of soil science.

facts.text: He is commonly called the father of soil science and was perhaps the first to investigate different soil types across broad geographic areas.
He showed that besides parent material, climate, topography and the length of soil formation explain how soil types vary from place to place.
He saw soil as a natural body with its own genesis and history, distinct from the bedrock that becomes soil under climate, vegetation, parent material, relief and age.
Building on these ideas, he produced the very first soil classification, which described five factors of soil formation.
He reached his theory after extensive field studies of Russian soils in 1883; his most famous work is Russian Chernozem (1883).
His research brought Russian terms such as chernozem, podsol, gley and solonets into the international vocabulary of soil science.
From 1869 to 1901 he published 285 works, including 61 books and 4 maps.
His ideas were taken up by many soil scientists, including Hans Jenny, and the IUSS's Dokuchaev Award, likened to a Nobel Prize for soil science, honours him.

Vasily Dokuchaev (1846–1903) was a Russian geologist and geographer credited with laying the foundations of soil science. He is commonly called its father. He was perhaps the first to investigate different soil types across broad geographic areas. After extensive field studies of Russian soils in 1883 he reached his theory, and his most famous work, {{ref:soil-hist-002}}, appeared that same year. Soil, he argued, is a natural body with its own genesis and history, distinct from the bedrock beneath it. Climate, vegetation, parent material, relief and age turn that bedrock into soil. Parent material alone could not explain why soil types vary from place to place. Climate, topography and the length of soil formation mattered too. On these ideas he built the very first soil classification, which described five factors of soil formation. His output was vast: from 1869 to 1901 he published 285 works, including 61 books and 4 maps. Many soil scientists took up his ideas, {{ref:soil-hist-010}} among them. The IUSS's Dokuchaev Award, likened to a Nobel Prize for soil science, honors him.

entries.title: Justus von Liebig brings chemistry to the farm

definition.text: German chemist (1803–1873), a principal founder of organic chemistry, who made major contributions to agricultural and biological chemistry.

facts.text: He is called the "father of the fertilizer industry" for stressing nitrogen and minerals as essential plant nutrients and for popularizing the law of the minimum.

His 1840 book Organic Chemistry in its Application to Agriculture and Physiology argued that chemistry could revolutionize farming; it was widely translated, fiercely criticized and highly influential.
The early concept of soil as a store of plant nutrients rested on his ideas, refined by agricultural scientists in laboratories and field plots.
Around 1840 he suggested dissolving animal bones in sulphuric acid to make fertilizer, a process first used in Britain in 1841.
Seeing both synthesis and decay in living systems made him an early advocate of conservation, including recycling sewage.
Despite criticism of his inexperience in practice, his writings spurred agricultural experiment and debate in Germany, England and France.

entries.title: Hans Jenny gives soil formation its variables

definition.text: Swiss-born soil scientist (1899–1992) and expert in pedology, above all in the processes of soil formation.

facts.text: He took a doctorate at ETH Zurich in 1927 on ion exchange reactions and joined the University of California, Berkeley, in 1936.
International recognition followed his 1941 book Factors of Soil Formation: A System of Quantitative Pedology.
It combined field studies with the formalism of physical chemistry to relate soil properties to climate, biota, relief, parent material and time, leaving room for further variables.
In The Soil Resource, Origin and Behaviour (1980) he recast the factors as state variables and extended their effects to ecosystem properties.
His factors underlie the CLORPT model of soil-landscape modelling and, adapted for description rather than explanation, the scorpan approach of digital soil mapping.
He studied the Mendocino pygmy forest, whose stunted plants grow on a 500,000-year-old marine terrace; a reserve there bears his name.
In his 1980 article "Alcohol or Humus" he argued against turning crop residues and forest humus into fuel, which would curtail carbon and nitrogen cycles and speed humus oxidation.
He was President of the Soil Science Society of America in 1949.

entries.title: Sergei Winogradsky takes microbes out of the clinic

definition.text: Ukrainian and Russian microbiologist, ecologist and soil scientist (1856–1953) who pioneered the cycle-of-life concept.

facts.text: He discovered several biogeochemical cycles and parts of them, and was among the first to study microbes outside medicine, making him an early student of microbial ecology.
In 1887 he found that Beggiatoa oxidizes hydrogen sulfide as an energy source, the first known form of lithotrophy.
From 1888 in Zürich he identified Nitrosomonas and Nitrosococcus, which oxidize ammonium to nitrite, and Nitrobacter, which oxidizes nitrite to nitrate; he described this two-step process in 1890.
He identified Clostridium pasteurianum, a free-living anaerobe that fixes atmospheric nitrogen without living in legume root nodules.
From 1922 he led the Pasteur Institute's agricultural bacteriology division, studying iron and nitrifying bacteria, Azotobacter, cellulose decomposers and culture methods for soil microbes.
His student Vasily Omelianski spread his concepts and methods in the Soviet Union in the following decades.

entries.title: Martinus Beijerinck, from root nodules to viruses

definition.text: Dutch microbiologist and botanist (1851–1931), one of the founders of virology and environmental microbiology.

facts.text: He investigated nitrogen fixation, revealing the symbiosis between legumes and the nodule bacteria that fix nitrogen, a reaction vital to soil fertility and agriculture.
He fully described the fixation process found by Hellriegel and Wilfarth, and in 1901 showed that Azotobacter chroococcum fixes atmospheric nitrogen.
He discovered bacterial sulfate reduction, in which bacteria use sulfate instead of oxygen as the terminal electron acceptor, a finding important for understanding biogeochemical cycles.
He isolated Spirillum desulfuricans, now Desulfovibrio desulfuricans, the first known sulfate-reducing bacterium.
He invented the enrichment culture, a fundamental method for studying microbes from the environment.
In 1898 his filtration experiments showed that tobacco mosaic disease is caused by an agent smaller than a bacterium, which he named a virus.
He founded the Delft School of Microbiology; the maxim "everything is everywhere, but the environment selects", often credited to him, was Lourens Baas Becking's.

entries.title: Friedrich Fallou, the tax assessor who named pedology

definition.text: German lawyer and land tax assessor (1794–1877) considered one of the founders of modern soil science.

facts.text: Evaluating forest and farmland for Saxony for most of his career, he grew concerned about declining soil quality and related soil profiles to their formation.
In 1862 he argued that soil was separate in nature from geology and introduced the term pedology to found soil study as an independent science.
His First Principles of Soil Science (1857) and Pedology or General and Special Soil Science (1862) turned his field observations into a systematic approach.
The 1862 book proposed a way to describe soil profiles, discussed soils' physical and chemical properties and classified soils by their mineral properties.
He separated pedology, a natural description of soil regardless of plants or use, from agrology, the study of soil in relation to plants and farming.
Dokuchaev proved more influential, but Glinka regarded Fallou as the founder of modern soil science, and Yarilov's 1904 article called him "Founder of Soil Science".

entries.text: A land tax assessor gave soil science one of its names. Friedrich Albert Fallou (1794–1877) was a German lawyer who spent most of his career evaluating forest and farmland for Saxony. The work worried him. Soil quality was declining, and he began relating soil profiles to how they formed. His First Principles of Soil Science (1857) and Pedology or General and Special Soil Science (1862) turned his field observations into a system. The 1862 book proposed a way to describe soil profiles, discussed soils' physical and chemical properties and classified soils by their minerals. That year he argued that soil was separate in nature from geology. He introduced the term pedology to found soil study as an independent science. Pedology described soil regardless of plants or use; agrology studied soil in relation to plants and farming. Dokuchaev proved more influential. Still, {{ref:soil-hist-008}} regarded Fallou as the founder of modern soil science, and Yarilov's 1904 article called him "Founder of Soil Science".

entries.title: Konstantin Glinka carries Russian soil science west

definition.text: Russian soil scientist (1867–1927), a student of Dokuchaev who carried the Russian school's ideas to the wider world.

facts.text: From 1889 he did geological and soil research under Dokuchaev, including work in Poltava and on the Forest Department expedition.
He was the first director of the Dokuchaev Soil Science Institute and wrote over 150 works on soil, geography, mineralogy and geology.
His 1908 soil science textbook included the first schematic soil map of the world.
Language barriers kept the Russian team's work from Western Europe until his German publication of 1914; Marbut translated a version from German into English.
By the 1920s he had found Russian soils that did not fit present climates and were seen as relics of warmer past climates.
In 1927 he became the first soil scientist elected to the USSR Academy of Sciences and led the Soviet delegation to the First International Congress of Soil Scientists in Washington.

conflicts.text: Glinka published the first world soil map in 1906.
conflicts.note: The lead gives 1906; the Career section dates the first schematic world soil map to his 1908 textbook.

entries.title: Eugene Hilgard puts climate into American soil science

definition.text: German-American expert on pedology (1833–1916), considered the father of modern soil science in the United States.

facts.text: He was an authority on climate as a soil-forming factor, on soil chemistry and on the reclamation of alkali soils.
In 1860, in Mississippi, he studied how rock material, climate and vegetation relate to the type of soil that develops.
From 1875 to 1904 he was professor of agricultural chemistry at the University of California, Berkeley, and directed the state agricultural experiment station.
For the Northern Transcontinental Survey of 1881–1883 he studied soils of the southwestern states and Pacific slope in relation to geology, composition, native flora and farming.
His 1892 Relations of Climate to Soils won the Liebig medal in 1894; with his 1906 book Soils it established climate as a soil-forming factor in US thinking.
He and Hopkins greatly influenced Marbut's shift from seeing soils as reflections of geology to treating soil science as a distinct field.

entries.title: Curtis Marbut builds the first US soil classification

definition.text: American soil scientist (1863–1935) who directed the Soil Survey Division of the US Department of Agriculture from 1913 until his death.

facts.text: He developed the first formal soil classification scheme for the United States, beginning the work in 1920.
Trained as a geologist and geographer, he first saw soils as surface reflections of the geology beneath but came to see soil science as distinct from geology.
In 1927 he translated Glinka's The Great Soil Groups of the World and their Development into English and applied the Russian ideas to a national classification.
His scheme became the 1935 system, modified and published in the 1938 Yearbook of Agriculture as the 1938 USDA soil taxonomy.
At its highest level it divided soils into pedocals, carbonate-rich soils of drier climates, and pedalfers, rich in aluminium and iron; "alfer" became the root of alfisol.
He died of pneumonia in 1935 on his way to advise the Chinese Geological Survey on organizing a soil survey.

entries.title: Lorenzo Richards measures the water in soil

definition.text: American soil physicist (1904–1993), one of the most influential figures in 20th-century soil physics.

facts.text: His 1931 Cornell thesis on capillary conduction through porous media made the first decisive advance beyond Buckingham in extending Darcy's law to unsaturated soils.
In it he set out the partial differential equation now called the Richards equation, though Lewis Richardson had published it in 1922.
He described the principles, construction and operation of the tensiometer and proposed the tension plate apparatus for measuring capillary potential in soil.
In 1941 he described the pressure-membrane apparatus, mainly for extracting soil solution for salinity analysis.
Working at the USDA Salinity Laboratory, he and colleagues fixed the accepted limits for plant growth: field capacity at −1/3 bar (−33 J/kg) and permanent wilting point at −15 bar (−1500 J/kg).
He remarked that the concept of available water is oversimplified.
His apparatus and methods moved the study of soil water from a qualitative stage to one based on measurement and mathematics.

Yet he remarked that the concept of available water is oversimplified.

entries.title: Minerals, not humus: how plants really feed

definition.text: The theory, synthesized and promoted by Liebig, that plants draw essential nutrients as inorganic minerals from the soil, and carbon and hydrogen from air and water.

facts.text: It opposed the humus theory, which held that decayed plant matter was plants' main carbon source and that fertilizers worked by breaking humus down.
De Saussure's experiments of 1804 suggested plants took carbon from the air and that their mineral content reflected the soil they grew in.
Using more precise measurements, Liebig showed that the humus in a soil could not supply enough carbon for the plants growing on it.
By the late 1830s Karl Sprengel had used Liebig's combustion analysis to show that manures owed their value to their minerals.
Liebig named nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium as essential to plant growth, and held that inorganic materials could feed plants as well as organic ones.
He also popularized Sprengel's law of the minimum: growth is limited by the scarcest essential resource, not by the total available.

entries.title: John Bennet Lawes and the first artificial fertilizer

definition.text: English entrepreneur and agricultural scientist (1814–1900) who founded the experimental farm that became Rothamsted Research.

facts.text: Before leaving Oxford in 1832 he began testing manures on plants in pots at Rothamsted, soon extending the trials to field crops.
In 1842 he patented a manure made by treating phosphates with sulphuric acid, a superphosphate that began the artificial fertilizer industry.
From the following year he worked with Joseph Henry Gilbert for more than half a century on crop and animal-feeding experiments.
He and Gilbert jointly received the Royal Society's Royal Medal in 1867.
In 1889 he endowed the Lawes Agricultural Trust to keep the experimental farm going; Rothamsted is the oldest agricultural research facility in the world.

entries.title: Guy Smith and the making of Soil Taxonomy

definition.text: American soil scientist (1907–1981) who originally developed the USDA soil classification system, Soil Taxonomy.

facts.text: After wartime service he joined the USDA, working from 1946 as a soil correlator for the Soil Conservation Service and from 1952 as Director of Soil Survey Investigations.
Tasked with developing a way to classify soils, he produced the first of seven iterations of what became a system used worldwide.
He developed Soil Taxonomy in collaboration with European soil scientists.
More than 15 years of his work led to the system made official in 1965 and published in 1975.
After retiring in 1973 he advised international partners on applying Soil Taxonomy, and he died in 1981 in Ghent, where he taught.

entries.title: Rattan Lal and the carbon in farm soils

definition.text: Indian-American soil scientist (born 1944), a pioneer of soil-centred farm management for food security and climate-resilient agriculture.

facts.text: Working in Nigeria from 1970 to 1987, he found organic carbon and nutrients disappeared after deforestation, and studied mulching, cover crops and no-till farming to restore them.
His most cited paper, in Science in 2004, was the first report that restoring soil organic matter both improves soil health and lowers atmospheric carbon dioxide.
Departing from the 1970s reliance on commercial fertilizer, his work showed how no-till, cover crops, residues, mulching and agroforestry rebuild degraded soils and sequester carbon.
His models suggest that restoring soil health could by 2100 double global grain yield, cut the land used for grain by 30% and reduce fertilizer use.
He founded the Rattan Lal Center for Carbon Management and Sequestration at Ohio State and launched the C-FARM carbon farming project in 2021.
He was IUSS president in 2017–2018 and won the Japan Prize in 2019 and the World Food Prize in 2020.

entries.title: Hugh Hammond Bennett, crusader against erosion

definition.text: Pioneer of soil conservation in the United States (1881–1960) and head of the federal soil erosion agency now called the Natural Resources Conservation Service.

facts.text: Working as a soil surveyor from 1903, he came to see soil erosion as a serious problem for the planet, first linking soil quality and erosion in a 1905 Virginia survey.
He co-wrote the USDA's Soil Erosion: A National Menace (1928), his most influential work, against colleagues who held soil to be a resource that cannot be exhausted.
Congressman James P. Buchanan then secured funds in 1929 for erosion studies and a 1930 amendment creating USDA soil erosion experiment stations, whose sites Bennett chose.
He directed the Soil Erosion Service from September 1933; his Dust Bowl advocacy helped pass the act of 27 April 1935 creating the Soil Conservation Service, which he led until 1951.
In the hardest-hit Dust Bowl region, nearly 40,000 farmers had put 5.5 million acres under terraced and contour-listed cultivation by May 1936.
The Coon Creek Watershed Project in Wisconsin was the first of many watershed projects set up to show farmers soil conservation practices.
Creating the Soil Conservation Service marked the US government's acceptance of interpreting soils for soil and water conservation.
He was also instrumental in forming the Soil Conservation Society of America, now the Soil and Water Conservation Society.

entries.title: Franklin Hiram King, father of American soil physics

definition.text: American agricultural scientist (1848–1911) who has been called the father of soil physics in the United States.

facts.text: As professor of agricultural physics at the University of Wisconsin–Madison from 1888 to 1902 he applied physics to agriculture, and his greatest impact was on soil science.
He studied soils' water-holding capacity, plants' moisture needs, aeration, the movement of soil water and groundwater and the draft of ploughs, and began studies of soil fertility.
At the USDA Bureau of Soils from 1902, he found nutrient concentration in the soil solution correlated with crop yields, undermining the views of bureau chief Milton Whitney; he was forced to resign.
He is best remembered for Farmers of Forty Centuries, an account of traditional Asian farming now regarded as an organic farming classic.

entries.title: Jean-Baptiste Boussingault and the first experiment station

definition.text: French chemist (1801–1887) who made major contributions to agricultural science.

facts.text: From 1836 he worked mainly on agricultural chemistry and plant and animal physiology.
In 1836 he set up the first agricultural experiment station on his wife's estate at Pechelbronn in Alsace, some seven years before Rothamsted.
He revived the quantitative methods first used by de Saussure and is called the father of field plot technique.
He made the first analysis of crops grown in a rotation and showed that soil nitrogen rises after legume crops.
He found plant growth proportional to the available nitrogen, so applying phosphorus and nitrogen together gives greater growth.
He asked whether plants can take up free nitrogen from the air; he answered no, laying a basis for what became the nitrogen cycle.
In 1839 he was given the chair of agricultural and analytical chemistry at the Conservatoire des Arts et Metiers in Paris.
Liebig hailed him as a pioneer of soil and plant chemistry, and his work on nitrogen in plant growth prepared the way for nitrogen fertilizers.

entries.title: Edmund Ruffin and the marl that revived worn-out fields

definition.text: American planter, politician and scientist (1794–1865), known for pioneering methods to preserve and improve soil productivity.

facts.text: He is best known as an early advocate of secession of the Southern slave states, and farmed his plantations with enslaved labour.
In his twenties he began experimenting with marl to rejuvenate land worn out by more than a century of tobacco monoculture.
He recommended crop rotation and amendments for exhausted soils, and studied bogs and swamps to learn how to correct soil acidity.
He experimented with lime to raise the pH of peat soils.
His book An Essay on Calcareous Manures explained how calcareous earths (marl) had cut soil acidity and raised corn and wheat yields.
His advice to use marl was not widely followed in his own time, but he has since been called the father of soil science in the United States.

entries.text: More than a century of tobacco monoculture had worn the land out when a young planter began spreading marl on it. He recommended crop rotation and amendments for exhausted soils. He studied bogs and swamps to learn how to correct soil acidity, and he tried lime to raise the pH of peat soils. His book An Essay on Calcareous Manures explained how marl had cut acidity and raised corn and wheat yields. Few farmers took his advice in his own time. He has since been called the father of soil science in the United States. Yet he is best known as an early advocate of secession of the Southern slave states, and he farmed his plantations with enslaved labor.

entries.title: Edgar Buckingham names the pull of soil on water

definition.text: American physicist (1867–1940) who worked as a soil physicist at the USDA Bureau of Soils from 1902 to 1906.

facts.text: His first soil physics work was on soil aeration: the loss of carbon dioxide from soil and its replacement by oxygen.

He found the rate of gas diffusion in soil did not depend much on structure, compactness or water content, and gave the diffusion coefficient as an empirical function of air content, a relation still cited in textbooks.
He concluded that soil gas exchange takes place by diffusion and is largely independent of changes in outside barometric pressure.
His soil water work appeared in 1907 as Bulletin 38 of the USDA Bureau of Soils, Studies on the movement of soil moisture.
He showed that soils can strongly inhibit evaporation, especially where capillary flow through the uppermost layers is cut off.
Arid soils first lost more water than humid ones but then less, which he put down to the soil forming a natural mulch.
He named the capillary potential arising from soil–water interactions, now called the matric or water potential.
He was the first to set out how hydraulic conductivity depends on capillary potential, and applied a formula equivalent to Darcy's law to unsaturated flow.

entries.title: Liebig's long argument over nitrogen

definition.text: The long dispute over Liebig's claim that plants feed on nitrogen compounds from the air, and over whether crops need nitrogen fertilizer.

facts.text: The claim was contested for many years and turned out true for legumes but not for other plants.
The 1840 and 1842 editions of his book said the air held too little nitrogen and that nitrogen fertilizer, perhaps as ammonia, was needed.
He later decided ammonia in rain supplied enough and argued for years against nitrogen fertilizer; his own nitrogen-poor fertilizer had no appreciable effect in a field test.
By the seventh German edition he admitted mistakes and again called nitrogen fertilizer beneficial or even necessary; in 1863 he came to appreciate biological nitrogen fixation.

entries.title: Selman Waksman finds medicine in soil microbes

definition.text: Russian-born American biochemist and microbiologist (1888–1973) whose research on the decomposition of soil organisms enabled the discovery of streptomycin and other antibiotics.

facts.text: As a graduate student he researched soil bacteriology at the New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station and studied soil fungi at the USDA.
He wrote Principles of Soil Microbiology (1927) and Humus (1936); his classical view of humus as distinct from decomposing organic matter long featured in soil science textbooks.
His lignin theory of 1932 is one of three main historical theories of how humic substances form.
His Rutgers team found several antibiotics, including actinomycin, streptomycin and neomycin, and he introduced the modern sense of the word antibiotic.
Streptomycin, from Streptomyces griseus and isolated by his student Albert Schatz, was the first antibiotic used to cure tuberculosis.
He won the 1952 Nobel Prize for systematic studies of soil microbes that led to streptomycin; Schatz contested the credit in 1950 litigation and was recognized as co-discoverer.

entries.contested_note: Credit for discovering streptomycin was disputed between Waksman and his student Albert Schatz, who won recognition as co-discoverer.

entries.title: Carl Sprengel, who stated the law of the minimum first

definition.text: German botanist and agricultural scientist (1787–1859) who first stated the law of the minimum.

facts.text: He trained in agriculture under Albrecht Thaer and then with Heinrich Einhof at Möglin from 1804 to 1808.
He studied natural sciences at Göttingen from 1821 to 1828 and became a professor there.
He was the first to state the 'theory of minimum' in agricultural chemistry: plant growth is limited by the essential nutrient present at the lowest concentration.
The rule is often credited to Justus von Liebig as Liebig's law of the minimum, but Liebig only popularised it later.
He founded the Academy of Agriculture at Regenwalde (Resko), where he taught and researched until his death in 1859.
His books include an 1839 study of manures and their action and the 1844 Die Bodenkunde, with a full guide to the chemical analysis of field soils.

entries.title: Joseph Henry Gilbert, the chemist behind Rothamsted's long trials

definition.text: English chemist (1817–1901) who spent a long career improving the methods of practical agriculture.

facts.text: A former doctoral student of Justus von Liebig at Giessen, he became director of the chemical laboratory at Lawes's Rothamsted experiment station in 1843.
He worked there from June 1843 until his death, and conducted most of the meticulous studies published under both names.
In 1843 Lawes and Gilbert began long-term field experiments at Rothamsted, some still running.
They found that cereal crops take up nitrogen from the soil, contrary to Liebig's view that it came only from the air.
Their work made Rothamsted a leading centre of agricultural research.

entries.title: Life powered by rock: the discovery of chemosynthesis

definition.text: Winogradsky's discovery of chemoautotrophy, popularly called chemosynthesis: organisms drawing energy from inorganic compounds and carbon from carbon dioxide.

facts.text: Until then, autotrophs were believed to get their energy only from light.
Organisms that oxidize hydrogen sulfide or ammonium for energy split autotrophs into photoautotrophs and chemoautotrophs.
His 1887 Beggiatoa work gave the first example of lithotrophy but not autotrophy; his nitrifying bacteria gave the first chemoautotrophy, fixing carbon dioxide into organic compounds.
This form of metabolism is believed to occur only in prokaryotes.

entries.title: Konstantin Gedroits and the soil that holds on

definition.text: Russian soil scientist (1872–1932) of Lithuanian origin, founder of colloidal soil chemistry in Russia.

facts.text: He introduced the concept of the soil absorbing complex and distinguished mechanical, physico-chemical and biological types of soil absorption capacity.
He classified soils by composition, separating soils unsaturated with cations from those saturated with calcium or with sodium ions.
He explained the evolution of saline soils chemically and laid the theoretical basis of liming and of adding gypsum to soil.
He led the chemistry laboratory of the Dokuchaev Soil Institute (1915–17) and headed the institute in 1929–30.
He was president of the International Union of Soil Sciences from 1927 to 1930 and received the Lenin Prize in 1927.

entries.title: Peter Erasmus Müller reads the forest floor

definition.text: Danish forester and naturalist (1840–1926) whose studies of forest soils laid early foundations for the study of humus forms.

facts.text: His seminal work on Danish forest soils described mor humus for the first time, calling it beech peat by analogy with sphagnum peat.
His Studies on Forest Soil appeared as a series in 1878–84 in the journal he founded in 1875, the first independent Danish forestry journal, and was translated into German and French.
These studies showed how plant communities and their animals shape the ground surface, as in heathland formation and soil change beneath surface peat.
His last major work, in 1924, concluded that the Danish heaths continue the tundra that arose after the ice age and were never forested like nearby land.

entries.title: Charles Darwin and the worms beneath the loam

definition.text: English naturalist, geologist and biologist (1809–1882), best known for his contributions to evolutionary biology.

facts.text: His five-year voyage on HMS Beagle from 1831 to 1836 established him as an eminent geologist.

When shown ground where cinders had vanished under loam, he suggested earthworms were responsible, a theory of their role in soil formation that he presented to the Geological Society on 1 November 1837.
His final book was The Formation of Vegetable Mould, through the Actions of Worms (1881), counted among his works of great importance.

entries.title: Nicolas-Théodore de Saussure finds plant carbon in the air

definition.text: Swiss chemist and plant physiologist (1767–1845), a major pioneer in the study of photosynthesis.

facts.text: He studied plant gas exchange and how different soils affected plant growth, work gathered in Recherches chimiques sur la Végétation (1804).
He based his conclusions on extensive quantitative data, unlike some predecessors.
He showed plants take their carbon from atmospheric carbon dioxide, not from soil humus as most of his immediate predecessors believed.
He showed plants need mineral nutrients taken up from the soil, disproving the idea that plant minerals arose by transmutation inside the plant.
His findings were largely neglected for decades until Liebig revived them and Boussingault's field research confirmed the importance of soil mineral nutrients.
Liebig used de Saussure's results to critique humus theories.

That disproved the idea that plant minerals arose by transmutation inside the plant. His findings were largely neglected for decades. Then Liebig revived them and used them to critique humus theories, and Boussingault's field research confirmed the importance of soil mineral nutrients.

entries.title: Heath: shrubland on poor, acid ground

definition.text: A shrubland habitat found mainly on free-draining, infertile, acidic soils, with open, low-growing woody vegetation.

facts.text: Heathland is favoured by hard, dry climates, especially in summer, and by acidic, low-fertility, often sandy and free-draining soils; a small mire may form where drainage is poor.
Heaths are dominated by low shrubs 20 cm to 2 m tall and range from very species-rich in Australia and South African fynbos to depauperate in Europe, where heather, heath and gorse dominate.

Many heaths are anthropogenic, made by centuries of clearing woodland by grazing and burning, and are kept by grazing and periodic burning (swailing) or rarely mowing, or they are recolonised by woodland.
Heaths are widespread but rapidly disappearing and rare in Europe; tree incursion after traditional management stopped and urban sprawl threaten them.

entries.title: Albert Bernhard Frank names the fungus-root

definition.text: German botanist, plant pathologist and mycologist (1839–1900) who coined the term mycorrhiza.

facts.text: He named the mycorrhiza in an 1885 paper on the root-symbiosis nutrition of certain trees by underground fungi.
A failed royal commission to develop truffle cultivation led him to work out the nature and development of mycorrhizae.
In 1877 he coined the term symbiosis to describe lichens.
The bacterial genus Frankia is named after him.

entries.title: Albert Atterberg sets the size of clay

definition.text: Swedish chemist and agricultural scientist (1846–1916) who created the Atterberg limits still used by geotechnical engineers.

facts.text: Around the age of fifty-four he turned to the classification and plasticity of soils, the work he is most remembered for.
He proposed the first texture classification, the international system, in 1905, and was apparently the first to set 0.002 mm as the upper size of clay particles.
Finding plasticity characteristic of clay, he devised in 1911 the consistency limits named after him; Terzaghi brought them into geotechnics and Casagrande standardized the tests in 1932.
The International Society of Soil Science formally recognized his soil classification work at Berlin in 1913, and his grain size scale is still the one used in Sweden.

entries.title: Albrecht Thaer puts farming into a system

definition.text: German agronomist (1752–1828) and supporter of the humus theory of plant nutrition.

facts.text: A physician by training, he turned from flower gardening to agriculture and became known across Europe for applying science to farming practice.
He is described as the first agricultural scientist to arrange the existing facts and theory of agriculture into a proper system.
In 1802 he founded the first German agricultural training institute at Celle, where he experimented with crop rotation to raise yields.
In 1804 he founded the first German agricultural academy at Möglin, renamed the Royal Prussian Academy of Agriculture in 1819.
His academy analysed many soils and classified specimens by their dominant components, such as sand, lime or red and blue clay, marking each with coloured labels.
Thaer's soil classification came into common use on large German estates.
His four-volume Grundsätze der rationellen Landwirthschaft (1809–1812), covering the theory of soil, ploughing, manuring and irrigation, appeared in English in 1844 as The Principles of Agriculture.
The humus theory set out in that work was still accepted in the period 1800–1860.

entries.text: Albrecht Thaer trained as a physician and loved flower gardening before he turned to agriculture. The German agronomist (1752–1828) became known across Europe for applying science to farming practice. He is described as the first agricultural scientist to arrange the existing facts and theory of agriculture into a proper system. In 1802 he founded the first German agricultural training institute at Celle, where he experimented with crop rotation to raise yields. In 1804 came the first German agricultural academy, at Möglin, renamed the Royal Prussian Academy of Agriculture in 1819. The academy analyzed many soils and classified them by dominant component, such as sand, lime or red and blue clay, each marked with a colored label. This classification came into common use on large German estates. His four-volume Grundsätze der rationellen Landwirthschaft (1809–1812) covered the theory of soil, plowing, manuring and irrigation. It appeared in English in 1844 as The Principles of Agriculture. Its humus theory of plant nutrition was still accepted in the period 1800–1860.

entries.title: Lorenz Hiltner names the rhizosphere

definition.text: German agronomist and microbiologist (1862–1923) who developed the concept of the rhizosphere and helped found microbial ecology.

facts.text: At the Tharandt research station he studied the symbiosis of legumes with root-nodule bacteria, work that produced the first cultures of rhizobium bacteria.
He also showed the importance of root nodules for the nitrogen nutrition of black alder.
In 1893 he and F. Nobbe published 'Inoculate the Soil!'.
In an April 1904 lecture he introduced the term rhizosphere for the soil directly affected by root secretions and their microorganisms.

entries.title: Francis D. Hole, the pedologist who gave Wisconsin a state soil

definition.text: American pedologist, educator and musician (1913–2002), known for mapping Wisconsin's soils and for popularizing soil science.

facts.text: He created the periodical Soil Survey Horizons in 1960 and co-created the Soils of Wisconsin Map published in 1968.
He co-authored the textbook Soil Genesis and Classification with Stanley Buol and Ralph McCracken, first published in 1973 and used in courses worldwide.
His Soils of Wisconsin (1976) explained soil development following Hans Jenny's factors of soil formation and divided the state into regions A to J.
He campaigned for Antigo silt loam, which the Wisconsin legislature named the official state soil in 1983.

entries.title: Cyril Hopkins and the soils of Illinois

definition.text: American agricultural chemist (1866–1919) at the University of Illinois, noted for his research and writing on Illinois soils.

facts.text: From 1894 until his death in 1919 he was chemist at the University of Illinois Agriculture Experiment Station, latterly heading its Department of Agronomy.
With Hilgard, he greatly influenced Marbut's change from seeing soils as reflections of geology to recognizing soil science as distinct from geology.
In 1896 he began the Illinois long-term selection experiment.
