entries.title: Roy Simonson, soil surveyor and historian

definition.text: American soil scientist (1908–2008) who studied soils across the United States and on islands of the Western Pacific.

facts.text: Trained under Charles E. Kellogg and Emil Truog, he joined the USDA soil survey programmes after teaching at Iowa State College.
During World War II he mapped soils on Western Pacific islands for the Military Geology Unit.
He was the soil survey's Director for Soil Classification and Correlation from 1953 to 1971.
He became editor-in-chief of the journal Geoderma in 1967 and wrote a history of US soil survey and classification from 1899 to 1970.

entries.title: Thomas Lyttleton Lyon and the Cornell field plots

definition.text: American soil scientist (1869–1938) who wrote on the nitrogen cycle.

facts.text: He headed the department of soil technology at the Cornell University College of Agriculture from 1912.
At Cornell's Caldwell Field he ran many field studies, including lysimeter and plot experiments.
In 1913 he and James A. Bizzell won the Howard N. Potts Medal for a paper on how certain non-leguminous plants relate to soil nitrate content.
From 1907 he published soil science textbooks; his Principles of Soil Management went through 10 editions.

entries.title: Enrichment culture: coaxing microbes into the lab

definition.text: A fundamental method of culturing microbes taken from the environment so that they can be studied.

facts.text: Martinus Beijerinck invented it; with the discovery of viruses it was one of his two major contributions to microbiology.
Early nitrification researchers, among them Warington, Winogradsky and the Franklands, could at first only enrich cultures of nitrifiers rather than isolate them pure.
Seven of the ten described anammox species are available in laboratory enrichment cultures.

entries.title: Farmers of Forty Centuries, King's lessons from Asia

definition.text: Franklin Hiram King's book on the long-sustained traditional farming of China, Korea and Japan, now regarded as a classic of organic farming.

facts.text: It recounts his nine-month tour of Asia in 1909, studying what would now be called organic farming or sustainable agriculture.
It discussed the advantages of sustainable agriculture and warned that such practices would be vital to farming in the future.
His wife Carrie Baker King finished the last chapter after his death and published the book in 1911.
Lord Northbourne called it a "classic" that no student of farming or social science can afford to ignore.

entries.title: Milton Whitney, a chief whose views met resistance

definition.text: The first chief of the US Division of Agricultural Soil, forerunner of the federal soil survey.

facts.text: Franklin Hiram King's finding that nutrient concentration in the soil solution correlated with crop yield undermined Whitney's firmly held views on soil chemistry and fertility.
George Nelson Coffey's map was not released as an official Bureau map because it did not fit Whitney's prevailing soil classification concepts.

entries.text: Milton Whitney was the first chief of the US Division of Agricultural Soil, the forerunner of the federal soil survey. He held firm views on soil chemistry and fertility, and the evidence did not always agree. Franklin Hiram King found that nutrient concentration in the soil solution correlated with crop yield, which undermined those views. Whitney's ideas also shaped what the Bureau released. George Nelson Coffey's map never became an official Bureau map, because it did not fit Whitney's prevailing soil classification concepts.

entries.title: Nikolai Sibirtsev, Dokuchaev's partner in a new science

definition.text: Russian soil scientist (1860–1900) who led the Russian school of soil science with Dokuchaev.

facts.text: From 1870 the school under Dokuchaev and Sibirtsev developed a new concept of soil.
He taught soil science as a professor; Konstantin Glinka took over his teaching when he fell ill.
He is also counted among the Russian geographers who made great contributions to physical geography.

entries.title: Russian Chernozem, the book that named soils by color

definition.text: Vasily Dokuchaev's 1883 book, his most famous work, a complete study of the chernozem soils of European Russia.

facts.text: It came out of his extensive field studies of Russian soils in 1883, from which he arrived at his theory of soil formation.
Studying the steppe soils of the Poltava region, he found that peasants named all soils by colour, and he began to use such names himself.
An English translation by N. Kaner was published in Jerusalem in 1967 for the USDA and NSF.

entries.title: The Soil Science Society of America and its grand challenges

definition.text: The largest soil-specific scientific society in the United States, formed in 1936.

facts.text: It was formed in 1936 by merging the Soils Section of the American Society of Agronomy with the American Soil Survey Association.
The ASA Soils Section became the official Americas section of the International Union of Soil Sciences in 1934, a role the society still fills.
Based in Madison, Wisconsin, it publishes peer-reviewed journals, magazines and books, led by its official Soil Science Society of America Journal.
Its voluntary certifications set standards for Certified Professional Soil Scientists and Certified Professional Soil Classifiers.
In 2011 it named soil science's grand challenges: climate change, food and energy security, waste treatment and water quality, and human and ecosystem health.
In 2017 it updated its definition of soil to cover loose material shaped by physical, chemical or biological processes at or near any planetary surface.
Its outreach includes the 'Secrets of Soil' exhibition, first shown at the Smithsonian's National Museum of Natural History, and the school websites Soils4Teachers and soils4kids.
Past presidents include William Albrecht in 1939, Hans Jenny in 1949 and Rattan Lal in 2007.

entries.title: From Dust Bowl emergency to a national conservation agency

definition.text: An agency of the United States Department of Agriculture, formerly the Soil Conservation Service, that gives technical help to farmers and other private landowners and managers.

facts.text: It began as the Soil Erosion Service, formed in the Department of the Interior on September 13, 1933, with Hugh Hammond Bennett as chief.
Bennett, driven by his knowledge of the soil erosion behind the 1930s Dust Bowl, led the founding and remained chief until he retired in 1952.
Moved to the Department of Agriculture on March 23, 1935, it was soon combined with other USDA units to form the Soil Conservation Service.
The SCS ran 500 Civilian Conservation Corps camps between 1933 and 1942, mainly for erosion control, and promoted practices such as contour plowing.
It was renamed the Natural Resources Conservation Service in 1994 to reflect its broader mission.
It gives farmers and ranchers technical and financial help, the money authorized by the Farm Bill, which is renewed every five years.
It leads the federal soil survey through the National Cooperative Soil Survey, with products such as the Web Soil Survey and the SSURGO database.
In 2015 it began broad support of soil health, promoting less tillage and more cover crops to reduce erosion and improve soil diversity.

conflicts.text: The agency currently has about 12,000 employees.

entries.title: Rothamsted, where wheat has grown in one field since 1843

definition.text: One of the oldest agricultural research institutions in the world, founded in 1843 at Harpenden, England, and formerly the Rothamsted Experimental Station.

facts.text: John Bennet Lawes, who had founded one of the first artificial fertilizer factories in 1842, set it up on his Rothamsted Manor estate to study how fertilizers affect crop yields.
With Joseph Henry Gilbert, who had trained under Liebig, Lawes began long-term field experiments; over 57 years they laid the foundations of scientific agriculture and crop nutrition.
The Broadbalk Experiment has been sown with winter wheat every year since 1843, and the Park Grass Experiment has been monitored continuously since 1856.
Thomas Way and Lawes discovered the principle of cation exchange there in the 19th century.
Its research led to single superphosphate fertilizer in the mid-nineteenth century, and in 1878 Robert Warington confirmed soil nitrification there.
In 1919 Ronald Fisher was hired to analyse its accumulated field data and stayed to create the theory of experimental design.
E. John Russell directed it from 1912 to 1943 and William Gammie Ogg until 1958, as staff grew from 140 to 471 and new departments, including pedology, were created.
Merged into the Institute of Arable Crops Research in 1987, it now operates as Rothamsted Research, funded mainly through the Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council.

entries.title: The National Cooperative Soil Survey maps a nation's soils

definition.text: A nationwide US partnership of federal, regional, state and local agencies and institutions that investigates, inventories, classifies and interprets the nation's soils and publishes the results.

facts.text: Led by the USDA's Natural Resources Conservation Service, it joins federal land agencies, state agricultural experiment stations, counties and conservation districts.
It inventories soils to judge land capability and conservation needs, and supplies soil information to the public, mainly through maps.
More than 90% of private lands have been mapped; in FY2001 maps were made or updated for 21,900,000 acres.
Federal authority for the soil survey comes from the Agricultural Appropriations Act of 1896, and the survey has involved several partners since its inception that year.
Survey work moved among USDA units, from an 1894 Division of Agricultural Soil to the Bureau of Soils in 1901, before passing to the Soil Conservation Service in 1952.
Land-grant universities have been close partners from the start, and conservation districts and Cooperative Extension are partners today.
Soil series established through the NCSS form a level of the USDA Soil Taxonomy hierarchy.
The first surveys cost about 3/10ths of a cent per acre; by 1999 a survey cost about $3 an acre.

entries.title: How the world's soil scientists organized in 1924

definition.text: The international scientific union of soil scientists, founded in 1924 as the International Society of Soil Science and a member of the International Science Council.

facts.text: Its purpose is to promote all branches of soil science and their applications, foster contacts among soil scientists, and stimulate research and its use.
It has 86 national and regional member societies with about 60,000 scientists, plus individual members in 57 countries.
Every four years it holds the World Congress of Soil Science; after its founding meeting in Rome in 1924, the first congress met in Washington, D.C., in 1927.
Its commissions, grown from six set up in 1924, range from soil morphology and soil fertility to degradation control, soil education and the history of soil science.
Since 2014 the IUSS Council has elected its President for a two-year term; before that, the national society hosting the next World Congress designated the President.
It endorses the World Reference Base as the international standard for soil classification.
It publishes the monthly IUSS Alert and the twice-yearly IUSS Bulletin, and is a founding partner of the International Year of Planet Earth.
Since January 2023 its secretariat has been run by Italy's Council for Agricultural Research and Economics.

Its commissions, grown from six in 1924, cover soil morphology, fertility, degradation control, education and the field's own history. It endorses the World Reference Base as the international standard for soil classification. Since 2014 its Council has elected the President for a two-year term. Since January 2023 Italy's Council for Agricultural Research and Economics has run its secretariat.

It houses the World Soil Museum and the World Soil Reference Collection, and ISRIC's Otto Spaargaren was nominated to help draft the World Reference Base.

entries.title: How the United States began mapping its soils

definition.text: The beginnings of systematic soil survey in the United States, from the first field mapping in 1899 to the consolidation of all USDA survey work in 1952.

facts.text: Milton Whitney began field work on May 3, 1899, with $16,000, mapping about 720,000 acres that year in tobacco lands and alkali areas slated for irrigation.

The first surveyors, geologists or chemists without agronomy training, separated soils mainly by texture, later adding colour, organic content, structure and drainage, and grouped soil types into series.
Influenced by Hilgard, Hopkins and Glinka's Russian school, Curtis Marbut, in charge from 1913, came to treat soil science as distinct from geology and to describe soils by horizons.
From 1933 to 1952 the Soil Conservation Service clashed with the Bureau of Chemistry and Soils over survey methods, until all USDA soil survey work was consolidated under the SCS.

entries.title: Lunar regolith, the gunpowder-scented ground of the Moon

definition.text: The unconsolidated material covering the surface of the Moon, whose finer fraction is called lunar soil.

facts.text: Lunar soil usually means grains 1 cm across or less, and lunar dust the still finer fraction, under one millimetre.

It forms mainly by mechanical weathering, as impacts and charged solar and interstellar particles grind basaltic and anorthositic rock ever finer, unlike Earth's soil formation driven by oxygen, water and life.
Its density is about 1.5 g/cm³, rising with depth; by mass half is finer than 60–80 μm, 10% finer than 10 μm and 10% coarser than 1 mm.
Seven elements make up 98–99% of lunar rocks and soil: oxygen (41–45%), silicon, aluminium, calcium, iron, magnesium and titanium.
Its composition largely reflects the local bedrock: it divides into highland and mare regolith, and by ilmenite content into high-, low- and very low-titanium types.
Its main minerals include plagioclase, olivine and pyroxenes, with abundant impact-melt glass, and ice in permanently shaded craters.
Its fine particles are sharp, very adhesive and electrically charged, and reportedly taste and smell of spent gunpowder.
It could serve as a lunar resource, as building material such as lunarcrete and as a medium for growing plants.

conflicts.text: Lunar soil has a relatively low density of 0.9–1.1 g/cm³.

entries.title: Martian regolith, studied from afar under a rusty sky

definition.text: The fine blanket of loose, varied surface deposits covering Mars, whose finer fraction is called Martian soil.

facts.text: No samples have yet been returned to Earth; the soil has been studied remotely by rovers and orbiters.
Mars is covered with sand and dust and littered with rocks; fine dust lifted in planet-wide storms stays aloft and tints the sky reddish from rusted iron minerals.
Easily weathered olivine is still present, suggesting that physical rather than chemical weathering now dominates on Mars.
Water and carbon dioxide ices are thought to lie frozen in the regolith, and Mars Odyssey measured water content up to 5% by weight.
Ice-rich regolith is thought to speed soil creep, rounding the 'softened terrain' of the Martian midlatitudes.
In 2008 the Phoenix lander found the regolith basic, at pH 8.3, and containing nutrients such as magnesium, sodium, potassium and chloride.
In 2012 Curiosity's first X-ray diffraction of Martian regolith found feldspar, pyroxenes and olivine, resembling the weathered basaltic soils of Hawaiian volcanoes.
Research on Earth relies on simulants such as Exolith Lab's MGS-1, and planned sample-return missions beginning with Mars 2020 should allow more accurate ones.

entries.title: Fake moon soil, and the surprise it failed to predict

definition.text: An Earth material made to approximate the chemical, mechanical, engineering, mineralogical or particle-size properties of lunar regolith.

facts.text: Researchers use simulants to study handling, excavating, transporting and using lunar regolith, since real samples are scarce, small and contaminated by Earth's atmosphere.
Before Apollo, crushed Earth rocks stood in for lunar soil; some differed greatly from the real thing, and the Moon's pervasive sharp, fine dust came as a surprise.
Later simulants, such as MLS-1 and JSC-1, were split into highland and mare types made by crushing and sieving anorthosite or basalt, matched to returned Apollo and Luna samples.
JSC-1, developed by NASA and the Johnson Space Center in 1994 to approximate mare soil, came from a glass-rich basaltic ash.
The lunar scientist Larry Taylor criticised many simulants for poor quality control and money wasted on features with no documented purpose.
JSC-1A geopolymerises in alkaline solution into a rock-like material with compressive and flexural strength comparable to conventional cements.
Recent simulants include Exolith Lab's highland LHS-1 and mare LMS-1, and the Indian Space Research Organisation's highland LSS-ISAC1 for its Chandrayaan programme.

entries.title: Space weathering, the slow aging of airless worlds

definition.text: The weathering of any object exposed to the harsh environment of outer space.

facts.text: Airless bodies such as the Moon, Mercury and asteroids are altered by cosmic rays, by solar wind irradiation, implantation and sputtering, and by meteorite and micrometeorite bombardment.
Much of what is known comes from lunar soils returned by Apollo, where impacts and particles comminute, melt, sputter and vaporize the soil.
Micrometeorite melt welds glass and mineral fragments into agglutinates, which make up as much as 60 to 70% of mature lunar soils.
Vaporised iron-bearing minerals such as olivine and pyroxene redeposit tiny blebs of metallic nanophase iron in agglutinates and thin grain rims.
As lunar soil matures it grows darker, redder and loses absorption-band depth, so young crater rays fade with time.
Understanding it is needed to interpret remotely sensed data from planetary surfaces.
It works more slowly on asteroids, yet soil grains returned by Hayabusa from Itokawa show definite space-weathering alteration.
Impacts on Mercury are expected to make 13.5 times the melt and 19.5 times the vapour per unit area as on the Moon.

entries.text: With no air to shield them, the Moon, Mercury and the asteroids take the full force of space. Space weathering is the weathering of any object exposed to that harsh environment. Cosmic rays strike these airless bodies. The solar wind irradiates their surfaces, implants particles in them and sputters atoms away. Meteorites and micrometeorites bombard them. Much of what is known comes from lunar soils returned by Apollo. There, impacts and particles comminute, or crush, the soil, and also melt, sputter and vaporize it. Micrometeorite melt welds glass and mineral fragments into agglutinates, clumps that make up as much as 60 to 70% of mature lunar soils. Iron-bearing minerals such as olivine and pyroxene vaporize, then redeposit tiny blebs of metallic nanophase iron in agglutinates and in thin rims on grains. The effect shows from afar. As lunar soil matures it grows darker and redder, and its absorption bands grow shallower, so the bright rays of young craters fade with time. Reading remotely sensed data from planetary surfaces therefore requires understanding this process. On asteroids it works more slowly, yet grains that Hayabusa returned from Itokawa show definite alteration. Mercury should take a far harder beating. Impacts there are expected to make 13.5 times the melt and 19.5 times the vapor per unit area as on the Moon.

entries.title: Astropedology, soil science for deep time and other worlds

definition.text: The study of very ancient paleosols and meteorites relevant to the origin of life, and of soil systems on other planets.

facts.text: It is a branch of pedology concerned with soils of the distant geologic past and of other planetary bodies, to understand Earth's place in the universe.
If soil is a planetary surface altered in place by biological, chemical or physical processes, the question for Martian soils and paleosols becomes whether they were alive.
Better understanding of soil formation on other planetary bodies helped lead the Soil Science Society of America in 2017 to define soil as loose material altered at or near a planetary surface.
Astropedology symposia are a new focus of scientific meetings on soil science.
Paleopedology underpins both the study of ancient ecosystems on Earth and the emerging field of astropedology in exoplanet research.

entries.title: Perchlorates, the salts that make Martian soil toxic

definition.text: The chlorine-bearing perchlorate salts whose relatively high concentrations make Martian regolith toxic.

facts.text: NASA's Phoenix lander first found perchlorates, such as calcium perchlorate, on Mars in 2008; later landers and the Mars Odyssey orbiter showed they are spread across the planet.
Levels of around 0.5% in the regolith are considered toxic to humans, and even trace amounts interfere with human thyroid function.
In a 2013 study, 0.5 g per litre of perchlorate cut leaf chlorophyll, root oxidizing power and plant size, and the salts built up in the leaves.
The water hyacinth Eichhornia crassipes tolerated perchlorates and could help remove them, though the plants then held high concentrations.
Without an ozone layer, ultraviolet light reaches the surface and makes perchlorates more lethal to bacteria, and soil iron oxides and hydrogen peroxide add to their toxicity.
Some bacteria adapt to perchlorate or even live off it; a NASA-funded project from 2022 is studying Dehalococcoides mccartyi to break perchlorates into chlorides and oxygen.
Perchlorates may also make life-related organic molecules harder to detect.

conflicts.text: Perchlorate levels on Mars are 0.05 wt %.
conflicts.note: Astropedology's figure is a tenth of the 'around 0.5%' given on Martian regolith.

entries.title: Moon dust, a hazard to machines and lungs
entries.article: Lunar regolith#Harmful effects of lunar dust

definition.text: The harm that fine, easily disturbed lunar dust can do to equipment and to the health of crews.

facts.text: It can darken surfaces and raise heat absorption, abrade materials by friction, and degrade seals, lenses, solar panels, windows and wiring.
Reactive particles in the lungs may cause respiratory disease, and long-term exposure possibly a disease similar to silicosis.
Apollo crews reported coughs, throat irritation, watery eyes and blurred vision from dust after moonwalks, though symptoms cleared within 24 hours.
A 2005 NASA study ranked dust the top challenge to study before a human Mars expedition, concerns that apply equally to lunar dust.

entries.text: Apollo crews came in from moonwalks with coughs, throat irritation, watery eyes and blurred vision, though the symptoms cleared within 24 hours. Fine lunar dust is easily disturbed, and it can harm both equipment and crews. It darkens surfaces so they absorb more heat, abrades materials by friction, and degrades seals, lenses, solar panels, windows and wiring. In the lungs, reactive particles may cause respiratory disease, and long exposure possibly a disease similar to silicosis. A 2005 NASA study ranked dust the top challenge to study before a human Mars expedition, and its concerns apply equally to the Moon.

entries.title: Bringing the Moon home, a few kilograms at a time

definition.text: The bringing of lunar rock and regolith back to Earth by space missions, beginning with Apollo.

facts.text: Apollo astronauts brought back some 360 kg of lunar rocks from six landing sites.
Every returned sample has been contaminated by Earth's air and humidity: the dust has rusted and lost its chemical reactivity, so it no longer matches conditions on the Moon.
On 16 December 2020 China's Chang'e 5 returned about 2 kg of lunar rock and soil, the first sample since 1972, making China the third country to do so.
Chang'e 6 returned samples from the far side of the Moon in 2024.

entries.title: How the Moon makes soil without water or life

definition.text: The making and continual alteration of lunar regolith by impacts and space radiation, known as space weathering.

facts.text: Its main processes are comminution by meteorite and micrometeorite impacts, agglutination of fragments by impact-melt glass, and solar wind sputtering and cosmic ray spallation.
Soils begin as a coarse, poorly sorted blanket of impact ejecta; micrometeoroids then grind it finer and add agglutinates and metallic iron, darkening it over time.
Soil forms far more slowly than on Earth: crater production rates suggest about 81 thousand years to overturn the top 2 cm.
Fire fountaining of lava also left glass-bead deposits, such as the orange soil at Shorty Crater found by Apollo 17 and Apollo 15's green glass.

entries.text: Lunar soil forms at a crawl. Crater production rates suggest it takes about 81 thousand years to overturn just the top 2 cm. This making and remaking is a case of {{ref:soil-hist-079}}. Each soil begins as a coarse, poorly sorted blanket of debris thrown out by impacts. Micrometeoroids then grind it finer, weld fragments into agglutinates with impact-melt glass, and add metallic iron, darkening it over time. Solar wind sputtering and cosmic ray spallation, which knocks fragments off atoms, keep altering the grains. Lava fire fountains also left glass beads, such as the orange soil Apollo 17 found at Shorty Crater and Apollo 15's green glass.

entries.title: Living off the land on the Moon and Mars

definition.text: The collection, processing and use of materials found on other bodies, such as the Moon or Mars, in place of materials brought from Earth.

facts.text: It could supply life support, propellants, construction materials and energy, reducing the payload launched from Earth.
Settling planets or moons will need local building materials such as regolith.
Water bound in regolith, ice or permafrost can be recovered by heating, though ice and permafrost may be harder than rock to mine.
Oxygen can be extracted from iron oxide in lunar regolith by heating it above 900 °C in hydrogen gas.

entries.text: Future crews could lighten what they launch from Earth by living off the land. In situ resource utilization means collecting, processing and using materials found on the Moon, Mars or other bodies, in place of materials brought from home. It could supply life support, propellants, construction materials and energy. Anyone settling a planet or moon will need local building materials such as regolith. Water bound in regolith, ice or permafrost can be recovered by heating, though ice and permafrost may be harder than rock to mine. Heating lunar regolith above 900 °C in hydrogen gas pulls oxygen out of its iron oxide.

entries.title: Is there soil on the Moon? It depends on the definition

definition.text: The unsettled question of what counts as soil on other planetary bodies, where the usual Earth definition, which includes organic content, may not fit.

facts.text: Planetary scientists use a functional definition: rocks are fragments of about 10 cm or more, larger than cobbles on the Wentworth scale, and soil is all other, typically loose material.
The planetary science community often adopts 'medium for plant growth', while a fuller definition calls soil altered surface material that records its environmental history and needs no life to form.
Under Earth systems many extraterrestrial soils would be Entisols in Soil Taxonomy or Regosols in the WRB, but applying Earth-based systems to such different settings is debatable.
An alternative would put all non-Earth soils in a new order or reference group, tentatively called Astrosols.

entries.contested_note: Sources disagree on what soil means off Earth, from a medium for plant growth to any altered surface material, and on whether Earth classifications or a new Astrosol group should cover it.

entries.title: Martian dust, lifted again and again

definition.text: The finest fraction of Martian regolith, under 30 micrometres across, much of it carried into the atmosphere.

facts.text: Atmospheric dust particles are generally about 3 μm across; dust from the 2001 global storms stayed aloft only 0.6 years, against about two years for Mount Pinatubo's.
On Earth soil moisture and oceans gather settled dust into larger particles, but neither works on Mars, so deposited dust is free to be lifted again.
Its composition, dominated by plagioclase feldspar and zeolite, suggests it is ground mechanically from basaltic rock with little chemical alteration.
A study found that it reacts with water to form highly reactive molecules like those that cause lung disease in quartz miners.

entries.text: On Mars, dust that settles rarely stays put. Martian dust is the finest fraction of the regolith, under 30 micrometers across, and much of it rides in the atmosphere as particles about 3 μm across. On Earth, soil moisture and oceans gather settled dust into larger particles. Neither works on Mars, so deposited dust is free to rise again. Dust from the 2001 global storms stayed aloft only 0.6 years, against about two years for Mount Pinatubo's. Plagioclase feldspar and zeolite dominate it, which suggests it is ground mechanically from basaltic rock with little chemical alteration. One study found that it reacts with water to form highly reactive molecules, like those that cause lung disease in quartz miners.

entries.title: Lunarcrete, concrete made from the Moon itself

definition.text: A proposed concrete-like building material made from lunar regolith to cut the cost of building on the Moon.

facts.text: Like concrete it would use aggregate, water and cement, with lunar regolith as aggregate and cement from calcium-rich lunar rock.
In 1986 Lin and colleagues made lunarcrete from 40 g of Apollo 16 regolith; it withstood 75 MPa of compression.
A waterless version binds regolith simulant with sulfur; a mix of 65% JSC-1 simulant and 35% sulfur averaged 33.8 MPa compressive strength.
AstroCrete, proposed for the Moon or Mars, binds regolith with human serum albumin from blood.

entries.title: Making Mars soil on Earth

definition.text: An Earth material used to mimic the chemical and mechanical properties of Martian regolith for research and prototype testing.

facts.text: The first, JSC Mars-1, was made at NASA's Johnson Space Center in 1998 from palagonitic tephra, low-temperature-altered volcanic ash from Hawaii.
Mojave Mars Simulant (2007) was crushed basalt with minimal weathering, so unlike the clay-like JSC Mars-1 it did not attract water.
MGS-1 (from 2018), the first mineralogically accurate simulant, mixes pure minerals to match the Rocknest soil analysed by Curiosity in Gale crater.
No simulant includes the perchlorates Phoenix found in 2008, though users can add perchlorate salts; fine particles and crystalline silica pose some health risk.

entries.title: Impact gardening, how meteorites till the Moon

definition.text: The stirring of the outer crust of airless moons and other bodies by impacts, called lunar gardening on the Moon.

facts.text: Lacking an atmosphere, such bodies have almost no erosion, so impact debris builds up at the surface as a rough soil, the regolith.
Later impacts, especially by micrometeorites, stir and mix this soil.
The top centimetre of the Moon was long thought to overturn every 10 million years, but a 2016 LRO study of impact ejecta put it closer to 80,000 years.

entries.title: Archean paleosols and early Earth's hints of soil life

definition.text: Soils preserved from early Earth's Archean eon, which give circumstantial evidence of life in soils 3.42 to 3.46 billion years ago.

facts.text: Soil profiles from the Pilbara region of northwestern Australia show distinct depletion of phosphorus.
Sulfur bacteria commonly oxidise sulfur to sulfates such as gypsum and barite, minerals of today's acid sulfate soils and a possible reason for sulfate build-up in Archean paleosols.

entries.title: Can a garden grow in moon dust?
entries.article: Astropedology#Growing plants on the Moon and Mars

definition.text: Research into whether lunar and Martian soils, or simulants of them, can support the growth of plants.

facts.text: All essential plant minerals appear to be present in both soils in sufficient amounts, except possibly reactive nitrogen, which Mars Pathfinder could not detect.
Nitrogen-fixing species could make up the shortfall, but fixation needs atmospheric nitrogen, absent on the Moon and only a trace on Mars.
In a large controlled experiment, plants germinated and grew for 50 days on Mars and Moon soil simulants without added nutrients, doing much better on the Mars simulant.
Plants struggle in real lunar soil, so long missions may need imported Earth soil, chemically treated regolith or plants bred for it.

entries.title: Ancient soils on Mars, and the open question of life

definition.text: Ancient soils on Mars, recognised from rover analyses and orbital remote sensing of the Martian surface.

facts.text: The Curiosity rover in Gale Crater found features like Earth's soil horizons and structures, including blocky angular peds, sand wedges, a shallow gypsic horizon and vesicular structure.
The Yellowknife Bay paleosols, about 3.7 billion years old, show olivine weathering to smectite and record a shift from possibly warm and wet to extremely cold and arid conditions.
Orbiters have detected phyllosilicate clays at thousands of sites dated to 4.0–3.7 Ga, explained either by hydrothermal activity or by surface weathering and pedogenesis.
Vesicular structures like those made by microbial gas in Earth's desert soils occur on Mars, but definitive evidence of life on Mars is still lacking.

entries.title: Was life born in the soil?

definition.text: The idea that life evolved in soil, where water held between clay grains forms countless microscopic reaction chambers.

facts.text: These chambers may also promote the making of organic compounds by mechanisms shown in the Miller–Urey experiment.
Clayey and organic soils resist erosion and so keep producing clay and organic matter, and early unicellular life would also have bound the soil.
The weathering cycle still supplies the ingredients that life requires.

entries.title: The Viking landers ask Martian soil if anything lives there

definition.text: Four biological experiments carried to the surface of Mars by the two Viking landers in 1976 to look for signs of microbial life.

facts.text: Each lander used a robotic arm to put soil samples into sealed test chambers; Viking 1 worked near the equator and Viking 2 further north.
The gas chromatograph–mass spectrometer, sensitive to a few parts per billion, found no significant organic molecules; Martian soil held less carbon than lifeless Apollo lunar soil.
The gas exchange experiment fed nutrients and water to soil under helium; oxygen disappeared on contact with the soil and carbon dioxide kept evolving.
The pyrolytic release experiment exposed soil to carbon-14-labelled CO and CO2, then baked it at 650 °C to detect any carbon fixed as biomass.
Any positive result was to be checked by heat-sterilizing a duplicate sample: persisting activity meant chemistry, a lost response meant biology.
The general view is that the results are best explained by oxidative reactions with the soil, which constant ultraviolet exposure has given a thin layer of very strong oxidant.
Perchlorate, found by Phoenix in 2008, destroys organics on heating and yields chloromethane and dichloromethane, the very compounds Viking detected, so whether Viking found organics remains open.
A 2018 reanalysis of the GC-MS data suggested organic compounds may in fact have been detected, matching Curiosity rover data.

entries.text: In 1976 two landers scooped up Martian soil to test it for life, and scientists still argue over the answer. The Viking landers carried four biological experiments to the surface of Mars to look for microbes. Viking 1 worked near the equator and Viking 2 farther north, each loading soil into sealed chambers with a robotic arm. A gas chromatograph–mass spectrometer, sensitive to a few parts per billion, found no significant organic molecules. Martian soil held less carbon than lifeless Apollo lunar soil. Fed nutrients and water under helium, soil in the gas exchange experiment made oxygen disappear on contact and kept giving off carbon dioxide. The pyrolytic release experiment exposed soil to carbon-14-labeled CO and CO2, then baked it at 650 °C to detect carbon fixed as biomass. Any positive result was to be checked on a heat-sterilized duplicate: persisting activity meant chemistry, a lost response meant biology. The general view blames oxidative reactions, since constant ultraviolet light has given the soil a thin layer of very strong oxidant. Yet perchlorate, found by Phoenix in 2008, destroys organics on heating and yields chloromethane and dichloromethane, the very compounds Viking detected. A 2018 reanalysis suggested organics may in fact have been detected, matching Curiosity rover data. Whether the results reflect soil chemistry alone or could include biology remains disputed.

entries.title: Bringing pieces of Mars back to Earth

definition.text: A proposed mission to collect rock and dust samples on Mars and bring them to Earth.

facts.text: Returned samples would allow far more extensive analysis than onboard sensors, focused on whether Mars once hosted life, and could be reanalysed by future instruments.
The Perseverance rover, landed in Jezero crater in February 2021, is caching rock, regolith (Martian soil) and atmosphere samples for return.
Back contamination of Earth by Martian organisms has been raised, but the scientific consensus is that the risk of large-scale effects is small.
Martian meteorites are another sample source: 356 had been identified by August 2023, out of over 79,000 known meteorites.

entries.title: Growing plants in space, and on the Moon

definition.text: The growing of plants in outer space, mostly in pressurized, weightless space gardens in low Earth orbit.

facts.text: The absence of gravity, important for root development, soil integration and watering, is the first challenge.
For long-term growth, nutrient supply to roots, biogeochemical cycles and microbial interactions in soil-based substrates are particularly complex.
In January 2019 cotton seeds sprouted in a sealed biosphere on the Chang'e 4 lander, the first plant grown on the Moon; it survived 2 days.
University of Florida tests showed Arabidopsis thaliana can germinate and grow in lunar soil, but slowly and with signs of stress.

entries.title: The labeled release test and its disputed signal

definition.text: A Viking life-detection test in which Martian soil was dosed with a dilute nutrient solution tagged with radioactive carbon-14 and the air above monitored for labelled gas.

facts.text: Both landers' first injections gave a steady stream of radioactive gas, from a sunlit surface sample and a sample from beneath a rock.
Samples heated 3 hours at 160 °C released no gas, and at 50 °C much less; but second and third nutrient doses released no more gas, unlike living terrestrial soil.
Superoxides formed by ultraviolet light, or hypochlorite from irradiated perchlorate, may explain the result chemically.
Its designer Gilbert Levin holds the positive results diagnostic of life, but most astrobiologists judge the experiments inconclusive or negative.

entries.contested_note: Levin and Straat maintain the results indicate life; most astrobiologists attribute them to oxidizing soil chemistry.

soil.text: A natural mixture of minerals, organic matter, gases, water and organisms that together support the life of plants and soil organisms; all of Earth's soil together is called the pedosphere.

soil science.text: The study of soil as a natural resource: its formation, classification and mapping, its physical, chemical, biological and fertility properties, and how these bear on soil use and management.

pedosphere.text: The outermost layer of Earth's crust, made of soil and subject to soil formation and erosion.

pedology.text: The branch of soil science that studies how soils form and evolve and builds frameworks for describing soil bodies, often in their natural environment.

soil composition.text: The proportions of solids (minerals and organic matter) and of pore space, shared between water and air, that make up a soil.

edaphology.text: The branch of soil science concerned with the influence of soils on living things, especially plants.

uses of soil.text: The many ways people rely on soil, from growing food and fibre to construction, mining and landscape work.

soil as a natural body.text: The view, developed by Dokuchaev, that soil is a natural body with its own genesis and history, distinct from the bedrock beneath it.

soil functions.text: The general capabilities of soils that matter for agriculture, the environment, nature protection, landscape architecture and urban uses.

soil health.text: The state of a soil meeting its range of ecosystem functions as appropriate to its environment.

soil quality.text: The condition of a soil judged by its capacity to perform ecosystem services that meet the needs of human and non-human life.

principles of pedology.text: The working principles pedologists use to explain soil genesis, starting from the idea that external factors drive soil-forming processes and create soil patterns.

soil science in practice.text: The practical work of soil scientists, traditionally mapping soils and increasingly addressing land and environmental problems across disciplines.

vernacular soil classification.text: Folk systems that name soils either with unique names or by obvious traits such as red, hot, fat or sandy.

atmospheric inputs to soil.text: What the pedosphere receives from the air, mainly wind-blown sediment, rainfall and diffusing gases.

forest soils.text: Soils formed under forest, usually well developed with thick humus layers.

grassland and desert soils.text: Soils formed where precipitation equals or falls short of evapotranspiration, so that soil development works under drought.

pioneer organisms in soil formation.text: The first colonisers of bare rock, such as lichens, mosses and microbes, whose acids begin turning rock into soil.

earth's critical zone.text: The near-surface environment where rock, soil, water, air and living organisms interact to regulate habitats and the availability of life-sustaining resources.

tropical forest soils.text: Soils of tropical forests, which receive more sunlight and rain over longer growing seasons than any other environment.

industrialization and edaphology.text: The ways industrialised production and farming have changed how soils interact with plants.

van helmont's willow experiment.text: An experiment in which Jan Baptist van Helmont (1577–1644) grew a willow tree in a pot of soil for five years, supplying only rainwater.

biological soil crust.text: A biological soil crust is a living surface community of fungi, lichens, cyanobacteria, bryophytes and algae in the open spaces between vascular plants.

mineral.text: A naturally occurring solid with a fairly well-defined chemical composition and a specific crystal structure.

weathering.text: The breakdown of rocks, soils and minerals through contact with water, atmospheric gases, sunlight and living things.

soil solution.text: The water held in soil pores together with the many organic and mineral substances dissolved or suspended in it.

what counts as soil.text: The unsettled question of where soil ends and other loose surface material begins, in particular whether lifeless regolith can be called soil.

chemical weathering.text: Weathering in which water, oxygen, carbon dioxide and other substances react with rock and change its composition.

biological weathering.text: Weathering started or sped up by living things, such as soil microorganisms, lichens and plant roots.

dissolution weathering.text: Chemical weathering in which a mineral dissolves completely without leaving any new solid; also called simple or congruent dissolution.

oxidation weathering.text: Chemical weathering by oxidation of metals in minerals, most commonly iron changing from Fe2+ to Fe3+.

physical weathering.text: Weathering that breaks rock into smaller pieces without changing its chemistry; also called mechanical weathering or disaggregation.

composition of plant residues.text: The water, elements and organic compounds that make up the plant debris from which soil organic matter forms.

soil organic carbon with depth.text: How the amount, age and makeup of soil organic carbon change between the surface layer, roughly the top 20 cm, and the deeper mineral soil.

frost weathering.text: Physical weathering caused by ice forming inside rock outcrops.

mineral hydration.text: Chemical weathering in which water molecules, or H+ and OH− ions, attach rigidly to the atoms of a mineral.

mineral chemistry.text: How the abundance of elements in the Earth's crust, and the swapping of one ion for another, control which minerals exist and how varied they are.

oxide minerals.text: Minerals in which oxygen or hydroxide is the main anion, divided into simple oxides, hydroxides and multiple oxides.

pressure release weathering.text: Physical weathering, also called unloading, that occurs when deeply buried rock is brought to the surface and the weight on it is removed.

salt weathering.text: The breaking up of rock when salty water seeps into cracks and evaporates, leaving salt crystals that grow there; also called haloclasty.

thermal stress weathering.text: Weathering caused by rock expanding and contracting as its temperature changes.

clay.text: A fine-grained natural soil material containing clay minerals, the hydrous aluminium phyllosilicates such as kaolinite.

rock-forming minerals.text: The mineral species and groups that are far more abundant in rocks than the rest.

silicate minerals.text: Minerals built from the silicon–oxygen tetrahedron, [SiO4]4−, grouped by how far those tetrahedra link together.

framework silicates.text: Silicate minerals whose tetrahedra share all four corners, the most polymerized class, including quartz and the feldspars.

phyllosilicates.text: Sheet silicates: minerals made of sheets of linked silica tetrahedra, a class that includes the mica, chlorite and kaolinite–serpentine groups.

soil texture.text: The quality of a soil set by its make-up of sand, silt and clay particles.

clay formation.text: The making of clay minerals, most commonly by long chemical weathering of silicate-bearing rocks, and their gathering into clay deposits.

hydrolysis and carbonation.text: Chemical weathering in which only part of a mineral dissolves and the rest turns into a new solid such as a clay mineral; carbonation is the form driven by dissolved carbon dioxide.

weathering in soil formation.text: The conversion of rock into soil material as weathering turns its minerals into clay minerals and iron oxides.

clay as a building material.text: The use of clay, the defining ingredient of loam, as one of the oldest building materials on Earth.

clay varieties.text: The main kinds of clay, grouped by their dominant clay minerals: kaolinite, montmorillonite–smectite and illite.

uses of clay.text: The shaping and firing of clay into pottery and construction products, and its use in many industrial processes.

mineralogy.text: The branch of geology that studies the chemistry, crystal structure and physical, including optical, properties of minerals.

biogenic minerals debate.text: The dispute among geologists and mineralogists over the International Mineralogical Association's exclusion of crystalline substances made by living things.

carbonate minerals.text: Minerals whose main anionic group is carbonate, [CO3]2−, chiefly calcite, aragonite and dolomite.

calcite.text: A carbonate mineral, the most stable polymorph of calcium carbonate (CaCO3).

mineral identification.text: Telling minerals apart by physical properties such as crystal habit, hardness, lustre, colour, streak, cleavage and specific gravity.

sulfate minerals.text: Minerals that contain the sulfate anion, [SO4]2−, of which gypsum is by far the most common hydrous member.

phytolith.text: A rigid microscopic mineral deposit, usually of silica, formed in plant tissue and often persisting after the plant decays.

soil ph.text: A measure of how acidic or basic (alkaline) a soil is.

soil horizon.text: A layer roughly parallel to the soil surface whose physical, chemical and biological characteristics differ from the layers above and below.

mineral-associated organic matter.text: Soil organic matter chemically stabilized by sticking to clay, iron oxide or other mineral surfaces.

weathering rind.text: A discoloured, chemically altered outer layer of a rock fragment, formed by weathering.

soil buffering capacity.text: A soil's resistance to a change in pH when acid or basic material is added.

soil color.text: The colour of a soil, often its most visually apparent property.

aluminium toxicity.text: Harm to plants from dissolved aluminium, the most widespread problem of acid soils.

factors affecting soil ph.text: The natural and human influences that set a soil's pH, starting with the minerals of its parent material and the weathering they have undergone.

measuring soil ph.text: The field and laboratory methods for determining a soil's pH, from reading the profile and its plants to electronic meters.

soil ph and nutrient availability.text: The control soil pH exerts over which ions are released or held, and so over the availability of plant nutrients.

master horizons.text: The main layers of a soil profile, marked with capital letters, most commonly O, A, E, B, C and R.

lowering soil ph.text: Reducing the pH of an alkaline soil by adding acidifying agents or acidic organic materials.

plant ph preferences.text: The soil pH ranges to which different plant species are adapted.

soil ph and soil organisms.text: The two-way relation between soil pH and the organisms living in the soil.

soil ph and water availability.text: The ways extreme soil pH reduces the water available to plants and organisms.

soil ph classes.text: The named soil pH ranges of the USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service, from ultra acidic to very strongly alkaline.

munsell soil color charts.text: The standard way soil surveys record soil colour, using the Munsell color system, which specifies a colour by hue, value and chroma.

soil color interpretation.text: Reading what a soil's colours reveal about its organic matter, iron chemistry, aeration and salts.

australian horizon designations.text: The horizon scheme of the Australian Soil and Land Survey Field Handbook (2009), which adds peaty P and D horizons, drops E, and numbers sub-horizons of A and B.

wrb horizon designations.text: The horizon and layer symbols set out in Chapter 10 of the World Reference Base for Soil Resources manual, 4th edition (2022).

bedrock.text: The solid rock beneath the weathered rock and loose surface deposits, together called regolith, in the near-surface crust of Earth or another terrestrial planet.

gleying.text: The development of gray or bluish, low-chroma colours in waterlogged soils as iron is reduced or removed.

core sample.text: A cylindrical section of a material such as sediment, rock or soil, usually obtained by drilling with a hollow tube.

trial pit.text: An excavation dug to study or sample the composition and structure of the subsurface, usually during a site investigation, soil survey or geological survey; also called a test pit.

regolith.text: A blanket of loose, unconsolidated and varied surface deposits covering solid rock.

saprolite.text: Chemically weathered rock, literally 'rotten rock', formed in the lower zones of soil profiles by deep weathering of the bedrock surface.

rock.text: Any naturally occurring solid mass or aggregate of minerals or mineraloid matter.

hydrolysis.text: Hydrolysis is any chemical reaction in which a water molecule breaks one or more chemical bonds.

sedimentary rock.text: Rock formed by the cementation of mineral or organic particles deposited at the Earth's surface.

limestone.text: A carbonate sedimentary rock made mostly of calcite and aragonite, and the main source of lime.

asteroid regolith.text: The loose surface layer of asteroids, produced by impacts and other surface-altering processes.

icy regolith on titan.text: Loose icy material on Saturn's moon Titan, called regolith because it behaves mechanically like regolith on other bodies.

igneous rock.text: One of the three main rock types, formed by the cooling and solidification of magma or lava.

deep weathering.text: Long-continued chemical weathering that builds thick, deeply weathered regolith over bedrock, the product of a region's long weathering history.

primary mineral.text: A mineral that formed during the original crystallization of its host igneous rock and has not been chemically altered since.

metamorphic rock.text: Rock transformed from an existing rock into a new type by heat and pressure, a process called metamorphism.

grus.text: An accumulation of angular, coarse sand and gravel produced by the granular disintegration of crystalline rocks, especially granitoids, through weathering.

lithology.text: The description of a rock unit's physical characteristics visible at outcrop, in hand or core samples, or under low magnification.

feldspar.text: A group of rock-forming aluminium tectosilicate minerals that also contain cations such as sodium, calcium, potassium or barium.

olivine.text: A magnesium iron silicate mineral, (Mg,Fe)2SiO4, of the nesosilicate type.

plagioclase.text: A continuous solid-solution series of framework silicate minerals within the feldspar group.

biotite.text: A common group of dark phyllosilicate minerals in the mica group, approximately K(Mg,Fe)3AlSi3O10(OH,F)2.

mafic.text: Describing silicate minerals, magmas and igneous rocks rich in magnesium and iron and relatively low in silica.

stone stripe.text: An elongated, unvegetated band of mostly talus-like basalt rock along a hillside or at the base of a cliff; also called a lava stringer.

orthoclase.text: A potassium feldspar, KAlSi3O8, an important tectosilicate mineral of igneous rock.

rock cycle.text: The geological concept describing the transitions, through geologic time, among sedimentary, metamorphic and igneous rock.

superficial deposits.text: Geologically recent, mostly unconsolidated deposits, typically of Quaternary age (less than 2.6 million years old).

parent material.text: The underlying geological material, generally bedrock or a superficial (drift) deposit, in which soil horizons form.

transported parent material.text: Loose, uncemented parent material moved by water, wind, ice or gravity, and classified by its last means of transport.

loess.text: A clastic, predominantly silt-sized sediment formed by the accumulation of wind-blown dust.

alluvium.text: Loose clay, silt, sand or gravel deposited by running water in stream beds, on floodplains, in alluvial fans or similar settings.

colluvium.text: Loose, unconsolidated sediment deposited at the base of hillslopes by rainwash, sheetwash, slow downslope creep or a combination of these.

glacial till.text: Unsorted sediment eroded and carried by a glacier and deposited directly from the ice.

loess plateau.text: A plateau of some 640,000 km2 around the upper and middle reaches of China's Yellow River, covered by loess.

loess soils and fertility.text: Soils developed on loess, which tend to be very rich and, under suitable climates, among the most agriculturally productive in the world.

residuum.text: Weathered rock that stays in place rather than being moved by erosion, and in time helps form soil.

loess–paleosol sequences.text: Stacked loess layers separated by buried soils, studied as archives of past climate and environmental change.

non-glacial loess.text: Loess that originates from deserts, dune fields, playa lakes or volcanic ash rather than from glacial outwash.

eluvial deposits.text: In geology, deposits and soils derived from weathering in place, or from weathering plus gravitational movement or accumulation.

river channel migration.text: The lateral shift of an alluvial river channel across its floodplain over time.

volcanic ash.text: Fragments of rock, mineral crystals and volcanic glass under 2 mm across, produced by volcanic eruptions.

cumulose parent material.text: Organic parent material built up in place from plant residues, such as sphagnum moss, preserved by a high water table or other conditions that slow decay.

glaciofluvial deposits.text: Boulders, gravel, sand, silt and clay from ice sheets or glaciers that meltwater streams have transported, sorted and deposited.

periglacial loess.text: Loess blown from the floodplains of glacial braided rivers that carried meltwater and sediment from melting ice sheets and ice caps.

lacustrine parent material.text: Sediment that settled in lakes, forming a well-sorted, fine-textured parent material rich in silt and clay.

glaciolacustrine deposits.text: Parent material formed from glacier-derived sediment carried into lakes, typically lakes at the ice margin.

marine parent material.text: Material carried by rivers to the sea that sank to the ocean floor and later became a parent material.

volcanic tephra parent material.text: Volcanic ash carried by the wind and settled at various distances from a volcano, the most common volcanic parent material.

lichens and soil formation.text: The part lichens, symbiotic colonies of algae or cyanobacteria and fungi, play in breaking down rock and building and stabilizing soil.

desert varnish.text: An orange-yellow to black coating, about one micrometre thick, on exposed rock surfaces in arid environments.

glacial drift.text: All sediment, from clay to boulders, carried by a glacier and deposited by or from the ice or by its meltwater.

moraine.text: Any accumulation of unconsolidated glacial debris, often till, in currently or formerly glaciated regions.

outwash plain.text: A plain of glaciofluvial deposits built by meltwater outwash at the end of a glacier; also called a sandur.

spheroidal weathering.text: Chemical weathering of jointed bedrock that produces concentric shells of highly decayed rock within saprolite; also called onion-skin weathering.

topsoil.text: The upper layer of soil, richest in organic matter and microorganisms, where most of the soil's biological activity takes place.

subsoil.text: The layer of soil beneath the topsoil, a mix of sand, silt and clay with much less organic matter and humus.

soil morphology.text: The branch of soil science that describes soils technically, above all their physical properties such as texture, colour, structure and consistence.

diagnostic horizon.text: A horizon defined by a set of criteria, whose presence or absence at a given depth is used to assign soils to taxonomic units.

o horizon.text: A surface layer of organic material, built from plant residues not mixed into the mineral soil and not waterlogged for long periods.

a horizon.text: The uppermost mineral horizon, at the surface or below an O horizon, where humified organic matter is intimately mixed with mineral material.

eluviation.text: The removal of soil material from upper layers by water percolating down through the profile.

e horizon.text: A mineral horizon that has lost clay, iron, aluminium, organic matter or a mix of these, leaving a concentration of sand and silt, mostly quartz.

hardpan.text: A dense, largely water-impervious soil layer, usually lying just below the topsoil.

soil profile.text: A vertical face of soil showing its horizons, layers roughly parallel to the surface; formally, one face of a pedon.

cryoturbation.text: Frost churning: the mixing of material from different soil horizons, down to bedrock, by repeated freezing and thawing in permafrost soils.

illuviation.text: The deposition in a lower soil layer of material, called illuvium, washed down by rainwater from a layer above.

b horizon.text: A subsurface mineral horizon, formed below an A, E, H or O horizon, where the original rock structure is largely gone and soil formation has altered or enriched the material.

c horizon.text: A layer below the soil horizons, other than hard bedrock, that is little affected by soil formation and lacks the properties of O, A, E or B horizons.

solum.text: The upper part of a soil, its surface and subsoil layers, that has developed under the same soil-forming conditions.

horizon designation.text: The code of letters and numbers that names each soil horizon: a capital master symbol, often followed by lowercase suffixes, with numbers for discontinuities and subdivisions.

h horizon.text: An organic layer, generally peat, that is saturated with water for long periods or has been artificially drained.

r layer.text: Hard, consolidated bedrock underlying the soil at the base of the profile.

horizon suffixes.text: Lowercase letters added to a master horizon symbol to record particular features or processes of soil formation.

lithologic discontinuity.text: A change in parent material within a soil profile, shown in horizon designations by a numerical prefix.

buried soil horizon.text: A genetic horizon that formed at the surface and was later covered by new mineral material, marked with the suffix b.

transitional horizon.text: A horizon combining the properties of two master horizons, written with both capital letters, the dominant one first, as in AB or BA.

fragipan.text: A diagnostic horizon of USDA soil taxonomy: an altered, dense subsurface layer that restricts water flow and root penetration.

commercial topsoil.text: Soil mixtures sold as topsoil, either natural topsoil mined and conditioned for use or manufactured from minerals, biosolids, compost or paper mill sludge.

ice wedge.text: A crack in the ground holding a narrow wedge of ice up to 3–4 metres long at the surface and reaching several metres down.

horizon boundaries.text: The lower border of a soil horizon, described in the field by how sharp it is (distinctness) and how its shape varies sideways (topography).

duripan.text: A diagnostic horizon of USDA soil taxonomy in which illuvial silica has cemented the subsoil into a hardpan.

petrocalcic horizon.text: A diagnostic horizon of USDA soil taxonomy and the WRB in which secondary carbonates have cemented the subsoil into a hardpan.

claypan.text: A dense, compact, slowly permeable subsoil layer with much more clay than the material above, from which a sharp boundary separates it.

silcrete.text: A hard soil duricrust formed when surface soil, sand and gravel are cemented by dissolved silica.

umbric horizon.text: A thick, dark, organic-rich surface horizon that is acid and low in bases; its name comes from Latin umbra, shade.

ferricrete.text: A hard, erosion-resistant layer of sedimentary rock, usually conglomerate or breccia, cemented into a duricrust by iron oxides.

cutans.text: Changes in soil texture or structure at natural surfaces of particles, pores or peds, caused by illuviation.

pedocal.text: A former class of the zonal soil order: soils of semiarid and arid regions rich in calcium carbonate and low in organic matter.

slickensides in soils.text: In pedology, the polished surfaces of cracks that form in soils with a high proportion of swelling clays.

cambic horizon.text: A diagnostic subsurface horizon showing early pedogenic change, recognized when it does not meet the requirements of any other diagnostic horizon.

tepetate.text: A Mexican term, from Nahuatl tepetlatl, for a horizon hardened by compaction or cementation in volcanic regions of Mexico.

albic horizon.text: A bleached, light-coloured subsurface diagnostic horizon left when soil formation moves clay minerals and oxides downward.

calcic horizon.text: A horizon of secondary carbonate accumulation, above 15% calcium carbonate equivalent and at least 5% more carbonate than the layer below.

epipedon.text: In USDA soil taxonomy, a diagnostic surface horizon, the upper part of the soil.

kandic horizon.text: An argillic horizon whose clays are mainly 1:1 silicate clays, giving it a low cation exchange capacity.

mollic epipedon.text: The fertile, dark surface horizon that is the defining diagnostic feature of Mollisols.

natric horizon.text: An argillic horizon in which large amounts of exchangeable sodium have accumulated.

pedon.text: The imaginary three-dimensional unit of soil large enough to show the full range of properties of a particular soil; a soil profile is one face of it.

soil monolith.text: A soil profile dug from the ground in one piece, without disturbing its layers, and preserved for study or display.

spodic horizon.text: An iron-rich diagnostic subsurface horizon of podzols, where iron and aluminium oxides accumulate with humus.

soil formation.text: The development of soil, also called pedogenesis, as shaped by the effects of place, environment and history.

leaching (pedology).text: The removal of soluble materials from one zone of a soil to another by water moving through the profile.

soil-forming factors.text: The five classic, intertwined influences that govern how a soil develops: parent material, climate, topography, organisms and time.

paleosol.text: An ancient soil that formed in the past.

climate as a soil-forming factor.text: The influence of climate on soil formation, chiefly through effective precipitation (precipitation minus evapotranspiration) and temperature, which set the rates of chemical, physical and biological processes.

organisms as a soil-forming factor.text: The influence of plants, animals, fungi, bacteria and humans on how a soil forms.

time as a soil-forming factor.text: The span over which the other soil-forming factors interact, which shapes how far a soil has developed.

topography as a soil-forming factor.text: The influence of relief (slope, elevation and aspect) on soil formation through its control of runoff, erosion and the formation of the surface profile.

dokuchaev's soil-forming equation.text: Vasily Dokuchaev's 1898 equation expressing soil as a function of climate, organisms and parent material over relative time.

jenny's state equation.text: Hans Jenny's 1941 equation treating soil formation as a function of climate, organisms, relief, parent material, time and further open-ended factors: S = f(cl, o, r, p, t, ...).

catena.text: A series of distinct but co-evolving soils arrayed down a slope, all in the same climate and on the same parent material.

pedoturbation.text: The mixing of material between soil horizons, an important factor in soil formation.

leaching model.text: A hydrological model of how irrigation water leaches dissolved substances, notably salt, from soil, depending on the water regime and the soil's properties.

soil biomantle.text: The organic-rich, bioturbated upper part of a soil, including the topsoil, where most soil organisms live, reproduce and die.

chronosequence.text: A set of sites that share similar attributes but differ in age, used to study change over time.

laterite.text: A soil type rich in iron and aluminium that often forms in hot, wet areas, mostly in the tropics.

sesquioxide.text: An oxide with two atoms of an element for every three of oxygen, such as the iron and aluminium oxides Fe2O3 and Al2O3.

podzolisation.text: An extreme form of leaching that eluviates iron and aluminium sesquioxides from the upper soil.

laterization.text: The prolonged chemical weathering of rock under tropical conditions that produces laterite.

stonelayer.text: A subsurface soil layer dominated by particles coarser than 2 mm that generally mimics the surface topography; also called a stone line.

biorhexistasy.text: A theory of the climatic conditions under which periods of soil formation alternate with periods of soil erosion.

paleoatmosphere reconstruction from pale.text: The use of paleosol chemistry to infer the past composition of the atmosphere, with which soils form in near-constant contact.

paleoclimate reconstruction from paleoso.text: The use of paleosols to gauge the climate they formed in, since rates and styles of weathering depend on climate.

paleosol classification.text: The naming of paleosols, which mostly borrows the orders of USDA soil taxonomy because modern systems fit ancient soils poorly.

paleosol identification.text: The recognition of a fossil or buried soil from criteria such as formation in place on bedrock and up-profile changes consistent with weathering.

pedodiversity.text: The variation of soil properties within an area, usually expressed through soil classes.

soil production function.text: The rate at which bedrock weathers into soil, expressed as a function of soil thickness.

laterite aquifers.text: Thick, porous and slightly permeable laterite layers that hold and yield groundwater, especially in rural tropical areas.

laterite building blocks.text: Laterite cut into blocks while moist and soft, which then harden on exposure to air into a durable building material.

laterite for phosphorus removal.text: The use of iron- and aluminium-rich laterite to remove phosphorus and heavy metals from wastewater.

laterite soils in farming.text: The agricultural behaviour of laterite soils, which are clay-rich but heavily leached.

lateritic ores.text: Metal ores concentrated in laterites, including aluminium, iron, manganese, nickel, copper and gold.

periglaciation.text: The geomorphic processes that result from seasonal freezing and thawing, very often in areas of permafrost.

lessivage.text: The washing of fine clay from the upper to the lower part of a soil by water moving down through the soil matrix; also called argilluviation.

ferrallitisation.text: The process by which rock is changed into a soil of kaolinite clay and sesquioxides, the hydrated oxides of iron and aluminium.

ecological succession.text: The change in species composition of an ecological community over time.

leaching efficiency.text: A leaching-model parameter that departs from unity where salt is unevenly distributed in the soil or the soil structure is irregular.

tree throw.text: A bowl-shaped pit in the subsoil made by a tree, through long root growth or when a toppled tree tears out its rootwad.

argillipedoturbation.text: Soil mixing caused by the shrinking and swelling of smectite clays, sometimes called self-mulching.

stone-line origin debate.text: The long controversy over whether stonelayers in soils formed by geological processes or by soil-forming, largely biological, processes.

biomantles and archaeology.text: The finding that most prehistoric cultural materials lie in the soil biomantle, where bioturbation has moved them out of their original context.

biomixing, biotransfer and biosorting.text: The three overlapping sub-processes of soil bioturbation, which together abrade and reduce particles (particle comminution).

dynamic denudation.text: The sum of all processes acting in the soil biomantle, in which bioturbation and other organic effects are commonly dominant.

soil age and profile development.text: How a soil's horizons, chemistry and productivity change as it ages from parent material to old soil.

soil-forming processes.text: The soil-forming factors work through four groups of processes: additions, losses, transformations and translocations.

cheluviation.text: The process in which metal ions in the upper soil bind with organic ligands into chelates that move downward by eluviation and are then deposited.

soil memory.text: The idea that soil keeps a record of past natural changes, environmental conditions and human activity.

slope, texture and runoff rate.text: A field method that estimates surface runoff from percent slope and the texture of the surface horizon.

hillslope positions.text: The named positions along a hillslope, from summit to toeslope, each with its own shape and role in moving soil material.

effective precipitation and leaching.text: Precipitation and temperature together decide how much water moves down through a soil and how strongly it is leached.

human activity as a soil-forming factor.term: Human activity as a soil-forming factor
human activity as a soil-forming factor.text: Human use transforms soils, mainly through land conversion, erosion, mining and construction.

microbial soil memory.text: The ability of soil microbial communities to change their structure, diversity and activity in response to natural or human factors and to keep those changes over time.

polygenetic soil.text: A soil, such as a paleosol, that shows evidence of continued soil development under later conditions.

soil geography.text: The branch of physical geography that deals with how soils are distributed across the terrain.

tropical soils.text: The soils of the humid tropics, most of them strongly leached and poor in nutrients, though some areas are fertile.

soils of british columbia and yukon.term: Soils of British Columbia and Yukon
soils of british columbia and yukon.text: British Columbia and Yukon have the greatest diversity of soils in Canada, from a varied geologic history, rugged mountain and valley terrain and wide climate range.

soils of ontario.text: Ontario soils formed mostly in parent materials left by the Wisconsinan Laurentide Ice Sheet, and their distribution follows three ecozones with different dominant soil-forming factors.

soils of quebec.text: Quebec has seven soil orders arranged in a zonal pattern from south to north, set by climate, vegetation, time since glaciation and parent material.

soils of the atlantic provinces.text: Seven of Canada's ten soil orders occur in Atlantic Canada, but heavy precipitation and coarse, acidic glacial till make Podzols the dominant soil.

soils of the prairie provinces.text: The soils of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba are the most heavily converted to farmland in Canada, with the soil pattern set by bedrock geology and the rain shadow of the Western Cordillera.

parkland and forest soil transition.text: Moving north from the grassland, soils change through the transitional Parkland zone to continuous Mixedwood forest, as tree litter replaces grass as the main organic input.

grain size.text: The diameter of individual grains of sediment, or of the lithified particles in clastic rocks.

prairie chernozem zonation.text: Chernozemic great groups across the Prairies follow the zonation of native grasses, which in turn follows the regional water deficit.

lithosequence.text: A set of soils formed under similar conditions on different parent materials, so that their profiles differ because of the parent material.

soils of australia.text: The soils of the Australian continent, many of them extremely ancient and naturally deficient in phosphorus.

sand.text: A granular material of finely divided mineral particles, defined mainly by grain size: coarser than silt and finer than gravel.

silt.text: A granular material finer than sand and coarser than clay, made mostly of broken quartz grains.

soil separates.text: Set ranges of particle size, sand, silt and clay, into which a soil's mineral particles are sorted.

clay size versus clay minerals.text: The difference between clay as a class of very fine particle sizes and clay as material made of clay minerals, two overlapping but distinct definitions.

plasticity of clay.text: Clay's capacity, when wet, to be moulded into a shape that it then keeps, its defining mechanical property.

usda soil texture classes.text: The twelve named categories into which the USDA groups soils by their percentages of sand, silt and clay.

loam.text: Soil made mostly of sand and silt with a smaller amount of clay.

clay soils in agriculture.text: How a high clay content shapes a soil's value for farming, trading poor drainage against greater fertility.

soil texture triangle.text: A triangular chart whose three sides give percent sand, silt and clay, used to read off a soil's texture class.

texture by feel.text: A qualitative field method that judges a soil's texture by moistening and working a small sample by hand.

shrink–swell capacity.text: The degree to which certain clay minerals in a soil expand when wet and contract when dry.

physical properties of soil.text: The measurable physical traits of a soil, which in falling order of importance for crops are texture, structure, bulk density, porosity, consistency, temperature, colour and resistivity.

gravel.text: A loose aggregation of rock fragments coarser than sand.

soil structure.text: The arrangement of a soil's solid particles and of the pore spaces left between them.

ped.text: A natural aggregate of soil particles, formed by soil-forming processes and separated from neighbouring units by pores or voids.

soil structure types.text: The grouping of soil structure by the shape and arrangement of its peds, with five major classes: platy, prismatic, columnar, blocky and granular.

particle-size distribution.text: A list of values or a mathematical function giving the relative amount, usually by mass, of particles of each size in a granular material.

sieve analysis.text: A procedure that measures the particle size distribution of a granular material by passing it through a stack of progressively finer sieves and weighing what each sieve holds.

hydrometer method.text: A laboratory sedimentation test that estimates a soil's percent sand, silt and clay from how fast dispersed particles settle, based on Stokes' law.

expansive clay.text: A clay soil that swells and shrinks greatly as its water content changes.

international soil texture system.text: The first soil particle-size classification, proposed by Albert Atterberg in 1905 from his studies in southern Sweden.

soil aggregation.text: The joining of primary soil particles into larger aggregates through rearrangement, flocculation and cementation.

soil aggregate stability.text: A measure of how well soil aggregates resist breaking apart under forces such as water and wind erosion, shrinking and swelling, and tillage.

x-ray sedimentation.text: A hybrid particle-sizing technique that combines sedimentation with X-ray absorption.

soil gradation.text: An engineering classification of a coarse-grained soil according to the range of particle sizes it contains.

tilth.text: The physical condition of a soil, especially how well it suits planting and growing a crop.

soil dispersion.text: The breakdown of soil, especially sodium-rich clay, into separate fine particles that water easily washes away.

soil crust.text: A surface layer of soil, often hardened and platy, that differs from the bulk soil beneath it.

improving soil structure.text: Practices that move soil toward a granular, crumb structure by raising its porosity, organic matter and microbial and faunal activity.

stokes's law.text: A law giving the drag force on a sphere moving through a viscous fluid at very small Reynolds numbers.

soil consistency.text: The ability of soil to stick to itself or to other objects and to resist deformation and rupture.

hardsetting soil.text: A soil that loses its structure when wet and sets hard into a structureless mass as it dries.

hydrophobic soil.text: A soil whose particles repel water.
