thermal desorption.text: A remediation technology that heats contaminated soil or other solids so that contaminants volatilize and can be separated, then collected or destroyed.

soil reclamation.text: The part of land reclamation that rebuilds soil on a disturbed site, usually after infrastructure removal, recontouring and contaminant cleanup and before revegetation.

light non-aqueous phase liquid.text: A hydrocarbon groundwater contaminant that does not dissolve in water and is less dense than it, so it forms a separate floating phase.

biosorption.text: A passive physicochemical process by which certain biomass concentrates and binds contaminants such as heavy metals onto its cell structure.

remediation of metal-contaminated soil.text: The cleanup of soils contaminated by heavy metals through isolation, immobilization, toxicity reduction, physical separation or extraction.

pesticide leaching.text: The movement of dissolved pesticides through the soil to sites beyond their target, a major source of groundwater pollution.

soil amendments in reclamation.text: Materials added to a reclamation soil to correct chemical, physical or biological properties that do not meet the end land use.

cadmium poisoning.text: Poisoning by cadmium, a naturally occurring toxic metal met in industry, in plant soils and in tobacco smoke.

bioslurping.text: A technique combining bioventing with vacuum pumping of floating free product (LNAPL) to recover it from groundwater and soil and bioremediate the soil.

dual-phase vacuum extraction.text: A high-vacuum technology, also called multi-phase extraction, that removes both contaminated groundwater and soil vapor through one well.

rhizofiltration.text: Phytoremediation that filters contaminated groundwater, surface water or wastewater through a mass of roots to remove toxic substances or excess nutrients.

pneumatic fracturing.text: A remediation method that injects gas into contaminated ground at a pressure above that of the gases already there, cracking the subsurface.

total petroleum hydrocarbon.text: A measure of the total amount of the mixture of hydrocarbons found in crude oil present at a site.

electrical resistance heating.text: An intensive in situ remediation method that passes alternating current through soil and groundwater between buried electrodes, heating them until contaminants evaporate.

microbial biodegradation.text: The harnessing of microbes' natural ability to degrade, transform or accumulate pollutants such as oil, PCBs, PAHs, pharmaceuticals, radionuclides and metals.

ecotoxicity testing.text: Standardized acute and chronic toxicity tests on terrestrial and aquatic organisms, including earthworms, used to rate a chemical's ecological hazard.

pesticide transformation products.text: The compounds a pesticide breaks down into, which may keep or even exceed the parent's harmful activity.

hydrocarbon biodegradation in soil.text: The breakdown of petroleum hydrocarbons by native soil microbes that use them for energy and carbon.

raymond process.text: An accelerated in situ bioremediation method, developed by Richard Raymond, that adds nutrients and electron acceptors to contaminated groundwater.

organic and inorganic soil contaminants.text: Soil contaminants are grouped as organic (pesticides, solvents, industrial products) and inorganic (metals, salts, nutrients, radionuclides).

remediation strategy selection.text: Choosing a remediation method depends on the contaminant, the site and soil properties.

soil vitrification.text: Heating soil to 1400 to 2000 °C so its silica melts into stable glass and crystalline solids.

soil washing.text: An ex situ treatment that may separate silt and clay fines from coarse material to cut the soil mass needing treatment.

bioremediation of pcbs.text: The use of microorganisms, working in sequence, to degrade polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) at contaminated sites.

geochemical background.text: The natural levels of elements and other substances in soil, water and air, set by processes such as weathering, against which contamination is judged.

contaminants of emerging concern.text: Pollutants found in environmental monitoring that may harm ecosystems or health and are usually not yet regulated.

bioremediation of radioactive waste.text: The use of bacteria, plants and fungi to catalyze reactions that decontaminate soil, water and sediment affected by radionuclides.

bioreduction of radionuclides.text: The enzymatic reduction of radionuclides by bacteria to lower oxidation states, changing their solubility, mobility and radiotoxicity.

phytoextraction of radionuclides.text: The removal of radionuclides from soil by plants that carry them from the roots into their shoots.

sustainable remediation.text: An approach to cleaning up contaminated land that weighs a remedy's environmental, economic and social effects and seeks to minimize the footprint of the cleanup itself.

vapor intrusion.text: The migration of volatile chemicals, usually VOCs, from contaminated soil or groundwater into the indoor air of buildings above or nearby.

medical geology.text: The interdisciplinary science of how natural geological factors affect the health of people and animals.

geophagia.text: The deliberate eating of earth or earth-like substances such as clay, chalk or termite-mound soil, by animals and people.

itai-itai disease.text: The mass cadmium poisoning in Toyama Prefecture, Japan, from about 1912, named for the severe spine and joint pain it caused.

coccidioidomycosis.text: Valley fever: a fungal disease of mammals caused by inhaling spores of the soil fungi Coccidioides immitis or C. posadasii.

iodine deficiency.text: A lack of the essential dietary trace element iodine, which the thyroid hormones need.

selenium deficiency.text: A shortage of selenium, a critical nutrient, below the levels an organism requires.

melioidosis.text: An infectious disease caused by the soil-dwelling bacterium Burkholderia pseudomallei, caught by contact with contaminated soil or water.

soil-transmitted helminthiasis.text: Infection with roundworms spread through soil contaminated with human faeces: ascariasis, hookworm and whipworm.

prion.text: A misfolded protein that makes normal copies of the same protein misfold, causing fatal, transmissible neurodegenerative diseases.

podoconiosis.text: A disease of the lymphatic vessels of the lower legs, also called nonfilarial elephantiasis, caused by long-term barefoot contact with irritant soils.

keshan disease.text: A congestive cardiomyopathy caused by dietary selenium deficiency together with a mutated strain of Coxsackievirus, named after Keshan County in China.

one health.text: An integrated approach that seeks to balance and optimize the health of people, animals, plants and ecosystems together.

avian geophagy.text: The eating of clay-rich soil by birds, notably South American parrots at clay licks.

soil ingestion by livestock.text: The swallowing of soil by grazing animals such as cattle and sheep, pressed onto pasture plants by their hooves.

chronic wasting disease.text: A fatal transmissible spongiform encephalopathy caused by prions that naturally affects deer, elk, moose and their relatives.

mycobacterium vaccae.text: A nonpathogenic bacterium of the Mycobacteriaceae that lives naturally in soil.

jinzū river soil restoration.text: The cleanup of cadmium-polluted farmland along Japan's Jinzū River after the itai-itai disease lawsuit.

biofortification.text: Breeding crops, conventionally or by genetic engineering, so that they contain more nutrients as they grow.

hygiene hypothesis.text: The idea that early-childhood exposure to certain microorganisms protects against allergies by properly tuning the immune system.

photosynthesis.text: The biological process by which plants, algae and cyanobacteria convert light energy into chemical energy stored in organic compounds.

geochronology.text: The science of finding the age of rocks, fossils and sediments from signatures held in the materials themselves.

radiocarbon dating.text: A method of finding the age of material containing organic carbon from how much of its radioactive carbon-14 is left.

palynology.text: The study of acid-resistant microscopic organic remains, such as pollen and spores, found in sediments and sedimentary rocks.

luminescence dating.text: A group of methods that find how long ago mineral grains were last exposed to sunlight or strong heating.

cosmogenic nuclide.text: A rare isotope created when a high-energy cosmic ray strikes an atom's nucleus in the Solar System and knocks out protons and neutrons.

evolution of photosynthesis.text: Photosynthesis began early in Earth's history, probably as anoxygenic forms using hydrogen or sulfur rather than water.

factors limiting photosynthesis.text: Photosynthesis is limited by light, leaf area for capturing light, CO2 supply to chloroplasts, water and temperature.

light-dependent reactions.text: The first stage of photosynthesis, in which chlorophyll absorbs light, electrons flow down a transport chain, and ATP and NADPH are made.

δ13c.text: A normalized ratio of the stable carbon isotopes carbon-13 and carbon-12, reported in parts per thousand (per mille, ‰).

calvin cycle.text: The light-independent stage of photosynthesis, in which RuBisCO captures CO2 and uses NADPH to make three-carbon sugars.

photorespiration.text: When CO2 is low, RuBisCO binds oxygen instead, a wasteful process that uses energy and makes no sugar.

c4 and cam photosynthesis.text: Some plants raise CO2 concentration at RuBisCO using PEP carboxylase, in C4 plants by separating steps in space and in CAM plants by separating them in time.

optically stimulated luminescence.text: A method of measuring the radiation dose a mineral has absorbed from the light it emits when stimulated, used to date sediments.

tephrochronology.text: Dating and correlating sequences and events by their position between layers of volcanic ash (tephra) of known date.

thermoluminescence dating.text: Dating by the accumulated radiation dose of the time since crystalline material was last heated, as in lava or ceramics, or exposed to sunlight, as in sediments.

radiocarbon calibration.text: The use of a calibration curve of past atmospheric carbon-14 to convert a sample's radiocarbon measurement into an estimated calendar age.

radiocarbon dating of soil and peat.term: Radiocarbon dating of soil and peat
radiocarbon dating of soil and peat.text: Radiocarbon dating of the organic matter in soils and peat, which is hard to do reliably because younger humic acid tends to contaminate it.

surface exposure dating.text: A set of techniques for estimating how long a rock has been exposed at or near Earth's surface.

beryllium-10 as a soil tracer.text: The use of beryllium-10, a cosmogenic isotope with a half-life of 1.387 million years formed in the atmosphere, to trace soil formation and erosion.

bomb pulse.text: The sudden rise of carbon-14 in Earth's atmosphere caused by above-ground nuclear tests from 1945 until the 1963 Limited Test Ban Treaty.

lead-210 dating.text: The use of lead-210, a radioactive isotope in the uranium-238 decay chain with a half-life of 22.20 years, to date recent sediments and trace soil movement.

rhizolith.text: An organosedimentary structure formed by plant roots in soils or fossil soils (paleosols).

marine isotope stages.text: Alternating warm and cool periods of Earth's climate deduced from oxygen isotope data in deep-sea cores.

clumped isotopes.text: Clumped isotopes are heavy isotopes bonded to other heavy isotopes within a molecule such as carbonate; their abundance depends on temperature.

silurian-devonian terrestrial revolution.text: The rapid spread and diversification of land plants and fungi between 428 and 359 million years ago, in the Silurian and Devonian periods.

geoarchaeology.text: A multidisciplinary field that applies the theories and techniques of the geosciences to archaeology.

taphonomy.text: The study of how organisms decay and become fossilized or preserved.

environmental dna.text: DNA collected from environmental samples such as soil, sediment, water, snow or air rather than from an individual organism.

soil mark.text: A difference in soil colour caused by archaeological features beneath it.

midden.text: An old dump for domestic waste.

stratigraphy (archaeology).text: The study of a site's sequence of superimposed units, or contexts, to learn when and how its deposits formed.

forensic geology.text: The study of earth materials as evidence to answer questions raised by the legal system.

forensic soil comparison.text: The comparison of a questioned soil sample of unknown origin with control samples, such as soil from the crime scene, to find similarities or differences.

law of superposition.text: The principle that in undeformed layered sequences the oldest layers lie at the bottom and newer material stacks on top.

celtic field.text: An old name for traces of prehistoric field systems in north-west Europe.

ridge and furrow.text: A pattern of ridges and troughs left by a ploughing system used in medieval Europe, typical of the open-field system.

forensic palynology.text: The use of pollen, spores and other palynomorphs to prove or disprove a link between objects, people and places in criminal and civil cases.

forensic archaeology.text: The branch of forensic anthropology that uses archaeological methods in legal cases, such as finding overlooked graves and processing mass graves.

geotaphonomy.text: The study of how a decomposing body and its burial affect the surrounding environment.

magnetic susceptibility analysis.text: Measurement of how readily a material becomes magnetised in an external magnetic field, used on soils and sediments.

geophysical survey (archaeology).text: Ground-based physical sensing techniques used to image or map buried archaeological features.

soil phosphate survey.text: Measuring and mapping phosphate in soil, which comes from people, their animals, rubbish and bones, to find former activity areas and sites.

cropmark.text: A pattern in growing crops, visible from the air or high ground, that reveals buried archaeological, natural or recent features.

raised field.text: A large cultivated mound, usually bounded by water-filled ditches, used to control moisture, frost damage and flooding.

history of soil science.text: How ideas about soil developed, starting from concepts built on Justus von Liebig's chemistry and refined by agricultural scientists in laboratories, greenhouses and small field plots.

the formation of vegetable mould through.term: The Formation of Vegetable Mould Through the Action of Worms
the formation of vegetable mould through.text: Charles Darwin's 1881 book on earthworms, their habits and their part in forming and moving the soil.

world congress of soil science.text: The International Union of Soil Sciences' conference, held every four years apart from a break for World War II.

world soil museum.text: A museum in Wageningen, the Netherlands, that displays soil profile monoliths representing the world's major soil types.

international year of soils.text: The year 2015, declared by the United Nations General Assembly on 20 December 2013 to raise worldwide awareness of soils.

development of soil taxonomy.text: The move from the qualitative soil classifications of Marbut and of 1938 to the quantitative Soil Taxonomy built under Guy D. Smith.

russian school of soil science.text: The school led by V. V. Dokuchaev and N. M. Sibirtsev from 1870, which treated soils as independent natural bodies with their own properties.

agricultural chemistry.text: The chemistry, especially organic chemistry and biochemistry, of agriculture.

australian society of soil science incor.term: Australian Society of Soil Science Incorporated
australian society of soil science incor.text: Australia's not-for-profit professional association for soil scientists and others concerned with managing the country's soils, publicly known as Soil Science Australia.

soil and water conservation society.text: A professional and scientific membership society that fosters the science and art of managing natural resources sustainably.

marbut's soil profile concept.text: The American adaptation of the Russian soil concept, led by C. F. Marbut, which put the individual soil profile ahead of external soil features and surface geology.

park grass experiment.text: A long-term field study at Rothamsted set up to test how fertilizers and manures affect hay yields.

german soil science society.text: Germany's non-profit society of soil science experts and others interested in the field, the Deutsche Bodenkundliche Gesellschaft (DBG).

burial of objects by earthworms.text: The slow sinking of surface objects, from stones to Roman ruins, as earthworms bring up earth from below and leave it as castings.

on the formation of mould.text: Darwin's 1837 paper to the Geological Society of London on the role of earthworms in forming soil.

world soil day.text: An annual day, 5 December, that celebrates the importance of soil in people's lives.

v.v. dokuchaev central museum of soil.term: V.V. Dokuchaev Central Museum of Soil
v.v. dokuchaev central museum of soil.text: A soil museum in Saint Petersburg, founded in 1902 by Vasily Dokuchaev.

opal soil centre.text: One of five centres of expertise of the Open Air Laboratories Network, based at the Centre for Environmental Policy, Imperial College London.

long-term agricultural experiments.text: Field experiments run for decades, some for more than 100 years, to test the sustainability of farming practices from yield trends.

central soil salinity research institute.text: An autonomous Indian institute under the Indian Council of Agricultural Research for research on salt-affected soils.

indian institute of soil science.text: An autonomous Indian research institute under the Indian Council of Agricultural Research, set up for advanced research in soil science.

history of bioturbation research.text: The study of how burrowing and mixing by living things shapes soil, from Darwin's earthworm work to its re-evaluation by soil geomorphologists from the 1980s.

modern study of soil formation.text: The shift, from about 1940, to treating soil formation as many interrelated physical, chemical and biological processes open to quantitative study.

soil surveys for nonfarm uses.text: The broadening of soil survey after 1950 from farming, ranching and forestry to information on how soils affect nonfarm uses.

broadbalk experiment.text: A long-running field experiment at Rothamsted Research, sown with winter wheat every year since 1843.

humus theory.text: The once-prevalent view that decayed plant matter, humus, was plants' main source of carbon.

soil map of the world.text: The world soil map published by FAO and UNESCO from 1971 to 1981 in 10 volumes at a scale of 1:5 million.

virgin lands campaign.text: Nikita Khrushchev's 1953 plan to boost Soviet farm output by ploughing new land in southern Western Siberia and northern Kazakhstan.

vasily dokuchaev.text: Russian geologist and geographer (1846–1903) credited with laying the foundations of soil science.

justus von liebig.text: German chemist (1803–1873), a principal founder of organic chemistry, who made major contributions to agricultural and biological chemistry.

hans jenny (pedologist).text: Swiss-born soil scientist (1899–1992) and expert in pedology, above all in the processes of soil formation.

sergei winogradsky.text: Ukrainian and Russian microbiologist, ecologist and soil scientist (1856–1953) who pioneered the cycle-of-life concept.

martinus beijerinck.text: Dutch microbiologist and botanist (1851–1931), one of the founders of virology and environmental microbiology.

friedrich albert fallou.text: German lawyer and land tax assessor (1794–1877) considered one of the founders of modern soil science.

konstantin glinka.text: Russian soil scientist (1867–1927), a student of Dokuchaev who carried the Russian school's ideas to the wider world.

eugene w. hilgard.text: German-American expert on pedology (1833–1916), considered the father of modern soil science in the United States.

curtis f. marbut.text: American soil scientist (1863–1935) who directed the Soil Survey Division of the US Department of Agriculture from 1913 until his death.

lorenzo a. richards.text: American soil physicist (1904–1993), one of the most influential figures in 20th-century soil physics.

mineral theory of plant nutrition.text: The theory, synthesized and promoted by Liebig, that plants draw essential nutrients as inorganic minerals from the soil, and carbon and hydrogen from air and water.

john bennet lawes.text: English entrepreneur and agricultural scientist (1814–1900) who founded the experimental farm that became Rothamsted Research.

guy d. smith.text: American soil scientist (1907–1981) who originally developed the USDA soil classification system, Soil Taxonomy.

rattan lal.text: Indian-American soil scientist (born 1944), a pioneer of soil-centred farm management for food security and climate-resilient agriculture.

hugh hammond bennett.text: Pioneer of soil conservation in the United States (1881–1960) and head of the federal soil erosion agency now called the Natural Resources Conservation Service.

jean-baptiste boussingault.text: French chemist (1801–1887) who made major contributions to agricultural science.

franklin hiram king.text: American agricultural scientist (1848–1911) who has been called the father of soil physics in the United States.

edmund ruffin.text: American planter, politician and scientist (1794–1865), known for pioneering methods to preserve and improve soil productivity.

edgar buckingham.text: American physicist (1867–1940) who worked as a soil physicist at the USDA Bureau of Soils from 1902 to 1906.

carl sprengel.text: German botanist and agricultural scientist (1787–1859) who first stated the law of the minimum.

liebig's nitrogen debate.text: The long dispute over Liebig's claim that plants feed on nitrogen compounds from the air, and over whether crops need nitrogen fertilizer.

selman waksman.text: Russian-born American biochemist and microbiologist (1888–1973) whose research on the decomposition of soil organisms enabled the discovery of streptomycin and other antibiotics.

joseph henry gilbert.text: English chemist (1817–1901) who spent a long career improving the methods of practical agriculture.

konstantin gedroits.text: Russian soil scientist (1872–1932) of Lithuanian origin, founder of colloidal soil chemistry in Russia.

discovery of chemosynthesis.text: Winogradsky's discovery of chemoautotrophy, popularly called chemosynthesis: organisms drawing energy from inorganic compounds and carbon from carbon dioxide.

peter erasmus müller (forester).text: Danish forester and naturalist (1840–1926) whose studies of forest soils laid early foundations for the study of humus forms.

charles darwin.text: English naturalist, geologist and biologist (1809–1882), best known for his contributions to evolutionary biology.

nicolas-théodore de saussure.text: Swiss chemist and plant physiologist (1767–1845), a major pioneer in the study of photosynthesis.

albrecht thaer.text: German agronomist (1752–1828) and supporter of the humus theory of plant nutrition.

heath.text: A shrubland habitat found mainly on free-draining, infertile, acidic soils, with open, low-growing woody vegetation.

albert bernhard frank.text: German botanist, plant pathologist and mycologist (1839–1900) who coined the term mycorrhiza.

albert atterberg.text: Swedish chemist and agricultural scientist (1846–1916) who created the Atterberg limits still used by geotechnical engineers.

lorenz hiltner.text: German agronomist and microbiologist (1862–1923) who developed the concept of the rhizosphere and helped found microbial ecology.

francis d. hole.text: American pedologist, educator and musician (1913–2002), known for mapping Wisconsin's soils and for popularizing soil science.

cyril g. hopkins.text: American agricultural chemist (1866–1919) at the University of Illinois, noted for his research and writing on Illinois soils.

roy w. simonson.text: American soil scientist (1908–2008) who studied soils across the United States and on islands of the Western Pacific.

thomas lyttleton lyon.text: American soil scientist (1869–1938) who wrote on the nitrogen cycle.

enrichment culture.text: A fundamental method of culturing microbes taken from the environment so that they can be studied.

farmers of forty centuries.text: Franklin Hiram King's book on the long-sustained traditional farming of China, Korea and Japan, now regarded as a classic of organic farming.

milton whitney.text: The first chief of the US Division of Agricultural Soil, forerunner of the federal soil survey.

nikolai sibirtsev.text: Russian soil scientist (1860–1900) who led the Russian school of soil science with Dokuchaev.

russian chernozem.text: Vasily Dokuchaev's 1883 book, his most famous work, a complete study of the chernozem soils of European Russia.

soil science society of america.text: The largest soil-specific scientific society in the United States, formed in 1936.

natural resources conservation service.text: An agency of the United States Department of Agriculture, formerly the Soil Conservation Service, that gives technical help to farmers and other private landowners and managers.

rothamsted research.text: One of the oldest agricultural research institutions in the world, founded in 1843 at Harpenden, England, and formerly the Rothamsted Experimental Station.

national cooperative soil survey.text: A nationwide US partnership of federal, regional, state and local agencies and institutions that investigates, inventories, classifies and interprets the nation's soils and publishes the results.

international union of soil sciences.text: The international scientific union of soil scientists, founded in 1924 as the International Society of Soil Science and a member of the International Science Council.

international soil reference and informa.term: International Soil Reference and Information Centre
international soil reference and informa.text: ISRIC, an independent, science-based foundation that provides quality-assessed soil information to address global environmental and societal challenges.

pochvovedenie.text: A Russian journal of soil science, published in English translation as Eurasian Soil Science.

soil science society of poland.text: The scientific and professional society of Polish soil scientists (Polskie Towarzystwo Gleboznawcze).

early united states soil survey.text: The beginnings of systematic soil survey in the United States, from the first field mapping in 1899 to the consolidation of all USDA survey work in 1952.

international humic substances society.text: A scientific society devoted to research on natural organic matter in soil and water.

soil science society of america journal.term: Soil Science Society of America Journal
soil science society of america journal.text: A bimonthly peer-reviewed journal publishing research on all aspects of soil science.

journal of soil and water conservation.term: Journal of Soil and Water Conservation
journal of soil and water conservation.text: A bimonthly peer-reviewed journal of conservation science, practice and policy.

international committee on anthropogenic.text: ICOMANTH, a committee active from 1995 to 2013 that worked on classifying soils derived from human activity.

european soil bureau network.text: A network of national soil science institutions, created in 1996 at the European Commission's Joint Research Centre in Ispra, that collects and harmonises soil information for Europe.

national society of consulting soil scie.term: National Society of Consulting Soil Scientists
national society of consulting soil scie.text: A North American professional society of soil scientists, mainly environmental consultants, merged into the Soil Science Society of America in August 2011.

lunar regolith.text: The unconsolidated material covering the surface of the Moon, whose finer fraction is called lunar soil.

martian regolith.text: The fine blanket of loose, varied surface deposits covering Mars, whose finer fraction is called Martian soil.

lunar regolith simulant.text: An Earth material made to approximate the chemical, mechanical, engineering, mineralogical or particle-size properties of lunar regolith.

space weathering.text: The weathering of any object exposed to the harsh environment of outer space.

astropedology.text: The study of very ancient paleosols and meteorites relevant to the origin of life, and of soil systems on other planets.

perchlorates in martian soil.text: The chlorine-bearing perchlorate salts whose relatively high concentrations make Martian regolith toxic.

lunar dust hazards.text: The harm that fine, easily disturbed lunar dust can do to equipment and to the health of crews.

lunar sample return.text: The bringing of lunar rock and regolith back to Earth by space missions, beginning with Apollo.

lunar soil formation.text: The making and continual alteration of lunar regolith by impacts and space radiation, known as space weathering.

in situ resource utilization.text: The collection, processing and use of materials found on other bodies, such as the Moon or Mars, in place of materials brought from Earth.

extraterrestrial soil definition.text: The unsettled question of what counts as soil on other planetary bodies, where the usual Earth definition, which includes organic content, may not fit.

martian dust.text: The finest fraction of Martian regolith, under 30 micrometres across, much of it carried into the atmosphere.

lunarcrete.text: A proposed concrete-like building material made from lunar regolith to cut the cost of building on the Moon.

martian regolith simulant.text: An Earth material used to mimic the chemical and mechanical properties of Martian regolith for research and prototype testing.

impact gardening.text: The stirring of the outer crust of airless moons and other bodies by impacts, called lunar gardening on the Moon.

archean paleosols.text: Soils preserved from early Earth's Archean eon, which give circumstantial evidence of life in soils 3.42 to 3.46 billion years ago.

growing plants on the moon and mars.term: Growing plants on the Moon and Mars
growing plants on the moon and mars.text: Research into whether lunar and Martian soils, or simulants of them, can support the growth of plants.

martian paleosols.text: Ancient soils on Mars, recognised from rover analyses and orbital remote sensing of the Martian surface.

viking lander biological experiments.text: Four biological experiments carried to the surface of Mars by the two Viking landers in 1976 to look for signs of microbial life.

origin of life in soil.text: The idea that life evolved in soil, where water held between clay grains forms countless microscopic reaction chambers.

mars sample-return mission.text: A proposed mission to collect rock and dust samples on Mars and bring them to Earth.

plants in space.text: The growing of plants in outer space, mostly in pressurized, weightless space gardens in low Earth orbit.

labeled release experiment.text: A Viking life-detection test in which Martian soil was dosed with a dilute nutrient solution tagged with radioactive carbon-14 and the air above monitored for labelled gas.

soil-found-077.q: What are the two main historical branches of soil science, and how do they differ?
soil-found-077.a: Pedology studies soil in its natural setting, while edaphology studies soil in relation to the uses that depend on it.

soil-found-097.q: In a typical soil, how is the volume shared between solids and pores?
soil-found-097.a: About half is solids (45% mineral and 5% organic matter) and half is pores, split equally between water and gas.

soil-found-091.q: Before Fallou and Dokuchaev, how was soil generally seen?
soil-found-091.a: As a product of chemical transformations of rocks: a dead substrate from which plants draw nutrients.

soil-found-096.q: Why do classifications not rest on soil genesis alone?
soil-found-096.a: Soil-forming processes are seldom observed and change over time, so genesis aids classification but cannot be its only basis.

soil-found-089.q: Why do tropical soils turn rusty red instead of showing podzolized layers?
soil-found-089.a: Fast decomposition leaves little fulvic acid to leach metals, so mobile magnesium, iron and aluminium precipitate as oxide minerals.

soil-found-098.q: What did van Helmont conclude from his willow experiment?
soil-found-098.a: Seeing the tree gain more weight than the soil lost, he concluded the willow was made of water, which was only partly correct.

soil-found-052.a: Weathering happens in place, while erosion carries rock and mineral material away by water, ice, wind, waves or gravity.

soil-found-063.q: True or false: rainwater can dissolve quartz.
soil-found-063.a: True: given enough time even quartz dissolves, going into solution as silicic acid.

soil-found-048.q: Which three elements make up most of the dry weight of plant debris, and how much of it?
soil-found-048.a: Carbon, oxygen and hydrogen, which together make up about 92% of the dry weight.

soil-found-056.q: How does pressure release make rock break into sheets?
soil-found-056.a: When erosion strips the rock above, the outer parts of deep-formed rock expand, opening fractures parallel to the surface along which sheets break away.

soil-found-037.q: Why does a quartz-rich rock count as mature?
soil-found-037.a: Quartz is the primary mineral that survives heavy weathering, so its abundance shows long weathering.

soil-found-051.q: Unlike soil structure, can farming change a soil's texture?
soil-found-051.a: No: texture is fixed by the soil's mineral component and does not change with farming.

soil-found-043.q: Why do igneous minerals weather in roughly the order they formed?
soil-found-043.a: Acid hydrolysis breaks the weakest cation–oxygen bonds first, following Bowen's reaction series.

soil-found-038.q: Why is a pH of 3.5 so much more acidic than a pH of 9.5?
soil-found-038.a: The pH scale is logarithmic, so a solution at pH 3.5 has one million times more hydronium ions than one at pH 9.5.

soil-found-024.q: Why does a clay- and humus-rich soil need more lime to change its pH?
soil-found-024.a: Its colloids buffer strongly, and lime must also neutralise the exchangeable acidity they hold, or the stored cations restore the original pH.

soil-found-016.q: What does litmus paper show when dipped in a soil–water mix?
soil-found-016.a: It turns red if the soil is acidic and blue if it is basic.

soil-found-022.q: Why can roots in strongly acidic soil suffer moisture stress even when the soil is fairly moist?
soil-found-022.a: Aluminium toxicity limits root growth so much that the plant cannot take up enough water.

soil-found-026.q: In the Munsell notation 10R 4/8, what do the three parts stand for?
soil-found-026.a: 10R is the hue, 4 the value and 8 the chroma, written as hue, then value/chroma.

soil-form-100.q: How does saprolite differ from saprock?
soil-form-100.a: Saprolite is weathered rock, oxidised in its upper part and partly weathered below, while saprock is fractured bedrock weathered only along its fractures.

soil-form-087.q: Which plant nutrients does rock not supply to soil?
soil-form-087.a: Nitrogen, hydrogen and carbon; rock is the source of every other plant nutrient.

soil-form-113.q: What is the soil of the Loess Plateau known for?
soil-form-113.a: It has been called the most highly erodible soil on Earth.

soil-form-108.q: How does residuum differ from saprolite?
soil-form-108.a: Saprolite keeps its bedrock's structural features, while residuum has lost them, being transformed further and shrunk in volume.

soil-form-095.q: Why do soils formed in lake deposits tend to have low permeability?
soil-form-095.a: Lacustrine material has a high clay content.

soil-form-092.q: How do inflowing rivers sort sediment in a lake?
soil-form-092.a: They drop larger rocks and stones near the lake edge, while suspended sediment settles across the whole lake bed.

soil-form-021.q: How is the depth of topsoil measured, and what horizons does it correspond to?
soil-form-021.a: From the surface to the first densely packed layer, the subsoil; classification systems call it the O or A horizon.

soil-form-017.q: How do hardpans made by people differ in origin from natural ones?
soil-form-017.a: Natural pans form when deposits such as silica, iron oxides or calcium carbonate bind soil particles; man-made ones are compacted by repeated ploughing, heavy traffic or pollution.

soil-form-034.a: Illuviation moves material basically vertically within the soil, while alluviation is the horizontal transfer by running water.

soil-form-024.q: In a horizon label such as 2Bt2, what do the leading and trailing numbers mean?
soil-form-024.a: The prefix 2 marks a lithologic discontinuity, a change in parent material; the suffix 2 marks a subdivision of one horizon.

soil-form-014.q: What does a sequence like O, A1, A2, B2, 2A2, 2B21 reveal about a soil's history?
soil-form-014.a: A fully formed profile was buried by sediments that later formed a new profile; the buried one starts at 2A2.

soil-form-028.q: How can a fragipan be told apart from a duripan?
soil-form-028.a: Air-dry fragipan fragments slake in water, unlike duripans and petrocalcic horizons.

soil-form-020.q: Why do micromorphologists use thin sections rather than a hand lens?
soil-form-020.a: A petrographic polarizing microscope shows far more in thin sections, including the relation of components to one another, often invisible in a hand specimen.

soil-form-030.q: What do the old terms pedocal and pedalfer distinguish?
soil-form-030.a: Marbut split soils into pedocals, with calcite building up as caliche in the B horizon, and pedalfers, rich in aluminium and iron.

soil-form-031.q: What does a cambic horizon become as a soil develops into an Alfisol?
soil-form-031.a: An argillic (Bt) horizon, which holds more clay than the cambic horizon.

soil-form-042.q: Which soil-forming factor is regarded as dominant?
soil-form-042.a: Climate: soils show the distinctive characteristics of the climate zones in which they form.

soil-form-044.q: How do animals that mix soil affect the horizons?
soil-form-044.a: Their mixing, sometimes called pedoturbation, tends to undo the processes that create distinct horizons.

soil-form-049.q: Why are crest soils on a catena drier than toeslope soils?
soil-form-049.a: Crests drain freely, while toeslopes are wetter, poorly drained and richer in clay and organic matter.

soil-form-055.q: What key assumption does a chronosequence make, and why is it debated?
soil-form-055.a: It assumes nothing but age differs between sites, which often cannot be tested.

soil-form-061.q: In Erhart's theory, what happens to soils during rhexistasy?
soil-form-061.a: A drier climate thins vegetation, physical weathering dominates, and intense rains erode soils into layers of sand and silt.

soil-form-064.q: Why is the mean soil taxonomic distance a better measure of pedodiversity than conventional indices?
soil-form-064.a: Conventional indices ignore how similar soil classes are, while the mean soil taxonomic distance accounts for it.

soil-form-073.q: Why can laterite be cut from the ground yet serve as durable building stone?
soil-form-073.a: It is mined below the water table while wet and soft; as it dries, iron compounds lock into a rigid lattice that resists the weather.

soil-form-067.q: How is ferrallitisation the reverse of podsolisation?
soil-form-067.a: In ferrallitisation silica is leached away and iron and aluminium sesquioxides remain; in podsolisation silica remains and iron and aluminium are removed.

soil-form-052.q: In biosorting, why do large stones end up at the base of the biomantle?
soil-form-052.a: Burrowers move only particles smaller than their burrows, so larger stones settle and form a stonelayer.

soil-form-062.q: How does soil memory in soils differ from memory in layered sediments?
soil-form-062.a: Soils store records palimpsest-wise, with features overprinting each other, while sediments store them book-wise, in datable order.

soil-phys-014.q: Why do geotechnical engineers separate silts from clays by plasticity rather than size?
soil-phys-014.a: Size does not fix mineral makeup, so engineers use plasticity measured with the Atterberg limits instead.

soil-phys-053.q: What makes loam the only distinctive class in the USDA texture triangle?
soil-phys-053.a: It is the only class not dominated by sand, silt or clay.

soil-phys-046.q: In the ribbon test, what does the length of the unbroken ribbon indicate?
soil-phys-046.a: How much clay the sample holds.

soil-phys-003.q: What is the difference between a ped and a clod?
soil-phys-003.a: A ped forms naturally as particles clump into aggregates, while a clod is a mass of soil made artificially, for example by cultivation.

soil-phys-019.q: Why can sieving alone not complete a soil's particle-size analysis?
soil-phys-019.a: Silt and clay below 60 μm need a second method, usually the hydrometer or pipette, on the material from the bottom sieve.

soil-phys-051.q: Why does laser diffraction usually size platy clay larger than sedimentation analysis does?
soil-phys-051.a: Its theories assume spherical particles, so a clay plate is sized by its cross-section.

soil-phys-021.q: In the USCS symbol CH, what do the two letters mean?
soil-phys-021.a: C names the main material, clay, and H means a high liquid limit.

soil-phys-017.q: How is cumulative percent passing found from cumulative percent retained?
soil-phys-017.a: It equals 100% minus the cumulative percent retained.

soil-phys-026.q: What do the liquidity and consistency indices always add up to?

soil-phys-024.q: Why does sodium make clay deflocculate?
soil-phys-024.a: Clay flocculates when the slightly positive edges of plates stick to the negative faces of others, and sodium displacing polyvalent cations weakens this.

soil-phys-039.q: Above what exchangeable sodium percentage does dispersion become highly likely?

soil-phys-011.q: Is every crusting soil also hardsetting?
soil-phys-011.a: No: a hardsetting horizon is thicker than a crust, often as thick as the cultivated layer or more.

soil-phys-057.q: When is a sand classed as well graded (SW) under the USCS?
soil-phys-057.a: When Cu ≥ 6 and 1 < Cc < 3; otherwise it is poorly graded (SP).

soil-phys-063.q: How do bulk density and porosity relate in a dry soil?
soil-phys-063.a: Inversely: the more pore space a soil has, the lower its bulk density.

soil-phys-069.q: Why is compaction harder to manage than salinization or erosion?
soil-phys-069.a: It is mainly a hidden, sub-surface problem, so special methods are needed to locate it.

soil-phys-073.q: Why does higher pore water pressure make soil weaker?
soil-phys-073.a: Strength comes mainly from friction proportional to normal stress, and effective stress is total stress minus pore water pressure.

soil-phys-116.q: Why does a saturated clay settle so much more slowly than a sand under load?
soil-phys-116.a: Clay's extremely low hydraulic conductivity lets water drain only slowly, while coarse soils drain readily and settle at once.

soil-phys-109.q: Why does a wet sandcastle stand but collapse when submerged?
soil-phys-109.a: Water above the water table is at negative pressure, pulling grains together so friction holds them; submerged, that pull is lost.

soil-phys-094.q: What do relative densities of 100% and 0% mean?
soil-phys-094.a: 100% means very dense sand or gravel; 0% means extremely loose, unstable soil.

soil-phys-091.q: Why are fine-textured, wet soils most easily compacted?
soil-phys-091.a: Water films shield the contacts between particles, and clay-rich soils are more susceptible than coarse ones.

soil-phys-068.q: Why can clay be highly porous yet conduct water poorly?
soil-phys-068.a: It stores much water per volume but releases it slowly through narrow pore throats.

soil-phys-133.q: Why does pumping groundwater make the land surface sink?
soil-phys-133.a: Pumping changes the effective stress on compressible silt or clay layers, which consolidate, often irreversibly, and lose volume.

soil-phys-104.q: Why is the cohesion intercept c′ not treated as a fundamental soil property?
soil-phys-104.a: It often comes from forcing a straight line through data that actually curve, so its value depends on the stress range.

soil-phys-072.q: How are a soil core's cracks made visible for image analysis?
soil-phys-072.a: The core is impregnated with resin carrying a fluorescent dye, ground back step by step, and each face is lit with ultraviolet or blue light and photographed.

soil-phys-111.q: Which clay mineral has the highest compression index: kaolinite, illite or montmorillonite?
soil-phys-111.a: Montmorillonite, at 1.0 to 2.6, against 0.50 to 1.10 for illite and 0.19 to 0.28 for kaolinite.

soil-phys-129.q: True or false: clay has a higher specific yield than coarse sand.
soil-phys-129.a: False: clay averages about 2%, while coarse sand averages about 27%.

soil-water-180.q: What usually happens when rain arrives faster than the soil can take it in?
soil-water-180.a: Runoff usually follows, unless a physical barrier holds the water.

soil-water-214.q: Who is credited with inventing hollow-pipe drainage?
soil-water-214.a: Sir Hugh Dalrymple, who died in 1753.

soil-water-201.q: Darcy's law is often compared with which law from electricity, and why?
soil-water-201.a: Ohm's law: both relate flow linearly to a potential difference, with hydraulic conductivity playing the part of electrical conductivity.

soil-water-187.q: Why does a single-ring infiltrometer tend to give misleading readings?
soil-water-187.a: Driving the ring in deforms the soil, and with only one ring the water can spread sideways.

soil-water-178.q: At what suction is the permanent wilting point set by convention?
soil-water-178.a: At −1,500 kPa (−15 bar), as Lorenzo A. Richards proposed.

soil-water-231.q: How does paving over soil contribute to urban flooding?
soil-water-231.a: It seals the surface, ending rainwater infiltration and natural recharge.

soil-water-228.q: In the Nile Delta, which tolerates a shallower water table, wheat or cotton?
soil-water-228.a: Wheat, at 45 cm, is very tolerant; cotton is sensitive and needs 90 cm.

soil-water-217.q: How does Seattle's Street Edge Alternatives Project handle runoff?
soil-water-217.a: Roadside ditches, plantings and uncurbed sidewalks let runoff flow onto permeable ground.

soil-water-183.q: Why must the Green–Ampt equation for cumulative infiltration be solved iteratively?
soil-water-183.a: Because F(t) appears on both sides of the equation.

soil-water-237.q: What four reservoirs does SaltMod track?
soil-water-237.a: The surface, the root zone, a transition zone that holds any horizontal drains, and the aquifer.

soil-water-197.q: Why are field methods preferred over laboratory samples for measuring hydraulic conductivity?
soil-water-197.a: They give the most reliable values with the least disturbance, whereas disturbing laboratory samples undermines their results.

soil-water-199.q: Why does an unconfined aquifer's transmissivity change as the water table moves?
soil-water-199.a: Layers above the water table are unsaturated and add nothing, so the saturated thickness changes.

soil-water-192.q: According to Allen Hazen, how does permeability depend on particle size?
soil-water-192.a: It is proportional to the square of particle size, so coarse sand may be over a million times more permeable than clay.

soil-found-071.q: What is a percolation test's result used for?
soil-found-071.a: Its result, in minutes per inch, is matched to local health codes to size a leach field.

soil-found-105.a: During peak events such as heavy rain, at rates set by the hydraulic conductivity of the medium.

soil-water-220.q: Why might irrigated land need subsurface drainage?
soil-water-220.a: To leach salts brought in with irrigation water; models such as SaltMod help set the drainage requirement.

soil-water-209.q: How does the biomantle show soil hydrology at work?
soil-water-209.a: Loosened by bioturbation, it speeds percolation through biopores and carries throughflow downslope above dense subsoil horizons.

soil-water-188.q: Under what conditions does a double-ring infiltrometer's rate approximate saturated hydraulic conductivity?
soil-water-188.a: When flow is steady and one-dimensional with a unit gradient below.

soil-water-226.q: What advantages do capacitance and impedance sensors have over TDR, and what is their drawback?
soil-water-226.a: They are cheaper and respond faster, but usually need calibrating for each soil type.

soil-water-229.q: How did Veihmeyer and Hendrickson define readily available water?
soil-water-229.a: As the difference between the water content at field capacity and at the permanent wilting point.

soil-water-236.q: How can soil moisture sensors act like a thermostat for irrigation?
soil-water-236.a: They trigger irrigation only when soil moisture drops below a set depletion threshold.

soil-water-179.q: Why can the capillary fringe stay saturated much higher in some soils than others?
soil-water-179.a: Small, uniform pores can keep soil saturated several feet above the water table, while large pores limit the saturated part to a few inches.

soil-water-213.q: Why is groundwater recharge hard to quantify?
soil-water-213.a: Evaporation, transpiration and infiltration must first be measured or estimated to close the water balance.

soil-phys-137.q: Why does a pale soil stay cooler than a dark one?
soil-phys-137.a: Paler soils have a higher albedo, so they stay cooler than dark soils.

soil-phys-140.q: Why are soil moisture and soil thermal properties often measured together?
soil-phys-140.a: Thermal properties depend strongly on volumetric water content, so the two are closely linked.

soil-phys-159.q: What temperature conditions produce needle ice?
soil-phys-159.a: Soil above 0 °C under surface air below 0 °C, so water rises by capillary action and freezes onto the growing column.

soil-phys-155.q: Why are clean sands and gravels not frost susceptible?
soil-phys-155.a: Their pores are too open for capillary flow.

soil-phys-139.q: Why does wet soil warm more slowly than dry soil?
soil-phys-139.a: Water raises its specific heat, and evaporating water takes up a great deal of energy.

soil-phys-138.q: On a day when the surface is warmer than the soil below, which way does heat flow?
soil-phys-138.a: Into the soil, since heat flows against the temperature gradient.

soil-chem-076.q: Who is considered the father of soil chemistry?
soil-chem-076.a: J. Thomas Way, who ran many experiments on ion exchange in soils in the early 1870s.

soil-chem-104.q: What chemical change in iron accompanies the formation of goethite?
soil-chem-104.a: Ferrous iron, iron(II), is oxidized to ferric iron, iron(III).

soil-chem-088.a: Tight hydrogen bonding between its layers keeps water from entering.

soil-chem-077.q: Why does it matter to know the reactions a chemical undergoes once it reaches soil?
soil-chem-077.a: They can raise or lower its toxicity, so knowing them helps predict a contaminant's fate and design cost-effective clean-up.

soil-chem-083.q: Why do clay minerals feature in theories of the origin of life?
soil-chem-083.a: Montmorillonite has been shown to catalyse joining nucleotides into RNA and forming lipid membranes.

soil-chem-098.q: In what kind of soil is imogolite found?
soil-chem-098.a: In soils formed from volcanic ash.

soil-chem-110.q: How does palygorskite's structure differ from that of layered smectites?
soil-chem-110.a: It has a ribbon structure of continuous silica chains with long water channels inside, and it does not swell.

soil-chem-091.a: Its layers are not rigidly joined, so water and hydrated cations can enter the interlayer reversibly.

soil-chem-092.q: What happens to smectite in contact with potassium-rich groundwater?
soil-chem-092.a: Potassium replaces sodium and collapses the interlayer, turning it into non-swelling illite.

soil-chem-058.q: What three fractions make up humic substances, and how do they differ?
soil-chem-058.a: Humic acid, fulvic acid and humin, which differ in solubility.

soil-chem-073.q: How can leonardite help on metal-contaminated ground?
soil-chem-073.a: Added to the soil, especially with compost, it reduces the uptake of metals by plants.

soil-chem-072.q: Why do micronutrient fertilizers need a chelating agent such as EDTA?
soil-chem-072.a: Without one, the phosphate salts in most fertilizers turn the metal ions into insoluble solids of no use to plants.

soil-chem-066.q: Besides serving as a soil amendment, what geological role may humate deposits play?
soil-chem-066.a: They may play an important role in forming uranium ore bodies.

soil-chem-074.q: Which source gives the best potassium humate, and why?
soil-chem-074.a: Well-oxidised lignite (leonardite), since the less oxidised the coal, the less potassium humate it yields.

soil-chem-053.q: In what kind of soil can anion exchange capacity exceed cation exchange capacity?
soil-chem-053.a: In highly weathered soils such as ferralsols (oxisols).

soil-chem-050.q: Why does adding salt destabilise a clay suspension?
soil-chem-050.a: Higher electrolyte concentration thins the double layer around the particles, destabilising the colloid.

soil-chem-118.q: Which variable, alongside pH, is called a master variable of soil reactions?
soil-chem-118.a: Redox potential, expressed as Eh or pe.

soil-chem-116.q: In a redox reaction, is the reducing agent oxidized or reduced?
soil-chem-116.a: Oxidized: it passes electrons to the oxidant, which is reduced.

soil-chem-131.q: How are oxidants delivered underground where permeability is low?
soil-chem-131.a: By soil mixing or hydraulic fracturing, rather than only direct-push rods or injection wells.

soil-chem-129.q: In sediments, where do methanogens dominate over sulfate reducers?
soil-chem-129.a: In the lower layers, where sulfate has been depleted.

soil-chem-126.q: Where do organic pollutants break down fastest, and why?
soil-chem-126.a: At the oxic–anoxic interface, such as the groundwater capillary fringe, where electron donors and acceptors abound.

soil-chem-002.q: How does acid rain harm trees such as sugar maple through the soil?
soil-chem-002.a: Its hydrogen ions displace calcium and magnesium from clay, leaching these base cations and mobilizing aluminium.

soil-chem-039.q: What is the dominant mineral in a calcrete, and in a silcrete?
soil-chem-039.a: Calcium carbonate in calcrete, and silica in silcrete.

soil-chem-012.q: Above what ECe is a soil classed as saline?
soil-chem-012.a: Above 4; it is severely saline above 16.

soil-chem-007.q: What is the trade-off between deep liming and surface liming?
soil-chem-007.a: Deep liming works better but is costlier and harder.

soil-chem-038.q: Why is gypcrete found mostly in very dry regions?
soil-chem-038.a: Gypsum is moderately soluble and leaches away under higher rainfall.

soil-chem-015.q: In the sacrificial-strip method, why do the dry strips become salty?
soil-chem-015.a: Groundwater rises in them by capillarity and evaporates, leaving its salts behind.

soil-chem-026.q: Why can a soil that enters winter dry reduce recharge to groundwater?
soil-chem-026.a: The drier it starts, the more water it can store instead of leaking to groundwater.

soil-chem-034.q: What happened when potentially acid sulfate soils were aggressively drained?
soil-chem-034.a: The results were disastrous: barren land and clear, lifeless water.

soil-chem-020.q: How does fly ash from coal-fired boilers raise alkalinity downstream?
soil-chem-020.a: Its calcium oxide dissolves to slaked lime, Ca(OH)2, which runoff carries into rivers and irrigation systems.

soil-bio-001.q: What counts as soil life, or edaphon?
soil-bio-001.a: Every organism that spends a significant part of its life cycle in the soil profile or at the soil-litter interface.

soil-bio-078.q: Since analysers measure only total carbon, how is organic carbon found?
soil-bio-078.a: The inorganic carbon is subtracted, or first driven off with acid.

soil-bio-040.q: How do earthworms breathe, given that they have no special respiratory organs?

soil-bio-041.q: Which ecological group of earthworms builds deep vertical burrows and pulls leaves down into mineral soil?
soil-bio-041.a: Anecic worms, such as Lumbricus terrestris, which come up from permanent vertical burrows to gather leaves.

soil-bio-075.q: Which two groups of microbes produce geosmin?
soil-bio-075.a: Cyanobacteria such as Anabaena, and actinomycetes, mainly Streptomyces.

soil-bio-043.q: What can invading earthworms do to the banded profile of a podzol?
soil-bio-043.a: They can erase it, mixing the organic, E and upper B horizons into a single dark Ap horizon.

soil-bio-070.q: Which bacterium is the most commonly applied microbial inoculant, and what does it do?
soil-bio-070.a: Rhizobium, which fixes nitrogen in legume root nodules.

soil-bio-009.q: Why do soil microbes respire less as salinity rises?
soil-bio-009.a: Because they have less available water.

soil-bio-085.q: If springtails do not decompose organic matter directly, how do they speed decomposition?
soil-bio-085.a: By fragmenting it and by controlling and spreading soil microbial communities.

soil-bio-016.q: How does a lysogenic phage differ from a lytic one?
soil-bio-016.a: A lytic phage kills its host to release virions; a lysogenic phage joins the host genome.

soil-bio-081.q: What largely sets the stature of tropical montane elfin forests?

soil-bio-036.q: What is the difference between basal and substrate-induced respiration?
soil-bio-036.a: Basal respiration is measured with nothing added; substrate-induced respiration adds nutrients and sugars.

soil-bio-066.q: How far below the sea floor have mineral-forming microorganisms been found?

soil-bio-010.q: Why is the diversity of soil life hard to measure?
soil-bio-010.a: Most soil microbes have never been cultured and remain undescribed.

soil-bio-032.q: Why can isopods die if kept from eating their own faeces?
soil-bio-032.a: On nutrient-poor litter, the microbes colonising their pellets enrich the food.

soil-bio-027.q: Which energy channels carry the largest flow in soil flow webs?
soil-bio-027.a: The bacterial and fungal channels; the root-herbivory channel carries much less.

soil-bio-062.q: On the sandplains of southern Western Australia, what do most plants rely on to get phosphorus and sulfur?

soil-bio-193.q: True or false: nematodes decompose organic matter.
soil-bio-193.a: False: they feed on living material, regulating bacterial numbers and community composition.

soil-bio-088.q: Why do copiotrophs lose out to oligotrophs once nutrients run out?
soil-bio-088.a: They live a feast-and-famine life, using nutrients fast but surviving poorly when supplies run out.

soil-bio-068.q: Why is biocementation unsuited to soils rich in fines?
soil-bio-068.a: Bacteria cannot pass pore throats smaller than about 0.4 μm.

soil-bio-080.q: How can extracellular polymeric substances lower a soil's hydraulic conductivity?
soil-bio-080.a: Together with microbial cells they block soil pores, a process called bioclogging.

soil-bio-139.q: Name a crop whose taproot serves as a storage organ.
soil-bio-139.a: Carrot, radish or turnip: many taproots are storage organs.

soil-bio-135.q: Why do most roots of most plants lie fairly close to the surface?
soil-bio-135.a: Nutrients are more available and aeration is better there.

soil-bio-198.q: What happens to a root's growth if its cap is removed?
soil-bio-198.a: It grows at random, because statoliths in the cap's statocytes drive gravitropism.

soil-bio-149.q: Compared with the rhizosphere, are microbes in bulk soil more varied or more abundant?
soil-bio-149.a: More varied; they are more abundant in the rhizosphere.

soil-bio-173.q: What does an ectomycorrhizal fungus supply its host in return for food?
soil-bio-173.a: Nitrogen: it gets about 15% of the host's food and supplies up to 86% of its nitrogen needs.

soil-bio-202.q: When can a non-systemic endophyte turn pathogenic?

soil-bio-168.q: How does tillage reduce a crop's phosphorus supply from arbuscular fungi?
soil-bio-168.a: It breaks up soil macrostructure and the hyphal network, leaving the network non-infective.

soil-bio-192.q: When do microbes switch on siderophore production?

soil-bio-145.q: Why can strigolactones released by roots backfire on a plant?
soil-bio-145.a: The parasitic plant Striga germinates when it detects them.

soil-bio-185.q: What is traded across the Hartig net?
soil-bio-185.a: Nutrients from the fungus's outer mycelium pass into the root's apoplast, and plant sugars pass back to feed the fungus.

soil-bio-169.q: For restoring desertified land, which worked best: a native fungal mixture, a single exotic species or no inoculum?
soil-bio-169.a: The mixture of native arbuscular fungi, which improved soil quality more over the long term.

soil-bio-200.q: Which enzyme lets Frankia turn atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia?

soil-bio-189.q: What can happen to arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi under high nitrogen?

soil-bio-190.q: Which two symbioses use the common symbiosis signalling pathway?
soil-bio-190.a: Arbuscular mycorrhiza, its ancestral user, and the younger root-nodule symbiosis with rhizobia.

soil-bio-106.q: What separates the L, F and H litter layers?
soil-bio-106.a: How decomposed they are: L is little decomposed, F partly and H fully.

soil-bio-112.q: On land, where does detritus occur?
soil-bio-112.a: As plant litter and as organic matter mixed into the soil, such as the humic soil beneath fallen leaves.

soil-bio-094.q: How does humus help a soil withstand drought?
soil-bio-094.a: It can hold the equivalent of 80–90% of its weight in moisture.

soil-bio-095.q: Why do humus profiles change faster than whole soil profiles?
soil-bio-095.a: Soil organisms drive them, so they change over a few years, while pedons take decades to centuries.

soil-bio-110.q: Give one way a plant has adapted to life in the leaf litter layer.
soil-bio-110.a: Bluebell shoots pierce the layer in spring, and rhizomatous wood sorrel thrives there.

soil-bio-117.q: What is the difference between positive and negative priming?
soil-bio-117.a: Positive priming speeds mineralization; negative priming causes immobilization, leaving nitrogen unavailable.

soil-bio-121.q: What evidence suggests that glomalin-related soil protein comes from fungi?
soil-bio-121.a: It declines when arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi are removed from soil or fungicides are applied.

soil-bio-128.q: Which dissolved organic molecules stay on soil minerals longer, hydrophobic or hydrophilic ones?

soil-bio-197.q: How does coarse woody debris on slopes help the soil?
soil-bio-197.a: It slows the downslope movement of organic matter and mineral soil, traps leaves, improves infiltration and slows evaporation.

soil-bio-122.q: Why may the soil-glue effect credited to glomalin not come from glomalin?
soil-bio-122.a: The heated citrate extraction also co-extracts humic substances.

soil-bio-092.q: What do supporters of the Soil Continuum Model say the evidence does not support?
soil-bio-092.a: The formation of large, persistent humic molecules in soils.

soil-class-016.q: What are the two levels of the World Reference Base?
soil-class-016.a: Reference Soil Groups, each refined by adding qualifiers.

soil-class-023.q: Which category does the Canadian system drop from the U.S.-style hierarchy?
soil-class-023.a: The suborder: its levels are order, great group, subgroup, family and series.

soil-class-012.q: In the 1938 U.S. system, how did intrazonal soils differ from zonal soils?
soil-class-012.a: Zonal soils reflected climate and vegetation; intrazonal soils reflected a local factor of relief or parent material strong enough to override them.

soil-class-007.q: At which level of USDA soil taxonomy do soil moisture regime names act as modifiers?

soil-class-038.q: Which soil is the state soil of North Carolina?
soil-class-038.a: The Cecil soil, which runs from Virginia to Alabama.

soil-class-019.q: In a WRB map unit, how much area must a dominant soil cover?

soil-class-034.q: In the Polish system, what three things describe each soil?
soil-class-034.a: Its type, from genesis and diagnostic horizons; its kind, the bedrock's geological origin; and its texture class.

soil-class-025.q: What property separates the great groups of Canada's Organic soils?
soil-class-025.a: Their degree of decomposition, measured by fibre content.

soil-class-031.q: What splits Canada's Luvisolic soils into two great groups?
soil-class-031.a: Soil temperature: Gray Brown Luvisols are at 8 °C or more, unlike Gray Luvisols.

soil-class-026.q: What tells the two great groups of Canada's Vertisolic order apart?
soil-class-026.a: The darkness of the A horizon, which separates Vertisols from Humic Vertisols.

soil-class-046.q: What has superseded the Handbook of Australian Soils?

soil-class-101.q: What base saturation must a Mollisol have?

soil-class-098.q: Why does organic matter build up to form a Histosol?
soil-class-098.a: It accumulates faster than it is destroyed, usually because poor drainage prevents aerobic decay.

soil-class-100.q: What horizon usually lies beneath the epipedon of an Inceptisol?

soil-class-095.q: Why are most skeletal soils so shallow on steep mountain slopes?
soil-class-095.a: Erosion strips material too fast for deep soil to form.

soil-class-107.q: Which Vertisol suborder is the most extensive worldwide?
soil-class-107.a: Usterts, whose cracks stay open at least 90 cumulative days a year.

soil-class-114.q: Why is a baseline needed to judge how far a soil has formed?
soil-class-114.a: Soils start much like their parent material and lose its features over time.

soil-class-138.q: What does the name podzol mean, and why?
soil-class-138.a: 'Under-ash' in Russian, after peasants who ploughed up what looked like a layer of ash.

soil-class-148.q: What mainly decides where arid areas lie?
soil-class-148.a: The general circulation of the atmosphere, which shifts with climate change.

soil-class-122.q: Why are Cambisols widespread in lands glaciated in the Pleistocene?
soil-class-122.a: There the parent material is young and soil formation is slow.

soil-class-118.q: Why can Alisols poison intolerant plants?
soil-class-118.a: At their low pH, aluminium and manganese dissolve.

soil-class-130.q: Where does the name Kastanozem come from?
soil-class-130.a: From the Russian and Latin words for chestnut, after the colour of the chestnut's husk.

soil-class-140.q: Why are most Retisols left under forest or pasture?
soil-class-140.a: Water drains through their clay-poor tongues while the dense clay parts are often too dry and hard to root, and earthworms avoid them.

soil-class-124.q: What does the high magnetic susceptibility of chernozem suggest about how it formed?
soil-class-124.a: Heat turns goethite and ferrihydrite into maghemite, so it points to fire, likely set by early humans.

soil-class-074.q: Why does draining a peatland release carbon dioxide?
soil-class-074.a: Drainage exposes organic carbon, built up underwater over thousands of years, to the air, where it decomposes to CO2.

soil-class-053.q: Why does terra preta resist leaching when the soils around it do not?
soil-class-053.a: Its charcoal stays in the soil for thousands of years, binding minerals and nutrients.

soil-class-078.q: Which kind of peat is the least decomposed: fibric, hemic or sapric?
soil-class-078.a: Fibric peat, which consists of intact fibre; sapric peat is the most decomposed.

soil-class-051.q: Why is terra rossa popular for growing wine?
soil-class-051.a: The karstic rock beneath gives it high internal drainage, surprisingly good for a clay-rich soil.

soil-class-081.q: How does tropical peat differ in origin from the temperate kind?
soil-class-081.a: It forms mostly from dead trees rather than the sphagnum typical of temperate peat.

soil-class-049.q: Why do brown podzolic soils lack the continuous E horizon of a true podzol?
soil-class-049.a: Soil creeping downslope keeps supplying iron and aluminium oxides, which build up as an orange-brown B horizon.

soil-class-067.a: A shallow depression of heavy clay floods after seasonal rains, and as the water evaporates a dried, fissured crust forms on the surface.

soil-class-052.q: Why does a latosol lose its fertility once the rainforest above it is felled?
soil-class-052.a: Its fertility lies in a thin humus layer fed by the forest; once that is no longer replaced, the nutrients leach away quickly.

soil-fert-181.a: An organism needs it for normal function but cannot make it itself, at all or in sufficient amounts.

soil-fert-169.q: Which plant nutrients do not come originally from the soil's mineral fraction?
soil-fert-169.a: Carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, supplied by carbon dioxide and water, and nitrogen, supplied by nitrogen fixation.

soil-fert-153.q: What did Albert Howard call the basis of the public health system of the future?
soil-fert-153.a: Soil fertility; he wrote that all future studies of disease must begin with the soil.

soil-fert-150.q: Why do inorganic fertilizers act at once?
soil-fert-150.a: Plants take up nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium in inorganic forms, which these fertilizers supply directly.

soil-fert-197.q: Why do legumes short of molybdenum fix less nitrogen?
soil-fert-197.a: Molybdenum is needed for nitrogenase, the enzyme of nitrogen fixation.

soil-fert-157.q: How do root hairs free cations held on soil particles?
soil-fert-157.a: They pump hydrogen ions into the soil, which displace cations held on negatively charged particles.

soil-fert-188.q: What does liming a garden soil to pH 6.5 do about lead?

soil-fert-159.q: Is iron part of the chlorophyll molecule?
soil-fert-159.a: No, but it is essential for making chlorophyll.

soil-fert-161.q: How can heavy phosphate applications cause zinc deficiency?

soil-fert-180.q: Why can cobalt matter to legumes though it seems inessential for most plants?
soil-fert-180.a: It is essential for nitrogen fixation by bacteria associated with legumes.

soil-fert-194.q: Why is nitrogen usually the hardest nutrient to manage?
soil-fert-194.a: Plant-available nitrogen changes quickly with soil water.

soil-fert-191.q: What does a soil nitrate test reading above the optimal range tell a corn grower?
soil-fert-191.a: Adding more nitrogen will not increase yield.

soil-fert-099.q: If nitrogen gas is the largest nitrogen store, why is usable nitrogen scarce in many ecosystems?
soil-fert-099.a: Little of the atmosphere's nitrogen gas is available to living things.

soil-fert-121.q: Why can ploughing in straw leave a crop short of nitrogen?
soil-fert-121.a: High-carbon straw stimulates microbes, which raise their nitrogen demand and out-compete the crop for ammonium and nitrate.

soil-fert-113.q: Which two groups of nitrifying bacteria work together, and what does each make?
soil-fert-113.a: Ammonia-oxidizing bacteria make nitrite, and nitrite-oxidizing bacteria turn it into nitrate.

soil-fert-143.q: Why is iron a limiting nutrient in most regions despite being abundant in the crust?
soil-fert-143.a: Where oxygen is present iron takes the stable ferric form, which dissolves poorly.

soil-fert-123.q: How does a build-up of ammonium in farm soil make it more acid?
soil-fert-123.a: Nitrification of the ammonium releases hydrogen ions that acidify the soil.

soil-fert-141.q: What separates a reservoir from an exchange pool in an element cycle?
soil-fert-141.a: A reservoir, generally abiotic, holds a chemical for a long time, while an exchange pool, generally biotic, holds it only briefly.

soil-fert-115.q: Why might ammonia-oxidizing archaea contribute more to ammonia oxidation in soils than bacteria do?
soil-fert-115.a: They outnumber ammonia-oxidizing bacteria in soils.

soil-fert-148.q: What gives salt marshes and mud flats their rotten-egg smell?
soil-fert-148.a: Hydrogen sulfide expelled by sulfate-reducing microorganisms.

soil-fert-130.q: What can the activity of phosphate-releasing enzymes in soil indicate?
soil-fert-130.a: The soil's potential for phosphorus mineralization and its phosphorus availability.

soil-fert-126.q: Why does the final microbial step to nitrogen gas matter for reactive nitrogen?
soil-fert-126.a: The atmosphere is the ultimate sink for reactive nitrogen, and denitrification returns it there as nitrogen gas.

soil-fert-110.q: What is unusual about the comammox Nitrospira found in 2015?
soil-fert-110.a: A single organism carries out complete nitrification, where two groups were long thought necessary.

soil-fert-001.q: Why do legumes generally need no nitrogen fertilizer?

soil-fert-050.q: What lets biochar serve for carbon removal?
soil-fert-050.a: Its refractory stability lets it persist in soils for thousands of years.

soil-fert-004.q: How does a compound NPK fertilizer differ from an NPK blend?
soil-fert-004.a: A compound binds the three nutrients chemically, while a blend is a physical mixture of single-nutrient fertilizers.

soil-fert-023.q: What did the once-common term artificial manure mean?
soil-fert-023.a: What are now called artificial fertilizers.

soil-fert-055.q: Where does the acidity of most acid soils generally come from?
soil-fert-055.a: From aluminium hydrolysis, since most acid soils are saturated with aluminium rather than hydrogen ions.

soil-fert-029.a: Aerobic bacteria need oxygen above 5%, so turning keeps up oxygen and the right moisture.

soil-fert-071.q: Why is ammonium nitrate a greater security risk than urea?
soil-fert-071.a: It forms explosive mixtures with fuels, while urea is not an oxidizer.

soil-fert-048.q: Can biofertilizers replace synthetic fertilizers today?
soil-fert-048.a: Not yet; they can reduce the use of synthetic fertilizers and pesticides but cannot yet replace them.

soil-fert-039.q: Why do nutrients in vermicompost wash away less readily?
soil-fert-039.a: The worm mucus coating the castings slows nutrient release and keeps nutrients from washing away.

soil-fert-084.q: Why does rain soon after spreading urea reduce nitrogen loss?
soil-fert-084.a: It moves urea into the soil, where the ammonia it forms can react with water to become ammonium instead of escaping.

soil-fert-032.q: What is the trade-off of cold composting in a small home heap?
soil-fert-032.a: It needs no turning, but it can take up to a year and parts may go anaerobic.

soil-fert-088.q: Why might a new hügelkultur bed be less fertile at first?
soil-fert-088.a: Wood has one of the highest carbon-to-nitrogen ratios, so its decay may tie up soil nitrogen for perhaps one to two years.

soil-fert-069.q: How does a living mulch differ from a cover crop?
soil-fert-069.a: A living mulch keeps growing with the crop, whereas a cover crop is worked into the soil or killed.

soil-fert-087.q: Why can soils farmed by slash-and-char keep cropping when slash-and-burn soils are abandoned?
soil-fert-087.a: Slash-and-char keeps much of the organic carbon as stable char, and such biochar-enriched soils can sustain cropping indefinitely, while slash-and-burn soils soon lose their nutrients.

soil-fert-204.q: How does Azolla fertilize a rice paddy?
soil-fert-204.a: Its partner cyanobacterium fixes atmospheric nitrogen, which Azolla releases to the rice as it dies.

soil-fert-091.q: Why does lime have to neutralize more than the acid in the soil water?
soil-fert-091.a: Acid-forming ions held on soil colloids will otherwise restore the original pH.

soil-fert-027.q: What goes wrong if green manure is worked in too short a time before planting?
soil-fert-027.a: Nitrogen immobilization can leave too little nitrogen for the next crop.

soil-fert-060.q: Why must agricultural lime be finely ground?
soil-fert-060.a: Soil acids are weak, so only fine particles react well: those finer than 60 mesh are fully effective, while those over 8 mesh are of little value.

soil-fert-037.q: Why does adding urine help a humanure compost heap?
soil-fert-037.a: It raises the heap's temperature, helping destroy pathogens and seeds.

soil-fert-044.q: Which part of human excreta carries most of its nitrogen?
soil-fert-044.a: Urine, which can hold up to 90% of the nitrogen in human excreta.

soil-fert-202.q: What is the main advantage of coated urea?
soil-fert-202.a: It releases urea gradually, lowering the risk of fertilizer burn and allowing less frequent applications.

soil-fert-017.q: Why does fluoride from phosphate fertilizers concern livestock more than crops?
soil-fert-017.a: Plants take up little fluoride, so the risk lies with livestock that eat contaminated soil.

soil-fert-046.q: Name an alternative to mined phosphate ore.
soil-fert-046.a: Phosphorus recovered from excreta, for example as struvite from urine.

soil-water-019.q: What are the two reasons rain can fail to soak in and become surface runoff?
soil-water-019.a: The soil is already saturated, or rain arrives faster than the soil can absorb it.

soil-water-089.q: Why does the US EPA prefer silt fences to straw bales for construction sediment control?
soil-water-089.a: Straw bales often protect water quality poorly and need much upkeep.

soil-water-020.q: Why can Horton overland flow erode soil extensively?
soil-water-020.a: The flow is shallow, sheetlike and fast, especially on steep terrain and loose, flat farmland.

soil-water-023.q: Why can paving a town both worsen droughts and cause floods?
soil-water-023.a: Less water reaches groundwater, so the water table falls, while more water left on the surface causes flooding.

soil-water-085.q: Why can felling a tree on clay soil damage a nearby building?
soil-water-085.a: The soil the tree had dried heaves as the deficit reverses, rising and spreading for years, and shallow foundations move with it.

soil-water-088.q: What does a low curve number say about an area?
soil-water-088.a: Its soil is more permeable and its runoff potential low.

soil-water-050.q: How do many erosion controls work physically?
soil-water-050.a: They are barriers of vegetation or rock that absorb some of the energy of the wind or water.

soil-water-045.q: Why does long cultivation make a soil more erodible?
soil-water-045.a: It depletes organic matter, which coagulates colloids into a stronger, more stable structure.

soil-water-004.q: Why do crop residues and plant cover reduce splash erosion?
soil-water-004.a: They soften the impact of raindrops, whose kinetic energy is what throws soil particles out of the crater each drop makes.

soil-water-043.q: How does a process-based erosion model differ from an empirical one?
soil-water-043.a: A process-based model solves equations for detachment, transport and deposition, while an empirical model relates soil loss statistically to environmental and management factors.

soil-water-095.q: Why are the pale, eroded hilltops in many fields wrongly blamed on water erosion?
soil-water-095.a: They are actually made by tillage erosion, which strips organic-rich topsoil from convex spots.

soil-water-113.q: What left prairie soil open to erosion once settlers plowed it?
soil-water-113.a: Plowing replaced the prairie grasses and their extensive fibrous roots with crops, exposing the topsoil to wind and rain.

soil-water-005.q: What are the two steps of sheet erosion?
