soil-water-005.a: Rainsplash first loosens small particles, then a thin, uniform sheet flow carries them a short distance.

soil-water-039.q: Why is a change in soil organic matter an unreliable sign of tillage erosion?
soil-water-039.a: Many other factors also affect organic matter, so a change does not necessarily mean soil was lost.

soil-water-029.q: Why does wind build separate sandy and silty deposits?
soil-water-029.a: Wind sorts sand from silt and clay, laying sand down as ergs and carrying silt further from the source to form loess.

soil-water-064.q: How does heavy rain make a slope more likely to fail?
soil-water-064.a: Pore water pressure on the slip surface lowers effective normal stress and friction, while the added groundwater makes the soil heavier.

soil-water-008.q: How does chemical erosion differ from physical erosion?
soil-water-008.a: Physical erosion removes rock or soil as solid sediment particles, whereas chemical erosion is usually measured from the dissolved load streams carry.

soil-water-049.q: What share of eroded sediment reaches rivers in Europe, according to WaTEM/SEDEM estimates?
soil-water-049.a: About 15%: that is the estimated sediment delivery ratio.

soil-water-252.q: A debris flow is as dense as other landslides; why does it flow almost like water?
soil-water-252.a: High pore-fluid pressure liquefies the sediment.

soil-water-031.q: Why do silt fences often give poor results in the field?
soil-water-031.a: Fine particles soon clog the fabric, and fences are often badly placed, installed or maintained.

soil-water-062.q: Why do shallow landslides often occur where permeable soil lies over less permeable soil?
soil-water-062.a: The lower layer traps water, pressure builds, and the saturated topsoil slides off.

soil-water-076.q: Which agency did the Soil Erosion Service become, and who led it?
soil-water-076.a: Hugh Hammond Bennett led it; it became the Soil Conservation Service, now the NRCS.

soil-water-101.q: What is one of the best defences against earthflows?
soil-water-101.a: Draining slopes, since saturated clay, fine sand and silt begin to flow and more water means faster flow.

soil-water-052.q: Why are anionic rather than cationic flocculants best practice in open systems?
soil-water-052.a: Cationic flocculants such as chitosan can cause hypoxia in fish.

soil-water-066.q: How does vegetation help stabilize a slope with shallow landslides?
soil-water-066.a: Roots reinforce the upper soil, and interception and transpiration dry it.

soil-water-108.q: Why does harvesting trees on a slope raise the risk of sloughing and slope failure?
soil-water-108.a: Roots hold the surface, and losing their strength can lower the safety factor so far that a moderate storm brings failure.

soil-water-250.q: Why is a desert pavement taken as a sign of a surface's relative age?

soil-water-257.q: When might gabions be chosen over riprap to protect a bank?
soil-water-257.a: On steep banks where the flow is too fast for riprap.

soil-water-124.q: What separates a marsh from a swamp?
soil-water-124.a: A marsh has herbaceous plants, while a swamp has woody plants.

soil-water-129.q: How do marsh plants cope with wet mud low in oxygen?
soil-water-129.a: Many have aerenchyma that carry air down to their roots.

soil-water-121.q: Why does peat accumulate in bogs even though plant growth there is slow?
soil-water-121.a: Decay is slower still in the oxygen-poor, saturated bog soil.

soil-water-147.q: What makes minerotrophic water neutral or alkaline?
soil-water-147.a: Dissolved bases such as calcium or magnesium ions make it base-rich.

soil-water-126.q: What keeps the pH of a rich fen relatively stable?
soil-water-126.a: Bicarbonate from calcium carbonate that groundwater dissolves as it passes limestone buffers the pH.

soil-water-138.q: What is the main control on whether a peatland releases carbon dioxide?
soil-water-138.a: The water table: a high one submerges the peat and slows respiration, while a falling one speeds aerobic decomposition and CO2 release.

soil-water-266.q: How does a palsa begin to grow?
soil-water-266.a: Where thin snow lets frost go deeper, an ice lens draws in water and lifts the surface by frost heave, a positive feedback.

soil-water-118.q: What sets landscape ecology apart from other branches of ecology?

soil-water-261.q: Why does draining peat add to carbon dioxide emissions?
soil-water-261.a: It exposes carbon stored for thousands of years to air, where it decomposes to CO2.

soil-water-137.q: Why is a drained peatland that still has a peat layer no longer a mire?
soil-water-137.a: Because new peat no longer forms there.

soil-water-142.q: How does suffosion differ from suffusion?
soil-water-142.a: Suffosion collapses the soil structure, losing mass and volume, while suffusion removes fines from between coarse grains that stay in contact, with no change in volume.

soil-agri-013.q: Besides growing crops, name two other uses of irrigation.
soil-agri-013.a: It revegetates disturbed soils in dry areas, protects crops from frost, suppresses weeds in grain fields and prevents soil consolidation.

soil-agri-046.q: How can farmers slow the evolution of herbicide-resistant weeds?
soil-agri-046.a: By using herbicides with different modes of action.

soil-agri-049.q: In surface irrigation, what decides the depth of water applied at any point?
soil-agri-049.a: The opportunity time, how long water stands on the surface there.

soil-agri-017.q: How do self-watering containers and wicking beds supply water to plants?
soil-agri-017.a: They draw water up from a reservoir by capillary action.

soil-agri-007.q: In a crop rotation, what should precede a nitrogen-depleting crop?

soil-agri-022.q: How do catch crops reduce nitrate leaching?
soil-agri-022.a: They take up the nitrogen left over from fertilizing the previous crop, so it is not leached.

soil-agri-010.q: How does following GPS guidance lines help the soil?

soil-agri-023.q: Why does newly added phosphorus leach from soils with 'legacy phosphorus'?
soil-agri-023.a: Decades of surplus phosphorus have filled their sorption sites, so the new phosphorus cannot adsorb.

soil-agri-032.q: Why is field soil steaming only a partial disinfection?
soil-agri-032.a: Heat-resistant spore-forming bacteria survive it; true sterilization needs laboratory autoclaving.

soil-agri-036.q: Which geological raw material is used against copper deficiency, and which to conserve nitrogen?
soil-agri-036.a: Malachite against copper deficiency, and zeolite to conserve nitrogen.

soil-agri-051.q: How does surge irrigation speed the advance of water down a furrow?
soil-agri-051.a: Pulsing the flow on and off wets and dries the surface, sealing it and reducing infiltration.

soil-agri-134.q: Why are Inga trees suited to alley cropping on acid tropical soils?
soil-agri-134.a: They fix nitrogen, grow on acid tropical soils and drop a thick mulch that protects the soil and shades out weeds.

soil-agri-056.q: What compounds make brassicas useful for biofumigation?
soil-agri-056.a: Isothiocyanates released from their glucosinolates, which are toxic to soil bacteria, fungi and nematodes.

soil-agri-025.q: What unit is soil salinity most often expressed in?
soil-agri-025.a: As ECe in decisiemens per metre, formerly millimhos per centimetre.

soil-agri-106.q: Why does ploughing turn over the uppermost soil?
soil-agri-106.a: To bring fresh nutrients to the surface and bury weeds and crop remains to decay.

soil-agri-114.q: How does the soil disturbance of a harrow differ from that of a cultivator?
soil-agri-114.a: A harrow disturbs the whole surface, while a cultivator disturbs only narrow tracks between rows.

soil-agri-104.q: What might explain copper and iron deficiencies in white spruce on burned clearcuts?
soil-agri-104.a: Burning raises soil pH, and the higher pH may cause them.

soil-agri-117.q: Why may no-till delay spring planting?
soil-agri-117.a: Light-coloured residue absorbs less solar energy than bare soil, so the soil warms and dries more slowly.

soil-agri-109.q: How do a mouldboard plough's coulter and share work together?
soil-agri-109.a: The coulter cuts down into the soil and the share cuts horizontally, freeing a strip of sod that rolls over upside down.

soil-agri-107.q: Why did fields worked with an ard tend to become squarish?
soil-agri-107.a: The ard left undisturbed strips between furrows, so fields were cross-ploughed both ways.

soil-agri-115.q: How do the teeth of a toothed cultivator differ in purpose from chisel plough shanks?
soil-agri-115.a: The teeth work near the surface against weeds, while chisel shanks work deep to break hardened layers.

soil-agri-120.q: What does strip tillage combine from conventional tillage and from no-till?
soil-agri-120.a: The soil drying and warming of conventional tillage with the soil protection of no-till.

soil-agri-059.q: How does irrigation leave soils saline?
soil-agri-059.a: Salt is left behind when irrigation water evaporates or rises from shallow saline water tables.

soil-agri-140.q: How do trees in agroforestry help water enter the soil?
soil-agri-140.a: They slow runoff and evaporation, so more water infiltrates.

soil-agri-065.q: How has the view of tillage changed in conservation agriculture?
soil-agri-065.a: Once thought to raise fertility through mineralization, it is now seen to destroy organic matter and cause erosion and crusting.

soil-agri-064.q: What three things raise soil carbon sequestration?
soil-agri-064.a: More biomass inputs, smaller losses of soil organic carbon and a longer mean residence time of that carbon.

soil-agri-075.q: How does a contour trench help crops in the drier growing season?
soil-agri-075.a: It catches downhill runoff so it soaks into the soil, and crops between trenches draw on that subsoil reserve.

soil-agri-141.q: If a check dam is not mainly a sediment trap, how does it reduce erosion?
soil-agri-141.a: It flattens the channel gradient and slows the flow, which induces infiltration.

soil-agri-082.q: Where are US soil surveys published now, and how does that differ from before?
soil-agri-082.a: On the NRCS Web Soil Survey, where changes go live in moments, rather than as county books that could take years to publish.

soil-agri-089.q: How does digital soil mapping differ from traditional soil mapping?
soil-agri-089.a: Traditional mapping has field soil scientists draw boundaries by hand, while digital mapping links observations to environmental data by quantitative relationships.

soil-agri-091.q: What does pedometric mapping produce instead of polygon maps of soil types?
soil-agri-091.a: Continuous grids of measured soil properties, with maps of prediction error.

soil-env-102.q: What is the main route by which carbon dioxide leaves the atmosphere for living things?
soil-env-102.a: Photosynthesis, which moves it into land and ocean life.

soil-env-212.q: How is carbon sequestration different from carbon capture and storage?
soil-env-212.a: Carbon capture and storage separates CO2 from industrial sources and stores it underground or under the sea bed, whereas biological sequestration captures CO2 through living processes such as photosynthesis.

soil-env-111.q: Why have peatlands such as those in East Anglia and the California Delta subsided?
soil-env-111.a: Tillage and drainage exposed their organic matter to oxygen.

soil-env-168.q: Why can biochar lock away carbon for so long?
soil-env-168.a: It retains half the carbon of the biomass it is made from and can endure in soil for thousands of years.

soil-env-112.q: How does a healthy soil with good water holding capacity protect waterways?
soil-env-112.a: It cuts overland flow, and nutrients and sediment stay in the soil instead of leaching or washing into waterways.

soil-env-114.q: What is the main reason warming soils release more carbon?
soil-env-114.a: Faster soil respiration: warming speeds up decomposition of soil organic matter.

soil-env-213.q: Does a positive climate feedback mean a good one?
soil-env-213.a: No. Positive or negative says nothing about good or bad; methane from wetlands, for example, is a positive feedback that adds to warming.

soil-env-152.q: Why does thawing yedoma matter for the climate?
soil-env-152.a: It may hold about 210 to 500 Gt of carbon, and as it thaws it becomes a significant methane source.

soil-env-136.q: How do palsas and pingos push the ground up?
soil-env-136.a: Meltwater trapped over deep permafrost freezes into ice lenses that lift the ground into mounds.

soil-env-132.q: Why is subsea permafrost slowly shrinking?
soil-env-132.a: It formed on land during the last Ice Age when sea levels were low, and has declined since being submerged under warmer, saltier conditions.

soil-env-140.q: Will permafrost thaw cause runaway warming?
soil-env-140.a: No. There is widespread agreement that its emissions will be smaller than human emissions and too small for runaway warming.

soil-env-163.q: How does warmer soil lose its ability to hold water and nutrients?
soil-env-163.a: Warmth speeds the decomposition of organic matter, lowering soil organic carbon and with it the soil's capacity to hold nutrients and water.

soil-env-119.q: What shrinks the soil carbon sponge, and what builds it?
soil-env-119.a: Bare soils, heavy cultivation, fertilizers, biocides and irrigation shrink it; afforestation, reforestation and cover cropping build it.

soil-env-215.q: Why does permafrost thaw at waterlogged sites produce methane?
soil-env-215.a: Methanogenesis needs fully anaerobic conditions, so thaw that exposes organic material without oxygen lets methanogens make methane.

soil-env-160.q: Why did climate models long overlook abrupt permafrost thaw?
soil-env-160.a: Abrupt thaw is hard to model, so models focused on gradual thaw.

soil-env-125.q: How does enhanced weathering store carbon dioxide?
soil-env-125.a: Through carbonic acid it removes CO2 from the air and stores it permanently in solid carbonate minerals or as ocean alkalinity.

soil-env-124.q: How do ectomycorrhizal fungi increase soil carbon storage?
soil-env-124.a: They reduce decomposer activity, for example by taking organic nitrogen and leaving decomposers nutrient-limited.

soil-env-065.q: Do densely populated areas always suffer land degradation?
soil-env-065.a: No. High population density is not always linked to degradation; it is people's practices that degrade a landscape.

soil-env-101.q: Why is land take also called land loss?
soil-env-101.a: The activities that consume land, such as building on it, are virtually irreversible.

soil-env-072.q: What is the immediate cause of desertification?
soil-env-072.a: The loss of most vegetation, which leaves dry topsoil unprotected to blow away or wash off.

soil-env-086.q: What is the best-known approach to halting desertification?
soil-env-086.a: Large tree-planting belts, such as China's Green Wall and the African Union's Great Green Wall along the Sahara.

soil-env-073.q: Does desertification mean that deserts are physically expanding?
soil-env-073.a: No. That original idea has been rejected; the UNCCD defines it as land degradation in drylands caused by climatic variations and human activities.

soil-env-082.q: How has cashmere demand worsened desertification in Mongolia?
soil-env-082.a: Herders shifted from sheep to goats, which eat roots and flowers and so degrade grazing land.

soil-env-064.q: Name two types of soil degradation that emerged only in the last 50 years.
soil-env-064.a: Any two of pollution, loss of arable land to construction, artificial radioactivity, and land-use limits from armed conflict.

soil-env-074.q: How does overcultivation turn soil to desert?
soil-env-074.a: It drains nutrients, so the soil loses organic matter and its ability to hold moisture, then hardens and cracks.

soil-env-207.q: How do bush encroachers differ from invasive species?
soil-env-207.a: Encroachers are native to the ecosystem; they count as encroachers when they outcompete other native species.

soil-env-098.a: Severely degraded grassland, also called black beach: bare, unusable black soil.

soil-env-208.q: According to the two-layer theory, why does overgrazing favour woody plants?
soil-env-208.a: Grasses use topsoil moisture and woody plants subsoil moisture, so removing grass lets more water reach the subsoil for woody plants.

soil-env-185.q: What carbon to nitrogen ratio must be kept for optimal plant growth?

soil-env-178.q: What did soil quality mean before soil health replaced it?
soil-env-178.a: Fitness for a use, such as quality of soil for maize production or for roadbed preparation.

soil-env-188.a: Each crop takes up or returns only its own set of nutrients, so carbon and nutrients run down.

soil-env-187.q: Which holds more carbon: the top two meters of soil, or the atmosphere and vegetation together?
soil-env-187.a: The soil, with an estimated 3,012 billion tonnes against 879 billion in the atmosphere and 600 billion in vegetation.

soil-env-216.q: Why does a septic tank need pumping out from time to time?
soil-env-216.a: Sludge builds up faster than it decomposes, so it is pumped out by vacuum truck.

soil-env-190.q: What body did the partnership's First Plenary Assembly establish?
soil-env-190.a: The Intergovernmental Technical Panel on Soils, whose experts advise the partnership on science.

soil-env-019.q: Why does phosphorus reach water mostly through erosion, while nitrate travels in water?
soil-env-019.a: Many forms of phosphorus adsorb onto soil particles, whereas nitrate moves in water flowing through the soil, such as tile drainage.

soil-env-033.q: Why can fungi break down pollutants that bacteria degrade poorly?
soil-env-033.a: Their non-specific enzymes attack substances such as pharmaceuticals and fragrances.

soil-env-020.q: Why does excess phosphorus drive eutrophication in lakes but nitrogen in the sea?
soil-env-020.a: Phosphorus usually limits plant growth in fresh water and nitrogen in the sea.

soil-env-026.q: Why can the same amount of a contaminant be toxic in one soil and harmless in another?
soil-env-026.a: Soil pH, organic matter and texture change how mobile, bioavailable and toxic a pollutant is, so risk assessment must be soil-specific.

soil-env-010.q: How does biomagnification differ from bioaccumulation?
soil-env-010.a: Bioaccumulation is build-up within one organism from its food and surroundings; biomagnification is the increase across food-chain levels.

soil-env-055.q: What is the main advantage of biostimulation?
soil-env-055.a: Native microbes, already suited to the subsurface and spread through it, do the work.

soil-env-025.q: How does biosparging differ from bioventing?
soil-env-025.a: Bioventing aerates the unsaturated zone, while biosparging targets the saturated zone below the water table.

soil-env-053.q: Why is landfarming unsuitable for metal-polluted soil?
soil-env-053.a: Inorganic contaminants are not degraded by it.

soil-env-041.q: How do plant roots help microbes clean contaminated soil?
soil-env-041.a: Roots release carbohydrates and acids that stimulate microbes, which then biodegrade the contaminants.

soil-env-204.q: Why can a factory outfall be modelled as a mathematical point?
soil-env-204.a: A point source has negligible extent, unlike nonpoint and area sources.

soil-env-036.q: How do mycorrhizal fungi lower the bioavailability of heavy metals?
soil-env-036.a: They produce proteins that bind the metals.

soil-env-051.q: Why has phytomining had limited commercial success?
soil-env-051.a: A review judged it slow and inefficient; by mid-2024 one nickel project had extracted less than a kilo of usable nickel.

soil-hist-040.q: Which classification system has had its editions launched at World Congresses of Soil Science?
soil-hist-040.a: The World Reference Base, first at Montpellier in 1998 and in its fourth edition at Glasgow in 2022.

soil-hist-043.q: What accreditation can members of the Australian Society of Soil Science gain?
soil-hist-043.a: They can become Certified Professional Soil Scientists.

soil-hist-029.q: Why did Marbut base classification on morphology rather than genesis?
soil-hist-029.a: He saw theories of soil genesis as ephemeral and dynamic.

soil-hist-046.q: What did the Park Grass Experiment reveal about ordinary field trials?
soil-hist-046.a: They probably underestimate long-term threats such as soil acidification.

soil-hist-030.q: Which soil-forming factor gained much more weight after 1940?
soil-hist-030.a: Time, with geomorphology used to find how long material has undergone soil formation.

soil-hist-004.q: Why is Liebig called the father of the fertilizer industry?
soil-hist-004.a: He stressed nitrogen and minerals as essential plant nutrients and popularized the law of the minimum.

soil-hist-008.q: What did Glinka's 1908 soil science textbook contain for the first time?
soil-hist-008.a: The first schematic soil map of the world.

soil-hist-024.q: When did Guy Smith's soil classification become official?
soil-hist-024.a: In 1965, after more than 15 years of work; it was published in 1975 as Soil Taxonomy.

soil-hist-073.q: What did Boussingault show about legumes in a crop rotation?
soil-hist-073.a: Soil nitrogen rises after legume crops.

soil-hist-014.q: What did chemoautotrophy overturn about how autotrophs get energy?
soil-hist-014.a: Autotrophs were thought to get energy only from light; some instead oxidize hydrogen sulfide or ammonium.

soil-hist-075.q: What did Hiltner mean by the rhizosphere?
soil-hist-075.a: The soil directly affected by root secretions and their microorganisms.

soil-hist-048.q: Which two bodies merged to form the Soil Science Society of America?
soil-hist-048.a: The Soils Section of the American Society of Agronomy and the American Soil Survey Association.

soil-hist-049.a: The World Soil Information Service (WoSIS) and SoilGrids.

soil-hist-055.q: Why does the society keep standard samples of humic and fulvic acids?
soil-hist-055.a: So scientists in many countries can work from the same reference materials, drawn from leonardite, river water, a mineral soil and peat.

soil-hist-059.q: How does lunar soil form differently from Earth's soil?
soil-hist-059.a: Mainly by mechanical weathering, as impacts and charged particles grind rock finer, not by oxygen, water and life.

soil-hist-079.q: Why do young crater rays on the Moon fade over time?
soil-hist-079.a: Space weathering makes lunar soil darker and redder as it matures.

soil-hist-083.q: How can oxygen be extracted from lunar regolith?
soil-hist-083.a: By heating its iron oxide above 900 °C in hydrogen gas.

soil-hist-080.q: Why does impact debris build up as regolith on airless bodies?
soil-hist-080.a: Lacking an atmosphere, they have almost no erosion to remove it.

soil-found-115.q: Where does the critical zone end at depth?
soil-found-115.a: At some depth in bedrock, where life and water cease to change the chemistry significantly.

soil-found-047.q: How long does mineral-associated organic matter typically persist, compared with particulate organic matter?
soil-found-047.a: Typically for centuries, whereas particulate organic matter, mostly little-decomposed plant remains, lasts only a few years to decades.

soil-form-097.q: Which part of the regolith is conventionally called soil?
soil-form-097.a: Its uppermost part, which typically holds significant organic matter.

soil-form-146.q: What silica content and enrichments mark mafic rocks?
soil-form-146.a: They have 45 to 55 wt% silica and are enriched in iron, magnesium and calcium.

soil-form-105.q: What features typically mark a meandering river?
soil-form-105.a: Point bars, cut banks, meanders, floodplains and oxbow lakes.

soil-form-023.q: Why does the subsoil get most of its colour from iron oxides?
soil-form-023.a: Because it holds little organic matter.

soil-form-019.q: What is the defining feature of Mollisols?
soil-form-019.a: A fertile mollic epipedon, built by long additions of root-derived organic matter.

soil-form-070.q: How much phosphorus did laterite remove from solution in laboratory tests and at pilot scale?
soil-form-070.a: 99% in laboratory tests and 96% in a pilot-scale facility.

soil-form-127.q: Why is phosphorus often the most deficient nutrient in tropical soils?
soil-form-127.a: Intense leaching and weathering deplete the mineral pool, and unlike nitrogen it cannot be replenished from the air.

soil-phys-189.q: How much surface per gram do clay minerals typically have?
soil-phys-189.a: Typically 10 to 1,000 square metres per gram, as they form thin plates.

soil-phys-125.q: Over what range does hydraulic conductivity vary from clays to gravels?
soil-phys-125.a: From about 10−12 m/s in clays to about 10−1 m/s in gravels.

soil-phys-064.q: Why are clay soils called heavy, despite their high porosity?
soil-phys-064.a: The word reflects their moisture weight and the extra force needed to pull tillage tools through them.

soil-phys-114.q: How is the overconsolidation ratio (OCR) defined?
soil-phys-114.a: It divides the preconsolidation stress, the highest stress a soil has carried, by the current stress.

soil-water-182.q: Why is Richards' equation hard to use for infiltration?
soil-water-182.a: It is computationally expensive, not guaranteed to converge, and sometimes struggles to conserve mass.

soil-phys-210.q: What is the general basin form of the water balance?
soil-phys-210.a: P = Q + ET + ΔS: precipitation equals streamflow plus evapotranspiration plus change in storage.

soil-water-174.q: Why does a high salt content restrict water uptake by roots?
soil-water-174.a: Solutes lower the osmotic potential of the soil solution, which severely restricts uptake by roots.

soil-phys-221.q: What is the pressure head at the water table?
soil-phys-221.a: There it equals atmospheric pressure; below it pressure head exceeds atmospheric pressure, and above it is negative.

soil-phys-201.q: Why are karst aquifers more sensitive to contamination than porous aquifers?
soil-phys-201.a: Their fast flow, through limestone fissures widened by carbonic acid, makes them far more sensitive.

soil-phys-194.q: Why do less soluble contaminants travel only short distances?
soil-phys-194.a: Adsorption holds them back, so they can move hundreds or thousands of times slower than water.

soil-phys-180.q: What does Fick's first law state?
soil-phys-180.a: J = −D dφ/dx: diffusive flux equals the diffusion coefficient times the concentration gradient, with a minus sign.

soil-phys-145.q: How deep do annual temperature cycles penetrate in wet and dry clay?
soil-phys-145.a: About 18.0 m in wet clay but only 6.5 m in dry clay.

soil-chem-107.q: What size are the particles of the colloidal fraction of soil?
soil-chem-107.a: Tiny clay and humus particles under 1 μm across, whose charges vary with soil pH.

soil-chem-097.q: What does allophane alter to when silica is added, and when it is removed?
soil-chem-097.a: To halloysite where silica is added and to gibbsite where silica is removed.

soil-chem-085.q: Why is the cation exchange capacity of kaolinite low?
soil-chem-085.a: Kaolinite has undergone almost no isomorphous substitution.

soil-chem-071.q: How many milliequivalents are 1 mmol of Na+ and 1 mmol of Ca2+?
soil-chem-071.a: 1 milliequivalent for Na+ but 2 for Ca2+, since equivalents are moles multiplied by valence.

soil-chem-130.q: When and where was biofiltration first introduced?
soil-chem-130.a: In England in 1893, as a trickling filter for wastewater.

soil-chem-180.q: Between which two lines is water stable on a Pourbaix diagram?
soil-chem-180.a: Between EH = −0.05916 pH and EH = 1.229 V − 0.05916 pH; outside them it is reduced to hydrogen or oxidized to oxygen.

soil-chem-142.q: How does alkalinity differ from basicity?
soil-chem-142.a: Basicity is an absolute position on the pH scale, while alkalinity is measured by titrating with an acid to an endpoint.

soil-chem-021.q: How does gypsum reclaim an alkali soil?
soil-chem-021.a: It supplies Ca2+ to replace sodium on the exchange complex and turns sodium carbonate into neutral sodium sulphate.

soil-bio-212.a: They are primarily detritivores, eating dead plants at any stage of decay.

soil-bio-071.q: What did a 2007 study find to be the main global determinant of bacterial diversity?

soil-bio-225.q: Which compound gives soil its earthy odour?
soil-bio-225.a: Geosmin, a volatile compound released by soil bacteria that mostly also produce spores.

soil-bio-054.q: How fast do bacteria turn over in the rhizosphere?
soil-bio-054.a: In just 12–19 hours, shorter on younger roots, because root exudates make the rhizosphere a special case.

soil-bio-178.q: What do rhizobia and legumes exchange in their mutualism?
soil-bio-178.a: The bacteria supply ammonia or amino acids and receive organic acids, mainly malate and succinate, as their carbon and energy source.

soil-bio-240.a: Hyphae aggregated into durable, water-repellent transport structures that work like xylem.

soil-bio-248.a: Secreted by mycorrhizal hyphae, it builds stable aggregates that resist erosion and accounts for about 5% of global organic carbon and nitrogen storage.

soil-bio-196.q: Why do autumn leaves decompose more slowly than most compost ingredients?
soil-bio-196.a: They are low in nitrogen and made largely of cellulose and lignin, which resist decay.

soil-bio-258.q: What does the Michaelis constant Km represent?
soil-bio-258.a: The substrate concentration at which the reaction rate is half of the limiting rate V.

soil-class-021.q: What system replaced the FAO soil classification, and when?
soil-class-021.a: The World Reference Base replaced it in 1998.

soil-class-155.q: Where does the ustic moisture regime sit relative to the aridic and udic?
soil-class-155.a: It is wetter than the aridic and drier than the udic.

soil-class-116.q: Which soil order covers the largest share of U.S. land?
soil-class-116.a: Mollisols, at an estimated 21.5%, followed by Alfisols at 14%.

soil-class-139.q: Which soils are excluded from the Regosols?
soil-class-139.a: Weakly developed soils that qualify as Leptosols, Arenosols or Fluvisols; Regosols are a leftover group for soils that fit no other.

soil-class-065.q: Why must fill be as free of organic matter as possible?
soil-class-065.a: Decomposing organic matter leaves voids that make the fill settle and can damage structures built on it.

soil-fert-165.q: At what concentration in soil water is boron toxic to most plants?

soil-fert-195.q: What do preplant and late-spring soil nitrogen tests show?
soil-fert-195.a: Preplant tests show the soil's nitrogen-supplying power, and late-spring or pre-side-dress tests decide whether more is needed.

soil-fert-119.q: What do denitrifying bacteria use in place of oxygen?
soil-fert-119.a: Nitrate and nitrite, as the final electron acceptor.

soil-fert-138.q: What share of soil potassium is in the soil solution, the form plants absorb most readily?
soil-fert-138.a: Only 0.1–0.2% of the total; fixed potassium makes up 96–99%.

soil-fert-082.q: Why does excess salt around roots make a plant respond as in drought?
soil-fert-082.a: When salts outside the root exceed those inside, water stops entering and may even leave the roots.

soil-fert-067.q: Why can straw or sawdust mulch briefly slow plant growth?
soil-fert-067.a: Their wide carbon-to-nitrogen ratio lets decomposing microbes draw nitrogen from the soil.

soil-fert-013.q: What do the numbers of a fertilizer grade such as 10-10-10 give?
soil-fert-013.a: The percentages of nitrogen, P2O5 and K2O.

soil-water-079.q: What two fates await rain that reaches land?
soil-water-079.a: It either flows over the ground as surface runoff or soaks in by infiltration, becoming soil moisture or groundwater.

soil-water-083.q: Why are planners advised to avoid karst for new development?
soil-water-083.a: Under a roof of competent limestone there is often no surface warning before an opening collapses.

soil-water-042.q: Why must drop size and terminal velocity be simulated accurately on bare soil?

soil-water-006.q: How do earth and debris differ in landslide classification?
soil-water-006.a: Earth has less than 20% by weight of particles over 2 mm; debris has more.

soil-water-098.q: Why are anionic flocculants best practice in open systems?
soil-water-098.a: Cationic flocculants such as chitosan can cause hypoxia in fish.

soil-water-253.q: What does a well-developed desert pavement indicate?
soil-water-253.a: Aridity and an older surface, since older surfaces carry better-developed pavements.

soil-water-280.q: What share of damaging landslides in the year to September 2003 were triggered by heavy rainfall?

soil-water-267.q: How does tropical peatland forest compare with forest on mineral soil as a carbon store?
soil-water-267.a: It holds far more carbon as soil organic matter, among the largest near-surface stores of land organic carbon.

soil-water-297.q: How do dead plankton help fill in a pond?
soil-water-297.a: They decay into humus that mixes with inwashed silt and clay to form soil, making the pond shallower.

soil-agri-030.q: What is the difference between monoculture and monocropping?
soil-agri-030.a: Monoculture describes crop diversity in space, whereas monocropping describes diversity over time.

soil-agri-011.q: In what units is soil salinity most often expressed?
soil-agri-011.a: As ECe in decisiemens per metre, formerly millimhos per centimetre.

soil-agri-110.q: Why did the heavy carruca plough make farming communal?
soil-agri-110.a: Pulling it took four to eight oxen, more than one peasant household had.

soil-agri-067.a: The ability of cover crops, such as nitrogen-fixing legumes, to stand in for chemical nitrogen fertilizer.

soil-agri-159.q: How wide do filter strips need to be?
soil-agri-159.a: At least 15 feet (4.6 m), and they can often serve as a cheap substitute for terraces.

soil-agri-167.q: What do the two Not Suitable land classes, N1 and N2, mean?
soil-agri-167.a: N1 has limitations that might be overcome in time but not at acceptable cost now; N2 has limitations ruling out any sustained use.

soil-meth-007.q: Which exponent of distance did Shepard settle on for inverse distance weighting?
soil-meth-007.a: Near -2, close to the gravity model.

soil-env-283.q: How can lowering a wetland's water table affect its methane balance?
soil-env-283.a: It increases methane consumption by soil methanotrophs and can turn the wetland into a methane sink.

soil-env-085.q: How does contour trenching prevent erosion?
soil-env-085.a: Trenches 150 m long and 1 m deep are dug along the contour and edged with stone walls, so water cannot flow.

soil-env-090.q: How much agricultural land had unsustainable farming degraded by 2025?
soil-env-090.a: 996 Mha, over 60% of all human-induced land degradation.

soil-env-217.q: In what order are materials replaced when an open-cut mine is reclaimed?
soil-env-217.a: Rock backfills the pit, stored pre-mining soil goes on top, then topsoil, and finally vegetation is restored.

soil-env-038.a: Adding a chelator to make heavy metals, often too immobile for plants to absorb, more soluble.

soil-env-034.q: Why can ligninolytic fungi degrade many organic pollutants?
soil-env-034.a: Lignin and cellulose are long-chain carbon compounds much like many organic pollutants.

soil-env-252.q: Which nanoparticle has been used in most field applications of nanoremediation?

soil-env-229.q: Why does electrical resistance heating (ERH) work in any soil type?
soil-env-229.a: Current travels mainly through the thin water film on grains, which is also why it cannot dry the ground out.

soil-env-296.q: How does Finland raise soil selenium?
soil-env-296.a: It adds selenium salts to chemical fertilizers.

soil-hist-127.q: What is the half-life of beryllium-10, and what does it date?
soil-hist-127.a: 1,387,000 years; it dates exposure of rocks, soils and ice cores.

soil-hist-096.q: Who first proposed the law of superposition, and when?

soil-hist-042.q: What did Darwin's chalk experiment near Down House show?
soil-hist-042.a: Chalk spread in December 1842 ended up buried 18 centimetres deep, a rate of 6 millimetres per year.

soil-hist-016.q: Which bacterium was shown in 1901 to fix atmospheric nitrogen?
soil-hist-016.a: Azotobacter chroococcum, in work that fully described the fixation process found by Hellriegel and Wilfarth.

soil-hist-107.q: Which soil did the Wisconsin legislature name the official state soil in 1983?

soil-hist-068.q: How do planetary scientists functionally separate rock from soil?
soil-hist-068.a: Rocks are fragments of about 10 cm or more, larger than cobbles; soil is all other, typically loose material.

soil-found-017.q: How does plant species diversity tend to change across the soil pH range, and why?
soil-found-017.a: It tends to increase from pH 3.5 toward pH 9, because there are more calcicole species, which prefer lime-rich soils, than calcifuge species, which prefer acid ones.

soil-form-147.q: Why does limestone erode into karst landscapes?
soil-form-147.a: It is partly soluble, especially in acid: water and organic acid from the soil slowly widen its joints over thousands or millions of years, dissolving the calcium carbonate into pavements, caves and gorges.

soil-form-103.q: What materials make up superficial deposits, and how do they usually lie onshore?
soil-form-103.a: Mostly gravel, sand, silt and clay, forming relatively thin, often discontinuous patches.

soil-form-107.q: How did periglacial loess come to be deposited?
soil-form-107.a: As meltwater dwindled each autumn and winter, bare floodplains dried and wind winnowed their glacially ground silt and clay, depositing it downwind.

soil-form-008.q: What is bioturbation in the A horizon?
soil-form-008.a: The mixing of organic matter into the mineral matter by burrowing animals.

soil-form-118.q: Besides a mollic epipedon, what must a Mollisol have, and where are Mollisols common?
soil-form-118.a: A base saturation above 50%; they are common in grasslands.

soil-form-125.q: How does primary succession differ from secondary succession?
soil-form-125.a: Primary succession colonizes new surfaces with no life, such as bare rock, lava flows or freshly exposed till; secondary succession follows a disturbance.

soil-phys-001.a: How individual particles clump, bind and aggregate, which in turn sets the pattern of pores between them.

soil-phys-030.q: How does gilgai form in Vertisols?
soil-phys-030.a: Repeated shrinking and swelling churns the soil and heaves underlying material to the surface.

soil-phys-118.q: What kind of fluid is quicksand, and how does it respond to stress?
soil-phys-118.a: A shear-thinning non-Newtonian fluid: undisturbed it looks solid, but a change in stress of less than 1% suddenly lowers its viscosity.

soil-phys-099.q: How does heavy rain affect slope stability through matric suction?
soil-phys-099.a: Raising infiltration lowers matric suction along the soil water characteristic curve, cutting the soil's shear strength and slope stability.

soil-phys-175.q: How does recreational trampling change alpine soils?
soil-phys-175.a: It raises bulk density and lowers porosity, altering soil moisture and temperature and increasing runoff and erosion.

soil-water-156.q: Over what suction range does saturated flow occur, and what drives it?
soil-water-156.a: Between 0 and 33 kPa suction, up to field capacity, with gravity and differences in water pressure pushing water away from where it was applied.

soil-water-195.q: How is hydraulic conductivity found in a constant-head test?
soil-water-195.a: The volume of water passing in a set time is measured, and K follows by rearranging Darcy's law with the specimen's length, cross-section and head.

soil-water-176.q: What do the parameters α and n describe in the van Genuchten model?
soil-water-176.a: α relates to the inverse of the air-entry suction, and n, greater than 1, measures the pore-size distribution.

soil-water-157.q: By how much can tree roots raise infiltration rates through preferential flow?
soil-water-157.a: Up to 27 times, because living or dead roots open preferential channels for rainwater.

soil-phys-202.q: How do confined aquifers store water, and how large are their storativities?
soil-phys-202.a: By matrix expansion and water compressibility, with storativities far below 0.01 and as low as 10−5.

soil-phys-200.q: When was fluorescein first developed, and what is its sodium salt called?
soil-phys-200.a: In 1871; its sodium salt is uranine, and both remain among the best dye tracers.

soil-phys-160.q: How large are frost boils, and where do they occur?
soil-phys-160.a: Typically 1 to 3 metres across, in periglacial or alpine areas with permafrost.

soil-chem-187.q: Who derived the Goldich dissolution series, and when?
soil-chem-187.a: S. S. Goldich, in 1938, after studying soil profiles and their parent rocks.

soil-chem-095.q: How does vermiculite form from biotite or phlogopite?
soil-chem-095.a: By weathering or hydrothermal alteration: the micas lose the potassium between their sheets, which is replaced by magnesium and iron.

soil-chem-158.q: What are the two fates of growing agglomerates during particle aggregation?
soil-chem-158.a: They settle out as sediment, or in concentrated suspensions link into a colloidal gel.

soil-chem-102.q: Which minerals are products sold as fuller's earth usually made of?

soil-chem-051.q: Which exchanger cations are frequently used to measure cation-exchange capacity?

soil-chem-177.q: Name some substances in soil that can act as electron donors.
soil-chem-177.a: Soil organic matter, petroleum hydrocarbons, less chlorinated solvents such as vinyl chloride, and reduced inorganic compounds.

soil-chem-005.q: Which nitrogen fertilizers do not acidify the soil?
soil-chem-005.a: Nitrate sources with little or no ammonium, such as calcium, magnesium, potassium and sodium nitrate.

soil-chem-033.q: How is net acidity calculated in acid base accounting?
soil-chem-033.a: Potential sulfidic acidity plus titratable actual acidity plus retained acidity, minus the acid neutralising capacity, in mol H+ per tonne of dry soil.

soil-bio-044.q: Which earthworms are usually used in vermicomposting?
soil-bio-044.a: The brandling worm Eisenia fetida or Eisenia andrei, which live in manure heaps rather than soil.

soil-bio-013.q: How do soil algae survive below the surface, out of the light?
soil-bio-013.a: Given steady temperature and moisture, they feed heterotrophically on easy carbon sources such as glucose.

soil-bio-229.q: Why do many northern forests of North America have a deep detritus layer that invasive earthworms can disrupt?
soil-bio-229.a: Most northern forests lost their native earthworms to the Wisconsin glaciation, so a deep detritus layer is typical and many native plants rely on it.

soil-bio-214.q: How much soil do small burrowers such as ants, termites and earthworms move worldwide?
soil-bio-214.a: So much that the global total matches the global rate of tectonic uplift.

soil-bio-187.q: Which way do roots move water during drought in hydraulic redistribution?
soil-bio-187.a: Groundwater is drawn up the taproot and released from the lateral roots into the dry surface soil; under flooding, roots move water the other way.

soil-bio-176.q: Where do ericoid mycorrhizal fungi trade nutrients with the plant, and how long do these sites last?
soil-bio-176.a: In coils inside the epidermal cells of fine hair roots, where soil nutrients are traded for plant sugars; the coils work for only a few weeks before degrading.

soil-bio-246.q: Which genera of mycorrhiza helper bacteria are most commonly reported?
soil-bio-246.a: Pseudomonas and Streptomyces; Bacillus is another.

soil-bio-093.q: Why has much humus persisted for more than 100 years?
soil-bio-093.a: It is hidden inside small soil aggregates or tightly sorbed or complexed to clays, out of reach of microbes and enzymes.

soil-bio-098.q: On what substrates do tangel and mor humus each develop in cold, humid mountains?
soil-bio-098.a: Tangel develops on alkaline substrates and mor on acidic ones.

soil-bio-256.q: What reaction does the acid enzyme that unlocks bound phosphorus catalyse, and at what pH does it work best?
soil-bio-256.a: It hydrolyses a phosphate monoester with water to give an alcohol and phosphate, at an optimum pH below 7.

soil-class-003.q: Why are natural soil classes useful?
soil-class-003.a: Experience shows that natural classes, based on morphology, behaviour or genesis, can be interpreted for many different uses.

soil-class-014.q: Why do soils on river flood plains stay azonal, or immature?
soil-class-014.a: New alluvium arrives every year, so the soils stay immature even though the farmland is fertile.

soil-class-112.q: How does soil climate differ between well-drained and waterlogged soils?
soil-class-112.a: In well-drained soils it is a subdued version of the regional climate; in waterlogged soils it depends more on local groundwater than on the atmosphere.

soil-class-135.q: On what materials and under what vegetation do Phaeozems form?
soil-class-135.a: On loess and glacial till under humid and sub-humid tall-grass steppe.

soil-class-156.q: Why do conditions in the acrotelm swing between aerobic and anaerobic?
soil-class-156.a: Its lower boundary usually coincides with the lowest level of the water table, which fluctuates within it.

soil-fert-185.q: What carbon-to-nitrogen ratio do composting microbes prefer in their feedstock?

soil-fert-232.q: At what pH range is the least soil phosphorus bound up?

soil-fert-218.q: Which paper is counted a milestone of biogeochemistry?
soil-fert-218.a: An 1844 paper by Dumas and Boussingault.

soil-fert-012.q: What share of fertilizers is applied as solids, and which are most common?
soil-fert-012.a: About 90%, most commonly urea, diammonium phosphate and potassium chloride.

soil-fert-092.q: How fast did Tukey and Wittwer find leaf-sprayed nutrients moving through the plant?
soil-fert-092.a: About one foot per hour, tracing radioactive phosphorus and potassium sprayed on leaves in the 1950s at Michigan State.

soil-fert-045.q: What proportion of biosolids is organic matter?

soil-fert-210.q: How did Peru treat guano from 1840, and what did that mean for its finances?
soil-fert-210.a: Peru made guano an exclusive state resource, and its royalties became the country's largest source of revenue.

soil-water-086.q: What three conditions cause surface runoff to form?
soil-water-086.a: Water cannot infiltrate fast enough because the soil is saturated, rain arrives faster than it can be absorbed, or surfaces are impervious.

soil-water-011.q: What is the main climatic control on water erosion?
soil-water-011.a: The amount and intensity of precipitation, especially when the soil surface lacks plant cover.

soil-water-044.q: What erosion index does the Conservation Reserve Program require land to have?

soil-water-071.q: Why does quick clay lose so much strength once remolded?
soil-water-071.a: Its clay particle structure is highly unstable, so it keeps far less strength than it had on first loading.

soil-water-028.q: Which structures carry water safely down to a gully floor?
soil-water-028.a: Drop structures, pipe structures, grass chutes and rock chutes.

soil-water-097.q: When are gabions chosen over riprap for river bank protection?
soil-water-097.a: On steep banks where flow is too fast for riprap; gabions are stone-filled wire boxes.

soil-water-263.q: How does a riparian zone protect water?
soil-water-263.a: It acts as a natural biofilter, shielding water from excess sediment, polluted surface runoff and erosion.

soil-water-259.q: What decides whether a wetland carries aquatic, marsh or swamp vegetation?
soil-water-259.a: How long flooding or groundwater saturation lasts.

soil-agri-016.q: What is Low Energy Precision Application (LEPA) in centre pivot irrigation?
soil-agri-016.a: Hanging drop heads just above the crop, or dragging hoses that wet the ground directly, to limit evaporation.

soil-fert-208.q: What forms of nitrogen are most commonly supplied by fertigation?
soil-fert-208.a: Anhydrous ammonia, ammonium nitrate or urea; nitrogen is the most common nutrient supplied.

soil-agri-003.q: Whose 1974 concept is considered the foundation of modern agroecology?
soil-agri-003.a: Harper's 1974 concept of agroecosystems, perhaps inspired by Tansley's process ecology of the 1930s.

soil-agri-125.q: For several soils, how does the optimum water content for tillage relate to the plastic limit?
soil-agri-125.a: The optimum equals 0.9 times the lower plastic limit.

soil-agri-081.q: According to the traditional theory, how do lynchets form?
soil-agri-081.a: Long ploughing makes soil slip downslope, building a positive lynchet where the surface rises and a negative lynchet where it drops.

soil-agri-088.a: It has the soil quality, growing season and moisture supply to give economically sustained high yields under acceptable farming methods, including water management.

soil-meth-029.q: What role does gas chromatography play in the Dumas nitrogen method?
soil-meth-029.a: The method ends with a gas chromatography column that separates nitrogen from carbon dioxide and water.

soil-meth-008.q: What does geomorphometry extract from digital elevation models?
soil-meth-008.a: Surface parameters and objects such as watersheds, stream networks and landforms.

soil-env-161.q: What did preliminary 2011 analyses estimate permafrost emissions to be, and what could they not account for?
soil-env-161.a: Around 15% of human emissions, but they could not account for abrupt thaw.

soil-env-269.q: What share of Earth's land do forests now cover, and how does that compare with before agriculture spread?
soil-env-269.a: About 31%, one-third less than before agriculture spread, with half that loss in the last century.

soil-env-075.q: What is Sahel drought now thought to stem from mainly?
soil-env-075.a: Rainfall variability set by sea surface temperatures, which are driven by natural variability, sulphate aerosols and greenhouse gases.

soil-env-313.q: Why did rangeland management develop in the United States?
soil-env-313.a: In response to rangeland deterioration from overgrazing and misuse of arid lands, shown by the Dust Bowl.

soil-env-037.q: What are the main mechanisms of phytoremediation?
soil-env-037.a: Phytoextraction, phytostabilization, phytovolatilization and phytofiltration, along with breakdown of pollutants by plants and by root-zone microbes.

soil-env-047.q: Which two migrations drive electrokinetic remediation, and which dominates?
soil-env-047.a: Electromigration (electrophoresis) of charged particles, the dominant one, and electro-osmotic flow of pore fluid running the opposite way.

soil-env-241.q: What limit does the WHO recommend for arsenic in drinking water, and why is it often unattainable?
soil-env-241.a: 10 μg/L; it is often unattainable in problem areas because arsenic is hard to remove.

soil-env-243.q: Above what fluoride concentration can groundwater cause dental fluorosis?

soil-env-263.q: How does the Raymond process circulate groundwater?
soil-env-263.a: Groundwater is pumped up downstream, infused with nutrients and oxygen, and re-injected upstream in a loop.

soil-env-297.q: What caused Keshan disease across its belt of China, and when did it peak?
soil-env-297.a: Selenium-deficient soil; it peaked in 1960–1970, killing thousands.

soil-hist-126.q: How is an age calculated in thermoluminescence dating?
soil-hist-126.a: The dose measured by heating is divided by the yearly dose rate, found from uranium, thorium and potassium contents plus cosmic rays.

soil-hist-100.q: How did non-reversible ploughs build ridge and furrow?
soil-hist-100.a: They turned soil toward the centre of the same strip each year, gradually building a ridge with a furrow between strips.

soil-hist-033.q: Who extended Darwin's idea of bioturbation to ants and trees, and when?

soil-hist-009.q: When did Curtis F. Marbut begin developing the first formal soil classification scheme for the United States?

soil-hist-021.q: What journey does Farmers of Forty Centuries recount?
soil-hist-021.a: A nine-month tour of Asia in 1909, studying what would now be called organic farming or sustainable agriculture.

soil-hist-066.q: Why would clayey and organic soils have kept producing clay and organic matter on the early Earth?
soil-hist-066.a: They resist erosion, and early unicellular life would also have bound the soil.

soil-found-060.q: In what order do igneous minerals weather, and why?
soil-found-060.a: Roughly in the order they formed, Bowen's reaction series, because the weakest cation–oxygen bonds go first.

soil-found-011.q: How is a soil colour written in Munsell notation?
soil-found-011.a: As hue, then value/chroma, as in a Cecil soil horizon recorded as red (10R 4/8) clay.

soil-form-137.q: At weathering rates of 20 m per million years, how long do deep regoliths take to form?
soil-form-137.a: Several million years, and longer still in cooler climates.

soil-form-112.q: How does alluvium differ from colluvium in sorting, and why?
soil-form-112.a: Running water lays down alluvium, so it is generally fine-grained and well sorted; colluvium moves without running water and is poorly sorted.

soil-form-096.q: How much richer in manganese is black rock varnish than the Earth's crust?
soil-form-096.a: It holds manganese 50 to 60 times more abundantly than the crust's 0.12%.

soil-form-027.q: Which test separates a duripan from petrocalcic horizons and fragipans?
soil-form-027.a: A duripan slakes in KOH but not in HCl.

soil-form-076.q: Why does modern soil classification fit paleosols poorly?
soil-form-076.a: Geology, life and the atmosphere changed greatly over the record, notably at the Great Oxidation Event 2.42 billion years ago; an alfisol, a forest soil, could not exist before trees.

soil-form-124.q: In biosorting, why do large stones end up at the base of the biomantle?
soil-form-124.a: Burrowers move only particles smaller than their burrows, so larger stones settle and form a stonelayer there.

soil-phys-052.q: What law is used to calculate particle size from terminal settling velocities?

soil-phys-092.q: How does the dry bulk density of a mineral soil compare with the density of quartz?
soil-phys-092.a: Quartz is about 2.65 g/cm3, but a mineral soil's dry bulk density is normally about half that, between 1.0 and 1.6 g/cm3, because the more pore space a soil has, the lower its bulk density.

soil-phys-115.q: What do relative densities of 100% and 0% mean?
soil-phys-115.a: 100% means very dense sand or gravel; 0% means extremely loose, unstable soil.

soil-phys-123.q: Why is a soil's bulk density always less than its particle density?
soil-phys-123.a: Bulk density includes the pores; particle density, typically 2.60 to 2.75 g/cm3, does not.

soil-water-153.q: Why do clay soils hold more water than sandy soils?
soil-water-153.a: Water clings more tightly to fine clay particles than to coarse sand grains, so clays hold more water while sands let it pass more easily.

soil-water-223.q: Why does a capacitance probe's reading depend mostly on soil water?
soil-water-223.a: Water's dielectric constant (80) is far above that of mineral soil (4), organic matter (4) and air (1).

soil-water-200.q: How quickly do plants recover from water stress after rewatering?
soil-water-200.a: Mildly stressed plants recover in 1–2 days, but after severe stress they regain only 40-60% of maximum photosynthesis the day after rewatering.

soil-water-208.q: How much can development cut infiltration?
soil-water-208.a: Felton and Lull (1963) found a potential 80 percent cut, and Taylor (1982) found construction cut infiltration rates by more than 77 percent.

soil-phys-218.q: At what suction is field capacity conventionally defined?
soil-phys-218.a: At −33 kPa (−0.33 bar), or −10 kPa for sandy soils.

soil-phys-206.q: Where does subsurface water return to the surface?
soil-phys-206.a: At lower elevations through springs, seeps, wells or streams, sometimes after thousands of years in an aquifer.

soil-phys-158.q: Why can't the expansion of freezing water explain frost heave?
soil-phys-158.a: Water expands only about 9%, too little; by 1930 Stephen Taber had shown that water migrates to the freeze line, and that benzene, which contracts on freezing, also heaves.

soil-phys-185.q: How does wetting change a soil's thermal conductivity?
soil-phys-185.a: It raises it: dry soil conducts about 0.2–0.4 W·m−1·K−1 and wet soil 1–3, and varying moisture largely determines a soil's conductivity because air conducts heat poorly.

soil-chem-198.q: How do soil minerals retain phosphorus in acid and in calcareous soils?
soil-chem-198.a: In acid soils by adsorption onto iron and aluminium oxyhydroxides; in neutral to calcareous soils by precipitation onto calcite.

soil-chem-108.q: What conditions does bauxite formation need?
soil-chem-108.a: Intense weathering and very good drainage, which dissolve kaolinite and precipitate gibbsite.

soil-chem-161.q: Which iron(III) oxyhydroxides matter most in soils?
soil-chem-161.a: Goethite and lepidocrocite, the commonest forms and the most important mineral carriers of iron in soils.

soil-chem-103.q: Rank AlCl3, CaCl2 and NaCl by how well they flocculate colloids.
soil-chem-103.a: AlCl3 > CaCl2 > NaCl, because multivalent cations flocculate colloids more efficiently than monovalent ones.

soil-chem-203.q: What does the Langmuir isotherm predict at low and high pressure?
soil-chem-203.a: θ = Kp/(1 + Kp), the fraction of sites occupied, is about Kp at low pressure and approaches 1 at high pressure.

soil-chem-174.q: Below what redox potential do methanogens grow, and to which domain do they belong?
soil-chem-174.a: Below −0.3 V; all known methanogens belong to the domain Archaea.

soil-chem-028.q: Why did land clearing bring salt to the surface in Australia?
soil-chem-028.a: Deep-rooted native vegetation had used groundwater year-round; once crops and pasture replaced it, rising groundwater brought stored salt up, and evaporation left it in the soil.

soil-chem-025.q: How do seeps differ from scalds?
soil-chem-025.a: Both are saline discharge areas: seeps are where groundwater meets the soil surface, scalds where water is lost by evaporation only.

soil-bio-067.q: What do Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter each oxidize?
soil-bio-067.a: Nitrosomonas oxidizes ammonia to nitrite, and Nitrobacter oxidizes nitrite to nitrate.

soil-bio-065.q: Why are earthworm casts taken as a sign of healthy soil?
soil-bio-065.a: Casts often hold more plant-available nutrients than the surrounding soil and build stable soil aggregates, marking biologically active soil.

soil-bio-030.q: Which energy channels did soil flow webs reveal?
soil-bio-030.a: The bacterial and fungal channels, which carry the largest flow, and the root-herbivory channel, which carries much less.

soil-bio-208.q: Why do the pines of the pygmy forest stay so small?
soil-bio-208.a: Their podzol, the Blacklock series, is very acid, nutrient-poor and high in exchangeable aluminium, and its iron hardpan blocks deep roots and internal drainage.

soil-bio-151.q: How do mycorrhizal hyphae reach soil that roots cannot?
soil-bio-151.a: Most are far finer than the smallest root or root hair, so they explore soil that roots cannot reach and add absorbing surface.

soil-bio-163.q: Why do orchid seedlings depend on a fungus?
soil-bio-163.a: Orchid seeds, 0.35–1.50 mm long, carry virtually no energy reserve, so seedlings get their carbon from the fungus.

soil-bio-153.q: How much nitrogen do grain legumes fix each year?
soil-bio-153.a: Grown on about 1.5 million km2 a year, they fix about 44–66 million tons, almost half of the nitrogen used in agriculture.

soil-bio-111.q: How do detritivores and microbes break detritus down together?
soil-bio-111.a: Detritivores digest mainly the protein-rich microbes and excrete the detritus barely changed; microbes regrow on that dung and it is eaten again, until the detritus is fragmented and its complex carbohydrates disappear.

soil-bio-101.q: How much of the carbon in soil can microbial necromass make up?
soil-bio-101.a: 30 to 80%, because microbes cycle soil carbon so extensively.

soil-bio-270.q: What does a Q10 of 2 to 3 mean for a biological rate?
soil-bio-270.a: The rate doubles or triples with every 10 °C, as in most biological systems.

soil-class-017.q: What organic carbon content separates mineral from organic material?
soil-class-017.a: Mineral material has less than 20% soil organic carbon; organic material has 20% or more.

soil-class-106.q: What base saturation separates Alfisols from Ultisols?
soil-class-106.a: Alfisols have at least 35% base saturation; the more leached Ultisols fall below 35%.

soil-class-120.q: In the WRB, what decides whether redox features make a Gleysol or a Stagnosol?
soil-class-120.a: Features from rising groundwater make a Gleysol; those from stagnant surface water make a Stagnosol or Planosol.

soil-class-146.a: Repeated wetting and drying: plinthite, a red clay-rich material sometimes over 80% iron oxides, then hardens irreversibly.

soil-fert-184.q: Why does residue with a C:N above 30:1 lower the nitrogen available to plants?
soil-fert-184.a: Microbes are left short of nitrogen, so they take up soil ammonium and nitrate and immobilize them; below 15, mineral nitrogen is freed for plants.

soil-fert-231.q: Why do older leaves yellow first when nitrogen runs short?
soil-fert-231.a: The plant moves nitrogen out of them to younger tissue.

soil-fert-227.q: Why does calcium deficiency show first in new, fast-growing parts?
soil-fert-227.a: Calcium does not move in the phloem, so low-transpiring tissues and new, fast-growing parts suffer first.

soil-fert-137.q: Why does potassium leach from plants faster than nitrogen or phosphorus?
soil-fert-137.a: It exists only as the small soluble K+ ion.

soil-fert-079.q: Why may marled crops show magnesium deficiency?
soil-fert-079.a: Marl's carbonate is mostly calcium carbonate, so magnesium must be supplied as well.

soil-fert-026.q: How much nitrogen does a green manure release?
soil-fert-026.a: Depending on the species, 45 to 224 kg/ha (40 to 200 lb/acre), and usually 40-60% of the crop's nitrogen becomes available to the next crop.

soil-fert-057.q: Why must agricultural lime be finely ground?
soil-fert-057.a: Soil acids are weak: particles over 8 mesh are of little value, 8–60 mesh somewhat effective, and finer than 60 mesh fully effective.

soil-fert-207.q: How much phosphogypsum does making phosphoric acid leave behind?
soil-fert-207.a: Five tons for each ton of phosphoric acid, an impure radioactive waste; 100 to 280 million tons are produced yearly.

soil-water-091.q: What happens to soil under buildings and roads?
soil-water-091.a: It is sealed off from rainfall and the nutrient cycle, so it is in effect consumed and made infertile.

soil-water-014.q: Why do clay-rich soils resist erosion better than sandy or silty ones?

soil-water-055.q: What safety factor makes a slope stable, and which values call for monitoring?
soil-water-055.a: A slope is globally stable if the safety factor exceeds 1 along every potential sliding surface; values between about 1 and 1.3 mark marginally stable slopes that need monitoring or stabilization.

soil-water-030.q: How high does wind usually lift sand?
soil-water-030.a: Most stays within 50 cm of the surface, and practically none rises above 2 m.

soil-water-106.q: How much can active pore water pressure cut a soil's shear strength?
soil-water-106.a: By up to 60%, because rising water content weakens shear strength and so cohesion.

soil-water-269.q: What does the Shields number compare?
soil-water-269.a: It is proportional to the ratio of the fluid force on a particle to the particle's weight.

soil-water-146.q: Why does a rich fen keep a fairly stable pH?
soil-water-146.a: Groundwater passing limestone dissolves some calcium carbonate, and the bicarbonate produced buffers the fen's pH.

soil-phys-162.q: In Penck's slope replacement, where does flattening begin?
soil-phys-162.a: At the lowest slope, spreading upward and backward: flattening always occurs from the bottom up.

soil-agri-006.q: Why is crop rotation not a form of intercropping?
soil-agri-006.a: Its crops grow in separate seasons.

soil-agri-057.q: Why does filling planting pits with manure and compost raise yields so much?
soil-agri-057.a: The organic matter attracts termites whose tunnels break up the soil; yields of trees, sorghum and millet can rise by up to 500 percent.

soil-agri-098.q: How much can no-till cut nitrous oxide emissions?
soil-agri-098.a: By 40–70% depending on rotation, which matters because nitrous oxide is 300 times stronger than CO2 and lasts 120 years.

soil-agri-112.q: How deep does a subsoiler work compared with most tillage tools?
soil-agri-112.a: Most tools work the top 15–20 cm (6–8 in); a subsoiler loosens soil to twice that depth, usually 45–75 cm (18–30 in) or more.

soil-agri-158.q: How do buffer strips protect surface waters?
soil-agri-158.a: By slowing surface runoff, they trap sediment and filter out nutrients and pesticides before these reach the water.

soil-agri-083.q: How does a digital terrain model differ from a digital surface model?
soil-agri-083.a: A digital terrain model shows the bare ground surface, while a digital surface model may include tree canopy and buildings.

soil-meth-019.q: How does the Kjeldahl method measure nitrogen?
soil-meth-019.a: Concentrated sulfuric acid at 360–410 °C digests the sample and holds its nitrogen as ammonium sulfate; sodium hydroxide turns this into ammonia gas, which is distilled into a standard acid and measured by titration.

soil-meth-012.q: Why can soil moisture shift the NDVI without any change in vegetation?
soil-meth-012.a: Wet soil darkens, and bare soils themselves give small positive values of about 0.1 to 0.2.

soil-env-273.q: How much CO2 does silicate weathering sequester per mole of calcium or magnesium released?
soil-env-273.a: In theory 1 mol of CO2 for each mol of Ca2+ or Mg2+, though natural ratios vary with temperature and CO2 pressure.

soil-env-070.q: How much land do drylands cover, and how many people live there?
soil-env-070.a: 41.3% of Earth's land surface, home to more than 2 billion people.

soil-env-091.q: Why did soils improve under agrivoltaic systems in the Kubuqi Desert?
soil-env-091.a: Panel shade cut soil temperature and evaporation, and the panels acted as windbreaks that stopped sand burying plants, creating a better microclimate with the vegetation.

soil-env-097.q: What removal rates do bioretention systems typically achieve?
soil-env-097.a: About 80% of suspended solids and 50–60% of heavy metals; a 2025 meta-analysis found nitrogen and phosphorus loads cut by about 55% and 62%.

soil-env-002.q: How long does DDT persist in soil?
soil-env-002.a: Its half-life in soil is 2–15 years, so residues are still found in people, though at levels 5 to 10 times lower than in the 1970s.

soil-env-031.q: Why can heavy metal pollutants never biodegrade?
soil-env-031.a: Almost all compounds biodegrade given time, but elements do not.

soil-env-013.q: Which fuels does air sparging suit, and which does it not?
soil-env-013.a: It suits light gasoline constituents such as benzene, toluene, ethylbenzene and xylene, but not heavier fuels such as kerosene and diesel.

soil-env-221.q: Why are LNAPLs easier to locate and remove than DNAPLs?
soil-env-221.a: An LNAPL is buoyant, so it stops at the water table and floats on it.

soil-env-266.q: How much caesium did mustard greens remove in the Chernobyl zone?
soil-env-266.a: Up to 22% of average caesium activity in one growing season.

soil-env-299.q: What most likely drives parrots on the Manu River to eat soil?
soil-env-299.a: Sodium: consumed soils are consistently higher in it, and geophagy increases with distance from the ocean.

soil-hist-129.q: How does lead-210 reveal soil erosion?
soil-hist-129.a: Excess lead-210 from fallout builds up in surface soils, and its activity profile with depth reconstructs soil redistribution over the past century, giving erosion and deposition rates.

soil-hist-091.q: How do a buried wall and a buried ditch show up as cropmarks?
soil-hist-091.a: A buried wall diverts water and displaces fertile soil, stunting crops, while an organic-rich ditch fill holds water and boosts growth.

soil-hist-115.q: Why did grain output on the Kazakh steppe fall after early success?
soil-hist-115.a: Only 200 to 350 mm of rain fell a year, the soils were salty, winds caused erosion in spring, and grain monoculture, on 83% of cropland in 1958–1959, depleted nutrients.

soil-hist-108.q: Where did Lawes and Gilbert find that cereals get their nitrogen?
soil-hist-108.a: From the soil, contrary to Liebig's view that it came only from the air.

soil-hist-078.q: Since when has the Soil Science Society of America's flagship journal appeared only online?
soil-hist-078.a: Since 2013, with double-blind review of its articles.

soil-found-118.q: How can a drop of acid help identify calcite?
soil-found-118.a: Acid dissolves calcite and releases carbon dioxide, giving a characteristic fizz.

soil-found-028.q: Why do gleyed soils show yellow-brown or orange mottles on a gray background?
soil-found-028.a: Under saturation microbes reduce iron to its soluble ferrous form, which can be removed and leaves gray silicate minerals; when the soil dries and oxygen returns, iron re-oxidises locally into the coloured mottles.

soil-form-141.q: Why are clays such abundant weathering products in soils?
soil-form-141.a: Feldspars make up about 60% of the Earth's crust, and hydrolysis turns them into clays such as illite, smectite and kaolinite.

soil-form-109.q: What happens to the fertility of Iowa's Loess Hills once their topsoil erodes?
soil-form-109.a: Their fertility comes from 10,000 years of prairie humus, so the loess left beneath is infertile without fertilizer.

soil-form-150.q: How does a terminal moraine differ from a recessional moraine?
soil-form-150.a: A terminal moraine forms at the glacier's foot and marks its furthest advance; a recessional moraine is a small ridge left where a retreating glacier paused.

soil-found-072.q: What does the name paralithic mean?
soil-found-072.a: Akin to stony: from the Greek para, "akin to", and lithic, "stony".

soil-form-057.q: Which pedogenic process appears to be the most active in many soils?
soil-form-057.a: Bioturbation, which dominates the upper part of most soils, except possibly vertisols and cryosols.

soil-phys-009.q: How does fast wetting destroy soil structure by slaking?
soil-phys-009.a: Water entering aggregates displaces air from their pores and aggregates with trapped air burst; the faster the wetting, the more slaking occurs.

soil-phys-082.q: How did wheel traffic change the soil in one cotton field?
soil-phys-082.a: Tilled surface soil had a bulk density of 1.3 g/cm3 and 51% pore space, while wheel-trafficked inter-rows had 1.67 g/cm3 and 37%.

soil-phys-070.q: Which pores are the largest still water-filled at field capacity, and why do they matter?
soil-phys-070.a: Mesopores, 30–75 μm; called storage pores, they hold water that plants and soil organisms can use.

soil-phys-093.q: How is a soil's water content w measured?
soil-phys-093.a: As the mass of water over the mass of solids, found by weighing a sample before and after oven drying.

soil-found-094.q: How does depression storage capacity help govern Horton overland flow?
soil-found-094.a: Together with infiltration capacity: once both are exceeded, water flows across the land, possibly causing flooding and soil erosion.

soil-water-185.q: What is the main limitation of the Kostiakov equation, and how is it fixed?
soil-water-185.a: It implies a final intake rate of zero, whereas infiltration usually approaches a finite steady value; the Kostiakov–Lewis equation adds a steady intake term.

soil-water-202.q: When does Darcy's law stop holding?
soil-water-202.a: Above Reynolds numbers of about 1 to 10, when inertial effects become significant.

soil-water-243.q: What is the premise of a soil inference system?
soil-water-243.a: That a soil's basic properties are enough to infer all its other physical and chemical properties, through logically linked pedotransfer functions.

soil-water-234.q: How do soil-based irrigation controllers decide when to water?
soil-water-234.a: They either skip a timed cycle when the soil is wet or start watering only when moisture falls to a set threshold.

soil-phys-212.q: In the Netherlands, how large is the winter drainage requirement, and where does it come from?
soil-phys-212.a: About 180 mm: 720 mm of precipitation against 540 mm of evaporation.

soil-env-129.q: Why can thawing permafrost add to climate change?
soil-env-129.a: Dead biomass has built up in it over millennia without fully decomposing; as warming thaws it, decomposition restarts and releases carbon dioxide or methane.

soil-phys-184.q: Which changes temperature more over a day: a material of low or high thermal effusivity?
soil-phys-184.a: One of low effusivity; a material of high effusivity changes much less.

soil-chem-191.q: What can electron probe microanalysis reveal inside a mineral grain?
soil-chem-191.a: Chemical zoning from core to rim, which records the grain's history.

soil-chem-111.q: Why can ferrihydrite hold so much arsenic, lead or phosphate?
soil-chem-111.a: Its nanoporous particles give several hundred square metres of surface per gram, which adsorb these substances.

soil-chem-164.a: When iron-bearing substances rust underwater, and commonly where primary iron minerals weather.

soil-chem-146.q: What does the Langmuir isotherm assume about a surface?
soil-chem-146.a: Equivalent sites holding one molecule each, an energetically uniform surface and at most a monolayer, assumptions seldom all true.

soil-chem-205.q: How does surface heterogeneity explain the Freundlich equation?
soil-chem-205.a: High-energy sites fill first, then low-energy ones, so the heat of adsorption weakens with coverage.

soil-chem-124.a: With a platinum electrode, read relative to the standard hydrogen electrode.

soil-chem-014.q: How does controlled drainage save irrigation water?
soil-chem-014.a: Where wet and dry seasons are marked, drains run only in the wet season.

soil-chem-043.q: In the Maas–Hoffman model, what is the breakpoint?
soil-chem-043.a: The salinity up to which yield is unaffected; beyond it, yield falls.

soil-bio-217.a: In two stages: its hyphae secrete enzymes that break polymers into small units such as monomers, which are then absorbed.

soil-bio-059.q: How do bacteria such as Acidithiobacillus ferrooxidans cause acid mine drainage?
soil-bio-059.a: They use iron sulfide to generate sulfuric acid, which drains from the mine with runoff and can drive the pH of groundwater and streams down to 2–3.

soil-bio-205.q: How does a chemoautotroph differ from a chemoheterotroph?
soil-bio-205.a: A chemoautotroph builds all its organic compounds from carbon dioxide; a chemoheterotroph, like most animals and fungi, cannot fix carbon into its own organic compounds.

soil-bio-209.q: Why can microarthropod communities be used as bioindicators?
soil-bio-209.a: They are very sensitive to changes in ecosystems.

soil-bio-166.q: How widespread is arbuscular mycorrhiza among plants?
soil-bio-166.a: It is the most widespread plant symbiosis known, found in about 80% of plant species, on every continent except Antarctica.

soil-bio-181.q: What do endophytic fungi give a plant in exchange for carbohydrates?
soil-bio-181.a: They can increase its water or nutrient uptake and protect it from insects, birds or mammals.

soil-bio-252.q: How does a rhizotron let researchers watch roots?
soil-bio-252.a: A central corridor usually has viewing windows into the soil profiles on either side.

soil-bio-131.q: Which kind of kerogen yields oil, which yields gas, and which yields none?
soil-bio-131.a: Labile kerogen yields mainly oil, refractory kerogen mainly gas, and inert kerogen no hydrocarbons but graphite.

soil-bio-253.q: Why do bacteria and fungi release exoenzymes into their surroundings?
soil-bio-253.a: Breaking macromolecules into small pieces lets their constituents pass through the cell membrane and be used inside the cell.

soil-class-001.q: What traits do soil classification systems group soils by?
soil-class-001.a: Measurable traits such as texture, structure, mineral composition and the way the soil formed.

soil-class-044.q: Why were human-made soils long left out of classification systems?
soil-class-044.a: Criteria built for natural soils often do not apply to them.

soil-class-093.q: What is the defining trait of an Aridisol?
soil-class-093.a: Water deficiency: an aridic moisture regime, with fewer than 90 consecutive moist days in the growing season, and no leaching.

soil-class-131.q: Which Leptosols are the most extensive on Earth?
soil-class-131.a: Lithic Leptosols, less than 10 cm deep, in mountain regions.

soil-class-058.q: What gives red soils their colour?
soil-class-058.a: High iron content, which gives colours from reddish brown to reddish yellow.

soil-fert-175.q: How does potassium help a plant tolerate drought?
soil-fert-175.a: It opens and closes stomata through an ion pump, so it controls water loss from leaves.

soil-fert-171.q: How much of a plant's dry mass is carbon?

soil-fert-146.q: How does a nutrient cycle differ from the flow of energy through an ecosystem?
soil-fert-146.a: Energy flows one way through ecosystems, but mineral nutrients cycle.

soil-fert-125.q: What did a 15-year nitrogen-addition study at Harvard Forest find?
soil-fert-125.a: More leaching, higher pine mortality and an end to biomass accumulation.

soil-fert-030.q: Which compost organisms are the most abundant and important?
soil-fert-030.a: Bacteria, which excrete plant-available nitrogen, phosphorus and magnesium; mesophilic or thermophilic kinds dominate depending on the phase.

soil-fert-209.q: Why did demand for guano fall rapidly after 1910?

soil-fert-215.q: What does wood ash supply as a fertilizer?
soil-fert-215.a: Potassium, and calcium carbonate, which acts as a liming agent to neutralise acid soils.

soil-fert-040.q: How does phosphate rich organic manure free the phosphorus locked in rock phosphate?
soil-fert-040.a: Microbial organic acids slowly dissolve its insoluble tricalcium phosphate, and the organic matter stops other ions locking the phosphorus into insoluble forms.

soil-water-021.q: Why does saturation-excess overland flow start sooner after earlier rain?
soil-water-021.a: Antecedent soil moisture sets how soon soil saturates: the wetter it starts, the sooner runoff begins.

soil-water-036.q: How are unpaved lots and dirt roads kept from raising dust?
soil-water-036.a: They are paved or gravelled, or stabilized with water, vegetable oil, calcium chloride or other suppressants.

soil-water-284.q: How can as little as 1 mm of silt harm coral?
soil-water-284.a: Suspended sediment disrupts filter-feeding organisms and deposits bury them; 1 mm of accumulation may kill coral polyps.

soil-water-249.q: How does bed load move along a stream?
soil-water-249.a: It rolls, slides and hops along the bed at a small fraction of the flow speed.

soil-water-069.q: How do roots crossing a potential failure plane stabilize a slope?
soil-water-069.a: They raise shear strength by binding particles and anchor unstable surface soil to deeper stable layers or bedrock.

soil-water-293.q: Why does an alluvial fan form where a channel opens out?
